  • Population-genomics study of carrot domestication (2023) — Central Asian origin, purple and yellow first cultivars
  • Imperial War Museum and Smithsonian accounts — the wartime night-vision story as radar cover
  • University of Kentucky extension guidance — cooking, storage and variety notes
  • Plants For A Future — Daucus carota: seed oil and root dye
  • Kew Plants of the World Online — Daucus carota: flower and seed heads in fresh and dried arrangements
  • Tisserand & Young (2014) — Essential Oil Safety — carrot seed oil for dry skin

Cabbage

Brassica oleracea (var. capitata)

Culinary

Digestive Health

FreshCooked

A cool-season leaf vegetable bred into a tight head — and one branch of the most versatile species in the vegetable garden. Cabbage is cheap, keeps for weeks, feeds a crowd, and turns into something new again in the fermenting crock.

Cultivars

Golden Acre

Skin
Flesh

The classic early green: round, tight 3–4 lb heads, sweet and tender, ready sooner than most. Fresh eating and slaw; an heirloom standard for smaller gardens.

Ruby Perfection

Skin
Flesh

A fall red: deep purple-red, firm heads bred to store into winter. Higher in vitamin C, it colours salads and slaws and braises to a deep wine shade.

Savoy (such as Famosa)

Skin
Flesh

Crinkled, blistered deep-green leaves; milder and more tender than smooth cabbage, and the leaves wrap without cracking. The cook's cabbage for rolls and gentle braises.

Napa

Skin
Flesh

A close cousin rather than a true cabbage (a different species, Brassica rapa): pale, barrel-shaped, mild and juicy. The kimchi cabbage of Korea and a stir-fry staple in China.

Germany — sauerkraut: cabbage salted and fermented in its own juice, served with everything — the ferment that crossed oceans.
Korea — kimchi: napa cabbage salted, seasoned with chilli, garlic and ginger, and fermented; so central that gimjang, the communal making of the winter supply, is its own season.
El Salvador — curtido: a lightly fermented relish of cabbage, carrot, onion and oregano, spooned over pupusas to cut their richness.
Poland — gołąbki: cabbage leaves wrapped around meat and rice and simmered in tomato sauce; and bigos, the hunter's stew of fresh and fermented cabbage together.
  • Cabbage's ancestor is wild cabbage, a loose-leafed plant of the sea cliffs along the coasts of southern and western Europe. People gathered it and grew it for thousands of years before anyone bred it into a head.
  • Cabbage belongs to Brassica oleracea, one single species that growers have pulled in every direction. Pick the leaves and you get kale and collards. Pick the side buds and you get Brussels sprouts. Pick a swollen stem and you get kohlrabi. Pick the flower clusters and you get cauliflower and broccoli. Cabbage is the branch bred for one great bud: a head of leaves wrapped around the growing point, the tip the plant grows from.
  • Cabbages with heads took shape in Europe in the Middle Ages. The crinkled savoy kind was refined in Italy's Savoy region in the 16th and 17th centuries, and red cabbage travelled the same European roads.
  • A whole head keeps for months in a cool store, and turned into sauerkraut — cabbage salted and left to ferment, to sour in its own juice — it keeps far longer. So cabbage became the winter vegetable of whole continents. Sauerkraut's vitamin C made it famous at sea, too: it was carried on long voyages, on Captain Cook's ships among them, to guard against scurvy, the disease sailors got from too little vitamin C.

Craft

  • Red cabbage is a dye plant. Its leaves give pink, purple and blue shades on eggs and cloth, and the colour shifts with acid and alkali — the same pigments that make cabbage water a kitchen test for acids. It is a home dye — the Easter-egg dye of the kitchen — rather than a dye of the dyers’ trade.
  • It gives a lot of nutrients for very few calories: 25 kcal per 100 g raw, with vitamin C at about 37 mg (roughly 40% of the daily value), vitamin K at 76 µg (about 63%), folate at 43 µg and fibre at 2.5 g.
  • The colours divide the strengths. Red cabbage carries more vitamin C (about 57 mg per 100 g) and adds anthocyanins, the purple pigments that also colour blueberries. Green cabbage leads on vitamin K and folate; savoy leads on fibre (3.1 g) and folate (80 µg). Colour is a fair guide, as it is with sweet potatoes.
  • Cabbage carries glucosinolates — the sharp, mustardy sulfur compounds behind its bite. When the leaves are chopped or chewed, these convert into isothiocyanates, compounds studied for how they help the body deal with harmful substances. Population studies link eating cruciferous vegetables regularly with lower rates of some cancers; that is an observed pattern across the whole vegetable family, not a proven prevention by cabbage alone.
  • Fermented cabbage — sauerkraut, kimchi — keeps much of the vitamin C and, in unpasteurised versions, carries the live cultures of a true ferment.
  • Caution: cabbage is high in vitamin K, so people taking warfarin or similar blood thinners should keep their intake steady rather than swinging between none and a great deal, and mention it to their clinician.
  • Caution: very large amounts of raw cabbage can interfere with the thyroid's use of iodine — a realistic concern mainly where iodine is already lacking. Ordinary portions, and cooking, are not a problem for most people. If raw cabbage makes you gassy, cooked and fermented forms are usually gentler.
  • When to plant: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost, or sow outside in spring; sow again in late summer for autumn heads
  • Sun: Full sun
  • Soil: Rich, firm soil that holds moisture — a hungry crop
  • Environment: Cool-season; flavour sweetens after a light frost. Net from planting day against cabbage white butterflies
  • Planter or ground: Ground best; one plant to a very large pot
  • Spacing and depth: 45 cm apart; sow 1 cm deep
  • Water: Likes water — steady moisture makes solid heads
  • Companion plants: Onions, garlic, and herbs such as rosemary and sage are good neighbours
  • When to pick: About 70–90 days; cut when the head feels firm and solid

Garden notes

  • A cool-season, hungry crop: plant for spring or late summer, give it rich soil and steady water, and it heads up as the weather cools — flavour sweetens after a light frost.
  • More of the plant is food than the head alone: the loose outer leaves cook like any green, and the core is sweet eaten raw. The roots and the woody stalk base are for the compost heap, not the kitchen.
  • Expect company: cabbage white butterflies lay their eggs on the leaves, and their caterpillars are the price of an unnetted crop. Fine mesh from planting day is the simple answer.
  • Cabbages are biennial — left to a second year they bolt, flower and set seed. Rotate them around the beds, because the soil disease clubroot follows brassicas grown in one place too long.

Propagation

Sow seed ¼–½ inch deep, 2–3 weeks before the last frost, or start indoors 4–6 weeks earlier and set plants out when they have 4–6 leaves. Space plants 12–18 inches apart. Cabbage is a cool-weather crop — sown late in spring it matures in the heat and forms poor heads, so time it for spring or fall.

Sources

  • USDA FoodData Central — nutrient values for green, red and savoy cabbage
  • Kew — cabbage, kale, collards and their kin as one species, Brassica oleracea
  • Captain Cook's journals and naval histories — sauerkraut carried against scurvy at sea

Banana

Musa (chiefly Musa acuminata and its hybrids)

Culinary

Digestive HealthHeart Health

FreshCooked

The banana is a staple food for much of the tropics and a snack for everywhere else — and one of the strangest crops on earth. The “tree” is a giant herb, not a tree at all; the fruit is seedless and sterile; and almost every banana in every shop is a cutting of a cutting of a single variety, the Cavendish. That sameness is the banana's triumph, and its danger.

Cultivars

Cavendish

Skin
Flesh

The world's banana: medium-sized, mild and sweet, shipped green and ripened to yellow on arrival. Nearly half of all bananas grown. Its dwarf form is the one sold for pots and small gardens.

Gros Michel

Skin
Flesh

The lost export king. Larger, creamier and more fragrant than the Cavendish, with a thick peel that shrugged off sea voyages. Panama disease ended its trade by the 1960s, but it still grows in gardens and small farms from Thailand to Latin America. To taste one is to taste the banana your great-grandparents knew.

Lady Finger

Skin
Flesh

Small, thin-skinned and very sweet, with pale flesh that does not brown when cut. A favourite in Australia, and the banana for fruit salads.

Blue Java (“Ice Cream Banana”)

Skin
Flesh

Fruit with a silvery blue-green bloom that ripens to plain yellow; the flesh is soft and creamy, nicknamed for vanilla ice cream. Unusually cold-tolerant for a banana, so it is the variety most often attempted in cooler gardens.

Red (Red Dacca)

Skin
Flesh

Short, plump fruit in a deep red-purple skin; the flesh inside is cream to pale pink, sweet, with a slight raspberry taste. Eaten fresh wherever it grows.

Plantain

Skin
Flesh

Not a dessert banana at all, but a starchy cooking banana (an AAB hybrid) that must be cooked: fried green into tostones, or black-ripe into sweet maduros. For hundreds of millions of people, this — not the sweet banana — is the banana that matters.

Uganda — matooke: green highland bananas peeled with a knife, wrapped in banana leaves and steamed for hours into a soft, pale mash. It is the national dish, eaten daily, with beans or groundnut stew.
Puerto Rico & the Caribbean — green plantains fried twice into crisp, salted tostones; ripe ones caramelised into maduros; and banana leaves lining the pasteles of the Christmas table.
Philippines — turon: saba bananas and jackfruit wrapped, fried and coated in caramelised sugar; and banana cue, skewered bananas grilled in the same crackling sugar.
India — meals served on banana leaves across the south; the blossom (vazhaipoo) chopped and spiced; the stem cooked as a vegetable; and in Kerala, thin banana chips fried in coconut oil.
  • Bananas were among the first fruits ever farmed. At Kuk Swamp, in the highlands of New Guinea, traces of banana growing reach back about 7,000 years. Wild bananas are packed with hard seeds and have little flesh. Early farmers found rare plants with no seeds, and kept them alive by planting the side shoots — suckers — that rise around the parent stem.
  • The sweet dessert banana comes mostly from Musa acuminata, crossed in places with the hardier Musa balbisiana. Breeders still mark the family lines with letters — A for acuminata, B for balbisiana — so a plantain is AAB and the Cavendish is AAA. Hundreds of local kinds branch from those crosses across Asia, the Pacific and Africa.
  • Bananas reached Africa well over a thousand years ago, and settled in so deeply that East Africa bred its own highland cooking bananas. Spanish and Portuguese ships carried the plant to the Americas in the 1500s.
  • The export trade first ran on one single variety, the Gros Michel. It was larger than today's banana, richer in taste, and had a thick peel that suited long sea voyages. A fungus in the soil, called Panama disease, destroyed its plantations through the first half of the 1900s. By the 1960s the trade had torn it out and replanted with a variety the fungus could not kill: the Cavendish.
  • The Cavendish now makes up nearly half of all the bananas grown in the world, and almost the whole of the export trade. And every one of those plants is a clone — an exact copy — traced back to a single plant grown under glass at Chatsworth House in England in the 1830s. A newer strain of the same fungus, Tropical Race 4, kills the Cavendish, and it is spreading through Asia, Africa and Latin America. With no variety inside the crop, there is no resistant plant to select from. That is the banana's lesson, written twice in a century: variety is not decoration. It is insurance.

Craft

  • The stem — really a tight roll of leaf sheaths — gives a strong fibre. Stripped and dried, it is woven into cloth, mats and baskets, twisted into rope and made into paper, above all in India and the Philippines, where banana fibre has been worked for centuries.

The fruit

  • A medium banana (about 118 g) provides about 105 kcal, 3.1 g of fibre, and 422 mg of potassium — about 9% of the daily value. Bananas are famous for potassium, and the fame is only half earned: the amount is genuinely useful, but beans and leafy greens give more. What a banana offers is potassium in the most portable package in the fruit bowl.
  • Its standout vitamin is B6 — about 0.43 mg per fruit, a quarter of the daily value. Vitamin B6 helps the body release energy from food and build the chemical messengers the brain runs on.
  • Also provides vitamin C (10.3 mg, about 11% of the daily value), manganese and a little magnesium.
  • Ripeness rewrites the fruit. A greener banana holds much of its starch as resistant starch — starch that passes through the small intestine undigested and is fermented by gut bacteria in the large intestine, working much like fibre. As the banana yellows, that starch turns to sugar: sweeter, softer, faster to digest.

The leaves and flowers

  • Nearly the whole plant is used somewhere in the world: the blossom is cooked as a vegetable, the leaves wrap and serve food, the stem is eaten in parts of India, and the peel goes into regional dishes and compost. See Around the World.
  • Caution: people with advanced kidney disease are often told to limit potassium-rich foods, bananas among them. That is a matter for their own clinician — it is not a reason for anyone else to pass the fruit bowl by.
  • When to plant: Plant pups — the suckers that rise around the parent stem — in spring or early summer in warm climates; in pots, start any time and move out after frost
  • Sun: Full sun
  • Soil: Rich, deep, well-drained soil with plenty of compost
  • Environment: Tropical through and through: heat and abundant water, frost cuts it to the ground, and the great leaves need shelter from wind
  • Planter or ground: Ground in the tropics; elsewhere a dwarf kind in a big pot, wheeled under cover for winter
  • Spacing and depth: Give a clump room — 3 m or more from other plants
  • Water: Likes water — never let it dry out for long
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: The bunch is ready 3–6 months after the flower appears; cut it when the fruits plump out and their edges round, and ripen indoors

Garden notes

  • Bananas are tropical through and through: heat, abundant water and rich feeding, and frost cuts them to the ground. Outside the tropics they are a container adventure — a dwarf variety in a big pot, wheeled under cover for winter.
  • They grow not from seed but from suckers, called pups, that rise around the parent stem. A clump of stems of different ages is a mat, and a well-fed mat can live and crop for decades.
  • Each stem fruits once and then dies back. Cut the spent stem out and the pups around it take its place — the planting renews itself, as long as the mat is fed, watered and thinned to a few strong stems.
  • Shelter them from wind. Those enormous leaves tear in a gale — a torn leaf looks dramatic and harms nothing; the plant simply grows through it.

Propagation

In spring, when the weather warms, dig up a sword sucker — a young shoot with narrow, blade-like leaves, 4 to 5 feet tall, with good roots — cut it from the parent with a clean spade and replant it. Do not use water suckers, with broad leaves and a weak join — they make weak plants. Most eating bananas make no usable seed, so seed is not a home route.

Sources

  • USDA FoodData Central — nutrient values for bananas, raw
  • Denham et al. (2003) — early banana cultivation at Kuk Swamp, about 7,000 years ago
  • FAO — Cavendish share of world production and exports, and Tropical Race 4 reporting

Apple

Malus domestica

Culinary

Digestive HealthHeart Health

FreshCooked

The apple is a fruit of the rose family with the most branching family tree of any food plant: every named variety in the world descends in part from wild forests still standing in the mountains of Kazakhstan. It is also a fruit with a rule — an apple never grows true from its own seed, so every variety in existence is a clone, carried down the centuries by grafting from one original tree.

Terpenes in this plant:

Cultivars

Honeycrisp

Skin
Flesh

Red over yellow, exceptionally crisp and juicy, sweet with a balancing tartness. Bred by the University of Minnesota and released in 1991; the apple that reset what shoppers expect from crunch. Best eaten fresh.

Granny Smith

Skin
Flesh

Bright green, hard and very tart, with dense flesh that holds its shape in a pie. From a chance seedling raised by Maria Ann Smith in Australia in 1868. The classic cooking and salad apple, and it keeps for months.

Fuji

Skin
Flesh

Dense, very sweet and crisp, red-blushed over yellow-green. Bred in Japan from Red Delicious and Ralls Janet and released in 1962. Stores exceptionally well; a lunchbox standard around the world.

Gala

Skin
Flesh

Mild, sweet and aromatic, striped orange-red over yellow. Bred in New Zealand in the 1930s and now among the most planted apples on earth. An easy first apple for children.

Cox's Orange Pippin

Skin
Flesh

Russet-flecked and orange-red, with a complex, almost spiced flavour no modern apple quite matches. Raised by Richard Cox in England around 1830. The connoisseur's eating apple — and famously temperamental to grow.

France — Normandy turns its apples into cider and Calvados brandy, and the tarte Tatin — apples caramelised in butter and sugar under pastry — comes from the Loire Valley.
Austria — Apfelstrudel: spiced apple and raisin rolled in pastry stretched thin enough, bakers say, to read a newspaper through.
United States — apple pie became the emblem of home cooking, though the pie itself, the apples and the saying all have older and wider roots.
England — cider orchards in the West Country, and a long tradition of named dessert apples eaten by the hand — Cox's Orange Pippin, above, first among them.
  • The apple's wild ancestor is Malus sieversii. It still grows in great forests on the wooded slopes of the Tian Shan mountains in Kazakhstan. The name of the country's largest city, Almaty, is often translated as “father of apples.” The apple was first tamed and grown there somewhere between 4,000 and 10,000 years ago.
  • Seeds travelled west along the Silk Road — in saddlebags and in thrown-away cores. Along the way, the young tame apple crossed with the local crabapples of Siberia, the Caucasus and Europe. Today's apple carries that mixed family history in every fruit.
  • Greek and Roman growers became masters of grafting: joining a living cutting from a good tree onto the roots of another tree, so the fruit stays exactly itself. Without grafting there could be no named varieties at all, because a pip — an apple seed — grows into a new apple that nobody knows, and it is usually sour.
  • More than 7,500 named varieties are now recorded around the world — eating apples, cooking apples, cider apples — yet shops stock only a handful. The old orchard varieties live on mostly in the care of collectors and small growers.
  • In North America, John Chapman — Johnny Appleseed — planted orchards of seed-grown trees across the frontier in the early 1800s. Because trees grown from seed do not come true to their parent, most of his apples were cider apples. The famous eating varieties crossed the ocean as grafted trees.

Craft

  • The wood is a craft wood: hard, dense and fine-grained, it is carved and turned, and used for tool handles. It comes from pruned branches and felled orchard trees — the craft use follows the fruit, not the other way round.
  • Apples themselves were a folk craft: the apple-head doll. A peeled apple was carved into a face and dried for weeks until it shrank into a wrinkled old face, then set on a cloth body. Native American makers began the craft, colonists and Appalachian families took it up, and apple-head dolls were sold across America from 1913 into the 1960s.
  • A medium apple (about 182 g, eaten with its skin) provides about 95 kcal and 4.4 g of fibre — much of it pectin, a soluble fibre, meaning the kind that forms a gentle gel in the gut. That fibre supports digestion and can modestly help keep LDL cholesterol — the “bad” cholesterol — in check.
  • Eat the peel. Nearly half the apple's fibre and most of its quercetin — a plant pigment studied for its antioxidant effects — sit in or just under the skin. Peel the apple and the fibre falls by almost half (from 2.4 g to 1.3 g per 100 g).
  • Provides vitamin C (8.4 mg per medium apple, about 9% of the daily value) and potassium (195 mg) — modest amounts that add up across a diet with fruit in it daily.
  • In large population studies, people who eat apples and pears regularly tend to have lower rates of type 2 diabetes and heart disease than people who rarely eat them. These are patterns across whole diets, not proof that an apple by itself prevents disease — but they point the same way as the fibre and pigment content.
  • The whole tree gives in turn: blossom for the bees in spring, fruit for people in autumn, and pruned wood sweet enough for the smoke of a barbecue. The seeds are the one part not eaten — see the caution below.
  • Caution: apple seeds contain a compound called amygdalin, which can release cyanide when seeds are chewed and crushed. The dose in one apple is tiny — a fruit holds only five to eight seeds, and seeds swallowed whole pass through undigested. A person would have to chew the seeds of dozens of apples at one sitting to approach harm. Spit the seeds out or swallow them whole, either is fine; just do not grind up seeds on purpose.
  • When to plant: Plant a grafted tree while dormant, in spring — or autumn in mild districts. Only grafting keeps the variety true, and the rootstock decides the tree's final size
  • Sun: Full sun
  • Soil: Well-drained soil; most garden soils suit if they are not waterlogged
  • Environment: Needs winter chill to fruit well, and varieties are bred for different amounts of it — match the tree to your winters
  • Planter or ground: Ground; dwarf rootstocks suit a large patio pot
  • Spacing and depth: By rootstock: dwarf trees 2.5–3.5 m apart, full orchard trees 6 m or more
  • Water: Water well in the first two years and in dry spells; settled trees need little
  • Companion plants: Chives, garlic and nasturtiums are the classic orchard neighbours. Most kinds also need a different apple variety flowering nearby to set fruit
  • When to pick: Pick when the fruit parts from the tree with a gentle twist and the pips are brown — autumn for most kinds

Garden notes

  • Buy a grafted tree. The variety name is a promise only grafting can keep, and the rootstock — the roots the variety is grafted onto — decides the tree's final size, from a full orchard tree down to a patio dwarf.
  • Most varieties cannot pollinate themselves and need a different apple variety flowering nearby. One tree alone may blossom beautifully and set almost nothing; bees do the carrying between the two.
  • Apples need winter chill to fruit well, and varieties are bred for different amounts of it. Match the tree to your winters before you plant.
  • Plant in full sun, prune in winter to keep the centre of the tree open to light, and thin the young fruit in early summer to one apple per cluster — the tree will size those well and bear every year instead of every other.

Propagation

Graft a named variety onto a bought rootstock — whip-and-tongue grafting in late winter or early spring is the home-gardener way. Collect the shoot wood while dormant in February or early March and keep it cool until grafting. A tree grown from a pip does not come true, so it will not give the same apple.

Sources

  • USDA FoodData Central — nutrient values for apples, raw, with skin
  • Encyclopedia of American Folk Art — the apple-head doll tradition, from Native American makers to the dolls sold from 1913
  • USDA flavonoid data — quercetin concentrated in the peel
  • Nature Genetics genome consortium (2010) — apple origin from Malus sieversii in the Tian Shan
  • Pooled Nurses' Health Study / Health Professionals cohort data — apple intake and diabetes and heart associations, stated as population patterns
  • Bolarinwa et al. (2014) — amygdalin content of apple seeds

Arnica

Arnica montana

MedicinalOrnamental

Skin HealthMovement and Support

External use only

A bright yellow mountain flower with a serious warning on it. Arnica grows in the poor, high meadows of Europe, and its flowers have been rubbed on bruises, sprains and sore muscles for centuries — it is one of the oldest injury herbs in the European tradition. But it works only on the skin, and only on skin that is not broken. Arnica is poisonous if eaten: never swallow it, in any form — no tea, no tincture by mouth, no exceptions. Every use below follows that rule.

Cultivars

  • Arnica is not really grown in named varieties — there are no garden cultivars to list. What exists instead is a family of related species, and two of them matter to anyone meeting this plant.
  • Meadow arnica (Arnica chamissonis) — a North American species from the western mountains and meadows, and the arnica of modern commerce. True A. montana is protected and refuses to farm well, so growers turned to this cousin: it grows willingly in fields, its flowers carry the same family of compounds, and the European and German pharmacopoeias — the official drug books — accept it as a substitute. Most arnica creams and oils on sale today are made from cultivated meadow arnica, even when the label just says "arnica."
  • Heartleaf arnica (Arnica cordifolia) — the common arnica of western North American woods and mountain slopes, named for its heart-shaped leaves. This is the species in the Indigenous record above, used in poultices for bruises and swelling by the peoples of British Columbia and the northern Rockies.
  • Beyond these, the genus holds around thirty species across the northern mountains of the world — nearly all of them yellow-flowered mountain plants, and several of them rare. The name "arnica" on a product in Mexico, it is worth knowing, usually means a different plant altogether, Heterotheca inuloides, no relation beyond the daisy family they share.
Germany, Austria and Switzerland — arnica's heartland. A bottle of arnica tincture or a tube of arnica salve is a standard household item, kept for the knocks and sprains of mountain life; the plant is gathered in memory and story as much as in fact, since wild picking is now restricted.
France — in the Vosges mountains the dried leaves were smoked as "mountain tobacco," and the flower's French name, panacée des chutes, cure-all for falls, matches the German one idea for idea.
North America — homeopathy made arnica a household word here: the little tubes of homeopathic arnica are sold everywhere for sports knocks and gym soreness — the diluted product, not the herb, with the evidence as stated above. Herbal arnica gels and oils are sold alongside them, and the two are easily confused — but they are not the same thing.
Mexico — "árnica" in Mexican markets is usually Heterotheca inuloides, a local daisy-family plant with its own tradition. Same name, different plant — a standing lesson in why the Latin name matters.
Cosmetics — arnica extracts appear in shampoos, hair tonics and skin products, a trade use that follows the flower's reputation rather than its trials.
  • Arnica is a plant of the high, hungry ground: the mountain meadows of Europe, from Spain and Scandinavia across the Alps and Carpathians to western Siberia. It grows where the soil is poor, sour and thin — roughly 500 to 2,800 metres up — and it vanishes from meadows that are fertilised or improved. Its very presence is a sign of an old, untouched meadow.
  • The Greeks and Romans never knew it; it is a mountain plant, far from their world. It enters the written record in the 1500s, in the German herbals, already famous as the herb for falls and blows. In 1588 the herbalist Tabernaemontanus described ordinary Saxon country people using it after falls and injuries at work — the use was old before it was ever written down.
  • Its German names tell the story. Wohlverleih — in full, Bergwohlverleih, "the mountain bestower of well-being." Fallkraut — "fall herb." In the 1600s the physician Johann Michael Fehr called it panacea lapsorum, Latin for "cure-all for falls." The French called it panacée des chutes, the same words in another tongue, and tabac des Vosges — Vosges tobacco — because the dried leaves were smoked in the mountains in place of tobacco.
  • The most famous arnica story belongs to Goethe, Germany's great poet. In old age, troubled by a heart complaint, he is said to have drunk arnica tea and believed the plant had saved his life, praising it warmly to the end of his days. It is told here as the story it is — a piece of history from a time before the plant's dangers were understood. Nobody should copy it: the safety section below explains why arnica is never taken by mouth today.
  • Arnica also stands at the very beginning of homeopathy. Samuel Hahnemann, homeopathy's founder, tested arnica — the root — on himself and his students in 1805, making it one of the first homeopathic remedies, and homeopathy carried the plant's name around the world. Homeopathic arnica is a different thing from the herb itself, diluted past the point where any of the plant remains; the two are kept separate in Health Benefits, because their evidence is separate too.
  • North America has its own arnicas — the genus is richest there, with around thirty species — and the peoples of that continent found the same uses on their own. Moerman's record of Indigenous plant use describes the Nlaka'pamux (Thompson) people of British Columbia applying a poultice of mashed heartleaf arnica (Arnica cordifolia) to swellings, bruises and cuts, and arnica roots were used in washes for back pain. Two continents, no contact, the same yellow flower put to the same work.
  • In the herb trade, the flowers were traditionally steeped into oils and salves for bruises and sore muscles — the use that carries on today. That is history, told as history; what the studies support is in Health Benefits.
  • The wild plant has paid for its fame. Picking, and the fertilising and ploughing of its meadows, have thinned it across Europe. It is now protected by law in many countries, named in the European Union's Habitats Directive, and in Germany collecting it from the wild for trade is not permitted. Much of the arnica in modern products is no longer this species at all — see Cultivars.
  • What is in the flower: the working compounds are a group called sesquiterpene lactones — bitter plant chemicals — chief among them one named helenalin. In laboratory work helenalin damps down inflammation signals in cells. It is also the plant's poison and its main skin irritant, which is why everything about arnica is a balance between a real effect and a real risk. The flowers hold about 0.3–1% of these compounds; the leaves hold less; the root and underground stem hold none of the helenalin type, which is one reason the flower is the part the official herb books use.
  • The official standing, plainly: the European Medicines Agency (2014) accepts arnica flower preparations on the skin for relief of bruises, sprains and localised muscle pain — as a traditional use. That word matters: the registration rests on the plant's long, documented history of use, and the agency's reviewers found the clinical studies too small and too loosely run to prove the effect on their own. Arnica's honest position is "used for centuries, plausibly helpful, not firmly proven."
  • Joint pain — the best single study. Widrig et al. (2007) gave 204 people with osteoarthritis of the finger joints either arnica gel or ibuprofen gel for three weeks, in a trial where neither patients nor doctors knew which was which. Pain and hand function improved the same in both groups — the arnica gel matched a standard pain gel. The Cochrane reviewers (Cameron et al., 2013) called this moderate evidence from that one study, while noting there was no comparison against a dummy gel, so how much of the effect is the arnica itself stays an open question.
  • Bruises — small and mixed. In one small study (Leu et al., 2010), a strong 20% arnica ointment sped up the clearing of bruises made by laser treatment, more than a dummy ointment. Other small bruise studies have found nothing. The fair summary is that arnica on a bruise may help it fade a little faster; it is not settled, and it cannot honestly be promised.
  • Muscle pain and swelling after surgery — a handful of small studies, results pointing both ways. Nothing here rises above "possibly, a little."
  • Homeopathic arnica is not herbal arnica. Homeopathic tablets and drops are diluted so far that no molecule of the plant is expected to remain in them. When researchers gathered all the placebo-controlled trials (Ernst et al., 1998), homeopathic arnica came out no better than the dummy pills — and a careful later trial in hand-surgery patients (Stevinson et al., 2003) found the same: no difference in pain, bruising or swelling. This matters because the two products sit side by side on shop shelves and are constantly confused.
  • Safety — the part that matters most. Never swallow arnica. The plant is poisonous by mouth: it can bring on severe stomach and bowel inflammation, vomiting and diarrhoea, muscle weakness, an irregular heartbeat, collapse, and in quantity it can kill. The United States Food and Drug Administration lists arnica as an unsafe herb; the only food use allowed there is as a flavouring in alcoholic drinks, at levels too low to act as anything but a taste. Old books describe arnica teas and drops taken by mouth — those uses were abandoned in the 1900s as the poisonings mounted, and they belong to history, not practice.
  • On the skin, the rules are: unbroken skin only — never on wounds, cuts or grazed skin; short-term use; and stop if it irritates. The same compounds that act on a bruise can inflame the skin itself, and repeated use can bring on a lasting allergic rash, especially in people sensitive to the daisy family — ragweed, chrysanthemums, marigolds and their kin. Arnica may also slow blood clotting a little, so anyone on blood-thinning medicine should ask their clinician before using it regularly. There is not enough safety knowledge for pregnancy or breastfeeding, so the standard advice is to leave it alone in both.
  • A hardy perennial, 20–60 cm tall. It starts the year as a flat rosette — a ring of soft, slightly hairy leaves lying on the ground — and sends up one slim stem, usually carrying a single flower head 6–8 cm across, golden-yellow, in June to August. After flowering the plant dies back to its underground stem and returns the next spring.
  • It wants what its meadows have: full sun, and soil that is poor, sour (acidic), and quick to drain — a sandy or gritty soil with no lime in it. Rich soil and fertiliser do not pamper it; they finish it. A plant of fertilised ground is a plant on its way out, which is why it is disappearing from farmed country.
  • Honest warning for gardeners: this is a difficult plant to grow, and the books say so. The seed needs light and a cold spell before it will stir, germination is patchy, and the seedlings grow slowly and lean on fungi in the soil that a garden bed may not have. A plant can take two or three years to flower. Lowland gardens with warm summers and heavy soil defeat it most of the time; a cool, gritty rock garden or alpine bed is its best chance.
  • Never dig or pick it wild. It is protected across much of Europe, its meadows are a protected kind of ground in their own right, and a picked plant is one of the year's few seed parents gone. Buy plants or seed from specialist alpine nurseries — and know that many nurseries sell meadow arnica, A. chamissonis, under the arnica name: it is the willing grower of the family, flowers its first or second year, and is the sensible garden choice.
  • If you do grow true arnica, the flowers are the part gathered, picked just as they fully open on a dry day — and the warning at the top of this page goes with every flower you pick: skin only, never swallowed.

Propagation

Sow seed in a cold frame in autumn, or in early spring, barely covering it — keep the compost moist and never let it dry out. Or divide an established clump in spring, with each piece keeping roots and shoots.

Sources

  • European Medicines Agency (2014) — Community herbal monograph on Arnica montana L., flos — skin use for bruises, sprains and local muscle pain, accepted as traditional use
  • Widrig et al. (2007) — arnica gel against ibuprofen gel for osteoarthritis of the hands: a randomised, double-blind trial in 204 patients
  • Cameron et al. (2013) — Cochrane review: topical herbal therapies for treating osteoarthritis — arnica gel rated against the trial evidence
  • Leu et al. (2010) — arnica ointment and the clearing of bruises after laser treatment: a small controlled study
  • Ernst et al. (1998) — systematic review of placebo-controlled trials of homeopathic arnica — no effect beyond placebo
  • Moerman (1998) — Native American Ethnobotany — Indigenous uses of North American arnica species, including the Nlaka'pamux poultice record

Mango

Mangifera indica

Culinary

Digestive HealthEye HealthImmune HealthSkin Health

FreshDried

The mango is the fruit of a big evergreen tree in the cashew family — kin to cashew and pistachio, and a far-off cousin of poison ivy. It has been grown in South Asia for more than 4,000 years, and it is now the everyday fruit of the tropics: eaten ripe and sweet, green and sour, dried, juiced and pickled — and even its seed is pressed into a butter for the skin.

Terpenes in this plant: ·

Cultivars

Alphonso

Skin
Flesh

The prized mango of India's west coast, around Ratnagiri in Maharashtra: rich, creamy, almost fibre-free flesh with a scent nothing else matches. Its season is short — April to June — and it is priced like it. The mango other mangoes are judged by.

Kesar

Skin
Flesh

From Gujarat, named for its saffron-coloured flesh — kesar is the word for saffron. Sweet, smooth and juicy, it is India's other great eating mango, and the one most often canned as pulp.

Haden

Skin
Flesh

The Florida grandfather: raised in Coconut Grove in 1910 from an Indian Mulgoba seed, it parented most modern shipping mangoes. Firm, mild, sweet flesh under a red-blushed skin.

Tommy Atkins

Skin
Flesh

The supermarket mango of the Americas, a Florida seedling of Haden from the 1920s. Very firm, fibrous and mild, with a long shelf life and colour that promises more than the flesh gives — bred for shipping, not for taste. Best in smoothies, salsas and salads.

Kent

Skin
Flesh

A Florida variety of the 1940s: big, rich and sweet, with soft, low-fibre flesh. It stays mostly green even when ripe, so it is judged by feel and scent, not colour. A late-season fruit.

Keitt

Skin
Flesh

Another Florida variety of the 1940s, and the latest of all: large fruit that stays green when ripe, sweet with a little tartness and almost no fibre. It stretches the mango season into early autumn.

Ataulfo (Honey)

Skin
Flesh

Mexico's small golden mango, named for the grower Ataulfo Morales: smooth, fibre-free, honey-sweet flesh and a thin seed, so there is more fruit to the bite. Sold as the honey mango, or champagne mango.

Nam Dok Mai

Skin
Flesh

Thailand's best-known mango: long and slender, very sweet, with smooth, low-fibre flesh. Eaten ripe with coconut sticky rice — and eaten green and crisp, dipped in chilli sugar.

India — aamras, pressed Alphonso pulp eaten with puffed puris in Maharashtra; and the green mango at work everywhere: sharp pickles, and amchur powder seasoning dishes all year.
Thailand — khao niao mamuang: ripe Nam Dok Mai over sweet coconut sticky rice; and crisp green mango with chilli-sugar dips at street stalls.
Mexico — mango on a stick from street carts, cut like a flower and dressed with lime, salt and chilli; the golden Ataulfo comes from the Soconusco coast of Chiapas.
Philippines — the Carabao mango, eaten ripe and sweet, dried into chewy export sweets; and green mango with bagoong, a salty shrimp paste.
  • The mango's first home is the land between north-east India, Bangladesh and Myanmar, where wild mango trees still grow in the foothills. Growers there took it into gardens more than 4,000 years ago, and India has been its heartland ever since — it is the country's national fruit.
  • The name tells the journey: from the Tamil word for the fruit, māṅkāy, through Portuguese manga to mango. The Latin name, Mangifera indica, means roughly "the mango-bearer of India".
  • From India the mango travelled both ways. Traders and monks carried it east through Southeast Asia well over a thousand years ago. Persian and Arab sailors took it to the East African coast by about the 900s. Much later, Portuguese ships carried it to Brazil in the 1700s. Spanish galleons brought Southeast Asian seed from the Philippines to Mexico, and it reached Florida in the 1800s.
  • There are two great families of mango. Indian kinds carry one embryo — one young plant — in each seed, and give rich, coloured, strong-flavoured fruit. A seedling grows up different from its parent, so every named Indian variety is kept alive by grafting: joining a piece of the named tree onto another tree, so it grows true. Southeast Asian kinds carry several embryos in a seed and grow true from seed. They give paler, very sweet fruit, with less resin in the taste.
  • Florida breeders crossed the two families in the early 1900s and produced the firm, colourful shipping mangoes — Haden first, in 1910, then its seedlings Kent, Keitt and Tommy Atkins — that fill supermarket shelves today.
  • Tradition in India holds that the Buddha was given a mango grove at Vaishali by the courtesan Amrapali, and rested in its shade. That is tradition, told here as it is told.
  • Fresh mango leaves are still strung over doorways across India at festivals — a toranam, a hanging of leaves for welcome and good fortune — and mango leaves and blossom appear in offerings. The tree is treated as a tree of plenty.
  • The Mughal emperor Akbar, in the 1500s, is said to have planted the Lakhi Bagh near Darbhanga: an orchard of a hundred thousand mango trees. A lakh is a hundred thousand — the name alone tells the scale of the planting.
  • In Ayurveda, India's old system of medicine, the ripe fruit, the leaves and the bark each had their uses. Unripe mango was dried into amchur — a sour powder — to keep its tang in the kitchen all year. These are historical uses, recorded as history.
  • The paisley pattern's curved teardrop is widely said to be drawn from the shape of a mango. The claim is repeated so often that it is best carried as tradition.

Traditional medicine

  • The leaves, taken as a tea, are a folk remedy in parts of Asia and the Caribbean — tradition, not tested medicine.
  • The bark is astringent, was used in folk medicine, and gives a brown dye. Neither leaf nor bark is a food.

Craft

  • Mango is a making tree as much as a fruit tree. The bark and leaves give a yellowish-brown dye used for silk. The wood is a worked timber — furniture, carpentry, flooring, boxes and dugout canoes. The seed kernel is pressed into mango butter, used in skin care and soap making.
  • Vitamin C leads: about 36 mg per 100 g of flesh, roughly 40% of the daily value, at only about 60 kcal per 100 g.
  • The deep orange colour is carotenoids, chiefly beta-carotene — the pigment the body turns into vitamin A. A 100 g serving gives about 54 µg of vitamin A, roughly 6% of the daily value. This flesh is where the mango's vitamins A and C truly live.
  • Fibre is modest but real — about 1.6 g per 100 g, much of it soluble — and it supports digestion. Against that, the flesh is sweet, about 14 g of sugar per 100 g, so portions are worth a thought for anyone watching blood sugar.
  • In the background: potassium (about 168 mg per 100 g) and folate (about 43 µg, roughly a tenth of the daily value).
  • Green, unripe mango is a food in its own right — crisp, sour and rich in vitamin C — eaten with salt and chilli across Asia, and dried into amchur, the sour powder that seasons Indian cooking.
  • Inside the flat stone sits the kernel. Pressed, it gives a pale, nearly scentless fat — mango butter — that melts at 32–36 °C, right around skin temperature, so it spreads on skin and melts in.
  • The butter carries a little vitamin E (tocopherols, up to about 148 mg in a kilogram of the fat) — a modest amount. It does not carry the fruit's vitamins A or C in any real amount: those stay behind when the fat is pressed out of the kernel, so claims that mango butter is rich in vitamins A and C mix up the flesh with the fat.
  • The kernel itself is ground into flour and eaten in parts of India, mostly in lean times. It is bitter and astringent, and it is not a common food.
  • When to plant: Plant a grafted tree in spring, after all frost risk — a grafted tree can bear in about three years; a seedling is an unknown tree and may take six to eight
  • Sun: Full sun
  • Soil: Deep, well-drained soil; it tolerates poor soil once settled
  • Environment: It wants the tropics: heat and no frost — a young tree is damaged near freezing. A dry spell helps it flower
  • Planter or ground: Ground only in frost-free places; small grafted kinds such as Cogshall and Pickering suit large pots elsewhere
  • Spacing and depth: Garden trees need 6–10 m; prune to picking height
  • Water: Water young trees regularly; settled trees stand drought but fruit better with summer water
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Pick mature and firm, about 3–5 months after flowering, and ripen on the counter — a ripe mango gives a little under the thumb and smells sweet at the stem end

Garden notes

  • In the ground, a mango belongs only in the warmest places — south Florida, Hawaii, Puerto Rico and their like — and even an old tree suffers in a hard frost. Elsewhere, a small grafted variety in a large pot, moved under cover for winter, is the way.
  • Left alone, a seedling tree can pass 30 m (100 ft) tall with a canopy as wide, and trees said to be 300 years old still fruit. Garden trees are grafted kinds, pruned to picking height.
  • It flowers in the dry season and ripens its fruit in summer. Wet weather at flowering feeds anthracnose, a fungal disease that spots blossom and fruit, and the mango grower's main enemy.

Propagation

Sow a fresh seed at once, soon after eating the fruit — take it out of the stone and plant it about 1 inch deep in a pot. A seed-grown tree may not give the same fruit as its parent, and can take 6–10 years to fruit. To keep a named type true, it must be grafted onto a seedling rootstock — veneer grafting is the usual way, and grafted trees fruit in 3–5 years.

Safety

  • The peel, and the milky sap in the fruit's stem, carry small amounts of the same family of irritant oils found in poison ivy — the mango's own family. Most people eat mango without trouble, but anyone who reacts strongly to poison ivy, cashew or pistachio may find the peel makes the lips or skin itch. The flesh inside is the safe part: peel the fruit and keep the sap off your skin. If your mouth or throat swells, stop — that is an allergy, and it should be taken seriously.

Sources

  • USDA FoodData Central — nutrient values for mangoes, raw
  • Plants For A Future — Mangifera indica: bark and leaf dye for silk, timber uses, seed butter
  • Morton (1987) — "Mango", in Fruits of Warm Climates; origin, spread and the Florida varieties
  • Mwaurah et al. (2020) — mango kernel fat reviewed; tocopherols (vitamin E) up to about 148 mg/kg of the fat
  • Berghea et al. (2021) — mango in the cashew family; skin reactions in people already sensitive to poison ivy

Burdock

Arctium lappa

MedicinalCulinary

Skin Health

Cooked

A biennial pioneer of disturbed ground — waste places, roadsides and field edges. The root is a food as much as a medicine, eaten as a vegetable in Japan, and the purple, thistle-like flowers feed bees through the summer.

  • Burdock was used as a medicine in Europe for centuries. The old herbals — books about healing plants — called it a blood purifier, a herb taken to clear the blood, and used it for skin troubles and stiff joints. That name records a belief, not a tested finding.
  • China used a different part. The seed, called niubangzi, held a long place in Chinese medicine, where it was used for sore throats, colds and skin rashes.
  • Japan turned the root into food. It has been grown there for centuries as gobo, bred long and thin, dug while young and cooked as a vegetable — the same root that Europe took as a medicine.
  • Herbals from the Middle Ages used the root and leaves for swellings and sores, and the leaf stayed in folk use long after, laid on the skin as a poultice — a soft mash of plant matter held against the body.
  • The plant comes from Europe and Asia. It crossed to North America with European settlers, and now grows on waste ground across the temperate world.

Traditional medicine

  • European regulators recognise the root as a traditional herbal medicine to increase the flow of urine and flush the urinary tract, as an aid in minor urinary complaints.
  • The same monograph lists it for temporary loss of appetite.
  • It is also traditionally used for seborrhoeic skin conditions — oily, flaky skin.

Craft

  • Burdock is a dye plant: its leaves, chopped and simmered long, give beige-tan shades with vinegar, light yellow with alum and a strong yellow with tin — soft, earthy colours from a plant most people only dig out.
  • The root is a food as much as a medicine — in Japan it is eaten as a vegetable, called gobo, and it is rich in the fibre inulin.
  • The young leaves can be cooked and eaten, though they are bitter.
  • Caution: buy burdock root rather than gathering it wild — the root is easily confused with the root of deadly nightshade (belladonna), and commercial burdock teas have been poisoned by that mix-up. Burdock is in the daisy family, so avoid it if you are allergic to daisy-family plants such as chrysanthemums, and avoid it in pregnancy, as it may stimulate the womb. Take care alongside diabetes medicines — burdock lowered blood sugar in animal studies — and herbal references advise care with blood-thinning medicines too.
  • When to plant: Usually gathered wild. To grow it, sow seed outside in spring where it will stay — the deep taproot resents moving
  • Sun: Full sun or some shade
  • Soil: Deep, loose soil, so the long root can grow straight; it tolerates poor, disturbed ground
  • Environment: A hardy biennial — leaves the first year, flowers the second; a pioneer of waste places and roadsides
  • Planter or ground: Ground only — the root grows to about three feet
  • Spacing and depth: Sow 1 cm deep; thin to 45 cm apart
  • Water: Average — drought-tolerant once the taproot is down
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Dig the root in the autumn of the first year, while it is still tender; young leaves are picked in spring

Garden notes

  • A biennial pioneer of disturbed ground — waste places, roadsides and field edges — covering bare soil where little else is established.
  • Its deep taproot, growing to about three feet, drives down through compacted soil and helps break it up.
  • The purple, thistle-like flowers feed bees and other pollinators through the summer.
  • An honest downside: the hooked burrs — the fastening that inspired Velcro — tangle in fur and feathers and have trapped small birds and bats, and the long-lived seed makes burdock hard to remove once it settles in.

Propagation

Sow seed in place in autumn, or in spring once the soil has warmed. Press seed shallowly into deep, loose, stone-free soil and keep it moist until seedlings show. Do not start it in pots and move it — the long taproot hates being disturbed and will fork. Dig first-year roots in autumn, before the plant flowers in its second year.

Sources

  • European Medicines Agency, burdock root monograph — traditional use for urinary flushing, loss of appetite and seborrhoeic skin
  • Memorial Sloan Kettering, About Herbs — no evidence for cancer, infection or diabetes claims
  • Bryson et al. (1978) — burdock tea contaminated with belladonna root (atropine)
  • NC State Extension, Plant Toolbox — plant habit, taproot and seed dispersal

Calendula

Calendula officinalis

MedicinalCulinary

Skin HealthWound Care

FreshCooked

The classic salve flower — calendula-infused oil is the heart of many herbal salves and balms. The petals are edible too, with a mild peppery tang.

  • The name is a calendar. Calendula is tied to the Latin calendae, the first day of the month, because the plant flowers through so much of the year that blooms could be found at the start of almost any month.
  • “Marigold” itself means Mary's gold: in the Middle Ages the flower was linked to the Virgin Mary and used at her feast days. And its second name, officinalis, marks it as an official apothecary plant — the name given to plants kept in the apothecary's store, which is why this species, of some 15–20 Calendula species, is the one in medicine. Its written record goes back at least to the 1100s. Hildegard of Bingen, a German abbess and writer on healing plants, described it in her book of medicines.
  • In the gardens of the Middle Ages it was the pot marigold: a kitchen-garden flower whose petals coloured broths, rice and cheese a golden yellow — the poor cook's saffron.
  • Herbalists used the flowers on the skin for wounds, burns and sores, and that use for wounds carried on through the centuries, into the salves it is still known for.
  • Because it flowers from late spring to the first frosts, it became one of the most planted cottage-garden flowers in Europe, and travellers carried it to gardens all over the world.
  • Its wild origin is honestly not known for certain. It is thought to come from southern Europe and the eastern Mediterranean; it is not found as a clear wild plant, and gardeners have carried it worldwide, where it now escapes and grows on its own in cool, temperate climates.
  • One name trap: the orange marigolds of Mexico's Day of the Dead and of Indian garlands are Tagetes, a different genus from the Americas. They share the name “marigold” and the daisy family with this plant — nothing more.

Traditional medicine

  • European regulators recognise the flower as a traditional herbal medicine for minor inflammations of the skin, such as sunburn.
  • The same monograph lists it as an aid in the healing of minor wounds.
  • It is also traditionally used for minor inflammation in the mouth or throat, as a gargle or rinse.

Craft

  • The petals dye wool and cloth a clear yellow, and were once used to colour butter and cheese.
  • Calendula-infused oil — petals steeped in oil until it turns deep gold — is the base of homemade salves, balms and soaps.
  • The petals are edible, with a mild peppery tang, and have long been used to add golden colour to foods — the “poor man's saffron”.
  • The best-studied human use is skin during radiotherapy, and the result is mixed. In a French trial of 254 women having radiotherapy after breast-cancer surgery, calendula ointment gave severe skin reactions in 41% against 63% on the comparison cream, with less pain (Pommier et al., 2004). In a larger, blinded Swedish trial of 420 women, calendula cream did no better than a plain aqueous cream (Sharp et al., 2013), and a smaller 2021 trial also found no clear difference. One large trial favoured calendula over one comparison cream; later trials against plain moisturisers found no advantage. That is not proof that calendula prevents radiation skin damage.
  • For wound healing overall, a review of 14 studies found the animal work stronger than the human work: animal studies showed faster early healing, while human results were uneven, with no benefit in one diabetic leg-ulcer trial and one burns trial, and a call for larger, better trials (Givol et al., 2019). The Skin Health and Wound Care tags rest on traditional use, with mixed human trial results — stated at that strength.
  • Caution: calendula is in the daisy family — do not use it if you are allergic to daisy-family plants such as ragweed or chamomile. The EMA does not recommend it in pregnancy or while breastfeeding, as its safety there has not been established.
  • Caution: the European monograph sets age limits for lack of safety data — skin use only over age 6, mouth and throat use only over age 12. And see a doctor if symptoms last longer than a week, or sooner if the skin looks infected or gets worse.
  • When to plant: Sow outside in spring, or start indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost; it self-seeds freely and returns year after year
  • Sun: Full sun, or a little shade in hot summers
  • Soil: Ordinary, well-drained soil; not fussy
  • Environment: A hardy annual, in bloom from late spring to the first frosts
  • Planter or ground: Both — pots suit it well
  • Spacing and depth: Sow ¼ to ½ inch deep and cover the seed — light stops it sprouting; germination takes about 5–15 days. Set plants 25–30 cm apart
  • Water: Average
  • Companion plants: A valued companion among vegetables: it works as a decoy, drawing aphids onto itself, and pulls in the hoverflies and lacewings whose young hunt aphids
  • When to pick: Pick the flowers as they open fully, after the dew has dried, all season — keep picking to keep them coming. Dry them in a ventilated place out of direct sunlight

Garden notes

  • One of the longest-flowering plants in the garden — in bloom from late spring to the first frosts, feeding bees and other pollinators for months.
  • The flowers draw in hoverflies and lacewings, whose larvae hunt aphids — a standing patrol for the vegetable garden.
  • Grown as a companion plant among vegetables, it also works as a decoy, drawing aphids onto itself and away from crops.
  • It self-seeds freely and returns year after year in the same spot, though the seedlings are shallow-rooted and easy to pull where they are not wanted; its taproot helps loosen the soil.
  • Pinch the growing tips when plants are a few inches tall for bushier growth, feed lightly — plants flower best when not heavily fertilised — and deadhead regularly to keep flowers coming, leaving heads only where self-sowing is wanted.
  • It may fade in long, hot summer weather and recover when cooler weather returns. Its real problems are few: aphids, powdery mildew and occasionally cucumber mosaic virus, and slugs and snails on young plants. Good air flow and watering at the soil help against mildew.

Propagation

Sow seed directly in the garden after the last frost, or start indoors 6–8 weeks earlier. Cover with only a thin layer of soil, about ¼ inch, and keep it evenly moist — seedlings show in 7–14 days. Thin to 8–16 inches apart. It self-seeds freely, so new plants often appear on their own the next year.

Cultivars

  • 'Pacific Beauty' is a tall series, to about 18 inches, in yellow, orange and apricot, with long stems good for cutting. 'Bon Bon' is a compact series, about 12 inches tall and wide, in apricot, yellow and orange — suited to pots and the front of a border.
  • 'Radio' is an old variety, introduced in 1931, less sticky and less strongly scented than the wild type. 'Indian Prince' carries flowers 2 to 3 inches across on plants 14 to 24 inches tall.
  • The POWERDAISY series is long-blooming and sterile, grown from cuttings rather than seed, and bred to resist powdery mildew.

Sources

  • Mahr (2008) — University of Wisconsin Extension guide to calendula cultivars, origin and care
  • Pommier et al. (2004) — phase III trial, calendula ointment versus trolamine in radiotherapy skin reactions, 254 women
  • Sharp et al. (2013) — randomised blinded trial, calendula cream versus aqueous cream, 420 women, no difference
  • Givol et al. (2019) — systematic review of calendula extract for wound healing, animal and human studies
  • European Medicines Agency, calendula flower monograph — traditional use for minor skin inflammation, minor wounds, and mouth and throat inflammation
  • European Medicines Agency, calendula assessment report — documented skin use since the 12th century; Commission E approval (1986)
  • Garden Planner companion guide — pollinator value and aphid trap-crop use

Cannabis

Cannabis sativa

MedicinalCulinary

Digestive HealthMental Health

A tall, fast-growing annual in the hemp family, Cannabaceae — the same family as hops — native to Central Asia and now grown in temperate regions all over the world. Cannabis is a single species with two very different crops bred from it: hemp, grown for fibre and seed and bred to make almost none of the intoxicating compound THC, and drug cannabis, bred to make a great deal of it. Which of the two a plant is depends on its breeding and its chemistry, not on a different species name. Most plants are either male or female, and it is the female flower that carries the plant's richest store of active compounds, held in a sticky resin coating the flowers.

The parts divide by purpose. The female flower is the medicinal and intoxicating part. The seed — hemp seed — is a straightforward food, rich in protein and oil, and carries no meaningful amount of THC or CBD, because those compounds are made in the flower, not in the seed. The stem gives one of the oldest textile fibres in the world. The leaf holds far less of the active compounds than the flower and is mostly a by-product, and the root has a small place in old medicine and in modern laboratory research.

The plant makes over a hundred related compounds called cannabinoids. Two dominate. THC (tetrahydrocannabinol) is the one that intoxicates: it changes perception, mood, appetite and the sense of time. CBD (cannabidiol) does not intoxicate, and is the basis of one licensed medicine. The plant also makes terpenes — the aromatic compounds that give many plants their scent, the same family of compounds found in lemon peel, pine resin and lavender. Terpenes give each cannabis variety its characteristic smell; whether they change the plant's effects in people is not established.

Terpenes in this plant: · · · · · ·

  • Cannabis is one of the oldest farmed plants in the world. It was first tamed in Central or East Asia thousands of years ago. Hemp was among China's earliest fibre crops: its seed was eaten and its stem was spun, and the plant appears in the earliest Chinese traditions of herbal medicine.
  • The Greek historian Herodotus, writing around 440 BCE, described the Scythians of the steppe throwing cannabis seed onto hot stones inside tents and breathing in the vapour. It is an early written record of the intoxicating use, standing alongside the fibre use.
  • From Asia the plant travelled along every trade route: into India, where it became part of Ayurvedic medicine and ritual; through the Middle East; into Europe as a fibre crop; and to the Americas with the colonists, who grew hemp for rope and sailcloth.
  • Western medicine took it up in the 1840s, when the Irish doctor William O'Shaughnessy brought cannabis medicines back from India and reported their use for pain, spasm and convulsions. Cannabis tinctures — strong plant extracts made with alcohol — then sat in Western pharmacies for the rest of the century.
  • The twentieth century turned that around. The United States taxed cannabis out of ordinary trade in 1937, and banned it outright in 1970. The United Nations Single Convention of 1961 spread the ban around the world. Hemp farming was mostly swept up along with the drug plant.
  • In recent decades the two crops have parted again in law. The United States took hemp out of its controlled-substances law in 2018. Several countries license medicines made from cannabinoids, the plant's active compounds. And a few countries — Uruguay and Canada first — have made the drug plant itself legal for adults.
  • Hemp oil, steam-distilled from the flowers, is breathed in for calm: in one very small study of five people, it left them feeling more relaxed. It holds no THC or CBD, and it is not CBD oil. Human · small

Craft

  • The stem gives hemp fibre, one of the oldest textile fibres in the world: stripped, retted and spun, it makes cloth, rope, twine and paper. Fibre hemp is bred tall and straight for exactly this — a separate crop from drug cannabis.
  • The strongest evidence belongs not to the plant but to medicines made from single compounds taken out of it. A purified CBD medicine, Epidiolex, is licensed for seizures in two rare, severe childhood epilepsies — Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and Dravet syndrome — where trials showed it reduced seizure frequency substantially more than placebo. That is evidence for that medicine, at that dose, in those conditions. It is not evidence for over-the-counter CBD oil, and not for the plant.
  • Laboratory-made versions of THC (dronabinol and nabilone) are licensed medicines for the nausea and vomiting caused by cancer chemotherapy, and dronabinol also for appetite loss in people with HIV/AIDS. The trial evidence behind them is older and moderate in strength.
  • A mouth spray combining THC and CBD (nabiximols) is licensed in several countries — though not the United States — for muscle stiffness and spasm in multiple sclerosis. Reviews find it probably reduces how severe the spasticity feels in the short term; measured stiffness improves less clearly.
  • For long-term pain, pooled reviews find that cannabis and cannabinoid medicines give a small average benefit: in one large review of non-cancer pain, 29% of people taking them achieved a meaningful 30% reduction in pain, against 26% on placebo. Real, but small — and bought with more side effects, such as dizziness and drowsiness.
  • For sleep, the evidence is modest and mixed. A major evidence review found moderate support for short-term sleep improvement in people whose sleep is disturbed by particular conditions — chronic pain, multiple sclerosis, fibromyalgia and sleep apnoea — and little beyond that. Cannabis is not an established treatment for insomnia, and heavy long-term use can make sleep worse.
  • For anxiety, the evidence points both ways. Small, short studies suggest CBD alone may ease anxiety in specific situations, such as public speaking. THC, by contrast, commonly causes anxiety and panic at higher doses, and heavy cannabis use is associated with higher rates of anxiety disorders. No anxiety treatment is established.
  • Hemp seed is a food, and a good one: roughly a quarter protein and a third oil, with an unusually favourable balance of the essential fats omega-6 and omega-3, plus a rarer fat, gamma-linolenic acid, that few foods carry. It does not intoxicate, and it is not a medicine.
  • Caution — dependence: cannabis can be habit-forming. About one in ten people who use it develop dependence, rising to roughly one in six among those who start as teenagers, and higher still in daily users. Withdrawal is real but milder than with alcohol or opioids — irritability, poor sleep and low appetite for a week or two.
  • Caution — mental health: the most serious risk sits with the mind. Large studies consistently link cannabis use — above all daily use of high-strength, high-THC cannabis, and use beginning in the teenage years — with higher rates of psychosis, including schizophrenia. Whether cannabis causes the illness or brings it forward in people already vulnerable is still argued, but the association is strong and grows with dose and strength, and it is the reason teenagers and anyone with a family history of psychosis are advised to avoid cannabis entirely.
  • Caution — pregnancy: do not use cannabis in pregnancy or while breastfeeding. THC crosses the placenta and passes into breast milk, use in pregnancy is linked with lower birth weight, and obstetric guidance advises against it outright.
  • Caution — driving: cannabis impairs driving and machinery use — reaction time, attention and coordination all suffer, and crash risk rises. The impairment outlasts the feeling of being affected.
  • Caution — interactions and lungs: CBD and THC interfere with the liver system that clears many medicines, and can change blood levels of blood thinners such as warfarin, some epilepsy and transplant medicines, and some antidepressants; CBD at medicine doses has also been linked with liver injury. Their effects add up with alcohol and sedative medicines. Smoked cannabis irritates the airways, and regular smoking is linked with chronic bronchitis.
  • Caution — the law: the law on cannabis differs sharply from place to place and changes often. The same plant that is a licensed medicine or a legal product in one jurisdiction is a criminal offence in another. Hemp is the legal exception in many places, defined by a cap on THC — 0.3% in United States law. Check the law where you are.
  • When to plant: Sow or set out in spring, after frost. Check the law where you are first — it differs sharply from place to place
  • Sun: Full sun
  • Soil: Deep, fertile, well-drained soil close to neutral; it sulks in wet, heavy ground
  • Environment: A temperate annual with a deep taproot that breaks up compacted soil; wind-pollinated, and the pollen is a notable allergen for some people
  • Planter or ground: Ground; large pots for single plants
  • Spacing and depth: 1 m or more apart — set out in spring, it can pass three metres by late summer
  • Water: Average — water young plants in dry spells
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Seed is gathered when the hulls harden, in autumn; fibre hemp is cut at flowering

Garden notes

  • Native to Central Asia and happiest in temperate climates: it wants full sun and a deep, fertile, well-drained soil close to neutral, and sulks in wet, heavy ground.
  • A true annual with a deep taproot: set out in spring it can pass three metres by late summer, and the root breaks up and aerates compacted soil as it goes.
  • The fast, dense canopy shades out weeds — one reason fibre hemp is usually grown with few pesticide sprays, since few pests trouble it.
  • Wind-pollinated: male plants shed clouds of pollen in late summer, a notable allergen for some people. The seed is rich bird food, and hemp seed has long gone into bird feed.
  • The plant takes up heavy metals from the soil into its tissues, which is why it is studied for cleaning contaminated land and has been trialled for that purpose, including around Chernobyl. That same appetite is a reason food crops of it belong on clean soil.

Propagation

Grow from seed, or take a cutting from a healthy mother plant in its leafy growth stage, dip the cut end in rooting hormone, and keep it warm and humid in a moist rooting mix until roots form. A cutting is an exact copy of its mother, while seed-grown plants vary. Only grow it where the law allows.

Safety

  • Essential oils are concentrates, many times stronger than the plant itself. Always dilute in a carrier oil before putting one on skin, and never swallow an essential oil.
