Chickweed

Stellaria media

MedicinalCulinary

Digestive HealthSkin Health

FreshCooked

A low, mat-forming spring plant. The whole plant is edible and has long been eaten as a spring green, and it has a traditional place on the skin as well as in teas.

  • The name tells you who ate it first. Chickweed is named for chickens, because chickens eat it eagerly. People who kept birds also gathered it for caged birds.
  • People ate it too. For hundreds of years in Europe, it was a spring green. People picked it young and ate it raw or cooked, at a time of year when little else was growing.
  • Writers on herbs in the 1500s and 1600s — Gerard and Culpeper among them — praised it as a cooling herb. People laid it on hot, itchy skin.
  • That use on skin stayed in folk practice — the everyday healing people did at home. A fresh poultice — a soft, wet mass of the plant held against the skin — made of chickweed, for rashes, bites and skin irritation, is still its best-known home remedy. It rests on tradition, not on trials — no careful tests have proved it.
  • Chickweed is native to Eurasia and is now naturalised almost everywhere in the temperate world, travelling with settlers, seed and soil. In Japan it is hakobera, one of the seven herbs of spring eaten on 7 January in nanakusa-gayu, a rice porridge cooked for health in the year ahead and to rest the stomach after New Year feasting — a living custom, still kept, with the herb sets sold in shops for the day.
  • The name is a description: Stellaria comes from the Latin stella, a star, for the small white star-shaped flowers, and media means “in between”.
  • It is a very old European plant: its remains have been found at pre-Neolithic sites in Britain, placing it among the wild plants present at the very start of farming in Europe.

Traditional medicine

  • Traditionally used on the skin — as a fresh poultice, wash or salve — to soothe itching, minor rashes, irritation and insect bites. This use rests on tradition; it has not been tested in controlled human trials.
  • Traditionally taken as a tea to soothe the throat and digestive tract.
  • The whole plant is edible and has long been eaten as a spring green. It contains vitamin C, flavonoids and minerals including calcium, iron and potassium.
  • Contains natural saponins, the soap-like compounds behind its soothing, slippery feel on the skin.
  • The modern research record is animal and laboratory work, claim by claim. In mice, chickweed extract reduced food intake and fat absorption in an obesity model, and leaf extract lowered blood sugar in diabetic mice — animal only. In rats, chickweed tea protected the heart muscle in diabetes without lowering blood sugar — animal only, and worth stating exactly: it did not do the headline thing. In the laboratory, extracts showed anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity, and one was active against hepatitis B virus in cultured cells — laboratory only.
  • There are no controlled human trials of chickweed for any use — not for skin, digestion, weight, blood sugar or cholesterol.
  • Caution: eaten in large amounts, the saponins can upset the stomach. Gather only from clean ground — plants from heavily fertilised soil can build up nitrates — and avoid medicinal use in pregnancy, as its safety has not been established.
  • Caution — the look-alike that matters: chickweed is confused with scarlet pimpernel, sometimes called poison chickweed, which is toxic to livestock and can upset people and pets. Pimpernel has square, hairless stems, dark spots under its leaves, and salmon-orange (sometimes blue) flowers. Chickweed has round stems with a single line of fine hairs, and small white flowers whose five deeply split petals look like ten. If the flowers are orange, it is not chickweed — do not eat it.
  • Caution: young spurges grow in the same patches and bleed a milky white sap when snapped; that sap is an irritant. Chickweed has no milky sap — if it bleeds white, leave it.
  • Caution: in one reported case, a patch test to fresh chickweed leaves was positive in a woman with recurring skin reactions after handling weeds — a single case, at case-report strength.
  • When to plant: Usually gathered wild. To grow it, scatter seed in spring on fertile, moist ground and let it form its mat
  • Sun: Some shade suits it; it grows in sun where the soil stays moist
  • Soil: Fertile, moist soil — its presence is a sign of both
  • Environment: A cool-season plant; it fades in hot, dry weather and returns in autumn
  • Planter or ground: Ground; a wide pot keeps it tidy
  • Spacing and depth: Scatter seed on the surface and press it in — it needs light to sprout
  • Water: Likes water — keep it moist
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Gather the leafy tops while they are fresh and green, in spring and again in autumn

Garden notes

  • Forms a dense, low mat that works as a living mulch, shading the soil, holding moisture and protecting the surface from erosion.
  • The tiny seeds are eaten by songbirds such as sparrows, finches and doves, and the flowers give early nectar and pollen to small bees and hoverflies.
  • When it dies back or is turned into the soil, it returns the minerals it gathered to the topsoil.
  • Its stems root where a joint touches damp soil, which is how one plant becomes a mat, and its seed can stay alive in the soil for more than 20 years — which is why it returns every cool season even where it was cleared.
  • The surest field check for true chickweed: a single line of fine hairs runs down one side of the stem and switches sides at each leaf joint.

Propagation

Scatter seed on the surface of moist soil in early spring or in fall, press it in lightly, and keep it damp until seedlings appear in about a week. It needs light to sprout, so do not bury it. It seeds itself with great ease — snip off the flowers before they set seed if you do not want it spreading through the whole bed.

Cultivars

  • Chickweed has never been bred — no named varieties exist. What does exist is a small group of very close species that books long lumped together as Stellaria media: Stellaria media in the strict sense; Stellaria neglecta, greater chickweed, larger, flowering April to July; and Stellaria pallida, lesser chickweed, smaller and paler, with petals tiny or absent. Tradition uses them the same way.

Sources

  • Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries — the nanakusa tradition: chickweed (hakobera) among the seven herbs of spring
  • Rani et al. (2012) — anti-obesity activity of Stellaria media in mice
  • Demján et al. (2022) — chickweed tea and the diabetic rat heart; no effect on blood sugar
  • Ma et al. (2012) — chickweed extracts against hepatitis B virus in cultured cells (laboratory only)
  • Singh et al. (2022) — review of chickweed pharmacology; evidence from animal and laboratory models
  • Kew, Plants of the World Online — Stellaria media: native to Eurasia, naturalised throughout the world
  • Drugs.com, chickweed monograph — traditional uses; no clinical evidence to guide dosage
  • WebMD, chickweed — no good scientific evidence for metabolic claims
  • Plants For A Future — ground cover, erosion control and wildlife value

Cilantro

Coriandrum sativum

Culinary

Vitamin AVitamin C

FreshDried

Cilantro is a fast-growing herb in the carrot family, grown for two parts that barely taste related: the fresh leaf — bright, green and citrus-sharp — and the dried seed, called coriander — warm, nutty and lemony, with no soap in it at all. The leaf tastes of soap to a real minority of people, for a genetic reason set out below. And it is not only leaf and seed: somewhere in the world every part of this plant is cooked with, roots and flowers included.

Cultivars

  • "Variety" means two different things for this plant: leaf varieties, bred to hold their leaves longer before flowering, and seed types, shaped by the regions that grow them. The forms are told apart by leaf, seed and use, because unlabelled photographs cannot honestly separate them.
  • 'Santo' — the slow-bolt standard for leaf, and the commercial grower's choice. Also sold as Long Standing or California Long Standing. It stands weeks longer than ordinary strains before flowering, and gives leaf in about 50–55 days from sowing.
  • 'Leisure' — a slow-bolt leaf variety prized for uniformity and dependability: even stands of medium-green, flat, feathery leaves with a strong, pungent flavour. About 50–55 days to leaf, 90–105 days to ripe seed.
  • 'Slow Bolt' (also sold as 'Slo-Bolt') — a seed-catalogue name rather than a single bred cultivar: strains selected simply for flowering late. Worth knowing for what it is — the name is the whole description, and it buys extra weeks of leaf, not immunity from bolting.
  • 'Calypso' — a bushy, slow-bolt leaf variety with high yields that regrows well after cutting, bred for repeated harvests.
  • Moroccan seed type — the big round seed of the spice trade: botanists' large-fruited form (var. sativum, fruits 3–5 mm across), light yellow-brown with strong ribs, mild in flavour and low in oil. Because it is large and handsome it is the seed sold whole — for pickling spice and crab boils — and most of Canada's large coriander crop is this type.
  • Indian seed type (dhania) — the elongated, oval seed (var. indicum), yellower and more lemony-sweet than the Moroccan. India grows it in quantity and keeps most of it: ground with cumin it is the base of countless curries, and the spice trade estimates that a quarter to two fifths of the world's coriander goes into Indian curry powders alone.
  • European small-seeded type — the small-fruited form (var. microcarpum, fruits 1.5–3 mm) grown in temperate Europe — Romanian and Russian seed. It looks less, but it is richer in oil (about 0.4–1.8%, against 0.1–0.4% in the large types), so it is the distiller's seed, grown for coriander oil and for flavouring gin.
Mexico — the leaf's second home. Cilantro is scattered over tacos, stirred through salsa and guacamole, floated on pozole. The plant came with Spanish cooking and met a cuisine that made it indispensable; the American name "cilantro" arrived at the table by the same route.
Thailand — the only kitchen that insists on all three parts. Leaves garnish; seeds go into curry pastes; and the root — rak phak chi — is pounded with garlic and white pepper as the base of curry pastes, soups and chilli dips, and of the marinade for grilled chicken. Thai cooks say there is no true substitute; chopped stems, at three times the amount, are the accepted stand-in.
India — dhania, both ways at once: the leaf whizzed into green chutneys and scattered fresh over finished dishes by the handful, and the seed ground with cumin (dhania-jeera) as the warm base under countless curries, and a member of garam masala. No country grows or uses more of it.
The Middle East and Yemen — the leaf chopped into salads and falafel mixtures, the seed through spice blends such as baharat; and Yemen's zhug, a fiery sauce of cilantro, chillies, garlic and spices, eaten with almost everything.
China — xiangcai, "fragrant greens": leaves in soups, noodle dishes and cold-dressed salads — the source of the English name Chinese parsley.
Vietnam — rau mùi, coriander leaf scattered over phở and salads at the table, torn by the eater into the hot broth.
Portugal — coentros, the European exception: most of northern Europe historically kept coriander for its seed, but Portugal — above all the Alentejo — cooks with the leaf, in açorda, the garlic-and-bread soup, and with pork and seafood.
Northern Europe — the seed's old territory: in German and Scandinavian baking and sausages, in British pickling spice and mixed spice, and in the distillery — coriander seed is second only to juniper among the flavourings of many gins.
  • Cilantro / coriander comes from the lands between the eastern Mediterranean and western Pakistan, and grows wild across western Asia and southern Europe. It is one of the oldest herbs people grow. Its name already appears in Mycenaean Greek — ko-ri-ja-da-na — in the second millennium BCE, and coriander seeds have been recovered from the Neolithic cave of Nahal Hemar in Israel, among the earliest spice finds anywhere in the world.
  • Egypt took to it early and valued it highly. Coriander fruits were placed in the tomb of Tutankhamun, who died about 1323 BCE — a spice worth sending with a king — and the plant is named in Egyptian medical writings, including the Ebers papyrus. The Roman writer Pliny, much later, said the finest coriander to reach Rome came from Egypt.
  • It is one of the very few foods the Old Testament names. In Exodus, the manna that fed the Israelites in the desert is described as "like coriander seed, white" — the seed was familiar enough to be the comparison everyone would know.
  • Greece grew it from at least the second millennium BCE, and Rome cooked with both parts: the leaf and seed went into moretum, the Romans' pounded spread of herbs, cheese and garlic, and Pliny praised the plant as a medicine. In Greek, Indian (Ayurvedic) and Middle Eastern traditional medicine the seed was a standing household remedy, above all for the digestion, and the leaf a cooling herb. Those uses are history; what the studies actually support is in Health Benefits.
  • Coriander reached Britain at the very end of the Iron Age. Seeds found in a well at Silchester date to just before the Roman invasion of AD 43 — the spice was already arriving by trade — and coriander turns up again and again in the deposits of Roman London. It has been grown in British gardens ever since.
  • The names carry the story. Greek koriandron (also koriannon) may come from koris, a bedbug — the green plant's smell reminded people of the insect, the first recorded version of the complaint some people still make. Latin coriandrum became French coriandre and English "coriander"; Spanish "cilantro" grew from the same Latin word. In India the plant is dhania, in China xiangcai, "fragrant greens," and English sometimes calls it Chinese parsley. The names also mark the part that is meant. In North America the fresh leaves and stems are cilantro — the Spanish word for the plant, carried into English by Mexican cooking — while the dried seed is coriander. In Britain and much of the rest of the world the whole plant is coriander, and the leaf is "fresh coriander."
  • Coriander seed oil — distilled from the seed — is rubbed, diluted, on the belly for digestive comfort, and breathed in for calm. Traditional use
  • The leaf first, by the numbers. Fresh cilantro leaves, per 100 g: 23 kcal, protein 2.13 g, fibre 2.8 g. The standout is vitamin K at 310 µg — about two and a half times the whole day's value — with vitamin A at 337 µg (about a third of the day's value), vitamin C at 27 mg (about a third), and useful folate and potassium (521 mg) besides. Vitamin K is the vitamin the body uses to clot blood normally and to build bone. The honest scale: nobody eats 100 g of cilantro at a sitting in a garnish — but in Indian chutneys and Mexican salsas it is eaten by the handful and the cupful, so the numbers are real food value where the plant is used generously.
  • The seed is a different food on paper. Per 100 g: 298 kcal, fibre 41.9 g, calcium 709 mg, iron 16.3 mg, magnesium 330 mg, potassium 1,267 mg. But a teaspoon of coriander seed weighs under 2 g, so in the kitchen the seed is a flavouring, not a mineral source. The figures describe the spice honestly; they do not make a serving of it a supplement.
  • Leaf and seed taste unrelated because they are built from different chemistry. The leaf's scent is dominated by compounds called aldehydes (2-decenal and 2-dodecenal among them). The seed's scent is dominated by linalool — about two thirds of its oil — the same compound that scents lavender, and it gives the seed its warm, citrus, floral flavour. That is why the seed never tastes soapy, and why many people who cannot eat the leaf enjoy the seed without noticing any connection.
  • The soap divide is real, and it is partly in the genes. In a 2012 study of 14,604 people, about one in seven said cilantro tasted soapy. The soap-tasters were more likely to carry a small variation in their DNA beside a cluster of smell-receptor genes — among them OR6A2, which builds a smell sensor that responds strongly to the very aldehydes that scent the leaf. A second 2012 survey found dislike of cilantro ranging from 3% of people with Middle Eastern backgrounds to 21% of people with East Asian backgrounds — the groups that cook with it most tend to dislike it least. The gene explains only a small part of the difference; habit and exposure do the rest. Neither side is wrong. They are, literally, smelling different leaves.
  • Blood sugar and cholesterol are the seed's most studied claims, and the honest summary is: promising in rats, unsettled in people. Two small trials of coriander seed powder in type 2 diabetes disagree with each other. The larger one — 150 people, 2 g a day for six weeks — found the seed no better than the dummy capsules for blood sugar, HbA1c or blood fats. A smaller one — 40 people, 1 g a day for six weeks — reported improvements, but reviewers note weaknesses in how it was designed and reported. Until a bigger, better trial settles it, coriander seed is a spice, not a diabetes treatment, and the evidence supports nothing more. Human · small
  • One claim is simply dropped: that cilantro pulls heavy metals — lead, mercury, aluminium — out of the body. It rests on studies in mice and on one doctor's case reports from the 1990s, measured with a finger-pressure test that has never been validated; a trial in children exposed to lead found coriander made no difference, and the percentages repeated online ("removes 87% of lead…") appear in no study at all. A proper review of the evidence concludes coriander is unlikely to remove heavy metals from the body. Anyone worried about metal poisoning needs a doctor and a blood test, not a herb.
  • When to plant: Sow in early spring, at the same time as lettuce, and again from late summer into autumn; in frost-free warm climates, autumn through winter is its best season. Sow a short row every two to three weeks through the cool seasons, so a young planting is always coming ready as the last one bolts
  • Sun: Full sun for the spring crop; a little afternoon shade suits summer sowings
  • Soil: Rich soil that holds moisture but drains, with a pH around 6.2–6.8
  • Environment: A cool-season annual: young plants shrug off a light frost, but a hard freeze kills them, and heat and long days — roughly above 80 °F (27 °C) — send it racing to flower
  • Planter or ground: Both — in a pot, choose a deep one, at least 8–10 inches, for the taproot
  • Spacing and depth: Sow where it is to grow, about ¼–½ inch deep — cilantro has a long taproot and hates being moved; thin seedlings to about 6 inches apart
  • Water: Keep it evenly watered — drying out hurries bolting
  • When to pick: Leaf from about 6 inches tall, roughly three to four weeks from sowing; seed at about three months — roughly 100 days — when about half the pods on a plant have turned tan-brown

Garden notes

  • Cilantro is a cool-season annual that lives fast. A plant in leaf stands about 50 cm (20 in) tall, taller once it flowers, and its whole leafy life is six to eight weeks before it bolts — sends up a flower stalk, turns feathery, and sets seed. Everything about growing it follows from that hurry.
  • Each "seed" is really a small dry fruit holding two seeds; rolling it gently under a rolling pin to crack the husk, or soaking it overnight, speeds sprouting, which otherwise takes about one to two weeks.
  • Slow-bolt varieties buy a week or a few, afternoon shade and mulch buy a little more, and pinching out a flower stalk buys days. A bolted plant cannot be unbolted — but it is not a failure. It is the coriander seed crop arriving, and the flowers in the meantime are excellent for bees and hoverflies.
  • Harvesting the leaf: cut the outer stems, take no more than about a third of the plant at once, and pick in the morning. The leaves are at their best before the flower stalk rises; the fine, feathery leaves that come with bolting taste harsher and more bitter.
  • The flowers are edible — small white-to-pale-pink umbrellas with a mild version of the leaf's flavour — and the soft green seeds that follow them, bright and citrusy before they harden, are used fresh by cooks as a seasoning in their own right. Letting a few plants flower also feeds the insects that keep aphids down; the plant's old garden reputation as a companion that discourages aphids rests on this flowering stage.
  • Harvesting the seed: wait until the pods smell warm and lemony when rubbed; green seed is harsh. Cut the heads into a paper bag, dry them fully, then rub and shake the seed free. Stored whole, in a jar away from light, it keeps its scent far longer than ground. Let a few pods fall where they grew and the plant sows next season's crop itself.
  • In a pot: a pot on a cool, bright windowsill stretches the leaf season at both ends of the year. Pots dry fast, and dry plants bolt.
  • Keeping the leaf: cilantro wilts and yellows quickly. Stand the stems in a jar of water, cover loosely, and refrigerate for up to a week; or chop and freeze in ice-cube trays with a little water or oil. It dries badly — the scent that makes it worth eating is the first thing to leave — which is why this plant's dried herb has always been its seed.

Propagation

Sow seed directly where it will grow, ¼–½ inch deep, in spring or late summer when the soil is 55–68°F. Keep the soil moist until seedlings appear in 7–21 days, then thin to 6–8 inches apart. Sow a fresh patch every 2–3 weeks for a steady supply. Do not move seedlings — cilantro grows a taproot that hates being disturbed — and it runs to flower fast once hot weather comes.

Safety

  • In cooking amounts this is a safe, ordinary food eaten by millions daily. A small number of people are allergic to it, as happens with other members of the carrot family. The concentrated essential oil is not the leaf or the seed and should not be swallowed as if it were; and seed taken by the spoonful as a supplement is a different act from seed ground into a curry.
  • People who take warfarin or a similar blood thinner are told to keep their vitamin K intake steady, so a sudden new daily chutney habit is worth mentioning to the clinician who manages the dose.

Sources

  • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: coriander (cilantro) leaves, raw, and spices, coriander seed — the nutrition figures
  • Diederichsen (1996) — Coriander (Coriandrum sativum L.), IPGRI — names, origin and the classification of the seed types
  • Saul et al. (2013) — Phytoliths in pottery reveal the use of spice in European prehistoric cuisine (PLOS ONE) — the earliest finds, from Nahal Hemar to Tutankhamun's tomb
  • Lodwick (2014) — Condiments before Claudius: new plant foods at the Late Iron Age oppidum at Silchester — coriander seed reaching Britain before the Roman invasion
  • Eriksson et al. (2012) — A genetic variant near olfactory receptor genes influences cilantro preference (Flavour) — the soap-taste genetics
  • Mauer & El-Sohemy (2012) — Prevalence of cilantro disliking among different ethnocultural groups (Flavour) — how widely the dislike varies
  • Abascal & Yarnell (2012) — Cilantro — culinary herb or miracle medicinal plant? — the heavy-metal claim examined against the evidence
  • Aga et al. (2001) — Cilantro against lead deposition in mice (Journal of Ethnopharmacology) — the animal study behind the detox claim
  • Zahmatkesh & Khodashenas Roudsari (2013) — Cinnamon, fenugreek and coriander compared in type II diabetic patients — the larger trial, which found no effect beyond placebo
  • Zamany et al. (2025) — Coriander seed supplementation in type 2 diabetes: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial — the smaller trial, which reported improvements

Cleavers

Galium aparine

MedicinalCulinary

Skin Health

Fresh

A scrambling, tangled spring herb — also called goosegrass, because geese and poultry graze the leaves. It is gathered fresh in spring, as a classic spring tonic herb in European tradition.

  • Writers in Greece and Rome knew this plant. Dioscorides wrote about a clinging Galium — a plant in this same group — that people used in medicine in his time.
  • Cleavers belongs to the coffee family, the Rubiaceae. Coffee and madder belong to the same family.
  • People once roasted its seeds and ground them as a stand-in for coffee. It was the closest thing to coffee that the hedgerow could offer.
  • In the herb books of Europe, it was a spring herb. Gerard recommended it in 1597, a generation before Culpeper, who wrote it down as a spring tonic — a drink taken to refresh the body. People took it when the plant came up fresh, to clear the body after winter. America's Eclectic physicians of the 1800s prescribed it as a diuretic and for skin eruptions — the bridge between the herb books and the country practice that followed. Indigenous nations in North America used Galium species — this plant's close relatives — as skin washes and kidney teas.
  • Country practice kept that same rhythm. Each spring, people gathered cleavers for teas and spring greens. They also used it as a wash for irritated skin.
  • Cleavers is native across Europe, North Africa and Asia, from Britain and the Canary Islands to Japan, and is now naturalised throughout North and South America, Australia and New Zealand. Whether it is also native to North America is honestly debated — Kew lists it as introduced there, while the USDA treats it as native. Everywhere, it follows people: hedgerows, field margins, gardens and waste ground. It is a noxious weed in many places and a serious weed of cereal crops.
  • The name explains the plant: Galium comes from the Greek gala, milk — a relative, Galium verum, was used to curdle milk for cheese — and aparine from a Greek word meaning “to seize”, the clinging plant. Its other everyday names are sticky willy, stickyweed and catchweed.

Traditional medicine

  • Traditionally used as a gentle diuretic — to support urine flow and ease minor fluid retention and urinary discomfort.
  • Herbalists traditionally class cleavers as a lymphatic herb, used for swollen glands. This rests on traditional practice alone; there are no human trials showing that it changes lymph flow.
  • Traditionally used as a wash or poultice to calm irritated skin.

Craft

  • Cleavers sits in the madder family, and like madder its roots hold a red dye. The roots are thin and fiddly to gather, so it was always a small-scale dye — pink-red shades on wool for those with patience.
  • The stems were a tool, not just a plant: Dioscorides recorded Greek shepherds matting the rough, hooked stems into a sieve for straining milk, and Linnaeus reported the same use still practised in Sweden in his day. The dried foliage was also stuffed into mattresses — the clinging hairs held the filling even instead of lumpy — which is where the family name “bedstraw” comes from.
  • The young shoots have traditionally been eaten as a spring green, and the plant contains vitamin C.
  • The modern research record is animal-level, and each piece needs its label. For the diuretic use, no study measuring urine output in people was found; rodent work reports only a mild increase — the reputation rests on tradition. In mice with drug-suppressed immune systems, a cleavers extract injected into the abdomen for three days raised natural-killer cell activity — in groups of three mice; injected, tiny and animal-only, it supports no claim for tea. And rats given cleavers extract for five days had less liver damage from a toxic dose of paracetamol than untreated rats — one animal overdose model, with no human meaning yet.
  • Caution: cleavers has not had formal safety testing. It is not recommended in pregnancy or while breastfeeding, and care should be taken alongside diuretic medicines.
  • Caution: the hooked hairs are a mechanical irritant, and a rash from handling cleavers is reported — worth knowing for a plant gathered fresh by hand.
  • Caution: do not gather from roadsides or sprayed field edges. The sticky surface collects dust and dirt, and as a major crop weed the plant is a routine herbicide target.
  • When to plant: Usually gathered wild. To grow it, sow seed in spring or autumn in a corner where it can scramble
  • Sun: Some shade — it is a hedgerow plant
  • Soil: Moist, rich soil — clay and loamy soils rich in nitrogen and phosphorus suit it best, which is why it thrives in manured beds and farm fields
  • Environment: A hardy annual that climbs and tangles over its neighbours, giving low cover for wildlife
  • Planter or ground: Ground — give it a fence or shrubs to climb
  • Spacing and depth: Sow 1 cm deep — the seed needs covering, as light stops it sprouting, and seedlings can emerge from as deep as 3 inches in loose soil; a few plants fill a corner. It germinates in cool, moist soil in late winter and early spring and can flower within eight weeks
  • Water: Likes moisture
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Gather the young shoots in spring, before the stems toughen

Garden notes

  • A food plant for the caterpillars of many moths and butterflies, including the hummingbird hawk-moth.
  • Birds eat the seeds, and geese and poultry graze the leaves — the source of its other name, goosegrass.
  • Its scrambling, tangled growth gives low cover and shelter for small insects and other wildlife.
  • Quickly covers bare, disturbed ground, helping to hold the soil in place.
  • In cereals it can cut yields by 30–60% and tangle in harvesting machinery. In a garden the same facts read simply: pull it before it seeds — the burrs travel on fur, clothing and boots — though seed in the soil stays viable only a few years, about three, so stopping seeding does clear it.
  • Gather the newest tender tips before the plant toughens and the fruits harden, and wash them well — the sticky hairs trap dust and dirt.

Propagation

Scatter ripe seed onto moist soil in autumn or early spring, in partial shade, and keep it moist until seedlings appear. It grows fast with no fuss and sets seed by summer, then dies back. Pull plants before the seed ripens if you do not want it spreading — it sows itself freely and can crowd nearby plants.

Sources

  • Kew, Plants of the World Online — native range from the Canary Islands and Britain to Japan; introduced across the Americas and Australasia
  • UC Statewide Integrated Pest Management — Catchweed Bedstraw Pest Notes: germination, seed depth and light, crop losses and control
  • Lee et al. (2024) — cleavers extract and natural-killer cell activity in immunosuppressed mice (injected extract, animal study only)
  • Sahin et al. (2022) — cleavers extract and liver markers in a rat paracetamol-overdose model (animal study only)
  • EarthWise, Cleavers Clinical Guide — traditional spring tonic and diuretic use; almost no modern human research
  • Herbal Reality and PeaceHealth herbal references — mild diuretic traditional use
  • Plants For A Future — larval food plant and wildlife value
  • Dowlati Beirami et al. (2024) — cleavers extract and wound closure in cultured skin cells (laboratory only)

Clover

Trifolium repens

MedicinalCulinary

Dried

White clover is a creeping perennial in the pea family, native to Europe and Central Asia and now naturalised in lawns and pastures worldwide, rooting as it spreads to form a soft green carpet. Its flowers and leaves are the parts traditionally used — and it should not be confused with red clover, a different plant with different uses.

  • In folk practice — everyday home healing — people made a tea of the flowers and leaves. They used it as a spring tonic, a drink to refresh the body, and as a remedy for coughs and colds. It was a gentle home herb, not a strong medicine.
  • Tradition says the rare four-leaf clover brings luck. Most leaves have three small leaves, called leaflets. The four-leaf ones are uncommon — and because they are hard to find, finding one became a sign of good fortune.
  • Tradition also links clover to Ireland's shamrock, the three-leafed plant of St Patrick. People have argued for hundreds of years about which plant the true shamrock is. White clover is one of the plants people claim it is, and the question is still open.
  • Its history on farms spread it around the world. In the 1600s and 1700s, farmers began to sow white clover into their grass fields. Wherever this kind of farming went, clover went with it.
  • White clover itself began as a hybrid. Genetic work (Griffiths et al., 2019) shows it arose roughly 15,000–28,000 years ago, in the depths of the last Ice Age, when two wild clovers — Trifolium pallescens and Trifolium occidentale — grew together in glacial refuges and joined into one plant carrying both their genomes.
  • New Zealand is the country white clover remade. Brought from England in the 1800s, it became the low-cost base of the country's farming — but it would not set seed there without its pollinators, so honeybees were deliberately introduced in the 1840s expressly so the clover could seed. New Zealand went from importing white clover seed every year to exporting it, and clover honey is now its most common honey.
  • It is also a modern study plant: researchers sampled more than 110,000 white clover plants in 160 cities in 26 countries and found its chemical defence shifting with distance from city centres in the same way worldwide.

Traditional medicine

  • In folk herbalism, a tea of the flowers and leaves has traditionally been used as a gentle expectorant — a remedy that helps loosen phlegm — for coughs, colds and chesty congestion. This is a traditional use; white clover has barely been studied in clinical research.
  • The flowers and leaves are edible and mildly nutritious: foraging guides note small amounts of vitamins A and C, and the plant contains a range of antioxidant plant compounds.
  • One boundary matters. Red clover's reputation rests on its isoflavones and on trials in menopausal women. White clover is a different species; those trials are not evidence for it, and the two clovers' records must not be mixed. No menopause, bone or heart claim carries over.
  • White clover's own record is laboratory-level: twelve flavonoids have been isolated from its flowers and leaves, several strongly antioxidant in laboratory tests (Kicel & Wolbiś, 2012). There are no human trials of white clover tea for coughs, colds or anything else — which is why white clover carries no benefit tags.
  • Safety — the look-alike that harms horses: alsike clover looks like a tall white clover but has no pale chevron on its leaflets, serrated leaf edges, and flower heads pink at the base fading to white. In horses it causes a sunburn-like skin damage on unpigmented skin, and, after weeks of eating a diet with a large share of alsike, liver damage — the “big liver” syndrome; the toxin is still unknown. White clover itself is low, creeping and rooting, with the chevron on its leaflets.
  • Safety: a pasture of mostly white clover can cause bloat in cattle and sheep; sowing it mixed with grass, as farmers do, lowers the risk.
  • Safety: some white clover forms carry compounds (linamarin and lotaustralin) that can release cyanide — a defence against being eaten. Ladino types are almost entirely free of them, which is one reason they were bred. In the amounts a person eats as a tea or a few flowers, this is not a poisoning risk.
  • Safety: red and white clover themselves are not toxic to horses, but a fungus that causes “black patch” disease on clover can produce a toxin that makes horses drool heavily — the “slobbers”.
  • Safety for people: eat raw leaves only in small amounts — they are hard to digest raw in quantity — eat them fresh, and never gather from sprayed lawns or roadsides.
  • When to plant: Sow seed outside in spring, or late summer, into a prepared patch or lawn
  • Sun: Full sun or some shade
  • Soil: Ordinary soil, even poor — it fixes its own nitrogen and feeds the soil as it grows. It wants soil around pH 6 or above (lime it if it falls below 6), answers strongly to potassium, and has low tolerance of salty soil
  • Environment: A hardy perennial; its creeping roots and dense cover loosen and protect the surface soil
  • Planter or ground: Ground — lawns, patches and green cover
  • Spacing and depth: Scatter seed thinly and rake it in lightly
  • Water: Average — drought-tolerant once settled
  • Companion plants: Grass is its classic partner in lawns and pasture; it feeds the plants growing with it
  • When to pick: Pick the flowers as they open through summer; the leaves are gathered young

Garden notes

  • Bacteria living in nodules on its roots take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form plants can use, steadily fertilising the clover itself and the plants growing with it — the reason clover has been sown into pastures for centuries.
  • Its creeping roots and dense cover loosen and protect the surface soil, and ground under clover is typically lively with earthworms.
  • The flowers are one of the most important nectar sources for honeybees and bumblebees in many regions.
  • In pasture it commonly fixes about 110–170 kg of nitrogen per hectare per year, with much higher figures — up to about 545 kg — reported at the top end.
  • It does best with about 600 mm or more of rain spread through the year, yields most in spring and autumn, and persists by its creeping stems rooting at the joints and by reseeding itself — which is why a patch outlives the grass sown with it.

Propagation

Sow seed in spring, barely covered, and keep the soil damp until it sprouts — or lift a piece of runner that already has roots and replant it. It spreads fast by runners, so give it a spot where it can roam.

Cultivars

  • White clover is bred and sold in three forms, by leaf size. The small, wild type has tiny leaves and is the toughest in close-grazed turf and lawns. The intermediate, or Dutch, type has mid-sized leaves — “Dutch white clover” in seed catalogues — and is the standard lawn and pasture type. The large, or Ladino, type has big leaves, grows taller and yields more, was bred from an Italian selection, and is grown for hay and rich pasture, though it is less long-lived under hard grazing.
  • Named kinds a reader can actually buy or meet: 'Durana' and 'Patriot', persistent intermediate pasture kinds bred for grazing; 'Regal' and 'Osceola', Ladino types; and 'Grasslands Huia', the New Zealand kind, certified from 1932 and long sold simply as “New Zealand white clover”. Microclover — very small-leaved lawn selections of the Pirouette and Pipolina type — is bred to blend into a lawn, stay low and need less mowing.

Sources

  • Mississippi State University Extension — white ladino clover: the three types, named varieties, pH, potassium and bloat
  • CSIRO, Register of Australian Herbage Plant Cultivars — Trifolium repens cv. Grasslands Huia: New Zealand origin, rainfall and persistence
  • Ontario Ministry of Agriculture — alsike clover poisoning in horses: identification and the two syndromes
  • Science Learning Hub, University of Waikato — the role of clover in New Zealand: introduction and pasture importance
  • Santangelo et al. (2022) — white clover adaptation across 160 cities worldwide, Science
  • Griffiths et al. (2019) — the two wild ancestors of white clover, Plant Cell
  • Kew, Plants of the World Online — accepted name and native range (Europe and Central Asia; introduced and naturalised worldwide)
  • Ogle & St. John (2008) — USDA NRCS Plant Guide for white clover: root-nodule nitrogen fixation, erosion-control cover, pasture use, and honeybees collecting nectar and pollen
  • Plants For A Future — white clover entry: leaves and flowers edible; an infusion traditionally used for coughs and colds; the plant classed as a tonic
  • van Eekeren et al. (2009) — earthworm abundance and burrowing greater under white clover than under grass alone
  • Kicel & Wolbiś (2012) — twelve flavonoids isolated from the flowers and leaves, several showing strong antioxidant activity in laboratory tests

Comfrey

Symphytum officinale

Medicinal

Skin Health

External use only

Comfrey is for the skin only — never eat it, and never drink it as a tea. Its old folk name is “knitbone”, from its traditional use on injuries, and its root and leaves contain allantoin, a compound also used in skin creams.

  • People have used comfrey on injuries for about 2,000 years. Dioscorides, a Greek doctor whose book on herbs guided medicine for hundreds of years, wrote about it in the first century. People used it for wounds and broken bones.
  • Its Latin name carries that old claim. Symphytum comes from the Greek word symphyo, which means “to grow together”. The name points to a plant that was meant to knit flesh and bone back together.
  • In England, that claim became its folk name: knitbone. For hundreds of years, country practice laid comfrey poultices — soft, wet masses of the plant held against the skin — on sprains, bruises and fractures.
  • Through the Middle Ages, people grew it in monastery gardens and physic gardens — gardens kept for medicine plants. The writers on herbs who came after kept it in their books as a wound herb.
  • The old use was on the skin, and that is where it has stayed. The root and leaves were poultice herbs — herbs used as poultices. Comfrey today is for use on the skin only, never inside the body.

Traditional medicine

  • European regulators recognise the root as a traditional herbal medicine for the skin: for the relief of minor sprains and bruises, applied as a thin layer twice a day.
  • A broken bone needs medical care, not a poultice.

Craft

  • The leaves give a dye for wool and cloth — simmered in a dyebath, with alum as the mordant, they give khaki, gold-brown and green shades. Dyers rate comfrey among the best plants for a green dye, and the same leaf bath colours handmade soap. Stranger still, an encyclopaedia of 1802 records the root’s sticky juice made into a glue that Angora goat-keepers used to spin fleece into very fine yarn for shawls. One more use for a plant that makes leaves faster than most gardens can use them.
  • Comfrey is for the skin only — never eat it, and never drink it as a tea.
  • In clinical trials of regulated pharmacy ointments made from comfrey root, it eased ankle sprains about as well as a standard anti-inflammatory gel, and helped back and knee pain — that evidence belongs to those tested preparations, not to home-made poultices.
  • The root and leaves contain allantoin, a compound also used in skin creams, which is part of why comfrey has long been a salve herb.
  • Caution: comfrey contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids that can seriously damage the liver. In 2001 the US Food and Drug Administration advised makers to take comfrey products meant to be swallowed off the market, and regulators require “External Use Only” warnings. Use it only on unbroken skin — never on cuts or broken or irritated skin — for no more than 10 days at a time, and not in pregnancy or while breastfeeding, or for anyone under 18. Be certain of the plant before using it: comfrey leaves have been mistaken for foxglove, which is poisonous.
  • When to plant: Plant root cuttings or a young plant in spring. Plant the sterile kind Bocking 14, which does not spread by seed
  • Sun: Full sun or some shade
  • Soil: Deep, rich, moist soil; the taproot can go down several feet, drawing up minerals other plants cannot reach
  • Environment: A very hardy perennial — and extremely vigorous, and very hard to remove once established, so plant it where it can stay for good
  • Planter or ground: Ground only — far too deep-rooted and vigorous for pots
  • Spacing and depth: 90 cm apart — one plant makes a large clump
  • Water: Likes water, though the deep roots find much of their own
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known — but its cut leaves feed the whole garden as a mulch, a compost activator and a liquid feed
  • When to pick: Cut the leaves from late spring, two or three times a season, leaving some for the bees

Garden notes

  • A “dynamic accumulator”: its deep taproot — often several feet down — draws up potassium, calcium and phosphorus from deep in the soil where other plants cannot reach.
  • The cut leaves are rich in potassium and are used as a mulch, a compost activator and a liquid plant feed.
  • The hanging bell flowers are worked through spring and summer by long-tongued bumblebees, which can reach the nectar.
  • An honest warning for the garden: comfrey is extremely vigorous and very hard to remove once established — the sterile variety ‘Bocking 14’ is the one to plant, as it does not spread by seed.

Propagation

Lift a clump in spring and split the fleshy roots, or cut roots into short pieces in early winter and plant them. Seed sown in autumn or spring also grows. Once in, it spreads fast and is hard to dig out — give it a spot of its own.

Sources

  • European Medicines Agency, comfrey root monograph — external use only, minor sprains and bruises, with the 10-day and unbroken-skin limits
  • US Food and Drug Administration (2001) — manufacturers advised to remove comfrey products for internal use; liver damage from pyrrolizidine alkaloids
  • Memorial Sloan Kettering, About Herbs — hepatotoxicity and confusion with foxglove
  • Cochrane review of topical herbal therapies (2013) — trial support limited to regulated comfrey root ointments

Curly Dock

Rumex crispus

Medicinal

Digestive Health

Dried

Also called Yellow Dock. A pioneer of disturbed ground with a strong taproot that can reach about four feet down, and tall stems of reddish-brown seed.

  • People used dock roots in medicine in Greece and Rome. Dock has stayed in herbal practice — the use of plants as medicine — ever since. People used it as a tonic, a drink or food taken to refresh the body, and as a gentle laxative — a medicine that helps the bowels move.
  • Native American peoples used curly dock in their own practice too. They used the root as a tonic, and the plant for skin troubles and sores — the Zuni, named plainly, used a poultice of the powdered root on sores, rashes and skin infections, and a root infusion for athlete's foot.
  • In lean times — times when food was short — its seeds were food. People gathered them in large amounts and ground them into a dark flour. They made bread and porridge from it when grain ran short.
  • The root was once a shop herb. People dried it and sold it as a tonic and a laxative. Its other name, yellow dock, comes from the yellow root.
  • It crossed the Atlantic with European settlers. It spread across North America, where it now grows on waste ground almost everywhere.
  • Its home range is far wider than that one crossing suggests: it is native across Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia from the Middle East to China, Korea and Japan, and introduced almost everywhere else — counted a weed in about 40 countries, growing above the Arctic Circle and on all continents. It has been called one of the world's most successful colonising plants that nobody planted on purpose.
  • In Armenia, young dock leaves — dock species as a group, including curly dock — were gathered in spring, braided and dried to make aveluk. Drying and a light fermentation made them less bitter, and the braids were later boiled and used through winter in soups and salads, often with grains, potatoes and walnuts.

Traditional medicine

  • The root was a traditional gentle laxative, listed by the British Herbal Pharmacopoeia for constipation — its anthraquinone compounds, a family of plant compounds that stimulate the bowel, are what move the bowels.
  • The same pharmacopoeia listed the root for liver congestion and for skin eruptions associated with constipation — the old idea that clearing the bowels clears the skin.
  • Native American tribes used the root as a general tonic and “blood purifier”, and as a source of iron for women. The root does contain iron, but in moderate amounts, and dock is not a treatment for anaemia.

Craft

  • The roots give yellow, dark green, brown and dark grey dyes for wool and cloth — and unusually for a dye plant, they need no mordant to hold the colour. The whole plant is dyer’s material: leaves and stalks give yellow with alum. It is the same strong root that medicine uses, put to the dyer’s work.
  • The honest centre: there are no human clinical trials of curly dock for any use. The standard drug reference states it plainly — the roots have a laxative effect, but research reveals no clinical data on using yellow dock to treat any condition, and no clinical evidence supports a dose. The pharmacopoeia listing in Traditional Uses is a traditional-use listing, not trial proof.
  • The chemistry is known at laboratory strength: the root holds anthraquinones — emodin, chrysophanol and physcion among them — the same compound family as senna. In animals, root preparations increased bowel movement; in the laboratory, extracts acted against Staphylococcus aureus and Bacillus subtilis. Neither is a finding in people.
  • Caution: the plant contains oxalates, natural compounds found in many plants that can add to kidney stones in people prone to them. As a laxative it is for short-term use only — overuse causes diarrhoea and digestive disturbance — and it should be avoided in pregnancy and while breastfeeding, and not combined with other laxatives.
  • Caution: yellow dock products should not be used by people with kidney disease, an intestinal blockage, or belly pain of unknown cause. Large amounts of root can cause diarrhoea, nausea and passing much more urine than usual, and large amounts of uncooked leaves should be avoided.
  • Caution, at the extreme end: fatal oxalate poisoning after eating very large amounts of curly dock leaves has been reported in people and in sheep, with low blood calcium and kidney damage. That is a large-amount poisoning record, not a normal-use risk.
  • When to plant: Usually gathered wild. To grow it, sow seed in spring in a contained corner — its seed stays alive in the soil for decades
  • Sun: Full sun or some shade
  • Soil: Almost any soil, including heavy, compacted ground; the strong taproot can reach about four feet down
  • Environment: A hardy perennial, and a pioneer of disturbed ground
  • Planter or ground: Ground only
  • Spacing and depth: Sow on the surface or just below; 45 cm apart
  • Water: Average — the deep root finds moisture
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Pick the leaves young, in spring; dig the root in autumn

Garden notes

  • Its strong taproot can reach about four feet down, drawing up moisture from deep in the soil and helping to break up and aerate compacted ground.
  • The tall stems carry masses of reddish-brown seed that songbirds — sparrows and red-winged blackbirds among them — feed on.
  • The leaves are food for caterpillars, and the plant is a larval host for copper butterflies.
  • A pioneer of disturbed ground whose seeds stay viable in the soil for decades — one plant can produce up to 60,000 seeds, and seed has stayed alive in soil for over 80 years — which is why dock keeps reappearing in gardens.
  • It resprouts from buds and pieces of the crown and root, and does not stand up well to tillage or close competition. For a sparse patch, removing the crown about 2 inches below the soil surface is the simple control. Dock species are listed as noxious weeds in some US states.

Propagation

Sow seed in spring, barely covered, and keep it damp until it sprouts. It self-seeds freely and can take over — grow it where it can spread, or cut the flower stalks off before they set seed.

Cultivars

  • There are no named garden varieties of curly dock — it grows wild and is not commonly grown, so none have been developed. Wild subspecies exist, as forms, not varieties: subsp. crispus on waste and farm ground, subsp. littoreus on coasts, and subsp. uliginosus on tidal estuary mud. It also hybridises freely with other docks, most often with broad-leaved dock.

Sources

  • Ohio State University Weedguide — curly dock seed production, seed life and worldwide weed record
  • Drugs.com — yellow dock monograph: no clinical data for any use; contraindications and adverse effects
  • Moerman — Native American Ethnobotany database: Zuni uses of Rumex crispus root
  • GLOBINMED, curly dock monograph — root constituents and traditional uses
  • British Herbal Pharmacopoeia — dock root for constipation and related traditional uses
  • Plants For A Future — gentle purgative and tonic actions recorded
  • University of Colorado — larval host for copper butterflies; seed longevity and oxalate toxicity to livestock

Dandelion

Taraxacum officinale

MedicinalCulinary

Digestive HealthUrinary Health

FreshDried

The dandelion is a daisy-family perennial from Europe and Asia, carried by wind and people to lawns and roadsides on every continent. Almost uniquely among familiar plants, the whole thing is used — leaves, root and flowers are all food, and the root and leaf are both traditional medicines, in different ways.

  • The name is French. Dent-de-lion means lion's tooth. It points to the jagged edges of the leaves.
  • Doctors in the Arab world wrote about the dandelion about 1,000 years ago. From their books, it passed into European medicine.
  • In Europe, it became a spring food and a home remedy. People ate the young leaves as a salad green. They used the bitter root and leaf to wake up digestion.
  • The roasted root made a drink of its own. People dried it, roasted it and ground it, then brewed it as dandelion coffee. It is a coffee stand-in with no caffeine. It was well known by the 1800s.
  • The flowers made a drink too: dandelion wine. It is a country wine made in spring from the yellow heads. Making it is a long tradition in Britain.
  • Settlers carried the plant to North America. There it spread into every lawn. It kept its place in the kitchen and the herb cupboard.

Traditional medicine

  • The root’s bitter compounds are traditionally used to wake up digestion: bitter tastes prompt the flow of saliva, stomach juices and bile, and dandelion root is a recognised traditional remedy in Europe for mild indigestion, fullness and temporary loss of appetite.
  • The leaf is the part traditionally used to increase urine flow and flush the urinary tract in minor urinary complaints.

Craft

  • The flowers dye wool and cloth a soft yellow with alum, and the roots give browner shades — a dye plant hiding in the lawn. Dyers know its yellows are gentle rather than lightfast, and the entry claims no more than that.
  • The root stores inulin, a gentle fibre that passes undigested to the large intestine, where it feeds beneficial gut bacteria — the kind of fibre called a prebiotic. Roots dug in autumn can be up to 40% inulin.
  • The leaves are a nutritious green, rich in beta-carotene (which the body converts to vitamin A), vitamin K and potassium, and the whole plant contains antioxidant polyphenols — protective plant compounds.
  • In laboratory and animal studies, dandelion extracts show anti-inflammatory activity; this has not been established in people.
  • In laboratory studies, dandelion extracts have prompted cell death in certain cancer cell lines — this has not been shown in people, and dandelion is not a cancer treatment.
  • When to plant: Usually gathered wild. To grow it, sow seed in spring wherever you want it — it asks for nothing
  • Sun: Full sun or some shade
  • Soil: Any soil, even heavy and compacted — the long taproot opens channels through it
  • Environment: A hardy perennial, and a pioneer of bare, poor ground; its flowers open early in spring, when bees need them most
  • Planter or ground: Ground; a deep pot keeps it contained
  • Spacing and depth: Sow on the surface and press it in
  • Water: Average — drought-tolerant once the taproot is down
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Leaves are best young, in spring, before flowering; roots are dug in autumn, when they hold the most inulin

Garden notes

  • The long taproot grows down through heavy, compacted soil, opening channels that improve aeration and drainage, and draws minerals up from deep layers; when leaves and roots die back, those minerals are returned to the surface soil for other plants.
  • The flowers open early in spring, when little else is blooming, and give bees, butterflies and other insects a crucial early source of nectar and pollen.
  • It is a pioneer plant — one of the first to colonise bare, poor ground — holding the soil and beginning the process that lets other plants follow.

Propagation

Sow seed on the surface in spring and keep it damp — it sprouts within two weeks. The seed blows far on the wind, so pick the flower heads off if you do not want it everywhere.

Sources

  • European Medicines Agency, dandelion root, leaf and root-with-herb monographs and assessment reports — traditional use for mild indigestion, appetite and urinary flushing; root inulin content
  • NCCIH — dandelion evidence summary: no compelling scientific evidence for any condition
  • USDA FoodData Central — nutrient values for dandelion greens, raw

Echinacea

Echinacea purpurea

Medicinal

Immune HealthSkin Health

Fresh

One of North America's classic medicinal plants — better known in the garden as purple coneflower. It is a native of the rocky prairies and open woodlands of central and eastern North America.

  • Echinacea is one of North America's classic healing plants. In the garden, most people know it as purple coneflower.
  • Native American peoples used it in the past for coughs, colds, sore throats and toothache.
  • That long use is why it is still the herb most people reach for at the first sign of a cold.
  • The named record is richer — and it belongs first to a sister species. Coneflower root was one of the most widely used medicines of the Great Plains, and the ethnobotanist Melvin Gilmore recorded that the tribes of the upper Missouri used it for more ailments than any other plant. The Lakota took the root for toothache and bellyache; the Cheyenne and Kiowa chewed a piece of root for a sore throat and let the saliva run slowly down; the Dakota laid freshly scraped root on festering wounds; peoples across the Plains used the root against snakebite and stings — a record of past use, not a treatment: a snakebite is a medical emergency. The Omaha and Ponca also used the dried seed head as a comb; their name for the plant, mika-hi, means comb plant. Most of this Plains record is for Echinacea angustifolia, the narrow-leaved coneflower — not for Echinacea purpurea — and it is told here with that fence standing.
  • Lewis and Clark met it in 1804–05: at their winter camp at Fort Mandan, William Clark recorded a root prized as a remedy for rattlesnake bite, and in spring 1805 Lewis sent roots to President Jefferson described in the same words. Modern editors identify the root as Echinacea angustifolia.
  • It entered settler medicine from about 1870, when H. C. F. Meyer of Pawnee City, Nebraska — who had learned of the root from Sioux and Pawnee peoples — sold it in his Meyer's Blood Purifier. He sent the root to John King and John Uri Lloyd of the Eclectic school; Lloyd Brothers of Cincinnati began making echinacea tinctures at scale in the 1880s, and echinacea stayed listed in the United States Pharmacopeia and National Formulary until the late 1940s, when it fell away as antibiotics arrived.
  • How Echinacea purpurea became the research plant is a seed mix-up. In 1938 the German maker Gerhard Madaus obtained American seed he believed was Echinacea angustifolia. It was Echinacea purpurea. Angustifolia would not grow reliably in Germany and purpurea would, so the fresh-pressed juice products that followed were purpurea, and most European research since has been on purpurea — while the Plains tradition behind it was angustifolia. That one story explains the whole species split in the evidence.
  • The common cold is its most studied use. Reviews of the trials find that taking echinacea may slightly reduce the chance of catching a cold — but the results are mixed, and whether it shortens a cold once you have one is still unclear.
  • European regulators accept the pressed juice of the fresh flowering herb for the short-term prevention and treatment of colds, taken for no more than ten days. Traditional uses they recognise include the root for cold symptoms and for spots and pimples from mild acne, and the juice in ointments for small superficial wounds.
  • It is sold as an immune-support herb, on the idea that it stimulates the immune system. Laboratory studies support immune activity, but the effect seen in people so far is modest.
  • The size of the cold record: the Cochrane review (Karsch-Völk et al., 2014) covered 24 double-blind trials with 4,631 people. No single prevention trial found a significant fall in colds; pooling the prevention trials afterwards suggested a 10–20% relative fall in risk, which the authors called of questionable importance in real life. Of the treatment trials that measured how long a cold lasted, only one of seven found a significant effect. A 2019 review (David & Cunningham) found the same shape: a possible effect on how many infections people caught, of unclear real-world importance, and no evidence that echinacea changed how long an infection lasted.
  • The European standings split exactly: the pressed juice of the fresh flowering herb holds well-established use in the EU for the short-term prevention and treatment of colds — a higher standing than the traditional use held by the root preparations for cold symptoms, and by the juice ointment for small superficial wounds.
  • Caution: echinacea is in the daisy family and closely related to ragweed. Allergic reactions are possible and can occasionally be severe, so do not use it if you are allergic to daisy-family plants such as ragweed, chamomile or chrysanthemums.
  • Caution: because it may stimulate the immune system, it can work against medicines that suppress immunity, such as those taken after an organ transplant — talk to a clinician first if you take immunosuppressants or have an autoimmune condition. The named medicines in the references are tacrolimus and cyclosporine. Its safety in pregnancy and while breastfeeding is not established, so it is best avoided then too.
  • Caution: the reported side effects are headache, dizziness, nausea, constipation, mild stomach pain and skin rash; stomach upset is the most common.
  • Caution, labelled theoretical: echinacea affects some liver enzymes in test systems, so in theory it could change levels of medicines handled by those enzymes. The clinical importance is unclear.
  • When to plant: Sow seed in autumn, or in spring after a few weeks in the cold of a fridge — the seed needs a spell of cold to sprout well. Young plants can go out in spring
  • Sun: Full sun
  • Soil: Lean, dry, well-drained soil; rich, wet ground shortens its life
  • Environment: A hardy perennial of the rocky North American prairies; drought-tolerant once established. Leave the seed heads standing — goldfinches feed on them
  • Planter or ground: Ground best; large pots work
  • Spacing and depth: Sow on the surface or just below; 45 cm apart
  • Water: Dry once settled — water only in long droughts
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Cut the flowers in summer; dig the root in autumn from plants three or four years old

Garden notes

  • A native of the rocky prairies and open woodlands of central and eastern North America, growing wild across the Great Plains and eastward — a natural fit for prairie-style and wildlife plantings.
  • A first-rate pollinator plant: the US conservation service rates its value to pollinators as high, and the flowers feed bees, butterflies and skippers from midsummer into autumn.
  • Leave the seed heads standing when the flowers fade — goldfinches and other songbirds feed on the seed through autumn.
  • Happy in lean, dry, well-drained soil in full sun, and drought tolerant once established. Wild echinacea has thinned with habitat loss and over-harvesting, so garden-grown plants help take the pressure off wild stands.
  • The whole genus is North American and small: nine species, all native to the prairies and open woods of central and eastern North America and nowhere else wild. The three used in medicine are Echinacea purpurea (east and central), Echinacea angustifolia (the dry plains from Texas into Canada) and Echinacea pallida, the pale purple coneflower, between the two.
  • Conservation can be named, not just hinted at: United Plant Savers lists echinacea as At-Risk, with a score of 44, driven by wild root harvest and habitat loss. The Tennessee coneflower was one of the first plants listed as endangered in the United States, in 1979, and was removed from the list in 2011 after its populations recovered; the smooth coneflower is still listed as threatened. Garden-grown purpurea, which grows easily from seed, carries no such burden.
  • Named kinds do not come true from seed — a 'Magnus' seedling is not 'Magnus'. Buy named forms as plants, or divide them, every three to four years in spring or autumn to keep clumps vigorous.
  • The disease to name is aster yellows: spread by leafhoppers, it twists and greens the flowers, it has no cure, and affected plants should be dug out so it does not spread.

Propagation

Sow seed in spring in warm soil, or lift a clump in spring or autumn and split it. Seed-grown plants may not match the parent plant, and they take two years or more to flower.

Cultivars

  • Named kinds of Echinacea purpurea itself: 'Magnus', the standard purple — larger flowers than the species, with petals held flat instead of drooping; Perennial Plant of the Year 1998, at 2–3 feet. 'White Swan', the reliable white form, white petals around an orange-brown cone, about 2 feet, and as long-lived as 'Magnus'. 'PowWow Wild Berry', compact at 16–24 inches, deep magenta-purple, and unusual in blooming in its first year from seed — an All-America Selections winner in 2010; its pair, 'PowWow White', does the same in white. 'Kim's Knee High' is a dwarf purple form for the front of a border and for pots.
  • The other coneflower species, labelled as species, not varieties: Echinacea angustifolia — narrow-leaved and shorter, the Plains medicine species, slow and hard to grow, with a deep taproot. Echinacea pallida — pale purple, with long, thin, drooping petals, blooming later. Echinacea paradoxa — the only naturally yellow coneflower, and the parent of most modern orange and yellow hybrids; those bright hybrids are crosses, are often short-lived at two to three years, and are not Echinacea purpurea.

Sources

  • United Plant Savers — echinacea At-Risk assessment: wild harvest and habitat loss
  • Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Echinacea purpurea 'Magnus' and 'White Swan'
  • Kew, Plants of the World Online — Echinacea: nine North American species
  • NCCIH — echinacea evidence summary: may slightly reduce the chance of catching a cold
  • European Medicines Agency, echinacea herb and root monographs — cold prevention and treatment; traditional uses
  • Karsch-Völk et al. (2014) — Cochrane review of echinacea for preventing and treating the common cold
  • David & Cunningham (2019) — systematic review and meta-analysis of echinacea and respiratory infections
  • Memorial Sloan Kettering, About Herbs — immunosuppressant interaction and allergy cautions
