Eggplant

Solanum melongena

Culinary

Digestive Health

Cooked

Three names for one plant: eggplant in America, aubergine in Britain, brinjal in South Asia. It belongs with the other great nightshade foods, beside its cousins the tomato, the potato, the peppers and the goji. Botanically the fruit is a berry — a glossy, spongy berry that soaks up oil, smoke and sauce like nothing else in the kitchen. Asia has loved it for thousands of years. Europe feared it for centuries as the "mad apple." Both stories are true.

Cultivars

  • 'Black Beauty' — the classic American globe: large, plump, glossy fruit of the deepest purple, almost black. The supermarket standard for a hundred years, and still the eggplant most readers picture first.
  • 'Ichiban' — a Japanese type: long, slim, dark-purple fruit with thin skin and few seeds. Early, heavy-bearing, and tender — bred for grilling and quick cooking.
  • 'Rosa Bianca' — an Italian heirloom: round, plump fruit blushed rose-lavender over white, with mild, creamy flesh and little of the bitterness older types were known for.
  • 'Listada de Gandia' — a Spanish heirloom from Gandia, near Valencia: oval fruit striped violet and white, thin-skinned and tender, beautiful enough that it is grown as an ornament as well as a food.
  • The white types — 'Casper', 'Clara' and their kin, descendants of the little egg-shaped whites that gave the plant its English name. Mild and thin-skinned. The honest trade-off: no purple skin means no nasunin.
  • The Thai types — small round fruit, green, white or striped, no bigger than a golf ball, eaten in curries where their firm bite and slight bitterness are the point. (The pea eggplant in Thai cooking, smaller still, is a different species, Solanum torvum, and a different plant altogether.)
The Levant — baba ghanoush: eggplant roasted or charred whole until it collapses, then mashed with tahini, lemon and garlic. The smoke is an ingredient.
Greece — moussaka: layers of eggplant with spiced minced meat under a béchamel top. The dish is old; the creamy top is a 20th-century addition, credited to the chef Nikolaos Tselementes.
France — ratatouille, the Provençal stew of eggplant with tomato, pepper, courgette and herbs.
India — baingan bharta: the whole fruit fire-roasted, its smoky flesh mashed with onion, tomato and spices. Brinjal curries run the length of the country, and the plant is often called the king of vegetables in India.
Turkey — imam bayildi: eggplant stuffed with onion and tomato and poached in olive oil. The name means "the imam fainted," and the story told with it — labelled as a story — is that he fainted either from pleasure or from horror at how much olive oil the dish had used.
Italy — parmigiana di melanzane, eggplant layered with tomato and cheese; and in Sicily, caponata, a sweet-sour stew with capers, olives and celery.
China — yuxiang qiezi, "fish-fragrant eggplant": no fish anywhere in it — the name is the pickled-chilli, garlic and ginger seasoning first made for fish, turned onto eggplant instead.
Japan — nasu dengaku: halved eggplant broiled under a sweet miso glaze.
The Philippines — tortang talong: a whole roasted eggplant, skin charred and slipped off, flattened into an omelette.
  • The wild ancestor is a thorny, bitter little nightshade of the Solanum incanum group — the "bitter apple" — whose line began in Africa and spread through the Middle East into Asia. In Asia, farmers tamed it. Genetic studies suggest the plant was domesticated twice, independently: once in South Asia and once in East Asia. India still holds the deepest variety of eggplants in the world, from thumb-sized rounds to fruits a foot long.
  • It has been grown in southern and eastern Asia since prehistoric times. The first written record that survives is Chinese: the Qimin Yaoshu, a farming manual finished in 544 CE, describes the plant.
  • The name travelled as far as the plant. From an old Indian word came Persian bādingān, then Arabic al-bādinjān, then Catalan albergínia, then French aubergine. "Brinjal" came by the same road through Portuguese beringela. "Eggplant" is the odd one out — a plain English coinage of the 1700s, when the fashionable varieties in England were small, white and egg-shaped, the size and colour of a goose egg.
  • Arab farmers carried the plant across North Africa and into Spain in the 700s. By the 1100s, Ibn al-Awwam's farming book in Arabic Spain was explaining how to grow it. Through the Arab world it became a Mediterranean staple — the food of Spain, Sicily, the Levant and Turkey.
  • Northern Europe, meeting it late and mostly as a garden curiosity, was suspicious. In Italy the name melanzana was misheard as mela insana — "mad apple" — and in 13th-century Italy people held that eating it caused insanity. Gerard's English herbal of 1597 called it the "madde or raging Apple" and doubted it was safe to eat. The fear itself is part of the plant's real history: for centuries, much of Europe grew this plant to look at, not to eat. In India, meanwhile, the brinjal was used in Ayurvedic practice, and the plant has a place in old Chinese folk medicine too — traditional uses, not advice.
  • Europeans carried it to the Americas, where it was grown at first as an ornamental curiosity — "guinea squash" — and Thomas Jefferson grew it at Monticello in the early 1800s. It became an ordinary market vegetable in America only toward the end of that century. Today China and India together grow about 86% of all the eggplants in the world.
  • Raw eggplant, per 100 g: 25 kcal, about 92% water, carbohydrate 5.9 g, sugars 3.5 g, fibre 3.0 g, protein about 1 g, potassium 229 mg, folate 22 µg, manganese 0.23 mg — and very little vitamin C, 2.2 mg. It is a light food: bulk, water and fibre for very few calories.
  • The purple skin is the interesting part. Its colour is nasunin, a pigment in the family called anthocyanins — the same kind of pigment that colours blueberries and blackberries. In laboratory work (Noda and colleagues, 1998 and 2000), nasunin proved a strong antioxidant: it mopped up damaging oxygen radicals, and it bound iron so the iron could not drive further damage, protecting fatty material in laboratory preparations from oxidation. That is test-tube work, honestly labelled: no trial in people has shown that eating eggplant protects the brain, the heart, or anything else. What can be said plainly is that the pigment is in the skin — so eggplant eaten skin-on keeps it, and peeling throws it away. White and green types carry little or none of it.
  • The pale flesh holds another studied compound, chlorogenic acid — again, laboratory-stage interest, not a proven benefit in people.
  • The fibre is real and ordinary: 3.0 g per 100 g, the steady, unglamorous kind of good that vegetables do.
  • The nightshade question, answered plainly. Eggplant belongs to the nightshade family and does carry small amounts of the bitter compounds called glycoalkaloids — far less than a greened potato — and ordinary servings of the fruit are safe food, eaten daily by hundreds of millions of people. Bitterness in a fruit is a sign it stayed on the plant too long and its seeds matured; young, glossy fruit is mild. The leaves and flowers are a different matter: they carry enough solanine — the nightshade poison — to be harmful in quantity, and they are never eaten. This is a fruit plant, not a greens plant.
  • One kitchen honesty: the spongy flesh drinks oil. Fried eggplant can carry many times the calories of the vegetable itself, because the oil comes with it. Grilled, roasted or stewed, skin on, it stays the light food the numbers describe.
  • Eggplant is a tropical perennial grown as an annual almost everywhere — frost kills it outright, and in frost-free country it lives on for a few seasons. The plant is a bushy 2–4 ft (0.6–1.2 m), with big soft leaves and star-shaped violet flowers pretty enough that, as the history above tells, whole countries grew it just for show.
  • Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost. The seed is slow and wants warmth to sprout — soil at 75–85 °F (24–29 °C) does it. Set the plants out only when the ground has warmed to about 60–70 °F and nights stay mild; eggplant set into cold soil simply sits and sulks.
  • Full sun, and rich, well-drained soil. Space plants 18–24 inches apart, and stake or cage them: a loaded plant is top-heavy, and fruit dragging on the ground rots and marks.
  • Water steadily — about an inch a week — and mulch under the plants. Uneven water makes misshapen fruit.
  • The plant's classic pest is the flea beetle, which chews the young leaves full of tiny holes, lace-style. Healthy plants usually outgrow the damage; it is the holes in the leaves of nearly every garden eggplant photo ever taken.
  • Picking is the whole skill. Fruit is ready 60–85 days after setting out (100–120 days from seed), and the sign is the skin: glossy, firm, and springing back a little under a thumb. Dull skin means the fruit waited too long — the seeds inside have browned and the flesh is turning bitter. Cut the fruit off with its green cap on; never pull. Pick every few days and the plant keeps setting new fruit until the cold stops it.
  • In a pot: one plant in a 5-gallon pot, in full sun, grows and fruits well — the short-season gardener's answer, and the pot can be chased after the sun.
  • Save the skin in the kitchen and the rule in the garden is the same plant, honestly: eat the fruit, admire the flowers, and leave the leaves alone.

Propagation

Sow seed indoors about eight weeks before you plan to set plants out, a quarter inch deep, and keep it warm. Do not set plants outside until the nights stay warm — cold soil stops the seed from sprouting.

Sources

  • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: eggplant, raw — the nutrition figures
  • Noda et al. (2000) — Antioxidant activity of nasunin, an anthocyanin in eggplant peels — the laboratory evidence for the skin pigment
  • Daunay & Janick (2007) — History and iconography of eggplant — the plant's history, names and long suspicion in Europe
  • Sękara et al. (2007) — Cultivated eggplants: origin, breeding perspectives and germplasm resources — domestication and the world's variety wealth
  • University of Minnesota Extension (2024) — Growing eggplant in home gardens — warmth, timing and harvest guidance

Goldenrod

Solidago spp.

Medicinal

Urinary Health

Dried

One of the most important late-season flowers in North America. Goldenrod is usually blamed for late-summer hay fever, but its pollen is heavy and sticky and carried by insects — wind-pollinated ragweed, flowering at the same time, is the usual culprit. The flowering tops are the part used.

  • The Latin name makes a claim. Solidago comes from solidare, which means to make whole. People gave it that name because they used goldenrod on wounds that would not heal.
  • European goldenrod was a wound herb in European practice for centuries, and people also drank it as a urinary tea.
  • Native American peoples used the North American goldenrods in their own medicine. They made teas and poultices for wounds, fevers and sore throats. A poultice is a soft mash of plant laid on the skin.
  • After the Boston Tea Party of 1773, American colonists turned away from taxed British tea. They brewed goldenrod instead. The drink was called Liberty Tea. In those years, goldenrod was even shipped abroad as a tea.
  • One thread runs through its whole history: it was a wound herb first, and a tea herb after.
  • The genus is mostly North American: Solidago holds about 100 to 120 species, most native to North America, and only a few to South America and Eurasia. The medicine species is the exception — Solidago virgaurea is the Eurasian one, native across Europe and temperate Asia and into North Africa.
  • North American goldenrods then travelled the other way and became a problem in Europe. Canada goldenrod was brought to England as a garden plant as early as 1645, spread through European gardens in the 1800s, and is now counted invasive in parts of Europe and in China, where it pushes out native plants. Giant goldenrod has done the same.
  • Its strangest chapter is industrial. In 1927 Thomas Edison, Henry Ford and Harvey Firestone set up the Edison Botanic Research Corporation in Florida to find a home-grown source of rubber in case imports were cut off. Edison's team tested more than 17,000 plants; goldenrod came out best. By cross-breeding and feeding, he grew goldenrod about 12 feet tall with leaves holding up to about 12% rubber, most of it from Solidago leavenworthii, and one form was named Solidago edisoniana for him. Ford is said to have given him a Model T fitted with goldenrod-rubber tyres — that tyre story is a well-loved tradition, told as such, not a tested fact. Edison died in 1931 before any factory use, and later work reached only about 7% rubber, which was tacky and stretched poorly, so goldenrod rubber never went into production.
  • It is also a state symbol four times over: the state flower of Kentucky (adopted 1926) and of Nebraska (adopted 1895), the state wildflower of South Carolina, and — as sweet goldenrod — the state herb of Delaware (1996).
  • The distilled flower oil is breathed in for coughs, colds and a blocked nose, and rubbed, diluted, on the skin for spots and bites. Traditional use

Traditional medicine

  • European regulators recognise goldenrod herb as a traditional herbal medicine to increase the flow of urine and flush the urinary tract, as an aid in minor urinary complaints — a use that rests on long-standing tradition; the diuretic effect has not been proven in proper trials.
  • The monograph covers European goldenrod (Solidago virgaurea); the North American goldenrods share the same folk tradition as urinary teas.
  • The monograph's traditional course runs two to four weeks, with plenty of fluids drunk alongside.
  • The animal record has a name, and it also proves the species differ. In rats, parts of Solidago virgaurea — above all a compound called leiocarposide — raised urine output while losing less sodium and potassium than ordinary water tablets; researchers call this an aquaretic effect. Leiocarposide is completely absent from Canada goldenrod and giant goldenrod, so the North American species in many American products are chemically different herbs from the monograph species, and the rat result cannot be carried across to them — or to people.
  • The human record is open studies with no comparison group: German follow-up studies reported that about 7 in 10 users felt better after two to four weeks, and one small open study in 22 healthy people recorded more urine on goldenrod drops. The European assessors found these studies too poorly reported to judge and kept goldenrod at traditional use only. No randomised trial has measured urine output in people. Germany's older Commission E approval — for flushing the urinary tract in infections, and for kidney and bladder gravel — is a traditional regulatory approval, not trial proof.

Craft

  • Goldenrod is one of the leading natural dye plants: the flowering tops give strong, clear yellows on wool — among the brightest yellows a home dyer can get. With iron in the bath, the same flowers shift to olive-green, so one harvest gives the dyer two colours.
  • Goldenrod is usually blamed for late-summer hay fever, but that blame is misplaced: its pollen is heavy and sticky and is carried by insects, not wind. Wind-pollinated ragweed, which flowers at the same time, is the usual culprit.
  • Caution: goldenrod is in the daisy family — do not use it if you are allergic to daisy-family plants. The EMA does not recommend it for children under 12, does not recommend combining it with synthetic water tablets (diuretics), and advises against it where fluid intake must be restricted, as in severe heart or kidney disease. It is not recommended in pregnancy or while breastfeeding, where there is no safety information.
  • Caution: the monograph names warning signs — if fever, blood in the urine, painful spasms or trouble passing urine appear, or symptoms last beyond the traditional course, see a doctor. Goldenrod tea is an aid in minor complaints only, not a treatment for a kidney or bladder infection.
  • Caution: in the United States, goldenrod products are sold as supplements with no check on which species they hold, so a product may contain Canada or giant goldenrod — species the European monograph does not cover.
  • When to plant: Plant young plants or divide clumps in spring; seed can be sown in spring too
  • Sun: Full sun
  • Soil: Ordinary, well-drained soil, even poor
  • Environment: A hardy perennial that spreads — give it room, or a contained corner. Spread depends on the species: Canada and tall goldenrods run fast by underground stems and can take over, while Solidago rugosa and blue-stem goldenrod form clumps and spread slowly, and named garden kinds are in general less aggressive than the wild forms. European goldenrod is a smaller plant, about 60 cm tall. Its autumn flowers feed migrating monarchs and fill the bees' winter stores
  • Planter or ground: Ground; large pots for the smaller kinds
  • Spacing and depth: 45–60 cm apart
  • Water: Dry once settled
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Gather the flowering tops as they open, in late summer and autumn

Garden notes

  • Conservation groups list goldenrods among the top autumn nectar plants, fuelling migrating monarch butterflies and filling honey bees' winter stores.
  • Specialist bees that collect pollen from almost nothing else — several mining bees and their relatives — depend on goldenrod in the autumn.
  • More than a hundred kinds of insects have been recorded visiting the flowers, and the seed feeds goldfinches, sparrows and juncos well into winter.
  • Left standing, the dry stems shelter overwintering insects through the cold months.

Propagation

Lift a clump in autumn or early spring and split it into pieces, each with roots and shoots, then replant at once. Goldenrod spreads fast and seeds itself freely — cut the flower stems back after flowering to keep it where you want it.

Cultivars

  • Goldenrod is a whole genus, so its varieties are species forms and their named garden kinds, each with its species stated. Solidago rugosa 'Fireworks' is the best-known garden goldenrod: arching sprays of tiny bright yellow flowers like a firework burst, about 3 to 3½ feet tall, clump-forming and slower to spread than the wild running species; it likes moist soil.
  • Solidago sphacelata 'Golden Fleece' is compact, about 15–18 inches, with flat yellow heads and semi-evergreen leaves, said to resist mildew — suited to small gardens and pots. Solidago 'Little Lemon' is a dwarf hybrid, about 12–14 inches tall, with pale lemon-yellow plumes on upright stems — the smallest choice for containers and edges.
  • Species forms worth one line each: blue-stem goldenrod (Solidago caesia), with arching purple-blue stems, no aggressive spread, and some shade tolerance; sweet goldenrod (Solidago odora), with anise-scented leaves — the tea species — standing poor dry soil without spreading aggressively; and showy goldenrod (Solidago speciosa), upright with dense, showy clusters at 1 to 3 feet.

Safety

  • Some goldenrod oils are high in estragole, a compound regulators say exposure to should be kept low — the distilled oil is not the flower, and the pure oil must never be swallowed.

Sources
