  • Xerces Society — goldenrod as a keystone fall nectar plant; insect-pollinated, not a hay-fever cause
  • University of Illinois Extension — ragweed, not goldenrod, causes late-summer hay fever
  • Monarch Joint Venture — goldenrod nectar for migrating monarchs
  • Lawless (2014) — Encyclopedia of Essential Oils — goldenrod flower oil for coughs, colds and skin
  • Tisserand & Young (2014) — Essential Oil Safety — goldenrod oil and its estragole chemotypes

Ground Ivy

Glechoma hederacea

MedicinalCulinary

Digestive HealthSkin Health

An evergreen perennial ground cover for shady places. Before hops took over, ground ivy was used to flavour, clarify and preserve ale — one of the oldest brewing herbs in Britain.

  • People in Britain used ground ivy to make ale long before hops became the usual brewing herb. They used it to give the ale its flavour, to clear it, and to help it keep. It was one of the oldest herbs used for brewing in Britain.
  • Ground ivy is native to Europe and western Asia. European settlers carried it to North America on purpose, as part of a standard stock of household herbs — which is how a European plant became the lawn weed North Americans know as creeping Charlie, now recorded in almost every US state.
  • Its brewing names preserve its history: alehoof and tunhoof (a tun is a brewing cask), and gill-over-the-ground, where “gill” comes from a French word meaning to ferment. In the 18th century, strong ale infused with the herb was sold as gill ale and said to be medicinal, and gill tea — the leaves infused and sweetened — was sold by street criers in London as a tea to “purify the blood”, drunk in wineglassful doses three or four times a day for long-standing coughs.
  • Gerard carried older uses forward: he recommended it for ringing in the ears, for kidney diseases, and — following Dioscorides — for sciatica and eye inflammation. In 19th-century America it was used for lung and kidney diseases, asthma and jaundice, was snuffed for persistent headache, and was given to painters to treat lead colic — poisoning from lead paint.
  • Two pieces of folklore, told as folklore: wreaths of its trailing stems were once laid on the dead, and in Switzerland it was believed that wearing it with rue, agrimony, maidenhair and broom straw would sharpen sight and reveal witches.
  • It is still in living traditional use: an Austrian folk-medicine survey recorded it taken as salad or tea for disorders of the liver and bile, gut, chest, kidneys and urinary tract, and for fever and flu.
  • Two garden forms exist, both ornamental: ‘Variegata’, its leaves edged and splashed with cream-white and sold for hanging baskets and pots, and ‘Dappled Light’, finely dappled light green. Neither differs as a medicine — they are grown for their leaves.

Traditional medicine

  • A traditional herb for coughs and chesty complaints — long used as an expectorant and anticatarrhal, to help loosen phlegm in coughs and bronchial complaints. Health Canada's herbal monograph allows these uses on the basis of tradition; ground ivy taken by mouth has not been tested in clinical trials.
  • Traditionally used as a stomachic — a bitter digestive aid — and as an astringent — a drying, tightening herb — for diarrhoea.
  • Traditionally used as a diuretic, and for haemorrhoids.
  • On the skin, it has traditionally been used to help heal minor cuts and wounds and to soothe inflammation — Health Canada has a separate monograph for this use on the skin.
  • Taken by mouth, ground ivy has not been tested in clinical trials. The only research to add is animal-level: in mice, a ground ivy extract given for three weeks reduced the size and number of cholesterol gallstone crystals — a rodent result that shows no effect in people and does not prove the traditional gallstone use.
  • Caution: not for use in pregnancy or while breastfeeding, and avoid it if you have a kidney condition. The reason sits in its oil: it holds a small amount of pulegone, the compound that makes pennyroyal oil dangerous — but at less than one-thirtieth of pennyroyal's concentration. Pulegone irritates the gut and kidneys and harms the liver at high doses, which is why the concentrated essential oil should never be swallowed; a tea never reaches that strength.
  • Caution: ground ivy is poisonous to horses if they eat a lot of it, fresh or in hay, and cattle are also recorded as poisoned by large amounts — other livestock mostly leave it alone for its bitter taste.
  • When to plant: Plant rooted pieces in spring, in a shady corner where it can spread — it is vigorous and can swamp smaller plants
  • Sun: Shade or some shade — a plant for banks and under trees
  • Soil: Moist soil; it holds ground where grass struggles
  • Environment: An evergreen, hardy perennial ground cover; its violet flowers open early, from March to May
  • Planter or ground: Ground; a pot keeps it contained
  • Spacing and depth: Set pieces 30 cm apart — they soon knit into a mat
  • Water: Likes moisture
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Gather the leaves and flowering tops in spring, as the flowers open

Garden notes

  • An evergreen perennial ground cover for shady places — it mats over banks and under trees, holding the soil where grass struggles.
  • Its violet flowers open early, from March to May, and are worked by bees — a good early bee plant, visited by species such as Anthophora and Osmia.
  • The foliage is rich in iron, and the plant has been recommended as an addition to the compost heap.
  • It spreads vigorously and can swamp smaller plants, so it needs room or watching; it is listed as a noxious weed in Connecticut.
  • It spreads by stems up to 75 cm long that root at every joint, forming a mat about 15 cm tall that can cover some 2 square metres per plant. Its one weakness is summer drought — in cool, moist soil almost nothing else stops it. To clear it, every rooted joint must be lifted, or it regrows.
  • Before it flowers it is often confused with violets, henbit and mallow. The square, mint-family stem and the kidney-shaped, scalloped leaves are the check. Its old name “creeping Jenny” properly belongs to a different plant, Lysimachia nummularia.

Propagation

Lift a rooted piece of runner in spring or early autumn and plant it where you want it — it roots wherever its stems touch soil, so this almost always works. Ground-ivy spreads fast and can smother its neighbours, so keep it in a pot or an edged bed, not loose in a mixed border.

Sources

  • Mitich (1994) — history of ground ivy, Weed Technology
  • Vogl et al. (2013) — Austrian folk-medicine survey record for ground ivy
  • Royal Horticultural Society — ‘Variegata’ cultivar profile
  • Health Canada, Natural Health Products monographs — traditional uses of ground ivy, oral and topical, with pregnancy and kidney warnings
  • Kew, Plants of the World Online — Glechoma hederacea: native Europe and western Asia, naturalised across temperate North America
  • USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Plant Guide — Ground Ivy: Saxon brewing, name origins and settler introduction
  • Barnes, Anderson & Phillipson, Herbal Medicines — traditional properties and livestock poisoning record
  • USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Plant Guide — ale flavouring before hops; toxic to horses in quantity
  • Bond, Davies & Turner (2007) — biology of ground ivy; iron content and ground-cover habit

Lamb's Quarters

Chenopodium album

CulinaryMedicinal

Bone HealthSkin Health

Cooked

Valued first as a food: a wild spinach whose leaves are eaten as a green, and whose seeds — from a wild relative of quinoa — were gathered and cooked like a grain for thousands of years.

  • People have eaten this plant for thousands of years. They gathered its seeds and cooked them like a grain. That was long before the plant had a name in any book.
  • In North America, people did more than gather it. Thousands of years ago, farmers in the east grew a farmed chenopod, Chenopodium berlandieri, as a seed crop. It was one of the crops of the Eastern Agricultural Complex, the farming built there before maize — corn — arrived.
  • The European record is just as old, and unusually direct. Seeds of this plant were found in the stomach contents of the Tollund Man and the Grauballe Man, Danish bog bodies of the early Iron Age, among many other weed seeds. Researchers read that mix — weed seeds, charcoal, sand — as threshing waste or a ritual meal, not proof of a prized crop. But a first-century AD granary at Fjand in Jutland held a cleaned, stored supply of the seed, which does show deliberate gathering and storage. Seed finds run from Neolithic and Bronze Age settlements onward.
  • In Europe and Asia, the leaves were a pot herb — a green cooked in the pot. The seeds were a famine food, eaten when other food ran short. In hard years, people ground them into flour.
  • In Britain it was also called fat hen. The name says it plainly: this plant fed people well.
  • Then maize and wheat farming spread, and people gave up the farmed chenopod. The plant went back to being a weed of waste ground. It is the wild spinach that gardeners still pick today.
  • In North India the same plant is not a weed but a crop: as bathua, it is grown on purpose as a winter green and cooked as saag, folded into yogurt raita and stuffed into paratha flatbreads. In the Ayurvedic tradition its Sanskrit name is Vastuka, a named food and remedy. One plant, a crop on one continent and a weed on another.
  • It is native to Europe and western Asia, and spread with farming until it became almost worldwide in temperate regions. In hard times it was eaten widely: leaves and seeds in China, seed bread in Russia, and the leaves boiled — the water thrown away — by the Nandi people in Kenya.
  • The seed needs one piece of care the leaf does not: its coat carries bitter saponins, so the traditional preparation is to soak it overnight and rinse it well before cooking. Pick leaves young, too — nitrate and oxalate levels are highest in older leaves and in plants from heavily fertilised ground.

Traditional medicine

  • Traditionally used as a mild laxative, and as a poultice to soothe minor burns and insect bites.

Craft

  • The young shoots give a green dye, and the crushed fresh roots work as a mild soap substitute — a washing plant as well as a food plant.
  • Valued first as a food: a wild spinach whose leaves are rich in vitamins A, C and K, and a good source of calcium, potassium, iron and protein.
  • The figures behind that, per 100 g of raw leaves (USDA): 43 kcal, protein 4.2 g — more than spinach, gram for gram — fibre 4 g, calcium 309 mg (about 31% of the daily value), vitamin C about 96% of the daily value, vitamin A about 73%, riboflavin about 37%, manganese about 37% and vitamin B6 about 21%. Two honest riders: the calcium figure is total calcium — the leaf's own oxalates bind some of it, so not all of it is absorbed; and boiling lowers the protein a little, to about 3.2 g, as it lowers the oxalates.
  • The seeds carry their own food value: about 13–16% protein, with a balanced amino-acid pattern and plenty of lysine for a plant food.
  • Beyond food, the laxative and poultice uses rest on tradition. Laboratory and animal work on extracts exists, but there are no human trials of lamb's quarters as a treatment.
  • Caution: the leaves are high in oxalates, natural compounds found in many plants that can add to kidney stones in people prone to them, so eat in moderation — and people prone to kidney stones should limit them. Cooking, especially boiling, lowers the oxalate content.
  • Caution: it can build up nitrates from rich or contaminated soil, so gather only from clean ground, away from sprayed or heavily fertilised areas.
  • Caution: there is a report that eating very large quantities of the raw leaves has caused light sensitivity of the skin in some people — reported at that strength only: raw leaves, very large amounts.
  • When to plant: Usually gathered wild. To grow it, scatter seed in spring on rich ground and thin the seedlings into the kitchen
  • Sun: Full sun or some shade
  • Soil: Rich soil — it often appears where nitrogen is plentiful
  • Environment: A hardy annual, and a pioneer of bare, disturbed ground
  • Planter or ground: Ground; a pot works
  • Spacing and depth: Scatter thinly; thin to 25 cm apart — the thinnings are the first harvest
  • Water: Average
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Pick the young leaves and tips through summer, before the plant flowers

Garden notes

  • A pioneer plant — one of the first to arrive on bare, disturbed ground, where its growth helps stabilise the soil.
  • Its many seeds are an important food for birds such as finches, sparrows and doves, and for small mammals.
  • Deep roots draw up minerals from below the surface, which return to the topsoil as the plant breaks down.
  • Its foliage supports insect life, and it often appears in nitrogen-rich soil.
  • One plant makes on average about 72,000 seeds — a large plant over 100,000 — and the seed can stay alive in the soil for decades. Pick before it seeds if you do not want it everywhere next year, and expect volunteers for years.
  • The seed sprouts best at or near the surface, in light; seed buried 2 cm or deeper rarely emerges. It germinates across a wide range of soil acidity and tolerates salty soil better than many crops. Many populations now resist common farm herbicides, which is part of why this weed is studied so much.

Propagation

Sow seeds in spring, a quarter inch deep in moist soil — they sprout in 7 to 14 days. Lambs-quarters seeds itself freely and the seed stays alive in the soil for decades, so pull up spare seedlings and do not let it set seed where you do not want it.

Cultivars

  • There are no named varieties of Chenopodium album. Botanists treat it as a variable group of close forms, which is why books disagree about it. The magenta-dusted “tree spinach” sold as 'Magenta Spreen' is not this plant — it is a tall relative, Chenopodium giganteum. Quinoa is another relative, named here as a relative only.

Sources

  • Helbaek (1959) — Chenopodium album as a food plant in prehistory: Tollund and Grauballe stomach contents, the Fjand seed store
  • Tang et al. (2022) — germination ecology of Chenopodium album: surface sprouting, acidity and salt tolerance
  • Rutgers Cooperative Extension — common lambsquarters: seed output, decades of soil survival, herbicide resistance
  • Indian Food Composition Tables (2017) — bathua leaves, the North Indian winter crop
  • USDA FoodData Central — nutrient values for lambsquarters, raw
  • Purdue University, Famine Foods database — Chenopodium album: bathua in India, and recorded uses in China, Russia and Kenya
  • Plants For A Future — Chenopodium album: green dye from the young shoots, roots used as a soap substitute
  • Cornell University weed identification programme — lamb's quarters as a nitrate-accumulating plant
  • Foster & Duke, Peterson Field Guide to Medicinal Plants and Herbs — traditional poultice use
  • Published compositional reviews of Chenopodium album — high leaf oxalate content; boiling reduces soluble oxalates

Mallow

Malva sylvestris

MedicinalCulinary

Digestive HealthSkin Health

FreshCooked

A soft-leaved flowering plant in the same family as hibiscus and okra, native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia and now found almost everywhere. Leaves, flowers and roots are all used, and the whole plant is edible; what it gives is mucilage, the slippery gel it makes when soaked, which coats and soothes.

  • Greek doctors used mallow early. About 2,000 years ago, Dioscorides, a Greek doctor, described mallows among his remedies.
  • The Romans took it up as food and as medicine. Pliny, the Roman writer on nature, described its uses. The poet Horace counted mallows among his own simple country foods.
  • Its name fits it well. Malva is linked to the Greek word for “soft”. Softening and soothing is what this plant has always been used for.
  • Through the Middle Ages, it was a standard herb of monastery gardens and cottage gardens. People used it for coughs, sore throats and sore, irritated skin.
  • It stayed a cottage remedy into modern times — an herb for tea and for poultices, used for coughs and sore skin. A poultice is a soft, wet mass of herb laid on the skin. It is still gathered wild across Europe.

Traditional medicine

  • The mucilage in the leaves and flowers coats the lining of the mouth and throat, easing irritation and the dry cough that comes with it. European regulators accept this as a traditional use, based on long-standing practice rather than clinical trials.
  • A tea or rinse held in the mouth was used to soothe mouth sores and a sore, irritated throat in the same way, by coating the tissue.
  • The same coating action was traditionally used to calm mild discomfort in the stomach and gut.
  • In traditional herbal practice, mallow was also used as a mild, soothing diuretic — a substance that gently increases urine flow.
  • On the skin, mallow has a long traditional use as a softening poultice or wash for irritated, inflamed skin, minor wounds and insect bites; early laboratory and animal research supports its soothing, wound-supporting character, but it has not been well tested in people.

Craft

  • The flowers give a soft purple-blue dye for cloth. The colour is gentle and fades with time, but it is a true dye from a common plant.
  • The bigger craft is the stems: their fibre was used for cordage, textiles and paper — mallow is a fibre plant as well as a dye plant.
  • The whole plant is edible — young leaves in salads, older leaves and shoots cooked as greens — and the leaves supply vitamin C, carotenoid antioxidants (the plant pigments the body can turn into vitamin A), vitamin E compounds, and minerals such as potassium, calcium and iron. The leaves also contain small amounts of alpha-linolenic acid, a plant omega-3 fat, though not in amounts that make mallow a rich source of it.
  • The root carries the same soothing mucilage as the leaf. Marsh mallow root — from a close kin of this plant — was the original base of the French marshmallow sweet.
  • When to plant: Sow seed outside in spring, where it will grow
  • Sun: Full sun or some shade
  • Soil: Ordinary soil, even poor and disturbed ground
  • Environment: Hardy; its strong roots help hold soil in place on banks, and the flowers draw bees through a long season
  • Planter or ground: Both
  • Spacing and depth: Sow 1 cm deep; 30–45 cm apart
  • Water: Average — drought-tolerant once settled
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Pick the leaves young, through the season, and the flowers as they open in summer

Garden notes

  • Mallow is unusually sensitive to ozone, a form of air pollution: its leaves show visible speckled injury at levels other plants tolerate, so scientists have used it as a living warning sign — a bioindicator — of ozone in the air.

Propagation

Sow seed in spring or autumn, or take softwood cuttings from stems or new shoots at the base in early summer. Plants are short-lived, so raise new ones each year. Seed-grown plants may not match the parent — take cuttings to keep a named type true.

Sources

  • European Medicines Agency, mallow flower and leaf monographs — traditional use for mouth and throat irritation, dry cough and mild gut discomfort
  • Barros et al. (2010) — nutrient composition of mallow leaves, flowers and stems
  • Gasparetto et al. (2012) — review of mallow phytochemistry and pharmacology
  • Bergmann, Bender & Weigel (1995) — mallow as the most ozone-sensitive native species tested; ozone bioindicator

Mullein

Verbascum thapsus

Medicinal

Respiratory Health

Dried

A classic pioneer of open, disturbed ground — dry, sandy or gravelly soils, rail banks and waste places. Its tall yellow flower spikes are visited by bees through the summer.

  • Mullein is an old medicine. Dioscorides described it about 2,000 years ago, and it has been used for coughs and chest complaints ever since.
  • Its tall dried stalks had a second use. Dipped in tallow — hard animal fat — they burned as torches, a kind of country candle carried at funerals and processions in parts of Europe. The plant's old name, hag taper, comes from this custom.
  • The soft leaves were used as insoles in worn shoes, to cushion and warm the feet.
  • In Ireland it became a valued remedy for consumption — tuberculosis — and was grown and sold for that use in the 1800s.
  • European settlers carried mullein to North America, and Native American peoples took it up — some smoked the leaves for coughs. There it escaped to roadsides and dry ground everywhere, the same pioneer — a plant that moves first into bare, open ground — it had always been in Europe.

Traditional medicine

  • The flowers are a traditional remedy for the symptoms of sore throat that come with a dry cough and a cold — this is the use in the European Medicines Agency's herbal monograph, and it rests on long-standing use, not clinical trials.
  • Mullein leaf and flower have a long tradition in teas for coughs and chest complaints generally.

Craft

  • The flowers give a yellow dye for wool and cloth.
  • The soothing effect is the flower's mucilage — a few percent of slippery, coating plant fibres that calm an irritated throat.
  • Strain mullein teas well, through fine cloth: the fine hairs on the leaves can irritate the throat and mouth.
  • Herbal ear drops containing mullein eased children's ear pain as well as anaesthetic drops in two clinical trials — but mullein was one of several herbs in olive oil, so the effect cannot be credited to mullein alone.
  • Caution: the seeds are poisonous and must never be eaten — they were once used to stun fish. The EMA does not recommend mullein flower for children under 12, or in pregnancy and while breastfeeding, where its safety has not been established, and advises using it for no more than a week at a time.
  • When to plant: Usually gathered wild. To grow it, scatter seed in spring on bare, dry ground — it needs light to sprout, and it spreads freely by seed
  • Sun: Full sun
  • Soil: Dry, sandy or gravelly soil; rich soil makes it soft
  • Environment: A hardy biennial — a flat rosette the first year, a tall flower spike the second. It is classed as a noxious weed in Colorado and Hawaii, so watch it where it is not wanted
  • Planter or ground: Ground only — too tall and deep-rooted for pots
  • Spacing and depth: Scatter on the surface; 60 cm apart
  • Water: Dry once settled
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Gather the leaves in the first year; pick the flowers as they open in the second summer

Garden notes

  • A classic pioneer of open, disturbed ground — dry, sandy or gravelly soils, rail banks and waste places — covering bare soil where little else will grow.
  • Its seed is very long-lived: in a buried-seed experiment begun in 1879, mullein seeds were still sprouting after more than 140 years, and a single plant can leave a seed bank that outlasts the gardener.
  • The tall yellow flower spikes are visited by bees and other pollinators through the summer, and the seed is eaten by finches and sparrows, including the American goldfinch.
  • Left standing, the dead stems shelter overwintering insects, and the plant hosts the mullein moth. It spreads freely and is classed as a noxious weed in Colorado and Hawaii, so it needs watching where it is not wanted.

Propagation

Sow seed in late spring to early summer, in a cold frame, and only just cover it — the seed needs light to sprout, and comes up in 2–3 weeks. Plant out in late summer. It makes a low rosette in its first year, flowers in its second year, then dies — so let it set seed if you want more plants.

Sources

  • European Medicines Agency, mullein flower monograph — traditional use for sore throat with dry cough and cold
  • Sarrell et al. (2001) — combination herbal ear drops and ear pain in children
  • Sarrell et al. (2003) — combination herbal ear drops compared with anaesthetic drops
  • Kew, Grow Wild — seed toxicity, fish-stunning history and the long-running buried-seed experiment

Nettle

Urtica dioica

MedicinalCulinary

Bone HealthHormone HealthUrinary Health

FreshDriedCooked

The stinging nettle is a tall perennial of rich, damp ground, native to temperate Europe and Asia and now found worldwide; its hollow hairs act like tiny needles, injecting a sting that cooking or drying completely removes. Its leaf, root, stem fibre and seed are all used. Its genus holds roughly 80 species, and the wider nettle family over 2,600.

  • Nettle is one of the oldest cloth plants in Europe. A cloth found in a Bronze Age burial in Denmark, about 2,800 years old, was woven from nettle fibre.
  • Nettle cloth went on being woven in northern Europe and Scotland for centuries — a linen-like cloth for sheets, shirts and table linen, made from a weed of the hedgerow.
  • When cotton ran short in the First World War, Germany turned back to nettle: the fibre was gathered on a large scale and woven into cloth.
  • As food, the young spring leaves were eaten as a tonic after winter. Nettle soup and nettle tea became old spring customs across Europe.
  • As medicine, folk practice used it widely. People made teas for the joints and for the waterworks — the body's urinary system. They also rubbed the fresh sting itself on painful joints — a harsh remedy, recorded for centuries.
  • One plant, three trades — cloth, food and medicine — which is why the nettle patch by the cottage was kept, not cleared.

Traditional medicine

  • The leaf is traditionally used as a mild diuretic, increasing urine flow to flush the urinary tract in minor urinary complaints — a use European regulators accept on the basis of long-standing practice.
  • The leaf has a traditional use as a rinse for an oily scalp and hair.
  • In folk medicine, the seed was used as a tonic.

Craft

  • The stems give one of the great plant fibres. Stripped, retted and spun like flax, nettle fibre makes cloth, rope, twine and fishing nets.
  • Nettle is a dye plant too, in two colours: the leaves and stems give a strong, lasting green for wool, and the roots, boiled with alum, give yellow.
  • The root — not the leaf — is the part used for the prostate: nettle root preparations are traditionally used, and recognised by European regulators, for easing the urinary symptoms of a benign enlarged prostate (such as a weak stream and frequent night-time trips), once a doctor has ruled out anything serious. A large six-month trial found root extract improved those symptoms more than a placebo, though the evidence overall is still rated limited.
  • The leaf is a genuinely rich food: high in vitamins A, C and K, calcium, iron and protein for a leafy green, and full of antioxidant plant compounds.
  • The leaf is also a traditional remedy for minor joint pain, and rubbing the fresh plant on painful joints is an old folk practice that one small trial found helpful for thumb-joint arthritis pain.
  • For hay fever, nettle leaf is often called a natural antihistamine: in laboratory tests its extract blocks histamine receptors, and one small early trial of freeze-dried leaf suggested it may ease symptoms — promising, but not yet well proven.
  • The seed is eaten too, sprinkled on food.
  • When to plant: Plant root pieces or young plants in spring, in a contained corner — a patch spreads and stays for years
  • Sun: Full sun or some shade
  • Soil: Rich, moist soil — nettles follow nitrogen
  • Environment: A hardy perennial; a patch is a nursery for butterflies, whose caterpillars feed on the leaves, so leave some standing
  • Planter or ground: Ground; a large sunken pot contains the roots
  • Spacing and depth: 30–45 cm apart
  • Water: Likes moisture
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Pick the young tops in spring, with gloves, before flowering; dig the roots in autumn

Garden notes

  • Nettle patches are nurseries for butterflies: the caterpillars of the small tortoiseshell, peacock, red admiral and comma butterflies feed on nettle leaves, and few other plants can replace it for them.
  • A patch also shelters aphids early in spring, which gives ladybirds and other aphid-eating insects an early meal and gets them established before garden pests build up.
  • Nettle stems also serve as animal bedding.
  • Chopped nettles are rich in nitrogen and minerals, which makes them a fine compost activator and the base of the traditional nettle liquid feed for the garden.
  • Dried nettle is a nutritious animal feed, fed to poultry and livestock.

Propagation

Sow seed on the surface of moist soil in spring, or divide the roots in spring through to late summer — dig up a piece of underground stem with shoots and replant it at once. Wear thick gloves — it stings. Grow it in a pot or behind a root barrier, as it spreads fast by its roots.

Sources

  • European Medicines Agency, nettle leaf and nettle root monographs — traditional uses for urinary flushing, minor joint pain and prostate urinary symptoms
  • Plants For A Future — Urtica dioica: green dye from the leaves, yellow dye from the roots
  • NCCIH — nettle root evidence for prostate symptoms rated limited
  • Safarinejad (2005) — six-month trial of nettle root extract in 620 men
  • Roschek et al. (2009) — nettle extract and histamine receptors (laboratory)
  • Mittman (1990) — small trial of freeze-dried nettle leaf for hay fever
  • Randall et al. (2000) — fresh nettle rub for thumb-joint arthritis pain

Plantain

Plantago major

Medicinal

Digestive HealthRespiratory HealthSkin HealthWound Care

Fresh

Broadleaf plantain — no relation to the banana-like fruit — is a low rosette of wide, ribbed leaves native to Europe and Asia that has followed people around the world, springing up in lawns, paths and compacted ground everywhere. The leaf is the main medicinal part; the seeds are used too.

  • Plantain was one of the nine sacred herbs of Anglo-Saxon England. The Nine Herbs Charm, a healing poem about 1,000 years old, names it as waybread and calls on it against poison and infection.
  • Greek and Roman doctors used it even before that. Dioscorides described it in the first century, for wounds and bites — the same skin uses it keeps today.
  • Later, it travelled with Europeans wherever they settled. It sprang up along their paths and wagon tracks. Its seed was carried in mud and on boots.
  • It is native to Europe and temperate Asia, and is now naturalised across North America, South America, Africa, Australia and New Zealand — believed to be one of the first plants to reach North America after European colonisation. Native Americans saw it arrive with the settlers. They gave it a name that tells the story: white man's footprint.
  • The name was true then, and it is still true now. Plantain still grows thickest where feet and wheels have packed the ground hard.
  • It was familiar enough to be a joke on stage: in Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost, Costard falls and breaks his shin and calls for “a plain plantain” — no salve, sir, but a plantain. Plantain was the everyday broken-skin remedy of its time.

Traditional medicine

  • The leaf is traditionally used in skin washes and toners, where its astringent tannins gently tighten and cleanse the skin’s surface.
  • The seeds are rich in mucilage, a swelling fibre similar to psyllium (which comes from a close plantain relative), traditionally used to keep the bowels moving gently.

Craft

  • The leaves are the classic salve herb: plantain leaves infused in oil and set with wax make the homemade plantain salve, the best-known balm in folk craft.
  • The tough veins of mature leaves are a fibre too: stripped out and twisted, they were made into small cords, thread and fishing line.
  • The leaf is the classic wayside first-aid plant: bruised fresh and laid on the skin, or made into a salve, it has been used for centuries on minor wounds, scrapes and insect bites. It contains allantoin, a compound that supports skin repair, and aucubin, which acts against microbes; one very small study of a plantain ointment on burns — only 15 people — found results much like a standard treatment cream, but the difference was not statistically significant, so it is a hint, not proof.
  • A larger wound trial followed. In a randomised, open-label trial, 94 people with diabetic foot ulcers or pressure ulcers used a 10% plantain leaf gel once a day for two weeks alongside routine care, or routine dressings alone (Ghanadian et al., 2024). Wound size fell by 86.9% in the gel group against 52.9% in the control group, and 64% healed completely against 20.5%. Its limits, stated with it: people knew which treatment they were getting, it ran only two weeks, and it is one trial in one setting. It strengthens the Wound Care and Skin Health tags with this species' own human evidence.
  • Plantain major also has its own cough trial. In a double-blind randomised trial, 80 adults with acute bronchitis took plantain syrup for 10 days or a placebo (Naderi et al., 2024). Bronchitis severity, cough frequency, sputum and chest-wall pain all improved significantly more on plantain, and no significant side effects were reported in either group. One trial, one centre, 80 people, 10 days — stated at that strength. (A combined aloe-and-plantain gel trial exists too; as a two-plant result it is not counted for plantain alone.)
  • The leaf’s tannins — the astringent compounds that make strong tea taste dry — and its flavonoid antioxidants are behind its traditional use for digestive upsets. In animal studies, plantain extracts have protected the stomach lining, but plantain has not been shown to prevent stomach ulcers in people.
  • In laboratory tests, plantain extracts act against a range of bacteria and some viruses. That is a laboratory finding, not proof that the plant fights infections in the body.
  • Safety: plantain leaf is generally considered safe as a food and a skin herb, and serious side effects are not documented. As with any wild plant, gather it from clean ground away from sprayed verges and roadsides, and be sure of the plant before eating it — the young leaves of foxglove, a poisonous plant, can be mistaken for plantain before either flowers. Plantain's leaves have strong parallel ribs and a leafless flower spike; foxglove's are softly hairy with net-like veins. Wash wild leaves well — this plant grows on paths and lawns, where dogs, spray and road dirt are part of its life.
  • Safety, with a species fence: the European monograph in this family covers ribwort plantain, Plantago lanceolata — narrow leaves — as a traditional remedy for mouth and throat irritation and dry cough. It does not cover this plant, Plantago major, and its cough standing must not be transferred here. Major's own evidence is the two trials above.
  • Safety: people allergic to plantain or to others in the plantain family should not use it; reactions are rare. Plantain pollen is wind-blown and is a known hay-fever trigger — a point about the pollen, separate from eating or rubbing the leaf.
  • Safety: there is not enough reliable information on taking plantain by mouth in pregnancy or while breastfeeding, so internal use is not recommended then; its safety there has not been established. Use on small areas of skin is a different, lower concern.
  • Safety: the leaf and seed are rich in mucilage, a gel-forming fibre which in theory can slow how fast other medicines are taken up. That has not been studied for this plant; as a precaution, take other medicines one to two hours apart from plantain preparations, above all medicines where the dose has to be exact. Large amounts may cause bloating, gas or loose stools.
  • When to plant: Usually gathered wild. To grow it, sow seed in spring in a patch of poor, trampled ground where little else thrives — a single plant makes thousands of seeds in a season and sows itself freely wherever ground is bare and trodden, which is why a pot or a contained patch is the honest advice
  • Sun: Full sun or some shade
  • Soil: Almost any soil, including compacted ground — its fibrous roots help bind it
  • Environment: A hardy perennial; the ground-hugging rosette tolerates mowing and foot traffic
  • Planter or ground: Ground; a pot works
  • Spacing and depth: Sow on the surface; 25 cm apart
  • Water: Average
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Pick leaves through the season — the youngest for eating, any size for a poultice; the seed heads ripen in late summer

Garden notes

  • Its strong fibrous roots and ground-hugging rosette help bind soil and slow erosion, and the plant tolerates the compacted, trampled ground where little else will grow.
  • The dense mat of leaves shades the soil surface, helping it hold moisture.
  • In laboratory studies, an extract of plantain seed worked as a natural coagulant — a substance that makes fine particles in dirty water clump together so they can be removed — clearing industrial wastewater about as well as some conventional treatments.

Propagation

Sow seed in spring, in a cold frame or straight outside in mid to late spring, on the soil surface — it needs light to sprout. Keep the soil damp until the seedlings show. Once it is settled, it seeds itself freely, so cut the flower spikes off before they ripen if you do not want it spreading.

Cultivars

  • 'Rubrifolia' (also sold as 'Atropurpurea') is the same broad rosette with bronze, burgundy to almost black-purple leaves, the colour deepening in autumn and strongest in full sun — grown for its leaves, not for medicine. 'Rosularis', the rose plantain, makes instead of the usual thin flower spike a tight rosette of ruffled green bracts, like a green rose — a curiosity grown in cottage gardens for centuries. 'Variegata' has leaves variegated with cream and white.

Sources

  • European Medicines Agency — herbal monograph on Plantago lanceolata (2025), cited to keep the two plantain species apart
  • Ghanadian et al. (2024) — randomised trial of Plantago major gel in diabetic foot and pressure ulcers, 94 people
  • Keshavarzi et al. (2022) — case-control study of Plantago major ointment in second-degree burns, 15 people
  • Naderi et al. (2024) — double-blind randomised trial of Plantago major syrup in acute bronchitis, 80 people
  • Royal Horticultural Society — Plantago major cultivars Rubrifolia, Rosularis and Variegata
  • Samuelsen (2000) — review of Plantago major traditional use and pharmacology (allantoin, aucubin)
  • Pharmaceuticals review of Plantago major (2023) — antimicrobial and antiviral activity in laboratory tests
  • Clinical study of plantain ointment on burns (2022) — very small trial (15 people); the difference from a standard cream was not statistically significant
  • Zarei Mahmoudabadi et al. (2018) — plantain seed extract as a water coagulant (laboratory)

Purple Dead-Nettle

Lamium purpureum

MedicinalCulinary

Skin Health

FreshCooked

A member of the mint family, and one of the earliest flowers of the year. It has no sting and is safe to handle.

  • The “dead” in its name means stingless — unlike its cousin the stinging nettle, it has no stinging hairs.
  • Purple dead-nettle is a European folk herb with a quiet past. It was never a famous medicine. Country people used it, and the great herbals — the big old books of healing plants — mostly passed it by.
  • People used it in simple ways. They took it as a spring tonic — a food or drink taken to wake the body up after winter — and ate it as one of the first greens of the year.
  • That is most of its history: a spring food, a small remedy, and one of the first flowers of the year for bees.

Traditional medicine

  • In European folk tradition it was used mostly on the skin, as a poultice or wash for cuts, scrapes and minor irritation.
  • Folk practice also describes it as astringent and as a gentle diuretic, though these are traditional descriptions, not tested ones.
  • The whole plant above ground is edible — leaves, stems and flowers — with a mild, earthy taste. Foraging guides describe the leaves as a source of vitamins A, C and K, iron and fibre.
  • It is a gentle folk herb rather than a tested medicine — research on this species itself is still very limited, and most laboratory work has been done on its relatives.
  • When to plant: Usually gathered wild. It is a winter annual: seed scattered in autumn gives plants that flower from late winter
  • Sun: Full sun or some shade
  • Soil: Ordinary, moist soil
  • Environment: Hardy; it covers bare soil through the cold months, then recedes by summer. Its early flowers are a critical nectar source for queen bumblebees just out of hibernation
  • Planter or ground: Ground; a pot works
  • Spacing and depth: Scatter seed on the surface in autumn
  • Water: Average
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Gather the leaves and flowers in late winter and spring, while it blooms

Garden notes

  • Honeybees and digger bees work the flowers too, when almost nothing else is in flower.
  • Its crimson-red pollen is an early source of protein for bees raising their first brood.
  • As it recedes by summer, it makes room for later plants.
  • Its seeds carry a small oily parcel (an elaiosome, a fatty attachment that ants eat) that ants carry off, planting the seed as they go.

Propagation

Sow seed where it is to grow, as soon as it is ripe, or in spring — press it lightly into damp soil and barely cover it, as it needs light to sprout. It seeds itself freely, so pull plants out before they set seed if you do not want it spreading through the garden.

Safety

  • Large amounts — a strong tea, for example — can have a laxative effect. Take care with identification: its closest lookalikes are henbit, which is also edible, and ground ivy, and while none of the usual lookalikes is toxic, it is still worth waiting for the square stem, the purple-tinged top leaves and the pink-purple flowers to be sure you have the right plant.

Sources

  • Kew, Plants of the World Online — accepted name and native range (Europe, Asia and North Africa; naturalised in North America)
  • Plants For A Future — purple dead-nettle entry: young leaves eaten raw or cooked as a potherb; the whole plant traditionally astringent, diuretic and purgative; fresh bruised leaves applied to cuts and wounds
  • Cornell University, College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — deadnettle weed profile: identification (square stems, purple-tinged upper leaves), separation from henbit, and pollination by bumblebees, solitary bees and honeybees
  • Penn State Extension — purple dead nettle, henbit and ground ivy as look-alike winter annuals; spring flowers visited by honeybees and bumblebees
  • Hodges (1952) — The Pollen Loads of the Honeybee: a prominent March–April pollen source, when bees need protein to build up their nests; the pollen crimson red
  • Pemberton & Irving (1990) — elaiosomes on the seeds of weeds including red dead-nettle, and the potential for their dispersal by ants

Purslane

Portulaca oleracea

Culinary

FreshCooked

Purslane is a fleshy, low-spreading succulent with spoon-shaped leaves and small yellow flowers, eaten as a vegetable since ancient times and now found in gardens and warm ground all over the world; its exact wild origin is debated, somewhere in the Old World. Leaves, stems and seeds are all edible — and it is a nutrient-rich garden plant.

  • Purslane has been eaten since ancient times, around the Mediterranean and across Asia. It is one of the oldest greens in the kitchen.
  • Greek medicine wrote about it early. Dioscorides described it in his herbal about 2,000 years ago, as a food and as a medicine.
  • In China, it has its own long record. There it is called ma chi xian, and it was used as a herb for cooling and for the gut.
  • It travelled with trade and settlement to every warm country. In most of them, people treated it the same way. They gathered it as a free green — and just as often, they pulled it out as a weed.
  • That double standing is its whole history. It was prized in some kitchens and pulled as a weed in others. And in every age, somewhere in the world, people were eating it.

The leaves

  • Purslane leaves carry more alpha-linolenic acid — the plant form of omega-3 fat — than any other leafy green vegetable measured, about 300–400 mg in a 100 g serving. (The body converts only a little of this plant omega-3 into the fish-oil forms, EPA and DHA.)
  • It is mineral-rich for a leafy green: a good source of potassium and magnesium, with useful amounts of calcium, plus vitamins A, C and E.

The stems and seeds

  • The stems are eaten raw or cooked like the leaves. The tiny black seeds are edible, and were ground into seed cakes by Aboriginal Australians.
  • In animal studies, purslane extracts have protected the liver against damage. This effect has not been shown in people.
  • In animal studies, purslane extracts have also protected brain and nerve cells — the kind of early research sometimes described as neuroprotective. This, too, has not been shown in people.
  • Caution: purslane is high in oxalates — natural compounds found in many plants that can add to kidney stones in people prone to them — so if that is a concern, keep portions moderate.
  • When to plant: Sow outside in late spring, once the soil is warm — it hates cold ground
  • Sun: Full sun
  • Soil: Poor, dry, sandy soil suits it; it is a pioneer of bare ground
  • Environment: A heat-loving annual; its dense, fleshy mat shades the soil and slows evaporation, helping the ground beneath hold water
  • Planter or ground: Both — a wide, shallow pot suits it
  • Spacing and depth: Sow on the surface or just below; 25 cm apart
  • Water: Dry once settled — the fleshy leaves store water
  • Companion plants: A recognised living ground cover beneath corn, tomatoes, peppers and potatoes, keeping the soil cool and moist around them
  • When to pick: Pick the stems and leaves through summer

Garden notes

  • It is a pioneer plant, among the first to take hold on bare, poor or dry ground, covering and stabilising soil where little else will grow.
  • Its dense, fleshy mat shades the soil and slows evaporation, helping the ground beneath it hold water.
  • Gardeners often let it grow as a living ground cover among taller crops — it is a recognised companion beneath corn, tomatoes, peppers and potatoes, keeping the soil cool and moist around them while its deeper roots draw up minerals from below.
  • Its small flowers are visited by bees and other small pollinating insects.

Propagation

Sow the tiny seed on the surface of warm, damp soil in late spring, after the last frost — do not bury it, as it needs light to sprout. Or push a stem cutting into damp soil in warm weather; it roots in about a week. It seeds itself freely, so keep it where it cannot take over.

Sources

  • Uddin et al. (2014) — purslane omega-3 (alpha-linolenic acid) content, highest of leafy greens measured; oxalate content
  • USDA FoodData Central — nutrient values for purslane, raw
  • Iranshahy et al. (2017) — review of purslane pharmacology; liver and nerve effects in animal studies
  • NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — omega-3 fact sheet: limited conversion of plant omega-3 to EPA and DHA
  • University of Nevada, Reno Extension — purslane as a companion plant and living ground cover

Red Clover

Trifolium pratense

Medicinal

Hormone HealthSkin Health

A nitrogen-fixing legume: bacteria in its root nodules take nitrogen from the air and add it to the soil, which is why farmers grow it as a cover crop and green manure. The flower heads are the part used.

  • Red clover's big story is on the farm. In the 1600s and 1700s it was grown across Europe to feed farm animals — cut for hay, and grazed by livestock.
  • It earned its place in the rotation. Rotation means growing different crops in turn on the same ground. Grown in turn with grain crops, it rested the soil and made it richer — its roots add nitrogen to the soil — and the harvests that came after clover were better for it.
  • Farmers carried it around the world. It became one of the standard plants of grazing land in North America, Australia and New Zealand.
  • In folk medicine, the flower heads were a remedy for skin troubles such as eczema and psoriasis, and for coughs, including whooping cough.
  • It is the state flower of Vermont — a small honour that shows how much the plant meant to farming country.
  • Red clover is native to Europe, western and central Asia and north-west Africa — the USDA places its origin more narrowly in Asia Minor and south-eastern Europe. It reached the British Isles from Germany in the 1600s and was brought to North America by English colonists. At its peak it was the most important legume hay crop in the north-eastern United States — as much as 10 million acres were grown in the northern states in the 1940s.
  • It is grown as two distinct farm types — medium and mammoth — set out under Cultivars below.
  • In the herbals it was Meadow Trefoil: Gerard noted a poultice of it for skin conditions, and Culpeper classed it as cooling, for inflamed surfaces, eye complaints and swellings. America’s Eclectic physicians of the 1800s made it a first-line skin herb — King’s American Dispensatory gave it a long reputation as an “alterative”, the old word for a blood-cleansing tonic, used chiefly for chronic skin diseases such as eczema and for whooping cough; Felter, in 1922, listed the same uses, plus scrofula, the swollen neck glands of tuberculosis. That record is the documented root of its folk skin use. At home, the flower infusion sweetened with honey was a household tea for persistent and spasmodic coughs, including in children, and a spring “blood purifier” tonic in European folk practice.

Craft

  • The flowers give a yellow dye — a small craft use for a plant grown by the field rather than the garden.
  • Contains isoflavones — plant compounds, including biochanin A and formononetin, that are structurally similar to the hormone estrogen.
  • Supplements are promoted for menopausal hot flushes, but studies have had inconsistent results, and the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health finds no conclusive evidence of benefit for any condition.
  • The trial record behind that verdict: a Cochrane review (Lethaby et al., 2013) pooled 43 randomised trials with 4,364 women and found no significant difference from placebo in daily hot-flush frequency for the standard red clover extract. In the large American ICE trial (Tice et al., 2003; 252 women), neither of two red clover products did clinically better than placebo over 12 weeks.
  • A later pooling (Kanadys et al., 2021) disagreed, finding about 1.7 fewer flushes a day than placebo — but the results varied greatly between studies, so the honest summary is a possible small effect, at low certainty, against the most rigorous review finding none.
  • For skin, there are no human trials of red clover for eczema or psoriasis at all. The Skin Health tag rests on the traditional record above, not on trials.
  • Caution: because of its estrogen-like activity, avoid red clover supplements in pregnancy and while breastfeeding, and talk to a healthcare provider first if you have a hormone-sensitive condition or take hormone-related medication.
  • Caution: red clover may increase the risk of bleeding alongside blood-thinning medicines such as warfarin.
  • In trials, standardised red clover extracts were used for up to two years and were generally well tolerated (NCCIH) — the cautions here are about who should avoid it, not about the extract being harsh. People with a history of hormone-sensitive cancer, including breast cancer, are advised to avoid it.
  • The famous “clover disease” that made sheep infertile in 1940s Western Australia came from subterranean clover, a different species eaten in very large amounts — not from red clover pasture at normal levels.
  • When to plant: Sow seed outside in spring, or late summer, into pasture, a patch, or a bed you want fed
  • Sun: Full sun or some shade
  • Soil: It grows in slightly acid soil (pH 5.5–6.0) but yields best at pH 6.0 or higher, in well-drained loamy soil; it tolerates wetter ground that alfalfa will not. It fixes nitrogen, and a deep taproot helps break up compacted layers
  • Environment: A hardy perennial, often short-lived; its flowers are an important nectar source for bumblebees and honeybees
  • Planter or ground: Ground
  • Spacing and depth: Sow ¼ to ½ inch deep into a firm, weed-free seedbed — on farms, 8–12 lb of seed per acre alone, or 2–4 lb per acre in a grass mix. It is commonly frost-seeded: broadcast onto frozen ground in late winter, and the freeze and thaw work the seed in
  • Water: Average
  • Companion plants: Grass is its classic pasture partner; it feeds the soil for whatever follows it
  • When to pick: Pick the flowers as they open through summer; the leaves are gathered young

Garden notes

  • Its flowers are pollinated by bumblebees and honeybees, and it is an important nectar plant and source of honey.
  • A deep taproot helps break up compacted layers of soil.
  • Grown as a living cover, it protects the soil surface from erosion.
  • Cut or graze at a quarter to half bloom, leave at least 2 inches of growth, and allow 45 days after the last autumn cut for the roots to store reserves before hard frost — late cutting is a main cause of stands dying out. A stand typically lasts 3–4 years. Anthracnose and powdery mildew are the named diseases in humid areas; resistant kinds reduce them.

Propagation

Sow seed in spring, in April to early May, no deeper than a quarter inch, on firm, moist soil. Red clover lives only a couple of years, so sow again to keep the patch going.

Cultivars

  • Medium red clover (double-cut) flowers earlier, establishes fast and usually gives two cuts a year; its stems average about 18 inches, and it is the common type. Named kinds include ‘Kenland’, ‘Pennscott’ and ‘Chesapeake’.
  • Mammoth red clover (single-cut) flowers two to three weeks later, grows coarser and taller — 24–30 inches, with more branches per stem — and recovers too slowly for more than one crop a year; it is often sown with timothy, because the two mature together. Named kinds include ‘Altaswede’, ‘Norlac’ and ‘Craig’.
  • The seed of the two types looks identical — which type you have is only known once it has grown.

Sources

  • Tice et al. (2003) — ICE trial, 252 women: neither red clover product clinically better than placebo
  • University of Maine Cooperative Extension, Bulletin #2259 — seeding rates, frost-seeding and harvest timing
  • Kew, Plants of the World Online — native range in Europe, Asia and north-west Africa
  • NCCIH — red clover evidence summary: no conclusive benefit for any condition; hot-flush studies inconsistent
  • Lethaby et al. (2013) — Cochrane review of phytoestrogens for menopausal symptoms: no significant benefit of red clover extract over placebo
  • USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Plant Fact Sheet — Red Clover: origin, medium and mammoth types and named cultivars
  • Plants For A Future — Trifolium pratense: yellow dye from the flowers (also recorded in the IUCN Red List species account)
  • Memorial Sloan Kettering, About Herbs — traditional uses, hormone-sensitive cancer and anticoagulant cautions
  • USDA Agricultural Research Service — red clover as a cover crop: nitrogen contribution and pollinator value

Rose

Rosa species

CulinaryOrnamental

Immune HealthMovement and Support

FreshCookedDried

The rose is two plants wearing one name. One is the garden rose, in tens of thousands of named varieties. The other is its wild ancestor, the dog rose (Rosa canina), a scrambling hedgerow shrub whose pale flowers are followed in autumn by the hip: a small red fruit very rich in vitamin C. Both give food: the petals you can cook with, the water and oil drawn from them, and the hips that are the rose's true food.

Terpenes in this plant:

Cultivars

  • There are no "varieties" here in the pineapple sense — there are whole classes of rose, built over centuries, and more than 40,000 named garden roses registered within them. The classes are the honest way to meet them. With tens of thousands of look-alike garden roses, no unlabelled photo can honestly carry a variety name.
  • Species roses — the wild ones, unchanged by breeders: single flowers of five petals, one flush in early summer, and the best hips of all. The dog rose (Rosa canina) is the hip-picker's species, and the rugosa rose (Rosa rugosa), a tough, salt-proof seaside shrub from north-east Asia, makes the biggest, fleshiest hips of any rose — the gourmet's hip.
  • Gallica roses — among the oldest garden roses in Europe, deep pink to purple, richly scented, flowering once. 'Officinalis', the Apothecary's Rose of Provins, is this class's famous name.
  • Damask roses — the roses of the attar stills, named for Damascus: intensely fragrant, pale pink, the source of nearly all the world's rose oil and much of its rose water.
  • Centifolia roses — the "cabbage roses" of Dutch flower paintings, a hundred petals packed into a globe; the perfume rose of Grasse in France, where it is called Rose de Mai, the May rose.
  • Alba roses — tall, graceful, white and blush-pink, scented, hardy, and among the toughest of the old roses.
  • China and tea roses — the repeat-flowerers from China that changed everything: more delicate, flowering again and again, with a scent likened to tea. Crossed with the European roses they produced the hybrid perpetuals and then the moderns.
  • Hybrid tea roses — the modern era opens in 1867 with 'La France', bred in Lyon by Jean-Baptiste André Guillot and generally counted the first hybrid tea, and so the first modern rose: long buds, one flower to a stem, repeat flowering — the florist's rose, and the largest class of all. 'Peace', released at the end of the Second World War, became the most famous rose of the twentieth century.
  • Floribunda roses — hybrid teas crossed back toward cluster-flowering kinds: smaller flowers carried in sprays, bushier plants, bred for a bed of colour rather than one perfect bloom.
  • Modern shrub and English roses — the late twentieth century bent back toward the old roses: breeders such as David Austin crossed modern repeat-flowering stock with the old gallicas and damasks to recover their scent and flower shape, and landscape breeders produced tough, disease-resistant shrubs that ask little care.
Bulgaria — the Rose Valley around Kazanlak, between two mountain ranges, is the world's rose-oil heartland: fields of damask roses picked at dawn in May and June, distilled the same day, and a rose festival every year. Bulgaria's oil sets the world standard.
Turkey — the lakes town of Isparta grows damask roses on a huge scale and rivals Bulgaria in oil, while rose water — gül suyu — scents the national sweet, lokum, known in English as Turkish delight.
Iran — rose water is a kitchen staple, stirred into sweets, sherbets and the saffron rice pudding sholeh zard; the town of Kashan holds a rose water festival each spring as the stills fire up.
Morocco — at Kelaat M'Gouna, in the Dadès valley, damask roses are grown in hedges around the fields and celebrated with a festival of roses; the harvest goes to water, oil and dried buds.
India — the rose flavours gulab jamun, the milk dumplings soaked in rose syrup; the city of Kannauj has distilled rose attar into sandalwood oil for centuries, in the Mughal tradition — legend says the attar was discovered in the emperor's household, at the bath of the empress Nur Jahan, and the story is told as legend.
Sweden — nyponsoppa, rose hip soup: a sweet, deep-orange soup of dried hips, eaten as a dessert and given to children — the hip as an ordinary, beloved food, not a remedy.
Poland and Hungary — rose hip jam fills pączki, the filled doughnuts of Polish bakeries, and hips are gathered for tea and preserves across central Europe; in Hungary the jam is a pantry staple.
England — the hedgerow itself: dog rose in every lane, hips for the wartime syrup described above, and petals once made into preserves in country kitchens.
  • Roses are old beyond gardens. Fossil roses tens of millions of years old have been found in North America, and the wild species — botanists count somewhere between about 140 and 300, because wild roses cross with each other so freely that even the experts argue — grow all across the northern half of the world: Europe, Asia and North America. Every garden rose ever bred descends from a handful of these wild species.
  • The garden story has two roots. In Europe and western Asia, growers worked with their own roses — the gallica, the damask, the alba, the centifolia — big, fragrant, and flowering once, gloriously, in early summer. In China, gardeners had spent centuries breeding roses that flower again and again through the season. When China roses and tea roses reached Europe around 1800, breeders crossed the two worlds together: European scent and hardiness, Chinese repeat flowering. Almost every rose in a garden today carries both inheritances.
  • Persia made the rose a culture. Rose water — golab — flavoured sweets, drinks and rice dishes, cooled the skin, and scented mosques and homes; the rose became the central flower of Persian poetry, the beloved that the nightingale sings to. Tradition credits the physicians of the medieval Islamic world with perfecting the steam distillation of rose water, and the damask rose itself carries a city's name: Damascus. Under the Ottomans the craft spread through Turkey and the Balkans, where it lives on as an industry — see Around the World.
  • Attar of roses — also called rose otto — is the essential oil distilled from damask rose petals, and it takes roughly three and a half tons of fresh petals, well over a million flowers, to make a single kilogram of it. That is why real rose oil has always cost more than gold by weight, and why the water left from the still — rose water — became the everyday form in which most people met the rose's scent.
  • France kept the medicine rose. At Provins, south-east of Paris, the apothecaries grew Rosa gallica 'Officinalis' — the Apothecary's Rose — dried its petals, and sold them across Europe; the town's name survives in the rose's other name, the Rose of Provins. The same deep red gallica is the rose heraldry remembers: the Red Rose of Lancaster is thought to be this very flower.
  • The dog rose carries its name from a belief, not a compliment. The ancients held that its root could cure the bite of a mad dog — rabies — and the Greek name for it, kynorrhodon, "dog rose," passed into Latin and stuck. The cure was never real; the name is two thousand years old and counting. What the dog rose genuinely gave was its hips, gathered across northern Europe for centuries as a winter food and a folk remedy against colds and weakness — a use that turned out to rest on something real, as Health Benefits explains.
  • England fought, or says it fought, under this flower. The white rose was truly the badge of the House of York. The matching red rose of Lancaster, though, was mostly created after the wars ended: Henry VII, who took the crown in 1485 and married Elizabeth of York, joined the two into the Tudor rose — white petals inside red — as a picture of peace restored, and had it painted everywhere. Shakespeare invented the famous scene of the rivals plucking red and white roses in a garden, and Sir Walter Scott's novels gave the wars their name, the Wars of the Roses, three centuries after the fact. The story everyone knows is largely a Tudor invention that worked — told here as exactly that.
  • And everywhere, the rose became the flower of love. Sappho is said to have called it the queen of flowers twenty-six centuries ago; Roman feasts were strewn with petals and Roman brides wore rose garlands; in Persia and India the rose spoke of longing in poem after poem. No other flower carries the meaning in so many languages at once: to give a red rose is understood from London to Lahore.
  • The hips' finest hour came in 1941. Britain was at war, ships carrying oranges were being sunk, and the Ministry of Food needed a home-grown source of vitamin C for the nation's children. It organised a national rose hip campaign: schools, Women's Institutes, Guides and Scouts picked the hedgerows in autumn — paid threepence a pound — and gathered some 200 tons of hips in the first campaign, to be made into rose hip syrup and sold cheaply in chemists' shops. The hedgerow harvest ran through the war, and a generation of British children grew up on the syrup's sharp, fruity taste.
  • Rose oil — attar, distilled from damask petals — is breathed in for worry and low mood, and rubbed, diluted, on the skin: pooled trials found it eased anxiety and stress in the moment, and helped sleep. Human · small
  • The hip is the rose's nutritional heart, and its numbers are remarkable. Wild rose hips, per 100 g (USDA figures): 162 kcal, carbohydrate 38.2 g, fibre 24.1 g — a quarter of the fruit is fibre — protein 1.6 g, and vitamin C at 426 mg, more than four times the daily value and about eight times what an orange gives, weight for weight. There is also vitamin A (217 µg, about a quarter of the daily value), vitamin E (5.8 mg) and calcium (169 mg). Two honest cautions belong with the numbers: they are for wild hips, and nobody eats 100 g of raw hips at a sitting. Hips are met as tea, syrup, soup and jam — and heat and drying cost some of the vitamin C, so a cup of hip tea is a smaller thing than the raw figure suggests. It is still one of the richest vitamin C foods in the temperate world.
  • Joint pain — the one claim with human trials, stated at its strength. A standardised powder of dog rose hips and seeds, 5 g a day, has been tested against dummy capsules in people with osteoarthritis. A review that pooled the three trials (Christensen et al., 2008; 287 patients, about three months each) found a small-to-moderate reduction in pain — patients on the powder were about twice as likely to feel a real improvement, and used less ordinary pain medicine. The fencing matters: all three trials were paid for by the powder's manufacturer, the trials were short, and the reviewers themselves said the result needs confirming by independent, larger, longer trials. Germany's Commission E, reviewing the evidence in 1990, had found it insufficient and gave rose hip a negative monograph. The fair summary: promising, not proven — and the evidence belongs to that measured powder, not to a mug of hip tea. Human trials
  • What may be doing the work: the hips carry a fat-like compound named GOPO, which in laboratory tests calms some of the chemical signals of inflammation. That is laboratory evidence — a reason the trials were worth running, not a promise about any product. Lab studies
  • Petals and rose water, honestly: rose petals are food — they flavour jam, Turkish delight, drinks and desserts — and rose water is a gentle, pleasant splash for skin and a flavouring in the kitchen. But there are no good clinical trials showing that rose water or petals heal skin, lift mood, or treat anything. Their value is flavour, scent and pleasure, which is value enough. Traditional use
  • Rose hip seed oil — the oil pressed from the seeds inside the hips, often sold as rosa mosqueta — is widely marketed for scars and ageing skin. The studies behind it are few and small, and they do not prove the claims. It is a light, pleasant skin oil; it is not a demonstrated treatment. Human · small
  • Garden roses are shrubs, from miniatures knee-high to climbers covering a house wall; most are sold grafted — a named variety joined onto a tough wild rootstock, usually dog rose — though own-root plants are common for species and shrub roses. Wild species like the dog rose are simply themselves: a scrambling shrub 1–5 m tall that will climb into a hedge or a small tree if it is allowed.
  • Sun and soil: roses flower best on at least six hours of direct sun a day, and morning sun matters — it dries the dew off the leaves, and dry leaves resist the fungal diseases that are the rose's main trouble. They want fertile, well-drained soil that holds moisture without staying wet, around neutral to mildly acid (pH about 6.0–6.5). Sitting in winter wet rots them; a raised bed is the fix on heavy clay.
  • Planting: bare-root roses go in while dormant, in late winter or early spring, soaked first and set with the graft union at about soil level; container roses can go in almost any time the ground is workable, watered well.
  • Pruning is the rose's one real demand, and the rule splits by class. Repeat-flowering roses — hybrid teas, floribundas, modern shrubs — are pruned in late winter or early spring, before growth starts: out come dead, weak and crossing stems, and the rest is cut back to strong outward-facing buds. Once-flowering old roses are pruned after they flower, since they bloom on last year's wood.
  • Flowers or hips — the gardener chooses. Snipping off faded flowers (deadheading) pushes a repeat-flowerer into making more flowers instead of fruit. If you want hips, stop deadheading and let the flowers stand: the hips ripen in September and October, and pickers traditionally wait until after the first frosts, when the fruit softens and sweetens a little. Leave some for the birds either way — hips are winter food for them.
  • Trouble, honestly: black spot, a fungal leaf disease, is the common one in wet summers; open planting, air around the bush, watering at the base rather than over the leaves, and clearing up fallen leaves all hold it down better than any spray. Choosing disease-resistant modern shrubs and the tough species roses avoids most of it.
  • For hips and for wildlife, plant the species: a dog rose in a hedge or a rugosa by a path will feed bees in June, birds in winter, and a picker in autumn, and asks almost nothing in return.

Propagation

Take softwood cuttings from this year's shoots in early to mid spring, or hardwood cuttings in mid autumn to late winter. New plants take about a year to move to the garden and two to three years to flower. Cuttings from a grafted rose may not grow the same as the parent plant.

Safety

  • Hips are a traditional food and safe as food. One rule is absolute, though: the seeds inside the hip are wrapped in fine, stiff hairs that irritate the mouth, throat and gut — every traditional recipe, wartime ones included, strains them out, and anything you make from hips must be strained the same way. Eat petals only from roses grown without sprays — florist roses are treated with chemicals and are not food. The hip powder in the trials caused only mild stomach upset in a few people, but concentrated hip products have not been safety-tested in pregnancy, so food amounts are the sensible line there.
  • Essential oils are concentrates, many times stronger than the plant itself. Always dilute in a carrier oil before putting one on skin, and never swallow an essential oil.

Sources

  • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: rose hips, wild — the nutrition figures
  • Christensen et al. (2008) — rose hip powder and osteoarthritis pain: a meta-analysis of the three randomised controlled trials
  • Winther et al. (2005) — a powder of rose hip seeds and shells in osteoarthritis of the hip and knee: a randomised controlled trial
  • Chrubasik et al. (2008) — Rosa canina effect and efficacy profiles: a systematic review — traditional uses, the Commission E verdict, and the trial record
  • Encyclopaedia Britannica — Attar of roses — the oil, the roses it comes from, and the yield of petals behind it
  • Proceedings of the Nutrition Society (1977) — the promotion of nutrition and food by the Ministry of Food, 1940–54 — rose hip syrup among Britain's home-produced vitamin C foods
  • Penn (2011) — Winter King: Henry VII and the Dawn of Tudor England — the Tudor rose as Henry VII's invention
  • American Rose Society (2023) — rose classifications — species, old garden roses and modern roses, and the registry of named roses
  • University of Georgia Extension (2023) — Basic Rose Culture — sun, soil, pH, pruning and deadheading
