Roselle

Hibiscus sabdariffa

MedicinalCulinary

Heart Health

Dried

This is Jamaican sorrel — the plant behind the ruby-red Christmas drink. It is a hibiscus, and no relation at all to wood sorrel or to garden sorrel: three different plants that share a name because they share a tart taste. The part used is the fleshy red calyx — the cup that swells around the seed pod after the flower falls.

  • Roselle comes from West Africa. There, its sour red calyces and its leaves have long been food and drink.
  • Trade carried it across the Atlantic a few centuries ago. In the Caribbean it found its famous role: sorrel, the spiced red Christmas drink, brewed with ginger and cloves.
  • In Mexico the same drink is agua de jamaica — Jamaica water — named for the island it came by.
  • In Sudan and Egypt it is karkade. It is served hot or cold, at home and at celebrations. Sudan is still one of its biggest growers.
  • Wherever it landed, it kept the same use — a sour, cooling drink for hot climates — and picked up a local name each time.

Craft

  • The stems yield a jute-like fibre — rosella hemp — spun and woven for rope, twine, cord and sackcloth in the tropics: a second crop from a plant grown for its calyces. There is even a whole fibre form of the plant, variety altissima, grown for the stems alone, with calyces too poor to eat. The petals give a yellow dye as well.
  • Dried and brewed, it makes the cooling drinks known across the tropics as sorrel in the Caribbean, bissap in Senegal, karkadé in Egypt and Sudan, zobo in Nigeria and agua de Jamaica in Mexico. The calyces are rich in vitamin C and in the red anthocyanin pigments that give the drink its colour.
  • Blood pressure is its most studied use. Pooled analyses of the trials find that hibiscus tea and extracts lower blood pressure modestly — on average around seven points off the top reading — with the clearest effects in people whose pressure was raised to begin with. The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health stresses that the evidence is limited and the effects small beside prescribed medicines. Roselle is not a treatment for high blood pressure, and it must never be used in place of prescribed medication.
  • It has also been studied for cholesterol and blood sugar, with weaker and mixed results: a pooled review of the cholesterol trials found no significant effect, and the blood-sugar findings are inconsistent. Neither effect is established.
  • The leaves are eaten as a sour green, including in Burmese cooking (chin baung).
  • Caution: avoid roselle in pregnancy. It has never been properly tested in pregnant women, and animal studies raise concerns that strong extracts can affect the womb and the development of offspring. Its safety while breastfeeding is likewise unknown.
  • Caution: roselle can add to the effect of blood-pressure medicines, so pressure may fall too far — talk to a clinician first if you take them. It can sharply reduce how much of the antimalarial medicine chloroquine the body absorbs, and it can change how the body handles some other medicines, including the cholesterol medicine simvastatin. Take care alongside diabetes medicines, as it may lower blood sugar a little, and note that very large doses of strong extracts have raised liver enzymes in animal studies.
  • When to plant: Sow after all frost has passed — or start indoors 6–8 weeks earlier where summers are short
  • Sun: Full sun
  • Soil: Good, well-drained soil
  • Environment: A true tropical annual: it needs warmth and a long season, grows fast to two metres or more, and is killed by the first frost
  • Planter or ground: Ground best; a very large pot where summers are hot
  • Spacing and depth: 60–90 cm apart
  • Water: Likes water while it is growing fast
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Pick the fleshy red calyces by hand as they swell around the seed pods, in late summer and autumn

Garden notes

  • A plant of West Africa originally, carried across the tropics centuries ago and now grown wherever summers are long and hot — Sudan, Nigeria, Mexico, Egypt, Thailand and China are among the biggest producers.
  • A true tropical annual: sown after all frost has passed, it needs full sun, warmth and a long season, grows fast to two metres or more in good, well-drained soil, and is killed by the first frost.
  • The harvest is gathered by hand — the fleshy red calyces are picked as they swell around the seed pods. The stems have a second use, yielding a jute-like fibre.
  • The large flowers each open for a single day and are visited by bees and other pollinating insects through the flowering season.

Propagation

Sow seed in early spring in a warm place, and plant out after the last frost, once the soil is warm. Cuttings of half-ripe wood in July or August also root. Frost kills it, so do not plant out too soon.

Sources

  • NCCIH — roselle (hibiscus) and blood pressure: evidence limited, effects small, not a substitute for prescribed treatment
  • Ellis et al. (2022) — meta-analysis of hibiscus and blood pressure: systolic about 7 mmHg lower
  • Serban et al. (2015) — pooled blood-pressure reductions with hibiscus
  • McKay et al. (2010) — hibiscus tea trial in adults with pre- or mild hypertension
  • Cochrane review of roselle for hypertension (2021) — evidence judged insufficient under strict criteria
  • Aziz et al. (2013) — meta-analysis: no significant effect of hibiscus on blood lipids
  • Memorial Sloan Kettering, About Herbs — hibiscus interactions with blood-pressure medicines, simvastatin and chloroquine
  • Kew, Plants of the World Online — name and native range (West Africa)

Rosemary

Salvia rosmarinus

CulinaryMedicinal

Digestive HealthMental Health

FreshDried

Rosemary is a woody, evergreen shrub from the dry coasts of the Mediterranean, all narrow needle-like leaves and small blue flowers, with a strong scent of pine and resin. It belongs to the mint family, Lamiaceae — kin to Sage, Thyme, Lavender and Basil in this library.

Terpenes in this plant: · · ·

Rosemary is one of the three plants in Crown Recovery Oil.

Cultivars

  • All rosemary is the one species, and every variety is edible. What differs is shape, flower colour, flavour — and, above all, how much cold the plant can stand. Named varieties are grown from cuttings, because seedlings vary and a named type does not come true from seed.
  • 'Tuscan Blue' — the classic cooking rosemary of warm climates: upright, 4–6 ft, with broad leaves, deep blue flowers and a warm, clean flavour low in harshness. It is tender — damaged when temperatures fall below about 20 °F (−7 °C) — so it belongs to zones 8 and up.
  • 'Spice Islands' — an upright plant of 4–5 ft, prized by cooks for an exceptionally strong flavour; the one to hunt down if the herb is for the kitchen first. Warm climates, zones 8 and up.
  • 'Arp' — the hardy one. Found growing near Arp, Texas, in 1972, where it had survived winters that killed the rosemary around it, it is the most cold-hardy variety in common use, coming through about −10 °F (−23 °C) in well-drained ground — zone 6, where ordinary rosemary dies. Grey-green leaves and a slightly sharper, more camphor-like flavour.
  • 'Hill Hardy' ('Madelene Hill') — another Texas selection, named for the herb grower Madelene Hill. Hardiness close to 'Arp', a smaller plant at 3–4 ft, and a flavour cooks rate among the best of the hardy types.
  • 'Miss Jessopp's Upright' — a narrow, columnar plant, 4–6 ft tall but only about 2 ft wide: the rosemary for a tight space, a hedge line or a formal row.
  • 'Prostratus' — the trailing type: 1–2 ft tall, spreading 4–8 ft, made to spill over walls and cover sunny banks. Edible like the rest, with a milder flavour; grown mostly for the ground it covers.
Italy — rosmarino is everywhere: scattered on focaccia with salt and olive oil, tucked under the skin of roast chicken, cooked with roast potatoes, white beans and lamb. Whole woody stems are also stripped and used as skewers on the grill, flavouring the meat from inside.
Greece — rosemary goes over roast lamb and potatoes with lemon and olive oil, and onto grilled meats — the same pairing of herb, fire and fat found all around its home sea.
France — one of the herbs of Provence, dried into herbes de Provence blends for grilling and roasting; and the country that made Hungary water famous, when the Montpellier distillers' version became the one to buy.
Spain — romero seasons roast meats and potatoes, and in the countryside its flowering branches have long been gathered for bees — rosemary honey is a Spanish speciality, pale and delicately scented.
Britain — the partner of roast lamb above all, and of roast potatoes; a few sprigs in the roasting tin is the whole recipe in many kitchens.
The United States — rosemary bread and focaccia in every bakery, rosemary salt on roasts and fries, and sprigs in lemonade and cocktails — the herb travelled from the roast to the glass.
  • Rosemary is native to the dry, rocky country around the Mediterranean Sea, where it grows wild on sunny slopes and cliffs near the coast. Its old Latin name tells the story: ros marinus, "dew of the sea" — a plant of the shore, said to be able to live on sea mist and dew alone.
  • The Greeks and Romans knew it well. Greek students were said to twine rosemary in their hair while studying for examinations, in the hope it would sharpen their memory — the first chapter of a reputation that has never left the plant. It was burned as incense, carried at ceremonies, and laid with the dead. The physician Dioscorides included it in De Materia Medica, his great book of medicines of the first century, as a warming herb — those uses are history; what the studies actually support is in Health Benefits.
  • Out of that memory reputation grew its meaning. For centuries in Europe rosemary stood for remembrance, and it appeared at the two occasions where remembrance matters most: weddings, where brides wore it as a sign of fidelity and of the life they were leaving, and funerals, where mourners carried sprigs and threw them into the grave so the dead would not be forgotten.
  • Shakespeare wrote the meaning down, and his line is still the one everybody quotes. In Hamlet (about 1600), Ophelia, handing out flowers, says: "There's rosemary, that's for remembrance. Pray you, love, remember." He was recording what everyone already understood, not inventing it — in Romeo and Juliet he has the Friar tell mourners to "stick your rosemary on this fair corse," the funeral custom again.
  • Rosemary also stands behind one of Europe's first perfumes. By legend, in the late 1300s a rosemary spirit — rosemary distilled in alcohol — was made for Queen Elizabeth of Hungary, and "Hungary water" was sold across Europe for centuries afterwards, as a perfume and as a cure-all for everything from headaches to gout. The story is a legend, written down long after the queen's time, but the water was real, and rosemary was always its heart.
  • The remembrance meaning is still alive. Rosemary grows wild on the Gallipoli peninsula in Turkey, where Australian and New Zealand soldiers fought in the First World War, and a sprig of rosemary is worn in Australia and New Zealand on Anzac Day, 25 April, in memory of the fallen.
  • The name change is recent and worth explaining plainly. Linnaeus named the plant Rosmarinus officinalis in 1753. In 2017, DNA studies showed rosemary sits inside the sage genus, Salvia, so botanists moved it (Drew et al. 2017). It could not take the name Salvia officinalis — that name already belongs to Sage — so it took the older replacement name Salvia rosmarinus. Gardeners may go on saying Rosmarinus for years; the plant does not mind.
  • Rosemary oil, distilled from the leaves, is breathed in for memory and clear thinking — the old student habit, now tested in small trials. Human · small
  • The leaf, fresh, per 100 g: 131 kcal, carbohydrate 20.7 g, fibre 14.1 g, protein 3.31 g, calcium 317 mg, iron 6.65 mg, potassium 668 mg, vitamin C 21.8 mg, folate 109 µg. Read those numbers with the serving in mind: a tablespoon of fresh rosemary is under 2 g, and nobody eats 100 g of it. Rosemary is a flavouring used by the sprig and the teaspoon; the figures show a leaf that is rich for its size, not a food to eat by the handful for its minerals.
  • The memory claim is the famous one, and it has been tested — in small studies, with mixed results, and the honest picture is narrower than the headlines. Three findings, each at its real strength:
  • Smelled: In 2003, Moss and colleagues tested 144 adults in rooms scented with rosemary oil, lavender oil, or nothing. The rosemary group scored better on the overall quality of their memory — and worse on the speed of it, in the same study. In 2012, Moss and Oliver sat 20 volunteers in a rosemary-scented cubicle and measured 1,8-cineole — one of rosemary's main scent compounds — in their blood: the more they had absorbed, the better their scores for speed and accuracy. That is a link across 20 people with no comparison group, not proof the scent caused the scores.
  • Eaten: Pengelly et al. (2012) ran the strongest test — a placebo-controlled trial in 28 older adults, average age 75, given dried rosemary leaf powder. The smallest dose, 750 mg (about a culinary amount, a scant half-teaspoon of dried leaf), improved the speed of memory. The largest dose, 6,000 mg, made speed of memory significantly worse. With rosemary, the studies say the dose matters, and more is not better.
  • Drunk: A 2018 study of 80 adults drinking a rosemary water found a few small improvements on some thinking tasks. Small, and on its own.
  • What this adds up to: a handful of small, short studies in healthy adults, pointing in a promising direction and sometimes in two directions at once. Nothing in them shows that rosemary treats memory loss or dementia. The kitchen sprig is food; the scent is a pleasure; the medicine is not proven. Human · small
  • One use does carry an official standing, of the traditional kind. The European Medicines Agency's herbal monograph accepts rosemary leaf as a traditional herbal medicine — a status that rests on long-standing use, not on clinical trials — for indigestion and mild cramps of the gut, taken as a tea, and added to bath water for minor muscle and joint pain and minor circulation trouble. And that is exactly what it is: tradition, recognised, and labelled as tradition. Traditional use
  • The leaf also works quietly in the modern food industry. An extract of rosemary, rich in a compound called carnosic acid, is an approved antioxidant food additive in the European Union (listed as E392): it slows the fats in oils, meats and snacks from going rancid, and food makers use it in place of synthetic preservatives. If a label says "antioxidant: rosemary extract," that is this leaf at work.
  • An evergreen, woody shrub. Upright types stand 2–6 ft tall; the trailing types stay low and spread wide. It is a perennial in USDA zones 8–10. The hardy varieties, 'Arp' and 'Madelene Hill', stretch that to zone 7 and, in a sheltered spot with sharp drainage, into zone 6. Everywhere colder, grow it in a pot and bring it under cover for winter.
  • Sun and soil decide everything. Give it full sun — at least six hours — and light, sandy or gravelly soil that drains fast. It thrives in poor, rocky ground where richer plants sulk, tolerates drought once its roots are down, and even stands salt spray near the sea. What kills rosemary is not cold alone but wet: roots sitting in wet soil, above all in winter, rot, and the plant dies from the ground up. In heavy soil, plant it in a raised bed or a pot.
  • Grow it from cuttings, not seed. Seed is slow and patchy to sprout, and a named variety will not come true from it. Take tip cuttings about 3–4 inches long in spring, strip the lower leaves, and set them in a gritty, free-draining mix kept lightly moist; roots form in about four to eight weeks. Set young plants out after the last frost, about 2 ft apart.
  • Water young plants until they settle, then water sparingly — this is a plant that prefers to be thirsty rather than wet. Feed little or not at all; lean soil keeps the flavour strong.
  • Prune lightly after flowering to keep the bush dense, and take sprigs for the kitchen as you need them, never stripping more than about a third of the plant at once. Do not cut hard back into old, bare wood: rosemary often refuses to sprout again from it, and a hard-pruned old bush may simply die.
  • The flowers are part of the plant's use. Small blue flowers — some varieties pink or white — open mainly from late winter into spring and on into summer, and bees work them eagerly. The flowers are edible, milder than the leaves: scatter them over salads, drinks and desserts, or stir them into sugar.
  • In a pot: choose a clay pot with drainage holes and a gritty mix, and water only when the soil has dried. Indoors over winter it wants the sunniest, coolest bright spot you have and very little water — indoor winters are honestly hard on rosemary, and many gardeners treat a potted plant as one to enjoy, replace, and start again from cuttings taken in summer.

Propagation

Take softwood cuttings from new growth in late spring or summer, or semi-ripe cuttings in summer. Low stems can also be pegged down to root in spring or autumn. Seed-grown plants do not come true for named varieties, and seed takes years to give a usable plant — cuttings keep the parent plant's traits.

Safety

  • As a seasoning, rosemary is food and safe. The medicines are another matter — the European monograph says rosemary leaf medicines are not for children under 12 and should not be used in pregnancy or while breastfeeding. The essential oil is a concentrate, many times stronger than the leaf: it is not a food, and it should not be swallowed. Amounts far beyond cooking can upset the stomach. Nobody needs more rosemary than the recipe asks for — the memory studies above say the same.

Sources

  • Moss et al. (2003) — rosemary and lavender aromas and cognition in 144 adults: memory quality up, memory speed down
  • Moss & Oliver (2012) — blood levels of 1,8-cineole and thinking performance after rosemary aroma, in 20 volunteers
  • Pengelly et al. (2012) — dried rosemary leaf powder and memory in older adults: the low dose helped, the high dose harmed
  • Moss et al. (2018) — drinking rosemary water and thinking performance: small effects in 80 adults
  • European Medicines Agency (2024) — EU herbal monograph on rosemary leaf: the recognised traditional uses, and who should not use the medicines
  • North Carolina State Extension — Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox: Salvia rosmarinus — zones, growing and propagation

Sage

Salvia officinalis

CulinaryMedicinal

Blood Sugar HealthDigestive HealthHormone HealthMental Health

FreshDried

A low, evergreen subshrub — woody at the base, soft and leafy above — in the mint family, Lamiaceae, alongside lavender, peppermint, lemon balm and thyme. Sage is native to the dry, rocky ground around the northern Mediterranean, and it has been carried into gardens everywhere since. It is a kitchen herb first: the grey-green, wrinkled leaves, strongly scented and slightly bitter, flavour stuffings, sausages, beans and brown butter across Europe, and the leaf is the part that is used.

The other parts play small roles. The violet-blue flower spikes that rise in early summer are edible and go into salads as a garnish, but no medicine is made from them. The seed is occasionally eaten in a few regional dishes and is not a remedy. The root is not used at all. What the leaf carries is a strong essential oil, and one compound in that oil matters for safety: thujone, which in quantity is toxic to the nervous system. The amounts in a seasoning of leaves are small; the amounts in the concentrated oil are not, and the two should never be confused.

Terpenes in this plant: ·

  • The name is the reputation. Salvia comes from the Latin salvere — to be well, to be saved. Officinalis marks a plant kept in the officina, the apothecary's storeroom. This was an official medicine, not a wayside herb.
  • Greek and Roman doctors used it widely. Theophrastus described sages in the fourth century BCE. Dioscorides put sage in his herbal. The Romans are said to have gathered it with ceremony, and they called it herba sacra — the sacred herb.
  • Around the year 800, Charlemagne's Capitulare de villis named sage. That was the ordinance — the official list — of what every imperial estate had to grow. Monastery physic gardens — gardens of healing plants — then carried it across Europe.
  • The medieval medical school at Salerno gave it the most quoted line in herbal history, in its Regimen of Health: "Cur moriatur homo cui salvia crescit in horto?" — "Why should a man die who has sage growing in his garden?" An old English saying runs the same way: "He who would live for aye must eat sage in May." Both record a reputation for keeping people alive — not a finding.
  • Sage was one of the herbs steeped in the Four Thieves vinegar. Legend says that blend protected a band of thieves who robbed plague houses. The story is legend. The herb's place in it shows how deep the trust in sage ran.
  • In the kitchen, it settled into the cooking of several countries. In Italy it goes with veal in saltimbocca. It is crisped in brown butter over pasta and pumpkin. In Britain it is minced with onion into the stuffing for roast pork and poultry. The grey-green of its leaves also gave the English language a colour: sage.
  • Sage oil, distilled from the leaf, is breathed in for a clear head and a lifted mood. Traditional use

Traditional medicine

  • For digestion and the mouth and throat, European regulators accept sage leaf at traditional-use strength: a tea for mild indigestion, heartburn and bloating, and a gargle for inflammation of the mouth and throat. Traditional use means the standing rests on long use rather than on trials.

Craft

  • The leaves are a dye plant. With different mordants — the salts that fix a dye to cloth — sage gives yellow-buff, yellow and greeny-grey shades. A sage rinse was also used to darken greying hair.
  • For memory and thinking, the human evidence is real but small, and it belongs to extracts, not to the kitchen herb. In one trial, single doses of a sage extract improved memory and attention scores in 20 healthy volunteers over 65, with a middle dose (333 mg) working best. In another, 42 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease took a sage tincture for 16 weeks and scored better on cognitive tests than those on placebo. Each is a single small trial, none has been repeated at scale, and nothing here shows that sage prevents or treats dementia.
  • For menopausal hot flushes, sage stands on a long tradition of use against sweating, which European regulators recognise at traditional-use strength. The one dedicated trial gave a fresh sage preparation to 71 menopausal women for eight weeks and watched the combined score for the number and intensity of flushes fall by half at four weeks and by about two-thirds at eight. There was no placebo group, so how much of that fall was the sage cannot be separated from the large improvement hot-flush trials routinely show on dummy treatment. A later, smaller placebo-controlled trial also favoured sage, and a pooled analysis of the few trials found flushes came less often on sage without a clear change in their severity. Promising and preliminary — not proven.
  • For blood sugar, one research group in Iran has run small trials of sage leaf extract in people with type 2 diabetes: in the largest, 80 people took 500 mg of extract three times a day for three months and finished with lower fasting glucose and lower HbA1c — a measure of average blood sugar — than the placebo group. The reported effects were unusually large for a herb, the trials all come from that one group, and no independent team has repeated them. Sage is not a diabetes treatment, and the finding stands at exactly that strength.
  • Caution — the oil and thujone: sage essential oil is a concentrate rich in thujone, and thujone in quantity attacks the nervous system. Sage oil swallowed in amounts corresponding to more than about 15 g of leaf has caused a racing heart, vertigo and convulsions. European regulators cap the thujone in sage medicines at under 6 mg a day. The oil is not a food and is never a substitute for the leaf.
  • Caution — pregnancy and breastfeeding: medicinal amounts of sage are not recommended in pregnancy or while breastfeeding, because safety has not been established and thujone is the standing concern. The amounts used in cooking are not the issue; concentrated teas, extracts and the oil are.
  • Caution — medicines: because sage extract can lower blood sugar, it can add to the effect of diabetes medicines and push blood sugar too low. And because thujone can provoke seizures, anyone with epilepsy, or taking medicines for seizures, should keep away from medicinal sage preparations.
  • When to plant: Sow seed in spring — it is slow to sprout — or take cuttings in summer, which root readily; plant out once growing well
  • Sun: Full sun
  • Soil: Poor to middling soil with sharp drainage — rich, wet ground makes it soft and short-lived
  • Environment: A plant of dry, stony Mediterranean hillsides; drought does it no harm once the roots are down, but wet winter soil rots the roots — a raised bed or a gravelly corner suits it best
  • Planter or ground: Both — a pot of gritty mix suits it very well
  • Spacing and depth: 45–60 cm apart
  • Water: Dry once settled
  • Companion plants: Cabbage-family plants, carrots and rosemary are its classic neighbours
  • When to pick: Pick the leaves from spring into autumn, at their strongest just before the flowers open; renew plants every four or five years, as they grow woody

Garden notes

  • A plant of dry, stony Mediterranean hillsides: it wants full sun, sharp drainage, and poor to middling soil. Rich, wet ground makes it soft and short-lived.
  • Evergreen and woody-based, it holds its grey leaves through winter in mild districts and sends up violet-blue flower spikes in early summer that bees work heavily.
  • Drought, once the roots are down, does it no harm. The usual way to kill sage is wet winter soil, which rots the roots — a raised bed or a gravelly corner suits it best.
  • Plants tire after four or five years, growing woody and sparse; cuttings root readily in summer and renew the plant exactly.
  • Leaves are picked from spring into autumn and are at their strongest just before the flowers open.

Propagation

Take softwood cuttings from new growth in late spring or early summer. Low stems can also be pegged down to root in spring or autumn. Seed can be sown in spring, but seed-grown plants do not come true for named varieties, so use cuttings to keep the plant you have.

Sources

  • European Medicines Agency (2016) — European Union herbal monograph on Salvia officinalis L., folium: traditional uses, thujone limits and pregnancy warning

  • Scholey et al. (2008) — sage extract and memory and attention in healthy older volunteers, Psychopharmacology
  • Bommer et al. (2011) — fresh sage preparation for menopausal hot flushes, open multicentre trial, Advances in Therapy
  • Kianbakht & Dabaghian (2013) — sage leaf extract and blood sugar in type 2 diabetes, Complementary Therapies in Medicine
  • Lopresti (2017) — review of the human trials of sage for cognition, Drugs in R&D

Self-Heal

Prunella vulgaris

Medicinal

Skin Health

Dried

One of the great traditional wound herbs — its old name is “heal-all” — used for centuries across Europe, Asia and North America for wounds, sores and sore throats. In Chinese medicine the dried flower spike, called xiakucao, is a long-standing traditional remedy in its own right.

  • Its old name is heal-all. For centuries, people across Europe, Asia and North America used it for wounds, sores and sore throats.
  • In Chinese medicine, the dried flower spike has a long history of its own. It is called xiakucao, and it is a long-standing traditional remedy there.
  • The name Prunella is itself a record: it comes from the German die Bräune, the old name for a severe throat inflammation the plant was used to treat — which is why a wound herb was also a throat herb. Gerard wrote in 1597 that for healing wounds there was no better herb in the world, and that the bruised leaves alone, worked into a salve, would heal a green wound. Culpeper kept the same reputation a generation later. Its other old names — carpenter's herb and hook-heal — came from its use on cuts from sharp tools.
  • In China the record is older and more specific: the dried spike, xiakucao — “summer-dry herb” — was recorded in Shen Nong’s Classic of the Materia Medica, compiled around AD 25–220. Chinese medicine classed it as bitter, acrid and cold, acting on the liver and gallbladder, and used it to clear liver fire, brighten red or sore eyes, ease dizziness and headache, and soften hard swellings and lumps, including goitre. It is still an ingredient in southern Chinese herbal teas, including the well-known drink Wong Lo Kat.
  • Indigenous peoples of North America used it in their own ways. In the Pacific Northwest, Quileute, Quinault and Coast Salish people put juice from the plant on boils; the Nuxalk boiled the whole plant as a weak tea; the Nlaka'pamux drank a cold infusion as an everyday drink. Cherokee people used an infusion as a wash for bruises, sores and cuts, and Blackfoot people used it as an eyewash for people and horses. In Kashmir, where it is called kalyuth, a decoction was used as a wash for muscle pain.
  • It was food as well as medicine: young leaves and stems were eaten raw in salads, the whole plant was boiled as a leaf vegetable, and the powdered herb was brewed as a cold drink. The bitter taste kept it a minor food — the USDA notes it is not generally eaten for that reason.
  • Self-heal is native across the temperate Northern Hemisphere — Europe, Asia, North Africa and North America. The Eurasian form is the low lawn plant introduced around the world in the 1800s; the North American native form is taller and more upright, with narrower leaves. In its new homes it has spread beyond gardens — it is now invasive in Pacific islands, including Hawaii.

Traditional medicine

  • Human research on self-heal is very thin. The one small trial — 40 volunteers with gingivitis, over 84 days — tested a toothpaste combining self-heal extract with another herb, Macleya cordata; gum scores improved more with the herbal toothpaste, but because two herbs were combined, the result cannot be credited to self-heal alone. Everything else behind its uses is tradition and laboratory work, not trials in people.

Craft

  • The flowers and stems give an olive-green dye for wool and cloth.
  • The plant contains rosmarinic acid, ursolic acid and flavonoids, and in laboratory studies these show anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and antimicrobial activity — interesting chemistry, but laboratory results are not the same as benefit in people.
  • It has a gentle safety record in traditional use; a mild stomach upset is possible.
  • Caution: its safety in pregnancy and while breastfeeding has not been studied, so medicinal use is best avoided then.
  • Caution: do not gather it from roadsides — the USDA warns that plants growing there can take up pollutants from the ground and passing traffic.
  • There is no European Medicines Agency monograph for self-heal, so no European assessment of it exists — its record rests on tradition and laboratory work.
  • When to plant: Sow seed in spring, or plant rooted pieces — it creeps and roots as it goes
  • Sun: Full sun or some shade
  • Soil: Ordinary, moist soil — neutral to slightly alkaline suits it; its creeping roots hold banks, stream edges and pond sides
  • Environment: A hardy perennial; low and lawn-friendly, it stays green and flowers even when mown short — though it can turn weedy if left entirely unmanaged
  • Planter or ground: Ground; a wide pot works
  • Spacing and depth: Sow seed about 2 mm deep — it is slow, and can take up to eight weeks to sprout; set pieces about 25–30 cm apart
  • Water: Likes moisture
  • Companion plants: No strong companions known
  • When to pick: Gather the flowering spikes in summer, as they open

Garden notes

  • Its fibrous, creeping roots and spreading habit hold soil together — the US Department of Agriculture recommends it for erosion control along roadsides, stream banks and pond edges.
  • The purple flower spikes give nectar and pollen to butterflies — whites, sulphurs and skippers — and to native bees, including bumblebees, digger bees, small carpenter bees and sweat bees.
  • Ground-foraging birds eat the small nut-like seeds, and the caterpillars of the gray marvel moth feed on the leaves.
  • A low, lawn-friendly plant that stays green, flowers even when mown short, and spreads into a living ground cover — though it can become weedy if left entirely unmanaged.
  • Deadhead as soon as flowering finishes if you want to hold it back — left alone, it self-seeds freely through a lawn. It is generally free of pests and diseases, but taller neighbours can crowd it out, so cut them back at the end of the season.

Propagation

Sow seed in mid spring, or divide clumps in spring or autumn. It seeds itself and spreads by runners, so cut off the flower heads if you do not want it to spread.

Cultivars

  • There are no named medicinal varieties. Gardeners grow two colour forms of the species itself: a white-flowered form (f. leucantha, sold as 'Alba') and a pink-flowered form sold as 'Rose Pearl'. The large-flowered garden prunellas sold as 'Pagoda' or the 'Bella' series are a different species, Prunella grandiflora — not this plant.

Sources

  • Bensky et al. — Chinese Herbal Medicine: Materia Medica — xiakucao actions and traditional indications
  • Moerman (1998), via BRIT Native American Ethnobotany Database — Pacific Northwest, Cherokee and Blackfoot records
  • Royal Horticultural Society / BBC Gardeners' World — white and pink garden forms; sowing and deadheading practice
  • USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Plant Fact Sheet (2012) — erosion control, pollinator value and ground-cover use
  • Kew, Plants of the World Online — native temperate range and 1800s introduction of Prunella vulgaris
  • Adámková et al. (2004) — double-blind trial of a combined self-heal and Macleya toothpaste for gingivitis (40 people, 84 days)
  • Frontiers in Pharmacology review (2022) — Prunella vulgaris traditional uses, chemistry (rosmarinic and ursolic acids, flavonoids) and laboratory pharmacology
  • Chinese Pharmacopoeia (2020 edition) — the dried flower spike, xiakucao, listed as an official traditional medicine

Shepherd's Purse

Capsella bursa-pastoris

CulinaryMedicinal

Hormone Health

One of the commonest weeds in the world — a pioneer of disturbed ground, gardens, paths and field edges, and one of the first plants to colonise bare soil. It can flower in almost any month of the year. The whole above-ground plant is the part used, gathered while in flower.

  • Its fame as a herb that stops bleeding is centuries old. In the First World War, when supplies of ergot and goldenseal — the standard anti-bleeding drugs — ran short, shepherd's purse was recommended in British and German medical publications as the home-grown substitute, and its extract was used in place of ergot preparations. Grieve called it “one of the best specifics for stopping haemorrhages of all kinds”. But when European assessors looked for proof, they found no studies showing a real clotting effect. So that reputation is history, not established fact.
  • Its official standing grew rather than shrank: it held a German Commission E monograph, gained a European monograph in 2011, and in 2023 it was added to the European Pharmacopoeia as Bursae pastoris herba. A plant can be traditional-use only and still be pharmacopoeial.
  • The name is a picture: the flat, heart-shaped pods look like the leather pouch shepherds carried food in, and the Latin bursa pastoris means exactly “shepherd's purse”. In England and Scotland it was also called “mother's heart”, from a children's trick — pick a pod, it bursts, and you were accused of breaking your mother's heart.
  • Shepherd's purse is native to temperate Eurasia — eastern Europe and Asia Minor across to China and India — and to North Africa. In Britain it is an archaeophyte, an ancient introduction rather than a true native, and it is now naturalised on nearly every continent, especially in cooler climates. It is often called the second most prolific wild plant in the world — a pioneer of cultivated ground, waysides and gardens everywhere people disturb soil.

    • Traditional medicine

    • European regulators recognise shepherd's purse as a traditional herbal medicine for reducing heavy menstrual bleeding in women whose cycles are regular — and only after a doctor has ruled out serious causes. Heavy bleeding always needs checking first.
    • Following the monograph, the traditional course begins three to five days before the period is due.

    As food

    • Half of this plant’s story is missing from most herb books: it is a major food plant in East Asia. In China, as jìcài, it has been eaten since the Zhou dynasty; today it is a prized spring vegetable around Shanghai, stir-fried with rice cakes and folded into wontons. In Japan it is one of the seven herbs of the spring festival Nanakusa-no-sekku, eaten in a seven-herb rice porridge. In Korea, as naengi, it is seasoned as a spring green and cooked in soybean-paste soup. The young leaves are rich in iron, calcium and vitamin C for a wild green. A Ming-dynasty famine-survival guide, the Jiuhuang bencao, recommended it mixed into bread-like cakes, and Indigenous peoples of North America ground it into meal and made a drink from it.
    • People have eaten and used this plant for a very long time — its seeds were found in the Neolithic settlement at Çatalhöyük in Turkey, dated to about 5950 BC, among the oldest direct records for any plant in this library.
    • For food, pick the leaves young, before flowering, when they are mild and peppery like cress; older leaves toughen. As a mustard-family plant it holds glucosinolates, so large amounts eaten raw can irritate digestion — the documented food use is normal cooked portions of a spring green.
    • In two small clinical trials, an extract added to a standard painkiller (mefenamic acid) was reported by the trial authors to reduce menstrual bleeding more than the painkiller alone. European assessors who reviewed the same trial for the official monograph read it more cautiously: they found no significant difference between the groups in the main blood-loss scores in the first two months, and judged the trial not usable for the monograph because the extract’s strength was not reported. The honest summary is that the evidence is early and disputed, not settled.
    • Caution: the EMA does not recommend shepherd's purse in pregnancy or while breastfeeding — extracts made womb tissue contract in laboratory studies, and its safety in pregnancy has never been tested. It is also not recommended for anyone under 18.
    • Caution: because this is traditionally a bleeding herb, take care alongside blood-thinning medicines and check with a clinician first — though it is fair to say the EMA itself reports no documented interactions and no known side effects. The leaf is also rich in vitamin K, the nutrient that works against warfarin — a second reason, in the opposite direction, why the clinician-first advice is right. That is a nutrient fact, not a proven interaction.
    • Caution: gather it from clean ground — it grows exactly where soil is disturbed, which includes sprayed and polluted edges.
    • When to plant: Usually gathered wild. To grow it, scatter seed in spring on any spare patch — it asks for nothing
    • Sun: Full sun or some shade
    • Soil: Almost any soil, even poor and disturbed ground
    • Environment: A hardy annual; its early spring flowers feed small bees and flies when little else is out
    • Planter or ground: Ground; a pot works
    • Spacing and depth: Scatter on the surface
    • Water: Average
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Gather the whole plant in spring, while it flowers; the leaves are best young

    Garden notes

    • Its early spring flowers feed small bees and flies when little else is out.
    • Birds are fond of the seeds — chaffinches and other small birds eat them — and the seed can survive in the soil for decades, waiting for its chance.
    • It is being studied for cleaning contaminated soils, as part of phytoremediation research — using plants to draw contaminants out of soil.
    • A curiosity, labelled as research: its seeds are described as protocarnivorous — the sticky coating on a wet seed traps tiny nematode worms, which the seedling may then draw nutrients from. It is also used as a laboratory model plant, as a close relative of Arabidopsis thaliana.
    • Because the seed can lie in the soil for decades, the plant will reappear for years in a bed where it has once seeded — pull it before the pods form if it is not wanted.

    Propagation

    Scatter seed thinly on bare, loosened soil in spring, barely covered, and keep it moist until it sprouts. It seeds itself fast and can spread like a weed, so pull plants up before the pods ripen if you do not want more.

    Sources

    • German Commission E monograph — approved traditional uses of shepherd's purse herb
    • Korean Food Composition Table, National Institute of Agricultural Sciences — naengi nutrition, including vitamin K
    • European Medicines Agency, shepherd's purse monograph — traditional use for heavy menstrual bleeding, after serious conditions are excluded
    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — native Eurasian and North African range; naturalised almost worldwide
    • Plants For A Future — Capsella bursa-pastoris: food use, leaf nutrition and mustard-family caution
    • Naafe et al. (2018) — two small trials of shepherd's purse extract with mefenamic acid for menstrual bleeding
    • EMA/HMPC Assessment Report on Capsella bursa-pastoris — European assessors’ reading of the same trial: no significant difference in the main blood-loss scores
    • Botanical Society of Scotland (2022) — distribution and seed persistence
    • Royal Horticultural Society — shepherd's purse as a seed food for small birds
    • Nutrients review of Capsella bursa-pastoris (2024) — phytoremediation studies

    Sorrel (Wood Sorrel)

    Oxalis spp.

    Culinary

    Fresh

    Wood sorrel — the little lawn weed with three heart-shaped leaflets — is not the garden salad herb of the same name. Jamaican sorrel is a different plant again — a hibiscus, sharing nothing with this one but the name and the sharp taste.

    • Wood sorrel has been a wayside nibble for centuries. People chewed the sour leaves on walks, to freshen the mouth, and gathered them as a spring green across Europe.
    • After winter, when scurvy threatened, sour spring greens rich in vitamin C were valued, and wood sorrel was one of them. That is history and tradition — not a modern treatment claim.
    • It was a kitchen herb too. In parts of Europe, the sour leaves went into spring sauces and salads. They did the work lemons do now.
    • Tradition links it to Ireland. Wood sorrel is one of the plants claimed as the true shamrock — the three-leafed plant of St Patrick. The claim is old, but so are the claims of its rivals, and no one knows for certain.
    • Its Latin name tells its taste. Oxalis comes from the Greek oxys — sharp, or sour.
    • The European woodland species, Oxalis acetosella, was called Alleluia, because it flowers between Easter and Whitsuntide, when the Alleluia psalms were sung. Its other old names were cuckoo bread and cuckoo's meat, because it appears when the cuckoo arrives.
    • Old herbals recorded it in a green sauce served with fish, and boiled in milk or water as a cooling drink in fevers — a record of past practice, not a recommendation.
    • Because its leaflets are heart-shaped, old herbal writers classed it as a heart herb under the doctrine of signatures — the belief that a plant's shape pointed to its use. That was belief, not fact.
    • “Wood sorrel” is not one plant. The genus Oxalis holds about 550 species, found almost worldwide except the polar regions, richest in tropical Brazil and Mexico and in South Africa — which is why it looks different in different places. A relative, Oxalis tuberosa — oca, sold in New Zealand as the New Zealand yam — has long been grown in the northern Andes for its edible tubers, alongside the potato.
    • Another relative travelled the other way. Bermuda buttercup, Oxalis pes-caprae, from South Africa, was brought to European gardens in the mid-1700s and is now a major weed of Mediterranean climates, California and Australia, spreading by underground bulbils. In its home country its sour leaves are a traditional ingredient in waterblommetjie, a water-lily flower stew.

    Craft

    • The oxalate salt drawn from the leaves was sold as “salt of lemons”, or salt of sorrel, and used to take ink and rust stains out of linen — a household craft that also explains why large amounts were never a food.
    • The boiled plant gives a yellow to orange dye.
    • The leaves, flowers and young seed pods are eaten in small amounts as a wayside nibble; the sharp, lemony taste comes from oxalic acid.
    • Eaten in small amounts as a sour green, it gives vitamin C like other fresh spring greens. There are no human trials of wood sorrel as a medicine — it has not been tested in people as a treatment for anything. (The European herbal monograph for “sorrel” concerns Rumex acetosa, a different plant, and none of it belongs here.)
    • Caution: the same oxalic acid that gives the flavour binds calcium and can interfere with absorbing it, so wood sorrel is a small-amounts plant only. People with kidney stones, gout, kidney problems or rheumatoid arthritis should avoid it or be especially careful. Cooking reduces the soluble oxalates.
    • Caution for pets and livestock: all wood sorrels are listed as toxic to dogs, cats and horses. A nibble usually causes no more than drooling and an upset stomach, but grazing animals that eat a lot of it are at real risk. Stock forced to eat large amounts of Oxalis in pasture — the classic case is Bermuda buttercup — can be poisoned by the oxalates.
    • Telling it from clover: wood sorrel is most often confused with clover, which grows beside it in the same lawn. Wood sorrel leaflets are heart-shaped and fold down; its flowers are small, yellow in the lawn kinds, with five petals, and its seed pods are upright capsules. Clover leaflets are oval, often with a pale chevron mark, and its flowers are round heads.
    • When to plant: Usually gathered wild. Wood sorrel spreads by seed and thin underground stems — to grow it, sow in spring in a corner where its spread is welcome
    • Sun: It depends on the species — the European woodland kind is a deep-shade plant, while the lawn kinds want sun to part shade
    • Soil: Poor, disturbed, even compacted soils
    • Environment: A hardy perennial that spreads fast — it makes a quick living cover on bare ground, and needs watching in beds where it is not wanted
    • Planter or ground: Both — a pot keeps it in bounds
    • Spacing and depth: Sow on the surface or just below; the plants spread to fill their corner
    • Water: Average
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Gather the leaves and flowers fresh through the season — small amounts only

    Garden notes

    • The ripe seed capsules are spring-loaded — touched, they fling their seeds several feet, which is one reason wood sorrel turns up everywhere.
    • It spreads by seed and by thin underground stems, and will grow in poor, disturbed and compacted soils, in anything from full sun to shade.
    • The small yellow flowers are visited by small bees through a long season.
    • The leaflets fold down at night, and in rain and harsh sun — a habit that also helps tell the plant from clover.
    • The creeping and Bermuda-buttercup kinds store food in small bulbs underground, so pulling the top growth leaves the plant alive below — one more reason a pot is the safer home for them.
    • It makes a quick living cover on bare, poor ground where little else volunteers — though that same fast spread means it needs watching in beds where it is not wanted.

    Propagation

    Divide a clump in spring, or separate the small bulbils at its base and replant them. Seed can be sown in spring, but it sprouts unevenly. It spreads by its roots and by seed, so give it room or it will take over a bed.

    Cultivars

    • There are no named culinary varieties of the lawn wood sorrels. What a reader actually meets is a set of distinct species. Oxalis stricta, common yellow wood sorrel, is upright and green with yellow flowers — the common North American lawn plant. Oxalis corniculata, creeping wood sorrel, is low and mat-forming, roots along its stems, and often has purple-flushed leaves; it is now worldwide, and its purple-leaved form is named var. atropurpurea. Oxalis acetosella is the European woodland species, white-flowered with pink veins, a plant of deep shade — the “Alleluia” plant above. Oxalis violacea, violet wood sorrel, is a North American woodland perennial with pink-purple flowers. Oxalis triangularis, the false shamrock from Brazil, has purple triangular leaflets and is grown as a houseplant, often sold around St Patrick's Day; its named form 'Atropurpurea' is a houseplant selection.

    Sources

    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — the Oxalis genus: about 550 species, worldwide, centred on America and South Africa
    • Grieve (1931) — A Modern Herbal: wood sorrel names (Alleluia, cuckoo bread), green sauce, salt of lemons
    • Castro et al. (2007) — spread and reproduction of invasive Oxalis pes-caprae in the western Mediterranean
    • Oxford University Herbaria, Plants 400 — Oxalis profile: oca, Bermuda buttercup history, bulb spread, livestock oxalates
    • NC State University Extension — wood sorrel oxalate caution and seed dispersal
    • ASPCA — Oxalis species toxic to dogs, cats and horses
    • Plants For A Future — oxalic acid binding calcium; small-amounts advice

    St. John's Wort

    Hypericum perforatum

    Medicinal

    Mental HealthSkin Health

    Fresh

    A sunny meadow and wayside perennial whose flowers offer no nectar but give bees plenty of pollen through the summer. Its medicine interactions are the first thing to know about it. The flowering tops are the part used.

    • The plant was used in ancient Greek medicine — for wounds, and for troubled nerves. Greek and Roman writers kept it in their herbals.
    • Its name comes from St John's Day, June 24, in midsummer. That is when the plant is in full flower, and when it was gathered for the year.
    • Tradition says bunches of it were hung over doors and windows on St John's Eve, to protect the house — against lightning, fire and evil spirits.
    • The flowers, steeped in oil, turn the oil red. That red oil was a household remedy for wounds, burns and nerve pain for centuries.
    • It has kept both lives into modern times: the midsummer herb of folklore, and a medicine still studied today for low mood.

    Craft

    • The flowers are a dye plant with a wide range: yellow, gold and brown shades, turning red after the dyebath is acidified. The colour follows the liquid it sits in — red in oil or alcohol, yellow in water — the same red pigment that colours the plant’s infused oil.
    • Caution — prescription medicines: St. John's wort speeds up the liver enzymes that clear many medicines from the body, so those medicines can stop working. The list includes the contraceptive pill — breakthrough bleeding and unplanned pregnancies have been reported — transplant anti-rejection medicines, HIV medicines, cancer medicines, the blood thinner warfarin, digoxin, and some antidepressants, whose levels it lowers.
    • Caution — serotonin syndrome: combined with antidepressant medicines (SSRIs, SNRIs and triptans among them), St. John's wort can cause serotonin syndrome — a potentially life-threatening reaction with agitation, fever, fast heartbeat, confusion and muscle stiffness. Anyone taking any prescription medicine must talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using it.
    • St. John's wort has been studied for mild to moderate depression, with mixed results: a large Cochrane review of 29 trials found its extracts worked better than placebo and about as well as standard antidepressants for mild to moderate depression, with fewer side effects — but two large US trials in major depression found no benefit over placebo, and the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health calls the evidence not definitive. Depression is a serious illness that needs medical care; this is not a casual tonic, and it is never a substitute for treatment.
    • European regulators accept specified extracts for mild to moderate depressive episodes as a well-established use, and list traditional uses for temporary mental exhaustion, minor skin inflammation such as sunburn and minor wounds (as an infused oil), and mild digestive discomfort.
    • Caution: it increases the skin's sensitivity to sunlight, and that applies to the infused oil on the skin as well as to taking it. It may be unsafe in pregnancy, and European regulators do not recommend it for anyone under 18.
    • When to plant: Sow seed in spring, or plant young plants — and plant it only where its spread can be watched: it is classed as a noxious weed in several western US states and parts of Australia, and it is poisonous to grazing livestock
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Well-drained soil, even poor; its deep roots can hold soil on banks
    • Environment: A hardy perennial that spreads by seed and creeping roots
    • Planter or ground: Ground, in a contained spot
    • Spacing and depth: 45 cm apart
    • Water: Dry once settled
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Gather the flowering tops as they open, around midsummer

    Garden notes

    • An honest downside: away from its home ground it can take over — it is classed as a noxious weed in several western US states and parts of Australia, spreads by seed and creeping roots, and is poisonous to grazing livestock, making their skin painfully sensitive to sunlight.
    • In California it was famously brought back under control by two leaf beetles introduced from Europe — one of the classic success stories of biological weed control.
    • Its deep roots can hold soil on banks, but its spreading habit means it needs watching wherever it is planted.

    Propagation

    Sow seed in autumn when ripe, or in spring, barely covered — it can take one to three months to sprout. Or divide clumps in spring or autumn. It spreads fast by seed and by roots, so keep it in check and do not let it seed where you do not want it.

    Sources

    • Linde et al. (2008) — Cochrane review: extracts superior to placebo and comparable to standard antidepressants for mild to moderate depression
    • European Medicines Agency, St. John's wort monograph — well-established use for mild to moderate depressive episodes; traditional uses
    • NCCIH — evidence not definitive; two large US trials in major depression found no benefit over placebo
    • Memorial Sloan Kettering, About Herbs — full interaction profile: contraceptive pill, transplant, HIV and cancer medicines, warfarin, digoxin, serotonin syndrome
    • USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Plant Guide — noxious-weed status and biological control

    Violet

    Viola spp.

    MedicinalCulinary

    Skin HealthSleep

    FreshDried

    The leaves and flowers are the parts used — in syrups, teas and salads, and in skin preparations. Among the earliest spring flowers, violets feed emerging bees, including a mining bee that specialises in violets.

    • The violet was the emblem flower of ancient Athens. Poets called the city "violet-crowned Athens". Violets were sold in its markets and worn in garlands.
    • Greek and Roman households used violets in wine and in garlands. Later, the flowers settled into syrups and sweets.
    • In France, Toulouse became the violet city. From the 1800s, its growers made candied violets — whole flowers coated in sugar. They are still the city's signature sweet.
    • Napoleon took the violet as his emblem. When he was exiled to Elba in 1814, his supporters wore violets as a secret sign. They said he would return when the violets bloomed.
    • He came back in March 1815, as the violets flowered. The flower stayed a sign of loyalty to him long after.
    • Under the Athens story sit older layers. Sappho's poems wove violets into garlands of love and longing, and in the Greek myth Persephone was gathering violets when Hades took her — which is why the violet has carried both love and loss ever since.
    • In medieval and Renaissance Christian art the violet stood for humility and modesty and was linked to the Virgin Mary — it appears low at the edge of paintings for that reason. In the Victorian language of flowers, the sweet violet meant modesty and the blue violet faithfulness — “I will always be true” — so a bunch worn on a coat was a readable message.
    • In Persian medicine the sweet violet, Viola odorata, is Banafsha — a named drug, named by Avicenna among others, used for coughs, fevers and sleeplessness. It is the tradition the modern trials below actually come from.
    • The genus Viola holds more than 500 species, mostly in the temperate Northern Hemisphere. The two a reader meets most: sweet violet, Viola odorata, native to Europe and western Asia and now spread through North America; and common blue violet, Viola sororia, native to eastern and central North America — the state flower of Illinois, Rhode Island, New Jersey and Wisconsin, and the provincial flower of New Brunswick.
    • The famous double, heavily scented Parma violets of the 1800s flower trade — grown around Parma, Toulouse and the Riviera and shipped by train to city florists — are now known from genetic work to belong not to Viola odorata but to Viola alba subsp. dehnhardtii. They rarely set seed and can flower for up to seven months. Toulouse grew both sweet and Parma violets.

    Traditional medicine

    • Violet syrup is a traditional cough remedy, long given for coughs and sore throats, especially to children.

    Craft

    • The flowers scent perfumes — violet was a classic perfume flower of the 1800s — and they are candied: brushed with sugar and dried, as a sweet decoration. The perfume also came from the leaves: violet leaf absolut is one of the most concentrated materials in perfumery — about 1,000 kg of leaves yield only 300–400 g of it. Grieve also recorded a violet ointment among the plant's preparations.
    • (The roots and seeds are a different matter — see Safety below.)
    • The cough syrup has one real trial behind it, and it is bigger than “small”: Qasemzadeh et al. (2015) ran a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial in 182 children aged 2–12 with intermittent asthma. Violet syrup, added to a standard short-acting inhaler, shortened the time to cough easing and to full cough suppression compared with placebo plus the inhaler. One trial, one country, as an add-on to standard treatment — not a replacement for it. Human trials
    • Violet has also been tested for sleep. Feyzabadi et al. (2018) ran a double-blind, randomised trial in 75 adults with chronic insomnia: three drops of violet oil — violet extracted in almond oil — in each nostril nightly for 30 days improved insomnia and sleep-quality scores more than almond oil alone or placebo, though all three groups improved, and the gain was stronger for sleep quality than for sleep length. No serious side effects were reported. A later review pooling five placebo-controlled insomnia trials (224 patients; Huang et al., 2022) found the same direction of effect. One moderate trial plus a pooling review — promising, not proven — is the strength behind violet's Sleep tag. Human trials
    • The leaves provide vitamins A and C, and the plant's slippery mucilage is soothing to irritated throats and skin — the traditional reason it is classed as a demulcent, a substance that coats and soothes. Traditional use
    • Violet contains natural salicylate compounds, the aspirin family of chemicals, which fits its old folk use for aches and inflamed skin. Traditional use
    • When to plant: Plant young plants or divide clumps in spring, in a shady corner
    • Sun: Some shade — a plant for under trees and shady edges
    • Soil: Fertile, humus-rich soil, moist but well-drained, neutral to alkaline, with leaf mould worked in. Propagate by division in spring or autumn, or by cuttings in spring or late summer
    • Environment: A hardy perennial that spreads by runners and self-seeding into a ground cover; violets are the only food of fritillary caterpillars, so a patch is a butterfly nursery
    • Planter or ground: Both
    • Spacing and depth: 25–30 cm apart
    • Water: Likes moisture
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Pick the flowers as they open in spring; gather the leaves through the season

    Garden notes

    • The fritillaries that feed only on violet leaves include the great spangled, variegated and regal fritillaries.
    • The seeds carry a small oily parcel (an elaiosome, a fatty attachment that ants eat) that ants carry back to their nests, planting the violets in rich nest soil as they go.
    • A mining bee, Andrena violae, specialises in violets.
    • It holds soil under trees and along shady edges where grass struggles.
    • After the showy spring flowers, violets produce small, closed, bud-like flowers in summer that never open. These pollinate themselves and set most of the plant's seed — which is why a patch spreads even with no bees about.
    • Parma violets are the exception to the family's hardiness: unlike sweet violet, the Parma group is frost-tender and was grown under glass or in warm climates.

    Propagation

    Divide a clump in spring or autumn — break off a small piece with roots and replant it. That is the easiest way. Seed can be sown in autumn, but it needs a cold spell first and sprouts unevenly. Named kinds may not come true from seed.

    Cultivars

    • Named sweet violets (Viola odorata) include 'Alba', with white flowers and a gentle scent; 'Coeur d'Alsace', dusky pink, flowering late winter to early spring at about 15 cm; 'Queen Charlotte' (also 'Königin Charlotte'), deep purple with a strong scent, flowering twice — spring and late summer; 'Reine des Neiges', the “Snow Queen”, near-white with an ice-blue rinse, a sport of 'Queen Charlotte'; and 'Sulphurea', uncommon yellow to sulphur-yellow flowers tipped purple.
    • Two relatives, named as species, not varieties: Viola sororia, the common blue violet — the lawn violet of North America, scentless or nearly so; the candied and syrup violet of Europe is the scented Viola odorata, and confusing the two is the commonest violet mistake. And Viola tricolor, heartsease or wild pansy, purple-yellow-white — the ancestor of the garden pansy.

    Safety

    • Only the leaves and flowers are eaten. The roots and seeds are not food — the root contains an alkaloid, violine, and is strongly sickening and purgative in larger doses, and some violets are high in saponins, which can cause nausea if too much is eaten.
    • The houseplant sold as an “African violet” is not a violet at all — it belongs to a different family, from Tanzania and Kenya, and is not an edible Viola. The windowsill plant is a different plant entirely.

    Sources

    • Qasemzadeh et al. (2015) — violet syrup and cough in 182 children with intermittent asthma: double-blind randomised trial
    • Feyzabadi et al. (2017) — Viola odorata in traditional Persian medicine: critical review of its chemistry and pharmacology
    • Huang et al. (2022) — violet extract for insomnia: systematic review and meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials
    • Malécot et al. (2007) — Parma violet cultivars belong to Viola alba subsp. dehnhardtii: genetic study
    • Royal Horticultural Society — Viola odorata 'Coeur d'Alsace': cultivar record, cultivation and propagation
    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — the Viola genus; Viola odorata and Viola sororia ranges
    • Mittal et al. (2015) — peer-reviewed review of Viola odorata: its mucilage, salicylates and vitamin C, and the traditional cough and skin uses
    • Feyzabadi et al. (2018) — randomised trial of violet oil nose drops for insomnia

    Vitex

    Vitex agnus-castus

    Medicinal

    Hormone Health

    Dried

    A deciduous shrub or small tree in the mint family, Lamiaceae — older books shelve it with the verbena family, and it was moved on modern evidence — native to the Mediterranean and east into Central Asia, where it grows along riverbanks and on coastal ground. In summer it carries long spikes of lilac flowers over leaves divided into narrow leaflets spread like the fingers of a hand, and the whole plant smells peppery when brushed. Its other names — chaste tree, chasteberry, monk's pepper — all point at the fruit: small, hard, dark berries the size of peppercorns, and the only part modern medicine uses.

    The parts divide cleanly. The ripe fruit is the medicine, gathered in autumn and dried, and every trial used a standardised extract of it. The leaves were used in ancient practice and in the old chastity customs, but no modern preparation is made from them. The flowers are garden ornament and bee forage. The root is not used. What the fruit does in the body is unusual for a plant: some of its compounds act on dopamine, a chemical messenger in the brain. Dopamine is the brake on prolactin, a hormone best known for driving milk production; prolactin running slightly high in the days before a period is one of the drivers linked to premenstrual breast pain and other symptoms. Ease the brake's target down, and those symptoms ease with it — that is the working explanation, and it is also why this plant comes with medicine interactions most herbs do not have.

    • Vitex is one of the oldest medicines for women's complaints ever written down. Hippocrates, in the fourth century BCE, recommended it for injuries, inflammation and use after childbirth. Four centuries later, Dioscorides described it in his herbal — his book of healing plants — for complaints of the womb and for bringing on milk. He also recorded its reputation for cooling sexual desire.
    • The name tells that second story twice over. The Greek word for the plant, agnos, meant chaste. It was heard as the Latin agnus, a lamb, and castus — chaste — was added. So the plant's Latin name reads "chaste lamb".
    • At the Thesmophoria, the women-only festival of Demeter at Athens, women strewed chaste tree leaves on the beds they slept on through the rites, to keep chastity for the festival's length. Pliny records the custom.
    • In medieval monasteries, monks ate the peppery berries, and used them in the kitchen in place of pepper. They believed the berries helped them keep a vow of celibacy. That is the whole origin of the name monk's pepper.
    • The genus name is older and plainer. Vitex comes from the Latin vieo, to weave or plait — a name that fits the plant's tough, flexible branches.
    • The modern chapter is German. Physicians there took vitex up for cycle complaints in the twentieth century. German and Swiss firms produced the standardised fruit extracts — extracts made to a fixed strength, named in the trials as Ze 440 and BNO 1095 — that let an ancient remedy be tested in modern randomised trials.
    • Vitex oil, distilled from the leaves and berries, is breathed in or rubbed, diluted, on the skin for cycle-related mood and PMS. Traditional use

    Craft

    • The long, flexible young branches bend without breaking, and are woven into fences, hurdles and baskets.
    • The leaves, seed and roots give a yellow dye, the flowers are used in perfume, and the wood is hard and close-grained.
    • For premenstrual syndrome, vitex has strong trial evidence. In the landmark trial, 170 women took a standardised fruit extract (20 mg a day) or a dummy preparation for three menstrual cycles; 52% of the vitex group had their symptoms at least halved, against 24% on placebo. Reviews gathering the randomised trials since point the same way — one pooled analysis of the three strictest trials found women on vitex about two and a half times more likely to see their symptoms clear than women on placebo — though trial quality varies and the benefit, while real, is modest: symptoms ease; they do not go away fully. European regulators give the specified extract their "well-established use" standing for premenstrual syndrome, the strongest category a herbal medicine can hold in that system, and Germany's Commission E approved the fruit for premenstrual complaints.
    • For breast pain that comes and goes with the cycle, several placebo-controlled trials find vitex eases it, and reviews of those trials agree. It is the symptom that fits the plant's action on prolactin most directly.
    • For irregular cycles, Germany's Commission E approved the fruit, and the plant has a long record of use for cycles that run long, short or missing. The trial evidence here is thinner than for premenstrual syndrome — reviewers who praise the PMS data call the cycle data weak beside it — and the evidence stands at that strength.
    • For menopause, vitex is sometimes sold for hot flushes and other symptoms, but the trials are few and small and reviewers find the evidence insufficient. No benefit has been shown.
    • Caution — dopamine medicines: vitex acts on the same brain messenger as medicines that raise or block dopamine — treatments for Parkinson's disease on one side and antipsychotic medicines on the other. It can work against either kind, and the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health advises people taking dopamine-related medicines to avoid it.
    • Caution — contraceptives and hormone therapy: vitex changes hormone signalling, and regulators advise that it may interfere with hormonal contraceptives and hormone replacement therapy — a pregnancy has been reported to an Australian regulator in a woman taking vitex alongside a contraceptive pill. It is also best avoided by anyone with a hormone-sensitive condition, such as a cancer that responds to hormones.
    • Caution — pregnancy and breastfeeding: vitex is not recommended in pregnancy — its safety there has not been established — and not while breastfeeding, where lowering prolactin can cut the milk supply. The same action that makes it useful before a period makes it the wrong plant here.
    • In the trials, side effects were usually mild and uncommon: nausea, headache, digestive upset, and occasionally itching or a rash.
    • When to plant: Plant a young shrub in spring, in a warm, sheltered place
    • Sun: Full sun — it likes its crown in full sun
    • Soil: Well-drained soil; at home on the stony, seasonally dry ground along watercourses
    • Environment: Deciduous and fast-growing, reaching one to five metres; in cold districts winter kills the top growth back, and it simply flowers on the new wood the following summer
    • Planter or ground: Ground; a large pot in warm districts
    • Spacing and depth: Give it room — 2–3 m across
    • Water: Average — it stands drought well once established, but flowers and fruits most freely with summer water
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Gather the berries through autumn, as they ripen

    Garden notes

    • A plant of Mediterranean riverbanks and stream sides: it likes its roots near water but its crown in full sun, and it tolerates the stony, seasonally dry ground along watercourses.
    • Deciduous and fast-growing, it reaches one to five metres. In cold districts winter kills the top growth back to the ground, and the plant simply flowers on the new wood the following summer.
    • It asks for well-drained soil and sun; once established it stands drought well, though it flowers and fruits most freely with summer water.
    • The lilac flower spikes open in summer, when few other shrubs are in bloom, and are rich in nectar — bees and butterflies work them heavily.
    • The berries ripen through autumn and are gathered then; a shrub in a warm, sheltered place will fruit reliably year after year.

    Propagation

    Take softwood or semi-hardwood cuttings 4 to 6 inches long in summer, dip in rooting hormone, and keep them covered until they root in 4 to 6 weeks. Seed also works — soak it for 24 hours first — but it sprouts unevenly over 2 to 7 weeks, and seed-grown plants will not match a named kind.

    Safety

    • Essential oils are concentrates, many times stronger than the plant itself. Always dilute in a carrier oil before putting one on skin, and never swallow an essential oil.

    Sources
