    • van Die et al. (2013) — systematic review of vitex for premenstrual syndrome, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, cyclical breast pain and menopause, Planta Medica
    • Cerqueira et al. (2017) — systematic review of vitex for premenstrual syndrome and premenstrual dysphoric disorder, Archives of Women's Mental Health
    • Halaska et al. (1999) — vitex against placebo for cyclical breast pain, The Breast
    • European Medicines Agency (2018) — European Union herbal monograph on Vitex agnus-castus L., fructus: well-established use in premenstrual syndrome
    • German Commission E (1992) — monograph approving agnus castus fruit for menstrual cycle irregularities, premenstrual syndrome and breast pain
    • National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health — Chasteberry: Usefulness and Safety, interactions and pregnancy cautions

    Yarrow

    Achillea millefolium

    Medicinal

    Digestive HealthSkin Health

    One of the oldest traditional wound herbs — long used on small cuts and superficial wounds, and known as “soldier's woundwort” from its battlefield history. The flower heads and leaves — the parts above ground — are the parts used.

    • Legend tells that Achilles used yarrow on his soldiers' wounds at Troy. The story is legend, not record. But it gave the plant its Latin name, Achillea.
    • Greek and Roman writers listed yarrow among their wound herbs. The legend only says, in story form, what people did in real life.
    • The oldest written record has names and dates. In the 1st century AD, Dioscorides described a plant his editors identify as yarrow — a span high, with leaves like a young bird's feather and small white flowers by the roadside — and wrote that it was very good for bleeding and for old and fresh sores. A little later, Pliny told the Achilles story as a discovery: Achilles, taught by the centaur Chiron, found the herb and healed Telephus with it.
    • For centuries after, it stayed a battlefield herb. In English folk speech it was called soldier's woundwort. People were still gathering it for wounds in the American Civil War.
    • In China, yarrow had a different honour. Its straight stalks were the classic stalks thrown to read the I Ching, the old book of changes. That use was kept for thousands of years.
    • Its other Latin name is a plain description. Millefolium means thousand leaves — for the leaf, cut into a thousand fine parts.
    • Yarrow is native across temperate Eurasia — most of Europe, east through Turkey, the Caucasus and Central Asia to Siberia and the Himalayas. Carried to herb gardens around the world, it is now naturalised in North and South America, Australia and New Zealand. North America also has its own closely related native forms, which is why botanists disagree about where the species boundary sits.
    • Its folk names were instructions for use: it was also called nosebleed plant and staunchweed, because crushed leaves were put up the nose or on a cut to stop bleeding.
    • In North America, Indigenous peoples used yarrow and its native varieties widely — Ojibwe people placed the florets on coals and inhaled the smoke to break a fever, Cherokee people drank a tea for fever and sleep, and Zuni people used a poultice of it on burns.
    • It carried love lore too. In Suffolk a leaf in the nose was said to bleed if love was true, and in Devon and County Donegal girls put yarrow under the pillow or in a stocking on May Eve to dream of a future husband. That is lore, told as it was believed — not a use.
    • In the Scottish Highlands it was made into an ointment for wounds, and in Dalarna, Sweden, people brewed ale with yarrow in place of hops, believing it made the ale stronger.
    • Blue yarrow oil, distilled from the flowering tops, is rubbed, diluted, on the skin for wounds and inflamed skin. Traditional use

    Traditional medicine

    • European regulators list this among its traditional uses.
    • Traditionally used for temporary loss of appetite, and for mild, cramping digestive complaints such as bloating and wind.
    • Traditionally used for minor cramps associated with menstrual periods.
    • These uses are traditional, based on long-standing use: the European Medicines Agency notes there is not enough clinical-trial evidence to confirm them.

    Craft

    • The flowers give yellow and green dyes for wool and cloth.
    • The leaves were used as a cleansing wash for greasy skin, and the fragrant seeds were kept indoors for their pleasant smell.
    • The tall, flat flower heads are also cut for fresh and dried flower arrangements.
    • One small human trial exists. In Iran, 50 students with period pain took yarrow or chamomile capsules over two cycles (Radfar et al., 2019). Both reduced the pain; yarrow's reduction was a little larger and lasted longer, but the difference between the two herbs was not statistically significant, and there was no placebo group. Promising and early — not proof.
    • Beyond that, clinical studies of yarrow are limited, and no quality trial confirms a dose for any condition. The digestive and skin uses above rest on tradition and the European traditional-use listing, not on trials.
    • Caution: do not use if you are allergic to plants in the daisy family, such as ragweed or chamomile. Avoid in pregnancy and for children under 12. Take care alongside blood-thinning medicines and check with a clinician first — an added effect is possible, though interactions are not well documented.
    • Caution: handling the plant can cause a skin rash (contact dermatitis) in some people — the most commonly reported side effect. Wear gloves if your skin reacts.
    • Caution: the herb holds only small amounts of thujone, but the concentrated essential oil is a different strength — never take yarrow oil by mouth. Thujone is the reason the monographs advise against use in pregnancy.
    • Caution: in one reported case, drinking about five cups of yarrow tea a day for a week brought on dry mouth, a racing heart and confusion. A single case — and a plain lesson that more is not better.
    • When to plant: Sow seed in spring, or divide clumps — it spreads and self-seeds
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Dry, poor soil where many plants struggle; rich soil makes it floppy
    • Environment: A hardy perennial for USDA zones 3–9, drought-tolerant once established, and used for erosion control on steep slopes. It grows 30–100 cm tall — the richer the soil, the taller and floppier
    • Planter or ground: Both
    • Spacing and depth: Sow on the surface or just below; 30–45 cm apart
    • Water: Dry once settled
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Gather the leaves young, and the flowering tops as they open, through summer

    Garden notes

    • The flat flower heads attract pollinators and beneficial insects, including hoverflies, ladybirds, lacewings and tachinid flies that help control garden pests.
    • Its flowers also feed butterflies and other wildlife.
    • Used in land restoration.
    • Divide clumps every 3–4 years in spring to keep them vigorous. Deadhead spent heads to stop self-seeding and coax out a second, smaller flush of flowers.
    • Winter wet kills more yarrow than cold does — it needs sharp drainage in winter, even where it tolerates clay in summer.

    Propagation

    Divide a clump in spring or autumn, every few years, each piece with roots and shoots. Seed can be sown on the surface in spring — do not cover it, as it needs light. It spreads by roots and by seed, so give it room or it will take over a bed.

    Cultivars

    • Garden yarrows are picked for flower colour. 'Paprika' flowers red with yellow centres, fading to pink, at 45–60 cm. 'Red Velvet' is a rich red, 60–90 cm, and holds its colour better than most reds. 'Cerise Queen' is deep pink, about 75 cm. 'Summer Pastels' is a seed mix in soft cream, peach, pink and lavender. 'Terracotta' opens orange-brown and fades to terracotta, at 75–90 cm.
    • Two famous garden yarrows are hybrids, not straight Achillea millefolium: 'Moonshine', with silver-grey leaves and pale lemon-yellow flowers, and 'Coronation Gold', with large golden-yellow heads. Hybrids like these are sterile — they do not self-sow or spread like the species.

    Sources

    • European Medicines Agency, yarrow herb and flower monographs — traditional-use indications; daisy-family allergy and pregnancy cautions
    • BRIT Native American Ethnobotany Database — Ojibwe, Cherokee and Zuni records for yarrow
    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — native Eurasian range and worldwide introduction of Achillea millefolium
    • European Medicines Agency, yarrow public summary — conclusions rest on traditional use
    • USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Plant Guide — beneficial-insect value, erosion control and drought tolerance
    • Tisserand & Young (2014) — Essential Oil Safety — blue yarrow oil for wounds and inflamed skin

    Garlic

    Allium sativum

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Heart Health

    FreshCooked

    A bulb of the onion family, and one of the oldest flavourings in the world — a plant people have grown for at least 5,000 years less as a vegetable than as a force: the pungency that makes it indispensable in the kitchen is the plant's own chemical defence, and it is also where nearly everything studied about garlic begins.

    Cultivars

    Music (hardneck, Porcelain type)

    the gardener's standard: big bulbs of four to six fat cloves in white wrappers, strong, clean garlic flavour, and it peels easily. Cold-hardy; stores moderately.

    Chesnok Red (hardneck, Purple Stripe type)

    purple-striped wrappers over cloves with a rich, sweet depth that keeps its flavour in cooking. One of the best roasting garlics.

    Inchelium Red (softneck, Artichoke type)

    a mild, well-balanced heirloom from Washington state, with many cloves in layers. An award-winner in taste tests, and the soft neck braids well.

    Silver White (softneck, Silverskin type)

    the longest keeper of all: dense white bulbs that can store ten months or more. The last garlic in the pantry before the new harvest.

    Elephant garlic

    not garlic at all, honestly labelled: it is a leek relative (Allium ampeloprasum) bred to grow enormous, mild bulbs. Gentle and sweet roasted, but a different plant with a fraction of true garlic's pungency.

    Lebanon — toum: garlic whipped with oil, lemon and salt into a white, light sauce, eaten with grilled chicken and fries — garlic as the main event, not the seasoning.
    China — Laba garlic: cloves pickled in vinegar until they turn emerald green, made for the Laba festival and eaten with dumplings through the New Year season.
    Spain — sopa de ajo, the Castilian garlic soup of bread, paprika, garlic and a poached egg; and ajo blanco, a chilled white soup of garlic, almonds and bread from Málaga.
    Korea — garlic at nearly every meal: pickled whole cloves (jangajji), cloves grilled and wrapped in lettuce with barbecue, and black garlic — bulbs aged warm until black, soft and sweet as balsamic.
    • Garlic's wild ancestor grew in Central Asia, in the mountains of what is now Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. From there, it travelled every road there was. It went into Egypt, where it fed the pyramid builders and was buried with Tutankhamun. It went into Greece and Rome, where soldiers and athletes ate it before hard effort. And it went east along the Silk Road into China.
    • Spanish, Portuguese and French ships carried it to the Americas in the 1500s. It took root in every kitchen it met. Few plants are as widespread: it is hard to name a major way of cooking that does not begin, somewhere, with garlic in hot oil.
    • All garlic falls into two great families. Hardneck garlic bolts — that means it sends up a flower stalk. It forms a single ring of large cloves around a stiff stem. It is the kind that stands up to cold, and it has the deepest flavour. Softneck garlic does not bolt. It forms many smaller cloves in layers. It keeps far longer, and it is the kind that braids.
    • Garlic barely flowers and almost never sets true seed. Like the banana, it is a clone crop: every bulb ever planted is a piece of an older bulb. So a kind of garlic is a living line, carried hand to hand for centuries.

    Craft

    • Softneck garlic is braided: the soft stems are plaited into strings with the bulbs hanging along them — a way of storing the harvest that doubles as a kitchen ornament. Hardneck kinds, with their stiff stems, are bundled or netted instead.
    • A whole bulb is concentrated nutrition — per 100 g, garlic provides vitamin B6 (about 1.2 mg, over 70% of the daily value), manganese (about 1.7 mg), vitamin C (about 31 mg) and selenium. But honesty about portions matters: garlic is eaten in grams, not hundreds of grams, so its real gift is its compounds, not bulk nutrition.
    • The signature compound is allicin — and allicin does not exist in a whole clove. Inside the intact clove, a substance called alliin sits in one compartment and an enzyme in another; crushing or chopping breaks the walls between them, and the enzyme makes allicin, the source of raw garlic's bite. Heat destroys the enzyme within moments, which is why raw garlic is fiercest. Crushed garlic left to rest about ten minutes before cooking lets the allicin form first — the cook's trick that keeps more of it.
    • Blood pressure: pooled analyses of clinical trials find that garlic supplements — aged garlic extract or standardised powder, roughly 600–1,200 mg a day taken for months — lower the top blood-pressure number by about 5 points on average, and by around 8 points in people who start with high blood pressure. Those are concentrated supplement doses, not the clove or two in a stir-fry, and garlic in any form is not a substitute for prescribed blood-pressure medicine.
    • Cholesterol: the same trial literature finds small reductions in total and LDL cholesterol from garlic supplements — real, but modest, and again at supplement doses.
    • Colds: one trial found fewer colds in people taking a daily garlic supplement, but it stands nearly alone; reviewers judge the evidence too thin to promise anything. Garlic's reputation against colds is older than its proof.
    • Caution: garlic supplements thin the blood slightly, and at supplement doses they can add to the effect of blood-thinning medicines and are usually stopped before surgery. That caution belongs to concentrated supplements — ordinary cooking amounts are food, and are not the concern. Raw garlic can also burn an empty stomach, and raw garlic paste left on skin can blister it.
    • When to plant: Plant cloves in autumn, pointed end up — garlic needs winter cold to divide into cloves properly; a bulb planted in spring often grows as one round, undivided ball
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Well-drained, fertile soil; wet winter ground rots the bulbs
    • Environment: Fully hardy — the winter cold is required, not just endured
    • Planter or ground: Ground best; wide pots work
    • Spacing and depth: Cloves 15 cm apart, about 5 cm (2 in) deep
    • Water: Average — water in dry springs, and stop as the leaves yellow
    • Companion plants: Carrots and lettuce are good neighbours. Keep apart from beans and peas, which garlic holds back
    • When to pick: Harvest in early summer when the lower leaves have yellowed but a few green ones remain; cure dry, with air moving around the bulbs, for several weeks

    Garden notes

    • Plant cloves in autumn, pointed end up, a few inches deep, in full sun and well-drained soil. Garlic needs winter cold to divide into cloves properly; a bulb planted in spring often grows as one round, undivided ball.
    • Hardneck types announce summer with the scape — a curling flower stalk that loops like a pig's tail. Cut it when it has curled once: the plant then puts its energy into the bulb, and the scape itself is a harvest — mild, green garlic flavour for pesto, stir-fries and grilling.
    • Young garlic leaves are eaten too, snipped like chives in spring cooking — the whole plant gives, from green leaf to scape to bulb.
    • Harvest when the lower leaves have yellowed but a few green ones remain, loosen with a fork rather than pulling, and cure the bulbs dry with air moving around them for several weeks before storing.
    • Save your biggest, healthiest bulbs as next year's seed garlic. Because garlic is a clone, your planting stock is quite literally your harvest, continued.

    Propagation

    Break a bulb into cloves and plant each one pointy-end up, about 2 inches deep, in autumn, 4 to 6 weeks before the ground freezes. Each clove grows into a full bulb by next summer. Garlic needs a cold winter to form a proper bulb — cloves planted in spring give smaller heads.

    Sources

    • Song & Milner (2001) — how allicin forms when a clove is crushed
    • Ried et al. (2016) — pooled trials of garlic supplements and blood pressure
    • Ried et al. (2013) — garlic supplements and cholesterol
    • Lissiman et al. (2014) — Cochrane review of garlic for the common cold
    • NCCIH — Garlic: usefulness and safety

    Ginger

    Zingiber officinale

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Digestive Health

    FreshDried

    The knobbly "root" in the produce aisle is not a root at all — it is a rhizome, a thick underground stem that creeps sideways through the soil, sending leaves up and true roots down. Ginger is a tropical plant of the same family as turmeric and cardamom, and one of the first spices ever traded across the world.

    Terpenes in this plant: ·

    Cultivars

    Jamaican

    pale, thin-skinned and silky, with a fine, lemony heat. The classic export ginger, long prized for ginger beer and for preserving.

    Cochin (Indian)

    from Kerala's coast: plump hands with a warm, lemon-touched pungency. Much of it is dried for the spice trade; the fresh form is a staple of Indian kitchens.

    Chinese (Canton)

    the supermarket standard: big, plump, mild and juicy, with skin thin enough to scrape off with a spoon. Bred by centuries of selection for size and mildness.

    Nigerian

    smaller, darker and very pungent, with an unusually high oil content. West African cooking's ginger, and increasingly exported for its strength.

    Young ginger

    not a variety but a harvest stage: rhizomes lifted early, at four to six months, before the skin toughens. Pink-tipped, almost skinless, mild and juicy — the ginger that pickles into the pale slices served with sushi.

    India — fresh ginger pounded with garlic into the paste that begins half the curries of the subcontinent; adrak chai, tea boiled strong with ginger; ginger in sweets and in the digestive chew of the after-dinner tray.
    Japan — gari, the sweet-pickled young ginger eaten between bites of sushi to clear the palate; and beni shōga, red pickled ginger strips over fried noodles and rice bowls.
    China — ginger-scallion sauce over poached chicken; ginger fried in sesame oil for the restorative dishes of the month after childbirth; brown-sugar ginger tea taken for chills.
    Jamaica & the Caribbean — fiery homemade ginger beer, brewed strong enough to bite; ginger worked into jerk seasoning and into sorrel drink at Christmas.
    • Ginger was first grown in maritime Southeast Asia — the lands of coasts and islands in the south-east of Asia. It spread very early. Austronesian voyagers carried it in their canoes across the Pacific and west to India, thousands of years ago. That made it one of the travelling plants of the ancient world.
    • From India, it moved along the Silk Road and the sea routes to Persia, Arabia and the Mediterranean. By Roman times, it was a costly import in Europe. By the medieval period, it was common enough that a pound of ginger cost about as much as a sheep — and people still prized it enough to pay that.
    • Spanish ships carried it to the Caribbean and South America in the 1500s. Jamaica became so famous for its pale, silky-skinned ginger that "Jamaican ginger" set the standard for the export trade.
    • Grown ginger almost never flowers or sets seed. So — like garlic and banana — every plant is a piece of an older plant: a rhizome divided and replanted. A rhizome is the thick underground stem. Its kinds are regional forms, not bred varieties. They are the same plant, shaped by the soils and tastes of Jamaica, India, China and West Africa.
    • Ginger oil is breathed in for nausea and rubbed, diluted, on aching muscles: in one trial of 301 people after surgery, breathing it in eased nausea. Human · small
    • Nausea is ginger's strongest ground. Pooled analyses of clinical trials find that about 1 to 1.5 grams of ginger a day — roughly a thumb-sized piece of fresh rhizome, grated — measurably eases nausea in pregnancy, and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists lists ginger among the non-drug options for it. For motion sickness and for nausea during chemotherapy, the trial results are mixed but lean positive, as an addition to standard care rather than a replacement for it. Human trials
    • The pungency comes from gingerols — the bite compounds of the fresh rhizome. Drying or cooking converts some gingerols into shogaols, which are more pungent still. Dried ginger is not weaker ginger; it just works differently, which is why fresh and dried are not interchangeable in a recipe.
    • Per 100 g fresh, ginger provides about 80 kcal, potassium (415 mg), magnesium (43 mg) and a little vitamin C — but as with garlic, ginger is eaten by the spoonful, not the plateful. Its value is what a small amount does: flavour, warmth and the studied effects above, at almost no caloric cost.
    • Ginger also speeds the emptying of the stomach in clinical studies — food moves on rather than sitting — which fits its long traditional place at the end of rich meals. Human trials
    • Trials of ginger for joint pain and for exercise muscle soreness find small reductions in pain — worth having, honestly stated as small. Human trials
    • When to plant: Start a plump rhizome indoors in late winter, grow it on in a wide pot through summer, and bring it in before the first frost
    • Sun: Some shade — light shade suits it best
    • Soil: Rich, moist, well-drained soil
    • Environment: Tropical and slow: it wants eight to ten warm months
    • Planter or ground: Pots — a wide container suits the spreading rhizome
    • Spacing and depth: Set the rhizome just under the surface, its pale buds (the eyes) facing up
    • Water: Likes water — keep it moist and warm while it wakes; sprouts can take weeks
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Young ginger can be lifted from about four months; mature ginger is ready at eight to ten months, when the leaves yellow and fall

    Garden notes

    • The leaves are not a food. With ginger, the harvest is the rhizome alone — the green top is the plant's engine, not an ingredient.

    Propagation

    Cut a firm rhizome into pieces 1 to 1½ inches long, each with at least one eye (bud), and let the cut faces dry for a few days so they callus over. Plant about 1 inch deep in early spring, once frost is past. Ginger does not grow from seed — a piece with no eye will rot, not sprout.

    Safety

    • In the amounts used in food and in the trials above, ginger is considered safe, including in pregnancy. High-dose ginger supplements are a different matter — they can cause heartburn, may add to the effect of blood-thinning medicines, and their use late in pregnancy is debated — so concentrated supplements are worth a word with a clinician first.
    • Essential oils are concentrates, many times stronger than the plant itself. Always dilute in a carrier oil before putting one on skin, and never swallow an essential oil.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — Ginger root, raw
    • Viljoen et al. (2014) — pooled trials of ginger for nausea in pregnancy
    • American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists — ginger among non-drug options for nausea in pregnancy
    • NCCIH — Ginger: usefulness and safety
    • Hunt et al. (2013) — inhaled ginger essential oil for postoperative nausea, in 301 people

    Kale

    Brassica oleracea (Acephala Group)

    Culinary

    Bone HealthEye Health

    FreshCooked

    Kale is what cabbage was before it learned to fold. It belongs to one of the most remarkable species in the garden: Brassica oleracea, the wild cabbage of Europe's coasts, which human hands have bred into cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, kohlrabi and kale — one plant, many bodies. Of them all, kale stayed closest to the wild leaf.

    Cultivars

    Curly kale ('Winterbor', 'Blue Curled Scotch')

    the standard: tightly frilled blue-green leaves on sturdy plants, sweetest after frost. The kale of Dutch stamppot and German Grünkohl.

    Lacinato ('Nero di Toscana', dinosaur kale)

    long, strap-shaped leaves of blue-black green, blistered like reptile skin, from Tuscany. Milder and sweeter than curly kale, and the leaf for ribollita soup and for kale salads.

    Red Russian

    flat, oak-shaped leaves with purple stems and veins, tender enough to eat raw when young. It came from Siberia with Russian traders to Canada around 1885, and it is the mildest of the common kales.

    Redbor

    curly kale in deep wine-purple, bred in the Netherlands: ornamental enough for a flower border, fully edible, and its colour deepens with cold.

    Siberian

    very large, gently frilled leaves on exceptionally cold-hardy plants; the kale for the shortest seasons and the deepest winters.

    Netherlands — boerenkoolstamppot: curly kale boiled and mashed through potatoes with a knob of butter, served with smoked sausage and gravy — the Dutch winter national dish.
    Germany — Grünkohl: kale braised low and slow with onions and served with Pinkel sausage and cured pork, traditionally after the first frost, and the centre of north German kale festivals and kale tours.
    Portugal — caldo verde: potatoes simmered and mashed into a broth, with kale (the flat couve) shaved into ribbons so fine they cook in a minute, and a slice of chouriço on top.
    Scotland — kale as the household green for centuries: kail broth with barley, kale with oatmeal, and the kale yard outside every cottage door.
    • Kale's wild parent still grows on limestone cliffs along the coasts of Europe, by the Mediterranean Sea and the Atlantic Ocean. It grows as a loose rosette — a low, flat ring of leaves — with waxy blue-green leaves. It can live with salt in the air, and it is tough.
    • The Greeks and Romans grew leafy kales. More than 2,000 years ago, Cato the Elder, a Roman writer, praised leaf cabbage above all other vegetables.
    • Curly kale became the winter green of northern Europe. It turns sweeter after frost, and it stands in the garden when little else will grow. In Scotland, the kale yard — the kail yairt in the old Scots tongue — was the household garden itself. For a long time, the word “kail” meant the dinner, not just the plant.
    • Colonists carried kale to North America. There it stayed a local green for hundreds of years — for a long time it was the garnish leaf laid under salad-bar bowls. Then people learned how rich in nutrients it is, and in the 2010s it became famous. The plant had not changed. The attention had.
    • Its brothers and sisters tell the family's story. Cabbage is the same leaf folded into a ball. Brussels sprouts are buds that grow along its stem. Broccoli and cauliflower are its flowers, bred to grow huge. Kale kept the first, simple shape — an open ring of leaves. A Roman farmer would still know it at a glance.
    • Vitamin K above everything: raw kale carries about 390 µg per 100 g — more than three times the daily value in a single serving's worth of leaves. Vitamin K is the vitamin the body uses to clot blood normally and to maintain bone.
    • At only about 35 kcal per 100 g, kale also provides vitamin C (about 93 mg, a full day's worth), vitamin A (about 241 µg RAE, from beta-carotene) and folate — the nutrient profile that put it at the top of the nutrient-density rankings.
    • Calcium worth counting: about 254 mg per 100 g, and kale's calcium is unusually well absorbed. Kale is low in oxalates — the compounds that lock calcium away in spinach — and studies find roughly 40% or more of kale's calcium is taken up by the body, comparing well with the calcium in milk.
    • Kale carries the eye pigments lutein and zeaxanthin in quantity (about 6 mg per 100 g) — the yellow pigments that gather in the retina, shared with green beans and sweet corn.
    • Like all its cabbage kin, kale contains glucosinolates — the family's sulphur defence compounds — which break down when the leaf is chopped into the pungent compounds studied for their protective effects in the diet. Population studies link diets rich in these vegetables with lower rates of several cancers; that is a dietary pattern, not a promise from any single leaf.
    • Caution: kale is one of the richest vitamin K foods there is, so people who take warfarin are advised to keep their intake of it steady from week to week — not to avoid it, but not to swing between none and a great deal either.
    • Caution: kale contains goitrogens, compounds that can interfere with the thyroid's use of iodine. At honest strength: in ordinary servings this is not a concern for healthy people; the risk belongs to eating very large amounts of raw kale day after day, especially where iodine is short. Cooking reduces the goitrogens, and kale is among the milder brassicas for them.
    • When to plant: Sow indoors in early spring or outside from spring; sow again in late summer for autumn and winter picking
    • Sun: Full sun, or a little shade in hot summers
    • Soil: Rich, firm soil that holds moisture
    • Environment: Cool-season and very hardy — frost converts some of the leaf's starches to sugars, so kale picked after a frost is sweeter. Net against cabbage white caterpillars
    • Planter or ground: Both — one plant to a large pot
    • Spacing and depth: 45 cm apart; sow 1 cm deep
    • Water: Likes water in dry spells
    • Companion plants: Onions, garlic and herbs are good neighbours
    • When to pick: From about 55 days, pick the outer leaves and leave the growing crown — one plant gives for months

    Garden notes

    • Pick it as cut-and-come-again: take the outer leaves and leave the growing crown, and one plant gives for months. Kale is biennial — in its second spring it flowers, and those flowers are early, generous food for bees; let one plant go and you can save seed.
    • Eat the stems too. The thick midrib is the part cooks strip out for salads — but chopped and cooked a few minutes longer than the leaf, or pickled, the stems are crisp and good. With kale, leaf and stem are both food; only the oldest woody base is for the compost.
    • It shares the cabbage family's pests, above all the cabbage white butterfly, whose caterpillars can skeletonise a plant. A fine net over the row is the simple answer, and it keeps the harvest clean without sprays.

    Propagation

    Sow seeds ½ inch deep outdoors as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, or start them indoors about four weeks before setting them out. Kale likes cool weather and soil between 55 and 75°F. Keep the soil damp until the seedlings are up — a dry crust on the surface stops them sprouting evenly.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — Kale, raw
    • Heaney & Weaver (1990) — how well kale's calcium is absorbed
    • NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Vitamin K fact sheet

    Corn

    Zea mays

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Urinary Health

    DriedCooked

    First, the plain fact: corn is a grain. Botanically it is a giant grass, and its ear is a cluster of grains — seeds — on a cob. Sweet corn is eaten young and milky, as a vegetable, but the plant's life and history are the life of a cereal, kin to wheat, rice and sorghum, and one of the three grains that feed the world.

    Cultivars

    Sweet corn ('Golden Bantam' and the modern supersweets)

    bred to hold sugar in the kernel and eaten young, in the milk stage, as a vegetable. Golden Bantam (1902) made yellow sweet corn America's standard; modern supersweet types stay sweet for days after picking instead of hours.

    Dent corn

    the world's bulk corn, named for the dent that dimples each kernel as it dries. Field corn: ground for meal and masa, fermented, and fed to livestock. Most corn grown on earth is dent.

    Flint corn

    hard, glassy kernels in bright colours — reds, blues, oranges, calico mixes. Traditional for polenta meal in Italy and for the ornamental ears of autumn; modern selections like 'Glass Gem' are grown for their beauty and still grind into meal.

    Flour corn

    soft, starchy kernels that grind easily to fine flour. The corn of the Hopi and other Pueblo peoples, whose blue varieties are bred from centuries of dryland selection.

    Popcorn

    the oldest type of all, close to teosinte's form: a hard hull seals each kernel so steam builds inside until it bursts. Popped corn has been found in ancient Peruvian and Mexican sites thousands of years old.

    Blue corn (Hopi types)

    flour corn in deep blue-purple, carrying the anthocyanin pigments; the corn of blue cornmeal, tortillas and Hopi piki bread.

    Mexico — the homeland: nixtamal ground to masa for tortillas and tamales — the tamales steamed in corn's own husks — pozole of whole hominy kernels, and elote, corn on the cob grilled and dressed with lime, salt, chilli and cheese.
    Italy — polenta: cornmeal stirred to a thick porridge in the north, where corn arrived in the 1600s and became the poor person's staple — with pellagra in the regions that never learned nixtamalization.
    American South — grits, ground from hominy — which is nixtamalized corn, the old technique surviving under another name — and cornbread from stone-ground meal.
    Africa — stiff cornmeal porridges under many names: ugali in East Africa, nsima in Malawi, sadza in Zimbabwe, eaten by hand with greens and relishes — corn, an American plant, become an African staple within a few centuries.
    • Corn was bred from teosinte, a wild grass that grew in the Balsas River valley in Mexico. This began about 9,000 years ago. Teosinte's ear is hard to recognise — it is only a few centimetres long, with about a dozen kernels, and each kernel is sealed in a hard, stony case. Indigenous farmers — the first peoples of the Americas — chose the best plants, generation after generation. In time, they turned it into an ear with hundreds of bare kernels. Those kernels cannot scatter on their own, and the plant cannot live without human hands. Corn is a plant that exists only because people do.
    • It spread the length of the Americas — the whole way up and down the two continents. Everywhere it landed, people changed it: corn with giant kernels in the Andes, flour corns in the Southwest, and flint corns in the north. The Maya and Aztec worlds ran on it. Even the word maize comes from mahís, the Taíno name for it, which passed into Spanish.
    • The cooks of Mesoamerica — the region of Mexico and Central America — made a discovery as important as the plant itself. It is called nixtamalization. They soaked and cooked the kernels in water made alkaline — the opposite of acid — with slaked lime (calcium hydroxide, made from burned limestone) or with wood ash. This loosens the hulls so they slip off. It adds calcium from the lime. And it frees the niacin — vitamin B3 — which corn that has not had this treatment keeps locked in a form the body cannot use. Later, corn travelled to poor parts of Europe and the American South without this way of cooking it. There, a sickness called pellagra followed it. Pellagra comes from not having enough niacin. Where the way of cooking travelled with the corn, the sickness did not come.
    • After 1492, corn crossed the oceans. Within two hundred years, it had become a staple food — a main food people depend on — from Africa to China. Today, its descendants fall into five great kernel types: dent, flint, flour, sweet and popcorn. All of them come from one Mexican grass.

    Traditional medicine

    • The rest of the plant has its traditional uses: corn silk — the strands from the ear's tip — is dried for a mild traditional tea, and the husks and cobs work in the kitchen (see Around the World and the Growing Guide). The silk tea's reputation as a diuretic is folk use; the evidence for it is thin, and it is stated here as tradition, not treatment.

    Craft

    • The husks are a craft material: soaked until soft, they are woven and braided into mats, baskets, dolls and chair seats — a craft carried from Indigenous American makers into folk tradition today.
    • The dried cobs became smoking pipes — hollowed out and fitted with a stem — in the Missouri meerschaum tradition that began in the 1860s. And purple corn gives a dye: the dark pigment in the purple kernels and cobs colours cotton and wool, a use dyers and researchers have brought back in recent years.
    • As a vegetable, sweet corn provides about 86 kcal per 100 g, fibre (about 2 g), vitamin C (about 7 mg), folate and B vitamins — a modest, useful profile, and yellow corn carries the eye pigments lutein and zeaxanthin (about 0.6 mg per 100 g), shared with kale and green beans.
    • As a grain, judge it whole: whole-grain cornmeal carries about 7 g of fibre per 100 g, with iron and magnesium — but only if the whole kernel, germ included, is ground. Degerminated meal, stripped for shelf life, loses much of both fibre and minerals. The whole kernel is the point.
    • Blue and purple corns carry anthocyanins — the same pigment family that colours blueberries and Okinawan sweet potatoes — in the outer layers of the kernel. Colour, again, is a fair guide to content.
    • Nixtamalization is that rare thing, a processing step that adds nutrition: masa and hominy gain calcium from the lime and niacin the body can actually use. The tortilla is nutritionally more complete than the raw kernel it came from.
    • Corn's starch makes it an energy food first. Sweet corn's glycaemic index is moderate — around the low 50s — so it raises blood sugar at a middle pace, neither the spike of white bread nor the steadiness of beans. Eaten as one part of a mixed plate, as it almost always is, that is an ordinary place for a staple grain to sit.
    • When to plant: Sow outside after the last frost, into warm soil, or start in pots a few weeks earlier
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Rich soil — a hungry crop; work in compost before sowing
    • Environment: Warm-season, with no patience for frost; plant in blocks, not single rows, so the wind can carry the pollen from the tassels to the silks
    • Planter or ground: Ground — it needs a block of plants to pollinate well
    • Spacing and depth: Sow 2.5 cm deep, 30 cm apart, in blocks
    • Water: Likes water, above all while the ears are swelling
    • Companion plants: Beans and squash are the classic partners — the Three Sisters: corn gives the beans their pole, and squash shades the soil
    • When to pick: About 70–90 days; an ear is ready when the silks have browned and a thumbnail pressed into a kernel gives milky juice

    Garden notes

    • A warm-season, hungry, thirsty grass: full sun, rich soil, steady water, and no patience for frost. It grows fast enough to watch.
    • Corn is wind-pollinated, so plant it in blocks, not single rows. The tassels at the top are the male flowers; their pollen must fall on the silks below, and every single strand of silk leads to one kernel — a gap-toothed ear is a map of the silks the pollen missed. This is also the Three Sisters' pole: corn gives the beans their trellis.
    • The whole plant works. Husks wrap tamales and dry into crafts and braided goods; spent cobs simmer into stock and corn-cob jelly and smoulder for smoke flavour; the stalks chop down into mulch and compost that return the plant's bulk to the soil.
    • Save seed from open-pollinated varieties only, and from many plants at once — corn inbreeds quickly, and seed from a handful of ears weakens within a few generations. Hybrid sweet corn seed will not come true, and its kernels are the one part of this plant that belongs to the seed companies.

    Propagation

    Sow seed straight where it will grow, once frost is past and the soil is warm, about an inch deep. Corn is pollinated by wind, so plant a block of several short rows, not one long row, or the ears come out patchy.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — Corn, sweet, yellow, raw
    • USDA FoodData Central — Cornmeal, whole-grain, yellow
    • Matsuoka et al. (2002) — corn's domestication from teosinte
    • Grobman et al. (2012) — ancient popped corn in Peru

    Collard Greens

    Brassica oleracea var. viridis

    Culinary

    Bone HealthEye Health

    Cooked

    A loose-leafed brassica that never learned to make a head — and never needed to. Collards are cabbage's older, plainer branch: broad flat leaves on a sturdy stalk, bred for the leaf alone, and one of the oldest greens in cultivation. In the American South they became far more than a vegetable.

    Cultivars

    Georgia Southern (Georgia)

    the heirloom standard of the South: tall plants with large, smooth, blue-green leaves and a mild flavour that sweetens after frost. Slow-cooked greens and big harvests.

    Vates

    a compact, blue-green type bred in Virginia (the name carries the state's experiment station initials): shorter plants, tender leaves, and notably slow to bolt in spring. Gardens and smaller spaces.

    Champion

    a Vates-type hybrid selected for dark blue-green colour, heavy yields and extra bolt resistance, with leaves that hold well in the field. Market gardens.

    Morris Heading

    an old North Carolina heirloom that half-folds its leaves into a loose, open rosette — as close as a collard comes to heading. A curiosity with true heritage flavour.

    Tiger Hybrid

    fast and vigorous, with bright green, slightly savoyed leaves; ready sooner than the heirlooms. Early harvests.

    American South — the classic: greens simmered with smoked turkey or ham hock, finished with vinegar and pepper sauce, the pot liquor soaked up with cornbread. A New Year's plate with black-eyed peas and pork is eaten for luck and prosperity.
    Brazil — couve: collard leaves rolled tight, shaved into the thinnest ribbons and flash-cooked with garlic — the green that always sits beside feijoada, the black-bean stew.
    East Africa — in Kenya, sukuma wiki — "stretch the week" — is kale's close kin cooked with onion and tomato to make a small piece of meat feed everyone; collards step into the same role wherever they grow.
    Portugal — caldo verde, the green soup: potato broth with collard-family leaves shaved hair-fine and stirred in at the last moment, so they stay bright.
    • Collards come from wild cabbage that grew on the coasts of Europe. They keep that oldest form. Long before anyone grew a cabbage with a tight head, people in Greece and Rome grew loose-leafed brassicas — cabbage-family plants — of just this kind. Collards are one of the earliest branches of the Brassica oleracea family tree. They are kin to kale. Like kale, people chose and grew them for their leaves, not for a bud.
    • The plant crossed the Atlantic early. Collards were growing in North America by the 1600s. People also grew them in Africa, where leafy brassicas fitted well into long traditions of greens cooked for a long time.
    • In the American South, enslaved African cooks made collards their own. They cooked the greens low, for a long time, with smoked meat. They saved the cooking liquid — called pot liquor — and prized it. It was cooking built on patience and on making much from little. It turned a hardy garden green into a key part of African diaspora foodways — the food traditions carried across the ocean by African people, and kept through the crossing and the hundreds of years after it. Collards are still a dish of gathering and memory. People cook them for New Year's Day — where, by tradition, their green colour is said to promise money in the year ahead — and for tables where everyone is fed.
    • Today's varieties grow out of that heritage — that history handed down. They include flat-leafed Southern standards, blue-green types bred to stand up well to frost, and hybrids — crosses bred on purpose — bred for tender leaves and for bolting late. To bolt is to rush up into flower and seed.
    • Per 100 g raw, collards give: 32 kcal per 100 g raw, with vitamin K at 437 µg — more than three and a half times the daily value — vitamin C at about 35 mg (39% of the daily value), folate at 129 µg (about a third of the daily value) and fibre at about 4 g.
    • Unusually rich in calcium for a leaf: about 232 mg per 100 g, rivalling kale. And unlike spinach, collards are low in oxalates — the compounds that lock calcium away — so more of that calcium is available to the body. That pairing is rare among greens.
    • Rich in vitamin A (about 251 µg RAE per 100 g) in the form of beta-carotene, which the body converts as needed, and in lutein — a pigment concentrated in the eye, where it helps filter light. Collards carry about 4,300 µg of lutein and its partner zeaxanthin per 100 g, among the highest of any common vegetable.
    • Like all their brassica kin, collards carry glucosinolates — the sharp sulfur compounds behind the family bite — which convert as the leaves are chopped and cooked into compounds studied for how they help the body deal with harmful substances. Population studies link regular eating of cruciferous vegetables with lower rates of some cancers; that is a pattern across the whole family, not a proven prevention by collards alone.
    • The whole plant earns its place: the thick stems are food too — chopped fine and cooked a little longer than the leaves, or pickled — and long cooking is not waste here, because the pot liquor holds the vitamins that leach out. Tradition drinks it for good reason.
    • Caution: collards are very high in vitamin K, which matters for blood clotting. People taking warfarin or similar blood thinners should keep their intake of greens like these steady from week to week rather than swinging between none and a great deal, and mention it to their clinician — the same note that applies to kale.
    • When to plant: Sow in spring for summer picking, or in late summer in the South for autumn and winter greens
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Rich, firm soil that holds moisture
    • Environment: One of the toughest vegetables in the garden: it takes light frost easily and turns sweeter after it, and endures hot Southern summers. Net young plants against cabbage whites
    • Planter or ground: Ground best; large pots work
    • Spacing and depth: 45–60 cm apart; sow 1 cm deep
    • Water: Likes water in dry spells
    • Companion plants: Onions, garlic and herbs are good neighbours
    • When to pick: From about 55 days, pick the lowest leaves first — the plant keeps growing from its crown and gives greens for months

    Garden notes

    • One of the toughest vegetables in the garden: a cool-season crop that takes light frost easily, and in fact turns sweeter after it — the plant moves sugars into its leaves as protection against the cold.
    • Pick from the bottom up: harvest the lowest leaves first and the plant keeps growing from its crown, giving greens for months from one sowing. The thick stems go to the pot chopped fine, or to the compost.
    • Collards are biennial and share the brassica family's troubles — cabbage white caterpillars above ground, clubroot in the soil — so net young plants and rotate the bed, as with cabbage.
    • In hot Southern summers collards simply endure where other greens bolt and bitter, which is one reason they became the South's green in the first place.

    Propagation

    Sow seed in early spring or midsummer, about half an inch deep. Keep the top of the soil damp while the seeds sprout — if it dries out, they fail.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — Collards, raw
    • Davis & Morgan (2015) — Collards: A Southern Tradition from Seed to Table; the green's origins in Europe and West Africa and its place in Southern foodways
    • NC State Extension — collard growing: a biennial, cool-season crop that stands frost, bottom-up picking, and the standard Southern varieties

    Potato

    Solanum tuberosum

    Culinary

    DriedCooked

    A starchy tuber in the nightshade family — kin to the Tomato and Peppers — and the most consequential vegetable ever to leave the Americas. The tuber is the food, and it feeds more of the world than any crop but the grains. The rest of the plant, though, is not food at all.

    Cultivars

    Russet Burbank

    America's baking potato: long, brown, netted skin, fluffy dry flesh that falls apart into mash and fries crisp. Bred in the 1870s from Luther Burbank's work and still the standard baker and chip potato of North America.

    Yukon Gold

    a Canadian-bred golden: thin yellow skin, yellow flesh, buttery and moist, holding its shape better than a russet. The all-rounder — mash, roast, soups — and it needs less butter to taste rich.

    Kennebec

    a smooth, thin-skinned white potato with dense, flavourful flesh; the chipping standard and a fine roaster. An old Maine-bred variety still widely grown.

    Purple Majesty

    purple skin over deep purple flesh that keeps its colour cooked, and carries anthocyanins, the blueberry pigments, that white potatoes lack. Roasting and salads, for the colour as much as the eating.

    French Fingerling

    small, finger-shaped, with rose skin and yellow flesh shot through with red; waxy and firm, nutty in flavour. Roasted whole in their skins.

    Peru — the homeland: papa a la huancaína, cold sliced potatoes under a golden chilli-cheese sauce; and chuño, potatoes freeze-dried by Andean nights and days as they have been for centuries, keeping for years.
    Ireland — colcannon: mashed potato folded with cabbage or kale and butter, and champ, mashed with spring onions.
    India — aloo gobi, potato with cauliflower and turmeric; potato is so at home in Indian kitchens that its name, aloo, is the everyday word for the vegetable itself.
    Spain — tortilla española, eggs set around slow-cooked potato and onion; and patatas bravas, fried potatoes under a spicy sauce in every tapas bar.
    • The potato was first grown as a crop in the high Andes, in what is now Peru and Bolivia, near Lake Titicaca. That was some 7,000 to 10,000 years ago. Andean farmers bred thousands of kinds. The region still grows several thousand native kinds, in every colour and shape, suited to high ground, frost and thin soil.
    • Spanish ships took the potato to Europe in the late 1500s. It spread slowly at first. It is a nightshade — a plant in the same family as its cousin the tomato — and people did not trust it. Then things changed. It gave more food per acre than grain, and it grew in poor, cool ground. It became the main crop of northern Europe, and of Ireland above all.
    • Ireland's story must be told plainly. By the 1840s, a third of Ireland's people lived almost wholly on the potato. Most of them grew just one kind, the Irish Lumper, because it gave a big crop in poor soil. In 1845, potato blight arrived. Blight is a water mould, Phytophthora infestans — a tiny living thing that grows in water and rots the plant. It destroyed the crop year after year, in fields where nearly every plant was the same, grown from the same stock. Around a million people died, and more than a million left the country. The blight lit the fire. A food system built on one crop and one kind made it a disaster, in a country that sent other food abroad all through the famine. The lesson still stands: having many kinds is not decoration. It is survival.
    • Today's kinds grow out of that history. Russets were bred in America. Golden kinds came from the old European stock. Purple kinds keep the Andean colours. Now breeders go back to those Andean thousands, to look for strength against blight and toughness in a changing climate.
    • More than starch: a medium baked potato eaten in its skin (about 173 g) gives about 161 kcal with 3.8 g of fibre, about 926 mg of potassium — more than a medium banana — about 17 mg of vitamin C (roughly a fifth of the daily value) and a useful share of vitamin B6, which the body uses in energy metabolism and the nervous system. Per 100 g baked in skin: 93 kcal, potassium 535 mg, vitamin C 9.6 mg.
    • Much of the good sits in and just under the skin — fibre, potassium and B vitamins are concentrated there — so baking, boiling and roasting in the skin keeps what peeling throws away.
    • Cooked and then cooled, potatoes change in a useful way: some of their starch converts to resistant starch, a form that passes to the large intestine and feeds its microbes much as fibre does. Potato salad made ahead is not a lesser dish for it. The effect is real but modest — a point in the potato's favour, not a transformation.
    • Plainly stated: a baked potato raises blood sugar quickly — it is a high-glycaemic food eaten alone. Eating it with its skin, with fat, protein or vegetables alongside, and letting it cool, all blunt that rise. Portion and company matter more than fear.
    • Caution: potatoes defend themselves with glycoalkaloids — the plant's own bitter chemical defences, mainly solanine and chaconine — concentrated in the skin when it greens in the light, and in sprouts. Ordinary sound potatoes carry far too little to matter, but green, sprouted or bitter potatoes should not be eaten: trim nothing and hope; throw them out. Store potatoes in the dark to stop the greening.
    • Caution, for the whole plant: only the tuber is food. The leaves, stems, flowers and the little green berries the plant sometimes sets carry the same defences at full strength and are not food in any preparation.
    • When to plant: Plant seed potatoes — small tubers, or cut pieces each carrying an eye — in spring, a few weeks before the last frost
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Loose, rich, well-drained soil; earth up soil around the stems as they grow, so the tubers stay covered — a tuber that reaches the light turns green, and green is a warning sign
    • Environment: Cool-season; hard frost kills the tops. Rotate the bed on a three-to-four-year cycle with its kin, the tomatoes and peppers
    • Planter or ground: Both — grow bags and big pots give clean, easy crops
    • Spacing and depth: 30–40 cm apart, about 10 cm deep
    • Water: Likes water while the tubers are swelling
    • Companion plants: Beans, corn and marigolds are good neighbours. Keep apart from tomatoes — they share blight and other diseases
    • When to pick: New potatoes when the plants flower; maincrop when the tops die back, about 90–120 days. Store dark, cool and dry

    Garden notes

    • Potatoes are grown from seed potatoes — small tubers, or cut pieces each carrying an eye — planted in spring, never from the plant's true seed in an ordinary garden. Earth up soil around the stems as they grow: the tubers form on buried stems, and hilling keeps them covered, because a tuber that reaches the light greens — and greens are the warning sign named in the cautions above.
    • They are hungry, thirsty plants in mid-season, and they share the nightshade family's pests: Colorado potato beetle above ground, blight in wet summers. Rotate the bed on a three-to-four-year cycle with the tomatoes and peppers, their kin.
    • Harvest new potatoes when the plants flower, maincrop when the tops die back. Handle them gently and store them dark, cool and dry.
    • What the garden leaves behind: the haulms — tops — go to the compost only if blight-free, and never to any animal's feed. Only the tuber comes to the kitchen.

    Propagation

    Plant certified seed potatoes in spring, once the soil has warmed. Cut big tubers into pieces, each with at least one eye, and let the cut sides dry for a day or two before planting. Use certified seed potatoes only — shop potatoes can carry disease and may have been treated to stop them sprouting.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — Potatoes, baked, flesh and skin
    • International Potato Center (CIP) — domestication near Lake Titicaca about 8,000 years ago, and more than 4,000 native varieties still grown in the Andes
    • Spooner et al. (2005), PNAS — genetic evidence that the cultivated potato traces to a single domestication in Peru
    • Encyclopaedia Britannica — the Great Famine in Ireland: blight from 1845, about a million deaths and mass emigration
    • EFSA (2020) — risk assessment of the potato glycoalkaloids solanine and chaconine in food

    Pumpkin

    Cucurbita pepo

    Culinary

    Eye HealthImmune Health

    DriedCooked

    A true squash wearing a famous name. "Pumpkin" is not a species — it is what we call the round, orange, hard-shelled members of the squash family, and the best-known of them belong to Cucurbita pepo, the same single species as zucchini, acorn squash and spaghetti squash. One plant family, many forms — and nearly every part of this one is food.

    Cultivars

    Small Sugar (New England Pie)

    the pie standard since the 1800s: small, deep-orange, with dense, sweet, fine-grained flesh and little string. The pumpkin to cook with, not to carve.

    Connecticut Field

    one of the oldest American varieties, grown since the 1700s: large, tall, orange fruit. This is the jack-o'-lantern pumpkin — bred for size and show, with thinner, more watery flesh. Carve it; cook with its smaller cousins.

    Rouge Vif d'Étampes (Cinderella)

    a French heirloom, scarlet-red and flattened, said to be the model for Cinderella's carriage. Deep-flavoured flesh for soups and roasting, and the most ornamental fruit in the patch.

    Jarrahdale

    an Australian type in a slate blue-grey skin, with golden, dense flesh and a fine sweet flavour; it stores for months. Roasting and soups — and a reminder that "pumpkin" need not be orange.

    Kabocha

    a cousin rather than a true C. pepo pumpkin (from the C. maxima line): squat, dark green, with chestnut-sweet, dry, fluffy flesh. Japan's winter squash, now at home everywhere; simmered, roasted and in tempura.

    Mexico — the seeds take the lead: pepitas ground into pipián, the green seed sauces; and calabaza en tacha, pumpkin candied in piloncillo syrup for the Day of the Dead.
    Japan — kabocha simmered in dashi and soy until tender (kabocha no nimono), and cut thin for tempura; a winter staple eaten with the skin on.
    Italy — tortelli di zucca in Mantua: pumpkin pasta filling with amaretti and mostarda, sweet against savoury; and the blossoms, stuffed with cheese and fried, all summer.
    United States — pumpkin pie, the Thanksgiving dish: spiced custard in pastry, descended from the early colonial pumpkin cookery that once filled hollowed shells with milk and spices and baked them in the fire.
    • The squash story is one of the oldest in the Americas. Seeds of Cucurbita pepo grown by people were found in Guilá Naquitz cave in Oaxaca, Mexico, and they date back about 10,000 years. So squash was one of the very first plants grown as a crop on the continent. At first, people grew it for its seeds, in the days when the flesh was thin and bitter. Over thousands of years, growers bred it into the sweet, thick-walled fruit we know.
    • The Indigenous peoples of North America grew squash in the Three Sisters: corn, beans and squash planted together. The corn gave the beans a pole to climb. The beans fed the soil. The squash's big leaves shaded the ground and held its moisture. Pumpkin fields were part of that way of growing long before there was a name for it in English.
    • The word travelled too. The Greek word pepon, a large melon, became the French word pompon, and then the English word "pumpkin". Colonists met the fruit in the 1600s and leaned on it hard. Early New England cooks stewed it, dried it and baked it into everything, because it kept through the winter, when little else did.
    • The kinship is the surprise. Zucchini, acorn squash, delicata, spaghetti squash and the classic field pumpkin are all one species, C. pepo. They were bred in different directions — some for eating young and tender, some for growing huge, hard and orange. The great blue Hubbard and the kabocha of Japan are close cousins, from sister species, C. maxima and C. moschata. The butternut is in the C. moschata line.
    • The Halloween lantern custom came from Ireland and Scotland. There, people carved turnips first. In America, the bigger, softer pumpkin took their place.

    Craft

    • The craft use is carving: the thick shell is cut into lanterns at Halloween.

    The fruit

    • The orange is beta-carotene and its close relation alpha-carotene, which the body converts into vitamin A as needed: raw pumpkin carries about 426 µg RAE per 100 g — roughly 47% of the daily value — at only 26 kcal. Vitamin A supports normal vision and the immune system.
    • Pumpkin also carries lutein — a pigment concentrated in the eye, where it helps filter light — at about 1,500 µg per 100 g, alongside vitamin C (9 mg), vitamin E and potassium (340 mg per 100 g). A light food that is not an empty one.
    • Fibre is the flesh's quiet weakness: pumpkin flesh itself carries only about 0.5 g per 100 g — it is a watery, light vegetable, and its strengths are its carotenes and minerals, not bulk. Eat the seeds, and eat pumpkin alongside beans and grains, for the fibre it lacks.

    The seeds

    • The seeds are a second food inside the first. Pumpkin seed kernels — pepitas — are dense and rich: about 30 g of protein per 100 g, with magnesium at well over the full daily value per 100 g and a strong showing of zinc. A small handful is the sensible portion of a concentrated food.

    The flowers

    • The blossoms are food too: squash flowers, stuffed and fried in Italy as fiori di zucca and folded into quesadillas in Mexico, are eaten the day they open. Few vegetables offer fruit, seed and flower on one plant.
    • Caution: canned "pumpkin" deserves a plain word — the big commercial brands' purée is legally pumpkin but is mostly made from Dickinson squash, a tan C. moschata cousin bred for dense, sweet, deep-orange flesh. It is a good food and honestly labelled under the rules; it simply is not the round orange fruit on the label's picture. Fresh sugar pumpkins and canned purée can stand side by side with nothing to hide.
    • When to plant: Sow outside after all frost, into warm soil, or start indoors 3–4 weeks earlier
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Rich ground with plenty of compost — a hungry crop
    • Environment: Warm-season; the first frost ends it. Bees are essential — squash flowers are pollinated almost entirely by them
    • Planter or ground: Ground — field pumpkin vines can run 3–6 m; bush kinds fit smaller gardens and big pots
    • Spacing and depth: Sow 2.5 cm deep; 90 cm or more between plants
    • Water: Likes water while the fruit is swelling
    • Companion plants: Corn and beans are the classic partners — the Three Sisters; nasturtiums and marigolds draw in pollinators
    • When to pick: About 90–120 days; ripe when the shell resists a thumbnail and the stem turns corky. Cure in a warm, sunny spot for a week or two

    Garden notes

    • A warm-season giant: sow after frost into rich ground and give it room — the vines of a field pumpkin can run 10 to 20 feet, though bush and half-bush types fit smaller gardens. Bees are essential; squash flowers are pollinated almost entirely by them, and the native squash bees are first on the job at dawn.
    • Pick the blossoms male: the plant makes far more male flowers than it needs, and those — not the females with their tiny fruit behind the petals — are the ones for the kitchen, so the harvest costs nothing.
    • Fruit is ripe when the shell resists a thumbnail and the stem turns corky. Cure pumpkins in a warm, sunny spot for a week or two to harden the skin, and a pie pumpkin keeps for months in a cool room.
    • Save the seeds twice over: a bowlful roasted for eating, and the best fruit's seed dried for next year's sowing — C. pepo kinds cross freely with each other, so grow one variety at a time if you want the seed to come true.

    Propagation

    Sow seed in spring, once the frost has passed and the soil is warm — at least 60°F. Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks early, one seed per pot, or sow straight outside, 1 inch deep. Give each plant lots of room — the vines run far — and thin to the strongest seedling.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — Pumpkin, raw
    • USDA FoodData Central — Pumpkin and squash seed kernels, dried
    • Smith (1997) — early squash domestication at Guilá Naquitz, Oaxaca

    Strawberry

    Fragaria × ananassa

    Culinary

    Immune Health

    Fresh

    The garden strawberry is a newcomer wearing an ancient name, and it is not, in the botanist's sense, a berry at all. The red flesh we eat is the swollen base of the flower; the true fruits are the little seeds, the achenes, studded over its surface. None of that changes the eating.

    Cultivars

    Chandler

    a June-bearing classic from California: large, glossy, deep-red berries in one heavy early-summer flush, sweet with a little tang. The pick-your-own farm standard; eating fresh by the bowlful.

    Seascape

    a day-neutral that fruits from spring to frost: medium-large, firm, bright berries with dependable flavour all season. The home gardener's steady supply.

    Albion

    another day-neutral, bred in California: long, conical, very firm berries with high sugar, keeping quality commercial growers prize. Fresh eating and any use where the berry must hold its shape.

    Mara des Bois

    a French variety bred to taste like the wild woodland strawberry it descends from: small, soft, strong-smelling berries. Fragile and perishable — grown for flavour above all, and eaten the day they are picked.

    Pineberry (White Soul type)

    a white-fruited strawberry with red achenes and a flavour many describe as pineapple-tinged, after the species name itself. A novelty, and a reminder of the white Chilean parent in every strawberry's ancestry.

    England — strawberries and cream at Wimbledon, where the pairing has been the tournament's dish since the 1870s and tonnes of berries are eaten across the fortnight.
    Japan — the strawberry as luxury fruit: perfect berries given as gifts, layered into Christmas cakes, and folded into ichigo daifuku, a whole berry wrapped in sweet rice cake.
    Mexico — fresas con crema, strawberries in sweetened cream, sold at markets everywhere; the city of Irapuato, in Guanajuato, is known as the country's strawberry capital.
    France — the gariguette, an early, elongated, aromatic variety that opens the French season, and the Breton town of Plougastel, which has grown strawberries since Frézier's Chilean plants arrived in its region.
    • Wild strawberries are very old. The little woodland strawberry, Fragaria vesca, grows across Europe, Asia and North America. People gathered it for thousands of years, and Roman writers praised it. Gardeners in the Middle Ages grew it. Its flavour is strong, but its fruit is only the size of a thumbnail.
    • The big strawberry came from an ocean crossing and an accident of gardening. In 1714 a French officer, Amédée-François Frézier, carried plants of the Chilean strawberry (F. chiloensis) home to France. It was a white-fruited kind with large berries, long grown by the Mapuche. Planted in Brittany near the North American F. virginiana — brought over earlier for its hardiness and its scarlet fruit — the two American species crossed.
    • The hybrid appeared in Breton gardens in the 1750s: Fragaria × ananassa. It took size from one parent and flavour and colour from the other, and every garden strawberry on earth descends from that crossing. Its species name, ananassa, means "pineapple-like" — early growers thought its flavour recalled a pineapple.
    • Today's varieties branch from that one hybrid, into June-bearers that crop in one heavy flush and day-neutral types that fruit steadily all season. And breeders keep going back to the wild species for the flavour genes — the flavour built into the plant — that the hybrid has lost.

    Traditional medicine

    • The leaves have a folk history of their own: strawberry-leaf tea — from the wild woodland plant especially — is a mild, pleasant traditional infusion, long used as a gentle everyday tonic. That is folk strength, not trial evidence, and the page offers it as tradition only.
    • Vitamin C is the headline: about 59 mg per 100 g (65% of the daily value) — more, gram for gram, than an orange — at only 32 kcal per 100 g, with about 2 g of fibre and under 5 g of sugar. Sweetness without much sugar is the strawberry's real trick.
    • The red is anthocyanins, the pigment family that colours blueberries and red cabbage, and strawberries also carry ellagic acid and a spread of other plant compounds studied for their antioxidant roles — compounds that help protect the body's cells from damage. Trials feeding strawberries to volunteers have found modest improvements in some blood-vessel and cholesterol measures; promising results, stated at that strength — a good food, not a medicine.
    • Useful everyday minerals and vitamins in the background: manganese (about 0.39 mg per 100 g, 17% of the daily value), folate (24 µg) and potassium (153 mg).
    • Caution: strawberry allergy is real, though uncommon. It is kin to the rose family allergies, and some people who react to birch pollen find raw strawberries make their mouth itch — a cross-reaction that cooking usually settles. Anyone whose lips or throat swell with berries should take that seriously and stop.
    • Caution, a small one: strawberries sit near the top of the lists for pesticide residues on conventionally grown fruit, year after year. Wash them well; buy from growers you trust or grow your own where you can.
    • When to plant: Plant crowns or runners in spring; the crown must sit exactly at soil level — buried crowns rot, lifted ones dry out
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Rich, slightly acid soil that drains well
    • Environment: A hardy perennial; net the bed against birds, and mulch with straw under the fruit to keep it clean
    • Planter or ground: Both — pots and hanging baskets suit it well
    • Spacing and depth: 30–45 cm apart
    • Water: Likes water while the fruit is swelling — water the soil, not the fruit
    • Companion plants: Lettuce, spinach, onions and borage are good neighbours. Keep apart from cabbage-family plants
    • When to pick: Pick fully red, in the morning; June-bearing kinds crop heavily for a few weeks, day-neutrals give a steady handful from spring to frost

    Garden notes

    • Strawberries are perennial: a June-bearing bed crops heavily for a few weeks; day-neutrals give a steady handful from spring to frost. Full sun and rich, slightly acid soil; the crowns must sit exactly at soil level — buried crowns rot, lifted ones dry out.
    • The plant multiplies by runners, long stems that root new plants where they touch the ground. Pin the best runners down to renew the bed for free; cut the rest away so the mother plants feed fruit, not family.
    • The honest enemies: birds, who know the hour a berry ripens — net the bed — and grey mould in wet weather, beaten by spacing, air and picking ripe fruit promptly. Straw and mulch under the fruit keep it clean; the fruit's old English name may carry the memory of that straw.
    • Wash the harvest gently and only just before eating — water hastens mould — and hull after washing, so the flavour stays in the berry.

    Propagation

    Peg a runner's young plant down onto soil in summer, after fruiting, and cut it free from the parent once it has rooted. Only use runners from healthy plants, or you will pass disease on to the new plants. The first young plant on a runner, nearest the parent, is usually the strongest.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — Strawberries, raw
    • Darrow (1966) — The Strawberry: History, Breeding and Physiology; Frézier's Chilean plants of 1714 and the Brittany crossing that produced Fragaria × ananassa
    • Giampieri et al. (2012) — review of the strawberry's nutrition and health effects: vitamin C, anthocyanins and ellagic compounds

    Lemon Balm

    Melissa officinalis

    MedicinalCulinary

    Digestive HealthSkin HealthSleep

    FreshDried

    A lemon-scented perennial in the mint family, native to southern Europe and Central Asia and grown in herb gardens for well over a thousand years. The leaf is the part used — fresh, dried for tea, or as an extract — and it is also the plant's gift to bees: Melissa is the Greek word for honey bee, and bees work the small white flowers all summer.

    • People have used lemon balm since the time of the ancient Greeks. Greek doctors wrote about it more than 2,000 years ago. They used it for wounds and stings, and to calm the nerves.
    • About 1,000 years ago, the Persian doctor Avicenna praised it. He said it was a herb that lifts the spirits.
    • Through the Middle Ages, monastery gardens grew it. It became a standard herb of the European physic garden — a garden kept for medicine plants.
    • In Paris in 1611, Carmelite nuns began to make Eau de Mélisse — Carmelite water. It is a lemon balm spirit, a strong drink made from the herb. People took it for nerves and digestion. It became famous all over Europe, and it is still made today.
    • Gardeners carried the plant everywhere they settled. It spread far beyond its first home in southern Europe. Now it grows as a garden escape — a garden plant that has spread on its own — on roadsides across Europe and North America.
    • Melissa oil, rubbed on as a lotion, eased agitation in one small trial of 72 people with severe dementia — but a later review of aromatherapy in dementia found no strong evidence overall, so this rests on that one trial. Human · small

    Traditional medicine

    • Traditionally used to ease mild symptoms of stress and to help with sleep. European regulators accept both as traditional uses, resting on long-standing practice rather than strong trial proof.
    • Traditionally used for mild digestive discomfort such as bloating and wind, in line with its calming reputation.

    Craft

    • The leaf scents perfumes and soaps. It is also distilled with spices into Carmelite water, still sold as a scented water. The dried leaves also go into potpourri — the scented mixtures kept in bowls and sachets around the house.
    • In small laboratory studies in healthy volunteers, single doses of lemon balm extract increased self-rated calmness and took the edge off the mood effects of a stress test. These were short, small studies of single doses — they show a gentle calming effect is plausible, not that lemon balm treats anxiety.
    • In one small, open pilot trial — with no placebo group for comparison — adults with mild-to-moderate anxiety and sleep disturbance reported less anxiety and less insomnia after fifteen days of a lemon balm leaf extract. Without a comparison group, how much of that was the herb itself is unknown.
    • Lemon balm is often combined with valerian in sleep remedies, and the pair has been studied together, including in children with restlessness and sleep problems — again in studies without placebo controls, so the results are encouraging rather than proven.
    • On the skin, a cream made from lemon balm extract is a well-established traditional treatment for cold sores. In placebo-controlled trials, the cream shortened healing time and eased symptoms when applied early, at the first tingle.
    • Caution: lemon balm may add to the effect of sedative medicines and alcohol. Laboratory studies suggest it could interfere with thyroid hormone activity, so people with thyroid conditions or on thyroid medication should check with a clinician before using it medicinally. Its safety in pregnancy and while breastfeeding has not been established, so medicinal use is best avoided then.
    • When to plant: Sow seed in spring, or divide a clump; it self-seeds freely, so cut it back after flowering to limit the seedlings
    • Sun: Full sun or some shade
    • Soil: Ordinary soil
    • Environment: A hardy perennial that holds its ground well — and spreads fast, by root and by seed, so give it a contained corner
    • Planter or ground: Both — a pot keeps it in bounds
    • Spacing and depth: Sow on the surface — it needs light to sprout; 45 cm apart
    • Water: Average
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Harvest the leaves before flowering, for the strongest lemon scent; cut back after flowering for a fresh flush

    Garden notes

    • A strong bee plant: the flowers give nectar through a long season, and beekeepers have rubbed hives with the leaves for centuries to help keep bees settled.
    • A hardy perennial that holds its ground well, shading the soil through the summer.
    • Like its mint relatives it spreads fast — by root and by self-sown seed — which makes it good cover but means it can take over a bed if left unchecked.
    • The fresh leaves make a pleasant tea and can be used in the kitchen wherever a soft lemon flavour fits.

    Propagation

    Divide an old clump in spring or early autumn, or sow seed in early spring. Layering also works: pin a low, bendy stem under a little soil and it roots in 1–2 months. Keep it in a pot or cut the flowers off before they set seed — it spreads fast by seed and by runners.

    Safety

    • Essential oils are concentrates, many times stronger than the plant itself. Always dilute in a carrier oil before putting one on skin, and never swallow an essential oil.

    Sources

    • European Medicines Agency — Melissa officinalis (lemon balm leaf) monograph
    • Kennedy et al. (2002) — lemon balm and calmness in healthy volunteers
    • Cases et al. (2011) — pilot trial of lemon balm in anxiety and sleep disturbance
    • Koytchev et al. (1999) — lemon balm cream for cold sores
    • Shakeri et al. (2016) — review of Melissa officinalis
    • Ballard et al. (2002) — Melissa oil lotion for agitation in severe dementia, in 72 people

    Chamomile

    Matricaria chamomilla

    MedicinalCulinary

    Digestive HealthSkin HealthSleep

    FreshDried

    A feathery annual in the daisy family, native to Europe and western Asia, with small daisy-like flowers whose hollow, apple-scented centres give the plant away — the name comes from the Greek for "ground apple." The flower heads are the part used, picked fresh and dried for tea, or made into extracts. (This is German chamomile; the perennial Roman chamomile is a different plant.)

    Terpenes in this plant:

    • Chamomile is one of the oldest medicines ever written down. People in Egypt used it long ago and thought highly of it. Doctors in Greece and Rome gave it for fevers, for pains, and for women's health problems.
    • In England in Anglo-Saxon times — about 1,000 years ago — it was one of the Nine Herbs. These were sacred herbs named in an old healing charm, a kind of spoken spell for healing. There, chamomile was called maythe.
