    • In the Middle Ages, people grew it in monastery gardens and in physic gardens — gardens kept for medicine plants. They also scattered it on floors as a strewing herb, so its scent would sweeten the air in the room.
    • It became one of the everyday home teas of Europe. People drank it to help sleep, to settle the stomach, and to calm fretful — restless, upset — children. It has kept that place ever since.
    • Most of this history is about German chamomile. Its close cousin, Roman chamomile, lives for many years instead of one. It shares the same name, and people used it in much the same way.
    • The distilled oil is breathed in for calm and rubbed, diluted, on irritated skin. Human · small

    Traditional medicine

    • Traditionally used to aid sleep and ease mild anxiety and restlessness. European regulators accept chamomile flower for a range of traditional uses based on long-standing practice.
    • Traditionally used for mild digestive complaints — bloating, wind and mild cramping — and as a mouthwash for minor mouth and throat irritation.
    • On the skin, chamomile preparations are traditionally used for minor irritation and inflammation.

    Craft

    • The flowers are a dye: they give a clear, soft yellow on wool and cloth, and chamomile was one of the old European dye plants of the home dyer.
    • Chamomile’s best-known craft is the hair rinse: a strong infusion of the flowers, poured through fair hair, brightens blonde hair — the use that made it a bathroom staple long before it was a tea.
    • In the best-known trial, 57 adults with mild-to-moderate generalised anxiety took a standardised chamomile extract or a placebo for eight weeks. Anxiety scores fell somewhat more with chamomile — a modest effect, in a single small trial.
    • In a longer follow-up study, people with more severe anxiety who had responded to chamomile kept lower anxiety scores when they continued it than when switched to a placebo, though it did not clearly prevent relapse. Promising, but still one research group's work.
    • For sleep, reviews pooling the small trials find chamomile improves how people rate their sleep quality — but not how long they sleep — and the one trial in people with chronic insomnia found no benefit. A cup of chamomile tea at bedtime is a reasonable ritual; it is not a proven treatment for insomnia.
    • Caution: do not use if you are allergic to plants in the daisy family, such as ragweed, chrysanthemums or marigolds — allergic reactions, rarely serious, are documented. Chamomile may add to the effect of sedatives, and there is a published case report of it interacting with the blood thinner warfarin, so check with a clinician if you take blood-thinning medicine. It may have mild estrogen-like effects. Medicinal amounts are best avoided in pregnancy, as safety has not been established.
    • When to plant: Sow seed in spring, on the surface, in a sunny spot; it self-sows freely once established
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Poor, sandy, well-drained soil — a light feeder that grows happily where richer feeders struggle
    • Environment: A hardy annual, flowering through a long season
    • Planter or ground: Both
    • Spacing and depth: Scatter on the surface and press in — it needs light to sprout; thin to 25 cm
    • Water: Average — drought-tolerant once settled
    • Companion plants: A traditional companion in vegetable gardens, valued for drawing in the hoverflies and lacewings whose young eat aphids
    • When to pick: Pick the flower heads on dry days, just as they open fully — keep picking to keep the flowers coming; dry them quickly out of direct sun for tea

    Garden notes

    • The flowers are worked by bees, hoverflies and other small beneficial insects through a long flowering season.

    Propagation

    Scatter the tiny seed on the soil surface in spring after the last frost, or start indoors 4–6 weeks earlier — do not cover it, as it needs light to sprout. Keep the soil moist until seedlings appear in 1–2 weeks, then thin to 8–12 inches apart. It reseeds itself freely, so new plants often return on their own.

    Sources

    • Amsterdam et al. (2009) — chamomile extract for generalised anxiety
    • Mao et al. (2016) — long-term chamomile for generalised anxiety
    • Hieu et al. (2019) — review of chamomile for sleep quality and anxiety
    • European Medicines Agency — Matricaria chamomilla (chamomile flower) monograph
    • NCCIH — Chamomile: usefulness and safety
    • National Association for Holistic Aromatherapy — German Chamomile profile — the distilled oil, its chemistry and uses

    Valerian

    Valeriana officinalis

    Medicinal

    Sleep

    Dried

    A tall perennial native to Europe and Asia, with flat heads of sweet-scented pink-white flowers in early summer. The root — dug in autumn, and strong-smelling once dried, with a smell often compared to old socks — is the medicinal part, used for sleep and nervous tension since the time of Hippocrates and Galen. It is the classic herbal sleep herb, and also the one whose trial record most plainly disagrees with itself.

    Terpenes in this plant: ·

    • Valerian has been used as a medicine for about 2,000 years. Hippocrates wrote of its uses, and Galen, the Roman physician, prescribed it for sleeplessness.
    • Its name is usually traced to the Latin word valere — to be strong, to be well.
    • In medieval England it was called all-heal, a name that says how widely it was used. It was grown in physic gardens — gardens of healing plants — all across Europe.
    • It kept its place as the herb for troubled nerves. In the First World War it was given to soldiers with shell shock. In the Second World War it was given to civilians shaken by air raids.
    • That long record is why regulators still list it for sleep and nervous tension — even though its modern trials, read fairly, disagree with each other.
    • Valerian root oil is breathed in for sleep and nervous tension. Traditional use

    Craft

    • The root gives an oil for perfumery — only about 1% of the root, with a deep, earthy, mossy smell that perfumers use as a base note. Dried valerian roots were also laid among stored linen to scent it.
    • Traditionally used — and accepted by European regulators as a well-established medicine — for sleep disorders and for mild nervous tension. That regulatory standing reflects its long history and the overall balance of studies, not consistent proof.
    • The honest summary of the sleep research is that the trials disagree. One large analysis of 16 trials found people taking valerian more likely to say their sleep improved — but the studies were of mixed quality, and there were signs that positive results were more likely to be published. Other rigorous reviews found no significant effect on sleep, and people who feel they sleep better on valerian rarely show matching changes in sleep-lab measurements.
    • Because of that mixed record, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends against valerian as a treatment for chronic insomnia. Valerian is not a sleeping pill and should not be expected to work like one.
    • Where benefit appears, it tends to build over two to four weeks of nightly use rather than arriving on the first night.
    • Caution: valerian can cause headache, dizziness, stomach upset, vivid dreams and next-morning dullness in some people. A few people have the opposite reaction — feeling restless or stimulated rather than sleepy.
    • Caution: do not combine valerian with alcohol or sedative medicines, as the effects can add up. Stopping suddenly after long, heavy use has, in rare reports, caused withdrawal-like symptoms, so it is best tapered rather than stopped abruptly. Its safety in pregnancy and while breastfeeding is not established — avoid medicinal use then, and it is not recommended for children under 12. Rare cases of liver injury have been reported, mostly with products combining several herbs.
    • When to plant: Sow seed in spring, on the surface, or divide the roots; give it room at the back of a bed — it grows up to five feet
    • Sun: Full sun or some shade
    • Soil: Moist, rich soil — a plant of damp ground
    • Environment: A hardy perennial; its deep roots hold banks and heavy soils together
    • Planter or ground: Ground best; a large pot at a pinch
    • Spacing and depth: 45–60 cm apart
    • Water: Likes water — keep it moist
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Dig the root in the autumn of the second year; the flowers open in early summer

    Garden notes

    • The flowers are rich in nectar and draw bees, hoverflies and butterflies, including swallowtails, through early summer.
    • A deep-rooted perennial of damp ground that holds banks and heavy soils together.
    • Gardeners have long valued it in the compost heap, where the roots and leaves are said to draw earthworms and add minerals — a traditional practice rather than a tested one.
    • Cats are drawn to the root, which holds a compound much like the one in catnip.

    Propagation

    Sow seed in spring, barely covering it, as it needs light to sprout, or divide a clump in spring or autumn. It seeds itself freely, so cut off faded flowers if you do not want new plants popping up all over.

    Safety

    • Essential oils are concentrates, many times stronger than the plant itself. Always dilute in a carrier oil before putting one on skin, and never swallow an essential oil.

    Sources

    • Bent et al. (2006) — review of valerian for sleep
    • Taibi et al. (2007) — review of valerian trials
    • American Academy of Sleep Medicine (2017) — guideline recommends against valerian for chronic insomnia
    • European Medicines Agency — Valeriana officinalis (valerian root) monograph
    • NCCIH — Valerian: usefulness and safety
    • Plants For A Future — Valeriana officinalis: root oil used in perfumery
    • Battaglia — The Complete Guide to Aromatherapy — valerian root oil breathed in for sleep and nervous tension
    • Tisserand & Young (2014) — Essential Oil Safety — valerian root oil for sleep and nervous tension

    Papaya

    Carica papaya

    Culinary

    Digestive HealthImmune Health

    FreshCooked

    The fastest fruit tree that is not quite a tree. Papaya is a giant soft-stemmed herb with a single hollow trunk, a crown of huge hand-shaped leaves, and its fruit hanging in a column against the trunk — and it can go from seed to ripe fruit in little more than a year. It is really two foods in one skin: green, it is a crisp, firm vegetable for salads and pickles, full of a milky sap; ripe, it turns gold or orange, soft and sweet. That milky sap carries papain, an enzyme that breaks down protein, and half of this plant’s story — the tenderisers, the supplements, the cautions — hangs on that one enzyme.

    Cultivars

    • The world’s papayas fall into two great groups: the small Hawaiian ‘Solo’ types, one fruit for one person, and the large Mexican and Central American types, where one fruit feeds a family. The sex of the tree shapes the fruit — round from female trees, long and pear-shaped from hermaphrodite trees — which is why the same variety can look like two different fruits.
    • ‘Solo’ — the original Hawaiian type: 0.5–1 kg fruit with golden-orange skin and flesh, sweet and firm. Seed came from Barbados in 1911; it was named in 1919 and had Hawaii’s whole trade by 1936. Its seed breeds true and gives only female and hermaphrodite plants — no males.
    • ‘Kapoho’ (‘Kapoho Solo’) — a yellow-fleshed Solo selection from the 1950s, bred for the wet Puna rainforest: firm flesh that keeps and ships well. It is not engineered, and growers still plant it for markets, like Japan, that have been slow to accept the engineered fruit.
    • ‘Sunrise’ (‘Sunrise Solo’) — a red-pink fleshed Solo type, about 565 g a fruit, sweet, from the University of Hawaii; Jamaica exports it as its ‘Sunrise’ papaya.
    • ‘Maradol’ — the big papaya of Cuba and Mexico, and of the large-fruit shelf in American shops: long fruit of about 1.5–2.6 kg with salmon-red flesh and a thick skin that travels well.
    • ‘Red Lady’ — a hybrid from Taiwan (the ‘Red Lady 786’ of the Known-You seed company): fruit of 1.5–2 kg with red flesh, bearing from about nine months after planting, and tolerant of ringspot virus — it catches it less badly than most, though it is not immune. Grown commercially around the tropics.
    • ‘Tainung No. 1’ — another Taiwan hybrid: vigorous plants, red-fleshed fruit of about 1.1 kg with a pointed tip on the hermaphrodite fruit, grown widely across the Caribbean, Asia and Africa.
    • ‘Rainbow’ — the engineered one, named plainly as such. Rainbow is a first-generation cross of ‘SunUp’ and ‘Kapoho’: yellow-fleshed, pear-shaped fruit of about 650 g, carrying the ringspot-resistance gene described above. Released in 1998, it is most of Hawaii’s crop. Its parent ‘SunUp’ — red-fleshed, the first resistant line — is barely grown itself now; its importance is as Rainbow’s parent.
    Laos and Thailand — the green papaya’s greatest dish. In Laos it is tam mak hoong, “pounded papaya,” a national dish: shredded unripe papaya pounded in a mortar with chilli, lime and fermented fish. Carried into Thailand’s Lao-speaking Isan region, it became som tam, and from there a staple of all Thai cooking. An honest footnote: papaya and chilli both reached Asia from the Americas only a few centuries ago, so this ancient-tasting dish is, at most, a few hundred years old.
    The Philippines — atchara, green papaya pickled sweet-and-sour, served beside fried and grilled food; and green papaya wedges cooked into tinola, the ginger chicken soup.
    Vietnam — gỏi đu đủ, green papaya salad, shredded crisp with herbs.
    Puerto Rico and the Caribbean — ripe lechosa eaten fresh and in juices, and dulce de lechosa at Christmas: papaya simmered slowly in spiced syrup until it turns amber and chewy. Green papaya is candied the same way in Mexico.
    Mexico — ripe fruit with lime juice and a shake of chilli salt; agua fresca of papaya; and the big Maradol types as the everyday market fruit.
    India — the world’s largest producer: ripe fruit fresh everywhere, green papaya into curries, and the unripe fruit’s latex behind the tenderiser trade.
    Indonesia — the leaves, cooked as a bitter green — papaya is one of the few plants in this library eaten for fruit, seed and leaf alike.
    Hawaii — the breakfast fruit: half a Solo with a squeeze of lime, and the whole Solo and Rainbow story told above.
    • Papaya was first farmed in Mesoamerica — the lowlands of what is now southern Mexico and Central America — long before Europeans arrived. The Maya grew it and called it ababai; the word “papaya” itself came through Spanish from the Caribbean, where the Taíno word is usually given as paapaía. Both roots are still argued over, and both peoples had the fruit long before it had a European name.
    • The first European to describe it in writing was Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, in the 1520s: he recorded that seeds had been carried from the coast beyond Panama to Hispaniola, and from there to the other Caribbean islands. Columbus is said to have called papaya “the fruit of the angels” — the line is repeated everywhere and pinned on him, though it is a story attached to the fruit rather than a documented quote. It has followed the fruit ever since.
    • In the Caribbean it stayed what it had always been: a yard fruit, eaten ripe off the plant. Puerto Rico calls it lechosa. Cuba calls it fruta bomba — because in Cuba “papaya” is a rude slang word, so the polite name had to change.
    • The Spanish carried it across the Pacific to Manila in the mid-1500s, and from the Philippines it spread to Malaya and India by the end of that century; the Portuguese took it into Africa. Few crops have ever travelled so fast: within about two hundred years of Columbus it was growing around the whole tropical world. Today India grows more papaya than any other country — over a third of the world’s supply.
    • Hawaii got its first papayas in the early 1800s. The turning point came in 1911, when Gerrit Wilder brought seed of a small-fruited papaya from Barbados. Named ‘Solo’ in 1919 — one fruit, one person — it was Hawaii’s only commercial papaya by 1936, and its descendants, like ‘Kapoho’ in the 1950s, built the islands’ export trade.
    • Then the virus came. Papaya ringspot virus, spread by aphids, had already driven Hawaii’s growers from Oahu to the clean rainforest district of Puna. In May 1992 the virus was found in Puna itself, where almost all the islands’ papaya grew, and within two years the industry was in crisis. The answer came from a team led by Dennis Gonsalves: they gave the plant a piece of the virus’s own coat gene, which works like a vaccination — the plant becomes resistant to the virus. From that work came ‘SunUp’, and from SunUp crossed with Kapoho came ‘Rainbow’. Seed was released to growers on 1 May 1998, and it saved the Hawaiian industry. Rainbow is one of the first genetically engineered fruit crops ever sold for food, and most of Hawaii’s papaya is Rainbow today.
    • Around the tropics the plant was used as medicine as well as food — the milky latex, the seeds against worms, the leaves in fever remedies. Those uses are history; what the studies actually support is in Health Benefits.
    • Ripe papaya, per 100 g: 43 kcal, carbohydrate 10.8 g, sugars 7.8 g, fibre 1.7 g, protein 0.47 g. Its standout is vitamin C at 60.9 mg — about two-thirds of the daily value — with folate at 37 µg (about a tenth of the daily value) and a little vitamin A and potassium besides. Red-fleshed fruit also carries lycopene, the red pigment, at about 1.8 mg per 100 g. It is a light, sweet fruit, and the numbers say exactly that.
    • Green papaya is a different food from ripe: firm, crisp, barely sweet, and rich in the milky latex and its enzyme. It is cooked or pounded raw into salads — never eaten as a sweet fruit — and the latex largely fades as the fruit ripens. Almost everything below turns on which papaya you mean.
    • Papain is an enzyme — a substance that speeds up chemical work — that cuts protein apart. It is strongest in the latex of the unripe fruit. Its kitchen work is plain to see: papaya tenderises meat, green papaya and its leaves have been used to wrap and soften tough cuts across the tropics for centuries, and powdered papain is still sold as a meat tenderiser. That is a fact about an enzyme, not a health claim.
    • The supplement claims run ahead of the evidence. Papain and papaya preparations are sold for digestion, but there are no trials of whole ripe papaya for digestion. One small trial tested a made papaya product (not the fruit) in people with indigestion and found less constipation and bloating while they took it; the effect did not last after they stopped. The fruit itself offers nothing for digestion beyond its modest fibre — 1.7 g per 100 g, and modest is the right word for it.
    • Papaya leaf juice is a folk remedy for dengue fever across South Asia, and it has been studied. Reviews of the trials find that platelet counts — the blood cells that help clotting, which dengue drives down — rose faster in patients given leaf extract, but the trials were small and low in quality, and whether the higher counts actually help patients is unclear. The 2019 review’s conclusion was that the evidence is insufficient to recommend it. The claim is neither hidden nor oversold: it is not a treatment to rely on.
    • The seeds are food too, in their place: fresh or dried, they are peppery — hot like mustard or watercress, because papaya belongs to the same plant order as the mustards and carries the same family of sharp compounds. They are eaten as a seasoning, in pinches. Two cautions belong with them. In traditional practice the seeds were used against intestinal worms, and in one small trial in Nigerian children, air-dried papaya seeds with honey cleared worms in more children than honey alone — one small trial, stated at that size. And seed extracts have been studied in male rats and monkeys as a possible contraceptive: at concentrated extract doses, far beyond any seasoning use, sperm stopped and then returned when the extract stopped. That is animal research on extracts, not an effect of eating seeds — but it is a fair reason the seeds stay a pinch, not a bowlful.
    • Pregnancy, stated carefully, because this is where papaya warnings come from. In parts of Asia, papaya is traditionally avoided in pregnancy. The one proper study (in rats, 2002) found that ripe papaya juice had no effect on the womb and did the animals no harm — while crude papaya latex, the concentrated sap of the unripe fruit, made the womb contract strongly, the way the body’s own labour signals do. There is no human study either way. So the study’s line stands: ripe papaya is a normal food; unripe and half-ripe papaya, and above all its latex, are best avoided while pregnant.
    • One more caution, on the skin: papain ointments were used for decades to clean dead tissue from wounds, but in 2008 the US Food and Drug Administration ordered the unapproved ones off the market, after reports of severe allergic reactions, and noted their effectiveness was not supported by sound studies. Papain can also trigger reactions in people allergic to latex. The latex is a working chemical, not a home remedy.
    • First, what it is: not a true tree. Papaya is a giant herb — a single soft, hollow trunk with no real wood, topped by a crown of huge lobed leaves on long hollow stalks. Fruit hangs in a column against the trunk, under the leaves. Plants reach 5–10 m (16–33 ft) if they live that long, but they are short-lived, and most garden plants are replaced after three or four years, when the fruit is too high to pick.
    • The three sexes, plainly. Papaya plants come in three kinds: male plants, whose flowers hang on long branching stalks and which make no fruit; female plants, with big flowers held close to the trunk, which make round fruit but need a male or hermaphrodite nearby for pollen; and hermaphrodite plants, whose flowers carry both parts, pollinate themselves, and make the long, pear-shaped fruit the shops prefer. You cannot tell a seedling’s sex until it flowers, so growers sow several seeds in one hole and, once the flowers show, cut away all but one fruiting plant. Bred lines like Solo save the trouble: their seed gives no males at all.
    • Speed is the joy of it. Seed sprouts in about two weeks in warm soil, and in warm ground the first ripe fruit comes 9–14 months after planting — among the fastest of all fruit plants. After that, a healthy plant fruits nearly all year where frost never comes.
    • Climate: it wants heat, 70–90 °F (21–32 °C) for best growth. Below about 59 °F (15 °C) flowering falters and fruit can come misshapen. It is frost-tender in earnest — damaged or killed below 31 °F (−0.6 °C). Outdoors it belongs in USDA zones 9b–11, and even there a hard winter can take it. In cold climates it is a summer pot plant, handsome but rarely fruiting indoors.
    • Soil and water decide more than feeding does. Full sun; well-drained soil, always — papaya rots at the root and stem in standing water, and wet feet kill more garden papayas than cold does. Give steady water in dry weather, never a bog. Shelter it from strong wind: the stem is soft and shallow-rooted, and a laden plant topples.
    • Space plants 7–12 ft (2–3.7 m) apart, and keep them at least that far from buildings — the roots are not destructive, but the crown is wide and the fruit drops.
    • Picking: pick at colour break, when the first yellow streaks show on the green skin, and ripen the fruit at room temperature — it will sweeten and soften indoors. For home eating, fruit left to half-yellow on the plant tastes best, if the birds and fruit flies allow it. A scratched green fruit runs milky latex; a ripe one runs nearly clear — the plant’s own ripeness gauge.
    • The virus, for gardeners: ringspot virus is spread by aphids and has no cure. In virus country the practical answer is the growers’ one — plant fresh plants often (Florida guidance is to replant every 18–24 months) and take the fast crop while it lasts.

    Propagation

    Take the seeds from a ripe fruit, rub off the jelly-like sac round each seed and rinse them, then sow 2–4 seeds in a pot of clean mix. They come up in 2–3 weeks — keep the strongest seedling and snip the rest off. Grow 2–3 plants: seed can give male, female, or both-sex plants, and only female and both-sex plants bear fruit.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: papayas, raw — the nutrition figures
    • Adebiyi et al. (2002) — ripe papaya and papaya latex tested in pregnancy, in a rat model — the pregnancy caution and the ripe-fruit finding
    • Rajapakse et al. (2019) — papaya leaf extract in dengue: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the trials — platelet counts rose, evidence low in quality, insufficient to recommend
    • U.S. Food and Drug Administration (2008) — unapproved topical papain products ordered off the US market — the wound-ointment chapter and the allergy reports
    • Gonsalves (2004) — transgenic papaya in Hawaii and beyond — the ringspot virus, SunUp and Rainbow story
    • Crane (2016) — Papaya Growing in the Florida Home Landscape, UF/IFAS Extension (HS11/MG054) — the plant, its three sexes, climate, frost and growing

    Parsley

    Petroselinum crispum

    Culinary

    Vitamin KVitamin CVitamin A

    FreshCooked

    The world's most underrated leaf. Parsley spent the last century pushed to the edge of the plate as a garnish, a green sprig nobody ate — yet it is a real vegetable in the world's great food cultures, chopped by the cupful into salads, and one of the most nutrient-packed leaves in the whole kitchen. It is a bright green plant in the carrot family, with a fresh, clean, faintly peppery taste, grown in two leaf forms — tightly curled, and flat. It is also famously slow: its seed can take a month to sprout, and gardeners have told stories about where it goes in the meantime for hundreds of years.

    Terpenes in this plant:

    Cultivars

    • Garden parsley is sorted into three groups by what you harvest — the curled leaf, the flat leaf, and the root. The forms are told apart by leaf and use, because unlabelled photographs cannot honestly separate them.
    • Curly leaf (the Crispum group) — leaves tightly ruffled and crimped into a bright green moss, on a compact, tidy plant. The flavour is the milder of the two leaf types. This is the garnish parsley, and the prettiest edging plant in the herb garden — the kind Pliny already described in Roman times. 'Moss Curled' is its classic named form, bred for an extra-tight curl.
    • Flat leaf, or Italian (the Neapolitanum group) — flat, divided leaves like small celery tops, with a stronger, cleaner, fuller flavour that stands up to cooking. This is the cook's parsley: the one for tabbouleh, sauces and stews, and the type most kitchens mean when a recipe just says parsley.
    • 'Giant of Italy' ('Gigante d'Italia') — a flat-leaf form bred big: oversized leaves on long stems, plants reaching 2 ft (60 cm) or more, cropping heavily and regrowing fast. The choice for a kitchen that uses parsley by the bunch rather than by the sprig.
    • Hamburg, or root parsley (the Tuberosum group) — grown not for its leaf but for its root: a thick, white taproot like a pale parsnip, 6–8 in (15–20 cm) long, tasting of parsley crossed with celeriac. It is a standard soup vegetable in Germany, Poland and the Netherlands, dug in autumn and cooked in broths and stews. Its leaves can be used like flat-leaf parsley but are coarser.
    • One name to keep apart: Japanese parsley, or mitsuba, is a different plant (Cryptotaenia japonica) that merely looks similar — not Petroselinum crispum.
    Lebanon and Syria — tabbouleh, the salad that settles the garnish question for good: parsley is the main ingredient, chopped by the cupful, with a little bulgur wheat, tomato, mint, lemon and olive oil. Parsley here is not decoration; it is the dish.
    Italy — gremolata, Milan's finishing sprinkle of finely chopped parsley with lemon zest and garlic, spooned over braised veal (ossobuco) in the last minutes; and salsa verde, the green sauce of parsley pounded with capers, garlic and oil, served with boiled meats.
    Argentina and Uruguay — chimichurri, the standing sauce of the grill: parsley chopped with oregano, garlic, vinegar and oil, made by the bowlful wherever meat is roasted.
    France — persillade, parsley chopped with garlic and breadcrumbs for a crust; and the bouquet garni, parsley stems tied with thyme and a bay leaf into the little bundle that flavours French stocks, soups and stews and is lifted out at the end.
    The Jewish Passover table — karpas: a sprig of parsley sits on the seder plate and is dipped in salt water at the start of the meal — the green of spring and new growth, tasted with the salt of tears.
    Germany and Poland — root parsley goes into the soup pot as part of the classic bundle of soup greens, and the leaves go everywhere: over potatoes, into salads, and into Frankfurt's Grüne Soße, the green sauce of seven herbs in which parsley is a standing member.
    Turkey — maydanoz is sold in great bunches and eaten as a table green in its own right, tucked into wraps and salads and chopped through köfte mixtures — another kitchen where parsley was never a garnish.
    • Parsley comes from the central and eastern Mediterranean, where it still grows wild on rocky ground, cliffs and old walls — a plant of stony places, which its name remembers. It has been grown around the Mediterranean for more than 2,000 years.
    • The name is a description. Greek petroselinon joins petros, rock, to selinon, the Greeks' word for this family of plants — "rock celery," the celery-like plant of the rocks. Crispum is Latin for curled, after the curly type. English "parsley" came down through French from the same Greek word. One wrinkle matters for the story below: selinon covered both celery and parsley, two close kin in the same family, and old tellings do not always separate them.
    • Its great story is a sad one. At Nemea in Greece, the infant prince Opheltes — son of King Lycurgus — was under an oracle's warning: he must not touch the ground before he could walk. His nurse Hypsipyle, asked by seven passing heroes to show them a spring, set the child down for a moment on a bed of this plant. While she was gone a serpent killed him. The heroes slew the serpent, buried the boy, and renamed him Archemorus — "beginner of doom," a warning of their own fate. In the story as later generations told it, the first parsley sprang from the child's blood. The funeral games they held for him became the Nemean Games, one of the four great games of Greece, and the victors there were crowned with wreaths of the plant — in Hyginus's telling, parsley outright; the judges wore dark clothes in mourning. So parsley belonged to the dead in Greece: it was strewn on graves and woven into funeral wreaths, and to say of a dying man "he has need of nothing now but parsley" was to say he was as good as gone.
    • Homer knew the plant — in the Iliad, the horses of the Greeks graze in meadows where it grows. The Romans brought it to the table: they wore garlands of it at feasts, in the belief that it kept off drunkenness and ill luck, chewed it to sweeten the breath after garlic and strong food, and put it in sauces — Pliny, the Roman naturalist, already knew a curled kind. It crossed into the gardens of the early Middle Ages: Charlemagne's list of plants to be grown on his estates, drawn up around the year 800, names it.
    • In Britain the plant gathered a dark reputation of its own, all of it hanging on that slow seed. Gardeners said the seed went to the devil and back seven times — some said nine — before it would sprout, and that the devil kept a share of it for himself, which is why so much of it never came up. They said only the wicked could grow it well, or only a witch could make it germinate; that it was bad luck to transplant it, or to give away a root; that it grew best in a household where the woman was the boss; and that the safe day to sow it was Good Friday, the one day the devil had no hold on the soil. None of it stopped anyone growing it — but everyone who has waited five weeks over a parsley row understands where the stories came from.
    • In the old herbals, parsley was a medicine as well as a food: the herb and the root were used to make more urine and flush the waterways, and for kidney gravel, while the seed and its oil were used to bring on a woman's courses. Those uses are the background to the evidence — and to the safety line — in Health Benefits.
    • Fresh parsley, per 100 g: 36 kcal, protein about 3 g, fibre 3.3 g. The standout is vitamin K at 1,640 µg — more than thirteen times the whole day's value in that 100 g, and among the highest figures for any common food. Behind it: vitamin C at 133 mg, about one and a half times the day's value and more than the same weight of orange; vitamin A at 421 µg, about half the day's value; folate at 152 µg, over a third; iron at 6.2 mg, about a third; with useful calcium and potassium besides. Vitamin K is the vitamin the body uses to clot blood normally and to build bone. Now the honest scale: 100 g is about a cup and a half of chopped leaves — nobody garnishes at that scale, but tabbouleh eats parsley at exactly that scale, and even one cup (about 60 g) brings roughly 1,000 µg of vitamin K and 80 mg of vitamin C. Eaten as a vegetable, parsley is not a garnish's rounding error; it is one of the strongest leaves in the kitchen.
    • That vitamin K cuts both ways: people who take warfarin or a similar blood thinner are told to keep their vitamin K intake steady, because sudden changes work against the medicine. Eating parsley in suddenly much larger amounts than usual — a new daily tabbouleh habit, say — is worth mentioning to the clinician who manages the dose.
    • The water claim, at its real strength. Parsley has a long-standing name as a diuretic — something that makes the body pass more water. Germany's Commission E, the expert panel that judged herbal medicines, approved parsley herb and root for flushing the urinary tract in minor complaints and for kidney gravel — an acceptance of a traditional use, based on long use rather than on trials in people. The one solid experiment is in rats: rats drinking a parsley seed extract passed significantly more urine, apparently because the extract slowed a pump in the kidney that normally pulls sodium and potassium back into the body (Kreydiyyeh & Usta, 2002). No good human trial exists. So: a mild flushing effect is plausible and traditional — it is not a proven treatment for the kidneys, and parsley tea is not a medicine.
    • The plant is also rich in apigenin, a compound studied in laboratory dishes and in animals, where it calms inflammation and protects cells from damage. Those are dish and animal results. They are not proof that eating parsley does the same in a person.
    • And an old kitchen habit, kept honest: chewing a sprig of parsley after garlic does freshen the mouth for a while. The further claim — that its green pigment hunts down and neutralises garlic through the body — has never been properly tested.
    • The safety line, stated plainly: the leaf is food; the concentrated oil is not the leaf, and the two should never be swapped. Parsley seed oil is rich in a compound called apiol, which in concentrated amounts stimulates the womb and damages the kidneys and liver. The oil was misused in the past to end pregnancies, and it poisoned women who took it — the German panel gave parsley seed a negative verdict, and the distilled oil is not used as a medicine at all. Ordinary cooking amounts of leaf and stem are the normal, safe use of this plant. Medicinal amounts — strong teas taken as a treatment, extracts, and above all the oil — are not for pregnancy, and the oil should not be swallowed. One garden note: like several of its carrot-family kin, parsley carries compounds that can react with strong sun on skin — people who handle a great deal of it on bright days can get a blistering rash where the juice touched. Wash hands after a big harvest.
    • There is no human proof that parsley detoxes or cleanses the kidneys, dissolves kidney stones, or lowers blood pressure or blood sugar in people. The findings behind those claims are animal and laboratory work.
    • Parsley is a biennial, and the word needs one plain sentence: in its first year it makes a leafy rosette of leaves and a taproot; in its second year it sends up a flower stalk, makes seed, and dies. For leaves, it is grown as an annual — sow fresh each year. A plant that has started to flower turns bitter and stops making good leaves.
    • The seed, and its famous slowness: parsley seed takes two to five weeks to come up, and comes up unevenly. The seed coat carries natural compounds that hold sprouting back until they wash away. Gardeners fight back three ways: soak the seed overnight — up to a day — in warm water before sowing; sow shallow, about ¼ in (6 mm) deep, and keep the soil moist the whole time; and mark the row, because a row that looks empty for a month gets weeded or dug over by mistake — the old trick is to sow a pinch of radish in the same row, which comes up fast and shows where the parsley will follow. Buy fresh seed: parsley seed loses its strength quickly, and old seed is the commonest reason a row fails.
    • Starting: sow indoors eight to ten weeks before the last frost, or sow outside a few weeks before it — young parsley takes light frost well. Set plants out once they are growing strongly. Parsley grows a taproot and dislikes being moved once it is established, so transplant young, and handle the root gently.
    • Sun, soil and space: full sun, or part shade — parsley takes more shade than most herbs, which makes it useful at the edge of a bed. It wants rich soil that holds moisture but drains, around pH 6.0–7.0. Plants stand 12–18 in (30–45 cm) tall in their first year. Space leaf parsley about 6–8 in (15–20 cm) apart; root parsley wants deep, loose, stone-free soil — a forked root is what a stone does to it — and a little more room in the row.
    • Water and picking: keep the soil evenly moist in dry spells; a thirsty plant runs to seed early. Pick by cutting the outer stems at the base, a few from each plant, and never take more than about a third of a plant at once — the centre keeps growing and replaces them. Picking starts about 70–90 days after sowing and runs until hard frost: parsley is a hardy plant, shrugging off light frosts and staying green and pickable late into the cold months, and in mild gardens (zones 5–9) it often stands through winter under a light cover. It grows well in a deep pot of a gallon or more — deep, because of the taproot.
    • Second-year gifts: if you let one plant live into its second year, it repays you twice. Its flat-topped flower heads are a landing table for tiny parasitic wasps and hoverflies — the gardener's allies, which hunt aphids and caterpillar eggs. And its leaves are the food of black swallowtail caterpillars; many gardeners plant a spare plant for them on purpose and count the butterflies as part of the crop.
    • Seed of your own: seed is ripe when the flower heads have browned. Shake it out dry, keep it cool, and use it the next season — freshness is everything with this seed. Left alone, a second-year plant also sows itself, and a parsley patch can renew its own row for years.

    Propagation

    Sow seed where it will grow, ½ cm deep, in early spring and again in late spring and late summer for a steady supply. Use fresh seed. It takes a month or more to come up, so do not give up on it too soon. Sow it in place — it does not like its roots disturbed by moving.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: parsley, fresh — the nutrition figures
    • Kreydiyyeh & Usta (2002) — Diuretic effect and mechanism of action of parsley, Journal of Ethnopharmacology — the rat study behind the water claim
    • Bahramsoltani et al. (2024) — Parsley: an updated review of its traditional uses, chemistry and pharmacology, Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry — the evidence and safety picture, reviewed
    • Apollodorus (c. 2nd century CE) — The Library, Book 3 — Opheltes, renamed Archemorus, and the founding of the Nemean Games
    • Hyginus — Fabulae, 74 — the telling in which the child's bed, and the victors' wreath, are parsley
    • University of Minnesota Extension (2024) — Growing parsley in home gardens — types, sowing, spacing and harvest

    Passionflower

    Passiflora incarnata

    MedicinalCulinary

    Sleep

    Dried

    A vigorous climbing vine native to the southeastern United States, bearing intricate flowers — Spanish missionaries read the parts of the flower as symbols of the Passion of Christ, which gave the plant its name. The parts above ground — leaves, stems and flowers — are the medicinal part, dried for tea or made into extracts. Its golf-ball-sized fruit, the maypop, is edible and was a food long before the vine was a medicine.

    • The peoples of the southeastern Americas used passionflower long before Europeans arrived. They ate the fruit, the maypop, as food, and used the leaves in their medicine.
    • In the 1500s, Spanish missionaries in the Americas read the flower as a picture of the Passion of Christ — the story of his suffering and death on the cross. They saw the fringe as the crown of thorns, and the three stigmas — the tips at the centre of the flower — as the nails of the cross.
    • That reading gave the plant its name — the Passion flower — and carried it back to Europe, where gardeners grew it as a wonder by the 1600s.
    • As a medicine, it came late to Europe and America. Herbal practice took it up in the 1800s as a calming herb for nerves and sleep.
    • Its two histories still meet in one plant — an American food and folk remedy, wearing a name given by missionaries.

    Traditional medicine

    • Traditionally used to relieve mild symptoms of mental stress and to aid sleep; European regulators accept both as traditional uses based on long-standing practice.
    • In one small pilot trial, 36 adults with generalised anxiety took a passionflower extract or the prescription sedative oxazepam for four weeks. Both groups' anxiety improved by about the same amount, and the passionflower group reported fewer problems with impaired job performance. The trial was small and had no placebo group, so it cannot show how much of the benefit came from the herb itself — a Cochrane review of the anxiety trials concluded there were too few to draw conclusions.
    • In small trials, a dose of passionflower before surgery or dental work eased patients' anxiety beforehand. These are single-dose, hospital-setting studies of specific extracts.
    • For sleep, the evidence is thin: in one small study, people who drank passionflower tea for a week rated their sleep quality slightly better. That is the current state of the sleep evidence — a nudge, not a demonstration.
    • Caution: passionflower can cause drowsiness, dizziness and confusion. Do not combine it casually with sleeping pills, anti-anxiety sedatives, or alcohol, and tell your care team if you have taken it before surgery, as it may add to the effects of anaesthesia.
    • Caution: passionflower is not recommended in pregnancy — it may stimulate the uterus — nor while breastfeeding, and not for children under 12, as safety has not been established in any of these groups.
    • When to plant: Sow seed in spring — it can be slow to sprout — or plant young plants after frost, with room to climb
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Well-drained soil
    • Environment: A fast-growing vine; it dies back to the root in cold winters and returns late in spring — late enough that gardeners often think it dead
    • Planter or ground: Ground, against a fence or trellis; a large pot with support works
    • Spacing and depth: Give it metres of fence or a strong trellis
    • Water: Average
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Harvest the leaves and stems while the plant is flowering; the fruit ripens in late summer

    Garden notes

    • The flowers are pollinated by carpenter bees and other large bees, and hummingbirds visit them too.
    • It is a vital wildlife plant in its home range: the caterpillars of the Gulf fritillary and zebra longwing butterflies feed on passionflower leaves, and few other plants can replace it for them.
    • Birds and mammals eat the maypop fruit and spread the seed.
    • A fast-growing vine that quickly covers fences and banks, shading and holding the ground beneath it.

    Propagation

    Take a stem cutting in early spring, before it flowers, and set it in damp potting mix in a shady, warm spot. Seed also works — sow fresh seed in spring — but it sprouts unevenly and can take months, and a seed-grown plant may take years to flower. Give it room: it spreads fast by suckers.

    Sources

    • Akhondzadeh et al. (2001) — passionflower versus oxazepam pilot trial
    • Miyasaka et al. (2007) — Cochrane review of passionflower for anxiety
    • Ngan & Conduit (2011) — passionflower tea and sleep quality
    • European Medicines Agency — Passiflora incarnata monograph
    • NCCIH — Passionflower: usefulness and safety

    Lavender

    Lavandula angustifolia

    MedicinalCulinary

    Sleep

    FreshDried

    A compact, grey-leaved shrub from the dry hills of the Mediterranean, in the mint family, grown for its spikes of violet buds — the part used, picked just before the flowers fully open. Lavender is at once a medicine, a perfume and a food: the buds flavour sugar, syrups, baking and the herb blend herbes de Provence. It is also the herb with the strongest trial evidence — provided the evidence is credited to the exact preparation that was studied, and to nothing else.

    Terpenes in this plant: · · ·

    Cultivars

    • Garden lavender comes in two kinds. True lavender, Lavandula angustifolia, is hardy and sweet-scented, and its named varieties are garden plants. The lavandins are hybrids of true lavender with spike lavender (Lavandula latifolia): bigger, later-flowering plants grown for oil.
    • 'Hidcote' is a true lavender, picked out by Major Lawrence Johnston in the 1920s in his Gloucestershire garden, Hidcote Manor. Small and neat, with deep violet-purple flowers and a strong, sweet scent, it is the variety for low hedges, edging and drying, and it is fully hardy.
    • 'Munstead' is the other classic true lavender, linked with Gertrude Jekyll's garden at Munstead Wood in Surrey and sold under the name from the early 1900s. Its flowers are a paler lavender-blue than 'Hidcote', its shape a little looser, and it flowers early; it is among the hardiest lavenders of all, and the one cooks reach for most.
    • 'Grosso' is a lavandin, not a true lavender — a French field plant selected by the grower Pierre Grosso in 1972. It gives far more oil than any true lavender, and most of the world's lavandin oil is 'Grosso'; but the oil carries camphor, so the scent is sharper and less sweet, and it goes into soap, candles and scented goods rather than food. Lavandins are also less hardy than true lavenders.
    • The name comes from washing. It is traced to the Latin word lavare, which means “to wash”, because the Romans put lavender in their bath water to scent it.
    • Rome used it in many ways — in baths, on bedding, and as a medicine. As the Romans travelled, they carried the plant across Europe.
    • In the Middle Ages, people used it as a strewing herb. They scattered it on the floors of castles and cottages to scent the room and to keep insects down.
    • Monastery gardens kept it growing through those hundreds of years. After them, herb gardens everywhere took it up.
    • By the 1800s, the hills of Provence, in the south of France, were planted with lavender for the perfume trade. Those are the fields it is still pictured in today.
    • Lavender oil, distilled from the buds, is breathed in for sleep and worry, and rubbed, diluted, on the skin. Human trials

    Traditional medicine

    • Traditionally used to relieve mild symptoms of mental stress and exhaustion and to aid sleep; European regulators accept lavender flower and lavender oil as traditional herbal medicines on that basis.

    Craft

    • Lavender is a maker's herb: the dried buds fill sachets and pillows and scent soaps and candles.
    • The fresh stems are woven into lavender wands — bundles tied with ribbon so the flowers are caged inside their own stems, made to scent drawers and cupboards.
    • The strongest evidence belongs to one specific product: Silexan, a standardised lavender oil made to be swallowed, in 80 mg capsules. In five placebo-controlled trials with more than 1,200 adults with anxiety, it eased anxiety symptoms significantly more than a placebo over ten weeks, without causing sedation or dependence in the trials. One large trial found it comparable to a low dose of a common antidepressant.
    • That evidence belongs to that preparation, at that dose. It does not carry over to lavender tea, to breathing in the scent, to bath oil, or to other lavender oil products — and it is not a reason to stop or replace prescribed treatment for anxiety.
    • For the scent itself, pooled trials of lavender aromatherapy show small reductions in anxiety scores, mostly in short studies of situations like medical procedures. Gentle and pleasant, but a thinner record than the capsule trials.
    • In the kitchen, lavender buds are simply a food: a little flavours syrups, sugars, shortbread and grilled dishes, and lavender is a traditional component of herbes de Provence.
    • Caution: swallowing lavender oil can cause burping, nausea, headache and diarrhoea. Lavender may add to the drowsiness of sedative medicines and alcohol. A small number of cases of breast swelling in young boys were reported with lavender oil products used on the skin, which reversed when the products were stopped — a reason for care with concentrated oil on young children. Lavender oil is not recommended in pregnancy; the flowers used as a food or tea in ordinary amounts are a different matter from the concentrated oil.
    • When to plant: Sow seed in spring — slow and patchy to sprout — or take cuttings in summer; plant out into the sunniest, driest spot you have
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Poor, dry, stony soil — it asks for drainage rather than feeding, and holds sunny banks where richer plants fail
    • Environment: Wet winter soil kills more lavender than cold does; the scented foliage is largely left alone by deer and rabbits
    • Planter or ground: Both — a pot of gritty mix suits it very well
    • Spacing and depth: 45–60 cm apart, by kind
    • Water: Dry once settled
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Pick the buds when the spikes show colour but before most flowers open, for the best scent and flavour; trim after flowering to keep the bush compact

    Garden notes

    • A strong pollinator plant: bees and butterflies work the flowers for weeks, and lavender is a genuine honey plant.

    Propagation

    Take a non-flowering shoot 2 to 4 inches long in early summer, strip the lower leaves, and set it in gritty, free-draining potting mix, kept moist but never wet. Roots form in about a month. Cuttings stay true to the parent plant — seed-grown plants, even from a named type like Hidcote, will vary.

    Sources

    • Dold et al. (2023) — pooled trials of Silexan lavender oil for anxiety
    • Kasper et al. (2014) — Silexan compared with paroxetine and placebo
    • Donelli et al. (2019) — pooled trials of lavender inhalation and anxiety
    • Henley et al. (2007) — case reports of breast swelling in boys using lavender oil products
    • European Medicines Agency — Lavandula angustifolia monograph
    • NCCIH — Lavender: usefulness and safety

    Bisabolol

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also calledα-bisabolol, also called levomenol

    The scent

    Mild, sweet and gently floral. The research literature also describes it as fruity and nutty, a little like coconut — sources differ on the details.

    (Matricaria chamomilla — also listed as Matricaria recutita); Candeia tree (Eremanthus erythropappus), the main commercial source; also Vanillosmopsis arborea and some Nectandra species.

    Found in: · Candeia tree · Vanillosmopsis arborea · Nectandra species

    What the Research Shows

    Soothes irritated skin Human · small

    The best-supported use. In one small trial, a 1% bisabolol spray helped venous leg ulcers heal completely where the control group saw none heal; trials in children with atopic dermatitis found fewer flares and less itching and inflammation. An 8-week cream trial in 28 women also lightened pigmented skin.

    Calms inflammatory pathways Lab studies / Animal studies

    In cells and animals it acts on well-known inflammatory signals (NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, COX-2), with antimicrobial and antioxidant effects alongside — the mechanism behind the skin findings, not yet proof in people.

    Helps other ingredients absorb Lab studies

    Bisabolol is a penetration enhancer — it helps other active ingredients pass through skin — and is typically used at 0.1–1% in cosmetics. The studied form is α-bisabolol; the β form is a different compound.

    What to Keep in Mind

    The evidence supports bisabolol soothing irritated skin and supporting healing — from small trials plus preclinical work — but it is not a proven wound treatment. Claims that it treats eczema, ulcers or melasma, or that it is anti-cancer or neuroprotective in people, come from cell and animal findings only.

    Generally well tolerated and regarded as low in toxicity, with no dermal irritation or photosensitivity reported. If you are allergic to the daisy family (Asteraceae — ragweed, chamomile), patch-test chamomile-derived products first; rare contact allergy is possible.

    Sources

    • Eddin et al. (2022) — review of alpha-bisabolol: skin, safety and plant sources
    • Lee et al. (2010) — 8-week cream trial in 28 women, pigmented skin

    Borneol

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also calledBorneo camphor. A bicyclic monoterpene alcohol. Its two mirror forms are (+)-borneol and (−)-borneol; isoborneol is a close relative, not the same compound.

    The scent

    Cool and camphor-like, with pine and a gentle minty freshness. Borneol is unusual among terpenes in being a solid crystal at room temperature, and it activates the same cold-sensing receptor (TRPM8) as menthol — which is why it feels cooling on the skin without being cold.

    Borneo camphor tree (Dryobalanops aromatica) — the classic source of (+)-borneol, drawn from the trunk resin. Ngai camphor plant (Blumea balsamifera) — the main source of (−)-borneol. Camphor tree (Cinnamomum camphora) oils, and in rosemary, , and ginger-family plants. A minor terpene in .

    Found in: Borneo camphor tree · Ngai camphor plant · Camphor tree · Rosemary · · · Ginger family ·

    What the Research Shows

    Pain relief on the skin, tested in people Human trials

    In a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 122 patients recovering from spinal surgery had a single application of a concentrated (25%) (+)-borneol solution around the wound for 30–60 minutes. Two-thirds of the borneol group (66%) achieved at least a 50% reduction in pain intensity, against 35% on placebo. The same team traced the mechanism to the TRPM8 cooling receptor — in mice. The authors call the human study preliminary: one application, one kind of pain.

    A 'messenger' that helps other substances through barriers Animal studies

    Borneol has been used in traditional Chinese medicine for centuries (as bing pian) less as a medicine in itself than as the ingredient that carries a formula where it needs to go. Modern animal research supports that role: borneol helps substances cross skin and the blood–brain barrier. A 2018 meta-analysis pooled 58 animal studies and found consistent improvement in delivery of co-administered drugs — but rated the studies' quality low, so this is a research direction, not a proven therapy.

    Anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial activity Laboratory

    In cell and animal work, borneol reduces inflammatory signals and inhibits some bacteria and fungi. None of this has been tested as a treatment in people.

    What to Keep in Mind

    Borneol's one human trial is narrow — a single, concentrated, skin application for post-surgical pain. It says nothing about inhaled or swallowed borneol, and claims about brain protection or stroke recovery rest on animal studies only. Most borneol writing online borrows the reputation of the traditional formulas it appears in; those formulas were never borneol alone.

    Borneol is permitted as a flavouring substance in the US, but it is not an approved pain treatment. Two honest cautions. First, synthetic borneol contains isoborneol, which is more irritating and more toxic than natural borneol — the natural and synthetic materials are not interchangeable. Second, because borneol helps other substances absorb through skin, it can also increase absorption of anything applied with it, including medicines — a reason for care with medicated creams. Traditional Chinese sources advise caution in pregnancy.

    Sources

    • Wang et al. (2017) — randomised trial of borneol for post-surgical pain, 122 patients
    • Zheng et al. (2018) — meta-analysis of 58 animal studies: borneol helping other substances reach the brain

    Camphene

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also calledNo common synonym. A bicyclic monoterpene (C10H16), a close structural relative of pinene and borneol. It is sometimes confused with camphor, which is a different, oxygen-containing compound made from it.

    The scent

    Pungent and camphor-like — damp earth, fir needles and forest floor after rain. It is one of the terpenes behind the sharp, resinous smell of a conifer forest, and like borneol it is a solid at room temperature rather than a liquid.

    Camphor oil (fractions of Cinnamomum camphora oil). Fir, cypress and other conifer oils; also turpentine fractions. , , rosemary, nutmeg and sage, in smaller amounts. A minor terpene in .

    Found in: Camphor oil · Fir · Cypress · · · Rosemary · Nutmeg · Sage ·

    What the Research Shows

    Cholesterol and blood fats — in animals Animal studies

    Camphene lowered total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol and triglycerides in animals with raised blood lipids. Follow-up work in liver cells suggests it works through cholesterol-production pathways (SREBP-1 and related proteins), a different route from statin drugs. There is no human trial of camphene for cholesterol.

    Pain and itch signals — in mice Animal studies

    A 2021 study in Molecular Brain found camphene quiets the Cav3.2 calcium channel, a pain-signalling pathway, in laboratory cells and mouse nerve cells, and reduced both inflammatory and nerve-related pain responses in mice. A 2025 follow-up found it reduced scratching in mice — an effect that disappeared in mice bred without the Cav3.2 channel.

    Antioxidant and antimicrobial activity Laboratory

    Camphene scavenges free radicals in laboratory assays and protected LDL cholesterol from oxidation in vitro; antimicrobial effects are also laboratory findings.

    What to Keep in Mind

    Every camphene result above is from cells or animals. The cholesterol findings used doses far beyond anything scent or flavour exposure provides, and there is no human evidence that camphene lowers cholesterol, relieves pain or calms itching in people. Camphene is best understood today as an interesting research compound and an industrial starting material — much of the world's camphene goes to make synthetic camphor.

    Camphene has low acute toxicity in animal testing (oral LD50 in rats reported above 5 g/kg in toxicology summaries) and a long history in flavour and fragrance use at low levels. Concentrated camphor-family oils are irritants to skin and eyes, so the usual essential-oil cautions apply: dilute, and never use concentrated material undiluted on skin. Safety at supplement-level doses in people is not established.

    Sources

    • Vallianou et al. (2011) — camphene lowered cholesterol and blood fats in animals
    • Gadotti et al. (2021) — camphene and pain signals in mice, through the Cav3.2 channel

    Caryophyllene

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also calledβ-caryophyllene, often shortened to BCP.

    The scent

    Woody and spicy — peppery and dry, like cloves, with a slightly camphor-like edge.

    Black pepper (Piper nigrum) and cloves (Syzygium aromaticum). Copaiba (Copaifera species) — the richest source, up to about 53%. , rosemary, basil, oregano and cinnamon. Far more abundant in kitchen spices than in .

    Found in: Black pepper · Cloves · Copaiba · · Rosemary · Basil · Oregano · Cinnamon ·

    What the Research Shows

    Switches on the CB2 receptor Lab studies / Animal studies

    Caryophyllene selectively activates CB2 — the cannabinoid receptor found mainly in the immune system — and not CB1, the receptor behind the cannabis “high”, so it is non-intoxicating. This is the best-supported explanation for its effects, though one 2019 cell study did not reproduce the direct activation, so it isn't settled fact.

    Eases pain and inflammation — in mice Animal studies

    Consistently reduced inflammatory and neuropathic pain behaviour in mice, without tolerance developing, and the effect disappeared in mice bred without CB2 receptors. Anxiety-like behaviour also eased in mice. There is no human trial for pain or stress.

    One small human trial Human · small

    In an 8-week trial, 52 women taking 100 mg a day scored lower on food-addiction measures — but their appetite, body composition and food intake did not change. Trial doses like this are also far above anything eaten in food.

    What to Keep in Mind

    Caryophyllene reduced pain behaviour in mice; no human chronic-pain trial exists. The stress evidence is mouse only, and there is no evidence that it improves sleep. Caryophyllene is a terpene, not a cannabinoid — “dietary cannabinoid” is a nickname, not a classification.

    Recognised as safe (GRAS) as a food flavouring, and rats tolerated high doses for 90 days without significant toxicity — but safety at supplement doses in people is not established. Don't equate copaiba oil with pure caryophyllene: the oil also contains diterpenes with liver-toxicity signals.

    Sources

    • Gertsch et al. (2008) — caryophyllene switches on the CB2 receptor, not CB1
    • Klauke et al. (2014) — caryophyllene eased pain in mice, without tolerance

    Eucalyptol

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also called1,8-cineole (its chemical name — the same compound), also written 1,8-cineol. A monoterpene ether (oxide). When a page says “cineole”, it means eucalyptol.

    The scent

    Fresh, cooling and camphor-like, with a minty sweetness — the clean, clearing smell of eucalyptus leaves and of traditional chest rubs and mouthwashes. It is one of the most recognisable scents in this guide.

    Eucalyptus oils — the major component, commonly more than two-thirds of the oil in Eucalyptus globulus; — amounts vary widely by chemotype, a leading part of many rosemary oils; Bay laurel, and sage; Tea tree oil, in small amounts (its standard caps eucalyptol at 15%); a minor terpene in .

    Found in: Eucalyptus oils · · Bay laurel · · Sage · Tea tree oil ·

    What the Research Shows

    Airway inflammation in asthma Human trials

    Unusually for a terpene, isolated eucalyptol has been through randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials — as a pharmaceutical capsule (200 mg, three times a day), taken alongside normal medication. In the first trial, 32 patients with steroid-dependent asthma reduced their daily prednisolone dose by 36% over 12 weeks, against 7% on placebo. A later six-month multicentre trial in 247 asthma patients found improved lung function, symptoms and quality of life when cineole was added.

    COPD flare-ups Human trials

    In a six-month placebo-controlled trial, 242 patients with stable COPD who added the same cineole capsules had fewer, shorter and less severe exacerbations, with better lung function and less breathlessness. Effects like these are why cineole is a licensed herbal medicine ingredient in Germany.

    The rosemary “clarity” link — promising, not proven Human · small

    In a small study of 20 volunteers, people who had sat in a rosemary-scented room had more 1,8-cineole in their blood, and higher levels tracked with faster, more accurate answers on mental tasks. But the study used whole rosemary aroma, had no unscented comparison room, and measured a correlation — it does not show that eucalyptol itself sharpens thinking.

    What to Keep in Mind

    Eucalyptol's strong human evidence is narrow and specific: a drug-dose capsule (600 mg a day), for airway inflammation, in patients already on standard treatment, and much of it from overlapping research groups studying the same commercial product. It does not show that diffusing eucalyptus oil treats asthma or COPD, and there is no good human evidence that isolated eucalyptol improves memory or mental clarity.

    Eucalyptol is recognised as safe (GRAS) as a food flavouring, and the capsule doses used in trials were generally well tolerated. Concentrated eucalyptus oil is a different matter: it can be dangerous if swallowed, especially for children, and should be kept out of their reach and never taken by mouth at home. High doses of cineole can irritate the stomach and airways, and asthma or COPD use in the trials was supervised add-on treatment, not self-treatment.

    Sources

    • Juergens et al. (2003) — cineole capsule trial in asthma, steroid dose cut
    • Worth et al. (2009) — six-month cineole trial in COPD, 242 patients

    Geraniol

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also calledAn acyclic monoterpene alcohol. It is the (E) form of 3,7-dimethyl-2,6-octadien-1-ol; its mirror-geometry partner, the (Z) form, is nerol, which smells similar but fresher and greener.

    The scent

    Sweet, soft rose — the heart of rose and geranium fragrance, with a faint fruity, almost peachy edge. Geraniol is one of the most widely used fragrance materials in the world, and your nose already knows it from soaps, lotions and gardens alike.

    Palmarosa oil — mostly geraniol, often 70% or more of the oil; Geranium and oils — a leading part of both scents; Lemongrass and citronella oils; also in many fruits and herbs in small amounts, and a minor terpene in .

    Found in: Palmarosa oil · Geranium oil · oil · Lemongrass · Citronella oil ·

    What the Research Shows

    Anti-tumour and anti-inflammatory signals Lab studies / Animal studies

    In rodent studies and cancer cell lines, geraniol slowed tumour growth and calmed inflammatory pathways. There are no human trials of geraniol for cancer, inflammation or any other condition.

    Antimicrobial and antifungal activity Laboratory

    Geraniol inhibits a range of bacteria and yeasts in laboratory tests, including Candida, and can disrupt Candida biofilms — the protective films yeasts build. These are dish-and-culture results; they are why geraniol is studied for preserving products, not evidence that it treats infections in people.

    A working natural insect repellent Animal studies

    Geraniol is used commercially in mosquito and tick repellents, and controlled repellency tests show it keeps biting insects away — though protection is shorter-lived than conventional repellent ingredients and needs reapplying.

    What to Keep in Mind

    Geraniol's evidence is preclinical throughout. Its reputation in skincare comes from fragrance, not therapy — and, as the safety note shows, its best-documented effect on skin in people is actually allergy, not healing. Nothing here supports using geraniol as a treatment.

    Geraniol is recognised as safe (GRAS) as a food flavouring. On skin, it is a declared fragrance allergen in the EU: it must be named on cosmetic labels above small thresholds, because a minority of people become sensitised to it — it is even one of the standard substances used in patch testing for fragrance allergy. Fresh geraniol is a weak sensitiser, but it oxidises in air and the oxidised material is more irritating, so old, air-exposed oils deserve the same caution as oxidised linalool and limonene: store cool, dark and sealed, and patch-test first.

    Sources

    • Chen & Viljoen (2010) — review of geraniol as a fragrance material, covering its laboratory antimicrobial/antifungal work and rodent anti-tumour and anti-inflammatory findings (South African Journal of Botany)
    • Müller et al. (2009) — controlled repellency tests comparing geraniol, citronella and linalool candles and diffusers against mosquitoes; the geraniol diffuser gave the highest repellency (97% indoors) (Journal of Vector Ecology)

    Humulene

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also calledα-humulene, also called α-caryophyllene.

    The scent

    Earthy, woody and herbal — hoppy, with a spicy edge. It is the terpene that gives beer its hoppy character.

    (Humulus lupulus) — humulene is named after them; Sage, coriander and ginseng; Cloves, , basil, balsam fir and black pepper.

    Found in: · Sage · Coriander · Ginseng · Cloves · · Basil · Balsam fir · Black pepper

    What the Research Shows

    Anti-inflammatory — in animals and the lab Animal studies / Lab studies

    In rodent studies, α-humulene (tested with caryophyllene from the Brazilian plant Cordia verbenacea) had effects comparable to the steroid dexamethasone, and it reduced allergic airway inflammation in mice. Anti-tumour and antimicrobial findings are laboratory and animal work only. There are no human clinical trials of isolated humulene.

    A close relative, but a different compound Lab studies

    Humulene is caryophyllene’s isomer — the same chemical formula, a different structure. Unlike β-caryophyllene it does not meaningfully activate the CB2 receptor, so it doesn’t share that story. Most studies also test the two together, which makes humulene’s solo effects hard to separate.

    What to Keep in Mind

    Two things sometimes said about humulene have no evidence behind them. “Appetite suppression”: the human hop trials behind this idea tested a bitter hop-acid extract (Amarasate) whose active ingredients are hop bitter acids — humulone and lupulone — not the terpene humulene; no study of humulene itself on appetite was found, in people or — in reviews that searched specifically — in any convincing animal food-intake study either. There is no human dose of humulene for appetite, because the trial has never been run. “Mental clarity”: no evidence found at all.

    There is no human safety data for isolated humulene at supplement doses, so the honest wording is “not established” rather than “proven safe”. At ordinary food and flavour levels it has no specific warning signal. The usual essential-oil cautions apply — dilute, and don’t use undiluted oils on skin.

    Sources

    • Fernandes et al. (2007) — rodent study of α-humulene with trans-caryophyllene from Cordia verbenacea; anti-inflammatory effects comparable to dexamethasone
    • Rogerio et al. (2009) — mouse study; α-humulene reduced allergic airway inflammation
    • Gertsch et al. (2008) — receptor-binding work (PNAS) behind the point that α-humulene, unlike β-caryophyllene, does not meaningfully activate CB2
    • Walker et al. (2024) — human trial of the bitter hop extract Amarasate (125/250 mg) in 30 women; the appetite findings belong to the hop extract, not to α-humulene itself (Obesity Pillars)

    Limonene

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also calledd-limonene, the common citrus form.

    The scent

    Fresh citrus — lemon and orange, bright and clean. Its mirror-image form, l-limonene, smells piney, like turpentine — so “limonene = citrus” is only half the story.

    Citrus peel — orange, lemon, lime and grapefruit, where it is the major component of the peel oil; peppermint and fir needles; also , juniper and .

    Found in: Citrus peel · Peppermint · Fir needles · · Juniper ·

    What the Research Shows

    Calming signals — in mice Animal studies

    Inhaled limonene reduced anxiety-like behaviour in mice in maze tests, and injected limonene did the same through adenosine, dopamine and GABA pathways. There is no human trial of limonene on its own for stress or anxiety.

    Whole citrus oils in people Human · small

    Human aromatherapy research does exist for anxiety and nausea — but it tests whole citrus oils (orange, bergamot, lemon), which contain many compounds, not isolated limonene. In one small study, inhaling sweet-orange oil (up to about 98% limonene) raised heart rate and subjective alertness in 24 young volunteers — a whole-oil, short-term result, not an energy or fatigue trial. Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects are laboratory and animal findings.

    Isolated limonene in people — flat alone, useful beside THC Human trials

    In a rigorous double-blind trial of 20 adults, vaporised d-limonene on its own at 1 or 5 mg did not differ from placebo on any measure — no energy, mood or alertness effect. Its one clear human result is as a partner: 15 mg of limonene with 30 mg of THC significantly reduced ratings of feeling anxious/nervous and paranoid, without changing THC’s blood levels.

    What to Keep in Mind

    “Anti-stress” rests on mouse studies — reduced anxiety-like behaviour in mice only. Claims about cholesterol, blood sugar, cancer or heartburn rest on animal, laboratory or uncontrolled work — the one human cancer study (43 women taking 2 g a day for 2–6 weeks) measured tolerability and biomarkers, not whether limonene treats anything.

    Limonene itself is not phototoxic. The sun sensitivity of cold-pressed bergamot, lime and lemon oils comes from different compounds in those oils (furocoumarins such as bergapten); steam-distilled lemon and lime oils and sweet orange oil are not phototoxic. The real skin caution is oxidation: limonene breaks down quickly in air and light, and oxidised limonene is a potent skin sensitiser (1.6% of patch-tested patients reacted) — which also makes antioxidant claims for old oil unreliable. It is recognised as safe (GRAS) as a food flavouring, and is a declared fragrance allergen in the EU.

    Sources

    • Lima et al. (2013) — inhaled limonene reduced anxiety-like behaviour in mice in maze tests
    • Song et al. (2021) — injected limonene calmed mice through adenosine, dopamine and GABA pathways
    • Spindle et al. (2024) — double-blind trial in 20 adults; vaporised d-limonene alone matched placebo, and with THC it reduced anxious and paranoid ratings
    • Miller et al. (2013) — 43 women with early breast cancer took 2 g of limonene a day for 2–6 weeks; the study measured tissue levels and biomarkers, not treatment

    Linalool

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also calledLinalool has two mirror-image forms — one sweeter and more floral, the other woodier and more lavender-like. It is found in more than 200 plant species.

    The scent

    Soft, sweet and floral with a woody lavender note. Its two mirror-image forms differ slightly — one sweeter and more floral, the other woodier and more lavender-like.

    Linalool is one of the most common scent compounds in the plant world. Lavender (Lavandula angustifolia) is its best-known source. It is also found in sweet basil and coriander; rosewood, bergamot and citrus blossom.

    Found in: · Sweet basil · Coriander · Rosewood · Bergamot · Citrus blossom

    What the Research Shows

    Calms anxiety — as lavender oil Human trials

    The strongest human evidence for a terpene, with an important catch: it belongs to lavender oil, not linalool alone. A standardised oral lavender-oil preparation (Silexan, 80 mg) reduced anxiety across randomised trials and meta-analyses — in one analysis of 697 people with subthreshold anxiety, and in a 539-person trial of generalised anxiety disorder — performing comparably to low-dose lorazepam and paroxetine in head-to-head trials, without sedation. Many of these trials were linked to the manufacturer.

    Supports sleep quality — as lavender scent Human · small

    A meta-analysis of 11 trials (628 adults) found breathing lavender oil improved sleep quality, though the authors call for higher-quality studies to confirm it. Europe's herbal regulator, the EMA, is more cautious: it lists lavender flower and oil as traditional use only for mild mental stress and exhaustion and to aid sleep, judging the trials too small to establish the effect.

    Linalool on its own Animal studies

    Isolated linalool shows calming and sedative effects in mice, acting on GABA pathways. That has not been demonstrated in people.

    “Improves sleep” and “anti-anxiety” belong to lavender oil and to one standardised oral product — not to linalool alone, not to inhaled linalool, and not to lavender products in general. The meta-analyses themselves warn the results can't be generalised to other products, linalool is not a proven sedative in people, and the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH, February 2025) states it is unclear whether lavender aromatherapy helps sleep quality or insomnia at all.

    What to Keep in Mind

    Fresh linalool is only a weak skin sensitiser, but once it oxidises in air, its breakdown products are potent ones — in a large patch-test study, 3.1% of patients reacted to oxidised linalool. Keep oils fresh, dark and cool, and never use old, oxidised oil on skin; in the EU it must be declared on fragrance labels. A disputed 2007 report linked lavender products to breast swelling in three prepubertal boys — causality is unproven, but avoiding concentrated daily topical lavender in young boys is a reasonable precaution. It may also add to the effect of sedatives, alcohol and sleep aids.

    Sources

    • Kasper et al. (2014) — lavender oil capsule for anxiety, head-to-head trial
    • Lucena et al. (2024) — review of lavender scent and sleep quality
    • NCCIH (2025) — lavender and sleep, plain-language summary
    • Contact Dermatitis (2026) — patch-test study of oxidised linalool, 6,719 patients

    Myrcene

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also calledβ-myrcene, the common natural form.

    The scent
