    Herbaceous, resinous and green, like fresh hops and balsam; in cannabis it also reads as spicy, earthy and musky, and mildly sweet.

    (Humulus lupulus) — up to about 70% of hop essential oil; lemongrass, , bay and thyme; verbena and .

    Found in: · Lemongrass · · Bay · Thyme · Verbena ·

    What the Research Shows

    Pain, inflammation, calm — in animals Animal studies / Lab studies

    A consistent preclinical picture: in a classic 1990 study, myrcene reduced pain responses in mice, and later work shows anti-inflammatory, sedative and anxiety-easing effects in animals. Sedative effects are also part of why hops appear in traditional sleep preparations. But a 2021 review states it plainly: studies in humans are lacking. There are no human trials.

    What to Keep in Mind

    “Pain relief” rests on mice — reduced pain responses in mice, with no human evidence that it relieves pain in people, and the animal doses were injected, not inhaled or eaten at food levels. The cannabis idea that strains over 0.5% myrcene are sedating (“couch-lock”) is an industry correlation, not a tested effect.

    A genuinely split picture: US government rodent studies found increased kidney and liver tumours at high doses, and in 2018 the FDA removed β-myrcene as a food additive under the Delaney Clause — while stating at the same time that there was no safety concern at intended-use levels. Other expert bodies consider it safe as a flavouring at those levels, it remains naturally present in many permitted foods, and it is not mutagenic in standard tests. Neither “proven carcinogen” nor “proven safe” is a fair one-line summary; the regulatory position is split and dose-dependent. Myrcene is also a workhorse of the flavour industry, used to make menthol, geraniol and linalool.

    Sources

    • Rao et al. (1990) — mouse study; myrcene reduced pain responses (writhing and hot-plate tests)
    • Surendran et al. (2021) — review of myrcene's pharmacology (Frontiers in Nutrition); states plainly that studies in humans are lacking
    • do Vale et al. (2002) — mouse study; myrcene, citral and limonene increased barbiturate sleeping time (Phytomedicine)
    • Chen et al. (2024) — mouse study; β-myrcene showed sedative–hypnotic effects in a PCPA-induced insomnia model (Pharmaceuticals)
    • National Toxicology Program (2010) — two-year gavage studies of β-myrcene in rats and mice; kidney tumours in male rats and liver tumours in male mice (NTP Technical Report 557)

    Nerolidol

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also calledperuviol or penetrol.

    The scent

    Woody and floral — often described as a faint rose-and-apple softness, sometimes with fruity, citrus notes.

    , jasmine and tea tree; , lemongrass and neroli (bitter-orange flower); The Brazilian Piper claussenianum, whose leaf oil can be over 80% nerolidol.

    Found in: · Jasmine · Tea tree · · Lemongrass · Neroli · Piper claussenianum

    What the Research Shows

    A wide preclinical portfolio Lab studies / Animal studies

    Reviews from 2016 and 2025 collect antimicrobial, antifungal, anti-biofilm, anti-parasitic, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and pain-related findings, plus calming effects in animals. All of it is preclinical: there are no human efficacy trials of nerolidol.

    Its best-documented job: helping things through skin Lab studies

    Nerolidol ranked first among the terpenes tested for enhancing skin penetration — in tests it carried a common anti-inflammatory drug (diclofenac) through skin better than the others. That, rather than a health benefit, is its most concrete documented property.

    What to Keep in Mind

    No benefit was listed for nerolidol originally, and none is claimed here. Wording such as “relaxes”, “fights infection” or “heals skin” would only be true as far as lab and animal studies go — it has not been tested in people, and it should not be called a sedative in humans.

    Safety

    Permitted as a food flavouring and widely used in cosmetics and detergents, with low toxicity in preclinical reviews. Two cautions follow from its talents: as a penetration enhancer it may increase absorption of other substances applied to the same skin, including topical medicines; and early evidence suggests it may affect a drug-metabolising enzyme (CYP3A4). That interaction is preliminary, not confirmed — but if you use medicines, it is worth a conversation with a clinician rather than assuming nerolidol is risk-free.

    Sources

    • Chan et al. (2016) — review of nerolidol’s preclinical pharmacology: antimicrobial, anti-parasitic, anti-inflammatory and other laboratory/animal findings (Molecules)
    • Li et al. (2025) — updated review of nerolidol research (Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry)
    • Nokhodchi et al. (2007) — laboratory study comparing terpene enhancers for diclofenac sodium across rat skin; at the highest concentration tested, nerolidol produced the greatest permeation of the terpenes compared (International Journal of Pharmaceutics)

    Ocimene

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also calledAn acyclic monoterpene (C10H16). It comes in several close forms — alpha-ocimene, (Z)-beta-ocimene and (E)-beta-ocimene — and plant oils usually contain a blend of them.

    The scent

    Sweet, herbaceous and green, with a soft floral warmth — often described as orchid-like. Ocimene is named after basil (genus Ocimum), where it is a major part of the fresh green aroma. It is not built to last: ocimene oxidises quickly in air, so its scent is at its best in the living plant and in fresh oil.

    — a major component of many basil oils, and the source of its name; Mint, , and orchids; Kumquats, bergamot and ; Also hops, black pepper and some cannabis varieties.

    Found in: · Mint · · · Orchids ·

    What the Research Shows

    Whole oils, not ocimene itself Laboratory

    Almost every study cited for ocimene actually tested a whole essential oil that happened to contain it. In laboratory work, a Citrus unshiu flower oil rich in ocimene showed anti-inflammatory effects in cells; a Ferulago carduchorum oil that was 43.3% (Z)-beta-ocimene was antifungal against Candida in the laboratory, but only weakly; and a bay laurel (Laurus nobilis) oil showed activity against a SARS coronavirus in vitro (2008). In each case the oil contained many compounds, so none of the effect can be credited to ocimene alone.

    A messenger molecule in nature Laboratory

    (Z)-beta-ocimene is a genuine communication chemical for insects and plants: it is a honey bee brood pheromone, released by bee larvae, and plants release it when their leaves are attacked, as part of their defence signalling. This is real, well-documented — but it is insect and plant biology, not a human benefit.

    “Uplifting” — by association only

    Animal studies are not even the basis here: ocimene’s energising reputation comes from cannabis strain descriptions and perfume writing, not from any trial. There are no human studies of ocimene, and no established animal evidence for mood or energy.

    What to Keep in Mind

    Of all the terpenes in this guide, ocimene has some of the thinnest human-relevant evidence. Every “benefit” attached to it online traces back to a whole oil, a strain description, or its role in insect communication. Enjoyed as a scent, it is lovely and well documented as part of basil and orchid fragrance — as a treatment, nothing has been shown.

    Safety

    Ocimene’s main practical caution is freshness: because it oxidises readily in air — like myrcene — old ocimene-rich oils are not the same material as fresh ones. Very little formal toxicology exists for ocimene on its own.

    Sources

    • Maisonnasse et al. (2010) — study identifying (Z)-β-ocimene as a honey bee brood pheromone (insect/plant biology, not a human study)
    • Kim et al. (2014) — laboratory study of Citrus unshiu flower essential oil, in which ocimene was one constituent among several; the whole oil suppressed inflammatory mediators in stimulated macrophages (Natural Product Communications)
    • Golfakhrabadi et al. (2015) — laboratory study of Ferulago carduchorum essential oil (43.3% (Z)-β-ocimene); weak activity against Candida (Journal of Arthropod-Borne Diseases)
    • Loizzo et al. (2008) — laboratory study of bay laurel (Laurus nobilis) essential oil, with β-ocimene a main constituent; activity against SARS coronavirus in vitro (Chemistry & Biodiversity)

    Phytol

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also calledSometimes nicknamed the “chlorophyll alcohol”. Phytol is an acyclic diterpene alcohol (C20H40O) — a larger molecule than the monoterpenes in most of this guide, and the side chain that anchors chlorophyll in the leaf.

    The scent

    Mild, soft and green, with a faint floral-balsamic note. Phytol is not really a fragrance ingredient in its own right — you will rarely see it listed for its scent. Its importance is structural: almost every green plant on earth holds it inside chlorophyll, and it is also the industrial starting material for making vitamins E and K1.

    Chlorophyll itself — present in every green plant, leaf and alga; Green vegetables — a normal, small part of the human diet; Green tea and leafy herbs; Released as chlorophyll breaks down in leaves and in the sea.

    What the Research Shows

    A sleep claim that cannot be credited to phytol Human · small

    A 2025 trial tested a capsule combining CBD 300 mg with 1 mg each of eight terpenes, including phytol. Deep-plus-REM sleep rose by about 1.3 percentage points versus placebo, but total sleep time did not change — and with nine active ingredients, nothing can be attributed to phytol itself. The study was industry-funded.

    Calming and pain signals in animals Animal studies

    In rodent studies, phytol showed anxiolytic-like, pain-reducing (antinociceptive), antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. These are preclinical findings; no trial of phytol alone in people has tested any of them.

    Skin-care interest Laboratory

    Phytol is used in cosmetic formulas, and recent reviews discuss anti-ageing and skin-barrier potential. The suggested route — that skin converts phytol to phytanic acid — has not been directly shown in human skin, so this remains preclinical.

    What to Keep in Mind

    There are no human trials of phytol on its own, for anything. The one human study mentioning it tested a nine-ingredient product. Everything else — calm, pain, skin — rests on animal and laboratory work. Phytol’s everyday significance is real but quieter: it is part of the chlorophyll in every green food you eat.

    Safety

    Phytol from the diet is normal and its fragrance safety has been formally assessed. One specific caution: the body converts phytol to phytanic acid, and people with Refsum disease — a rare inherited condition — cannot break phytanic acid down and must limit it. That is a reason for people with that condition to be wary of concentrated phytol supplements; it is not a concern for ordinary dietary exposure.

    Sources

    • Wang et al. (2025) — double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial in 125 adults with insomnia; a capsule of CBD 300 mg plus 1 mg each of eight terpenes including phytol raised deep-plus-REM sleep share by ~1.3 percentage points, with no change in total sleep time and nothing attributable to phytol itself (Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine)
    • Islam et al. (2015) — review of phytol’s pharmacological potential: anxiolytic-like, pain-reducing, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in animal and laboratory work (Biomedicine & Pharmacotherapy)
    • Wu et al. (2026) — review of phytol in skin care, covering its pharmacological mechanisms and cosmetic applications (International Journal of Molecular Sciences)

    Pinene

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also calledTwo forms, α-pinene and β-pinene; α is the studied one.

    The scent

    Fresh pine — resinous, woody, crisp and green, slightly camphor-like and herbal.

    Pine (Pinus species) — α-pinene is often 30–50% of Scots pine oil; and ; , eucalyptus and frankincense.

    What the Research Shows

    Memory support — in rodents Animal studies

    Injected α-pinene improved memory in mice and rats whose memory had been chemically impaired, working through brain growth-factor pathways (BDNF/TrkB/CREB).

    Tested in people — and it did nothing Human trials

    Pinene is one of the few terpenes put directly to a human test. In a 2025 double-blind trial (19 healthy adults, six sessions), inhaled α-pinene at 15 mg — at or above the doses naturally found in cannabis flower — produced no significant effects compared with placebo, and when combined with THC it did not soften THC’s impairment of memory or working memory.

    The wider picture Lab studies / Animal studies

    Anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, airway-opening (bronchodilator) and antimicrobial effects appear across laboratory and animal studies.

    What to Keep in Mind

    “Improves cognitive function” rests on rodents — improved memory in brain-impaired rodents given injected pinene — and a 2025 human trial has since tested it directly and found no effect, alone or against THC-impaired memory. “Boosts energy” has no evidence behind it at all, not even in animals; the fresh pine scent is described as alerting, which is a scent association, not a measured effect. Rosemary-aroma memory studies can’t be credited to pinene either: they test whole rosemary oil, in which a different compound (1,8-cineole) is usually dominant.

    Safety

    Fresh pinene is low-risk at fragrance and flavour levels, but oxidised pinene and pine oil are significant skin sensitisers — discard old pine oil and never use oxidised oil on skin. Undiluted oil irritates skin and airways, so take care with asthma. Pine oil (not isolated pinene) is generally not recommended for children under 6 or during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

    Sources

    • Lee et al. (2017) — mouse study; injected α-pinene improved scopolamine-induced memory impairment
    • Hashemi & Ahmadi (2023) — rat study; α-pinene moderated kainic-acid memory impairment via BDNF/TrkB/CREB pathways
    • Spindle et al. (2025) — double-blind human trial in 19 healthy adults; inhaled α-pinene (15 mg) produced no significant effects vs placebo and did not reduce THC’s memory impairment (Medical Cannabis and Cannabinoids)

    Sabinene

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also calledA bicyclic monoterpene (C10H16), built on the thujane skeleton — the same family framework as thujone, though sabinene itself is a different and milder compound. A close relative, sabinene hydrate, appears alongside it in some oils.

    The scent

    Warm, woody and spicy, with black-pepper heat softened by pine and a bright citrus top. It is one of the defining notes of juniper and a quiet contributor to the warmth of black pepper and nutmeg — the sort of terpene you recognise as “spice” before you could ever name it.

    Juniper berries and juniper oil — one of the dominant terpenes; Black pepper — levels vary widely by source and harvest; Nutmeg — typically around 15–35% of the oil, varying by origin; seed oil — a major component; Also Norway spruce, holm oak, marjoram and tea tree oil (0.2–12%).

    What the Research Shows

    Anti-inflammatory signals in cells Laboratory

    In laboratory work, sabinene reduced nitric oxide production in stimulated immune cells (macrophages) — a standard early marker of anti-inflammatory activity (summarised in Molecules, 2024, via secondary sources). This is a cell-culture finding, several steps from any human effect.

    Antifungal and antimicrobial activity in dishes Laboratory

    Sabinene has shown activity in vitro against fungi including Candida, Trichophyton and Aspergillus species, and related work on sabinene hydrate (2024) reports antimicrobial effects. Nothing here has been tested on people, and laboratory strength does not predict a useful treatment.

    Antioxidant readings Laboratory

    Sabinene scores in standard antioxidant assays. As with most terpenes, these test-tube readings are the weakest form of evidence and are routinely overstated in marketing.

    What to Keep in Mind

    There are no human trials of sabinene, and no animal studies establishing a benefit either — the entire evidence base is laboratory work. Most claims attached to sabinene online trace back to whole juniper, pepper or nutmeg oils, or to traditional uses of those plants; none of that transfers to sabinene on its own.

    Safety

    Sabinene is used at low levels as a flavouring component. Formal toxicology data for sabinene alone is thin — published safety assessments lean on read-across from related compounds such as camphene — so there is no strong safety dossier in either direction, and concentrated isolated sabinene is not a well-studied material for skin use.

    Sources

    • Kim et al. (2024) — cell study; Chamaecyparis obtusa leaf essential oil and pure sabinene both reduced inflammatory signalling (iNOS expression, nitric oxide production, JNK/p38 phosphorylation) in LPS-stimulated macrophages (Molecules)
    • Valente et al. (2013) — laboratory study of Oenanthe crocata essential oil and its constituent sabinene; the oil was antifungal and antioxidant, and sabinene itself inhibited nitric-oxide production in stimulated macrophages (Food and Chemical Toxicology)
    • Judžentienė et al. (2024) — laboratory study of the antimicrobial properties of sabinene hydrate (Molecules)

    Terpineol

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also calledTwo close relatives share this page, both monoterpene alcohols (C10H18O). Alpha-terpineol is the lilac-scented form, a leading component of pine oil. Terpinen-4-ol is the form tea tree oil is known for — the standard for tea tree oil (ISO 4730:2017) sets it at 35–48% of the oil.

    The scent

    Alpha-terpineol is soft and floral — lilac and lily with a gentle pine freshness, a classic soap and perfume note. Terpinen-4-ol smells different: warm, earthy, woody and slightly peppery — the clean, medicinal heart of tea tree oil. The two are often confused because their names are nearly identical; their scents and sources are not.

    Tea tree oil — terpinen-4-ol is its main component (35–48%); alpha-terpineol is a small part (2–5%); Pine oil — alpha-terpineol is a leading component; Lilac — alpha-terpineol contributes to the flower's scent; Also cajuput, petitgrain and some eucalyptus oils.

    What the Research Shows

    The most active single piece of tea tree oil Laboratory

    In the standard review of tea tree oil research, terpinen-4-ol was the most active single component against bacteria and fungi in laboratory tests, working by disrupting microbial cell membranes. Alpha-terpineol is also antimicrobial in vitro. All of this is laboratory evidence for the isolated compounds.

    Human trials exist — for the whole oil only Human trials

    Tea tree oil itself has been trialled in people: a 5% tea tree gel improved acne comparably to 5% benzoyl peroxide, though more slowly and with fewer side effects, and a 5% tea tree shampoo reduced dandruff. Those results belong to the whole oil, with its hundred-plus compounds — they cannot be credited to terpinen-4-ol or alpha-terpineol alone, and neither compound has been trialled in people on its own.

    Calming and anti-inflammatory signals Animal studies

    In rodent work, alpha-terpineol shows anti-inflammatory and sedative-like signals. Preliminary, animal-only, and not a basis for sleep or calm claims in people.

    What to Keep in Mind

    This is the page where the discipline matters most: tea tree oil's human evidence is real, but it is the oil's, not the single terpene's. No human trial has tested isolated terpinen-4-ol or alpha-terpineol for skin, scalp or anything else.

    Safety

    Tea tree oil is toxic if swallowed and should never be taken by mouth. Oxidised tea tree oil — old oil exposed to air and light — is more likely to sensitise skin, so freshness and dark, cool storage matter; terpinen-4-ol itself shows low sensitisation potential in testing. Alpha-terpineol is a long-used fragrance ingredient; as with any fragrance material, patch-test first if your skin is reactive.

    Sources

    • Carson et al. (2006) — review of tea tree oil research; terpinen-4-ol identified as the most active single component against bacteria and fungi in laboratory tests (Clinical Microbiology Reviews)
    • Bassett et al. (1990) — human trial of 5% tea tree oil gel vs 5% benzoyl peroxide for acne (whole oil, not the isolated terpene) (Medical Journal of Australia)
    • Satchell et al. (2002) — human trial of 5% tea tree oil shampoo for dandruff (whole oil, not the isolated terpene) (Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology)
    • ISO 4730:2017 — the tea tree oil standard setting terpinen-4-ol at 35–48% of the oil (standard, not a study)

    Terpinolene

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also calledδ-terpinene — not the same as terpineol.

    The scent

    Fresh pine first, then floral, herbal and citrus — the comparisons you will see most often are green apple and lilac.

    Nutmeg, and cumin; Lilac, tea tree, and ; Lemon and conifers (Pinus species); The dominant terpene in fewer than 1 in 10 cannabis cultivars.

    What the Research Shows

    A systematic review, honestly summarised Lab studies / Animal studies

    A 2021 systematic review (in Phytomedicine) gathered 57 studies and found the strongest signals for antioxidant, larvicidal and insecticidal activity, with antifungal, antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, anti-spasmodic and anti-proliferative findings alongside. All of it is laboratory, computer-model or animal work, the mechanisms are unclear, and there is no clinical trial behind any of it.

    Calming or energising? The honest answer Animal studies

    Inhaled terpinolene made mice move less — a sedative-like effect. Yet cannabis strains rich in terpinolene are often described as energising. Those strain descriptions are not evidence about the isolated compound: a whole plant's effect involves THC and many other terpenes at once. The evidence doesn't pick a side.

    What to Keep in Mind

    Terpinolene arrived with no description, and the literature supports an honest short entry rather than a benefit list: no claims about relaxation, focus, anxiety relief or anti-cancer effects in people are supported. One mix-up to avoid — terpineol is a different compound (an alcohol with a lilac and pine-sap scent), despite the similar name.

    Safety

    In the systematic review's own assessment, terpinolene's safety in the body is poorly evaluated — so it should not be described as safe at supplement or therapeutic doses. It is used as a food flavouring, it degrades with heat, oxygen and UV light, and the general essential-oil cautions apply.

    Sources

    • Menezes et al. (2021) — systematic review of 57 terpinolene studies (from 2,449 screened); strongest signals antioxidant, larvicidal and insecticidal, all preclinical (Phytomedicine)
    • Ito & Ito (2013) — mouse study; inhaled terpinolene reduced motor activity, a sedative-like effect (Journal of Natural Medicines)

    Valencene

    Most benefits below come from early, animal, or lab studies — not human trials.

    Also called(+)-valencene. A bicyclic sesquiterpene (C15H24) of the eremophilane family — a larger, heavier molecule than the monoterpenes, which is why its scent lingers longer. It takes its name from the Valencia orange.

    The scent

    Sweet, warm orange peel with a soft woody depth — the part of orange aroma that stays after the bright top notes fade. Valencene is also the immediate natural stepping-stone to nootkatone, the compound that gives grapefruit its character: in the fruit, and slowly in stored oil, valencene converts toward nootkatone, and the scent shifts from sweet orange toward grapefruit.

    Sweet orange and Valencia orange peel oil — its defining source; Grapefruit and tangerine peel; Trace amounts in some cannabis varieties.

    What the Research Shows

    Anti-inflammatory activity in cells Laboratory

    In macrophage cell studies, valencene reduced inflammatory output (including iNOS/nitric oxide pathways and suppression of the HMGB1 signal) — summarised in a 2018 review of sesquiterpene health effects. Laboratory findings only.

    Skin-cell protection under UV light Laboratory

    The same review literature reports valencene protecting skin cells against UVB damage in vitro. Interesting for cosmetic research; not a sunscreen claim, and not tested on human skin.

    One animal survival study Animal studies

    A secondary source reports improved survival in a single mouse sepsis model. One study, in mice, for a critical-care condition — it supports no everyday claim. There are no human trials of valencene for anything.

    What to Keep in Mind

    Valencene is often marketed using its neighbour's résumé: nootkatone (its conversion product) is an EPA-registered insect repellent with real testing behind it — but that evidence is nootkatone's, not valencene's. On its own evidence, valencene is a well-loved orange flavour and scent ingredient with early laboratory findings only.

    Safety

    Valencene is listed as FEMA 3443 and recognised as safe (GRAS) as a food flavouring. The practical point is storage: valencene slowly oxidises toward nootkatone in air, so an old valencene-rich orange oil will smell more grapefruit-like and less sweetly orange than a fresh one — a quality change, well documented in citrus-oil handling.

    Sources

    • Nuutinen (2018) — review of the medicinal properties of terpenes in Cannabis sativa and hops, covering valencene's anti-inflammatory and UVB skin-cell laboratory findings (European Journal of Medicinal Chemistry)
    • Tsoyi et al. (2011) — mouse study; (+)-valencene and (+)-nootkatone from Cyperus rotundus increased survival in septic mice, linked to heme oxygenase-1 induction (Journal of Ethnopharmacology)

    Hops

    Humulus lupulus

    MedicinalCulinary

    Hormone HealthSleep

    Dried

    A vigorous perennial climbing plant — a bine, twisting clockwise up any support — native across Europe, western Asia and North America, and a cousin of cannabis in the hemp family. The medicinal and brewing part is the strobile: the cone-like cluster of female flowers, papery green and rich in the bitter, resinous yellow powder called lupulin that gives beer its bite and its keeping quality.

    Terpenes in this plant: · ·

    Cultivars

    • Hops are sold by variety, and the variety decides what a beer tastes like. Brewers split them by work: aroma hops, added late for scent, and bittering hops, boiled long for bite — bitterness is measured as alpha acid, and the aroma kinds run low. The old European varieties are landraces, shaped by one place over centuries; the modern American ones were bred on purpose.
    • Saaz, from around the town of Žatec in Bohemia, is the classic noble hop: very low in alpha acid, with a fine, spicy, floral scent. It is the hop of Czech pilsner, the variety other lager hops are judged against.
    • Hallertau Mittelfrüh, the old landrace of Bavaria's Hallertau region, is Germany's noble hop: mild, floral and herbal, low in bitterness — a hop for pale lagers and wheat beers.
    • Fuggle is England's old ale hop: a chance seedling found in Kent in 1861 and sold by Richard Fuggle from 1875. Earthy, woody and gentle, it shaped English ales for a century.
    • East Kent Goldings, grown only around Canterbury in Kent, are the other great English aroma hop: soft, sweet and honeyed, used in pale ales and bitters.
    • Cascade is the American break with all that: bred by the USDA in Oregon from Fuggle and a Russian hop, and released in 1972. Its grapefruit-and-pine scent defined the American pale ale and set off the craft-beer hop race.
    • Hops grow wild across the temperate parts of the northern half of the world — the lands with mild summers and cold winters. People began to use them in beer in Europe some time between the 800s and the 1000s. Hops took the place of the older herb mixes that brewers had used before. Hops also gained a name for making people sleepy. That came from the hop-pickers: at harvest time, people noticed that the pickers grew tired very easily.
    • Hop oil is breathed in for sleep and nervous tension — the old hop pillow, filled with the dried cones, works the same way. Traditional use

    Traditional medicine

    • Traditionally used to relieve mild symptoms of mental stress and to aid sleep; European regulators accept hop strobiles as a traditional herbal medicine on that basis. Germany's Commission E recognised hops for restlessness, anxiety and sleep disturbances as long ago as 1984.

    Craft

    • The cones are sewn into hop pillows — small cloth pillows filled with dried strobiles, a folk craft long said to help sleep. That is tradition, not evidence: what little sleep research exists tests extracts, not pillows.
    • The long bines, cut back in autumn, are woven into wreaths and garlands.
    • The flowers also give a brown dye. And the stems are a fibre: in Sweden they were soaked through the winter and worked like flax into cloth and rope, and hop stems were made into paper.
    • Hops' sleep reputation grew up alongside valerian, and almost all of the human sleep research tests the two together rather than hops alone. In the largest trial of the combination, 184 adults with mild insomnia slept somewhat better by their own rating after four weeks — a modest benefit, and sleep-laboratory measurements showed no difference.
    • European regulators accept specific valerian-and-hops extract combinations as well-established medicines for sleep disorders — but what the combination does cannot be credited to hops alone, or to hop tea, or to a hop pillow. There are no adequate trials of hops by itself for insomnia, and one placebo-controlled trial of a hops preparation in chronic insomnia found no benefit.
    • In one small trial, a hops extract taken for four weeks eased self-rated stress, anxiety and low mood in young adults — a single small study, worth noting rather than leaning on.
    • The strobiles also carry one of the most potent plant estrogens known, a compound called 8-prenylnaringenin. At the amounts in beer or tea it is far below the doses used in trials, but concentrated hop extracts are not a casual choice for anyone with a hormone-sensitive condition.
    • Caution: traditional sources and the European assessment advise people with depression to avoid hops, as a sedative may deepen low mood. Hops can cause drowsiness and add to the effects of alcohol and sedative medicines — do not drive if affected. Use in pregnancy and while breastfeeding is not recommended, and not for children under 12.
    • Caution for the household: hops are dangerous to dogs. A dog that eats hops — including spent hops from home brewing — can develop a severe, sometimes fatal rise in body temperature. Keep fresh, dried and spent hops well away from dogs.
    • When to plant: Plant rhizomes in spring, with strong supports ready — a bine can climb twenty feet in a season. Grow female plants for the cones
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Rich, moist, well-drained soil
    • Environment: A hardy perennial that dies back to the crown each autumn; its deep, spreading roots hold banks, but the vigour means it needs a place where spreading is welcome
    • Planter or ground: Ground — far too vigorous for pots
    • Spacing and depth: 1–2 m apart, along the support
    • Water: Likes water while it is climbing
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Pick the cones in late summer, when they feel papery and smell resinous

    Garden notes

    • The leaves are a food plant for the caterpillars of the comma butterfly, and the dense summer growth shelters birds and insects.
    • A fast, tall screen of living green through the summer, shading ground and structures, then dying back to the crown each winter.
    • The deep, spreading roots hold banks and rough ground, though the plant's vigour means it needs a place where spreading is welcome.

    Propagation

    In January or February, while the plant is asleep, dig beside an established plant and cut a rhizome into pieces about 3 inches long, each with buds, then plant them just below the soil. Only female plants bear cones, and plants grown from seed may turn out male and bear none — so take rhizomes or cuttings from a known female plant.

    Safety

    • Essential oils are concentrates, many times stronger than the plant itself. Always dilute in a carrier oil before putting one on skin, and never swallow an essential oil.

    Sources

    • European Medicines Agency — Humulus lupulus (hop strobile) monograph
    • Morin et al. (2005) — valerian–hops combination trial in mild insomnia
    • Kyrou et al. (2017) — hop extract and self-rated stress in young adults
    • Milligan et al. (1999) — 8-prenylnaringenin, the hop phytoestrogen, identified
    • Lawless (2014) — Encyclopedia of Essential Oils — steam-distilled hop oil for sleep and nervous tension

    Thyme

    Thymus vulgaris

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Digestive HealthRespiratory Health

    Fresh

    A small, woody mint-family shrub from the dry, rocky hillsides of the western Mediterranean, where it grows in poor, sun-baked soil. The leaves and flowering tops are the parts used — in the kitchen, and for much longer than that, in the cough remedies of European households. Its hot, medicinal smell comes from thymol, the compound that does most of its work.

    • The Egyptians used thyme in embalming, mixing it among the herbs that preserved the dead.
    • In ancient Greece it was burned as incense in temples. Its name is tied to the Greek word thymos — linked both to smoke, from that burning, and to courage and spirit.
    • The Romans spread it across their empire — a kitchen herb, a medicine, and a plant for bees. Roman roads carried it into northern Europe.
    • In the Middle Ages it was a strewing herb — an herb scattered on floors to sweeten the air — and a symbol of courage. It was grown in monastery gardens and castle yards.
    • Through all of it, its use in the kitchen and its use as a cough remedy ran side by side — the double life it still leads.
    • The kitchen record is long and named. In French cooking thyme became a fixed part of the bouquet garni — a tied bundle of thyme with bay and parsley, put into soups, sauces and stews and lifted out before serving — and of herbes de Provence, the dried herb mix of the south of France. In Lebanon, Syria, Jordan and Palestine, thyme is a main part of za'atar, the mix of dried thyme with sumac, sesame and salt eaten with bread and oil; the Arabic word za'atar names both the herb and the mix.
    • The Romans also used it around the house: to purify rooms, and to give an aromatic flavour to cheese and liqueurs, and Roman soldiers bathed in thyme water for courage. In the Middle Ages, women embroidered a sprig of thyme on a knight's scarf to bring him courage, and thyme was placed under pillows to aid sleep and ward off nightmares. Thyme's essential oil, rich in thymol, was still being used on surgical dressings and battle wounds in the First World War.
    • Today thyme is grown in gardens in temperate climates all over the world, while wild thyme still grows across the dry hills of the Mediterranean and the Levant.
    • Thyme oil, rich in thymol, is the antiseptic form: rubbed, diluted, on the skin for wounds, and breathed in for coughs. Traditional use

    Traditional medicine

    • Thyme also has a quieter traditional use for mild digestive discomfort and wind.

    Craft

    • Thyme's making uses are old ones. It was burned as incense in Greek temples — the smoke was the offering — and in the Middle Ages it was strewn on floors to sweeten the air of a room. Its oil, rich in thymol, went onto surgical dressings as an antiseptic into the First World War.
    • Thyme's established place is in coughs: European regulators accept thyme preparations as a traditional remedy for the productive, chesty cough that comes with a cold — a use based on long-standing practice, not on clinical trials of thyme itself.
    • The trial evidence that does exist belongs to licensed combination medicines — thyme paired with ivy or with primrose root — which eased coughing fits in adults with acute bronchitis. Those results are for those ready-made products, not for thyme alone and not for a home-brewed tea.
    • Their numbers, with that warning attached: in the thyme–ivy syrup trial (Kemmerich et al., 2006; 361 adults with acute bronchitis), eleven days of the syrup cut daytime coughing fits by about 69%, against about 48% on placebo, and the halfway fall in fits came about two days sooner. In the thyme–primrose tablet trial (Kemmerich et al., 2007; 361 adults), coughing fits fell by about 67%, against about 51% on placebo. No trial of thyme on its own, as a single herb, for cough in people was found in the European assessment — the single-herb standing is traditional use only.
    • Thymol, its main active compound, is the same antiseptic used in medicated mouthwashes. In laboratory studies, thyme's oils act against microbes and relax the muscle around the airways, which is part of why regulators find the traditional cough use plausible — laboratory findings, not proof in people.
    • In ordinary cooking amounts, thyme is simply a safe and flavourful food.
    • Caution: do not use thyme medicines if you are allergic to thyme or to other plants of the mint family, such as oregano, sage or lavender.
    • Caution: most thyme medicines are not recommended for children under 12 — though two named liquid extracts are covered from age 4 at lower doses. Never swallow thyme essential oil — the concentrated oil can irritate the mouth, throat and stomach and is harmful in quantity. In pregnancy, keep to the amounts used in food; the safety of medicinal doses has not been established, and medicinal preparations are not recommended while breastfeeding either, for the same reason. Food amounts are a normal food in both cases.
    • Caution: no interactions with other medicines have been reported for thyme herb preparations in the European monograph — worded as reported, not as none existing. Stomach upset may occur with medicinal thyme preparations; how often is not known. And if a cough lasts longer than a week, or breathlessness, fever or pus-like sputum appear, seek medical advice.
    • When to plant: Sow seed in spring, on the surface, or divide plants; give it the driest, sunniest corner you have
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Poor, dry, stony, gritty soil that drains freely — rich, wet ground gives it weaker flavour and a shorter life
    • Environment: A hardy evergreen perennial that asks almost nothing of the soil — no feeding, and little water once established
    • Planter or ground: Both — pots suit it perfectly
    • Spacing and depth: 25–30 cm apart
    • Water: Dry once settled
    • Companion plants: Cabbage-family plants and strawberries are its classic neighbours
    • When to pick: Snip sprigs through the season, at their strongest just before flowering; trim lightly after flowering, and replace plants after three to four years as they grow woody

    Garden notes

    • Thyme thrives where many herbs fail: poor, dry, stony soil in full sun. Rich, wet ground gives it weaker flavour and a shorter life.
    • Its small flowers draw bees and other pollinating insects over a long season — thyme honey is a classic of the Mediterranean.
    • The low, dense growth holds dry banks and edges, protecting thin soil from washing away.
    • It asks almost nothing of the soil, needing no feeding and little water once established.
    • Named kinds must be grown from cuttings or division, not seed — seed-grown thyme varies a lot from plant to plant, and only cuttings keep a named kind's flavour and form. Winter wet kills more thyme than winter cold: it rots in wet, heavy soil, and established plants need no fertiliser at all — heavy feeding makes tall, weak, spindly growth. A harder cut back of woody stems in spring keeps the plant from opening out into a bare middle. It is hardy in USDA zones 5–9.

    Propagation

    Take softwood cuttings 2 to 3 inches long from new growth in late spring or early summer, or divide a clump in spring or autumn. Cuttings and divisions keep the parent plant true. Seed works too, but named kinds will not come true from seed.

    Cultivars

    • Named kinds of Thymus vulgaris itself: 'Narrow Leaf French' — narrower leaves and a lighter, sweeter taste; the form chefs prefer, and the classic bouquet garni thyme. 'Broadleaf English' — broader leaves and the most robust growth; the standard strong kitchen thyme. 'German Winter' — a very winter-hardy form with good culinary flavour; the one to pick in cold gardens.
    • Lemon thyme is a different plant with its own Latin name — Thymus × citriodorus, a hybrid whose lemon scent comes from citral-rich oil rather than thymol. It is used fresh for fish, poultry, salads and desserts, and is best added fresh, as its lemon scent fades when dried. Its named forms include 'Silver Queen', with silver-edged leaves, and 'Archer's Gold', with gold-tipped leaves.
    • Two more kinds, one line each: Spanish thyme, Thymus zygis, sits inside the European thyme monograph beside vulgaris — shop “thyme herb” may be either species. Creeping thyme, Thymus serpyllum, is a low groundcover for paths and rock gardens with much weaker oil — a groundcover plant, not a kitchen substitute.

    Sources

    • Penn State Extension — Herb Garden Plants: Thyme — cultivars Narrow Leaf French, Broadleaf English and German Winter
    • NC State Extension, Gardener Plant Toolbox — lemon thyme and its cultivars; harvest at peak oil just before flowering
    • McCormick Science Institute — thyme history: bouquet garni, herbes de Provence and za'atar
    • Herb Society of America — Herb of the Month: Thyme — Roman, medieval and First World War uses
    • European Medicines Agency — Thymus vulgaris (thyme herb) monograph
    • Kemmerich et al. (2006) — thyme–ivy syrup trial in acute bronchitis
    • Kemmerich et al. (2007) — thyme–primrose tablet trial in acute bronchitis

    Peppermint

    Mentha × piperita

    MedicinalCulinary

    Digestive HealthRespiratory Health

    FreshDried

    Peppermint is a natural hybrid — a cross between watermint and spearmint that arose in England and was first described there in 1696. It is sterile: it never sets viable seed, so every peppermint plant in the world is a piece of an older plant, spread by runners. The leaf is the part used for teas, and the strong oil distilled from the leaves and flowering tops is a medicine in its own right. Its cooling bite is menthol.

    Peppermint is one of the three plants in Crown Recovery Oil.

    • Peppermint is a young plant, as herbs go. The mints that Greek and Roman writers knew were its parents — spearmint and watermint — not peppermint itself.
    • The cross first appeared in England. In 1696 the botanist John Ray described it there. That was the first written record of the plant.
    • Peppermint is sterile — it never makes seed that can grow. So every peppermint plant since then has come from a runner or a cutting. Every peppermint plant in the world is a piece of an older plant.
    • Mitcham, in Surrey, made it famous. From the 1700s Mitcham grew peppermint for its oil, and Mitcham mint was prized as the finest.
    • Growers took it to America in the 1800s. The United States became a great producer, and the Pacific Northwest is still one of the main oil regions.
    • The distilled oil is also rubbed, diluted, on the forehead and temples for a tension headache: in one small trial of 41 people, a 10% oil solution eased the pain about as well as paracetamol. Human · small

    Traditional medicine

    • The leaf, drunk as a tea, is a traditional remedy for mild digestive cramps, bloating and wind — a use European regulators accept on the basis of long-standing practice.

    Craft

    • The oil scents soaps, candles and bath goods — the sharp, clean smell makers reach for when a product should smell fresh.
    • The oil is a stronger and different thing from the tea. Enteric-coated capsules of peppermint oil — coated so they pass through the stomach and release in the bowel — are the form tested for irritable bowel syndrome: a pooled analysis of 12 trials with 835 people found the capsules eased overall IBS symptoms and abdominal pain better than placebo, and European regulators accept this use. Peppermint tea has never been tested that way, and the capsule results should not be transferred to it.
    • Menthol explains peppermint's reputation for clearing the head. Menthol switches on the cold sensors in the nose, so breathing feels freer and clearer, while careful measurement shows the actual airflow through the nose does not change. It is a genuine comfort during a cold, but it is not a decongestant and does not clear a blocked nose.
    • Caution — reflux: peppermint relaxes the valve at the top of the stomach, so it commonly triggers or worsens heartburn. If you live with reflux or a hiatus hernia, peppermint — tea, oil or capsules — may make it worse; heartburn is also the most common side effect of the oil capsules.
    • Caution: never apply peppermint oil to the face of a baby or young child, and keep it away from their nose — menthol vapour can trigger a spasm of the airways in the very young. The oil is not for children under 2, and the capsules are not recommended under 8. In pregnancy, keep to ordinary food and tea amounts; the safety of medicinal doses has not been established.
    • When to plant: Plant runners or rooted pieces in spring — never seed: true peppermint is sterile, and every new plant comes from a runner or cutting, so a patch stays true to its parent
    • Sun: Full sun or some shade
    • Soil: Moist, rich soil — true to its watermint parent
    • Environment: A hardy perennial that spreads vigorously by runners and can take over a bed
    • Planter or ground: A pot, or a contained corner — this is the rule with mint
    • Spacing and depth: Set pieces 30 cm apart — they soon fill their space
    • Water: Likes water — keep it moist
    • Companion plants: Cabbage-family plants are its classic neighbours — but always from its pot, never loose in the bed
    • When to pick: Harvest the leaves before flowering, for the best flavour; cut it back hard whenever it strays — it always returns

    Garden notes

    • True to its watermint parent, peppermint loves moist, rich soil and spreads vigorously by runners — a patch can take over a bed, which is why it is usually grown in a pot or a contained corner.
    • Because it is sterile, it never self-seeds; every new plant comes from a runner or cutting, so a patch stays true to its parent.
    • When it flowers, the small lilac blooms are worked by bees, and the foliage shelters ground insects through the season.
    • Its roaming roots knit damp soil together at the edges of ponds and ditches where it has escaped gardens.
    • In the garden, give it moisture and containment, harvest the leaves before flowering for the best flavour, and cut it back hard whenever it strays — it always returns.

    Propagation

    Peppermint makes no good seed, so grow new plants from cuttings, runners or division. In spring, pull a rooted runner or a piece of the clump apart and replant it, or set a stem cutting in water or damp mix until it roots. Keep it in a pot — the runners spread fast and take over a bed.

    Sources

    • European Medicines Agency — Mentha × piperita (peppermint leaf and oil) monographs
    • Alammar et al. (2019) — pooled trials of peppermint oil for irritable bowel syndrome
    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — Mentha × piperita, the sterile hybrid described in 1696
    • Göbel et al. (1996) — 10% peppermint oil for tension headache, in 41 people

    Elecampane

    Inula helenium

    Medicinal

    Respiratory Health

    Dried

    A tall, bold daisy-family perennial from Europe and western Asia — big leaves, yellow sunflower-like heads, and a thick, aromatic root. The root is the part used, dug in autumn from plants two or three years old, when it is at its richest. Legend ties its Latin name to Helen of Troy, said to have held the plant when she was carried off to Troy; what is certain is that it has been a household lung herb in Europe for well over two thousand years. Its evidence, though, is thin.

    • An old story tells that Helen of Troy held elecampane in her hand when she was carried off to Troy. This is a story from tradition, not a proven record. But it gave the plant its Latin name, helenium.
    • What is certain is the long use. Greek and Roman doctors wrote about elecampane about 2,000 years ago. It has been a household lung herb in Europe ever since.
    • The Romans also candied the root — they cooked it in sugar to keep it. Candied elecampane was still sold as a sweet for coughs in the 1800s.
    • In 1804, a chemist drew a new substance out of the root. He named it inulin, after the plant's group name, Inula. The fibre still carries that name.
    • People grew it in cottage gardens and physic gardens — gardens of healing plants — for centuries. It was a first remedy for chesty coughs. It kept that standing on tradition alone, as it still does today.

    Traditional medicine

    • Elecampane's reputation rests on tradition: for centuries it has been used as an expectorant — a remedy to loosen phlegm and ease chesty, mucus-heavy coughs and bronchitis. That is a long folk record, and it is only a folk record: elecampane has not been properly tested in human trials for coughs or for anything else.
    • The official verdicts match that thinness. Germany's Commission E reviewed elecampane root and concluded its benefit was not proven well enough, partly because of its allergy potential, and there is no European Medicines Agency monograph for it. It is carried in older herbals and the British Herbal Pharmacopoeia as an expectorant, but no regulator endorses it today.

    Craft

    • The root is a dye plant: softened with ashes and whortleberries (bilberries), it yields a blue dye — and the leaves give blue as well. A rare colour, from a garden root.
    • The root is genuinely remarkable in one measurable way: up to about 44% of the dried root is inulin, a gentle fibre that passes through the stomach undigested and feeds beneficial bacteria in the large intestine. Inulin was first isolated from this very root in 1804, and it is named after the plant's genus, Inula. The root's soothing mucilage — the slippery coating substance — is the most plausible part of its cough tradition.
    • Its bitter compounds, the sesquiterpene lactones such as alantolactone, act against microbes in laboratory tests. That is a laboratory finding only; it has not been shown to fight infections in people.
    • Caution — the daisy family: those same lactones are the characteristic allergens of the daisy family. Do not use elecampane if you are allergic to ragweed, chamomile, marigolds or their relatives, and note that handling the plant can irritate sensitive skin.
    • Caution: avoid elecampane in pregnancy and while breastfeeding — its safety has not been established and traditional references advise against it. Large doses are sickening, causing vomiting, diarrhoea and stomach cramps.
    • When to plant: Sow seed in spring, or divide the roots; give it room — it grows to two metres and is not a plant for a small bed
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Moist, rich, moisture-holding soil; its deep, fleshy roots work heavy ground
    • Environment: A hardy perennial that self-seeds freely into a long-lived, self-maintaining patch
    • Planter or ground: Ground only
    • Spacing and depth: 60–90 cm apart
    • Water: Likes water
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Dig the roots in autumn of the second or third year, when the inulin store is at its peak

    Garden notes

    • A plant of moist, rich ground: its deep, fleshy roots work heavy soil, and the plant itself grows to two metres, giving a patch of ground real structure.
    • The broad yellow flowers open through the summer and are visited by bees and butterflies.
    • It self-seeds freely and holds a long-lived, self-maintaining patch once established — worth knowing before you plant it, as the root harvest means digging the plant up.

    Propagation

    Split a clump in autumn or spring, making sure each piece has a growth bud, or sow seed in spring. It spreads by creeping roots and self-seeding, so give it room.

    Sources

    • Kenny et al. (2022) — review of Inula helenium (elecampane)
    • German Commission E — elecampane root monograph (benefit not proven well enough)
    • British Herbal Pharmacopoeia — elecampane root listed as an expectorant
    • Plants For A Future — Inula helenium: blue dye from the root and leaves

    Fenugreek

    Trigonella foenum-graecum

    MedicinalCulinary

    Blood Sugar Health

    FreshDried

    One of the oldest cultivated plants in the world — a small legume of the Mediterranean and western Asia, grown since the Bronze Age. The seed is the part used as spice and medicine: hard, yellow-brown and sharply aromatic. The leaves are food too, eaten fresh or dried as the herb methi across South Asia. Its Latin species name, foenum-graecum, means "Greek hay", after its ancient use as a fodder crop.

    • Fenugreek is a crop from the Bronze Age. Its seeds have been found in Bronze Age settlements. That makes it one of the oldest farmed plants still in use.
    • In ancient Egypt, people used it as food, as medicine and as fodder — food for farm animals. Fenugreek seeds were placed in Tutankhamun's tomb, among the goods buried with him.
    • The Romans used it to flavour hay for cattle. That use sits behind its Latin name, foenum-graecum, which means Greek hay.
    • From the Mediterranean, it travelled the trade routes east, into the kitchens and the medicine of Persia, India and China.
    • It never left the kitchen in any place it reached. Today, India grows more of it than any other country. It is a staple spice from Ethiopia to Iran.
    • The distilled seed oil is rubbed, diluted, on the skin for boils and eczema, and used in prepared mixtures for indigestion. Traditional use

    Traditional medicine

    • Across South Asia and the Middle East, the seed has a long traditional use for supporting milk flow in breastfeeding mothers — a folk use whose trial evidence is thin and mixed.

    Craft

    • In India the ground seed is soaked and mixed into a paste for hair and skin — a traditional cosmetic, used to soften and condition hair and as a face pack. It is a beauty tradition, not a medicine.
    • Blood sugar is fenugreek's most studied use, and the honest summary is "real but modest". Pooled analyses of trials in people with type 2 diabetes or prediabetes found that fenugreek seed lowered fasting blood sugar by roughly 1 mmol/L and the long-term marker HbA1c by up to about 0.85 points — but the trials were small, mostly of low quality, used medium-to-large daily amounts of seed, and the analyses do not all agree on which measures improve. Fenugreek is a food with a measurable effect, never a treatment for diabetes and never a substitute for diabetes medicine.
    • The seed explains itself: about half of it is a soluble fibre that forms a gel in the gut and slows the absorption of sugar from a meal, and it is roughly a quarter protein, with useful iron.
    • The leaves, eaten as methi, are a nutritious green in their own right.
    • Caution — pregnancy: do not use fenugreek in medicinal amounts during pregnancy. It can stimulate the womb at those doses, regulators advise against more-than-food amounts, and animal studies raise concerns about effects on the developing baby. Ordinary culinary amounts in food are a different matter.
    • Caution — blood sugar medicines: because fenugreek itself lowers blood sugar, it can add to the effect of diabetes medicines and push blood sugar too low. If you take such medicine, treat medicinal use of fenugreek as something to raise with your clinician and watch your readings.
    • Caution — allergy: fenugreek is a legume, a relative of peanut, chickpea and soya, and people allergic to those foods may react to it; the seed dust can also irritate the nose and chest.
    • Caution — blood thinners: case reports link fenugreek taken alongside warfarin with a stronger blood-thinning effect, so take care with anticoagulant medicines.
    • One harmless quirk, documented in medical references: at medicinal doses, fenugreek can make your sweat and urine smell of maple syrup. It fades when you stop, and it is the seed's aroma compound, sotolon, passing through.
    • When to plant: Sow seed outside in spring, in a sunny, well-drained spot
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Well-drained soil, even poor — as a legume it fixes its own nitrogen and leaves the soil richer than it found it
    • Environment: A fast annual in the tradition of an ancient dryland crop; it tolerates dry conditions once established
    • Planter or ground: Both
    • Spacing and depth: Sow 1–2 cm deep, 10–15 cm apart
    • Water: Average — dry once settled
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Cut the leaves young for greens; harvest the pods when they yellow if seed is what you want — about three months from sowing

    Garden notes

    • As a legume, fenugreek fixes nitrogen — bacteria in its root nodules take nitrogen from the air and leave the soil richer than they found it, which is why it is grown as a green manure and fodder crop as well as a spice.
    • Its small white-to-yellow flowers are visited by bees, and the plant asks little: it tolerates dry conditions once established, in the tradition of an ancient dryland crop.
    • The whole plant returns to the soil readily, and surplus plants make a useful nitrogen-rich addition to compost.

    Propagation

    Soak the seed in warm water for twelve hours, then sow it where it will stand in spring. It dislikes being moved, so do not start it in pots and move it.

    Safety

    • Essential oils are concentrates, many times stronger than the plant itself. Always dilute in a carrier oil before putting one on skin, and never swallow an essential oil.

    Sources

    • Neelakantan et al. (2014) — pooled trials of fenugreek and blood sugar
    • Kim et al. (2023) — review of fenugreek trials in diabetes and prediabetes
    • NCCIH — Fenugreek: usefulness and safety
    • USDA FoodData Central — Fenugreek seed
    • Lawless (2014) — Encyclopedia of Essential Oils — steam-distilled fenugreek seed oil for skin and digestion

    Hawthorn

    Crataegus monogyna / C. laevigata

    MedicinalCulinary

    Heart Health

    FreshCooked

    A thorny hedgerow tree native across Europe — common hawthorn and its close cousin the Midland hawthorn — white with blossom in May and red with berries in autumn. Two parts are used: the leaf together with the flower, the "flowering tops", which is the standard medicinal form in Europe, and the ripe red berries, the haws, which are the gentler traditional hedgerow part. Both carry flavonoids and procyanidins — protective plant pigments of the same broad family that colours berries and tea.

    • Common hawthorn grows all across Europe and into western Asia. The Midland hawthorn grows mostly in old woods and on heavier soils — soils with more clay in them. Where the two grow side by side, they cross with each other freely and make mixed trees.
    • Its blossom is tied to May Day. People called hawthorn the “May tree”, and its flowering marked the turn of the year. That link is old — it was there long before hawthorn was used as a medicine.

    Traditional medicine

    • European regulators accept hawthorn leaf with flower as a traditional remedy for temporary nervous cardiac complaints — palpitations and a fluttery, anxious heartbeat — only after a doctor has checked the heart and excluded anything serious. They also list it traditionally for mild stress and to help sleep. These are traditional uses, based on long practice.
    • The berries are the traditional home part — hedgerow jellies and syrups, and country people once ate the young spring leaves in the hedge, the old "bread and cheese". The trial evidence above belongs to leaf-and-flower extracts, not to the berry, and not to teas; the stones inside the haws are not eaten and should be strained out.

    Craft

    • The wood is hard, heavy and fine-grained — a carver’s wood, used for tool handles, walking sticks and small turned pieces. The tree is too small for timber, so its wood goes to small, lasting things. Its charcoal was prized too — hawthorn charcoal burns hotter than oak charcoal.
    • Hawthorn's real trial record concerns one thing: standardised extracts of the leaf and flower, tested as an addition to ordinary treatment in mild heart failure. A Cochrane review of 14 trials found that people taking the extract alongside their usual treatment could exercise a little further and reported less breathlessness and fatigue than those on placebo. The trials were mostly small and short.
    • Against that, the largest single trial — 2,681 people followed for two years — found no clear benefit on its main measure, and the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health calls the heart-failure evidence conflicting. The fair summary is: modest symptom benefits in smaller trials, unconfirmed by the biggest one, always alongside conventional medicine, never instead of it.
    • Caution — never a substitute: hawthorn must never be used in place of prescribed heart or blood-pressure medicine, and heart failure is a condition for doctors, not for self-treatment. Do not stop, reduce or replace any heart medicine because of this herb.
    • Caution — interactions with heart medicines: hawthorn can add to the effect of digoxin and other heart medicines, of beta-blockers, of nitrates, and of blood-pressure medicines — heart rate or blood pressure may fall too far. Anyone taking any of these must talk to their doctor or pharmacist before using hawthorn in medicinal amounts, and use it, if at all, only with their knowledge. (European regulators' own monograph reports no known interactions, and one small study found hawthorn did not change digoxin levels in the blood — but the concern is its added effect on the heart itself, and cancer and heart centres advise medical supervision.)
    • Caution — warning signs come first: swollen ankles or legs, pain in the chest that spreads to the arms, neck or upper abdomen, or new breathlessness are reasons to see a doctor at once. They are never reasons to take an herb.
    • Caution: the safety of hawthorn in pregnancy and while breastfeeding has not been established, and regulators do not recommend it then, nor for heart complaints in anyone under 18. Side effects in the trials were uncommon and mild — dizziness, nausea and digestive upset.
    • Caution — buy carefully: in 2024 the US Food and Drug Administration warned that some products sold as "tejocote root" (Mexican hawthorn) actually contained yellow oleander, a poisonous plant. Buy hawthorn only from reputable sources.
    • When to plant: Plant a young tree, or hedging plants, while dormant — in late winter or spring
    • Sun: Full sun or some shade
    • Soil: Almost any soil, even poor; it tolerates poor soil and exposure
    • Environment: A long-lived, deep-rooted small tree that holds banks and field edges and forms the backbone of laid hedges; few trees give wildlife more — blossom for bees, haws for birds deep into winter, thorny branches for nesting
    • Planter or ground: Ground only
    • Spacing and depth: Hedging plants 30–45 cm apart; a tree needs 4–5 m
    • Water: Water through the first year; settled trees need little
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Gather the flowering tops in May, as the blossom opens, and the haws in autumn, when they are fully red and softening

    Garden notes

    • Few trees give wildlife more. The May blossom feeds bees and other pollinating insects; the haws feed thrushes, fieldfares and redwings deep into winter; and the dense, thorny branches are safe nesting cover for small birds.
    • A long-lived, deep-rooted tree that holds banks and field edges, tolerates poor soil and exposure, and forms the backbone of laid hedges across the countryside.
    • Its leaf litter and fallen fruit return minerals to the soil beneath the hedge, feeding the whole hedgerow community.

    Propagation

    Sow fresh seed in autumn in a pot outdoors and leave it through winter — the seed needs a warm spell, then a cold spell, before it will sprout, and it can take up to 18 months. A tree grown from seed will not match its parent, and it takes years to fruit.

    Sources

    • Guo et al. (2008) — Cochrane review of hawthorn extract for chronic heart failure
    • Holubarsch et al. (2008) — the SPICE trial of hawthorn in heart failure
    • European Medicines Agency — Crataegus (hawthorn leaf with flower) monograph
    • NCCIH — Hawthorn: usefulness and safety

    Arrowhead

    Syngonium podophyllum 'Gold Allusion'

    Ornamental

    Also called the goosefoot plant and American evergreen. The 'Gold Allusion' form has golden-green, arrow-shaped leaves traced with pink veins. A young plant sits in a neat, bushy mound made for tabletops and shelves — but it is a vine by birth, and given time it will start to trail and climb.

    • The plant comes from the tropical rainforests of southern Mexico, the West Indies, and Central and South America.
    • In the wild it begins life on the shaded forest floor, then climbs tree trunks toward the light. It is a hemiepiphyte — a plant that starts in the ground and spends its adult life climbing, rooting into the bark as it goes. Wild vines can climb ten metres or more.
    • The forest floor it comes from is deep in fallen leaves, so the soil there stays rich, moist and loose, and its roots spread through that soft, rotting layer.
    • Its leaves change as it climbs. Young leaves are simple arrows; older leaves divide into lobes — rounded parts — often five. 'Gold Allusion' is a bred variety in the Allusion series, chosen for its gold-green colour and pink veining. Its name, Syngonium, comes from Greek words for the plant's fused reproductive parts — the parts for making seed, grown together as one.
    • In feng shui — the Chinese practice of arranging a space to keep its energy in balance — the arrowhead is a favoured plant. The five lobes of its mature leaves are said to stand for the five elements — wood, fire, earth, water and metal — held in balance, and it is placed near sharp corners to soften their harsh energy.
    • It is also read as a symbol of steady growth and new beginnings, and is often given to someone starting something — a home, a venture, a next chapter.
    • The genus has a dated, named history. The name Syngonium was first used by the Austrian aroid specialist Heinrich Wilhelm Schott in 1829; the first plant later placed in it had been described by Linnaeus in 1763, as Arum auritum. Thomas Croat's revision of 1981 — the first full revision since 1920 — recognised 33 species; work since has raised the genus to about 40 accepted species, most of them in Central America, with Costa Rica and Panama the richest ground.
    • As a genus, Syngonium runs from Mexico south to Bolivia, Brazil and Paraguay, from dry forest to wet forest, from sea level to about 2,000 metres. Botanists recognise two natural varieties of this one species: var. podophyllum, from Mexico to Brazil, and var. peliocladum, from Costa Rica and Panama.
    • Of the roughly 40 species, this is the one that fills the shops: Syngonium podophyllum is the most widely produced species in the indoor foliage trade, and most named houseplant forms come from it.
    • When to plant: Indoors any time — new plants and cuttings settle fastest in spring
    • Light: Bright, indirect light indoors; it tolerates lower light, though the gold colour fades in the dim
    • Soil: A well-draining mix that still holds moisture — 2 parts potting soil, 1 part perlite or pumice, 1 part orchid bark
    • Environment: Warm rooms, 60–85°F, with steady indoor conditions away from cold drafts. The foliage looks best at about 40–60% humidity — dry winter room air is the usual reason leaf edges brown. Chilling injury can start below about 55°F; outdoors it is frost-tender, USDA zones 10–12 only
    • Pot: Pots — pinch the tips to keep it bushy, or give it a support to climb
    • Water: Keep the mix evenly moist — water when the surface has dried slightly, and let the excess drain away; less often in the colder months

    Care in detail

    • Light: bright, indirect light suits it best; it tolerates lower light, though the gold colour fades in the dim. Variegated forms grown in shade can revert to plain green, and their pale patches scorch first in strong sun.
    • Water: keep the mix evenly moist — water when the surface has dried slightly, and let the excess drain away; water less often in the colder months. A plant kept to “completely dry” will sulk.
    • Feed: a balanced liquid fertilizer into the soil through spring and summer — commercial growers feed at roughly a 3-1-2 ratio.
    • Soil: a well-draining mix that still holds moisture — 2 parts potting soil, 1 part perlite or pumice, 1 part orchid bark. A slightly acid mix, about pH 5.5–6.5, suits it — the bark and perlite mix already lands there.
    • Temperature: 60–85°F.
    • Pruning and climbing: prune the tips to keep it bushy, or give it a support to climb. A moss pole does more than hold it up: given something to climb and root into, the plant produces its large, divided adult leaves, of 5 to 11 leaflets; kept trailing or pinched, it stays in the small arrow-leaf form.

    Toxicity

    Toxic if eaten — all parts contain calcium oxalate crystals, tiny needle-shaped crystals that irritate the mouth and digestive tract. Keep out of reach of children and pets; it is listed as toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

    The sap can irritate sensitive skin — wear gloves when taking cuttings or pruning.

    Never plant it out in a frost-free climate: in Florida it has escaped from gardens, and the Florida Invasive Species Council lists it as a Category I invasive. Keep it in a pot indoors, and never dump cuttings or soil where they could root outdoors in warm climates.

    Propagation

    In spring or summer, cut a 4–6 inch stem just below a node — the bump where a leaf joins the stem — and root it in water or moist potting mix in bright, indirect light. A leaf on its own, with no node, will not make a new plant. Wear gloves — the sap irritates skin and eyes.

    Cultivars

    • 'White Butterfly' is the standard, most common form — mostly white to pale-green leaves with green margins and white veins, and a compact, reluctant-to-vine habit.
    • The Allusion series — the family 'Gold Allusion' belongs to — includes 'Berry Allusion' (white centre fading to green, light red veins), 'Bold Allusion' (large cream leaves, olive splashes at the edges, pink veins), 'Maria Allusion' (new leaves bronze-pink, maturing coppery-green), 'Pink Allusion' (light olive-green with deep pink veins) and 'Cream Allusion'.
    • Pink forms: 'Neon Robusta', whose new leaves open solid bright pink and mature green, bred from 'White Butterfly'; 'Regina Red', blushing red with olive speckles; 'Strawberry Cream', opening creamy blush-pink and mellowing to green with pink veins; and 'Pink Splash', pale green with light pink speckles.
    • Speckled forms: 'Confetti' (light green with large pink splotches), 'Milk Confetti' (frosted green with many small pink patches and the odd large blotch) and 'Three Kings' (each leaf patterned dark green, light green and white).
    • White-variegated forms: 'Albo-variegatum' (green with mottled white variegation, pink-tinted stems), 'Holly' (compact, leaves nearly solid white with small dark-green speckles at the edges) and 'Batik' (dark green with white veins).
    • Small, compact forms: 'Pixie', with white radiating from the veins into dark green, and 'Glo-Go', dark green with striking light-cream veins and limited vining.
    • Two other species are sold beside it, named here as species, not varieties: Syngonium wendlandii, deep green with a silver centre stripe, and Syngonium angustatum, with narrow leaves that later divide deeply.

    Sources

    • Croat (1981) — a revision of Syngonium: genus history from 1829, 33 species, the two varieties of S. podophyllum
    • Croat et al. (2019) — the genus at about 40 species, centred on Central America
    • Clemson University Extension, HGIC — arrowhead vine: popular species and variegated cultivars, with descriptions
    • Chen et al. (2004) — cultural guidelines for commercial production of Syngonium, UF/IFAS: cultivar table, humidity, temperature, feeding
    • NC State University Extension, Plant Toolbox — Syngonium podophyllum: watering, mature leaf division, hardiness
    • University of Florida IFAS Extension — Syngonium podophyllum in Florida: Category I invasive listing
    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — Syngonium podophyllum, native range
    • ASPCA — Syngonium podophyllum toxicity (calcium oxalate crystals)
    • Cummings & Waring (2019) — review of sealed-chamber plant air studies and real rooms

    Heartleaf Philodendron

    Philodendron hederaceum

    Ornamental

    The sweetheart plant: a trailing or climbing vine with glossy, heart-shaped leaves, two to four inches across, that unfold bronze and settle to deep green. One of the most forgiving houseplants ever sold — and one of the first to be sold to everyone.

    • This plant comes from southern Mexico. Its home runs through Central America and the Caribbean and into tropical South America — the hot, wet lands near the equator.
    • In the wild, it starts life on the forest floor. A plant that lives this way is called a hemiepiphyte: it starts in the ground, then climbs. Its seedlings crawl across the floor until they find a tree trunk. Then they climb up into the canopy — the leafy top of the forest — rooting at every node as they go. A node is the point on a stem where a leaf grows. They root into bark and fallen leaves. The higher the plant climbs into the light, the bigger its leaves grow.
    • The soil on that forest floor is a thin, rich layer of rotted leaves over poor ground below. That is why this plant feeds happily from a light, airy potting mix. It can even take in water through the roots that grow in the air along its stems.
    • Its trailing stems can run many feet long — well past thirteen feet, given time and something to climb.
    • Captain William Bligh — the captain known for the ship Bounty — carried a plant of it from the Caribbean to Kew Gardens in London in 1793.
    • The plant was first named Arum hederaceum by Nikolaus von Jacquin in 1760. In 1829, Heinrich Schott moved it into the group called Philodendron. The name Philodendron means “tree-loving”, which fits the way it climbs.
    • For many years it stayed a plant of botanic gardens only. Then, in 1936, Woolworth's five-and-dime stores — shops that sold cheap everyday goods — began selling it for five cents a plant. That started the first great houseplant craze, a time when almost everyone wanted plants in the home. This is the plant that taught ordinary families to keep plants.
    • It has a tangle of old names — scandens, oxycardium and micans. They show how much it changes across its wide home range. In 2012, plant scientists settled hederaceum as the right name. The soft, velvet-leaved form sold as 'Micans' is this same plant in a softer form.
    • When to plant: Indoors any time — new plants and cuttings settle fastest in spring
    • Light: Bright, indirect light indoors gives the fastest growth and the biggest leaves; it tolerates low light, growing more slowly. Keep it out of direct sun, which scorches the leaves
    • Soil: A mix with strong drainage and air in it — 2 parts potting soil, 1 part perlite or pumice, 1 part orchid bark or coco coir
    • Environment: 65–85°F, and always above 55°F
    • Pot: Pots — it trails from shelves and hanging baskets, or climbs a support
    • Water: Water thoroughly when the top soil feels completely dry — every one to two weeks; less in the cold season

    Care in detail

    • Light: bright, indirect light gives the fastest growth and the biggest leaves; it tolerates low light, growing more slowly. Keep it out of direct sun, which scorches the leaves.
    • Water: water thoroughly and discard what drains through, or bottom-water by standing the pot in shallow water; repeat every one to two weeks, when the top soil feels completely dry. Water less in the cold season.
    • Feed: a balanced liquid fertilizer once a month in spring and summer.
    • Soil: a mix with strong drainage and air in it — 2 parts potting soil, 1 part perlite or pumice, 1 part orchid bark or coco coir.
    • Temperature: 65–85°F, and always above 55°F.

    Toxicity

    Toxic if eaten — the leaves and stems contain calcium oxalate crystals, tiny needle-shaped crystals that irritate the mouth and digestive tract. Keep out of reach of children and pets.

    Propagation

    Cut a stem 3 to 6 inches long just below a leaf joint (node) in spring or early summer, strip the lower leaves, and stand it in a glass of water or moist potting mix in bright, indirect light. Roots show in a few weeks. A leaf on its own will never root — the cutting must carry a node, where the leaf joins the stem.

    Sources

    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — Philodendron hederaceum
    • Wolverton (1989) — NASA Clean Air Study, sealed-chamber tests
    • Cummings & Waring (2019) — review of sealed-chamber plant air studies and real rooms
    • ASPCA — Philodendron hederaceum toxicity (calcium oxalate crystals)

    Pothos

    Epipremnum aureum

    Ornamental

    Golden pothos — also called devil's ivy and hunter's robe. A glossy vine with heart-shaped green leaves marbled in gold, so hard to kill that folklore gave it the devil's name. A common first houseplant.

    • Kew's Plants of the World Online gives this plant just one true home: Mo'orea, a volcanic island in the Society Islands of French Polynesia. There it climbs in wet tropical forest, on rich volcanic soil deep in fallen leaves.
    • People carried it from there to everywhere. It now grows wild across the tropics — the Caribbean, Florida, Hawaii, South and Southeast Asia, and northern Australia. In some of those places it escapes from gardens and smothers the native forest, so it should never be planted outdoors in a warm climate.
