    • In the wild, it climbs high into the tops of the trees. The leaves on a climbing stem can grow huge, and they split into deep lobes — deep cuts in the leaf. They look nothing like the small hearts on a houseplant. A potted pothos almost never flowers. It stays young for ever, and that is part of why it is so easy to keep.
    • Nearly all of the dozens of named kinds came from this one species. They began as sports — chance changes in one plant, spotted by a grower and then copied from cuttings. Marble Queen, with white marbling, is one kind. Neon, a solid bright yellow-green, is another.
    • Its name is a fossil of its own history — a piece of the past that stayed. It was first described in 1880 as Pothos aureus, which is why we still call it pothos. In 1908 it was moved to Scindapsus aureus. In the early 1960s, a rare flowering moved it again, to Rhaphidophora aurea. Then, in 1964, the botanist George Bunting settled it as Epipremnum aureum.
    • Its toughness earned it the name devil's ivy. Tradition says it can survive even in "the depths of Hell", and it can stay green in near-darkness.
    • In India and China, people know it as the money plant. They believe it draws money and good fortune. In feng shui and in Vastu Shastra — two old systems for how things are placed in a home — it is used to clear bad, stuck energy. People place it in the southeast of a room, the corner of prosperity, to invite wealth and success.
    • When to plant: Indoors any time — new plants and cuttings settle fastest in spring
    • Light: Bright, indirect light indoors keeps the gold marbling strong; it adapts to low light but may lose its variegation there
    • Soil: A chunky mix that breathes while holding some moisture — 2 parts potting soil, 1 part perlite or bark, 1 part vermiculite or moss
    • Environment: 65–85°F, in ordinary warm rooms
    • Pot: Pots — it trails, or climbs a pole or trellis, which rewards it with larger leaves
    • Water: Water when the topsoil is completely dry, then drain well; reduce water in colder weather

    Care in detail

    • Light: bright, indirect light keeps the gold marbling strong; it adapts to low light but may lose its variegation there.
    • Water: water when the topsoil is completely dry — slowly, or by bottom-watering, standing the pot in a shallow bowl until the soil is visibly wet, then draining. Feed monthly, and reduce both feed and water in colder weather.
    • Soil: a chunky mix that breathes while holding some moisture — 2 parts potting soil, 1 part perlite or bark, 1 part vermiculite or moss.
    • Support: pothos climbs by nature; a pole or trellis rewards it with larger leaves.
    • Temperature: 65–85°F.

    Toxicity

    Toxic if eaten — all parts contain calcium oxalate crystals, tiny needle-shaped crystals that irritate the mouth and digestive tract. Keep out of reach of children and pets.

    Propagation

    Cut a healthy stem just below a node — the little bump where a leaf joins the stem — in spring. Set the cutting in water or damp potting mix with at least one node under the surface and no leaves in the water. Roots show in a few weeks; pot it up once they are an inch or two long. Keep cuttings away from pets and children — the plant is toxic if eaten.

    Sources

    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — Epipremnum aureum, native to Mo'orea
    • Wolverton (1989) — NASA Clean Air Study, sealed-chamber tests
    • Cummings & Waring (2019) — review of sealed-chamber plant air studies and real rooms
    • ASPCA — Epipremnum aureum toxicity (calcium oxalate crystals)

    Snake Plant

    Dracaena trifasciata

    Ornamental

    Snake plant — also called mother-in-law's tongue and Saint George's sword. Stiff, upright swords of leaves, deep green with darker bands and, on the best-known form 'Laurentii', bright yellow edges, rising two to four feet from thick underground stems. A plant built for dry country and forgetful waterers.

    • It is native to tropical West Africa, from Nigeria east to the Congo. There it grows in dry, rocky ground and at the edges of open woodland.
    • Its home soil is thin, sandy and poor, and rain there comes in seasons. The plant answers with rhizomes — thick underground stems — that store water and spread slowly outward into new rosettes of leaves.
    • It also breathes on a dry-country schedule. Its leaves open their pores at night, when the air is cooler, and close them by day. That way it loses far less water to the heat. Botanists call this CAM photosynthesis — short for crassulacean acid metabolism. It is a large part of why the plant shrugs off drought and neglect indoors.
    • For two centuries, its name was Sansevieria trifasciata. The genus was named by Carl Peter Thunberg for Raimondo di Sangro, Prince of San Severo — an Italian prince, alchemist and inventor. In 2017, DNA evidence folded the sansevierias into Dracaena. It has carried its present name since.
    • Before it was a houseplant, it was a working plant. In Africa, people worked the tough fibres of its leaves by hand. That work gave it an old name: viper's bowstring hemp.
    • In Brazil and Portugal it is the espada de São Jorge — Saint George's sword. Tradition ties the name to Saint George, the saint who slew a dragon with his sword's tip, and the leaves are shaped like swords. People grow it outside their houses and by their doors, to ward off evil and protect the home.
    • Across many cultures, it stands for resilience and strength. In feng shui it is placed near entrances for its rising, protective energy, and is said to encourage prosperity.

    Craft

    • The leaves hold a strong fibre — bowstring hemp. It has been twisted into bowstrings, rope and nets, and woven into baskets and mats in the plant's home regions.
    • When to plant: Indoors any time — new plants and divisions settle fastest in spring
    • Light: Brightest in bright, indirect light indoors, and extremely adaptable to low light
    • Soil: A chunky, free-draining mix — 2 parts potting soil, 1 part perlite or bark, 1 part vermiculite or moss; a cactus or succulent mix suits it too
    • Environment: 65–85°F; it tolerates dry indoor air
    • Pot: Pots — a snug, heavy pot balances the upright leaves
    • Water: Water only when the soil is completely dry, then generously, and let it drain completely — overwatering, not thirst, is what kills it

    Care in detail

    • Light: brightest in bright, indirect light, and extremely adaptable to low light.
    • Water: water only when the soil is completely dry, then water generously and let it drain completely. Overwatering, not thirst, is what kills it — its rhizomes rot in wet soil.
    • Feed: fertilize monthly, and decrease feed and water in colder weather.
    • Soil: a chunky, free-draining mix — 2 parts potting soil, 1 part perlite or bark, 1 part vermiculite or moss. A cactus or succulent mix suits it too.
    • Temperature: 65–85°F.

    Toxicity

    Toxic if eaten — the leaves contain saponins, soap-like compounds that cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea in people and pets. Keep out of reach of children and pets.

    Propagation

    Divide the clump in spring, so each piece has leaves and roots, or root leaf sections in damp, gritty mix. Leaf cuttings from yellow-edged types like 'Laurentii' usually grow back plain green — divide those to keep the yellow edge. Wear gloves, as the sap can irritate skin.

    Sources

    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — Dracaena trifasciata
    • Wolverton (1989) — NASA Clean Air Study, sealed-chamber tests
    • Cummings & Waring (2019) — review of sealed-chamber plant air studies and real rooms
    • ASPCA — Dracaena trifasciata toxicity (saponins)

    Spider Plant

    Chlorophytum comosum

    Ornamental

    Spider plant — also called the airplane plant and the ribbon plant. A fountain of long, arching leaves, each striped cream or pale yellow down its centre, that sends out trailing stems tipped with small white flowers and baby plantlets — "spiderettes" — every one of them a new plant. Fast, forgiving, and safe to keep around pets.

    • It is native across a wide sweep of Africa, from the tropics down to South Africa. There it is common from the Western Cape to Limpopo.
    • In the wild, it grows on forest margins and in coastal thicket, often in the shade of trees, in soil enriched by fallen leaves. Its thick, tuberous roots store water against dry spells — one reason it forgives a missed watering.
    • Carl Peter Thunberg, the Swedish naturalist known as the father of South African botany, collected it on his expeditions into the eastern interior. He gave it its first scientific name in 1794.
    • In the Victorian era it was the "ribbon plant". Its striped leaves echoed the ribbons in fashion at the time. The spider name came later, from the plantlets dangling at the ends of their stems like spiders on silk.
    • In South Africa, the plant holds a tender place in Nguni tradition. It is kept in the room where a mother and her newborn stay, as a protective charm for them both. Water in which the roots have been dipped is drunk by the mother, in the belief that it protects the infant. An infusion — a drink made by soaking the plant in water — is traditionally given to the baby as a purgative, to clear the bowels.
    • The best-known cultivar — a named garden form — is 'Vittatum': green leaf edges around a broad cream centre stripe. 'Variegatum' reverses the pattern, with white edges and a green centre. 'Fire Flash', sold alongside them with bright orange stems, is a close relative — Chlorophytum orchidastrum — rather than this species.
    • When to plant: Indoors any time — plantlets root fastest in spring
    • Light: Bright, indirect light indoors; prolonged direct sun scorches the leaves
    • Soil: A chunky, nutrient-rich mix with strong drainage — 2 parts potting soil, 1 part perlite or pumice, 1 part orchid bark
    • Environment: 55–80°F, with consistent warmth and moderate humidity; it is sensitive to fluoride in tap water, so rainwater or distilled water keeps the leaf tips cleaner
    • Pot: Pots and hanging baskets — the plantlets trail over the edge
    • Water: Water when the top one to two inches of soil feel dry — thoroughly, discarding the excess

    Care in detail

    • Light: bright, indirect light; prolonged direct sun scorches the leaves.
    • Water: water when the top one to two inches of soil feel dry — thoroughly, discarding the excess, or by bottom-watering, standing the pot in shallow water to drink from below.
    • Feed: a balanced, water-soluble fertilizer once a month in spring and summer; reduce feeding in fall and winter as growth slows.
    • Soil: a chunky, nutrient-rich mix with strong drainage — 2 parts potting soil, 1 part perlite or pumice, 1 part orchid bark.
    • Temperature: 55–80°F, with consistent warmth and moderate humidity.
    • Brown leaf tips are common and usually harmless; the plant is sensitive to fluoride in tap water, so rainwater or distilled water keeps the tips cleaner.

    Toxicity

    Non-toxic — spider plant is listed as safe for cats and dogs and is not known to be toxic to people, which makes it a good choice for homes with children and pets.

    Propagation

    Pot up the small plantlets at the ends of the runners — pin one still joined to the parent onto moist mix until it roots, then cut the runner, or pot a plantlet that already has roots. Any time of year indoors, best in spring and summer. Cut the runner only once the plantlet holds firm when you tug it gently.

    Sources

    • SANBI, PlantZAfrica — Chlorophytum comosum, collected and named by Thunberg (1794)
    • Hutchings et al. (1996) — Zulu Medicinal Plants: Nguni uses of spider plant
    • Wolverton (1989) — NASA Clean Air Study, sealed-chamber tests
    • Cummings & Waring (2019) — review of sealed-chamber plant air studies and real rooms

    Monstera

    Monstera deliciosa

    Culinary

    Fresh

    Swiss Cheese Plant, Ceriman, Mexican Breadfruit, or — mistakenly — Split-Leaf Philodendron. A Monstera grows large and bold indoors. In the wild it is a climbing vine of the tropical forest, scrambling up tree trunks toward the light. It grows the same way indoors, growing fast through the warm months and unfurling leaf after enormous leaf.

    Appearance

    • Young Monstera leaves are smooth, glossy and heart-shaped. As the plant matures and climbs toward brighter light, each new leaf arrives larger, deeply split along its edges and pierced with natural holes — the fenestrations that earned it the Swiss Cheese name. Botanists think the splits and holes serve the plant in its forest home, letting wind pass through the huge leaves without tearing them, and letting light filter down to the leaves below. Thick aerial roots grow from the stems — the same roots that grip tree bark in the wild. A mature leaf can approach three feet long outdoors; indoors, leaves of one to two feet are usual.
    • Monstera deliciosa comes from the humid tropical forests of southern Mexico, south through Central America to Panama. Its range takes in Guatemala, Belize, Honduras and Costa Rica. It grows from the lowland forests up into the lower mountain slopes.
    • In the wild, a Monstera begins life on the dark forest floor. Its seedling does something remarkable: it grows toward the darkest shadow it can find, because darkness usually means the base of a tree. Once it reaches a trunk, it turns upward and climbs toward the light at the top of the forest, holding on with its aerial roots — roots that grow out into the air. Botanists call it a hemi-epiphyte. That means it starts life in the soil but spends much of it in the air, rooted into bark and pockets of fallen leaves, drinking in the warm, wet forest air. The light it loves best is the forest's own: bright, but filtered through leaves.
    • A climbing Monstera barely lives in soil at all. Its first roots sit in the thin, spongy layer of fallen leaves that covers the forest floor. Its climbing roots press into cracks in the bark stuffed with decaying leaves and moss. What feeds it is that layer of fallen leaves. Fungi and microbes — tiny living things — break the leaves down, without pause, into a rich, dark humus. The plant's roots tap straight into it: some still reach the ground, and others take in moisture and food from the debris packed around them. Rain passes through quickly, so its roots are used to water that arrives often but never stands. That is exactly what a chunky, airy potting mix imitates indoors.
    • The genus name Monstera was coined by the French botanist Michel Adanson in 1763. It is usually traced to the Latin monstrum — a monster — a fitting word for leaves of such size and strangeness. The species was described for science in 1849 by the Danish botanist Frederik Liebmann, who found it growing in Mexico. Deliciosa means "delicious" — for its fruit.
    • That fruit is famous in its homeland. It is called piñanona, a blend of piña (pineapple) and anona (custard apple). It has been eaten in Mexico since long before botanists arrived, and in the 1800s it was sold in the markets of Veracruz. Fully ripe, it tastes of pineapple and banana. Only the fully ripe fruit is eaten. The unripe fruit is full of irritating crystals and is not to be eaten, and the rest of the plant is not food either: its leaves carry calcium oxalate crystals, and the plant is toxic if eaten. In Spanish the plant is also called Costilla de Adán — "Adam's rib" — for the cut of its leaves.
    • Brought to Europe in the 1840s, it caused a sensation in Victorian glasshouses, and it has stayed popular since. It is often called a split-leaf philodendron, but that is a case of mistaken identity. Monstera is its own genus — its own branch of the family — a cousin of the philodendrons, not one of them.

    Craft

    • The big cut leaves are a florist's material: they last well in water and are used in bold, tropical flower arrangements.
    • The older craft is in the roots: the long aerial roots were used as ropes in Peru, woven into baskets in Mexico, and wound into frames for “mimbre” furniture in Guatemala — a working fibre long before the leaf became a florist’s decoration.
    • A Monstera is a generous presence in a room. Its broad leaves give off moisture as they breathe, gently raising the humidity around them — a kindness in dry, heated homes, and to the other tropical plants grouped nearby. And there is a simple pleasure in tending a plant that visibly rewards you, with a new leaf unfurling every few weeks in the growing season. It is often sold as an air purifier, but no houseplant can meaningfully clean a room's air — grow it for its leaves.
    • When to plant: Indoors any time — new plants settle fastest in spring
    • Light: Bright, indirect light indoors — an east or west window, or a few feet back from a sunny south one; too little light and the new leaves arrive plain and hole-less
    • Soil: Chunky and airy, like the forest litter it roots into at home — 2 parts potting soil, 1 part orchid bark, 1 part perlite; free-draining and slightly acidic
    • Environment: 65–85°F; it sulks below 60°F, so keep it clear of cold drafts
    • Pot: Pots — give it a moss pole, coir pole or sturdy trellis to climb, and it grows bigger, better leaves
    • Water: Water thoroughly when the top inch or two of mix feels dry, and let the excess drain away — never leave it standing in water; less in winter

    Care in detail

    • Potting Mix: Chunky and airy, like the forest litter it roots into at home. A good mix: 2 parts potting soil, 1 part orchid bark, 1 part perlite — free-draining and slightly acidic.
    • Support: Monstera is a climber, and it grows bigger, better leaves when it can climb. Give it a moss pole, coir pole or sturdy trellis, and tie the stems in loosely as it grows. Left to sprawl, it stays smaller-leafed and leggy.
    • Water, Feed, & Frequency: Water thoroughly when the top inch or two of mix feels dry, and let the excess drain away — never leave it standing in water. It drinks most in spring and summer and needs less in winter. Feed monthly with a balanced liquid fertilizer through the growing season, and rest it in winter.
    • Light & Temperature: Bright, indirect light — an east or west window, or a few feet back from a sunny south one. Too little light and the new leaves arrive plain and hole-less; harsh midday sun scorches them. Monstera thrives in temperatures ranging between 65-85°F, and sulks below 60°F, so keep it clear of cold drafts.

    Toxicity

    Toxic if eaten — the leaves contain calcium oxalate crystals. Keep out of reach from children and pets

    Propagation

    Cut a stem piece 1–2 inches below a node in spring or early summer and root it in water or a light mix, or wrap damp moss round a node on the plant until roots form, then cut it off. Each piece must have a node — a leaf on its own will never make a new plant and will rot. New leaves can take 2–3 months to show.

    Sources

    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — Monstera deliciosa, native from southern Mexico to Panama
    • Plants For A Future — Monstera deliciosa: aerial roots used for rope, baskets and furniture frames
    • Madison (1977) — revision of the genus Monstera
    • Cedeño-Fonseca et al. (2020) — Monstera of Costa Rica and Panama
    • ASPCA — Monstera deliciosa toxicity (calcium oxalate crystals)
    • RHS — Monstera deliciosa care guidance

    Peace Lily

    Spathiphyllum wallisii

    Ornamental

    White Sails, Spathe Flower, or most commonly the Peace Lily — and, despite the name, not a lily at all. A tropical forest-floor plant, it settles happily into the shadier corners that other plants refuse, and rewards steady, simple care with glossy leaves and white blooms. It also has a famous way of asking for water: let it get too dry and the whole plant wilts dramatically — then perks up again within hours of a drink.

    Appearance

    • Its leaves are deep green, glossy and lance-shaped, arching out from the base of the plant in a soft fountain. The white "flowers" are not flowers at all: each is a spathe, a modified leaf curved like a little sail or spoon around a creamy spike — the spadix — which carries the true, tiny flowers. A happy plant blooms most freely in spring and summer, though it may send up spathes at almost any time of year.
    • The genus Spathiphyllum — the group this plant belongs to — comes from the tropical Americas, from Mexico through Central America to Brazil. It has the most species in Colombia and Venezuela. Across the Pacific, a smaller group of species reaches Southeast Asia and the western Pacific islands. The peace lilies in our homes come mostly from the American species, above all those of Colombia and Venezuela.
    • In the wild, peace lilies grow on the floor of humid tropical forests, in the deep shade of the tree canopy — the roof of leaves overhead. They grow very often along the banks of rivers and streams, in ground that stays moist and is sometimes flooded for part of the year. The light there is dim and dappled, the air is warm and wet, and their shallow roots sit in soft, rich forest soil. That is why a peace lily is so content in a shady room, and so unhappy in a dry one.
    • The ground beneath a wild peace lily is barely mineral at all. It is mostly fallen leaves at every stage of decay. Fungi, bacteria and small creatures work them over into a dark, spongy humus — rich, rotted plant matter — that holds water like a sponge, yet still lets floodwater drain through. Its shallow, fibrous roots live in that top layer. They drink steadily, and feed on the slow release of nutrients from the fallen leaves. A potting mix that holds moisture and is rich in organic matter is the indoor match for that forest floor.
    • The name Spathiphyllum was given by the Austrian botanist Heinrich Wilhelm Schott in 1832. It comes from the Greek spathē, a broad blade or spathe, and phyllon, a leaf: the plant with a leaf-like spathe. The best-known species, Spathiphyllum wallisii, honours Gustav Wallis, the German plant collector who found it growing in Colombia.
    • The common name is pure symbolism. The white spathe, held high above the leaves, is said to look like the white flag of truce. So the plant came to stand for peace. It is also linked with purity and sympathy, which is why peace lilies are so often given at times of loss, and placed in memorial gardens and quiet corners. And despite the lily in its name, it belongs to the arum family — the same family as Monstera, Pothos and the ZZ Plant — not to the true lilies at all.
    • When to plant: Indoors any time — new plants settle fastest in spring
    • Light: Medium to low indirect light indoors — it is one of the most shade-tolerant flowering houseplants, though brighter indirect light brings more blooms. Keep direct sun off the leaves
    • Soil: A rich, moisture-holding mix that still drains freely — 2 parts potting soil, 1 part perlite, 1 part compost or bark; keep the drainage hole clear
    • Environment: 65–80°F; cold below about 55°F damages it, so keep it away from drafts and chilly windowsills. It appreciates humidity
    • Pot: Pots — it wants moisture, not a swamp
    • Water: Keep the mix evenly moist, and water when the top inch feels dry; if the leaves wilt, water promptly — it usually recovers within hours

    Care in detail

    • Potting Mix: A rich, moisture-holding mix that still drains freely. A good mix: 2 parts potting soil, 1 part perlite, 1 part compost or bark. It wants moisture, not a swamp, so keep the drainage hole clear.
    • Water, Feed, & Frequency: Keep the mix evenly moist, and water when the top inch feels dry. If the leaves wilt, water promptly — it usually recovers within hours, though it is kinder not to let it faint often. It appreciates humidity: misting, a pebble tray, or a spot among other plants all help, and rainwater or filtered water can prevent the brown leaf tips that hard tap water sometimes causes. Feed lightly every six to eight weeks in spring and summer; it needs little.
    • Light & Temperature: Medium to low indirect light suits it — it is one of the most shade-tolerant flowering houseplants — though brighter indirect light brings more blooms. Keep direct sun off the leaves, which scorch easily. It thrives in temperatures ranging between 65-80°F, and cold below about 55°F damages it, so keep it away from drafts and chilly windowsills.

    Toxicity

    Toxic if eaten. It is not a true lily, but its calcium oxalate crystals irritate the mouth — keep out of reach from children and pets

    Propagation

    Divide a full, healthy plant in spring. Lift it from its pot and gently pull the clump apart so each piece keeps its own shoots and roots, then pot each piece in fresh mix. Wear gloves — the sap can irritate skin. A leaf in water will not root, so do not try cuttings.

    Sources

    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — the genus Spathiphyllum
    • Missouri Botanical Garden — Spathiphyllum, Greek for leaf-spathe
    • Wolverton (1989) — NASA Clean Air Study, sealed-chamber tests
    • Cummings & Waring (2019) — review of sealed-chamber plant air studies and real rooms
    • RHS — peace lily care guidance

    ZZ Plant

    Zamioculcas zamiifolia

    Ornamental

    Zanzibar Gem, Aroid Palm, Emerald Palm, Eternity Plant — or simply the ZZ. The ZZ Plant is built for neglect. From the dry grasslands and forest edges of eastern Africa, it stores its own water underground, shrugs off dim rooms, and asks for almost nothing. Give it a corner and an occasional drink and it will stand there, glossy and upright, for years.

    Appearance

    • Smooth, fleshy stems rise from the base, each carrying pairs of glossy, deep-green leaflets so polished they are often mistaken for plastic. The leaves themselves hold an astonishing amount of water — over ninety percent of their weight — and below ground sits a thick, potato-like rhizome, full of stored water, that carries it through drought. It grows slowly and steadily, usually reaching two to four feet indoors given time.
    • Zamioculcas zamiifolia is the only species in its whole genus — its whole group of close plant relatives. It is native to eastern Africa: from southern Kenya through Tanzania, Malawi, Mozambique and Zimbabwe, and south to KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa.
    • Its homeland is country that is dry for part of the year: open grassland, rocky outcrops, and the edges and lower layer of dry forests. Rain comes with a wet season, then vanishes for months. The plant's whole design answers that rhythm. In a hard drought, it may let its leafy stems die back. It waits, hidden in its rhizome — its thick underground stem — until the rains return. The light is bright, the air is dry, and when water comes, it drains away fast.
    • Wild ZZ plants root in thin, sandy, stony ground. The soil is weathered and mineral, with very little organic matter in it. Water passes through in hours, not days. There is no rich humus layer — no layer of rotted leaves — to feed from. Instead, the plant banks its own reserves in its rhizome and leaves. It lives frugally between rains, in a soil where life is sparse and slow. The ZZ is in no hurry either. Indoors, that means a gritty, fast-draining mix and a light hand with the watering can matter far more than feeding.
    • The ZZ Plant waited a long time for fame. It was first described in 1829 by Conrad Loddiges, a London nurseryman and botanist. He named it Caladium zamiifolium. In 1856, Heinrich Wilhelm Schott moved it into a brand-new genus, Zamioculcas. That name blends Zamia — the cycad its leaflets look like — with culcas, an old name for a related plant. In 1905, Adolf Engler settled it into its modern name, Zamioculcas zamiifolia. Then, for nearly a hundred years, it sat quietly in botanical collections. Only in the mid-1990s, when Dutch nurseries began growing it on a large scale, did the ZZ take off. It is now one of the most planted indoor plants in the world.
    • In the lands where it grows wild, it holds a small place in traditional medicine. Botanists and ethnobotanists — scientists who record how people use plants — have written it down. In Malawi and in Tanzania's East Usambara Mountains, juice from the leaves was traditionally used for earache. The Sukuma people of north-western Tanzania applied the roots to ulcers.
    • Its nickname, the Eternity Plant, speaks to its near-indestructible patience. In feng shui practice, it is linked with steady growth and prosperity. It is a fitting symbol for a plant that simply endures.
    • When to plant: Indoors any time — new plants settle fastest in spring
    • Light: It tolerates low light indoors — even a room lit mostly by fluorescent light — and simply grows more slowly there; bright, indirect light keeps it fullest. Keep direct sun off the leaves
    • Soil: Any free-draining potting mix, the grittier the better — 2 parts potting soil to 1 part perlite or coarse sand. A pot with drainage holes is non-negotiable
    • Environment: 65–85°F, and it should not sit below 60°F for long
    • Pot: Pots
    • Water: Water only when the mix has dried out completely — about twice a month in summer, once a month or less in winter. Its rhizomes store water, so err on the dry side

    Care in detail

    • Potting Mix: Any free-draining potting mix will do, the grittier the better. A good mix: 2 parts potting soil to 1 part perlite or coarse sand. A pot with drainage holes is non-negotiable — its rhizomes rot if they sit wet.
    • Water, Feed, & Frequency: Water only when the mix has dried out completely — about twice a month in summer, and once a month or less in winter. Its rhizomes are full of stored water, so err on the dry side: overwatering is the one reliable way to kill it. Feed very sparingly, once or twice a year in the growing season; it needs little food.
    • Light & Temperature: It tolerates low light — even a room lit mostly by fluorescent light — and simply grows more slowly there; bright, indirect light keeps it fullest and happiest. Keep direct sun off the leaves, which can scorch. It thrives in temperatures ranging between 65-85°F and should not sit below 60°F for long.

    Toxicity

    Toxic if eaten — contains calcium oxalate crystals. Keep out of reach from children and pets

    Propagation

    Divide a crowded plant when you repot it, each piece with a rhizome, roots and a leaf. Or push single leaflets base-first into moist, free-draining mix. Leaflets take months — a small rhizome forms first, then roots, then a new leaf. Wear gloves: the sap irritates skin and eyes.

    Sources

    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — Zamioculcas zamiifolia, native to eastern Africa
    • Flora of Zimbabwe — ZZ plant habitat and recorded traditional uses
    • NC State Extension — ZZ plant care guidance

    Almond

    Prunus dulcis

    Culinary

    Heart Health

    FreshDried

    The almond is the seed inside the stone of a small flowering tree — a close cousin of the peach, the plum and the cherry, grown for the opposite part. In a peach the flesh is the food and the stone is thrown away; in an almond the flesh is a thin, leathery green hull that dries, splits open and is discarded, the stone is a pitted shell, and the food is the kernel inside it. One warning about a name before anything else: the sweet almond of the shops has a wild-tasting twin, the bitter almond, the same species in a bitter form. Bitter almonds carry a compound called amygdalin, which turns into cyanide in the body. They are not sold as food, and even a few can be dangerous. Every almond sold to eat is a sweet almond.

    Cultivars

    • Almonds are not one tree but hundreds of named cultivars, and in California a short list does most of the work. Unlike peas or beans, the cultivars are told apart by kernel, shell and harvest date — a photograph of a tree in leaf cannot honestly name one.
    • 'Nonpareil' — the standard everything else is measured against, about 40% of California's plantings. Thin, papery shell, a large smooth pale kernel, and the flavour the market pays most for. It ripens in mid-August and cannot pollinate itself, so it is always planted with other cultivars flowering beside it.
    • 'Carmel' — the classic partner for 'Nonpareil', planted to pollinate it and widely cropped in its own right: a well-filled kernel in a slightly harder shell, harvested a little after 'Nonpareil'.
    • 'Butte' and 'Padre' — a late pair, usually planted and harvested together in September, with smaller, richly flavoured kernels; 'Butte' came out of the University of California's breeding work. 'Monterey' is later still, with a large kernel, and stretches the harvest toward October.
    • 'Independence' — the change in the modern orchard: a cultivar that can set a full crop with its own pollen, released in 2008, so a block of it needs no second cultivar and far fewer bees. 'All-in-One' does the same job for gardens — self-fertile and semi-dwarf, one tree in a backyard will crop on its own.
    • 'Marcona' — Spain's prized kernel: rounder and richer than the California types, traditionally fried in olive oil and salted, and the almond of good turrón, the Spanish Christmas sweet. 'Largueta', long and flat, is Spain's other classic. The Spanish trees are mostly old, dry-farmed and low-yielding beside California's irrigated orchards, and their kernels are prized anyway.
    • The wild almond grows on dry, stony hills from the Levant through Iran and into Central Asia, and the weight of botanical evidence puts the tree's home — and the likeliest place it was first farmed — in Iran and the lands around it. Almonds were among the earliest domesticated fruit trees anywhere. Domesticated almonds turn up at Early Bronze Age sites in the Middle East, among them Numeira in Jordan, between about 3000 and 2000 BCE, and almonds were among the foods placed in Tutankhamun's tomb in Egypt around 1325 BCE.
    • Domestication started with a taste. Wild almonds are mostly bitter, and bitter means poisonous: the amygdalin that makes them bitter is the plant's defence. Somewhere a rare tree bore sweet kernels, and people kept seed from trees like it. The almond could be farmed early for a simple reason — it grows well from seed and comes up good, in the centuries before grafting existed to copy a chosen tree exactly.
    • From its home the almond travelled the shores of the Mediterranean into North Africa and southern Europe, carried by traders and settlers, and the Greeks and Romans grew it widely. In Spain and the islands it settled so deeply that whole hillsides of old, dry-farmed trees are still harvested by hand.
    • The tree stands early in the Bible's stories. Jacob sent almonds down to Egypt as a gift for a governor he did not know was his own son Joseph. Aaron's staff, left overnight among the staffs of the other tribes, was found in the morning budded, blossomed and bearing ripe almonds — the sign, in the story, that his house had been chosen. The Hebrew name for the almond, shaqed, sounds like the word for watching or waking, and the tree earned it honestly: it is the first tree of the year to wake and flower.
    • The English word is a traveller too: Greek amygdalē became Latin amygdala, then Old French almande, then almond — the "l" crept in late and was never really sounded. In California many growers say "amond" to this day, and their joke explains it: they are almonds while they are on the tree, and amonds once the harvest shaker has knocked the L out of them.
    • Almonds ground with sugar became marzipan, the sweet paste of Toledo in Spain and of festival baking across Europe, modelled into fruits and figures for feast days. Almond milk — ground almonds steeped in water and strained — was a staple of medieval kitchens, used in place of cow's milk through Lent and on fast days, when animal foods were set aside. And in spring, across the Mediterranean and the Middle East, the young green almonds were eaten whole, hull and all, before the shell hardened — dipped in salt, sharp and crisp, for the few weeks they lasted.
    • Spanish missions brought the tree to California in the 1700s, but the crop only found its ground in the middle 1800s, in the Central Valley, where the climate matched its home: mild wet winters, long hot rainless summers. That valley now grows about four-fifths of the world's commercial almond supply. Spain and Australia are the next producers, on a much smaller scale. When Vincent van Gogh's nephew was born in 1890, the painter made him a picture of almond blossom against a blue sky — branches of the same late-winter flowers that now open over a million acres of California orchards each February.
    Spain — turrón, the almond-and-honey sweet of Christmas, in hard white slabs and soft golden ones; 'Marcona' almonds fried in olive oil and salted as a tapa; and almond trees across Mallorca and the dry mainland hills, blossoming in January and February and shaken down by hand in late summer.
    Italy — Sicily runs on almonds: granita for breakfast, sweet almond-milk drinks, and marzipan modelled and painted as fruit. Amaretti, the bitter-edged almond biscuits, take their flavour from apricot kernels and bitter almond — the flavour is treasured; the dose in a biscuit is tiny and regulated.
    The Middle East and North Africa — almonds scattered over rice dishes and stuffed into dates and pastries; green almonds in spring, eaten whole with salt; and in Morocco, amlou, a spread of ground roasted almonds, honey and argan oil, eaten with bread.
    India — badam: almonds soaked overnight and peeled for the morning, a custom in many households; warm spiced almond milk (badam doodh); and almonds through festive sweets and rich dishes, with India among the world's biggest buyers of California's crop.
    California — the modern almond at full scale. Bloom runs from mid-February into March, and for those weeks more than two million honeybee colonies — most of the commercial hives in the United States — are trucked into the valley to pollinate the flowers, the largest movement of livestock most people have never heard of. In late summer the shakers come: a machine grips each trunk and shakes the nuts down onto the orchard floor, where they dry in the sun before being swept up and carried away to be hulled and shelled.
    • Almonds, raw, per 100 g: 579 kcal, protein 21 g, fat 50 g — most of it monounsaturated, the same family of fat that olive oil is known for — fibre 12.5 g, and carbohydrate about 22 g. The standout nutrients are vitamin E at 25.6 mg, well over a full day's worth and more than almost any other common food, and magnesium at 270 mg, about two-thirds of a day's worth, with calcium (269 mg), potassium (733 mg) and riboflavin besides. A standard handful is about 30 g, and it carries roughly a third of those figures.
    • Cholesterol Human trials
      Cholesterol is where the human evidence is strongest. Many randomised trials have fed people almonds daily and measured their blood fats, and when the trials are pooled the result is consistent: total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol — the kind linked to heart disease — both fall by a modest amount, on the order of 5 mg/dL for LDL in the largest recent pooling of 36 trials and nearly 2,500 people. HDL cholesterol, the protective kind, does not change. The United States Food and Drug Administration allows a carefully fenced claim on nut packages: scientific evidence suggests but does not prove that eating about 42 g (1.5 oz) of almonds a day, as part of a diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol, may reduce the risk of heart disease. Suggests, not proves — that is the true size of it.
    • Usable calories Human trials
      The label overstates the calories. In feeding studies where everything eaten and passed was measured, a serving of almonds gave the body about 130 usable calories per ounce against the roughly 170 the label arithmetic predicts — some of the fat stays locked inside the nut's tough cell walls and passes through undigested. In the pooled feeding trials, people given almonds every day did not gain weight, and one large pooling found a small average loss. That is a finding about almonds eaten in place of other food, not a licence to add handfuls on top of everything else.
    • Blood sugar Human · small
      On blood sugar the evidence is thinner. Trials in people with type 2 diabetes are small and short. Some pooled analyses found a small fall in HbA1c, the long-term blood-sugar measure; others found no change in blood sugar at all. A possible small effect is the honest summary, and almonds are not a treatment for diabetes.
    • The gut Human · small
      The gut has one careful trial behind it. In a 2022 study, 180 adults snacked on whole or ground almonds for four weeks, and the almond groups produced more butyrate — a fuel for the lining of the gut, made by gut bacteria from fibre — than the control group eating muffins. The same trial's main hope, a rise in bifidobacteria, did not happen, and both halves of that result belong in the record.
    • Almonds are traditionally praised as a food for the brain, and almond compounds are studied for cancer and memory in laboratories. Neither claim has a good trial in people behind it. What is proven is narrower and still worth having: a food that lowers LDL cholesterol a little, carries a day's vitamin E in a small handful, and does not fatten the people who eat it in trials.
    • When to plant: Bare-root trees in winter, while they are dormant
    • Climate: Zones 7–9
    • Winter chill: 200–500 hours below 45 °F (7 °C), depending on the cultivar
    • Soil: Deep and draining freely — a sandy loam is ideal, around pH 6.0–7.5
    • Pollination: Plant two different cultivars that flower at the same time, or a self-fertile cultivar for one tree alone
    • First nuts: In the third or fourth year; a full crop by the fifth to seventh
    • When to pick: Late summer, when the green hulls dry, split open and show the shell inside

    Care in detail

    • The almond is a small deciduous tree. Left to itself it can reach 7 metres or more; orchards prune it to about 4–6 metres so the crop can be shaken and caught. It wants the Mediterranean pattern it evolved in: a mild, wet winter and a long, hot, rainless summer.
    • Winter cold is a requirement, not a hardship: without its spell of chill the tree flowers raggedly and sets few nuts, and too little chill is the usual failure in mild coastal gardens.
    • The flowers are the risk. Almond blooms in late winter, weeks before the apple, and a single hard frost on open blossom can take the whole year's crop. Plant away from low frost pockets where cold air pools, and expect some years to fail even in good country. Wet springs are the second enemy: rain on the bloom brings fungal diseases — brown rot and shot hole among them — which is why the crop belongs to dry-summer climates and struggles in humid ones.
    • The tree tolerates poor and stony ground better than wet ground: roots sitting in water invite root rot, and heavy wet clay kills more garden almonds than cold does.
    • Pollination is the point most often missed. Nearly all cultivars cannot use their own pollen. 'Nonpareil' with 'Carmel' is the classic pairing, and bees do the rest; commercial orchards rent about two hives to the acre for the bloom weeks.
    • Garden and orchard trees are grafted — the named cultivar grows on roots borrowed from a peach or a peach–almond cross, chosen for the soil. A well-kept tree goes on cropping for twenty-five years and more.
    • An established tree in deep soil is drought-tough by orchard standards, but nuts fill and size best with deep watering through the dry summer, and young trees need regular water while they establish. In dry country a thick mulch helps, kept away from the trunk.
    • Harvest is written on the fruit. Orchards shake the tree and let the nuts finish drying on the ground. In a garden, shake or knock the branches over a sheet, gather the nuts, peel off the hulls, and dry the nuts in their shells in a warm airy place before storing. In the shell, kept cool and dry, they keep for months; shelled kernels go rancid fastest of all and belong in a sealed jar somewhere cool.

    Propagation

    Buy a rootstock and bud or graft a bud from the variety you want onto it in spring — T-budding is the usual way. A tree grown from a nut does not come true, and the nuts may be bitter. Almonds also need a second, different variety nearby to set nuts.

    Safety

    • Almond is a tree nut, and tree-nut allergy can be severe — for someone allergic, almonds are dangerous at any dose, and labels list them for that reason. Bitter almonds, the wild-tasting form, are a different risk: their amygdalin releases cyanide, food-safety authorities warn that even a small number can poison, and they are not a food. Sweet almonds from the shop carry neither risk beyond the allergy one. In the United States, almonds sold as raw are steam-treated before sale — a rule brought in after two salmonella outbreaks traced to raw almonds — so "raw" on an American label means untreated-tasting, not untreated.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture — FoodData Central: nuts, almonds, raw — the nutrition figures
    • Musa-Veloso et al. (2019) — meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials: almond eating lowered total and LDL cholesterol — the cholesterol figures
    • U.S. Food and Drug Administration (2003) — qualified health claim for nuts, including almonds, and heart disease — the fenced wording of the claim
    • Novotny et al. (2012) — measured energy value of almonds in human diets — the usable-calorie finding
    • Creedon et al. (2022) — randomised trial of almond snacking and the gut, King's College London — the butyrate result and the bifidobacteria result
    • European Food Safety Authority (2019) — cyanogenic glycosides in foods — the bitter almond warning
    • Zohary & Hopf (2000) — Domestication of Plants in the Old World — origin and early farming of the almond
    • Almond Board of California — California's share of world supply, bloom and pollination figures

    Aloe Vera

    Aloe vera

    MedicinalCulinary

    Skin Health

    Fresh

    Barbados Aloe, Burn Plant, First Aid Plant. Aloe vera is a desert succulent with thick, fleshy leaves full of clear gel. It has been grown for thousands of years. It needs bright light and very little water. One warning first: the yellow latex just under the rind is a strong laxative and is not safe to eat — the gel is the part used, and only on skin.

    Appearance

    • Aloe vera grows as a stemless rosette of thick, fleshy, lance-shaped leaves. The leaves are grey-green, often flecked with white when young, with small pale teeth along the edges. Inside a leaf is clear gel. The gel is the plant's water store, and it is how the plant survives months of drought. A mature plant sends up a tall spike of yellow, tubular flowers in summer, but this is rare indoors.

    How to Prepare the Gel

    • Cut a thick outer leaf close to the base of the plant.
    • Stand the leaf upright in a cup or bowl for a little while and let the yellow latex drain away. This yellow part is bitter and harsh — you do not use it.
    • Lay the leaf flat and slice off the green rind from both sides.
    • Take out the clear gel inside. You can use it fresh, just as it is.
    • Plant research today points to one wild home: the south-east of the Arabian Peninsula, in the Hajar Mountains of north-east Oman and the eastern Emirates. From there, people carried it widely, and it now grows wild in dry places around the world — from the Mediterranean to India, China and the Caribbean.
    • It grows at the desert's edge: rocky, sun-baked slopes and dry, gravelly ground, where rain is rare and brief. Days are hot, nights are cooler, the air is dry, and there is almost no shade. The plant stores water in its leaves, and it opens its pores at night, in the cool dark, to take in air — so it loses as little water as possible.
    • The soil there is mostly mineral: sand, gravel and broken-down rock, with almost no organic matter in it. It drains fast and dries fast. There is little humus, life in the soil is lean, and nutrients are scarce. Aloe is suited to that poor soil. Rich, wet potting soil can rot it indoors, and a gritty cactus mix suits it well.
    • Aloe is one of the oldest medicinal plants ever written down. It appears in the Ebers Papyrus, an Egyptian medical text from about 1550 BCE, and tradition holds that the Egyptians prized it as a "plant of immortality". The Greek physician Dioscorides described it in his herbal in the first century CE. From the ancient world it travelled along the trade routes into Ayurvedic medicine in India, where it is known as kumari, and was used in traditional practice across Asia and Africa.
    • Aloe is thought to come from the Arabic alloeh, meaning a bitter, shining substance — the latex. Vera is Latin for "true". Linnaeus first described it in 1753. In 1768 it was published twice, within days of each other — as Aloe vera by Nicolaas Burman, and as Aloe barbadensis, "the aloe from Barbados", by Philip Miller, from plants then grown in the Caribbean. Kew keeps Aloe vera as the accepted name, and barbadensis as a synonym for the same plant.
    • The latex was used for centuries as a strong laxative.

    Craft

    • The gel is worked into soaps and skin preparations — aloe soap is a staple of home soap making, the clear gel stirred into the mix for a smooth bar.
    • The leaves give a dye as well: in Africa, aloe leaf dye is recorded used alongside henna, as around Zarzis in Tunisia.
    • The clear gel inside the leaves is used on skin for sunburn and minor kitchen burns. This is a traditional home remedy, used for centuries; many households keep a plant for it. Traditional use
    • Burns Human trials
      Clinical research suggests the gel, spread on the skin, may help minor burns heal faster and hurt less. The trials are small and used different products, so this is promising rather than settled.
    • Acne Human · small
      Two small studies suggest the gel, used alongside other treatment, may improve acne.
    • Psoriasis Human · small
      A small amount of research suggests the gel may also help psoriasis.
    • Blood sugar Human · small
      A small amount of research suggests aloe gel taken by mouth may lower blood sugar and HbA1c a little in people with diabetes. Taking aloe by mouth carries real cautions — see Safety below.
    • When to plant: Indoors any time — offsets (pups) are potted up in spring
    • Light: Your brightest spot indoors — a south or west window with several hours of direct sun; introduce a new plant to full sun gradually, so its leaves do not scorch
    • Soil: A cactus or succulent mix, or 1 part potting soil, 1 part sand, 1 part perlite or lava rock; a clay pot with a drainage hole is ideal
    • Environment: 55–85°F; frost will kill it, so bring outdoor plants in well before the first cold nights
    • Pot: Pots
    • Water: Water deeply, then wait until the soil is completely dry before watering again — roughly every three weeks in the growing season, and much less in winter
    • When to pick: Cut a plump outer leaf at the base when you need the gel

    Care in detail

    • A clay pot balances the top-heavy rosette.
    • Soak, drain and empty the saucer; wet roots rot fast.
    • One light feed in spring is plenty, and many plants are never fed at all.

    Propagation

    In spring or early summer, lift a plant that has pups at its base and cut a pup away with its own roots, once it is a few inches tall with several leaves. Let the cut end dry for a day or two, pot it in dry cactus mix, and wait about a week before watering. Wear gloves — the sap can irritate skin. A single leaf on its own rarely roots, so do not use that.

    Safety

    • The yellow latex just under the rind is a strong laxative. It is harsh and hard to predict, and in 2002 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration removed aloe latex from over-the-counter laxatives. Do not eat the leaves. The clear gel is the part used, on skin only. Aloe is toxic to dogs and cats if eaten, so keep the plant out of reach of pets and children.
    • Aloe taken by mouth is a different matter from gel on skin. Whole-leaf extract is classed as a possible cause of cancer, leaf extracts taken by mouth have been linked to cases of hepatitis, and aloe by mouth may be unsafe during pregnancy and while breastfeeding. Talk to a clinician before taking aloe by mouth, especially if you take diabetes medicine.

    Sources

    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — Aloe vera, accepted name and Arabian Peninsula origin
    • Ebers Papyrus (c. 1550 BCE) — aloe among Egyptian remedies
    • U.S. Food and Drug Administration (2002) — aloe latex removed from over-the-counter laxatives
    • National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) (2025) — Aloe Vera: usefulness and safety

    Fiddle Leaf Fig

    Ficus lyrata

    Ornamental

    Banjo Fig, Lyre-Leaf Fig — the Fiddle Leaf Fig is the statement tree of the modern home. A rainforest tree from western Africa with enormous, violin-shaped leaves, it became the defining houseplant of the last decade. It has a reputation for drama, but the truth is simpler: it loves routine, and it rewards the keeper who gives it a bright spot and then leaves it in peace.

    Appearance

    • The leaves are its main feature: huge, leathery and glossy, each one shaped like a fiddle or a lyre — broad and rounded at the tip, narrower at the base — with prominent veining and a gently wavy edge, up to eighteen inches long on a mature tree. In the wild it can reach forty to fifty feet; indoors it typically grows as a single upright trunk of six to ten feet, though it can be encouraged to branch into a fuller tree. New leaves unfurl from a pointed bud at the top — a small event worth watching for.
    • Ficus lyrata comes from the lowland rainforests of western Africa. Its home runs from Sierra Leone east to Cameroon. It also takes in Guinea, Liberia, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Togo, Benin, Nigeria and Gabon.
    • It grows in hot, wet lowland rainforest. The air is warm all year, and rain is plentiful. Kew calls it a hemi-epiphytic tree. That means a seed may sprout high in the branches of another tree and send roots down to the soil — or the tree may grow straight from the forest floor. Either way, it ends as a tree that stands on its own and reaches up for the light at the top of the forest. That double life explains how it acts indoors.
    • Rainforest soil surprises people. Under all that green, it is thin and poor. Almost all of the forest's food is locked up in the living plants and in the layer of fallen leaves on top. What feeds the forest is speed. In the heat and the wet, fungi shred fallen leaves within weeks. Some of these fungi are mycorrhizal partners — fungi that thread through tree roots and trade food with them. Bacteria and insects help too. The fig's roots drink the freed food straight from that recycling layer, before the rain washes it away.
    • The plant was first described for science in 1894, by the German botanist Otto Warburg, from the plants of Africa. Its name is its portrait. Ficus is the Latin word for a fig. Lyrata means shaped like a lyre — the ancient Greek instrument the leaf looks like. Fiddle is simply the plainer English word for the same shape. For years, some nurseries sold it under a second name, Ficus pandurata. That name is now set aside as a duplicate name that is not accepted.
    • In its West African home, great fig trees are landmarks. They are shade trees and places where people gather. Across Africa, fig trees carry deep cultural weight as trees of meeting and shelter. The fiddle leaf's own fame, though, is fully modern. In the 2010s, it became one of the most photographed houseplants in the world, and a fixture of home design. It holds the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. Few plants have travelled so fully from rainforest to icon.
    • When to plant: Indoors any time — new plants settle fastest in spring
    • Light: The brightest room you have, with the light filtered — near an east window, or behind a sheer curtain at a south or west one; a little gentle morning sun is welcome. Turn it a quarter turn when you water, so it grows evenly
    • Soil: A rich, well-drained mix that holds some moisture without staying soggy — 2 parts potting soil, 1 part bark, 1 part perlite; it likes to be slightly snug in its pot
    • Environment: 65–75°F, kept steady, and away from drafts, radiators and air-conditioning vents — sudden change is the surest way to make it shed its leaves
    • Pot: Pots — it can stay in the same one for several years
    • Water: Water thoroughly when the top two inches of mix feel dry, let it drain fully, and empty the saucer — keep the rhythm steady, as irregular watering is a classic cause of dropped leaves

    Care in detail

    • Potting Mix: A rich, well-drained mix that holds some moisture without staying soggy. A good mix: 2 parts potting soil, 1 part bark, 1 part perlite. It likes to be slightly snug in its pot and can stay in the same one for several years.
    • Water, Feed, & Frequency: Water thoroughly when the top two inches of mix feel dry, let it drain fully, and empty the saucer — overwatering is the most common way to lose one. Keep the rhythm steady, because irregular watering is a classic cause of dropped leaves. Feed monthly with a balanced fertilizer in spring and summer, and ease off in winter.
    • Light & Temperature: The brightest room you have, with the light filtered — near an east window, or behind a sheer curtain at a south or west one. A little gentle morning sun is welcome; harsh afternoon sun can scorch. Turn the plant a quarter turn when you water, so all sides get their share of light and it grows evenly. It thrives in temperatures ranging between 65-75°F, kept steady and away from drafts, radiators and air-conditioning vents — sudden change is the surest way to make it shed its leaves.

    Toxicity

    Toxic to pets if eaten, and the milky sap can irritate skin. Keep out of reach from children and pets

    Propagation

    Take a stem cutting in spring or summer, with a leaf joint and its bud, and root it in water or mix. For a tall plant, air layer instead: wound the stem, wrap it in damp moss and plastic, and cut it free once roots show. A single leaf alone will not make a new plant. Wear gloves — the milky sap irritates skin.

    Sources

    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — Ficus lyrata, native to western tropical Africa
    • NC State Extension — Ficus lyrata care and toxicity
    • New York Botanical Garden — fiddle-leaf fig growing guide

    Basil

    Ocimum basilicum

    Culinary

    FreshCooked

    Sweet basil is a soft, glossy-leaved plant with a sweet scent of clove and anise, grown for its leaves: torn over tomatoes, pounded into pesto, stirred into curries at the last second. It is a tropical plant that grows for one warm season and is killed by the first frost. Pinched through the summer, it stays leafy and keeps giving leaves.

    Terpenes in this plant: ·

    Cultivars

    • There are hundreds of basil cultivars — bred forms of the one species, with a few close hybrids among them — and most of what a cook calls basil is one of these. The forms are told apart by leaf, scent and use, because unlabelled photographs cannot honestly separate them.
    • 'Genovese' — the pesto basil, and the standard against which the others are judged. Large, glossy, slightly cupped leaves, sweet with a warm clove note and — the point of pride — no mintiness. It is the basil of Liguria, in north-west Italy: basil grown in that region under set rules carries the protected name Basilico Genovese (a DOP, protected designation of origin, since 2005), and the leaves from Prà, a district of Genoa, are the most prized of all.
    • Thai Sweet (var. thyrsiflora) — Thai basil: narrower, sturdier leaves on purple stems, with purple flower stalks and a clear anise-liquorice scent that stands up to hot, spiced dishes where Genovese would fade. It is the basil stirred through Thai red and green curries and served raw with Vietnamese phở. 'Siam Queen', an All-America Selections winner, is its best-known garden form.
    • 'Lemon' — lemon basil (Ocimum × citriodorum) — a hybrid between sweet basil and American basil (O. americanum), with smaller, paler leaves and a true, clean lemon scent over the basil warmth. This is the kemangi of Indonesia and Malaysia, eaten raw with sambal and rice dishes, and used in Laos and Thailand too. 'Sweet Dani', a strongly lemon-scented form, was an All-America Selections winner in 1998.
    • 'Purple Ruffles' — the show plant of the family: big leaves of deep purple, heavily ruffled and fringed, with pink-purple flowers. It was bred in the United States (by Ted Torrey, crossing 'Green Ruffles' with 'Dark Opal'), introduced in 1984, and won an All-America Selections award. The flavour is real basil but spicier and more anise-like than Genovese, and the leaves turn herb vinegars a clear pink-purple. Its smooth-leaved elder, 'Dark Opal' (1962), is the other classic purple.
    • 'African Blue' — a hybrid, not a seed variety: camphor basil (O. kilimandscharicum) crossed with 'Dark Opal', found in Ohio in 1983. It is sterile — it never sets seed, and every plant is grown from a cutting of the original cross. Where frost never comes (zones 9–11) it is a true perennial, growing 3–4 ft tall with purple-veined leaves and flower spikes that open all season and are worked constantly by bees. Its scent carries real camphor from its African parent, so cooks use it lightly, if at all; it is grown for bees, for looks, and for the pot only in small doses.
    • And briefly, the bush basils — 'Spicy Globe' and the Greek types: tight mounds of tiny leaves, bred for pots, edges and small gardens, with the same sweet scent in miniature. The 2024 tomato study in In the Garden used one of these small-leaved bush forms.
    Italy — pesto alla genovese: basil pounded in a marble mortar with garlic, pine nuts, two hard cheeses and olive oil. Basil pastes appear in Genoese cookbooks from 1852, and the first printed recipe in its modern form is Giovanni Battista Ratto's, in La Cuciniera Genovese in 1863. Basil is also the leaf of the caprese salad, laid with tomato and mozzarella, and the green leaf on a pizza Margherita. Cooks add it at the last moment — heat dulls it fast.
    France — pistou, Provence's close cousin of pesto, traditionally made without pine nuts and stirred by the spoonful into soupe au pistou, the summer vegetable soup of the south.
    Thailand — Thai sweet basil stirred into red and green curries in the last minute of cooking, and served raw with noodles and salads. (The famous stir-fry phat kaphrao belongs to holy basil, the different species named above — in Thai kitchens the two are never confused.)
    Vietnam — a bunch of Thai basil on the herb plate that comes with phở, torn by the eater into the hot broth at the table, where it perfumes the soup without cooking.
    Indonesia and Malaysia — kemangi, lemon basil, eaten raw by the handful in lalapan — the platter of raw herbs and vegetables served with sambal and rice — and folded through rice dishes such as nasi ulam.
    Iran — reyhan, basil, is a standing member of sabzi khordan, the platter of fresh herbs — with bread, cheese and walnuts — that sits on the table at almost every meal, eaten by the leaf alongside the food.
    India — sweet basil's seeds, sabja, swollen in water and stirred into falooda and rose sherbets, where they drift like soft pearls. The leaf itself plays second place here to its sacred cousin, tulsi.
    Georgia and the Caucasus — purple basil, rekhani, is a table herb in its own right, eaten fresh with cheese and folded into summer salads.
    • Basil comes from tropical Asia — India and the lands towards Iran are the usual candidates for its first home — and it has been grown in India for about 5,000 years. Its wild kin grow across tropical Asia and Africa. From Asia it travelled the old trade routes west, and it was known in the Mediterranean world early: the Greek writer Theophrastus described it, under the name okimon, around 300 BCE.
    • The name tells its standing. Ocimum comes from the Greek okimon, the old name for the plant, linked to a word for smelling — a plant named for its scent. Basilicum comes from basilikos, "royal," from basileus, a king. Basil is still called the king of herbs by cooks, and in France it is herbe royale — the royal herb.
    • Its meanings were not always kind. In ancient Greece basil carried associations of hatred and mourning, and Greek gardeners held that it had to be sown with curses and abuse if it was to sprout well. Scorpions haunt its old stories both ways: a sprig of basil left under a pot was said to turn into a scorpion — yet Dioscorides, the Greek physician whose herb book guided medicine for fifteen centuries, prescribed basil for scorpion stings. In ancient Egypt, by long tradition, basil was used in embalming, the preparing of the dead — one more link between this bright herb and the world of funerals.
    • Christian legend softened the story. St Helena, mother of the Emperor Constantine, was said to have found the True Cross where basil was growing, and in Greek tradition basil is still brought to church for the Feast of the Cross in September, in memory of that finding.
    • In Italy basil became a sign of love — the opposite of the Greek reading. In Renaissance Italy a pot of basil on a young woman's windowsill quietly told suitors she welcomed them. And Italy gave basil its saddest story: in Boccaccio's Decameron (about 1353), Lisabetta of Messina learns that her brothers have murdered her lover Lorenzo. She finds his body, takes his head home, and hides it in a great pot planted with the finest basil of Salerno, watering the plant with her tears until she wastes away beside it. The poet John Keats retold the tale in 1820 as "Isabella, or the Pot of Basil," and the pot of basil has meant love and grief together ever since.
    • One plant must not be confused with this one. In India the sacred basil is holy basil, or tulsi — Ocimum tenuiflorum, a different species, sacred to the gods Vishnu and Krishna, grown at temples and doorsteps and rarely cooked with, precisely because it is holy. Its sacred stories, and the modern research published under the name tulsi, belong to that plant, not to sweet basil. Sweet basil is eaten in India — its seeds go into drinks — but it is a food there, not a god.
    • The distilled oil is rubbed on the skin for head pain: in one small trial of 144 people with migraine, it eased attacks over three months. Human · small
    • Fresh basil leaves, per 100 g: 23 kcal, protein 3.15 g, fibre 1.6 g. The standout is vitamin K at 414.8 µg — more than three times the whole day's value in that 100 g — with vitamin A at 264 µg (about a third of the day's value), manganese at about half the day's value, and useful amounts of copper, folate, calcium and vitamin C besides. Now the honest scale: 100 g of leaves is a big heap, several packed cups. A cook's handful is more like 10–25 g. But basil is eaten by the heap in one place — a generous serving of pesto is built on roughly 50 g of leaves — so its vitamin K is real food value, not a garnish's rounding error. Vitamin K is the vitamin the body uses to clot blood normally and to build bone. One caution comes with that vitamin K — see Safety below.
    • The scent is chemistry. Basil's perfume comes from a small amount of essential oil — less than 1% of the fresh leaf — made of compounds that include linalool (the scent of lavender), eugenol (the bite of cloves) and estragole (the anise note of tarragon), in mixes that change from variety to variety. In laboratory dishes and in animal studies, basil extracts and basil oil do interesting things — they slow some bacteria and fungi, and they calm inflammation in animal tissue. Those are dish and animal results. They are not proof that eating basil treats infection or inflammation in a person. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • What has actually been tried in people is small, and it used extracts and oil, not leaves on a plate. A few single, small trials exist: a leaf extract taken by 60 women around menopause, which reported better sleep scores after a month; an extract syrup added to a prescribed antidepressant in one small trial, which reported better mood and anxiety scores; and basil oil rubbed on arthritic knees in one trial, which eased pain about as well as a standard pain gel. Each of these is one small study, none has been repeated, and none of them tested eating basil as food. They are reasons for researchers to keep looking — they are not proven benefits. Human · small
    • The seeds are a food in their own right — small black beads that, soaked in water, swell fast into jelly-coated pearls. Across Asia they are stirred into sweet drinks and desserts — falooda in India, sherbets in Iran — where they are eaten as much for the slippery texture as anything. The seeds are mostly fibre. Claims that they slim are not supported: in a 12-week trial, 10 g of basil seeds a day before meals changed neither weight nor body fat against the comparison group. Human · small
    • The concentrated essential oil is not the leaf, and the two should not be swapped. Some basil oils are rich in estragole, a compound European regulators say exposure to should be kept low, after high doses damaged genes in rodents. Ordinary cooking amounts of the leaf are the long-standing, normal use of this plant; swallowing the oil is a different act, and there are no sound clinical trials behind the oil's advertised uses.
    • Some claims do not hold up at all: that basil lowers blood pressure, treats anxiety, or boosts the immune system in people. No good human trial shows any of these for sweet basil.
    • Basil is a tender annual — a tropical plant grown for one warm season. It hates cold in a way few herbs do: leaves blacken in cold air and cold soil, growth stalls below about 50 °F (10 °C), and the first frost kills it outright. Only in frost-free ground (zones 9–11) do perennial forms like 'African Blue' live on.
    • Sowing: start seed indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost, or sow outside once nights stay reliably above about 50 °F and the soil is warm. The seed sprouts best warm — about 70–85 °F (21–29 °C) — and comes up in roughly 5–10 days. Set plants out only when the nights are warm; a plant chilled young never quite recovers.
    • Sun, soil and space: full sun, six to eight hours or more. Rich soil that holds moisture but drains — basil is thirsty and hates drying out, yet rots in sodden ground. A pH around 6.0–7.0 suits it. Space plants about 12–18 inches apart; 'Genovese' grows 18–24 inches tall and as wide if it is pinched well.
    • Water at the base, not over the leaves — wet leaves in cool weather are an open door to disease — and mulch the soil to keep moisture even.
    • Pinching is the whole craft of basil. Pinch the growing tip off just above the second set of leaves, and the plant answers with two branches instead of one; keep doing it, and a single stem becomes a bush. Pinch off every flower head as it forms: once basil flowers freely, the leaves turn harsher and the plant begins to wind down. Harvest by cutting stems back to a pair of leaves, taking no more than about a third of the plant at once, and pick in the morning, when the leaves carry the most scent.
    • Companions — the famous pairing, at its real strength. Basil and tomato are the classic couple of the vegetable garden, and the Okra, Peppers and Tomato entries in this library name basil as a companion too. What the research actually shows: in controlled tests, the scent compounds drifting off basil plants switched on the tomato's own wound defences, so the tomato responded faster and more strongly when bitten (Yoshida et al., 2024); and in some field plantings, tomatoes grown with basil carried fewer whiteflies. What it does not show: that basil makes tomatoes taste better. No taste trial has found that — it is a story gardeners pass on, not a tested finding. Peppers and eggplant pair with basil in the practical way: same season, same sun, same thirst.
    • Trouble to watch for: basil downy mildew, a disease that arrived in North America in the 2000s — leaves yellow on top with a grey-purple fuzz beneath, and a plant can collapse in days in warm, wet weather. Space plants for air, water at the base, and where the disease is common, choose resistant forms such as 'Rutgers Obsession DMR' or 'Prospera'. Fusarium wilt, a soil fungus that wilts one stem at a time, is the other enemy; there is no cure, so start with clean seed and healthy plants.
    • In a pot: basil does well in a pot of a gallon or more, in the sunniest spot there is, and the pot is the cold-country answer late in the season — bring it in before the nights turn cold. Cut stems keep best standing in a glass of water at room temperature; the fridge is too cold and blackens the leaves. Surplus leaves are best kept as pesto, or frozen in oil.
    • Flowers and seed: let one plant flower at the end of the season and the bees will find it within the day — basil in bloom is a small festival for pollinators. The flowers themselves are edible, mild and pretty in salads and drinks. Seed is ripe when the flower heads have browned; shake it out dry and keep it for next year.

    Propagation

    Sow seed indoors in spring on a warm, sunny sill, or sow direct outside after May, once nights are warm. Or root a stem cutting that has not flowered — cut just below a leaf node and stand it in water or moist mix until roots form. Basil hates cold and frost kills it, so keep new plants warm.

    Safety

    • People who take warfarin or a similar blood thinner are told to keep their vitamin K intake steady, because sudden changes work against the medicine. Basil is rich in vitamin K, so eating it in suddenly much larger amounts than usual — a new daily pesto habit, say — is worth mentioning to the clinician who manages the dose.

    Sources

    • Jansen (1981) — Ocimum basilicum, in Plant Resources of South-East Asia (PROSEA) — names, origin and spread
    • Azizah et al. (2023) — Sweet basil (Ocimum basilicum L.): botany, phytochemistry and pharmacological activity, reviewed — what the studies do and do not show
    • Askari et al. (2024) — Topical basil oil for knee osteoarthritis: a randomised trial against diclofenac gel
    • Yoshida et al. (2024) — Companion basil primes the tomato wound response through scent signals (Plant Cell Reports)
    • Ratto (1863) — La Cuciniera Genovese — the first printed pesto recipe in its modern form
    • Boccaccio (c. 1353) — The Decameron, Day IV, story 5 — Lisabetta and the pot of basil
