    Beets

    Beta vulgaris

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Digestive HealthEye HealthHeart Health

    FreshCooked

    The beet is four crops wearing one Latin name. Beetroot, chard, sugar beet and the fodder beet fed to cattle are all Beta vulgaris, bred in different directions from the same seaside plant — for the root, for the leaf, for sugar, for bulk. The red root is the branch that reached the kitchen, and it colours everything it touches: hands, boards and the plate itself.

    Cultivars

    Detroit Dark Red

    Skin
    Flesh

    The standard red beet since 1892: round, deep red to the centre, sweet and earthy. The canning and pickling benchmark.

    Chioggia

    Skin
    Flesh

    An old Italian variety from Chioggia, the fishing town near Venice, grown since the 1800s. Cut across, the flesh shows rings of red and white like a target. The rings fade in cooking; raw or lightly pickled, they stay.

    Golden

    Skin
    Flesh

    Golden-yellow flesh, sweet and mild, carrying the same pigment family in its yellow form. It does not stain hands and boards the way red beets do.

    Bull's Blood

    Skin
    Flesh

    An heirloom grown since the 1800s as much for its leaves as its roots: the tops are deep red-purple and are picked young for salads; the roots are small and sweet.

    Albina Vereduna

    Skin
    Flesh

    A white beet: all the sweetness, none of the pigment, for dishes where the red would muddy everything it met.

    Ukraine and Eastern Europe — borscht, the deep-red beet soup, served hot with sour cream or cold in summer; a national dish of Ukraine with versions across the whole region.
    Poland — ćwikła, grated beetroot with horseradish beside roasted meats, and barszcz, the clear beet broth.
    Britain — pickled beetroot in vinegar, sliced into salads and sandwiches; the form in which many Britons first meet the plant.
    Australia — a slice of pickled beetroot inside the hamburger, a fixture of the Australian burger since the middle of the last century.
    India — beetroot poriyal in the south, the root cubed and stir-fried with coconut and spices, and beetroot raita, its colour turning the yogurt pink.
    • The beet's ancestor is the sea beet, Beta vulgaris subsp. maritima, a sprawling plant of the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts that still grows wild on stony beaches and cliff edges. Its leaves were eaten first — Greeks and Romans grew beets as a leaf vegetable — and the swollen root came later.
    • Root beets took shape in the gardens of Italy and Germany in the 1500s and 1600s. Growers chose them for a round, sweet, deeply coloured root. Then they spread across Europe and to North America. By the 1800s the red beet was a standard vegetable for pickling and preserving: it keeps well, and it pickles well.
    • The family's other career is sugar. In 1747 the chemist Andreas Marggraf showed that beet juice holds the same sugar as cane. His student Franz Achard built the first beet-sugar factory in Silesia in 1801. When wartime blockades cut France off from cane sugar under Napoleon, beet fields followed. Today's sugar beets have white roots and are bred to about a fifth sugar by weight, and they now supply roughly a fifth of the world's sugar.
    • Chard is the leaf branch, grown for its stems and leaves, with no swollen root at all. The mangelwurzel is the fodder branch — fodder is feed for farm animals — a giant, coarse beet once fed to livestock across Europe. One species, four answers to four different needs.

    Craft

    • The root is a dye plant. Beetroot colours cloth and Easter eggs red; its pigment, betanin, is used as a red colourant, and beetroot dye has even been used in ink. One honest limit: on cloth the colour is short-lived, fading and washing out fast — on eggs and in food it serves far better.
    • The root, per 100 g raw: 43 kcal, fibre 2.8 g and sugars 6.8 g — sweet for a root vegetable — with folate at 109 µg (about a quarter of the daily value), potassium at 325 mg and a useful share of manganese.
    • The colour is betalains, the pigment family that makes the root red or golden. Beets are one of the few foods that carry them. The pigments are studied for antioxidant roles; the honest summary is that the root is a nutritious food whose pigments are interesting, not a medicine.
    • Beetroot and blood pressure is the beet claim with real trials behind it, and its limits matter. The root is rich in natural nitrate, which the body converts — through bacteria in the mouth — into nitric oxide, a compound that relaxes blood vessels. Pooled across trials, beetroot juice and nitrate concentrates lower systolic blood pressure (the top number) by roughly 4 points on average over days to weeks; in one four-week trial, people with hypertension drinking 250 mL of beetroot juice a day saw clinic readings fall by about 8 points systolic. Those are juice and concentrate studies, at set doses, over short periods — a modest effect, not a treatment, and no reason to change any prescribed medicine. The cooked root carries the same nitrate in smaller, unmeasured amounts.
    • Athletes drink beetroot juice for the same nitrate: trials in recreational athletes find small improvements in how long hard effort can be sustained, with smaller or absent effects in the highly trained.
    • The greens are a second vegetable on the same plant, and by the numbers the stronger one: 22 kcal per 100 g, with vitamin K at 400 µg (more than three times the daily value), vitamin A at 316 µg RAE (about a third), vitamin C at 30 mg, potassium at 762 mg, calcium at 117 mg, and lutein — a pigment concentrated in the eye — at about 1,500 µg. Cook them as spinach is cooked. Their vitamin K is high enough that people taking warfarin should keep their intake of greens like these steady and mention it to their clinician.
    • Beeturia: in roughly one person in ten, the red pigment passes straight through and colours urine and stools red. It is harmless, but it alarms anyone not expecting it — worth knowing before, not after.
    • Caution: beetroot sits among the higher-oxalate vegetables. Oxalates are natural compounds that can add to the load in people who form calcium-oxalate kidney stones. Anyone advised to limit oxalates should treat beets — and especially beet greens — as occasional foods and ask their clinician. The root's sugar (nearly 7 g per 100 g) also counts in a careful eater's sums.
    • When to plant: Sow outside from spring, in succession, and again in late summer.
    • Sun: Full sun.
    • Soil: Loose, stone-free soil that drains well.
    • Environment: A cool-season crop; roots swell best in cool weather.
    • Planter or ground: Ground, or deep planters.
    • Spacing and depth: Sow 2–3 cm deep; thin the seedlings to about 10 cm apart — each beet "seed" is a cluster holding several seeds, so seedlings come up in tufts.
    • Start inside or outside: Sow outside where they are to grow.
    • Water: Keep evenly moist; dry spells make roots woody.
    • Companions: Onions and lettuce are classic companions.
    • When to pick: Pull at golf-ball to tennis-ball size for tenderness; let the biggest keep for storage.

    Garden notes

    • The thinnings from a beet row are the first greens of the year — nothing need be wasted.
    • The tops are harvest too: a leaf or two from each plant as it grows, and the whole crown at pulling. Twist the tops off roots meant for storage — left on, the leaves draw moisture out of the root.
    • Biennial for seed: a root that survives winter flowers in its second year. Garden beet crosses freely with chard and sugar beet — all one species — so seed-savers keep the branches apart.

    Propagation

    Sow seed direct in early spring, as soon as the soil can be worked, about ¾ inch deep and 1 inch apart in rows 12 to 18 inches apart. Each wrinkled seed ball holds 2 to 4 seeds, so thin the seedlings to 3 to 4 inches apart — cut the spare seedlings off rather than pulling them, so you do not disturb the roots of the ones left. Sow again every 3 weeks until midsummer for a steady crop.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — nutrient values for beets, raw, and beet greens, raw
    • Siervo et al. (2013) — review of 16 trials: beetroot juice and nitrate lowered systolic blood pressure
    • Kapil et al. (2015) — four-week trial of beetroot juice in people with hypertension
    • Hoon et al. (2013) — review of trials: nitrate and exercise endurance
    • Kew Plants of the World Online — Beta vulgaris: beetroot used as a natural dye

    Parsnip

    Pastinaca sativa

    Culinary

    Digestive Health

    Cooked

    A pale, sweet root that was Europe's staple before the potato arrived and its sweetener before sugar was cheap — then was quietly set aside for both. The parsnip kept its place at the roast dinner and in the soup pot, where its sweetness, deepened by frost, still earns it.

    Cultivars

    Hollow Crown

    Skin
    Flesh

    The old standard, grown since the 1800s: long, smooth, thick-shouldered roots for deep soil.

    Harris Model

    Skin
    Flesh

    An American type: shorter, blockier roots, bred for heavier ground where Hollow Crown would fork.

    Gladiator

    Skin
    Flesh

    A modern hybrid: vigorous, uniform roots with resistance to canker, the parsnip's main root disease.

    Tender and True

    Skin
    Flesh

    A British variety kept for flavour: slender roots, sweet and fine-grained.

    Guernsey

    Skin
    Flesh

    A shorter, half-long root from the Channel Islands tradition, suited to shallow soils.

    Britain — roast parsnips beside the Sunday roast and the Christmas turkey, their edges caramelised; and parsnip soup, often curried in its modern form.
    Ireland — carrots and parsnips mashed together with butter, the orange-and-cream mash that sits beside roasts and stews.
    France — a supporting player in pot-au-feu, the great boiled dinner, where the parsnip sweetens the broth.
    United States — part of the New England boiled dinner, and of Thanksgiving tables in the north, where the frost that sweetens it is guaranteed.
    • Wild parsnip grows across Europe and western Asia. The parsnip we grow is that same species, Pastinaca sativa, with its root bred thick and sweet. Greeks and Romans grew it. Pliny, the Roman writer, records that parsnips were carried to Rome from the Rhine country for the emperor Tiberius's table — which says something about how highly it was valued.
    • Through the Middle Ages the parsnip was a European staple: a starchy root for the pot, and a sweetener for cakes and preserves, in a world where honey was precious and cane sugar a luxury. Parsnip wine was a British country drink.
    • The potato ended its reign. Potatoes arrived from the Americas in the 1500s and spread through the 1700s. They yielded more, stored as well, and asked less of the cook. The parsnip retreated to the winter garden and the northern table, where its frost-sweetness kept it loved. Settlers carried it to North America in the 1600s, where it spread into the wild so thoroughly that its wild form is now a common roadside plant across the continent.
    • Its kin are the carrot family. Carrot is its closest relative on the shelf, and parsley and celery share the family's divided leaves and umbels — flower heads shaped like umbrella spokes.
    • The most energy-dense of the common roots after the potato: 75 kcal per 100 g raw, with fibre at 4.9 g — among the highest of any root vegetable — vitamin C at 17 mg (about a fifth of the daily value), folate at 67 µg, vitamin K at 22.5 µg and potassium at 375 mg.
    • The fibre is the honest headline: nearly 5 g per 100 g of mixed fibre, the kind that feeds the gut and slows the sugar of a meal into the blood. For a starchy root, the parsnip digests gently.
    • The sweetness is real sugar — about 4.8 g per 100 g — formed as the plant converts starch to sugar in cold weather. That conversion is why a parsnip dug after frost tastes like a different vegetable from one dug in autumn warmth.
    • Caution, from the plant's own defences: parsnip foliage carries a sap that can irritate skin, and the wild plant's sap is a genuine hazard — in sunlight it can raise blisters, a reaction called phytophotodermatitis (phyto means plant, photo means light: the sap makes skin light-sensitive). Garden parsnip leaves are far milder, but gloves for pulling tops on a sunny day are cheap insurance, and only the roots come to the kitchen. The wider family holds deadly look-alikes such as poison hemlock, so no wild carrot-family plant should ever be eaten on a guess.
    • When to plant: Sow outside in spring.
    • Sun: Full sun.
    • Soil: Deep, stone-free soil; stones and fresh manure make roots fork.
    • Environment: A long, cool season; cold is its friend — frost sweetens the root.
    • Planter or ground: Ground — the roots run deep.
    • Spacing and depth: Sow 1–2 cm deep; thin to about a hand's width (15 cm) apart.
    • Start inside or outside: Sow outside where they are to grow, and use fresh seed — old seed germinates poorly.
    • Water: Keep the seedbed evenly moist; germination is slow.
    • Companions: No strong companions known.
    • When to pick: Harvest from autumn onward, after the first frosts; dig as needed through winter.

    Garden notes

    • The slowest of the roots to start: parsnip seed germinates slowly even when fresh, so patience at sowing is part of the crop.
    • In hard climates, mulch the row after the first frosts and keep digging into winter — the ground itself is the store.
    • Biennial for seed: a root left to a second spring sends up tall yellow umbels and sets seed freely. Parsnip crosses with wild parsnip, so seed-savers grow one variety at a time.
    • Pull the tops with gloves on bright days; the leaves carry the same light-sensitive sap as the wild plant, in milder form.

    Propagation

    Sow fresh seed direct in spring, March to April, 1 cm deep, in deep, light soil that drains well. Use fresh seed each year — old seed sprouts poorly — and sow more than you need, as it comes up in 2–4 weeks and can be patchy. Never move seedlings — the tap root forks if it is disturbed.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — nutrient values for parsnips, raw
    • Pliny the Elder (1st century CE) — Roman account of parsnips carried from the Rhine country for the emperor Tiberius

    Turnip

    Brassica rapa

    Culinary

    Bone HealthEye HealthImmune Health

    FreshCooked

    Two vegetables on one plant, and the humbler of the pair carries the stronger numbers. The turnip's white root is mild and quick; its greens are among the most nutritious leaves in the garden. For most of its long history the turnip was poor people's food and cattle food — which is another way of saying it kept people and animals alive.

    Cultivars

    Purple Top White Globe

    Skin
    Flesh

    The American standard since the late 1800s: round white roots with a purple shoulder where the sun touches them, grown for root and greens together.

    Hakurei

    Skin
    Flesh

    A Japanese hybrid bred in the 1950s that changed the plant's reputation: small, white, sweet roots eaten raw like a radish, ready in little over a month, with mild greens.

    Golden Ball

    Skin
    Flesh

    An old round variety with golden-orange flesh, denser and sweeter than the white types, and a good keeper.

    Seven Top

    Skin
    Flesh

    Grown in the American South for greens alone: it makes a crown of leaves and no root worth the name, which is the point.

    Purple Top Milan

    Skin
    Flesh

    An early Italian type, flattened and fast, for spring sowing and quick pulling.

    France — navets in pot-au-feu and glazed beside roast duck (canard aux navets), the turnip treated as a delicacy rather than a filler.
    Japan — kabu simmered in dashi until tender, and pickled; the little white turnips are a winter staple.
    American South — turnip greens simmered with smoked pork, pot likker soaked up with cornbread: a dish of the late-autumn and winter table.
    Scotland — the famous "neeps" served beside haggis are usually rutabagas, not true turnips; the true turnip's Scottish role is the older, smaller white root in broths.
    • The turnip is Brassica rapa in its root form. It is the same species that, bred in other directions, gives bok choy and Chinese cabbage. Studies of its genes place the first growing of the root turnip in Central Asia, several thousand years ago. From there it travelled both ways, becoming a staple food of the Greek and Roman world, and reaching Japan by about 700 CE.
    • In Europe it fed poor people and farm animals for centuries. Then, in England in the early 1700s, it became part of a farming revolution. Charles "Turnip" Townshend championed turnips in a four-course crop rotation — a set order of crops grown one after another in the same field. The turnips fed cattle through the winter, and the soil rested between grain crops. Turnips grown as animal feed changed what farming could do.
    • One mix-up is worth clearing up, because recipes blur it. The rutabaga — called swede in England and neep in Scotland — is not a turnip. It is Brassica napus, a cross of turnip and cabbage. It is bigger and denser, with yellow flesh and a short stem neck above the root. A true turnip is smaller, with white flesh, and its leaves grow straight from the root's shoulder, with no neck at all. In Scotland "neep," and often "turnip" too, means the rutabaga — which is why the two are so often mixed up.
    • In the American South, the greens took the lead. Turnips planted on new ground gave leaves within weeks. The greens were simmered with smoked pork, and their cooking liquid — pot likker — was soaked up with cornbread. It became a foundation dish of the region.

    Craft

    • Before the pumpkin, there was the turnip. In Ireland and Scotland — and on the Isle of Man, at Hop-tu-Naa — big turnips (often the swede type, from the same Brassica rapa family) were hollowed out, carved with faces and lit with a candle or ember at Samhain, the old Halloween, to ward off spirits and light the way. The National Museum of Ireland keeps a famous carved “ghost turnip” from Fintown, County Donegal, made around 1900. Irish and Scottish emigrants carried the custom to America, where the bigger, softer pumpkin took the turnip’s place — the jack-o’-lantern began as a turnip.
    • The root is a light food: 28 kcal per 100 g raw, fibre 1.8 g, vitamin C at 21 mg (about a quarter of the daily value) and potassium at 191 mg. Mild, quick-cooking, and easy on a plate that needs bulk without weight.
    • The greens are the strong half, and it is not close: per 100 g raw, vitamin A at 579 µg RAE (nearly two-thirds of the daily value), vitamin K at 251 µg (about twice the daily value), vitamin C at 60 mg (two-thirds), folate at 194 µg (about half) and calcium at 190 mg — more than six times the root's calcium, in a leaf that costs 32 kcal. Root and greens belong in one conversation because they are eaten from one plant, but their numbers are different foods' numbers.
    • Like the rest of the cabbage family, turnips carry glucosinolates — the sulphur compounds behind the brassica bite — which convert as the plant is chopped and cooked into compounds studied for how they help the body deal with harmful substances. Population studies link regular cruciferous eating with lower rates of some cancers; that is the family pattern, not a promise from this plant.
    • Caution: the greens' vitamin K is high enough to matter for blood clotting. People taking warfarin or similar medicines should keep strong greens like these at a steady level rather than swinging between none and a feast, and say so to their clinician.
    • When to plant: Sow outside in spring for early roots and again in late summer for the autumn crop that stores.
    • Sun: Full sun.
    • Soil: Loose soil that drains well.
    • Environment: A cool-weather plant; heat makes roots woody and sharp.
    • Planter or ground: Ground, or deep planters.
    • Spacing and depth: Sow 1–2 cm deep; thin firmly to about 10–15 cm apart.
    • Start inside or outside: Sow outside where they are to grow.
    • Water: Keep evenly moist for tender roots.
    • Companions: Peas are the classic companion.
    • When to pick: Roots are ready in about two months, greens in half that.

    Garden notes

    • Sow where they are to grow, thin firmly, and keep the thinnings for the pot.
    • Take a few leaves from each plant as it grows, or cut the whole crown at harvest.
    • Turnips share the brassica troubles — flea beetles on the seedlings, clubroot in the soil — so cover young rows, and keep brassicas out of the same ground for a few years.
    • Roots store in a cool place for weeks. The greens do not store at all and are best cooked the day they are cut.

    Propagation

    Sow seed straight where it will grow, from early spring to late summer, ¼ to ½ inch deep, then thin plants to 4 to 6 inches apart. It does not move well, so do not start it in pots to transplant.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — nutrient values for turnips, raw, and turnip greens, raw
    • McAlvay et al. (2021) — genomic study of Brassica rapa diversity: Central Asian origin of the root turnip
    • National Museum of Ireland — the carved “ghost turnip” of Fintown, Co. Donegal (c. 1900) and the Samhain lantern tradition

    Radish

    Raphanus sativus

    Culinary

    Digestive HealthImmune Health

    FreshCooked

    The sprinter of the vegetable garden — seed to plate in a month for the little spring kinds — and one of the oldest cultivated plants in the world. The radish's bite is the cabbage family's bite, concentrated: a crisp root that announces itself.

    Cultivars

    Cherry Belle

    Skin

    The round red standard: an All-America Selections winner in 1949, quick, crisp and dependable.

    French Breakfast

    Flesh

    An elongated red-and-white type sold in Paris markets since the 1800s, mild and quick; traditionally eaten with butter and salt.

    White Icicle

    A long white spring radish, crisp and mild, ready almost as fast as the round kinds.

    Daikon

    Skin

    The great white winter radish of Japan (Minowase type): roots a foot long or more, mild and juicy, for pickles, salads and simmering. A different season and a different kitchen from the spring kinds.

    Black Spanish

    Watermelon

    Skin

    A Chinese heirloom type: plain green-white outside, magenta at the centre when cut. Mild and sweet, grown for the surprise.

    Japan — daikon grated fresh (oroshi) beside grilled fish and tempura; simmered in dashi until tender; and pickled as takuan, the yellow pickle that ends meals.
    Mexico — radishes sliced over tacos and pozole for crunch and heat; and in Oaxaca, the Night of the Radishes (Noche de Rábanos) — the radish-carving festival told under Traditional Uses.
    Korea — mu, the Korean radish, cubed into kkakdugi kimchi and sliced into the clear winter broth dongchimi.
    France — radis beurre: spring radishes split, buttered and salted, eaten with bread as a first course.
    India — mooli grated into salads and folded into parathas, the flatbreads stuffed with spiced radish.
    • Raphanus sativus was first grown as a crop so long ago that its exact home is still argued over. Wild radishes of the Mediterranean and Black Sea coasts are its kin. People grew it in both Egypt and China thousands of years ago. Its Greek name, raphanos, means "quickly appearing". It is a gardener's name, earned in the seedbed, where the seed comes up fast.
    • Herodotus wrote that words carved on Egypt's Great Pyramid listed the radishes, onions and garlic eaten by the men who built it. The carving cannot be checked now, and the story may be a guide's tale. But radishes were certainly eaten in the ancient world, at both ends of Asia.
    • From China, the radish travelled to Japan. There, hundreds of years of choosing the best plants bred the daikon, the great white winter radish, long and mild, made for pickling and simmering. In Europe, choosing ran the other way, toward the small, quick, peppery spring radish. The big black winter radishes are the old European storage kind.
    • The seed is a crop too. Radishes left to flower make pods. Picked green, the pods are eaten crisp and peppery. One Indian kind, the rat-tail radish, is grown for its pods alone. It makes no root worth eating.

    Traditional medicine

    • In Japan, grated daikon has long been served beside fried and fatty foods in the belief that it helps the meal digest. Daikon does carry starch-splitting enzymes (diastase), and the pairing is centuries old — tradition with a plausible mechanism, offered as tradition.

    Craft

    • In Oaxaca, Mexico, radishes are carved — not for the table, but for show. Every 23 December since 1897, the Night of the Radishes (Noche de Rábanos) fills the city’s main square: growers raise big white radishes specially for the night and carve them, still fresh, into figures, scenes and whole landscapes, competing for prizes before the crowds. It is one of the world’s great vegetable-carving traditions, and it belongs to this plant alone.
    • The spring radish is mostly water and crunch: 16 kcal per 100 g raw, fibre 1.6 g, vitamin C at 14.8 mg (about a sixth of the daily value), folate at 25 µg and potassium at 233 mg. A food that adds bite and bulk to a plate for almost nothing.
    • The daikon runs a little higher on vitamin C: 18 kcal per 100 g, vitamin C at 22 mg (about a quarter of the daily value), folate at 28 µg and fibre at 1.6 g.
    • The bite is glucosinolates — the same sulphur compounds as in the rest of the cabbage family — converted as the root is chewed into the sharp, mustard-like oils that clear the nose. Population studies link regular cruciferous eating with lower rates of some cancers; that is the family's pattern, stated at the family's strength, not a claim for the radish alone.
    • The leaves are food: young radish tops, cooked like other brassica greens or pounded into a pesto, carry the family's vitamins in smaller measure than turnip greens. The seed pods, picked green, are a crisp, peppery vegetable in their own right.
    • Caution: the radish is a gentle food and needs no strong warnings. Eaten in very large amounts raw, its sharp compounds can irritate an empty stomach — a portion note, not a danger.
    • When to plant: Sow spring kinds outside from early spring, little and often; sow winter kinds in mid-to-late summer.
    • Sun: Full sun.
    • Soil: Loose soil that drains well.
    • Environment: The quickest crop in the garden; crowded or dry roots turn woody and hot.
    • Planter or ground: Ground, or shallow planters for the spring kinds.
    • Spacing and depth: Sow 1–2 cm deep; thin so each root has room to swell.
    • Start inside or outside: Sow outside where they are to grow.
    • Water: Keep evenly moist.
    • Companions: Sown with slow carrots and parsnips, radishes mark the row — they come up fast and are eaten before the slow crop needs the room.
    • When to pick: Pull spring kinds in three to five weeks, young and often; winter kinds in autumn.

    Garden notes

    • Sow little and often, a small batch every fortnight through the season.
    • Daikon's deep root is used by gardeners to break up heavy soil — grown as a tool as much as a crop.
    • Let a few plants flower if seed or pods are wanted. They cross freely with other radishes and with wild radish, so one variety at a time keeps seed true.

    Propagation

    Sow seed straight where it is to grow, in early spring, 3 to 6 weeks before the last frost, about half an inch deep. Keep the soil damp and thin the seedlings to about 2 inches apart. Sow a small batch every week or two for a steady supply — radishes go to seed fast in hot weather.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — nutrient values for radishes, raw, and daikon radish, raw
    • Herodotus, Histories (5th century BCE) — account of the radishes eaten by the builders of the Great Pyramid
    • Oaxaca cultural record — Noche de Rábanos (Night of the Radishes), the radish-carving festival held every 23 December since 1897

    Cucumber

    Cucumis sativus

    Culinary

    FreshDried

    A vining annual grown for a fruit eaten unripe and raw, while the skin is still green and tender. Cucumber is about 95% water, and its gift is refreshment rather than nourishment: crisp, cool and mild, it hydrates and flavours salads, sandwiches and drinks while adding very few calories. The fruit is the part eaten, fresh or pickled; the yellow flowers are edible, and the seeds are eaten with the fruit and dried for use in some cuisines. Its relatives are the other gourds — pumpkin, zucchini, winter squash and watermelon — though cucumber's own line runs through Asia, not the Americas or Africa.

    Cultivars

    Slicing

    Skin
    Flesh

    Long and thick-skinned, bred for salads and sandwiches. Marketmore 76 and Straight Eight are the long-standing garden standards.

    Pickling

    Skin
    Flesh

    Shorter, blockier and thin-skinned, picked small for brining: Boston Pickling, National Pickling. The tiniest are the cornichons of French kitchens.

    Burpless and Asian

    Skin
    Flesh

    Long, slender and thin-skinned, with small seeds, bred for low bitterness and easy digestion; the Japanese and Chinese long cucumbers are the classic form.

    Persian

    Skin
    Flesh

    Short, smooth and nearly seedless, eaten whole, skin and all — the snacking type.

    English (Hothouse)

    Skin
    Flesh

    The long, wrapped cucumbers of supermarkets, grown in greenhouses; many set fruit without pollination, which keeps them nearly seedless.

    Lemon

    Skin
    Flesh

    A round, yellow heirloom that looks like a lemon and tastes like a mild cucumber.

    One impostor to know: the Armenian "cucumber" is a melon — Cucumis melo — long, ribbed and mild, but a melon by family record, not a cucumber.

    India — folded into raita, cucumber in spiced yogurt, and chopped into kachumber salad.
    Greece — tzatziki: grated cucumber with garlic, dill and yogurt.
    China — pai huang gua: cucumbers smashed and dressed with garlic, black vinegar and sesame oil.
    Japan — sunomono: cucumber sliced thin into sweet vinegar.
    The pickle jar — for most of its history, cucumber's second life was pickling, which kept a perishable summer fruit edible for months: dill pickles in North America and Germany, ogórki in Poland, cornichons in France.
    • Cucumber was first grown as a crop in India. Its wild ancestor still grows there, in the foothills of the Himalayas. Studies of its genes point to a single start there, about 3,000 years ago.
    • From India, it travelled along the trade routes. It reached China by about 2,000 years ago, and the lands around the Mediterranean in ancient times. Roman writers tell of cucumbers grown for the emperor Tiberius out of season — at the wrong time of year. They grew in frames on wheels, covered with sheets of see-through stone. It was an early greenhouse, built around this plant.
    • Columbus carried cucumber seed to Haiti in 1494. From there, the plant spread through the Americas.
    • In plant science, the fruit is a pepo — the fruit type of the gourd family. It is a berry with a firm rind, with the seeds set in soft flesh.

    Traditional medicine

    • In India, cucumber holds a place in Ayurvedic tradition as a cooling food for hot weather — a traditional use that still shapes how it is eaten there.
    • Slices laid on the eyes and skin are a long-standing folk practice. What soothes is the cool water in the slice; no treatment claim is made.
    • Hydration is the headline. Cucumber is about 95% water, and a 100 g serving carries only 15 kcal. Eating it contributes to the day's fluid intake; that, honestly stated, is its main health role.
    • Vitamin K: 16.4 µg per 100 g with the peel on — about 14% of the daily value. Vitamin K is needed for normal blood clotting and for maintaining bone. Most of it sits in and just under the peel, which is a reason to eat slicing cucumbers unpeeled.
    • Modest extras: potassium 147 mg, vitamin C 2.8 mg and fibre 0.5 g per 100 g. Cucumber is not a nutrient-dense food, and no disease claim is made for it.
    • Caution — bitterness: cucumbers carry cucurbitacins, intensely bitter defensive compounds concentrated near the stem end and the peel. Cultivated types are bred to hold very little, but heat and drought stress raise the level. A cucumber that tastes strongly bitter should be spat out, not eaten — a heavy dose of cucurbitacin can bring on stomach cramps and diarrhoea.
    • When to plant: Sow outside after the last frost; the first frost kills the plant.
    • Sun: Full sun.
    • Soil: Rich soil that holds moisture and drains well.
    • Environment: A warm-season vine; drought and heat stress are what turn fruit bitter.
    • Planter or ground: Ground, or up a trellis — a trellis keeps fruit straight, clean and easy to find, and saves ground.
    • Spacing and depth: Sow 1–2 cm deep; space plants about 30–45 cm apart on a trellis, wider on the ground.
    • Start inside or outside: Sow outside where they are to grow, or start inside shortly before the last frost.
    • Water: Water steadily.
    • Companions: Beans, peas and corn are classic companions.
    • When to pick: Pick often and pick young.

    Garden notes

    • Standard types need bees — each female flower needs pollen carried from a male flower — while greenhouse types set fruit without them.
    • A cucumber left to swell and yellow tells the vine to stop setting new ones, so picking is also pruning.
    • Cucumber climbs by tendrils and takes happily to fences and netting as well as trellises.

    Propagation

    Sow seed straight where it will grow, once frost is past and the soil is warm, about an inch deep. The roots dislike being moved, so do not start it in pots and move it.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — nutrient values for cucumber, with peel, raw
    • Chomicki et al. (2020) — genomic evidence for cucumber's domestication in India
    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — Cucumis sativus: family and native range
    • Pliny the Elder (77 CE) — Roman account of cucumbers grown out of season for Tiberius

    Zucchini

    Cucurbita pepo

    Culinary

    Eye HealthImmune Health

    Cooked

    A summer squash picked young, while the rind is tender and the seeds still soft — the same fruit that, left on the vine, would harden into a marrow. Zucchini is mild, watery and quick-cooking: it grills, sautés, bakes into breads and disappears into sauces, and its golden flowers are a food in their own right. The fruit is the main part eaten; the blossoms are prized, and the seeds are eaten with the young fruit. It is the same species as pumpkin — Cucurbita pepo — and shares that species with acorn and spaghetti squash as well.

    Cultivars

    Black Beauty

    Skin
    Flesh

    The long-standing standard: dark green, glossy and heavy-yielding.

    Golden Zucchini

    Skin
    Flesh

    Bright yellow fruit on a compact plant, picked just as young; Gold Rush is the best-known name.

    Ronde de Nice

    Skin
    Flesh

    A French heirloom picked round and tiny, made for stuffing.

    Costata Romanesco

    Skin
    Flesh

    An Italian ribbed heirloom, nutty-flavoured when small, and grown as much for its large blossoms as for its fruit.

    Cocozelle

    Skin
    Flesh

    An old Italian type, green with pale stripes, at its best very young.

    Cousa

    Skin
    Flesh

    Short, pale and bulbous-ended, the stuffing squash of Middle Eastern kitchens.

    Italy — the flowers lead: fiori di zucca, blossoms stuffed with ricotta or mozzarella, battered and fried — and the fruit goes into pasta, frittata and slow-cooked summer stews.
    France — the courgette is one of the pillars of ratatouille, with tomato, pepper and aubergine.
    Turkey — grated zucchini becomes mücver, crisp fritters with herbs and cheese.
    Lebanon and the Levant — cousa squashes are hollowed and stuffed with spiced rice or meat as kousa mahshi.
    Mexico — calabacitas cooks summer squash with corn, green chile, tomato and cheese — a dish whose roots run straight back to the milpa, where squash grew beside maize and beans long before Europe knew any of the three.
    • Zucchini's deep roots are American. Cucurbita pepo was domesticated — tamed and bred by people — in two places on its own: in Mexico, and in eastern North America, thousands of years ago. After Columbus, its seed crossed to Europe.
    • In the Americas, the early squashes grew in the milpa. That is a field where maize, beans and squash are planted together. The seeds were a valued food in their own right, ground into sauces. That seed tradition lives on in Mexican cooking today.
    • But the zucchini itself — the slender green fruit picked small — is an Italian creation. It was selected near Milan in the late 1800s, from older European summer squashes. Its name is the diminutive of zucca, the Italian word for squash — a diminutive is a word form that means "little". In France and Britain it is the courgette, which means "little squash" in French.
    • Italian immigrants carried it to the United States in the 1920s. There it kept its Italian name, and in time it took a permanent place in summer gardens.
    • Light eating: 17 kcal per 100 g, and mostly water. Zucchini fills a plate without filling a calorie budget.
    • Vitamin C: 17.9 mg per 100 g with the skin on — 20% of the daily value.
    • Eye pigments: lutein and zeaxanthin, 2,125 µg per 100 g, concentrated in the skin. These are the same pigments that collect in the human retina; stated as content.
    • Also present: potassium 261 mg, folate 24 µg and fibre 1.0 g per 100 g.
    • Caution — bitterness: zucchini grown from home-saved seed can cross with ornamental gourds and turn dangerously bitter with cucurbitacins. In 2015 a man in Germany died after eating a stew made with a bitter home-grown zucchini, and Germany's Federal Institute for Risk Assessment issued a public warning. Shop-bought and seed-catalogue zucchini is bred safe; any zucchini that tastes intensely bitter should be spat out and thrown away, never cooked into submission.
    • When to plant: Sow outside after the last frost.
    • Sun: Full sun.
    • Soil: Rich soil.
    • Environment: A warm-season bush — the most generous plant in a summer garden; one or two bushes out-produce most households.
    • Planter or ground: Ground, or large planters.
    • Spacing and depth: Sow 2–3 cm deep; give each plant about a square metre.
    • Start inside or outside: Sow outside, or start inside a few weeks before the last frost.
    • Water: Water steadily, at the base of the plant.
    • Companions: Corn and beans — the Three Sisters planting.
    • When to pick: Pick at 15–20 cm (6–8 in), every day or two.

    Garden notes

    • Fruit left on the vine swell into marrows and slow the plant down — picking keeps it producing.
    • The flowers open in the morning; once the bees have worked them, spare male blossoms can go to the kitchen.
    • Late in the season, watch for powdery mildew on the leaves, and in North America for the squash vine borer in the stems.

    Propagation

    Sow seed straight where it will grow, once frost is past and the soil has warmed to at least 65 to 70°F, about 1 inch deep. Thin to one strong plant per hill. The roots dislike being moved, so direct sowing beats transplanting.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — nutrient values for zucchini, with skin, raw
    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — Cucurbita pepo: family and origin
    • Paris (2001) — history of the cultivar groups of Cucurbita pepo, including zucchini's Milanese origin
    • BfR (2015) — German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment warning on bitter home-grown zucchini

    Watermelon

    Citrullus lanatus

    Culinary

    Heart Health

    FreshDriedCooked

    A trailing African vine grown for the largest fruit in the garden: a hard-rinded berry that can pass 10 kg, filled with sweet, watery flesh — red in most modern varieties, yellow in some — and flat, dark seeds. Watermelon is eaten fresh by the slice, but the plant gives more than the slice: the seeds are roasted and eaten in many countries, and the rind is cooked and pickled where nothing is wasted. Among the gourds it is a more distant cousin, from another continent entirely.

    Cultivars

    Seeded

    Skin
    Flesh

    The original form: full-sized fruit with mature dark seeds, and the fullest flavour range of any group.

    Seedless

    Skin
    Flesh

    Not seed-free by magic but by chromosome count. A parent plant with doubled chromosomes (four sets) crossed with a normal plant (two sets) gives a plant with three sets, whose fruit grows normally but whose seeds never mature — only soft white traces remain. The method came out of Japanese breeding work begun in 1939; seedless fruit became common in shops from the 1990s. Seedless vines still need a seeded variety planted beside them for pollination.

    Yellow- and Orange-Fleshed

    Skin
    Flesh

    Older than the red standard in some regions, and honey-sweet; Yellow Crimson is the best-known name. Red flesh is itself a bred trait — wild and early watermelons were pale.

    Icebox

    Skin
    Flesh

    Bred small, at 2–7 kg, to fit a refrigerator and a small household. Sugar Baby, released in 1959, made the type a garden standard.

    Giant

    Skin
    Flesh

    Grown for contests rather than kitchens; the heaviest watermelon on record stands near 159 kg.

    West Africa — some watermelons are grown not for sweet flesh at all but for their seeds: the seed-grown egusi melons of this same species are harvested, dried and ground into the thickening heart of egusi soup in Nigeria and its neighbours.
    China — watermelon seeds are roasted and salted as a snack, and the rind is stir-fried rather than discarded.
    American South — the rind is pickled, sweet and spiced.
    Egypt and the Levant — roasted seeds are a standard snack, in lands that have eaten the fruit since antiquity.
    Russia — in the lower Volga, tradition boiled the juice down to nardek, a watermelon "honey."
    Japan — square watermelons are grown in boxes as gifts — priced as objects, not as lunch.
    • Watermelon comes from Africa. In 2021, scientists studied its genes — the plant's inherited code — and found its closest wild relative: the Kordofan melon of Sudan, a pale, non-bitter wild watermelon that still grows there. It is likely the crop's ancestor. This settled a long argument. People had placed the origin in southern Africa, but that was based on a relative that had been wrongly identified.
    • Paintings in Egyptian tombs suggest that watermelon was already eaten as a sweet dessert fruit in the Nile Valley some 4,000 years ago.
    • Its oldest use was simpler than dessert. In the dry Kalahari, wild watermelons were a stored drink — a source of water for people and animals through the dry season.
    • From Africa, the fruit travelled to India and to China. China is now the world's largest grower. Watermelon reached the Americas in the 1600s, carried by Europeans and by enslaved Africans.
    • Even its chemistry carries its name. Citrulline is an amino acid — one of the building blocks of protein. It was first taken out of watermelon juice in 1914, and it was named for Citrullus, the watermelon's Latin name.
    • Hydration and lightness: 30 kcal per 100 g, about 92% water, and 6.2 g of natural sugars. Sweet refreshment at low energy cost.
    • Lycopene: 4,532 µg per 100 g — more, gram for gram, than raw tomato (2,573 µg). Lycopene is the pigment that makes the flesh red. It is stated here as content: studies of lycopene and of watermelon juice exist, but no disease claim is made for eating the fruit.
    • Citrulline: watermelon is the richest common food source of this amino acid — a few hundred milligrams in a cup of flesh, and more in the rind than in the flesh. The body converts citrulline to arginine, which plays a part in normal blood-vessel function; that pathway is stated, not promised. Small trials of concentrated watermelon extracts and juices are not trials of eating the fruit.
    • Also present: vitamin C 8.1 mg, potassium 112 mg and vitamin A 28 µg RAE per 100 g.
    • Seeds and rind: the seeds are edible and nourishing roasted, and the rind is edible cooked or pickled — in much of the world neither is treated as waste.
    • When to plant: Sow outside after all danger of frost.
    • Sun: Full sun.
    • Soil: Rich, sandy, well-drained soil.
    • Environment: A heat-lover that needs a long, warm season; the vines spread for metres.
    • Planter or ground: Ground — the vines need room to run.
    • Spacing and depth: Sow 2–3 cm deep; space hills about 2 m apart.
    • Start inside or outside: Start inside a few weeks before the last frost, or sow outside after it.
    • Water: Water deeply while fruit is sizing.
    • Companions: Corn is the classic companion.
    • When to pick: Read ripeness three ways together — the tendril nearest the fruit dries and browns, the pale ground spot where the melon rests turns creamy yellow, and the rind loses its shine.

    Garden notes

    • Bees are essential: only the female flowers fruit, and each needs several bee visits to set well.
    • Seed for saving comes only from seeded types, taken from a fully ripe fruit.

    Propagation

    Sow seed 1 inch deep once the soil is warm, 68 to 95°F. Start seed indoors 3 to 4 weeks before setting out if you want a head start, and move seedlings with care, as the roots dislike being disturbed. Seedless kinds sprout poorly and need a seeded kind planted nearby to set fruit.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — nutrient values for watermelon, raw
    • Renner et al. (2021) — genomic study identifying the Sudanese Kordofan melon as the watermelon's closest relative
    • Rimando & Perkins-Veazie (2005) — measurement of citrulline in watermelon flesh and rind
    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — Citrullus lanatus: family and native range

    Winter Squash

    Cucurbita pepo, C. moschata, C. maxima

    Culinary

    Eye HealthImmune Health

    DriedCooked

    Winter squash is not one plant but a harvest: the mature, hard-shelled fruit of three Cucurbita species, picked fully ripe in autumn and able to keep for months in a cool room. Where summer squash is eaten young and tender, winter squash is eaten mature — the rind hard, the flesh dense, sweet and deep orange, and the seeds large enough to roast. The flesh is the main part eaten; the seeds — pepitas — are a food in themselves, and the blossoms are eaten in season. Pumpkin is the family's most famous member, and it belongs to this same hard-shelled tribe, alongside butternut, acorn, spaghetti, kabocha, delicata and their kin.

    Cultivars

    Butternut

    Skin
    Flesh

    Tan and bell-shaped (Cucurbita moschata), with all the seeds in the bulb and a long neck of solid flesh. Bred by Charles Leggett in Stow, Massachusetts, in the 1940s, from a gooseneck squash crossed with a Hubbard type; the name is said to be his — "smooth as butter, sweet as a nut." Sweet, smooth, and the easiest of the group to peel.

    Acorn

    Skin
    Flesh

    Small, ribbed and dark green (Cucurbita pepo), with an acorn's shape. Grown in North America long before it had a variety name; the Table Queen type, sold from 1913, made it a household squash. Halved and baked, it is its own serving bowl.

    Spaghetti

    Skin
    Flesh

    A pale yellow cylinder (Cucurbita pepo) whose cooked flesh separates into strands. Bred in China in the 1930s and slow to catch on; it became common in North America only in the 1970s. The mildest and least sweet of the group.

    Kabocha

    Skin
    Flesh

    A squat, dark-green Japanese squash (Cucurbita maxima) with dense, almost chestnut-sweet flesh. Its name is said to come from Cambodia, the seed carried to Japan by Portuguese traders in the 1500s.

    Delicata

    Skin
    Flesh

    Small and cream-and-green striped (Cucurbita pepo), with a rind thin enough to eat. Introduced by a New York seed house in 1894, shelved for decades as too delicate to ship, and revived in recent years for its sweetness.

    Hubbard

    Skin
    Flesh

    The giant of the group (Cucurbita maxima): blue-grey or green, warty, thick-shelled, and able to keep half a year. Named in the mid-1800s for Elizabeth Hubbard of Marblehead, Massachusetts, who brought the seed to gardeners' attention.

    Japan — kabocha is simmered in dashi as kabocha no nimono and fried as tempura.
    Italy — winter squash fills pasta: cappellacci di zucca in Ferrara, tortelli in Mantua.
    Argentina — winter squash thickens locro, the maize, bean and squash stew.
    New England — acorn halves are baked with butter and maple syrup.
    Caribbean — calabaza runs through soups and stews such as sancocho.
    Mexico — the seeds take the lead: pepitas are ground into pipián sauces and into sikil p'ak, the Yucatecan pumpkin-seed dip — seed dishes older than the Spanish arrival, and the direct survival of the squash's oldest use.
    • All three species are American. Each was domesticated — tamed and bred by people — from wild gourds thousands of years ago. Cucurbita pepo was tamed in Mexico and in eastern North America. C. moschata was tamed in the warm lowlands further south. C. maxima was tamed in South America.
    • Indigenous growers bred them into squashes that keep. That keeping quality was the whole point of the plant in the past: a fruit that could feed a household through winter, without refrigeration.
    • Squash grew with maize and beans in the Three Sisters planting of the Haudenosaunee and many other peoples. People dried the flesh in strips for storage. They ate the seeds as food, and ground them into sauces.
    • Europeans first met winter squash in the 1500s. Within a hundred years, they had carried the seed all over the world. Kabocha's line runs from the Americas to Japan, carried by Portuguese traders.
    • One member of the family took on a second life. In the 1800s, Irish and Scottish immigrants brought to North America their custom of carving lanterns for Halloween — at home, the lantern had been a turnip. Here they found the pumpkin, a native C. pepo: bigger, softer and far easier to hollow out than a turnip. The turnip lantern gave way to the pumpkin jack-o'-lantern, and the carved pumpkin has marked Halloween ever since.
    • The named varieties are much newer work. Butternut was bred in Massachusetts in the 1940s. Delicata dates to 1894.
    • Vitamin A: butternut carries 532 µg RAE per 100 g raw — 59% of the daily value — almost all of it as beta-carotene (4,230 µg), the pigment that makes the flesh orange. The body converts beta-carotene to vitamin A, which is needed for vision and for the immune system. The winter squashes as a group average less — 68 µg RAE per 100 g across all varieties — with butternut at the rich end.
    • Vitamin C: 21 mg per 100 g in butternut; 12.3 mg across winter squashes generally.
    • Potassium and fibre: butternut carries 352 mg of potassium and 2.0 g of fibre per 100 g, at 45 kcal.
    • The seeds: pepitas are a concentrated food — protein, magnesium and zinc in a small package — roasted from the cavity of any of these squashes.
    • Caution — bitterness: a winter squash that tastes intensely bitter carries too much cucurbitacin and should not be eaten. Documented cases include two women in France who lost much of their hair after eating bitter squash soup (Assouly, 2018). Bred varieties are safe; the warning belongs to home-saved seed that has crossed with ornamental gourds, and to any squash that tastes wrong.
    • When to plant: Sow outside after the last frost.
    • Sun: Full sun.
    • Soil: Rich soil, with room for the vines to run.
    • Environment: A long, warm season; vining types spread for metres, bush forms take less room.
    • Planter or ground: Ground is best — the vines need room.
    • Spacing and depth: Sow 2–3 cm deep; space hills about 1–2 m apart.
    • Start inside or outside: Start inside a few weeks before the last frost, or sow outside after it.
    • Water: Water deeply while fruit is sizing.
    • Companions: Corn and beans — the Three Sisters planting.
    • When to pick: When the rind resists a thumbnail and the stem has corked and dried.

    Garden notes

    • Cure the harvest in a warm, airy spot for ten days to two weeks: the skin hardens further, and the flesh sweetens as starches convert — winter squashes measurably gain sweetness and carotenoids in the first weeks of storage.
    • Store cool and dry. Most keep two to six months: delicata and acorn at the short end, Hubbard and butternut at the long end.
    • Save seed only where the plant grew away from ornamental gourds and from other Cucurbita of the same species, or next year's fruit may come up bitter.

    Propagation

    Sow seed straight where it will grow, once frost is past and the soil has warmed to at least 65 to 70°F, about 1 inch deep. Thin to 2 to 3 plants per hill. Seed saved at home may not come true, as squash cross-pollinate easily.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — nutrient values for butternut squash, raw, and winter squash, all varieties, raw
    • Kew, Plants of the World Online — Cucurbita pepo, C. moschata and C. maxima: species and origins
    • Assouly (2018) — case reports of hair loss after eating bitter squash, JAMA Dermatology

    Acerola

    Malpighia emarginata

    Culinary

    Immune Health

    Fresh

    A small red cherry that is not a cherry at all — and the richest natural source of vitamin C most people have never tasted. One small handful of acerola holds more vitamin C than a whole bag of oranges, and the fruit is gone in a day or two: it bruises at a touch and spoils fast, so it is best eaten straight from the tree, or frozen or juiced within hours.

    Cultivars

    • The fruit runs from bright red to deep red, and from sharp to almost sweet, depending on the tree — most acerola is grown from seed, so trees vary, and growers pick the best ones and grow them from cuttings. Named varieties are local to Brazil and the Caribbean; what matters for the reader is the ripeness rule — slightly underripe for the most vitamin C, fully red for the sweetest eating.
    Brazil — juice and frozen pulp, the form in which most Brazilians meet the fruit; it is also eaten fresh from the tree and made into jams and liqueurs.
    Puerto Rico and the Caribbean — cereza, eaten fresh, pressed into juice, and cooked into jams and sauces.
    Florida and Texas — backyard trees, grown for the fruit and for the pink flowers; the fruit is eaten fresh or frozen the same day.
    Elsewhere — grown as an ornamental shrub and for hedges, and kept small as a bonsai subject for its small leaves and fruit.
    • Acerola is Malpighia emarginata, a tropical fruit-bearing shrub or small tree in the family Malpighiaceae. It is native to the Caribbean — the Lesser Antilles of the southern Caribbean Sea — and to Central America and northern South America, especially Brazil.
    • Its name comes from the Arabic az-zu'rūra, through Spanish, for a similar-looking old-world fruit. Other names are Barbados cherry, West Indian cherry, Puerto Rican cherry and cereza.
    • Brazil is the largest producer of acerola in the world, and it was in Brazil that the fruit's vitamin C was first measured and the plant first grown on a large scale. It has since been planted across the tropics and subtropics, and has naturalised in southern Florida and the Lower Rio Grande Valley of Texas.
    • The raw fruit, per 100 g: 32 kcal, carbohydrate 7.69 g, fibre 1.1 g, protein 0.40 g, and vitamin C at 1,677.6 mg — about eighteen times the daily value. It also carries manganese at 26% of the daily value and a little vitamin A.
    • The vitamin C is the story, and its range matters: the amount runs from roughly 1,000 mg to over 4,000 mg per 100 g depending on the variety and how ripe the fruit is. It is highest when the fruit is slightly underripe, and it falls as the fruit reddens and sweetens. The USDA's number sits inside that range.
    • A small handful is plenty. The US National Institutes of Health set the upper limit for vitamin C at 2,000 mg a day for adults aged 19 and over — a 100 g serving of acerola can approach or pass it. Extra vitamin C leaves the body in the urine, but very high intakes can upset the stomach. More is not better.
    • The fruit is 91% water and very low in sugar for a fruit, which is why it tastes sharp and sour rather than sweet. Eaten fresh it is a bright, tart mouthful; juiced or cooked with sweeter fruit, it is easier to love.
    • Caution from the plant itself: the leaves and their short stalks carry minute stinging hairs that can irritate skin. Handle the branches with care, and wash after picking.
    • When to plant: Plant in a sheltered spot — its roots are shallow, and it dislikes wind
    • Sun: Full sun, six to eight hours a day
    • Soil: Well-drained soil
    • Environment: A compact tropical evergreen of USDA zones 9b–11, and frost-tender: young plants die below about 30 °F (−1 °C), and mature trees survive only a brief dip to about 28 °F (−2 °C)
    • Planter or ground: Ground — a compact shrub or small tree, 6–20 ft tall, with spreading branches on a short trunk; it is also kept small as a bonsai
    • Spacing and depth: A compact tree, 6–20 ft tall — allow room for the spreading branches
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Flowers and fruit run from April to November, and fruit ripens three to four weeks after flowering; pick often and handle gently

    Garden notes

    • Trees start fruiting in their first year, but real crops begin around the third year, reaching up to about 47 kg per plant in the sixth year.
    • Ripe fruit bruises at a touch and spoils within a day or two: eat it straight from the plant, juice it, or freeze it at once. Semi-ripe fruit keeps for several days in the fridge.

    Propagation

    Grow a new tree from air layering or a hardwood cutting, not from seed. In spring or summer, air-layer a branch — roots form in 6 to 8 weeks — or root leafy hardwood cuttings, which root within about 2 months. Seed-grown trees do not come true, so the fruit may be poor.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — Acerola, raw (FDC ID 171686); nutrient values per 100 g
    • Vendramini & Trugo (2000) — vitamin C in acerola by variety and ripeness, Food Chemistry
    • NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — vitamin C upper limit of 2,000 mg a day for adults aged 19 and over

    Achote

    Bixa orellana

    Culinary

    The red seed that colours food. Achote — also called annatto and achiote, and nicknamed the lipstick tree — is a small tropical tree grown for one thing: the brick-red coating on its seeds. Rub a seed between your fingers and your skin turns orange-red. That colour, a pigment called bixin, has painted bodies, dyed cloth and coloured food for thousands of years. It is why cheddar cheese is orange, why Puerto Rican rice is gold, and why the seeds sit in spice jars across the Caribbean and Latin America. The flavour is mild and earthy; the colour is the point.

    Cultivars

    • The seed in the shop is sold by origin, not by variety name — a jar of achote never names the tree it came from. Named varieties do exist, but they belong to growers and breeders, who select for one thing: how much bixin the seed carries. Good seed runs about 2–4% bixin. Brazil's best-known variety, 'Piave Vermelha', carries about 3.5–5%, which is why growers prize it; Brazil's breeding programme also produced the line Embrapa 37. In Mexico, regional types are known as Peruvian red, Peruvian green and Criolla. For the cook, none of this is on the label — what matters is fresh seed, brick-red and strongly coloured, not faded brown.
    Puerto Rico — the heart of achote cooking. Cooks warm the seeds in oil or lard until the fat turns deep red-orange, strain the seeds out, and keep the coloured fat: aceite de achiote. It is the colour of arroz con gandules, rice with pigeon peas, the island's national dish; it tints the masa of pasteles, the filled plantain-and-root parcels wrapped in banana leaf; it colours alcapurrias and starts the sofrito base that begins so many pots. Beside it in the pantry sits recaíto, the green herb paste — green base first, then the red-gold oil. Ground achote is also in sazón, the seasoning blend sprinkled through island cooking.
    Mexico — in Yucatán, ground achote is the base of recado rojo, the red paste — achiote with sour orange juice, garlic and spices — rubbed on pork for cochinita pibil, the slow-roasted pig cooked in banana leaves, and on chicken for pollo pibil.
    The Philippines — atsuete, carried across the Pacific by Spanish galleons, colours pancit Malabon noodles and their sauce a bright orange, and gives kare-kare, the peanut stew, its warm tint.
    Venezuela — onoto, the local name, colours the corn masa of hallacas, the filled parcels steamed at Christmas.
    Brazil — urucum, ground to a powder called colorau and shaken over rice, beans and stews as an everyday colour; the same seed that painted bodies long before it seasoned pots.
    Britain and the cheese world — annatto is the quiet reason Red Leicester is red, Cheshire and cheddar are gold, and much of the world's processed cheese is orange. Most people who have eaten orange cheese have eaten achote without knowing its name.
    • Achote is Bixa orellana, a shrub or small tree in the family Bixaceae. It is native to tropical America — the warm country from Mexico through the Amazon basin to Brazil — and its wild ancestor, which botanists call variety urucurana, still grows in open forest there. The second half of its scientific name honours Francisco de Orellana, the Spanish explorer who first sailed the length of the Amazon in the 1540s.
    • Its names carry its history. Achiote comes from āchiyōtl, the word in Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs. In Brazil it is urucum, from the Tupi word for red. Achote is the name used in Puerto Rico and parts of the Caribbean. English took annatto, and the nickname "lipstick tree" came later, from the seed paste's likeness to lipstick — and its real use in cosmetics.
    • Long before Europeans arrived, the peoples of tropical America used the red seed paste on skin. It was body paint for ceremony and for war, and the colour red itself stood for the sun, fire, blood and life. The paste was also practical: smeared on skin, it was believed to keep insects off and the sun from burning. The men of the Tsáchila people of Ecuador still dye their hair bright orange-red with crushed achote seeds, as they have for centuries, and peoples in Brazil, such as the Wari', still paint their bodies with it.
    • The colour went into food early, too. By some accounts, the Maya coloured their chocolate drinks with achote, and in the 1500s it was used to paint Mexican manuscripts. The seeds and leaves were also part of traditional medicine across the region — teas and washes for fevers, wounds and stomach troubles. Those uses are history; what the studies actually support is in Health Benefits.
    • Europeans wanted the dye. In the 1600s, Dutch traders bought annatto from the Indigenous peoples of the Guyana coast and sold it in the Netherlands as paint. Spanish and Portuguese colonisers carried the plant itself around the world in the 1500s and 1600s — to the Philippines, to Africa, to India — and everywhere warm, it took root and took on local names and local dishes.
    • The modern chapter is the food factory. Annatto became the natural colour behind orange cheese, golden butter and margarine, snacks, cereals and drinks — listed on labels in Europe as E160b. Cheesemakers had coloured cheese with it for centuries before the factories: winter milk is pale, and a little annatto made every cheese the same warm gold. It is still one of the most used natural food colours in the world.
    • The honest headline: achote is a colour, not a medicine, and it has no proven health benefit. The seeds are barely eaten — they are warmed in oil or ground into a paste, and in most dishes they are strained out or eaten in pinches. Nobody eats achote by the spoonful, which is why there is no standard nutrition table for the seed itself.
    • What is inside the red coating is real chemistry, and it is worth stating plainly. Bixin and its partner norbixin are carotenoids — the same family of pigments that colours carrots and tomatoes — and in laboratory tests they behave as antioxidants, soaking up the reactive molecules that damage cells. The seeds are also one of the richest known sources of tocotrienols, a form of vitamin E. All of that is true of the seed in a test tube. None of it has been shown to make people healthier.
    • The human evidence, stated at its strength: the Natural Medicines database, which grades herbal remedies on their trial evidence, rates every use of annatto as "insufficient reliable evidence" — too little good research in people to say it helps with anything. The studies behind the claims are nearly all in laboratories or animals: bixin improving cholesterol readings in rats, extracts slowing bacteria in a dish, seed compounds killing cancer cells in glassware. One use was tested properly in people and failed: powdered annatto leaf, taken three times a day for twelve months by men with an enlarged prostate, did no better than a dummy pill. Supplements of annatto tocotrienols are sold for bones and cholesterol, but the benefit in people is not proven.
    • Safety, plainly: in the small amounts used in food, annatto is considered safe — the US Food and Drug Administration lists annatto extract as a colour that may be used in foods generally, and Europe's food safety panel set daily limits for bixin and norbixin that normal food use stays well under. The one real caution is allergy. A small number of people react to annatto with hives, swelling, or stomach trouble, and rare severe reactions have been reported. Anyone who has reacted to it before should read labels — it hides in cheese, snacks and drinks under "annatto", "E160b", or simply "colour".
    • The plant: An evergreen shrub or small tree, 2–8 m (about 6–26 ft) tall, often wider than it is tall, with a domed crown of heart-shaped leaves. It is grown as much for its looks as for its seeds: clusters of pink flowers, each about 5 cm across, open at the ends of the branches, followed by the showy pods.
    • The pods: The plant's signature: oval capsules covered in soft red bristles, ripening from bright red to brown. When ripe, each pod splits in two and shows 30–50 small seeds, every one wrapped in its red coating.
    • Climate: A true tropical. It is hardy outdoors only in USDA zones 10–12 and is frost-tender — frost damages or kills it. It wants full sun for the best flowering and pods, though it tolerates light shade, and it likes warm, humid air.
    • Soil and water: It is not fussy — it grows in most soils if they drain well, and does best in rich, moist ground. Once settled it can ride out dry spells of some months, but it flowers and fruits better with regular water, and it prefers drier ground while the pods ripen.
    • Growing it: Sow fresh seed — it sprouts in about one to two weeks — or take cuttings of mature wood, which flower sooner than seedlings do. A young plant can carry its first pods in about two years. Prune after harvest to keep it bushy; it is often grown as a hedge.
    • Harvest: Pick the pods when they dry and begin to split, rub the seeds out, and dry them. Kept dry and out of the light, the seed keeps its colour well.
    • In a cool climate: It can be grown in a large pot and brought indoors before the nights turn cold — a sunny windowsill plant for the winter, back outside for the summer, with pods a hope rather than a promise.

    Propagation

    Sow fresh seed at the start of warm, wet weather — fresh seed from a ripe pod sprouts in 7 to 10 days in moist soil. Or root a hardwood cutting at least 8 mm thick with rooting hormone; roots form in 7 to 9 weeks. Cuttings keep the parent's yield and flower sooner; seed-grown plants take longer and vary more.

    Sources

    • Jansen & Cardon (eds.) (2005) — Plant Resources of Tropical Africa 3: Dyes and Tannins — the plant, its history, production and uses
    • Vilar et al. (2014) — traditional uses, chemical constituents and biological activities of Bixa orellana: a review — what the plant contains and what the studies show
    • EFSA ANS Panel (2016) — safety of annatto extracts (E 160b) as a food additive — the daily limits for bixin and norbixin
    • U.S. Food and Drug Administration — 21 CFR 73.30: annatto extract listed as a colour additive for foods
    • Ortiz Cuadra (2013) — Eating Puerto Rico: a history of food, culture and identity — achiote in the island's cocina criolla

    Cassava

    Manihot esculenta

    Culinary

    Digestive Health

    Cooked

    The root that feeds half a billion people. Cassava is a woody shrub grown for the thick starchy roots under it — a staple food across the tropics, the third-largest source of food carbohydrate there after rice and maize. It grows where other crops fail: poor soil, little rain, no fuss. It also carries a warning no other root in this library carries: never eat it raw. The roots — and the leaves — hold compounds that release cyanide, the poison, unless the plant is peeled, soaked and cooked properly. Cooked right, it is safe, filling food. Raw or rushed, it is dangerous.

    Cultivars

    • The real split is sweet versus bitter. Sweet types are low in the cyanide compounds and are cooked and eaten like a vegetable — boiled, fried, mashed. Bitter types are high in them and are never eaten fresh; they are grated, pressed and dried into flour and foods like gari and farinha. The bitterness is not a flavour quirk; it is the warning sign.
    • Named varieties are local — every cassava country has its own, bred for its soil and its dishes. What matters for the reader is the sweet/bitter split and the processing, not a variety list.
    Brazil — farinha, the toasted cassava flour sprinkled over almost every meal; tapioca crepes, thin pancakes of cassava starch filled with cheese or coconut; and pão de queijo, cheese bread made with cassava starch instead of wheat flour.
    West Africa — gari, the roasted granules eaten with water or soup; fufu, the pounded dough scooped with the hand; attiéké, the steamed, slightly sour couscous of Côte d'Ivoire.
    Central Africa — saka-saka, cassava leaves pounded and simmered with palm oil and peanuts; chikwangue, the wrapped cassava loaf of Congo.
    East Africa — cassava flour stirred into ugali, the stiff porridge eaten with greens and stew.
    South-East Asia and the Pacific — tapioca pearls in bubble tea; cassava cake in the Philippines, baked with coconut milk; steamed and fried cassava as a snack food across Indonesia and Thailand.
    • Cassava comes from South America. Its wild ancestor, Manihot esculenta subsp. flabellifolia, still grows in west-central Brazil, and the plant was domesticated there no more than about 10,000 years ago — one of the oldest farmed crops of the Americas.
    • It was a staple of the peoples of the Americas long before Europeans arrived, grown in gardens and fields from Brazil to the Caribbean, and the knowledge of how to make it safe — grating, soaking, pressing, cooking — travelled with the plant.
    • Portuguese traders carried it from Brazil to Africa in the 1500s, and to Asia in the same period. In Africa it spread fast, because it grows in poor soil and stores in the ground: a family can leave roots standing and dig them as needed, which matters where the rains fail.
    • Today more than 500 million people depend on it, and Nigeria grows more of it than any other country. Its family is the spurges, Euphorbiaceae — the same family as the poinsettia and the rubber tree.

    Craft

    • The root’s starch is a maker’s material: a glue can be made from it — cassava-starch glue has been used on postage stamps — and the starch serves as a size, the stiffening finish worked into cotton fabrics.
    • The root, per 100 g raw: about 160 kcal, about 38 g of carbohydrate, fibre 1.8 g and protein 1.4 g, with vitamin C at about 20.6 mg (roughly a fifth of the daily value). It is an energy food first: it fills you up. It is not a vitamin food, and it is low in protein — a diet built on cassava alone is short on protein, which is why it is always eaten with beans, fish, meat or greens.
    • The leaves are also eaten, cooked, in parts of Africa — simmered into dishes like saka-saka in Congo and matapa in Mozambique. They are a green vegetable, not a root, and they follow the same rule as the root: cooked only, never raw.
    • Safety — read this before anything else. Raw or under-processed cassava contains cyanogenic glycosides, mainly a compound called linamarin (with a smaller amount of lotaustralin). These are natural compounds that release hydrogen cyanide — a poison — when the plant's cells are crushed or chewed. Sweet types hold under 50 mg of cyanide per kilo; bitter types hold up to about 400 mg per kilo. That is why the rules are absolute: never eat cassava raw; peel it completely; cut it small; soak it; boil it thoroughly; throw the cooking water away. The leaves follow the same rule — they are cyanogenic too and are eaten only after long cooking.
    • What happens when the rules are broken: a large amount of poorly processed cassava can poison within hours — dizziness, headache, stomach pain, vomiting and diarrhoea. Over years, a diet heavy in poorly processed cassava is linked to konzo, a sudden paralysis of the legs, and to goitre, a swelling of the gland in the neck. Both are diseases of poverty and poor processing, not of cassava eaten properly.
    • Cassava is naturally free of gluten, which is why its flour and starch — tapioca — are used in gluten-free baking. Tapioca pearls, the chewy balls in bubble tea, are cassava starch.
    • When to plant: Grow from stem cuttings, not seed — lengths of stem about 20 cm are pushed into the ground in spring, after the last frost, in warm soil, and they root
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Well-drained soil; it tolerates poor soil, but waterlogged ground rots the roots
    • Environment: A tropical perennial, grown as an annual where winters bite; it needs warmth, and frost kills it outright
    • Planter or ground: Ground; in a cool climate, a large pot in a greenhouse or sunny room, kept warm and dry through winter — but it is a big plant for a pot, and the roots will stay small
    • Spacing and depth: About a metre of space per plant
    • Water: It grows with little rain; keep the ground drained, as waterlogged soil rots the roots
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Roots are ready in 8–12 months, sometimes longer; dig when the stems are thick and the roots have swollen

    Garden notes

    • In warm ground it grows 2–3 m tall on woody stems, with hand-shaped leaves on long stalks.
    • Roots can be left standing in the ground and dug as needed — the ground itself is the store. Left in the ground too long, though, the roots turn woody, and a test plant tells you when they have swollen.

    Propagation

    Cut a hardened stem from a healthy, disease-free plant at least 10 months old into pieces about 20 cm long, each with 1–2 nodes. Push them into warm, well-drained soil at the start of the growing season and keep them moist until they sprout, in 7–10 days. Cassava needs a long, frost-free season of 8–11 months. The roots must be peeled and cooked well before eating.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — Cassava, raw (FDC ID 169985); nutrient values per 100 g
    • FAO — cassava origin, spread and production; the standard account of the crop in the tropics
    • Plants For A Future — Manihot esculenta: glue and textile size from the root starch

    Goji

    Lycium barbarum

    Culinary

    Eye Health

    FreshDried

    A small red berry from a tough, thorny shrub — the wolfberry. Goji has been grown in the dry country of Ningxia, in north-central China, for centuries, and written about as a valued herb there for far longer. Today the berries are sold dried all over the world, sweet and chewy, in trail mix and teas. The honest picture is a good dried fruit with one small, real eye study behind it — and a lot of bigger claims that the evidence does not support.

    Cultivars

    • The two species: Lycium barbarum is the main commercial goji, grown in Ningxia and Xinjiang; Lycium chinense is the other cultivated goji, with similar fruit that tastes a little different and holds a little less sugar. Most dried goji on sale is L. barbarum.
    • Named garden varieties exist, but the berry on the shelf is sold by origin — Ningxia first — rather than by variety name.
    China — the berries are simmered into soups and congee (rice porridge), steeped as tea, and cooked with chicken and pork; they are also soaked in wine. In old herb practice they were eaten for the eyes and for long life — a claim of tradition, not of trials.
    Tibet and the Himalayas — “Tibetan goji” is a trade name for berries grown in the high country; the plant is the same species.
    The West — dried berries in trail mix, granola and smoothies, and as a tea; the form in which most readers will meet the plant.
    • Goji is Lycium barbarum, one of two boxthorn species whose fruit is sold as goji (the other is Lycium chinense). It belongs to the nightshade family, Solanaceae — the same family as the tomato, the potato and the pepper.
    • Its home is Ningxia, in north-central China, where it has been grown for more than 600 years. Its first written mention is far older: about 200 BCE, in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing, the old Chinese book of herbs, where it appears as gouqi, listed among the top-grade herbs — the ones considered safe for long use.
    • It reached England in 1730, where it was at first mistaken for a tea plant. It has since spread as a garden shrub across Europe and North America, valued as much for its toughness — it survives cold, drought and poor soil — as for its fruit.
    • The dried berries, per 100 g: 349 kcal, protein 14.3 g, carbohydrate 77.1 g, sugars 45.6 g, fibre 13.0 g, vitamin C 48.4 mg, iron 6.8 mg, calcium 190 mg, and vitamin A at 26,822 IU (8,040 µg RAE). Read those numbers with the serving in mind: a small handful of dried berries is about 28 g, not 100 g — and even so, the sugar is real. Dried goji is a sweet food.
    • Goji is the richest food source of zeaxanthin, a yellow-orange pigment that collects in the eye — in the macula, the small spot at the back of the eye that does the sharp seeing. That is the reason for the eye claims, and the evidence is one small trial, honestly stated: Li et al. (2021) gave 27 healthy adults aged 45–65 a 28 g serving five times a week for 90 days, and the density of the eye pigment rose. That is a measurement of pigment, not proof against macular degeneration or any eye disease. No larger trial has shown that goji protects sight.
    • The wider evidence is thin.
