A systematic review of the plant's polysaccharides — the complex sugars credited with most of its supposed benefits — found only two randomised controlled trials among twenty papers. Most of what is claimed for goji rests on laboratory and animal work, not on people.
    • Caution for anyone on blood thinners: there are case reports of the INR — the blood test that measures how thin the blood is — rising after goji tea or juice alongside a steady warfarin dose. Anyone taking warfarin should ask their clinician before taking goji regularly.
    • The dried berry's vitamin A is high enough to count: 8,040 µg RAE per 100 g is far above the daily value, so a large daily serving is not a casual habit. A small handful, now and then, is the sensible way to eat it.
    • When to plant: Plant a young bush where it has room, with a fence or wall to lean on
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Well-drained, slightly alkaline soil, pH 6.5–8.0
    • Environment: A cold-hardy perennial shrub, hardy in USDA zones 3–9, down to about −20 to −23 °C; drought-tolerant once settled
    • Planter or ground: Ground — it grows 2–3 m tall on weak, arching, thorny stems
    • Spacing and depth: Give it room — it throws up suckers from the roots and will spread if left alone; prune it hard
    • Water: Low once settled — it is drought-tolerant
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: Fruit ripens from August to October; pick the berries when they are bright orange-red and soft, handle them gently — they bruise easily — and dry them quickly if you are keeping them

    Garden notes

    • One bush can crop for 15–20 years.
    • It is a tough plant — it survives cold, drought and poor soil — but it spreads by suckers from the roots, so give it a place where spreading is welcome, or prune it hard to keep it in bounds.

    Propagation

    Take a softwood cutting 4 to 6 inches long in early summer, strip the lower leaves, and set it in a half-perlite, half-peat mix, kept moist and out of direct sun. Roots form in a few weeks. Seed-grown plants take about three years to fruit and may not match the parent — cuttings fruit sooner and stay true.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central — Goji berries, dried (FDC ID 173032); nutrient values per 100 g
    • Li et al. (2021) — goji berries and macular pigment density in 27 healthy adults, Nutrients
    • Systematic review of Lycium barbarum polysaccharides — two randomised controlled trials among twenty papers

    Miracle Fruit

    Synsepalum dulcificum

    Culinary

    Fresh

    A small red berry that is barely sweet itself — and yet makes a lemon taste like lemonade. Chew one miracle berry, and for about half an hour sour foods taste sweet: lemons, limes, vinegar, sour gruel. The berry does not add sugar. It carries a protein that changes how the tongue reads sourness, and the effect fades on its own. One caution: the berry changes how sour food tastes, not what it is — the acid is still there.

    Cultivars

    • The plant is usually grown from seed, so plants vary in size and in how much fruit they carry, and nurseries pick the best ones. Named varieties are not part of the public record for this plant. The berry is the same in all of them: small, red, about 2 cm long, with one seed like a coffee bean.
    West Africa — chewed before sour meals, as Marchais recorded in 1725: sour gruel and palm wine made sweet by a berry.
    The United States — “flavour-tripping” parties, where guests chew the berry and then taste lemons, limes and vinegar for the surprise of it; and a small trade in fresh berries and freeze-dried tablets.
    Japan — sold as a novelty and a sweetener, and grown in warm gardens and greenhouses.
    • Miracle fruit is Synsepalum dulcificum, a slow-growing evergreen shrub in the family Sapotaceae. It is native to tropical West and West-Central Africa, where it is known in Yoruba as àgbáyun, and as taami, asaa and ledidi in other languages of the region.
    • The first European account comes from 1725, when the French explorer Chevalier des Marchais, travelling in West Africa, noted that local people chewed the berry before meals — sour gruel, palm wine — so that the sour food would taste sweet. The plant was formally described in 1852 by Daniell.
    • The secret inside the berry is miraculin, a glycoprotein — a protein with sugar chains attached — 191 amino acids long and about 24.6 kDa in size. It was isolated in 1968 by Kurihara and Beidler. Miraculin is not sweet itself. It binds to the tongue's sweet receptors, and when acid touches those receptors, they fire as if sugar were there. Sour food tastes sweet, but only while the mouth stays acidic.
    • The berry's modern history is a regulatory one. The US Food and Drug Administration denied miraculin as a food additive in 1974; a 1980s attempt to sell it in the United States stalled; and in 2011 the FDA imposed a ban on importing S. dulcificum (specifying miraculin) from Taiwan. The fresh berry itself is still sold as a novelty fruit.
    • The berry itself is a light food: low in sugar, with a mildly sweet tang of its own. Its value is not nutrition; it is the taste effect.
    • The effect lasts about 30 minutes to an hour or two after chewing a berry. It fades on its own. A picked berry kept cold holds its effect for a day or so.
    • People have tried the berry as a way to make food taste better when taste is dulled — including during chemotherapy, when food can taste flat or metallic. That use is not proven. It is a thing people have tried, not a thing trials have shown.
    • When to plant: Start from seed or a nursery plant — it is slow: about 3–5 years from seed to first fruit, and 2–3 years for a nursery plant
    • Sun: Full sun to partial shade
    • Soil: Acidic soil, pH 4.5–5.8 — a peat-based mix of the kind blueberries like; in alkaline soil, or with hard water, it yellows and dies back
    • Environment: Frost-tender — damaged near 32 °F, and it suffers below about 50 °F (10 °C); it wants high humidity, and it is self-fertile, so one plant alone will fruit
    • Planter or ground: Ground in warm, humid climates; in most of the United States it is a pot plant, brought inside for the winter
    • Spacing and depth: A slow-growing shrub, 1–2.5 m tall in cultivation and up to about 5.5 m in its native home, with dense, glossy leaves
    • Water: Rain water or distilled water suits it better than tap water in hard-water places
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: In its native home it gives two large crops a year after the rainy season, and in warm, humid climates it bears fruit through the year; eat the berries fresh — the taste effect is lost within 2–3 hours at room temperature after picking

    Garden notes

    • One plant can hold hundreds of berries at a time — ripe red berries among glossy green leaves, with green unripe berries beside them.

    Propagation

    Sow fresh seed at once, just barely covered, in rich, acid soil. Seed comes up in about 8–10 weeks, but the plant stays tiny in its first year — only a few inches tall — and fruit starts at about 4 years. Do not dry or store the seed — it loses life fast once out of the berry.

    Safety

    • Miraculin changes how food tastes, not what the food is. A lemon still holds its acid, and vinegar is still vinegar. Anyone who must be careful with acid — for the stomach, or for the teeth — should treat sour food as sour, however sweet it tastes in the moment.

    Sources

    • Kurihara & Beidler (1968) — miraculin, the taste-changing protein, isolated and described
    • US Food and Drug Administration — miraculin denied as a food additive (1974); import ban on S. dulcificum from Taiwan (2011)
    • World Agroforestry — miracle fruit growing, soil and first-crop timing

    Pineapple

    Ananas comosus

    Culinary

    Digestive HealthImmune Health

    FreshCooked

    A pineapple is a bromeliad — the only one in its family grown around the world for food. The plant is a rosette of stiff, sword-shaped leaves, and the fruit it makes is not one fruit but hundreds of small fruits joined together: each "eye" on the shell was once a single flower. It is sweet, sharp and juicy fresh, and it carries one famous passenger — bromelain, a group of enzymes that break down protein. Fresh pineapple has it; canned pineapple, heated in the tin, does not.

    Cultivars

    • Growers group the world's pineapples into four classes — Smooth Cayenne, Red Spanish, Queen and Abacaxi — and the fruit in the shops belongs to one of them, even when the label never says so.
    • MD-2 ('Del Monte Gold') — the pineapple in almost every supermarket now. Bred in the 1990s and released for the fresh trade, it is a cylindrical fruit of about 3–4 lb (1.3–1.8 kg) with deep yellow flesh, high sugar, low acid and high vitamin C, and it keeps well and resists browning inside after cutting — which is why it took over the fresh market. Its leaves are mostly smooth, spiny only at the tip.
    • Smooth Cayenne — for a century the world's main pineapple, and still one of the most widely grown. A big fruit, 5–6 lb (2.3–2.7 kg), with pale yellow to yellow flesh that is both sweet and sharp. It was the classic canning pineapple and the main fresh export to the United States mainland in the plantation years; MD-2 has pushed it aside in the fresh trade.
    • Queen — a smaller fruit, 2–3 lb (0.9–1.4 kg), with golden yellow, crisp flesh and a mild, delicate flavour; it keeps well after ripening. The leaves are spiny. Grown in South Africa, Australia and India, and as Queen Victoria on Réunion and Mauritius.
    • Red Spanish — the pineapple of the Caribbean and Latin America. A squarish, barrel-shaped fruit of 2–4 lb (0.9–1.8 kg) with pale yellow flesh that is more fibrous and less juicy than the others, and a tough shell that ships well. Its leaves matter beyond the fruit: the Philippine piña cloth described below is woven from the leaves of this type, grown there as Philippine Red.
    • Sugarloaf ('Kona Sugarloaf', 'White Sugarloaf') — a sweet, low-acid fruit of 5–6 lb with white flesh and a core soft enough to eat. Grown in Hawaii and parts of Africa and the Caribbean, mostly for local eating rather than export.
    • Singapore Spanish — a fruit of about 3½–5 lb with golden yellow flesh, grown in Malaysia and used mostly for canning.
    • Pernambuco — Brazil's fresh-eating pineapple of the Abacaxi class, pale-fleshed, sweet and fragrant, eaten where it grows and rarely exported.
    Hawaii — the symbol of the islands, and for much of the 1900s the centre of the world trade: Dole and Del Monte plantations, the Ginaca machine, and canned pineapple shipped everywhere. The trade has moved on; the symbol has not.
    The Philippines — the leaves. Piña is a cloth woven from the fibre of pineapple leaves, above all the Red Spanish type: the leaves are scraped by hand with a coconut shell or a shard of pottery, the fine fibres knotted strand by strand and woven on hand looms into a lustrous, lace-like cloth. It has been made since the 1600s, centred on Kalibo in Aklan, and is sewn into the Barong Tagalog, wedding dresses and formal dress. In 2023 Aklan piña handloom weaving was placed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
    Mexico — tepache, a lightly fermented, gently fizzy drink made from the peels and core — the parts the knife leaves behind — with raw sugar and cinnamon or clove, left a few days to turn. The peel is food here, not waste.
    Brazil — abacaxi eaten fresh and juiced everywhere, and grilled at churrasco barbecue with cinnamon until the edges caramelise.
    Costa Rica and Thailand — two of the biggest pineapple countries of the modern trade: Costa Rica leads the fresh export market with MD-2, and Thailand is a giant of growing and canning.
    Puerto Rico — the piña colada, pineapple with coconut and rum, created in San Juan in 1954 and named the island's national drink.
    West Africa — pineapples grow across the region and are eaten fresh and juiced; Nigeria is among the world's larger producers, mostly for its own tables.
    • Pineapple comes from the river country between southern Brazil and Paraguay, around the Paraná and Paraguay rivers, where its wild relatives still grow. The peoples of South America spread it across the continent as a crop long before Europeans arrived — there is evidence of it in Peru from 1200–800 BCE, and the Maya and Aztec peoples grew it in Mexico in the centuries after. By the late 1400s it was a staple food across tropical America.
    • Its name in the Guaraní language was naná, "excellent fruit" — that word became the scientific name, Ananas. The Spanish called it piña, for its likeness to a pine cone. English speakers took "pine" and added "apple," the old word for any fruit, and made "pineapple."
    • Christopher Columbus met the fruit on Guadeloupe on 4 November 1493, on his second voyage — the first European encounter on record. Carried back to Europe, it could only be grown there in heated glasshouses called pineries, at great cost, and it became a symbol of wealth and luxury: a fresh pineapple was set on the dinner table as a display piece rather than eaten, passed from party to party and even rented out for an evening until it rotted. King Charles II of England was painted being presented with one. The pineapple shape was carved into gateposts, furniture and buildings — including the great stone Pineapple folly at Dunmore in Scotland — and in time it came to stand for hospitality: a welcome, offered in stone or wood where the real fruit could not be.
    • The Portuguese and Spanish spread the plant fast in the 1500s — to the island of St Helena, to Africa, to the Philippines, Guam and Hawaii. It travelled so well because the plant itself travels: a crown or sucker stays alive for weeks and roots wherever it is set in warm ground.
    • In Hawaii the fruit was called hala kahiki, "foreign hala," after the similar-looking fruit of the native hala tree. The first commercial plantation there was planted in 1886. James Dole arrived in 1899, planted in 1900, and built the company that still carries his name; Del Monte planted on Oahu from 1917; and in 1911 Henry Ginaca's machine, which peeled and cored the fruit in one pass, made canning fast enough to feed a world market. Hawaii's share of world production has since shrunk to almost nothing, but the pineapple remains its symbol.
    • In South and Central America, the plant was traditionally used for medicine as well as food — the root of the bromelain story told below. Those uses are history; what the studies actually support is in Health Benefits.

    Craft

    • The leaves of the Red Spanish type — grown in the Philippines as Philippine Red — give one of the world’s finest cloth fibres. The long fibres are scraped free with a coconut shell or a shard of pottery, knotted strand by strand and woven on hand looms into piña, a lustrous, lace-like cloth. It has been made since the 1600s, centred on Kalibo in Aklan, and is sewn into the Barong Tagalog, wedding dresses and formal dress. In 2023, Aklan piña handloom weaving was placed on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
    • Fresh raw pineapple, per 100 g: 50 kcal, carbohydrate 13.1 g, sugars 9.85 g, fibre 1.4 g, protein 0.54 g. Its two standout nutrients are vitamin C at 47.8 mg — about half the daily value — and manganese at 0.93 mg, about 40% of the daily value, with a little copper and vitamin B6 besides. It is a sweet fruit with real sugar in it; the numbers say so.
    • Bromelain is a group of enzymes — substances that speed up chemical work in the body and in food — that break down protein. It is found in the stem and the fruit; most bromelain sold in supplements is taken from the stem. In the kitchen its work is easy to see: fresh pineapple juice tenderises meat, and fresh pineapple stops jelly from setting, because the enzyme cuts the protein in both. Heat destroys it. Canned pineapple and cooked or canned juice have little or no active bromelain left, which is why canned pineapple works in jelly and fresh does not.
    • What the studies support, stated at their strength. Bromelain supplements have been studied for sinus swelling, joint pain, muscle soreness and recovery after wisdom-tooth surgery. The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) finds there is not enough good research to recommend bromelain for sinusitis; some studies suggest it might ease some symptoms after wisdom-tooth surgery; and for most other uses the research is very thin, or used mixtures of ingredients, so the effect of bromelain alone is unclear. Eating fresh pineapple is eating food — it is not a supplement dose.
    • One bromelain use is real medicine, and it is not a home remedy: in 2022 the US Food and Drug Administration approved a bromelain skin treatment that removes dead tissue from severe burns. It is used by professionals in burn care. It is not something to try at home.
    • Fresh versus canned matters beyond the enzyme. Canned pineapple in heavy syrup carries about 78 kcal per 100 g — the extra is syrup sugar — and less vitamin C than fresh. Juice loses the fibre. Fresh fruit is the full food.
    • And one claim does not hold: pineapple does not burn fat, melt fat, or slim anyone. No study shows that.
    • When to plant: Set out in warm weather, once the ground is warm — never from seed, but from a piece of the plant itself: the crown, the leafy top twisted off the fruit; slips and hapas, small shoots from the stalk just under the fruit; suckers, shoots from the joints of the leaves; or ratoons, shoots from the underground stem. Twist or cut the piece off and let it dry in the shade for a day or two before planting; the bigger the piece, the faster it fruits — a sucker is the quick start, a crown the slow one
    • Sun: Full sun, for the best fruit
    • Soil: Moderately fertile, sandy, well-drained soil, neutral to mildly acid; it will not tolerate flooding — standing water rots the roots
    • Environment: Frost-tender in earnest: growth slows below about 60 °F (16 °C), a light frost burns the leaves and can rot the fruit, and cold at about 28 °F (−2 °C) kills it; its comfort range is about 68–86 °F (20–30 °C)
    • Planter or ground: Ground, or a 3–7 gallon pot in the same well-drained mix — the pot is the cold-country answer: bring it indoors before nights fall below about 50 °F (10 °C), keep it in the sunniest window, and expect a small fruit, eventually
    • Spacing and depth: Space plants 12–36 inches apart; wider spacing gives larger fruit
    • Water: It tolerates drought once settled, though growth and fruit suffer without water
    • Companion plants: No strong companions known
    • When to pick: A pineapple does not gain sugar after it is picked — it can soften and colour, but it cannot sweeten. Let the shell turn gold from the bottom up on the plant, smell the base for sweetness, and pick then; cut or twist the fruit off, and save the crown: it is next year's plant

    Garden notes

    • A pineapple plant is a herbaceous perennial — it lives for years — standing 3–6 ft (0.9–1.8 m) high and as wide, a spiral rosette of stiff, sword-like leaves. It is a true bromeliad, kin to the air plants and Spanish moss, and like them it is built to catch and hold water.
    • How the fruit forms: when the plant has made about 70–80 leaves, the centre flowers — a head of 50 to 200 small flowers — and the flowers fuse into a single fruit, the syncarp, topped by the leafy crown. The fruit ripens about 5–7 months after flowering.
    • One stem makes one fruit; then side shoots carry the plant on, and a planting usually gives one main crop and one ratoon crop — a second crop from the regrowth — before it is renewed.
    • Time is the price: from planting to a ripe fruit takes about 18–24 months, and longer in cooler places — a crown in a pot can take two years just to flower. This is a plant for patient gardeners.
    • The shop-bought crown in a pot is how most home gardeners meet this plant, and it works, slowly.

    Propagation

    Twist the leafy top off a ripe pineapple, or pull a slip or sucker from the parent plant, and let it dry in the shade for a day or two. Then plant it in clean, free-draining soil or a pot. Plant in spring, after the last frost. Fruit takes 18 to 24 months, so be patient.

    Safety

    • A lot of fresh pineapple at one sitting can leave the mouth sore — the bromelain and the fruit's acid together do that. Bromelain supplements, which are a different thing from the fruit, can upset the stomach and cause diarrhoea, can interact with medicines, and little is known about their safety in pregnancy. Anyone taking regular medicine should talk to their clinician before taking bromelain supplements.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: pineapple, raw, all varieties — the nutrition figures
    • National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (2024) — Bromelain: usefulness and safety — what the studies do and do not show
    • Liu et al. (2019) — oral bromelain after wisdom-tooth surgery: a systematic review of the trials
    • Bartholomew et al. (2003) — The Pineapple: Botany, Production and Uses — origin, history, varieties and growing
    • UNESCO (2023) — Aklan piña handloom weaving, Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity

    Bromeliad

    Bromeliaceae

    Ornamental

    A bromeliad is not one plant. It is a whole family — about 3,700 species in some 80 groups (genera) — and almost all of them come from the tropical Americas. What they share is the rosette: stiff leaves set in a spiral, often forming a cup in the middle that holds water. Some grow in the ground. Some grow on trees, with no soil at all. One of them, the pineapple, feeds the world. The rest are grown for how they look — bright bracts that last for months, leaves striped, spotted, silvered or blushing red — and for the fibre some of them give.

    Cultivars

    The ornamental bromeliads fall into a few clear types. These are the main ones; the family holds many more.

    Guzmania — the Scarlet Star

    Guzmania lingulata and its hybrids. The classic shop bromeliad: a rosette of wide, glossy green leaves with a tall spike of bright bracts — red, orange, yellow or pink — that lasts three to six months. The true flowers are small and short-lived; the colour is the bracts. It likes shade and humidity, and is the most low-light tolerant of the tank types.

    Aechmea — the Urn Plant

    Aechmea fasciata, the Silver Vase. Sturdy, with silver-grey banded leaves and a bold pink flower spike. Its leaves are spiny-edged, and it tolerates brighter light than Guzmania.

    Vriesea — the Flaming Sword

    Vriesea splendens. Smooth-edged leaves with dark cross-bands, and a flat, sword-shaped spike of bright red bracts with yellow flowers. Introduced to Europe in 1840 and still one of the most widely grown.

    Neoregelia — the Blushing Bromeliad

    Neoregelia carolinae, and 'Fireball'. Grown for its leaves, not its flowers: the centre of the rosette blushes red, pink or purple as it comes into flower, and the leaves may be striped, spotted or mottled. Compact, and happy in brighter light.

    Tillandsia — the air plants

    Including Spanish moss (Tillandsia usneoides). These grow with no soil at all, clinging to trees, rocks, wires or driftwood, and drink through tiny silver scales on their leaves. Spanish moss hangs in grey-green garlands up to 6 m (20 ft) long from live oaks and bald cypress across the American South. Tillandsia ionantha and Tillandsia xerographica are the best-known potted air plants.

    Billbergia — Queen's Tears

    Billbergia nutans. Slender, arching leaves and drooping clusters of pink, green and blue flowers. One of the toughest of the family — it is among the few that can live outdoors all year in very mild, frost-free places.

    Cryptanthus — the Earth Star

    Flat to the ground, with star-shaped rosettes in stripes of green, pink, cream and brown. It grows in soil, holds no water cup, and is grown for its leaves alone.

    Dyckia and Hechtia — the desert bromeliads

    Spiny, grey-green rosettes built for dry, sunny ground — the family's answer to a succulent. They want sun, sharp drainage and very little water.

    Puya — the giants

    Puya chilensis makes a dense clump of spiny leaves and a flower spike up to 1.5 m (5 ft) tall, packed with yellow-green bell flowers. A garden plant for warm, frost-free ground, not a windowsill.

    Brazil — the family's heartland. The Atlantic rainforest holds the most kinds, and many of the best-known ornamentals — Aechmea, Vriesea, Neoregelia — come from its trees. Bromeliads grow there on branches, on rocks and in the ground, from sea level to high mountains.
    The Andes — the second centre of kinds, on the mountain slopes of Peru, Colombia and Ecuador, where bromeliads grow from low forest to 4,200 m (nearly 14,000 ft) up.
    Mexico and Central America — the third centre, and the home of many Tillandsia air plants, which grow on trees, cacti and even telephone wires.
    The American South — Spanish moss country. It hangs from southern live oak and bald cypress from coastal Virginia to Florida and west to Texas, and its grey garlands are the picture of the old Southern landscape. It takes nothing from its tree — it is not a parasite — and it shelters bats, warblers and spiders among its strands.
    Hawaii — the pineapple is the islands' symbol, though the plant is not native there; it was brought as a crop.
    • The family began in the Guiana Shield, the old high country of northern South America, about 100 million years ago. It spread across the tropical Americas from there, and only much later — about 19 million years ago — split into the eight subfamilies recognised today. Three places hold the most kinds: the Atlantic rainforest of Brazil, the Andean slopes of Peru, Colombia and Ecuador, and Mexico with Central America.
    • Nearly every bromeliad is American. The one exception is Pitcairnia feliciana, a single species in tropical West Africa, thought to have reached Africa by long-distance dispersal about 12 million years ago.
    • The family is named for Olof Bromelius (1639–1705), a Swedish doctor and botanist. The French botanist Charles Plumier described some of the first bromeliads known to European science in 1703, and Linnaeus gave the genus Bromelia its name in 1753.
    • Europeans first met the family through the pineapple: Columbus found it grown by the Carib people in the West Indies on his second voyage in 1493, and within fifty years it was being grown in India and other warm countries. The ornamental kinds came later and caused a stir of their own — Guzmania lingulata reached Europe in 1776, Aechmea fasciata in 1828, and Vriesea splendens in 1840. In the 1800s, breeders in Belgium, France and the Netherlands began crossing them for the flower trade, and the hybrids they made are still among the most widely grown bromeliads today.
    • Indigenous peoples of the Americas used bromeliads long before any of that — for food, for fibre, for protection and for ceremony — and still do. Ceremony, above all, means Tillandsia: in highland Chiapas, Maya flower gatherers collect a red-leaved Tillandsia to decorate the arches that mark ceremonial sites, and house crosses and shrines. The same kinds are gathered for Day of the Dead altars and, at Christmas, into flower offerings for Baby Jesus. No health benefit from bromeliads has been confirmed in studies of people.

    Craft

    • Spanish moss (Tillandsia usneoides) was the most used bromeliad of the old South. Native peoples — including the Houma, Seminole, Natchez and Koasati — stripped away its outer coat to get the tough, black, curly fibre inside. The fibre lashed together the poles of house frames, was mixed with mud to plaster walls, was woven into clothing and ropes, and was stuffed into mattresses, chairs and saddles. It was also mixed into clay for pottery — there is evidence of that use more than 3,000 years ago — and fresh moss was soaked and stuffed into dugout canoes to keep them from drying out and splitting.
    • In the 1920s and 1930s, picking Spanish moss was steady work in Florida and Louisiana. The moss was baled, cleaned in moss gins, and sold to furniture and car makers for stuffing cushions and seats — Henry Ford stuffed the seats of the Model T with it. Foam brought that trade to an end. The moss is still gathered today for flower arranging and for craft, and by the Houma and Koasati for the making and decorating of small dolls.
    • Chaguar fibre comes from Bromelia serra and Bromelia hieronymi, two spiny bromeliads of the Gran Chaco in Argentina. Their strong fibre is a mainstay of the Wichí people's economy, woven into bags, nets and cloth.
    • Piña cloth is woven from pineapple leaves, above all the Red Spanish type.
    • Spanish moss was boiled to make a tea for chills and fever, and used on sprains, swollen joints, insect stings, cuts and muscle strains. No trial supports those uses, and they are not recommended.
    • When to plant: In spring for pups and new plants; move them outdoors for the summer only once nights stay above 10 °C (50 °F), and bring them in before autumn nights fall to that
    • Light: Bright light, but shaded from strong summer sun, which scorches the leaves — Guzmania and Vriesea want bright, indirect light; Aechmea and Neoregelia take a little more, including an hour or two of gentle morning sun; air plants want strong, filtered light and good airflow
    • Soil: A small pot and a free-draining mix — equal parts fine bark or orchid compost, grit and coir; their roots are small and mostly hold the plant in place, and soggy soil rots them
    • Environment: About 21 °C (70 °F) in summer to flower, and a cooler spot of about 12 °C (54 °F) once the flower head has formed, to make it last longer; keep them above 10 °C (50 °F) in winter — Guzmania and Vriesea above about 15 °C (59 °F); they will not take frost; they like humid air — a bright bathroom or kitchen suits them, or stand the pot on a tray of damp gravel with the water below the base of the pot
    • Planter or ground: Pots for most kinds; a few — Billbergia and Puya among them — live outdoors all year only in very mild, frost-free ground
    • Water: Know which kind you have, because the watering is different — tank types (Guzmania, Aechmea, Vriesea, Neoregelia) hold water in the cup at the centre of the rosette: keep the cup topped up with rainwater or distilled water, tip it out and refill it every month or two so the water does not go stale, and water the potting mix lightly too, letting it dry a little between waterings; air plants (Tillandsia) have no cup and no soil: soak or mist them, then let them dry fully, or they rot; terrestrial types (Cryptanthus, Dyckia) grow in soil and are watered like ordinary plants, with sharp drainage

    Garden notes

    • A bromeliad is a perennial — it lives for years — but each rosette flowers only once in its life. The coloured bracts can last for months, and then the mother rosette slowly fades over the following months. That is not a failure: while it fades it makes pups — small copies of itself around its base — and the pups are the next plant.
    • Feed very little — too much feed dulls the leaf colour.
    • Pups: wait until a pup is about a third the size of the mother plant, then cut it off in spring with a clean, sharp knife, keeping some roots with it. Pot it in a small pot of free-draining mix, keep it warm and bright out of direct sun, and be patient — a pup flowers only once it is mature, which takes a few years (about three to five years for Vriesea). If there is only one pup, you can cut the old rosette away once it has died back and let the pup grow on in the same pot.

    Propagation

    After a bromeliad flowers, small plants called pups grow at its base. Wait until a pup is about one-third the size of the mother plant, then cut it away with a clean, sharp knife, keeping any roots it has, and pot it on its own in loose, fast-draining mix. The mother plant fades and dies after flowering — that is normal, and the pups carry on.

    Sources

    • Givnish et al. (2011) — Genetics, evolution and conservation of Bromeliaceae — family size, origin and centres of kinds
    • Marie Selby Botanical Gardens — Bromeliad Programs — family named for Olof Bromelius, range and growth habits
    • Royal Horticultural Society — How to grow bromeliads — light, warmth, watering, potting mix and pups
    • USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Spanish Moss Plant Guide — Native American fibre uses, pottery, tea as folk use
    • University of Florida IFAS Extension (2026) — Spanish Moss: Curse or Blessing? — folk remedies, the moss trade, wildlife
    • Wikipedia — Bromeliaceae; Bromelia — family size, history, European introductions, chaguar fibre
    • Guess & Guess (1998) — Tillandsia guatemalensis in ritual adornment, Maya flower gatherers in Chiapas

    Blueberry

    Vaccinium corymbosum

    Culinary

    Digestive HealthHeart HealthMental Health

    FreshCookedDried

    One of the very few major fruits the world farms that began in North America — and it was farmed there only yesterday, as plant history goes. For thousands of years the blueberry was a wild fruit, gathered and never planted; the first cultivated crop was sold in 1916. The berries grow in clusters on a long-lived bush, each one wearing a dusty pale coating called the bloom, and each one marked at its end with a neat five-pointed star — the scar left by the flower. Sweet, mild and only gently sharp, they are eaten fresh by the handful, baked into pies and muffins, dried like raisins, and frozen without losing much of what they carry.

    Cultivars

    • Northern highbush (Vaccinium corymbosum) — the blueberry of the shops. A tall bush, 4–6 ft (1.2–1.8 m) in a garden and taller left alone, from the swamps and uplands of the east. It needs a real winter — roughly 800–1,000 hours of cold — to flower and fruit well, and it is hardy through cold that would kill most fruit bushes. Most named varieties below are this kind.
    • Southern highbush — northern highbush crossed with evergreen southern cousins, bred to fruit where winters are mild: some need as little as 150–500 hours of cold. The kind for the warm south and for mild coastal gardens; the berries come early in the season.
    • Lowbush (Vaccinium angustifolium) — the wild blueberry of Maine and eastern Canada, a creeping plant barely knee-high. It is not really planted at all: wild stands are managed, pruned by burning or mowing, and raked at harvest. The berries are small, dark and intensely sweet, and most of the crop is frozen or canned rather than sold fresh.
    • Rabbiteye (Vaccinium virgatum) — the south-eastern native, named for its unripe fruit, which blushes pink like a rabbit's eye before it blues. The tallest and toughest kind, shrugging off heat and poorer soil that would trouble highbush, though it still wants acid ground. The fruit ripens berry by berry over a long season and the skin is a little firmer.
    • Half-high — highbush crossed with lowbush, giving a short, very cold-hardy bush of 2–4 ft, made for cold gardens and big pots.
    • 'Bluecrop' — the standard northern highbush of the world: mid-season, heavy-cropping, dependable, the variety most commercial plantings are built on.
    • 'Duke' — the early one, ripening at the front of the season with firm, mild fruit; the bush needs careful pruning to keep its strength.
    • 'Patriot' — bred for cold and for ground that stays wet longer than other blueberries like; very hardy, early to mid-season, with large berries.
    • 'Jersey' — one of the old varieties from Coville's own breeding years (released 1928), still widely grown: late-season, upright, tough and reliable rather than fancy.
    • 'Rubel' — history in a bush: the wild plant found by Rube Leek and named in the Whitesbog work, an ancestor of much of the modern crop. Its berries are small and dark with the intense flavour of the wild fruit, grown mostly for processing.
    • 'Elliott' — the very late one, bred to stretch the season's end, firm and tart until fully ripe.
    • 'Sharpblue' and 'Misty' — two southern highbush standbys for mild-winter gardens, among the first to ripen anywhere.
    • 'Premier' and 'Climax' — classic rabbiteyes of the south-east, early for their kind and heavy-bearing where summers are long and hot.
    Maine, USA — the wild lowbush barrens: tens of thousands of acres of creeping blueberry, owned but never planted, pruned by fire as they were for generations, and harvested with hand rakes in late summer. Nearly all of it is frozen within hours; it is the small, dark, intensely flavoured berry of pancakes and pies.
    New Jersey, USA — the birthplace of the farmed blueberry. Whitesbog, where White and Coville did their work, still grows berries among the cranberry bogs, and the town of Hammonton calls itself the Blueberry Capital of the World.
    Michigan and the Pacific Northwest, USA — the great highbush states of the modern trade, with British Columbia across the line in Canada: big plantings of 'Bluecrop' and its kin, machine-harvested for processing and hand-picked for the fresh trade.
    Quebec, Canada — wild lowbush country like Maine's, where the bleuet is a point of provincial pride and the harvest is a summer institution.
    Peru and Chile — the season turned upside down. Plantings in Peru's coastal desert, watered by irrigation, made Peru the world's biggest blueberry exporter within the last few years, shipping fresh berries north through the northern winter; Chile built the same trade a generation earlier.
    Poland and northern Europe — among the world's larger highbush growers now, though there the gathered wild berry of the woods is still the bilberry, the blueberry's small dark cousin — a different fruit on the same family tree.
    • The blueberry is native to eastern North America, growing wild in bogs, wet woods, pine barrens and mountain slopes from Canada down the Atlantic side to Florida and the Gulf. It belongs to a wide family of kin: the highbush of the swamps, the low, creeping lowbush of the northern barrens, the tall rabbiteye of the south-east, and across the Atlantic a small dark cousin, the bilberry, which has its own story told below.
    • The Indigenous peoples of the east knew the plant long before anyone thought of farming it. Berries were eaten fresh in their short season and dried in the sun for winter; dried berries went into pemmican, the travelling food of pounded dried meat and fat, and kept it sweet and sound. The juice stained cloth and baskets a deep blue-purple, and the berries, leaves and roots were all used in the medicine of the time — teas of the leaf and root were brewed for coughs and as tonics, and the fruit itself was food and remedy together. Those uses are history; what the studies actually support is in Health Benefits.
    • The Wabanaki peoples of the far north-east told how the berries came to them: in a time of hunger, the Great Spirit sent the "star berries" down from the sky to feed the children — the star being the five-pointed mark every blueberry still carries on its blossom end. The story is part of the plant's real history, and the mark is there on every berry to this day.
    • In Maine, the lowbush barrens were looked after for generations by careful burning, which cleared the ground and brought the berries back thicker — a managed wild harvest, not a farm. In the later 1800s that harvest became an industry: the berries were raked by hand with scoop rakes, and canneries in Maine packed them by the ton. The highbush of the swamps, though, defeated everyone who tried to plant it. Bushes dug up and set in good garden soil sickened and died, and the blueberry was written off as a fruit that could not be tamed.
    • The answer came from a government botanist. Frederick Coville, of the US Department of Agriculture, spent years failing with the plant before he found its secret: the blueberry demands sour, acid soil — the very bog ground farmers thought worthless — and it needs a cold winter before it will flower well. Rich, sweet garden soil is poison to it. He published the method in 1910, in a bulletin called Experiments in Blueberry Culture.
    • Elizabeth White read that bulletin at Whitesbog, New Jersey, where her family farmed cranberries in the acid sands of the Pine Barrens. In 1911 she invited Coville to work there, and she paid the local people of the pines — who knew the wild bushes as no scientist could — to find and mark the finest wild highbush plants in the woods. About a hundred were brought in, each named for the person who found it: one famous bush, found by Rube Leek, became 'Rubel'. Coville crossed the best of them, and in 1916 White and Coville sold the first commercial crop of cultivated blueberries in the world. Every highbush blueberry in every shop today descends from that work in the New Jersey pines.
    • One story must be kept apart from this plant, because it is not this plant's story. In the Second World War, British night-fighter pilots were said to eat bilberry jam to sharpen their night vision. The bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus) is the blueberry's small, dark European cousin, not the blueberry. The tale was most likely cover for a real secret — the new airborne radar the night fighters carried, the same trick the British played with carrots — and when bilberry was later tested properly, in controlled trials, it did not improve night vision at all. It is a good story about a cousin; the blueberry itself gains nothing from it.

    Craft

    • The juice is a real dye, not just a stain. Native American peoples used blueberry juice to dye baskets and cloth a deep blue-purple — deliberate work, with the colour itself as the point.
    • Blueberries, raw, per 100 g: 57 kcal, carbohydrate 14.5 g, sugars 10.0 g, fibre 2.4 g, protein 0.74 g. A cup of them (148 g) gives about 84 kcal and 3.6 g of fibre. The honest nutrient picture: vitamin K at 19.3 µg (about a sixth of the daily value) and manganese at 0.336 mg (about 15%) are its best figures; vitamin C is modest at 9.7 mg — the blueberry is not a vitamin C fruit. Its fame rests on its colour: the deep blue-purple skin is loaded with anthocyanins, the pigments that colour it, at roughly 160 mg per 100 g — among the richest of any common fruit. Those pigments are what nearly all the research below is really about.
    • Blood vessels and blood pressure hold the strongest human evidence. In one trial (Johnson et al. 2015), 48 postmenopausal women whose blood pressure was already raised ate 22 g of freeze-dried blueberry powder a day — about a cup of fresh berries' worth — for eight weeks. Their blood pressure fell by about 5–6% and their arteries grew less stiff, while a comparison group on a dummy powder did not change. In the longest trial (Curtis et al. 2019), 115 older adults with metabolic syndrome — the cluster of weight, blood-sugar and blood-pressure risks — took a cup's worth of blueberry a day for six months: the lining of their blood vessels worked measurably better and arterial stiffness improved, while half a cup a day did nothing at all. But the same trial found no change in blood pressure and no change in insulin resistance, which the first trial's blood-pressure result has to sit beside: the two do not fully agree, and the fair reading is that a cup a day seems to help blood vessels work, with the blood-pressure question still open.
    • Two fences belong on all of this. First, nearly every trial used freeze-dried powder, measured out — a cup of fresh berries is the same fruit, but it is not the same tested dose — the trials' results hold for the fruit only as far as that goes. Second, several of the blueberry trials were paid for by the blueberry industry. That does not undo them, but it is part of the record.
    • Memory and mind: the early signs are promising and the studies are small. In the first human trial (Krikorian et al. 2010), just nine older adults with early memory changes drank wild blueberry juice daily for twelve weeks and improved on two memory tests — a real result in a very small, preliminary study, whose comparison group came from a sister study rather than the same trial. A later trial (Miller et al. 2018) gave 37 adults aged 60–75 a cup's worth of blueberry powder a day for 90 days: they made fewer errors on a memory test and switched tasks more cleanly than the placebo group, though their walking and balance did not change. And in the records of 16,010 nurses followed into old age (Devore et al. 2012), the women who ate blueberries most often lost their mental sharpness more slowly — but that is an association in health records, not a trial: people who eat berries often differ from people who don't in a hundred other ways. Put together: there is a consistent, hopeful signal for memory in old age, from small short trials, and no trial shows that blueberries prevent dementia.
    • Blood sugar, plainly: for all the talk, the best trial found no improvement in insulin resistance from a cup a day (Curtis et al. 2019), and there is no proven blood-sugar benefit. Blueberries are a sweet fruit with fibre, eaten instead of dessert they are a kind choice — but they are not a treatment.
    • The eyes: nothing solid. The night-vision story belongs to the bilberry, and even for the bilberry it failed its tests, as the history above tells. Blueberry itself has not been shown to improve sight.
    • The leaf: blueberry leaf teas and extracts are sold, and the leaf carries some of the same family of pigments and acids as the fruit. What exists is laboratory and animal work — including blood-sugar effects in rodents — and no proper human trials. Traditional leaf teas belong to the history; no benefit has been shown in people.
    • Cautions are few, because this is a food: a rare few people are allergic to blueberries. The fruit at the table needs no warning. Concentrated leaf extracts are a different matter from the fruit — untested in pregnancy and best left alone there.
    • When to plant: In spring or autumn; set bushes 4–5 ft (1.2–1.5 m) apart for highbush, 6 ft for rabbiteye
    • Sun: Full sun gives the most fruit; the bush tolerates a little shade and fruits less
    • Soil: Acid soil, about pH 4.5–5.5, moist and rich in organic matter, and well drained — ordinary garden soil is almost never acid enough, and in sweet or limy soil the leaves yellow and the bush starves no matter how it is fed; test the soil before planting, work in peat or composted pine bark, and use sulphur to bring the pH down where the test says it is needed
    • Environment: Match the kind to your winter: northern highbush needs a real winter — roughly 800–1,000 hours of cold — southern highbush and rabbiteye suit mild winters, and half-highs the severest cold
    • Planter or ground: Ground, or a pot in ericaceous (acid-loving) compost — in a pot the acid-soil problem is solved in a bag
    • Water: Steady moisture — its roots are shallow and fine, so give a deep watering in dry weeks — under a thick mulch of bark or pine needles; it hates both drought and standing water, and where tap water is hard and alkaline, rainwater is the kinder drink
    • When to pick: The berries on a cluster ripen one after another over several weeks, and the colour lies a little — wait until the blue is deep with no green or red at the stem end, then roll the ripe ones off with your thumb into a cupped hand; pick every few days through the season, and net the bush as the fruit colours if you mean to eat any yourself

    Garden notes

    • First, what it is: a deciduous shrub — it drops its leaves in winter — with small white or pink bell flowers in spring, berries in summer, and leaves that turn scarlet and crimson in autumn, which is half the reason it earns a place in ornamental gardens. A good bush crops for decades; some of White and Coville’s original plants at Whitesbog still bear.
    • Pollination: a blueberry bush is self-fertile and will crop alone, but two different varieties of the same kind, flowering together, give bigger berries and more of them — the bees do the carrying between the bell flowers.
    • Planting and patience: for the first year or two, rub off the flowers and let the bush spend itself on roots and wood — it feels wasteful and it pays. A first real crop comes in the third or fourth year, and a bush is in its prime from about year six, cropping a few kilos of berries a season.
    • Pruning: in winter, while the bush sleeps. Cut out the oldest, thickest canes at the base — a bush should always be renewing itself, with young, middle-aged and old wood in balance — and take out twiggy, crossing growth so light reaches the middle. Lowbush ground is renewed the old way, by mowing or burning half the patch each year.

    Propagation

    Take a 10–15 cm softwood cutting from new growth in late spring, or a semi-ripe cutting in early summer. Strip the lower leaves and set it in moist, acidic potting mix under cover, kept damp but not wet. New plants take a year or more before they are ready to plant out. Cuttings keep the same variety — seed-grown plants will not.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: blueberries, raw — the nutrition figures
    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2015) — USDA Database for the Flavonoid Content of Selected Foods — the anthocyanin figures
    • Johnson et al. (2015) — daily blueberry consumption and blood pressure and arterial stiffness in postmenopausal women: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial — 22 g of freeze-dried powder for eight weeks
    • Curtis et al. (2019) — blueberries improve biomarkers of cardiometabolic function in participants with metabolic syndrome: a 6-month, double-blind, randomized controlled trial — one cup a day improved blood-vessel function; no change in blood pressure or insulin resistance
    • Krikorian et al. (2010) — blueberry supplementation improves memory in older adults — wild blueberry juice for twelve weeks in nine adults
    • Miller et al. (2018) — dietary blueberry improves cognition among older adults in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial — 37 adults, 90 days of freeze-dried blueberry
    • Devore et al. (2012) — dietary intakes of berries and flavonoids in relation to cognitive decline — 16,010 women of the Nurses' Health Study, an observational record
    • Canter & Ernst (2004) — anthocyanosides of Vaccinium myrtillus (bilberry) for night vision: a systematic review of placebo-controlled trials — the rigorous trials found no effect
    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2016) — Celebrating the Highbush Blueberry's Centennial — Coville, White, Whitesbog and the first cultivated crop of 1916

    Raspberry

    Rubus idaeus

    Culinary

    Digestive HealthImmune Health

    FreshCookedDried

    A raspberry is not one fruit but a cluster: dozens of tiny bead-like fruits, each with its own seed, joined around a hollow centre. Pick it and the cluster slips off its white core, which stays on the plant — that hollow is the raspberry's signature, and the quickest way to tell it from a blackberry, which keeps its core. The plant is a thicket of upright canes that lives for years by its roots, though each cane lives only two. And the raspberry leads a double life: the fruit is a food, eaten fresh around the world, while the leaf is a remedy with a history of its own — the two are told separately here, because their stories and their evidence are not the same.

    Cultivars

    • Garden raspberries fall into two kinds, and the kind decides both the harvest and the pruning. Summer-bearing kinds fruit once, in summer, on canes that grew the year before. Autumn-bearing kinds — also called primocane or everbearing — fruit in late summer and autumn on the new canes of the same year, and can give a second, smaller crop the following summer if the canes are kept. The named varieties below say which kind each is.
    • 'Heritage' — the classic autumn-bearing red, bred in New York and released in 1969. It fruits from late summer until the frosts on the year's new canes, which makes its pruning the simplest of all (see In the Garden), and for decades it has been the home gardener's standard autumn raspberry: reliable, well-flavoured, and hardy.
    • 'Glen Ample' — Scotland's summer-bearing standard, bred at the Scottish Crop Research Institute. Its canes are thornless, which pickers bless, and it crops heavily with big, firm fruit — the variety behind much of Britain's fresh raspberry trade.
    • 'Tulameen' — a summer-bearing kind bred in British Columbia, Canada, and the flavour benchmark: large, bright, sweet fruit that gardeners rate among the best-tasting of all. It is less hardy than most and sulks in hard winters, so it is grown where winters are moderate or under cover.
    • 'Meeker' — Washington State's berry, released by Washington State University in 1967. A summer-bearing red with deep colour and rich flavour, grown above all for freezing, juice and purée — most of America's processed raspberries are this one variety.
    • 'Autumn Bliss' — an English autumn-bearer, bred at East Malling, and one of the earliest of its kind to fruit: big, well-flavoured berries from late summer onward, on a compact plant that suits smaller gardens.
    • 'Anne' and 'Fall Gold' — the gold raspberries. A yellow raspberry is a red raspberry with the red pigment switched off, and the flavour gives the secret away: softer, honeyed, often sweeter-tasting than the reds. 'Anne' is a pale-gold autumn-bearer; 'Fall Gold' an older gold of the same fruiting kind. Birds, it is often said, leave gold fruit alone longer, mistaking it for unripe.
    • Black raspberries — not a colour of this species but a species of their own, Rubus occidentalis, from North America: 'Jewel' and 'Bristol' are the long-grown kinds. The fruit is nearly black under a whitish bloom, smaller and seedier than the red, with a deeper, wilder flavour, and the canes arch over and root where their tips touch the ground. Picked, the fruit comes away hollow, like the red — it is a true raspberry.
    • Purple raspberries — crosses between the red and the black, such as 'Royalty' and 'Brandywine': dusky purple, large and tart, grown mostly for cooking, jam and pies rather than the punnet.
    • Wineberry — a relative worth naming, Rubus phoenicolasius, from Japan and northern Asia, grown for its glossy red fruit and stems dressed in sticky red hairs. It is handsome and tasty, and it has escaped from gardens in eastern North America and now spreads where it is not wanted — admire it, and plant it, if at all, with that record in mind.
    • And the famous crosses: the loganberry (California, 1881, raised by James Harvey Logan) and the tayberry (Scotland, named for the River Tay) are raspberry × blackberry hybrids, and the boysenberry is a deeper tangle of the same family. They are their own fruits, not raspberries — they keep the blackberry's core when picked — but the raspberry is in their blood.
    Russia — the world's largest raspberry grower, with about a quarter of the world crop (2023 figures), grown mostly for its own tables and freezers. The raspberry — malina — holds a place in Russian cooking and folk song alike, as the taste of the summer garden.
    Serbia — the raspberry as a national crop. Around Arilje, in the west of the country, whole valleys grow it, most of the crop is one American variety, 'Willamette', and nearly all of it is frozen for export. Serbians call the fruit "red gold," and it is among the country's best-known exports.
    Scotland — soft-fruit country: the fields of Tayside and Angus, the Glen varieties bred for them, and at the table cranachan — raspberries folded through whipped cream with toasted oatmeal, honey and a little whisky — the classic Scottish raspberry dessert.
    Washington, United States — the northwest corner of the state, around Whatcom County, grows most of America's red raspberries, and most of them are 'Meeker', picked by machine and frozen, juiced or puréed within hours.
    Poland — one of the world's largest producers, strong in autumn-bearing varieties and in the frozen trade that supplies Europe's freezers through the winter.
    Mexico — now the world's second-largest producer, growing in the highlands for the fresh market, much of the crop travelling north to American shops.
    Prince Edward Island, Canada — raspberry cordial country. The sweet red cordial was the island's celebration drink, and L. M. Montgomery made it famous worldwide in Anne of Green Gables (1908), in the scene where Anne serves her friend Diana the drink she believes is raspberry cordial — it was currant wine. The cordial itself is still made and sold on the island.
    • The raspberry is a plant of the northern woods: it grows wild across Europe and northern Asia, and in North America in its own American form, along woodland edges, banks and clearings, wherever birds drop its seed. People have eaten it far longer than they have grown it — raspberry seeds turn up in Stone Age settlements, gathered from the wild thousands of years before anyone planted a cane.
    • Its scientific name is a place. The Roman writer Pliny, in the first century, described the fruit as growing on Mount Ida, and the Greeks called it the bramble of Ida; Linnaeus took idaeus, "of Ida," from that account. Which Mount Ida Pliny meant is not certain — there is one on Crete and one in Asia Minor. Rubus, the wider name, comes from the Latin for red.
    • The prettiest telling of the name is a story set down by the French plant writer Henri Leclerc. The nymph Ida, so the story goes, was nurse to the infant Zeus on Crete, and reached into a raspberry bush to pick the crying child a berry — the berries were snow-white then. A thorn pricked her breast, her blood fell on the fruit, and raspberries have been red ever since. It is a story people told to explain a name and a colour — a story, and nothing more.
    • The English name is younger and plainer: "raspberry" is thought to come from raspise, a sweet, rose-coloured wine of the 1400s — the berry may simply have been named for the wine's colour.
    • The fruit was slow to be tamed. A Roman farming writer of the fourth century already listed it among cultivated fruits, and medieval monasteries grew it, but for most of its history it was gathered, not gardened. Gerard described it in his Herball of 1597, and by 1629 Parkinson was listing red, white and thornless kinds for English gardens. Serious breeding is younger still: nearly every variety grown today was bred in the last hundred years or so.
    • In North America the plant was already home. The American red raspberry — a close form of the same species — was eaten fresh and dried by Indigenous peoples, and its leaf and root were brewed in their remedies, long before European varieties were carried across and crossed with it.
    • The leaf built the second reputation. Raspberry leaf tea — the leaf, not the fruit — was a household remedy in Europe and America for centuries: brewed as a bracing, astringent tea for loose bowels, used as a gargle for sore throats and mouth sores, and taken for women's complaints of every kind. Above all it became the pregnancy herb: midwives recommended it in the last weeks before birth, in the belief that it toned the womb and made labour shorter and easier. That belief was strong enough that in the 1940s laboratory researchers took the leaf apart to test it, naming a compound, fragarine, that was long credited with the effect. What the one proper trial of the leaf in pregnancy actually found is in Health Benefits — the tradition is history.
    • The fruit had a household medicine of its own: in Britain it was preserved as raspberry vinegar, kept in the house and drunk diluted in water for fevers and sore throats — a way of holding the harvest's flavour and sharpness through the winter.

    Craft

    • The fruit gives a purple to dull-blue dye. And the stems give paper: harvested in summer after fruiting, stripped of their leaves and steamed until the fibres come free, then cooked and beaten — the paper comes out light brown.
    • Raw raspberries, per 100 g: 52 kcal, carbohydrate 11.9 g, sugars just 4.4 g, fibre 6.5 g, protein 1.2 g. Vitamin C stands at 26.2 mg — about 29% of the daily value — and manganese at 0.67 mg, about the same share, with a little potassium and folate besides. A cup of berries (123 g) gives about 8 g of fibre and 32 mg of vitamin C. Two numbers carry this fruit: the fibre is among the highest of any common fruit — strawberries carry about 2 g per 100 g, blueberries about 2.4 g — and the sugar is low for something that tastes this sweet.
    • The fibre is the honest strength. It feeds the gut and keeps the bowels moving, and it is why the raspberry's digestive reputation needs no dressing up: 6.5 g in every 100 g is a fact, not a claim. The vitamin C figure stands the same way — a real contribution, stated as a number and left at that.
    • The deep red colour comes from pigments called anthocyanins, and the fruit also carries a family of compounds called ellagitannins. Both are studied keenly — in dishes and in animals, for effects on blood vessels, inflammation and cancer cells. None of that has been shown to happen in people eating raspberries. The pigments are why the fruit is red; what they do in a body is, so far, a laboratory question.
    • After-meal blood sugar has one real study behind it, and it is stated at its size. In a small trial (Xiao et al. 2019), 32 adults — 21 of them with prediabetes and insulin resistance — ate a set breakfast on three separate days, with no raspberries, with 125 g, or with 250 g of frozen red raspberries. In the prediabetes group, both raspberry portions lowered the amount of insulin the body needed after the meal, and the larger portion lowered the peak blood sugar too. That is one small study of single meals, paid for by a raspberry industry body, and it showed nothing about lasting effects. Raspberries are a sensible fruit for anyone watching blood sugar — high fibre, low sugar — but they are not a treatment for diabetes.
    • The leaf, tested. Raspberry leaf in pregnancy has been put to a proper trial exactly once. In Sydney, 192 first-time mothers were given either raspberry leaf tablets (two 1.2 g tablets a day) or a dummy tablet, from 32 weeks of pregnancy until the birth (Simpson et al. 2001). The leaf caused no harm that the trial could find, for mother or baby. But contrary to the popular belief, it did not shorten the first stage of labour. The second stage was shorter by about ten minutes on average, and fewer women in the leaf group needed forceps (19.3% against 30.4%) — differences the researchers called clinically interesting but which were not large enough, in a trial of this size, to rule out chance. A review of everything published (Bowman et al. 2021) concluded that studies in women show neither clear benefit nor clear harm, and that in laboratory and animal work the leaf can both tighten and relax the muscle of the womb — which is why its effects are hard to predict. The fair summary: a strong tradition, a thin record, and no proof of harm at the doses the trial used.
    • The caution follows from that unpredictability, and it is the standard one. Because the leaf may act on the womb, the usual guidance is to keep away from it in the first three months of pregnancy, and if it is used at all, to begin only in the last stretch — most midwife guidance says from about 32 weeks — and to check with a midwife or doctor first. That matters most for anyone who has had a caesarean or other womb surgery, labour that came early, placenta problems, or twins. The trial's clean safety result belongs to its own terms: low-risk first pregnancies, a measured dose, started at 32 weeks.
    • And one famous claim does not hold: raspberry ketone does not burn fat. Raspberry ketone is the compound that gives the fruit its scent, and the fruit holds very little of it — about 1 to 4 milligrams in a whole kilogram of berries — so the capsules sold for weight loss, at doses of 100 milligrams and more, are filled with a factory-made version, and a person would need to eat dozens of kilograms of raspberries to swallow one capsule's worth from fruit. The claim rests on mice fed the compound at up to 2% of everything they ate, and on fat cells in dishes. The only human trial ever run was of a six-ingredient product — raspberry ketone alongside caffeine, capsaicin, garlic, ginger and bitter orange — taken with a diet and exercise programme (Lopez et al. 2013), so nothing in its result can be credited to raspberry ketone; and the safety of these doses in people has never been properly tested.
    • When to plant: Set bare-root canes in early spring, as soon as the ground can be worked — in mild districts, autumn planting also succeeds; red kinds 2–3 feet apart in rows 6–8 feet apart, black and purple kinds a little wider
    • Sun: Full sun — six to eight hours at the least, more for the sweetest fruit — and shelter from strong wind, which whips the canes
    • Soil: Deep, rich, well-drained soil, slightly acid — about pH 5.5–6.5; they will not tolerate standing water — roots left flooded can suffocate within a day — and on heavy soil, plant in a raised bed
    • Environment: Most kinds are hardy through USDA zones 3–8, some to zone 9, and the plant needs a real winter chill to fruit well; it is a northern fruit and does not thrive where winters are warm
    • Planter or ground: Ground, with support from the start: two posts and two wires, or a fence, and tie the canes in loosely as they grow
    • Water: About an inch of water a week, and more while the fruit is swelling — a dry spell at fruiting makes crumbly berries that fall apart in the fingers; mulch the row to hold moisture and keep weeds down, keeping the mulch a little clear of the cane bases, and feed once in early spring
    • When to pick: In season, pick every two or three days, in the cool of the day: a raspberry is ripe when it is deeply coloured, plump, and slips off its white core with the gentlest pull; pick dry, use a shallow container, chill the pickings quickly, and wash them only just before eating — and net the patch if the birds find it first

    Garden notes

    • First, the plant’s rhythm, because everything else follows from it. The roots and the crown — the knotted base at ground level — live for years, and a well-kept patch can crop for ten to fifteen years. Each cane lives two years. A cane in its first year is a primocane: green, leafy, growing. In its second year the same cane is a floricane: woody, flowering and fruiting — and once it has fruited, it dies. Raspberry pruning is nothing more than acting on those two facts.
    • Pruning summer-bearing kinds: straight after the harvest, cut every cane that fruited down to the ground — it will not fruit again. Then thin the new canes: take out the weak and crowded ones and leave the strongest standing a few inches apart, so air can move through the row. In late winter, shorten the kept canes a little and remove any that winter killed.
    • Pruning autumn-bearing kinds, the easy way: in late winter, cut all the canes to the ground. The new canes that grow in spring will fruit in late summer and autumn of the same year — one crop, no sorting of canes at all.
    • Spread: red raspberries sucker freely and will walk out of their row into paths and lawns. Plant them where the spread is welcome, or mow and dig the edges to hold the line. Keep the patch away from ground where tomatoes, potatoes, peppers or eggplants grew recently — those crops share soil diseases with raspberries — and away from wild brambles, which share their viruses. Buy certified disease-free plants; a cheap cane from an old patch can bring its diseases with it.

    Propagation

    Red and yellow raspberries: dig up a young sucker with its own roots in spring, cut it free with a spade, and replant it. Black and purple raspberries: in late summer, bend a cane tip down, bury it in a few inches of soil, and cut it free the next spring once it has rooted. Only take suckers from healthy plants — virus passes on to the new plant.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: raspberries, raw — the nutrition figures
    • Simpson et al. (2001) — raspberry leaf in pregnancy: its safety and efficacy in labor — the one randomised trial of the leaf
    • Bowman et al. (2021) — biophysical effects, safety and efficacy of raspberry leaf use in pregnancy: a systematic integrative review — what the whole evidence record shows
    • Xiao et al. (2019) — attenuation of postmeal metabolic indices with red raspberries in individuals at risk for diabetes: a randomized controlled trial — the after-meal blood sugar study
    • Lopez et al. (2013) — eight weeks of supplementation with a multi-ingredient weight loss product — the only human trial of a product containing raspberry ketone
    • Morimoto et al. (2005) — anti-obesity actions of raspberry ketone — the mouse study where the ketone claim began
    • Jennings (1988) — Raspberries and Blackberries: Their Breeding, Diseases and Growth — origin, history and varieties
    • Montana State University Extension (2019) — Growing Raspberries in Montana Gardens — planting, pruning and care
    • FAO (2023) — FAOSTAT: world raspberry production — the country figures
    • Plants For A Future — Rubus idaeus: fruit dye and stem-fibre paper

    Blackberry

    Rubus fruticosus agg.

    Culinary

    Digestive HealthImmune Health

    FreshCooked

    The hedgerow fruit. A blackberry is not one fruit but a cluster of tiny fruits, each with its own seed, and it comes away from the plant with its soft core still inside — that is how you tell it from a raspberry, which leaves its core behind. Nor is it one species: Rubus fruticosus is an aggregate, a family of hundreds of microspecies that set seed without fertilisation, so each one breeds true and every hedge has its own local kind. The plant — the bramble — is a scrambling thicket of arching, thorny canes, and the fruit ripens green, then red, then black. Red is not ripe. Only the black ones are sweet, and they have been gathered from the hedge for as long as there have been people living beside it.

    Cultivars

    • Garden blackberries are not the wild aggregate. They are bred hybrids, raised over the last 150 years from several Rubus species, European and American. They sort three ways by habit — erect kinds stand on stiff canes of their own, semi-erect kinds arch and need wires, and trailing kinds run along a trellis — and two ways by fruiting: most fruit on last year's canes, while the newer primocane kinds also fruit on the current season's growth, in late summer and autumn.
    • 'Navaho' — the milestone. Released by the University of Arkansas in 1989, it was that programme's first thornless blackberry, and an erect one: stiff, spineless canes that stand without a trellis, and medium berries, about 5 g, rated the sweetest of the Arkansas line. It ripens through mid to late summer. 'Navaho' is the variety that made thornless home growing ordinary.
    • 'Ouachita' — another Arkansas erect thornless kind, earlier than 'Navaho', with firm fruit and steady yields year after year. The modern all-rounder for a small garden.
    • 'Chester Thornless' — semi-erect, from the United States Department of Agriculture's programme in Maryland. Late-season and heavy-cropping, and the hardiest of the thornless kinds where winters bite — the one to choose in cold country. It needs its wires.
    • 'Triple Crown' — semi-erect and thornless, also from the USDA programme. Very large berries with a rich, sweet-tart flavour and heavy crops on a vigorous plant; give it a strong trellis and room.
    • 'Loch Ness' — Scotland's thornless semi-erect, bred at the Scottish Crop Research Institute. Neater and less rampant than most of its kind, with heavy crops of glossy fruit from late summer. The standard British garden blackberry.
    • 'Prime-Ark Freedom' — Arkansas again, released in 2013: the world's first thornless primocane-fruiting blackberry. It fruits on the new canes in late summer and autumn and again on the old canes the following summer — two crops from one plant. The fruit is large and sweet but soft, so it was bred for gardens and local markets, not for shipping.
    • 'Marion' — the marionberry — the trailing kind, thorny, released in Oregon in 1956 from a cross of 'Chehalem' and 'Olallie' made by the USDA breeder George Waldo. It is the most widely planted trailing blackberry in the world, and cooks hold its intense, winey flavour above every other blackberry's. Its bloodline runs back through the loganberry to the Himalayan blackberry and Oregon's own wild blackberry, with a little raspberry in it. It wants a trellis and a mild winter.
    • The hybrid berries — blackberry crossed with raspberry gave a small family of its own. The loganberry appeared in 1881 in the Santa Cruz, California garden of Judge James Harvey Logan, a chance seedling where a blackberry and a raspberry grew together; the boysenberry followed in 1930s California, a deeper mix raised by Rudolph Boysen; and the tayberry is a later Scottish cross. All three are grown like trailing blackberries and eaten like softer, sharper blackberries.
    • The wild aggregate itself — still there in every hedge, and not to be despised: because each microspecies is its own line, one bush gives small sour fruit and the next, ten yards on, gives large sweet ones. Good bushes are worth remembering and returning to. One warning belongs here: the "Himalayan" blackberry is not a garden variety at all, however it is sold — it is the invader told in Origin & Lineage, and it should not be planted.
    Britain and Ireland — blackberrying is a late-summer ritual with its own rules: a hooked stick to pull the high canes down, stained fingers, the best berries always just out of reach. In the kitchen the classic pairing is blackberry and apple — the apple softens and stretches the berries in pies and crumbles — and bramble jelly, strained clear of the seeds, is the traditional preserve. The last of the crop went into the Michaelmas pie, eaten before the deadline in the story above.
    France — the mûre. Wild blackberries are gathered for jam and tarts, and Burgundy makes crème de mûre, a blackberry liqueur in the same family as Dijon's famous cassis.
    Oregon and the Pacific Northwest — marionberry country: marionberry pie is Oregon's official state pie, and the berry goes into jam, ice cream and wine across the region. Alongside it runs the region's double life with the wild Himalayan blackberry — cursed as the coast's worst weed and picked by the bucketful from every roadside in August, sometimes by the same people on the same day.
    Mexico — zarzamora. Mexico is one of the world's great blackberry exporters, centred on Michoacán, where bred thornless kinds are picked through the winter to supply northern markets out of season — the supermarket blackberry in January is likely to be Mexican.
    Chile — the mora, carried by settlers and now thoroughly at home: loved in the German-influenced south, where it fills kuchen and jam, and spreading wild through the countryside as it did in Australia. One plant, two reputations, on every continent it has reached.
    Australia — the pantry and the weed war, side by side: blackberry jam and a day's picking in the hills remain part of country life, in the same states where the plant is a declared weed and landholders are required to control it.
    • The aggregate is native across Europe, into north-west Africa and western Asia, and brambles of some kind grow wild on nearly every continent. This is the European blackberry and the garden kinds bred from it and its American cousins.
    • Its pips are among the commonest plant remains on European archaeological sites. In the British record they turn up from prehistoric settlements onward and appear at nearly half of medieval sites — some sown by birds, no doubt, but a gathered food across thousands of years, eaten by people who never planted it.
    • Greek and Roman writers knew the bramble as medicine as much as food. Hippocrates, around 400 BCE, recommended it; the bramble stands in Dioscorides' De Materia Medica in the first century CE; and the earliest surviving European picture of a blackberry is in the Juliana Anicia Codex of 512 CE, a painted copy of Dioscorides' work. Pliny the Elder wrote that dyers in northern Italy took a violet colour from the berries — a poor man's purple, and one that faded in the sun.
    • The names are plain English: "blackberry" is simply the black berry, and "bramble" is the old word for the prickly bush itself. In Britain the plant is the bramble, the fruit the blackberry, and late-summer picking is "blackberrying."
    • The leaves and the bark of the root are rich in tannins — the mouth-drying substances in strong tea — and for centuries they were the household remedy for loose bowels. Herbals from Gerard onward praised the bramble as an astringent; the dried leaves were infused for dysentery and diarrhoea, the stronger root bark was boiled down for the same purpose, and the leaf tea was gargled for sore throats and mouth ulcers. In nineteenth-century America the root bark was an official medicine, listed in the United States Pharmacopoeia, and Germany's Commission E approved blackberry leaf as late as 1990 — for mild, short-lived diarrhoea and mild inflammation of the mouth and throat. All of that rested on tradition and on the tannins, not on clinical trials, and it is history; what the studies actually support is in Health Benefits.
    • People also passed sick children under a bramble arch — a cane that had bent down and rooted at its tip, making a natural hoop — as a cure for whooping cough. The practice was recorded in the 1680s and lived on in country districts for two centuries after.
    • Then there is the deadline, the best-known blackberry story of all. Michaelmas, 29 September, is the feast of St Michael, who in the old telling threw Lucifer out of heaven. Lucifer landed in a bramble, and in his temper he cursed the fruit — spat on it, stamped on it, scorched it, the tellings differ — and so after Michaelmas the berries were his, and nobody should pick them. When Britain changed its calendar in 1752 and dropped eleven days, country people who kept the old reckoning moved the deadline with it, to Old Michaelmas, 10 or 11 October; in Ireland the spoiling was often laid on the púca, a spirit of the countryside, sometimes at Samhain, the start of November. The story was already old when it first reached print, in an Irish plant catalogue of 1727 whose author called it a fable. Underneath it sits a plain fact anyone can check: the last berries ripen into cold, wet weather, and by October they are mouldy, frost-nipped, watery and full of insects. The story drew the line where the fruit itself draws it.
    • The bramble travelled, and travelling is where its story darkens.
