Settlers carried it to New South Wales in the 1840s, for the fruit and for hedges; it escaped, and Australia now counts it among its worst weeds — a Weed of National Significance, declared in every state, covering some nine million hectares. In 1885 the American plant breeder Luther Burbank brought in seed from India and sold the plant as the "Himalaya Giant." It was not Himalayan at all — the species, Rubus armeniacus, is from Armenia and northern Iran — but it was enormously vigorous, and by 1945 it had taken the Pacific Coast. It rules roadsides and riverbanks across the Pacific Northwest to this day, picked by the bucketful and fought by the state, both at once.

    Craft

    • The dye comes from more than the berries. In the bramble family, the root boiled with salt gives an orange dye, alongside the purple-to-dull-blue dye of the fruit.
    • Raw blackberries, per 100 g: 43 kcal, carbohydrate 9.61 g, sugars just 4.88 g, fibre 5.3 g, protein 1.39 g. The fibre is the headline — 5.3 g in 100 g is high for a fruit, about a fifth of a day's need, and a cup of berries (about 144 g) gives roughly 7.6 g. With it come vitamin C at 21 mg, about a quarter of the daily value; manganese at 0.65 mg, over a quarter; and vitamin K at 19.8 µg, with smaller amounts of copper and folate. For a fruit it is low in sugar — about half the sugar of pineapple, weight for weight. The seeds you crunch are part of the fibre, not a flaw in it.
    • Fibre is the solid, everyday benefit, and it needs no dressing up: it feeds the gut, keeps the bowels regular, and slows the meal down. That is the whole of the claim, and it is enough.
    • The near-black colour is anthocyanins — pigments, the same family that colours blueberries and black grapes — and they carry most of the excitement in the research. Stated at its true strength, that research is mostly laboratory and animal work. In the best-known animal study, aged rats fed a diet with 2% blackberry for eight weeks did better on tests of balance and coordination, and on short-term memory, than rats on the plain diet (Shukitt-Hale et al. 2009). Rats are not people. No human trial has tested blackberries for memory or brain health.
    • There is one proper human trial, and it deserves its exact weight. Twenty-seven overweight or obese men, in a randomised crossover trial, ate 600 g of blackberries a day — a very large bowlful, about four cups — for one week, alongside a high-fat diet, against a matched gelatin control. On the blackberries their insulin response improved: they needed less insulin to handle the same meal, and a standard measure of insulin resistance got better, and they burned slightly more fat (Solverson et al. 2018). Their blood glucose itself did not significantly change. One small, short trial, in men only, at a dose few people would eat — a promising result, not a proven benefit, and no basis for a blood-sugar claim.
    • The old leaf-and-root medicine is fenced the same way. The tannins are real, and an astringent tea is a plausible household remedy — but there are no clinical trials of blackberry leaf or root for diarrhoea or anything else. The Commission E approval of 1990 was given on traditional use, and Europe's medicines agency has issued no monograph for blackberry leaf at all. Diarrhoea that lasts more than a few days, or comes with fever or blood, is a case for a doctor, not a tea.
    • Cautions, plainly: eat the fruit black. Red and half-red berries are sour and astringent and can upset the stomach. The ripe fruit itself is an ordinary, safe food.
    • And the large claims do not hold: blackberries have not been shown to prevent or treat cancer — extracts killing cells in a dish is not evidence about eating the fruit — and they do not "detox" anything. The fibre, the vitamin C and the low sugar are the honest story.
    • When to plant: Plant bare-root or potted plants in spring, or in autumn where winters are mild; space erect kinds 3–4 feet apart, semi-erect about 5 feet, trailing kinds 6–8 feet, with 8–10 feet between rows
    • Sun: Full sun — six to eight hours at the least — gives the fruit; shelter from hard wind helps the long canes
    • Soil: A fertile, well-drained loam, slightly acid (about pH 5.5–6.5), with plenty of compost worked in; brambles forgive many soils but not wet feet — ground that stays soggy rots the roots
    • Environment: Most garden kinds suit USDA zones 5–9: the erect thorny kinds are the hardiest, the thornless semi-erect kinds can be cut back by a hard winter (‘Chester’ stands cold best), and the trailing kinds want the mildest winters of all
    • Planter or ground: Ground, with support: erect kinds mostly stand alone, though one wire steadies them; semi-erect and trailing kinds need posts and wires — two wires, at about 3 and 5 feet, is the usual frame — with the canes tied in as they grow
    • Water: About an inch of water a week through the growing season, and more while the fruit is swelling; a mulch over the roots keeps the moisture in and the weeds down; feed with a general fertiliser in spring, and again after the harvest is in
    • When to pick: A blackberry does not ripen after it is picked, so pick it ripe or not at all: fully black, plump, and softening — at its sweetest the shine turns dull; pick in the cool of the morning, every two or three days, into shallow containers so the fruit is not crushed, chill it fast, and wash it only when you are about to eat it

    Garden notes

    • First, how it grows, because everything else follows: the roots and crown live for years — a patch fruits well for a decade or more — but each cane lives two years. A first-year cane, the primocane, only grows; over winter it hardens, and in its second year, as the floricane, it flowers, fruits, and dies. Next year’s fruit is already growing beside this year’s while you pick.
    • Pruning is the one job that matters, and it is simple: as soon as a cane has fruited, cut it out at the ground — it will die anyway, and its room belongs to the new canes. In summer, tip the new primocanes to make them branch and carry more fruit; in winter, thin each plant to its strongest canes and shorten the side branches. Primocane-fruiting kinds allow a shortcut: cut the whole plant to the ground in late winter and take one late crop off the new canes — the easier system where winters are hard.
    • Birds will find the patch the day the first berry colours; a net thrown over the row is the honest answer. A newer pest asks for prompt picking: the spotted-wing drosophila, a small fruit fly that reached North America in 2008 and Britain in 2012, lays its eggs in ripening fruit rather than rotten fruit. Picking ripe berries as they ripen and clearing fallen fruit is the home gardener’s defence.
    • And the warning, stated plainly, because this plant has earned it: a bramble spreads. Canes root wherever a tip touches the ground, suckers travel underground, and birds sow the seed in every fence line. Plant it where it can be mown around, keep the cane tips off the soil unless you want a new plant there, and think twice before planting any blackberry near open country. In Australia and New Zealand, where the wild plant is a declared weed, plant only named garden varieties and keep them at home.

    Propagation

    In mid to late spring, bend a long, arching cane down and bury its tip about 3 inches deep in the soil, pegging it down and keeping it moist. Roots form by the following autumn or spring — then cut the new plant free from the parent and replant it. Wear thick gloves for thorny kinds, and keep the buried tip watered in dry spells or it will not root.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2019) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: blackberries, raw — the nutrition figures
    • Solverson et al. (2018) — blackberry feeding increases fat oxidation and improves insulin sensitivity in overweight and obese males — the one human trial
    • Shukitt-Hale et al. (2009) — effects of blackberries on motor and cognitive function in aged rats — the animal study, animal evidence only
    • Blumenthal et al. (1998) — The Complete German Commission E Monographs — blackberry leaf approved on traditional use, for mild acute diarrhoea and mild inflammation of the mouth and throat
    • Edees & Newton (1988) — Brambles of the British Isles — the aggregate and its hundreds of microspecies
    • Tomlinson & Hall (1996) — plant remains on British archaeological sites — blackberry pips through the record
    • Hummer & Janick (2007) — Rubus iconography: antiquity to the Renaissance — Hippocrates, Dioscorides and the earliest pictures
    • Threlkeld (1727) — Synopsis Stirpium Hibernicarum — the first printed record of the Michaelmas belief
    • Finn et al. (1997) — 'Marion' trailing blackberry — the marionberry's parentage and 1956 release
    • Clark (2014) — 'Prime-Ark Freedom' primocane-fruiting thornless blackberry, HortScience — the first thornless primocane-fruiting kind
    • NC State Extension (2024) — Blackberries for the Home Garden — soil, spacing, support, water and harvest
    • Weeds Australia — European blackberry profile — a Weed of National Significance, and its spread in Australia

    Cranberry

    Vaccinium macrocarpon

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Urinary Health

    CookedDried

    The sourest berry in North America, and one of only a few fruits the continent gave the world. The cranberry grows as a low, trailing evergreen vine in cold bogs, and its fruit is so sharp that almost nobody eats it fresh — it reaches the table cooked into sauce, sweetened into juice, or dried with sugar. What it does have, beyond the sourness, is the best-tested health record of any berry in this library: not a cure for anything, but real human evidence, from dozens of trials, that it helps some people keep urinary infections from coming back.

    Cultivars

    • 'Stevens' — the cranberry of the world. A hybrid bred in the 1940s and released in 1950, it is now the most widely planted variety anywhere: vigorous vines, large, firm, deep-red berries, heavy crops, ripening mid-to-late season. If a cranberry product has a variety behind it at all, it is usually this one.
    • 'Ben Lear' — picked out of the wild in Wisconsin in the early 1900s and still a standard there. It ripens early, colours a deep red, and carries large berries — a short-season grower's friend, with somewhat softer fruit than 'Stevens'.
    • 'Early Black' — one of the first named varieties, chosen in Massachusetts in the 1840s. Smaller, dark red-purple berries that ripen before everything else; the vines fill a bed more slowly, and the fruit's flavour is rated among the best of the old kinds.
    • 'Howes' — selected in 1843 by Eli Howes of Dennis, Massachusetts — Captain Hall's own town. A late-ripening berry, firm and pale red, famous for keeping: it was the shipping berry of the hand-scoop era, and its keeping quality still recommends it.
    • 'Pilgrim' — a 1961 release, a cross of two older kinds, with large purple-red fruit and heavy yields; widely planted in the Pacific Northwest and the east alike.
    • 'Crimson Queen' and 'Mullica Queen' — the modern generation, released from the Rutgers breeding programme in the 2000s: bred for very high yields and early, deep colour, and planted widely in new bogs since.
    • Behind all of them stands the wild plant itself, and one close kin worth naming: the small cranberry, Vaccinium oxycoccos, a finer, smaller-fruited species of the same wet ground across northern Europe and Asia, gathered there for centuries under its own local names. It is a different species, not a variety of this one.
    Massachusetts — the cranberry's first farm country and still its symbolic home: Cape Cod bogs, Captain Hall's sanded vines, the growers' cooperative that became Ocean Spray, and the sauce at the Thanksgiving table.
    Wisconsin — the working centre of the modern crop: the state grows roughly three-fifths of all the cranberries in the United States, around towns like Warrens, where the autumn harvest turns whole districts red.
    New Jersey — the Pine Barrens, a vast acid sand-and-pine wilderness, were wild cranberry country for centuries and an early cultivated region; the berries bouncing as they were sorted earned them the local nickname "bounceberries."
    Quebec and British Columbia, Canada — Canada is the second cranberry country: Quebec's bogs supply a large share of the world's processed and organic fruit, and the berries were gathered by First Nations there long before they were farmed.
    The Netherlands — the shipwreck's legacy: cranberries from that washed-up barrel still grow wild in the dune hollows of Terschelling and Vlieland, gathered each autumn as a local tradition on islands that never had a bog.
    • The cranberry is native to northern North America, growing wild in bogs and wet ground from Newfoundland and the Maritime provinces west to Minnesota, and south in the mountains to North Carolina. Its bogs are a gift of the ice age: as the glaciers melted back, they left shallow kettle ponds that filled with sand, peat and acid water — exactly the ground this plant wants, and ground almost nothing else does.
    • The Indigenous peoples of the northeast knew it for thousands of years. The Wampanoag of what is now Massachusetts called it sasumuneash — "very sour berry" — and the name they used tells the truth about the taste. They ate the berries fresh and dried, and dried them into pemmican: berries pounded together with dried meat and melted fat, a food that kept for months and carried travellers and hunters through winter. The berries coloured rugs and blankets with a red dye, and Wampanoag healers used them in traditional healing — for fever, for swelling, and on wounds. For some peoples the berry stood as a symbol of peace. Those uses are history; what the studies actually support is in Health Benefits.
    • The berry keeps well because it carries its own preservative — a natural acid in the fruit that slows spoiling — and that keeping quality made it valuable far beyond the bog. Early European settlers took cranberries aboard ship on long voyages against scurvy, and barrels of them were traded like stores that would not rot.
    • The English name is a picture. Settlers called it the craneberry because the flower, nodding on its thin stalk with its petals swept back, looks like the head and neck of a crane — the birds fed in the same bogs. In time the word shortened to cranberry.
    • Cranberry sauce appeared in colonial accounts in the 1600s and in print in the first American cookbook in 1796; by the 1800s the sweetened sauce had its lasting place at the harvest table, where it sits at Thanksgiving still.
    • Cultivation began by accident in 1816, on Cape Cod. Captain Henry Hall of Dennis, Massachusetts, noticed that wild vines in his bog grew better where beach sand had blown over them — thicker, fruiting harder. He began transplanting vines and spreading sand on purpose, and the practice he stumbled on, called sanding, is still part of cranberry farming today: a thin layer of sand every few years settles the vines, roots the runners and buries weed seeds and pests.
    • In 1930 the growers' cooperative that became Ocean Spray was formed in Massachusetts, and the juice drink it built — cranberry sweetened into a cocktail — turned a seasonal sauce fruit into a year-round one. The industry had one famous fright: in November 1959, weeks before Thanksgiving, the US government warned that part of the crop carried traces of a weedkiller, and sales collapsed overnight; most of the crop was cleared and the scare passed, but growers remembered it for decades.
    • The cranberry also travelled. Around 1845, by the usual account, a barrel of cranberries washed ashore on the Dutch island of Terschelling from a wrecked ship — and the berries took hold in the damp dune hollows, where cranberries grow wild in the Netherlands to this day, an American bog plant naturalised in European sand.

    Craft

    • The berries were a dye. Wampanoag people coloured rugs and blankets red with cranberry — a true textile dye tradition. It is the whole of this plant’s craft story, and it is enough: the dye is the craft.
    • Fresh raw cranberry, per 100 g: 46 kcal, carbohydrate 12 g, sugars just 4.3 g, fibre 3.6 g, protein 0.5 g, vitamin C 14 mg — about a sixth of the daily value — with a little vitamin E, vitamin K and manganese besides. Now the honest part: almost nobody eats fresh cranberries by the 100 grams. They are too sour. Most people meet this berry sweetened — as juice cocktail, which by the standard recipe is about a quarter cranberry juice and the rest sweetened water, or as dried cranberries with sugar added until they eat more like a sweet than a fruit. The fresh berry's numbers are good; the forms on the shelf are a different food, and the fresh berry's good numbers do not carry over to them.
    • The one claim with real weight behind it is the urinary one, and it is a claim about prevention, not treatment — that line matters. Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are most often caused by E. coli bacteria gripping the wall of the bladder. Cranberries carry a group of compounds called proanthocyanidins — PACs for short — of a type that makes it harder for those bacteria to grip. Bacteria that cannot hold on are flushed out when the bladder empties, so an infection never gets started.
    • The evidence, at its true current strength. In 2023 the Cochrane Collaboration — the body that gathers all the trials on a question and weighs them together — published its fifth review of cranberry for preventing UTIs: 50 randomised trials, 8,857 people. Its finding: cranberry products (juice, tablets or capsules) probably reduce the risk of a symptomatic, confirmed infection in women whose UTIs keep coming back — by about a quarter — in children, and in people left prone to infection by a medical procedure, such as bladder radiotherapy. Just as plainly, the same review found little or no benefit in elderly people in care homes, in pregnant women, and in adults whose bladders do not empty properly. It is a real effect, in some people, and no effect found in others. Human trials
    • The United States Food and Drug Administration read the same evidence and, in 2020, allowed a qualified claim on labels — the kind a regulator permits when the science is there but not settled. For cranberry supplements the label word is "limited" evidence; for juice drinks, "limited and inconsistent." That is the claim at its official strength, and no more should be claimed for it.
    • An older idea needs correcting plainly, because it is still repeated: cranberry was long said to work by making the urine acid, too acid for bacteria. At the amounts anyone actually eats or drinks, the urine does not turn acid enough to matter. The working explanation is the anti-grip one above — the PACs — and even there, processing matters: turning berries into tablets and capsules can lower the PACs, and products vary widely.
    • And the boundary, in plain words: cranberry does not treat an infection that has already started. No good evidence supports that, in anyone. A urinary infection is a job for a doctor and, usually, antibiotics — anyone who thinks they have one should be seen, not reach for juice instead of treatment.
    • When to plant: Set rooted cuttings or small plants in spring, about 12 inches (30 cm) apart, pressed into the sand; the bed is slow — runners take two to three years to knit into a full mat, a first light crop comes in the second or third year, and full crops from the third or fourth
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Very acid — pH about 4.0 to 5.5 — made of sand and peat, low in nutrients; ordinary garden soil is too rich and too sweet (too high a pH) for it, so build a small bed of peat and sand, or use a large container of the same mix, and water with rainwater where the tap water runs alkaline
    • Environment: Cold is a requirement, not a hardship: the plant needs a real winter — roughly 1,000 to 2,500 hours of cold between freezing and about 45 °F (7 °C) — to set its flower buds properly, which is why it belongs to the cool north (about USDA zones 2–7)
    • Planter or ground: Ground in a built bed of peat and sand, or a large container of the same mix — a home bed never needs a bog
    • Water: Constant moisture — about an inch of water a week, the bed kept moist like a wrung sponge — but the vines are not under water while they grow: growers flood a bed only in winter, to wrap the vines against killing cold, briefly in spring, to shield blossom buds from a late frost, and at harvest
    • When to pick: The fruit ripens from mid-September into November, deep red and firm — and ripe cranberries bounce, because each berry carries small pockets of air inside it; at home, pick by hand when the colour is full; sound fresh berries keep for weeks in the fridge and freeze exactly as they are

    Garden notes

    • First, what it is: an evergreen trailing perennial of the heath family — a true kin of the blueberry it shares its family section with. Wiry runners run 1–6 ft (0.3–1.8 m) along the ground and root as they go; from them rise short upright stems, only a few inches tall, that carry the flowers and fruit. The whole plant stays under about 8 inches (20 cm) high and spreads into a dense, glossy mat. A planting is nearly permanent: vines live for decades, and some commercial beds planted in the 1800s are still cropping.
    • Sanding: every few years, spread a thin layer of clean sand over the bed, as Hall found by accident in 1816. The sand roots the runners, holds back weeds, and buries some pests and diseased leaves. It is the oldest trick in cranberry growing because it still works.
    • Commercial growers pick two ways: dry harvest, raking the berries off with scoops for the fresh market, and wet harvest, the famous one — the bed is flooded until the water covers the vines, machines knock the berries loose, and the floating fruit is corralled on the surface and lifted out, bound for juice and sauce. A home bed never needs flooding to pick.

    Propagation

    Push stem cuttings into moist, acid soil in spring, or pin a runner down onto damp soil until it roots, then cut it free. It needs very acid, damp soil, and cuttings take two to three years to fruit — seed-grown plants do not come true.

    Safety

    • Cranberry in food amounts is safe for most people; very large amounts can upset the stomach and cause diarrhoea, especially in young children. There is conflicting evidence about cranberry and the blood-thinner warfarin — case reports suggest the two may interact, studies disagree — so anyone taking warfarin should talk to their clinician before using cranberry products beyond ordinary food. In pregnancy, food amounts are thought safe; the evidence for larger, supplement amounts is not settled.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: cranberries, raw — the nutrition figures
    • Williams et al. (2023) — Cranberries for preventing urinary tract infections, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews — 50 trials, 8,857 people; who benefits and who does not
    • National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (2024) — Cranberry: usefulness and safety — prevention not treatment; the warfarin question; food amounts in pregnancy
    • U.S. Food and Drug Administration (2020) — Letter of enforcement discretion: qualified health claims for cranberry juice beverages and cranberry dietary supplements — "limited" and "limited and inconsistent"
    • Cape Cod Cranberry Growers' Association — the history of cranberries in Massachusetts — Wampanoag use, the craneberry name, Hall's 1816 sanding

    Elderberry

    Sambucus nigra

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Digestive HealthImmune Health

    FreshCookedDried

    The elder is a hedgerow shrub — in Europe it can grow into a small tree — that gives two harvests a year. In early summer it covers itself in flat plates of creamy, sweet-scented flowers; by late summer those plates have become heavy, drooping clusters of small purple-black berries. Both harvests are food, and both are medicine in the old records. But this plant has a rule, and it comes first: the berries are eaten cooked, never raw. Raw or unripe elderberries — and the leaves, bark, stems and roots in any form — carry cyanide-making compounds and gut-irritating proteins that bring on nausea, vomiting and severe diarrhoea. Cooking destroys them, which is why every traditional preparation, from syrup to jam to wine, heats the fruit. Follow that rule and the elder is generous; ignore it and the elder bites.

    Cultivars

    • The varieties split by homeland between two elders. The European elder (S. nigra) grows into a large shrub or small tree, commonly to about 20 ft (6 m). The American elder (subsp. canadensis) is a smaller, suckering shrub of 5–12 ft (1.5–3.6 m) that spreads into a thicket, and it is the hardier of the two. Their berries are used the same way, under the same cooking rule.
    • Adams (American) — the old standard, released in 1926 and still planted: vigorous, productive, the benchmark the newer varieties are measured against.
    • York (American) — among the largest berries of any elder, ripening late; pair it with an earlier variety so the two flower together and crop well.
    • Nova (American) — an early-ripening, heavy-bearing variety, a natural partner for York.
    • Bob Gordon (American) — a 2011 release, selected from a wild plant found near Osceola, Missouri. Among the sweetest elderberries grown, with heavy crops on drooping heads that hang face-down — which the birds find harder to strip.
    • Wyldewood (American) — released in 2010 by the University of Missouri, with extra-large flower heads; a first choice where the flowers are harvested as well as the fruit.
    • Ranch (American) — a tough, upright grower that tolerates poorer ground and wind better than most.
    • Haschberg (European) — Austria's orchard elder, the backbone of the European elderberry juice trade: large clusters of dark, juice-rich berries on a vigorous tree.
    • Samdal and Sampo (European) — Danish selections bred for the juice crop, heavy-bearing and grown commercially in northern Europe.
    • Black Lace and Black Beauty (European) — the garden elders: deep purple, almost black foliage (finely cut, like lace, in Black Lace) with pink flowers. They fruit like any elder, but they are planted for their looks — the elder as an ornamental in its own right.
    Britain — the hedgerow elder. Elderflower cordial and elderberry wine are the twin drinks of the British summer and autumn, and Pontack sauce is the old keeper: a sharp sauce of elderberries, vinegar and spice, named for Pontack's Head, a London tavern of the late 1600s, made to be laid down for years and used as a ketchup on meat and fish.
    Germany and Austria — Holunder country. Austria grows Haschberg in orchards; much of the European crop goes to juice, and the berry's dark pigment is used to colour other foods. In early summer the flowers are dipped in batter and fried as fritters — Hollerküchle — and elderflower syrup stands in every kitchen.
    Scandinavia — elderflower cordial (Danish hyldeblomstsaft, Swedish fläderblomssaft) is the taste of early summer, drunk diluted all season. This is also the Elder Mother's home ground, where the asking-before-cutting custom was strongest.
    Hungary — bodza: elderflower syrup (bodzaszörp) is a standard home-made drink, and the berries go into jams and the fruit soups of the region.
    North America — the American elder's country: elderberry pie, jelly and wine from farm kitchens, a small and growing Midwest farm crop (the Missouri breeding work behind Bob Gordon and Wyldewood), and behind all of it the far older Indigenous use of the plant.
    • The elder is native across Europe, North Africa and western Asia, growing in hedgerows, wood edges and waste ground wherever the soil is rich and damp. North America has its own branch of the same species — the American elder, Sambucus nigra subsp. canadensis — a suckering shrub of the eastern half of the continent. The two are the same plant in two homelands, with the same rule about cooking.
    • The names are old. Sambucus comes from the Greek sambuca, a harp-like instrument the Romans knew; Pliny used the name nearly two thousand years ago. "Elder" itself is traced to the Anglo-Saxon æld, fire — because the plant's hollow stems, their soft pith pushed out, were used as blowpipes to kindle a fire. The same hollow stems gave it the country names Pipe Tree and Bore Tree.
    • Few plants were used for so much. Flowers, berries, bark, leaves and root all stood in the old herbals, and the elder was called the medicine chest of the country people. The writer John Evelyn put it in 1664: if the medicinal properties of elder's leaves, bark and berries were fully known, there was hardly an ailment for which a countryman could not fetch a remedy from every hedge. Those uses are history; what the studies actually support is in Health Benefits.
    • In Denmark, the tree was held to be lived in. The Elder Mother — Hyldemoer, in the old Danish — dwelt in the elder, and no one cut the tree or took its wood without asking her leave first. A cradle made from elder wood was said to bring her anger down on the child lying in it. Hans Christian Andersen put her into a story of his own, "The Elder-Tree Mother" (1845), in which she rises from a pot of elderflower tea and shows a sick boy the whole of his life in the flowers. An elder growing by the house — by the back door, people said — was held to guard the home.
    • The same tree carried darker stories. Legend said that Judas hanged himself from an elder, and elder was one of the trees accused of giving the wood for the Cross. Its wood was not burned on the fire: people said it spat and screamed as it burned, and that burning it brought ill luck. And to stand beneath an elder on Midsummer's Eve, it was said, was to see the King of the Fairies ride past with his court.
    • In North America, the Indigenous peoples of the continent had their own long knowledge of their elder: the berries cooked for food, the flowers and other parts in their medicine, centuries before Europeans arrived. Settlers took the plant up, and elderberry pie, jelly and wine became staples of the American country kitchen.
    • The medicine tradition ran on two tracks. The berry became syrup — elderberry syrup stood in an official British pharmacopoeia of 1788, listed for coughs, colds and constipation — and syrup is what the modern flu trials tested. The flower became tea, the old sweating tea for a cold, and dried elder flower is the part Europe's herbal regulators accept today. Berry and flower have separate records, and neither one's record is borrowed for the other.

    Craft

    • The hollow stems were craft as much as story. With the pith pushed out, a length of elder stem became a pipe, a whistle, a flute or a boy's pop-gun — Culpeper joked that every boy with a pop-gun knew the elder tree. Pliny recorded the country belief that the shrillest pipes were cut from elders growing out of earshot of a cock's crow. The hard wood beneath the pith was worked into pegs, spindles and combs, and the berries, bark and leaves all gave dyes — purple, black and green.
    • What is in the berry: per 100 g of ripe raw berries — 73 kcal, carbohydrate 18.4 g, fibre 7.0 g, protein 0.66 g. The standout nutrient is vitamin C at 36 mg, about 40% of the daily value, with potassium at 280 mg, a little iron (1.6 mg) and vitamin B6 besides. Two honest notes: those figures are for the raw berry, and cooking — which is not optional — costs some of the vitamin C, though the fibre stays; and a syrup's sweetness is the maker's sugar, not the berry's. The deep purple-black colour is anthocyanins, plant pigments that behave as antioxidants in laboratory tests; that is chemistry, not a promise.
    • Flu — the claim this plant is famous for, and its full record. In 1995, during an outbreak of influenza B in an Israeli farming community, 27 people were given either a standardised elderberry syrup (sold as Sambucol) or a dummy syrup: nearly 90% of the elderberry group were well within two to three days, while the dummy group took at least six. In 2004, a Norwegian trial of 60 people with influenza A or B, run the same way, found symptoms easing on average four days earlier on the syrup, with less use of other medicine. A 2009 trial of elderberry lozenges in 64 people pointed the same way. Gathered together in a 2019 meta-analysis (Hawkins et al.), the four trials held only 180 people in total, and the reviewers found that elderberry substantially shortened and softened upper-respiratory symptoms — the effect clear for flu, and resting on a single trial for the common cold.
    • The other side of the record, at the same size. In 2020 an independent American trial (Macknin et al.) gave 87 people aged five and up, all with laboratory-confirmed flu, the same syrup at the same dose as the 2004 trial — and found no benefit at all: symptoms lasted the same on elderberry as on the dummy syrup. One after-the-fact analysis hinted that those on elderberry without the flu drug oseltamivir did slightly worse; it was an unplanned analysis, and the authors drew no firm conclusion from it. The honest summary of the whole record: several small early trials said yes, the largest independent trial said no, and the question is still open.
    • The funding is part of the record too. The positive flu trials tested one company's syrup, and that syrup's developer was among the researchers behind them; the air-traveller trial below used a commercial extract with its maker's support. That does not make the results false — it is context a reader is owed, and it is why the independent 2020 trial matters.
    • Colds and prevention. In a 2016 trial (Tiralongo et al.), 312 long-haul air travellers took elderberry capsules around their flights. They caught colds at the same rate as the group on dummy capsules — elderberry did not prevent colds — but those who did catch one had a shorter, milder illness. Nothing in the record shows elderberry preventing flu either, and it is not a substitute for the flu vaccine. The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health puts it plainly: some preliminary research suggests elderberry may relieve symptoms of flu and colds; there is not enough good evidence to recommend it.
    • COVID-19, both directions handled plainly. Elderberry was promoted for COVID-19; there is no good evidence it helps, and US regulators took action against companies that claimed it did. The opposite fear — that elderberry might over-stir the immune system into a dangerous "cytokine storm" — rests on one laboratory finding, in which the syrup raised immune signalling chemicals in blood cells in a dish. A 2021 review of the human evidence (Wieland et al.) found no sign of that overstimulation in people. Neither the hope nor the fear has been shown in people.
    • The flower's own standing. Dried elder flower, taken as a tea, is accepted by the European Medicines Agency for the relief of early symptoms of the common cold — as a traditional use. That phrase has a precise meaning: the acceptance rests on the flower's long, documented history of use, and the agency's committee noted the lack of clinical trials behind it. It is a standing the berry does not hold, and the berry's trials do not transfer to the flower.
    • Safety — the part that matters most. Cook the berries, and eat nothing else of this plant. The cyanide-making compound is chiefly one called sambunigrin, and it is not spread evenly: measured amounts run highest in the leaves and in green, unripe berries, far lower in the ripe fruit, and lowest of all in the flowers — which is one reason the flowers have their own gentler tradition. Strip ripe berries from their stalks before cooking, because the stalks carry more of it than the fruit. Heat destroys both the cyanide-makers and the lectins, the gut-irritating proteins the raw plant also holds.
    • The documented case. In August 1983, at a gathering in Monterey County, California, wild elderberries were pressed raw for juice with their leaves and branches crushed in. Of the 25 people there, 11 fell ill within minutes — nausea and vomiting — and eight were flown to hospital by helicopter; one was kept in, and all recovered. The US Centers for Disease Control reported the case in 1984, and its advice still stands: the berries may be safe, particularly cooked; leaves and stems must never be crushed in.
    • The American berry, measured. Modern laboratory analysis of the American subspecies found its cyanide-making compounds low in every part of the plant, and none measurable in commercial juice — the ripe American berry sits at the mild end of its family. The rule stands anyway, for both subspecies: ripe, stripped from the stalks, and cooked.
    • Know the plant before you pick it. Dwarf elder (Sambucus ebulus), a knee-high, non-woody relative, carries more poisonous berries and is never food. In North America, pokeweed's dark berries grow on a tall plant with thick magenta stems — a different plant entirely, and a dangerous confusion. If you are not certain of the plant, do not pick.
    • Pregnancy and breastfeeding: little is known about elderberry's safety in either, so medicinal use is best left alone. Anyone taking regular medicine — above all medicines that damp down the immune system — should talk to their clinician before using elderberry products.
    • When to plant: Plant two different varieties growing near each other — within about 60 ft (18 m) — because elder is only partly self-fruitful and two kinds flowering together set far heavier crops; space American plants about 6 ft (1.8 m) apart and let the thicket form
    • Sun: Full sun gives the best fruit; part shade is tolerated
    • Soil: Moist, fertile, well-drained ground, mildly acid to neutral (about pH 5.5–6.5); the American elder in particular will grow in damp ground that defeats other fruit
    • Environment: The American elder is hardy in zones 3–9; the European in about zones 4–7
    • Planter or ground: Ground: the American elder makes a multi-stemmed thicket 5–12 ft (1.5–3.6 m) tall and spreads by suckers — new stems rising from the roots — so give it a corner it can own; the European elder grows larger, into a small tree of about 20 ft (6 m)
    • Water: Keep young plants watered in their first years; settled plants are tough
    • When to pick: Flowers: pick whole heads on a dry morning, just as they fully open, and use them the same day for cordial or fritters, or dry them for tea. Berries: pick a cluster only when every berry on it is fully dark — purple-black and soft — and the head hangs heavy; clip whole clusters, strip the berries off with a fork or your fingers, pick out any green berries and bits of stalk, and cook the berries before eating them, always

    Garden notes

    • A deciduous, fast-growing plant that asks for little. Both flower in flat, creamy plates — May to June in Europe, June into July in North America — and the berries ripen from late summer, roughly August to September. A settled bush yields roughly 3–15 lb (1.4–6.8 kg) of berries in a season.
    • Pruning is simple and forgiving. Fruit comes on young canes. Each winter, cut out dead wood and any cane older than three years, and keep the strongest young canes standing. Or take the renovation route: cut the whole plant nearly to the ground every few years and let it regrow — it fruits on the new growth.
    • New plants are easy: push hardwood cuttings into the ground in winter and most will root, or dig up a sucker and move it.
    • Birds love the ripe fruit and will strip a bush in days; net the plant, or pick promptly, or plant enough to share. Every flower head picked is a berry cluster given up, so pick a share and leave the rest.

    Propagation

    In early spring, before buds open, cut pencil-thick pieces about seven inches long from last year's growth and set them in damp, free-draining mix — they root in about six weeks. Seed-grown plants vary a lot, so use cuttings to keep the kind you want.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2019) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: elderberries, raw — the nutrition figures
    • National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (2024) — Elderberry: usefulness and safety — what the studies do and do not show, and the raw-berry warning
    • Hawkins et al. (2019) — black elderberry and upper respiratory symptoms: a meta-analysis of the randomised, controlled trials
    • Zakay-Rones et al. (2004) — elderberry syrup in influenza A and B: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
    • Macknin et al. (2020) — elderberry extract for influenza in emergency-room patients aged five and above: a randomised trial that found no benefit
    • Tiralongo et al. (2016) — elderberry supplementation and colds in air travellers: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
    • Centers for Disease Control (1984) — Poisoning from elderberry juice — California, MMWR — the 1983 Monterey County case
    • European Medicines Agency (2018) — European Union herbal monograph on Sambucus nigra L., flower — traditional use for relief of early symptoms of the common cold

    Mulberry

    Morus spp.

    Culinary

    Digestive HealthImmune Health

    FreshCookedDried

    A mulberry is not one fruit but a crowd. Each berry-shaped cluster is dozens of tiny fruits joined together — every bump on it was once a single flower — and it ripens soft, sweet and so full of dark juice that it stains fingers, tongues and pavements on contact. Three species share the name: the white mulberry of China, grown for five thousand years as the one food of the silkworm; the black mulberry of Persia, grown for the fruit itself and the richest-flavoured of the three; and the red mulberry, North America's own. Between them they fed an industry that dressed emperors and bankrupted speculators — and the fruit was almost a by-product.

    Cultivars

    • The three species below are the kinds to choose between, because with mulberries the species is the choice that matters — each is a different tree with a different home, habit and fruit.
    • White mulberry — Morus alba — the silkworm tree of China, and now the most planted mulberry on earth. A fast-growing, tough tree of 30–50 ft (9–15 m). The fruit is ½–1 in (1.5–2.5 cm) long, ripening white, pink, red or purple-black by variety, sweet and mild — beside the black mulberry, often called plain. Named forms: 'Tehama', a California selection with large white fruit; and the fruitless males, planted by the thousand as shade trees in dry cities — all leaf and pollen, no fruit at all.
    • 'Pakistan'A named form of the white mulberry whose fruit runs several inches long, kin to the long-fruited Himalayan mulberry.
    • 'Pendula'A weeping form of the white mulberry, grown purely for looks.
    • Black mulberry — Morus nigra — the fruit tree of Persia and the Mediterranean, and the connoisseur's mulberry. A slow-growing, wide-spreading tree of 20–30 ft (6–9 m) that can live for centuries and grows gnarled and hollow with age. The fruit is about 1 in (2.5 cm) long, dark purple-black, with deep red juice and the richest flavour of the three — sweet and sharp together, and only fully itself when completely ripe; an under-ripe black mulberry is sour enough to pucker. It ripens late: midsummer, and into September in cool districts.
    • Red mulberry — Morus rubra — North America's own, a woodland understorey tree of 35–50 ft (10–15 m) with large, rough, hairy leaves. The fruit ripens dark red to black and tastes between the white and the black — sweet with some bite. It is now the rarest of the three in the wild: in Canada it is listed as endangered, with only a few hundred wild trees known, and across its range it is being crossed out of existence by its own cousin (told below).
    • 'Illinois Everbearing' — the backyard favourite of cold-winter country: an American selection, a cross between the white and red mulberries, hardy and heavy-cropping, with dark, flavourful fruit that ripens a few at a time from early summer well into autumn instead of all at once. For a home garden in a cold district it is the usual recommendation, and the long season is the reason.
    • Telling the three apart, in the hand: white mulberry leaves are smooth and somewhat glossy; red mulberry leaves are rough and hairy, like fine sandpaper; black mulberry leaves are rough with short, stiff hairs and sit on very short stalks, the fruit hugging the branch. Fruit colour alone will not tell you — all three can ripen dark.
    China — the homeland of the white mulberry and of silk: five thousand years of planting the tree for its leaves, with the fruit eaten fresh and dried, the leaf drunk as tea, and every part of the tree in the old medicine books.
    Japan — China's great silk rival in its day, when raw silk was among Japan's top exports and mulberry fields covered whole districts. The sericulture has shrunk; the leaf tea, kuwa-cha, is still drunk.
    Turkey — white mulberry country. The harvest is shaken down in early summer and boiled into dut pekmezi, a thick, dark mulberry molasses second only to grape pekmez among Turkey's fruit syrups, eaten at breakfast with tahini; the rest is dried into pale, raisin-sweet dut kurusu, sold in every market, or spread into pestil, a sun-dried fruit leather. Anatolia's villages are full of the trees.
    Iran — toot: dried white mulberries kept in a bowl beside the tea, nibbled in place of sugar cubes, as they have been for centuries. The black mulberry is shah toot, "the king's mulberry," eaten fresh in its short season and prized above the white for flavour.
    Central Asia — along the old Silk Road the dried fruit was travel food and winter food at once: light, sweet, keeping for months without spoiling. In high valleys such as Hunza, dried mulberries were a staple of the winter store, even ground into a sweet flour.
    India — the other great silk land: the mulberry fields of Karnataka, in the south, feed silkworms to this day, and India remains one of the world's two great silk producers. The fruit is eaten in the north, where black mulberries are a brief summer pleasure.
    England — the black mulberry as a garden monument: gnarled veterans stand in the grounds of old houses, colleges and rectories, some of them planted in James I's era or grown from those that were. The garden of Buckingham Palace, on the ground of the king's own mulberry plantation, now holds the national collection of mulberries.
    United States — two mulberries at once: the native red, foraged for pies, jam and eating out of hand wherever it still grows wild; and the escaped white, bird-sown along every fencerow, feeding birds and staining sidewalks from coast to coast — plus its fruitless male form, the shade tree of the desert Southwest, whose other side is told in the garden notes below.
    • Three trees, three homes. The white mulberry (Morus alba) comes from China. The black mulberry (Morus nigra) comes from south-western Asia, most likely the highlands around Iran, the Caucasus and Armenia, though it has been planted for so long that its wild home is guesswork. The red mulberry (Morus rubra) is native to eastern North America, from Ontario and Minnesota down to Florida and Texas. All three belong to the fig family, Moraceae — kin to figs, jackfruit and breadfruit.
    • The Latin names are simply the colours: alba white, nigra black, rubra red. They mislead a little. The names record the fruit of the kind first described, not of every tree — a "white" mulberry's fruit can ripen white, pink, red or purple-black, and plenty of white mulberries bear dark fruit. The species tells you the tree's home and habits, not always the colour in the bowl.
    • Like the pineapple, the mulberry fruit is a multiple fruit: a whole spike of tiny flowers swells and fuses into one cluster. That is why it looks like a blackberry but has no core and no single berry's structure — and why it is so soft. There is almost nothing holding it together, which is also why it cannot be shipped fresh and is so rarely sold.
    • The silk story begins in China more than five thousand years ago — silk cloth survives from Neolithic sites there. The story China told about its discovery is this: the Empress Leizu, wife of the Yellow Emperor, was drinking tea beneath a mulberry tree when a silkworm cocoon fell into her cup. In the hot tea the cocoon loosened into a single shining thread, and she saw that it could be wound and woven. She is remembered as the Silkworm Mother. It is a story, told as a story — but the tree at its centre is real, and so is what the story explains.
    • The silkworm, Bombyx mori, is a moth caterpillar that eats mulberry leaves and, in practice, nothing else — and it does best on the white mulberry above all. One cocoon is a single thread hundreds of metres long. So wherever silk was wanted, white mulberries were planted: the tree and the worm travelled together, west along the roads that took silk's name, the Silk Road. For thousands of years China guarded the secret of how silk was made, and the cloth travelled without the knowledge.
    • The knowledge escaped around 550 CE — by the account the Byzantine historian Procopius told, two monks who had lived in the silk country hid silkworm eggs in their hollow bamboo canes and carried them to the Emperor Justinian in Constantinople. Historians doubt eggs could have survived the journey; what is certain is that silk-making reached the Byzantine world in that era, and the white mulberry came with it, then spread through the Mediterranean and into Italy, France and Spain as the food of Europe's silk industries.
    • Rome gave the fruit its most famous story. In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Pyramus and Thisbe, lovers in Babylon kept apart by their families, arranged to meet at night under a white mulberry tree. Thisbe fled a lioness; Pyramus, finding her bloodied veil, believed her dead and killed himself beneath the tree, and Thisbe, returning, did the same. Their blood soaked the roots, and the mulberry's fruit, white before, turned dark red — which is why, the story says, ripe mulberries carry the colour of blood. Shakespeare retold it as the bungled play inside A Midsummer Night's Dream. A mulberry at his own home, New Place in Stratford, was by tradition planted by Shakespeare himself; in 1756 a later owner, tired of visitors, had it cut down, and the wood was carved into keepsakes.
    • The black mulberry belonged to the Mediterranean world: grown there since ancient times for the fruit, praised by Roman writers, and planted so thickly in Greece for silk that some derive the name of the Morea — the Peloponnese — from its mulberry trees. It travelled north as a garden fruit tree, slow-growing and very long-lived, the mulberry of old walled gardens.
    • In 1609 King James I of England tried to found an English silk industry to rival France and Italy. He wrote to landowners across the country offering mulberry trees at three farthings each, planted a four-acre royal mulberry garden on ground now under Buckingham Palace and Green Park, and had some ten thousand trees imported. The trees that came were black mulberries. The story usually told is that the king planted the wrong tree. The truth has more give in it: silkworms will eat black mulberry leaves, though they thrive best on white; and the black is by far the hardier tree in a cold, wet England, so it may have been chosen with open eyes. Either way the English silk scheme failed — and the fruit trees stayed. Ancient, gnarled black mulberries in old English gardens, some planted in that era, are its living legacy.
    • North America already had the red mulberry, and its peoples ate the fruit and, in places, wove the inner bark into cloth. The colonists wanted the white one, for silk: Virginia's assembly passed laws in the 1600s requiring settlers to plant mulberry trees, and in the 1730s Georgia's trustees required plantings and shipped small lots of Georgia raw silk to London. Silk stayed a cottage craft — Connecticut became the young republic's silk centre, with the first American silk mill at Mansfield in 1810 — but the tree-planting habit it started never left.
    • Then came the bubble. In the 1830s a fast-growing Chinese mulberry, Morus multicaulis, was promoted as a silkworm feed that could be cut again and again for leaves, and its trees became a speculation: one tree bought for $25 in Massachusetts was sold for $50 in Connecticut, and its new owner refused $450 for a quarter share of it. After the financial Panic of 1837 the price of the trees collapsed — from $1.25 apiece to a few cents within a year — and a killing winter in 1840–41 and blight in 1844 finished the orchards. Farmers tore the trees out and the "multicaulis fever" became a byword for a swindle. The white mulberry escaped anyway: bird-sown from all that planting, it naturalised along fencerows and woodland edges across the continent, where it grows still.
    • In China the whole tree was a medicine chest for well over a thousand years, and those uses are history: the leaf was used for fevers and coughs, the root bark — sang bai pi, "mulberry white bark" — for coughs and laboured breathing, the twigs for aching joints, and the fruit to nourish the body and, the medicine books said, darken grey hair. Persian and Indian medicine used the fruit and leaf in their own ways, and in China and Japan the leaf was drunk as a tea, including against sugar sickness — the tradition standing behind the modern leaf-extract studies told in Health Benefits.
    • One name to keep separate, in one line: the paper mulberry is a different tree, Broussonetia papyrifera — a cousin in the same family, the bark-cloth and paper tree of Asia and the Pacific. It is not a true mulberry and bears nothing like this fruit.
    • The nutrition figures are USDA's, measured on the black mulberry. Per 100 g of raw fruit: 43 kcal, carbohydrate 9.8 g, sugars 8.1 g, fibre 1.7 g, protein 1.44 g. The standouts are vitamin C at 36.4 mg — about 40% of the daily value — and iron at 1.85 mg, about 10% of the daily value and unusually high for a fruit, with potassium (194 mg), calcium (39 mg) and a little vitamin K besides. Serving honesty: mulberries are eaten by the handful under the tree, and a full cup (140 g) gives about 51 mg of vitamin C. Dried white mulberries, the form in most shops, concentrate everything including the sugar — they are a sweet dried fruit, closer to raisins than to a health food.
    • The iron and the vitamin C arrive in the same fruit, and that pairing is genuinely useful: vitamin C helps the body absorb iron from plant foods eaten at the same meal, and here the fruit brings both. That is ordinary nutrition, stated at its size — a good fruit, not a treatment for anything.
    • Now the blood-sugar story, told at its exact strength, because it is the claim this tree is famous for and it is usually told wrong. The compound behind it is called DNJ (1-deoxynojirimycin), and it lives in the leaf — above all the white mulberry's leaf — not in any useful amount in the fruit. DNJ blocks some of the gut's tools for splitting sugars and starches (enzymes called alpha-glucosidases), so sugar from a meal enters the blood more slowly. What has actually been tested in people is a standardised leaf extract, not the tree as anyone eats it. In the best-known early trial, healthy volunteers and people with type 2 diabetes drank 75 g of sugar water with or without a gram of leaf extract: the rise in blood sugar over the next two hours was about a quarter to a third smaller with the extract — and more undigested sugar reached the lower gut, the trade-off of the method (Mudra et al. 2007). In a later double-blind trial, 37 healthy adults took a branded leaf extract with a starch drink and their blood-sugar rise was 14–22% smaller (Lown et al. 2017). A pooled analysis of 12 small trials, 615 people in all, found small average falls in fasting blood sugar and HbA1c over weeks of leaf or leaf extract (Cui et al. 2023). The fences, plainly: these were short, small trials, several of them funded or co-authored by the maker of the extract; a cup of leaf tea has never been shown to deliver a tested dose; and no trial shows that eating the fruit lowers blood sugar — the fruit itself carries 8.1 g of sugar in every 100 g. Human · small
    • The dark fruit's colour comes from anthocyanins — plant pigments that are studied in laboratories for all kinds of effects — and the fruit carries a little resveratrol, the red-wine compound. Both are present in small amounts, and no human trial shows a benefit from eating mulberries for either. There is no human evidence behind the "superfood" claims built on them. Lab studies
    • When to plant: Plant in spring; give them room — 15–30 ft (5–9 m) from other trees by species and size — and keep them well away from paths, drives, patios and washing lines, because the fallen fruit stains everything under the tree for weeks
    • Sun: Full sun for fruit
    • Soil: Mulberries are famously unfussy — almost any soil that drains will do, including poor and alkaline ground
    • Environment: White and red mulberries are hardy to USDA zone 4; the black is the tender one, zone 5 and warmer, and in cool districts it wants the sunniest, most sheltered spot you have — it will grow, but it fruits late and lightly where summers are short
    • Planter or ground: Ground: white — fast, tough, 30–50 ft (9–15 m), fruit within a few years of planting; black — slow, spreading, 20–30 ft (6–9 m), a tree you plant for your grandchildren as much as yourself, and the best fruit; red — a woodland tree for a shady edge, grown as much for the tree itself as the crop
    • Water: Water young trees regularly while they establish; once settled they stand drought well
    • When to pick: The fruit ripens unevenly — one branch carries white, red and black fruit at once — and ripe fruit lets go at a touch: spread an old sheet under the tree and shake the branches; the ripe fruit falls, the unripe stays. White and red ripen from late spring into early summer; black from midsummer on; ‘Illinois Everbearing’ straggles across the whole season. Eat within a day or two, or cook, dry or freeze the same day

    Garden notes

    • Male and female: most mulberries are one or the other — male trees make pollen and no fruit; female trees make the fruit, and a lone female fruits without any male nearby, the fruit simply being seedless. Nurseries sell named female or self-fertile forms for fruit, and male clones where only shade is wanted. Know which you are buying.
    • Pruning: prune in the depths of winter, while the tree is fully dormant — mulberries bleed sap heavily if cut once the sap rises in spring. Young trees need shaping; an old black mulberry needs almost none and resents hard cutting. Leave veterans alone.
    • The honest problems, stated plainly. The tree self-seeds: white mulberry seedlings spring up in every fence line and flower bed, and pulling them is a yearly job. And in North America the white mulberry crosses freely with the native red, and the hybrids outgrow the pure reds — red mulberry is endangered in Canada largely for this reason. A gardener in red-mulberry country who wants to help can plant a red or a named hybrid, and pull white seedlings near wild woods.
    • Finally, the pollen: male mulberries shed clouds of it in spring, and mulberry pollen is among the worst hay-fever offenders known. Several desert cities — Albuquerque since 1994, and Las Vegas, El Paso and Tucson as well — ban planting mulberries altogether for this reason. Check your local rules before planting in the Southwest, and plant a female if hay fever lives in your house.

    Propagation

    Take cuttings 22–30 cm long with at least three buds at pruning time, in June or July, and plant them at once. Or sow fresh seed as soon as it is ripe. Cuttings keep the parent's fruit; a tree grown from seed can take 10 years or more to fruit and may not match the parent.

    Safety

    • Eat mulberries ripe: the unripe fruit and the tree's milky sap can upset the stomach.
    • Mulberries are not a diabetes treatment, and leaf products are not a substitute for diabetes medicine. Anyone who takes medicine for blood sugar should talk to their clinician before using mulberry leaf products at all, since the leaf's effect could add to the medicine's.

    Sources

    • National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (2023) — White Mulberry Leaf: usefulness and safety — the leaf evidence and its limits
    • Mudra et al. (2007) — mulberry leaf extract and the blood-glucose response to 75 g of sucrose, in healthy adults and people with type 2 diabetes
    • Lown et al. (2017) — mulberry leaf extract improves glucose tolerance in healthy adults: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study
    • Cui et al. (2023) — mulberry leaf and leaf extract and blood-sugar measures: a systematic review and meta-analysis of twelve trials
    • Morton (1987) — Fruits of Warm Climates: the mulberries — the species, their homes and their uses
    • COSEWIC (2014) — assessment and status report on the Red Mulberry in Canada — the endangered status and the crossing with white mulberry
    • City of Albuquerque (1994) — the Pollen Control Ordinance — mulberry among the trees that may not be planted in the city

    Black Currant

    Ribes nigrum

    Culinary

    Eye HealthImmune Health

    FreshCooked

    The most intensely flavoured berry in this library, and the richest in vitamin C by a wide margin. The black currant is a small, glossy, near-black berry that hangs in dangling strings — called strigs — from a thornless northern bush. Raw, it is tart, musky and resinous, too much for most people straight off the bush; cooked, juiced or made into the French liqueur cassis, it is one of the great fruit flavours of the cold countries. It also carries the strangest history of any berry here: for much of the 1900s it was against the law to grow it in the United States.

    Cultivars

    • 'Ben Lomond'The first of Scotland's Ben varieties, released in 1975 from the Scottish Crop Research Institute at Invergowrie and named, like all the Bens, for a Scottish mountain. Bred for cold springs and even ripening, it crops heavily with the full, traditional black currant flavour, and it became the commercial standard — the variety behind much of the world's juice.
    • 'Ben Connan' — a later Ben, with some of the largest berries of any variety, on a compact bush; early and heavy-cropping, a favourite where it is grown.
    • 'Ben Hope' — the Ben bred to answer the bush's worst enemy: it resists the black currant gall mite, the tiny pest whose swollen "big buds" spread reversion disease, the virus that slowly ends a bush's cropping life.
    • 'Ben Sarek' — the small-garden Ben: a naturally compact bush, about 3 ft (1 m) tall, with good mildew resistance and full-sized fruit.
    • 'Titania' — a tall, vigorous Swedish variety, released around 1980. Its rust resistance descends from Canada's 'Consort', a grandparent, and with mildew resistance and large crops besides, it is one of the safest plantings for North America.
    • 'Consort' — the variety that changed the law's facts. Released at Ottawa in 1952, it was bred from the Siberian Ribes ussuriense, which cannot carry white pine blister rust, crossed with an ordinary black currant — so 'Consort', and its sister releases 'Coronet' and 'Crusader', are immune to the rust. Its fruit is smaller and its flavour strong and old-fashioned, but where state rules still restrict black currants, the immune varieties are the ones allowed.
    • 'Noir de Bourgogne' — the old French variety of the Dijon cassis fields: small berries of exceptional scent and intensity, grown for the liqueur rather than the table, and written into the rules of Cassis de Bourgogne to this day. 'Blackdown', its usual partner in the maceration tanks, is the rounder, sweeter half of the classic blend.
    • Behind all of them: red and white currants are a different species (Ribes rubrum), cousins rather than varieties of this one, and the gooseberry shares the black currant's genus — its own entry sits beside this one in the family section.
    France — cassis country. Dijon and Burgundy turn the harvest into crème de cassis for the kir and the kir royale, and the berry flavours sorbets, coulis and pâtisserie across the country; the bushes traditionally grew at the ends of the vineyard rows, a second crop from the wine land.
    Britain — the Ribena generation's fruit. Most of the British crop is grown for juice; at the table it is jam, cordial, and the black currant layer of summer pudding, and its flavour is the country's default for anything purple.
    Russia — smorodina is a garden institution: bushes behind every dacha fence, five-minute jam (pyatiminutka) made by the potful, fruit drinks and kissel, and the leaves going into pickle crocks and teapots as a matter of course.
    Poland — the quiet giant: Poland grows more black currants than any other country in the world, most of them frozen or turned into juice concentrate for export — a large share of the world's black currant products begins in a Polish field.
    Scandinavia — svartvinbär in Sweden, mustaherukka in Finland: the bush is at home in the short northern summer, and the berries are made into saft, the strong cordial diluted at every table, and into fruit soups and winter drinks.
    New Zealand — the modern research home of the fruit: Canterbury growers and scientists made black currants a studied crop there, and much of the recent extract and supplement work begins with New Zealand fruit.
    North America — the comeback. Since the bans fell, small farms in New York, the Pacific Northwest and the Northeast have planted the bush again, and craft makers are producing American cassis for the first time in a century — a flavour the continent is relearning.
    • The black currant is native across the cool middle of the world — central and northern Europe and northern Asia, east to Siberia and the foothills of the Himalayas. Wild, it grows where the ground stays damp: stream banks, wet woodland edges, alder thickets and hedgerows. It is a plant of cold winters and mild summers, and everything in its later history follows from that.
    • One name trap is worth clearing at the start. The little dried "currants" sold for baking — Zante currants — are not this fruit at all; they are tiny dried grapes that borrowed the name because of their size. The black currant is a true berry on a bush, kin to the gooseberry, and no relation to the grape.
    • The first cultivation on record is Russian: by the standard account, monastery gardens were growing black currants in the 1000s, and the bush became a fixture of Russian gardens and village plots, where it stays beloved — smorodina — to this day. Western Europe took it up later; it was in gardens there by the late 1500s, and the English herbals of the 1600s knew it well.
    • Those herbals gave the berry a nickname that tells its oldest medical story: quinsy berries. Quinsy was a severe, swollen sore throat, and black currant juice and syrup were the household gargle and soother for it — a use country practice kept for centuries, and the reason a bottle of black currant syrup lived in so many medicine cupboards. Those uses are history; what the studies actually support is in Health Benefits.
    • The leaf had its own parallel career. Across Europe, black currant leaf tea was the traditional drink for making the body pass more water and for easing rheumatic aches and gout. That tradition is still on the books: Europe's medicines agency (the EMA) keeps an official monograph for the leaf as a traditional remedy — for minor joint pain, and to increase urine to flush the urinary tract — while stating plainly that no studies in patients have been done. It is a record of long use, not a proof.
    • The leaf also worked in the kitchen. In Russia, fresh black currant leaves went into the pickle crock with cucumbers for their scent, and were dried for tea; the winter buds, intensely aromatic, were gathered for flavouring and for perfumery, where cassis bud remains a prized material.
    • English settlers carried the bush to the Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1629, and through the 1800s it was an ordinary American garden fruit — by 1899 the United States had nearly 7,000 acres of currants and gooseberries. Then came the disease that undid it.
    • White pine blister rust is a fungus that cannot complete its life without two hosts: a five-needle pine and a Ribes bush. On the currant it does little harm; on the pine it can kill the tree. Of all the Ribes, the black currant is the most susceptible — the best host the fungus has. With the white pine timber industry at stake, the federal government banned the cultivation, sale and transport of black currants in 1911, and funded eradication: government crews, and in the 1930s thousands of Civilian Conservation Corps workers, spent years spraying and uprooting currant and gooseberry bushes across the country.
    • The science softened before the law did. It became clear the rust threatens pines mainly where the two hosts grow close together in damp conditions, and plant breeders answered with currants that cannot carry the rust at all — Canada's 'Consort' of 1952, bred from a Siberian species, heads that line. The federal ban was lifted in 1966 and the question handed to the states. Most states let go over the following decades; New York, once the centre of American growing, lifted its ban only in 2003, after a grower's long campaign. A handful of states still ban or restrict the bush today, which is why the garden section below tells American readers to check their state rules.
    • France gave the fruit its most famous form. In 1841, in Dijon, Auguste-Denis Lagoute made the first crème de cassis — black currants steeped in spirit and sweetened into a thick, dark liqueur, from the bushes that grew at the ends of Burgundy's vineyard rows. A century later Dijon's mayor, Canon Félix Kir, popularised a splash of cassis in the local white wine, and the drink took his name: the kir.
    • Britain gave it its other famous form. In 1938 the Bristol firm H. W. Carter launched Ribena, a black currant syrup developed from research by Dr Vernon Charley of the University of Bristol, who had found just how much vitamin C the fruit holds. When war cut off oranges, the government encouraged black currant growing, bought nearly the whole crop, and from 1941 gave black currant syrup free to young children under the Vitamin Welfare Scheme. A generation of British children grew up on the taste — which is why black currant, not grape or cherry, is Britain's default purple flavour to this day.

    Craft

    • The winter buds are a perfumery treasure. Gathered in winter, mostly in Burgundy and the Loire country in France, they are soaked in solvent to draw out their scent — about 30 kg of buds make just 1 kg of the dark, intense extract called cassis bud absolute. Perfumers have used it in fine fragrance since the 1960s and 1970s, and a very little goes a long way.
    • Fresh raw black currant, per 100 g: 63 kcal, carbohydrate 15.4 g, protein 1.4 g — and the headline number of this whole library: vitamin C 181 mg, about twice the full daily value, roughly three times what oranges carry, weight for weight. Behind it: potassium 322 mg, iron 1.54 mg, vitamin E 1.0 mg, calcium 55 mg, and vitamin A 230 IU. The honest serving note: 100 g is a good handful of a very tart berry, and most people meet black currant cooked with sugar, as jam, or diluted as cordial and juice — those forms carry added sugar, and the fresh berry's good figures do not carry over to them. What can be said for the berry is that its vitamin C held up well enough in syrup to carry a wartime children's scheme; that is history's evidence, and it is in the history above.
    • The near-black skin is coloured by anthocyanins — the same family of pigments as in blueberries, here in stronger kinds: mostly delphinidin and cyanidin joined to a sugar called rutinose. Pigments are chemistry, not benefits: they are simply what the eye studies below actually tested.
    • The eyes are where the human evidence sits, and it is real but small, and it tested concentrated anthocyanin extracts, not bowls of berries. In one small double-blind crossover trial, healthy volunteers taking black currant anthocyanins adjusted to the dark better and had less of the temporary focusing shift that screen work causes than on placebo. In one two-year trial — 38 patients with open-angle glaucoma, all on their normal pressure-lowering drops — 50 mg a day of black currant anthocyanins went with slower worsening of the visual field than placebo, and with better blood flow at the optic nerve; eye pressure itself did not change. That is the record at its true strength: two small trial programmes, promising, unproven at scale, and no substitute for glaucoma treatment. Nobody's drops should ever be swapped for currants. Human · small
    • Circulation claims rest on smaller ground still: a few short studies, mostly from the same Japanese research group, found black currant anthocyanin drinks increased blood flow in the forearms and shoulders and eased muscle fatigue after typing work. Small numbers, short periods, supplement doses — a hint, not a finding. Human · small
    • The seed is a separate story. Pressed, the tiny seeds give an oil that is about 15–20% gamma-linolenic acid — GLA, an omega-6 fat the body turns into inflammation-calming compounds — with some omega-3 fat besides, a rare combination. The oil has been tested: in one small six-month trial (34 people with rheumatoid arthritis, about 10 g of the oil a day), joint tenderness improved significantly against placebo. For eczema, GLA oils as a group have been tested more and found wanting — the balance of the evidence is that they do not help. So the seed oil's record: one small positive trial for joints, a negative record for skin, and in both cases a supplement — not something eating the fruit provides in any amount. Human · small
    • And some claims simply do not hold: black currant does not detox anything, has not been shown to prevent cancer, lower blood pressure or slim anyone, and its vitamin C — a genuine nutrient fact — is not a tested cold cure. The sore-throat syrup of the old herbals sits in the history, where the evidence leaves it.
    • When to plant: Set bare-root bushes in autumn or early spring while dormant, and plant them an inch or two deeper than they grew in the nursery — the buried stem throws up the new shoots the bush fruits on; space bushes 4–6 ft (1.2–1.8 m) apart
    • Sun: Full sun where summers are cool; a little afternoon shade where they are hot
    • Soil: Rich soil that holds moisture without drowning — deep, fertile, well-drained, about pH 6–6.5 — and a thick mulch every year, because its roots run shallow and like to stay cool and damp
    • Environment: Cold is a requirement, not a hardship: roughly 800 to 1,500 hours of cold between freezing and about 45 °F (7 °C) before the buds will break and flower properly — about USDA zones 3–7 (into zone 8 where summers stay cool); dormant, it shrugs off −40 °F (−40 °C), but it flowers early, so plant it out of frost pockets, where cold air drains away
    • Planter or ground: Ground — a deciduous, thornless, multi-stemmed shrub, 3–6 ft (1–1.8 m) tall and about as wide, sending up stems from the base; black currants are self-fertile — one bush fruits on its own — though bees working the flowers make for fuller strigs
    • Water: This is a hungry, thirsty bush by berry standards: a yearly mulch of compost or well-rotted manure, and steady water while the fruit is swelling, are most of its care; dry fruiting wood and drought give small, dropping berries
    • When to pick: The fruit ripens in July in the northern hemisphere, the top berries of a strig colouring first and the string finishing over about two weeks; berries sweeten for a few days after they turn black, so pick whole strigs when the last berries have blackened, strip them with a fork over a bowl — the fruit freezes perfectly, exactly as picked

    Garden notes

    • Pruning is the one skill, and it follows from how the bush fruits: the best crops come on one- and two-year-old wood. Each winter, cut out about a third of the oldest, darkest stems at ground level, and take out anything weak or crossing, leaving eight to twelve strong stems of mixed ages. Done yearly, the bush renews itself forever; left undone, it fades into old wood and small fruit.
    • Troubles, honestly: the gall mite — invisible, living in the buds, which swell round and fail (“big bud”) — spreads reversion disease, the slow end of many old bushes; resistant varieties like ‘Ben Hope’ are the answer, and swollen buds are picked off and burned where they appear. Powdery mildew whites the leaves of susceptible varieties; aphids curl the shoot tips; birds take ripe fruit unless it is netted.
    • And the rust: the bush itself is barely harmed by white pine blister rust, but where five-needle pines grow and state or provincial rules restrict Ribes, plant only the immune varieties — ‘Consort’, ‘Coronet’, ‘Crusader’, ‘Titania’ — and check the local law first. The rule exists to protect the pines, and it is still on the books in a few states.

    Propagation

    In the dormant season, from late autumn to late winter, take hardwood cuttings about 8 inches long from this year's healthy young wood. Push them two-thirds deep into moist soil in a sheltered spot and leave them a year before moving them. Take cuttings only from young, healthy bushes, and pick off any flowers in the first year so the young plant puts its strength into roots.

    Safety

    • The fruit in food amounts is safe for most people. The seed oil in trials caused occasional mild stomach upset and headache; like other GLA oils it is a supplement to check against regular medicines before taking. The leaf teas of tradition are a separate matter from the fruit: they are history, not a recommended treatment.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2019) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: currants, European black, raw — the nutrition figures
    • Nakaishi et al. (2000) — effects of black currant anthocyanosides on dark adaptation and screen-work eye strain in healthy volunteers, Alternative Medicine Review
    • Ohguro et al. (2012) — two-year randomised, placebo-controlled trial of black currant anthocyanins on visual field in glaucoma, Ophthalmologica
    • Leventhal et al. (1994) — treatment of rheumatoid arthritis with black currant seed oil, British Journal of Rheumatology
    • European Medicines Agency (2010) — Community herbal monograph on Ribes nigrum L., folium — the leaf's traditional uses, and the absence of patient studies
    • Bratsch & Williams (2009), via Ohio State University — Specialty Crop Profile: Ribes (currants and gooseberries) — the rust, the bans and the state rules
    • Lejay Lagoute, Dijon — the house history of crème de cassis: Lagoute, 1841, and the kir
