    • Ribena / Suntory (2024) — Our Story: Dr Vernon Charley, 1938, and the wartime children's syrup

    Gooseberry

    Ribes uva-crispa

    Culinary

    Digestive HealthImmune Health

    FreshCooked

    A small, tart berry on a fiercely thorny bush, and for two hundred years the most competed-over fruit in Britain. Gooseberries live two lives: picked hard and green in late spring, they are a sour cooking fruit for sauces, pies and jam; left to ripen in summer, the dessert kinds turn sweet enough to eat from the bush. The berries come green, yellow, white and red, smooth or softly hairy, and in Britain they are still called goosegogs in the garden. One name to keep separate: the Indian gooseberry, or amla, is a different fruit from a different tree, and none of its story belongs to this plant.

    Cultivars

    • 'Roaring Lion' — a red giant of the show era, dating to about 1805. A 'Roaring Lion' berry took first prize at a Nottingham show in 1819 at just under 20 pennyweights, about 30 grams — a monster for its day, and about half what the record weighs now. It stands for the hundreds of big show varieties the clubs bred, most of them now lost.
    • 'Leveller' — the classic large dessert berry of the Victorian shows: smooth, green-yellow fruit of great size and good flavour, as happy in a pie as on the show bench. Still grown and still a byword for a big gooseberry.
    • 'Careless' — the standard green cooking gooseberry since the mid-1800s: pale green-white berries, heavy crops, reliable in ordinary gardens. If a recipe simply says gooseberries, this is the kind it means — picked green and sour for pies, sauces and jam.
    • 'Whinham's Industry' — a red variety raised in Northumberland in 1835 and named for its raiser, Robert Whinham. Hardy, heavy-cropping and tolerant of shade and poor spots where other kinds sulk; its berries cook well and ripen to a dark, sweet red.
    • 'Whitesmith' — an old white-fruited dessert kind: smooth, pale, almost translucent berries, early and sweet eaten ripe from the bush.
    • 'Invicta' — the modern answer to mildew, raised at East Malling in Kent: a very vigorous bush with some resistance to American gooseberry mildew, bearing heavy crops of pale green berries that cook well and ripen sweet. The variety that brought gooseberries back into ordinary gardens.
    • 'Hinnonmäki Red' — a Finnish-bred variety with mildew resistance in its parentage: medium red berries with a genuinely sweet flavour ripe, on a hardy bush. Finland's breeding programme produced a family of these — red, yellow and green — built for short northern summers.
    • 'Pixwell' — the American answer: released in North Dakota in 1932, bred from the wild American gooseberries. Nearly thornless, mildew-resistant, with pink-red fruit when ripe — the gooseberry for gardens where the European kinds struggled, and easier picking than any of them.
    Britain — the gooseberry's home stage: the club shows of Yorkshire and Cheshire, gooseberry fool (the crushed fruit folded through cream, in print by 1747), crumbles, pies and jam, and the first green berries of the year cooked as a rite of late spring. The traditional sauce went with rich food — roast goose and pork — the sharpness cutting the fat.
    France — the mackerel currant: green gooseberries cooked into a sharp sauce for grilled mackerel, a pairing old enough to name the plant. The fruit is groseille à maquereau; sweet ripe dessert gooseberries never took hold in France the way they did in Britain.
    Germany and Austria — the Stachelbeere, the "prickle berry": baked into cakes and the classic gooseberry meringue torte, made into compotes and preserves, and grown in cottage gardens across the German-speaking lands.
    Scandinavia — gooseberries suit the short, cool summer: grown in Finland, Sweden and Norway, eaten ripe in the brief season and preserved against the winter. Finland's Hinnonmäki breeding station gave the fruit some of its hardiest modern varieties.
    Russia and Eastern Europe — gooseberry jam is a classic of the region, above all the green gooseberry jam cooked to a clear emerald — in its most famous form with walnuts, a preserve with a royal reputation — and the berries are bottled and frozen for winter across Russia, Poland and Ukraine.
    North America — the comeback still under way: after the federal ban lifted in 1966 and the states followed, gooseberries returned slowly to American gardens and farmers' markets, mostly the American-bred kinds like 'Pixwell' and 'Poorman'. Many American gardeners have still never tasted one — the lost half-century is the reason.
    • The gooseberry is native to Europe, the Caucasus, northwestern Africa and southwestern Asia, a plant of woods, hedgerows and rocky ground. The classical writers of Greece and Rome never mention it — it is a northern fruit, and its recorded story starts in the north.
    • The first record of it in England is a purchase: in 1276, gooseberry bushes were bought for the Westminster garden of King Edward I, brought from France. For a long time it stayed a minor garden plant, then spread fast in the 1500s — by 1597 the herbalist John Gerard could write that gooseberries grew "in our London gardens and elsewhere in great abundance."
    • Old medicine valued the berry for its sharpness. Its acid juice was held to cool fevers — one of its old English names is feaberry, the fever berry — and the unripe fruit was used in the kitchen the way verjuice was, as a souring for sauces. Those uses are history; what the fruit offers as food is in Health Benefits.
    • Then came the craze, and it was a working people's craze. From the 1700s, and above all in the 1800s, amateur growers — many of them mill workers and miners in Lancashire, Cheshire, Yorkshire and the Midlands — formed gooseberry clubs and competed to grow the single heaviest berry. The clubs met in pubs, kept careful registers, and bred hundreds of new varieties chasing weight: the Horticultural Society's London garden held 360 different gooseberry varieties by 1831, and The Gooseberry Growers' Register, the annual record of the shows, listed 171 separate shows in 1845 alone. Growers thinned each branch to a few berries, fed them, and shaded them from sun and rain under little shelters as they swelled.
    • The shows weighed in the old troy units — pennyweights and grains — and the record crept up across two centuries. In 2013 Kelvin Archer of Cheshire grew a berry of 64.49 grams, about the size of a large hen's egg and the first ever past 40 pennyweights. In 2019 Graeme Watson of Yorkshire beat it with a yellow variety called Millennium at 64.56 grams, and he has since weighed in a berry reported at 65.3 grams. Of the hundreds of shows, nine survive: the Egton Bridge Old Gooseberry Society in Yorkshire, founded in 1800 and the oldest of them, still meets on the first Tuesday of August, and eight clubs remain in Cheshire.
    • The same century that made the gooseberry also nearly unmade it, from two directions at once. Around 1900 a fungus native to North America, the American gooseberry mildew, took hold in Europe — it had been reported in Russia a decade earlier, and in 1900 it was found in Ireland — and spread across the continent. The big European dessert varieties had no defence against it: leaves and berries furred white, fruit cracked, and bushes weakened year on year. Commercial gooseberry growing collapsed across Britain and Europe in the early 1900s. The rescue came from the mildew's own home: breeders crossed the European gooseberry with the smaller wild American gooseberries, which had lived with the fungus and resisted it, and the modern mildew-resistant varieties descend from those crosses.
    • In America the gooseberry was caught in a different fight. A fungus called white pine blister rust needs two hosts to live: a five-needle pine, and any Ribes — currant or gooseberry. To protect the white pine timber forests, the United States government restricted Ribes from 1911, banned it federally under the plant quarantine laws, and sent crews out to dig up and destroy currant and gooseberry bushes, wild and planted, for decades. The federal ban was lifted in 1966 and left to the states; most states had lifted theirs by 2003, and a few still restrict Ribes today. The black currant took the worst of that story — it is told on its own page — but the gooseberry was swept up in it, and American growing lost half a century.
    • Even the name is uncertain. Nobody knows where "gooseberry" comes from: the likeliest story is that it is a worn-down form of the Dutch kruisbes, the German Krausbeere or the French groseille. The popular explanation — that the sharp sauce was served with roast goose — may be a reason invented after the word. In France the fruit kept the pairing that stuck: groseillier à maquereau, the mackerel currant, because its sour sauce was eaten with oily mackerel.
    • Raw gooseberries, per 100 g: 44 kcal, carbohydrate 10.2 g, fibre 4.3 g, protein 0.9 g, fat 0.6 g. The fibre figure is the fruit's quiet strength — more fibre, weight for weight, than most berries in this library — and it comes with the skins and seeds, which are eaten with the fruit. Gooseberries are also naturally rich in pectin, the setting agent of jam, which is part of the same fibre story and the reason gooseberry jam sets so willingly.
    • Its vitamin C is honest and middling: 27.7 mg per 100 g, about a third of the daily value. A full serving does better than the per-100 g figure suggests — a cup of berries, about 150 g, carries roughly 42 mg, near half the daily value — because ripe gooseberries are eaten by the bowlful, not by the spoonful. There is a little potassium (198 mg), a little vitamin A, and small amounts of several B vitamins besides. The red and purple varieties carry their colour as anthocyanins, the same family of pigments that colours blueberries; that is a fact about what is in the fruit, not a promise.
    • And the plain truth about research: the gooseberry itself has barely been studied in people. There are no clinical trials of eating gooseberries to point to — no tested effect on blood sugar, blood pressure, joints or anything else. What exists is laboratory work on extracts, which is not the same as eating the fruit, and a great many claims borrowed from the Indian gooseberry, amla, which is a different plant and whose evidence does not transfer. Its value is as a food: tart, high in fibre, with a fair measure of vitamin C.
    • Cautions, plainly: gooseberries in food amounts are safe for nearly everyone. Very unripe berries are sharply sour — that is their cooking purpose, not a danger. The one real hazard of the plant is in the garden, not the kitchen: the thorns are formidable, and picking is glove work.
    • When to plant: Set bushes 4–5 ft (1.2–1.5 m) apart, cordons about 15 in (38 cm) apart along their support; it fruits young — a bush can carry a real crop in its third year
    • Sun: Full sun gives the best ripe fruit, but the gooseberry tolerates part shade better than most fruit — in Britain it was traditionally grown against a north wall — and a little shade is a kindness where summers run hot
    • Soil: Fertile, moist and well drained, slightly acid to neutral; the bush dislikes both drought and standing water, and its roots run shallow, so keep the ground under the bush clear — hoeing damages them
    • Environment: Cold is its friend: one of the hardiest fruits in this library — dormant bushes stand winter cold to about −30 °F (−34 °C), in USDA zones 3–8 — and it needs a proper cold winter to fruit well; heat is its limit — in hot summers the leaves scorch, growth stalls and mildew thrives
    • Planter or ground: Ground, grown as an open bush on a short bare stem, or trained flat as a cordon or fan against a wall or fence, which saves space and makes picking kinder
    • Water: Mulch in spring to hold moisture and keep the roots cool, and water in dry spells while the fruit swells
    • When to pick: In two passes: from late spring, pick the berries hard and green, thinning the crop as you go — the thinnings go to the kitchen for sauce, pie and jam, and the berries left behind grow the larger for it; then in summer, let the rest ripen fully on the bush for eating fresh — a ripe dessert gooseberry gives slightly when gently squeezed and tastes sweet before it tastes sharp; net the bushes as the fruit colours, or the birds will hold their own show

    Garden notes

    • First, what it is: a small deciduous bush, 3–5 ft (0.9–1.5 m) high and as wide, of arching branches thickly set with sharp spines, alone or in twos and threes at the leaf joints. It is long-lived and undemanding once settled.
    • Pruning, in plain words: each winter, keep the centre of the bush open like a cup — take out crossing branches, weak growth and the oldest wood, and shorten the leaders a little. Air moving through the bush is the first defence against mildew, and fruit forms best on wood two and three years old and on the short spurs of older branches. Wear gloves. Every cut is made among thorns.
    • The mildew, honestly: American gooseberry mildew is still the bush’s main disease — a white powdery coat on young leaves and berries that turns brown and felty, cracking the fruit. The garden defences are the resistant varieties (‘Invicta’, ‘Hinnonmäki’, ‘Pixwell’), the open pruned centre, watering at the roots rather than over the leaves, and picking off the first furred tips when they appear. Fruit with the felt rubbed off is still edible, but a badly mildewed crop is a poor one.
    • The other enemy is smaller: gooseberry sawfly caterpillars can strip a bush to bare ribs of leaves in a few days in spring. Check the leaf undersides from April, and pick off the pale green larvae by hand at first sight — a defoliated bush fruits badly the next year. And a note for American gardeners: a few states still restrict Ribes to protect white pines — check the local rule before planting, and plant away from five-needle pines.

    Propagation

    Take a hardwood cutting 5 to 8 inches long from one-year-old wood in late autumn or early spring, before growth starts, and set it in moist soil or potting mix with at least two buds buried. Gooseberries take longer to root than currants, so take several cuttings — not every one will take.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2019) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: gooseberries, raw — the nutrition figures
    • Royal Horticultural Society — Fascinating facts: gooseberries — the 1276 record, 360 varieties by 1831, the Growers' Register's 171 shows of 1845, the mackerel name, and the mildew decline and resistant crosses
    • Salmon (1905) — On the present aspect of the epidemic of the American gooseberry mildew in Europe, Journal of the Royal Horticultural Society — the mildew's arrival and spread
    • Egton Bridge Old Gooseberry Society, with show reports in Country Life (2019) — the surviving shows and the record berries: Archer's 64.49 g of 2013 and Watson's 64.56 g of 2019
    • Benedict (1981) — History of White Pine Blister Rust Control, USDA Forest Service — the Ribes restrictions, eradication campaigns and the 1966 lifting
    • Barney & Hummer (2005) — Currants, Gooseberries, and Jostaberries: A Guide for Growers, Marketers, and Researchers in North America — varieties and growing

    Sea Buckthorn

    Hippophae rhamnoides

    Culinary

    Eye HealthImmune Health

    Cooked

    A thorny, silver-leaved shrub carrying dense ropes of orange berries so sour that almost nobody eats them raw by the handful — and so rich in what they hold that peoples across Asia and northern Europe have prized them for well over a thousand years. One berry carries two different oils: one in its seed, one in its flesh, and they are not the same oil. The plant itself is a survivor — it makes its own nitrogen fertiliser in its roots, holds sand dunes and broken riverbanks together, and fruits through winters that kill softer plants.

    Cultivars

    • Sea buckthorn is one species with a family of subspecies, and most of what growers call varieties are bred kinds drawn from three of them. The subspecies differ more than varieties of most fruits do — in size, sourness and vitamin C alike.
    • The European coastal kind (subsp. rhamnoides) — the wild plant of the Baltic and North Sea dunes: small, intensely sour berries, very thorny, and among the richest in vitamin C at around 300–400 mg per 100 g. Most German orchard kinds were selected from it.
    • The Siberian kind (subsp. mongolica) — from the Altai Mountains and Siberia: bigger, somewhat sweeter berries on a hardier plant, and the base of Russian breeding. 'Chuyskaya' — sold in North America as 'Star of Altai' — is its best-known kind: earlier and sweeter than most, with vitamin C near 170 mg per 100 g. 'Titan' is another Russian kind, with berries large by sea buckthorn standards — about the size of a large pea — and a milder flavour.
    • The Chinese kind (subsp. sinensis) — the plant of the Loess Plateau plantings: small, sour berries, and the source of the highest vitamin C measurements ever reported for the species. It is planted by the million hectares for soil holding first and fruit second.
    • 'Leikora' — a German orchard kind from the Berlin breeding programme begun in 1979: heavy-cropping, with deep orange fruit ripening in September.
    • 'Hergo'The most widely planted kind in German orchards, its fruit picked by machine.
    • 'Askola'Vigorous and rich in vitamins.
    • 'Frugana' — one of the earliest of the German orchard kinds, and less thorny.
    • The males — because the sexes are on separate plants (see In the Garden), growers also plant named males that make no fruit at all: the German 'Pollmix' kinds, bred only to flower at the right time and shed pollen over the females. A variety list for this plant honestly includes plants you will never pick a berry from.
    Russia and Siberia — oblepikha is a household staple: jam, a tart golden juice, and the oil kept as a home remedy for skin and stomach alike. The Altai region is its breeding heartland, and Siberian gardens grow it where apples fail.
    China — shaji juice is a mainstream drink, sold everywhere, and the state planting programmes that carpeted the Loess Plateau made China the centre of the world crop. Berry, oil and leaf tea all have industries behind them.
    Mongolia — sea buckthorn juice, chatsargana, is a beloved national drink, pressed in quantity in Uvs province and served sweetened; the plant is a traditional remedy there as it is in Tibet.
    Tibet and Ladakh — the high-altitude home: berries gathered from wild thickets along the rivers, juiced and dried, a winter store of vitamins where almost no other fruit will grow.
    Germany and the Baltic — the juice, Sanddornsaft, is a northern speciality, sour enough to be sold sweetened or blended; wild bushes are harvested along the coasts, and the bright bushes are part of the autumn dune landscape.
    Finland — the research home of the berry's chemistry: the Turku programme measured what is actually in the fruit and ran the dry-eye trial described above.
    Canada and the northern United States — a new orchard frontier: prairie plantings of Russian and German kinds, grown for juice and oil in climates too cold for most fruit.
    • Sea buckthorn is native in one long band across the cold half of Eurasia: from the Atlantic coasts of Britain, the Netherlands and the Baltic, across Russia and Central Asia to Siberia, Mongolia, northern China and the Himalayas. Its richest ground — where the plant is most varied — is the high country around Tibet and the Himalaya. In the wild it grows where little else will: sea dunes, gravel riverbanks, dry mountain slopes and cold deserts.
    • Its scientific name is a story in itself. Hippophae comes from two Greek words: hippos, horse, and phaos, light or shining. The tradition behind it, repeated since ancient times, is that the Greeks fed the leaves and young shoots to their horses, and the horses' coats came to shine. The name is the plant's oldest testimonial — told here as the tradition it is.
    • The English name is plainer and slightly misleading. It is not a true buckthorn — that is a different plant, Rhamnus, in a different family — and it does not grow in the sea. It is a thorny bush that grows beside the sea, and the name stuck; the Latin ending rhamnoides simply means "looks like buckthorn."
    • In Asia the plant's written record is long and serious. It is written into the rGyud bzhi, the Four Tantras, the founding text of Tibetan medicine, and it held a place in Mongolian medicine too — used above all for the lungs and coughs, for the stomach, and to keep strength up at high altitude. Chinese medicine took it up in the same spirit, for coughs, digestion, blood circulation and pain. In the Indian Himalaya, in Ladakh, it is a home remedy and a food at once, known locally as tsermang. These are records of traditional use; what modern studies support is in Health Benefits.
    • The horse tradition travelled with the plant: across Central Asia the leaves and berry leftovers were fed to livestock, and herdsmen from Greece to Mongolia told versions of the same shiny-coat story.
    • The modern chapter opens in Russia. From the 1940s Soviet researchers studied the plant systematically, and breeders in Siberia — working with the big-fruited Siberian subspecies — raised kinds with larger, sweeter berries. The oil went further: it is reported to have been carried in the Soviet space programme, in the cosmonauts' food and as a skin cream meant to guard against radiation. Germany began its own breeding in 1979, selecting orchard kinds from wild stands; Finland built a research programme on the berry's chemistry.
    • China planted it on a scale nobody else attempted. Most of the world's sea buckthorn — well over two million hectares of it, wild and planted — is in China, much of it set out across the eroding Loess Plateau, where its roots hold crumbling soil and its berries give poor hill farms a crop. No other fruit shrub has been asked to do landscape repair as its day job.

    Craft

    • This is a dyer’s plant three times over: a yellow dye from the fruit, a yellow dye from the stems, roots and foliage, and a blackish-brown dye from the young leaves and shoots. The wood is a craft wood too — tough, hard, very durable and fine-grained, used for fine carpentry and turning.
    • First, an honesty note about numbers. The US Department of Agriculture's food database has no full entry for this fruit, so there is no single official table to quote. The figures below come from research analyses and European food tables, and they swing widely — because the plant itself swings widely. What is true of every kind measured: this is a genuinely vitamin-rich berry. What is not true is any single tidy figure printed on a juice carton.
    • Vitamin C is the headline, and it is real — but variable. Measured values run from under 100 mg per 100 g of berries in some kinds to around 300–400 mg in the wild European coastal kind, with bred Russian kinds near 170 mg and the highest Chinese kinds measured far above all of these. Even at the bottom of that range the berry matches an orange; at the top it carries many times more. Ripeness, place and variety move the number more than any processing does, and the honest figure is the range, not the biggest one.
    • The deep orange colour is carotenoids — the pigment family that colours carrots — including beta-carotene, which the body can turn into vitamin A. The berries also carry real vitamin E and useful potassium. The juice is sharply acid and low in sugar for a fruit juice; the sourness is mostly malic acid, the acid of apples.
    • One berry, two oils — and the difference matters, because the two are sold side by side and often mixed without the label saying so. The seed oil, pressed from the small dark seeds, is rich in the two essential fats linoleic acid (omega-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (omega-3), which together make up about 70% of it, and it carries much of the plant's vitamin E. It has almost none of the famous omega-7. The pulp oil, taken from the orange flesh, is the omega-7 oil: a large share of it — commonly around a third, measured anywhere from about an eighth to over half — is palmitoleic acid, an omega-7 fat that is rare in the plant world, though your own skin and body make it too. The pulp oil also carries the carotenoids, which is why it is deep orange and why it can tint skin orange for a while.
    • Dry eyes — the best single human study. In a Finnish trial (Larmo et al., 2010), 100 people with dry eye symptoms took either 2 g a day of sea buckthorn oil — a mix of the seed and pulp oils — or a dummy oil, for three months over autumn and winter, with neither patients nor researchers knowing who had which. Eighty-six finished. In both groups the tear film grew saltier as the cold season dried the air, but it rose significantly less in the oil group, and the worst redness and burning were somewhat lower. That is one trial, of a supplement oil, with a modest effect — stated at exactly that strength, it is the strongest human result this plant has. Human · small
    • Eczema — the trial that did not deliver. In a double-blind trial (Yang et al., 1999), 49 people with atopic eczema took capsules of seed oil, pulp oil or paraffin oil — the dummy — for four months. The skin of the pulp-oil group improved; but so did the skin of the dummy-oil group, by the statistics even more strongly, and the seed-oil group's improvement did not reach significance. The honest reading is that this trial does not show the oils work for eczema, whatever the tradition says, and the increases in omega-7 in the blood did not track with improvement either. No eczema benefit has been shown. Human · small
    • Burns, wounds and stomach ulcers — a strong tradition, thin human proof. In Russia and China the oil has a long record of hospital use on burns, slow-healing wounds and skin damaged by radiation, and it is still used there; animal studies support the wound use. But careful trials in people are lacking, so that use stays where the evidence puts it: a documented medical tradition, not a tested treatment. The stomach-ulcer work is likewise in rats, not people. Animal studies
    • Blood fats and the heart: a handful of small human studies of the berries and oils have mostly come out flat or mixed — no clear effect on cholesterol worth claiming. There is no cholesterol benefit to claim. Human · small
    • When to plant: Plant in spring: one male for roughly every six to eight females, within wind’s reach — the pollen travels on the wind, not on bees — and set the male on the side the spring wind blows from; only the females carry berries
    • Sun: Full sun, without compromise — it will not fruit in shade and fades under taller trees
    • Soil: Almost any well-drained soil suits it, sand and gravel included; a neutral to slightly acid soil, around pH 6–7, is its comfort. Its roots carry nodules holding Frankia bacteria — microbes that pull nitrogen out of the air and turn it into plant food — so the bush feeds itself and slowly enriches the poor ground around it
    • Environment: One of the hardiest fruit plants in the world — Siberian kinds stand cold near −40 °C — and it shrugs off heat, wind and salt spray that would strip other shrubs
    • Planter or ground: Ground — a deciduous shrub or small tree, usually 2–5 m tall and as wide, with stiff thorns along the branches
    • Water: Drought-tolerant once its roots are down, but water young plants through their first dry summers, and fruit is better with water in a dry spell
    • When to pick: Berries ripen from late August into October: snip short fruiting twigs, freeze them overnight, and knock the hard berries loose over a tray — the berries sit tight against the branch on almost no stalk, their skins burst at a squeeze, and the thorns guard all of it; berries picked after the first frosts are a little less sharp, and hand-harvesting this fruit is measured in hours, not minutes

    Garden notes

    • The first thing to understand is the plant’s love life: sea buckthorn is dioecious — male and female flowers grow on separate plants — and a female alone will never fruit. You cannot tell the sexes apart until the plants flower, at three or four years old, which is why named kinds, grown from cuttings of known plants, are worth their price.
    • The berries ripen from late August into October and, if left, hang on the bare branches deep into winter, which is when the bush looks its best and the birds get their share. Its narrow leaves are silvery-green — silvered with tiny scales that cut water loss.
    • The honest warning: it suckers. New shoots rise from the roots well away from the plant, and an unmown sea buckthorn becomes a thicket — which is the point on a dune and a problem in a small garden. Do not plant it beside a lawn you love unless you are prepared to patrol the edge.

    Propagation

    Easiest from seed, or from hardwood cuttings in late winter, or by digging up root suckers with roots on them in early spring. Plants are male or female, and only females bear fruit, so seed-grown plants are a gamble — cuttings and suckers keep the sex of the parent plant. Wear gloves — the branches are thorny.

    Safety

    • The berries are very acid — a lot at once can upset the stomach, and the acid is not kind to tooth enamel, which is one reason the juice is usually diluted or sweetened. The pulp oil's pigments can leave skin temporarily orange; harmless, but worth knowing before a wedding. The oils may slow blood clotting slightly, so anyone on blood-thinning medicine should ask their clinician before taking them as supplements, and there is not enough safety knowledge for the oils as supplements in pregnancy. The fruit eaten as food — juice, jam, sauce — is simply food.

    Sources

    • Larmo et al. (2010) — the dry-eye trial: sea buckthorn oil by mouth slowed the tear film's seasonal drying in 100 people
    • Yang et al. (1999) — seed oil and pulp oil tested against a dummy oil in eczema: the trial behind the caution above
    • Yang & Kallio (2001) — the fatty acids of the berry's two oils, measured across subspecies — seed oil versus pulp oil
    • Tiitinen et al. (2005) — sugars, acids and vitamin C measured in sea buckthorn berries
    • Suryakumar & Gupta (2011) — review of sea buckthorn in traditional medicine, Tibetan and Chinese records included, and in modern research
    • Li & Beveridge (2003) — Sea Buckthorn: Production and Utilization — growing, harvest and use, the standard production reference
    • Plants For A Future — Hippophae rhamnoides: dyes from fruit, stems and leaves; wood for carpentry and turning

    Schisandra

    Schisandra chinensis

    Culinary

    FreshDried

    A climbing vine from the cold forests of north-east Asia, grown for its red berries. The berries hold five flavours in a single bite — sweet, sour, bitter, pungent and salty: the skin and flesh are sweet and sour, the seed inside is bitter and peppery, and chewed whole the berry finishes faintly salty. In Korea the dried berries make omija, the five-flavour tea. One warning first, because it is the best-proven fact about this plant: schisandra changes how the body handles many medicines (see Safety below), so anyone on regular prescription medicine should be careful with the concentrated extracts.

    Cultivars

    • Schisandra is not a plant of named garden varieties in the West. In China and Korea, production plantings are raised from selected seed lines rather than named kinds. What a gardener actually meets is one named selection and two relatives worth knowing apart.
    • 'Eastern Prince' — the one cultivar widely sold. It was bred at the Vladivostok station of Russia's Vavilov Institute and is self-fertile: a single vine carries flowers that can set fruit on their own, which answers the male-and-female problem set out in In the Garden. Buy a plant grown from a cutting of it — seedlings raised from its seed may not keep the self-fertile trait.
    • Southern schisandra (Schisandra sphenanthera) — not a variety but the sister species, the southern fruit of the Chinese herb trade, from the mountains of central and southern China. Its berries are smaller and dry darker. It is an official drug in its own right and the source of the Wuzhi extract behind the interaction studies above.
    • Red-flowered schisandra (Schisandra rubriflora) — a Chinese relative grown purely as an ornamental climber, for deep red flowers quite unlike this plant's pale ones. It has no food or medicine tradition of its own and is listed here only so the names are not confused.
    Korea — omija-cha, the five-flavour tea: dried berries steeped in water — often cold water overnight, because hard boiling drags out harsh bitterness — and sweetened with honey. From the same ruby-pink juice comes omija-hwachae, a chilled summer punch served with slices of pear and a scatter of pine nuts, a drink of banquets and hot days. Berries are also layered with sugar into a syrup, omija-cheong, and made into wine.
    China — wu wei zi is first a medicine: the dried berries go into classic formulas for the chronic cough and as a tonic, and are drunk as a simple tea and steeped into medicinal wines. The trade form is the dried fruit, sun-dried until dark red and wrinkled.
    Russia — limonnik: the hunters' berry of the Far East, eaten fresh in season and made into juice, syrup, kissel — a fruit drink thickened to a soft jelly — and wine. A tea is brewed from the leaves and young stems as well as from the berries, and the pharmacopoeia tincture was the Soviet form of the medicine.
    Japan — gomishi, known through Chinese-style medicine (kampo) as a minor formula ingredient rather than a kitchen flavour.
    The West — schisandra arrived in the 1990s as a supplement, riding the "adaptogen" banner out of the Soviet research, and gardeners in cold countries have taken it up as a hardy climber that happens to fruit.
    • Schisandra is a forest vine of the cold north: northern China, Korea, Japan and the Russian Far East, where it climbs trees at the woodland edge and along streams. Its crushed leaves and stems smell of lemon, which earned it its Russian name, limonnik — "the little lemon plant."
    • The five flavours are the plant's heart, and the old books map them precisely. The Tang-dynasty physician Su Gong, quoted in Li Shizhen's great Compendium of Materia Medica (1596), wrote that the skin and flesh are sweet and sour, the kernel pungent and bitter, and the whole fruit has a salty taste — "so the five flavours are complete in this fruit." In Chinese medicine each flavour was held to find its own organ: sour to the liver, bitter to the heart, sweet to the spleen, pungent to the lungs, salty to the kidneys. A fruit carrying all five was therefore prized as one that could nourish the whole body at once. That is the tradition as it was held.
    • The plant stands near the very beginning of the written herb record. The Shennong Bencao Jing — the Divine Farmer's Classic of Materia Medica, compiled in China around the 1st–2nd century CE from older knowledge — lists wu wei zi in its top class, the "superior" herbs thought fit to take over a long life. The old text praises it for adding to the breath and strength of the body, settling coughs and panting, and making up what the body lacks. Through the centuries that followed it stayed a classic: prescribed for long-standing coughs, for night sweats, for wasting and weakness — history, told as history; what modern studies support is in Health Benefits.
    • In Korea the berry is omija — the same three characters, the same five flavours — and it lived a double life there as medicine and as a celebrated drink (see Around the World). The mountain district of Mungyeong became so known for it that the town holds an omija festival each autumn.
    • In the Russian Far East, the Nanai and other hunting peoples of the Amur river country carried the dried berries and seeds on long hunts, eating a handful against hunger, thirst and exhaustion, and they said the berries sharpened their sight in the dark. It was that hunters' record — a berry that kept men going — that drew scientists to the plant.
    • The Soviet chapter is real and large. From the 1940s, Soviet researchers studied the vine systematically. The word "adaptogen" — a substance said to help the body withstand stresses of many kinds without doing it harm — was coined by the pharmacologist Nikolai Lazarev in 1947 and built into a research programme by Israel Brekhman, with schisandra among the first plants put under the idea. By the early 1960s schisandra was an official medicine in the USSR, listed in its national pharmacopoeia, and it remains in the Russian and Chinese pharmacopoeias today. Soviet studies reported better endurance and mental performance in healthy people — but they were run to the standards of their time and place, and most cannot be checked the way a modern trial can. They should be taken at that strength, and no stronger.
    • Two fruits share this name, and the difference matters. Schisandra chinensis is the northern fruit, bei wu wei zi. Its sister species from central and southern China, Schisandra sphenanthera — the southern fruit, nan wu wei zi — is an official drug in its own right, and the old books already prized the northern above it. Much modern research, including the strongest medicine-interaction studies described in Safety below, was done on the southern species. Where that is so, the southern species is named.
    • What is in the berry: a family of plant chemicals called lignans — the schisandrins and gomisins — found in this form almost nowhere else in nature. They are concentrated in the seed, not the flesh, which is why extracts are made from the whole berry, seed and all, and why simply eating the fruit is a weaker thing than taking an extract. No standard food database lists this berry — the US Department of Agriculture's FoodData Central has no entry for it — so there are no settled nutrition figures for it. Schisandra is used by the spoonful — as tea, dried fruit or extract — not eaten by the bowlful; the fresh berry is sharply sour and mouth-drying.
    • The liver — the famous claim, fenced at its true strength. In animals, schisandra lignans protect the liver against chemical injury strongly and consistently: a 2025 review gathered 54 animal studies and they point the same way. In people, the record is far thinner. In 1970s China, schisandra preparations were found to lower a liver enzyme reading (ALT) in people with hepatitis, and chemists built a synthetic drug from schisandrin chemistry — bifendate — that is still used in China alongside hepatitis treatment. But a lower enzyme reading is not the same as a healed liver, and the reading climbs again when the drug stops. Modern trials of the berry itself are small and mixed: a mixture of schisandra extract and sesame (sesamin) lowered liver enzymes over five months in 40 people — a mixture, so the sesame may share the credit — while a 12-week trial of schisandra alone in 28 women found no significant change in liver enzymes. The honest position: genuinely promising in animals, not proven as a liver treatment in people. Animal studies
    • Strength and tiredness — the best modern human findings, and they are small. In two Korean trials, each lasting 12 weeks and each comparing the extract against dummy capsules, 1 g a day of berry extract increased leg-muscle strength more than the dummy: one in 45 women past the menopause, one in 54 adults over 50. Muscle size did not change in either. Two small trials, one country, an extract rather than the tea — stated at exactly that strength. Human · small
    • Menopause — one small trial. Thirty-six women finished a 12-week trial of a schisandra extract; hot flushes, sweating and heart palpitations eased more than with the dummy capsules. One trial, few women: a hint worth more research, not a settled use. Human · small
    • Stress and focus — the "adaptogen" claim in its modern dress. The human evidence rests on the Soviet-era studies described above and on mixture products: the best-known, ADAPT-232, blends schisandra with rhodiola and eleutherococcus, so its results on attention cannot be credited to schisandra alone. No strong modern trial has tested schisandra by itself for stress, calm or mental performance. The marketing runs far ahead of the evidence.
    • When to plant: Plant in spring, spacing vines about 4–6 ft (1.2–1.8 m) apart along their support; plant one male for every few females — or plant the self-fertile ‘Eastern Prince’ and have berries from a single vine
    • Sun: It fruits best with sun on its top growth while its roots stay cool, shaded and mulched — a forest-edge plant by nature
    • Soil: Rich, humus-filled soil that holds moisture yet drains — it is unhappy in a bog and unhappy in dust; slightly acid to neutral suits it (about pH 5.5–6.5)
    • Environment: Cold is this plant’s friend: hardy through USDA zones 4–8, it shrugs off winters down to about −30 °F (−34 °C); heat and drought check it more than frost ever will
    • Planter or ground: Ground, on a support it can wrap — a strong trellis, arbor, fence or wires, put up before the vine needs it; on a support it runs 15–25 ft (4.5–7.5 m) in gardens, and longer in the wild
    • Water: Water through dry spells, above all in the first years and while fruit is swelling
    • When to pick: Pick in autumn, when the whole hanging cluster has turned fully red — late August into September in Korea, later further north — and pick promptly, because the birds know the day as well as you do; the berries are dried in shade or gentle heat until dark and wrinkled, and dried, they keep for the year’s teas

    Garden notes

    • Male and female, in plain words: most schisandra vines are one sex or the other. The small, fragrant, cream-to-pale-pink flowers of late spring are male on one plant and female on another. Only female vines make berries, and only if a male flowers near enough for insects to carry pollen between them. A vine grown from seed keeps its sex secret until it first flowers, usually in its third or fourth year, so seed-growers plant several and keep the mix that results.
    • Patience is the price, as with so many cold-country fruits: two or three quiet years while the roots settle, first flowers around year three or four, and useful crops from year four or five. Prune lightly in early spring — shorten the side shoots and clear out tangles before growth starts.
    • From seed: the seed must be fresh, and it needs a long cold spell — about three months chilled and damp — before it will stir. Cuttings and layers are how named plants and known sexes are kept.

    Propagation

    Sow seed in autumn in a cold frame, or take half-ripe cuttings in August, or layer long shoots in autumn. Seed sprouts unevenly and can take a long time, and seed-grown plants may be male or female, so grow several if you want berries.

    Safety

    • The medicine interaction is the best-documented effect schisandra has. Its lignans slow down CYP3A4 — one of the body's main systems for clearing medicines — and block a pump called P-glycoprotein that moves drugs out of cells. In human studies, most of them using the southern species' extract (sold in China as Wuzhi capsules) given to transplant patients, blood levels of the anti-rejection drug tacrolimus roughly doubled to tripled, and levels of the sedative midazolam rose too. The two species share the same lignan chemistry, and the standard interaction references carry the warning for schisandra generally: anyone taking regular prescription medicine — transplant drugs, sedatives, and the long list of medicines cleared through CYP3A4 — should talk to their doctor or pharmacist before using schisandra extracts or strong preparations. A cup of omija tea at the table is a much weaker thing than a capsule of extract, but the caution grows with the dose.
    • Schisandra can cause heartburn, stomach ache, loss of appetite, itching or a skin rash in some people. In the Russian record it can stimulate the womb — it was once used to help a stalled labour along — so it is best avoided in pregnancy. The dried berry as food and tea has centuries of ordinary use behind it; it is the concentrated extracts where the care belongs.

    Sources

    • Panossian et al. (2008) — Pharmacology of Schisandra chinensis: an overview of the Russian research and uses in medicine — the Soviet pharmacology and clinical record
    • Shennong Bencao Jing (c. 1st–2nd century CE) — the Divine Farmer's Classic: wu wei zi listed among the superior herbs (historical source)
    • Li Shizhen (1596) — Bencao Gangmu, the Compendium of Materia Medica: the five flavours mapped to skin, flesh and kernel (historical source)
    • Park et al. (2016) — a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of Schisandra chinensis extract for menopausal symptoms
    • Park et al. (2020) — a randomised trial of Schisandra extract on muscle strength and fatigue in adult women
    • Chiu et al. (2013) — improvement of liver function in humans using a mixture of schisandra fruit extract and sesamin: a randomised, placebo-controlled study
    • Frontiers in Pharmacology (2025) — efficacy of Schisandra chinensis in liver injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 54 animal studies
    • Ridley (2026) — Schisandra chinensis: trials and interactions — a critical review of the human evidence and the CYP3A interaction studies
    • Korea.net — Omija hwachae punch: the Korean five-flavour punch and its making

    Fig

    Ficus carica

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Digestive Health

    FreshDried

    The fig is one of the oldest farmed fruits in the world — sweet, soft, eaten fresh or dried for more than eleven thousand years — and one of the strangest. What we call a fig is not a fruit in the usual sense at all. It is a hollow flower-head turned inside out, lined on the inside with hundreds of tiny flowers. In the wild, those flowers can only set seed with the help of a wasp two millimetres long, the fig wasp, which crawls inside through a small hole at the tip, pollinates the flowers, lays its eggs and dies there. The garden figs most people grow are different: they swell sweet and seedless with no wasp at all. This is the edible fig, Ficus carica. It is not the Fiddle Leaf Fig houseplant, Ficus lyrata — a different species, grown for its big glossy leaves and never for fruit. Nothing told here belongs to that houseplant.

    The tree is a small, spreading, deciduous tree of the mulberry family, native to the Mediterranean and western Asia, with big, rough, lobed leaves — the leaves of the old stories — and smooth grey bark. It grows 10 to 30 feet tall and as wide, and it can live for decades, even a century, fruiting every summer. A ripe fig is soft and heavy, its skin thin, its flesh pink or amber and full of tiny seeds, its sweetness deep and honeyed. Fresh figs spoil fast; dried, they keep for months, and drying concentrates everything in them — the fibre, the minerals and the sugar alike.

    Cultivars

    Growers sort figs two ways. First by how they set fruit: Common figs ripen with no pollination at all, and they are the ones most gardens grow; Smyrna figs drop every fruit unless a fig wasp pollinates them; San Pedro figs give a first crop that needs no wasp and a second crop that does; and the caprifig is the wild male fig that carries the wasps and is grown for pollination, not for eating. Second by skin and flesh, which is how a gardener picks one.

    Brown Turkey

    The most widely grown garden fig, and the hardiest of the common kinds. Medium fruit, brownish-purple skin, pinkish-red flesh, sweet and reliable, often two crops a year. Best eaten fresh; not the best for drying.

    Black Mission

    The old Spanish mission fig, the classic dried fig of California. Large fruit, purplish-black skin, deep red flesh, rich and honeyed. Two crops: an early one and a main late-summer one.

    Celeste

    Also called the Sugar Fig. Small, rose-brown to purple fruit, very sweet, with a small eye that keeps out souring and insects. A good cold-hardy choice for cooler gardens.

    Chicago Hardy

    The cold-hardy fig, bred for places where the top freezes back in winter and regrows from the roots. Medium purple-brown fruit on a smaller tree, well suited to a pot that can be moved under cover.

    Kadota

    An old green fig with amber flesh, nearly seedless, mild and honeyed. The backbone of the California fig-canning trade, good for drying and for eating fresh.

    Adriatic

    Light green skin, strawberry-pink flesh, rich and sweet. A common type, so it fruits with no wasp, and a steady bearer, good fresh or dried and happy in a pot.

    Calimyrna

    The Smyrna fig of Turkey, renamed in California. Large golden fruit with amber flesh and a nutty flavour, the finest dried fig of all — but a Smyrna type, so it needs the fig wasp and the caprifig, and it will not fruit in a garden without them.

    King

    A San Pedro type: a big early crop that needs no wasp, a second crop that does. Large greenish-yellow fruit with amber flesh, at its best in warm, long summers.

    • The fig may be the first plant people ever farmed on purpose. In the early Neolithic village of Gilgal I, in the Jordan Valley about 13 kilometres north of Jericho, archaeologists found nine charred figs dating to about 9400–9200 BCE — around 11,400 years ago. The figs were of a seedless kind, the sort that ripens with no pollination and so cannot grow from seed; a tree like that can only carry on if people plant cuttings of it. The team that dug them up argued that this makes the fig the first domesticated plant, tended about a thousand years before wheat and barley. Other scholars have questioned that reading, and the argument is still open — but no one doubts the fig's age as a farmed fruit. From the Jordan Valley it spread through the whole ancient Near East and the Mediterranean, carried by people who loved it and could grow it from a cutting pushed into the ground.
    • In ancient Egypt figs were a staple food, dried for keeping and carried on journeys, and the dead were buried with baskets of them. In ancient Greece they were so valued that at times the best fruit could not be exported by law — and the word "sycophant" is said to come from the men who informed on illegal fig exporters, sykon being Greek for fig. Pliny the Elder, writing in Rome in the first century, counted 29 kinds of fig known in his day. The Romans told that the twins Romulus and Remus, the founders of Rome, were found in a basket caught beneath a wild fig tree, the Ficus Ruminalis, at the foot of the Palatine Hill — and Romans tended that tree for centuries.
    • The fig runs through the holy books. In Genesis, Adam and Eve sew fig leaves together to cover themselves after eating the forbidden fruit — some commentators have even guessed the forbidden fruit itself was a fig. In Deuteronomy the promised land is praised as a land of figs, vines and olives. In the Quran a whole short chapter, Surah At-Tin — the chapter of the fig — opens with an oath by the fig and the olive. In Greek story the goddess Demeter is said to have given the fig to mortals, and Dionysus is credited with finding it.
    • As a food the fig travelled everywhere warm enough to grow it. Spanish missionaries carried it to the Americas — the Black Mission fig takes its name from the Franciscan missions of California, where it was planted in the 1700s — and California later became the great dried-fig country, its orchards built on the Smyrna fig from Turkey, renamed Calimyrna in California. Dried figs fed sailors, soldiers and travellers for centuries: light to carry, sweet enough to eat alone, and long-keeping.
    • In folk medicine the fig was used in three separate ways, matching its three parts. The dried fruit was eaten as a gentle laxative, a use that runs through Greek, Roman and Arab medicine alike. The leaves were brewed as a tea, in Spain and across the Mediterranean, for blood sugar — a use that has now had one small trial of its own. And the milky sap was dabbed on warts and corns, a remedy still used in rural Iran. The sap was also used to curdle milk for cheese, like rennet, and the leaves were laid on the skin as a poultice for sores. Much of that use was hope and habit, not tested proof. The tested part stands on its own, under Health Benefits.
    • What is in the fruit, first. A fresh fig is mostly water, with about 2.9 g of fibre per 100 g; a dried fig, with the water gone, holds about 9.8 g of fibre per 100 g, along with 680 mg of potassium and 162 mg of calcium — more calcium than most fruits — and about 48 g of natural sugars per 100 g. Dried figs are also rich in copper, manganese, magnesium and vitamin K. One old claim should go: figs are not a meaningful source of vitamin A or vitamin C. Dried figs hold almost none of either.
    • The strongest evidence is for constipation, and it is one trial. In a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 80 Korean adults with functional constipation ate 300 g of fig paste a day — three packs before meals — or a matched placebo paste for eight weeks. Colon transit time, the time food takes to pass through the large intestine, fell by 24.5 hours on fig paste against 15.0 hours on placebo, and stool softness and abdominal discomfort improved more on figs. Stool frequency did not differ between the groups. One trial of 80 people is a real result, not a body of evidence — and the dose, 300 g of paste a day, is far beyond a normal serving, so it is not something to copy at home. Prunes carry a larger and stronger trial record for the same job. Human · small
    • The fig-leaf blood-sugar story is genuinely mixed, and it is about the leaf, not the fruit. In 1998 Spanish researchers gave ten adults with type 1 diabetes a fig-leaf decoction — a boiled leaf tea — with breakfast for a month, then a plain tea for a month. After-meal blood sugar was lower in the fig-leaf month, and the average insulin dose was about 12% lower. Ten people, two of whom dropped out, no change in long-term blood sugar, and a later review found no difference in fasting glucose or HbA1c. A later trial in type 2 diabetes found no significant change at all. A small extract trial in healthy adults found that a fig fruit extract rich in abscisic acid lowered after-meal glucose and insulin a little — but that tested a made extract, not figs eaten as food. No trial has tested whole figs for blood-sugar control in people, and dried figs are sugary food. Nobody taking insulin or blood-sugar medicine should add fig-leaf tea without telling the doctor who manages their medicine, because two things that lower blood sugar can stack into a low. Human · small
    • The wart remedy has one small trial behind it. In 2007, in Iran, 25 people with common warts put fig-tree latex on the warts on one side of the body while the warts on the other side were frozen, the standard treatment. The latex cleared the warts completely in 11 of the 25 people (44%); freezing cleared them in 14 (56%). About one in five saw the warts come back within six months. It is one open trial of 25 people, never repeated at scale — interesting, slightly behind freezing, and not a promise. Human · small
    • Everything else said about figs sits further down the ladder. Laboratory work shows fig extracts killing germs and slowing cancer cells in dishes, and animal tests show leaf extracts easing blood sugar in diabetic rats. None of that shows what eating a fig or drinking the leaf does in a person, and none of it is carried as a benefit here. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • When to plant: Grow it from a cutting or a potted plant in spring, and plant it while young — it dislikes being moved once settled
    • Sun: Full sun is essential — six to eight hours a day, the hottest spot you have — for sweet fruit and a good crop
    • Soil: It grows in many soils but does best in deep, well-drained ground around pH 6.0 to 7.5, and it fruits better in lean soil than in rich ground: too much feeding makes leaves at the cost of figs
    • Environment: USDA zones 7 to 10 in the ground, and zone 6 with a cold-hardy kind like 'Chicago Hardy' and winter protection; it needs a long, hot summer to ripen its fruit, and it is damaged by hard frost when young, though an established tree can take short cold down to about −10 °C (14 °F)
    • Planter or ground: Ground, with room — a fig in warm ground grows into a broad, spreading tree or large shrub, 10 to 30 feet tall and as wide, with roots to match, away from walls, drains and paving it can lift; in cold places it stays smaller, or it can be kept in a pot and moved into an unheated garage or shed once it is dormant
    • Water: Water steadily for the first year or two while it settles, and water while the fruit is swelling; after that it asks for little, and it is drought-tough by fruit-tree standards
    • When to pick: Figs do not ripen after picking, so pick each one only when it is fully coloured, soft, and drooping a little on its stalk — and pick often, because a ripe fig spoils in a day or two

    Garden notes

    • Two crops are possible in a warm climate. The first, the breba crop, grows on last year's wood and ripens in early summer; the main crop grows on new wood and ripens from late summer into autumn.
    • Prune in late winter, while it is dormant, taking out dead wood, crossing branches and suckers at the base. Fruit grows on new wood, so pruning shapes the tree without losing the crop.
    • Wet feet kill more young figs than cold does.
    • The leaves are big and lobed, the bark smooth and grey, and the tree loses its leaves in winter, so a bare winter fig is a healthy fig, not a dead one.
    • One warning belongs here, from the safety note above: the sap stings and burns skin in sunlight. Wear gloves and long sleeves when pruning, and wash off any sap straight away.

    Propagation

    Take a woody stem cutting about 8 to 10 inches long in late winter, while the tree is still asleep, and push it into moist potting mix with one bud above the soil. New roots form in a few weeks. Wear gloves — the milky sap stings skin.

    Safety

    • The fruit is food, fresh or dried, and safe for almost everyone. Dried figs are very sweet — about half their weight is sugar — so they count as a sweet food, not a free one.
    • The sap is the part to respect. Fig sap and fig leaves hold chemicals called furocoumarins, which make the skin burn in sunlight. Sap on sun-exposed skin can cause a blistering burn that looks like a bad sunburn and takes days to appear — there are case reports of children needing hospital care after playing with fig leaves in the sun, and of adults badly burned after using fig-leaf mixtures as a tanning lotion. Anyone handling the leaves or pruning the tree should keep the sap off the skin, and wash it off and stay out of the sun if it touches. The same caution covers the wart remedy: sap on the wart only, off the skin around it, and out of the sun.
    • Unripe figs leak more sap than ripe ones, and the sap can sting the mouth. People with a fig allergy should avoid the fruit, and anyone who has had a reaction to the sap should not use the leaf tea or the wart remedy.

    Sources

    • Kislev et al. (2006) — Early domesticated fig in the Jordan Valley (Science) — the nine charred figs from Gilgal I, about 9400–9200 BCE, and the argument that the fig was the first domesticated plant
    • Baek et al. (2016) — Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of Ficus carica paste for the management of functional constipation (Asia Pacific Journal of Clinical Nutrition) — 80 adults, 300 g of fig paste a day for eight weeks
    • Serraclara et al. (1998) — Hypoglycemic action of an oral fig-leaf decoction in type-I diabetic patients (Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice) — 10 adults with type 1 diabetes, one month of leaf decoction with breakfast
    • Bohlooli et al. (2007) — Comparative study of fig tree efficacy in the treatment of common warts vs. cryotherapy (International Journal of Dermatology) — 25 people, latex against freezing
    • Atkinson et al. (2019) — Abscisic acid standardized fig extracts ameliorate postprandial glycemic and insulinemic responses in healthy adults (Nutrients) — small crossover trial of a made extract, not whole figs
    • USDA FoodData Central — Figs, raw and Figs, dried, uncooked — the fibre, potassium, calcium and sugar figures
    • Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — the accepted name Ficus carica, its place in the mulberry family, and its native range

    Grape

    Vitis vinifera

    CulinaryMedicinal

    FreshDried

    The grape is the oldest farmed fruit in the West, and one vine gives three foods at once: the fresh fruit, the raisin, and the wine. The plant here is the common grape vine, Vitis vinifera, a woody climber from the warm lands around the Mediterranean and south-west Asia. It climbs by curling tendrils, its leaves broad and lobed with toothed edges, its fruit hanging in bunches that ripen green, red or deep purple-black. A single cup of grapes — about thirty grapes — holds about 104 calories, is four-fifths water, and gives a good share of the day's copper and vitamin K. The skins of red and purple grapes carry the pigments and polyphenols — plant compounds with antioxidant action — that the whole health story turns on, above all resveratrol. The resveratrol story needs its size stated up front: it is mostly laboratory and animal work, and the amounts tested in trials are far above what a handful of grapes holds.

    Cultivars

    There are between 5,000 and 10,000 named cultivars of Vitis vinifera, but only a few dozen make up most of what the world grows and eats. They fall into three uses — table grapes for eating fresh, wine grapes for the press, and raisin grapes for drying — and many cross between them.

    Table grapes: 'Thompson Seedless' (sold as Sultana), the green, seedless grape that is also the great raisin grape, making about 90% of American raisins; 'Flame Seedless', red and seedless, crisp and sweet; 'Crimson Seedless', reddish-purple and seedless, a late-season favourite; 'Red Globe', large red seeded grapes, sweet and firm; 'Perlette', an early green seedless grape; and 'Muscat of Alexandria', an old, sweet, musky white grape eaten fresh and dried.

    Thompson Seedless

    Flame Seedless

    Crimson Seedless

    Muscat of Alexandria

    Wine grapes: 'Chardonnay', the white grape behind wines from light and crisp to rich and buttery, and the base of Champagne; 'Sauvignon Blanc', sharp, green and aromatic; 'Riesling', pale, fragrant and long-lived; 'Pinot Noir', delicate, light to medium red, the grape of Burgundy; 'Cabernet Sauvignon', deep-coloured, full-bodied, the great red of Bordeaux; 'Merlot', softer and rounder than Cabernet, with plum notes; 'Syrah' (called Shiraz in Australia), dark, spicy and full; 'Grenache', warm and fruity; 'Tempranillo', the red of Rioja; and 'Airén', the pale Spanish white grown over more land than any other wine grape.

    Chardonnay

    Pinot Noir

    Cabernet Sauvignon

    Merlot

    Grenache

    Tempranillo

    Airén

    Raisin grapes: 'Thompson Seedless' above all, dried in the sun into golden sultanas; 'Black Corinth', the tiny black grape dried into the currants of cakes and puddings; and 'Muscat of Alexandria', dried into large, sweet, musky raisins.

    One name that does NOT belong here: 'Concord'. Concord is the grape of American juice and jelly, but it is Vitis labrusca, the American fox grape, not Vitis vinifera — its skins slip off the pulp, its flavour is musky and "foxy", and it needs less heat to ripen. It is a different species, and none of what is told of V. vinifera belongs to it.

    • The grape was tamed in the South Caucasus, in what is now Georgia, where the wild vine, Vitis vinifera subsp. sylvestris, grew in the river valleys and damp woods. Chemical traces of wine — tartaric acid, the fingerprint of the grape — were found soaked into great clay jars at the villages of Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora, dated to about 6000–5800 BC, the oldest wine yet found anywhere. The jars were large enough to ferment, age and serve from, and the pottery itself was decorated with bunches of grapes. From that cradle the tamed vine travelled west with traders and settlers, and east along the land routes into Central Asia, splitting as it went into table grapes for eating and wine grapes for the press.
    • In Egypt the grape was already a familiar fruit by 2500 BC. Tomb paintings show vines on trellises, workers picking bunches and treading them in presses, and the fruit eaten fresh, dried into raisins, or made into wine for feasts and for offerings to the gods. In Greece the vine belonged to Dionysus, god of wine and festivity, who was said to have taught men to grow the vine and make the wine; the symposia — drinking gatherings where men talked philosophy over cups of wine — were a Greek institution, and the vine's leaf was his emblem. Rome took the vine and carried it across the empire, from Italy to Gaul and Spain, planting vineyards wherever the sun was warm enough, and the grape became the fruit of the whole Mediterranean table.
    • The leaves are food too, and have been for as long as the fruit. Across the Mediterranean, the Middle East and the Balkans, young vine leaves are wrapped around rice, herbs and sometimes meat and rolled into tight parcels — dolma in Turkish, dolmades in Greek — a dish that was already being made by the early Byzantine period. The leaves are picked young and tender, blanched, and filled; they give a gentle sour, lemony note of their own.
    • Drying the grape is as old as eating it fresh. Left in the sun, the fruit becomes the raisin — Thompson Seedless dried gives the golden sultana, and the small black Corinth grape dried gives the currant of cakes and puddings. Raisins kept through the winter when fresh fruit could not, travelled well on ships and caravans, and were eaten plain, baked into bread, and stirred into sauces. The juice, pressed and left unfermented, was the sweet must of Roman cooking; fermented, it was wine, vinegar, and the base of medicines.
    • The vine has a medicine history of its own. In the old medicine of India the grape was prescribed for coughs, chest catarrh, and swollen liver and spleen, and its juice went into fermented tonics. In Europe the red vine leaf — the leaf that turns red in autumn — became a medicine for tired, swollen legs, and the European Medicines Agency now accepts dried red vine leaf extract as a well-established medicine for long-term venous insufficiency: swollen legs, varicose veins, and a feeling of heaviness, pain and tiredness in the calves. That standing belongs to the leaf extract, made to a set strength, and not to the fruit on the table.
    • The vine's hardest chapter came in the 1800s. A tiny root aphid from America, phylloxera, reached Europe and ate the roots of the European vines; within a few decades it had killed most of the vineyards of France and spread across the wine world. The rescue came from the very place the pest came from: European vines were grafted onto American roots that the aphid could not kill, and nearly every wine vine grown today still stands on American roots. The old vines that survived ungrafted, on sandy soils the aphid could not live in, are prized to this day.
    • The grape also carries a story in the Hebrew Bible: after the flood, Noah planted a vineyard, made wine, and drank it — one of the oldest vineyard stories ever written down. And in Georgia, where the wine story began, the old way never died: wine is still fermented and aged in great clay jars buried in the ground, the qvevri, a way of making wine eight thousand years old and still in use.
    • What is in the fruit, first. A cup of red or green grapes (151 g, about thirty grapes) holds about 104 calories, 27 g of carbohydrate, 23 g of natural sugars, 1.4 g of fibre, and is about 80% water. Its best nutrients are copper, at about 21% of the daily value, and vitamin K, at about 18%; it also gives small amounts of potassium (288 mg), thiamin, riboflavin, vitamin B6 and vitamin C (about 5% of the daily value). Red and purple skins add anthocyanins — the pigments behind their colour — while green skins carry mainly flavan-3-ols. The seeds hold proanthocyanidins, and the skins hold resveratrol, but in small amounts: a cup of grapes holds well under a milligram of resveratrol, while trials test 75 to 500 mg a day.
    • The heart claim, at its true size. Pooled trials of grape products — fresh grapes, raisins, juice, powder and seed extract mixed together — show small drops in blood pressure and blood fats. A meta-analysis of 28 trials in 1,344 people found grape products lowered systolic blood pressure by about 3.4 mmHg and diastolic by about 1.7 mmHg; another of 48 trials found total cholesterol down about 6 mg/dL and LDL — the "bad" cholesterol — down about 5 mg/dL. These are small changes in blood markers, not proof of fewer heart attacks, the trials mixed many forms of grape together so the effect of fresh grapes alone is not clear, and the certainty of the evidence is low. No long trial has tested whether eating grapes prevents heart disease. Human trials
    • The seed extract is a separate story and must not be handed to the fruit. Grape seed extract — a concentrate from the seeds, not the fruit — lowered blood pressure in a meta-analysis of 16 trials in 810 people: systolic down about 6 mmHg, diastolic down about 2.8 mmHg, with the clearest drops in younger people, in people carrying extra weight, and in people with metabolic syndrome — a cluster of high blood pressure, high blood sugar and extra weight around the waist. The doses ran from 100 to 2,000 mg a day, far above what eating grapes gives, the trials were small and their results varied widely, and the authors themselves called for a large, long trial to confirm it. The extract is not the grape. Human trials
    • Resveratrol, plainly. Resveratrol is the compound the headlines are about, and the human evidence is thin. In the laboratory it switches on pathways linked to ageing in yeast and worms, and in mice on a high-calorie diet it cut deaths by about a third — but on an ordinary diet it did not extend mouse lifespan, and the mechanism behind the early excitement turned out to depend on how the laboratory test was set up. In people, the longest study of natural resveratrol intake — nearly 800 older adults followed for nine years — found no link between resveratrol in the diet and death, heart disease, cancer or inflammation. Human trials of resveratrol supplements show small, mixed effects: some report modest blood pressure drops in people with type 2 diabetes, and one 24-month trial found a small rise in bone density in women after the menopause, but the trials are small, the results disagree with each other, and none measured lifespan or heart attacks. Eating grapes is not taking resveratrol, and drinking wine is not either. Human · small
    • Blood sugar, honestly. In three large American cohorts of health professionals — 187,382 people followed for years — every three servings a week of grapes and raisins was linked to a 12% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes. That is a link in observational data: people who eat more grapes may live differently in other ways, and it cannot show cause. In trials, grape products lowered insulin resistance — a measure of how hard the body must work to handle sugar — but did not change HbA1c, the long-term blood sugar measure, or fasting insulin, and fasting glucose was slightly higher. A 24-week trial of 36 g of raisins a day in 48 people with type 2 diabetes changed neither weight, blood sugar control nor blood fats. Grapes are a sweet fruit, and no one with diabetes should treat them as a treatment. Human · small
    • The leaf medicine, kept separate. Dried red vine leaf extract, made to a set strength, is the one grape preparation with a formal medicine standing: the European Medicines Agency accepts it as a well-established medicine for chronic venous insufficiency, on the strength of clinical studies showing less leg swelling and easier legs. The leaf as a tea, and the fruit on the table, share none of that standing. Human trials
    • When to plant: Plant bare-root vines in late winter to early spring, or potted vines at any time the ground is workable, spacing vines 1.2 to 1.8 metres apart with rows 2 to 3 metres apart, and give the vine its trellis at planting
    • Sun: Full sun, 6 to 8 hours a day at least, ideally against a south- or south-west-facing wall that gives back heat at night; with less sun the grapes stay sour
    • Soil: Deep, stony, free-draining soil is ideal, around pH 6.0 to 7.5, and it takes lime well; the vine likes poor ground better than rich — rich, wet soil makes leaf and wood at the cost of fruit, and roots sitting in water rot
    • Environment: USDA zones 6 to 9, reliable in zones 7 to 9 and only in sheltered spots in zone 6; ripened wood takes cold down to about −18 °C (0 °F), but once the buds have broken in spring they scorch at −1 to −2 °C (30 to 28 °F), and a late frost can take the whole year's fruit; it needs a long, warm growing season — at least 170 frost-free days
    • Planter or ground: Ground, on a strong trellis, wires, an arbour or a pergola to climb on — a fence post will not hold a mature vine; trained and pruned it stands 2 to 3 metres tall and spreads 3 to 5 metres wide, and left alone it will climb a tree or a wall to 10 metres and more, and it lives for decades, so plant it where it can stay
    • Water: Water steadily through the first year while the roots settle; once settled the vine is drought-tough and asks for almost no watering — a deep drink every two to three weeks in a dry late spring is enough, and watering stops once the grapes begin to colour, so the sugar is not watered down
    • When to pick: Pick the bunches when they taste sweet and full — grapes do not ripen further once picked — and cut the whole bunch with secateurs rather than pulling it

    Garden notes

    • Pruning is the work that matters most, and it is not optional. Grapes fruit only on shoots from one-year-old wood, so every late winter, while the vine is still dormant and before the buds swell, cut away 80 to 90% of the last year's growth, leaving only 30 to 60 buds on a mature vine. Train the vine on a simple system — a high cordon, with two permanent arms along a wire at about 1.7 metres, is the easiest for a home grower — and tie the kept canes to the wire. In spring, rub off suckers from the trunk; in summer, pinch the shoots back to five or six leaves past the last bunch, and thin crowded bunches so the rest ripen well. A vine left unpruned makes a tangle of leaf, poor fruit and disease within two or three years.
    • Feed lightly — a little mature compost scratched in at the base in late winter is enough. Nitrogen fertiliser makes wood and leaves instead of fruit.
    • The vine is raised from cuttings, not from seed: take lengths of ripened cane 20 to 30 cm long with three or four buds at pruning time in winter, and root them. Seedlings do not come true to the parent, so a named cultivar is always a cutting of the original vine. Most vines give their first real harvest in their third year.
    • Waterlogged winter ground is the leading cause of a garden vine failing.
    • Disease is the honest warning. In humid country the European grape needs watching for powdery mildew, downy mildew and grey mould, and air flow through the vine — open pruning, no crowding — is the first defence. Where disease pressure is high, a resistant American or French-American hybrid will give a better harvest with far less spraying.

    Propagation

    Cut a pencil-thick cane from last year's growth into pieces 10 to 14 inches long in late winter, while the vine is asleep, and set them in moist potting mix with two buds buried. A vine grown from seed will not match its parent — use cuttings to keep the same grape. Do not propagate a patented type without permission.

    Safety

    • Grapes and raisins are poison to dogs. Even a single grape can make a dog ill, and they can cause sudden kidney failure; any dog that eats grapes or raisins needs a vet straight away, and there is no safe amount.
    • For people, grapes are a safe, ordinary fruit, but they are sweet — about 15 g of sugar per 100 g — so a large handful is a sugary snack, not a free one.
    • Wine is alcohol, and no health benefit of wine is a reason to drink it: the alcohol itself raises the risk of liver disease, some cancers and accidents, and the heart evidence for wine comes from observational studies that cannot separate wine from the lives of the people who drink it.
    • Grape seed extract and resveratrol supplements are not foods, and their safety in pregnancy, in children, and alongside blood-thinning and blood-pressure medicines is not settled — anyone taking them should ask a doctor first.

    Sources

    • McGovern et al. (2017) — Early Neolithic wine of Georgia in the South Caucasus (PNAS) — the oldest wine, about 6000–5800 BC, from tartaric acid in jars at Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora
    • International Organisation of Vine and Wine — the 5,000 to 10,000 cultivar figure and the ten wine varieties behind a quarter of the world's vineyards, via the Nature genomics review
    • Muraki et al. (2013) — Fruit consumption and risk of type 2 diabetes (BMJ) — three cohorts, 187,382 people; grapes and raisins, three servings a week, 12% lower diabetes risk (observational)
    • Asbaghi et al. (2021) — Effect of grape products on blood pressure: a systematic review and meta-analysis — 28 trials, 1,344 people; systolic down about 3.4 mmHg, diastolic down about 1.7 mmHg
    • Lupoli et al. (2020) — Impact of grape products on lipid profile: a meta-analysis — 48 trials; total cholesterol down about 6 mg/dL, LDL down about 5 mg/dL
    • Zhang et al. (2016) — The impact of grape seed extract treatment on blood pressure changes: a meta-analysis of 16 randomized controlled trials — 810 people; systolic down about 6 mmHg, diastolic down about 2.8 mmHg; extract doses 100–2,000 mg a day
    • Semba et al. (2014) — Resveratrol levels and all-cause mortality in older community-dwelling adults — nearly 800 older adults followed nine years; no link between dietary resveratrol and death, heart disease, cancer or inflammation
    • European Medicines Agency — European Union herbal monograph on Vitis vinifera L., folium (red vine leaf) — well-established use for chronic venous insufficiency; traditional use for heavy legs, haemorrhoids and skin capillary fragility
    • USDA FoodData Central — Grapes, red or green (European type, Thompson seedless), raw — the cup figures: 104 calories, copper 21% and vitamin K 18% of the daily value
    • Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine — Grape and raisin toxicity — grapes and raisins can cause sudden kidney failure in dogs; any ingestion is an emergency
