    • Penn State Extension / Cornell Cooperative Extension — grape growing guidance — zones 6–9 for V. vinifera, full sun, hard dormant pruning of 80–90% of growth, fruit on one-year-old wood

    Pomegranate

    Punica granatum

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Heart Health

    FreshCooked

    The pomegranate is a small, many-branched tree from the warm lands between Persia and northern India, and it is one of the oldest farmed fruits in the world — grown for five thousand years, carried from garden to garden across Asia, Egypt, Greece, Rome and Spain, and still eaten the same way: cracked open by hand, the jewel-red seeds picked out one by one. The fruit is a round, leathery ball the size of a large orange, crowned with a little dried flower-cup, and inside it are hundreds of seeds, each wrapped in a juicy, ruby-red coat called an aril. The arils are the part you eat — sweet, tart and crunching — and their juice stains everything it touches. The tree itself is a handsome thing, a deciduous shrub or small tree to about 3 to 5 metres, with glossy narrow leaves and bright orange-red trumpet flowers in spring, and it fruits in autumn, when the branches hang heavy with red.

    Cultivars

    There are more than 500 named pomegranate cultivars in the world, and only a handful are commonly grown. They differ in the colour of the skin and the arils, in sweetness and tartness, in how hard the seeds are, and in how much cold they can take. The ones a gardener is most likely to meet are these.

    Wonderful

    The standard. Large fruit with deep purple-red skin and deep crimson, juicy arils; rich and sweet-tart, firm seeds; the pomegranate of the shops and the juice trade, ripening in mid-autumn. It needs a long, warm season to colour and sweeten fully.

    Granada

    A bud sport of Wonderful, a chance change on a Wonderful branch. Darker red than Wonderful, a little less tart, and ripening about a month earlier.

    Early Wonderful

    Like Wonderful but earlier, for places where autumn comes fast.

    Angel Red

    Vivid red skin and arils, very juicy, with soft, chewable seeds; ripens early and is one of the best for eating fresh.

    Eversweet

    Red skin, pale pink arils, very sweet with almost no tartness and soft seeds; the one for people who dislike sharp fruit. Its juice is pale and does not stain.

    Parfianka

    Large red fruit from Central Asia, bright and sweet-tart with very small, soft seeds; often rated among the best-tasting of all.

    Utah Sweet

    Pink skin and pale arils, very sweet, with softer seeds than Wonderful.

    Salavatski

    Large orange-red fruit, semi-sweet with hard seeds; one of the hardiest, grown where winters bite.

    Kazake

    Yellow-orange to light red fruit, sweet-tart with rather hard seeds; another cold-hardy kind, from the Russian and Central Asian collections.

    Bhagwa

    Bright red arils, balanced sweet-sour, soft seeds; the leading commercial cultivar of India.

    Nana

    The dwarf pomegranate, 2 to 4 feet tall, grown for its small size and bright flowers, and for bonsai. Its fruit is edible but small and sour, and it is grown for looks, not for eating.

    • The pomegranate comes from the warm, dry lands of western and central Asia — from Iran through Afghanistan to northern India, with wild trees still standing in the Caucasus and Central Asia. Its Latin name tells a Roman story: Punica is the Roman name for Carthage, the city in North Africa from which the Romans wrongly thought the best pomegranates came, and granatum means seedy, or full of grains. In Persian it is anār, in Arabic rummān, in Hebrew rimmōn, and in Sanskrit dāḍima.
    • It is one of the first fruits people ever farmed. Charred pomegranate remains have been found at Bronze Age sites in Jericho and Arad, and the fruit sailed in the cargo of the Uluburun shipwreck off the Turkish coast some three thousand years ago. By 3000 BCE it was grown in Persia, and by 1600 BCE it had reached Egypt, where a pomegranate-shaped vase was buried with Tutankhamun and the oldest whole fruit ever found was laid in the tomb of Djehuty. The Phoenicians carried it around the Mediterranean to North Africa, Greece and Italy, and it reached China by about 100 BCE.
    • In Greece the pomegranate is the fruit of the Persephone story. In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, Hades gives Persephone a pomegranate seed to eat in the underworld, and because she has eaten the food of the dead she must return below for part of each year — the old telling of why the earth has seasons. At Argos the goddess Hera held a pomegranate in her hand, and the fruit stood for marriage, abundance and the many seeds of a full life.
    • The fruit runs through the holy books of three faiths. In the Hebrew Bible it is named among the fruits of the promised land, its red seeds woven into the hem of the high priest's robe and carved on the pillars of Solomon's temple, and in Jewish custom it is eaten at Rosh Hashanah, the new year — legend says it holds 613 seeds, one for each of the 613 commandments, though no fruit has ever been counted to hold exactly that. In the Song of Songs the beloved's cheeks are likened to a cut pomegranate. In the Quran it is named among the fruits of paradise. Whether it was the forbidden fruit of Eden is an old guess, and it stays a guess: the story names no fruit at all.
    • The city of Granada in Spain is named for it — granada is Spanish for pomegranate — and the fruit sits on the city's arms, a memory of the long Moorish centuries when the pomegranate grew in every Andalusian garden. From Spain the tree sailed to the Americas with the Spanish, and it has grown in California since the days of the missions.
    • In old medicine nearly every part of the tree had a use, and the uses split cleanly in two. The fruit and its juice were food and gentle medicine — cooling, in the Ayurvedic and Unani telling, given for thirst, fever and weak digestion. The rind, the flower buds and the root bark were the strong medicine: bitter and astringent, full of tannins. Dioscorides, the Greek physician of the first century, prescribed a decoction of the rind for worms, and the root bark was the great tapeworm remedy of the old pharmacopoeias, kept in official use into the nineteenth century. The bark holds alkaloids that can poison in too large a dose, which is why that remedy belonged to physicians, not to home kitchens.
    • The fruit gave its name to a weapon. The hand-thrown iron grenade of the sixteenth century was named for the pomegranate — granada — because the round, seed-packed iron ball bursting apart looked like the fruit splitting open.
    • What is in the fruit, first. A hundred grams of arils — the juicy seeds — give 83 calories, 4 grams of fibre, 236 mg of potassium, 38 micrograms of folate, 16.4 micrograms of vitamin K and 10.2 mg of vitamin C. The deep red colour comes from anthocyanins, the same colour compounds as in berries, and the rind and juice are rich in large polyphenols called ellagitannins, chiefly punicalagin. One plain fact belongs here: those big polyphenols are barely absorbed as they are. It is the gut's bacteria that break them down into smaller compounds, the urolithins, and people differ in how well their gut does it — which is one reason the same juice does not do the same thing in everyone.
    • Blood pressure is the one benefit with real human trials behind it, and the honest size of it is small and mixed. A 2017 pooling of 8 randomised trials of pomegranate juice found the top number of blood pressure fell by about 5 points and the bottom number by about 2 points. A bigger 2024 pooling of 22 randomised trials, of juice, extracts and capsules together, found larger falls — about 8 points on the top number and 3 on the bottom — but the trials disagreed with each other a great deal, and the authors themselves called for better trials before any firm claim is made. An Oxford review of the same early trials, also in 2017, read the same evidence the other way and judged it weak: only two of the eight trials showed a clear benefit, several were poorly reported, and the review concluded the trials so far do not convincingly show a benefit. Put together: the pooled numbers point down, the single trials are mixed, and the effect, if real, is modest — a small help alongside a heart-healthy diet, never a treatment for high blood pressure on its own. Human trials
    • Cholesterol and the arteries have been studied far less well. Small trials of pomegranate juice and cholesterol have given mixed results, and no single trial was strong enough to carry a claim here. The laboratory work — pomegranate compounds keeping fats from oxidising in a dish, easing swelling in animals — is laboratory work, and none of it shows what drinking the juice does in a person. Lab studies
    • Memory has one small, careful trial. In 2013, researchers at UCLA gave 32 older adults with mild memory complaints either 8 ounces of pomegranate juice or a flavour-matched dummy drink every day for four weeks, without anyone knowing who got which. Only the pomegranate group improved on a test of verbal memory, and their brain scans showed more activity during memory tasks. The authors called the trial preliminary, and it was: 28 people finished it, it lasted a month, and no one has repeated it at a bigger scale. One small trial is a beginning, not a proof. Human · small
    • Cancer is where the fence matters most. Pomegranate compounds slow the growth of cancer cells in dishes and in animals, and that laboratory work is often quoted as though it were a human result. It is not. The human trials in prostate cancer have been small, and they have not shown a clear benefit. No trial has shown that eating pomegranates or drinking the juice prevents or treats cancer in people. Lab studies
    • When to plant: Plant bare-root trees while they are dormant in late winter, or set out pot-grown plants in spring after the last hard frost; space trees 10 to 15 feet apart
    • Sun: Full sun, six to eight hours a day or more, and a long, hot summer to ripen its fruit; in shade it grows leaves and gives little fruit
    • Soil: It grows in many soils but does best in deep, well-drained ground, around pH 5.5 to 7.0; it tolerates poor, stony and even salty ground better than wet ground — roots sitting in water rot, and heavy wet clay kills more young pomegranates than cold does
    • Environment: USDA zones 8 to 10, with the hardiest kinds, Salavatski and Kazake, surviving in sheltered spots in zone 7; young trees are tender to frost, and an established tree can take short cold down to about −12 °C (10 °F)
    • Planter or ground: Ground, as a many-stemmed shrub or a small tree with one to three trunks — decide early, because the tree sends up suckers from the base all its life, and they must be pulled away or it turns back into a thicket; it also grows well in a large pot in a free-draining mix, and the dwarf Nana is the one for pots
    • Water: Water deeply but not often — steadily for the first year or two while it settles, and after that it is drought-tough by fruit-tree standards, but it fruits best with even moisture through the summer; keep the water steady while the fruit is swelling, because a dry spell followed by heavy watering or rain is what splits the fruit open on the tree
    • When to pick: Harvest in autumn, mostly September to November, when the fruit is fully coloured, feels heavy for its size and gives a metallic sound when tapped; cut it from the branch with secateurs, leaving a short stem, and do not pull — the fruit does not ripen further once picked, so leave it on the tree until it is ready, but pick promptly before rain splits it

    Garden notes

    • Grow it from cuttings, not from seed: seedlings do not come true to the parent, and a seedling's fruit is a surprise.
    • Feed lightly in late winter or early spring.
    • Prune in late winter while the tree is dormant, and prune lightly: take out dead, weak, crossing wood and the suckers at the base, and leave the rest alone. Fruit forms on short spurs on wood two to three years old, so heavy pruning cuts the crop.
    • The flowers come in spring — bright orange-red trumpets, some of which set fruit and some of which fall — and the fruit takes six to seven months to ripen. A tree usually begins to bear two to three years after planting, and reaches full bearing at about five years.
    • Whole fruit keeps for weeks in a cool spot and for a month or more in the refrigerator.

    Propagation

    Take a pencil-thick hardwood cutting, 6 to 12 inches long, from last year's growth in late winter, and set it in free-draining mix with a couple of buds showing. Seed also works — sow in spring — but seed-grown plants will not match the parent fruit, so use cuttings to keep a good variety true.

    Safety

    • The fruit and its juice are safe as food for most people. The juice is sweet: an 8-ounce glass carries about 32 grams of natural sugar, so anyone watching blood sugar should take a small glass with a meal, not a large one alone.
    • The juice also does real work on medicines, in the same way grapefruit juice does: it slows the liver enzymes that clear some drugs, so blood levels of some statins, some blood-pressure drugs and the blood thinner warfarin can rise. One case report describes severe muscle breakdown in a man on rosuvastatin after he started drinking pomegranate juice, and warfarin users have had their clotting measures shift. Anyone taking a statin, blood-pressure medicine or warfarin should ask their doctor before drinking pomegranate juice every day.
    • The rind, root bark and stem bark are not safe in large amounts, and the old bark remedy for worms should never be tried at home. Allergic reactions are rare but do happen. Juice as food is likely fine in pregnancy; concentrated extracts have not been studied there.

    Sources

    • Sahebkar et al. (2017) — pomegranate juice and blood pressure: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Pharmacological Research) — 8 trials, about 5 points off the top number, 2 off the bottom
    • Bahari et al. (2024) — pomegranate and blood pressure: a systematic review and meta-analysis (Phytotherapy Research) — 22 trials, about 8 points off the top number, 3 off the bottom, with high disagreement between trials
    • Gbinigie et al. (2017) — pomegranate and blood pressure: an Oxford systematic review of randomised trials (Nutrition Research) — 8 trials, evidence judged weak
    • Bookheimer et al. (2013) — pomegranate juice and memory: a small preliminary randomised trial in older adults with mild memory complaints — 32 people, 28 finishing, 8 ounces a day for four weeks
    • USDA FoodData Central — Pomegranates, raw — the nutrition figures per 100 g of arils
    • Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — the accepted name Punica granatum, its place in the loosestrife family, and its native range
    • American Botanical Council, HerbalGram 100 (2013) — pomegranate herb profile: botany, history, traditional uses and the old bark remedy
    • Clemson Cooperative Extension — home-garden pomegranate growing guide: feeding, pruning, harvest and fruit splitting

    Olive

    Olea europaea

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Blood Sugar HealthHeart Health

    The olive is one of the oldest farmed trees on Earth, and one of the most loved: a slow, gnarled evergreen of the dry Mediterranean hills, with narrow grey-green leaves, silver beneath, and small fruit that ripens from green to purple-black in the autumn sun. The tree here is Olea europaea, the European olive, in the olive family, Oleaceae — kin to lilac, jasmine, ash and forsythia. A single tree can live for hundreds of years, and some are said to be over a thousand, still bearing fruit on trunks so twisted and hollow that they look like old sculpture. The fruit is a drupe, a stone fruit like a cherry, and it is bitter beyond eating when raw: the compound that makes it bitter, oleuropein, has to be washed out by curing before the fruit can be eaten at all. From that one bitter fruit come two of the Mediterranean's great foods — the table olive, cured and salted, and olive oil, pressed from the ripe fruit — and from the leaves comes a bitter tea and extract that herbal medicine has used for centuries. One thing to know before anything else: the health trials behind the olive tested the oil, mostly extra virgin oil, and the leaf extract — not the olives on a plate. The salt in a table olive and the oil in a bottle are not the same story.

    Cultivars

    The olive has hundreds of named cultivars — well over five hundred worldwide — and the ones below are the names a reader is most likely to meet, in a nursery, on a bottle or on a jar. Most are named for the place they came from, and most fall into two uses: oil olives, small fruit with a high oil content, and table olives, large fruit with thick flesh.

    Arbequina

    Spain (Catalonia). Small, compact tree, the garden favourite: fruits young, usually fruits alone, and makes a mild, fruity oil. Small olives that can also be cured. The best cold tolerance of the common oil olives.

    Arbosana

    Spain. Small tree, grown for oil alongside Arbequina, often in dense modern groves. Mild oil.

    Koroneiki

    Greece (southern Peloponnese). Tiny fruit, but one of the highest oil yields of any olive, and a robust, peppery oil of exceptional quality. More tender to cold than most.

    Picual

    Spain. The country's leading oil olive, a large, vigorous tree with a pungent oil that keeps well.

    Frantoio

    Italy (Tuscany). The classic Tuscan oil olive, fruity with a strong finish; grown with Leccino, which pollinates it.

    Leccino

    Italy (Tuscany). The other half of the Tuscan pair: a mild, sweet oil, and a good pollinator for Frantoio.

    Coratina

    Italy (Puglia). One of Italy's most important oil olives, from the country's largest olive-growing region; a strong, bitter, peppery oil.

    Manzanilla (Manzanillo)

    Spain (Seville). The classic green table olive — manzanilla means little apple — large, round, thick-fleshed, and the olive behind most canned black olives in America. Needs a pollinator nearby.

    Kalamata (Kalamon)

    Greece. The large, almond-shaped, purple-black table olive, smooth and meaty, usually kept in wine vinegar or oil. Olives of this cultivar grown outside the Kalamata region are sold in the EU as Kalamon.

    Mission

    California, from the Spanish mission groves of the 1700s. A large, upright tree, good in the cold, and a true dual-purpose olive: black table olives and oil.

    Picholine

    France. Long, green table olives with a mild, sweet taste, also pressed for oil.

    Gordal

    Spain. Very large table olives, often stuffed with pimento or cheese.

    Hojiblanca

    Spain (Andalusia). A dual-purpose olive with white-backed leaves, used for both oil and the table.

    Nocellara del Belice

    Sicily. Large, green, buttery table olives, also pressed for oil.

    Chemlali

    Tunisia. Compact and cold-hardy, the main oil olive of Tunisia.

    Fruitless forms exist too — 'Swan Hill' is the best known — grown as ornamental trees that never set fruit. They are not fruiting cultivars, and none of what is told of the fruiting olive belongs to them.

    • The olive is a tree of the eastern Mediterranean, first farmed in the Levant — the lands of modern Syria, Lebanon, Israel and Jordan — some six to seven thousand years ago, in the valleys of the Jordan and along the Carmel coast. It is among the oldest fruit trees people ever tamed, and its spread follows the rise of whole civilisations: it took root in Crete around 3500 BCE, reached the Greek mainland and Cyprus, and travelled west with Phoenician and Greek traders and settlers until it stood in Iberia by about 1050 BCE, in Italy by about 600 BCE, and all around the shores of the sea. The Greeks carried cuttings and grafted them onto wild trees; the Romans planted cuttings in nursery beds and carried the tree across their whole empire. Spain, Italy and Greece remain the great olive countries to this day, and the tree now grows in about thirty countries, in the warm belt between roughly 30 and 45 degrees of latitude — California, Australia, South Africa, Chile, Argentina and more.
    • In the old story, the olive was Athena's gift to Athens. When the goddess and the sea god Poseidon competed for the city, Poseidon struck the rock and brought forth salt water, and Athena planted the first olive tree — food, oil and wood in one gift — and the city chose hers and took her name. The tree became the city's emblem, and its oil and branches ran through Greek life: victors at the Olympic games were crowned with wreaths of wild olive, the kotinos; oil filled the lamps, dressed the food, anointed kings and athletes, and was poured as an offering. The branch of the olive became the sign of peace, and it still is.
    • The oil was the ancient world's great multi-purpose product, and most of the crop went to the press, not the table. Olives were crushed underfoot, with pestle and mortar, under stone rollers and in presses — the first mechanical presses came from Klazomenai in Turkey, and the Romans used a great circular stone press, the trapetum — and the finest oil, then as now, came from the first pressing of fruit picked early, while still green. Table olives were made edible by salting. The oil lit the lamps, oiled the skin, carried perfumes, soothed wounds, and was traded in jars across the whole Mediterranean; under the laws of Solon, olive oil was the only export Athens allowed. The tree bears heavily only every other year, and the harvest runs from October to December.
    • The medicine of the olive was mostly the medicine of the leaf. Dioscorides, writing in the first century, called the pounded leaves astringent — drawing and drying — and said they stopped the spread of sores and stayed bleeding, while the juice of the leaves was good against sore eyes, and with honey it cleaned a suppurating ear. Hippocrates before him had used olive leaf on wounds. In the 1800s the leaf came back into European medicine as a fever remedy: in 1854 Daniel Hanbury told how he had used a tincture of the leaves against severe fever since 1843, Spanish doctors prescribed the leaves for intermittent fever, and French army doctors used them through the Peninsular War of 1808–1813, when quinine was scarce. By the 1830s the bark too had a name as a quinine substitute for fevers. The oil's place in medicine was quieter and steadier: a base for ointments and salves, a dressing for skin, a gentle purge, and the carrier that carried other medicines into the skin. The European Medicines Agency still holds the leaf as a traditional herbal medicine — a tea of the leaves, used to help the kidneys pass water in mild cases of water retention — a standing that rests on long use, not on trials.
    • The tree's later journey is the story of empire and migration. The Spanish carried it to the Americas in the 1500s and 1600s, and the Franciscan missions planted it in California from the 1700s — the Mission olive, still grown there, takes its name from those mission groves. In Australia it arrived with the early settlers and now grows wild in places, and in the far south of the old world it stands in the groves of Lun on the Croatian island of Pag, where some trees are said to be over a thousand years old. Wherever it travelled it became a tree of home and of patience: slow to grow, hard to kill, bearing fruit for generations on the same gnarled trunk, and so long-lived that Theophrastus, writing more than two thousand years ago, called it the longest-lived of trees, persisting by its trunk, its side shoots and its roots that are so hard to destroy.
    • The tree also fed a whole way of eating. The Mediterranean diet — vegetables, beans, bread, fish, and olive oil as the main fat — grew up around it, and the oil's place at the centre of that diet is what the modern trials set out to test. That tested part stands on its own, under Health Benefits.
    • What is in the fruit, first. Ripe canned olives carry about 116 calories per 100 grams, with about 11 grams of fat — most of it oleic acid, the monounsaturated fat that is also the heart of the oil — about 1.6 grams of fibre, and very little protein. Green pickled olives are much the same, at about 145 calories per 100 grams. What the table olive carries that the oil does not is salt: about 735 milligrams of sodium per 100 grams in ripe olives, and about 1,556 milligrams in green pickled ones — so a small handful of ten green olives holds about 420 milligrams of sodium, a fifth of a day's worth. The oil is the pressed juice of the fruit: about three-quarters oleic acid, with vitamin E and a family of bitter plant compounds — polyphenols — that refining strips away, above all hydroxytyrosol and oleuropein, and oleocanthal, the compound that gives good oil its peppery bite at the back of the throat. Extra virgin oil is the first pressing, made by pressing alone, cold, with no heat or chemicals; refined oil keeps the fat and loses most of the polyphenols. A tablespoon of oil holds about 120 calories.
    • The strongest evidence there is comes from one great trial, and it tested a whole way of eating, not the oil alone. The PREDIMED trial enrolled 7,447 men and women in Spain, aged 55 to 80, all at high risk of heart disease but without the disease itself, and gave them one of three diets for a median of nearly five years: a Mediterranean diet with a litre of extra virgin olive oil a week supplied for each family — about 50 grams a day — a Mediterranean diet with mixed nuts, or advice to eat a low-fat diet. The two Mediterranean diet groups had about 30% fewer major heart events — heart attack, stroke or death from heart disease — than the low-fat group: a hazard ratio of 0.70 for the olive oil group. That is a real, randomised trial in people, at a real-life dose, with hard outcomes. Two fences belong to it. First, the oil was tested inside a whole Mediterranean diet, so the oil's share cannot be separated from the rest of the eating pattern. Second, it tested the oil, not the olives on a plate — no trial has tested eating whole olives against heart attacks or strokes. The trial was also re-checked and published again in 2018, after a fault was found in how some people had been assigned to their groups; the re-checked result was the same. Human trials
    • The same trial found a second result worth telling plainly. Among the 3,541 people in the trial who did not have diabetes at the start, new diabetes was about 40% less common in the olive oil diet group than in the low-fat group — a hazard ratio of 0.60. This was a secondary finding, not the trial's main question, and again it belongs to the oil inside the whole diet, not to table olives. No trial has tested whole olives against diabetes. Human trials
    • A smaller trial tested the oil itself, and it is the clearest proof that the polyphenols matter, not just the fat. The EUROLIVE trial gave 200 healthy men three olive oils in turn — low, medium and high in polyphenols, but otherwise the same — at 25 millilitres a day, about two tablespoons, for three weeks each. As the polyphenol content rose, the good cholesterol, HDL, rose a little, and the oxidised form of the bad cholesterol, LDL — the form that burrows into artery walls — fell. The European Food Safety Authority has since allowed a precise claim on this point: the polyphenols in olive oil help protect blood fats from oxidative damage, where the oil gives at least 5 milligrams of hydroxytyrosol and its kin per 20 grams. The effect is modest, and it is an effect on blood markers, not on heart attacks — but it was shown in people, at a real-life dose, and it is why extra virgin oil, not refined oil, is the one the trials used. Human trials
    • The leaf extract has its own, smaller trial record, and it is mixed. In a randomised, double-blind crossover trial of 60 pre-hypertensive men, a leaf extract giving 136 milligrams of oleuropein a day for six weeks lowered daytime systolic pressure — the top number — by about 4 millimetres of mercury against the control, and total and LDL cholesterol and triglycerides fell a little. In a larger trial of 621 people already treated for high blood pressure, published in 2025, the leaf extract lowered 24-hour systolic pressure by 6.4 millimetres of mercury against 1.5 on placebo over twelve weeks. But a third trial, of 56 adults in 2026, found no significant difference between the extract and placebo on blood pressure at all. The honest size of it: small trials, pointing the same way more often than not, with one clear miss — and the leaf extract is not the fruit and not the oil. It is not a treatment for high blood pressure, and it is never a substitute for prescribed medicine. Human · small
    • The brain finding is an association, and it is told as one. In two large American studies followed for 28 years — 92,383 adults in all — those who ate more than 7 grams of olive oil a day, a little over half a tablespoon, had a 28% lower risk of dying with dementia than those who never or rarely ate it, and the link held whatever their overall diet quality. The same studies linked higher olive oil intake with lower total mortality. But these are observational studies: they watched what people ate and what happened to them, and they cannot show that the oil caused the difference — people who eat olive oil may differ in other ways too. The dementia link was also stronger in women than in men. There is no trial of olive oil against dementia, and no trial of whole olives against it either.
    • Two fences close the section. First, the laboratory work — oleuropein and hydroxytyrosol killing germs in dishes, calming swelling in animal tests, slowing the growth of cancer cells in dishes — is laboratory and animal work, and none of it shows what eating olives or taking the oil does in a person. Second, none of that is a claim about whole olives: the fruit's fibre and nutrients are real, but the trials that carry the weight here tested the oil and the leaf extract, and the salt in a table olive is a real cost that the oil does not carry. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • When to plant: Plant a grafted tree from a nursery, in spring after the last frost or in autumn in mild climates, and give it room
    • Sun: Full sun, at least six hours a day and eight is better; it also needs a cool winter to set fruit — roughly 200 to 400 hours below 45 °F (7 °C) — and a tree kept warm indoors all winter will leaf but never fruit
    • Soil: Lean, gritty, stony soil that drains freely, around pH 6.5 to 8.5; the olive grows in poor, rocky, even alkaline ground, but it cannot stand wet feet — standing water kills more olive trees than cold does, and rich, wet compost is the wrong ground for it
    • Environment: USDA zones 8 to 11, with the hardiest cultivars, Arbequina above all, reaching into zone 7 with shelter and winter protection; it is damaged by hard frost when young, though an established tree can take short cold down to about −12 °C (10 °F)
    • Planter or ground: Ground: an unpruned tree grows 25 to 30 feet tall with a spread of 15 to 25 feet, though pruning keeps it to 12 to 20 feet, and patio-sized selections stay around 8 to 10 feet; in cold country it grows well in a large terracotta pot — Arbequina is the best pot choice — brought under cover for winter, in a cool, frost-free place, not a warm room
    • Water: Water steadily for the first year or two while it settles; once settled it is genuinely drought-tough and asks for little, and too much water brings disease
    • When to pick: The fruit swells over summer and ripens in autumn, turning from green through straw yellow to purple-black, and the harvest runs from October into December; pick green for table olives and for early, peppery oil, or leave the fruit to ripen fully for a milder oil

    Garden notes

    • Most cultivars set some fruit alone, but nearly all bear better with a second cultivar within about 50 feet, and Leccino needs a pollinator. Expect the first fruit three to five years after planting a grafted tree; a tree grown from seed may take eight to twelve years and will not come true to its parent.
    • The tree flowers in late spring, on last year's wood, in sprays of small, creamy-white, four-petalled flowers, pollinated by the wind — thousands open at once, and only a few set fruit.
    • The tree bears heavily only every other year — a full crop one year, a light one the next — which is normal, not a fault.
    • Prune after the harvest, in late winter before growth starts: take out dead wood and crossing branches, open the centre to light and air, and never top the tree.
    • The leaves are narrow, green on top and silvery-white beneath, and evergreen, so the tree never stands bare. The bark grows gnarled and hollow with age, and old trees throw up shoots from the base that can be cut back or left. The tree is long-lived beyond any gardener's span: plant it for the next generation as much as for your own.

    Propagation

    Take semi-ripe cuttings 10–15 cm long in late summer (July–August), strip the lower leaves, and keep them in sandy, free-draining mix, just damp. Cuttings keep the parent's olives true; seed does not, and takes many years to fruit. Roots can take a few weeks or a few months to form — keep the mix damp, not wet, or the cutting rots.

    Safety

    • Table olives are salty — the brine is the point — so anyone watching salt should eat them in small handfuls, not by the bowlful.
    • Olive pollen is one of the strongest hay-fever allergens in the Mediterranean, and people allergic to the pollen can also react to the fruit, though a true olive fruit allergy is rare.
    • Leaf extract can lower blood pressure and blood sugar, so anyone taking blood pressure or diabetes medicine should talk to a doctor before using it, and the European monograph does not recommend leaf medicines for children or for people with severe heart or kidney disease.
    • The oil itself is safe as a food in ordinary amounts, but it is calorie-dense — about 120 calories a tablespoon — so it is a swap for other fats, butter or margarine, not something to add on top of them.

    Sources

    • Estruch et al. (2018) — Primary prevention of cardiovascular disease with a Mediterranean diet (New England Journal of Medicine) — 7,447 adults, Mediterranean diet plus extra virgin olive oil, median 4.8 years, major heart events about 30% lower
    • Ros et al. (2014) — Mediterranean diet and cardiovascular health: teachings of the PREDIMED study (Advances in Nutrition) — the diabetes finding among 3,541 people without diabetes, and the blood pressure and lipid findings
    • Covas et al. (2006) — The effect of polyphenols in olive oil on heart disease risk factors: a randomised trial, the EUROLIVE study (Annals of Internal Medicine) — 200 healthy men, 25 ml a day, HDL rose and oxidised LDL fell as polyphenol content rose
    • Lockyer et al. (2017) — Impact of phenolic-rich olive leaf extract on blood pressure, plasma lipids and inflammatory markers: a randomised controlled trial (European Journal of Nutrition) — 60 pre-hypertensive men, 136 mg oleuropein a day for six weeks
    • Lamti et al. (2025) — Efficacy of olive leaf extracts in controlling blood pressure in hypertensive patients: a double-blind randomized clinical trial (Journal of Hypertension) — 621 treated hypertensive patients, 24-hour systolic pressure down 6.4 mmHg against 1.5 on placebo at twelve weeks
    • Lauwers et al. (2026) — Evaluation of the effect of olive extracts on blood pressure and cardiovascular health markers in adults (PLOS One) — 56 adults, no significant difference from placebo
    • Tessier et al. (2024) — Consumption of olive oil and diet quality and risk of dementia-related death (JAMA Network Open) — 92,383 adults followed 28 years, more than 7 g a day linked to a 28% lower risk of dementia-related death
    • Guasch-Ferré et al. (2022) — Consumption of olive oil and diet quality and risk of mortality (Journal of the American College of Cardiology) — 92,383 adults, higher olive oil intake linked to lower total and cause-specific mortality
    • European Medicines Agency — European Union herbal monograph on Olea europaea L., folium (2017) — the traditional-use standing for olive leaf, mild water retention, adults only
    • European Food Safety Authority (2011) — Olive oil polyphenols and protection of blood lipids from oxidative stress — the allowed claim at 5 mg hydroxytyrosol per 20 g of oil
    • USDA FoodData Central — Olives, ripe, canned and Olives, pickled, canned or bottled, green — the nutrition and sodium figures
    • Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — the accepted name Olea europaea, its place in the olive family, and its native range
    • World History Encyclopedia — The Olive in the Ancient Mediterranean — first cultivation, the spread with Phoenician and Greek colonisation, Athena's gift, Olympic wreaths, and the ancient oil trade
    • Rhizopoulou (2007) — Olea europaea L.: a botanical contribution to culture — the tree's age, the fossil leaves of Santorini, and Theophrastus on its long life

    Kiwi

    Actinidia chinensis var. deliciosa

    Culinary

    Digestive HealthImmune HealthSleep

    Fresh

    Kiwi is a small brown fruit with bright green flesh and a ring of tiny black seeds — sharp, sweet and juicy, eaten with a spoon or peeled like a peach. It grows on a strong woody vine that climbs and twines, with big heart-shaped leaves and creamy white flowers in late spring. The fruit came from the mountain forests of China, and it only got its name in New Zealand, after the little flightless kiwi bird. One fruit holds more vitamin C than an orange, and two a day have been shown in a proper trial to keep the bowels moving.

    Cultivars

    The green kiwis, all of them Actinidia chinensis var. deliciosa — the green kiwi long known as Actinidia deliciosa:

    Hayward

    The standard — the big, egg-shaped, brown and fuzzy fruit with bright green flesh, the one in nearly every shop.

    Bruno, Abbott, Allison, Monty (Montgomery) and Greensill

    The older New Zealand green kinds, smaller or less rich in vitamin C, all overshadowed by Hayward.

    Blake

    A smaller, earlier green kind.

    Saanichton 12

    A large-fruited green kind grown in the Pacific north-west.

    Vincent

    The low-chill green kind for warm winters, needing only about 200 hours of winter cold.

    The gold kiwis are Actinidia chinensis var. chinensis, not var. deliciosa — a close kin, not a form of the green kiwi:

    Hort16A

    Sold as Zespri Gold, it was the first gold kiwi in the shops, launched in 2000, with smooth bronze skin and sweet yellow flesh; it is mostly out of commercial growing now, badly hit by the vine disease Psa.

    SunGold

    'Zesy002', the gold kiwi in the shops now, sweeter and less sharp than the green.

    Hongyang

    The red-fleshed kind from China, gold flesh with a red heart.

    The smooth-skinned, grape-sized "kiwi berries" sold to eat whole are Actinidia arguta, the hardy kiwi — a different species again, not a cultivar of this plant, and none of what is told here belongs to it.

    • Kiwi is a Chinese fruit through and through. It grows wild in the mountain forests of central and southern China, along the Yangtze River valley, climbing through the trees at 800 to 1,400 metres up. Its old Chinese name is mihoutao, which means macaque peach — monkey peach — because the monkeys of those forests eat the ripe fruit. Other old names call it the vine pear and the sheep peach.
    • The first writing that can be pinned to the plant is a poem from the Tang dynasty, in the 700s, by Cen Shen, describing a mihoutao plant growing above a well in what is now Shaanxi. The first clear written description of the fruit itself comes from the Song dynasty, in the 1100s. For centuries after that it was gathered from wild vines, not farmed. It was rarely grown on purpose, because it was picked as a wild food and a folk medicine, not as a crop.
    • In old Chinese practice the ripe fruit was given as medicine, not eaten for pleasure. It was given to children to help them grow, and to women who had just given birth to help them recover. The old books call it cooling: it was used to quench thirst, to settle a poor appetite, and to help slow digestion, with the fruit said to act on the stomach and the gut. The root, the vine and the branches were used in folk practice too — for aching joints, swellings and bruises — but those uses were never tested in people, and they are told here as tradition, not as proof.
    • The fruit reached the rest of the world through New Zealand. In 1904 Isabel Fraser, headmistress of Wanganui Girls' College, came home from visiting her missionary sister in China carrying kiwifruit seeds. A Wanganui nurseryman, Alexander Allison, planted them in 1906 and grew the first plants. For years the fruit was a garden novelty, sold under the name Chinese gooseberry.
    • The fruit that filled the shops came from one nurseryman's eye. Hayward Wright, an Auckland nurseryman, picked out vines whose fruit was big, tasty and kept well, and grew them by grafting. In 1956 that fruit was named Hayward after him, and by the late 1960s it was the standard fruit of the export trade — the green kiwi the world still buys.
    • The name changed in 1959. Auckland fruit packers Turners & Growers dropped "Chinese gooseberry" — first for "melonette", then for "kiwifruit", after New Zealand's kiwi bird — because the old name sounded dull and the new one sold the fruit. The name stuck, and "kiwi" became the short form in many countries. In China the fruit is still mihoutao, and it is counted as a national fruit.
    • From New Zealand the vine spread to orchards in Italy, Chile, Greece, Spain, Japan and the United States, and in the last decades of the 1900s China itself began growing it as a crop — by 1998 China held tens of thousands of hectares of kiwifruit orchards. In 1988 New Zealand set up the Kiwifruit Marketing Board, now called Zespri, to sell the fruit to the world.
    • In the kitchen the fruit is eaten raw, cut in half and scooped out, or peeled and sliced. Sliced kiwi crowns the pavlova, the meringue dessert of New Zealand and Australia. It goes into fruit salads, juices and smoothies, and into wine and vinegar in China and New Zealand. The fruit holds actinidin, an enzyme that breaks down protein — the same work a meat tenderiser does — so crushed kiwi softens meat in a marinade, and raw kiwi curdles milk and stops gelatin setting. That is why kiwi never goes into a milk pudding or a jelly unless it has been cooked first.
    • What is in the fruit, first. In 100 grams of green kiwi — about one and a half fruits — there are about 61 calories, about 3 grams of fibre, about 93 milligrams of vitamin C, about 312 milligrams of potassium, and useful amounts of vitamin K, folate and vitamin E. One fruit on its own holds around 70 milligrams of vitamin C, close to a whole day's need. Gold kiwi holds more vitamin C still, and less fibre.
    • The bowel effect is the best-tested thing about kiwi, and it rests on a real trial in people. In a trial across New Zealand, Italy and Japan, 184 adults — 63 healthy, 60 with long-term constipation, and 61 with constipation-type irritable bowel — ate two green kiwis a day for four weeks, then switched to a fibre powder (psyllium) for four weeks, so each person tried both. The kiwi weeks brought about one and a half more full, easy bowel movements a week in both constipated groups, and people said their guts felt more comfortable. Two kiwis hold about 6 grams of fibre, and the fibre holds water, which softens the stool — but fibre alone does not explain the whole effect, and the trial did not settle what else is at work. The people in the trial knew what they were eating — a kiwi cannot be disguised — so some of the comfort may come from knowing. Even so, the food safety authority of Europe looked at six human trials together in 2021 and found the link held, and in 2025 the European Union allowed the claim that eating green kiwi helps normal bowel function by making stools more frequent. Two large green kiwis, about 200 grams of flesh, is the amount the claim rests on. Human trials
    • Sleep has one small trial behind it, and it must be told at its true size. In 2011, 24 adults who said they slept badly ate two green kiwis one hour before bed every night for four weeks. They fell asleep about 35% faster, spent about 29% less time awake in the night, slept about 13% longer, and their sleep was rated about 5% more efficient. Those are real changes, but the trial had no comparison group — everyone knew they were eating kiwi, so hope and habit may have played a part. The researchers point to the fruit's serotonin, a brain chemical tied to the sleep cycle, and to its folate and antioxidants as a possible reason. A later small trial in 24 young men found kiwi shifted serotonin in the body and improved morning alertness, without proving a steady sleep gain. Two kiwis before bed is a cheap, harmless thing to try; it is not a proven sleep treatment. Human · small
    • Colds have one small trial behind it too, and it used gold kiwi, not green. In 2012, 32 healthy adults aged 65 and over ate the flesh of four gold kiwis a day — or two bananas, for comparison — for four weeks each. The kiwi did not stop colds coming. But when a cold did come, head congestion lasted fewer days and felt less severe, and sore throats lasted fewer days. Blood tests showed vitamin C, vitamin E and folate all rose, and one marker of damage from stress in the body fell. The body's own germ-fighting cells showed no change. Four kiwis a day is more than most people eat, and the trial was small — 32 people — so the gain is modest and needs a bigger trial to confirm. Human · small
    • Blood pressure has one trial as well, small and worth telling plainly. In 2015, 118 men and women with mildly raised blood pressure ate three green kiwis a day, or one apple a day, for eight weeks. Day-and-night blood pressure readings fell a little more in the kiwi group — about 3.6 points off the top number and 1.9 off the bottom one. But blood pressure taken in the clinic did not change, and the blood vessels themselves showed no change. Three kiwis a day is a lot of fruit, and one trial is not enough to call kiwi a blood-pressure food. It never stands in place of prescribed medicine. Human · small
    • Two fences belong here. First, vitamin C is needed to build collagen, the stuff that holds skin together — but no trial has tested kiwi itself on skin, so no skin claim is made. Second, the laboratory work — kiwi extracts calming swelling or killing germs in dishes, and easing signs of disease in animals — is laboratory and animal work, and none of it shows what eating the fruit does in a person. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • Sun: Full sun, in a warm spot sheltered from wind — give it room, sun and air, and keep it out of frost pockets and hard wind
    • Soil: Deep, fertile, well-drained ground on the acid side, pH about 5.6 to 6.5, with compost worked in
    • Environment: USDA zones 7 to 9 — mild winters and long warm summers; it needs a real winter to flower and fruit: Hayward needs several hundred hours of cold below 45 °F, while low-chill kinds like Vincent need only about 200; late frosts are the enemy — they kill the young shoots and flowers — and the vine needs a long, frost-free summer, 225 to 240 days, to ripen its fruit
    • Planter or ground: Ground, on something big and strong to climb on: a pergola, a stout trellis or a fence — it is a strong woody vine that climbs and twines, growing 20 to 30 feet long in a season, and a light frame will not hold it
    • Water: The vine is thirsty — water deeply so the soil is wet a foot down, and never let the roots dry right out — but never leave it standing in water, which rots the roots
    • When to pick: Pick the fruit hard in late autumn, as late as frost allows, once a cut fruit shows black seeds — it ripens indoors, not on the vine

    Garden notes

    • Male and female: the vine carries its sexes on separate plants. Only the female vines bear fruit, and only when a male vine flowers beside them and bees carry the pollen across. One male, planted in the middle, can serve up to eight females. Buy named plants, not seedlings, so you know which sex you are getting — Tomuri and Matua are the usual male partners for Hayward. A few kinds, like 'Jenny', set some fruit on their own, but even they fruit better with a male nearby.
    • Training and pruning: train one straight trunk up to a high wire, then two permanent side branches along it, like a T. Fruit grows on one-year-old canes, so prune the female hard every winter, cutting back to ten to twenty fruiting canes, and prune the male straight after flowering. Summer pruning keeps the shade off the fruit so it ripens.
    • A vine grown from a bought plant takes three to seven years to bear. The flowers are white to cream, opening in late spring; the leaves are big and heart-shaped, the young shoots covered in red hairs, and the leaves fall in winter.

    Propagation

    In midsummer, take a cutting 5 to 8 inches long with 2 or 3 joints from new wood, keep one leaf at the top, dip the base in rooting hormone, and set it in perlite under a clear cover to hold the damp in. Roots form in 6 to 8 weeks. Some types root poorly and may need grafting instead, and a plant grown from seed will not match its parent.

    Safety

    • Kiwi allergy is real and has grown more common as the fruit has spread. Most often it is a mouth allergy: itching, tingling and swelling of the lips, mouth and throat soon after eating. Some people get hives from touching the fruit, and a few have a severe whole-body reaction.
    • People allergic to birch pollen often react to kiwi, and so do people allergic to natural rubber latex — the latex-fruit link — because the proteins look alike to the body. The main culprit is actinidin itself, the fruit's own enzyme. Anyone who has reacted to kiwi should not test themselves with more of it, and anyone with a latex allergy should be careful with kiwi, banana, avocado and chestnut, which share the same cross-reaction. Cooking may weaken the proteins that cause the allergy, but it does not make the fruit safe for someone who is allergic.
    • Kiwi can sting and irritate the mouth if a lot is eaten at once, which is the actinidin at work.
    • Two large green kiwis hold about 80 micrograms of vitamin K, which matters for blood thinning — anyone taking warfarin should talk to their prescriber before making big changes to how much kiwi they eat regularly.

    Sources

    • Gearry et al. (2023) — two green kiwis a day for constipation and gut comfort, 184 adults in three countries
    • EFSA NDA Panel et al. (2021) — green kiwifruit and normal bowel function, the health-claim opinion
    • European Commission (2025) — Regulation (EU) 2025/1560, the authorised green kiwifruit bowel-function claim
    • Lin et al. (2011) — two kiwis before bed and sleep, 24 adults over four weeks
    • Hunter et al. (2012) — four gold kiwis a day, colds and vitamin C in 32 older adults
    • Svendsen et al. (2015) — three kiwis a day and blood pressure in 118 adults
    • Te Ara — the Encyclopedia of New Zealand — kiwifruit history, names and varieties
    • USDA FoodData Central — green kiwifruit food values per 100 g
    • Plants of the World Online, Kew — the accepted name and where it grows wild
    • DermNet NZ — kiwifruit allergy and the latex cross-reaction
    • GrowYourOwn — Kiwifruit: how to grow it (zones, chill hours, trellis and pruning, citing university extension guidance)

    Persimmon

    Diospyros kaki

    CulinaryMedicinal

    FreshCookedDried

    Persimmon is the bright orange autumn fruit of a small tree from China, and its name in Japan, kaki, is the name the tree carries in Latin too. The fruit hangs on bare branches late in the year, after the leaves have fallen, like lanterns left on the tree. One medium fruit is sweet and honey-like, soft to spoon when it is a Hachiya, crisp to bite when it is a Fuyu. The tree is a member of the ebony family, the family that gives the hard black wood called ebony, and it grows 15 to 25 feet tall in a garden, with broad, stiff, dark green leaves that turn gold and red in autumn. The name Diospyros is often read as "divine fruit", from Greek words for god and grain, and the fruit has lived up to the name in the places that grow it best: China, Japan and Korea, where it has been food, medicine and an autumn sign for more than two thousand years.

    Cultivars

    Persimmon kinds fall into two groups, and the group decides how the fruit is eaten. Non-astringent kinds lose their mouth-drying tannins early and are eaten firm and crisp:

    Fuyu

    The squat, tomato-shaped fruit most often sold, sweet and dense.

    Jiro

    Much like Fuyu but a little larger and flatter.

    Izu

    An early, smaller, rounder fruit that ripens two or three weeks before Fuyu.

    Gosho

    An older Japanese kind of the same group.

    Suruga

    An older Japanese kind of the same group.

    Astringent kinds stay full of soluble tannins — the plant compounds that dry the mouth — until the fruit turns completely soft:

    Hachiya

    The tall, acorn-shaped fruit, the classic drying kind and the one most often baked with.

    Saijo

    A smaller, very sweet Japanese kind, seedless.

    Tanenashi

    A seedless kind much used in the American South for pulp and baking.

    Hiratanenashi

    A flat, seedless Japanese kind.

    Tamopan

    A Chinese kind with a strange flat, turban-like shape.

    Pollination-variant kinds change with their seeds: a seeded fruit turns brown inside and loses its astringency, while a seedless fruit of the same kind stays astringent.

    Chocolate

    Also called Maru, it is the best known, named for the brown streaks in its flesh, not for a chocolate taste.

    Hyakume

    Belongs to the same group.

    Nishimura Wase

    Also sold as Coffeecake, and belongs to the same group.

    'Sharon Fruit' is not a kind of its own. It is a trade name for the astringent kind 'Triumph', grown in Israel and treated after picking to take the astringency out, so it can be eaten firm.

    • Persimmon is a tree of China first. It grew wild there and was first farmed there more than 2,000 years ago, and the earliest Chinese farm records of it reach back to the Han dynasty. From China it travelled to Japan in the 7th century and to Korea in the 14th century, and in all three countries it became one of the great autumn fruits. Marco Polo, travelling in the early 14th century, recorded the Chinese trade in persimmons. The tree reached California and southern Europe in the 1800s — seed first reached the United States in 1856, sent from Japan by Commodore Perry — and Brazil in the 1890s, carried there with Japanese settlers.
    • In Japan the fruit is kaki, and it is one of the great signs of autumn. It appears in haiku as a season word, in paintings and prints, and on the table through the cold months. The dried fruit, hoshigaki, is the heart of that autumn keeping: astringent fruit is peeled by hand, hung in the sun and wind for weeks, and rubbed and massaged as it dries, until it turns dark, sweet and soft, dusted with its own white sugar bloom. Hoshigaki keeps far longer than fresh fruit, and in the days before cold storage it was winter food. It is still served at New Year as a sign of good luck and long life, and it is used in sweet-making. Korea keeps the fruit the same way, as gotgam, dried persimmon, and soaks it in a spiced punch, sujeonggwa, with ginger and cinnamon for feasts and the Lunar New Year.
    • The leaves have a life of their own. In Japan the leaf tea is kaki no ha cha, in Korea gamnip-cha, in China shiye cha: dried leaves steeped in hot water, drunk as an everyday drink and, in folk medicine, linked with blood pressure, coughs and bleeding. In Nara, in Japan, pressed sushi of mackerel or salmon is wrapped in persimmon leaves — kakinoha-zushi — and the leaves are said to help keep the fish and to lend it a faint scent. In Chinese medicine the leaf, called Shi Ye, was first written down as a medicine in the Diannan Bencao, in the Ming dynasty, for long-lasting sores of the lower leg, and later books link it with cough, bleeding, thirst and high blood pressure. The dried fruit's white bloom was also used in Chinese medicine as a cooling remedy for the lungs, and the fruit stalk for hiccough. All of this is folk use, told as folk use: the leaf's place in medicine rests on long use, not on a trial in people.
    • The fruit is eaten fresh, dried, and cooked. Non-astringent kinds are sliced into salads, eaten out of hand, and cooked into puddings and breads. Astringent kinds, once jelly-soft, are spooned like a custard, or pulped for baking. The unripe fruit's tannins were also put to work outside the kitchen: the juice of unripe persimmon, rich in tannin, was used in Japan as a dye and a wood stain, and to stiffen cloth and fishing nets.
    • What is in the fruit, first. One medium raw Japanese persimmon, about 168 grams, holds about 118 calories, 31 grams of carbohydrate, 6 grams of fibre, and almost no fat. It gives about 136 micrograms of vitamin A, mostly as carotenoids — the yellow-orange pigments that give the fruit its colour, including beta-cryptoxanthin and beta-carotene, which the body can turn into vitamin A — plus 12.6 milligrams of vitamin C, 0.6 milligrams of manganese, and 270 milligrams of potassium. Drying the fruit keeps the fibre and the minerals but destroys nearly all of the vitamin C, and it packs the sugars and calories into a smaller bite.
    • The strongest human evidence is one small trial, and it tested a made ingredient, not the ripe fruit on a plate. In a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 40 adults with raised cholesterol, cookie bars holding tannin-rich fibre from young, unripe persimmon fruit — 3 grams or 5 grams, three times a day before meals, for 12 weeks — lowered total cholesterol at both doses, and lowered LDL, the "bad" cholesterol, at the 5-gram dose. HDL, the "good" cholesterol, and triglycerides, the fats in the blood, did not change. The fibre came from young fruit, not from a ripe persimmon eaten whole, and no second trial has repeated the result. Eating a ripe persimmon is not the same as eating those bars. Human · small
    • The blood-sugar evidence is thinner still, and it is a single-dose test, not a treatment. In a small placebo-controlled crossover test in healthy adults, 1.88 grams of a prepared persimmon tannin, taken half an hour before a starch drink, slowed the rise in blood sugar at 15 and 30 minutes, and lowered insulin at 15 minutes. The tannin was a prepared extract, the test was one drink on one day, and the people tested were healthy. It shows a tannin can slow starch digestion in the gut for a short while. It does not show that eating persimmons lowers blood sugar day to day, or helps anyone with diabetes. Human · small
    • The rest of the health story is laboratory and animal work, and it stays there. In dishes and in rats and mice, persimmon tannins and leaf extracts have shown antioxidant activity, slowed starch-digesting enzymes, and changed blood fats and blood sugar. None of that shows what eating the fruit does in a person, and none of it is carried here as a human benefit. The leaf tea's link with blood pressure is folk use, and the laboratory work behind it has never been tested as a treatment in people. The tea does not replace blood-pressure medicine. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • Fibre and the gut need a straight telling, because the two kinds pull in opposite directions. Ripe fruit adds useful fibre, and fibre in food generally helps keep the bowels moving. But the tannins in unripe, astringent fruit can firm the stools and slow the gut down, and that is why the old advice that persimmon suits constipation is only half true: ripe fruit helps, unripe fruit can do the opposite.
    • When to plant: Plant in late winter or early spring, 10 to 20 feet from other trees and buildings, to fit the kind's full size; buy a grafted tree, not a seedling — a seedling takes years longer to fruit and may never fruit well
    • Sun: Full sun, at least six to eight hours a day
    • Soil: Deep, well-drained ground — it grows in many soils but does best in a loam around pH 6.0 to 7.5, and it hates wet feet: standing water rots its fleshy roots faster than cold kills it, and heavy wet clay is the commonest cause of a young tree failing
    • Environment: USDA zones 7 to 10; it is hurt by cold below about 10 °F (−12 °C), and young trees are hurt sooner, so in the cold end of its range it wants the warmest, most sheltered spot in the garden; it needs only 100 to 200 chill hours, the cold hours in winter that wake the tree for spring, so a mild winter is no bar to fruit
    • Planter or ground: Ground: most kinds reach 15 to 25 feet tall and wide, though some stay smaller
    • Water: Water steadily through the first year or two while it settles, and through dry summers while the fruit swells; once settled it asks for little
    • When to pick: The fruit ripens in autumn, October into November: pick a Fuyu when it is fully coloured and still firm, and eat it crisp or let it soften a little; pick a Hachiya when it is fully coloured but still firm, and let it soften indoors until it is jelly-soft and the skin turns almost see-through — never eat it firm

    Garden notes

    • Many kinds set fruit without a pollinator, and some set seedless fruit from unfertilised flowers; a pollinator nearby gives larger, seeded fruit and a heavier crop in some kinds.
    • Prune little, and prune late, in late winter before the late bud-break. Thin the centre for air and light, take out dead wood and crossing branches, and never cut hard: the fruit grows on the current year's shoots, which grow from one-year-old wood, so hard pruning takes the next crop with it. Thin the young fruit in a heavy year — take up to half — or the branches will bend and break under the weight, and the fruit left will be small.
    • A fruit left on the tree after leaf-fall will keep colouring, and a hard frost will spoil it. The leaves turn gold and red before they fall, and the bare tree with its orange fruit is one of the fine sights of the autumn garden.

    Propagation

    Grow a seedling from a ripe fruit's seed in autumn, after a cold spell in the fridge, to make a rootstock. Then graft a cutting of a named variety onto it while the tree is still bare in winter. Seed alone will not give you the same fruit as the parent tree — grafting is the only way to keep a named variety true.

    Safety

    • An astringent persimmon, like Hachiya, is eaten only when it is completely soft, like jelly. A firm one will dry the mouth out and taste bitter.
    • Eating a lot of unripe, astringent fruit — especially the peel, and especially on an empty stomach — can, rarely, cause the tannins to knot food into a hard mass in the stomach called a bezoar, a diospyrobezoar, which can block the stomach or bowel and bring pain, vomiting and ulcers. Most cases follow a clear pattern: large amounts of unripe fruit, eaten with the peel, on an empty stomach, or in people with delayed stomach emptying.
    • Anyone with delayed stomach emptying, for example with diabetic gastroparesis, or who has had stomach surgery, should avoid persimmon or ask a doctor first. A ripe fruit, eaten in a normal amount, is safe food for most people.

    Sources

    • Gato et al. (2013) — Persimmon fruit tannin-rich fibre reduces cholesterol levels in humans (Annals of Nutrition and Metabolism) — 40 adults, tannin-rich fibre from young fruit in cookie bars, 3 or 5 grams three times a day for 12 weeks
    • Takemori et al. (2022) — Effects of persimmon fruit polyphenols on postprandial plasma glucose elevation in rats and humans (Journal of Nutritional Science and Vitaminology) — 1.88 grams of prepared kaki-tannin before a starch drink, small crossover test in healthy adults
    • Morton (1987) — Japanese Persimmon, in Fruits of Warm Climates — origin and spread, the two fruit kinds, the named cultivars, climate, soil and growing
    • Xie et al. (2015) — Persimmon (Diospyros kaki L.) leaves: a review on traditional uses, phytochemistry and pharmacological properties (Journal of Ethnopharmacology) — the leaf in Chinese medicine, first recorded in the Diannan Bencao, and the folk uses that follow
    • Hossain & Shahidi (2023) — Persimmon leaves: nutritional, pharmaceutical, and industrial potential — a review (Plants) — leaf tea in Japan and Korea, and the leaf's traditional uses
    • USDA FoodData Central — Persimmons, Japanese, raw — one fruit of 168 grams: 118 calories, 6 grams of fibre, vitamin A 136 micrograms, vitamin C 12.6 milligrams, manganese 0.6 milligrams, potassium 270 milligrams
    • Seattle Japanese Garden (2019) — Persimmon: the divine fruit of autumn — the name, hoshigaki, and the fruit's place in Japanese autumn

    Breadfruit

    Artocarpus altilis

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Blood Sugar Health

    CookedDried

    Breadfruit is a tall tropical tree whose fruit feeds whole islands. Its name is plain and true: when the big green fruit is baked or roasted, its soft, starchy flesh tastes and feels like fresh bread. The fruit grows on the tree — round, bumpy, green to yellow-green, often as big as a small football and weighing one to three kilos — and a single tree can bear 50 to 200 of them in a year. The tree is a member of the mulberry and fig family, and its kin are the jackfruit, the mulberry and the fig. In Hawaii it is called 'ulu, in Tahiti 'uru, in the Philippines rimas, and in French arbre à pain, the bread tree.

    Cultivars

    Breadfruit has more named kinds than almost any other food tree. The Breadfruit Institute in Hawaii keeps more than a hundred cultivars in its collection, and in Samoa alone 46 cultivar names were recorded from islanders in one study. Names change from island to island, and one name can cover different trees in different places. The kinds below are the best-known and best-described.

    Ma'afala

    From Samoa. A shorter, more compact tree than most, with small fruit and creamy, pale yellow flesh that turns tender when cooked. The kind most often planted in new breadfruit orchards, and the kind being introduced to the Caribbean, including Jamaica, for its high protein and mineral content.

    'Ulu

    The Hawaiian 'ulu, also called 'ulu maoli. The canoe plant brought to Hawaii by the first Polynesian settlers. Round fruit, rougher skin, with dried sap and scabbing on the rind, often weighing more than four pounds.

    Ulu Fiti

    From Fiji by way of Samoa. Yellow flesh, tender and a little sweet when mature, with a soft, moist texture when cooked. Good for chips and fries.

    Puou

    From Samoa and Tahiti. A large fruit with few seeds, good roasted, and in one study the kind with the highest levels of carotenoids, the orange plant pigments the body turns into vitamin A.

    Afara

    From Tahiti. Firm, dense, starchy flesh, white or creamy, and one of the highest-yielding kinds.

    Meion

    From Chuuk in Micronesia. Its name means "ease", for how easily the cooked fruit pounds soft. An early-bearing kind with light yellow, creamy flesh.

    Meinpadahk

    A natural cross between breadfruit and its close kin Artocarpus mariannensis. Bright, waxy green skin that does not scab or crust as it ripens.

    The first split in breadfruit is seeded or seedless. Most kinds grown for food are seedless, and seedless kinds are grown not from seed but from root shoots, root cuttings, air layering or grafting, so that each new tree is true to its kind. Seeded kinds are a delicacy on many islands, and their cooked seeds are eaten. The breadnut, Artocarpus camansi, is a different species with many large seeds — a close kin, not a breadfruit cultivar.

    • Breadfruit comes from the far west of the Pacific. It is thought to be native to New Guinea, and people have grown it there and across the islands for more than three thousand years. Long before any European saw it, island voyagers carried young trees with them in their canoes from island to island, planting them as they settled new shores — to Hawaii, to Tahiti, to Samoa, to Fiji and beyond. It became a staple food, the food a family could count on, because one tree feeds many people and asks for little care.
    • The tree is a handsome evergreen, 15 to 20 metres tall, sometimes more, with a straight trunk and a wide crown of huge, glossy, deeply lobed leaves, often a foot to three feet long. The leaves are so large they are used as plates and as wrapping for food. The fruit hangs from the branches on short, thick stalks. Most kinds carry no seeds at all. Seeded kinds carry small, brown, edible seeds that taste nutty when cooked.
    • Europeans first met breadfruit in 1769, when Captain Cook reached Tahiti and the botanist Joseph Banks saw islanders living well on the fruit. Banks saw a cheap, filling food for the enslaved people on the sugar plantations of the British West Indies, and he put the idea to King George III. The king agreed, and in 1787 Lieutenant William Bligh sailed on HMS Bounty to fetch the plants. Bligh reached Tahiti, collected just over a thousand young breadfruit plants, and set sail for the Caribbean. Three weeks out, on 28 April 1789, his crew mutinied under Fletcher Christian. Bligh and eighteen loyal men were set adrift in a small open boat, and the mutineers threw the breadfruit plants overboard. Bligh sailed that open boat 5,822 kilometres in 47 days to Timor, and lived to sail again. In 1792 he went back to Tahiti, collected more than 2,600 plants, and this time brought them safely to St Vincent and Jamaica. The tree he planted in the botanic garden at St Vincent in 1793 is said to still stand there. Breadfruit has grown in the Caribbean ever since.
    • Breadfruit is eaten at every stage of its ripening. Young fruit is cooked as a vegetable. Mature fruit, still green, is roasted, baked, boiled or fried, and eaten like potato or yam. Ripe fruit turns soft and sweet, and is eaten as a fruit. The seeds of seeded kinds are cooked and eaten. Dried fruit is ground into flour, which keeps well and can be baked into bread. The flour has no gluten in it.
    • Because the fruit ripens all at once and spoils within days, islanders long ago learned to keep it. On many islands the fruit was peeled, softened and packed into leaf-lined pits in the ground, where it fermented into a sharp-smelling paste called ma in Polynesia. Washed and cooked, the paste was good to eat, and it kept in the pit for a year or two, until the next harvest. Drying in the sun and freezing are the newer ways of keeping it.
    • The tree gives far more than food. Its light, strong timber is used for houses, canoes, furniture and surfboards. Its milky sap is used to caulk canoes, as a glue, and as a chewing gum. The smooth bark is fibrous and was once made into tapa cloth. The flowers are burned to keep mosquitoes away. The leaves, bark, sap and flowers are all used in island medicine: in Trinidad and the Bahamas a tea of the leaves is drunk for high blood pressure; sap thinned with rainwater is given for diarrhoea; chewed young leaves are used against food poisoning. That medicine use is tradition, and it is told as tradition.
    • What is in the fruit, first. Raw breadfruit, per 100 grams, holds about 103 calories, 27 grams of carbohydrate, nearly 5 grams of fibre, about 1 gram of protein and almost no fat. It is rich in potassium — 490 milligrams per 100 grams — and in vitamin C, 29 milligrams. A cup of the fruit, about 220 grams, gives around 227 calories, 11 grams of fibre, 1,080 milligrams of potassium and 64 milligrams of vitamin C, about 71% of a day's need. Its protein is unusual for a starchy food: it holds all the essential amino acids, the building blocks of protein the body cannot make for itself, with good amounts of leucine, isoleucine and valine.
    • The fruit's effect on blood sugar has been measured in people, and that is the strongest human evidence there is. Several researchers have measured the glycemic index — the measure of how fast a food raises blood sugar — and found breadfruit low, lower than wheat, cassava, yam and potatoes. The number shifts with how the fruit is cooked: flour and some cooked forms test in the high forties to low sixties, while fried forms can test higher. So the plain truth is that breadfruit, cooked plainly, raises blood sugar at a lower rate than most other starchy staples — and frying it can undo that advantage. No trial has tested breadfruit as a treatment for diabetes. Human trials
    • The one full diet study is in mice, not people. In a 2020 study, mice were fed for 21 days on a diet in which breadfruit flour replaced all the wheat. The mice grew well, showed no sign of sickness, and grew faster than the mice fed wheat. In a laboratory digestion model, breadfruit protein was easier to digest than wheat protein. The study found no harm from a breadfruit diet — and no harm in mice is not proof of a benefit in people. Animal studies
    • Two small trials tested the leaf, not the fruit, and the fence matters. In a 2023 trial in Indonesia, 39 adults with type 2 diabetes took 500 milligrams a day of breadfruit leaf extract for 21 days. Their fasting blood sugar fell by 88.5 milligrams per decilitre, against 33.9 in the group without the extract — a real difference, but from one small trial of 39 people over three weeks, of an extract, not the fruit. In a 2024 trial, 36 adults took leaf extract for 21 days and their blood pressure fell a little, but no more than in the group given the dummy capsules. The blood pressure claim fails its own test. Neither trial says anything about eating the fruit. Human · small
    • The laboratory work is laboratory work. In dishes, breadfruit seeds hold compounds that hold back the enzymes that break down starch, and the fruit holds phenols, the plant chemicals that mop up the damage of free radicals. None of that shows what eating the fruit does in a person, and none of it is claimed here as a human benefit. Lab studies
    • When to plant: Grow it from a young tree raised by root cutting, air layering or grafting, planted at the start of the warm, rainy season
    • Sun: Full sun, six to eight hours a day or more — less sun means no fruit
    • Soil: Deep, fertile, well-drained ground is best, a sandy loam around pH 5.5 to 7.5, fed with compost; it tolerates sandy and coral soils, but not waterlogged ground or salty soil — roots sitting in water rot
    • Environment: USDA zones 10 to 12 — south Florida and Hawaii at the cool edge, and the warm tropics beyond; frost kills it, growth stalls below 50 °F (10 °C), and damage starts below 40 °F (4 °C); it wants steady heat, 70 to 90 °F (21 to 32 °C), high humidity above 60%, and 60 to 150 inches of rain a year, in the lowlands below 2,000 feet, with shelter from strong wind, which tears its great leaves
    • Planter or ground: Ground, in a large piece of ground in a frost-free place — never in a small garden, never near a house or a power line; it grows 15 to 20 metres tall, sometimes more, with a crown as wide as a house
    • Water: Water steadily for the first two or three years while it settles; after that it asks for less, and drier places need steady watering
    • When to pick: Harvest when the skin turns yellow-green and yields slightly to pressure, and drops of milky sap appear on the rind; a fresh green fruit keeps seven to ten days, and a ripe one three to seven

    Garden notes

    • Be honest about the size and the warmth before anything else. Breadfruit is a tree for the true tropics, not for a temperate garden.
    • Mulch thickly around the base to hold moisture. A tree fruits in three to five years from planting, sometimes in two from a root cutting, and bears most heavily from five to twenty years old.
    • Prune to keep the fruit within reach and to let air move through the crown, and take out dead wood. The tree drops large leaves and fruit, so plant it where the fall does no harm.
    • In a cool store at about 12 °C, wrapped fruit keeps around twenty days — colder than that damages it.

    Propagation

    Breadfruit is grown from its own roots, not from seed — most eating types are seedless. When a shoot at least 30 cm tall grows from a surface root, cut the root 10–15 cm on each side of the shoot and pot it in well-drained soil, shaded and kept moist until it takes hold. Or cut a healthy root 1.5–6 cm thick into 12–30 cm lengths after fruiting ends and lay them in loose, moist soil. It needs a warm, frost-free place to grow.

    Safety

    • Breadfruit is a cooked food: the fruit is roasted, baked, boiled or fried, and it is not eaten raw as a rule, though the ripe fruit of seeded kinds is eaten raw as a snack in the Pacific.
    • The leaf extract may lower blood sugar and blood pressure, so anyone taking medicine for diabetes or for blood pressure should take care with leaf preparations and speak to a doctor first. The safety of breadfruit leaf preparations in pregnancy has not been studied.

    Sources

    • Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — the accepted name Artocarpus altilis, the mulberry family, the New Guinea origin, the tree's height, and the Bounty mission
    • Liu et al. (2020) — Breadfruit flour is a healthy option for modern foods and food security (PLOS ONE) — the low glycemic index findings, the mouse diet study, and the protein digestibility work
    • Ulandari et al. (2023) — Breadfruit leaf extract and fasting blood glucose in type 2 diabetes (Biomedical and Pharmacology Journal) — 39 adults, 500 mg a day for 21 days
    • Jariah et al. (2024) — Breadfruit leaf extract and blood pressure (Biomedical and Pharmacology Journal) — 36 adults, 21 days, no significant difference from placebo
    • Ragone et al. (2004) — Nomenclature of breadfruit cultivars in Samoa (Journal of Ethnobiology) — 46 cultivar names recorded from Samoan islanders
    • USDA FoodData Central — raw breadfruit nutrition per 100 g
    • Secretariat of the Pacific Community — Breadfruit (Healthy Pacific Lifestyle) — varieties, food uses, fermenting and drying, and the multipurpose tree
    • PROSEA — Plant Resources of South-East Asia, Artocarpus altilis — food and preservation, latex and timber uses, leaf medicine, yields and storage
    • National Geographic — Breadfruit and 'The Bounty' That Brought It Across the Ocean — the 1,015 plants, the mutiny, and the tree's yield and nutrition

    Artichoke

    Cynara scolymus

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Digestive Health

    Cooked

    The artichoke is a thistle you eat before it flowers. What lands on the plate is the flower bud itself, picked while it is still closed tight — a green, pine-cone-shaped head of overlapping leaves, with a soft heart at its centre. Pull the leaves off one by one, scrape the soft flesh from each with your teeth, and the heart underneath is the prize: tender, nutty and faintly sweet.
