Leave the bud on the plant and it opens into a huge purple thistle flower, as wide as a saucer, loved by bees and no longer any good to eat. The plant is a big, bold perennial from the Mediterranean, with long silvery-green leaves that can stand as tall as a person. Its wild ancestor is the cardoon, a spiny thistle of the same shores, and the artichoke is the cardoon bred over centuries for a fat, fleshy bud.

    Cultivars

    Green Globe

    The old standard, and still the one most often grown. Big, round, deep-green buds, 10 to 13 cm across, with thick, fleshy hearts. The plant grows about 1 to 1.5 m tall and needs a long, warm season. The form sold as Green Globe Improved is a refined selection of the same kind, bred for more even buds.

    Imperial Star

    Bred to crop in its first year from seed, which most kinds will not do. Nearly spineless, mild green buds, ready about 85 to 90 days after planting out. Smaller plants, 45 cm to 1.2 m tall, and the best choice where winters are too cold for the plant to live through — it is grown as an annual there.

    Purple of Romagna

    Also called Violetto di Romagna, an old heirloom from Emilia-Romagna in Italy. Large, round heads that run from green to deep purple, prized by cooks for their tenderness. Needs about 85 to 100 days, and lives through the winter in mild places.

    Violetto

    Also sold as Violetta di Chioggia, an Italian heirloom from the Veneto. Smaller, slightly long purple buds, tinged violet on the scales, with dozens of little side buds after the main ones. Tougher in the cold than Green Globe, hardy where winters are mild to moderate.

    Violet de Provence

    The small purple artichoke of southern France, eaten whole when young. Slim, violet-tipped buds with a nutty taste, picked small.

    Romanesco

    An old Italian kind with round, purple-silver buds that turn greener towards the stem, almost a ball in shape.

    Colorado Star

    A newer open-pollinated kind, bred for shorter seasons and cooler gardens, with green buds that colour purple in the sun.

    The names overlap and tangle: Violetto, Violetta and Violetta di Chioggia are sold as one kind as often as three, and Purple of Romagna is the same plant as Violetto di Romagna. Italian heirlooms are old regional kinds rather than uniform modern cultivars, so the same name can cover plants that differ a little from garden to garden. The Jerusalem artichoke is no kin at all — it is a sunflower grown for its knobbly root, and it has nothing to do with this plant.

    • The artichoke comes from the Mediterranean, and it has been grown there for a very long time. Theophrastus, a Greek writer on plants in the 3rd century BCE, wrote of artichoke-like plants grown in Sicily. The Greeks and Romans knew the wild cardoon and plants close to the artichoke, and ate them as food and as a help for digestion. Whether the fat-budded artichoke of today already existed then, or was bred later from the cardoon, is still argued over — the old writings may be describing the cardoon itself. The name carries the journey: from the Arabic al-kharshuf, through Italian articiocco, to the English artichoke.
    • The old story tells how the plant got its name. Zeus, king of the Greek gods, fell for a beautiful girl named Cynara, made her a goddess so she could stay near him, and when she grew homesick and slipped back to earth to see her family, he threw her down from Olympus and turned her into an artichoke. The Latin name Cynara keeps her name. It is a story, told as a story.
    • By the 1400s the artichoke was a luxury of the rich in Italy, Spain and France. Catherine de Medici, who married the future Henry II of France in 1533, brought her love of artichokes with her from Florence to the French court, and ate them openly though the court doctors warned against them — they called the artichoke a food that stirred desire, and said it was unfit for women. The court ladies followed her all the same, and the artichoke became the fashionable food of Paris. Henry VIII of England was said to be fond of them too.
    • The artichoke has always divided opinion and drawn strong feeling. In 1604 the painter Caravaggio attacked a waiter in Rome over a plate of artichokes — some say because they were served without butter, some say because they were served at all. Three hundred years later, in 1935, the artichoke was at the centre of a New York crime story: a gangster known as the Artichoke King forced sellers to hand over their crates cheap and sold them on at a high price, until the mayor, Fiorello La Guardia, banned the sale of artichokes in the city altogether. The ban lasted a week, and artichokes came back more popular than ever.
    • Spanish and French settlers carried the plant to the Americas, and it found its best home on the cool, foggy coast of central California. The town of Castroville calls itself the Artichoke Capital of the World, and before she was famous, Marilyn Monroe was crowned its first Artichoke Queen. Most of the artichokes eaten in the United States still come from that one stretch of coast.
    • As a medicine, the artichoke has an old name as a liver and digestion plant. Greek and Roman writers used artichoke-like plants for the digestion, and through the centuries the leaf was taken as a bitter tonic before rich meals — in France and Italy, people still drink the water the artichokes were cooked in, believing it wakes up the liver and readies the stomach for what follows. The leaf is rich in bitter compounds, above all cynarin, which prompts the liver to make more bile — the bitter fluid the body uses to digest fat. That old use is the reason the leaf was ever tested at all. What the tests found stands on its own, under Health Benefits.
    • One small wonder belongs in the kitchen, not the medicine chest. Cynarin briefly dulls the taste buds that sense sweetness, so water or wine drunk just after eating an artichoke can taste strangely sweet. It is a trick of the tongue, and it passes in minutes.
    • What is in the bud, first. A medium cooked artichoke, about 120 g of the edible part, gives around 64 calories, about 7 g of fibre — roughly a quarter of a day's fibre — and good amounts of folate, vitamin K, vitamin C, magnesium and potassium, with almost no fat. Much of the fibre is inulin, a kind of fibre the gut cannot digest, which feeds the friendly bacteria of the gut. The bud also carries the bitter compounds of the leaf in smaller amounts, including cynarin and chlorogenic acid. It is a genuinely nourishing vegetable, and that is the plainest and surest thing to say about it.
    • The leaf as a medicine has a formal traditional standing, and that is its true size. The European Medicines Agency accepts artichoke leaf as a traditional herbal medicine for relief of digestive troubles — a feeling of fullness, bloating and wind — based on long use, not on proof. The agency judged the clinical evidence as a whole too thin for a stronger standing, and kept the traditional one. Traditional use
    • The best trial of the leaf extract tested it against a dummy pill in people with functional dyspepsia — stomach complaints that keep coming back with no disease a doctor can find. In a six-week trial, 247 people took either a leaf extract, 640 mg three times a day, or a placebo, and 244 were counted in the results. Symptoms eased more with the extract than with the placebo, and the people's quality of life rose more too — a real difference, though a modest one. People whose main trouble was irritable bowel syndrome were not in the trial, so nothing here speaks to that. Human trials
    • The cholesterol trials are small, and they point the same way without settling the question. In a trial of 143 people with clearly raised cholesterol, a leaf extract of 1,800 mg a day for six weeks cut total cholesterol by 18.5%, against 8.6% on placebo. In a trial of 75 adults with mild to moderate high cholesterol, 1,280 mg a day for twelve weeks cut total cholesterol by 4.2% while it rose 1.9% on placebo — but the "bad" LDL cholesterol, the "good" HDL cholesterol and the blood fats did not move. In a trial of 92 overweight adults with mild high cholesterol, 500 mg a day for eight weeks raised HDL and lowered LDL and total cholesterol. A pooling of nine trials with 702 people found total and LDL cholesterol and blood fats lower on the extract, with HDL unchanged. A Cochrane review of the three trials then available, 262 people in all, judged the evidence promising but not convincing, and said better trials were needed. That review was later withdrawn by Cochrane for editorial reasons, not because its findings were wrong. No trial has asked whether artichoke leaf extract prevents heart attacks or strokes. Eating artichokes as food has never been tested for cholesterol at all — the trials all used leaf extract. Human · small
    • The liver story needs the same care. The old name of the artichoke is as a liver plant, and the leaf does prompt the liver to make more bile — that much is well shown. A small pooling of five trials with 333 people with fatty liver found liver enzymes and blood fats lower on the extract than in the comparison groups. But those trials were small, and no trial proves the leaf heals or protects the liver in a person. The European Medicines Agency lists liver disease among the conditions where leaf preparations must not be used. Anyone with liver trouble should ask their own doctor, not reach for the extract. Human · small
    • When to plant: Plant out after the last frost, from young plants or root divisions — seed-grown plants vary, and many will not bud in their first year; root divisions — young shoots with roots, cut from an old plant — are the surest way to keep a good kind true
    • Sun: Full sun; in hot places give it afternoon shade and steady water
    • Soil: Deep, rich, well-drained ground, full of rotted compost, around pH 6.5 to 7.5; dig the bed deep, a good spade's depth, and work in plenty of compost before planting — drainage matters more than richness, because roots sitting in wet ground rot
    • Environment: A plant of cool, mild coasts — its home is the Mediterranean; it lives through the winter as a perennial in mild places, about USDA zones 7 to 11, and is grown as an annual, replanted each spring, where winters are colder; it likes cool springs of 10 to 24 °C and mild winters, and it sulks in hard frost and in long, hot summers
    • Planter or ground: Ground, with room — a grown plant stands 1 to 1.5 m tall and spreads 1 to 1.8 m wide, with long, silvery leaves; give each plant 1.2 to 1.8 m of room, with rows 1.8 to 2.4 m apart, and do not crowd it against smaller vegetables it will shade out
    • Water: Water steadily through the growing season; dry plants make small, tough buds; the plant is a hungry feeder and drinks a lot
    • When to pick: Pick the buds while they are still tight and closed, when they are full-sized but the scales still hug the head — a bud that squeaks when you squeeze it is fresh and tight; cut with a short piece of stem, about 2 to 5 cm; the big bud at the top of each stalk comes first, and smaller side buds follow

    Garden notes

    • Be honest about the space before anything else. The artichoke is a big plant.
    • Young plants need a spell of cool weather to be tricked into flowering: a few weeks below 10 °C once they are about 30 cm tall, which is why spring-planted seedlings that meet a late cold snap often bud the same year, and why Imperial Star was bred to bud without it.
    • Feed through the season with compost or a balanced feed. Cut the stalks back after the harvest, and in cold places pile a thick mulch over the crown for winter, or lift the crowns and keep them cool and dry until spring. A strong plant crops for three to five years, then weakens — divide it and start fresh plants from its young shoots.
    • Leave a bud too long and it opens into a purple thistle flower — beautiful, beloved by bees, and past eating. A few left to flower on purpose are no loss: the flowers are among the finest in the vegetable garden.
    • Watch for aphids clustering on the young buds and leaves, and for slugs on young plants. The plant's worst enemy is winter wet at the crown, which rots it — good drainage and a mulch that does not sit soggy against the stem are the best defence.

    Propagation

    In spring, cut a young shoot (offset) from the base of a mature plant, keeping some root with it, and plant it at once. This keeps the parent's quality. Seed also works — sow indoors in late winter or early spring — but seed-grown plants vary in size and yield.

    Safety

    • As food, the artichoke is safe for most people — it is a common vegetable, eaten for centuries. The leaf preparations are another matter.
    • The European Medicines Agency says they must not be used by anyone allergic to the daisy family (daisy, chrysanthemum, marigold, ragweed and their kin), or by anyone with a blocked bile duct, gallstones, inflammation of the bile ducts, liver disease, or any other bile trouble that needs a doctor's care — because the leaf pushes bile flow, and that can bring on pain where the bile cannot flow freely.
    • Leaf preparations are not recommended in pregnancy or while breastfeeding, or in children under twelve, because their safety there has not been shown. The usual side effects are mild and pass quickly: wind, loose stools, a queasy stomach, heartburn.
    • One more caution for the vegetable itself: artichokes are rich in fructans, the family of fibres that includes inulin, so people with irritable bowel syndrome may find them gassy and uncomfortable.

    Sources

    • Holtmann et al. (2003) — leaf extract against placebo in functional dyspepsia, 247 people enrolled, 244 counted, six weeks
    • Bundy et al. (2008) — leaf extract against placebo in mild to moderate high cholesterol, 75 adults, 1,280 mg a day for twelve weeks
    • Englisch et al. (2000) — leaf extract against placebo in raised cholesterol, 143 people, 1,800 mg a day for six weeks
    • Rondanelli et al. (2013) — leaf extract against placebo in overweight adults with mild high cholesterol, 92 people, 500 mg a day for eight weeks
    • Sahebkar et al. (2018) — pooling of nine trials with 702 people, total and LDL cholesterol and blood fats lower on the extract
    • Wider et al. (2013) — Cochrane review of leaf extract for high cholesterol, three trials, 262 people, evidence promising but not convincing
    • Kamel & Farag (2022) — pooling of five small trials with 333 people with fatty liver, liver enzymes and blood fats lower on the extract
    • European Medicines Agency (2018) — herbal monograph on artichoke leaf, traditional use for fullness, bloating and wind, and the contraindications
    • USDA FoodData Central — cooked globe artichoke, nutrition per 100 g and per medium artichoke
    • Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online, the naming of Cynara scolymus and its Mediterranean home
    • Royal Horticultural Society — growing notes and history, Theophrastus, Catherine de Medici, Caravaggio, the 1935 New York ban

    Asparagus

    Asparagus officinalis

    Culinary

    FreshCooked

    Asparagus is the first green vegetable of spring: thick, tender spears that push straight up out of the bare soil, weeks before anything else in the vegetable garden is ready. The plant is a perennial — it lives for many years from one deep root crown — and the spear is its young shoot, cut while it is still short and its tip is still tightly closed. Left alone, the spear grows on into a tall, feathery green fern, taller than a person, that feeds the crown for next year's crop. Asparagus is native to Europe and western Asia, and it has been prized as food for thousands of years. It also carries the best-known quirk in the vegetable world: after eating it, many people's urine smells strongly of sulfur — and whether you can smell it comes down to your genes.

    Cultivars

    'Mary Washington'

    The old standard, released by the United States Department of Agriculture in 1949. An open-pollinated kind, meaning it sets seed freely and holds both male and female plants; the female plants spend strength on seed, so they yield less than the males. Thin to medium green spears, mild and classic in flavour, and still the most widely grown garden kind.

    'Martha Washington'

    The sister of Mary Washington, the other old open-pollinated standard, much the same in the garden: both male and female plants, steady rather than spectacular.

    'Jersey Knight'

    The modern garden favourite, an all-male hybrid from Rutgers University in New Jersey. All-male means every plant puts its strength into spears and none into seed, so it yields more and lives longer, and it resists Fusarium wilt, the soil disease that kills asparagus beds. Large, tender, sweet green spears.

    'Jersey Giant'

    Another all-male Rutgers hybrid, early and heavy-yielding, with very large spears; a good choice where spring frosts come late, since it emerges a little later than some.

    'Jersey King' and 'Jersey Supreme'

    Two more all-male Rutgers hybrids in the same family, both bred for yield and for resistance to rust and crown rot. Jersey King is an early kind; Jersey Supreme is valued for straight, uniform spears.

    'Purple Passion'

    The purple kind, with deep burgundy spears that are sweeter and more tender than the green kinds, and that turn green when cooked. An open-pollinated kind with both male and female plants, and a little less vigorous in hot, humid summers.

    'Sweet Purple'

    A second purple kind, much like Purple Passion in colour and sweetness, turning green in the pot.

    'Millennium'

    A newer all-male hybrid, bred for cold winters and for heavy yields, and a good choice in the coldest asparagus country.

    'Syn 4-56' and 'Syn 53'

    Synthetic kinds, bred in the same way as the Jersey hybrids and much like them in the garden, grown more by market farmers than by home gardeners.

    White asparagus is not a cultivar at all: any of these kinds will grow white spears if the shoots are kept in the dark under mounded soil. And the wild coastal form of the plant, treated by some botanists as Asparagus officinalis subsp. prostratus, is a low, sprawling plant of sea cliffs from northern Spain to Britain — a wild cousin, not a garden choice.

    • Asparagus is an old food. It is shown as an offering on an Egyptian wall carving from around 3000 BC, and it was known in Syria and Spain in ancient times. The Greeks and Romans ate the spears fresh in spring and dried them to keep for winter. The word itself is Greek — asparagos — meaning a young shoot picked before its leaves open.
    • The Romans loved it more than anyone. The emperor Augustus is said to have used "faster than cooking asparagus" as his order for speed — the Roman way of saying "at once" — and he kept a special fleet of boats, the Asparagus Fleet, to carry the vegetable to his table. The writer Pliny the Elder tells of spears from Ravenna so large that three of them weighed a pound. In the second century BC, Cato the Elder wrote one of the longest passages in his farming book about how to grow it: sow after the spring equinox, feed it well with sheep dung, and protect it with straw in its first winter. A recipe for cooking asparagus stands in the Roman cookbook attributed to Apicius, one of the oldest recipe collections to survive. Julius Caesar was served it dressed with scented oil instead of olive oil at a dinner in Milan, and ate it without complaint while his companions winced. The Greek physician Galen, writing in the second century AD, called it a beneficial herb.
    • Old herbal medicine used asparagus as a diuretic — a thing that makes the body pass more water — and as a supposed aphrodisiac, a food for desire. The root was the part used for medicine, dried and made into teas, while the spear was the food. The aphrodisiac name rests on the spear's shape and on old belief, not on any test. The diuretic use was real enough in practice that it carried through the centuries, and it is told under Health Benefits at its true size.
    • In the 1600s and 1700s, white asparagus came into its own in France and Germany. White asparagus is not a different kind of plant: it is the same spear grown under mounds of soil, shut away from the light so it never turns green. The work is done by hand, a stalk at a time, which made it a luxury for the tables of the rich. In Germany it is still the spring vegetable above all others — Spargelzeit, asparagus time, runs from April into June, and towns hold festivals for it. In France the white spears of Argenteuil were famous, and in the Netherlands the sandy soils of Limburg grow them still. King Louis XIV of France, a fanatical gardener, kept some 6,000 asparagus plants in heated beds at Versailles so the court could eat them as early as December.
    • Asparagus travelled with European settlers and is now grown all over the temperate world. In 2023 the world grew about 8.6 million tonnes of it, and most of that — nearly nine tenths — came from China. Peru grows much of the asparagus eaten out of season in the northern hemisphere, and the white spears are still a European specialty, above all German, French and Dutch.
    • The smell in the urine is an old observation, not a new one. Benjamin Franklin wrote in 1781 that "a few stems of asparagus eaten, shall give our urine a disagreeable odour." The French writer Marcel Proust put it more kindly, saying the spears turned his chamber pot into a flask of perfume. What neither of them could know is told under Health Benefits: the smell comes from sulfur compounds made when the body breaks down asparagusic acid, a compound found in no other vegetable, and whether you can smell it is written in your genes.
    • What is in a spear, first. Asparagus is light food: about 20 calories in 100 grams raw, with about 2 grams of fibre. Its best-known nutrient is folate — vitamin B9, the vitamin the body uses to build new cells — with 52 micrograms in 100 grams raw, and about 89 micrograms in four cooked spears, around a fifth of a day's need. It is also a good source of vitamin K, with about 42 micrograms in 100 grams raw, and it carries potassium, vitamin C and small amounts of iron. The raw and cooked figures come from two separate USDA records, so they are not lined up side by side as if one cooking pot tripled the folate.
    • The urine smell, plainly, because it is the question everyone asks. Asparagus holds asparagusic acid, a sulfur compound found in no other vegetable. When the body breaks it down, it makes sharp-smelling sulfur compounds, chiefly methanethiol and dimethyl sulfide — the same family of smells as onion, garlic and cooked cabbage. The smell can appear within half an hour of eating. Two things differ from person to person: some bodies make less of the smell, and some noses cannot detect it at all. The second difference is the bigger one, and it is genetic. In a study of 6,909 people published in the BMJ in 2016, about 58% of men and 61.5% of women could not smell the odour in their own urine, and the inability was tied to 871 small genetic differences near a cluster of smell-receptor genes on chromosome 1. An earlier study in 2011 found the same split — differences in both making the smell and smelling it — and tied the smelling side to one genetic variant near the smell-receptor gene OR2M7. The smell is harmless, and it fades within hours. Not smelling it is normal too.
    • The old diuretic use is tradition, and it is told as tradition. Asparagus root was used for centuries to make the body pass more water, and the spear carries the amino acid asparagine and saponins — bitter, soapy plant compounds — that were held responsible. No trial has tested whether eating spears as food makes a person pass more water, and the root preparations of old herbal medicine are not the spears on a plate. The standing of asparagus as a diuretic rests on long use, not on proof. Traditional use
    • The blood-pressure evidence is one small, open trial of a powder most people never eat. In a 2013 trial, 28 healthy volunteers took 6 grams a day of powder made from asparagus bottom stems or from the feathery green shoots — the parts usually thrown away at harvest — for ten weeks. The bottom-stem powder lowered both the upper and lower blood-pressure numbers and fasting blood sugar, and the shoot powder lowered the lower number and blood sugar. The trial had no placebo group and no blinding, so the people taking the powder knew what they were taking, and 28 people is a small number. A study in rats with high blood pressure found the same direction: asparagus in the diet lowered blood pressure and the activity of ACE, the enzyme that tightens blood vessels. None of this tested spears eaten as food, and none of it makes asparagus a treatment for high blood pressure. Human · small / Animal studies
    • Blood sugar and cholesterol sit in the same small trial, and nowhere else in people. The same 28 volunteers saw fasting blood sugar fall and total cholesterol fall on both powders. That is one small open trial of a waste-part powder, not a finding about the vegetable, and it has not been repeated in a larger trial. Human · small
    • The gut-health telling rests on inulin, a fibre that feeds good gut bacteria. Asparagus holds inulin-type fibres, and inulin in general has good human evidence behind it: trials of inulin from chicory and other sources show it raises the numbers of Bifidobacterium in the gut. No trial has tested asparagus itself for this — the evidence is for inulin as a fibre, not for asparagus as a food. The spear's own fibre still counts as ordinary good food, but the prebiotic claim belongs to the fibre family, not to this vegetable alone. Human trials
    • Two fences belong here. First, the cancer work is laboratory work only: asparagus saponins have killed liver-cancer cells in dishes, and that is where it stops — no animal or human trial has tested asparagus against cancer, and a dish is not a body. Second, the aphrodisiac name is old belief, not a finding: no trial has tested it, and the shape of a spear is not evidence. Lab studies
    • When to plant: Plant one-year-old crowns — dormant root clusters — in early spring, as soon as the soil can be worked; from seed is possible — sow indoors ten to twelve weeks before the last frost — but it adds a year to the wait
    • Sun: Full sun, in a permanent spot where the bed will not be dug over or shaded out
    • Soil: Deep, well-drained ground — a sandy loam is ideal — around pH 6.5 to 7.5, which is near neutral, neither acid nor alkaline; it rots in wet, heavy clay, and it likes its ground rich: work in plenty of compost or well-rotted manure before planting, and clear every perennial weed first, since you cannot dig the bed over once the crowns are in
    • Environment: USDA zones 3 to 8 — a plant for cold winters and warm summers; it needs a cold winter rest to grow well the next spring, and where winters are too mild, it grows weakly and yields poorly; some garden books stretch the range to zone 10, but the plant's need for winter cold is the safer guide
    • Planter or ground: Ground — you plant it once and pick from it for fifteen to twenty years or more; dig a trench about 12 inches wide and 6 to 8 inches deep, shallower in heavy soil, set the crowns 12 to 18 inches apart, buds up, roots spread out over a little mound of soil at the bottom, and cover them with just 2 inches of soil at first, filling the trench in as the spears grow; space the trenches 4 to 5 feet apart
    • Water: Water steadily while the bed settles, about an inch a week, rain counted in; once established the crowns are fairly drought-tough, but a dry bed gives thin spears
    • When to pick: Harvest spears when they are 6 to 10 inches tall and the tips are still tightly closed, cutting at soil level with a sharp knife or snapping them where they break naturally

    Garden notes

    • Be honest about the wait before anything else. Asparagus is a perennial that asks for patience: you take no spears at all in the first year, only a light picking in the second, and a full harvest from the third spring on.
    • Feed each spring with compost or a balanced fertiliser, and mulch to hold moisture and keep weeds down.
    • In the second spring pick lightly for two or three weeks only; from the third spring, pick for six to eight weeks, then stop. Stop for the year when most new spears come up thinner than a pencil. Every spear you do not cut grows into a fern, and the fern is the crop: it feeds the crown for next year, so never cut the ferns down in summer. When the ferns turn yellow or brown in autumn, cut them back to within 2 inches of the ground and mulch the bed for winter.
    • The asparagus beetle is the pest to watch for — a small spotted beetle that eats the spears and ferns, and whose dark grubs feed on the foliage. Pick beetles off by hand, and keep the bed clear of dead fern litter over winter, where the beetles shelter. Asparagus is said to grow well beside tomatoes, since the tomato plant is held to drive the beetle away, though that is garden lore rather than a tested finding.
    • The ferns grow 4 to 6 feet tall and cast shade, so put the bed on the north side of the vegetable garden, where it will not shade shorter crops. A well-kept bed yields about half a pound to a pound of spears per plant each season once it is mature, and it peaks when the plants are four to eight years old.

    Propagation

    Sow seed indoors in February, or outdoors in March or April, 1 inch deep. Plants from seed take 3 years before picking. Or divide a well-established crown in late winter or early spring, each piece keeping several growing points and roots — do this no more than once every 3 years.

    Safety

    • The spears are safe food. The small red berries that grow on female plants in autumn are a different matter: they are mildly poisonous and are never eaten — they can bring on sickness and vomiting if eaten in quantity.
    • Skin allergy to asparagus is rare, but it happens, mostly in people who handle it at work, and it can also bring on hay fever or asthma in sensitive people.
    • The old root medicines were not to be used by people with inflamed kidneys or with swelling caused by failing kidneys or heart — but that warning belongs to the root preparations, not to the spears as food.
    • Asparagus holds purines, the compounds the body turns into uric acid, at about 25 milligrams in 100 grams, so people with gout were traditionally told to keep it modest — a small amount in a food, not a danger in a single serving.

    Sources

    • USDA FoodData Central (2019) — Asparagus, raw, and Asparagus, cooked, boiled, drained — the folate, vitamin K and calorie figures
    • Nishimura et al. (2013) — Powdered asparagus bottom-stems and cladophylls in 28 healthy volunteers, 6 g a day for 10 weeks, open trial — the blood-pressure, blood-sugar and cholesterol findings
    • Markt et al. (2016) — Sniffing out significant "Pee values": genome-wide study of asparagus anosmia in 6,909 people — the genetics of who can smell the odour
    • Pelchat et al. (2011) — Excretion and perception of a characteristic odour in urine after asparagus ingestion — differences in both making the smell and smelling it, tied to a variant near the smell-receptor gene OR2M7
    • Olas (2024) — A review of the pro-health activity of Asparagus officinalis L. and its components — the saponin and laboratory evidence, and the fence that it is laboratory and animal work only
    • Drugs.com (2026) — Asparagus Uses, Benefits & Dosage — the clinical overview: little to no clinical evidence for the medicinal uses
    • Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — the accepted name Asparagus officinalis, its place in the asparagus family, and its native range
    • Bratsch (2009) — Virginia Cooperative Extension asparagus profile — the Jersey hybrids, the open-pollinated kinds, Purple Passion, and the planting advice
    • Wikipedia — Asparagus — the Egyptian offering, the Asparagus Fleet, the "faster than cooking asparagus" saying, Cato's growing advice, and the world production figure

    Spinach

    Spinacia oleracea

    Culinary

    Eye Health

    FreshCooked

    Spinach is the soft green leaf everybody knows from the salad bowl and the saucepan — a cool-season annual that grows as a low rosette of broad, dark green leaves, 20 to 30 cm tall, and is picked young for salads or full-grown for cooking. It belongs to the amaranth family, Amaranthaceae, which makes it a cousin of beet and Swiss chard. The leaves are eaten raw or cooked, and they carry a remarkable load of nourishment for so light a food: vitamin K, folate, vitamin C, beta-carotene (which the body turns into vitamin A), magnesium and potassium — and lutein, the yellow pigment the eyes use, in larger amounts than almost any other common food. China grows by far the most of it: in 2021 the world grew 32 million tonnes, and China grew 92% of that.

    Cultivars

    Spinach comes in three leaf shapes, and the garden kinds fall into one of the three. Savoy kinds have thick, deeply crinkled, dark green leaves — the classic spinach look, the hardiest in cold, and the hardest to wash clean. Smooth-leaf (flat-leaf) kinds have broad, flat, glossy leaves that rinse clean easily and are the kinds grown for freezing and canning and for bagged salads. Semi-savoy kinds sit between the two, lightly crinkled, and are the modern compromise.

    Named garden kinds worth knowing: 'Bloomsdale Long Standing' — the old savoy heirloom from the early 1800s, thick and very crinkled, one of the best-tasting kinds, about 48 days to pick, with no disease resistance; 'Tyee' — a savoy kind, late to bolt; 'Melody' — a semi-savoy kind that won the All-America Selections award in 1977, tender and dark green, about 42 days; 'Space' — a smooth-leaf hybrid, quick at about 39 days and resistant to downy mildew, good for baby leaves; 'Olympia' — smooth-leaf, very fast and late to bolt, about 46 days; 'Giant Nobel' — a big smooth-leaf kind, late to bolt, good for steaming and canning; 'Monstrueux de Viroflay' (often just 'Viroflay') — a French smooth-leaf kind from at least the mid-1800s, with leaves 8 to 10 inches long; 'Indian Summer' — a savoy hybrid, late to bolt, about 35 days; 'Acadia' — a semi-savoy hybrid, late to bolt and highly resistant to downy mildew, about 45 days; and 'Corvair' — a semi-savoy kind with strong downy mildew resistance.

    Two plants sold as spinach are not spinach at all. New Zealand spinach (Tetragonia tetragonoides) is a different plant from a different family, grown as a heat-proof stand-in for summer; Malabar spinach (Basella alba) is a climbing vine from Asia, also unrelated. Neither is spinach, and nothing told here applies to them.

    • Spinach is a latecomer to the world's tables. It was tamed from a wild plant of Central Asia, Spinacia turkestanica, which still grows wild around the Caspian Sea and through Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Afghanistan. The taming happened in the land that is now Iran — old Persia — about 2,000 years ago. No Greek or Roman writer mentions it. The oldest written records that name it come from Mesopotamia in the fourth century AD.
    • The name carries the journey with it. It comes from the Persian aspanakh, through Arabic into Latin, and so into English as spinach. Arab traders carried it east to India and on to China, where it arrived through Nepal in the seventh century and was called the Persian vegetable. It travelled west through the Muslim lands and reached Europe by way of Moorish Spain, where it was grown by the eleventh century. From Spain it spread across Europe, and by the fifteenth century it was a common spring green — welcome because it was ready so early in the year, when winter stores were running low and few fresh vegetables were about. Early settlers carried it to the Americas.
    • In the old medicine systems of Asia, spinach was food and medicine at once. In Ayurveda it was counted cooling and laxative, and the leaves were given as a pot herb to people recovering from illness; the seeds were used as a cooling laxative. Persian medicine called it nourishing, laxative and quick to digest, and used it for sore throats, aching backs and joints, and inflamed eyes. In Chinese medicine it was counted a blood and yin tonic that cools heat and helps the water pass. In the English kitchen garden it was known as the broom of the bowels, for the gentle loosening the fibre-rich leaves were thought to give. None of this was tested in the way modern medicine tests a treatment, and it is told here as tradition.
    • Two famous stories about spinach are not true, and both are worth telling straight because they are told everywhere. The first is Popeye. The sailor first appeared in the comic strip in 1929, and the strip first showed him eating spinach in 1932 — where he says it is "full of vitamin A an' tha's what makes hoomans strong and hefty." He never said his strength came from iron. The iron story grew up later: a 1977 article claimed a German chemist in 1870 had misplaced a decimal point and given spinach ten times its true iron, and a 1981 article in the British Medical Journal repeated it, adding that Popeye had raised spinach eating by a third. A careful check of the original papers by the criminologist Mike Sutton found no decimal-point error at all. The early iron figures were too high, most likely because the samples were contaminated with iron from laboratory equipment and because fresh and dried spinach were confused — a cup of dried spinach holds far more iron than a cup of fresh, because fresh spinach is mostly water — but the correct value was already well known before Popeye was ever drawn, and the claim about sales was never shown either. The second story is the Florentine one: that Catherine de' Medici, married from Florence to the King of France in 1533, loved spinach so much that she had it at every meal, and French dishes of spinach were named à la Florentine after her. Food historians have found no trace of it — no brigade of Florentine cooks, no spinach at every meal — and spinach was already an ordinary French vegetable long before she arrived. The name is real: in classic French cooking, à la Florentine still means a dish built on a bed of cooked spinach, often with eggs or fish and a cheese sauce. The story behind the name is a tale, not history.
    • What is true about the iron is plainer and less grand. Raw spinach holds about 2.7 mg of iron per 100 g, and a cup of cooked spinach holds about 6.4 mg — a fair amount against a daily need of about 8 mg for most adults. But spinach also holds oxalic acid, which binds iron (and calcium) in the gut and stops much of it being taken up, so the body gets far less of that iron than the number suggests. Cooking helps: boiling lowers the oxalate and frees more of the iron. Spinach is a good food. It is not an iron cure.
    • What is in the leaf, first. A cup of cooked spinach (about 180 g) gives far more than a day's vitamin K, about two-thirds of a day's folate, and a good share of vitamin A as beta-carotene, vitamin C, magnesium and potassium, for very few calories. It also gives about 20 mg of lutein and zeaxanthin — the two yellow pigments that gather in the eye. Raw spinach holds about 12 mg of lutein and zeaxanthin per 100 g, among the richest amounts in any common food.
    • The eye story is the one real health story spinach has, and it needs telling at its true size. Lutein and zeaxanthin are the pigments that make the yellow spot at the centre of the retina — the macula, the part of the eye we see fine detail with. They sit there and filter blue light and mop up the damaging fragments that light makes. The body cannot make them; they come only from food, and spinach is one of the richest sources.
    • In people, the link has been shown in two ways. First, in a small feeding study, 13 people ate extra spinach and corn every day for up to 15 weeks, adding about 11 mg of lutein a day, and the pigment in their eyes grew denser by about 19% on average. That is a small study, but it used the food itself, and it measured the eye directly. Second, in large observational studies — studies that watch what people eat and what happens to them, rather than testing a treatment — people with the highest intakes of lutein and zeaxanthin had a lower risk of age-related macular degeneration, the eye disease that steals central vision in old age: about half to two-thirds lower in the studies that measured it. Observational studies cannot prove the food caused the difference, because people who eat more greens differ in other ways too. Human · small
    • The big trial that tested lutein as a pill did not prove it prevents the disease. In AREDS2, a trial of 4,203 people aged 50 to 85 who were already at risk of advanced macular degeneration, adding 10 mg of lutein and 2 mg of zeaxanthin a day for five years did not significantly hold back the disease in the main analysis. In a closer look, the people who took lutein instead of beta-carotene, and the people who ate the least lutein in their ordinary diet, did seem to benefit — about 18% to 25% lower risk — but those were secondary looks, not the trial's main question, and they tested a pill, not spinach. So the honest size of it is this: spinach is one of the best food sources of the pigment the eye uses, eating it raises the eye's pigment, and people who eat more of these pigments have healthier eyes in observational studies — but no trial has shown that eating spinach prevents macular degeneration. Human trials
    • The rest of the health record is thinner, and it stays thin. Laboratory and animal studies have found antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in spinach extracts, and small studies have looked at blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol — but none of it amounts to a tested effect of eating spinach in people, so none of it is claimed here. The old medicine systems' wider claims — for the lungs, the liver, the joints, the blood — are tradition, told above as tradition. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • When to plant: Sow seed straight into the ground — it dislikes being moved — in early spring, four to six weeks before the last frost, and again in late summer for a fall crop; sow a little every two weeks for a steady supply
    • Sun: Full sun in the cool seasons, light shade as the days warm
    • Soil: Rich, moist, well-drained ground, with a pH of 6.5 to 7.5 — spinach is fussy about acid soil, and below pH 6.0 it grows stunted and pale; dig in compost before sowing — it is a hungry plant and wants nitrogen for big, dark leaves
    • Environment: A cool-season crop, and heat is its enemy: it grows best when the days are 35 to 75 °F (about 2 to 24 °C); seed sprouts in soil as cool as 40 °F, best near 70 °F, and fails in hot soil above about 85 °F; in mild-winter places it can be grown right through the cool months
    • Planter or ground: Ground — sow half an inch deep, in rows 12 to 18 inches apart, and thin the seedlings to 4 to 6 inches apart
    • Water: Keep the soil evenly moist — about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week — because dry soil and heat both push the plant to bolt
    • When to pick: Pick baby leaves from about 28 days, full leaves from 35 to 50 days, taking the outer leaves first and leaving the centre to keep growing

    Garden notes

    • Bolting is the thing to watch for. As the days lengthen past about 14 hours and the heat rises, the plant shoots up a tall stalk, flowers, and turns bitter. Late-bolting kinds ('Space', 'Olympia', 'Tyee', 'Indian Summer', 'Acadia') buy a little more time, and a little shade buys a little more, but no kind holds through a hot summer.
    • With mulch, a fall sowing can overwinter in the ground for an early spring picking.
    • Troubles: downy mildew is the main disease, worst in cool, wet weather — choose resistant kinds and give the plants air. Leaf miners tunnel pale trails through the leaves; row covers keep the flies off. Slugs like the low leaves. Wash every picking well, savoy kinds twice.

    Propagation

    Sow seed direct where it is to grow, half an inch deep, as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, and sow a short row every week or two for a steady crop, and again in mid to late summer for autumn. Seed fails to sprout in warm soil, and heat makes plants run to seed, so sow in cool weather and keep the soil moist.

    Safety

    • Spinach is one of the highest-oxalate foods, at roughly 750 mg of oxalate per 100 g raw. Oxalate binds calcium in the gut, which is why spinach is a poor source of calcium despite the calcium it contains, and in people who form calcium-oxalate kidney stones it can add to the risk. Boiling cuts the oxalate by roughly a third to a half — throw the water away — and most healthy people eating ordinary amounts need not worry.
    • Two cautions belong to everyone: people taking blood-thinning medicines should keep their spinach eating steady from week to week, because vitamin K affects clotting and sudden changes matter more than the amount; and spinach should not be leaned on as an iron treatment for anaemia, because so little of its iron is taken up — eating it with vitamin C, such as lemon juice, helps a little.
    • Wash the leaves well: the savoy kinds, with their crinkled leaves, hold grit in their folds.

    Sources

    • Sutton (2010) — Spinach, Iron and Popeye: ironic lessons from biochemistry and history — the check of the original papers: no decimal-point error, no iron claim by Segar, no shown rise in sales
    • Schwarcz (2017) — Setting the facts straight about iron in spinach (McGill Office for Science and Society) — the retelling of Sutton's findings, the fresh-versus-dried confusion, and the iron and oxalate figures
    • Bender (1977) — The 1977 article that first spread the decimal-point story, without evidence
    • Hamblin (1981) — The British Medical Journal article that repeated the decimal-point story and the 33% sales claim
    • Ribera et al. (2021) — On the origin and dispersal of cultivated spinach (Genetic Resources and Crop Evolution) — the wild ancestor S. turkestanica, domestication in Persia about 2,000 years ago, the oldest records, and the road to China through Nepal
    • Hammond et al. (1997) — Dietary modification of human macular pigment density — 13 people, spinach and corn adding 11.2 mg lutein a day, macular pigment up about 19%
    • Eye Disease Case-Control Study Group (1993) — Antioxidant status and neovascular age-related macular degeneration — higher blood lutein and zeaxanthin linked with lower risk
    • Seddon et al. (1994) — Dietary carotenoids, vitamins A, C, and E, and advanced age-related macular degeneration — higher dietary lutein and zeaxanthin linked with about 57% lower risk
    • AREDS2 Research Group (2013) — Lutein + zeaxanthin and omega-3 fatty acids for age-related macular degeneration (JAMA) — 4,203 people, five years, no significant effect on advanced disease in the main analysis
    • Chew et al. (2014) — Secondary analyses of the effects of lutein/zeaxanthin on age-related macular degeneration progression: AREDS2 Report No. 3 — the closer looks: about 18% lower risk against beta-carotene, about 25% lower in people with low dietary lutein
    • USDA FoodData Central — Spinach, raw and cooked: iron, vitamin K, folate, lutein and zeaxanthin, and oxalate figures
    • University of Wisconsin Extension — Spinach, Spinacia oleracea — the three leaf types and the named cultivars
    • University of Minnesota Extension — Growing spinach — sowing times, spacing, water, and bolting

    Fennel

    Foeniculum vulgare

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Digestive HealthHormone Health

    FreshCookedDried

    Fennel is one of the oldest flavours in the kitchen — sweet, warm and tasting of aniseed, the same taste as liquorice. It is a tall, feathery plant of the carrot family, and it gives three foods at once: a crisp white bulb to eat as a vegetable, fine green fronds to snip like a herb, and small ridged seeds to chew, grind or brew as a tea. In flower it stands as tall as a person, sometimes taller, its stems crowned with flat heads of tiny yellow flowers that bees work all summer. The smell is the giveaway: crush any part of it and the air fills with aniseed. That smell matters, because the one plant it must never be mixed up with — poison hemlock — smells foul and mousy instead, and has purple spots on a smooth stem.

    Cultivars

    Fennel comes in three garden forms of one species, and the form decides what you harvest. Common or herb fennel (F. vulgare var. vulgare, the bitter fennel of the medicine books) is the tall plant, grown for its fronds, flowers and seeds, and it makes no bulb at all. Sweet fennel (var. dulce) is the same tall plant with sweeter seed, grown for seed and for the oil pressed from it. Florence fennel (var. azoricum, called finocchio in Italian) is the short vegetable form, bred for the swollen, white, layered base of its leaf stalks — the "bulb", which is not a true bulb at all, but tightly packed leaf bases.

    The named Florence fennel cultivars are bred for big, round, un-split bulbs that hold back from bolting:

    'Zefa Fino'

    Bolt-resistant with large, flat-round bulbs, ready in about 80 days.

    'Orion'

    A hybrid, bolt-resistant with large bulbs that hold well, ready in about 80 days.

    'Finale'

    Open-pollinated, with very large, flattened bulbs and good bolt resistance, ready in 75 to 80 days.

    'Fino'

    Open-pollinated, best for autumn harvest, bolt-tolerant with large bulbs, ready in about 80 days.

    'Dragon'

    An F1 hybrid, even and late to mature, bolt-resistant, ready in about 90 days.

    'Preludio'

    High-yielding and even, good for autumn harvest, ready in about 80 days.

    'Trieste'

    A French hybrid, bolt-resistant, ready in about 90 days.

    'Romanesco'

    A large-bulbed Italian form.

    The leaf fennels are grown for looks and flavour, not for a bulb:

    'Bronze'

    Also sold as 'Purpureum' and as 'Rubrum', with deep bronze-purple feathery leaves that fade towards green with age.

    'Smokey'

    Another bronze-purple leaf form, good for eating and for the border.

    'Grosfruchtiger'

    A vigorous leaf fennel with a sweet flavour, ready in about 60 days.

    Bronze fennel's dark leaves make it the one fennel grown as much for the flower border as for the kitchen.

    One wild form is worth knowing by name so it is not mistaken for a garden plant: subsp. piperitum, wild pepper fennel, short-leaved with a very bitter seed, a plant of the dry Mediterranean hills, not of the vegetable bed.

    • Fennel is a plant of the Mediterranean shores, at home on dry ground near the sea and along riverbanks, and it has travelled from there to nearly every warm country on earth. Its Greek name is marathon or marathos, and the plain of Marathon in Greece — where the Athenians beat the Persians in 490 BCE — was named for it: the place name means, quite simply, a plain with fennel. The word is old enough to appear on a Mycenaean clay tablet from the 13th century BCE, among a list of spices, and the messenger's run from that battlefield to Athens is where the modern marathon race gets its name.
    • The old stories reach further back still. In Hesiod's Theogony, the fire-bringer Prometheus steals an ember from the gods and hides it in a hollow fennel stalk to carry it down to people. Theophrastus, the father of botany, described the plant in the 4th century BCE, and the writings given to Hippocrates, the father of medicine, already list it as a medicine. The Romans ate it, used it as a medicine, and hung it up to keep insects away; fennel leaves crowned the winners of games, and fennel tea was said to give warriors courage before battle.
    • In India the plant is saunf, and in the old Sanskrit writings madhurika, the sweet one. Its growing there goes back at least to 2000 BCE. The seeds are chewed after meals to this day, on their own or sugared and brightly coloured, and mixed with other seeds as mukhwas, the little after-meal mouth freshener passed round at the end of a meal in homes and restaurants — sweet on the tongue, fresh on the breath, and held to settle the stomach after rich food. India now grows more fennel than any other country.
    • Fennel travelled with monks, farmers and settlers. Charlemagne ordered it grown on every imperial farm. In the Anglo-Saxon Nine Herbs Charm of the 10th century it stands as finule, one of nine plants called on against sickness. Churchgoers once carried fennel seeds in their handkerchiefs to nibble through long services, and the seeds picked up the name "meeting seeds". When Portuguese settlers reached Madeira in the 15th century and found the hillsides thick with wild fennel, they named a new town for it: Funchal, from funcho, fennel, with the ending -al, a place of fennel.
    • In the old medicine of Greece, Rome, India and Iran, fennel was given for much the same things everywhere: for wind and bloating, for griping pains in the gut, for coughs, for scanty milk in nursing mothers, and to bring on a late monthly bleed. In Ayurveda it is counted a cooling, sweet digestive, kindling the digestive fire without heating the body the way hotter spices do. Much of that use was hope and habit, not tested proof. The tested part stands on its own, under Health Benefits.
    • Wherever it has landed, wild fennel has made itself at home — along roadsides and waste ground in California, Australia and South Africa, on the hills of Madeira, and on dry banks across southern Europe. In California it has spread so far that it is rated a moderate invader of grassland, scrub and wetland, crowding out native plants. The garden plant and the wild plant are the same species, and the wild one seeds itself freely.
    • Sweet fennel oil is the old remedy for colic and wind. One small trial of a prepared fennel seed oil mixture settled colic in 65% of 125 babies — but the mixture is not the pure oil, and the pure oil must never be swallowed. Human · small
    • What is in it, first. The seeds hold 3 to 6% essential oil, and most of that oil — commonly 50 to 90% of it — is one compound, trans-anethole, the same compound that gives anise its taste, with smaller amounts of fenchone, estragole and limonene. The bulb is a light vegetable: about 31 calories in 100 grams, with fibre, vitamin C and potassium. The leaf carries the same aniseed oil in smaller amounts, and the yellow pollen, gathered from the flower heads, is sold as a costly spice of its own.
    • The gut use has a formal traditional standing, and that is its true size. The European Medicines Agency accepts fennel fruit — the seed — as a traditional herbal medicine for mild, cramping gut complaints with bloating and wind, for minor cramp with monthly periods, and as a cough remedy in colds. The standing rests on long use, not on proof: the agency's own review found no good clinical trial of fennel tea behind it. No trial has tested fennel tea for indigestion in adults. That use is tradition, and it is told as tradition. Traditional use
    • The one proper trial of fennel for the gut was in babies with colic, and it is a small, single trial. In a placebo-controlled trial of 125 babies aged 2 to 12 weeks, a fennel seed oil mixture given for a week settled the colic — crying under nine hours a week — in 65% of the babies given fennel, against 24% of those given the dummy mixture, and weekly crying time fell from about 13.5 hours to about 8.8 hours. No side effects were seen in the week of the trial. But it is one trial, never repeated by another team, and it tested a made oil mixture, not fennel tea and not a chewed seed — and the same agency that accepts fennel for adults does not recommend fennel preparations for children under four, because of the estragole in the oil. A parent should ask a doctor before giving any fennel preparation to a baby, and never give the pure oil. Human · small
    • The period-pain trials are the strongest human evidence fennel has, and they are still small and uneven. A 2020 review that pooled 12 small randomised trials found fennel eased period pain about as well as ordinary painkillers, and better than a dummy treatment. But every trial was small, most were run in one country, the results varied widely from trial to trial, and the reviewers rated the risk of bias as moderate and saw signs that unfavourable results may never have been published. Fennel looks promising for period pain; it is not proven. Human trials
    • Two old claims do not hold up. Fennel tea is widely drunk by nursing mothers to bring more milk, but there is no good evidence that it works, and the milk authorities record weak evidence only, with no rise in the milk-making hormone. The old story that fennel sharpens the eyesight — Pliny told of snakes eating it to clear their sight — has no trial behind it at all, and it stays a story.
    • The rest of the laboratory work — fennel oil killing germs in dishes, easing swelling in animal tests, holding back the growth of cells in a dish — is laboratory and animal work, and none of it shows what eating the bulb or drinking the seed tea does in a person. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • When to plant: Sow where it is to stand, a quarter of an inch deep, after the last frost — it grows a long taproot that hates to be moved; Florence fennel is sown in early spring, or better in late summer for an autumn crop
    • Sun: Full sun — six hours a day or more
    • Soil: Light, well-drained ground, around pH 6 to 7, though fennel forgives a range of soils so long as the ground drains — wet feet rot it
    • Environment: Herb fennel is a short-lived perennial, hardy in zones 4 to 9, growing 4 to 6 feet tall and coming back year after year in mild winters; Florence fennel is grown as an annual in every zone, standing about 2 feet tall, and it is fussy where herb fennel is easy — it makes its bulb only in cool weather with steady water, about 60 to 65 °F while the bulb swells, and in heat or long days it runs straight to flower and makes no bulb at all
    • Planter or ground: Ground — give it room, and thin herb fennel to 12 to 18 inches apart
    • Water: Keep Florence fennel's ground evenly moist; herb fennel asks for far less — water it while it settles, then leave it mostly alone, for it is drought-tough once its taproot is down, and too much rich food makes floppy, tasteless growth
    • When to pick: Pick Florence bulbs when they are about the size of a tennis ball, 80 to 100 days from sowing, before they flower — a bulb left too long turns woody and splits; cut herb fennel seed heads when they turn brown and the seeds rattle, and dry them in a paper bag

    Garden notes

    • Be clear which fennel you are growing before you sow, because the two kinds want different things.
    • Snip the fronds all summer. Let some flower heads stand for the bees. The yellow flowers are a magnet for bees, hoverflies and other good insects, and the plant feeds the caterpillars of the anise swallowtail butterfly.
    • The spread is the warning that belongs in any garden note. Herb fennel seeds itself freely — one plant can shed thousands of seeds — and in warm countries it has escaped gardens and now grows wild along roadsides and coasts. Cut the flower heads before the seed drops unless you want a fennel patch, and check the local rules before planting it near open ground: in California it is rated a moderate invader, and in several western states it is listed as a troublesome weed. Florence fennel, picked before it flowers, hardly ever self-seeds.
    • Two garden habits are worth keeping. Do not plant fennel beside dill: the two cross, and the seed that results tastes of neither. And give fennel its own corner, away from the vegetable beds — gardeners have long found that fennel holds back the growth of the plants next to it, and a tall, self-seeding fennel in the middle of the beds is a nuisance, however good it looks.

    Propagation

    Sow seed straight where it will grow in spring, a quarter inch deep, once the soil has warmed. Its taproot dislikes being moved, so do not start it in pots and move it.

    Safety

    • Fennel as food is gentle, and the cautions are about the concentrated forms. Never swallow the pure essential oil. The oil holds estragole, a compound that damaged DNA and caused liver tumours in rats and mice at high doses, and the European Medicines Agency limits fennel tea to two weeks at a time, does not recommend fennel preparations in pregnancy or while breastfeeding, and does not recommend them for children under four.
    • Girls given fennel tea daily for months have developed breast tissue that faded once the tea stopped, and fennel's mild oestrogen-like action is the reason anyone with a hormone-sensitive condition, or on hormone treatment, should ask a doctor first.
    • People allergic to celery, carrot, anise or mugwort pollen can react to fennel too, since all are kin in the carrot family. Fennel can also change how the body handles some medicines — it holds back one of the liver's main drug-processing enzymes, and one report found it cut the uptake of the antibiotic ciprofloxacin.
    • A gut complaint that keeps coming back, lasts more than two weeks, or comes with pain, weight loss or a change in bowel habit needs a doctor, not more tea.
    • One warning belongs to anyone who gathers wild fennel: it grows beside poison hemlock, which can kill. Fennel smells strongly of aniseed when crushed and has no purple spots on its stem; hemlock smells foul and mousy and has a smooth, purple-spotted stem. Never eat a carrot-family plant you cannot name with certainty.

    Sources

    • European Medicines Agency (2007) — Community herbal monograph on Foeniculum vulgare, fructus — the traditional-use standing for gut complaints, period cramp and cough, the two-week limit, and the age and pregnancy cautions
    • Lee et al. (2020) — Fennel for reducing pain in primary dysmenorrhea: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Nutrients) — 12 trials, fennel similar to painkillers and better than placebo, small trials with moderate bias risk
    • Alexandrovich et al. (2003) — The effect of fennel (Foeniculum vulgare) seed oil emulsion in infantile colic: a randomised, placebo-controlled study (Alternative Therapies in Health and Medicine) — 125 babies, colic settled in 65% on fennel against 24% on placebo
    • Badgujar et al. (2014) — Foeniculum vulgare Mill: a review of its botany, phytochemistry, pharmacology, contemporary application, and toxicology (BioMed Research International) — the chemistry, the traditional uses and the safety record in one place
    • Touwaide & Appetiti (2022) — Herbs in History: Fennel (American Herbal Products Association) — the Marathon name, the Mycenaean tablet, Prometheus, Theophrastus and Hippocrates
    • Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — the accepted name Foeniculum vulgare, its place in the carrot family, and its native range
    • USDA FoodData Central — Fennel, raw — the bulb's food values
    • University of Wisconsin–Madison, Division of Extension — Fennel, Foeniculum vulgare — the named cultivars, the zones, and the Florence and bronze forms
    • North Carolina State Extension — Fennel (Foeniculum vulgare) — hardiness zones 4 to 9, full sun, and the two kinds grown in the garden
    • Drugs.com — Fennel monograph — the case reports of premature breast development, the CYP3A4 interaction and the ciprofloxacin report
    • Lawless (2014) — Encyclopedia of Essential Oils — fennel oil in aromatherapy and home use

    Cinnamon

    Cinnamomum verum

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Dried

    Cinnamon is the dried inner bark of a small evergreen tree, and it is one of the oldest spices in the world — sweet, warm and woody, the smell of baking, of chai, of Christmas. The tree here is Cinnamomum verum, true cinnamon, also called Ceylon cinnamon, a tree of the laurel family from Sri Lanka and the warm coast of southern India. Left alone it grows 10 to 15 metres tall, with glossy leaves 7 to 18 cm long, each leaf marked by three clear veins running from base to tip, and new leaves that open pink-red before they turn green. Its flowers are small, greenish and sweet-smelling, carried in loose sprays, and its fruit is a purple berry about 1 cm across with a single seed inside. The spice is the thin inner bark of young shoots, peeled by hand, scraped clean and rolled into soft, layered sticks called quills as it dries. The scent comes mostly from one compound, cinnamaldehyde. The warning that belongs up front: the jar in most kitchens does not hold this tree. What is sold as cinnamon in North America and much of Europe is almost always cassia, a thicker, harder, darker bark from a different tree, and cassia carries far more of a compound called coumarin, which can harm the liver when eaten in large amounts over time. True cinnamon holds only a trace of it. The difference is told in full below, because it is the honest heart of the story.

    Cultivars

    True cinnamon has no garden cultivars in the nursery sense — no named forms bred for a garden. What it has is Sri Lankan bark types, named for the taste of the bark, and these are the names a buyer meets: Pani-Miris Kurundu — sweet and spicy, the most prized; Miris Kurundu — spicy; Sewala Kurundu — smooth; Weli Kurundu — coarse; and Thiththa Kurundu — bitter. The spelling of the smooth type varies between sources — Sewala, Sevel and Sewele all appear — and the older lists name seven types, adding Pani Kurundu, Naga Kurundu and Kahata Kurundu. The names describe the bark's taste, not the look of the tree, and the same tree can be graded by the thickness of its quills.

    The Sri Lankan grading of quills is by diameter, not by cultivar, and it is worth knowing because the finest grade is the thinnest: Alba, under 6 mm across; Continental, under 16 mm; Mexican, under 19 mm; and Hamburg, under 32 mm. Alba is the finest and costliest, made of the thinnest inner bark.

    Cassia is not a cultivar of true cinnamon. Cinnamomum cassia (Chinese cassia), Cinnamomum burmannii (Indonesian cassia) and Cinnamomum loureiroi (Vietnamese or Saigon cinnamon) are separate species, and none of what is told of Cinnamomum verum belongs to them.

    • Cinnamon has been known since remote antiquity. It was carried into Egypt as early as 2000 BC, where it went into embalming oils and into kyphi, the scented mixture burned as incense, and it was counted a gift fit for kings and for a god — an inscription records cinnamon and cassia given to the temple of Apollo at Miletus. The first Greek mention of it is in a poem by Sappho, in the seventh century BC.
    • For centuries nobody in the Mediterranean knew where it came from, and the traders meant it to stay that way. Herodotus, writing in the fifth century BC, said cinnamon and cassia grew in Arabia, guarded by winged serpents, and that giant cinnamon birds carried the sticks from an unknown land to build their nests. Pliny the Elder, a century and a half later, called the bird story what it was: a traders' fiction, made up to charge more. The spice in truth came by sea from Sri Lanka and the Malabar Coast, through Arab middlemen who kept the source secret to hold their monopoly. Pliny also wrote that it was carried around the Arabian Peninsula on rafts without rudders or sails or oars, riding the winter trade winds, and that a Roman pound of it — about 327 grams — could cost up to 1,500 denarii, the wages of fifty months' labour. It was too costly for common use, and the emperor Nero is said to have burned a whole year's supply of the city's cinnamon at the funeral of his wife Poppaea in AD 65.
    • The mystery lasted into the Middle Ages. When the French nobleman Joinville went on crusade to Egypt in 1248, he reported — and believed — what he had been told: that cinnamon was fished up in nets at the source of the Nile, at the edge of the world. Marco Polo, who travelled further east than any European before him, was careful not to say where it grew.
    • The secret broke with the ships. The Portuguese took hold of Sri Lanka in 1536 and the Dutch took it from them in 1656, and each in turn held a near-monopoly on the trade. At first the bark was gathered from wild trees. Around 1770 it became a farmed crop in Sri Lanka, and the tree was carried to the Seychelles in 1771, where it grew so easily it went wild, and later to Madagascar, southern India and Zanzibar. Sri Lanka still grows 80 to 90% of the world's true cinnamon.
    • In Sri Lanka the tree is kurundu, and the harvest is hand work that has barely changed. The tree is cut back — coppiced — so it throws up straight young shoots, kept as a bush two or three metres tall. In the wet season, when the bark lifts most easily, a worker cuts the shoots, peels off the outer bark, and scrapes the thin inner bark free in long strips. The strips curl as they dry into quills: thin, papery, tan-coloured, made of many soft layers nested together, like a scroll of parchment. A true cinnamon quill crumbles easily between the fingers. A cassia stick does not — it is a single thick, hard, dark red-brown scroll, and it takes real force to break.
    • In the old medicine of India, Ayurveda, the bark was used against vomiting, diarrhoea and wind, and as a warming spice to wake a digestion that has gone quiet. Western herbal doctors used it in the same way, as a warming carminative — a spice that settles wind and cramping in the gut — and for loss of appetite. Germany's Commission E, the old official panel on herbal medicines, approved cinnamon bark for loss of appetite and for mild digestive complaints such as cramping, bloating and flatulence. The European Medicines Agency accepts cinnamon bark as a traditional herbal medicine for mild spasmodic digestive complaints such as bloating and flatulence, and for mild diarrhoea — on the strength of long use, not on trials. No trial has tested true cinnamon bark for digestion in people.
    • The spice travelled the world's kitchens as it travelled the trade routes: into Sri Lankan curries and hoppers, into Indian garam masala and chai, into Middle Eastern rice and meat dishes, into European baking, mulled wine and hot chocolate, and into Mexican chocolate and coffee. The leaf is distilled for a leaf oil, rich in eugenol, the clove-scented compound, which is used in flavouring and perfumery — a different oil from the bark oil, and not the spice.
    • Sri Lanka — the tree's home: the wet south-western lowlands and hills, where wild trees still grow and where the hand-peeling of quills is a craft passed down through families.
    • Southern India — the Malabar Coast, where the tree grows wild and is farmed alongside the Sri Lankan trade.
    • Seychelles — carried there in 1771, where it grew so easily it went wild and became part of the islands' landscape; a sizeable trade grew up there.
    • Madagascar and Tanzania — farmed on a commercial scale, including the spice farms of Zanzibar, where visitors are shown the tree and its scraped bark.
    • Indonesia — cassia country rather than true cinnamon country: the cassia grown in Indonesia and China is what fills most of the world's spice jars.
    • The bark oil is breathed in for its warm scent. It is a strong skin sensitiser: never put it on skin undiluted. Traditional use
    • What is in the bark, first. True cinnamon bark holds up to about 4% essential oil, mostly cinnamaldehyde (60 to 75%), with smaller amounts of eugenol, cinnamyl acetate and linalool. It also holds tannins and mucilage, the soft plant jelly that soothes the gut lining. The compound that decides safety is coumarin: true cinnamon holds about 0.004% of it, while cassia holds about 1% — roughly 250 times as much. The European Food Safety Authority sets a safe daily limit for coumarin of 0.1 mg per kilogram of body weight. For a 60 kg adult that is 6 mg a day, reached by about 2 grams of cassia — less than a teaspoon. The same amount of true cinnamon stays far below the limit. This is why the kind matters, and why the trials below must be read with the kind in mind.
    • The blood-sugar story is the one people ask about, and it must be told honestly, because it is mixed. Nearly every trial used cassia, not true cinnamon, in capsules or powder at 1 to 6 grams a day for four to eighteen weeks, and the trials disagree with each other.
    • The most-quoted trial of all can no longer be trusted as it stands. Khan and colleagues, in 2003, gave 60 people with type 2 diabetes in Pakistan 1, 3 or 6 grams of cassia a day for 40 days, and reported fasting blood sugar down by 18 to 29%, and the fats in the blood down by a similar share. In September 2025 the American Diabetes Association, which publishes the journal the trial appeared in, put a formal Expression of Concern on the paper: independent statisticians found differences between the trial groups at the start that do not fit proper randomisation, an unclear account of how people were randomised or blinded, and figures with so little variation they raised questions about how they were reported. The association could not reach the authors or see the underlying data. The paper has not been withdrawn, but its results can no longer be treated as settled, and the big percentages it reported have never been repeated at that size by any other trial. Human · small
    • The pooled trials — all the trials added together — give a smaller, muddier picture. A 2008 pooling of five trials (282 people) found no significant effect on HbA1c, the long-term blood-sugar measure, nor on fasting blood sugar or blood fats. A 2013 pooling of ten trials (543 people) found fasting blood sugar down by about 25 mg/dL, and the blood fats a little better, but still no significant effect on HbA1c — and the trials varied so widely in dose, length and result that the authors said the dose and length of treatment were unclear. A Cochrane review in 2012, pooling ten trials (577 people), found the effect on fasting blood sugar inconclusive and no significant effect on HbA1c, and concluded there was not enough evidence to support cinnamon for diabetes. A 2019 pooling of eighteen trials found fasting blood sugar down by about 19 mg/dL, with no significant effect on HbA1c, and again warned that the trials varied too much to read the result plainly. Human trials
    • Two smaller trials show what the mixed picture looks like up close. In a British trial of 58 people with type 2 diabetes, 2 grams of cassia a day for twelve weeks lowered HbA1c from 8.22% to 7.86%, against a rise from 8.55% to 8.68% on dummy capsules, and blood pressure fell a little — but fasting blood sugar did not fall significantly against the dummy capsules, and blood fats did not change. In an American trial of 109 people, 1 gram of cassia a day for ninety days, added to usual care without a dummy capsule to compare against, lowered HbA1c by 0.83 points against 0.37 points with usual care alone. Other trials found no change at all. No trial has tested true cinnamon bark on its own for blood sugar. Human · small
    • The mechanism offered for the effect comes from laboratory work, not from people: in dishes of cells, cinnamaldehyde and a cinnamon compound called MHCP switch on parts of the insulin signal, the message that tells cells to take in sugar. That is a laboratory finding, and it does not show what eating the spice does in a person. The same fence holds for the germ-killing work: cinnamon oil kills germs in a dish, which is not the same as treating an infection in a body. Lab studies
    • When to plant: Plant out young, in spring; grow it from fresh seed sown soon after harvest — the seed loses its power to sprout within days — or from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in warm weather, which root in six to eight weeks under cover
    • Sun: Full sun once established, with some shelter from hard wind when young
    • Soil: Deep, rich, well-drained soil that stays moist but never sits wet — a slightly acid soil, around pH 5.5 to 6.5, suits it best; wet feet rot the roots faster than cold does; in a pot, use a free-draining mix, a pot with holes in the bottom, and never let it stand in water
    • Environment: A strict tropical tree: it grows outdoors only where winters stay warm — the equivalent of USDA zones 10 to 12, at 20 to 30 °C (68 to 86 °F) through the year, with high humidity and generous rain; frost kills it, and even a short dip below 10 °C (50 °F) damages young growth; in cooler places it is a pot plant, moved outdoors for the warm months and brought inside before the first cold night
    • Planter or ground: Ground in the tropics, or a pot in cooler places; the tree is kept as a coppiced bush, two or three metres tall, by cutting the shoots back — left alone it will grow into a 10 to 15 metre tree, far too big for most gardens
    • Water: Water steadily for the first year or two while it settles
    • When to pick: The first thin bark can be taken from two- to three-year-old shoots, and the best bark comes later, after five years and more

    Garden notes

    • Be honest about the climate before anything else. True cinnamon is a strict tropical tree.
    • Feed lightly through the growing season.
    • To harvest bark at home, cut a straight two-year-old shoot at the base, peel off the outer bark, and scrape the thin inner bark free in strips. Dry the strips in shade with good air, and they will curl into quills on their own.
    • Indoors, give it the brightest window, keep the air moist, and keep it away from cold draughts.

    Propagation

    Sow fresh seed as soon as it comes from the fruit — it loses its power to sprout fast if stored. Plant in moist, well-drained mix in warm shade; seedlings show in about 20 days. Or take a partly mature shoot with at least one node from a healthy tree and root it under cover in a warm, humid place. Cinnamon needs warmth and high humidity and cannot take frost.

    Safety

    • Cinnamon as a spice in food is safe in the amounts people cook with. The risk sits with large daily amounts and with supplements, and it sits almost entirely with cassia, because of coumarin. High coumarin over time can raise liver enzymes and harm the liver, and people with liver disease should be careful.
    • Cinnamaldehyde is a known skin allergen: cinnamon oil can redden and burn the skin and cause an allergic rash, and it should never be put on the skin undiluted.
    • The "cinnamon challenge" — swallowing a spoonful of dry powder — has sent teenagers to hospital choking and struggling to breathe, and it is dangerous.
    • Cinnamon is not a treatment for diabetes, and no one should stop or change prescribed diabetes medicine on the strength of it. People taking blood-thinning medicines should ask a doctor before taking cinnamon in supplement amounts, because coumarin thins the blood.

    Sources

    • Allen et al. (2013) — Cinnamon use in type 2 diabetes: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis — 10 trials, 543 people, fasting glucose down about 25 mg/dL, no significant effect on HbA1c, high variation between trials
    • Baker et al. (2008) — Effect of cinnamon on glucose control and lipid parameters — 5 trials, 282 people, no significant effect on A1C, fasting glucose or blood fats
