    • Leach & Kumar (2012) — Cinnamon for diabetes mellitus (Cochrane review) — 10 trials, 577 people, effect on fasting glucose inconclusive, no significant effect on HbA1c, not enough evidence to support use for diabetes
    • Khan et al. (2003) — Cinnamon improves glucose and lipids of people with type 2 diabetes — 60 people, 1, 3 or 6 g of cassia a day for 40 days; with the American Diabetes Association Expression of Concern (2025) on the paper
    • Akilen et al. (2010) — Glycated haemoglobin and blood pressure-lowering effect of cinnamon in multi-ethnic type 2 diabetic patients in the UK — 58 people, 2 g of cassia a day for 12 weeks
    • Crawford (2009) — Effectiveness of cinnamon for lowering hemoglobin A1C in patients with type 2 diabetes — 109 people, 1 g of cassia a day for 90 days, added to usual care
    • European Medicines Agency — Assessment report and monograph on Cinnamomum verum bark — the traditional-use standing for mild digestive complaints, the oil content and the coumarin figures
    • European Food Safety Authority (2008) — Coumarin in flavourings and other food ingredients with flavouring properties — the safe daily limit of 0.1 mg per kilogram of body weight
    • PROSEA — Plant Resources of South-East Asia, Cinnamomum verum — the native range, the Portuguese and Dutch monopolies, cultivation from around 1770, and the Seychelles and Java plantings
    • Cinnamomum verum — Wikipedia — the tree's description, the bark-type names, the quill grades, and the history of the spice trade, including Herodotus, Pliny and Nero

    Black Pepper

    Piper nigrum

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Dried

    Black pepper is the most used spice in the world, and it comes from a vine, not a bush or a tree. Piper nigrum is a woody climbing vine from the warm, wet forests of the Malabar Coast in south-west India, in what is now Kerala. It climbs trees, poles and trellises, holding on with short roots that grip the bark, and it hangs long spikes of small round berries — green at first, then red as they ripen, each berry about 5 mm across, a stone fruit with one seed inside. The leaves are broad and glossy, 5 to 10 cm long, with clear veins running from the base to the tip. Black, white and green pepper all come from this one plant: black pepper is the unripe berry, picked green and dried in the sun until the skin wrinkles and turns black; white pepper is the ripe red berry with its skin soaked off; green pepper is the unripe berry kept fresh. The bite of all three comes from piperine, a sharp-tasting compound that is a different kind of heat from the capsaicin of chillies. Black pepper is not the plant of the Peppers entry: those peppers are Capsicum — chillies and sweet peppers — whose heat comes from capsaicin, and the two plants are not related. One warning cannot wait: piperine changes how the body handles some medicines. Anyone who takes regular medicine should ask their doctor before taking piperine capsules or large medicinal doses of pepper — the spice on food is a different matter, and it is covered under Health Benefits.

    Cultivars

    Black pepper has many named cultivars, and nearly all of them are Indian farm varieties, not garden forms. India grows more than 75 cultivars, and the best known are Karimunda, the most widely grown in Kerala; Kottanadan, from south Kerala, with the highest oleoresin — the thick, spicy extract — of the old varieties; Aimpiriyan from Wayanad; Narayakodi from central Kerala; Neelamundi from Idukki; Kuthiravally from Kozhikode and Idukki; Balancotta; Kalluvally from north Kerala; and Malligesara and Uddagare from Karnataka.

    Alongside the old farm varieties are newer improved varieties, bred in India for yield and disease resistance. The best known are the Panniyur series — Panniyur-1 to Panniyur-8 — bred at the Pepper Research Station at Panniyur in Kerala; Sreekara and Subhakara, selections from Karimunda; Panchami, a selection from Aimpiriyan; Pournami, tolerant of root-knot nematode; and IISR Girimunda, IISR Malabar Excel and IISR Thevam, bred at the Indian Institute of Spices Research in Kozhikode.

    One distinction must be kept clear, because the names look alike. Tellicherry, Malabar, Lampong, Sarawak, Kampot and Vietnamese are not cultivars. They are place names and trade grades: Tellicherry is the name for the largest, latest-picked berries of Malabar pepper from Kerala; Malabar is the standard Indian export grade; Lampong is pepper from Sumatra; Sarawak from Malaysia; Kampot from Cambodia. The berry in the jar is graded by where it grew and how big it is, not by a cultivar name, and the same vine can give berries sold under more than one of those names.

    • Black pepper comes from the Western Ghats, the mountain range behind the Malabar Coast, where wild pepper vines still climb the trees of the rainforest. The spice's name carries its journey: the Sanskrit word was pippali, which became piperi in Greek and piper in Latin, and from there pepper in English. The word first meant long pepper, a close cousin, before it settled on this vine.
    • The oldest sign of pepper outside India is a strange one. Ramesses II, the great pharaoh of Egypt, died in 1213 BCE, and when his mummy was examined in Paris in 1976–77, black peppercorns were found packed inside the nostrils, put there by the embalmers to keep the shape of the famous nose. How pepper reached Egypt so early is not known — it may have travelled through traders whose names are lost — but the peppercorns were there.
    • Rome fell in love with pepper. After Rome took Egypt in 30 BCE, ships learned to ride the monsoon winds straight across the Arabian Sea to the Malabar Coast, and a Greek merchant's handbook of the first century, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, describes the run to Muziris, the great pepper port of the Chera kingdom near the mouth of the Periyar river. The Roman writer Pliny the Elder, writing in the same century, priced pepper by the pound and grumbled at the money Rome spent on it. Pepper was weighed like gold, and it was used as money — to pay taxes, tributes, dowries and rent.
    • The most famous payment of all came in AD 410, when the Visigoths took Rome. As part of the ransom for the city, they demanded 3,000 pounds of pepper — a weight of spice worth more than the same weight of silver. That is where the name "black gold" comes from: a spice so prized that a sack of it could buy a house, and a king would ask for it before silver.
    • For a thousand years after Rome, the trade stayed in other hands. Arab merchants carried the pepper from India to the Mediterranean, and Venetian merchants sold it onward across Europe, at prices only the rich could pay. In 1498 Vasco da Gama sailed around the Cape of Good Hope and reached the Malabar Coast by sea, and the Portuguese took the trade by force; the Dutch and then the British followed them. As the trade opened up, the price fell, and by the 1700s pepper had moved from the tables of kings to the tables of ordinary people. Today the vine is grown across the warm tropics — Vietnam, Brazil, Indonesia and India among them — but it still comes home to Kerala, where the wild vine grows.
    • In India, black pepper has been medicine as long as it has been food. In Ayurveda it is called maricha, and it is one of the three pungent spices of trikatu — black pepper, long pepper and dried ginger — a formula for weak digestion, meant to kindle agni, the digestive fire, and to carry other medicines into the body. The old texts call pepper a yogavahi, a carrier: a small amount added to a formula to help the rest of it work. In Chinese medicine it is Hu Jiao, a hot, pungent herb for a cold stomach — for cold pain in the belly, vomiting and loose bowels from cold, and a poor appetite in the cold months. In the West, the nineteenth-century American eclectic doctors used it for a weak, sluggish stomach and for flatulence, and as a warming stimulant. All of that use is tradition, told as tradition. The tested part stands on its own, under Health Benefits.
    • The distilled oil is a warming rub for aching muscles, and it is breathed in for focus — in one small trial it eased the craving of smokers trying to quit. Human · small
    • What is in the berry, first. The dried berry holds about 5 to 9% piperine, the compound that gives pepper its bite, plus a scented oil and smaller amounts of other pepper compounds. A pinch of ground pepper on food carries only a few milligrams of piperine at most. The trials below used 20 mg of pure piperine in a capsule, taken on its own — a dose no meal reaches.
    • The piperine story is real, and it is smaller than the headlines say. In 1998, Shoba and colleagues gave healthy volunteers 2 grams of curcumin — the yellow compound of turmeric — on its own, and then with 20 mg of piperine. On its own, curcumin in the blood was undetectable or very low. With piperine, the blood levels were much higher, and the authors reported a 2,000% rise in bioavailability. That number is quoted everywhere, and it needs its full truth told with it. The study was small, and it measured total curcumin in the blood — including the forms the gut and liver have already tagged for removal, which cannot easily enter cells. A 20-fold rise on a starting level near zero can still be a small amount. Human · small
    • A later test, done with care, found no gain at all. In 2025, Kroon and colleagues gave nine healthy men 2,400 mg of curcumin with and without 20 mg of piperine, and measured the free, untagged curcumin — the form that can actually enter cells. Free curcumin stayed below 2 nanomoles per litre in most cases, with piperine and without it. Piperine added no benefit. The two studies measured different things, and they do not agree. What can be said plainly is this: piperine slows the gut and liver enzymes that clear some compounds, so it can change how much of another substance reaches the blood — and whether that change helps a person at all is not settled. No trial has shown that pepper, or piperine, improves a health outcome in a person. Human · small
    • The same enzyme-slowing is the reason piperine changes medicines, and that part is better proven than the curcumin part. In a small human trial in 1991, Bano and colleagues gave six healthy volunteers propranolol, a blood-pressure drug, and six others theophylline, an asthma drug, each with and without 20 mg of piperine a day for seven days. With piperine, both drugs reached higher blood levels and stayed longer. Piperine has also raised blood levels of phenytoin, a drug for seizures, in small human studies. These were small trials of a capsule dose, not of pepper on food — but the mechanism is real, and it is why the warning at the top of the entry is there. A pinch of pepper on a meal is not the same as a piperine capsule, and no one should guess at the line between them while taking regular medicine. Human · small
    • Digestion is the oldest claim for pepper, and it rests on animals and tradition, not on people. In animal studies, piperine given with food raised the digestive enzymes of the pancreas and moved food through the gut faster. No trial in people has tested black pepper, or piperine, for digestion, appetite or bloating. The Ayurvedic use for weak digestion is centuries old and is told as tradition. Animal studies
    • The rest of the laboratory record is laboratory work. In dishes and in animals, piperine has shown antioxidant effects — mopping up the reactive molecules that damage cells — and it has eased swelling in animal tests. None of that shows what eating pepper does in a person, and none of it is carried as a health claim here. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • When to plant: Plant cuttings in spring, and keep them warm and damp until they root
    • Sun: Dappled shade — not full midday sun, which scorches the leaves, and not deep shade, which stops it fruiting
    • Soil: Rich, moist, well-drained soil that is slightly acid, around pH 5.5 to 6.5, and never sitting in water
    • Environment: A plant of the hot, wet tropics: hardy outdoors only in USDA zones 10 to 11 — the warmest corners of the United States, such as south Florida and Hawaii — where the coldest it will take is around 35 °F (about 2 °C), and frost kills it; it wants steady warmth, about 24 to 30 °C (75 to 86 °F), and air dampness above 70% — dry air makes the flower buds drop; anywhere colder, it grows only indoors or in a heated greenhouse, where the warmth and damp it needs can be kept up
    • Planter or ground: Ground in the tropics, on a tree, a pole or a trellis; in cooler places, a large pot indoors or in a greenhouse, with a moss pole or trellis to climb
    • Water: Water steadily while the vine settles
    • When to pick: Pick the spikes when one or two berries at the base of the spike begin to turn red, and before the fruit is fully ripe — left to ripen, the berries lose their bite and fall

    Garden notes

    • Give it something to climb from the start — a tree, a pole or a trellis. The vine climbs to about 4 metres on its support, holding on with short roots, and it roots again wherever a trailing stem touches the ground. Grow it from cuttings about 40 to 50 cm long taken from a mature vine, not from seed: peppercorns from a shop will not grow.
    • Patience is part of growing it. The vine bears fruit from its fourth or fifth year, and then for about seven years. The flowers are small, on hanging spikes 4 to 8 cm long at the leaf joints, and the spikes lengthen to 7 to 15 cm as the berries grow.
    • For black pepper, spread the green spikes in the sun for several days until the berries shrivel and turn black, then strip them from the spike. For white pepper, wait until the berries are fully red, soak them until the skin comes off, and dry what is left. For green pepper, pick the berries unripe and keep them fresh in brine or by freeze-drying.
    • Indoors, grow it in the brightest, warmest, dampest spot in the house — a warm bathroom window or a greenhouse is better than a dry living room. Mist it often, or stand the pot on a tray of pebbles and water, and keep it away from cold draughts and radiators. An indoor vine may never fruit, and that is the honest expectation: the plant asks for tropical damp, and most houses cannot give it.

    Propagation

    Take a 6–8 inch cutting from a healthy runner shoot near the base of a mature vine, with 2 to 3 nodes, and root it in warm, humid air in moist, free-draining mix. Give it a tall support to climb. Dried peppercorns from a shop will not grow — only a fresh cutting, or fresh ripe berries, can start a plant.

    Safety

    • Pepper as food, in the amounts used for seasoning, is safe for most people. Large amounts can burn the stomach, bring on heartburn, and make a sore stomach or an ulcer worse. Ground pepper makes anyone cough and sneeze, and it should be kept away from a small child's nose and mouth. High-dose piperine capsules are a different matter from food: they have not been well studied in pregnancy or while breastfeeding, and anyone taking regular medicine — above all phenytoin, carbamazepine, propranolol or theophylline — should talk to their doctor before taking them, because piperine can raise the blood levels of those drugs.
    • Essential oils are concentrates, many times stronger than the plant itself. Always dilute in a carrier oil before putting one on skin, and never swallow an essential oil.

    Sources

    • Shoba et al. (1998) — Influence of piperine on the pharmacokinetics of curcumin in animals and human volunteers (Planta Medica) — 2 g curcumin alone or with 20 mg piperine; blood levels undetectable or very low alone, much higher with piperine; 2000% rise in bioavailability reported
    • Kroon et al. (2025) — A pharmacokinetic study and critical reappraisal of curcumin formulations enhancing bioavailability (iScience) — 9 healthy men, 2,400 mg curcumin with and without 20 mg piperine; free curcumin below 2 nM in most cases either way; piperine added no benefit
    • Bano et al. (1991) — Effect of piperine on bioavailability and pharmacokinetics of propranolol and theophylline in healthy volunteers (European Journal of Clinical Pharmacology) — 6 volunteers per drug, piperine 20 mg daily for 7 days; higher peak levels and longer stay for both drugs
    • Srinivasan (2007) — Black pepper and its pungent principle-piperine: a review of diverse physiological effects (Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition) — the piperine review: digestive enzymes in animals, antioxidant work in dishes and animals, and the enzyme-slowing that raises drug levels
    • McCormick Science Institute — Black Pepper — the "black gold" name, the AD 410 ransom of 3,000 pounds of pepper, pepper used as money for taxes, tributes, dowries and rent, and the Malabar, Tellicherry, Cochin, Sarawak, Lampong and Belem grades
    • Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — the accepted name Piper nigrum, its place in the pepper family, and its native range
    • Spices Board of India / ICAR-Indian Institute of Spices Research — Black pepper extension pamphlet — more than 75 cultivars in India, Karimunda the most popular in Kerala, and the improved varieties Panniyur-1 to Panniyur-8, Sreekara, Subhakara, Panchami, Pournami, IISR Girimunda and IISR Malabar Excel
    • Rose & Behm (1994) — inhaled black pepper oil and the craving of smokers trying to quit

    Vanilla

    Vanilla planifolia

    Culinary

    Dried

    Vanilla is the world's best-loved flavour, and it comes from an orchid. Vanilla planifolia is a climbing orchid from the rainforests of Mexico, and it is the one orchid the world grows for food. Its fruit is a long green pod — called a bean in the kitchen, though it is not a bean at all — and after months of careful curing that plain green pod turns dark, soft and wrinkled, and gives out the warm, sweet smell everyone knows from ice cream, cakes and custard. The pod holds more than two hundred scent compounds, and the best known of them, vanillin, makes up only 1 to 2% of a cured pod's weight. Vanilla is the second most costly spice in the world by weight, after saffron, and nearly all of it is grown far from its home, on farms in Madagascar and Indonesia, by hand — every flower pollinated by a person's fingers, because outside Mexico the bee that does the job does not live.

    Cultivars

    Vanilla has had almost no modern plant breeding, so there are very few named cultivars. The trade grows it from cuttings of the plain species, and what sets one vanilla apart from another is mostly where it was grown and how it was cured, not a cultivar name.

    The one named cultivar with a formal standing is 'Handa', bred by researchers on Réunion and patented in 2017, selected for better production. Whether its cuttings will ever be sold to growers is not known.

    There are also named Mexican types grown for the trade, the 'Mansa' types, long-grown vines from Mexico chosen for their pods. They are spoken of as types rather than as registered cultivars, and the line between a type and a cultivar here is not sharp.

    The variegated forms sold for looks are the same plant, grown for their leaves, and they are slower and less vigorous than the plain green vine because the pale parts of the leaf hold less green colouring and catch less sun:

    'Variegata'

    Green leaves striped in creamy yellow.

    'Albo-Variegata'

    White-splashed leaves.

    The names that sound like cultivars mostly are not. Bourbon and Mexican are origins of Vanilla planifolia — Bourbon from the Indian Ocean islands, Mexican from its home country — and their flavour differs because of the soil, the weather and the curing, not because the vine is a different cultivar. Tahitian vanilla is a different plant altogether, Vanilla × tahitensis, a natural cross between Vanilla planifolia and Vanilla odorata, with a more floral, fruity smell and less vanillin, and it breaks down faster in heat. Pompona vanilla, Vanilla pompona, is another species again, with broad pods and a deep, woody smell.

    • Vanilla is a climbing vine of the warm, wet lowland forests of south-eastern Mexico and Central America, growing in the shade under the trees. It roots in the ground and climbs with thick, fleshy aerial roots that grip the bark of its host tree, reaching 15 metres long in the wild and more. Its stems are thick and green and succulent, about as wide as a finger, with glossy, fleshy leaves 8 to 25 cm long. The flowers are pale green-yellow, waxy and sweet-smelling, and each one opens for a single day. The name comes from the Spanish vainilla, a little pod or little sheath, for the shape of the fruit.
    • The first people to grow vanilla were the Totonac people of Veracruz, on Mexico's Gulf coast, who called it tlilxochitl, the black flower, for the dark cured pod. A Totonac tale tells that the first vanilla vine grew where a princess and her lover were killed for their forbidden love, and the vine was a gift from the gods. The Maya before them called it zizbic and worked out the first curing of the pods, mixing cured beans with copal resin to perfume their temples, and using the green pods on venomous insect bites and wounds.
    • The Aztecs took vanilla from the Totonac as tribute, and they are the ones who first put it in food: they stirred ground vanilla into xocolatl, their drink of cacao, chilli and water, drunk by nobles, warriors and priests. The drink was thought to give strength and lift desire, and vanilla beans were paid to Aztec rulers as tribute. Most of what is known of these early uses comes from Spanish writers after the conquest, not from the peoples' own written records.
    • Vanilla reached Europe with the Spanish in the 1500s, carried home with chocolate, and for two hundred years it stayed a luxury flavour for chocolate, pastries and sweets. In Europe it was also listed in medicine books as a nerve stimulant and a love potion, and given for fever, low spirits, stomach troubles and tiredness. Thomas Jefferson brought vanilla to the United States in 1789 after his time in France. By the early 1900s those medicine listings had faded away, and vanilla lived on as a flavour, not a treatment.
    • The turn that made vanilla a world crop came from a flower that would not set fruit. In Mexico the flower is pollinated by a small stingless bee of the Melipona kind, and nowhere else in the world does that bee live. Vines carried to Europe and to the French colonies flowered and bore nothing, and botanists tried for years to pollinate them by hand and failed. In 1836 the Belgian botanist Charles Morren worked out how the flower was put together and pollinated it by hand with fine tools, but his way was too slow and delicate for a farm.
    • Then, in 1841, on the island of Réunion in the Indian Ocean — then called Île Bourbon — a 12-year-old enslaved boy named Edmond Albius worked out a quick way to do it with a fingertip and a small stick: lift the thin flap inside the flower, the rostellum, that keeps the male and female parts apart, and press the pollen-bearing anther against the stigma. Within days other planters came to see it, and Edmond was sent around the island to teach the trick. He was freed when slavery was abolished in 1848, took the name Albius from the Latin alba, white, for the vanilla flower, and died poor in 1880, never paid for the discovery that built the whole trade. His way of pollinating — a small stick or toothpick, one flower at a time, in the morning while the flower is open — is still the way every vanilla farm in the world does it today.
    • After 1841 vanilla farming spread from Réunion to Madagascar, the Comoros and beyond, and by 1898 Réunion alone was sending out 200 tonnes of dried pods a year, more than Mexico. The name Bourbon vanilla comes from Île Bourbon, and it still means Vanilla planifolia grown on the Indian Ocean islands — Madagascar, Réunion, the Comoros and Mauritius. Madagascar is now the largest grower, and Madagascar and Indonesia together grow about two-thirds of the world's vanilla. In its Mexican home the wild vine is in trouble: its forest is being cut, and the IUCN Red List counts Vanilla planifolia as Endangered in the wild.
    • A green pod has no smell. The flavour is made after the harvest, in the curing: the pods are heated, then sweated in blankets and dried in the sun, day after day for months, until they turn dark brown, soft and wrinkled, and the vanillin and the other scent compounds form. A pod takes eight to ten months to ripen on the vine after pollination, and months more to cure. In 1874 chemists first made vanillin in a laboratory, and most of the vanilla flavour sold today is that laboratory-made vanillin, not vanilla from a pod. It is the same molecule, but on its own, so its smell is simpler than a cured pod's.
    • What is in the pod, first. A cured pod holds about 1 to 2% vanillin by weight, alongside vanillic acid, p-hydroxybenzaldehyde and more than two hundred other scent compounds. The extract sold in bottles is cured pods soaked in alcohol and water; under the United States food standard it must hold at least 35% alcohol by volume. Imitation vanilla is laboratory-made vanillin, usually in a weaker alcohol base. The amounts of vanilla eaten in food are tiny — a teaspoon of extract, a scraped pod in a pan of custard — and that smallness matters for everything that follows.
    • The honest size of the health evidence is small. A 2020 review of the research by nutrition scientist Keith Singletary concluded that support for human health benefits of vanilla, vanillin and vanillic acid was "limited and preliminary." There is no controlled human trial showing that eating vanilla improves health, prevents disease or treats any condition, so no health tag here rests on a human trial, because there is none to rest it on.
    • The laboratory work is real and is told as laboratory work. In chemical tests in dishes, vanilla extract and its compounds acted as antioxidants — they neutralised the damaging molecules that rust and age living tissue — and in one 2007 test the extract showed far less antioxidant power than the reference antioxidant it was tested against. In animal tests, vanillin turned down signals linked to swelling and changed how cells handled sugar. None of that shows what eating a spoonful of custard does in a person, and no trial has carried any of it into people. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • The one human work that exists is about smell, not about eating vanilla, and it is about familiarity, not about vanilla itself. In small studies of newborn babies, a smell the baby had already spent time with — vanilla, or its mother's milk — calmed crying and grimacing during a blood test from a vein. In a 2003 study of preterm babies, a familiar vanilla smell kept crying from rising during a vein puncture, but did nothing during a heel prick, which hurts more. In a 2005 study of 44 full-term babies, a familiar vanilla smell or familiar mother's milk calmed babies during a heel prick, while an unfamiliar vanilla smell did not calm them at all. A later study of 69 full-term babies found an unfamiliar vanilla smell had no effect on pain at all. The calming came from the smell being known, not from vanilla being vanilla. There are no controlled studies showing that the smell of vanilla calms stress or worry in adults. Human · small
    • One small skin study is sometimes quoted and is not carried here as proof. A serum holding 1% vanilla extract and 1.5% bakuchiol extract, rubbed on the face and neck twice a day for 56 days, improved firmness in adult women with sagging skin — but there was no comparison group, and the effect cannot be separated from the bakuchiol or from the two together. The natural medicines database rates the evidence for vanilla in wrinkled skin as too little to judge. Human · small
    • Vanilla does have one plain, practical use in the kitchen, and it is about taste, not medicine. The smell of vanilla makes food taste sweeter than it is, and in taste tests a little extra vanilla let makers cut a quarter of the sugar from yogurt without people liking it less. That is a way to use less sugar, not a health benefit of vanilla itself.
    • When to plant: Grow it from a cutting, not from seed — a length of vine with several nodes, laid along damp mix so the nodes root
    • Sun: Bright, filtered light, like the shade under rainforest trees — morning sun is kind to it, and direct midday sun scorches its thick leaves
    • Soil: A loose, rich mix that drains freely — half orchid bark and half peat moss or coconut coir is the usual mix — around pH 6.0 to 7.0, kept evenly damp but never soggy; wet feet rot the roots faster than anything else
    • Environment: Outdoors only in USDA zones 10 to 11, and some garden guides say zone 11 only; daytime temperatures of 21 to 32 °C (70 to 90 °F), nights never below 15 °C (60 °F), and frost kills the vine outright; the air should stay damp, 70 to 85% humidity, with moving air so the leaves do not rot; in most of the world it can only be grown in a warm greenhouse or a bright, humid indoor room
    • Planter or ground: A tall support to climb — a tree, a post, a trellis or a moss pole, at least 2 to 3 metres high — in the ground in the warm tropics, or in a pot under cover
    • Water: Keep the mix evenly damp; mist the aerial roots as well as watering the pot, and feed lightly while it is growing
    • When to pick: Pick the pod when its tip begins to turn yellow, after eight to ten months ripening on the vine

    Garden notes

    • Be honest about the difficulty before anything else. Vanilla is one of the hardest food plants a home grower can try, and most attempts fail. It needs a warm, wet, shaded place all year, a tall support to climb, and a person's hand on every flower.
    • A cutting takes three to four years to reach flowering size, and the vine lives ten to twenty years. The vine only flowers once it has grown long, so prune it back to keep it within reach — a vine that climbs out of reach cannot be pollinated.
    • The flower is the heart of it. Each flower opens at dawn and wilts by the afternoon of the same day, and it must be pollinated that morning or it drops. Lift the little flap inside the flower with a toothpick or a small stick, and press the pollen-bearing anther against the stigma beneath it — Edmond Albius's move, still done by hand on every farm. Pollinate only a few flowers on each cluster, or the vine sets more pods than it can ripen well.
    • Cure the picked pod: scald it briefly in hot water, wrap it in blankets to sweat, and dry it in the sun a little each day for months, until it turns dark brown, soft and wrinkled and smells of vanilla. A pod that is not cured has no smell at all. Expect the first pods in the fourth year, and count a single pod as a triumph.
    • Watch for root rot and stem rot from overwatering, and for spider mites and mealybugs in dry indoor air. Keep the vine out of cold draughts, and never let it sit in water.

    Propagation

    Take a stem cutting with at least two nodes. Let the cut end heal for a day or two in dim light, then plant it upright with one node covered, tied to a support. A fresh, wet cut planted straight away will rot. It needs warmth and high humidity, and a cutting takes 2 to 4 years to flower.

    Safety

    • Vanilla in food amounts is safe for most people. The extract is alcohol-based, so it is used by the drop and the spoonful in cooking, never drunk straight, and kept where children cannot reach it. Allergy to vanilla is rare, but workers who handle pods day after day can develop a skin rash from them. One buying warning matters: very cheap bottles sold as Mexican vanilla to tourists are sometimes flavoured with tonka bean extract, which holds coumarin, a compound banned in food in the United States since 1954 because it can damage the liver and is a danger to people taking blood-thinning medicines. The United States Food and Drug Administration has warned buyers about it. Real vanilla lists vanilla bean extract on the label; a bottle that lists tonka, coumarin, or no ingredients at all is one to leave on the shelf. The problem is the tonka, not vanilla grown in Mexico, which is among the finest there is.

    Sources

    • Singletary et al. (2020) — Vanilla: potential health benefits (Nutrition Today) — human support "limited and preliminary"; traditional uses listed; vanillin 1–2% of cured pods
    • Bythrow et al. (2005) — Vanilla as a medicinal plant (Seminars in Integrative Medicine) — Maya, Totonac and Aztec history; European medicine listings; Jefferson 1789
    • Melbourne et al. (2019) — Edmond Albius: the boy who revolutionised the vanilla industry (Linnean Society) — the 1841 hand-pollination discovery and his life
    • Lubinsky et al. (2008) — Origins and dispersal of cultivated vanilla (Economic Botany) — Mexican origin and spread of the crop
    • Bory et al. (2008) — Patterns of introduction and diversification of Vanilla planifolia in Réunion (American Journal of Botany) — the Réunion story
    • Goubet et al. (2003) — Olfactory experience mediates response to pain in preterm newborns (Developmental Psychobiology) — familiar vanilla smell calmed crying during venipuncture, not heel stick
    • Rattaz et al. (2005) — The calming effect of a familiar odor on full-term newborns (Journal of Developmental & Behavioral Pediatrics) — 44 babies; familiar vanilla or mother's milk calmed, unfamiliar vanilla did not
    • Romantsik et al. (2014) — The effects of olfactory stimulation on pain responses in full-term infants (Acta Paediatrica) — 69 babies; unfamiliar vanilla smell had no effect on pain
    • University of Florida IFAS Extension (2024) — Vanilla growing in the South — few named cultivars; only 'Handa' patented; 'Mansa' types; variegated forms grown for looks
    • Oxford University Plants 400 — Vanilla planifolia — native range; vines to 30 metres; planifolia gives 95% of commercial vanilla
    • Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — the accepted name Vanilla planifolia, its place in the orchid family, and its native range
    • United States Food and Drug Administration (2008) — Mexican vanilla warning — tonka bean extract and coumarin in some cheap bottles; danger for people on blood thinners
    • IUCN Red List — Vanilla planifolia assessed as Endangered in the wild

    Saffron

    Crocus sativus

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Mental HealthHormone HealthEye Health

    Dried

    Saffron is the most costly spice in the world by weight, and the reason is plain to see in the flower. Each lilac-purple bloom holds just three deep-red threads — the stigmas, the part of the flower that catches pollen — and each thread must be picked by hand, on the morning the flower opens. About 150 flowers give a single gram of dried saffron; a kilo takes roughly 150,000. The plant is a small autumn crocus, Crocus sativus, of the iris family: a low plant, 15 to 20 cm tall, growing from a corm — a round, bulb-like stem base — with narrow grass-like leaves and a flower that opens in October, when most of the garden is shutting down. Three things give saffron its character: crocin, which turns food gold; picrocrocin, which gives the bitter-honey taste; and safranal, which gives the smell — warm, hay-like, a little like iodine and a little like honey. One warning cannot wait: saffron is not the same as meadow saffron, the autumn crocus Colchicum autumnale, which is poisonous. The two flowers look alike to a careless eye and share a common name, but only Crocus sativus is the spice.

    Cultivars

    Saffron has no named garden cultivars in the way a rose or a tulip does — none at all in the nursery trade. Because the plant sets no seed, every plant is a clone grown from corms, and what differs is not the variety but where the corms were grown and how the threads were dried. Corms sold for the garden are sold by origin, not by cultivar name.

    What the trade does name are regional kinds, told apart by the colour, length and strength of the threads:

    Kashmiri

    From the high valleys around Pampore in Kashmir, with the darkest red threads — its best grade is called Mongra, the next Lacha.

    Aquila

    From the Abruzzo province of Italy, with short, deep-red threads.

    Spanish saffron, from La Mancha, has threads running from red to orange and a milder smell, sold in the grades Superior and Creme. Iranian saffron, which is most of the world's crop, is sold by grade rather than by a regional name.

    One named strain appears in the research, not in the garden trade: Crocus sativus var. cashmerianus, a Kashmir selection tested in field trials in the Mediterranean, which flowered well and gave strong colour and scent. It is a trial strain, not a cultivar a gardener can buy by name.

    • Saffron has been grown for at least three and a half thousand years, and its story starts in the Aegean. The walls of Akrotiri, the buried town on the island of Santorini, carry frescoes from about 1600 BCE showing women picking crocus flowers and offering the threads to a goddess — the oldest pictures of the harvest we have. For a long time no one knew where the plant came from, because it sets no seed at all: it is a sterile triploid, a plant with three sets of chromosomes instead of two, and it can only be grown by splitting its corms. A 2019 study of its DNA settled the question: it descends from the wild crocus Crocus cartwrightianus, and its home is Attica, the land around Athens, and the nearby islands. The Greek word for it is krokos, thread — for the slender stigmas.
    • The Greeks told a story about the flower. The young Crocus was struck dead by a discus thrown by the god Hermes, and where his blood fell, three drops stained the stigmas of a nearby flower red. The Romans used saffron everywhere a rich colour or smell was wanted: in food, in wine, in perfume, scattered on the floors of banquet halls, and in the baths — Cleopatra is said to have bathed in saffron-scented water. In Persia it was grown for a thousand years before that, and Persian cooks made it the heart of their rice dishes, as they still do today. In India it coloured the robes of monks and the sweets of festivals, and in old Persian and Indian medicine it was given for low spirits, for women's troubles, and for pain.
    • After the fall of Rome the spice faded from Europe, and it came back with the Arabs, who carried it into Spain in the 8th to 10th centuries. The Spanish word for it, azafrán, comes from the Arabic az-za'farān, the yellow one. From Spain it spread through the whole of medieval Europe, and its price was so high that a pound of it could cost more than a horse. In the town of Saffron Walden in Essex, the crop was so important that the town took its name from it. The price also brought cheats: saffron was cut with dyed petals, with marigold, with turmeric, and with the stamens of other flowers, and towns punished the fraud harshly — in 14th-century Basel, stealing saffron could be punished by death.
    • In the kitchen, saffron has always been used the same way: a few threads steeped in warm water or milk, then stirred into rice, bread, fish stew or sweet milk pudding. Paella in Spain, risotto in Milan, tahchin and polo in Persia, biryani in Kashmir — the golden rice of each place is saffron's work. As a dye it coloured silk and wool a rich yellow-orange, and in the Middle Ages it stood in for gold leaf in illuminated manuscripts. As a medicine, the old herbals gave it for melancholy — low, heavy spirits — for painful monthly bleeding, for coughs, and to bring on sleep. Much of that use was hope and habit, not tested proof. The tested part stands on its own, under Health Benefits.
    • Today almost all the world's saffron comes from Iran — more than nine tenths of it — grown on the dry high plains of Khorasan. Spain's La Mancha, Kashmir, Greece, Morocco and Afghanistan grow the rest. The harvest has not changed in three thousand years: the flowers open at dawn, pickers gather them by hand in baskets, and the three red stigmas are pulled from each flower and dried. A single picker gathers perhaps a few thousand flowers a day, and a kilo of the dried spice needs about 150,000.
    • What is in the thread, first. Dried saffron is mostly the three compounds named above — crocin, picrocrocin and safranal — with small amounts of other plant chemicals. The colour, the taste and the smell are three different compounds, and the trials tested the whole stigma extract, not one compound on its own.
    • The mood trials are the strongest evidence saffron has, and they are small. In the mid-2000s a research group in Tehran ran a series of short trials in adults with mild to moderate depression: 30 mg a day of saffron stigma extract in capsules, against a dummy capsule or against a standard antidepressant, for six to eight weeks. The saffron groups improved more than the dummy groups, and about as much as the groups on fluoxetine or imipramine. Two reviews that pooled these trials — Hausenblas et al. (2013), five trials, and Lopresti & Drummond (2014), six trials — found the same: a large effect against placebo, and an effect close to the standard drugs. The honest limits, stated plainly: most of the trials came from one research group in Iran, the groups were small — typically 30 to 40 people — the trials lasted only six to eight weeks, and no trial followed people for months or years. Saffron is not a treatment for depression on its own, and no one should stop or change a prescribed antidepressant on the strength of it. Human trials
    • The premenstrual trial is one trial, and it is a good one. Agha-Hosseini et al. (2008) gave 30 mg a day of saffron, 15 mg twice a day, or a dummy capsule, to women aged 20 to 45 with premenstrual syndrome, for two menstrual cycles. Daily symptom scores and mood scores improved more on saffron than on placebo. A later review pooling the trials of saffron for premenstrual symptoms found the same direction of effect. It is one trial of one dose for two cycles — promising, not settled. Human · small
    • The eye trials are the smallest of all, and the most tentative. Falsini et al. (2010) gave 20 mg a day of saffron or a dummy capsule to 25 people with early age-related macular degeneration — the slow wearing of the centre of the retina in older age — for three months, then swapped the groups over. The retina's response to flickering light improved on saffron and not on placebo. A later trial in 100 people over 50 with mild to moderate macular degeneration found a small gain on the eye chart — less than one letter — and a faster retinal response. The authors of both trials said the results need repeating, and neither trial showed that saffron changes the course of the disease. Human · small
    • Two more findings are worth a sentence each, and no more. In a 16-week trial of 46 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, 30 mg a day of saffron gave better scores on memory and daily-function tests than placebo. In a six-week trial of an evening dose of saffron extract, sleep quality improved a little in adults with mild sleeplessness. Each is one small trial. Neither makes saffron a treatment for dementia or for sleeplessness. Human · small
    • When to plant: Plant the corms in late summer — August to early September — about 10 cm deep and 8 to 15 cm apart, pointed end up
    • Sun: Full sun, and a long, warm growing season
    • Soil: Light, well-drained ground — a sandy loam is ideal — around pH 6 to 8, and it grows happily in chalky, stony or poor soil; heavy wet clay is the one ground to avoid — on heavy ground, plant the corms on a ridge or in a raised bed with gravel mixed in
    • Environment: Sunny, dry summers and cool, wet winters — the equivalent of USDA zones 6 to 9; it takes frost well once settled, down to about −18 °C (0 °F); what it cannot take is a wet summer — the corms rest through the summer, and water sitting on them rots them
    • Planter or ground: Ground — on a ridge or in a raised bed where the ground is heavy
    • Water: Water while the plants are growing in autumn and spring, and keep them dry through the summer rest; feed little — a light dressing of compost in autumn is enough
    • When to pick: The flowers come in the same autumn, October into November, often before the leaves are fully out; pick the flowers in the morning, as soon as they open

    Garden notes

    • Be honest about the harvest before anything else. A garden bed of saffron gives a handful of threads, not a jar: about 150 flowers make a single gram. Grow it for the flowers and the pleasure of the harvest, not to fill the spice cupboard.
    • The leaves are narrow and grass-like, and they appear with or just after the flowers, staying green through winter and spring, then dying back in early summer as the corms rest. The flowers are lilac-purple, about 5 cm across, with three yellow anthers and three deep-red stigmas arching out of the centre — the threads.
    • Pull the three stigmas from each picked flower. Dry them in a warm, dark, airy place for a day or two, then keep them in a small sealed jar away from light.
    • Every three or four years, lift the corms in late summer, when they are resting, and divide the clusters — each mother corm will have made several daughters. Replant the biggest corms and give the small ones away. The chief enemies are mice and voles, which eat the corms, and slugs on the flowers; a wire basket sunk in the ground keeps the corms safe where voles are a problem.

    Propagation

    Lift and divide the corms in summer, once the leaves have dried, and replant in late summer to early fall. Do this every three to four years, when the clump gets crowded. Saffron makes no seed — corms are the only way. Throw away any soft or spotted corms.

    Safety

    • In food, saffron is safe: a pinch is tens of milligrams. The trials used 20 to 30 mg a day of extract for weeks, and the side effects were mild — a little nausea, headache, dry mouth, or drowsiness. Up to about 1.5 g a day is generally counted safe, but the margin narrows sharply above that: around 5 g a day can be toxic, bringing vomiting, dizziness, bleeding and a yellowing of the skin; about 10 g has brought on abortion; and 12 to 20 g can be fatal. Those amounts are hundreds of times the trial dose, but they are the reason the spice is never taken by the spoonful.
    • The sharpest warning is for pregnancy. Saffron in medicinal amounts can make the womb contract, and large amounts have been linked to miscarriage. A small pinch in food is the traditional use and is generally counted safe after the first three months, but saffron supplements are not taken in pregnancy, and never without a doctor's word. Saffron can also thin the blood a little, so it is used with care by anyone on blood-thinning medicine or with a bleeding disorder, and before surgery. People with bipolar disorder should not take it without a doctor, because it has been reported to bring on over-excited, manic states. Anyone allergic to crocus or to the iris family should avoid it.

    Sources

    • Hausenblas et al. (2013) — Saffron (Crocus sativus L.) and major depressive disorder: a meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials (Journal of Integrative Medicine) — five trials, large effect against placebo, close to standard antidepressants
    • Lopresti & Drummond (2014) — Saffron (Crocus sativus) for depression: a systematic review of clinical studies (Human Psychopharmacology) — six trials, 30 mg a day for six to eight weeks
    • Toth et al. (2019) — The efficacy of saffron in the treatment of mild to moderate depression: a meta-analysis (Planta Medica) — 30 mg a day against placebo and standard antidepressants
    • Agha-Hosseini et al. (2008) — Crocus sativus L. (saffron) in the treatment of premenstrual syndrome: a double-blind, randomised and placebo-controlled trial (BJOG) — 30 mg a day for two menstrual cycles, women aged 20 to 45
    • Falsini et al. (2010) — Influence of saffron supplementation on retinal flicker sensitivity in early age-related macular degeneration (Investigative Ophthalmology & Visual Science) — 25 people, 20 mg a day for three months, crossover
    • Broadhead et al. (2019) — Saffron therapy for the treatment of mild/moderate age-related macular degeneration: a randomised clinical trial (Graefe's Archive for Clinical and Experimental Ophthalmology) — 100 people over 50, 20 mg a day for three months, crossover
    • Akhondzadeh et al. (2010) — Saffron in the treatment of patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease: a 16-week, randomized and placebo-controlled trial (Journal of Clinical Pharmacy and Therapeutics) — 46 people, 30 mg a day
    • Negbi (1999) — Saffron cultivation: past, present and future prospects, and Mathew (1999) — the Crocus monograph — the sterile triploid origin from Crocus cartwrightianus
    • Nemati et al. (2019) — the phylogenetic analysis placing saffron's origin in Attica, from C. cartwrightianus — the origin of the plant
    • Touwaide & Appetiti (2022) — Herbs in History: Saffron (American Herbal Products Association) — the history, the harvest, and the 100,000 to 150,000 flowers per kilo
    • Metropolitan Museum of Art — Dyeing for Color: Saffron — the Minoan use, the dye, the 150,000 flowers, and the warning against meadow saffron
    • Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — the accepted name Crocus sativus, its place in the iris family, and its native range
    • Atlas-Flora — Saffron crocus (Crocus sativus), care & requirements — growing: zones 6a to 9b, planting depth and spacing, the dry summer rest, and the Basel story

    Bay Laurel

    Laurus nobilis

    CulinaryMedicinal

    FreshDried

    Bay laurel is the tree behind the bay leaf — the dark green, glossy leaf that goes into almost every stock pot, soup and stew in the Mediterranean kitchen, and the wreath that crowned poets and winners in the ancient world. It is an evergreen tree or large shrub from the Mediterranean, in the laurel family, Lauraceae, growing 7 to 18 metres tall in the open, sometimes to 20 metres, with smooth bark and stiff, leathery leaves 6 to 12 cm long, dark green and shiny on top, with wavy edges and a strong middle rib. The leaves smell warm and spicy when crushed. Male and female flowers grow on separate trees — small, pale yellow-green flowers in spring — and the female trees bear small black berries like olives. One rule cannot wait: the whole leaf comes out before eating. The leaf stays stiff and sharp-edged even after long cooking, and a swallowed leaf can choke, or scratch and lodge in the throat or gut. Use it whole so it is easy to find, and take it out before serving.

    Terpenes in this plant: · · ·

    Cultivars

    The plain species is the true culinary bay, and most cooks grow that. Four named garden forms are sold, and all of them are true Laurus nobilis — but the plain species is the safest pick for the kitchen, because the named forms can taste a little different.

    'Aurea'

    The golden bay. New leaves come out bright yellow, brightest in full sun, and turn greener as they age. It is fully usable in cooking, and it is grown as much for its colour as for its leaves.

    f. angustifolia

    The willow-leaf bay. Its leaves are much narrower than the plain species, long and willow-like, and it is prized for its fine texture when the tree is clipped. It is said to be the toughest of the forms in cold.

    'Undulata'

    Also sold as 'Crispa' — the wavy bay. Its glossy leaves have rippled, wavy edges, which makes it a handsome clipped shrub or pot plant.

    'Saratoga'

    A smaller, rounder-leaved tree, growing to about 20 to 25 feet, with broader, lighter green leaves that are good for seasoning food. Some sources treat it as a cross between Laurus nobilis and the Azores laurel, Laurus azorica, rather than a pure form of true bay — whether it is a pure form or a cross is not settled. It is also the form noted as resistant to the laurel psyllid, a small sap-sucking insect, and to soft scale.

    'Baby Bay'

    Also sold as 'Bay Junior', a shrub to about 4 to 6 feet. Little is recorded about it beyond its size.

    'Little Ragu'

    A dense form to 6 to 8 feet in ten years. Little is recorded about it beyond its size.

    • Bay laurel is a tree of the Mediterranean, native from southern Europe around the sea to North Africa and the Near East. It is a leftover of the old laurel forests that once covered much of the Mediterranean basin when the climate was wetter; as the land dried, those forests shrank back to damp ravines and sheltered hillsides, with remnants still standing in southern Turkey, northern Syria, southern Spain, north-central Portugal, northern Morocco, and the Canary Islands and Madeira. The Latin name tells its standing: Laurus is the old Latin name for the tree, and nobilis means noble and famous. In Greek the tree was daphne, which is simply the Greek word for laurel.
    • The tree belonged to Apollo. In the old story told most fully by the Roman poet Ovid, Apollo was struck by the love god Eros's golden arrow and fell for the river nymph Daphne, who had been struck by a lead arrow and wanted nothing to do with him. He chased her, she begged to be freed, and her father turned her into a laurel tree. Apollo took the tree as his own, made it evergreen, and wore its leaves. From that story the laurel became Apollo's tree, sacred at his sanctuary at Delphi, and the wreath of its leaves became the prize for winners at the Pythian Games held there in his honour — for athletes, poets and musicians. At Olympia the winners' wreaths were olive, not laurel; laurel was Delphi's crown, and in Rome it became the crown of a victorious general in his triumph, and of poets. The words still carry it: a laureate is someone crowned with laurel, and a poet laureate carries the title to this day. The tree was also set by doors and gates as a guard, and Pliny the Elder wrote that it was held to be never struck by lightning — a belief, not a fact, and told as one.
    • In the Roman kitchen the leaf was an everyday seasoning, as it still is. The cookbook attributed to Apicius roasts a suckling pig with green laurel inside, seasons sauces with crushed laurel berries, and has the leaves taken out before serving — the same rule cooks follow now. A whole leaf, fresh or dried, goes into stocks, soups, stews, sauces, pickles and slow-cooked meat and fish, and comes out at the end. Ground leaf is used too, in smaller amounts, and the leaf also flavours the bouquet garni, the little bundle of herbs simmered in French cooking. Turkey grows almost all of the world's bay leaves today — about 97% of the total — and the leaves are picked from wild and planted trees alike.
    • As a medicine the tree has a very long record, and the record is one of warming remedies. The Greek physician Dioscorides, writing around 60 CE, called laurel warming and softening: a decoction of the leaves — leaves simmered in water — was used for sitz baths for troubles of the bladder and womb, crushed fresh leaves were laid on wasp and bee stings, and the berries were given with honey for lung complaints and breathlessness. He also wrote that leaves taken in drink upset the stomach and caused vomiting. Pliny recommended a leaf decoction boiled down to a third for pains in the bowels, and both men warned against the root bark — Dioscorides wrote that it could end a pregnancy. In the twelfth century Hildegard of Bingen gave laurel a chapter of her Physica: a powder of bark and leaves in honeyed water or wine to cleanse the stomach, and an ointment made with goat tallow to ease pain in the head, chest, side and back. The Renaissance herbals carried the same preparations on, and Lonicerus recommended leaves boiled in wine against indigestion, belching and vomiting. Preparations of laurel for rheumatism and scabies are recorded into the twentieth century, as is its use as a strewing herb for its scent, and as a pantry guard — dried leaves scattered in a cupboard to keep moths and other insects away from stored food.
    • The leaf must not be confused with its look-alikes, and the old books are plain about the danger of the mix-up. Cherry laurel (Prunus laurocerasus) and Portugal laurel (Prunus lusitanica) are different plants, in the rose family, and their leaves are poisonous; they are hedging shrubs, never food. California bay (Umbellularia californica) looks like true bay and is used in cooking in its own country, but its leaf holds umbellulone, a compound that can cause headaches and, in larger amounts, a blood disorder, and it is stronger and sharper in flavour. Only leaves sold as Laurus nobilis are the true bay leaf of the kitchen.
    • The distilled leaf oil is breathed in for a blocked chest and rubbed, well diluted, on aching muscles. Traditional use
    • What is in the leaf, first. Dried bay leaves hold about 1 to 3% essential oil, and most of that oil is 1,8-cineole, also called eucalyptol — commonly 30 to 50% of the oil — with smaller amounts of terpinyl acetate, linalool, pinene, sabinene and eugenol. The leaf also carries flavonoids and tannins, and sesquiterpene lactones, the compounds that can cause skin allergy in sensitive people. The oil in a bottle is a separate thing: it is the concentrated scent oil, and it is never swallowed.
    • The blood-sugar story is the one human trial there is, and it is small. In a trial in Pakistan, 40 adults with type 2 diabetes who stayed on their usual tablets took capsules of ground bay leaf — 1, 2 or 3 grams a day — or a dummy capsule, for 30 days. Fasting blood sugar fell by 21 to 26% in the bay leaf groups, total cholesterol by 20 to 24%, and the harmful LDL cholesterol by 32 to 40%, with no significant change on the dummy capsules. The good HDL cholesterol rose in the 1- and 2-gram groups, and triglycerides — the fats in the blood — fell in those groups too. Higher doses did no better than lower ones. That is one trial, of 40 people, for 30 days, and it has not been repeated by a larger trial since. The report does not say whether the groups were picked by chance, the three-month blood-sugar marker was not measured, and nobody in the trial ate bay leaf the way a cook uses it — a single leaf in a pot is far less than a gram a day of ground leaf in capsules. Bay leaf is not a diabetes treatment, and no one should change their diabetes medicine on the strength of it. Human · small
    • The tea trials are smaller still, and one of them had no comparison group at all. In Tunisia, 30 healthy adults drank a tea made from 5 grams of dried bay leaf in 100 ml of water once a day for 10 days. Fasting blood sugar, LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol and triglycerides did not change in any meaningful way; only urea, a waste product in the blood, fell. The same group later reported lower stress scores and lower blood cortisol — the stress hormone — after the same 10-day tea, but with no dummy tea to compare against, expectation and repeat testing could explain much of the change. A newer trial, published in 2026, did use a dummy tea: 55 healthy adults drank bay leaf tea or a dummy tea once a day for 10 days, and the bay tea group had lower white blood cell counts and lower stress and anxiety scores at the end. That is a small, short trial in healthy people, measuring blood markers and questionnaire scores — not illness, and not a cure for anything. Human · small
    • One more small trial, in 20 healthy adults, baked bay leaf powder into cookies: blood sugar was lower at 30 and 45 minutes after eating the cookie with the most bay leaf in it, but the total blood-sugar rise over two hours was no different from the plain cookie, and appetite did not change. Human · small
    • The rest of the health story is laboratory and animal work, and it stays there. In dishes and in rats and mice, bay leaf extracts and the oil have killed germs, eased swelling, lowered blood alcohol after a dose, and, in one laboratory screen, helped rat fat cells use glucose better. None of that shows what a leaf in a soup does in a person, and the review of the human evidence says so plainly: few human studies exist, they are small and short, and the doses and forms differ so much that firm conclusions are hard to draw. The old digestive use — a tea after a heavy meal to settle the stomach — has never been tested in people at all. It is tradition, and it is told as tradition. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • When to plant: Grow it from seed sown in spring, or from heel cuttings taken in late summer, about 10 to 15 cm long, kept in a cold frame; plant out in early spring while the tree is still dormant
    • Sun: Full sun is best — at least six hours of direct sun outdoors, with a little afternoon shade in very hot, dry places; indoors it wants the brightest window in the house; the leaves taste strongest when the plant has had full sun for at least part of the year
    • Soil: Any ordinary garden soil that drains well — loam, sand, even clay, so long as water does not sit in it; it is not fussy about richness or acidity, tolerating a pH from about 4.5 to 8.3, and doing best around 6 to 8
    • Environment: A tree for warm, mild places — hardy outdoors in USDA zones 8 to 10, taking short cold down to about −9 to −12 °C once established, and suffering browned leaves in a hard frost when young; in colder places grow it in a pot and bring it indoors for the winter, into a bright, cool room
    • Planter or ground: Ground in warm places, or a pot — in a pot, or clipped once a year, it stays a shrub a few feet high for decades, which is how most cooks keep it
    • Water: Water to keep the soil moist but never soggy; once settled in the ground it is drought-tough, but a young tree needs steady water for its first year or two
    • When to pick: Leaves can be picked at any time of year, fresh or dried

    Garden notes

    • Bay laurel is slow-growing, and that is the first thing to know. Left alone in warm ground it becomes a tree 7 to 18 metres tall, sometimes to 20 metres, and 5 to 6 metres across.
    • Cuttings can take many months to root. Suckers from the base can also be lifted in spring, and a low branch layered in spring can be cut free a year later. Feed a potted plant lightly in spring, and a plant in the ground once in spring if the soil is poor; it is a light feeder and asks for little. Wet roots in winter are the commonest cause of loss, above all in pots, so a pot must have drainage holes and a free-draining mix.
    • Prune once a year, in late spring or summer, to shape it — cutting back to a branch fork rather than shearing across the top — and the clippings are the bay leaves for the kitchen. It clips well into a standard with a single stem and a ball-shaped crown, a hedge, or a topiary shape, and it reshoots from old wood. To dry leaves, press them flat so they do not curl, and keep them in a dark, airy room, then in a sealed jar.
    • Flowers come in spring, March to May, in small pale yellow-green clusters beside the leaves, and on female trees they are followed by the small black berries in autumn. The tree is dioecious, so a lone tree may never set berries at all. Bay laurel has few pests; scale can appear, and a small moth sometimes glues two leaves together with cottony fluff and lays eggs between them — pull the leaves apart and remove the eggs. It is listed as harmful to pets if eaten, so keep fallen leaves and berries away from dogs and cats.

    Propagation

    Take semi-ripe cuttings in late summer or early autumn — 4 to 6 inch shoots from this year's growth, keeping only the top leaves — and root them in free-draining mix in a shaded, humid spot. Take several, as many fail and rooting can take a year. Layering a low branch in spring, or dividing a rooted sucker in spring, also works. Seed forms only on female plants and often rots before it sprouts, so it is not the home route.

    Safety

    • The whole leaf is taken out before eating. The leaf is not poisonous, but it does not soften in cooking, and its stiff, sharp edges can choke, lodge in the throat or gullet, or, rarely, pierce the gut. Ground leaf in cooking amounts is fine. The berries hold far more aromatic oil than the leaves and are not eaten. The concentrated oil must not be swallowed; it holds methyleugenol, a compound classed as possibly causing cancer in people on the strength of animal studies, and its main compound, 1,8-cineole, can trigger a spasm of the voice box or breathing trouble if put near the face of a baby or small child. The leaf and the oil can cause allergic skin rash in sensitive people, through their sesquiterpene lactones, especially in people allergic to the daisy family. For pregnancy and breastfeeding there is no good data on medicinal doses or the oil, so the safe course is cooking amounts only, with the leaf taken out. Anyone taking blood-sugar medicine should talk to their doctor before taking bay leaf capsules or strong bay tea, because the capsule trial did lower blood sugar.

    Sources

    • Khan et al. (2009) — Bay leaves improve glucose and lipid profile of people with type 2 diabetes (Journal of Clinical Biochemistry and Nutrition) — 40 adults, 1, 2 or 3 g ground bay leaf a day in capsules for 30 days
    • Singletary (2021) — Bay leaf: potential health benefits (Nutrition Today) — the review of the human trials, the Tunisian tea study, the cookie trial and the type 1 diabetes trial, and the judgement that firm conclusions are hard to draw
    • Chbili et al. (2026) — Effects of daily Laurus nobilis tea on inflammatory biomarkers and stress/anxiety levels: a randomized controlled pilot in healthy North African participants (Scientific Reports) — 55 healthy adults, bay leaf tea or dummy tea once a day for 10 days
    • Paparella et al. (2022) — A review of the botany, volatile composition, biochemical and molecular aspects, and traditional uses of Laurus nobilis (International Journal of Molecular Sciences) — the botany, the leaf oil, Turkey's share of world production, and the traditional uses
    • Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — the accepted name Laurus nobilis, its place in the laurel family, and its native range
    • IUCN Red List — Laurus nobilis assessment — Least Concern, native across the Mediterranean from southern Europe to Israel and North Africa
    • Wisconsin Horticulture, University of Wisconsin–Madison — Sweet bay, Laurus nobilis — the wreaths for poets, athletes, soldiers and emperors, the zones, and the houseplant and container growing
    • The Spruce — How to grow and care for bay laurel — the four named cultivars, zones 8 to 10, soil pH range, and pruning
    • Tisserand & Young (2014) — Essential Oil Safety — the safety limits for bay leaf oil, including the 0.5% dermal maximum

    Lentils

    Lens culinaris

    Culinary

    Heart HealthBlood Sugar HealthDigestive Health

    Cooked

    The lentil is one of the oldest foods on Earth — a small, flat seed, shaped like a tiny lens, that people have been farming for around ten thousand years. The plant is a low, bushy annual, a member of the pea family, standing about knee-high, with small white to pale lilac flowers and short pods that hold one or two seeds each. The seed is the whole story: cheap, quick to cook, needing no soaking, and packed with protein, fibre, iron and folate. Its Latin name says what it looks like — lens is Latin for lentil — and the glass lens in a camera or a pair of spectacles is named after it, because a double-convex lens is lentil-shaped.

    Cultivars

    Lentils are not sold by garden variety names the way apples are. They are sold by colour and size, and the colour tells you how they cook. Two broad kinds are recognised: the large-seeded macrosperma and the small-seeded microsperma, and within those, the seed coat and the inside — the cotyledon — come in several colours.

    Red Lentils

    Small, with a red-orange inside, and usually sold hulled and split, bright orange-red. They cook fastest — 15 to 20 minutes — and fall apart into a thick, creamy purée, which is why they are the lentil of dal, soups and stews. Named forms include Red Chief and Petite Crimson. The brown-skinned red-inside lentil sold whole is masoor.

    Green Lentils

    Larger, with a yellow inside and a green or brown coat, and they hold their shape when cooked — the lentil for salads and side dishes. North American growers name them by size and by old variety names: small green lentils are Eston types, medium green Richlea types, and large green Laird types.

    Brown Lentils

    The familiar all-purpose bag simply labelled "lentils" in many shops — mild, earthy, and the cheapest. The small, dark, nutty Spanish brown lentil is Pardina, and large brown lentils are often Brewer types.

    French Green Lentils

    Also called Puy lentils — small, dark green with blue speckles, and hold their shape best of all. True Lentilles vertes du Puy come from the Le Puy region of France and carry a protected origin; a French-style green lentil grown elsewhere is not a Puy lentil.

    Black Lentils

    Sold as Beluga — the smallest of all, tiny, glossy and almost round, like beluga caviar, which is where the name comes from. The variety behind the trade name is the cultivar Indianhead, first selected at the Indian Head research station in Canada. Beluga lentils hold their shape well and cook in about 20 to 25 minutes.

    Yellow and Tan Lentils

    Red or green lentils with the coat removed and the yellow inside showing — sold as split yellow lentils, quick to cook and mild in flavour. Their colour is the cotyledon, not a separate kind of plant.

    • The lentil is one of the handful of plants that launched farming. It belongs to the Neolithic founder crops of Southwest Asia — the first plants people of the ancient Near East brought under cultivation, alongside emmer and einkorn wheat, barley, peas, chickpeas and flax. Wild lentils were gathered long before they were farmed: wild seeds turn up at Ohalo II in Israel, a camp some 23,000 years old, and at Abu Hureyra in Syria, around 13,000 years ago.
    • The farmed lentil was first grown in the Fertile Crescent, the arc of good land running through what is now south-east Turkey, Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Jordan and Iraq. Its wild ancestor is Lens culinaris subspecies orientalis, a small-seeded wild lentil that still grows across the region. Genetic and dig evidence puts the first farming of it 8,000 to 10,000 years ago, with people sowing it on purpose even earlier, in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic. At Yiftah'el in Israel, a store of more than a million charred lentils was found — a harvest, put by, around ten thousand years ago. Farming selected for bigger seeds, pods that held together instead of shattering, and seeds that sprouted together.
    • From the Fertile Crescent the lentil travelled with farming itself: into Europe and Egypt with the first farmers, into Central Europe by the fifth thousand years before Christ, and into the Indus valley, where it was a staple of the Harappan civilisation. Today the biggest grower is a surprise — Canada, on the prairies of Saskatchewan, grows about a third of the world's lentils, ahead of India and Australia. India eats the most, and still imports lentils to feed its kitchens.
    • The lentil's most famous story is in the Bible. In Genesis, Esau comes in from the field famished and begs his brother Jacob for some of "that red stuff" — the red pottage, the lentil stew — and Jacob will give it only if Esau sells him his birthright, the firstborn son's share. Esau swears it away, eats the bread and lentil stew, and walks off. That is why he was also called Edom, which means red.
    • In India the lentil has been daily food for thousands of years, cooked as dal — most often the red lentil, called masoor. Old Ayurvedic books name it masura and praise the red lentil as light, easy to digest and strengthening, a food for people getting their strength back after illness, cooked soft as a thin soup with warming spices like cumin, ginger and asafoetida. That is tradition, told as tradition — no trial has tested masura as a medicine.
    • Everywhere it settled, the lentil became the poor man's meat and the pot's backbone: Turkish mercimek soup, Ethiopian and Eritrean stews, Egyptian koshary, the lentil soups of the Mediterranean. It keeps for years dry, cooks in twenty minutes with no soaking, and feeds a family for pennies — which is why it has outlasted empires while fancier foods came and went.
    • The plant feeds the ground as well as the eater. Like all legumes, the lentil fixes nitrogen from the air through little nodules on its roots, leaving the soil richer for the next crop. Farmers have used it as a rotation crop for that reason for centuries, and Canada first grew it as a cover crop to rest the fields before it became a crop in its own right.
    • What is in the seed, first. A hundred grams of cooked lentils — about half a cup — gives 116 calories, 9 grams of protein, 7.9 grams of fibre, 3.3 mg of iron (18% of a day's need) and 180 micrograms of folate (45% of a day's need), with almost no fat. Folate is the B vitamin the body needs to make new cells, and it matters most in pregnancy. The iron is plant iron, not the iron in meat: the body takes it in poorly on its own, and much better when the meal also holds vitamin C — lentils with lemon, tomato or peppers — while tea or coffee with the meal holds it back.
    • The blood-sugar story is the strongest lentil-only evidence there is, and it is human evidence. In a trial of 10 people, eight cooked lentil varieties were tested one by one, and every one had a low glycemic index — the measure of how fast a food raises blood sugar — between 10 and 23, where white bread scores 100 and white rice around 73. In a trial of 48 healthy adults, replacing half the rice or potato in a meal with cooked lentils cut the blood-sugar rise after the meal by about a fifth with rice and about a third with potato. A wider review of pulses in people with and without diabetes found that pulses eaten alone lowered fasting blood sugar and insulin, and that pulses in low-glycemic-index diets lowered HbA1c, the long-term blood-sugar measure. The lentil trials are small and short — single meals, ten to fifty people — so the honest size of it is: lentils raise blood sugar far less than most starchy foods, meal by meal. Whether eating them daily lowers the long-term risk of diabetes is not settled. Human · small
    • The cholesterol story is real but mostly pulse-group evidence, and the fence matters. A review of 26 randomised trials in 1,037 people found that about one serving of pulses a day — around 130 grams cooked — lowered LDL cholesterol, the "bad" cholesterol, by 0.17 mmol/L, about 6.6 mg/dL, against the same diet without pulses. But only one of those 26 trials used lentils on their own; the rest used beans, chickpeas and peas. The lentil-only trial is small and new: in 2024, 38 adults with a large waistline ate either 980 grams of cooked green lentils a week or meat-based lunches with no lentils, for twelve weeks. The lentil eaters' fasting LDL and total cholesterol fell, and their blood sugar after meals rose less, while the meat eaters' cholesterol rose. Digestive complaints were no worse than on the meat meals. One trial of 38 people is a beginning, not a verdict. Human trials
    • The long-view evidence is from large groups of people followed for years, and it is about legumes generally, not lentils alone. In a study of 9,632 Americans followed for 19 years, people who ate legumes four or more times a week had a lower risk of heart disease than people who ate them rarely. A review of more than a million people found that eating more pulses was tied to a lower risk of dying overall. These are associations — people who eat legumes also tend to eat and live differently in other ways — so they point the same way as the trials without proving lentils alone do it.
    • The fibre does quiet work of its own. Lentils carry soluble fibre and resistant starch — starch that passes undigested into the large gut, where it feeds the gut's microbes. That is the likely reason for the gentle blood-sugar effect and part of the cholesterol effect. The same fibre is why lentils fill you up: in single-meal trials, legumes gave about a third more fullness than other foods. None of this is a treatment for any disease, and lentils are not a substitute for medicine. Human · small
    • When to plant: Sow in early spring, two to four weeks before the last frost, once the soil reaches about 40 °F (4 °C) — lentils can take a light frost when young; in warmer places, zones 8 to 10, sow in autumn instead and let it grow through the mild winter
    • Sun: Full sun, six hours or more a day
    • Soil: It must drain well — a sandy loam is ideal, around pH 6.0 to 7.5; heavy clay and waterlogged ground rot the seed and the roots — more young lentils are lost to wet feet than to cold
    • Environment: A cool-season annual: it wants a cool spring and a dry finish, and it hates summer heat — temperatures above about 85 °F (29 °C) while it flowers make the blossoms drop; it grows best where springs are cool, roughly zones 3 to 7 for a spring sowing
    • Planter or ground: Ground — a field crop, not a pot plant; in a pot a lentil will grow leaves and even flower, but it will rarely set a useful crop
    • Water: Water gently until the plants are up, then water only when the top two inches of soil are dry — the crop needs little water, and none at all in the last two weeks before harvest
    • When to pick: Let the pods dry on the plant — pick when about 80 to 90% of the pods have turned brown and papery and the seeds rattle inside

    Garden notes

    • Be honest about the harvest before anything else. A home patch gives a small harvest — a ten-foot row gives roughly half a pound to a pound of dried seed, enough for a few soups, not a winter's store. They are worth growing to know one of the oldest crops on Earth at first hand, and because they leave the soil richer than they found it.
    • Sow the seed about an inch deep, two inches apart, in rows about 18 inches apart, and thin the seedlings to three to six inches apart. Seed sprouts in 7 to 14 days. The plant stands 12 to 24 inches tall, bushy and low, needing no stakes and no trellis.
    • Do not feed it nitrogen: the lentil makes its own through the nodules on its roots, and rich soil grows leaves instead of pods. A little compost for drainage is enough.
    • The plant flowers in small white to pale lilac blooms, then sets short flat pods, each holding one or two seeds. Cut the plants at ground level on a dry morning, dry them further under cover for one to two weeks, then rub the pods between gloved hands to free the seeds and winnow the chaff away by pouring the seeds from one bucket to another in a light wind. Dry the seeds fully before storing, or they will spoil.
    • Pests and troubles are few in a home garden: aphids on the young growth, and mould if the season turns wet while the pods are ripening. Rotate the crop — do not grow lentils or their pea and bean cousins in the same ground more often than once every three years — and never follow a wet summer with lentils in the same bed. The whole season runs about 80 to 110 days from sowing to dry seed.

    Propagation
