    Sow seed direct where it will grow, in early spring, 1–2 inches deep. It is a cool-season annual, so sow in late April to early May in most places. Do not move seedlings — the roots do not like it — and give it soil that drains well, as it rots in wet ground.

    Safety

    • Lentils must always be cooked — dried lentils eaten raw can cause nausea and stomach pain, and undercooked lentils are hard on the gut. Cooked properly, the common complaint is wind and bloating, which most people find eases as their gut gets used to them. People who struggle with wind should start with small amounts and build up. Lentils are a moderate source of purines, the compounds that break down into uric acid, so anyone with gout who has been told to watch purines should ask their doctor how much fits.

    Sources

    • Liber et al. (2021) — The history of lentil domestication and spread, from genotyping of wild and landrace lentils (Frontiers in Plant Science) — first farmed in Southwest Asia 8,000–10,000 years ago; wild progenitor L. culinaris subsp. orientalis; wild seeds gathered at Ohalo II and Abu Hureyra; the Yiftah'el hoard of more than a million lentils
    • Chamberlin et al. (2024) — Twelve weeks of daily lentil consumption improves fasting cholesterol and postprandial glucose (Nutrients) — 38 adults, 980 g cooked green lentils a week for 12 weeks, lower fasting LDL and total cholesterol and gentler post-meal blood sugar
    • Ha et al. (2014) — Effect of dietary pulse intake on established therapeutic lipid targets (Canadian Medical Association Journal) — 26 randomised trials, 1,037 people, about one serving of pulses a day lowered LDL cholesterol by 0.17 mmol/L; only one trial used lentils alone
    • Sievenpiper et al. (2009) — Effect of non-oil-seed pulses on glycaemic control (Diabetologia) — pulses lowered fasting blood sugar and insulin, and lowered HbA1c in low-glycemic-index diets
    • Ramdath et al. (2017) — Lentil carbohydrate fractions and post-meal blood sugar (Journal of Nutrition) — eight cooked lentil varieties tested in 10 people, all with low glycemic index values of 10 to 23
    • Moravek et al. (2018) — Replacing rice or potato with lentils lowers the post-meal blood sugar rise (Journal of Nutrition) — 48 healthy adults, half the rice or potato replaced with lentils, blood-sugar rise cut by about a fifth with rice and a third with potato
    • Bazzano et al. (2001) — Legume consumption and risk of coronary heart disease (Archives of Internal Medicine) — 9,632 people followed for 19 years, legumes four or more times a week tied to lower heart disease risk
    • Shaikh et al. (2024) — Lentils: global trade and popular regional cuisines (Legume Science) — Canada the largest producer at about a third of world output, then India and Australia
    • USDA FoodData Central — Cooked lentils per 100 g: 116 kcal, 9.0 g protein, 7.9 g fibre, 3.3 mg iron, 180 mcg folate
    • Merriam-Webster — Lens, etymology: New Latin lent-, lens, from Latin, lentil, from its shape
    • Genesis 25:29–34 — Esau sells his birthright for bread and lentil stew

    Chickpea

    Cicer arietinum

    Culinary

    Heart HealthBlood Sugar HealthDigestive Health

    FreshCooked

    Chickpea is the round, beige seed of a small bushy plant, and one of the oldest foods people have ever farmed. It is the backbone of hummus and falafel, the heart of chana dal and gram flour in India, and a food that has fed the Middle East, the Mediterranean and South Asia for ten thousand years. The plant is a low annual legume, a member of the pea family, Fabaceae, standing 20 to 50 cm tall, with small feathery leaves, white or pink pea-like flowers, and short pods that each hold one to three seeds. The name of the seed tells its shape: arietinum means like a ram's head, for the little beak on the seed that looks like a ram's nose. The Latin word for it, cicer, gave Rome its most famous orator his name.

    Cultivars

    Chickpea has no garden cultivars in the way a rose or an apple does. It is a farm crop, and its named forms are farm varieties, bred for yield and disease resistance, not for a garden bed. What a gardener meets are the two great market kinds, and a third, smaller one.

    Desi

    The small, dark kind: small seeds with a rough, wrinkled coat in brown, black or green, with a strong beak. This is the kind closest to the wild parent, the kind of India and Ethiopia, split for chana dal and ground for besan flour. Named desi varieties include JG 11 and JG 74, BG 256, K 850 and Pusa 3043, all Indian releases.

    Kabuli

    The large, pale kind: big, smooth, cream-coloured seeds, the kind in most cans and in hummus and salads in the Mediterranean and the West. The name means "from Kabul", for the road by which these larger seeds reached the Middle East and Europe. Named kabuli varieties include CDC Frontier, CDC Leader and CDC Orion, bred in Canada; Sierra and Royal, grown in the northern United States; and Pusa 1053 (Pusa Chamatkar), Pusa 5023 and KAK 2, Indian releases.

    Green

    The green-seeded kind: seeds that stay green when ripe, eaten fresh as a green vegetable. Named green varieties include Sadabahar and BDG 112. Green chickpeas picked young and fresh from the pod are a different eating experience from the dried seed, and the same plant can be picked either way.

    More than 190 chickpea varieties have been released in India alone, and the names above are a small pick of the widely grown ones, not a full list. A seed packet labelled simply "chickpea" or "garbanzo" is most often a kabuli kind.

    • Chickpea is one of the founder crops of farming. It was first grown in the Fertile Crescent — the broad arc from south-east Turkey through Syria and Iraq to the Levant — about ten thousand years ago, alongside wheat, barley, peas and lentils, when people first began to farm instead of gathering wild food. Its wild parent is Cicer reticulatum, a plant that still grows wild in a small area of south-east Turkey and nearby Syria, and the two can still cross and bear seed together. The oldest traces of chickpeas eaten as food come from Syria, around 8,000 BCE, and by 3,300 BCE the crop was well recorded in Egypt and the Middle East.
    • From its home the chickpea travelled in every direction. It reached Greece by the late Stone Age and was grown across the Bronze Age world, from Crete in the west to India in the east, arriving in India by about 2,000 BCE and in Ethiopia by the Iron Age. Homer names it in the Iliad, around 800 BCE, and the Greek writer Theophrastus wrote of it in his book on plants in the fourth century BCE. In Rome it was everyday food, eaten boiled, roasted and ground, and the oldest surviving Roman cookbook, Apicius, gives a recipe for chickpeas cooked with leeks, honey and vinegar.
    • The name carries a story of its own. In Latin the chickpea was cicer, and the Roman orator Marcus Tullius Cicero took his family name from it. Plutarch, writing his life of Cicero, tells that the first Cicero had a small dent in the end of his nose like the cleft of a chickpea, and took his name from it — and that Cicero himself, when friends urged him to drop so humble a name as he entered public life, answered that he would make the name Cicero more famous than the grand old names of Rome. When he was quaestor in Sicily he had a silver offering engraved with his first two names and, in place of the third, a little chickpea.
    • In India the chickpea became chana, a food in a hundred forms: whole chickpeas in curries, split chickpeas as chana dal, and chickpea flour — besan, or gram flour — for breads, fritters and sweets. In the Levant and Egypt it became hummus, the Arabic word for chickpea itself, ground with tahini, the paste of sesame seeds; and falafel, the crisp fried patties of ground chickpeas with herbs and spices. Whether falafel began in Egypt with fava beans and moved to the Levant with chickpeas, or the other way round, is still argued over by food historians, and the honest telling is that both beans have a claim.
    • In old medicine the chickpea was used as food and as a simple remedy together, as most staple foods were: Homer and later Roman, Indian and medieval European writers mention it for food and for healing both. None of that old use was tested in the way a medicine is tested now, and it is history, not proof. The tested part stands on its own, under Health Benefits.
    • The chickpea's newest story is only ten years old, and it began with water that cooks used to throw away. In December 2014 the French musician Joël Roessel found that the water from a can of beans could be whipped into a foam like egg white, and in March 2015 the American cook Goose Wohlt made a meringue from nothing but chickpea liquid and sugar. Wohlt gave the liquid its name, aquafaba, from the Latin for water and bean. Two tablespoons stand in for one egg white, three for a whole egg, in meringues, mousses and cocktails — a use for what was once poured down the sink.
    • What is in the seed, first. A cup of cooked chickpeas (164 g) carries about 269 calories, 14.5 g of protein, 12.5 g of fibre and 4.2 g of fat, with 282 micrograms of folate — about 71% of a day's worth — plus iron, manganese, magnesium and potassium. Canned chickpeas, drained and rinsed, carry less folate and more salt than chickpeas cooked at home from dry, so the numbers above are for home-cooked, boiled without salt. The protein is good plant protein but, like all beans, it is short on one building block, methionine, so it pairs well with grains, which supply it.
    • Blood sugar: the effect is real after a single meal, and small over weeks. Boiled chickpeas have a glycaemic index of around 30 — low, meaning blood sugar rises gradually — and hummus scores about 15. In a trial of 19 healthy adults, a chickpea meal gave lower blood sugar at 30 and 60 minutes than the same amount of carbohydrate from wheat foods or white bread. But in the same research group's six-week trial, 20 healthy adults eating chickpea foods or wheat foods for six weeks each showed no difference in fasting blood sugar, insulin, or how their bodies handled a glucose drink. The wider evidence on pulses as a family is stronger: a pooled analysis of trials found pulses improved fasting blood sugar and HbA1c, the measure of average blood sugar over months, in people with and without diabetes. So the honest size of it is: chickpeas slow the rise after a meal, and as part of a pulse-rich diet they help blood sugar over time — chickpeas alone, over six weeks, did not move the longer-term markers in healthy people. Human · small
    • Heart: the cholesterol trials are small, and all from one research group, but they point the same way. In a randomised crossover trial of 47 adults, a chickpea diet for at least five weeks left total cholesterol 3.9% lower and LDL cholesterol — the kind that clogs arteries — 4.6% lower than a wheat diet. A second, tighter trial of 27 adults found LDL 0.20 mmol/L lower on chickpeas than on wheat matched for fibre. A third trial, 45 adults adding at least four cans of chickpeas a week to their normal food for twelve weeks, found LDL down 7.3 mg/dL. The authors themselves put much of the effect down to the fibre and the fats in the chickpeas rather than to anything special in the seed. Pooled across every pulse trial, a daily serving of pulses lowers LDL by about 0.17 mmol/L and systolic blood pressure by about 2 mmHg. A small fall in a blood marker is not the same as fewer heart attacks, and no trial has tested that. Human · small
    • Digestion and fullness: the fibre does the work, and the trial record is thin but friendly. A cup of chickpeas carries 12.5 g of fibre, close to half a day's worth, and fibre is what keeps the gut moving and feeds the gut's bacteria. In a three-week trial, 200 g of chickpeas a day raised the numbers of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, a bacterium that makes butyrate, a fuel the gut lining uses — but the same trial found no change in how often people opened their bowels. Meals with pulses leave people feeling about a third fuller than the same meal without them, though that fullness does not reliably make people eat less at the next meal. The wind is real: the sugars in chickpeas that gut bacteria ferment raise flatulence, and fewer than half of people notice extra wind in the first week of daily beans. Human · small
    • When to plant: Sow in spring, about the same time as garden peas, two to three weeks before the last frost, when the soil has reached 10 to 16 °C (50 to 60 °F); in mild places, zones 9 to 11, it can also be sown in late autumn for a winter harvest
    • Sun: Full sun, six to eight hours a day
    • Soil: Light, well-drained soil — a sandy loam is best — around pH 6.0 to 7.5
    • Environment: A cool-season crop that wants a long, dry finish; it grows best where days sit between 21 and 27 °C (70 and 80 °F), and seedlings stand a light frost; it needs 90 to 120 days from sowing to harvest — about 100 days is the usual figure
    • Planter or ground: Ground — sow the seed straight where it is to grow; chickpeas grow a deep taproot and hate being moved, so do not start them in pots
    • Water: Water steadily while it settles, then water little — it is drought-tough once established, and it wants a dry finish so the pods can ripen
    • When to pick: For fresh green chickpeas, pick the pods when they are plump and green, about 85 to 90 days after sowing; for dried chickpeas, wait until the plant turns brown and the pods are dry and rattle when shaken — about 100 to 120 days

    Garden notes

    • Sow the seed 3 to 5 cm deep (1 to 2 inches), 8 to 15 cm apart (3 to 6 inches), in rows 45 to 60 cm apart (18 to 24 inches). Thin the seedlings to 15 cm apart when they are about 8 cm tall.
    • Like all legumes it makes its own nitrogen, fixing it from the air through the nodules on its roots, so it wants little or no nitrogen feed; too much nitrogen grows leaf at the cost of pods, and too much water rots the roots. Wet weather at flowering brings blight, and water sitting round the roots brings root rot — the two troubles that kill more chickpeas than cold does.
    • The plant flowers in about six to eight weeks, small white, pink or purple pea flowers, and the pods follow over the next month. Each pod holds one to three seeds. For dried chickpeas, pull the whole plant and hang it upside down in a dry, airy place to finish drying before shelling.
    • Four to eight plants per person is the usual garden figure for a useful crop, and a single plant gives only a small handful of pods, so sow generously. The plant is self-pollinating, and a gentle shake of the flowering stems is all the help it needs.

    Propagation

    Sow seed directly where it will grow, a few weeks before the last frost, once the soil has warmed to at least 5°C. Plant 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart, in full sun and well-drained soil. Seedlings appear in 7–14 days. Do not start in pots and move them — chickpea roots hate being disturbed. Where legumes have never grown, dust seed with the right rhizobacteria before sowing.

    Safety

    • Chickpeas must be cooked: raw or undercooked chickpeas carry lectins, plant proteins that upset the stomach, and only proper boiling destroys them. Canned chickpeas are already fully cooked and are safe straight from the can. A true chickpea allergy exists, though it is far less common than peanut allergy; the main allergens are storage proteins that survive boiling, and people allergic to other legumes — most of all lentils and peas — are the most likely to react, because the proteins are alike. People with a peanut allergy should ask an allergist before eating chickpeas, as laboratory tests show cross-reaction between chickpea and peanut proteins, though how often that turns into a real reaction is not settled. Chickpeas are a food, not a medicine, and none of what is written above is a treatment for diabetes, heart disease or any other illness.

    Sources

    • Pittaway et al. (2006) — Dietary supplementation with chickpeas for at least 5 weeks results in small but significant reductions in serum total and low-density lipoprotein cholesterols in adult women and men — 47 adults, randomised crossover, at least 5 weeks each diet
    • Pittaway et al. (2007) — Effects of a controlled diet supplemented with chickpeas on serum lipids, glucose tolerance, satiety and bowel function — 27 adults, randomised crossover, 5 weeks each diet, LDL 0.20 mmol/L lower
    • Nestel et al. (2004) — Effects of long-term consumption and single meals of chickpeas on plasma glucose, insulin, and triacylglycerol concentrations — 19 adults single-meal, 20 adults six-week crossover; single meals lowered glucose, six weeks did not move fasting glucose or insulin
    • Sievenpiper et al. (2009) — Effect of non-oil-seed pulses on glycaemic control: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials in people with and without diabetes — pulses improved fasting glucose and HbA1c
    • Ha et al. (2014) — Effect of dietary pulse intake on established therapeutic lipid targets for cardiovascular risk reduction: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials — daily pulses lowered LDL by 0.17 mmol/L and systolic blood pressure by about 2 mmHg
    • Jukanti et al. (2012) — Nutritional quality and health benefits of chickpea (Cicer arietinum L.): a review — the seed's nutrients and the state of the health evidence
    • USDA FoodData Central — Chickpeas (garbanzo beans, Bengal gram), mature seeds, cooked, boiled, without salt (FDC 173757) — one cup: 269 kcal, 14.5 g protein, 12.5 g fibre, 282 mcg folate
    • Wangorsch et al. (2020) — Identification and characterization of IgE-reactive proteins and a new allergen (Cic a 1.01) from chickpea (Cicer arietinum) — allergens survive boiling; possible cross-reaction with peanut proteins
    • Abbo et al. (2003) — The chickpea, summer cropping, and a new model for pulse domestication in the ancient Near East — domestication in the Fertile Crescent with wheat, barley, peas and lentils
    • Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — A family affair: protecting the humble chickpea — desi and kabuli kinds, domestication about 10,000 years ago, earliest food traces in Syria around 8,000 BCE
    • Plutarch — Life of Cicero 1.1–3.5 — the chickpea dent on the first Cicero's nose, and Cicero's answer to friends who urged him to change the name
    • Wikipedia — Aquafaba — Roessel's December 2014 foam experiments and Wohlt's March 2015 meringue; the name from Latin aqua and faba; 2 tablespoons per egg white, 3 per whole egg

    Oats

    Avena sativa

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Blood Sugar HealthHeart HealthSkin Health

    Cooked

    Oats are the cool-climate grain — the one that grows where wheat gives up. The oat is a grass, a tall annual with loose, nodding heads of grain that turn gold as they ripen, and its story is the story of the cold north: scorned in the warm south as horse food, loved in Scotland as the staff of life, and now in nearly every kitchen in the world as porridge, muesli, oatcakes and oat milk. What sets oats apart from every other grain is one fibre inside the kernel, beta-glucan, and it carries one of the few health claims food regulators have actually allowed on a food — for cholesterol, at a measured daily amount. One caution cannot wait: ordinary oats are often grown, harvested and milled alongside wheat, barley and rye, so they can carry gluten. Anyone with coeliac disease needs oats labelled gluten-free, and a small number of people with coeliac disease react to the oat protein itself, so oats are best brought in with a doctor or dietitian's guidance.

    Cultivars

    Oats are a field crop, not a garden plant, and the named forms are farm varieties — bred for yield, straw strength, disease resistance and milling quality — rather than garden cultivars. They fall into two groups by sowing time, and into two kinds by the husk. Spring oats are sown in early spring and cut in late summer; winter oats are sown in autumn, stand through the winter, and are cut the next summer. Husked oats keep a tough hull around the grain that must be milled off; naked or hull-less oats shed the hull at harvest, so the groat comes out clean.

    Spring oats, husked — the common milling kinds

    'Canyon', the second most widely grown spring oat in the United Kingdom, the millers' steady choice, tall straw and early to ripen; 'Conway', 'Aspen' and 'Caledon', all on the United Kingdom's recommended lists; and 'Lion', a short, stiff-strawed milling oat with the best kernel content of the spring kinds; 'Yukon' and 'Delfin', short, strong-strawed kinds that stand well in poor ground, Delfin the highest yielding spring oat across Europe in its trials. In North America the long-standing milling kind is 'CDC Dancer'.

    Winter oats, husked

    'Mascani', 'Gerald' and 'Dalguise', the standard winter kinds in the United Kingdom, taller and later than the spring kinds; and 'Cromwell', a newer winter kind. Winter oats yield more than spring oats where the winters are mild enough for them, and they are the kinds most often grown for milling in the warmer oat country.

    Naked or hull-less oats

    The kinds a home grower wants, because the grain needs no milling to eat: 'Avalon', 'Fusion', 'Grafton' and 'Peloton' among the winter kinds, and 'Kamil' and 'Lennon' among the spring kinds, all listed in the United Kingdom's 2026 inspectors' guide; and in North America 'Hulless Paul', a hull-less kind bred for home growing, whose grain falls clean from the hull at threshing. Naked oats yield less than husked kinds — the hull makes up about 30% of a husked oat's weight — but they carry less of the mould toxins that gather in the hull, and for a home plot they are the practical choice.

    Older kinds

    Two older kinds worth knowing by name. 'Markton', an American kind of the 1920s, was the first oat bred to resist covered smut, a grain disease of the day. And the black oat of old English and Scottish farming — dark-hulled oats, grown in Orkney and Shetland into modern times — belongs mostly to the bristle-pointed oat, Avena strigosa, a different species from the common oat, not a cultivar of it. The naked oat of old English farming, called pilcorn, was a hull-less race of the common oat, grown in England in the thirteenth century.

    • Oats came to the human table by a side door. Unlike wheat and barley, which people set out to tame at the dawn of farming, the oat first travelled with those crops as an uninvited weed — tolerated, then gradually adopted — and was only grown as a crop in its own right thousands of years later, in the cool, wet north of Bronze Age Europe. People were already gathering wild oats long before any of that: a granary in the Jordan Valley, dated to about 11,400 to 11,200 years ago, held on the order of 120,000 wild oat seeds stored alongside wild barley. That was gathering, not farming — the oat was not yet a crop.
    • The wild oat most geneticists now hold to be the crop's closest ancestor is Avena sterilis, the wild oat of the Near East and the Mediterranean, a plant that carries six sets of chromosomes — the same six sets the cultivated oat carries. Farmers in the cooler, wetter parts of Europe began to pick out the oat plants that kept their grain instead of scattering it, and by about 1000 BCE the oat was a deliberate crop of the north. It thrived exactly where wheat failed: poor, acid soils, short growing seasons, and cool, damp, cloudy summers.
    • The Greeks and Romans knew the oat and thought little of it. To them it was animal feed and peasants' food, and the Roman writer Pliny recorded it as a weed of wheat fields. The Romans carried it to Britain, where the cool, wet climate suited it perfectly. By 1500 it was an important grain in England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales, and it had spread with settlers to the rest of northern Europe.
    • In Scotland the oat became the people's grain, and the Scots made a cuisine of it. Porridge — oatmeal simmered with water or milk — was the daily breakfast. Oatcakes, baked on a griddle, were the daily bread. Oats went into broths to stretch scarce meat, into haggis, and into bannocks for feast days. The grain's link with poverty in southern England only sharpened the Scottish pride in it: Samuel Johnson's Dictionary of 1755 defined oats as "a grain, which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people" — and the Scots wore the insult as a badge.
    • In Ireland and the north of England the story was much the same: porridge, oatcakes, and oats as winter feed for horses and cattle. Oats stored well, fed animals through the winter, and cooked into filling meals without the gluten that makes wheat bread rise — a lack that mattered, since oat flour on its own makes flat, dense loaves, and the oat's place was the pot and the griddle, not the oven.
    • Across the Atlantic, oats travelled with settlers and stayed a farm crop for a long time. In America they were grown mostly for animal feed until around 1900, when local mills and grocery stores began to sell oatmeal as a breakfast food. In 1888 seven American oat millers joined to form the American Cereal Company, later renamed the Quaker Oats Company, and its advertising — including the first trial-size boxes in 1890 — turned a farm grain into a packaged breakfast. Quick oats followed in 1922, instant oats in 1966, and the first flavoured oatmeal, maple and brown sugar, in 1970.
    • The modern table has given the oat a second life. Rolled oats, steel-cut oats and Scottish oats — the same grain, cut or flattened in different ways — sit beside muesli and granola. Overnight oats, soaked cold in a jar, became a fashion of the 2010s and after. And oat milk, first sold in Sweden in the 1990s, put the grain in the coffee cup: oats soaked and strained, a drink that foams like milk and carries no dairy.
    • Folk medicine used the oat gently, and mostly on the outside. Oatmeal baths and poultices were laid on itchy, irritated skin, and oat straw — the dried stems — was brewed as a tea in folk practice for nerves and tiredness. The skin use is the one that lasted: finely ground oatmeal is still the home remedy for itching, and it is the one folk use that modern regulators have taken up. The straw tea was hope and habit, not tested proof, and nothing is claimed for it here.
    • What is in the grain, first. A whole oat kernel — the groat — holds starch, protein, oil, and fibre, and the fibre that matters most is beta-glucan, a soluble fibre: soluble means it dissolves in water, and beta-glucan goes thick, which is what makes porridge gluey. About 60 grams of dry oats — a generous bowl — holds about 3 grams of beta-glucan, the amount the cholesterol evidence is built on.
    • Oats also carry avenanthramides, compounds found almost nowhere else, which calm swelling and itching in laboratory tests — laboratory tests, not proof in people. Lab studies
    • The cholesterol finding is the strongest thing oats have, and it is unusually honest for a food. In 1997 the United States Food and Drug Administration allowed a health claim on oat foods: that eating at least 3 grams of beta-glucan from oats a day, as part of a diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol, may reduce the risk of heart disease. The European Food Safety Authority reached the same conclusion in 2010 and allows the claim that oat beta-glucan helps keep blood cholesterol at a normal level, at the same 3 grams a day. Human trials
    • The number behind the claim comes from a pooling of 28 randomised trials, published by Whitehead and colleagues in 2014. At 3 grams of oat beta-glucan a day or more, LDL cholesterol — the "bad" cholesterol — fell by 0.25 millimoles per litre, about 10 milligrams per decilitre, and total cholesterol by 0.30 millimoles per litre, against the control diets. A larger pooling of 58 trials in 2016 found much the same: LDL down by about 4%, non-HDL cholesterol by about 5%. The effect is modest and real, and it was larger in people who started with higher cholesterol, and larger again in people with diabetes — though only three of the 28 trials in the first pooling recruited people with diabetes. More than 3 grams a day did not measurably add to the effect. The thick gel beta-glucan forms in the gut is thought to be the reason: it traps bile acids, the body makes bile from cholesterol, and the liver then draws more cholesterol from the blood to make new bile. Human trials
    • Blood sugar is the second regulator-backed finding, and it works meal by meal, not day by day. In 2011 the European Food Safety Authority concluded that beta-glucans from oats and barley reduce the rise in blood sugar after a meal, when a meal holds about 4 grams of beta-glucan for every 30 grams of digestible carbohydrate in it. The thick gel slows the stomach emptying and slows the meeting of food and digestive juices, so the sugar enters the blood more gently. The form of the oats matters here: instant oatmeal raises blood sugar far more sharply than steel-cut or large-flake oats — in the standard tables of glycaemic index, instant oatmeal scores around 79 while steel-cut oats score around 52 — because the finer the grain is cut and the more it is cooked, the faster its starch is reached and broken down. A bowl of instant oats is not the same food, for blood sugar, as a bowl of steel-cut oats. Human trials
    • The skin finding is the third, and it rests on a different form of the same grain. Colloidal oatmeal — the whole oat kernel milled to a very fine powder that spreads through bath water instead of sinking — is listed by the United States Food and Drug Administration as an over-the-counter skin protectant, allowed to say it temporarily protects the skin and helps relieve minor itching from rashes, eczema, poison ivy, oak or sumac, and insect bites. The American Academy of Dermatology lists a colloidal oatmeal bath among the home steps that give quick, short-term relief from itchy childhood eczema. Human trials are small but encouraging: in a 2017 trial of 90 children with mild to moderate eczema, a 1% colloidal oatmeal cream worked as well as a prescription barrier cream over three weeks, and in a 2020 trial of 61 people with mild to moderate eczema, the oatmeal cream improved skin hydration and barrier function and cut eczema scores by about half over two weeks, while a standard moisturiser improved hydration only. An oatmeal bath soothes the itch; it does not treat eczema itself, and it is not a replacement for the treatment a doctor prescribes for a flare. Human · small
    • Two things are often claimed for oats that the evidence does not yet carry. First, fullness and weight: beta-glucan's thickness can help a meal feel filling, but the trials on lasting fullness and on weight are small and mixed, and no regulator allows a weight claim for oats. Second, blood pressure: some trials suggest a small fall in blood pressure with oat eating, but the finding is far less settled than the cholesterol finding, and it is not carried as a benefit here.
    • When to plant: Sow spring oats outdoors two to six weeks before the last frost, as soon as the ground can be worked; winter oats are sown in late summer or early autumn
    • Sun: Full sun — six hours a day or more
    • Soil: Deep, well-drained, loamy ground, around pH 6.0 to 7.0; oats tolerate poor, acid ground better than wheat does
    • Environment: A cool-season crop that grows best at about 10 to 24 °C (50 to 75 °F), in USDA zones 2 to 8; it takes light frost when young, and hot, dry summers shorten the grain and thin the yield
    • Planter or ground: Ground — oats are not suited to pots; they need open ground and full sun
    • Water: Needs steady moisture rather than drought — water steadily while the plants settle and while the heads fill; dry spells thin the crop
    • When to pick: Harvest when the heads are golden and the grains feel hard and dry, and a thumbnail pressed to a grain leaves no dent — about 90 to 120 days after sowing for spring kinds

    Garden notes

    • Be honest about the scale before anything else. Oats are a field grain, not a garden vegetable. A home plot can grow them — a small bed gives a few bowls of porridge and a fine sight in late summer — but a family cannot live off a garden bed of oats. Grow them for the pleasure of it, for the grain, and for the soil: as a cover crop they smother weeds, hold the ground against erosion, and feed the soil when they are turned in.
    • Heavy wet clay is the enemy: roots sitting in water invite disease. A dressing of compost or aged manure before sowing is enough for a home bed; heavy feeding makes tall, weak straw that falls over in wind.
    • Sow spring oats outdoors two to six weeks before the last frost, as soon as the ground can be worked, broadcasting the seed evenly and raking it in, or sowing in rows 15 to 30 cm (6 to 12 inches) apart. Seed goes 1 to 2 inches deep. Winter oats are sown in late summer or early autumn, so they stand through the winter. Germination takes five to ten days in cool soil. Keep the bed weeded while the oats are young; once they are knee-high they shade out most weeds themselves.
    • The plant grows 60 to 120 cm (2 to 4 feet) tall, with flat, pale green leaves and a loose, open head of grain — a panicle — that hangs and nods as it fills, quite unlike the stiff upright ear of wheat or barley. Each little grain sits in a papery husk, and the whole head turns from green to gold as it ripens, about 90 to 120 days after sowing for spring kinds. Birds love the ripening grain, so a home bed may need netting in the last weeks.
    • Cut the stems close to the ground with a sickle or shears, tie them in bundles, and let them dry for a few days under cover. Then thresh — beat the bundles, or rub the heads between gloved hands — and winnow, pouring the grain from one bucket to another in a light breeze so the chaff blows away. Husked kinds need the hull milled off before eating; naked kinds are ready to cook as they come. Store clean, dry groats in sealed jars in a cool place; grain kept above 10 to 15% moisture will spoil.
    • As a cover crop, sow them thickly in late summer and turn them in before they set seed, or let them stand through winter where the frosts kill them, and the dead growth will feed the ground for the spring.

    Propagation

    Sow seed 1–2 inches deep in drills, in spring for grain or in autumn as a winter cover crop, and give it at least ten weeks of cool-season growth. After an oat cover crop has died down, wait at least three weeks before sowing other seeds — oats give off chemicals that stop other seeds sprouting.

    Safety

    • Oats themselves hold no gluten — the gluten in ordinary oats comes from wheat, barley and rye grown, harvested and milled alongside them — so people with coeliac disease must use oats labelled gluten-free, and a small number react to the oat protein avenin itself. A true allergy to oats is rare but real, and anyone allergic to oats should avoid them in food and on the skin. Oat products on the skin are gentle and widely used, including for babies, but a patch test on a small area of skin is wise before a new preparation is used widely, and oatmeal baths make the tub slippery. Oats are a food, not a medicine: the cholesterol effect needs about 3 grams of beta-glucan a day, every day, as part of a diet low in saturated fat — one bowl, now and then, does not do it.

    • Ho et al. (2016) — A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials on the effect of oat beta-glucan on cholesterol (British Journal of Nutrition) — 58 trials, median 3.5 g a day, LDL down about 4%

    • European Food Safety Authority (2011) — Scientific opinion on oat and barley beta-glucan and post-meal blood sugar — the claim at 4 g of beta-glucan per 30 g of available carbohydrate in a meal

    • Kurtz & Wallo (2007) — Colloidal oatmeal: history, chemistry and clinical properties (Journal of Drugs in Dermatology) — the FDA skin protectant standing and the 1945 first bath preparation
    • United States Food and Drug Administration — Skin protectant drug products for over-the-counter human use (21 CFR Part 347) — colloidal oatmeal as an allowed active ingredient
