    • Reynertson et al. (2020) — A 1% colloidal oatmeal cream against a standard moisturiser in mild to moderate eczema (Journal of Drugs in Dermatology) — 61 people, fourteen days
    • Britannica — Oatmeal, and the Quaker Oats Company — the Roman scorn, oats in Britain by 1500, the 1888 millers' union, quick oats 1922, instant oats 1966
    • National Institute of Agricultural Botany (2026) — Cereal Crop Inspectors Guide to Oat Field Characters, Oat 2026 — the named spring, winter, husked and naked varieties
    • Agrii — Canyon variety profile — the second most widely grown spring oat in the United Kingdom, and Quaker's favoured kind from Scottish growers
    • CPM Magazine — Rotational resilience: the cereal with health at its heart — Lion, Yukon and Delfin, and the millers' variety choices

    Quinoa

    Chenopodium quinoa

    Culinary

    Blood Sugar HealthHeart Health

    Cooked

    Quinoa (KEEN-wah) is a seed that eats like a grain but is not one. It is the seed of a tall, leafy plant from the high Andes, a cousin of spinach, beets and chard, and it carries its colour on its head: the seed clusters ripen in shades of cream, gold, pink, red and deep purple. It has fed mountain peoples for thousands of years, it was pushed aside under Spanish rule, and it is now grown and eaten all over the world. What sets it apart from every true grain is its protein: quinoa holds all nine of the amino acids the human body cannot make for itself, which few plant foods can claim.

    Cultivars

    Quinoa is sold by seed colour as much as by name — white, red and black seed in the shops — and the named garden forms below are the ones seed sellers and trial records agree on. Colours and habits differ by kind, and the seed colour of a named form is part of its name in the trade.

    Brightest Brilliant Rainbow

    The best-known garden form: a mix of seed heads in hot pink, burgundy, red, orange, yellow, white and green, grown as much for looks as for food. Takes 90 to 120 days to ripen.

    Cherry Vanilla

    Compact, early to ripen, with pink and cream seed heads and a mild, sweet flavour.

    Red Faro

    Deep red seed heads; in one trial of ten kinds it held the most grain protein, 14.0%.

    Titicaca

    A Danish-bred form, bred to ripen without waiting for short days, so it grows well in northern gardens.

    Dave 407

    Also sold as Colorado 407: bred in Colorado for high ground and high yield.

    Temuco

    A Chilean lowland form, from the warmer quinoa country of southern Chile.

    Red Head

    Deep red seed heads, a steady producer in temperate gardens.

    Oro de Valle

    Golden seed, noted as drought-tough.

    French Vanilla and Mint Vanilla

    Pale-seeded, mild-flavoured garden forms, sold alongside Cherry Vanilla.

    Biobio

    A Chilean form, one of the older garden kinds.

    The Andean landraces — the old farm kinds of the high plateau, kept by Quechua and Aymara growers for thousands of years — number in the thousands and have no single garden names. They are the source of the seed colours and the hardiness the named forms draw on.

    • Quinoa comes from the Altiplano, the high plateau of the Andes around Lake Titicaca, where Peru and Bolivia meet today, at about 3,800 metres above the sea. People there gathered the wild plant as far back as 7,000 years ago, and were growing it on purpose by about 5,000 BCE. Its wild ancestor is a weedy goosefoot, Chenopodium hircinum, that still grows across South America.
    • The Inca called it chisaya mama — the mother of all grains — and held it sacred. It stood beside corn, potatoes and coca leaf as one of the great gifts of Pachamama, Mother Earth. Each year the Inca ruler planted the first seeds of the season with golden tools, and at the solstice quinoa seed was offered to Inti, the sun god. Idols were shaped from quinoa flour. The seed fed the Inca armies, mixed with fat into a travelling food, and was ground into flour and made into bread, cakes, porridge and beer.
    • The Spanish came in 1532, and quinoa's sacred standing made it a target. The colonial rulers discouraged and in places forbade its growing, and pushed wheat and barley in its place. Quinoa growing fell away across the old Inca lands. It survived in the far highland villages — too high, too cold and too far for the Spanish to reach — where Quechua and Aymara farmers kept growing it as they always had, quietly, for centuries.
    • The way back began in the 1970s, when Western researchers took note of the seed's food value. Fields were planted in Colorado in the 1970s and 1980s, and health-food shops began to sell it. The United Nations named 2013 the International Year of Quinoa, and the American space agency NASA studied it as a food for long space flights. Today quinoa is grown far beyond the Andes — in North America, Europe, Asia and Australia — and its seed is sold white, red and black in shops everywhere.
    • In the Andes the seed was rinsed, then cooked into soups and porridges, ground into flour, or fermented into drink. The rinse matters and is still the rule today: each seed wears a bitter, soapy coat called saponin, which must be washed off before cooking, or the food tastes bitter. The young leaves were also eaten as a green, cooked like spinach. In Andean folk medicine the leaves and seeds were used for swelling, for gut troubles, for thin blood and for mountain sickness — uses told as tradition, not as tested medicine.
    • What is in the seed, first. A cooked cup of quinoa — about 185 grams — holds about 222 calories, 8 grams of protein, 5 grams of fibre and 39 grams of carbohydrate, with about 3.5 grams of fat, most of it unsaturated. It is a good source of magnesium, manganese, iron, folate, zinc and phosphorus, and it carries plant compounds called flavonoids, notably quercetin and kaempferol, which show antioxidant activity in laboratory tests.
    • The protein is the headline, and it holds up. Quinoa is one of the few plant foods that is a complete protein: it holds all nine essential amino acids — the building blocks of protein the body cannot make and must get from food. Most grains fall short on lysine, one of those nine; quinoa is rich in it. One honest limit belongs here: complete is not the same as plentiful. A cooked cup gives about 8 grams of protein — strong for a grain, but far less than a piece of meat or a cup of lentils. Quinoa is a strong helper in a plant-based diet, not the whole of it.
    • Quinoa is naturally free of gluten, because gluten is a protein found only in wheat, barley and rye. In a small trial, 19 adults with coeliac disease ate 50 grams of quinoa a day for six weeks as part of their usual gluten-free diet, and it was well tolerated — gut measures stayed normal and the condition did not worsen. Two cautions ride with that finding. In laboratory tests, 2 of 15 quinoa types set off coeliac immune cells, so the trial result is for the quinoa that was tested, not a promise for every kind. And quinoa can pick up traces of gluten where it is grown, moved or packed near gluten grains, so people with coeliac disease should choose quinoa marked certified gluten-free and follow their clinician's advice. Human · small
    • Blood sugar: the human trials are small, and they point the same way. A pooled analysis of 7 trials with 258 adults found that eating quinoa lowered fasting blood sugar, with no change in body weight. In a one-year trial of 207 adults whose blood sugar was already raised, 100 grams of quinoa a day in place of about half their usual staple food gave lower blood sugar two hours after eating and lower fasting insulin than a mixed-grain diet or a control diet. In a single-meal test with 18 healthy young women, cooked quinoa raised blood sugar less than white bread with the same amount of carbohydrate. These are real trials in people, but they are small and short, and they tested quinoa as a swap for other grains — not as a medicine. Human · small
    • Heart and blood fats: the same small-trial picture. In a trial of 40 adults aged 50 to 75, quinoa biscuits eaten for four weeks lowered total cholesterol by 0.30 and LDL cholesterol — the "bad" kind — by 0.25 mmol/L more than matched wheat biscuits. In 50 adults carrying extra weight, 50 grams of quinoa a day for twelve weeks left triglycerides — another blood fat — lower than in a group that ate no quinoa. A pooled analysis of 5 trials with 206 people found small falls in triglycerides, total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol. The falls are small, the trials are small, and one trial of bread with quinoa flour found no extra benefit at all. Quinoa as part of a good diet may help blood fats a little; it is not a cholesterol treatment. Human · small
    • Two fences belong here. First, the laboratory work — quinoa compounds killing germs in dishes, easing swelling in animal tests, and slowing cancer cells in dishes — is laboratory and animal work, and none of it shows what eating quinoa does in a person. Second, no trial has tested quinoa for sleep, memory, skin, wounds or breathing, and no such claim is made here.
    • When to plant: Sow after the last frost, straight where it is to grow, or start indoors four weeks before the last frost and plant out while young; sow shallow, about 1 to 1.5 cm deep, and thin the seedlings to about 25 to 30 cm apart
    • Sun: Full sun — six to ten hours a day
    • Soil: Well-drained, sandy loam, around pH 6.0 to 7.5; it tolerates poor and stony ground better than wet ground
    • Environment: A summer annual that grows, seeds and dies in one warm season, in 90 to 120 days from sowing, in USDA zones 4 to 10; a cool-weather crop that likes long days and cool nights, and sets seed badly when nights stay above 32 °C (90 °F)
    • Planter or ground: Ground — sow straight where it is to grow, or start indoors and plant out while young
    • Water: Steady water while it is young gives a better crop; once settled it is drought-tough by crop standards, but it is not a desert plant
    • When to pick: Harvest when the leaves have dropped and the seed heads are dry, and a seed pressed with a fingernail does not dent

    Garden notes

    • The plant grows 1 to 2 metres tall — 3 to 6 feet — some kinds taller, with broad, goosefoot-shaped leaves and a tall head of tiny clustered flowers that swell into the coloured seed heads. Young plants take a light frost; a hard frost kills them, below about −3 °C (28 °F).
    • Harvest when the leaves have dropped and the seed heads are dry, and a seed pressed with a fingernail does not dent. Cut the heads, dry them fully, and rub or thresh the seed free. Rinse the seed well to wash off the bitter saponin coat before cooking or storing. Birds love the ripening seed — harvest promptly, or cover the heads with netting.
    • The young leaves can be picked and cooked like spinach, but take only a few from each plant, or the seed head will suffer for it.
    • Go easy on nitrogen fertiliser: too much grows leaf at the cost of seed.

    Propagation

    Sow seed straight outside in spring, after the last frost, once the soil has warmed to at least 50°F. Sow shallow — about half an inch deep — and thin the seedlings to 8 to 12 inches apart. It does not like its roots disturbed, so direct sowing beats starting indoors.

    Safety

    • Rinse the seed well before cooking, until the water runs clear — the bitter saponin coat is the plant's own defence against birds and insects, and unrinsed quinoa tastes bitter and soapy. Quinoa holds oxalate, a compound that can add to kidney stones in people prone to them, so those people should keep portions moderate. A true allergy to quinoa is rare, but it has been reported, including severe reactions in case reports. The leaves are eaten as a green in the Andes, but they are not sold as a food in shops, and nothing here is a claim about the leaf as medicine.

    Sources

    • Zevallos et al. (2014) — quinoa in coeliac patients: 19 adults, 50 g a day for 6 weeks, well tolerated
    • Pourshahidi et al. (2020) — quinoa biscuits and cholesterol: 40 adults aged 50 to 75, 4 weeks
    • Navarro-Perez et al. (2017) — 50 g of quinoa a day and triglycerides: 50 adults, 12 weeks
    • Atefi et al. (2024) — pooled analysis of 7 trials, 258 adults: fasting blood sugar
    • Karimian et al. (2021) — pooled analysis of 5 trials, 206 people: blood fats and weight
    • Huang et al. (2025) — one-year trial, 207 adults with raised blood sugar: 100 g of quinoa a day
    • USDA FoodData Central — nutrition figures for cooked quinoa, per cup and per 100 g
    • MedlinePlus — quinoa as a complete protein and a gluten-free food
    • Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, The Nutrition Source — quinoa nutrition and history
    • Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations — International Year of Quinoa 2013
    • Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — the accepted name Chenopodium quinoa, its place in the amaranth family, and its native range
    • Kellogg & Murphy, Washington State University Extension — quinoa variety trials and seed sources

    Walnut

    Juglans regia

    Culinary

    Heart Health

    ManganeseOmega-3 (ALA)

    FreshDried

    The walnut is the seed of a great spreading tree — the common walnut, also called the English walnut or the Persian walnut, Juglans regia, of the walnut family, Juglandaceae. The nut falls from the tree in autumn inside a thick green husk; the husk splits and peels away to show a hard, wrinkled shell, and inside the shell sits the kernel in two halves, folded and creased like a small pale brain. It is that likeness that made the walnut famous long before anyone measured what is in it. The tree itself is a large deciduous tree, 25 to 35 metres tall with a broad crown, its leaves long and pinnate — one leaf made of five to nine smooth-edged leaflets — and it can live and bear for a hundred years and more.

    Cultivars

    Walnuts are grown as named cultivars, grafted onto rootstocks, because a tree grown from a nut does not come true to its parent. The cultivars are told apart by kernel, shell, harvest date and leafing time — a photograph of a tree in leaf cannot honestly name one.

    'Chandler'

    The standard of the modern orchard, released by the University of California in the late 1970s. Late to leaf out, so it dodges spring frosts, with a large, pale, easy-to-crack kernel. It now grows about two-thirds of California's crop.

    'Howard'

    Released alongside 'Chandler' by the same university breeding work. Earlier to bear and a heavy cropper, with a good light kernel; the usual partner planted beside 'Chandler'.

    'Hartley'

    The old California standard before 'Chandler', a large nut with a strong shell, long favoured for selling in the shell. Still grown, now a small share of the crop.

    'Franquette'

    The French cultivar, brought to California in the 1800s. Late leafing and late ripening, with a small, well-filled kernel; once the backbone of the California orchards, now grown in small amounts.

    'Tulare'

    An early Californian cultivar with a large nut, harvested ahead of 'Chandler'; the second-largest share of the crop after 'Chandler' and 'Howard'.

    'Serr' and 'Vina'

    Older Californian releases from the same university programme, 'Serr' mid-season and 'Vina' early, both now minor beside the big three. 'Payne' is older still, one of the early Californian selections. 'Ivanhoe' is a newer release, and 'Livermore' is the red-kernelled one — its kernel skin is a deep red, grown for the colour as much as the flavour.

    Seedling trees — ungrafted trees grown from nuts — still fill old gardens and farmyards, and their nuts vary from tree to tree: some thin-shelled and sweet, some thick-shelled and bitter. A garden tree from a nut is a gamble; a named cultivar, grafted, is the known thing.

    • The walnut's home is the mountains of Central Asia and the lands west of them — from the Balkans eastward through Iran to the Himalayas and south-west China. One centre of its origin is Iran, another lies further north-east in Central Asia, and the largest wild forests stand in Kyrgyzstan, at Arslanbob, where walnut trees grow in near-pure stands at 1,000 to 2,000 metres above sea level. Its exact wild range is hard to pin down now, because people have carried and planted it for so long.
    • In the fourth century BCE, Alexander the Great carried the "Persian nut" — the Greek writer Theophrastus called it karyā hē Persikē — from Iran and Central Asia into Macedonia and Greece. The Romans spread it further, across southern Europe and northern Africa, and the Latin name for it was nux Gallica, the Gallic nut. The Romans also gave the tree its lasting name: Juglans is Jovis glans, the nut of Jupiter, king of the gods, and regia means royal — the royal nut of Jupiter. The walnut is named once in the Hebrew Bible, in the Song of Songs, where the speaker goes down "into the garden of nuts"; the earliest walnut wood in the Levant comes from the Middle Bronze Age, found in northern Israel.
    • Eastward, the tree travelled along the Silk Road into China about two thousand years ago, where it is called hú táo, the Hu peach — the peach of the Hu, the peoples of the lands north and north-west of China. Westward, it reached Britain with the Romans, and France, where in the eighth century Charlemagne ordered walnuts planted in his orchards, and church tithes could be paid in walnuts. In America it is called the English walnut to tell it apart from the black walnuts native to the continent — the name possibly because English sailors were prominent in carrying the nuts about — and it reached the Americas in the seventeenth century with English colonists, then California with the Spanish missions. Today almost all of the United States crop comes from California's Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys, and China grows more walnuts than any other country.
    • The Greeks called the walnut karyon, meaning head, probably because the shell resembles a skull and the kernel a brain. That likeness became a whole way of reading plants: the doctrine of signatures, which held that a plant's shape showed what part of the body it healed. The Greek physician Dioscorides, writing in the first century, esteemed walnuts as medicine — eaten with rue and figs, and burned kernels ground with wine and oil and rubbed on an infant's head to make the hair grow. Galen, a century later, mixed them with garum, the fermented fish sauce, as a laxative. In the Renaissance the doctrine was revived and given new weight by Paracelsus, and the English herbalist William Coles, writing in 1657, found in the walnut "the perfect Signature of the Head": the green husk was the skin of the skull, the shell the skull itself, and the kernel the brain within. On that reading, walnuts were prescribed for head wounds, headaches, mental illness and epileptic fits.
    • Not everyone agreed, even then. Pliny the Elder, in the first century, warned that even sitting beneath a walnut tree brings on a heaviness of the head, since the leaves give off a poison that reaches the brain. The Ménagier de Paris, a household book of 1393, said walnuts cause headaches rather than curing them. The brain likeness was a guess dressed as a sign, and the trials that finally tested it are told under Health Benefits.
    • Walnuts were food long before they were medicine. They were among the foods left on the table in the Temple of Isis at Pompeii when Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE. Green, unripe walnuts — picked while the husk is still soft — are pickled whole in Britain, dark and sharp, and steeped in spirit in Italy to make nocino, the dark walnut liqueur. Ripe kernels are eaten as they come, baked into cakes and breads, scattered over salads, and pressed for a fragrant oil that goes rancid quickly and is kept cool. The tree's timber is prized too: walnut wood, dark and close-grained, is cut for fine furniture, veneer and gunstocks, and the tree has always been planted as much for its wood and its shade as for its nuts.
    • Kyrgyzstan — the wild walnut forests of Arslanbob, the largest in the world, where families still gather nuts from trees that have stood for centuries, and the forest itself is the crop.
    • France — the walnut country of the Périgord and the Dauphiné, where 'Franquette' was bred; walnut oil pressed in old mills, walnut cakes, and green walnuts steeped for liqueurs.
    • Italy — nocino, the dark walnut liqueur made from green walnuts picked on St John's Day, 24 June; walnuts through the cooking of Piedmont and Tuscany, in sauces, cakes and stuffings.
    • Britain — pickled walnuts, dark and sharp, eaten with cold meats and cheese; and the Victorian after-dinner walnuts with port and Stilton, the one place the English once kept them.
    • Persia and the Middle East — walnuts ground into sauces and sweets: fesenjan, the Persian stew of walnuts and pomegranate, dark and rich, served at feasts; walnuts through the baking and confectionery of the whole region.
    • China — the world's largest grower, where the walnut is the Hu peach of the old name, eaten as a snack food, pressed for oil, and given as a gift food; the oldest walnut tree in the world is claimed near Khotan, in Xinjiang.
    • California — the modern walnut at full scale. Orchards of 'Chandler' and 'Howard' across the Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys, shaken down in autumn by machines that grip each trunk, the nuts dried and hulled and cracked in sheds the size of warehouses.
    • Walnuts, raw, per 100 g: 654 kcal, protein 15 g, fat 65 g, carbohydrate about 14 g, fibre 6.7 g. The fat is what sets them apart: most of it is polyunsaturated — 47 g of the 65 — and of that, about 9 g is alpha-linolenic acid, called ALA, the plant form of omega-3, a fat the body cannot make and must get from food. No other common nut carries anywhere near that much ALA; a single ounce, about 14 halves, gives roughly 2.5 g of it, more than a day's worth. The same 100 g carries manganese at about three and a half milligrams, roughly one and a half days' worth, copper at about 1.6 mg, well over a day's worth, magnesium at 158 mg, phosphorus at 346 mg, and folate at 98 micrograms. The body turns only a small share of the plant omega-3 into the longer fish-oil forms, EPA and DHA, so walnuts are not a stand-in for oily fish.
    • Cholesterol is where the human evidence is strongest, and it is modest. A 2018 pooling of 26 controlled trials with 1,059 people found that walnut diets lowered total cholesterol by about 7 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol — the kind linked to heart disease — by about 5.5 mg/dL, and triglycerides by about 4.7 mg/dL, against the comparison diets. The longest single trial, the Walnuts and Healthy Aging study, known as WAHA, assigned 708 healthy adults aged 63 to 79 in Barcelona and California to eat 30 to 60 grams of walnuts a day, or none, for two years: total cholesterol fell by 8.5 mg/dL and LDL by 4.3 mg/dL in the walnut group, while triglycerides and HDL cholesterol did not move, and body weight barely changed. The LDL fall was larger in men, down 7.9%, than in women, down 2.6%. Human trials
    • The regulators have weighed the same evidence and fenced it carefully. In 2004 the United States Food and Drug Administration allowed a qualified claim on walnut packs: "Supportive but not conclusive research shows that eating 1.5 ounces of walnuts per day, as part of a low saturated fat and low cholesterol diet, and not resulting in increased caloric intake, may reduce the risk of coronary heart disease." Supportive but not conclusive — that is the true size of it. In Europe, the food safety authority authorised a claim at 30 grams a day — about an ounce — that walnuts help blood vessels widen as they should, a measure of vessel health; it did not accept a claim that walnuts lower LDL cholesterol on their own. Human trials
    • The largest trial of whole diets that included walnuts is PREDIMED, in Spain, which assigned 7,447 adults at high risk of heart disease to a Mediterranean diet with 30 grams of mixed nuts a day — 15 grams of walnuts with almonds and hazelnuts — or the same diet with extra olive oil, or advice to eat low-fat. Over a median of almost five years, the nut group had about 28% fewer major heart events — heart attack, stroke, or death from heart disease — than the low-fat group. That is a real result, and it is fenced: it tested mixed nuts inside a whole Mediterranean way of eating, not walnuts alone, and the first paper was withdrawn and republished in 2018 after errors in how people had been assigned to groups; the conclusions held in the corrected analysis.
    • The brain claim got its proper test, and it failed it. WAHA's main question was whether two years of daily walnuts would slow the decline of memory and thinking in healthy older adults. It did not: thinking scores in the walnut group and the no-walnut group changed no differently. A later look at the Barcelona group alone, who started with lower scores, hinted at slower decline, and brain scans in a small subgroup hinted at differences too — the researchers called that encouraging but inconclusive. Walnuts belong in a brain-friendly diet; they have not been shown to sharpen memory.
    • Two smaller findings, stated at their size. A 2020 review of the blood-pressure trials found too little evidence to call walnuts a blood-pressure food. And one small, careful gut trial — 18 healthy adults, 42 grams of walnuts a day for three weeks, with every meal provided — found more of the gut bacteria Faecalibacterium, Roseburia and Clostridium, which make butyrate, a fuel for the gut lining, and lower levels of two secondary bile acids linked to inflammation. Butyrate itself was not measured, so the trial shows a shift in the gut's tenants, not a proven benefit to the gut. It is one small, short trial. Human · small
    • When to plant: Plant a grafted tree of a named cultivar, bare-root in winter while it is dormant — a seedling tree is a gamble on the nut
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Deep, well-drained ground — a sandy loam is ideal — around pH 6.0 to 7.5
    • Environment: A tree for temperate places — the equivalent of USDA zones 5 to 9; it wants full sun and a long, warm summer to fill the nuts, and it needs a real winter cold to set its buds; it leafs out late in spring
    • Planter or ground: Ground — a large garden, a field edge or an orchard, never a small garden; orchards space trees 30 to 40 feet apart, and a garden tree wants at least that
    • Water: Deep watering through the dry summer once it is settled; nuts fill and size best with it
    • When to pick: In autumn, when the green husks split open and the nuts drop; gather them daily

    Garden notes

    • Be honest about the size before anything else. The walnut is a big tree, not a garden shrub. In the open it grows 25 to 35 metres tall with a broad crown as wide as it is tall, and it lives for a century. It belongs in a large garden, a field edge or an orchard, never in a small garden, never near a house, a drain or a power line. Give it room: orchards space trees 30 to 40 feet apart, and a garden tree wants at least that.
    • It wants full sun and a long, warm summer to fill the nuts, and it needs a real winter cold to set its buds; without enough winter chill it leafs out raggedly and crops poorly. It leafs out late in spring, which is a gift: late frosts that take the blossom of other fruit trees usually pass it by.
    • It tolerates poor and stony ground better than wet ground: roots sitting in water invite root rot, and heavy wet clay kills more young walnuts than cold does. Once settled it is drought-tough by tree standards, but nuts fill and size best with deep watering through the dry summer.
    • The walnut's roots and fallen leaves release juglone, a compound that stunts or kills some plants growing nearby — tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, apples and pears among them. Keep the tree well away from the vegetable garden and from beds of plants that dislike it; grasses, beans and many shrubs tolerate it. The shade is deep too, and little grows well directly beneath a big walnut.
    • Garden trees are usually grafted onto black walnut roots or a walnut hybrid, chosen for the soil. First nuts come in the fourth to seventh year, a full crop much later, and a well-kept tree goes on cropping for decades. Prune only in late summer, when the sap is down — pruning in winter or spring makes the tree bleed sap from the cuts.
    • Harvest is written on the fruit. In autumn the green husks split open and the nuts drop; gather them daily, wear gloves, peel off the husks, wash the nuts and dry them in their shells in a warm airy place for a fortnight before storing. In the shell, kept cool and dry, they keep for months; shelled kernels go rancid fastest of all and belong in a sealed jar somewhere cool. Squirrels take their share — expect it, and gather early rather than late.

    Propagation

    Grow it from a nut, not a cutting. Collect nuts in autumn, hull and wash them, and chill them in moist sand in the fridge for about 120 days. Plant in early spring, 2 to 3 inches deep. A seed-grown tree will not match a named kind — keeping a named kind takes grafting, which is skilled work.

    Safety

    • Walnut is a tree nut, and tree-nut allergy can be severe — for someone allergic, walnuts are dangerous at any dose, and labels list them for that reason. Walnuts are rich in oil and go rancid in warmth: keep them cool and dry, below 25 °C, and throw away any batch that smells stale or shows mould — mouldy walnuts can carry aflatoxin, a poison made by mould, and a mouldy batch should be discarded whole, not picked over. The green husks stain hands and cloth a deep brown that does not wash out easily, so hull fresh nuts with gloves. And walnuts are filling food, not light food: an ounce carries about 185 calories, and the trials' small benefit came from walnuts eaten as part of the day's food, not added on top of it.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture — FoodData Central: nuts, walnuts, English — the nutrition figures
    • Guasch-Ferré et al. (2018) — meta-analysis of 26 controlled trials: walnut diets and blood fats — the cholesterol figures
    • Rajaram et al. (2021) — the WAHA trial, cholesterol results (Circulation) — 708 adults, 30 to 60 g a day for two years
    • Sala-Vila et al. (2020) — the WAHA trial, cognition results (American Journal of Clinical Nutrition) — no effect on thinking in healthy older adults
    • U.S. Food and Drug Administration (2004) — qualified health claim for walnuts and coronary heart disease — the fenced wording of the claim
    • European Food Safety Authority (2011) — walnuts and blood-vessel widening at 30 g a day — the authorised claim, and the LDL claim not accepted
    • Estruch et al. (2018) — the PREDIMED trial (New England Journal of Medicine) — Mediterranean diet with mixed nuts, 7,447 adults, about 28% fewer major heart events
    • Holscher et al. (2018) — walnut eating and the gut bacteria (Journal of Nutrition) — 18 adults, 42 g a day for three weeks
    • Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — the accepted name Juglans regia, its place in the walnut family, and its native range
    • McGranahan & Leslie — the walnut's Central Asian origin and its spread; Arslanbob and the Kyrgyz forests
    • California Walnut Board — California's share of the United States crop and the cultivar shares, 'Chandler' about two-thirds

    Sunflower

    Helianthus annuus

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Blood Sugar HealthHeart HealthSkin Health

    CookedDried

    The sunflower is the tallest, sunniest food plant in the garden — a single stalk that can grow taller than a person, topped by one great golden face that can measure a foot across. The name is Greek: helios, the sun, and anthos, a flower. The Latin second name, annuus, means yearly: the plant lives for one summer only, sown in spring, in flower by high summer, and gone after its seeds ripen. Each head is not one flower but hundreds of tiny flowers packed together — the dark centre is a crowd of small tube flowers, ringed by the yellow petals, which are flowers too. The seeds sit in the centre in a spiral, each one turned about 137.5 degrees from the next, the golden angle, so more seeds fit in the head than any other packing would allow. The seed is the food, the oil pressed from it is one of the world's great cooking oils, and a field of them in bloom is a sight nothing else looks like.

    Cultivars

    The garden kinds fall into four groups, and the group matters more than any one name: giants grown for height and seed, branching kinds grown for armfuls of flowers, dwarfs grown for pots and small gardens, and pollen-free kinds grown for the vase.

    Giants, for height and seed

    'Mammoth', also sold as 'Mammoth Russian' — the old Russian oilseed type, 3 to 3.6 metres tall with a head up to 30 cm across, the classic seed sunflower; 'Russian Giant', much the same and sometimes taller; 'American Giant', which can pass 4 metres in good ground with heads past 40 cm; 'Mongolian Giant', tall with a little more branching; 'Titan' and 'Kong Hybrid', both bred for size; and 'Skyscraper', 3 to 3.6 metres, a steady grower for height without the fuss of the competition kinds.

    Branching and coloured kinds, for flowers over weeks

    'Lemon Queen' — soft pale yellow, branching, many flowers over a long season, and one of the best kinds for bees; 'Autumn Beauty' — gold, bronze, burgundy and mixed colours, 8 to 15 flowers on one plant; 'Velvet Queen' — deep red to mahogany; 'Italian White' — creamy white petals with a dark centre; 'Evening Sun' — gold, bronze and red mixed; 'Moulin Rouge', 'Chianti Hybrid' and 'Claret' — dark reds; and 'Prado Red', a strong red.

    Dwarfs, for pots and borders

    'Teddy Bear' — 60 to 90 cm tall, with fully double, fluffy golden flowers like pompoms, nothing like a plain sunflower; 'Sunspot', also sold as 'Dwarf Sunspot' — only 45 to 60 cm tall but with one big head up to 25 cm across; 'Little Becka' — 30 to 40 cm, red and gold two-tone; and 'Music Box' — 60 to 70 cm, gold, bronze and mixed colours, branching.

    Pollen-free kinds, for cut flowers

    The ProCut series — 'ProCut Orange', 'ProCut Lemon', 'ProCut Gold', 'ProCut White Lite' and 'ProCut Plum' among them — single stems bred for the florist, with no pollen to drop on tables; and 'Sunrich', of the same kind.

    Oil and birdseed kinds

    'Peredovik', a Russian oilseed kind; 'Black Oil', the small black seed sold for bird feeders and oil; and 'Large Grey Stripe', the big striped seed sold for eating. The oil kinds are farm kinds, not garden flowers, and their heads are smaller and their seeds darker than the eating kinds.

    • The sunflower is a North American native, one of the few great food crops first farmed in what is now the United States. Wild sunflowers grow across the Great Plains of the United States and Canada, and the plant was tamed once, about four to five thousand years ago, in the east-central part of the continent, in the country of the Mississippi valley. The oldest remains of the farmed kind come from Tennessee, about 4,600 years old. The people who tamed it chose a tall plant with one big head and seeds that stayed in the head when ripe, instead of scattering.
    • Native American nations ate the seeds straight, ground them into meal and flour, and mixed the meal with corn flour to make cakes. They pressed oil from the seed, used the dark hulls as a dye, used the leaves as medicine, and used the pollen in ceremony. The sunflower was not a staple food the way corn, beans and squash were, but it was grown by many nations from the east of the continent across the Midwest and into the south-west and Mexico.
    • Spanish explorers carried the seed to Europe in the early 1500s. For two centuries it was a garden wonder, not a crop. In 1597 the English herbalist John Gerard wrote, disappointed, that the sunflowers in his London garden had grown only fourteen feet tall, while his rivals on the Continent claimed twenty-four. The plant was grown for its looks and for its seed as a snack, and in folk medicine its flowers and leaves were given for fevers.
    • The plant's great turn came in Russia. The Orthodox Church forbade many oily foods during the long fasts of Lent and Advent, but the sunflower, a newcomer, was not on the forbidden list, so its oil could be eaten when other oils could not. Peasants in Ukraine and the Kuban began to grow it for oil, and the first crushing mills were built in 1830. Russian breeders spent the next hundred years raising the oil in the seed, past 40%, and breeding small-headed, single-stemmed oil kinds. By the late 1800s the Russian oilseed kinds, above all the one sold as 'Mammoth Russian', were carried back across the Atlantic, most likely by Russian settlers, and became the base of the sunflower oil trade in North America — the plant had gone home as a giant oilseed.
    • The sunflower's most famous story is Greek, and it is told here with one honest correction. In Ovid's poem the Metamorphoses, the sea nymph Clytie loves the sun god Helios, who leaves her for another. She sits on the rocks for nine days without food or drink, watching the sun cross the sky, and at last she is changed into a flower that turns its face to the sun for ever. The flower Ovid names is a heliotrope, a small sun-turning flower — the sunflower is an American plant, and no Greek or Roman could have known it. But from the 1600s on, painters told the story with a sunflower in Clytie's place, and the sunflower has carried her name ever since.
    • The turning itself is real, and it has a limit worth knowing. Young sunflowers do follow the sun: the head faces east at dawn, turns west through the day, and swings back east overnight, ready for morning. The movement comes from the stem growing faster on one side than the other, run by the plant's inner day-night clock. But once the flower opens and ripens, the turning stops, and the head sits facing east for good. An east-facing head warms sooner in the morning sun, and warm heads draw far more bees — in one study, five times as many as heads facing west.
    • The sunflower became a painter's flower in the late 1800s, above all in Vincent van Gogh's sunflowers of 1888 and 1889, painted in the south of France — great yellow heads in vases, cut and wilting, painted again and again. It is the national flower of Ukraine, and the sunflower field is the emblem of the country's farmland. Today Ukraine and Russia together grow a large share of the world's sunflower seed, and the crop is grown on every continent except Antarctica.
    • North America — the plant's home: wild sunflowers across the Great Plains, the first farming in the Mississippi valley, and today the great seed fields of the northern Plains of the United States.
    • Ukraine and Russia — the oil heartland: the Lent loophole, the first crushing mills in 1830, a century of breeding for oil, and still the centre of world sunflower oil, growing well over a third of the world's seed. The sunflower is Ukraine's national flower.
    • France — the painter's country: van Gogh's sunflowers in Provence, and the yellow fields of the south-west, in the Gers and the Languedoc.
    • Spain and the Mediterranean — the seed as a snack: roasted seeds eaten by the handful, and the oil in the kitchen beside olive oil.
    • Argentina — one of the world's great growers and exporters of sunflower oil, from the Pampas.
    • China and India — the oil in the kitchen, and the seed roasted and eaten as a snack, a use that has grown with the crop in both countries.
    • What is in the seed, first. One ounce (about 28 grams, a small handful) of dry-roasted sunflower kernels carries about 165 calories, 5.5 grams of protein, 14 grams of fat — most of it unsaturated — and just over 3 grams of fibre. It is one of the richest foods for vitamin E: that ounce gives about half an adult's daily need. It also gives copper, selenium, magnesium and thiamin in good measure. The fat in the old, classic oil is mostly linoleic acid, an omega-6 fat the body cannot make for itself; the newer high-oleic oil is mostly oleic acid, the same fat that fills olive oil.
    • The strongest human evidence is small, and it is told small. In a feeding study in New Zealand, 22 women past the menopause with type 2 diabetes ate a supplied healthy diet with 30 grams of sunflower kernels a day — about an ounce — for three weeks, and the same diet with almonds for another three weeks, in turn. On the sunflower kernels, the "bad" LDL cholesterol fell by about 9.5%, triglycerides (a blood fat) by 12%, and fasting blood sugar by 11%. Blood pressure eased a little too. That is one short study, in 22 women, all with diabetes, eating food supplied to them — not proof for everyone, and the almonds did much the same for cholesterol. No long study has followed sunflower seed eaters to see whether they have fewer heart attacks. Human · small
    • The oil's evidence is about what it replaces, not about the oil alone. A network meta-analysis that pooled 55 trials found sunflower oil among the best of the common cooking fats at lowering LDL cholesterol when it took the place of butter or lard — beside safflower, rapeseed and flaxseed oils — while butter and lard ranked worst. The trials measured blood fats, not heart attacks, and the authors would not name one winning oil. The American Heart Association, weighing the fear that omega-6 fats drive swelling in the body, concluded the fear was wrong: replacing saturated fat with polyunsaturated fat cut heart events by about a quarter across six trials, and it advised getting at least 5 to 10% of calories from omega-6 fats. In 2018 the United States Food and Drug Administration allowed a guarded claim for high-oleic oils, sunflower oil among them: supportive but not conclusive evidence that about one and a half tablespoons a day may lower heart disease risk — only when it replaces fats higher in saturated fat, and only without adding calories. Human trials
    • The seed and the oil are not the same food, and the two oils are not the same either. The classic oil is high in linoleic acid and goes stale faster in long, hot frying; the high-oleic kind stands up to heat better and keeps longer. The label to look for is "high oleic". A sunflower picture on the bottle does not say which kind it is.
    • The skin evidence is small and on the skin, not in the body. In a small trial in 19 adults, sunflower seed oil rubbed on the forearm twice a day for four weeks kept the skin's barrier sound, did not redden the skin, and left it better hydrated — while olive oil in the same trial damaged the barrier and caused mild redness. That is a small, short trial of the plain oil on healthy skin. Two later trials in people with eczema tested not the plain oil but fatty esters made from it, mixed into a cream with oatmeal, and found less itch and less steroid cream used — a promising result for a made product, not a result for the oil from a bottle. Human · small
    • The rest is weaker, and is told as weaker. In a study of more than 6,000 adults, people who ate seeds of any kind at least five times a week had about a third lower levels of C-reactive protein, a blood marker of swelling, than people who ate no seeds — but that was observation, not a trial, and it covered all seeds together, not sunflower alone. The old folk uses — flowers and leaves for fever and cough — have no trial behind them at all, and no safe dose has been worked out.
    • When to plant: Sow the seed where it is to grow, after the last frost, from mid-April into May in a temperate garden
    • Sun: Full sun — six to eight hours a day at least
    • Soil: Soil that drains well, around pH 6.0 to 7.5, with compost dug in on poor sandy ground
    • Environment: A summer annual; the flower opens in mid to late summer, and the seed ripens 70 to 100 days after sowing
    • Planter or ground: Ground or a planter — dwarfs suit pots and small gardens; a giant needs a sheltered spot, out of hard wind, where its shade will not fall on shorter vegetables
    • Water: Water steadily, most of all while the plant is young and while the head is filling with seed; tall kinds are thirsty in hot weather, and pots need water daily
    • When to pick: When the back of the head turns from green to yellow-brown, the petals have dried and dropped, and the head hangs down

    Garden notes

    • Sunflowers want full sun — six to eight hours a day at least — and in shade they flower poorly and grow weak.
    • Sow the seed where it is to grow, after the last frost, from mid-April into May in a temperate garden. The seed can also be started in pots from late March, but the plant grows a deep taproot and dislikes being moved, so direct sowing is best. Sow about 1 to 2.5 cm deep, in soil that drains well, around pH 6.0 to 7.5, with compost dug in on poor sandy ground. Seedlings come up in 7 to 10 days in warm soil. Thin to the kind's final spacing: about 30 cm apart for dwarfs, 45 to 60 cm for giants and branching kinds.
    • A rich bed with compost is usually feeding enough; if growth is slow, a potassium-rich feed, such as tomato feed, helps flowering. Stake anything over two metres, or the wind will take it when the head is heavy.
    • Birds and squirrels get there first if they can — once the petals start to brown, tie a paper bag or fine mesh over the head, then cut it with a length of stem, hang it somewhere warm, dry and airy, and rub the seeds out when they loosen. Dry the seeds fully before storing them in a closed jar.
    • For flowers to cut, take them in the morning and put them straight in water; the branching kinds are the best cut flowers, because one plant keeps making blooms for weeks. For bees, 'Lemon Queen' is the kind to plant. Watch for slugs on young seedlings, and for birds digging up newly sown seed — sow a few extra and thin later.

    Propagation

    Sow seed straight where it will grow, after the last frost, about 1 inch deep. Seedlings sprout in 7 to 10 days. Start seed indoors only in a pot you can plant whole, as the roots dislike being moved.

    Safety

    • A few people are allergic to sunflower seeds, and the reaction can be severe, even life-threatening — anyone who has reacted to a seed or nut should treat sunflower seeds with the same care. Salted seeds in the shell carry a lot of salt, and the kernels are rich in calories, so a small handful is the sensible daily amount, not a bagful. The oil is a cooking fat, not a medicine, and none of what is said here is a reason to change heart or diabetes medicine.

    Sources

    • Seiler et al. (2017) — the history of the sunflower: domestication, the Russian oilseed turn, and the return to North America
    • Richmond et al. (2013) — 30 grams of sunflower kernels a day in 22 postmenopausal women with type 2 diabetes, three weeks, crossover with almonds
    • Schwingshackl et al. (2018) — network meta-analysis of 55 trials comparing cooking oils and fats for blood lipids
    • Harris et al. (2009) — American Heart Association science advisory on omega-6 fats and heart disease
    • Danby et al. (2013) — sunflower seed oil and olive oil on the adult skin barrier, 19 volunteers
    • Atamian et al. (2016) — the circadian clock behind sunflower heliotropism, east-facing heads and pollinator visits
    • U.S. Food and Drug Administration (2018) — qualified health claim for oils with at least 70% oleic acid, high-oleic sunflower oil included
    • USDA FoodData Central — sunflower seed kernels, dry roasted, nutrients in one ounce
    • Ovid (c. 8 CE) — Metamorphoses, Book 4 — the Clytie story
    • Oxford University Plants 400 — the sunflower's history, Gerard's fourteen feet, and the 'Mammoth Russian' return

    Tea

    Camellia sinensis

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Heart Health

    FreshDried

    Tea is the most drunk prepared drink in the world after water, and it all comes from one plant: Camellia sinensis, an evergreen shrub of the tea family, Theaceae, also called cha. Green tea, black tea, oolong, white tea and pu-erh are not different plants. They are the same leaf, handled in different ways after picking. Green tea is heated soon after picking so the leaf stays green. Black tea is left to darken in the air until it turns brown. Oolong sits in between. White tea is made from young buds with little handling at all, and pu-erh is left to age and mellow. What is picked is the tender tip — a bud and the two young leaves below it. The leaf carries three things the research keeps coming back to: catechins, a family of sharp-tasting plant compounds led by EGCG; L-theanine, an amino acid found in almost no other food; and caffeine, in smaller amounts than coffee — about 30 mg in a cup of green tea and about 50 mg in a cup of black tea, against about 95 mg in a cup of filter coffee.

    Cultivars

    Tea has two botanical kinds that matter, and hundreds of named cultivars bred from them. The Chinese kind, var. sinensis, is the small-leaf, cold-hardy shrub of China, Japan and the high gardens — the parent of most green teas, oolongs and Darjeeling. The Assam kind, var. assamica, is the broad-leaf tropical tree of Assam, Yunnan and the low gardens — the parent of most strong black teas. A third kind, var. cambodiensis, is rare and little grown.

    The named cultivars on packets and in nurseries: 'Yabukita', Japan's green-tea standard — picked in Shizuoka in 1908, registered in 1953, now about three quarters of Japan's tea ground, grown for sencha; 'Saemidori', registered in 1990, prized for a sweet, rich taste and used for high-grade sencha and gyokuro; 'Okumidori', a late-sprouting kind that stretches the harvest and gives a gentle, mellow cup; 'Longjing 43', the Dragon Well green tea of Hangzhou; 'Tieguanyin', the Iron Goddess of Mercy, the great oolong of Fujian; 'Jinxuan', the milk oolong of Taiwan; 'TV1', the Tocklai-bred Assam kind grown across India and East Africa for strong black tea; and 'Sochi', a Russian-bred cold-hardy selection for gardens at the cold edge of tea country.

    For a home garden the choice is ruled by cold first, flavour second: the Chinese kind and its cultivars for temperate gardens, the Assam kind only where winters stay warm. Seed-grown plants vary from seedling to seedling; named cultivars are raised from cuttings, so each one holds true to its name.

    • Tea grows wild in the forested hills where south-west China meets Myanmar and north-east India, and the plant was first brought into gardens in that same country — Yunnan and Sichuan in China, and the hills across the border. Left alone it is a small tree; kept for picking it is a shrub, held low so the new shoots stay within reach. The Chinese kind, var. sinensis, is a small-leaf shrub, 1 to 3 metres tall, with leaves 3 to 6 cm long. The Assam kind, var. assamica, is a broad-leaf tree that can stand 10 to 15 metres, with leaves 10 to 20 cm long. Both are the same species, and they cross freely.
    • The old story says the legendary emperor Shennong found tea in 2737 BCE, when leaves blew into his pot of boiling water. It is a good story and it is told as a legend, not as a record: the date comes from a text put together some three thousand years later, and the earliest tellings do not always name the leaf as tea. What the ground and the written record do show is narrower and just as fine. Tea leaves were found in the tomb of a Han emperor of the 2nd century BCE, a servant's contract from 59 BCE lists buying tea among his duties — so it was already something bought and sold — and by about 760 CE Lu Yu had written The Classic of Tea, the first book on growing, making and drinking it. Tea began as medicine, for staying awake and settling the stomach, and became a drink for pleasure under the Tang dynasty (618–907 CE).
    • Buddhist monks carried tea to Japan. Seeds came with returning scholars in the 800s, but tea only took root in Japanese life after 1191, when the Zen monk Eisai came back from China with seeds and the Song way of whisking powdered green tea, and wrote Japan's first book on tea, praising it as a health drink. In the 1500s Sen no Rikyū shaped the tea ceremony, chanoyu, into the quiet, simple rite it still is — and the whisked powdered tea of that rite, matcha, is the old Chinese way, kept alive in Japan long after China had moved on to steeped leaves.
    • Tea reached Europe by sea. The Dutch East India Company shipped the first tea to Europe in 1610, and by 1662 Catherine of Braganza had made it fashionable at the English court. In the 1700s the British East India Company built its fortune on Chinese tea, and tea went from a luxury to a daily habit across Britain — helped along by smuggling that undercut the heavy tax on it. The same habit helped light two fires. In 1773 American colonists tipped 342 chests of Company tea into Boston Harbor, a protest against the Company's hold on the trade. And China would sell tea only for silver, wanting little Britain made, so the Company closed the gap by selling Indian opium into China — a trade that led to the Opium Wars of the mid-1800s.
    • Britain's answer was to grow its own tea and stop buying from China. Two things made that possible. In 1823 the Scottish trader Robert Bruce was shown tea growing wild in Assam, where the Singpho people had brewed the leaves for generations. And between 1848 and 1851 the botanist Robert Fortune travelled through China's tea country in disguise for the East India Company and carried out plants, seeds and trained Chinese tea makers — one of the great thefts of trade knowledge in history. Assam was planted for sale from 1839, Darjeeling from 1841, and Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, followed after 1867. Within a lifetime India had passed China as the world's biggest tea grower.
    • In folk medicine tea was used in much the same way wherever it travelled: to stay awake and clear-headed, to settle the stomach after a heavy meal, and as a wash for tired eyes and sore skin. In Assam the leaves were also eaten as a vegetable, boiled or with garlic and oil — a use a Dutch traveller noted as early as 1598. Much of that use was habit and hope, not tested proof. The tested part stands on its own, under Health Benefits.
    • What is in the cup, first. A cup of green tea carries catechins led by EGCG, L-theanine, caffeine, and small amounts of minerals. The amounts swing widely — by the kind of tea, the leaf, the water and how long it steeps — so no single number fits every cup. Black tea carries fewer catechins, because the darkening in air uses them up, and a little more caffeine. That is why most of the trials below used green tea, and why their results belong to green tea first.
    • The heart is where the evidence is strongest, and it is still modest. In the Ohsaki study, 40,530 Japanese adults were followed for up to 11 years. Women drinking five or more cups of green tea a day had a lower death rate than women drinking less than one cup — about 23% lower for death from any cause and about 31% lower for death from heart disease. Men showed the same direction, weaker. That is a study of people living their lives, not a trial: it cannot prove the tea caused the difference, and heavy tea drinkers in Japan may live differently in other ways too.
    • The trials point the same way, in small steps. A pooling of 14 trials found green tea lowered total cholesterol by about 5 to 7 mg/dL and LDL, the "bad" cholesterol, by about 2 to 5 mg/dL, with no change in HDL, the "good" kind. A pooling of trials on blood pressure found a fall of about 2 mmHg on the top number. Small, real, and consistent — a help on top of food, movement and medicine, never instead of them. Human trials
    • The calm alertness is real, short-lived, and smaller than the selling of it. In a trial of 27 healthy adults, 100 mg of L-theanine with 50 mg of caffeine — about the caffeine of one strong cup, with theanine added — improved speed and accuracy when switching between tasks, measured an hour after the dose. In a trial of 44 young adults, 97 mg of L-theanine with 40 mg of caffeine did the same and lifted self-rated alertness. A pooling of 11 such trials found the same shape: a moderate lift in attention in the first two hours, mostly on switching between tasks. Three fences belong here. The trials were small, each under 50 people, and each tested a single dose, not weeks of daily drinking. The theanine dose was several cups' worth — one cup holds only a small part of it, about a fifth. And some of the trials were run by tea-company researchers. Tea feels steadier than coffee; that feeling has some trial backing, at a dose above one cup. Human · small
    • Blood sugar moves a little. Poolings of 17 and 27 trials found fasting blood sugar fell by about 1 to 2 mg/dL with green tea — small, but steady across the trials. That is not a treatment for blood sugar, and no one should drink tea in place of care for it. Human trials
    • Two things tea is often sold for, it does not do. A Cochrane review of trials lasting at least 12 weeks found green tea gave little or no meaningful weight loss outside Japan — the average change was close to nothing. And on cancer, the picture is mixed and weak: a Cochrane review found the results varied by the kind of cancer and the way the study was done, the trial evidence was thin, and the Ohsaki study found no lower death rate from cancer among heavy tea drinkers. Tea is not a cancer treatment and is not shown to prevent cancer.
    • When to plant: Grow it from seed sown in spring, or from a cutting of a named cultivar, and plant out while young
    • Sun: Full sun in cool, damp climates; in hot summers give afternoon shade, or the leaves scorch
    • Soil: Sour, humus-rich, free-draining ground — pH about 4.5 to 5.5, the range tea gardens use, and garden guides allow up to about 6.5
    • Environment: A plant for warm, damp places — the Chinese kind grows outdoors in USDA zones 7 to 9, and hardy selections with shelter can manage zone 6; the Assam kind needs zones 9 to 11 and is killed by frost
    • Planter or ground: Ground, or a large pot or a raised bed filled with sour, bark-rich mix on lime-heavy or heavy wet ground; in colder zones than 7, grow it in a large pot and bring it into a bright, unheated shelter for hard frosts
    • Water: Steady moisture without ever standing in water; water when the top inch or two of soil dries out, and mulch thickly to hold the damp in
    • When to pick: Take the tender tip — a bud and the two young leaves below it — in spring, when the first flush is the finest, and again through the growing season as new shoots come

    Garden notes

    • Be honest about the climate before anything else. Tea is a plant for warm, damp places. The Chinese kind grows outdoors in USDA zones 7 to 9, and hardy selections with shelter can manage zone 6; the Assam kind needs zones 9 to 11 and is killed by frost. An established Chinese tea bush takes short cold down to about −10 to −12 °C (14 to 10 °F), but young plants need cover in their first winters.
    • Light: full sun suits it in cool, damp climates; in hot summers give afternoon shade, or the leaves scorch. Shelter from cold, drying wind matters more than anything in a temperate garden.
    • In lime-heavy or chalky soil the leaves yellow between the veins and the bush fades. Heavy wet clay is worse: roots sitting in water rot.
    • Water: tea comes from a land of heavy rain — 50 to 60 inches a year where it grows wild — and it likes steady moisture without ever standing in water. Water when the top inch or two of soil dries out, and mulch thickly to hold the damp in. It grows best between 60 and 80 °F (15 to 27 °C), and it sulks in long dry heat above 100 °F (38 °C) without shade.
    • Grow it from seed sown in spring, or from a cutting of a named cultivar, and plant out while young. It grows a deep root and dislikes being moved once settled. Prune each spring to keep the bush at waist to shoulder height, 3 to 4 feet, so the new shoots stay within reach — a picked bush is a pruned bush, and an unpruned one grows into a tree. Expect to wait about three years before the first real picking.
    • Picking: take the tender tip — a bud and the two young leaves below it — in spring, when the first flush is the finest, and again through the growing season as new shoots come. The bush flowers in autumn, small white flowers with a cluster of yellow stamens, sweet-smelling. In colder zones than 7, grow it in a large pot and bring it into a bright, unheated shelter for hard frosts.

    Propagation

    Take semi-hardwood cuttings in summer, or sow fresh seed in autumn. Cuttings keep the parent plant true; seed-grown plants vary. Only fresh seed will sprout — seed that has dried out will not grow.

    Safety

    • Brewed tea as it has been drunk for centuries is generally counted safe by Europe's food safety authority, EFSA, in its 2018 opinion. The danger is in concentrated extract pills. In trials, supplements giving 800 mg or more of EGCG a day raised liver enzymes, and case reports link extract pills — sometimes taken on an empty stomach — to liver injury, rarely severe. No supplement dose has been shown to be free of risk, and the European rule now keeps extract foods below 800 mg of EGCG a day, with warnings. A cup of tea is not a pill, and pill results do not belong to the cup — nor do cup results belong to the pill.
    • Caffeine is the ordinary limit — up to 400 mg a day is the usual ceiling for healthy adults, about eight cups of green tea or less once coffee and cola are counted, and 200 mg a day in pregnancy. Tea with a meal lowers how much iron the body takes from that meal, so anyone low in iron does best drinking tea between meals rather than with them. And let the cup cool a little: drinks taken scalding hot, above 65 °C, are classed as probably harmful to the gullet. Anyone pregnant, on blood-thinning medicine, or with liver trouble should ask a doctor before taking green tea extract pills — and the pills are best left alone altogether.

    Sources

    • Liu et al. (2014) — Effects of tea intake on blood pressure: a meta-analysis of randomised trials
    • Onakpoya et al. (2014) — The use of green tea extract in the management of blood pressure and cholesterol: a meta-analysis of 20 randomised trials
    • Jurgens et al. (2012) — Green tea for weight loss and weight maintenance in overweight or obese adults: a Cochrane review

    • Giesbrecht et al. (2010) — The combination of L-theanine and caffeine improves attention: 44 young adults, 97 mg L-theanine with 40 mg caffeine
    • Camfield et al. (2014) — A review of 11 trials of L-theanine with caffeine and attention in the first two hours
    • European Food Safety Authority (2018) — Safety of green tea catechins: brewed tea, extract pills and the 800 mg EGCG figure
    • Filippini et al. (2020) — Green tea and cancer: a Cochrane review
