    Coffee

    Coffea arabica

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Blood Sugar HealthDigestive HealthHeart HealthMental Health

    Cooked

    Coffee is the most drunk plant in the world after tea — and the plant behind it is a quiet, glossy-leaved shrub from the high forests of Ethiopia. Coffea arabica grows as an evergreen shrub or small tree, its leaves dark green and shining, its flowers white and sweet-smelling like jasmine, its fruit a cherry that ripens from green to yellow to a deep, glossy red. Inside each cherry sit two seeds, flat side to flat side. Those seeds, roasted and ground and brewed, are coffee. The plant carries about 60% of all the coffee grown in the world, and nearly everything sold as fine or single-origin coffee. Its beans hold about 1.2 to 1.5% caffeine by dry weight — roughly half what the tougher robusta coffee, Coffea canephora, holds. Caffeine is the most studied food compound there is, and it is the reason coffee wakes people up. One warning cannot wait: caffeine is a real drug in a friendly cup. Too much brings a racing heart, shaking hands, worry and sleepless nights, and coffee late in the day steals sleep. The safe amounts are set out under Health Benefits — read them before the fourth cup.

    Cultivars

    Coffee has no single garden form — it has a family tree of named varieties, and the names on coffee bags are the names of this family. The two old lines that nearly all the world's arabica comes from are Typica, the clean, sweet, delicate line that the Dutch carried from Yemen through Java to the Americas, and Bourbon, a sweeter, rounder line that grew on the island of Bourbon, now Réunion, and spread through Central and South America. Both yield little and fall sick easily, but their cup is the standard the rest are judged by.

    Caturra

    From Bourbon came the dwarf that changed farming: Caturra, a natural short mutation found in Brazil, which grows compact, yields heavily and lets farmers plant closer together.

    Catuaí

    From a cross of Mundo Novo and Caturra came Catuaí, the red-cherried variety in the hero photo, bred in Brazil for high yield and for standing up to wind and heavy rain.

    Mundo Novo

    Mundo Novo itself is a natural cross of Typica and Bourbon found in Brazil in the 1940s, tall and very productive.

    Pacamara

    Pacamara, a cross of Pacas and Maragogipe from El Salvador, is known for its very large beans.

    Maragogipe

    Maragogipe is a Typica mutation with beans so large they are called elephant beans.

    Gesha

    The most famous name of all is Gesha, also spelled Geisha — an Ethiopian landrace collected from the Gesha forest in the 1930s, made famous by farms in Panama in the 2000s, floral as jasmine and bergamot tea, very low yielding and often the most costly coffee on the shelf.

    SL28 and SL34

    Kenya's SL28 and SL34, chosen by the Scott Agricultural Laboratories in the 1930s, give the winey, blackcurrant cup Kenya is known for.

    Yellow Bourbon

    Yellow Bourbon is a Brazilian Bourbon mutation whose cherries ripen yellow, not red.

    Pink Bourbon

    Pink Bourbon, a Colombian favourite with pink-orange cherries, was found by genetic testing to be an Ethiopian landrace, not a Bourbon at all.

    Ethiopia itself holds thousands of local types, most never formally named, sold simply as heirloom — the most floral and fruity coffees there are. The rust-resistant modern varieties, Catimor and Castillo, are crosses with a robusta hybrid, bred for yield and for standing up to coffee leaf rust; their cup is plainer, and they are not pure arabica.

    • Coffee grows wild in the high forests of south-western Ethiopia, in the land of Kaffa — and the word coffee may well come from Kaffa itself. Long before anyone brewed it, people in those highlands knew the cherry's lift: they chewed the red cherries, and they ground the seeds and mixed them with animal fat into balls, a food that travelled well and kept a person going.
    • The best-known story of coffee is the tale of Kaldi, a goat herder who saw his goats dance and leap through the night after eating the red cherries of a certain bush, tried the cherries himself, felt the same lift, and carried them to a nearby monastery, where the monks found the brew kept them awake through long night prayers. It is a wonderful story, and it is a legend, not history. It was first written down in 1671, more than seven centuries after the events it describes, and the earliest written version does not even name the herdsman. The goats may be invention. The place is fact: the plant really does grow wild in the Ethiopian highlands.
    • The drink itself was born across the Red Sea, in Yemen. By the middle of the 1400s, Sufi monks in Yemen were brewing coffee to stay awake and clear-headed through their night prayers, and from Yemen the habit spread to Mecca, Cairo, Damascus and Istanbul, where the first coffeehouse opened in 1554. Coffeehouses were new places in the world — rooms where people met to talk, hear the news and do business over a cup — and they spread with the drink. The word came with it: from the Arabic qahwah, through the Turkish kahve, into the Dutch koffie and the English coffee.
    • Not everyone welcomed it. In Mecca in 1511, religious judges banned coffee for its stimulating effect; the ban was overturned in 1524 by the Ottoman sultan. Cairo banned it too, and its coffeehouses were sacked. The bans never held, and the drink only grew.
    • Until the end of the 1600s, nearly all the world's coffee came from Yemen, shipped through the port of Mocha. Then the plant slipped out: the Dutch carried it to Java in the 1600s, and a French officer, Gabriel de Clieu, carried seedlings to Martinique in 1720, from where it spread across the Caribbean and into South America. Brazil took it up, and by 1852 Brazil was the world's largest grower of coffee — a place it still holds. The plant now grows all round the warm belt of the earth, between the two tropics, wherever high, cool ground and steady rain allow.
    • Coffee also has a quieter old use that is easy to miss: the leaves. In Ethiopia, coffee leaves were brewed as a tea long before the bean drink spread, and leaf tea is still drunk in parts of Ethiopia and South Sudan today. It holds far less caffeine than the bean drink, and it is a drink, not a medicine — no trial has tested it for health.
    • What is in the cup, first. A cup of brewed coffee holds caffeine — about 95 mg in a standard mug, though the amount swings widely with the bean, the roast and the brew — and a family of plant compounds called chlorogenic acids, which give coffee much of its bitter edge and its antioxidant work in the body. The cherry's pulp and the green bean hold the most of these compounds; roasting cuts them back. The cup holds almost no calories on its own. Milk, sugar and syrup are what turn coffee into a sweet drink, and the research below is about plain coffee, not sweetened coffee drinks.
    • The one effect that is proven in people, in controlled trials, is the shortest one: caffeine wakes the brain up. The European Food Safety Authority, weighing the trial evidence, found that cause and effect had been established between caffeine and increased alertness and attention, for servings holding at least 75 mg of caffeine — about one ordinary cup. A 2025 pooling of 31 randomised, placebo-controlled trials in 1,455 healthy adults found the same pattern in smaller words: caffeine gave small but real gains in reaction speed and accuracy on attention tasks. The gains are for simple attention and staying awake, not for memory or hard thinking, and in people who drink coffee every day, part of the lift is simply the easing of overnight withdrawal — the morning cup returns them to normal rather than lifting them above it. Human trials
    • The longer story is different in kind: it comes from watching large groups of people over years, not from trials, and it shows links, not proof. The largest pooling of that work is a 2017 umbrella review in the BMJ, which gathered 201 meta-analyses of observational studies and 17 of trials, and found coffee drinking more often linked with benefit than with harm, with the largest lower risks at three to four cups a day against none: all-cause mortality about 17% lower, cardiovascular mortality about 19% lower, cardiovascular disease about 15% lower. The review's own warning stands with the numbers: observational work cannot prove cause and effect.
    • The blood-sugar link is the steadiest of the long-term findings. A 2014 meta-analysis of 28 prospective studies with more than 1.1 million people found each extra cup of coffee a day linked with about 9% lower risk of type 2 diabetes, and the link held for decaffeinated coffee too — about 6% lower per cup — which points to compounds other than caffeine doing part of the work. The link grows with the amount drunk, cup by cup, up to about six cups a day.
    • The liver findings are the strongest in size. In the BMJ umbrella review, any coffee against none was linked with about 29% lower risk of fatty liver disease, 27% lower risk of liver scarring, and 39% lower risk of cirrhosis, along with a lower risk of liver cancer. A 2015 cohort study of a multi-ethnic population in the United States found two to three cups a day linked with 38% lower risk of liver cancer and 46% lower risk of chronic liver disease. As with the rest, these are links seen in populations, not proof in a trial.
    • The brain findings are real and narrower. Coffee drinkers show a lower risk of Parkinson's disease across many studies — about 30% lower in a 2002 pooling — and the link follows caffeine, not the rest of the cup: caffeinated coffee and caffeine itself were linked with the lower risk, while decaffeinated coffee was not. The working idea is that caffeine blocks a docking point in the brain called the adenosine A2A receptor. Coffee drinking is also linked with a lower risk of dementia and of depression, by about a quarter in a pooling of 22 prospective studies — again, links, not proof.
    • Two fences belong here. First, unfiltered coffee — French press, Turkish coffee, boiled coffee — holds oily compounds called diterpenes, cafestol and kahweol, which raise blood cholesterol; a paper filter catches most of them, so filtered coffee does not carry the same effect. Second, coffee is not a treatment for any of these conditions. No one should drink coffee to treat diabetes, liver disease or Parkinson's, and no one should stop prescribed treatment because they drink coffee.
    • When to plant: Grow it from fresh seed sown in spring, or buy a young plant from a nursery — seed-grown plants take three to four years to bear, and nursery plants fruit sooner
    • Sun: Morning sun and dappled afternoon shade, or about 30 to 50% shade through the day; indoors it wants a bright spot out of direct midday sun
    • Soil: Deep, rich, well-drained ground, slightly acid — pH about 5.5 to 6.5; a sandy loam rich in humus suits it best
    • Environment: A plant of cool tropical highlands — outdoors year-round only in frost-free places, about USDA zones 10 to 11; it grows best between 15 and 24 °C (59 to 75 °F), and frost kills it
    • Planter or ground: Ground in frost-free places; everywhere cooler, a houseplant or a pot that comes under cover before the cold
    • Water: Water steadily so the soil stays evenly moist, never dry and never soaked; keep the ground mulched to hold moisture
    • When to pick: Pick the cherries only when fully red, cherry by cherry, as they ripen unevenly on the branch — eight to nine months after flowering

    Garden notes

    • Frost kills it, and even a chill below about 10 °C (50 °F) checks its growth. It is a plant for warm, humid, sheltered air.
    • Heat: the plant grows best between 15 and 24 °C (59 to 75 °F). Above about 30 °C (86 °F) it suffers, flowers drop and cherries ripen too fast and lose flavour. Cool nights slow the ripening and build the sugars that make a good cup. The finest coffee grows high: 1,200 to 2,500 metres in the tropics, where the air is cool and the ripening is slow.
    • Full sun scorches the leaves.
    • Soil: deep, rich, well-drained ground, slightly acid — pH about 5.5 to 6.5. A sandy loam rich in humus suits it best. It hates wet feet: water sitting round the roots brings rot, and heavy wet clay kills more young plants than cold does. Keep the ground mulched to hold moisture, and water steadily so the soil stays evenly moist, never dry and never soaked.
    • Grow it from fresh seed sown in spring, or buy a young plant from a nursery — seed-grown plants take three to four years to bear, and nursery plants fruit sooner. Space shrubs about 2 to 2.5 metres apart in the row. Prune once a year after harvest, taking out dead wood and crossing branches, and keep the plant to a height that lets the cherries be picked by hand. The flowers are white and sweet, opening in flushes after rain; the cherries take eight to nine months to ripen, and they are picked only when fully red, cherry by cherry, as they ripen unevenly on the branch.
    • The warning that belongs in any garden note is leaf rust, a fungus that turns the leaves orange underneath and strips the plant bare. Arabica is open to it, and in wet years it can ruin a crop. Good air flow, shade that is not too heavy, and clearing fallen leaves all help; the rust-resistant crosses exist for places where rust is a yearly fight. Scale insects, mealybugs and aphids trouble pot-grown plants indoors.

    Propagation

    Grow it from fresh seed, sown in a warm, damp mix, or from a stem cutting dipped in rooting powder and kept covered until it roots. Arabica seed grows true to its kind, but robusta and hybrids need cuttings. Only fresh seed sold for planting will grow — roasted beans will not sprout.

    Safety

    • The European Food Safety Authority judges up to 400 mg of caffeine a day — roughly four ordinary mugs of brewed coffee — as safe for healthy adults, and a single dose of up to 200 mg as safe. In pregnancy, the safe amount drops to 200 mg a day from all sources, and the same 200 mg a day applies while breastfeeding. For children and teenagers, the authority found too little evidence to set a safe daily amount at all. A single dose of 100 mg close to bedtime can already make it harder to fall asleep and shorten sleep. More than the safe amount brings a racing heart, shaking hands, worry, restlessness and stomach upset, and in people who are sensitive to caffeine, far less can do the same. Anyone with a heart rhythm problem, high blood pressure that is hard to control, severe worry, or a sleep problem should talk to a doctor about how much coffee suits them, and coffee never replaces sleep.

    Sources

    • Poole et al. (2017) — Coffee consumption and health: umbrella review of meta-analyses of multiple health outcomes (BMJ) — 201 observational meta-analyses and 17 trial meta-analyses; largest lower risks at three to four cups a day
    • Ding et al. (2014) — Caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee consumption and risk of type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and a dose-response meta-analysis (Diabetes Care) — 28 prospective studies, over 1.1 million people; about 9% lower risk per extra cup
    • European Food Safety Authority NDA Panel (2015) — Scientific Opinion on the safety of caffeine (EFSA Journal) — up to 400 mg a day for healthy adults, 200 mg a day in pregnancy and while breastfeeding, 100 mg near bedtime disturbs sleep
    • European Food Safety Authority NDA Panel (2011) — Scientific Opinion on the substantiation of health claims related to caffeine and increased alertness and attention (EFSA Journal) — cause and effect established for servings of at least 75 mg of caffeine
    • Encyclopaedia Britannica — History of coffee — Yemen in the 1400s, Sufi monks, coffeehouses in Mecca and Constantinople, the spread to Java and the Americas, Brazil largest since 1852
    • Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — the accepted name Coffea arabica L., its place in the Rubiaceae, and its native range in Ethiopia

    Vetiver

    Chrysopogon zizanioides

    Culinary

    A tall tropical grass grown for the part nobody sees: a dense mass of fine, scented roots that smell of earth, wood and rain. Almost every famous grass scent — lemongrass, citronella — lives in the leaf; vetiver's lives underground. In India, where the plant comes from, it is khus, and its roots have cooled houses, scented drinking water and flavoured summer drinks for centuries. The same roots, distilled, give one of perfumery's great base scents, and the same plant, set in a line across a slope, is one of the most planted erosion defences on earth. Its older scientific name, Vetiveria zizanioides, is still the one on most bottles and books.

    Vetiver is one of the three plants in Crown Recovery Oil.

    Cultivars

    Vetiver is not a bred vegetable, and there is no catalogue of named garden varieties to list. What a grower actually chooses between is types — and with this plant the type matters more than it does for almost any other plant, because the types behave differently.

    The sterile cultivated type ('Sunshine' and its kin)

    The plant of the world's hedges and oil fields: a southern Indian cultivated form, taken from place to place as clumps for centuries, which flowers without setting seed that grows. 'Sunshine' is the name attached to the clone the DNA work identified — one single plant, in effect, copied across the tropics. It never runs, never self-sows, and can only be planted by hand. Other named sterile selections exist in national collections, but 'Sunshine' is the one the world mostly grows.

    The wild northern khus

    The fertile, seed-bearing vetiver of the Ganges plain and the wild riverbanks: it grows untidily, seeds itself, and gives the oil Indian perfumery prizes most — ruh khus, distilled from wild-dug roots. It is the original of the species and the source of the sharbat and tatti tradition, and it is not the plant sold for garden hedges.

    The oil origins

    Perfumers sort vetiver the way wine is sorted, by place, because the same plant gives different oils in different soils: Haitian oil is the freshest and lightest, with a citrus brightness; Bourbon oil from Réunion is the warmest and most complex, and now the rarest; Javanese oil is the smokiest and most leathery. These are origins, not varieties.

    African vetiver (Chrysopogon nigritana)

    A separate, taller West African species, planted for the same erosion work in its home region. Its roots are not the perfume root, and it is not this plant.

    • Vetiver comes from India — the wild plant grows on riverbanks, floodplains and marshy ground across the subcontinent, and the cultivated plant was selected there. Its name carries its use: vetiver comes from the Tamil vettiveru, vetti, digging, and ver, root — "the root that is dug up." In northern India it is khus, and the two names mark two different plants in trade: the wild, seed-bearing khus of the northern plains, and the cultivated vetiver of the south.
    • The root was traded and taxed early. In the 600s CE, under the emperor Harshavardhana, the city of Kannauj became the great centre of India's aromatic trade, and a tax on vetiver root is recorded from that time — Kannauj is still a perfume town today, and its traditional distillers still make ruh khus, a deep green vetiver oil, from wild northern roots in copper stills.
    • In Ayurveda, India's traditional medicine, the root is ushira, classed among the cooling herbs. In the past, it was infused in water for thirst and summer fevers, ground into pastes for hot, irritated skin, and given for digestive upsets and urinary complaints. Those uses belong to the past and to tradition; what testing in people actually shows is much less.
    • The drink grew out of the fragrance. Khus sharbat — a syrup made from the root extract, stirred into chilled water or milk — became a fixture of the Indian summer, sold bottled across the country. The bottled syrup is usually coloured a startling green; the root's own colour is pale gold, and the flavour underneath the colour is the real thing.
    • Carried out of India, the root became a perfume crop. The French planted it on Mauritius in the mid-1700s and then on Réunion — then called Bourbon — where the first chemical analysis of the oil was made in 1809 and "Bourbon vetiver" became the prestige oil of the early 1900s. Java grew it on a large scale, and in the late 1930s the plant reached Haiti, which changed the trade for good.
    • One fact shapes everything about the modern plant. DNA fingerprinting (Adams et al., 1998) showed that almost all the vetiver grown outside South Asia is a single clone — the sterile type named 'Sunshine' — a southern Indian cultivated form that makes no useful seed and does not spread. It is planted by splitting clumps, it stays where it is put, and it cannot seed itself into new ground. The fertile wild type of the north is a different plant in behaviour, and the two are kept apart wherever it matters.
    • The second career began in sugar cane. In the 1950s the Fiji Sugar Corporation planted vetiver hedges to hold soil on steep cane fields; John Greenfield, who had worked with those hedges, carried the method to World Bank watershed projects in India in the early 1980s, and Richard Grimshaw at the World Bank championed it worldwide. A US National Research Council panel, chaired by Norman Borlaug, reviewed the evidence and reported in 1993 that vetiver hedges were a cheap, safe and effective way to slow erosion; Grimshaw went on to found The Vetiver Network to spread the method.
    • India — the home of it all: khus tattis dripping over doorways, roots in the water pot, sharbat in the summer, attars in Kannauj, and hedges on farm bunds that predate the modern erosion movement by centuries — the British colonial farm services were promoting vetiver hedges in the 1930s, and Indian farmers long before that.
    • Haiti — the modern centre of the oil. Vetiver arrived in the late 1930s and took hold around Les Cayes in the south; Haiti is now the world's largest producer, supplying roughly half the world's vetiver oil, and tens of thousands of small farmers grow it, digging the roots by hand. The money is real and so is the strain: a root crop dug out of hillsides can leave the soil it grew in worse off, and Haitian growers and buyers have been working on planting it in hedges so the harvest and the holding of the land go together.
    • Réunion — Bourbon vetiver: the prestige oil of the first half of the 1900s, warm and rosy, against which other oils were judged. Production shrank as land and labour found other uses, and true Bourbon oil is now a rarity that perfumers hunt for rather than a staple they order.
    • Indonesia — Java's oil, grown around Garut in West Java, is the smoky end of the vetiver range, distilled long and dark; in the middle of the 1900s Java was the trade's biggest source before Haiti passed it.
    • West Africa — in Mali and Senegal the roots were traditionally put with stored drinking water, to scent it and, it was held, to keep it sweet; the grass itself is planted for the same soil work as everywhere else, often using the African cousin named in Cultivars.
    • Vetiver oil, distilled from the roots, is breathed in for calm and rubbed, diluted, on the skin — the grounding oil, and a perfumer's base note. Traditional use

    Craft

    • The cooling was practical as well as medical. Across northern India, screens woven from the roots — khus tattis — were hung over doors and windows through the hot season and kept sprinkled with water; the air that passed through arrived cooler and carrying the root's scent, and tradition credits the device to the court of the emperor Akbar in the 1500s. The same principle later filled the pads of electric desert coolers.
    • Roots were also tucked into earthen water pots so the drinking water took up the scent, woven into hand fans, mats and baskets, and burned in incense; the leaves thatched roofs.
    • Vetiver is not a food with figures. It appears in no standard food-composition database, because almost nobody eats it — the one kitchen use, khus sharbat, is a sugared syrup, and its nutrition is the sugar's. There are no vitamin or mineral numbers for this plant.
    • The oil is where the measured interest sits. Vetiver oil is more than 90% sesquiterpenes — the large, heavy scent molecules that make it thick, slow to evaporate and long-lasting on skin — and the molecules that carry its smell are named: khusimol, and the two vetivones, alpha and beta. That chemistry is a fact about the oil. What the oil does for people's health is a separate question, and here the record is thin.
    • In the laboratory: vetiver oil and root extracts slow the growth of some bacteria and fungi in test tubes, and show antioxidant activity in bench assays. Lab studies
    • In animals: the oil, smelled or swallowed, has calming and sedative-like effects in rats and mice. Both kinds of result are real, and both are the kind of result that often does not carry over to people. Animal studies
    • In people: there are no completed randomised trials of vetiver for any medical use — not for anxiety, not for sleep, not for skin, not for anything else. A small trial of vetiver aromatherapy for anxiety and depression has been registered, but no results have been published. Aromatherapy calls the scent "grounding," and it is one of the most valued scents in that world; a valued scent is a fact about taste, not a tested effect on the mind.
    • The traditional medicine — the Ayurvedic cooling root — was never tested in the modern way, and none of it counts as a benefit. The plant's real, documented worth is in perfume, in craft and in holding soil.
    • When to plant: Plant slips in warm weather, at the start of the rains where rains are seasonal
    • Sun: Full sun, and lots of it — in shade the clumps thin, lean and lose the density that does the work
    • Soil: The plant's tolerance is genuinely wide — poor, stony, acid, alkaline and salty soils all grow it — though it does its best work in deep, open soil, and the claim sometimes printed that it thrives at any acidity from one extreme to the other comes from the promotional literature and is stronger than the trials behind it
    • Environment: A tropical grass: frost blackens the tops, the clump can regrow after a light frost, and a hard freeze kills it outright. It is a permanent plant only where winters are frost-free or nearly so; everywhere colder it is a summer curiosity that will not see the spring
    • Planter or ground: Ground — planted in rows for roots, or in a line along the contour of a slope for a hedge
    • Spacing and depth: For a hedge, slips go in about 15 cm (6 in) apart along the contour line of a slope
    • Water: It tolerates flooding for weeks and drought once established; new slips, though, must be kept watered until they take hold

    Garden notes

    • A densely tufted perennial grass: stiff, upright clumps 1.5–2.5 m (5–8 ft) tall — to 3 m in the best conditions — with long, thin, rigid leaves and brownish-purple flower heads on the fertile types. It has no runners and no creeping roots: the clump thickens where it stands and goes nowhere else.
    • The root system is the famous part. Where most grasses spread their roots sideways, vetiver's drive almost straight down — 2–4 m (7–13 ft) deep, much of that in the first year — a dense curtain of fine, strong roots. That curtain is what holds soil, and it is also the harvest: there is no way to take the roots and keep the plant.
    • It is never grown from seed in practice. The sterile types make none that grows, and even fertile seed is unreliable, so vetiver is planted as slips — small rooted pieces split from a mature clump. For a hedge, the clumps knit into a continuous barrier within a season or two; for root growing in India, slips are planted in rows at the start of the rains.
    • How the hedge works, at its documented strength: a line of vetiver across a slope slows running rainwater, spreads it, and drops the soil the water was carrying, so a low terrace builds up behind the hedge over the seasons while more of the rain soaks in instead of running off. In the Indian field trials of the 1980s, plots protected by vetiver hedges lost over 90% less soil than unprotected plots and kept far more of their rain — the result the 1993 National Research Council review examined and endorsed. The grander claims in the promotional literature — that vetiver pulls heavy metals out of polluted ground and water, that its roots have a measured share of the strength of steel — rest on much thinner evidence — they remain claims, not findings.
    • Harvest, two ways that cannot be combined. For roots: the whole clump is dug at a year and a half to two years old, when the roots carry the most oil — it takes roughly 150 kg of roots to yield a single kilogram of oil — and the planting is finished and begun again. A hedge planted to hold a slope is therefore never dug: the two uses are two separate plantings, and a gardener chooses which one a clump is for. The leaves, meanwhile, can be cut again and again without harming the plant — for mulch, for thatch, and in India traditionally for weaving — and trimming a hedge's tops is ordinary upkeep that keeps it dense.
    • One warning belongs to the fertile type: seed-bearing vetiver planted beside waterways in warm climates can sow itself where it was not invited. The sterile types carry no such risk, which is why they are the only ones sold for planting in most countries — buy slips under a name, and know which type you have.

    Safety

    • The oil is a long-standing perfume ingredient, used on skin at low strength in finished products, and serious reactions are uncommon; neat oil is strong and is diluted before it touches skin. There is no established safe dose for swallowing vetiver oil or root preparations, and no good safety record for them in pregnancy — so the firm line is the simple one: vetiver is a scent and a craft plant, not a home medicine, and it is not taken by mouth as a remedy.

    Sources

    • Yule & Burnell (1886) — Hobson-Jobson, the Anglo-Indian glossary — the tatty, the name vettiveru, and the tradition crediting Akbar's court
    • National Research Council (1993) — Vetiver Grass: A Thin Green Line Against Erosion — the expert review of the hedge evidence
    • Adams et al. (1998) — DNA fingerprinting reveals the clonal nature of vetiver — the 'Sunshine' clone and the sterility of the world's plantings
    • Bhushan et al. (2013) — Vetiveria zizanioides: a pharmacological overview — the Ayurvedic record and the laboratory pharmacology
    • Gunasekar et al. (2025) — Pharmacological and therapeutic potential of Chrysopogon zizanioides: a comprehensive review — traditional uses and the preclinical evidence, gathered
    • The Vetiver Network International (2026) — the plant and the Vetiver System — botany, planting practice and the documented-versus-promoted record

    Flax

    Linum usitatissimum

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Blood Sugar HealthDigestive HealthHeart Health

    Cooked

    Flax is one plant with three gifts, and its Latin name says so: usitatissimum means "most useful". From one slender annual come the seed you eat, called linseed, the oil pressed from that seed, and linen, the cloth spun from its stems. The plant itself is a quiet beauty — a thin, upright stem about knee to waist high, narrow grey-green leaves, and small sky-blue flowers, five petals each, that open in the morning and drop by the afternoon, so a field in flower looks like a pale blue sea that changes every day. Each flower leaves behind a small round pod, a boll, holding ten flat, glossy seeds, brown or golden. The seed is where the food story lives: it is rich in a plant omega-3 fat, in fibre, and in lignans — plant compounds found in flaxseed in far greater amounts than in any other common food. One caution cannot wait: the seed holds natural compounds that can release tiny amounts of cyanide, and the ground seed releases more than the whole seed. At the spoonfuls people normally eat, the body clears it without trouble, but large amounts, and raw ground seed eaten by small children, need care.

    Cultivars

    Flax has no named garden cultivars in the nursery sense — no named forms bred for a flower bed. What it has is farm varieties, bred for seed or for fibre, and those are the names that belong here.

    For linseed and for oil

    Short, branchy plants bred to carry many seed pods: 'Ingot', with small yellow seeds and tall, sturdy plants; 'Lirina', oil-rich and high-yielding, blue-flowered, ripening from August; 'LS Koral', a golden variety with pale yellow seeds and high oil content; and 'Serenade', white-flowered, with a higher seed yield but less oil. Brown seed and golden seed are the two seed colours sold for eating: golden seed tastes milder and keeps baking pale, brown seed is the common kind. They are the same species, not different plants.

    For fibre

    Tall, straight, unbranched plants bred for long stems: 'Avian', good fibre quality and high yields; 'Felice', high fibre yield and good disease resistance; and 'Lisette', quick to grow and steady in the field. Fibre types and seed types are the same species, bred in opposite directions: fibre plants grow tall with few branches and few seeds, seed plants grow short and branchy with many pods.

    The other blue-flowered flaxes sold for gardens — perennial blue flax, Linum perenne, and scarlet flax, Linum grandiflorum — are different species, not cultivars of this one. None of what is told of Linum usitatissimum belongs to them, and their seed is not linseed.

    • Flax is one of the oldest crops people ever grew. Wild flax fibre has been found in a cave in Georgia, in the Caucasus, worked into cord some 30,000 years ago, long before farming began. The plant was tamed as a crop about 8,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent — the river lands of the Near East — first for its seed and then for its fibre. From there it travelled with farmers into Egypt, across the Mediterranean and into Europe, and in time to every cool farming country in the world.
    • Egypt made flax famous. Flax grew along the Nile in great fields, and Egyptian weavers turned it into linen so fine it was almost see-through — cloth for the clothes of the living, for the wrapping of mummies, and for gifts sent from one king to another. Linen was so woven into Egyptian life that it was used for clothing, bedding, sails and burial cloths alike, and the finest pieces were kept for temples and for the dead. The seed was pressed for oil too, used for lamps, for embalming and for cooking.
    • In the ancient Near East, flax was a farm crop with a place in the farming year: the Gezer Calendar, a short Hebrew inscription from about the 10th century BC, names a month for harvesting flax, and at Jericho, Rahab hid two spies under stalks of flax laid out on her roof to dry — the drying step before the fibre was worked. In Greece and Rome, flax was food, fibre and medicine all at once, and by 1000 BC people in Greece and Jordan were baking bread from flaxseed.
    • The Greek physicians knew it well. The writings handed down under the name of Hippocrates, the Greek father of medicine, mention flax some seventy times. The seed was most often crushed and laid on the skin as a poultice — a warm, soft dressing — for boils, sores and swellings, and the stalk was softened in water and laid over open wounds as a bandage, sometimes soaked in wine or honey. Hippocrates also recommended the seed for pain in the gut, and later writers record its use for constipation. Charlemagne, the Frankish king, is said to have recommended flaxseed for gut trouble too, carrying the Greek advice into medieval Europe.
    • In the old medicine of India and the Middle East, linseed was used in much the same way: as a soothing, slippery seed for the gut, as a poultice for swelling and pain, and as a cough remedy — an infusion of the seed, sweetened with honey and lemon, was used by the Cherokee in North America for coughs and sore throats, and that use is still found today. Through the Middle Ages and into the herbal books of early modern Europe, the seed stayed a household remedy for constipation, for coughs and for sore, swollen skin. Much of that use was habit and hope, not tested proof.
    • The fibre side of the story never stopped either. Linen was the cloth of Europe for thousands of years — for shirts and sheets, for tablecloths and sails, for the sails of ships and the canvas of painters — until cotton, which was cheaper and easier to spin by machine, pushed it aside in the 1800s. In Ireland, Belgium and northern France, flax growing and linen weaving were whole ways of life, and the linen towns of Ulster and Flanders were famous for them. The seed oil had its own trade too: linseed oil was the base of paints and varnishes and of linoleum flooring, and in America the oil sold for wood and paint is still called linseed oil — that industrial oil is not food, and must never be eaten.

    Craft

    • Linen is made from the stem, not the seed. When the plants are nearly ripe, they are pulled up by the roots, so the full length of fibre is saved, and laid out to dry. Then the stalks are soaked in water, or left out in the dew, until the woody part begins to rot away from the fibres — this is called retting. The stalks are dried again, beaten to break the woody core, and combed to separate the long fibres, which are then spun into thread and woven. Linen made this way is strong, cool to wear and grows softer with washing. It was the cloth of Egypt, of Europe and of the sails of ships for thousands of years, and it is still woven today, in smaller amounts, for clothes, sheets and table linen.
    • What is in the seed, first. About a third to nearly half of the seed by weight is oil, and most of that oil is alpha-linolenic acid — ALA for short — a plant omega-3 fat. A level tablespoon of ground seed carries about 1.6 g of it, and flaxseed is the richest common food source of it. The seed is also about a quarter fibre by weight, much of it a slippery soluble fibre called mucilage, which turns to a soft gel when the seed meets water. And the seed is, by a very wide margin, the richest food source of lignans — plant compounds, mainly one called secoisolariciresinol diglucoside, which gut bacteria turn into weak, oestrogen-like molecules. The seed also carries protein, about a fifth of its weight, and small amounts of vitamins and minerals.
    • Ground beats whole, and the whole seed beats the oil. The seed coat is hard and glossy, and whole seeds often pass through the gut unbroken, so much of what is inside is never reached. Grinding cracks the coat open. In trials, ground seed raised blood levels of the omega-3 fat; whole seed did not. The oil carries the omega-3 but leaves the fibre and most of the lignans behind — and in the trials, that matters: the oil did not lower cholesterol, while the whole and ground seed did. Ground seed goes rancid faster than whole seed once it meets air, light and heat, so it is best ground fresh and kept cool and shut. Human trials
    • The heart evidence is the strongest there is, and it is human evidence. In a placebo-controlled trial of 110 adults with clogged leg arteries — peripheral artery disease — 30 g of milled flaxseed a day, baked into breads and muffins, for six months, left blood pressure about 10 points lower on the top number and 7 points lower on the bottom number than the dummy foods. In the people who started with a top number of 140 or more, the top number fell by 15 points. The authors called it one of the strongest blood-pressure effects ever seen from a food. But it is one trial, in sick people, and the pooled picture across many trials is smaller: on average, blood pressure fell by only about 2 to 3 points. The big trial result has not been repeated at that size. Human trials
    • Cholesterol moves a little, in the same direction. A meta-analysis — a pooling — of 28 trials found that flaxseed lowered total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol, the "bad" kind, by a small amount: whole or ground seed lowered them clearly, while the oil did not. The drop was bigger in women, especially after the menopause, and in people who started with high cholesterol. No trial has yet shown that eating flaxseed prevents a heart attack or a stroke — the trials measured blood pressure and cholesterol, which are risk factors, not the events themselves. Human trials
    • Blood sugar moves a little too, and again only with the whole seed. A meta-analysis of 25 trials found small falls in fasting blood sugar, in insulin and in a measure of insulin resistance with whole flaxseed, but not with the oil or with lignan extracts, and no clear change in HbA1c — the blood test that shows average blood sugar over two to three months. Flaxseed does not replace diabetes care, and it is not a treatment for diabetes on its own. Human trials
    • The gut benefit is real but small, and it rests on small trials. The fibre and mucilage add bulk and soften the stool, and in small trials flaxseed eased constipation — in one, 50 g of flaxseed flour a day worked at least as well as the laxative lactulose over four weeks, and in another, flaxseed baked into cookies eased constipation in people with type 2 diabetes. A small trial in people with irritable bowel syndrome found no benefit. The seed needs water with it: dry seed without enough fluid can swell and block the gut, and anyone with a narrowed gut should not take it. Human · small
    • The cancer story is the most interesting and the least settled. In a small, well-run trial, 32 women with newly found breast cancer ate a muffin with 25 g of flaxseed a day, or a plain muffin, for about a month before surgery. In the flaxseed group, the tumours grew more slowly — the growth marker fell by about a third — and more tumour cells died. But the trial measured markers inside the tumour, not whether anyone lived longer or stayed free of cancer, and it was only 32 women for one month. A similar small trial in men with prostate cancer found the same kind of slowing. Population studies point the same way without proving cause. That is not proof that flaxseed prevents or treats cancer. Human · small
    • When to plant: Sow direct in early spring, two to six weeks before the last frost, as soon as the soil can be worked
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Deep, well-drained, fertile loam, around pH 6.0 to 7.5; heavy wet clay is its enemy
    • Environment: A plant for cool summers, around 15 to 21 °C (60 to 70 °F); it fails in hot, humid weather
    • Planter or ground: Ground — sow where it is to grow; it dislikes being moved
    • Spacing and depth: About 6 mm (a quarter of an inch) deep; sow thickly for fibre, thinly for seed
    • Water: About an inch a week until settled, then little; stop watering two weeks before harvest
    • When to pick: Fibre at 90 to 100 days, when the stems are turning yellow from the bottom up; seed at 100 to 120 days, when nine in ten bolls have turned brown and rattle

    Garden notes

    • Flax is a cool-season annual, easy to grow and quick to finish: sow to harvest takes about 90 to 100 days for fibre and 100 to 120 days for seed. It is a plant for cool summers, not hot ones — it likes temperatures around 15 to 21 °C (60 to 70 °F), full sun, and it fails in hot, humid weather, where fungal diseases take hold.
    • Sow the seed straight where it is to grow, in early spring, two to six weeks before the last frost, as soon as the soil can be worked — about 6 mm (a quarter of an inch) deep. The seed needs light, moist soil to sprout, in 7 to 10 days. Sow thickly for fibre, so the plants grow tall and straight with no room to branch; sow thinly, with room between plants, for seed, so each plant branches and carries many pods. Flax dislikes being moved, because its roots are fragile and it grows a taproot.
    • Soil: it grows in many soils but does best in deep, well-drained, fertile loam, around pH 6.0 to 7.5. Heavy wet clay is its enemy — roots sitting in water invite disease. Do not feed it heavily: too much nitrogen makes tall, weak stems that fall over in wind and rain. Water steadily until the plants are settled, then little — about an inch a week — and stop watering two weeks before harvest.
    • The flowers open in the morning and drop by the afternoon, each lasting a single day, but new ones keep opening for two to three weeks, about 40 to 50 days after sowing. After flowering come the round bolls. For fibre, pull the whole plant, roots and all, when the stems are turning yellow from the bottom up and the bolls are still green. For seed, wait until nine in ten bolls have turned brown and rattle when shaken, then cut the stalks and dry them upright in bundles for two weeks before threshing out the seed.
    • Flax will self-seed where it is happy, and a patch left to itself often comes back the next spring. Watch for rust, wilt and blight in wet summers, and for cutworms and grasshoppers eating the young plants. It is an annual, so it must be sown fresh each year.

    Propagation

    Sow seed direct where it is to grow, in early spring — flax dislikes being moved, because its roots are fragile and it grows a taproot. It self-seeds where it is happy, and a patch left to itself often comes back the next spring. Sow fresh seed each year: it is an annual, and a plant left to itself gives seed, not a second year of growth.

    Safety

    • The seed holds cyanogenic glycosides — natural compounds that release small amounts of hydrogen cyanide when the seed is crushed or chewed. At normal amounts — a tablespoon or two a day — the body clears it without trouble: the liver turns the cyanide into thiocyanate, which leaves in the urine, and the European Food Safety Authority found that average eating did not pass its safety limit in any age group. At the very high end of eating, some children and teenagers passed it slightly, though the Authority judged harm unlikely. The ground seed releases the cyanide more easily than the whole seed, and heat plus water cuts it sharply: baking the seed into moist bread or muffins, or boiling it for a few minutes in porridge, removes most of it, while dry-roasting ground seed on a tray removes only a little. A sensible ceiling is about 30 to 40 g a day — two to three tablespoons — for an adult, and small children should not eat large amounts of raw ground seed.
    • Two more cautions. First, the seed can slow the uptake of medicines taken at the same time, because its fibre and mucilage coat the gut — take medicines an hour or two apart from a spoonful of flaxseed. Second, because the seed can lower blood sugar and blood pressure a little, people on diabetes or blood-pressure medicines should watch their readings when they start eating it regularly, and anyone pregnant should keep to food amounts — the lignans act weakly like oestrogen, and large supplement doses have not been tested in pregnancy. The oil sold for paints and wood is not food oil and must never be swallowed. The food oil, pressed for eating, goes rancid quickly and should be kept cold, dark and shut, and never heated for frying.

    Sources

    • Pan et al. (2009) — Meta-analysis of the effects of flaxseed interventions on blood lipids (American Journal of Clinical Nutrition) — 28 trials, whole seed lowered cholesterol, oil did not
    • Mohammadi-Sartang et al. (2018) — Flaxseed supplementation on glucose control and insulin sensitivity: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 25 randomized, placebo-controlled trials (Nutrition Reviews) — small falls in fasting blood sugar and insulin with whole seed, none with oil, no clear change in HbA1c
    • Thompson et al. (2005) — Dietary flaxseed alters tumor biological markers in postmenopausal breast cancer (Clinical Cancer Research) — 32 women, 25 g flaxseed muffin a day for about a month before surgery, tumour growth marker fell by about a third
    • EFSA Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain (2019) — Evaluation of the health risks related to the presence of cyanogenic glycosides in foods other than raw apricot kernels (EFSA Journal) — the acute reference dose of 20 micrograms of cyanide per kilogram of body weight, and ground linseed releasing more than whole
    • Goyal et al. (2014) — Flax and flaxseed oil: an ancient medicine and modern functional food (Journal of Food Science and Technology) — the seed's makeup, the traditional uses, and the whole-seed versus oil distinction
    • Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — the accepted name Linum usitatissimum, its place in the flax family, and its native range
    • Touwaide & Appetiti (2023) — Herbs in History: Flax (American Herbal Products Association) — the 30,000-year-old fibre, the Fertile Crescent taming, and the Hippocratic uses

    Peas

    Pisum sativum

    Culinary

    Blood Sugar HealthDigestive HealthImmune Health

    FreshCooked

    One of the oldest farmed foods on Earth, and still one of the sweetest things in a spring garden. The pea is a seed that grows in a pod on a climbing vine — eaten three ways: shelled fresh and green, whole in the pod (the snow and snap types), or dried down to a store-cupboard staple. It also holds a place no other vegetable holds: the science of genetics was worked out on this plant, in a monastery garden, one counted pod at a time. One warning about a name before anything else: the sweet pea of flower gardens is a different plant, Lathyrus odoratus, grown for its scented flowers — its seeds are not food, and it is not this pea.

    Cultivars

    Peas sort into three eating types, and the type decides how the plant is picked and eaten.

    Shelling peas (garden peas, English peas)

    Grown for the seeds alone; the pod is tough and is thrown away. 'Lincoln' — an old English favourite, vines about 2½–3 ft, tender and sweet, freezes well, and among the more heat-tolerant of the shelling peas. 'Green Arrow' — long, slim pods holding up to eleven peas, heavy crops, a classic freezer pea at about 68–70 days. 'Little Marvel' — a dwarf at about 2 ft that needs no trellis, ready in about 60 days, the one for small gardens and pots. 'Wando' — the shelling pea chosen where spring warms up fast, bred to keep cropping a little longer into warm weather than the others.

    Snow peas (Pisum sativum var. saccharatum)

    Flat, thin-walled pods picked while the seeds inside are still tiny; pod and all is eaten. The French name is mange-tout, "eat all." 'Oregon Sugar Pod II' — a dwarf snow pea, vines about 2½ ft, pods in pairs, bred for resistance to the common pea diseases. 'Mammoth Melting Sugar' — the tall old heirloom, 5–6 ft of vine and big flat pods; it is also a piece of breeding history, because it was a snow pea of this kind that Calvin Lamborn started from (below).

    Snap peas (Pisum sativum var. macrocarpon)

    The newest type: thick-walled, rounded pods eaten whole with full-size peas inside, crisp and sweet. They exist because of one cross. In Idaho, breeder Calvin Lamborn, working with M. C. Parker at the Gallatin Valley Seed Company, crossed a snow pea with a mutant shelling pea that had an unusually thick pod wall; after a decade of selecting, 'Sugar Snap' was released in 1979 and won the All-America Selections Gold Medal the same year. The original is a tall climber, 6 ft and more, and needs a real trellis. Lamborn's 'Sugar Ann' (1984, also an All-America Selections winner) is the dwarf answer — about 2 ft, the earliest snap, named for his daughter. 'Cascadia' is a bush snap of about 3 ft bred with resistance to pea diseases.

    Field peas

    Smooth-seeded types grown not for the table-fresh trade but to ripen and dry on the plant: split peas for soup, marrowfat peas for mushy peas, and the great prairie crop of Canada and Russia. A garden pea left unpicked becomes this — the same species, harvested at the other end of its life.

    • The pea was domesticated in the Fertile Crescent — the arc of land across the Near East where farming began — about 10,000 years ago. It is one of the eight founder crops, the short list of plants that started agriculture there: einkorn wheat, emmer wheat, barley, lentil, pea, chickpea, bitter vetch and flax. People had eaten wild peas long before anyone farmed them — pea remains at the Ohalo II site, in what is now Israel, are about 23,000 years old — and storage pits at the Neolithic village of Ahihud held peas alongside lentils and fava beans some 10,000 years ago, which means peas were already a crop worth storing.
    • The Greeks and Romans grew peas and ate pea soup; in Athens in the 400s BCE, street vendors sold hot pea soup to passers-by, and the playwright Aristophanes mentions it on stage. For most of the centuries that followed, though, the pea was eaten dried. Dried peas keep for years, travel well and cook down into filling food, and fresh green peas were a brief spring treat at best.
    • The old English word for the crop was pease — a word for the stuff as a whole, the way "oatmeal" names a stuff and not a thing. The singular "pea" and the plural "peas" were formed later, by back-formation, when people began hearing the end of "pease" as a plural. Boiled dried peas made pease pottage, then pease pudding: soaked, boiled, mashed and set, eaten hot or cold with salt pork, standard food for sailors because it kept and it filled. The rhyme remembers it — "Pease porridge hot, pease porridge cold, pease porridge in the pot, nine days old" — first printed in John Newbery's Mother Goose's Melody around 1760. Pease pudding is still made in the north of England, and mushy peas, its marrowfat cousins, still come with fish and chips.
    • Eating peas young, green and fresh was an invention of the 1600s, and at first it was a rich person's fashion. A hamper of green peas from Genoa was presented to King Louis XIV of France in January 1660, shelled before the court as a ceremony; by 1696 Madame de Maintenon was writing that peas at court were "a fashion, a fury" — ladies ate them after dinner, before bed, at the risk of indigestion. A fresh-pea soup, Potage Saint-Germain, took its name from the king's court. In England the same split opened between coarse "field peas," grown to dry, and tender "garden peas," grown to eat green.
    • Breeders were already reshaping the plant before science caught up with it. In England, Thomas Andrew Knight crossed pea varieties from the 1790s onward — some of the first deliberate plant breeding anywhere — and his wrinkled-seeded "marrow" peas were sweeter than the old smooth kinds. The reason for the wrinkles was only found in the 1990s: a faulty starch gene leaves more of the pea's sugar unconverted, and the seed wrinkles as it dries because of it.
    • Then the pea changed science. Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar at St Thomas's Abbey in Brno (now in the Czech Republic), chose peas to study how traits pass from parent to offspring — because pea flowers pollinate themselves, his varieties bred true, and because their traits come in clean either/or pairs. Between 1856 and 1863 he hand-crossed nearly 30,000 pea plants and counted everything: tall against short, round seed against wrinkled, yellow against green, purple flower against white, full pod against pinched, green pod against yellow, flowers along the stem against flowers at its tip. He showed that traits are passed on as separate units — what we now call genes — that some traits dominate and hide the other, and that the hidden trait is not lost: it came back in the next generation in about one plant in four. He presented the work in 1865 and published it in 1866, and the world ignored it for thirty-four years. In 1900 three botanists — Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak — independently reached the same results and found Mendel's paper waiting for them. Genetics, and everything built on it, starts with peas. The plant is still a laboratory subject: its full genome was published in 2019.
    • Thomas Jefferson's favourite vegetable was the English pea. At Monticello he grew fifteen types of it, staggered his sowing, and ate peas fresh from mid-May to mid-July. His neighbourhood kept an annual contest for the first peas of spring — the winner hosted the others at a dinner built around the dish — and by family account it was almost always won by his neighbour George Divers. The one year Jefferson's peas came first, he told his family to say nothing: it would please his friend more to think he never failed.
    • The last chapter is the freezer. A picked pea starts turning its sugar to starch within hours, which is why peas eaten straight from the pod taste sweeter than any shop pea. Clarence Birdseye, who had watched Inuit food freeze fast and keep its quality in Labrador winters, built quick-freezing into an industry; on 6 March 1930 the first Birds Eye "frosted foods" went on sale in Springfield, Massachusetts, and peas were in that first line. Frozen peas are picked and frozen within hours of harvest, at the moment of sweetness — which is why a bag of frozen peas can honestly taste better than "fresh" peas that spent days travelling.
    • Britain and Ireland — mushy peas beside fish and chips, pease pudding in the north-east cooked in the liquor from a ham, and pea and ham soup. The dried-pea tradition of the pease centuries, still on the plate.
    • The Netherlands — snert, also called erwtensoep: a split-pea soup with smoked sausage and pork, traditionally made so thick it is said a spoon should stand up in it; skating food, eaten through the Dutch winter.
    • Sweden and Finland — pea soup on Thursdays, with pancakes and jam after, is a custom centuries old in both countries; the Finnish armed forces still serve it on Thursdays.
    • Italy — risi e bisi in Venice: rice and the first fresh peas of spring, cooked loose, halfway between a soup and a risotto, with the empty pods simmered into the stock so nothing is wasted. By tradition it was served to the Doge on 25 April, the feast of St Mark, the city's patron.
    • India — matar, green peas, across the north Indian kitchen: aloo matar (peas with potato), matar paneer (peas with fresh cheese), peas through rice and snacks; dried white peas make ragda for chaat. India grows green peas on a huge scale and is also the world's largest buyer of dried peas.
    • China — the shoots. Dou miao, the tender young leaves, tips and tendrils of the snow pea plant, stir-fried fast with garlic, is a prized seasonal vegetable, picked by hand and priced like it; snow peas themselves go through stir-fries whole. China grows most of the world's green peas.
    • The dry-pea world — most of the planet's pea crop is still harvested dry. Russia and Canada lead world dry-pea production (about 3.25 and 3.0 million tonnes of a roughly 14-million-tonne world crop in 2024), grown across the northern plains and shipped worldwide — the founder crop of the Fertile Crescent is now a prairie commodity.
    • Fresh green peas, per 100 g: 81 kcal, protein 5.42 g, fibre 5.7 g, carbohydrate 14.4 g, sugars 5.67 g, fat 0.4 g. The standout vitamins are vitamin C at 40 mg — about 44% of the daily value — folate at 65 µg and vitamin K at 24.8 µg, with iron (1.47 mg) and potassium (244 mg) besides. For a green vegetable those protein and fibre figures are high, and the reason is simple: a pea is a seed, and it eats like one.
    • Dried peas are a second food from the same plant, and a much denser one. Split peas, per 100 g dry, run about 352 kcal with protein around 23.8 g and fibre around 25.5 g — among the cheapest sources of protein in the world, which is why pea soup has fed armies, navies and poor households for centuries. Dried peas are always soaked and cooked; they are never eaten raw.
    • Fresh peas are the opposite case: they are safe and sweet eaten raw, straight from the pod, and generations of gardeners have eaten more of the crop standing at the row than ever reached the kitchen.
    • On blood sugar, peas behave better than their sweetness suggests. Green peas carry their sugar with fibre and protein, and measured glycaemic index values are low: frozen green peas tested between 29 and 42 in the University of Sydney's database, and boiled peas sit in the low-to-middle range in the international tables. Those are measured values for the food. Peas do not treat diabetes or any other condition.
    • Pea protein powder is a different thing from the vegetable. It is made from dried yellow peas by concentrating the protein out of them — an isolate, a processed ingredient, not a serving of vegetables. A few small exercise studies have tested the powder alongside training, with results much like other protein powders; that is a finding about a supplement taken with workouts, not about eating peas. Human · small
    • Claims that peas fight cancer, clean the blood or detox anything rest on laboratory work with pea compounds, not on trials in people. Those claims have no trial in people behind them. Lab studies
    • When to plant: Sow direct as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, about four to six weeks before the last frost
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Well drained, around pH 6.0–7.5, and not rich in nitrogen
    • Environment: Best between about 55 and 75 °F (13–24 °C); stops flowering once days run past about 85 °F (29 °C)
    • Planter or ground: Ground, with support in place at sowing for the tall types
    • Spacing and depth: About 1 inch deep and 2 inches apart
    • Water: About an inch a week, evenly moist while flowering and the pods fill
    • When to pick: About 55–70 days from sowing; pick every day or two

    Garden notes

    • The pea is an annual that climbs by tendrils — thin curling threads that wrap around whatever they touch. Its flowers are white on most varieties (some are purple), and they pollinate themselves, usually before the flower has fully opened. That one fact explains a lot: it is why pea varieties stay true, why seed saved from your own plants grows out the same, and why Mendel had to open flowers by hand and cross them himself to do his experiments.
    • It is a cool-season crop, and timing is the whole game. Sow the seed directly in the ground — peas transplant badly — as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, about four to six weeks before the last frost. Seed will germinate in soil as cold as 40 °F (4 °C), though slowly, and young plants shrug off a light frost. Sow about 1 inch deep and 2 inches apart, in full sun.
    • Heat ends it. Peas grow best between about 55 and 75 °F (13–24 °C) and stop flowering once days run past about 85 °F (29 °C); the harvest window is a spring race of about two to three weeks of picking. Where summers are hot, sow again in late summer, about eight to ten weeks before the first fall frost, for an autumn crop — and in mild-winter country (zones 8–11) peas are a fall-to-spring crop, grown through the cool months and finished before the heat.
    • Give climbers their support at sowing, not later: tall types reach 5–7 ft and want a trellis, netting or fence in place from the start, while dwarf types at 2–3 ft manage with brushwood or a short fence. Set the support first and sow along its foot, and the tendrils do the rest.
    • Soil should be well drained, around pH 6.0–7.5, and not rich in nitrogen — for a reason that is the pea's best trick. Peas feed themselves. Bacteria called Rhizobium leguminosarum live in small knobs — nodules — on the roots, and they take nitrogen gas from the air in the soil and turn it into a form the plant can use; the plant pays them in sugars. A working nodule, cut open, is pink inside. When the crop is done, leave the roots in the ground and that nitrogen stays in the bed for whatever grows next. On ground where peas or beans have never grown, the bacteria may be missing; seed can be coated with inoculant — the bacteria themselves, sold as a powder — to start the partnership. Go easy with nitrogen fertiliser either way: it grows leaves, not pods, and a well-fed plant stops bothering with its nodules.
    • Water about an inch a week, and keep the soil evenly moist while the plants flower and the pods fill; a mulch helps hold the moisture and keeps pods off the soil.
    • Picking: the first pods come about 55–70 days from sowing. Pick every day or two — shelling peas when the pods are plump, bright green and full but not yet dull; snap peas plump and crisp; snow peas while the pod is still flat and the seeds are shadows inside. Picking is not just harvest; a plant whose ripe pods are left hanging takes the hint and stops flowering. Eat, cook or freeze what you pick the same day — the sugar in a picked pea starts turning to starch within hours, and no storage undoes it.
    • Saving seed and rotation: let a few of the best pods dry on the vine and shell out next year's seed — it will come true. And move peas around the garden: growing them in the same bed year after year builds up soil diseases, so give a bed a break of three or four years between pea crops where you can.

    Propagation

    Grow from seed, sown direct where the plants will grow — peas transplant badly. Let a few of the best pods dry on the vine and shell out next year's seed: it will come true, because pea flowers pollinate themselves. Move peas around the garden: growing them in the same bed year after year builds up soil diseases, so give a bed a break of three or four years between pea crops.
