    Rhubarb

    Rheum rhabarbarum

    Culinary

    Digestive Health

    Cooked

    A vegetable that lives as a fruit. Rhubarb is a hardy perennial grown for its thick, fleshy leaf stalks — red, pink or green, and sharp enough to make your mouth pucker — which are cooked with sugar and eaten as pies, crumbles and jams. Only the stalks are food. The big heart-shaped leaves above them are poisonous: they carry oxalic acid, and they are never eaten, by anyone, in any amount. Cut the leaf off every stalk you pick and put it on the compost heap. The stalks are the plant's spring gift; the leaves are not food at all.

    Cultivars

    'Victoria'

    The classic. Bred by Joseph Myatt in the 1830s and named for Queen Victoria, it is still the variety most gardens grow: medium stalks, light green speckled with pink, heavy crops and excellent flavour.

    'Timperley Early'

    Among the earliest of all to crop, outdoors in early spring — and one of the varieties the Yorkshire sheds use for forcing, so its stalks are among the first rhubarb of the year, in late winter.

    'Canada Red'

    A Canadian variety, bred in Winnipeg ('Chipman's Canada Red'). Its stalks are shorter and more slender than most, but deep red, tender and sweet, and the plant makes few seed stalks.

    'Glaskin's Perpetual'

    The long-season one. It is low in oxalic acid, so its stalks stay mild and can be picked over a longer season without turning harsh.

    The forcing varieties

    The Yorkshire sheds grow their own set, kept by families for generations: 'Stockbridge Arrow', 'Stockbridge Harbinger', 'Reed's Early Superb', 'Prince Albert' and 'Queen Victoria' among them, chosen for pale, tender stalks grown in the dark.

    A plain note on colour: red is not sweeter. Colour and sweetness are not linked — the green varieties are often the most productive, and a pink-stemmed plant can be tarter than a red one.

    • Rhubarb belongs to the buckwheat family, Polygonaceae — kin to buckwheat itself and to sorrel, which shares its sharp, lemony bite. Garden rhubarb, Rheum rhabarbarum, comes from the cold country of southern Siberia and Mongolia. It is one plant of a large family of Rheum species spread across Asia, and it is not the same plant as the rhubarb of the old medicine trade: that was the root of its cousins Rheum officinale and Rheum palmatum, from the mountains of China and Tibet. Food in the garden, medicine in the root — two different plants wearing one name.
    • In China the medicine root — da huang, "great yellow," for the colour of the cut root — was written down in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing, the oldest Chinese herbal, compiled about 2,000 years ago. It was a strong, valued drug, used above all to purge the gut. For thousands of years, "rhubarb" in most of the world meant that dried root, not anything you would put in a pie.
    • The name tells the journey. The Greeks called the plant rha, after the river Rha — the Volga — along whose banks it grew, in country foreign to them: rha barbaron, "the foreign rha." Latin kept it as rheubarbarum, and English softened it to rhubarb.
    • The dried root travelled west along the Silk Road for centuries, and it was costly — land carriage was slow and risky, and old accounts say the root was at times more costly than opium. In the 1600s Russia took the trade into its own hands: a state monopoly, run through the border town of Kyakhta in Siberia, where every root was inspected — bored through to prove it was sound inside — and the bad pieces were destroyed. "Russian rhubarb" became the finest grade in Europe, and private trade in it was banned outright. The monopoly faded in the 1800s as ships brought the root from Canton instead, but the episode had a strange echo: in the 1780s China banned rhubarb exports to Russia for a time, in the belief — mistaken, but widely held in Beijing — that the Russians could not do without their rhubarb.
    • Europe knew rhubarb as a drug in the apothecary's jar long before it knew it as a food. Garden species were grown in Europe before the 1700s, still for their roots. When the English first tried eating the plant in the 1600s, they chose the leaves — the poisonous part — and the cramps, sickness and deaths that followed put people off rhubarb for some two hundred years.
    • Sugar changed everything. In the early 1800s, with sugar finally cheap, cooks in England discovered the stalks: stewed sweet, they made a tart filling that tasted like the first fruit of spring, weeks before any fruit was ripe. The London market gardener Joseph Myatt bred and sold the new eating varieties — 'Victoria' in the 1830s, named for the young queen — and rhubarb tarts and pies swept the country. In America, where settlers had brought it by the 1820s, it earned the plain name "pie plant," and in 1947 a New York customs court formally ruled it a fruit, because fruit is how it is eaten.
    • In old Persian myth, the first man and woman were said to have grown from a single rhubarb plant, joined together — and wild rhubarb still grows across the high country of Iran and Central Asia, where the stalks are cooked savoury as well as sweet.
    • Forcing is rhubarb's second act. The story goes that in 1817, at the Chelsea Physic Garden in London, a crown was accidentally covered over — and when it was uncovered weeks later, it had grown pale, tender, sweet stalks in the dark. Growers in Yorkshire built an industry on that accident. In the Rhubarb Triangle — the nine square miles between Leeds, Wakefield and Bradford — crowns grow two years in the fields, are frosted, then are lifted in November and packed into long, dark, heated sheds. Fed only by the sugar stored in their roots, the stalks grow an inch a day, fast enough that growers say you can hear them creak and pop as they push upward. They are picked by candlelight, so that light never greens and toughens them. At its height the Triangle grew most of the world's forced rhubarb and sent special trains to London overnight; "Yorkshire Forced Rhubarb" was given protected-name (PDO) status in 2010. Of more than two hundred forcing growers, only a handful are left.
    • In both world wars rhubarb was a British garden standby — one of the few sweet things a rationed kitchen could grow. But the First World War also wrote the leaves' warning in earnest: in 1917, with green vegetables short, rhubarb leaves were recommended as a substitute, people were poisoned, some died, and the advice was withdrawn. The stalks were never the problem. The leaves always were.
    • Britain — rhubarb crumble with custard, rhubarb and ginger jam, and the forced stalks of the Yorkshire Triangle as a late-winter delicacy; Wakefield, in the Triangle, holds a rhubarb festival each year.
    • Germany — Rhabarberkuchen, rhubarb cake, often under a crumble or meringue top, and rhubarb juice and spritzers in spring.
    • Poland — kompot z rabarbaru, a sweet rhubarb drink, served cold through the season.
    • Iran — khoresh rivas, a savoury stew: rhubarb stalks simmered briefly with lamb or beef, parsley and mint, the tart stalks cutting the rich meat — proof the plant is not only a dessert.
    • Denmark — rabarberkage, rhubarb cake, a spring standard.
    • Iceland — rhubarb jam is a pantry staple, spread on bread and layered into the celebration cake vínarterta.
    • The United States — strawberry-rhubarb pie, the sweet strawberries softening the tart stalks; and rhubarb custard pie in Amish country.
    • The stalks, per 100 g raw: 21 kcal, carbohydrate 4.54 g, sugars just 1.1 g, fibre 1.8 g, protein 0.9 g. The standout nutrient is vitamin K at 29.3 µg — about a quarter of the daily value — with potassium at 288 mg, a little vitamin C at 8 mg, and calcium at 86 mg on paper. It is a tart, low-sugar, low-calorie food: nearly all the sugar in a rhubarb crumble is sugar that was added to it.
    • The calcium needs an honest note. Much of it is bound up with the plant's own oxalic acid, and oxalic acid stops calcium being absorbed — so in practice rhubarb is not a calcium food, whatever the table says.
    • The fibre has been tested once, in people, at its real size: Goel et al. (1997) gave ten men with high cholesterol 27 g a day of fibre prepared from rhubarb stalks, for four weeks. Total cholesterol fell 8% and LDL cholesterol 9% — and both returned to where they started within a month of stopping. That is one small, short trial of a concentrated fibre, not a finding about eating rhubarb. Later work on the same fibre was in mice. Human · small
    • The root of the Chinese species is a real and powerful laxative drug, carrying compounds called anthraquinones. It is not a food, and it is not the garden plant. Traditional use
    • When to plant: Set crown divisions in early spring (autumn works too)
    • Sun: Full sun, a little shade where summers are hot
    • Soil: Rich, fertile, well-drained; a heavy feeder that rewards a yearly mulch of compost or rotted manure
    • Environment: Needs a real winter; a perennial in USDA zones 3–8, failing where winters stay warm
    • Planter or ground: Ground
    • Spacing and depth: About 3 ft apart, with the buds about 2 inches below the surface
    • Water: Keep the ground moist but never waterlogged — crowns rot in wet soil
    • When to pick: From the third year, stalks 8–15 inches long, pulled with a twist; stop picking by midsummer

    Garden notes

    • A hardy herbaceous perennial: it grows from a thick crown — a knotted mass of roots and buds — sends up leaves 2–4 ft tall each spring, and dies back to the ground each winter. A well-kept crown crops for fifteen years or more. The stalks run up to about 18 inches long and 1–2 inches thick, red, pink or green by variety.
    • It needs a real winter. Rhubarb rests in the cold and will not thrive where winters stay warm — as a perennial it suits USDA zones 3–8, and in warm-winter country it fails or is grown as a short-lived annual. Give it full sun (a little shade where summers are hot), and rich, fertile, well-drained soil; it is a heavy feeder and rewards a yearly mulch of compost or rotted manure.
    • Plant crowns, not seed: seed-grown plants vary and often do not match the parent, while a crown division is the variety itself. Set divisions in early spring (autumn works too), spaced about 3 ft apart, with the buds about 2 inches below the surface. Keep the ground moist but never waterlogged — crowns rot in wet soil.
    • Harvest with patience. Take no stalks in the first year, only a few in the second, and freely from the third. Pick stalks when they are 8–15 inches long: pull each one with a twist at the base — do not cut, as a cut stump can rot — and cut the leaf off straight away. Never take more than about a third of the plant's stalks at a time, and stop picking by midsummer so the crown can rebuild for next year. Cut out any flower stalk the moment it appears; flowering drains the crown.
    • Two safety notes from the garden itself: after a hard late frost, do not eat the stalks — oxalic acid can move into them from the frost-damaged leaves. And every leaf you strip goes to the compost heap, never the pot.
    • Divide old crowns every four or five years to keep them vigorous: dig the crown in early spring and cut it into pieces, each with at least one strong bud, and replant.
    • Forcing at home: a rested crown can be forced in a dark shed or garage, or outdoors under a tall forcing pot that shuts out the light. Lift the crown after frost, pot it up, keep it dark, and pale sweet stalks follow in late winter. The crown gives everything it has to that one crop and is spent afterwards — the Yorkshire growers compost theirs, and home gardeners do the same.

    Propagation

    Divide old crowns every four or five years to keep them vigorous: dig the crown in early spring and cut it into pieces, each with at least one strong bud, and replant. Seed-grown plants vary and often do not match the parent, so plant crowns, not seed — a crown division is the variety itself. Forcing at home spends the crown: it gives everything it has to that one crop and is composted afterwards.

    Safety

    • Rhubarb leaves hold about 0.5–1.0% oxalic acid, along with other suspect compounds. Eaten, they can burn the mouth and gut and damage the kidneys. An adult would need to eat several kilos of leaves to take a lethal dose of the acid itself — but far smaller amounts have made people seriously ill, and poisonings and deaths are on record, including the 1917 cases. The rule has no exceptions: leaves are never food. They are safe on the compost heap, where the acid breaks down as they rot.
    • The stalks carry oxalic acid too, in far smaller amounts, and ordinary servings are safe. People who form calcium-oxalate kidney stones are often advised by their doctors not to eat large amounts of rhubarb often.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: rhubarb, raw — the nutrition figures
    • Goel et al. (1997) — cholesterol-lowering effects of rhubarb stalk fibre in hypercholesterolemic men — the one small human trial, at its size
    • Foust (1992) — Rhubarb: The Wondrous Drug — the medicine-root trade, the Russian monopoly and the drug years
    • European Commission (2010) — registration of 'Yorkshire Forced Rhubarb' as a protected name (PDO) — the Triangle, the sheds, the forcing varieties and the candlelight picking
    • University of Wisconsin–Madison Extension (2026) — Rhubarb, Rheum rhabarbarum — the plant, growing, harvest and the leaf warning

    Oregano

    Origanum vulgare

    Culinary

    CalciumIronMagnesiumPotassium

    FreshDried

    "Joy of the mountain" — that is what its Greek name is read to mean, and it fits: a tough, sun-loving perennial that carpets dry Mediterranean hillsides and asks almost nothing of the gardener. Oregano is the flavour of pizza and of the Greek village salad, a warm, peppery, slightly bitter leaf that does something almost no other herb does — it tastes stronger dried than fresh, so the bunch crumbled from a jar is the classic form, not a poor substitute. One warning before anything else: the name covers a family of types, and they are not equal. The Greek type, subspecies hirtum, is the cook's oregano, rich in the oils that give the bite. The common wild type of northern gardens can be so mild it disappoints in the pot. One plant must not be confused with this one. Mexican oregano is Lippia graveolens, a shrub of Mexico and Central America in a different family altogether (the verbena family, not the mints). Its flavour is earthier and more citrus-like, and it is the oregano of pozole, beans and chili in Mexican cooking. The two share a name and a dried-leaf trade, and nothing else.

    Cultivars

    Greek oregano (subspecies hirtum)

    The classic, and the one to grow for the kitchen. A compact plant with small, slightly hairy leaves — hirtum means hairy — and white flowers. Its oil is the richest in carvacrol of any oregano, which is the bite: peppery, warm, a little numbing on the tongue. This is the dried oregano of Greece and Italy, the one sold in bunches on its stems in Greek markets, and the type most shop jars of "oregano" claim to be. If a packet just says oregano, this is the flavour it is promising.

    Common oregano (subspecies vulgare)

    The wild marjoram of northern Europe: pink-purple flowers in generous heads, a pretty, spreading plant that bees and butterflies work all summer. As a garden plant it is lovely; as a seasoning it is the great disappointment of the herb garden, often so mild it has almost no flavour at all. It is grown for ground cover, for looks and for pollinators — and it is the reason gardeners are told to taste a leaf before buying a plant labelled simply "oregano."

    Italian oregano (Origanum × majoricum)

    A garden hybrid between oregano and sweet marjoram, sometimes called hardy sweet marjoram because it survives winters marjoram cannot. The flavour is the marriage of its parents: oregano's warmth rounded by marjoram's sweetness, milder and more floral than the Greek type. It is a fine all-round kitchen herb, good used fresh where the Greek type might shout, and a standard in Italian-American gardens.

    'Hot and Spicy'

    A bred form of the Greek type, selected for an extra peppery kick: all the oregano flavour, with a heat that reads almost like a mild chilli. Low and bushy, about 24–30 inches tall, hardy in zones 5–9. It is the oregano for Tex-Mex pots, salsas and bold bean dishes, and it keeps its bite late into the year.

    Golden oregano ('Aureum')

    A form grown for its leaves before its flavour: bright gold-green foliage in spring, softening to chartreuse by midsummer, in a low cushion about 6–12 inches tall. The flavour is mild but real, fine in salads and light dishes. It earns its place as edging, in pots, and anywhere a herb garden wants a patch of light.

    Syrian oregano (Origanum syriacum)

    A cousin worth knowing: a different species with large, velvety, pale leaves — the herb of Levantine za'atar.

    Garden centres also sell purely ornamental oreganos such as 'Kent Beauty', grown for their hop-like pink bracts and not for the kitchen.

    • Oregano is native to the hills and mountains around the Mediterranean and east into Central Asia, growing wild on dry, rocky, sun-baked ground — thin soil, sharp drainage, and long hot summers. That wild toughness is still in the garden plant.
    • The Greek name was origanon. It is traditionally read as oros, mountain, and ganos, joy or brightness — "joy of the mountain." (Philologists debate the word's deeper roots, but the mountain-joy reading is the one the plant has carried for centuries.)
    • Greek story gave the plant a goddess. Aphrodite, goddess of love, was said to have created oregano on Mount Olympus and grown it in her garden as a symbol of joy and happiness — a fitting maker for the "joy of the mountain," and the reason the herb belonged to love and weddings ever after.
    • So Greek and Roman brides and grooms were crowned with wreaths of oregano on their wedding day, for joy in the marriage. The same plant was laid on graves and planted over them, in the belief that it brought the dead peace and that life continued beyond the grave — joy at the wedding, rest at the grave.
    • Oregano was medicine early. It appears in the writings that carry Hippocrates' name, from the 5th century BCE onward, in dozens of preparations — above all for coughs, chests and breathing, and for stomach trouble. Those uses are history.
    • Aristotle recorded the plant's most famous animal story. In his History of Animals he wrote that when a tortoise has eaten a viper, it afterwards eats origanum — "this has been observed," he says — and he tells of a man who had often watched it happen and, meaning to test it, gathered up all the origanum within reach; when the plant was gone, the tortoise died. It is an ancient anecdote — but it fixed oregano's reputation as an antidote for a thousand years: Dioscorides, whose herb book guided medicine for fifteen centuries, duly listed oregano preparations against venomous bites and poisons.
    • The Romans, who liked the flavour as much as the medicine, carried the plant across their empire, and it settled into the cooking of southern Europe — above all Greece and southern Italy, where it never left the table. Through the Middle Ages it stayed in monastery and cottage gardens, more medicine than food in the north; its great kitchen centuries were still to come, and they would happen an ocean away.
    • The Spanish carried Mediterranean oregano to Latin America in colonial times — though the "oregano" that took root in Mexican kitchens was mostly the different native plant, Mexican oregano. Greek and Italian immigrants brought the true plant to the United States around 1900, but to most Americans it stayed a foreign word. M.F.K. Fisher's wartime cookbook of 1942 mentions it once.
    • Then came the war, and pizza. From 1943 to 1945, hundreds of thousands of American soldiers fought up through southern Italy, where oregano grows wild on the hills and is scattered generously over pizza and tomato dishes. They came home wanting that taste. American oregano sales rose by thousands of percent in the decade after the war, pizzerias spread from coast to coast, and the "pizza herb" became a staple of the American spice shelf — reported, in time, as the most-imported herb in the United States.
    • Greece — rigani is gathered wild from the hillsides, dried on the stem, and crumbled by hand over the food at the table: over the village salad and its slab of feta, over grilled lamb and chicken, into ladolemono, the lemon and olive oil dressing. A Greek bunch of oregano, stems and all, is a standard market sight.
    • Italy — the south is oregano country: scattered over pizza in Naples and Sicily, through tomato sauces, over grilled fish and vegetables. The north, broadly, prefers marjoram — the map of Italian oregano is the map of the old Greek and Arab south. And it was southern Italy's pizza that carried the herb to America.
    • Turkey — kekik, the everyday word covering oregano and its close thyme-like kin, is wild-gathered and heaped over grilled meats, salads and breakfast eggs, and brewed as a tea in the countryside.
    • The Levant — za'atar: the dried herb — classically Syrian oregano — mixed with sumac and sesame seed, and eaten the region's way: torn flatbread dipped first in olive oil, then in the green, tangy blend; or baked onto the bread itself as manoushe. Few spice blends on earth are eaten so plainly and so daily.
    • Mexico — the oregano here is a different plant, Lippia graveolens: earthier, with a citrus edge, dried and crumbled into pozole, beans, chili sauces and menudo. Mexican cooks are not using a substitute — they are using their own oregano, which was never the Mediterranean plant at all.
    • Argentina — dried oregano is a core ingredient of chimichurri, the parsley-and-oil sauce spooned over grilled beef, and Argentine pizza — a proud local tradition of its own — is dusted with it as freely as any in Naples.
    • The United States — the "pizza herb" of Italian-American cooking: in the red-sauce joints, the meatballs, the garlic bread, the shaker jar on the pizzeria table beside the chilli flakes. Oregano is reported to be the most-imported herb in the country, by both weight and value — an astonishing landing for a plant America barely knew in 1942.
    • Oregano's proven role is flavour.
    • The dried leaf is, by weight, remarkably stocked. Dried oregano, per 100 g: 265 kcal, fibre 42.5 g, vitamin K 621.7 µg — several times the whole day's value — calcium 1,597 mg, iron 36.8 mg, manganese about 5 mg, vitamin E 18.3 mg, potassium 1,260 mg and magnesium 270 mg. Now the honest scale: nobody eats 100 g of oregano. A teaspoon is about 1 g. A pizza's whole dusting adds almost nothing to the day's nutrition — the numbers describe what the leaf is made of, not what a serving delivers. Oregano earns its place by making other food taste good, and that is a real contribution: food people enjoy eating gets eaten.
    • The bite is chemistry. Oregano's flavour and scent come from its essential oil, and in the Greek type the leading compound is carvacrol, the same warm, pungent substance found in thyme. In laboratory dishes, oregano oil and carvacrol kill bacteria and fungi — that part is well shown, and it is why the oil is studied for food preservation. Animal studies point the same way. But a dish is not a body: no controlled trial has shown that eating oregano, or swallowing its oil, treats an infection in a person. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • Oil of oregano is a concentrate — the distilled essence of a great deal of leaf in a small bottle — marketed as a "natural antibiotic" and a cure for everything from colds to gut parasites. The evidence does not carry those claims: they rest on the laboratory results above, not on trials in people. Sprinkling dried oregano on food is eating a herb. Swallowing oregano oil by the dropper is a different act entirely. Lab studies
    • Oregano does not boost the immune system, cleanse parasites, or work as an antibiotic in people. No human evidence supports any of these.
    • When to plant: Set plants out after the frosts, about a foot apart
    • Sun: Full sun — six to eight hours or more
    • Soil: Sharp drainage, well-drained, even gritty or sandy soil, around pH 6.0–8.0
    • Environment: Hardy roughly in zones 4–10; winter wet, not cold, is what kills it
    • Planter or ground: Ground, or a pot of gritty mix in full sun
    • Spacing and depth: About a foot apart
    • Water: Sparingly once established; overwatering kills it or washes out its taste
    • When to pick: Cut stems for drying in midsummer, just before the flowers open

    Garden notes

    • Oregano is a hardy perennial — it lives for years. It grows 1–2 ft (about 30–60 cm) tall and spreads wider than that by creeping underground stems, into a loose, bushy mound. In cold-winter country it dies back to the crown and returns in spring; in mild winters it can stay half-evergreen. It is hardy roughly in zones 4–10, and the thing that kills it is not cold but winter wet.
    • Sun is the flavour. Give it full sun — six to eight hours or more. Oregano makes its oils as a defence against hot, dry, bright weather, so a plant grown lean in blazing sun tastes strong, and a plant pampered in rich, wet, shaded ground grows lush and bland. Poor, rocky, ordinary soil is not a problem for this plant; it is the point.
    • Soil and water: sharp drainage above all — well-drained, even gritty or sandy soil, around neutral to mildly alkaline (pH about 6.0–8.0). Water it while it settles in, then sparingly: once established it is properly drought-tolerant, and overwatering is the commonest way to kill it or to wash out its taste.
    • Starting: seed is easy but faithless — seedlings of oregano vary wildly in flavour, and a seed packet of the Greek type can give you plants from strong to nearly tasteless. For a flavour you can trust, buy a plant you have tasted a leaf of, or take cuttings or divisions from a plant you know, in spring. Set plants out after the frosts, about a foot apart, and let them spread.
    • Harvest: snip stems as you need them once the plant is well grown, taking no more than about a third at a time. The leaves carry their strongest flavour in midsummer, just before the flowers open — that is the moment to cut stems for drying, on a dry morning after the dew is off.
    • Drying is where oregano breaks the herb rule. Most herbs fade as they dry; oregano's flavour concentrates. Tie stems in small bunches and hang them in a dark, airy place for a week or two until crumbly, then rub the leaves off the stems and store them airtight, away from light. A jar of good Greek oregano keeps its bite for the better part of a year — this is why the dried leaf, not the fresh, is the classic form.
    • Flowers and bees: if you let some stems bloom, you will see why the plant is a pollinator favourite — the flower heads, white on the Greek type and pink-purple on the common, are worked by bees and butterflies for weeks. Cut the plant back by about half after flowering and it answers with a second flush of fresh leaves.
    • Care and keeping: cut the old stems down in spring as new growth starts. Clumps grow woody and tired in the centre after a few years — divide them in spring, replant the vigorous outer pieces, and compost the old heart. The plant spreads with intent, so give it a corner of its own, a raised bed, or a pot — it does very well in a pot of gritty mix in full sun, which is also the answer where winters are wet.
    • Companions: gardeners have planted oregano through the vegetable garden for centuries, saying it does its neighbours good; what can be said for certain is that a flowering oregano patch feeds the bees and butterflies that the whole garden depends on. It asks so little water that it keeps good company with the other dry-ground Mediterraneans — thyme, rosemary, sage and lavender.

    Propagation

    For a flavour you can trust, buy a plant you have tasted a leaf of, or take cuttings or divisions from a plant you know, in spring — seed is easy but faithless, and seedlings vary wildly in flavour. Clumps grow woody and tired in the centre after a few years: divide them in spring, replant the vigorous outer pieces, and compost the old heart. Give it a corner of its own: it spreads with intent.

    Safety

    • Undiluted oregano oil burns and irritates skin and gut; it can provoke allergy in people sensitive to the mint family (thyme, sage, basil and their kin); it is not established as safe in pregnancy; and it can interact with medicines.

    Sources

    • Touwaide & Appetiti (2024) — Herbs in History: Oregano, American Herbal Products Association — the name, the Aphrodite story, Hippocrates and Dioscorides, weddings and graves
    • Aristotle (4th century BCE) — History of Animals, Book IX — the tortoise that ate the viper, then the origanum
    • Soltani et al. (2021) — A review of the phytochemistry and antimicrobial properties of Origanum vulgare and its subspecies — what the laboratory work does and does not show
    • National Public Radio (2015) — GIs brought a taste for oregano home from Italy — the war, the pizza, and the sales that followed
    • University of California (2024) — Oregano, Home and Landscape — the culinary varieties and how they grow

    Marigold

    Tagetes spp.

    Culinary

    Eye Health

    Fresh

    Marigolds are the gold-orange annuals that edge half the world's vegetable beds — and in Mexico they are something more: cempasúchil, the flower of the dead, heaped on altars every November. The genus Tagetes holds about fifty species from the Americas, and the garden kinds are three of them, all Mexican: the tall African or Aztec marigold (Tagetes erecta), the compact French marigold (Tagetes patula), and the lacy signet marigold (Tagetes tenuifolia). Their leaves carry oil glands that give the whole plant a strong, sharp scent, loved by some gardeners and wrinkled at by others. One name needs clearing up at the start: this is not the pot marigold. The word "marigold" — Mary's gold — belonged first to Calendula officinalis, the European pot marigold, which has its own page in this library. The two plants share a name and a colour and nothing else; they are not close kin, and their uses are different.

    Cultivars

    African / Aztec marigold (Tagetes erecta)

    The tall one: 1–3 ft (30–90 cm), and old heirloom types taller still, carrying big pompon heads 2–4 in (5–10 cm) across in yellow, orange and cream. This is the cempasúchil of Mexico and the species grown for lutein. Garden series include 'Antigua' (compact, for bedding), 'Inca II', 'Moonsong' (deep orange), 'Vanilla' (creamy white heads) and the tall old mixture 'Crackerjack'.

    French marigold (Tagetes patula)

    The compact one: 6–18 in (15–45 cm), bushy, covered for months in smaller flowers — single, crested or double, often two-toned, mahogany red edged or splashed with gold. This is the companion-planting species, and the one whose roots do the nematode work. Series include 'Bonanza', 'Durango', 'Safari' and the single-flowered 'Disco'.

    Signet marigold (Tagetes tenuifolia)

    The delicate one: mounds 8–12 in (20–30 cm) of fine, lacy, lemon-scented leaves and masses of small single flowers. This is the food flower, the one whose lemony blooms are eaten. Cultivars include 'Lemon Gem', 'Tangerine Gem' and 'Paprika'.

    Triploid hybrids (T. erecta × T. patula)

    Crosses between the African and French kinds, sold in series such as 'Zenith': French-sized plants with near-African flowers. They set no fertile seed, so nothing tells them to stop flowering, and they bloom without pause until frost.

    Two relatives worth knowing. Mexican mint marigold (Tagetes lucida), called pericón in Mexico, is a perennial with sweet, anise-flavoured leaves used as a tarragon-like herb where true tarragon wilts in the heat; it flowers in autumn and has its own place in the Day of the Dead season in parts of Mexico. And huacatay (Tagetes minuta) is a tall, strong-tasting Peruvian cooking herb — and a stubborn weed in countries where it has escaped, which is the genus's other face: some of these plants travel too well.

    • Marigolds are American plants. The genus is centred on Mexico and Central America, and the tall T. erecta still grows wild in the centre of Mexico. The peoples of Mexico grew it long before Europeans arrived — it was raised in the chinampas, the "floating gardens" of Xochimilco, and it was already an old cultivated flower when the Spanish came.
    • Its Nahuatl name is cempoalxochitl — cempoalli, twenty, and xochitl, flower: "the flower of twenty petals," twenty standing for many. The Spanish spelling made it cempasúchil. The friar Bernardino de Sahagún described it among the flowers of Mexico in the Florentine Codex in the 1500s, the first written record of the plant.
    • In the world of the Mexica — the Aztecs — the flower belonged to the dead. It was offered in the Great Temple, and it had its place in the festivals honouring those who had died, long before those festivals met the Catholic days of All Saints and All Souls and became the Día de los Muertos, the Day of the Dead, kept on 1 and 2 November.
    • Mexico tells a story of how the flower came to be. Two children, Xóchitl — her name means "flower" — and Huitzilin, "hummingbird," grew up together and fell in love, and climbed a mountain to offer flowers to Tonatiuh, the sun, who blessed them. Then war came, and Huitzilin was killed. Xóchitl climbed the mountain again and begged the sun to join them. Tonatiuh threw down a ray of light and turned her into a flower bud that stayed closed — until a hummingbird settled on it, and the bud opened into the gold cempasúchil. As long as the flowers bloom and hummingbirds fly, the story says, the two are together — and it is why the flower stands for a love that death does not end.
    • That is the flower families still use. For Día de los Muertos they build the ofrenda — the home altar with photographs, candles, bread and the dead person's favourite foods — and cempasúchil is set all over it, and heaped on graves. Petals are scattered in paths, from the street or the cemetery gate to the altar, because the flower's strong colour and scent are said to guide the returning souls home. The flower blooms at the end of the rainy season, just in time: in many places the seed is sown around the feast of San Juan, 24 June, so the plants stand in full flower for the first days of November.
    • The plant's medicine belongs to that same old world. In Mexico the flowers were taken as a tea for stomach aches and other digestive troubles, and used in baths and washes; the herb trade across the Atlantic took up similar uses.
    • After the conquest the seed crossed the ocean. The flower reached Europe in the 1500s and was soon everywhere — in gardens, in herbals, in the flower paintings of Brueghel and Rubens. Its English names record the roads the seed travelled, not where the plant is from: "African" marigold came by way of North Africa, "French" marigold spread through the gardens of France. Both are Mexican. Linnaeus gave the genus its lasting name in 1753: Tagetes, after Tages, a prophet of the Etruscans who was said to have sprung up out of ploughed earth — a fitting name for a flower that sows itself so freely.
    • Carried east — probably by the Portuguese, in the same century — the flower found a second home in India, where it became genda, one of the country's essential festival flowers. Few plants have ever been taken up so completely by two cultures so far apart.
    • Mexico — cempasúchil above all: fields sown in June so the bloom lands on the first days of November, markets piled high with gold flowers, ofrendas and graves covered, petal paths laid to the door. The flower is also the country's lutein crop and a dye flower of long standing.
    • India — genda: strung into garlands (mala) by the million for temples, weddings, honoured guests and the festivals of Diwali and Dussehra, when whole markets turn orange. The flower that left Mexico in the 1500s is now one of the most-grown flowers in India.
    • Nepal — sayapatri: garlands for Tihar, the festival of lights, including the day of the festival that honours dogs, who wear marigold garlands around their necks.
    • Ukraine — chornobryvtsi, "black-brows," for the dark centres of the flowers: a beloved cottage-garden flower, sung about in songs as a sign of home, of mother, and of the land itself.
    • The lutein fields — Mexico, Peru, Ecuador, India and China grow T. erecta by the hectare as a crop, not a garden flower: harvested, dried and milled so that hens lay golden-yolked eggs and supplement makers get their lutein.
    • What is in the flower: the colour itself. The petals of T. erecta are one of the richest natural sources of lutein, a yellow pigment in the same family as the orange of carrots. Most of the pigment in the petals — close to nine parts in ten in commercial extracts — is lutein and its near relations. Lutein matters because the human eye gathers it: it collects in the macula, the small central spot of the retina that does the sharp seeing, where it is thought to work as a filter and a shield. The body cannot make it; it can only come from food.
    • The trade follows from that. Nearly all the lutein sold in the world — for eye supplements, and as the colouring that turns egg yolks and chicken skin gold in poultry feed — is taken from this flower. T. erecta is grown by the field for it in Mexico, Peru, India and China, picked, dried and ground into marigold meal or drawn out into extracts. When a supplement label says its lutein comes "from marigold," this is the plant.
    • The big test of lutein supplements was AREDS2 (2013), a large American trial in people at risk of advanced macular degeneration, the eye disease that takes central sight in old age. Adding lutein to the supplement formula did not clearly slow the disease for the group as a whole; it helped most in the people who ate the least lutein in their food, and it proved a safer stand-in for beta-carotene, which it replaced. That is the honest size of it: a real trial, a modest and uneven result, about supplement doses — not about eating flowers. A garnish of petals is food, not a dose. Garden marigolds do not treat eyes. Human trials
    • Eating the flowers, at food strength: the signet marigold is the food flower of the genus — its small blooms taste lemony with a hint of tarragon and are scattered over salads and desserts. Petals of T. erecta colour food in Mexico and elsewhere, and dried marigold colours feed and, in parts of Europe, some human foods as the colouring E161b (lutein). In the United States, by contrast, marigold meal is approved only as a colour in poultry feed, not as a food additive for people — a plain fact worth knowing before treating the big pompons as a vegetable.
    • Skin and other claims rest on thin evidence: marigold (Tagetes) extracts are sold in creams and oils, but the human evidence behind them is thin — mostly laboratory work on extracts, not trials on people. The skin marigold of the herbals is the other one, Calendula; the two are confused constantly. Lab studies
    • When to plant: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost, or sow in place once the soil has warmed; set out only when frost is finished
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Ordinary soil that drains; rich, heavily fed soil makes leafy plants with few flowers
    • Environment: Killed by frost; blooms from early summer to the first frost
    • Planter or ground: Ground or pots
    • Spacing and depth: French marigolds about a hand's span apart, signets a little more, tall Africans room to be tall
    • Water: Water at the base; give them air — crowded plants in wet, still weather can mildew
    • When to pick: Deadhead the faded heads to keep the plants flowering

    Garden notes

    • All three garden kinds are annuals — one season and done — and all are killed by frost. They want full sun and ordinary soil that drains; rich, heavily fed soil makes leafy plants with few flowers. Water at the base of the plants, and give them air: crowded marigolds in wet, still weather can mildew.
    • Sowing: start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost, or sow in place once the soil has warmed — the seed sprouts in about a week in warm ground. Set plants out only when frost is finished. Give French marigolds about a hand's span each way, signets a little more, and the tall Africans room to be tall. Bloom runs from early summer to the first frost.
    • Deadheading — picking off the faded heads — keeps the plants flowering; the signets need it least. Save seed from the open-pollinated kinds if you like; the named series are hybrids and will not come true from saved seed. Watch for spider mites in hot, dry spells and slugs on young plants; both find marigolds on their own, whatever the companion-planting reputation says.
    • Companion planting — the honest record, claim by claim. One part of that reputation is solidly documented:
    • Nematodes — the proven one. Root-knot and lesion nematodes are microscopic worms that gall and stunt the roots of vegetables. Living marigold roots fight them two ways: the worms cannot breed on marigold roots, and the roots give off a substance, alpha-terthienyl, that is poisonous to them. French marigold is the strongest of the genus at it, and the effect has been shown in trial after trial over more than sixty years (UF/IFAS Extension; Hooks et al., 2010). The conditions matter: the marigolds must be actively growing, the chemistry works from living roots, and the surest use is a solid stand of marigolds grown in the bed for two months or more before a nematode-prone crop goes in — or marigolds interplanted through the season. Results vary with the marigold variety and the nematode species, and a few plants dotted along a bed's edge will not clean infested soil.
    • Whitefly — one good study. In two large glasshouse trials (Conboy et al., 2019), French marigolds grown beside tomatoes from the start slowed the build-up of glasshouse whitefly; the active part of the scent proved to be limonene, the citrus-smelling compound the leaves release. Marigolds brought in after whitefly had already taken hold did little. Promising, and narrower than the legend: one pest, one setting, planted early.
    • Everything else — not proven. The broad claim that marigolds keep all pests off all vegetables has not held up under testing. Aphids colonise marigolds themselves, and no trial supports the flower as a general shield. Plant them for the nematodes, for the one studied whitefly effect, and because the single-flowered kinds — the signets above all — feed bees and butterflies all summer. The tight double pompons, bred for looks, offer pollinators almost nothing.

    Propagation

    Save seed from the open-pollinated kinds if you like; the named series are hybrids and will not come true from saved seed. Sow seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost, or sow in place once the soil has warmed — the seed sprouts in about a week in warm ground. Set plants out only when frost is finished: all three garden kinds are killed by frost.

    Safety

    • Marigolds are in the daisy family, and people allergic to ragweed, chrysanthemums and their kin can react to them too. Handling the plants bothers some gardeners — the sap and the strong oils can irritate sensitive skin, so gloves are sensible if your skin complains. And the flowers are eaten as a garnish, in small amounts, not by the bowlful.

    Sources

    • Linnaeus (1753) — Species Plantarum — the genus Tagetes described and named
    • Sahagún (1577) — Florentine Codex — cempoalxochitl described among the flowers of Mexico
    • Hadden et al. (1999) — the pigments of marigold flower extract: mostly lutein
    • Age-Related Eye Disease Study 2 Research Group (2013) — the AREDS2 trial: lutein supplements and macular degeneration
    • Setshogo (2005) — PROTA: Tagetes erecta — production for dye, feed pigment and lutein
    • Krueger et al. (2019) — UF/IFAS Extension: marigolds (Tagetes spp.) for nematode management
    • Hooks et al. (2010) — marigold as a cover crop to protect crops from plant-parasitic nematodes
    • Conboy et al. (2019) — French marigolds protect tomatoes from glasshouse whitefly through limonene

    Nasturtium

    Tropaeolum majus

    Culinary

    Immune Health

    Fresh

    The whole plant is the story. Nasturtium is a trailing garden plant from the Andes with round, shield-shaped leaves, bright trumpet flowers in orange, red and yellow — and a peppery bite in every part of it. The leaves go into salads like a green, the flowers go in whole for colour and the same warm, cress-like heat, and the unripe seed pods, pickled in vinegar, stand in for capers so well they earned their own name: poor man's capers. Few garden plants give a cook this much of themselves.

    Cultivars

    Garden nasturtiums come in two shapes, and choosing between them matters more than the flower colour. Climbing and trailing types send out stems 6 feet (about 2 m) or more, scrambling over the ground, spilling from baskets, or twining up netting and fences by their leaf stalks. Dwarf or bush types stay in a mound about a foot (30 cm) tall, made for pots, edging and small beds. Both flower from midsummer until the first frost.

    'Alaska'

    A dwarf type grown as much for its leaves as its flowers: each round leaf is marbled and splashed with cream. The flowers come in a mix of cherry, crimson, orange, salmon and yellow above the patterned leaves.

    'Empress of India'

    An old variety, and still a favourite. It makes a compact, cascading mound of deep blue-green leaves with brilliant crimson-red flowers. Cooks rate it among the best-flavoured nasturtiums, which is why it turns up in kitchen gardens as often as in flower beds.

    'Jewel' series

    Bushy dwarf plants with semi-double flowers — an extra layer of petals — in red, cherry-pink, yellow and orange shades. A tidy plant for containers and the front of a border.

    'Whirlybird' series

    Its flowers face upward and sit on top of the leaves instead of hiding under them, in cherry-rose, cream, gold, mahogany, scarlet and tangerine. If a nasturtium's blooms usually vanish beneath its own foliage, this is the one bred to fix that.

    'Glorious Gleam'

    A climbing mix with large, often fragrant, single and semi-double flowers in yellow, gold-orange and scarlet. This is the trailing kind that covered Monet's path: plant it where it is allowed to run.

    • Nasturtium comes from the high country of the Andes, from Bolivia to Colombia, where it grows on mountain slopes, often near streams. The peoples of the Andes grew it long before Europeans arrived — the Inca used it as a salad vegetable and as a herb.
    • Spanish travellers carried it from Peru to Europe in the 1500s, as a vegetable first and a flower second. The big garden species was recorded in Europe by the late 1600s, and the nasturtium in gardens today is mostly a hybrid — a cross of Tropaeolum majus with two smaller relatives, T. minus and T. peltophorum, bred over centuries into the climbers and dwarfs we grow now.
    • Its everyday name is borrowed. The plant is no relation of watercress, but its leaves hold a peppery oil much like watercress oil, and taste like it — so it took watercress's old Latin name, Nasturtium, which itself comes from nasus tortus, "twisted nose," for the face the sharp taste makes you pull. Its other old name, Indian cress, says the same thing twice: a cress from the "Indies," as Europeans then called the Americas.
    • The scientific name is a battlefield picture. When Linnaeus named the genus Tropaeolum in 1753, he was thinking of the Roman custom of raising a trophy pole — a tropaion — after a victory and hanging the beaten enemy's shields and helmets on it. The plant's round leaves were the shields; its flowers, the helmets. The word "trophy" comes from the same root.
    • A story the Linnaeus family told belongs here too: his daughter Elisabeth Christina said she had seen the flowers give off tiny sparks at dusk, like static. Nobody has repeated the sighting since, but the story travelled with the plant through two centuries of gardening books.
    • Sailors and settlers valued the leaves against scurvy, the disease of long voyages without fresh food — and for once the old use and the chemistry agree, because the leaves are rich in vitamin C, the very thing scurvy is a shortage of.
    • In France the plant found its most famous garden. At Giverny, Claude Monet planted nasturtiums along the central alley of his flower garden, the Clos Normand, and let them have their way: by the end of every summer they spilled out of the beds and spread across the path itself, until the walk to the house ran through a carpet of orange and green. The garden is still kept that way today, and the path of nasturtiums is the one in his paintings of the garden.
    • Peru and the Andes — the homeland. Leaves and flowers went into salads there long before the plant had a European name, and the plant still grows half-wild on Andean slopes and stream banks.
    • France — Monet's Giverny made the trailing nasturtium a painter's plant, and French cooks took the flowers into the kitchen: whole blooms in salads and mesclun, where their colour and pepper do the work of both garnish and seasoning.
    • Britain — the pickled pods. Unripe nasturtium seed pods, gathered while they are still green and soft, are pickled in vinegar and used exactly like capers — in sauces, salads and with fish. They were the poor man's capers: the garden answer when the real thing, imported from the Mediterranean, was dear or could not be had, and they were pickled most heavily in wartime, when capers stopped arriving at all.
    • Germany — Kapuzinerkresse, "Capuchin cress," named for the flower's hood, shaped like a monk's cowl. A standard of the cottage garden, eaten in salads and used in the German herbal tradition.
    • Wherever it has escaped — nasturtium seeds itself so willingly that it has gone wild far from gardens: along the California coast, in Australia and New Zealand and around the Mediterranean, it now grows on banks and waste ground as if it had always been there.
    • The leaves are rich in vitamin C — properly rich. In a careful measurement published in Nature in 1944, fresh nasturtium leaves held between 200 and 465 mg of vitamin C in every 100 g, and even the stalks held 100 to 160 mg. Amounts vary from plant to plant and season to season, and later measurements have often come in lower, but by any measure this is one of the strongest vitamin C leaves in the garden — the reason it was trusted against scurvy. A salad handful is only a few grams of leaf, so think of it as a strong contribution, not a day's supply in a garnish.
    • The peppery bite is a mustard oil. When the leaf is chewed or crushed, a stored compound called glucotropaeolin is broken down into benzyl isothiocyanate — a substance in the same family as the heat in mustard, horseradish and watercress. In laboratory tests this oil kills a range of bacteria, which is why nasturtium had a real place in European herbal medicine for infections of the urinary tract and the chest. Lab studies
    • What the human evidence supports is smaller. In one small trial in 2024, 30 healthy women took nasturtium for 14 days; a mild antibacterial effect showed in the urine, and a natural defence protein rose. That is a hint, not a treatment: there is no good evidence that eating nasturtium cures an infection, a cold, or anything else, and the salad leaf is food, not a measured dose of the oil. Human · small
    • The flowers carry the same peppery oil in milder form, and some vitamin C of their own — they are eaten for colour and taste, and that is honestly most of their value.
    • When to plant: Sow where it is to grow, after the last frost
    • Sun: Full sun for the most flowers; it will grow in part shade but bloom less
    • Soil: Well drained and poor — rich soil and fertiliser make leaves, not flowers
    • Environment: Frost kills it; flowers within about two months of sowing, until the first frost
    • Planter or ground: Ground, baskets or pots; trailing types climb by their leaf stalks on slim supports
    • Spacing and depth: About half an inch (1–2 cm) deep, about 12 inches (30 cm) apart
    • Water: Tolerates dry spells once settled, though steady water keeps it flowering strongly
    • When to pick: Pick flowers and leaves often — picking is pruning; pick pods for pickling while young, green and still soft

    Garden notes

    • Nasturtium is a tender perennial — it lives for years where winters are warm — but frost kills it, so in most gardens it is grown as an annual, sown fresh each spring. It flowers fast, often within about two months of sowing, and keeps going until the first frost cuts it down.
    • Sow it where it is to grow, after the last frost: the seeds are large — pea-sized, wrinkled — and easy to handle, which makes this one of the best plants for a child's first sowing. Push each seed about half an inch (1–2 cm) into the soil, keep it watered until it sprouts, and space plants about 12 inches (30 cm) apart — further for the trailing types, which need room to run.
    • Sun and soil: full sun for the most flowers; it will grow in part shade but bloom less. The soil should be well drained and — this is the plant's one famous rule — poor. Rich soil and fertiliser make leaves, not flowers: a well-fed nasturtium is a handsome green mound with hardly a bloom on it. Average-to-lean ground, no feeding, is what it wants. It tolerates dry spells once settled, though steady water keeps it flowering strongly.
    • The trailing types have no tendrils. They climb by curling their leaf stalks around anything slim — netting, wire, thin canes — and they will not grip a thick post or a flat wall. Or skip the support and let them do the other job: a trailing nasturtium makes fast, dense ground cover that smothers weeds under its leaves.
    • The aphid bargain: nasturtium's mustard oils make it a magnet for aphids, above all the black bean aphid, which will often settle on nasturtiums in crowds while leaving nearby beans and brassicas nearly alone. Gardeners plant it on purpose as a trap crop — a sacrifice that draws the pest to itself. The attraction is real, and extension services recommend the plant for it, but it is a tool, not a shield. It works by drawing aphids in, not by repelling anything; check the plants, pull and destroy stems that are black with aphids, or leave them and let the ladybirds and hoverflies — whose young live on aphids — find the feast. The same mustard oils also draw cabbage white butterflies to lay their eggs, so a nasturtium beside the cabbages needs watching from both sides.
    • Picking is pruning: the more flowers and leaves you pick for the kitchen, the more the plant makes. Pick pods for pickling while they are young, green and still soft — once they harden and turn, they are seed for next year instead. And it will sow that seed itself: nasturtium self-seeds freely, and a plant allowed to drop seed usually returns uninvited — and mostly welcome — the next spring.

    Propagation

    Sow seed where it is to grow, after the last frost: the seeds are large — pea-sized, wrinkled — and easy to handle. Pick pods for pickling while they are young, green and still soft — once they harden and turn, they are seed for next year instead. It will sow that seed itself: a plant allowed to drop seed usually returns uninvited — and mostly welcome — the next spring. Frost kills it, so sow fresh each spring.

    Safety

    • Nasturtium as food — leaves, flowers and pickled pods in normal amounts — is safe for most people. A lot at one sitting can be hot and harsh on the stomach, as mustard would be. Concentrated extracts and supplements are a different thing from the salad plant and are not covered by the food's record; anyone pregnant or on regular medicine should treat those with the usual care and ask their clinician.

    Sources

    • Sutherland et al. (1944) — vitamin C measured in nasturtium leaves and stalks, published in Nature
    • Pfäffle et al. (2024) — a small human trial of nasturtium and its mustard oil, published in Nutrients
    • Vrca et al. (2022) — the seed oil of nasturtium and its activity in laboratory tests
    • University of Wisconsin Extension (2026) — Nasturtium, Tropaeolum species: growing, care and varieties
    • Fondation Monet (2026) — Monet's gardens at Giverny: the central alley and its nasturtiums

    Chives

    Allium schoenoprasum

    Culinary

    Vitamin CVitamin A

    Fresh

    The smallest and mildest of the onion family — a clump of hollow green tubes with a gentle onion taste, snipped over eggs, potatoes and soft cheese. Chives are a true perennial: the clump dies back in winter, returns in spring, and can be cut again and again through the season. In late spring it flowers, and the whole clump crowns itself with round purple pom-poms that are edible too, and that bees work constantly. It is one of the oldest alliums in human use, and the only one native to both the Old World and the New.

    Cultivars

    Chive varieties differ in the thickness of the tube, the height of the clump and the strength of the flavour — fine tubes for garnish, coarse tubes for cooking by the handful. No variety photos are used: the forms are told apart by leaf and flower, because unlabelled photographs cannot honestly separate them.

    Common chives

    The species itself, and what nearly every garden grows: medium hollow tubes, mild sweet onion flavour, purple pom-pom flowers in late spring. Sold simply as "chives," it is the standard the named forms are measured against.

    'Purly'

    A selected garden form with medium, straight leaves held more upright than the common run of chives, and a mild, sweet onion flavour. It is sold by seed houses as an improvement for the kitchen garden: a tidier clump that stands up to cutting.

    'Staro'

    The large-leaved standard: coarser, broader tubes than common chives, bred for yield — the form to grow when chives are wanted by the handful for cooking rather than by the snip for garnish. 'Purly' was selected against it, and the two are often listed side by side.

    'Grolau'

    A Swiss-bred form with coarse, broad, dark green leaves, noted for standing drought better and yellowing less than other forms — a working chive for dry gardens.

    'Forescate'

    A bigger plant all round: 18–20 inches tall, with larger, brighter flowers than the species — grown as much for the flower display as for the leaf.

    The Siberian or giant form

    A larger, blue-green, more robust chive with bigger leaves and, to many tastes, a richer flavour. It travels under two names and an honest disagreement: some botanists make it a variety of common chives (A. schoenoprasum var. sibiricum — the name also given to the wild North American plants), and some give it its own species name, Allium ledebourianum. 'Pink Giant', with leaves about twice the size of the species and large clear pink flowers, is sold under the Siberian name. Whichever name is used, it is grown and eaten exactly like common chives, only bigger.

    Garlic chives (Allium tuberosum) — a different species, kept apart. This is the plant also sold as Chinese chives or nira. Everything about it differs once you look: the leaves are flat straps, not hollow tubes; the flavour is mild garlic, not onion; the flowers are white stars that open in late summer and autumn, not spring pom-poms; and it comes from eastern Asia, where it is a vegetable in its own right — stirred into dumpling fillings with egg, shrimp and pork in China, and used across East Asian cooking. It is a good plant in its own right; it is not a variety of chives, and its kitchen and its stories belong to itself. One gardener's warning travels with it: it seeds itself freely, so its flower heads are cut before they ripen unless more plants are wanted.

    • Chives grow wild across the whole northern world — Europe, Asia and North America — in meadows, on riverbanks and in rocky ground. It is the only member of the onion family native to both sides of the Atlantic, which makes its first home a genuinely open question: a plant that was already everywhere cannot be handed to one country. People have gathered and eaten it for thousands of years — use is often put at about 5,000 years — and it was grown in European gardens by the Middle Ages. Claims that it was first cultivated in China, and that Marco Polo carried it west from there, are told often; they are stories repeated from book to book, not records.
    • The name is a description. Schoenoprasum is Greek: schoinos, a rush, and prason, a leek — the rush-leek, for its hollow, rush-like leaves. In the Middle Ages the English called it exactly that: rush leek. The word chives comes through French cive from cepa, the Latin for onion. Linnaeus gave the plant its formal name in 1753.
    • Rome knew it well. The poet Martial, writing around 80 CE, joked about its effect on the breath — whoever has eaten chives, he said, should give kisses with the mouth closed. Pliny recorded that the emperor Nero ate chives preserved in oil on set days each month for the sake of his voice. Roman medicine used the plant too: it was believed to relieve the pain of sunburn and a sore throat, to work as a diuretic — a thing that makes the body pass more water — and to raise the blood pressure. Those are Roman beliefs, not tested findings.
    • Its later European life was quiet and domestic. Chives settled into cottage gardens and stayed there — a plant of the kitchen door, cut fresh because it keeps badly. The Swedish botanist Anders Jahan Retzius, in his Attempt at a Flora of 1806, described chives with pancakes, soups, fish and sandwiches, in the sauce served with the herring at midsummer, and farmers planting chives between the rocks of their flowerbed borders to keep the beds free of pests. Bunches of dried chives were hung about houses in the belief that they warded off sickness and ill luck, and Romani people are recorded using chives in fortune telling.
    • In the 19th century, Dutch farmers fed chives to their cattle on purpose, so the milk would take a different taste — an early, deliberate piece of flavour-making, and the Dutch dairy tradition attached to this plant. Dutch settlers are said to have carried the practice to America, planting chives in pastures so the milk for cheese came already scented.
    • Colonists brought chive seed to North America, where the plant joined a wild relative already growing there — the North American plants are sometimes separated as the Siberian variety (see Cultivars), though botanists dispute the split.
    • France — chives are one of the four fines herbes, the classic fresh-herb mixture with tarragon, chervil and parsley, folded through omelettes and soft cheeses at the last moment. Heat dulls chives fast, so French cooking adds them at the end or not cooked at all.
    • Sweden — chives belong to midsummer: snipped into the sour-cream sauce (gräddfil) served with the pickled herring of the midsummer table, and over new potatoes — a use Retzius was already describing in 1806.
    • Germany and Poland — chives are served stirred into quark, the fresh soft cheese, and spread on bread — a standing combination in both countries.
    • Britain and America — the baked potato's partner: chives snipped into sour cream, and into egg salads, potato salads and devilled eggs.
    • The flower border, everywhere — chives are planted as ornament as much as herb: edging paths and rose beds, where the purple pom-poms earn their place. Retzius's farmers planted them in the rocks of their borders against pests; gardeners still plant them beside roses, on the same reasoning.

    Craft

    • Chive flowers steeped in white wine vinegar turn it pink and lightly onion-scented — a small, pretty piece of kitchen craft. The dried flower heads are cut for winter bouquets.
    • Raw chives, per 100 g: 30 kcal, protein 3.27 g, carbohydrate 4.35 g, fibre 2.5 g. The standout is vitamin K at 212.7 µg — about one and three-quarter times the whole day's value in that 100 g — with vitamin C at 58.1 mg (about two-thirds of the day's value), vitamin A at 218 µg (about a quarter), folate at about a quarter of the day's value, and useful amounts of calcium, magnesium, manganese and potassium besides. Now the honest scale: chives are eaten by the tablespoon, not by the cup. A tablespoon of chopped chives is about 3 g — a few percent of those figures. A cook who snips chives over everything, every day, eats a genuinely useful amount of them over a week; a single garnish is flavour, not a supplement.
    • Vitamin K is the vitamin the body uses to clot blood normally and to build bone. Chives' high figure comes with the standard note: people who take warfarin or a similar blood thinner are told to keep their vitamin K intake steady, because sudden changes work against the medicine. At garnish amounts there is little to steady; anyone who starts eating chives by the cupful daily — in salads and sauces, say — is making the kind of change worth mentioning to the clinician who manages the dose.
    • What has actually been studied in chives themselves is laboratory work. In a 2017 comparison of the six most eaten onion-family vegetables, chive extracts showed the strongest antioxidant activity of the six in the test tube — antioxidant activity being the laboratory measure of how well a substance slows the chemical damage called oxidation — and some ability to slow blood platelets clumping in vitro, though garlic and shallot were far stronger at that. Other laboratory studies since have found the same kind of antioxidant and bacteria-slowing activity in chive extracts. These are dish results. No trial has tested eating chives for any condition in people, and there is no human evidence that chives lower blood pressure, thin the blood, or treat anything else. Lab studies
    • That fence matters because chives sit in a famous family. Garlic and onions have real human research behind some of their claims; chives are not garlic, their sulfur compounds — the family chemicals behind the onion smell and much of the research — are present in smaller amounts, and the family's evidence does not carry over to chives. The Roman uses, and the diuretic and blood-pressure beliefs that travelled with them, are history, not tested findings.
    • There is no evidence in people that chives detox the body, fight cancer, or strengthen the immune system beyond the vitamin C figure given above.
    • When to plant: Sow seed indoors a few weeks before the last frost, or outside once the soil is warm
    • Sun: Full sun gives the strongest growth and the most flowers; light shade is tolerated, with fewer flowers
    • Soil: Rich, moist but well-drained soil; once settled, tolerates drought, though it grows best with steady moisture
    • Environment: Hardy perennial, surviving winter in zones 3–9; dies back in winter in cold climates and is among the first green things to return in spring
    • Planter or ground: Ground or pots — a clump in a pot on a sunny step or windowsill cuts all season
    • Spacing and depth: Space clumps 12–20 inches apart
    • Water: Grows best with steady moisture; tolerates drought once settled
    • When to pick: Snip leaves from the outside of the clump all season, or shear the whole clump down and let it regrow; leaves are best fresh

    Garden notes

    • Chives are a hardy perennial — among the hardiest herbs, surviving winter in zones 3–9 — forming a dense clump of slender bulbs, each bulb sending up hollow, tube-like leaves 8–20 inches long. The plant stands about 10–20 inches tall. It dies back in winter in cold climates and is among the first green things to return in spring.
    • Sun and soil: full sun gives the strongest growth and the most flowers; light shade is tolerated, with fewer flowers. It likes rich, moist but well-drained soil and, once settled, tolerates drought — though it grows best with steady moisture. It asks little feeding; rich feeding is not needed.
    • Starting: chives grow easily from seed — started indoors a few weeks before the last frost, or sown outside once the soil is warm — but seed is slow to make a cutting-size clump, and the quick start is a division: a piece of someone else's clump, planted out, settles fast. Space clumps 12–20 inches apart.
    • Division is the plant's housekeeping. The bulbs multiply quickly and the clump crowds itself; lift and divide it every 2–3 years to keep it vigorous, in spring or autumn, making sure each piece carries at least a few bulblets with roots. Divided pieces are also the free way to spread chives along a whole border.
    • Cutting is the harvest and the care in one. Snip leaves from the outside of the clump, or shear the whole clump down and let it regrow — the plant answers cutting with fresh tubes all season. Leaves are best fresh; they keep badly, though they freeze acceptably, and they lose most of themselves dried.
    • Flowers: in late spring the clump sends up stiff stalks topped with the purple pom-poms — dense balls of 10–30 small star-shaped flowers, opening from papery buds. They are edible, mild and pretty scattered over salads, and bees work them constantly. The one decision they ask: let them stand for the bees and the look of the thing, or cut them before they set seed — a chive clump allowed to seed will scatter seedlings about the bed. Gardeners who cook from the plant often cut the flower stalks out to keep the leaves coming; gardeners who plant for the border leave them. Cutting the whole clump back after flowering brings a second flush of fresh leaves.
    • Trouble: very little. Chives have no significant insect or disease problems in most gardens, and deer and rabbits leave them alone — the onion smell that flavours our food defends the plant. Keep grass from invading the clump; the plant is shallow-rooted, so mulch rather than hoe close.
    • In a pot: chives are one of the easiest pot herbs — a clump in a pot on a sunny step or windowsill cuts all season, and a pot can be brought under cover in autumn to stretch the leaf season into winter. A potted clump needs the same division every few years, or it crowds itself out of its own pot.

    Propagation

    Lift and divide the clump every 2–3 years, in spring or autumn, making sure each piece carries at least a few bulblets with roots. Divided pieces are also the free way to spread chives along a whole border. Chives grow easily from seed too — started indoors a few weeks before the last frost, or sown outside once the soil is warm — but seed is slow to make a cutting-size clump, and the quick start is a division.

    Safety

    • Vitamin K is the vitamin the body uses to clot blood normally and to build bone. Chives carry a great deal of it — 212.7 µg per 100 g, about one and three-quarter times the whole day's value. People who take warfarin or a similar blood thinner are told to keep their vitamin K intake steady, because sudden changes work against the medicine. At garnish amounts there is little to steady; anyone who starts eating chives by the cupful daily — in salads and sauces, say — is making the kind of change worth mentioning to the clinician who manages the dose.

    Sources

    • Martial (c. 80 CE) — Epigrams — chives on the breath, and the closed-mouth kiss
    • Retzius (1806) — Attempt at a Flora (Försök til en flora) — Swedish table uses, and chives planted in the borders against pests
