    • Beretta et al. (2017) — six onion-family vegetables compared in the laboratory: chives' antioxidant and platelet activity, in vitro

    Leek

    Allium ampeloprasum

    Culinary

    Vitamin KVitamin A

    FreshCooked

    The mild giant of the onion family. A leek makes no bulb: what you eat is a tight bundle of leaf bases wrapped around each other into a thick white shaft — botanists call it a pseudostem, a "false stem" made of leaves — topped by a fan of flat blue-green leaves. Its flavour is onion softened and sweetened, and it melts into soups like no other allium. It is a hardy, slow, patient crop, in the ground for most of a year, and it carries more history than any other soup vegetable: an emperor ate it for his singing voice, and a whole nation wears it as an emblem. The leek is one crop from a species with several faces — the same species, Allium ampeloprasum, also gives elephant garlic, grown for its huge mild cloves, and kurrat, the Egyptian leek grown for its green leaves. They are one plant, bred three ways.

    Cultivars

    Leeks come in two working kinds. Summer leeks are sown early and grow long, thinner, paler shafts for late-summer and autumn eating, and they are the less hardy kind. Winter leeks are thick-shafted, blue-green and iron-hardy, bred to stand in frozen ground and be dug from autumn through spring.

    'Musselburgh' (also 'Giant Musselburgh', 'Scotch Flag')

    The great Scottish heirloom, named for the town of Musselburgh near Edinburgh and grown since the 1800s. Very thick white shafts, broad blue-green leaves, and hardiness above everything: this is the winter leek that stands through hard frosts and is still the standard against which hardy leeks are measured.

    'American Flag' (also 'Large American Flag', 'Broad London')

    The American standard since the late 1800s: thick white shanks, blue-green leaves, a long season of 120–150 days, adaptable across climates. Extension services still list it among their recommended varieties more than a century on.

    'King Richard'

    The early one: a summer leek ready in about 75–80 days, with an unusually long, slender, elegant white shaft and mild flavour, needing less earthing-up than most. It is the leek for cooks who want the long white look early — and the one to lift before hard winter, since it is not built for frost like the winter kinds.

    'Lancelot'

    A modern hybrid grown for a long, clean, uniform white shaft and upright leaves; the kind of leek much commercial and garden seed now aims at, sold for reliability rather than romance.

    Pot leeks and the show bench

    A British tradition of its own. In the North East of England, growing leeks for show became a working men's art: the working men's clubs of the mining towns kept their own leek clubs — Northumberland's archives hold one club's records back to the 1920s — and growers fed their plants on secret "special brews," the recipes guarded and passed from father to son. Pot leeks, grown in pots for thickness, are judged by volume; blanched leeks by their white length. Ashington held a World Championship Leek and Onion competition for years, the last in 2008, and the heaviest leeks ever weighed have passed 9 kg — over 20 lb — for a single plant: a leek the size of a small child, grown for pride, not for soup.

    The kinds are told apart by season, shaft and leaf colour, because unlabelled photographs cannot honestly separate them.

    • The wild plant grows around the Mediterranean and east into western Asia, on dry and rocky ground. Its name is a small map of where it lived: ampeloprasum is Greek, ampelos, a vine, and prason, a leek — the vineyard leek, the leek that grew between the vines. People in Mesopotamia and Egypt were growing it thousands of years ago; it stands among the oldest vegetables in cultivation anywhere.
    • Egypt held it in high esteem. Pliny, the Roman writer, says flatly that the most esteemed leeks were Egypt's, ahead of Rome's own. And the leek is one of the foods named in the Bible's wilderness story: in the Book of Numbers, the Israelites, tired of manna, look back on Egypt and remember "the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick" — ordinary Nile-side food, remembered with longing.
    • Greece wondered about the leek and the voice. A work handed down under Aristotle's name asks why leeks contribute to the loudness of the voice, noting that partridges — loud birds — eat a lot of them. Whether or not the reasoning convinces, the belief that leeks strengthen the voice was alive in Greece centuries before Rome tested it at the highest level.
    • Rome's test was the emperor Nero. Pliny records it in his Natural History: Nero, "to improve his voice, used to eat leeks and oil every month, upon stated days, abstaining from every other kind of food, and not touching so much as a morsel of bread even." The habit stuck to his name — later tradition calls him Porrophagus, the leek-eater. No study has ever tested leeks on a singing voice.
    • Wales took the leek for its own, and the story of how is a tradition Wales tells about itself, not a dated fact. The tale says that before a battle against the Saxons, Welsh soldiers were told to pull leeks and wear them in their helmets, so each man could tell friend from foe. One telling gives the advice to Saint David, the 6th-century monk who became Wales's patron saint; another gives the order to Cadwaladr, king of Gwynedd in the 600s. No writing from the time records it, and the two tellings cannot both be true as told — David died around 589, before Cadwaladr's reign began — so the story is a tradition Wales tells about itself, not a dated fact. A second story sets the emblem at the Battle of Crécy in 1346, where Welsh archers fought, it is said, in a field of leeks. What is documented is the wearing itself, and it is old: by the Tudor period the royal household guard wore leeks on Saint David's Day, and in Shakespeare's Henry V (1599) the Welsh captain Fluellen wears his leek in his cap and the king answers, "I wear it for a memorable honour; for I am Welsh, you know, good countryman." The leek is still worn across Wales every 1 March, Saint David's Day — the daffodil, its companion emblem, is a newcomer of the 1800s beside it.
    • Through all of this the leek stayed what it began as: a working vegetable of cool northern gardens, grown from Britain to Scandinavia precisely because it stands in the ground through winter when little else does.
    • Wales — the emblem is eaten as well as worn. Cawl, the Welsh broth of meat and vegetables, is built on leeks, and leeks go into Welsh cooking wherever a gentle onion is wanted — including the leek-filled pastries and the St David's Day table, where the emblem is dinner.
    • Scotland — cock-a-leekie, called Scotland's national soup: a clear broth of chicken and leeks, thickened if at all with rice or barley, and — the part that surprises everyone — traditionally finished with prunes, whose soft sweetness against the savoury broth is the dish's signature. It is old: a chicken-and-leek soup reached Scotland from France by the late 1500s, with leeks standing in for onions, and the name itself is first recorded in the Orchtertyre House accounts of 1737, "cockie leekie fowlls in it." It is still a traditional course at Burns Suppers.
    • France, by way of New York — leek and potato soup is an old French home dish, eaten hot. Its famous cold form, vichyssoise, is an American creation: Louis Diat, the French-born chef of the Ritz-Carlton in New York, took the leek-and-potato soup his mother used to make, enriched it with cream, served it chilled, and named it for Vichy, the spa town near his home. He told the story himself in Gourmet in 1951; the year usually given for the invention is 1917, when it was served at the opening of the hotel's roof garden. The garnish, traditionally, is chopped chives — one entry in this library sprinkled over another.
    • Egypt — the living link to the ancient world: kurrat, the leaf-form of this same species, is still grown and eaten in Egypt as it has been for centuries, the green leaves eaten fresh alongside fava-bean dishes. The leeks the Israelites remembered are, in this form, still on Egyptian tables.
    • Greece and Turkey — around the eastern Mediterranean the leek is a vegetable in its own right, not a seasoning: Greek prasopita, a leek pie in filo, and prasorizo, leeks cooked with rice; Turkish zeytinyağlı pırasa, leeks braised in olive oil with carrots and a little rice, eaten warm or cool.
    • Raw leeks — the bulb and lower leaf, which is how the standard figures are measured — per 100 g: 61 kcal, protein 1.5 g, carbohydrate 14.15 g, fibre 1.8 g, fat 0.3 g. The standouts are vitamin K at 47 µg, about 39% of the day's value, and folate at 64 µg, about 16%, with vitamin B6 at about 14%, manganese at about a fifth of the day's value, iron at 2.1 mg, and vitamin C at 12 mg besides. The green tops, which the standard record does not cover, are the richer part for some of this: the vitamin A (83 µg in the measured part) and the eye pigments lutein and zeaxanthin — about 1,900 µg per 100 g — live mostly in the green leaf. Eat the greens, not just the white.
    • Vitamin K is the vitamin the body uses to clot blood normally and to build bone. The standard note applies, in proportion: people who take warfarin or a similar blood thinner are told to keep their vitamin K intake steady, because sudden changes work against the medicine. Leeks at soup amounts are an ordinary part of a steady diet; nobody needs to fear them, and nobody should suddenly start eating them by the kilo either.
    • Leeks are a notably rich source of kaempferol, a flavonoid — one of the large family of plant compounds studied for how they interact with the body's chemistry. Kaempferol's interesting effects are laboratory and animal findings, and the human research behind flavonoid-rich diets is population research — people who eat more vegetables of many kinds fare better, which is not the same as a trial of leeks. No clinical trial has tested eating leeks for any condition in people, and leeks are not a cure for any condition. Lab studies
    • The same limit covers the family's fame. Leeks carry sulfur compounds of the onion kind, allicin among them, but in smaller measure than garlic, and garlic's and onion's research — such as it is — belongs to garlic and onions. None of it is evidence about leeks. Population studies that link allium vegetables as a group with lower rates of some cancers are studies of the whole family's eating habits, mostly garlic and onion; they are not evidence about leeks.
    • One part of the leek's chemistry cuts both ways. Leeks are rich in fructans — fermentable fibres that feed the bacteria of the gut, which is a normal and useful part of eating vegetables. Those same fructans are what some sensitive stomachs react to with gas and discomfort; the white shaft carries more of them than the green tops, so a stomach that objects to the white part often accepts the greens.
    • Leeks do not detox the body, protect the heart, or prevent cancer: the evidence for leeks themselves does not carry those claims. Nero's voice cure is Pliny's story, not a claim about leeks.
    • When to plant: Sow indoors in late winter, 8–12 weeks before the last frost; plant out in spring when seedlings are about pencil-thick
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Rich, fertile, well-drained soil that holds moisture; plenty of compost worked in before planting
    • Environment: A hardy, cool-season crop of cool northern gardens; hardy kinds stand in the ground through winter
    • Planter or ground: Ground, or deep containers of rich compost
    • Spacing and depth: About 15 cm (6 inches) between plants in rows about 30 cm apart; seedlings set into holes about 15 cm (6 inches) deep
    • Water: Steady water; roots are shallow, so steady water matters more than deep water
    • When to pick: When the shaft is about 2.5 cm (1 inch) thick or better; hardy kinds are dug as needed from autumn to spring

    Garden notes

    • The leek is a biennial — a two-year plant — grown as an annual. Left to itself into a second year it sends up a tall stalk topped with a round ball, an umbel, of many small pinkish-white flowers, which bees work and which then make seed. The crop is taken in the first year, long before that.
    • Time is the first fact: leeks are slow. From seed to a thick shaft takes the better part of a year — seed is usually sown indoors in late winter, 8–12 weeks before the last frost, in trays or modules. The seedlings look like blades of grass; if their tops flop, trimming them back to a few inches makes stockier plants. Nothing about the young plant hurries.
    • Planting out is the leek's own ritual, and it is how the white shaft is made. When the seedlings are about pencil-thick, they are set out into holes poked with a dibber — a pointed tool for making planting holes — about 15 cm (6 inches) deep, one seedling dropped into each hole so only the green tips show, and watered in. The hole is not filled with soil by hand; the watering and the rain wash it in gradually. Spacing runs about 15 cm between plants in rows about 30 cm apart. Buried in the dark, the shaft grows white: that is blanching — keeping light off a stem so it stays pale and tender — done by the hole itself.
    • Earthing up lengthens the white. As the plants grow, soil is drawn up around the shafts a few centimetres at a time, two or three times through the season, always stopping below the point where the leaves fan out — soil pushed higher washes down between the leaves, which is the grit problem below. A trench works the same way: seedlings set in a shallow trench, filled in as they grow.
    • Soil, water and feeding: leeks want rich, fertile, well-drained soil that holds moisture, in full sun, and they are hungry plants — plenty of compost worked in before planting, and nitrogen through the season, is what makes thick shafts. Their roots are shallow, so steady water matters more than deep water; they grow slowly and compete badly with weeds when young, so the bed is kept clean and mulched.
    • The grit, and the washing: a leek is a bundle of leaves, and soil and sand lodge between the layers as it grows, especially in earthed-up plants. There is no shortcut — the leek is cut lengthways, or sliced into rings, and rinsed under running water, fanning the layers so the grit washes out. Every cook who has crunched sand in a leek soup learns it once.
    • Harvest: a leek is ready when its shaft is about 2.5 cm (1 inch) thick or better. It is not pulled — the roots hold fast — but loosened with a fork and lifted. And then the leek's great virtue: it waits. Hardy kinds stand in the ground through winter, losing little, and are dug as needed from autumn to spring; in hard country a thick mulch of straw keeps the ground diggable. Few vegetables store themselves so obligingly in the soil.
    • Trouble: the honest list is short. Leek rust, an orange-spotted fungus, freckles the leaves in damp seasons — it spoils looks more than shafts, and spacing for airflow and rotating alliums to fresh ground each year are the defences. In some regions the leek moth and the allium leaf miner tunnel the leaves; netting the crop where they are known is the standard answer. Deer and rabbits mostly leave alliums alone.
    • In a pot: leeks can be grown in deep containers of rich compost, watered steadily — a modest shaft rather than a show one, but the flavour is the same, and a pot by the kitchen door cuts fresh all winter in mild climates.

    Propagation

    Sow seed indoors in late winter, 8–12 weeks before the last frost, in trays or modules, and plant the seedlings out when they are about pencil-thick. Left to itself into a second year, a leek sends up a tall stalk topped with a round ball, an umbel, of many small pinkish-white flowers, which bees work and which then make seed — but the crop is taken in the first year, long before that.

    Safety

    • Vitamin K is the vitamin the body uses to clot blood normally and to build bone. People who take warfarin or a similar blood thinner are told to keep their vitamin K intake steady, because sudden changes work against the medicine. Leeks at soup amounts are an ordinary part of a steady diet; nobody needs to fear them, and nobody should suddenly start eating them by the kilo either.
    • Leeks are rich in fructans — fermentable fibres that feed the bacteria of the gut, which is a normal and useful part of eating vegetables. Those same fructans are what some sensitive stomachs react to with gas and discomfort; the white shaft carries more of them than the green tops, so a stomach that objects to the white part often accepts the greens.

    Sources
