    Borage

    Borago officinalis

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Movement and SupportVitamin AVitamin C

    FreshCooked

    A bristly Mediterranean herb grown for two things that sound like unlikely partners: leaves that taste of cucumber, and flowers shaped like small blue stars. The young leaves go into salads, sauces and ravioli; the flowers garnish summer drinks — most famously a Pimm's cup — and are frozen into ice cubes. And the seeds give an oil that is the richest common source of a fatty acid called GLA. Borage sits in the borage family, Boraginaceae, beside its cousin Comfrey, which has its own entry in this library.

    Cultivars

    Borage is barely a bred plant. Seed catalogues mostly sell the species itself — there is no list of cultivars to give. What a gardener actually chooses between is the flower colour.

    Common blue borage

    The plant itself: true-blue, star-shaped flowers with a black cone of stamens at the centre. The buds open pink and the flowers turn blue as they open, so a plant in full swing carries both colours at once.

    'Alba' (white borage)

    A white-flowered form of the same plant, identical in leaf, habit and cucumber flavour. It tends to flower a little later in the season than the blue, and its stalks are said to stand a little sturdier. Gardeners grow it for the contrast — white stars over the same rough grey-green leaves.

    'Variegata'

    A form with cream-splashed leaves and the usual blue flowers, grown for its looks in herb and cottage gardens. Like most variegated plants it can throw plain green shoots, which are cut out if the pattern is to stay.

    One cousin worth a line: creeping borage (Borago pygmaea), a low, spreading perennial from Corsica and Sardinia with smaller, paler blue flowers, is sometimes grown in rock gardens. It is a different species, not a variety of this one.

    • Borage comes from the Mediterranean, where it still grows wild on dry, stony ground; some accounts point to the eastern end of that sea, around Syria, as its first home. It spread across Europe with herb gardens in the Middle Ages and has since sown itself into gardens and waste ground across the temperate world.
    • Nobody knows where its name comes from, and neither of the two old guesses is proven. One traces borago to corago, from the Latin cor, the heart, and ago, I bring — the heart-bringer. The other traces it to burra, a shaggy woollen cloth, for the plant's rough, hairy leaves. Either way, the name arrived carrying the plant's reputation with it.
    • The classical writers knew a plant they called bouglōsson in Greek and buglossos in Latin — “ox-tongue,” for the rough leaves. Dioscorides wrote that it was mixed into wine and thought to make people cheerful. Pliny wrote that put into wine it increased exhilaration, “and so it is also called euphrosynum” — the gladdener. Later herbalists identified that ox-tongue plant as borage, and the descriptions are too thin to prove them wrong or right; the identification is the standard one, held lightly. Some later writers went further and guessed that borage was the nepenthe of Homer's Odyssey, the drug that banished sorrow — a guess, and nothing more.
    • Out of that reputation came the saying the plant is still known by. The old Latin tag, quoted in Gerard's herbal of 1597, runs Ego borago, gaudia semper ago — “I, borage, always bring joy.” English turned the pun into its own version: borage for courage.
    • Tradition says Roman gladiators drank wine flavoured with borage before they fought, to steady their nerve. In the Middle Ages the story grew a farewell scene: knights leaving for the Crusades were handed stirrup cups — a last drink taken in the saddle — with borage flowers floating in them, and the women who stayed behind are said to have embroidered borage flowers on the scarves of the men going to war, a wish for courage worn into battle. These are traditions, not documented events; they show what the plant meant, which is its own kind of fact.
    • The herbals kept the theme. Gerard (1597): “The leaves and floures of Borrage put into wine make men and women glad and merry, driving away all sadnesse, dulnesse, and melancholy.” John Evelyn wrote that sprigs of borage are “of known virtue to revive the hypochondriac and cheer the hard student.” For centuries borage was the herb of gladness — a medicine for low spirits as much as for the body.
    • In ordinary medicine of the time, the leaf and flower were used in teas to bring on a sweat in fevers, as a soothing drink for coughs — the plant is full of mucilage, a slippery plant gel that coats and calms — and in poultices for swellings. Those uses are the past, not advice; what the studies actually support is narrower.
    • The modern chapter is about the seed. In the late 1900s researchers found that borage seed oil is exceptionally rich in GLA, and the plant became a field crop, grown for its seed in Britain, North America, New Zealand and elsewhere — an old herb-garden plant turned oilseed.
    • England — the Pimm's cup. A borage flower, and often a young leaf sprig, is the classic garnish of a Pimm's No. 1 cup, and was there in the older claret cups before it. The flowers are also frozen into ice cubes for summer drinks and candied for cakes — the cucumber note and the blue star doing equal work.
    • Germany — Frankfurt's Grüne Soße, the green sauce of Hesse: seven herbs, fixed by rule — parsley, chives, chervil, sorrel, cress, salad burnet and borage — chopped fine into sour cream and served with hard-boiled eggs and potatoes. The season traditionally opens on Maundy Thursday, and the sauce is protected: to carry the Frankfurt name, the herbs must be the seven, grown in the region.
    • Italy — in Liguria, borage is a headline green of preboggion, the gathered mix of wild and garden greens that fills pansoti, the region's triangular ravioli, served with walnut sauce. Here the leaf is not a garnish but a filling, cooked like spinach.
    • Spain — in Aragón, borraja is a vegetable in its own right, one of the few places in Europe where borage is a market crop rather than a garden extra: the leafy stems are cooked with potatoes and olive oil and eaten as a dish, not a decoration.
    • Iran — a name warning. The famous Persian “borage tea,” gol gavzaban, is usually made from a cousin, Echium amoenum, not from this plant. Same common name, different species — the Latin name is the one that counts.
    • The leaf as food, by the numbers: raw borage leaf, per 100 g, gives 21 kcal, vitamin C 35 mg, vitamin A 210 µg, calcium 93 mg, iron 3.3 mg and potassium 470 mg. That is a respectable leaf. The honest serving note: nobody eats 100 g of borage leaves at a sitting — a handful in a salad or a sauce is the real amount — so the numbers describe the leaf, not a serving.
    • The seed is where the measured interest is. The seeds are about a third oil, and that oil is roughly 20–25% GLA — gamma-linolenic acid, an omega-6 fat the body uses to build some of its own inflammation-calming messengers. It is the richest common plant source of GLA there is: evening primrose oil, the better-known source, carries only about 8–10%. GLA content is a fact about the oil. What taking it does for people is a separate question, and the answers below are mixed.
    • Rheumatoid arthritis — the best evidence borage has. In a placebo-controlled trial (Leventhal et al., 1993), people with rheumatoid arthritis who took 1.4 g of GLA a day in borage seed oil for 24 weeks had meaningfully fewer tender and swollen joints; the placebo group did not improve. A second trial at a higher dose (Zurier et al., 1996) pointed the same way, and when the Cochrane reviewers gathered the herbal trials for rheumatoid arthritis (Cameron et al., 2011), they rated the evidence for GLA oils — borage among them — as moderate for relieving pain and disability. Two fences belong on this: the trial doses were large, many capsules a day, nothing like a food use; and “moderate evidence of some benefit” is the ceiling, not a cure claim. Memorial Sloan Kettering's summary lands in the same place: moderate support for rheumatoid arthritis symptoms, and no good evidence for anything else. Human trials
    • Eczema — the clearest negative. Borage oil was widely sold for eczema, and it was properly tested. The Cochrane review (Bamford et al., 2013) gathered 27 studies with 1,596 people and found that borage oil and evening primrose oil taken by mouth improved eczema no more than the dummy oils they were compared against. The reviewers concluded the oils lack effect on eczema and that further studies would be hard to justify. No skin benefit is claimed for the oil. Human trials
    • Everything else — asthma, menopausal symptoms, diabetic nerve pain, premenstrual symptoms — has been promoted at one time or another and studied thinly or not at all. There is no good evidence for any of it.
    • When to plant: Sow direct in spring, where it is to grow; a second sowing in summer for a later run of flowers
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Any ordinary soil that drains; it tolerates poor, dry ground better than rich ground, where the plants grow lush and flop in the wind
    • Environment: A hardy annual, 60–90 cm (2–3 ft) tall and about as wide; flowers from early summer until the frosts
    • Planter or ground: Ground — sow where it is to grow; it makes a long taproot and sulks when moved
    • Spacing and depth: About 1 cm deep; thin or space plants to about 45 cm
    • Water: Little once settled — it tolerates poor, dry ground better than rich, wet ground
    • When to pick: Take the leaves young; pick flowers as they open. Both wilt fast — use within the hour, not to store

    Garden notes

    • A hardy annual, 60–90 cm (2–3 ft) tall and about as wide, with hollow, bristly stems and rough, hairy, grey-green leaves. It flowers from early summer until the frosts: the flower sprays uncurl as they bloom, buds opening pink and turning true blue, each flower a five-pointed star about 2 cm across with a black centre cone.
    • Sow it where it is to grow. Borage makes a long taproot and sulks when it is moved, so seed goes straight into the ground in spring, covered about a centimetre deep — the seed stirs best in the dark — with a second sowing in summer for a later run of flowers. Thin or space plants to about 45 cm; they are bigger than the seed packet suggests.
    • It self-sows freely. Each flower sets four hard, black seeds, and a plant left standing at summer's end will give you borage for years without another packet being opened. In a small garden that can be too much of a good thing: pull the seedlings you do not want while they are small, before the taproot takes hold.
    • Sun and soil: full sun is best, and any ordinary soil that drains will do — it tolerates poor, dry ground better than rich ground, where the plants grow lush and flop in the wind.
    • Bees: borage is a bee plant of the first rank, and the reason is mechanical — the flowers go on making nectar through the day and refill after a bee has emptied them, so the same plant can be worked again and again. A patch in flower hums from morning to evening, and hoverflies and other pollinators come with the bees.
    • Companions, at their real strength: gardeners plant borage near tomatoes and strawberries, and say it puts off the tomato hornworm and improves the fruit. The worm claim has no good test behind it. The real service is the bees — a plant that keeps bees busy in the vegetable garden is working for every crop there that needs pollinating.
    • Picking: take the leaves young; older leaves are coarser and more bristly, and the bristles can prickle sensitive skin, so gloves are sensible for a big harvest. Flowers are picked as they open, pinched off at the black centre cone. Both wilt fast — this is a plant to use within the hour, not to store.

    Propagation

    Sow seed direct where it is to grow, in spring — borage makes a long taproot and sulks when it is moved. It self-sows freely: each flower sets four hard, black seeds, and a plant left standing at summer's end will give you borage for years without another packet being opened. It is an annual, so each year's plants come from seed, not from a plant that lives on.

    Safety

    • The caution, plainly and in proportion. The leaf, flower and raw seed carry small amounts of pyrrolizidine alkaloids — liver-harming compounds found across this plant family. Borage's amounts are small, far below those of its cousin comfrey, and the occasional leaf in a salad or a flower on a drink is the centuries-old pattern of use. But proportion cuts both ways: borage leaf teas, juices and extracts taken daily or in quantity are a different exposure, and the standard advice is firm — do not take borage products by mouth during pregnancy or while breastfeeding; people with liver disease should avoid them; and the oil can slow blood clotting a little, so it is stopped before surgery. Borage seed oil itself, properly made, does not carry the alkaloids — but only buy oil that is certified PA-free, and treat “certified PA-free” as a requirement, not a bonus.
    • One look-alike warning: before it flowers, the hairy leaf rosette can be mistaken for foxglove, which is poisonous. Eat borage only from plants you grew yourself, or from plants you can see in flower.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: borage, raw — the leaf nutrition figures
    • Leventhal et al. (1993) — treatment of rheumatoid arthritis with gamma-linolenic acid in borage seed oil: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
    • Cameron et al. (2011) — Cochrane review: herbal therapy for treating rheumatoid arthritis — GLA oils rated as moderate evidence for symptom relief
    • Bamford et al. (2013) — Cochrane review: oral evening primrose oil and borage oil for eczema — no effect beyond placebo
    • Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (2026) — About Herbs: Borage — the evidence summary and the safety warnings, including certified PA-free oil and pregnancy
    • Touwaide & Appetiti (2024) — Herbs in History: Borage — the classical record, Dioscorides and Pliny, and the plant's documented history

    Coconut

    Cocos nucifera

    Culinary

    Digestive Health

    FreshCooked

    The tree of life, and for once the name is close to a plain description. The coconut palm is a single-trunked palm with no branches and no true wood, and nearly every part of it is used: the young nut holds a sweet, clear drink; the white flesh is food fresh, dried, or squeezed into milk and cream; the flesh gives an oil; the fibrous husk gives coir, a rope fibre that shrugs off salt water; the hard shell becomes bowls, cups and charcoal; the leaves thatch roofs and weave into mats; the trunk builds houses; the flower stalk gives a sweet sap; and even the soft heart at the crown is eaten — at the price of the tree itself. Botanically the coconut is a drupe, a stone fruit like a peach, not a true nut: skin outside, thick fibre under it, then the hard shell with its three dark "eyes," and inside that, the water and the flesh.

    Cultivars

    Every coconut in the world is the one species, Cocos nucifera — but growers divide it into two great kinds, the Talls and the Dwarfs, with bred hybrids between them. The kinds are told apart by the palm — its size, speed and trunk — as much as by the nut.

    The Talls

    The classic beach palm of every postcard: 20–30 m (65–100 ft) of leaning trunk topped with a crown of long fronds. Slow and long-lived — first nuts at six to ten years, full bearing at fifteen to twenty, and a working life of sixty years or more, sometimes a hundred. Talls are cross-pollinated, so their seedlings vary. On good soil a tall can give up to about 75 nuts a year, though fewer than 30 is commoner in neglected ground. Named talls include the Jamaica Tall (the Atlantic Tall, with its swollen trunk base and crooked trunk), the Panama Tall (the Pacific Tall) and India's West Coast Tall.

    The Dwarfs

    Smaller, earlier and shorter-lived: the trunk grows more slowly and stays slimmer, flowering begins at about three to five years, and the nuts hang within easier reach. Most dwarfs pollinate themselves, so they come true from seed — the dwarf habit itself is one of the Pacific domestication traits. A dwarf is not a houseplant-sized palm, though: given years, a "dwarf" can still reach 10–18 m (30–60 ft).

    'Malayan Dwarf'

    The best-known dwarf in the Americas, from Malaysia, in three colour forms told by the young fruit and leaf stalks: green, yellow and gold (the gold is called red in Jamaica). It flowers at about four years and was planted across Florida and the Caribbean for its reported resistance to lethal yellowing, the disease that destroyed the tall palms — though long Florida trials later found the resistance weaker than hoped: in test plots the Malayans died in large numbers too, just somewhat fewer than the talls.

    'King Coconut' (thembili)

    Sri Lanka's orange coconut, placed by Sri Lankan botanists in a group of its own between tall and dwarf. It is grown for one thing only: drinking. Its water is the sweetest of any coconut's, and the bright orange nuts are sold fresh at roadside stalls all over the island, cut open to drink on the spot. It is barely grown anywhere else.

    'Maypan'

    The bred answer to disease: a hybrid of Malayan Dwarf and Panama Tall, made in Jamaica, that grows with a tall's vigour and size while keeping much of the dwarf's early bearing and its reported disease resistance. Widely planted in Florida and the Caribbean alongside the Malayan Dwarf.

    No variety photo is used: a coconut palm in a photograph cannot be honestly assigned a variety — a Malayan Dwarf and a young tall are near-identical in a picture, and the colour forms need the grower's word. If variety pictures are wanted later, they need a named source: a research station or extension photo that states the variety. No variety is guessed from a photograph.

    • The coconut evolved in the central Indo-Pacific, and it was built to travel by sea. The thick fibrous husk is a float: a ripe nut that falls into the ocean bobs with the shell sealed inside, and in tests made in 1941 coconuts could still sprout after floating in sea water for up to about 110 days — long enough to drift thousands of kilometres between island groups. Drift alone probably did not carry it across the whole Pacific — ocean-current models say that crossing was too far — but it spread the palm along coasts and between neighbouring islands long before people, and people did the rest.
    • The DNA tells of two beginnings. A study of more than 1,300 coconuts from around the world (Gunn and colleagues, 2011) found two clearly different populations: a Pacific group and an Indo-Atlantic group. That pattern points to the coconut being taken into cultivation twice, independently — once in island Southeast Asia, and once along the southern edge of the Indian subcontinent. The clearest marks of farming — dwarf palms, self-pollination, and the round, sweet-watered fruit form the Samoan language calls niu vai — arose only in the Pacific group. The older wild form, niu kafa, is long and triangular with a much thicker husk: a fruit shaped for the sea, not for the table.
    • The great carriers were the Austronesian peoples, who first farmed the coconut in island Southeast Asia and took it with them as a canoe plant — food, drink and fibre packed in one floating package — as they settled the Pacific island by island, east to the far Polynesian islands and west to Madagascar and the Comoros. Where the two populations meet and mix, around Madagascar and the southwest Indian Ocean, is the fingerprint of that ancient sea route. Coconuts most likely reached the Pacific coast of the Americas before Columbus, carried from the Philippine side of the ocean; the Atlantic coconut came later, brought by the Portuguese to Cape Verde and on to the Caribbean and Brazil in the 1500s.
    • The name is a face. Sixteenth-century Portuguese sailors called the nut coco — "head" or "skull" — because the three dark spots on the shell make a little face, two eyes and a mouth; coco was also the name of a grinning ghost or bogey in Portuguese stories, which is what the face reminded them of. Nucifera simply means "nut-bearing." Before the Portuguese name stuck, the West knew the fruit as nux indica, the Indian nut — Marco Polo used that name for it in Sumatra in 1280.
    • In India the palm carries one of the great plant names of the world: in Sanskrit it is kalpa vriksha, "the tree of the necessities of life" — in tradition, a tree that provides everything needed. The coconut itself sits at the centre of Hindu worship and weddings, offered whole and broken open before the gods. The Malay name says the same thing in plainer words: pokok seribu guna, "the tree of a thousand uses." In the Philippines it is called, simply, the tree of life.
    • Across the tropics the palm was also a medicine chest — the water for the sick, the oil for skin and hair, preparations of the root and shell in local practice. Those uses are history; what the studies actually support is in Health Benefits.
    • The Philippines — where the palm is called the tree of life, and three countries (Indonesia, the Philippines and India) together grow about three-quarters of the world's coconuts. Young green nuts — buko — are opened for their water and soft jelly flesh, in drinks, salads and pies; the ripe flesh is grated and squeezed into gata, the coconut milk that runs through Filipino cooking; and the flower sap is tapped as tuba, drunk fresh or fermented.
    • Sri Lanka — the king coconut at every roadside stall, cut and handed over with a straw; coconut milk in nearly every curry; and a whole "coconut triangle" of groves between the main cities given over to the palm.
    • India — Kerala, in the south, is the coconut state, its name often linked to kera, the coconut tree. The flesh goes into chutneys and curries, the oil into cooking and hair care, and the whole nut into the temple — offered and broken in worship and at weddings, as it has been for centuries.
    • Thailand — coconut milk and cream are the base that carries the curries and the great soups like tom kha; young coconuts are sold chilled everywhere, the top cut away for the water and the soft flesh spooned out after.
    • Indonesia and Malaysia — santan, coconut milk, is the rich heart of rendang, laksa and a hundred curries; Indonesia is among the world's two largest producers.
    • Polynesia and the Pacific — the canoe plant that made settlement possible: drink, food, fibre for sails and lashings, all in one floating package. In the colonial era the dried flesh — copra — became the islands' cash crop, shipped away for oil, and copra money reshaped island life. The sprouted nut's spongy apple is still eaten fresh.
    • The Caribbean — coconut water and jelly flesh from roadside vendors; coconut milk in Jamaica's rice and peas; and the tall palms that once defined the coasts, thinned in living memory by lethal yellowing disease.
    • Brazil — água de coco, coconut water sold on every beach from green nuts cut to order, and cocada, the coconut sweet sold beside it.

    Craft

    • One plant, every part — the uses that built that name. The husk's fibre, coir, was twisted into rope and rigging that lasted in salt water when other ropes rotted, and is still made into mats, brushes and planting fibre. The shell was carved into cups, bowls and ladles, and burned into a fine charcoal. The leaves roofed and walled houses as thatch and were woven into baskets, mats and hats; their stiff midribs became brooms. The straight trunk served as posts and beams, and its dense outer wood is still cut as coconut timber. The unopened flower stalk, cut and bound, weeps a sweet sap — toddy — drunk fresh in the morning, fermented into palm wine by evening, boiled down into coconut sugar, or soured into vinegar. Inside a sprouting nut, the growing embryo swells into a soft, spongy ball, the coconut apple, eaten fresh in the Pacific. And the heart of palm — the palm's single growing point, cut from the crown — is a crisp delicacy whose dish earned the name "millionaire's salad," because a coconut palm has only one heart, and taking it kills the tree.
    • Coconut water — the clear liquid inside a young nut — per 100 g: 19 kcal, carbohydrate 3.71 g, sugars 2.61 g, fibre 1.1 g, protein 0.72 g. Its standout mineral is potassium at 250 mg — a full cup of coconut water gives about 600 mg, roughly an eighth of a day's needs. It also carries real sodium (105 mg per 100 g), so it is not the sodium-free drink it is sometimes sold as; and its vitamin C is small, 2.4 mg per 100 g. It is a pleasant, light drink with a useful amount of potassium. That is the whole claim.
    • The flesh of a ripe nut, per 100 g: 354 kcal, fat 33.5 g, carbohydrate 15.2 g, fibre 9.0 g, sugars 6.2 g, protein 3.3 g. The fibre is genuinely high — 9 g in 100 g is more than most nuts and seeds offer. Its minerals are led by manganese at 1.5 mg, about two-thirds of the daily value, with copper at about half the daily value and useful iron and potassium besides. It is also an energy-dense food: a cup of shredded coconut carries about as many calories as a small meal, and the numbers show it.
    • Coconut milk and coconut cream are not the liquid in the nut. The water is found; the milk is made, by grating the ripe flesh and squeezing it through cloth with water. Cream is the rich first squeeze, milk the thinner pressing after. Both carry the flesh's fat, which brings the story to the oil.
    • The fat: about 30 g of the flesh's 33.5 g of fat is saturated, and coconut oil is about 82% saturated fat — a higher share than butter (about 63%). One tablespoon of coconut oil holds more than 11 g of saturated fat, close to a full day's limit on the American Heart Association's advice.
    • The argument over that fat, both sides at their strength. In 2017 the American Heart Association reviewed the evidence and advised against coconut oil: in all seven controlled trials it examined, coconut oil raised LDL cholesterol — the "bad" cholesterol that drives artery disease — and the advisory concluded that because coconut oil raises LDL and has no known offsetting favourable effects, it advises against its use; swapping saturated fats for unsaturated vegetable oils cut heart and vessel disease by about 30% in the trials it reviewed. The other side answers with the biggest pooling of the trials (Neelakantan and colleagues, 2020, sixteen trials): coconut oil did raise LDL compared with vegetable oils, by about 10 mg/dL — but it also raised HDL, the "good" cholesterol, by about 4 mg/dL, and it showed no effect on body weight, body fat, inflammation or blood sugar; and measured against butter rather than seed oils, coconut oil comes out ahead, with lower LDL and higher HDL. Both sides are arguing from cholesterol numbers: no trial has yet tested coconut oil against actual heart attacks and strokes. And the oil is not the food — the Pacific peoples whose traditional diets were rich in coconut ate the flesh and cream, not bottled oil. No heart claim is made either way; the fat content is a fact, and the choice belongs to the reader. Human trials
    • The MCT claim, and its limits. MCTs — medium-chain triglycerides — are fats the body burns more quickly than most, and studies of them report modest effects on weight. But the oil used in those studies was a purified MCT oil made only of the two shortest of these fats. Ordinary coconut oil is a different thing: its biggest fat is lauric acid, a longer fat that the body handles only partly in the fast way, and the true MCTs of the studies make up only about 13–14% of coconut oil. Coconut oil is not MCT oil, and the MCT results do not carry over to it. Human trials
    • When to plant: Plant when the weather is warm and wet; in its true frost-free climate the palm plants and fruits all year round
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Sand or light soil with sharp drainage — happy in pure sand where almost nothing else crops
    • Environment: Strictly tropical — USDA zones 10b–11, frost-free coasts; cold injures it in the 40s °F (below about 7 °C), and at freezing, 32 °F (0 °C), it can be killed outright
    • Planter or ground: Ground outdoors in frost-free tropics; a summer pot plant at best where winters freeze
    • Spacing and depth: Give a tall its full room — 20–30 m of height and a wide crown; from a nut, lay it on its side and bury it about half deep
    • Water: Steady water in dry spells to crop well, though an established palm rides out drought
    • When to pick: Picked green at six to seven months for water and jelly flesh, or left to eleven or twelve months for the hard flesh, milk and copra; a healthy palm fruits nearly all year

    Garden notes

    • First, what it is: a palm, not a tree in the wood sense — one unbranched trunk growing from a single crown of fronds 4–6 m (13–20 ft) long. It grows only from that crown: if the crown is destroyed, the palm dies, which is why the heart is a one-time harvest. There is no pruning it smaller and no second chance.
    • Climate is the whole question. The coconut is strictly tropical — outdoors it belongs in USDA zones 10b–11, frost-free coasts. Cold injures it in the 40s °F (below about 7 °C), and at freezing, 32 °F (0 °C), it can be killed outright; the University of Florida's guidance is blunt that coconuts can be killed or injured at 32 °F. Frost kills it. If your winters freeze, this is a summer pot plant at best, and even dwarf kinds in pots need real warmth, light and room.
    • Site: full sun, and the beach is its home — it is one of the most salt-tolerant crop plants in the world, unbothered by salt spray and happy in pure sand where almost nothing else crops. It wants drainage, and steady water in dry spells to crop well, though an established palm rides out drought.
    • Growing from a nut: choose a ripe brown nut that sloshes, lay it on its side in sand or light soil, bury it about half deep, and keep it moist and warm. Then wait — sprouting takes months, commonly three to six, the shoot emerging from one of the three eyes. Seedlings grow fast once they start.
    • Time is the price, as with pineapple: a tall palm gives its first nuts at six to ten years and reaches full bearing at fifteen to twenty; dwarfs flower at three to five years. After that a healthy palm fruits nearly all year, each nut taking the better part of a year to ripen — picked green at six to seven months for water and jelly flesh, or left to eleven or twelve months for the hard flesh, milk and copra.
    • Space and safety: give a tall its full room — 20–30 m of height and a wide crown — and think about what falls. A ripe coconut is a heavy object dropping from a great height; falling nuts are a genuine hazard, so plant away from paths, roofs and parked cars, and clear ripe nuts overhanging anywhere people walk.
    • Disease, for gardeners in Florida and the Caribbean: lethal yellowing, spread by a small sap-sucking insect, kills palms within months and has no cure once a palm is infected — the practical answer is the growers' one: plant the kinds with reported resistance (Malayan Dwarf, Maypan), knowing from the Florida trials that the resistance is partial, not a promise.

    Propagation

    Choose a ripe brown nut that sloshes, lay it on its side in sand or light soil, bury it about half deep, and keep it moist and warm. Then wait — sprouting takes months, commonly three to six, the shoot emerging from one of the three eyes. Seedlings grow fast once they start.

    Safety

    • Coconut is rich food — the flesh and oil add up fast in calories. Coconut allergy is real, if uncommon; in the United States coconut is labelled among the tree nuts, and anyone with a nut allergy should take advice before eating it. And the oil is a food and a skin-and-hair oil with a long history of ordinary use — the sweeping cure claims made for it online are not supported by the evidence above.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: coconut meat, raw, and coconut water — the nutrition figures
    • Gunn et al. (2011) — independent origins of cultivated coconut in the Old World tropics — the two populations, and where coconut farming began
    • Sacks et al. (2017) — dietary fats and cardiovascular disease, the American Heart Association presidential advisory — the case against coconut oil
    • Neelakantan et al. (2020) — coconut oil consumption and cardiovascular risk factors: a meta-analysis of the clinical trials — what the pooled trials show for LDL, HDL, weight and inflammation
    • Harries & Clement (2014) — long-distance dispersal of the coconut palm within the coral atoll ecosystem — the floating fruit, and how the palm travelled
    • Broschat & Crane (2017) — The Coconut in Florida, UF/IFAS Extension (HS40) — varieties, fruiting age, lethal yellowing and growing in Florida

    Avocado

    Persea americana

    Culinary

    Heart HealthDigestive HealthPotassium

    Fresh

    A fruit built out of fat, on purpose. Almost every other fruit in this library sweetens itself with sugar; the avocado fills its flesh with oil instead — the same soft, mostly monounsaturated oil that makes olive oil famous — around one enormous seed. It never ripens on the tree: it hangs there hard for months and only softens after it is picked. It is a member of the laurel family, kin to bay laurel and cinnamon. And the fruit itself is a survivor from another world: a feast sized for giant animals that died out thousands of years ago, kept alive ever since by people who liked it too much to let it go.

    Cultivars

    Growers still sort avocados by the three races, because the races decide what a variety can bear. Mexican race: small fruit, thin smooth skin, the richest oil, leaves that smell of anise when crushed, and the hardiest against cold. Guatemalan race: thick, rough, warty skin, fruit that hangs longest on the tree, middling cold tolerance. West Indian race: big, smooth, glossy fruit with the least oil, a hint of salt tolerance, and the least cold tolerance of all — a true lowland tropical. Most shop varieties are crosses.

    'Hass'

    The world avocado: a Mexican–Guatemalan cross (about three-fifths Mexican by the 2019 genetic study), 200–300 g, with thick pebbly skin that turns from green to near-black as the fruit ripens after picking — a built-in ripeness signal no other variety matches as clearly. Rich, nutty flesh, high oil, keeps and travels well, and the tree bears heavily. Patented 1935; about 80% of the world's crop. Every one is a clone of Rudolph Hass's seedling.

    'Fuerte'

    The avocado 'Hass' dethroned. Found in 1911 at Atlixco, Mexico, a natural Mexican–Guatemalan cross; fuerte means "strong," a name it earned by surviving the hard California freeze of 1913. Smooth green skin that stays green when ripe, pear-shaped, excellent mild flesh. It was the world's leading variety for decades and is still widely grown, though its trees bear unevenly, heavily one year and lightly the next.

    'Bacon'

    A Mexican-race seedling raised by James Bacon in Buena Park, California, in 1928: smooth thin green skin, mild light flesh, and among the hardiest of the common varieties — a garden choice where winters bite.

    'Zutano'

    Another Mexican type, raised in Fallbrook, California, in 1926: shiny yellow-green thin skin, lighter, more watery flesh than 'Hass', hardy and fast-bearing, now used more as a polliniser and rootstock than as a shop fruit.

    'Pinkerton'

    A California variety (a 'Hass'-family seedling, found in the 1960s): long pear shape, rough green skin that stays green, a small seed and more flesh per fruit than most, on a compact tree.

    'Reed'

    A Guatemalan seedling from Carlsbad, California: round fruit like a green cannonball, thick rough skin, rich flesh, ripening in summer when 'Hass' is scarce.

    West Indian types ('Waldin', 'Pollock' and their kin)

    The big smooth avocados of Florida and the Caribbean: fruit that can pass a kilo, pale mild flesh with less oil, eaten where they grow and rarely shipped far.

    • Avocado comes from south-central Mexico and the lands below it into Central America. People were eating wild avocados in the Coxcatlán Cave in Puebla around ten thousand years ago, and over the following thousands of years the peoples of Mesoamerica bred the wild fruit — small, thin-fleshed, mostly seed — into the generous food it became. Three kinds, called races, were shaped in three homes: the Mexican race in the cool highlands, the Guatemalan race in the highlands further south, and the West Indian race in the warm lowlands. Nearly every avocado in the shops today is a child or a cross of those three.
    • The Nahuatl word was ahuacatl. The Aztecs mashed the fruit with sauce into ahuacamolli — ahuacatl plus molli, sauce — and that word, carried through Spanish, is "guacamole." Spanish speakers reshaped ahuacatl into aguacate; English speakers, wrestling with the Spanish, turned it into "avocado," and for a while also called it the "alligator pear," for its rough green skin and its shape.
    • The seed tells the oldest story. An avocado seed is far too big for any living wild animal in its homeland to swallow, and the leading explanation — first set out by Daniel Janzen and Paul Martin in 1982 — is that the fruit was built for giants: the gomphotheres, elephant cousins, and the giant ground sloths, some as heavy as a truck, that once roamed the Americas. They ate the fruit whole, walked away, and dropped the seed in dung far from the tree. The giants died out around thirteen thousand years ago, and the avocado should, by that logic, have followed them. Instead, people took over the giants' job — planting the seed wherever they went. Scientists call fruits like this "evolutionary anachronisms": foods still dressed for partners who are gone. It is the leading explanation — no avocado seed has ever been found in fossil dung.
    • Aztec and Maya farmers grew the tree in gardens and paid it in tribute; Spanish writers described it in the early 1500s, and the Spanish and Portuguese then carried it around the tropical world. But for centuries it stayed a local food in most places — a tree in the yard, not a crop in the shops. Its rise to a world fruit waited for one California tree.
    • In 1926 a mail carrier named Rudolph Hass, of La Habra Heights, California, planted avocado seeds he had bought from a nurseryman, meaning to graft the fashionable 'Fuerte' variety onto the seedlings. One seedling refused the graft — twice, then a third time. Hass was ready to chop it down; his grafter told him it was a good strong tree and to let it be. The tree bore rough, pebbly fruit his children liked better than any other, and in 1935 Hass patented it under his own name (it rhymes with "pass"). The patent earned him very little, but the tree earned everything: because avocados do not grow true from seed, every 'Hass' tree since has been grafted from that one's wood. The mother tree stood in La Habra Heights until root rot took it in 2002, at about seventy-six years old, and roughly four out of every five avocados eaten in the world today are her clones — a 2019 genetic study found the variety is a cross, about three-fifths Mexican race and two-fifths Guatemalan.
    • Around Mexico and Central America the tree was used as medicine as well as food — the leaves brewed as teas, the seed grated into remedies. Those uses are history; what the studies actually support is in Health Benefits, and the safety lines about leaves and seed below are not fine print.
    • Mexico — the homeland table: guacamole from the Aztec ahuacamolli, fruit eaten in tacos, soups and tortas, and the toasted Mexican-race leaf as a seasoning — in black beans, in quesadillas in Oaxaca, under barbacoa. Mexico still grows more avocados than any other country, roughly a third of the world's supply.
    • The world trade — after 'Hass', the map redrew itself: Mexico first, then the Dominican Republic, Peru, Colombia, Indonesia and Kenya among the large producers, with the fruit flown and shipped green-hard and ripened near the shops that sell it.
    • California and the United States — the tree's second home: the 'Fuerte' era, the 'Hass' patent, and a fruit that went from exotic to ordinary across the twentieth century.
    • Avocado toast — the modern chapter: smashed avocado on toast was served in Sydney cafés by the early 1990s (the chef Bill Granger is usually credited, from 1993), spread through café culture to Los Angeles and New York in the 2010s, and became so emblematic that in 2017 an Australian property developer's remark that young people might afford houses if they stopped buying it turned "avocado toast" into shorthand for a generation's spending. Whatever the argument, the dish marks the moment the fruit finished its journey from Aztec tribute to café staple.
    • Brazil — avocado eaten sweet: beaten with sugar and lime, or blended into a milkshake-like vitamina — a reminder that "savoury" is a local decision, not the fruit's nature.
    • Indonesia and the Philippines — the same sweet road: avocado blended with milk and chocolate or coffee into iced drinks (es alpukat, avocado shakes).
    • Japan — adopted late and wholeheartedly, sliced into salads and onto rice, sometimes with soy sauce in place of the tuna it resembles in richness.
    • Avocado flesh, per 100 g: 160 kcal, fat 14.7 g — of which about 9.8 g is monounsaturated, the kind that dominates olive oil, and only about 2.1 g saturated — fibre 6.7 g, potassium 485 mg (more, weight for weight, than banana), folate 81 µg (about a fifth of the daily value), with vitamin E, vitamin K and a little vitamin C besides. Sugars are almost absent: 0.7 g. It is a rich food — the fat is the point of it, and the numbers say so plainly.
    • Cholesterol, stated at trial strength. In one controlled feeding trial (Wang et al. 2015), 45 overweight adults ate three cholesterol-lowering diets in turn, five weeks each; the version with one whole avocado a day lowered LDL cholesterol — the "bad" kind — by 13.5 mg/dL, more than the same diet using other oils instead (8.3) or a lower-fat diet (7.4). One trial, 45 people, five weeks: a real finding, at that size. It fits the bigger picture without proving it: in two long Harvard cohorts following more than 110,000 adults for thirty years (Pacheco et al. 2022), people eating at least two servings of avocado a week had about a sixth lower risk of cardiovascular disease than people who rarely ate it — an association from watching people's lives, not a trial. The honest summary: swapping avocado in place of butter, cheese or processed meat is a swap the evidence smiles on; avocado is a food, not a treatment. Human trials
    • The fibre is the quiet half of the story: 6.7 g per 100 g is high for a fruit, and it comes with the fat, which is why avocado satisfies the way it does.
    • When to plant: Plant in spring, once frost is past
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Rich, loose, sharply drained; roots rot in heavy, waterlogged ground
    • Environment: Frost-tender; outdoors in USDA zones 9–11, and in zone 8 only with a Mexican-race variety, a sheltered wall, and luck
    • Planter or ground: Ground; a young tree grows in a big pot on a sunny patio and can be carried under cover for winter — but expect leaves, not fruit
    • Spacing and depth: Room — a mature canopy can spread 10 m or more, and roots run wide and shallow under it
    • Water: Deep, regular water in dry weather; water deep and let the surface breathe
    • When to pick: Pick by size and season, not softness — the fruit never ripens on the tree; it softens only after picking, over days at room temperature

    Garden notes

    • First, what it is: a fast-growing evergreen tree of the laurel family, 9–20 m (30–66 ft) tall left to itself, with glossy leaves that flush copper-red when young. In gardens it is usually kept pruned to a size a ladder can manage. A grafted tree can fruit in three to four years; a tree from a seed may take seven to fifteen, and there is no shortcut.
    • The seedling surprise, stated plainly: avocados do not come true from seed. A 'Hass' seed grows a tree, but not a 'Hass' tree — its fruit will be something new, usually worse, occasionally fine, never the same. That is why the seed a child sprouts in a jar of water is a houseplant and a science project, not an orchard tree — and why every shop avocado variety is grafted: a piece of the named tree joined onto seedling roots.
    • The A/B flowering system, in plain words. An avocado flower opens twice: once as a female, ready to receive pollen, and once as a male, shedding it — never both at once. Varieties fall into two timetables. Type A ('Hass') opens female in the morning and male the next afternoon. Type B ('Fuerte', 'Bacon', 'Zutano') opens female in the afternoon and male the next morning. Planting an A and a B together means that on any given morning, one tree's females meet the other's males, and bees moving between them set more fruit. A single tree still fruits — the timetables overlap enough on warm days — but a pair of opposite types is the grower's insurance.
    • Flowers come in thousands on a mature tree, and almost all of them fall: well under one flower in a thousand becomes a fruit. A tree carrying a hundred avocados has done its job well.
    • Picking is backwards from other fruit: an avocado never ripens on the tree. It matures there — full-sized, full of oil — and hangs hard for months, a living storage room, then softens only after picking, over days at room temperature. Growers pick by size and season, not softness; at home, pick one, let it soften indoors, and if it eats well, pick the rest. Squeezing fruit still on the tree bruises it and tells you nothing.
    • Cold, by race: the tree is frost-tender, but not evenly. Mexican-race varieties ('Bacon', 'Zutano', 'Hass' with its Mexican share) can shrug off brief dips to about −6 to −4 °C (low 20s °F) once mature; Guatemalan types are hurt around −4 to −2 °C; West Indian types are damaged near freezing itself. Young trees of any kind are tender — protect them their first winters. Avocado belongs outdoors in USDA zones 9–11, and in zone 8 only with a Mexican-race variety, a sheltered wall, and luck.
    • Water, honestly: this is a thirsty tree by fruit-tree standards. Groves are irrigated generously, and a home tree wants deep, regular water in dry weather — the more so in pots and sandy soil. Its roots are shallow and hungry for air, though, and they rot in heavy, waterlogged ground (root rot is what killed the 'Hass' mother tree). Rich, loose, sharply drained soil, mulch over the roots, water deep and let the surface breathe: that is the balance.
    • Sun and space: full sun, and room — a mature canopy can spread 10 m or more, and roots run wide and shallow under it. Keep the trunk's base clear of mulch, feed lightly and often rather than heavily at once, and prune after harvest to keep the tree at picking height.
    • In a pot: a young tree is handsome in a big pot on a sunny patio and can be carried under cover for winter — the cold-country answer — but expect leaves, not fruit; a potted avocado that fruits is a rare and patient achievement.

    Propagation

    Avocados do not come true from seed. A 'Hass' seed grows a tree, but not a 'Hass' tree — its fruit will be something new, usually worse, occasionally fine, never the same. That is why the seed a child sprouts in a jar of water is a houseplant and a science project, not an orchard tree — and why every shop avocado variety is grafted: a piece of the named tree joined onto seedling roots. A grafted tree can fruit in three to four years; a tree from a seed may take seven to fifteen, and there is no shortcut.

    Safety

    • Now the cautions, plainly, because this plant has two faces. The flesh is food. The rest of the tree is not. Avocado leaves, bark, skin and seed carry a substance called persin, the tree's own fungicide — it stops fungi attacking the tree, and it is dangerous to many animals. Birds are the most sensitive: caged birds have died within a day or two of eating avocado. In horses, cattle, goats and sheep, the leaves and bark can injure the heart and cause a painful inflammation of the udder in milking animals; the leaves are the strongest part. Dogs and cats are hardier, but the seed is exactly the size to lodge in a dog's gut. So: no avocado — flesh, leaves or trimmings — for pet birds or livestock, ever, and the seed and skin go to the compost, not to animals.
    • The seed is not a food for people either. Grated avocado-seed teas and powders are sold with health claims; none of those claims has been tested in people, the seed carries persin and bitter defensive compounds, and the California Avocado Commission itself advises against eating it. The seed has one use: planting it.
    • The leaves need the same care. In Mexican cooking, leaves of the Mexican race — the ones that smell of anise when crushed — are toasted and used as a seasoning, a flavouring in a pot of beans or under barbacoa, the way a bay leaf is used. That is a seasoning tradition, in small amounts, from one race of the tree. Leaf teas, drunk as medicine, are a different matter: they are history, not recommended, and avocado leaves should never be gathered for animals to eat.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: avocados, raw, all commercial varieties — the nutrition figures
    • Wang et al. (2015) — one avocado a day in a moderate-fat diet lowered LDL cholesterol more than matched diets without it: a randomised, controlled feeding trial in 45 adults
    • Pacheco et al. (2022) — avocado eating and cardiovascular disease over 30 years in two large US cohorts of more than 110,000 adults — an association, stated as one
    • Janzen & Martin (1982) — "Neotropical Anachronisms: the fruits the gomphotheres ate" — the giant-animal dispersal explanation for the avocado's great seed
    • MSD Veterinary Manual (2023) — avocado (Persea spp.) toxicosis in animals — persin, the leaves as the most toxic part, and the animals at risk
    • Hass Avocado Board / University of California accounts — Rudolph Hass, the 1926 seedling, the 1935 patent (US Plant Patent 139) and the mother tree's death in 2002

    Cacao

    Theobroma cacao

    Culinary

    Heart Health

    FreshCookedDried

    Chocolate does not begin as a sweet bar. It begins as a bitter drink — ground beans whisked to a froth with water, chilli and vanilla, no sugar at all — and for most of its five-thousand-year history, that drink is what cacao was. The plant is a small understorey tree of the Amazon rainforest that does something few fruit trees do: it flowers and fruits directly on its trunk, hanging its big ribbed pods from the bark itself. And its scientific name is a claim in Greek: Theobroma, “food of the gods,” a name Linnaeus gave it in 1753 — and once you know the plant’s story, the name reads less like praise and more like a report. The Aztec told how the god Quetzalcoatl brought cacao down to people as a gift. The name and the story say the same thing from two sides of the world.

    Cultivars

    Growers long sorted the world’s cacao into three great groups, and the names still run the trade — though the plant’s genes, mapped in 2008, draw the map more finely, into about ten populations. The classic three are the ones a buyer meets.

    Criollo

    The “native” cacao of Central America and northern South America, the type the Maya and Aztec drank. Pale, lightly coloured beans, mild and complex in flavour, the connoisseur’s cacao — and the hardest to grow: tender, disease-prone, and low-yielding. True Criollo is a small share of the world crop, a few percent at most, grown in places like Venezuela and Central America.

    Forastero

    The “foreigner,” the bulk cacao of the world: the great majority of all beans, hardy and heavy-yielding, with a strong, plain chocolate flavour. Its home is the Amazon basin, and its most planted form, the Amelonado type, is the cacao of West Africa’s farms. Almost all everyday chocolate is Forastero.

    Trinitario

    The cross. In Trinidad in the 1700s, plantings of Criollo were devastated — by disease, or by storm; the accounts differ — and Forastero was brought in to replant. The two crossed, and the hybrid that resulted, Trinitario, joined Criollo’s flavour to Forastero’s toughness. It is the fine-cacao workhorse of the Caribbean and is grown around the tropics.

    Nacional (‘Arriba’)

    Ecuador’s own. A distinct type with a famous floral note, named Arriba — “upriver” — for the beans floated down the Guayas River to the port of Guayaquil. Genetic work places Nacional among the distinct old populations, and it is a striking thought that the Mayo-Chinchipe, in whose pots the oldest cacao traces were found, lived in the same Ecuadorian country where Nacional’s line runs back: they may have had a hand in shaping it.

    A note on labels: “fine or flavour” cacao — Criollo, Trinitario, Nacional and their kin — is a small slice of the world crop next to bulk Forastero, and the single-origin bars of the craft chocolate trade are built on it. The variety names are real; the bean in an ordinary bar is almost never one variety, and labels that imply otherwise are marketing, not botany.

    • Cacao comes from the upper Amazon — the rainforest country where the great river’s tributaries run down from the Andes through what is now Ecuador, Peru, Colombia and Brazil. That is where the wild tree grows and where its family is most varied, and the science of the plant’s own genes points there as its home.
    • The oldest evidence of cacao in use anywhere comes from that country. At Santa Ana-La Florida in south-east Ecuador, a village of the Mayo-Chinchipe people, researchers found three separate traces of cacao in pottery and stone tools about 5,300 years old: starch grains that match cacao alone, remains of theobromine — a chemical found in ripe cacao beans — and fragments of cacao’s own DNA. The pots came from houses and from tombs: cacao was daily food and a funeral offering at once. This is about 1,500 years earlier than the oldest clear evidence in Central America, and it makes the upper Amazon the oldest known centre of cacao’s domestication.
    • From South America the plant travelled north, carried by people, into Central America and Mexico. By about 3,900 years ago the Olmec of Mexico’s Gulf coast were using it — traces of theobromine survive in their pottery — and the Olmec are usually credited with the word itself: kakawa, the root of “cacao.”
    • The Maya of the lowland forests made cacao central. They grew it in shaded forest gardens, drank it frothed — poured from one vessel to another from a height to raise the foam, which was the prized part — and wrote its name in their hieroglyphs. Painted pots in Maya tombs still show the foam being poured. Cacao went into marriage rites and offerings, and the beans themselves were money: a store of wealth you could also drink.
    • The Aztec of highland Mexico could not grow cacao — their capital was too high and too cold — so the beans came up from the warm lowlands as trade and as tribute, counted by the load in the empire’s tax records. Their drink, xocolatl, was bitter and rich: ground cacao with chilli, vanilla and other flavourings, beaten to a froth, served cold in fine cups. The emperor Montezuma’s court drank it in quantity. Beans were everyday currency in Aztec markets — and valuable enough that counterfeiters hollowed them out and filled the shells with clay, a fraud the Spanish recorded.
    • The Aztec story of where cacao came from tells its worth. They said the god Quetzalcoatl — the feathered serpent, god of wind and learning — brought the cacao tree to people, taking it from the mountain where the gods kept the foods, and taught them to roast and grind the beans. When he was driven out, the story goes, the cacao went with his blessing. The tree was a gift from a god, and the “food of the gods” name Linnaeus chose three thousand years later lands on the same idea.
    • Europeans met the beans in 1502, when Columbus’s fourth voyage stopped a great trading canoe off Honduras and found its cargo of strange “almonds” that the traders clearly treasured. The drink itself reached Europe through Mexico after Cortés; the Spanish, who at first found it bitter and strange, sweetened it with sugar and kept it hot, and for a century chocolate stayed a Spanish court secret before spreading to France and England, where chocolate houses opened in London in the 1650s. For two hundred years in Europe it remained what it had been in Mexico: a drink.
    • The bar came late, and it came from machines. In 1828 the Dutch chemist Coenraad van Houten patented a press that squeezed much of the fat — the cocoa butter — out of the ground beans, leaving a cake that could be milled into cocoa powder; his alkali treatment, “Dutching,” made the powder milder and darker and able to mix with water. In 1847 the English firm Fry’s used the new powder and the pressed-out butter to make the first solid chocolate that could be eaten rather than drunk. Daniel Peter in Switzerland added condensed milk in 1875 to make milk chocolate, and in 1879 Rodolphe Lindt’s conching machine — which kneads the chocolate for hours — gave it the smooth melt that bars are still judged by. The sweet bar is younger than the railway.
    • Cacao was also medicine in its old homes — the Maya and Aztec used it in remedies, and colonial-era texts list dozens of uses, from fevers to fatigue.
    • West Africa — where the world’s chocolate now grows. Cacao crossed the Atlantic in the 1800s, and Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana became the giants: together they grow more than half the world’s cacao, almost all of it on small family farms of a few acres, and almost all Forastero. The beans are fermented in heaps under banana leaves and dried in the sun, village by village.
    • Ecuador — the oldest home and the Nacional country: fine Arriba cacao for the craft trade, and in the pods themselves a second food — the sweet white pulp around the beans, eaten fresh and juiced where the trees grow.
    • Mexico — the drink never left. In Oaxaca and Chiapas cacao is still whisked to foam with water or milk, cinnamon and sugar in the modern manner, and in the old one with chilli; and in mole negro, the dark sauce of Oaxaca, chocolate is a seasoning — a spoonful of cacao deepening a sauce of chillies and spices, chocolate used the way its first cooks used it, unsweetened and savoury.
    • Brazil — cacao in Bahia’s shaded forest farms, the pulp juiced as suco de cacau, and the husks left to feed the soil.
    • The Caribbean and Central America — Trinitario country, small farms and the old estate tradition, Grenada and Trinidad and the Dominican Republic among the fine-cacao names; in parts of Central America a fermented cacao drink of the pulp and bean, bálsamo and its kin, still follows the old pattern.
    • Indonesia and Malaysia — the newest big growing region, bulk cacao from Sulawesi and beyond, proof the Amazon tree now circles the whole tropical world.
    • Everywhere, the road from pod to bar runs the same way: the pod is cut from the trunk by hand; the beans, still in their sweet pulp, are heaped or boxed and left to ferment for several days — the pulp feeds yeasts and bacteria, the heap heats, and the bean’s flavour is born there; the beans are dried in the sun, roasted, and cracked so the shell can be winnowed away; the broken bean, the nib, is ground until its own fat melts it into a thick liquid, chocolate liquor; and from there the road forks — press out the butter and mill the cake for cocoa powder, or sweeten, conche and mould the liquor into bars. Fermentation is the step no factory can skip: an unfermented bean never tastes like chocolate.
    • Start with the bean’s own numbers, in the form people actually buy it plain: unsweetened cocoa powder, per 100 g: 228 kcal, protein 19.6 g, fat 13.7 g, carbohydrate 57.9 g, fibre 37 g, and almost no sugar — 1.75 g. It is rich in minerals on paper: magnesium 499 mg, iron 13.9 mg, potassium 1,520 mg per 100 g. But nobody eats 100 g of cocoa powder. A tablespoon is about 5 g, and it gives about 12 kcal and 2 g of fibre — real, but a spoonful’s worth. Both numbers matter: the powder is concentrated, the serving is small.
    • The two stimulants, stated as fact. Cocoa powder carries caffeine at 230 mg per 100 g — about 12 mg in a tablespoon, a small fraction of a cup of coffee — and far more theobromine: about 2,060 mg per 100 g. Theobromine is caffeine’s gentler relative; it is most of the lift in chocolate, and it is also why chocolate is dangerous to dogs, who clear theobromine from their bodies far more slowly than people do. Chocolate is a people food; keep it from dogs entirely.
    • The flavanols are where the real research sits. Flavanols are a family of plant compounds in which cacao is unusually rich — one of them, epicatechin, is the most studied. Short trials find that cocoa flavanols help blood vessels widen and give small average drops in blood pressure. Europe’s food safety authority allows one careful claim: 200 mg of cocoa flavanols a day “helps maintain the elasticity of blood vessels, which contributes to normal blood flow” — a claim about a measured dose of flavanols, from high-flavanol cocoa, not about chocolate in general. Human trials
    • The biggest test is the COSMOS trial. Over 21,000 older adults in the United States took either a cocoa extract capsule — 500 mg of cocoa flavanols a day, a dose no one could eat from chocolate without a mountain of sugar and fat — or a dummy capsule, for about three and a half years. On the trial’s main measure, all cardiovascular events added together, the extract group did a little better but not by enough to rule out chance: the trial’s headline result was not significant. On one secondary measure, death from cardiovascular disease, the extract group was 27% lower, and among people who actually took their capsules faithfully the total-events result also turned favourable. That is a promising signal, honestly reported — and it is about a concentrated extract in a capsule. The trial’s own leaders said it plainly: COSMOS was not a chocolate trial. Human trials
    • Whatever flavanols may do at extract doses, a chocolate bar is not a flavanol supplement. What stands between the bean and the bar is sugar and fat. A typical milk chocolate is about half sugar by weight; even a strong dark chocolate, 70–85% cacao, runs about 600 kcal and roughly 24 g of sugar per 100 g, with over 40 g of fat — the cocoa butter itself, which is part of the bean’s honest makeup. Dark chocolate keeps more of the bean and less of the sugar, and the numbers say exactly that much and no more.
    • Processing matters too: the alkali “Dutching” that makes cocoa powder dark and mild also strips out much of its flavanol content, and roasting and fermenting each take their share. The bean starts rich; not everything survives the road to the bar.
    • Chocolate does not detox, does not burn fat, and is not shown to lift mood beyond the pleasure of eating it — studies of mood use flavanol extracts or the experience of chocolate itself, and neither makes a health claim a bar can carry. Cacao’s supported story is a good one without them: a genuinely flavanol-rich food, one strong trial with a promising secondary result, and a small authorised claim about blood vessels at a measured dose.
    • When to plant: Sow fresh seed straight from the pod — it dies within days of leaving the pod and cannot be dried or stored; seedlings are raised in nurseries near where the pods are cut
    • Sun: Part shade — about a quarter to a third shade suits it; grown in full tropical sun it crops heavily for a few years with heavy feeding, then exhausts and sickens
    • Soil: Deep, rich and moist but drained — the tree rots in standing water
    • Environment: True tropics only, within about 20 degrees of the equator; 21–32 °C (70–90 °F), steady, with no frost at all — cold below about 15 °C (59 °F) checks it, and a frost kills it; rain of roughly 1,500–2,500 mm a year, spread through the year, and humid air
    • Planter or ground: Ground where it grows; in cold climates a large pot under glass, where winters are warm, humid and frost-free indoors
    • Water: Plenty of rain, spread through the year — about 1,500–2,500 mm a year; dry wind and dry seasons are its enemies
    • When to pick: Pods ripen all year, with two harvest peaks; a pod takes about five to six months from flower to ripe, and ripeness is read by colour — green pods turning yellow, red pods turning orange, by type — and by a hollow sound when the pod is tapped

    Garden notes

    • First, what it is: a small evergreen tree of the rainforest understorey — the shaded floor beneath the tall canopy. In the wild it can reach 12–15 m (40–50 ft); on farms it is pruned to about 3–8 m so the pods can be reached. It is a tree of the true tropics only, grown within about 20 degrees of the equator, and it asks for the forest floor it evolved on: warmth, wet air, shade and shelter.
    • The trunk flowers. Cacao’s strangest habit has a name — cauliflory, flowering on the trunk. The tiny flowers, only 1–2 cm across, white to pale pink, grow in clusters straight out of the trunk and the older branches, from little pads of tissue called cushions that flower again and again for years. The pods follow in the same place, hanging from the bark — which is just as well, since a ripe pod can weigh half a kilogram, more than a thin twig could hold.
    • The pollinators are midges — biting midges of the genus Forcipomyia, flies the size of a pinhead, the only insects that work the flower’s small, hooded structure. They breed in the damp leaf litter of the shaded forest floor, which is one reason cacao fails in tidy, sun-blasted plantations: no litter, no midges, no pods. Of the thousands of flowers a tree opens in a year, only a small share are ever pollinated, and only a few dozen pods ripen. Cacao sets its own strict ration.
    • Climate, plainly: it wants 21–32 °C (70–90 °F), steady, with no frost at all — cold below about 15 °C (59 °F) checks it, and a frost kills it. It wants rain of roughly 1,500–2,500 mm a year, spread through the year rather than in one season, and humid air. Dry wind and dry seasons are its enemies.
    • Shade is a need, not a preference, above all for young trees: in its home the tree lives under taller trees, and on farms it is planted under banana, plantain, coconut or standing forest thinned to a canopy — about a quarter to a third shade suits it. Grown in full tropical sun it can crop heavily for a few years with heavy feeding, then exhausts and sickens; the shaded forest farm is the durable way, and it is how cacao was always grown.
    • Soil: deep, rich and moist but drained — the tree rots in standing water. It grows from seed, which must be fresh: cacao seed dies within days of leaving the pod and cannot be dried or stored like ordinary seed, so seedlings are raised in nurseries near where the pods are cut. Farms also graft and bud good varieties onto seedling roots.
    • Time: a seedling tree first flowers at about three to five years and is in full bearing by about ten; it can crop for decades — twenty-five to thirty good years is a fair span, though old trees live far longer. Flowers and pods at every stage stand on the tree together all year; there are usually two harvest peaks a year rather than one season. A pod takes about five to six months from flower to ripe, and ripeness is read by colour — green pods turning yellow, red pods turning orange, by type — and by a hollow sound when the pod is tapped.
    • Picking is by hand and always will be: the pods are cut, never pulled, with a knife or a long-handled blade, taking care not to wound the cushion, which must flower again. Cut the cushion and you cut next year’s crop.
    • In cold climates cacao is a conservatory plant, not a garden one: it can be grown in a large pot under glass where winters are warm, humid and frost-free indoors, and a potted tree may even pod — but this is a rainforest tree at the edge of its patience, and it is grown there for love of the plant, not for a chocolate harvest.

    Propagation

    It grows from seed, which must be fresh: cacao seed dies within days of leaving the pod and cannot be dried or stored like ordinary seed, so seedlings are raised in nurseries near where the pods are cut. Farms also graft and bud good varieties onto seedling roots.

    Safety

    • Cocoa powder carries caffeine at 230 mg per 100 g — about 12 mg in a tablespoon, a small fraction of a cup of coffee — and far more theobromine: about 2,060 mg per 100 g. Theobromine is caffeine’s gentler relative; it is most of the lift in chocolate, and it is also why chocolate is dangerous to dogs, who clear theobromine from their bodies far more slowly than people do. Chocolate is a people food; keep it from dogs entirely.

    Sources

    • Coe & Coe (2013) — The True History of Chocolate — Olmec, Maya and Aztec cacao, beans as money, the road to the bar

    • Sesso et al. (2022) — the COSMOS trial: cocoa extract and cardiovascular events in over 21,000 older adults
    • European Food Safety Authority (2012) — cocoa flavanols and the maintenance of normal blood-vessel elasticity: the authorised claim and its 200 mg dose
    • Wood & Lass (1985) — Cocoa — the tree, its flowers and midge pollinators, shade, climate and harvest

    Amaranth

    Amaranthus spp.

    Culinary

    Digestive HealthImmune HealthVitamin AVitamin CCalciumPotassiumIronMagnesium

    Cooked

    Two foods from one plant: a tiny seed cooked like a grain, and leaves cooked like spinach. The seed is not a true grain — amaranth is a broadleaf plant, kin to spinach, beets and quinoa, not to wheat — so cooks call it a pseudocereal, a seed that does a grain's job. Three species carry the seed crop: Amaranthus cruentus and A. hypochondriacus from Mexico and Central America, and A. caudatus from the Andes. Other species — A. tricolor, A. dubius, A. viridis, A. blitum — are grown for their leaves. The name comes from the Greek amarantos, "unfading," for flower heads that hold their colour long after picking. It is also an honest plant to meet with its family showing: its wild cousins are the pigweeds, some of the toughest weeds on Earth, and garden amaranth keeps a measure of that toughness — heat-proof, drought-proof, and generous to a fault with seed.

    Cultivars

    'Plainsman' (A. hypochondriacus × hybridus)

    The commercial grain type: bred at the Rodale Research Center in Pennsylvania and released in the mid-1980s, early and even-ripening, with pale seed — the variety behind most North American grain production.

    'Golden Giant' (A. hypochondriacus)

    A tall grain type, plants to about 7 ft, carrying big golden-yellow heads and heavy yields of mild-flavoured seed.

    'Burgundy' (A. hypochondriacus)

    Deep red heads, stems and leaves; grown for grain, for cut-and-come-again greens, and frankly for looks.

    'Hopi Red Dye' (A. cruentus)

    The Hopi dye plant of the Southwest: the reddest seedlings of any amaranth, flower bracts used to colour piki bread, seed and young leaves eaten as well.

    'Love-Lies-Bleeding' (A. caudatus)

    The Andean grain in its garden form, named for its long hanging crimson tassels; the seed is the same kiwicha the Andes has always eaten.

    'Tampala' (A. tricolor)

    A leaf type bred for hot, humid climates, picked young and often, the form of the species eaten across South and Southeast Asia as a spinach of the tropics. The same species, in red-and-gold forms, is the foliage plant sold as Joseph's coat — one species wearing two names in two trades.

    • People gathered wild amaranth seed in the Americas for thousands of years before anyone farmed it. Domestication happened more than once, roughly 6,000 to 8,000 years ago: the earliest domesticated seeds found so far, in a rock shelter at Peñas de la Cruz in Argentina, are about 7,200 to 7,900 years old, and seeds from the Coxcatlán Cave in Mexico's Tehuacán Valley date to about 4000 BCE. The wild ancestor behind the grain species is generally taken to be Amaranthus hybridus, a widespread American weed.
    • In the Aztec empire, amaranth — huauhtli in Nahuatl — stood with maize and beans as one of the great crops. Conquered provinces paid it to the capital, Tenochtitlan, as tribute, in quantities the tribute lists put at thousands of tons a year; some accounts say as much as 20,000 tons. It fed people daily, ground into tamales and drinks, and it also fed the gods. For the festival of Panquetzaliztli, amaranth flour was mixed with honey — and, in some rites, with sacrificial blood — into a dough called tzoalli, shaped into images of the god Huitzilopochtli, carried in procession, then broken and eaten by the people.
    • In the Andes, A. caudatus — kiwicha in Quechua — was grown for more than 3,000 years, a mountain grain for thin air and short seasons, eaten popped, ground and brewed.
    • After the Spanish conquest of Mexico in 1521, the crop's sacred role brought its fall. Franciscan friars condemned the tzoalli ceremonies as idolatry — a mockery, as they saw it, of communion — and amaranth growing was banned and fields were burned while wheat was pushed onto the land in its place. Popular accounts add savage penalties for anyone caught growing it; no such decree survives, and none was needed. The tribute system that had moved the seed was dismantled, epidemics killed farmers, and within a few generations an imperial crop had shrunk to hidden household plots in highland villages in Mexico, Guatemala and the Andes, where families quietly kept sowing it.
    • It never quite died. In Mexico the popped seed bound with honey or syrup became alegría — "joy" — a street sweet sold to this day, and a direct descendant of tzoalli with the god left out. In the American Southwest, the Hopi grew a deep-red A. cruentus as a dye plant, colouring their piki bread with its flower bracts, and other Pueblo peoples steamed the greens.
    • The leaves, meanwhile, travelled the world. In the centuries after Columbus, amaranths reached Asia and Africa and were taken up as a potherb wherever the climate was hot: a cooked green in India, China, Southeast Asia, West and East Africa and the Caribbean. A plant can be two different foods in two different hemispheres — seed in its homeland, leaf almost everywhere else — and amaranth is the clearest case of it.
    • Traditional medicine used the plant modestly: an astringent tea of the leaves for loose bowels, and a gargle for sore mouths and throats, are the uses the old records repeat. Those are records of practice; the tested evidence is a separate matter, and it is thin.
    • The modern revival is recent and deliberate. In 1950 the geographer Carl Sauer could still write that the crop was "practically unknown to everyone except to Indians who grow it." In 1975 the U.S. National Academy of Sciences picked amaranth as one of 36 underexploited tropical plants with promising economic value, the Rodale Research Center in Pennsylvania took up breeding and field trials, and in 1984 the Academy published a full report, Amaranth: Modern Prospects for an Ancient Crop. Seed companies followed. Today the grain is farmed commercially in Mexico, India, China and the American Great Plains — a small crop still, but a real one, and the leaf remains a daily green across the tropics.
    • Mexico — alegría: popped amaranth bound with honey or syrup into bars and skulls for the Day of the Dead, sold by street vendors everywhere; the grain also still goes into tamales and atole in the villages that never stopped growing it.
    • Peru and the Andes — kiwicha, popped for breakfast cereals and street snacks, ground into flour, and brewed into drinks; a grain of the high valleys, grown where maize gives up.
    • India — the seed as rajgira, "king seed," and ramdana, "seed given by God": because it is not a true grain, its flour is permitted in Hindu fasting food, and it is rolled into laddus and flatbreads through the festival calendar. The leaves, chaulai, are stir-fried with spices as an everyday green.
    • China — xian cai (A. tricolor), stir-fried or in soups; the red-centred forms bleed their colour into the cooking liquid and tint the broth pink.
    • The Caribbean — callaloo: in Jamaica the word names the amaranth green itself, steamed with onion, thyme and pepper. In Trinidad the same word names a different dish built on taro leaves — one word, two plants, and the difference matters in a market.
    • Greece — vlita (A. blitum), wild and garden amaranth boiled and dressed with lemon and olive oil, a standard plate of summer greens.
    • East and West Africa — leaf amaranth as an everyday potherb: mchicha in Swahili-speaking East Africa, cooked with onion and tomato and groundnut, a market green sold in bundles across the region.
    • The grain, uncooked, per 100 g: 371 kcal, protein 13.6 g, fibre 6.7 g, carbohydrate 65.3 g, fat 7.0 g. The minerals are the standouts: iron 7.61 mg — about 42% of the daily value — magnesium 248 mg (about 59%), calcium 159 mg, phosphorus 557 mg, potassium 508 mg, folate 82 µg and manganese 3.33 mg. Cooked, a 100 g serving runs 102 kcal with protein at 3.8 g — the seed takes up about two and a half times its weight in water.
    • The protein is better built than a true grain's. Amaranth protein carries all the essential amino acids, and it is notably richer in lysine — the amino acid wheat, maize and rice run shortest of — which is why the seed keeps being paired with maize in the countries that know both: each covers the other's gap.
    • The seed carries no gluten. That is a plain fact of what the plant is — a broadleaf, not a grass — and it is why amaranth flour and grain appear in gluten-free cooking for people with coeliac disease.
    • The leaves are a second, different food. Raw, per 100 g: 23 kcal, protein 2.5 g, calcium 215 mg, potassium 611 mg, vitamin C 43.3 mg, vitamin A 146 µg, folate 85 µg — and vitamin K at 1,140 µg, among the highest figures for any leafy green, higher than spinach. That last number is worth knowing plainly: people who take warfarin are usually told to keep their vitamin K intake steady rather than letting it swing, and a new habit of large daily servings of these leaves would swing it.
    • The leaves also carry oxalates, as spinach does, and amaranth greens are traditionally cooked, not eaten in large raw piles. Cooking is the custom everywhere the leaf is a staple.
    • The famous modern claim — that amaranth lowers cholesterol — has been tested in people, and it failed its best test. In a double-blind trial, 22 patients with moderately high cholesterol ate a 50 g amaranth snack or a matching corn snack daily for two months: total and LDL cholesterol fell no more on amaranth than on corn, and HDL cholesterol — the fraction usually counted as protective — fell significantly more on amaranth.
