Small trials of amaranth oil alongside a low-fat diet likewise found no cholesterol advantage. A 2019 review of 33 studies summed the record up: in animals the seed often lowers cholesterol; the pilot studies in humans were not convincing. Amaranth is a nutritious food. A cholesterol treatment is not among the things it has been shown to be. Human · small
    • Blood sugar, blood pressure and antioxidant claims rest on laboratory dishes and animal studies — on peptides, squalene and other compounds measured outside a human body. They have not been shown in people. And the seed itself is a starchy food that raises blood sugar the way other grains do; nothing in the human record supports a diabetes claim. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • The oil in the seed is unusually rich in squalene, a compound also taken from shark livers and olives and used in cosmetics and vaccine science. That is chemistry, and it explains research interest in the oil; it is not evidence that eating the grain changes anything in a person's health.
    • When to plant: Sow directly in the ground after the last frost, once the soil has warmed to about 60–65 °F (16–18 °C) or more
    • Sun: Full sun, and soil that drains
    • Soil: Tolerates poor soil and, once established, real drought
    • Spacing: Leaf types stand 6 to 10 inches apart; grain types want 12 to 18 inches
    • When to pick: For greens, begin picking young leaves and stem tips once plants are a foot or so tall; for grain, the crop takes about 90 to 120 days

    Garden notes

    • Amaranth is a warm-season annual, killed by frost and happiest in real heat. It runs on the same photosynthetic system as maize and sorghum — a form of photosynthesis tuned for hot, bright, dry weather — which is why it grows fastest exactly when lettuce and spinach give up.
    • Sow directly in the ground after the last frost, once the soil has warmed to about 60–65 °F (16–18 °C) or more; there is no prize for earliness, and seed sown into warm soil catches up fast. The seed is tiny, about a millimetre across: sow it barely covered, an eighth to a quarter inch deep, mixed with a little dry sand if that helps spread it evenly. It germinates in about a week in warm soil. In short-season gardens it can be started indoors four to six weeks before the last frost and set out once nights are warm.
    • Full sun, and soil that drains. Amaranth tolerates poor soil and, once established, real drought; it is one of the few vegetables that can be left to a hot dry week without sulking. Go easy on nitrogen fertiliser for the grain types — rich feeding grows leaves at the expense of seed heads. For leaf growing, richer soil and closer spacing are the point, and both are fine.
    • Thin without mercy; crowded plants make small heads. Leaf types stand 6 to 10 inches apart; grain types want 12 to 18 inches, and they use the room — expect 4 to 7 ft of plant, with flower heads in crimson, gold, green or bronze from midsummer until frost.
    • For greens, begin picking young leaves and stem tips once plants are a foot or so tall, about a month from sowing; pinching the tip keeps a plant bushy and delays flowering. For grain, the crop takes about 90 to 120 days.
    • Harvesting the grain is the fiddly part, and it is mostly timing. The seeds ripen unevenly along a head and shed as they ripen, so test by rubbing a head between your palms over a bowl: when seeds fall freely, cut the heads into a bag or over a sheet. Birds find ripening heads as reliably as people do, which argues for cutting a little early and often. Dry the cut heads indoors for another week or two, rub the seed out, and winnow it — pour it slowly from one container to another in front of a fan or in a light breeze, and the chaff blows off. A single plant can carry tens of thousands of seeds, so two or three plants are a household crop.
    • The seed needs no hulling and no washing: there is no inedible husk to remove and no bitter coating of the kind quinoa carries. It cooks in about 20 minutes into a soft porridge, grinds into flour, and pops in a hot dry pan like miniature popcorn.
    • One honest warning: amaranth self-seeds freely. A bed left to ripen will plant next year's bed, and the seedlings come up in paths and neighbouring rows. Many gardeners count that a gift; anyone who does not should cut the heads before they shed. Its wild pigweed cousins are among the most troublesome weeds in farming, and garden amaranth keeps the family habit of showing up uninvited — grow it where that is welcome.

    Propagation

    Saving seed is easy and keeping it pure is not. Amaranth is wind-pollinated and varieties cross freely, so grow one variety in a season if the seed is to come true; cleaned seed keeps three to five years in a cool, dry jar.

    Safety

    • The leaves carry vitamin K at 1,140 µg per 100 g — among the highest figures for any leafy green, higher than spinach. People who take warfarin are usually told to keep their vitamin K intake steady rather than letting it swing, and a new habit of large daily servings of these leaves would swing it.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: amaranth grain, uncooked and cooked, and amaranth leaves, raw — the nutrition figures
    • Sauer (1967) — The grain amaranths and their relatives: a survey of their history and classification — domestication, the Aztec crop, and the plant's spread
    • National Research Council (1984) — Amaranth: Modern Prospects for an Ancient Crop — the revival assessment, tribute and ceremony history, and the crop's prospects
    • Chávez-Jáuregui et al. (2010) — Effects of defatted amaranth snacks on lipid metabolism of patients with moderate hypercholesterolemia — the double-blind trial: no significant LDL benefit, HDL reduced
    • Baraniak & Kania-Dobrowolska (2019) — Amaranth as a potential dietary adjunct of lifestyle modification to improve cardiovascular risk profile — the review of the cholesterol, blood-sugar and blood-pressure evidence, animal against human

    Bleeding Heart

    Lamprocapnos spectabilis

    Ornamental

    Bleeding heart is a shade perennial from the cool woodlands of northeast Asia, grown for one thing above all: arching stems hung with pink heart-shaped flowers, each with a white drop beneath, like a row of little hearts on a string. The flowers open in late spring, the ferny leaves die back in the heat of summer, and the plant sleeps underground until the next spring. Its botanical name changed in living memory — gardeners still sell it as Dicentra spectabilis, but botanists moved it in 1997 to a genus of its own, Lamprocapnos, where it is the only species. One warning cannot wait: every part of this plant is poisonous. The sap irritates the skin, and eating the leaves or roots can bring vomiting, confusion and worse. Never eat any part of it, and keep it away from small children and pets.

    Cultivars

    The plain species is the pink and white one: bright pink outer petals with white inner drops, on green ferny leaves, about 60 to 120 cm tall.

    'Alba'

    The white form. Every flower is white, stem and all, on the same ferny leaves. It has the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

    'Valentine' ('Hordival')

    The red form. Deep cherry-red outer petals with white inner drops, on burgundy stems, with new leaves flushed pinkish-red before they turn green. It has the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

    'Gold Heart'

    The gold-leaved form. Bright golden-yellow leaves with the usual pink and white flowers, on red stems, to about 60 cm tall. It came from Hadspen Garden in England in 1997.

    'Ruby Gold'

    Golden-yellow foliage, with red outer petals flushed orange and small inner white ones, on a clump-forming perennial to about 90 cm tall.

    'White Gold' ('Tndicwg')

    Bright yellow foliage, with white outer petals and small inner ones, on a clump-forming perennial to about 90 cm tall.

    'Yellow Leaf'

    Bright yellow foliage, with bright pink outer petals and small inner white ones, on a clump-forming perennial to about 90 cm tall.

    'Cupid'

    Palish green foliage, with pale shell-pink outer petals and small white inner ones, on a clump-forming perennial to about 90 cm tall.

    Two names that look like cultivars of this plant are not. 'Luxuriant' and 'Sulfur Hearts' are hybrids of the North American Dicentra species, not forms of Lamprocapnos spectabilis, and they do not belong in this list.

    • Bleeding heart is a plant of the cool, moist woodlands of northeast Asia. It grows wild in northeast China — the provinces of Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang — and on the Korean Peninsula, in dappled shade and in rock crevices in the mountains. It has been grown in gardens across northeast Asia for so long, in Siberia and Japan as well as China and Korea, that no one can now say exactly where it is wild and where it was planted.
    • The names tell the story of the flower. Lamprocapnos is Greek for bright or shining smoke; spectabilis means spectacular, showy, worth seeing. The old name, Dicentra, means two spurs, for the two spurs on the flower. The common name comes from the shape itself: a pink heart with a white drop hanging beneath it, as if the heart were bleeding. Pull the two pink outer petals apart and the white inner petals show a shape gardeners called a lady in a bath.
    • In China the plant is called hébāo mǔdān, purse peony, because each flower looks like a little embroidered purse hanging on a bush with peony-like leaves. In Korea it is geum nang hwa, gold bag flower, for the same reason. In Japan it is taitsurisō, sea bream fishing rod, because the row of flowers looks like little fish hanging from a rod. The purse names are lucky names, tied to the New Year.
    • A Chinese legend tells how the purse peony came to be. A girl named Si Jun waited for a soldier love who had gone to war beyond the Great Wall. Each month she embroidered a purse for him and hung it on the peony outside her window, until the bush was covered in so many little purses that bees and butterflies tried to pollinate them, believing them real flowers. At last the immortals rewarded her patience by turning the purse-covered peony into a new plant, with leaves like a peony and flowers shaped like bridal purses. To this day a gift of purse peonies is a love token in China, much as a red rose is in Europe. The tale is a legend, not a fact.
    • The plant reached Western gardens through China. It was first brought to England in 1810 and died out, then brought again in 1846 by the Scottish plant hunter Robert Fortune, who found it growing in the Grotto Garden on the island of Chusan and bought it from a nursery in Shanghai. He sent it to the Royal Horticultural Society, and it flowered in England in May 1847. Fortune wrote that the mandarins of northern China grew it with pride in their "little fairy gardens". By 1852 it was growing in North America and across Europe, and it has been a cottage-garden favourite ever since.
    • In Traditional Chinese Medicine the root is the part used: taken by mouth for sores and stomach pain, and laid on the skin for bruises and swellings. The old books describe it as pungent, bitter and warm, and say it moves the blood and clears "wind". The Lingnan Medicine Collection of 1949 records it for dispersing blood, clearing sores, and settling pain. That is tradition, not tested proof — no trial has ever tested the root — and the same plant that supplies the root is poisonous if the dose is wrong, so the use stands as history, not as advice.
    • Two things it is not. The North American bleeding hearts, still in the genus Dicentra, are different plants — same family, different genus — and nothing told of this one belongs to them. And it is not a food plant. One plant database lists the young leaves as cooked food, but a Korean family was poisoned in 2015 after the leaves were eaten by mistake, and the plant's own chemistry says the risk is real. The leaves are not food.
    • The honest size of it first. There are no human trials of bleeding heart for anything, and no animal trial that shows a benefit in people. What exists is the traditional root use and laboratory work.
    • The root is used in Traditional Chinese Medicine for sores, stomach pain, bruises and swellings, and to move the blood. That is a long-standing traditional use, recorded in the books, and it is the whole of the evidence. No trial has tested whether it works, and the plant is poisonous. The root use is tradition, not proof. Traditional use
    • Extracts of the root and herb killed cancer cells in dishes, in four human cancer cell lines tested in the laboratory, and the plant's alkaloids were measured in the same study. Dishes are not people. Nothing about that says the plant treats cancer, and it is not a reason to take it. Laboratory
    • Safety, plainly, because with this plant the safety is the point. Every part is poisonous — leaves, stems, flowers, roots and sap. The plant carries isoquinoline alkaloids, including protopine and sanguinarine: about 0.17% of the dry weight above ground and 0.25% in the roots. The sap can irritate the skin, leaving a tingling, prickling feeling. Eating the leaves can bring vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion and irritability. A large amount can bring breathing failure and heart paralysis. In 2015 in Korea, four people fell ill half an hour after a meal in which bleeding heart leaves had been added by mistake, thinking they were radish leaves — dizziness, a dry mouth, a racing heart, confusion — and one man, who had eaten the most, needed hospital care. Small children and pets are at the greatest risk, because a small body takes a smaller amount to harm. Germany named bleeding heart its Poisonous Plant of the Year in 2017, to warn gardeners of exactly this risk. Anyone who eats any part of it should call a poison control centre straight away.
    • Environment: Zones 3 to 9. Hardy to at least −20 °C.
    • Sun: Part shade. Full sun only in a cool, moist place.
    • Soil: Moist, rich, well-drained soil, slightly acid, about pH 5.5 to 6.5.
    • Size: About 60 to 120 cm tall and 45 cm wide.
    • Flowers: Flowers late spring into early summer. Dies back in summer heat and drought.

    Garden notes

    • Plant it where it will not be disturbed. The roots are fleshy and brittle, and the plant resents being moved once it is settled — a clump can sit in the same spot for years without needing dividing. Mark the place, because the plant vanishes in summer and a spade can find it by accident.
    • Keep the ground moist and rich. In a hot, dry summer the leaves yellow and the plant goes dormant early — that is its nature, not a failure, and it returns the next spring. Aphids, slugs and snails sometimes feed on the leaves.
    • A late frost can catch the soft spring growth, so a sheltered spot suits it best.

    Propagation

    Grow it from seed sown while fresh, from root cuttings 7 to 10 cm long taken in spring in sandy soil, or by dividing a clump in late autumn or early spring. The seeds come in long pods with a pale, fatty attachment that ants carry away.

    Safety

    • Every part is poisonous — leaves, stems, flowers, roots and sap. The plant carries isoquinoline alkaloids, including protopine and sanguinarine: about 0.17% of the dry weight above ground and 0.25% in the roots. The sap can irritate the skin, leaving a tingling, prickling feeling. Eating the leaves can bring vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion and irritability. A large amount can bring breathing failure and heart paralysis.
    • In 2015 in Korea, four people fell ill half an hour after a meal in which bleeding heart leaves had been added by mistake, thinking they were radish leaves — dizziness, a dry mouth, a racing heart, confusion — and one man, who had eaten the most, needed hospital care. Small children and pets are at the greatest risk, because a small body takes a smaller amount to harm. Germany named bleeding heart its Poisonous Plant of the Year in 2017, to warn gardeners of exactly this risk. Anyone who eats any part of it should call a poison control centre straight away.

    Sources

    • Tebbit, Lidén & Zetterlund (2008) — Bleeding Hearts, Corydalis and their relatives (Timber Press) — the plant's story, names and garden history
    • Fukuhara (1997) — the revision that moved the plant from Dicentra to its own genus Lamprocapnos
    • Jeong et al. (2015) — anticholinergic syndrome after eating bleeding heart leaves (Clinical Toxicology) — the 2015 Korean poisoning case
    • Royal Horticultural Society — Lamprocapnos spectabilis plant finder — the cultivars and their Awards of Garden Merit
    • Plants For A Future — Dicentra spectabilis — growing facts, hardiness to −20 °C, and the cooked-leaves note
    • North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Lamprocapnos spectabilis — the poppy family, the native range, and the shady woodland home
    • HortTechnology (2012) — Bleeding Heart: A Review for Growers — the plant's history, culture and propagation
    • Israilov et al. (1984) — the alkaloids of Dicentra (Chemistry of Natural Compounds) — protopine, sanguinarine and the rest, with the amounts measured
    • Botanischer Sondergarten Wandsbek (2017) — Bleeding Heart named Poisonous Plant of the Year in Germany

    Lemon

    Citrus × limon

    Culinary

    Immune HealthUrinary HealthVitamin C

    FreshCooked

    The sourest fruit in the kitchen, and one of the most useful. A lemon is not a wild species at all — it is a hybrid, born from a cross between a citron and a bitter orange, and it exists only because people carried it, grafted it and planted it wherever the winters were kind. Almost nothing of it is wasted: the juice seasons food and drink, the zest carries the scent, the peel gives an oil used in polish and perfume, and even the leaves are cooked in one corner of Spain. It is also the fruit that beat scurvy — and then, through a swap nobody checked, briefly lost to it again.

    Cultivars

    'Eureka'

    The supermarket lemon of the world. It began in 1858 in Los Angeles, from seed of an Italian lemon planted there, and it still defines what most people picture: oval, bright yellow, a small nipple at the end, juicy and sharply sour, with few seeds. The tree is nearly thornless, grows fast, and in a kind climate flowers and fruits almost all year round, so 'Eureka' is picked in every month. It is also tender: of the common lemons it minds cold the most.

    'Lisbon'

    'Eureka's' close rival, and the other lemon in the shops. It came from Portugal, reached California by way of Australia in the 1870s, and in the fruit the two are hard to tell apart: the same size, the same sharp juice. The differences are in the tree — 'Lisbon' is thorny, dense and hardier, shrugging off both heat and a degree or two more cold, and it carries its main crop in winter and spring, with the fruit sheltered inside the canopy.

    'Meyer'

    The sweet one, and it is not a true lemon: it is a different cross, a lemon crossed with a mandarin, which is why it tastes the way it does. Frank N. Meyer, a plant explorer for the US Department of Agriculture, brought it from China in 1908, where it was grown as a potted house plant. Rounder than a true lemon, with thin, smooth skin ripening to deep yellow-orange, a scent almost like blossom, and juice that is sweet-tart rather than sour. Cooks prize it for desserts and preserves; gardeners prize the tree, which is smaller, hardier and made for a pot. Because the skin is thin it ships badly, so it stays a home and market-garden fruit.

    'Femminello'

    Italy's lemon, the main kind of Sicily and the Amalfi coast, grown there for centuries. A family of closely related forms rather than one single tree, picked in several flushes through the year — the tree flowers again and again, so fruit is gathered in nearly every season, the winter pick being the most prized. The giant, fragrant lemons of the Amalfi terraces belong to this group.

    'Fino' and 'Verna'

    Spain's pair, from the lemon country around Murcia. 'Fino' (also called 'Primofiori', "first flowers") is the early lemon, smooth-skinned and juicy, picked from autumn into winter. 'Verna' is the late one, thick-skinned and large, picked in spring and summer when the others are done — between them they keep Spanish lemons coming most of the year.

    'Ponderosa'

    The giant, and a lemon–citron cross, grown mostly as a curiosity and a pot plant. The fruit can reach grapefruit size, with very thick, bumpy skin and seedy, mild juice. A few fruits go a long way; most people grow it for the spectacle.

    Variegated Pink ('Pink Eureka')

    A sport of 'Eureka' found in a California garden in the 1930s: green-and-cream striped leaves, striped young fruit that ripens yellow, and flesh with a blush of pink. The juice runs clear; the pink is in the flesh, not the glass.

    • Lemons were never found wild. Genetic studies show the lemon is a cross between the citron — a big, thick-skinned, fragrant fruit grown more for its rind than its juice — and the bitter (sour) orange, which is itself a cross between a pummelo and a mandarin. So three old citrus kinds stand behind every lemon. The cross is thought to have happened in the country between north-eastern India, northern Burma and southern China, where all the parent kinds grew.
    • The citron travelled west first, reaching the Mediterranean in ancient times. The lemon followed much later, spreading west with Arab traders and farmers in the centuries around the year 1000, and taking root in Sicily and Spain, where Arab growers were masters of irrigation. By the 1100s Arab farming writers in Seville were describing how to grow it. From Spain and Italy it moved across Europe — a luxury for a long time, grown in glass orangeries by the rich of cold countries, who kept potted trees under cover all winter for a few fruits and the scent of the blossom.
    • The name came along the same road: from the Arabic laymūn and Persian līmūn, through the Old French limon, into English as "lemon" by the 1400s.
    • Columbus carried citrus seed to the Americas on his second voyage in 1493, and lemons were planted in the Spanish colonies as soon as there were settlements to plant them in. Wherever the climate matched the Mediterranean — California, South Africa, Australia, Chile — the lemon made itself at home.
    • Then comes the scurvy story, and it is worth telling at its true shape, because the lemon is usually given the wrong part in it. In May 1747, aboard HMS Salisbury, the Scottish naval surgeon James Lind took twelve sailors sick with scurvy and fed six pairs six different remedies. The pair given two oranges and one lemon a day recovered in about six days — one was fit for duty, the other nearly so — while the rest barely improved. Lind published the result in 1753, in A Treatise of the Scurvy. It still took until 1795 for the Royal Navy to order a daily ration of lemon juice for every sailor. When it did, scurvy — a disease that had killed sailors in their thousands — all but vanished from the fleet.
    • In 1860 the Navy switched its contract from Mediterranean lemons to limes grown in Britain's own West Indian colonies. The reasons were practical: the limes were cheaper, they were British-grown, and they tasted even sourer — and sourness was wrongly taken to be the measure of the medicine, because nobody yet knew what in the juice actually worked. The truth is that limes carry only about half the vitamin C of lemons, and the juice, pressed, stored and shipped for months, lost still more of its strength on the way. Scurvy crept back on long voyages and polar expeditions, in men drinking their ration faithfully. British sailors were nicknamed "limeys" after the lime juice — the weaker fruit is the one the name remembers. Vitamin C itself was not identified until 1932; only then could anyone measure what Lind's sailors had proved by getting well.
    • Around the Mediterranean and across Asia, the tree was used as medicine as well as food — the juice for fevers and sore throats, the fruit in Ayurvedic practice in India for the digestion, the peel and oil in household remedies of every kind. Those uses are history; the tested evidence is a separate matter.
    • In India, strings of lemons and green chillies — nimbu-mirchi — were hung over doorways and shopfronts, and still are, to turn away Alakshmi, the bringer of misfortune, and to keep a household from the evil eye. The lemon was thought to soak up bad luck the way it soaks up bad smells. It is a story people lived by, part of the plant's real history.
    • Sicily and the Amalfi Coast, Italy — the lemon as a landscape. On Amalfi the trees climb stone terraces built up the cliffs over centuries, trained on chestnut-wood frames, and the fruit — huge, thick-skinned, intensely scented — goes into salads eaten as a dish in their own right, into granita, and into limoncello, the sweet lemon liqueur made by steeping zest in spirit, which the coast has produced since the early 1900s by the usual account. Sicily's lemons were once so valuable that the trade in them — and in the citric acid drawn from their juice — was a serious business, fought over and taxed.
    • Spain — one of the world's great lemon exporters, centred on Murcia and Alicante, and home to a use of the leaf found almost nowhere else: paparajotes, fresh lemon leaves dipped in a sweet batter, fried, and dusted with sugar and cinnamon — the leaf gives the scent and is not itself eaten, peeled away like a bay leaf. It is the Murcian sweet above all others.
    • Morocco and North Africa — the preserved lemon: whole lemons packed in salt and their own juice and left for weeks until the peel turns soft, silky and intensely flavoured, the sharpness gone. Cut into tagines and salads, the peel is the part that matters — a way of keeping the harvest, invented long before cold storage, that became a flavour in its own right.
    • India — lemons and their close kin are everyday and sacred at once: squeezed over dals and chaat, pickled whole in salt and spice, offered in temples, and strung with chillies over doorways in the nimbu-mirchi strings told in the history above.
    • Menton, France — a town that built its name on the fruit: its lemons, sheltered by the hills behind the Riviera, were famous across Europe, and since 1934 Menton has held a Fête du Citron each winter, building vast sculptures from lemons and oranges — the fruit as civic pride.
    • California and Arizona — the lemon's second great home: 'Eureka' was born in Los Angeles, the desert valleys around Yuma and the Coachella grow winter lemons in irrigated sun, and between them the United States eats fresh lemons in every month of the year.
    • Mexico — one honest confusion worth clearing: in Mexico the word limón on a menu usually means the lime, not this fruit — the true lemon is limón amarillo, "the yellow limón," and is the rarer of the two at table.

    Craft

    • The peel gives an oil used in furniture polish, cleaning and perfume, and the juice was the historic source of citric acid.
    • Lemon flesh, per 100 g: 29 kcal, carbohydrate 9.3 g, sugars just 2.5 g, fibre 2.8 g, protein 1.1 g. The standout is vitamin C at 53 mg — about 59% of the daily value — with a little potassium (138 mg) and calcium (26 mg) besides. Now the honest part: nobody eats lemon by the 100 grams. One whole lemon gives about 31 mg of vitamin C, roughly a third of a day's need, and the juice alone carries less than the flesh — 38.7 mg per 100 g — and almost no fibre. Lemon is a seasoning with a real vitamin in it, not a fruit you eat for bulk nutrition.
    • Vitamin C and scurvy are the one proven medical chapter, and it is nutrition, not magic: the body cannot make vitamin C, and without any for a month or two the gums bleed, old wounds reopen and scurvy sets in. Lind's sailors recovered because the fruit replaced what their diet lacked. Anyone eating fruit and vegetables regularly gets enough; the lemon's glory is historical, and it is glory enough.
    • The vitamin C does one more everyday job that is solidly established: it helps the body absorb iron from plant foods — beans, lentils, leafy greens — when they are eaten at the same meal. A squeeze of lemon over a bowl of lentils or a plate of greens is not a garnish; it genuinely helps the iron in them get used. That is ordinary nutrition science, and it is one of the best reasons the fruit sits on the table.
    • Kidney stones, stated at the evidence's real strength — which is small and mixed. Lemon juice is rich in citric acid (about 5 g in 100 ml of juice, the richest of the common citrus juices), and citrate in the urine helps stop calcium stones forming. In two small studies of people who form calcium stones and pass too little citrate, drinking lemonade made from about 120 ml (4 oz) of lemon juice in 2 litres of water raised their urinary citrate a good deal (Seltzer et al. 1996; Kang et al. 2007, where the stone-forming rate also fell, though not by enough to be sure it was not chance). A third small study, a head-to-head crossover against the standard drug potassium citrate, found lemonade did not significantly raise citrate or urine pH, though it did help patients drink more fluid (Koff et al. 2007). The fair summary: lemonade is a reasonable food-level support that some doctors suggest alongside treatment; the proven treatment for low citrate is potassium citrate; and no one should treat stones with lemon juice instead of seeing a doctor. Human · small
    • The teeth pay for the acid, and this is a caution, not a benefit: straight lemon juice sits at about pH 2, and sipped often — lemon water all day, juice sucked from the wedge — it softens and wears tooth enamel, which does not grow back. Dilute it, drink it rather than sipping it for hours, rinse with plain water afterwards, and wait a while before brushing.
    • One folk practice needs the same plain treatment: lemon juice was rubbed on skin and hair to lighten them, and it still is. On skin it is a hazard as much as a cosmetic — citrus juice on skin followed by strong sun can raise a blistering, staining rash in some people. It is part of the plant's history; it is not recommended.
    • Lemon water does not "detox" anything. The liver and kidneys do that work, and no study shows lemon water helping them do it.
    • When to plant: Plant in spring, after the last frost, so the tree settles before its first winter
    • Sun: Full sun — six to eight hours at the least, more for fruit
    • Soil: Must drain freely; slightly acid soil suits them (about pH 5.5–6.5)
    • Environment: Outdoors year-round in USDA zones 9–11; fruit is damaged by a few hours around −2 °C (28 °F)
    • Spacing: Plant standard trees 4–6 m (12–20 ft) apart, and one tree is enough — lemons are self-fertile
    • When to pick: Fully yellow, heavy for its size, the skin beginning to give a little under the thumb

    Garden notes

    • First, what it is: a small evergreen tree, 3–6 m (10–20 ft) tall left to itself, with glossy oval leaves, purple-tinged flower buds opening to white, sweet-scented blossom, and thorns on most kinds — 'Eureka' has few, 'Lisbon' plenty. It can carry flowers, green fruit and ripe fruit all at the same time, which is why a healthy tree in a warm place is never quite out of season.
    • Cold is the limit, plainly: of the common citrus, the lemon is among the most tender. Fruit is damaged by a few hours around −2 °C (28 °F), and hard freezes injure or kill the wood. Outdoors year-round it belongs in USDA zones 9–11; in zone 8 only 'Meyer', in a sheltered spot, with protection on cold nights. Plant in spring, after the last frost, so the tree settles before its first winter.
    • Sun and soil: full sun — six to eight hours at the least, more for fruit. The soil must drain freely; lemons rot at the root in ground that stays wet, and root rot in soggy soil kills more home trees than cold does. Slightly acid soil suits them (about pH 5.5–6.5), and they are hungry feeders — a citrus feed, little and often through the growing season, keeps the leaves deep green.
    • Water: deep and regular, then let the surface dry — evenly moist, never soggy, and more often in pots and in heat. A mulch over the roots helps, kept clear of the trunk.
    • Space: plant standard trees 4–6 m (12–20 ft) apart, and one tree is enough — lemons are self-fertile and set fruit without a partner.
    • Picking is the reverse of the pineapple's rule: a lemon does finish ripening its colour on the tree and does not sweeten after picking, so pick by ripeness, not by the calendar — fully yellow, heavy for its size, the skin beginning to give a little under the thumb. The tree is its own store cupboard: ripe fruit holds on the branch for weeks without spoiling, so pick as you need. Cut or twist the fruit off with a stub of stem; torn skin invites rot. 'Eureka' and 'Femminello' pick across most of the year; 'Lisbon' and 'Fino' are winter-into-spring fruit; 'Verna' carries the late spring and summer.
    • In a pot: this is where the lemon has lived for centuries — the orangeries of Europe were built for it. A grafted 'Meyer' or 'Eureka' in a big pot of gritty, free-draining compost, in the sunniest place you have, moved under cover before the first frost and back out after the last, will flower and fruit where no outdoor tree could live. Expect a smaller tree, 1–2 m, and pick the fruit the same way.

    Propagation

    Buy a grafted tree. Lemons are grown by grafting a named variety onto seedling roots, so the fruit is true to its name and the tree fruits young — a grafted tree can bear in two to three years. A tree from a pip is a gamble and a long wait, though as a house plant it asks little.

    Safety

    • Straight lemon juice sits at about pH 2, and sipped often it softens and wears tooth enamel, which does not grow back. Dilute it, drink it rather than sipping it for hours, rinse with plain water afterwards, and wait a while before brushing.
    • Citrus juice on skin followed by strong sun can raise a blistering, staining rash in some people — lemon juice rubbed on skin to lighten it is a hazard as much as a cosmetic, and it is not recommended.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: lemons, raw, without peel, and lemon juice, raw — the nutrition figures
    • Curk et al. (2015) — new insights on limes and lemons origin from nuclear and cytoplasmic markers — the citron × sour orange parentage, and Meyer's different cross
    • Lind (1753) — A Treatise of the Scurvy — the 1747 trial aboard HMS Salisbury and its result
    • Seltzer et al. (1996) — dietary manipulation with lemonade to treat hypocitraturic calcium nephrolithiasis — urinary citrate more than doubled in 12 patients
    • Kang et al. (2007) — long-term lemonade-based dietary manipulation in patients with hypocitraturic nephrolithiasis — citrate rose; the stone-rate fall was not significant
    • Koff et al. (2007) — comparison between lemonade and potassium citrate in kidney stone patients — lemonade did not significantly raise citrate or pH; the drug did

    Lemongrass

    Cymbopogon citratus

    Culinary

    FreshCookedDried

    Lemongrass is a tall tropical grass that smells strongly of lemon without having any lemon in it. The scent is a compound called citral, and it lives above all in the swollen, pale base of the stalk — the part cooks bruise, slice and pound into the soups, curries and marinades of Southeast Asia. The stalk usually flavours the dish and is lifted out before eating; the long leaves are the tea part, fresh or dried. Its botanical nickname, West Indian lemongrass, points the wrong way: the plant is from the island world of Southeast Asia, and the name only records that it was planted early and widely in the Caribbean, where it is still called fever grass. One separation worth making at the start: this is not the citronella of mosquito candles. That is a different grass in the same family of scented grasses, grown for its oil, and nobody cooks with it.

    Cultivars

    "Variety" for lemongrass means species: two different grasses share the name, and two more cousins are worth separating from both, because they are not food at all. The species are told apart by origin, use and scent, because unlabelled photographs cannot honestly separate one scented grass from another.

    West Indian lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus)

    The world's kitchen lemongrass: the fresh stalk of Thai, Vietnamese, Malaysian and Indonesian cooking. Despite the name it is Southeast Asian. It almost never flowers and is grown from divisions of the clump. Its oil carries more myrcene than its cousin's, which rounds the scent — and also makes the oil keep less well, one reason the oil trade prefers the other species.

    East Indian lemongrass (Cymbopogon flexuosus)

    The oil plant, native to India and grown across India, Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Thailand, where it is also called Cochin grass or Malabar grass. Most lemongrass oil in world trade is distilled from this species; its oil runs about 75–85% citral. Unlike its cousin it grows readily from seed, and Indian growers have bred named varieties for oil yield. In India it is a medicine and perfume crop first; the cooking there leans on C. citratus, and in much of India even that is more a tea and remedy plant than a kitchen spice.

    Citronella grasses (Cymbopogon nardus and Cymbopogon winterianus)

    Not this plant, and not food. These two cousins are grown for citronella oil, the sharp lemon scent of mosquito candles and repellent sprays. The muddle is old and even official: the US Department of Agriculture files lemongrass itself under the name "lemon grass (citronella)". They are relatives, nothing more — citronella grass is never eaten, and its oil is not a flavouring.

    Palmarosa (Cymbopogon martini)

    One more cousin, completing the set: an Indian grass grown for a rose-scented oil that goes into soaps and perfumes. Not a kitchen plant either.

    • Where lemongrass began cannot be pointed to exactly. It is known only from cultivation — nobody has ever found it truly wild — and the likeliest home is Malesia, the island region of Malaysia and Indonesia, where it has been grown for centuries. Its local names map its home ground: serai and sereh in Malaysia and Indonesia, tanglad in the Philippines, takhrai in Thailand, sả in Vietnam.
    • The genus name is Greek and slightly unfair to the plant: Cymbopogon joins kymbe, a boat, and pogon, a beard, for the boat-shaped husks around its flower clusters — a sight most growers never see, because garden lemongrass almost never flowers.
    • In India's Ayurvedic medicine it was a standing remedy for fevers, troubled digestion and nervous complaints, and lemon-scented waters made from it were written about in India centuries ago. In Chinese medicine it was used for colds, headache, stomach-ache and rheumatic pain. Across Southeast Asia the tea of the leaves was a household answer to stomach ache and fever. Those uses are history; the tested evidence is a separate matter.
    • The plant travelled with trade and planting, and after the First World War it was taken up on a large scale in Central and South America, and later in Madagascar and Africa. In Brazil it became capim-limão and capim-santo, one of the country's most popular herbal teas, drunk in the evening as a calming tea under the name abafado. In the Caribbean it settled in as fever grass, the tea given for fevers and colds; in West Africa it became a common tea on the same terms.
    • Thailand — takhrai: stalks bruised whole into tom yum and tom kha soups and lifted out at the table, and pounded into the curry pastes, where the stalk is cut fine enough to disappear into the paste.
    • Vietnam — sả: minced into marinades for grilled meats, stirred through lemongrass chicken and beef, and simmered in curries in the south.
    • Cambodia — lemongrass is the backbone of kroeung, the pounded paste of lemongrass with galangal, turmeric, garlic and lime leaf that stands under a large share of the country's cooking.
    • Indonesia and Malaysia — serai and sereh: through rendang, laksa, sambals and satay marinades. In Java the plant is so much a household fixture that it is planted in nearly every home garden.
    • The Philippines — tanglad: in chicken tinola, in the marinade for grilled chicken inasal, and in the teapot as a household tea.
    • India — the oil species' home, and a tea country for this one: in Maharashtra lemongrass is boiled into gavati chaha, "grass tea", and the leaf goes into masala chai blends in the west of the country.
    • Brazil — capim-limão, capim-santo: the abafado, a covered-steeped evening tea taken to calm and to settle the stomach — the tradition the 1986 study tested — and a cold drink of the leaves blended with lime.
    • The Caribbean — fever grass: the tea of the plant given for fevers, colds and stomach trouble, a household remedy across the islands, under the name its West Indian title came from.
    • West Africa — a common tea in Nigeria and Ghana, drunk for fever and as an everyday drink, in the same household pattern as the Caribbean's.

    Craft

    • The oil made the plant an industry as well as a food. Distilled from the leaves, it went into soaps, perfumes and cosmetics, and its citral became a starting material for making ionones — compounds that smell of violets — for the perfume trade. Beekeepers found a use of their own: citral and geraniol, two of the oil's compounds, are also in the scent honeybees themselves use to call the colony together, so a little lemongrass oil in an empty hive box can draw in a passing swarm looking for a home.
    • By the numbers first. Raw lemongrass, per 100 g: 99 kcal, carbohydrate 25.3 g, protein 1.82 g. Its mineral figures are striking on paper — manganese at 5.24 mg, more than twice the whole day's value; iron at 8.17 mg, about 45% of the day's value; potassium at 723 mg, about 15% — with useful calcium, magnesium, zinc and folate besides. Its vitamin C is low, 2.6 mg: for all the lemon smell, it is not a lemon in nutrition. Then the honest scale, which matters more for this grass than for most foods: nobody eats 100 g of lemongrass. A stalk or two flavours a whole pot of soup and usually leaves the pot before the bowl; even sliced fine into a salad it is a few grams. The numbers describe the plant. What a serving delivers is the flavour — which is the real food value of this grass.
    • The lemon scent is citral, a pair of near-identical compounds that make up roughly three quarters of the plant's essential oil — and the oil is only a small part of the plant. In laboratory dishes citral kills microbes, and it has killed cancer cells in dishes too. So have a great many substances that do nothing of the kind in a body. There is no human evidence that eating or drinking lemongrass treats any infection or any cancer. Lab studies
    • Cholesterol is the plant's most repeated claim, and its whole human evidence is one small study from 1989. Twenty-two people with high cholesterol took capsules of the concentrated oil — 140 mg a day — for ninety days. There was no dummy-capsule group to compare against. Eight of the twenty-two saw their cholesterol fall; fourteen saw nothing; and in those who responded, levels rose again once the oil stopped. The study was never repeated to a modern standard, and later work is in rats, at doses nobody eats. Interesting, and unproven: no cholesterol benefit follows, and the oil capsules of that study are not the food in any case. Human · small
    • Blood pressure has been tested in people a few times, always small and always short. In the largest test, 105 healthy adults drank tea made from 2, 4 or 8 grams of leaf daily for a month, with no comparison group; their readings eased down a little, and they passed more water — the tea is a mild diuretic, as tradition always said. A review of all the human and animal work, published in 2022, concluded that the effect looks real but small, that the studies are still preliminary, and that the safety picture is not fully mapped — the same work notes that lemongrass can slow the heart rate. The plain verdict: a hint, not a treatment. Lemongrass tea is not a substitute for blood-pressure medicine, and anyone whose pressure is treated should mention a daily-tea habit to their clinician, since the two could add together. Human · small
    • The calming claim has been tested properly, and it did not hold. Brazil's evening abafado was put to fifty healthy volunteers under double-blind conditions — half the cups lemongrass, half a dummy tea — and it made no difference to how fast people fell asleep, how well they slept, or what they remembered of their dreams. Eighteen anxious volunteers, tested the same way, were no calmer for it. The same study found the tea harmless over two weeks of daily drinking, which is worth having on record. The concentrated oil does calm mice in laboratory tests; mice and oil are not people and tea. One small study of the smell itself found that volunteers who breathed the aroma during a stressful test said they felt calmer, though their body measures did not change. The calming reputation is history; as a benefit, it was tested and not confirmed. Human trials
    • Blood-building claims cut both ways, and they stay unsettled because they are. In one study of 105 volunteers, a month of daily lemongrass tea raised haemoglobin and red-cell counts. In a smaller study, young women drinking the tea twice a day for sixty days saw their haemoglobin slip slightly instead. Two small studies pointing in opposite directions settle nothing: lemongrass tea is not an anaemia treatment, and it is not shown to be a blood thinner either. Human · small
    • Safety, plainly. In cooking amounts this is a safe, ordinary food eaten by millions daily. The concentrated oil is a different thing from the plant: it can irritate skin and stomach, very high doses damaged the liver and stomach lining in rats, and it should not be swallowed as a home remedy. Pregnancy needs one careful line. Lemongrass as a flavouring in food is fine; the concentrated forms — the oil, supplements, and strong medicinal teas taken daily — are best avoided while pregnant. Two of the plant's compounds, citral and myrcene, caused harm to unborn rats at high doses — skeletal problems, and pregnancy loss at the highest doses — and lemongrass has an old reputation for bringing on menstruation. No study has been done in pregnant women, so this is a precaution, stated as a precaution, and it does not extend to a stalk in a soup.
    • When to plant: Plant after all danger of frost, in the warmest, sunniest place you have
    • Sun: Full sun makes thick, strongly scented stalks; shade makes thin, weak-flavoured ones
    • Soil: Rich soil that holds moisture but drains
    • Environment: A true perennial only where winters stay frost-free — about USDA zones 10–11, and it will overwinter in zone 9 with shelter and mulch in a mild year
    • Spacing: Set clumps about 3 ft (90 cm) apart
    • When to pick: When a stalk’s swollen base is about ½ inch (1.25 cm) thick or more, cut it or twist it off at ground level

    Garden notes

    • Lemongrass is a clump-forming perennial grass, about 3–6 ft (0.9–1.8 m) tall where it is happy, a fountain of long, arching, blue-green blades. The leaf edges are sharp enough to nick fingers — handle a big clump with gloves.
    • Plant it after all danger of frost, in the warmest, sunniest place you have. Full sun makes thick, strongly scented stalks; shade makes thin, weak-flavoured ones. Set clumps about 3 ft (90 cm) apart — one warm season makes a wide clump.
    • Soil and water: rich soil that holds moisture but drains. This is a thirsty, hungry grass in the growing season — water it regularly and it grows fast; let it dry out and it sulks; leave it standing in water and the base rots.
    • Cold is the hard limit. Frost blackens the leaves, and a hard freeze kills the clump. It is a true perennial only where winters stay frost-free — about USDA zones 10–11, and it will overwinter in zone 9 with shelter and mulch in a mild year. Everywhere else, grow it as a summer annual and harvest it down before the frost does, or keep it in a pot.
    • In a pot: give it room — at least a 5-gallon pot, 12 inches across or more — in the same rich, drained mix. Bring it indoors before the first frost, to the sunniest window; it rests through winter, looking tired, and grows again when the light returns. A potted clump can be divided each spring, which is how cold-climate growers keep it going year after year.
    • Harvesting the stalk: when a stalk's swollen base is about ½ inch (1.25 cm) thick or more, cut it or twist it off at ground level. Take the outer stalks and leave the centre of the clump growing; a settled clump in a warm summer gives stalks for months. The pale lower 4–6 inches are the cooking part; the tough green top goes to the teapot or the compost. Stalks keep a week or two in the fridge and freeze well, whole or chopped.
    • The leaves are the tea part, fresh or dried, and can be cut a few at a time all season without troubling the clump. And one garden note that belongs to this plant alone: beekeepers set a drop or two of lemongrass oil in an empty hive box in swarm season, because its scent speaks the bees' own language — a swarm looking for a home may move into a box that smells, to them, like bees already live there.

    Propagation

    It almost never flowers in a garden and sets no useful seed, so it is grown from pieces of itself: divide a clump, or root a shop stalk. A fresh stalk with its base intact, stood in a jar of water on a bright sill, roots in a week or two and pots up happily.

    Safety

    • In cooking amounts lemongrass is a safe, ordinary food eaten by millions daily. The concentrated oil is a different thing from the plant: it can irritate skin and stomach, very high doses damaged the liver and stomach lining in rats, and it should not be swallowed as a home remedy.
    • Lemongrass as a flavouring in food is fine in pregnancy, but the concentrated forms — the oil, supplements, and strong medicinal teas taken daily — are best avoided while pregnant. Two of the plant’s compounds, citral and myrcene, caused harm to unborn rats at high doses, and lemongrass has an old reputation for bringing on menstruation. No study has been done in pregnant women, so this is a precaution, and it does not extend to a stalk in a soup.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: lemon grass (citronella), raw — the nutrition figures
    • Elson et al. (1989) — lemongrass oil and serum cholesterol in 22 people with high cholesterol — the one human cholesterol study, uncontrolled
    • Leite et al. (1986) — Pharmacology of lemongrass III: the abafado tea tested in healthy volunteers — no hypnotic or calming effect found
    • Ekpenyong et al. (2015) — lemongrass tea and blood measures in 105 volunteers — haemoglobin and red-cell counts rose
    • Ekpenyong et al. (2016) — lemongrass tea and blood-pressure indices in healthy adults — small decreases, no comparison group
    • Silva & Bárbara (2022) — Exploring the anti-hypertensive potential of lemongrass: a comprehensive review — the blood-pressure evidence weighed, and found preliminary
    • Goes et al. (2015) — inhaled lemongrass aroma and anxiety in volunteers under stress — one small study
    • Nogueira et al. (1995) — the embryofetal toxicity of citral in rats — the basis of the pregnancy caution
    • Paumgartten et al. (1998) — myrcene and pregnancy in rats — harm only at very high doses
    • Plant Resources of South-East Asia (1999) — PROSEA No. 19, Essential-oil plants: Cymbopogon citratus — origin, names, spread and traditional uses

    Sweet Almond Bush

    Aloysia virgata

    Ornamental

    Sweet almond bush is a fast-growing shrub from northern Argentina, and its whole point is its smell. From midsummer into fall it carries long, drooping spikes of tiny white flowers, and on a warm evening one plant can perfume a whole garden — sweet, like almond and vanilla. The flowers draw bees, butterflies, hummingbirds and moths by the dozen. This is not the almond tree, and it grows no almonds. Its name comes from the scent of its flowers alone. It is a garden plant for warm places, not a food plant, and nothing of it is eaten.

    Cultivars

    Sweet almond bush has no named garden cultivars — none at all in the nursery trade. It is sold and grown as the plain species.

    Dwarf Sweet Almond

    A smaller selection of the same plant, kept tidy for a patio or a small garden, but it carries no cultivar name — it is a nursery’s selection, not a named variety.

    var. virgata and var. platyphylla

    Two botanical varieties, told apart by botanists from the shape of the leaves: var. virgata, the narrow-leaved form, and var. platyphylla, the broad-leaved form. The broad-leaved form is the one in the South American folk record and the one in the mouse study. The difference is a botanist’s distinction, not a gardener’s choice, and no named garden form of either of them exists.

    • Sweet almond bush is a South American plant through and through. It is native to northern Argentina, and grows from central Argentina up through Paraguay, Bolivia, Brazil and Peru, in open woodland and along forest edges. In the wild it is a woody shrub, often leggy, with stiff, slightly weeping branches. Gardeners in warm countries — Florida, Texas, California, Singapore — grow it as a large shrub or a small tree, and in 2008 it was named one of Florida's Plants of the Year. Its other names are sweet almond verbena, incense bush, white almond bush and tree verbena.
    • The name tells two small stories. The genus Aloysia honours Queen Maria Luisa of Spain, wife of King Charles IV, and the species name virgata means "with straight slender twigs," for the plant's long, wand-like flowering stems. It is a cousin of lemon verbena, Aloysia citrodora — but where lemon verbena's scent sits in its leaves, sweet almond bush's scent sits in its flowers.
    • In South America the broad-leaved form of the plant, var. platyphylla, is a folk medicine plant, known there as niño rupá guasú or salvia guasú. In Bolivia, Paraguay and Argentina it has been used as a carminative, to settle wind; as a diaphoretic, to bring on sweating; as a stimulant and a tonic; as a stomachic, for the stomach; against catarrh, the running nose and chest of a cold; and against rheumatism, the aching joints. That is the folk record, told as tradition — none of it has been tested in people.
    • Other folk uses are recorded in the same part of the world. The juice squeezed from the leaves has been put on the skin for skin troubles. The roots have been dried and powdered and used to make a fermented drink. The flowers have been used as an ingredient in perfumes, and the wood for walking sticks. These are recorded uses, not advice, and the plant is not eaten as food.
    • The scent is the reason the plant travelled. The flowers are small and plain to look at — white, bell-shaped, with four ruffled lobes — but their perfume carries across a yard, strongest in the late afternoon and evening, and the plant blooms in flushes from late spring to frost where it is warm. One plant can fill a garden with the smell of almond and vanilla, and the flowers are a steady source of nectar for butterflies and bees through the summer and fall.
    • What is in the plant, first. The leaves and young stems hold a scented oil, and its main parts are three scented compounds — beta-caryophyllene, germacrene D and bicyclogermacrene — with smaller amounts of sabinene and delta-elemene. The flowers carry the almond-vanilla perfume. The oil has been analysed, not tested as a medicine.
    • The one tested finding is small, and it belongs to mice, not to people. Two compounds were isolated from the broad-leaved form of the plant, var. platyphylla, and given by injection to mice. Both compounds acted on the same docking site in the brain that calming medicines use — the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor — and one of them made the mice behave more calmly in maze tests, spending more time in the open and lit-up parts of the maze. That is a real finding in animals, of two isolated compounds given by injection. It is not a finding about the plant as a tea, a sniff of the flowers, or a medicine for people, and no human trial of any kind exists. Animal studies
    • The laboratory work is laboratory work. The plant's oil has been tested against germs in dishes, and it slowed the growth of common germs such as Staphylococcus aureus and E. coli. That shows what the oil does in a dish, not what the plant does in a person. Lab studies
    • The folk uses — for wind, sweating, the stomach, colds and aching joints — are tradition, not tested proof. No trial has tested the plant itself in people for any of them.
    • Safety, plainly. The plant can cause allergic dermatitis — an itchy skin rash — in sensitive people, so handle it with care if your skin reacts to plants. A traditional record says the plant was used to bring on abortion, so it must not be used in pregnancy. It is not a food plant, and no part of it should be eaten or brewed as a tea. No drug interactions have been documented; none should be invented from the animal work.
    • Size: 5 to 15 feet tall and 3 to 8 feet wide, fast — it reaches its full size in three to five years
    • Environment: USDA zones 8 to 11; a hard freeze cuts it back to the ground, and it regrows from the base in spring. It stands cold down to about 15 °F (−9 °C).
    • Sun: Full sun — the flowers and the scent are both weaker in shade
    • Soil: Loamy, well-drained soil, around pH 5.6 to 7.8
    • Water: Once settled it is drought-tough and asks for moderate to low water

    Garden notes

    • Be honest about the size before anything else. Sweet almond bush is a big shrub, not a small one. In warm ground it grows 5 to 15 feet tall and 3 to 8 feet wide, fast — it reaches its full size in three to five years. It can be trained as a small tree with a single trunk, or kept pruned to a smaller shrub, but it is not a plant for a small bed, and it needs room to arch.
    • Climate: the shrub is a plant for warm places — the equivalent of USDA zones 8 to 11. It is frost-tender: a hard freeze cuts it back to the ground, and it regrows from the base in spring. It stands cold down to about 15 °F (−9 °C). In northern Florida it freezes back in winter and regrows as a 3- to 4-foot shrub; where winters stay mild it keeps its leaves all year.
    • Sun and soil: it wants full sun — the flowers and the scent are both weaker in shade. It likes a loamy, well-drained soil, around pH 5.6 to 7.8, and once settled it is drought-tough and asks for moderate to low water. Wet ground that stays soggy is the one thing it dislikes.
    • It blooms on new growth, so prune it hard in late winter or early spring to keep it full and low, and trim it after each flush of flowers — it regrows fast and blooms again within weeks. A light trim a few times a year keeps it from going leggy.
    • The flowers are small and white, bell-shaped with four ruffled lobes, carried in drooping spikes about 20 cm (8 inches) long at the tips of the stems. They open from midsummer into fall, and in warm climates from spring right through to frost. The leaves are oval with toothed edges, arranged in opposite pairs, slightly glossy and rough to the touch. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants, so a single shrub may carry only one kind. The fruit is a small, round, brown, dry capsule of no garden interest.

    Propagation

    Grow it from cuttings taken in spring or early summer, which root easily. Plant it in spring after the last frost.

    Safety

    • The plant can cause allergic dermatitis — an itchy skin rash — in sensitive people, so handle it with care if your skin reacts to plants.
    • A traditional record says the plant was used to bring on abortion, so it must not be used in pregnancy. It is not a food plant, and no part of it should be eaten or brewed as a tea. No drug interactions have been documented.

    Sources

    • Wasowski et al. (2011) — Two diterpenes from Aloysia virgata, calming-like effects in mice (Phytomedicine) — isolated compounds injected into mice, acting on the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor
    • Bassols et al. (1996) — Folk uses of Aloysia virgata in Bolivia, Paraguay and Argentina (as cited in Wasowski et al. 2011) — carminative, diaphoretic, stimulant, stomachic, tonic, anticatarrhal and antirheumatic
    • Ricciardi et al. (2005) — Essential oil of Aloysia virgata var. platyphylla from Corrientes, Argentina (Flavour and Fragrance Journal) — the oil's main parts: beta-caryophyllene, germacrene D and bicyclogermacrene
    • Pérez Zamora et al. (2018) — Essential oils of South American Verbenaceae, antimicrobial activity in dishes (Molecules) — Aloysia virgata oil tested against common germs in the laboratory
    • NParks, Singapore — Aloysia virgata (Flora & Fauna Web) — description, native range, and the recorded folk uses: leaf juice for skin troubles, roots for a fermented drink, flowers in perfumes, wood for walking sticks
    • Chicago Botanic Garden — Sweet almond verbena (Blooms Collection) — the allergic dermatitis caution

    Tamarind

    Tamarindus indica

    Culinary

    Digestive HealthPotassiumMagnesiumIron

    FreshCookedDried

    Tamarind is a great legume tree of the dry tropics whose pods carry one of the world's most travelled flavours: a sticky, sweet-sour pulp that sours curries in India, noodles in Thailand, drinks in Mexico and brown sauces in England. It is the only species in its genus — there is just the one tamarind — and almost everything about it holds a surprise. Its name means "Indian date," yet the tree is African. Its fierce sourness is not vitamin C, of which it has almost none, but tartaric acid, of which it has more than any other fruit. And the tree itself is a giant: slow-growing, wind-firm and able to live for two hundred years, shading a whole village square beneath one crown.

    Cultivars

    The world's tamarinds divide first by taste, and the divide is wide: sour types, grown for cooking, whose pulp is a seasoning; and sweet types, grown above all in Thailand, whose ripe pods are eaten fresh from the shell like a fruit. Pod shape divides them too: the tamarinds of Asia bear longer pods holding six to twelve seeds, while African and West Indian trees bear shorter pods with one to six. Most of the world's trees are unnamed seedlings, each one its own variety; the named varieties below come mostly from Thailand and India, where the tree is bred and selected in earnest.

    Makham Waan

    Thailand's sweet tamarind; the name is simply Thai for "sweet tamarind." Its ripe pulp runs as low as 2–3% acid against sugar up toward 40%, so the pod is cracked and eaten out of hand. Thailand is the sweet-tamarind country, and its sweet types, packed in boxes, are the tamarind most shoppers outside Asia ever meet fresh.

    'Si Thong'

    A named Thai sweet selection, "golden," one of the sweet cultivars behind Thailand's boxed fresh trade.

    'Manila Sweet'

    A sweet selection spread by the United States Department of Agriculture's subtropical research station in Miami, and grown in Florida and the Caribbean — a reminder that the sweet types were worth carrying and naming on the far side of the world too.

    PKM-1

    India's best-known bred variety, a sour cooking type released in 1992 by the horticultural research institute at Periyakulam in Tamil Nadu. It is a clonal selection chosen for the pulp trade: about 39% of the pod is usable pulp, against roughly 28% in local trees; its tartaric acid runs high, at 17.1%; a mature tree crops around 263 kg of pods; and grafted trees bear from their third year, years ahead of seedlings.

    Urigam

    A prized local type from the village of Urigam in Tamil Nadu: long, C-curved, fleshy pods with a high share of pulp, the kind of tree a district is known by.

    Prathisthan

    A high-yielding selection released from the fruit research station at Aurangabad in Maharashtra, sweet-leaning for a cooking type and planted for yield.

    The red types

    In some regions a tamarind with reddish flesh is told apart from the ordinary brown-fleshed kind and rated above it; India's 'Yogeshwari' is a red-pulped selection. The red types are a small, local thread in the story.

    • Tamarind comes from the dry savanna country of tropical Africa, the belt of Sudan and the lands below the Sahara, where it still grows wild. People carried it east to South Asia several thousand years ago, and it was grown in India for so long, and so completely made India's own, that it has often been reported as native there. It is not: India is its second home, and the deeper one in the kitchen, but Africa is its first.
    • The name tells that story by getting it backwards. The Persians and Arabs met the fruit through India and called the dried pulp tamr hindi — "Indian date," for the date-like look of the sticky brown flesh. Medieval writers shortened it to tamar indi; Marco Polo wrote of tamarandi; Latin made it Tamarindus, and Linnaeus added indica. So both the common name and the scientific one honour the wrong continent. The fruit itself was old in the wider world long before: it was known to the ancient Egyptians, and to the Greeks by the 4th century BCE.
    • In India the tree became imli, a fixture of the dry country — planted along roadsides and around villages and tanks, its shade public property. In Ayurveda the pulp, amlika, was classed as sour and was used above all as a gentle mover of the bowels and a cooling drink in fevers. That same pairing — the bowels and the fever drink — comes back in system after system that had little contact with one another: in traditional practice across Africa, in Thai medicine, in Filipino folk practice, and later in the Caribbean. The pulp was taken seriously enough as medicine to be official in the British and American pharmacopoeias into the modern era, imported in quantity for the drug trade. Those uses are history; the tested evidence is a separate matter.
    • The Spanish and Portuguese carried tamarind across the Atlantic in the 1500s, to Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, where it took root in the ground and in the cooking at once — Mexico plants more tamarind than almost anywhere outside India. From there and from Asia it spread through every warm country; one of the first tamarind trees in Hawaii was planted in 1797. Few food plants on earth are grown in so many places, and in most of them it is simply assumed to be local.
    • The tree also gathered meanings, and they are beliefs people held. Some African peoples held the tamarind sacred. In Burma — Myanmar — the tree was held to be the dwelling-place of the rain god, and some people believed it raised the temperature of the air around it. In parts of India a tamarind tree might be married, in ceremony, to a mango tree before the mango's fruits were eaten. And a caution ran through several countries that it was harmful to sleep beneath a tamarind or to tie a horse under one — a belief that probably grew from something real: the tree's fallen leaves are acid enough to mark and eat into cloth left damp beneath it. Few plants survive in its deep, acid shade, which can only have fed the stories.
    • India — the world's largest producer, and the pulp's deepest home. As imli it sours sambar, rasam and a hundred chutneys; the sweet imli chutney is spooned over chaat; tender green pods are cooked as a seasoning with rice, fish and meat; young leaves and flowers are cooked as greens and go into curries; and the pulp is pressed into salted blocks that keep without cold storage and travel to every market in the country.
    • Thailand — makham is the sour backbone of pad thai in its genuine form, and of soups and dipping sauces besides; and Thailand's sweet types are eaten fresh from the pod, a second life for the same species in the same country.
    • The Philippines — sampalok is the souring soul of sinigang, the sour soup that is close to a national dish, and the young leaves go into Filipino cooking too.
    • Indonesia and Malaysia — asam jawa, "Javanese sour," sours sayur asem, the sour vegetable soup, and sambals across the Malay world.
    • Mexico — tamarindo everywhere: agua de tamarindo, the sweet-sour drink sold in every market and bottled carbonated; and dulces de tamarindo, the pulp worked with sugar and chilli into candies — the candies whose lead history is told plainly in Health Benefits.
    • The Caribbean — tamarind balls, the pulp rolled with sugar into a sweetmeat, are a fixture of Jamaica, Cuba and the Dominican Republic; and in Puerto Rico street vendors pour tamarind syrup over cones of shaved ice.
    • Egypt and the Levant — tamr hindi, under its old Arabic name, is the dark, sweet-sour drink of Ramadan evenings, served cold when the fast breaks.
    • West Africa — in the tree's homeland the pulp is soaked into drinks and stirred into porridges and sauces, the oldest pattern of all.
    • Madagascar — the tamarind's most devoted eaters are not people: ring-tailed lemurs eat the fruit and leaves so heavily that, where the trees stand, tamarind can supply as much as half their food across the year.
    • England — the traveller in the sauce bottle. Worcestershire sauce, made since the 1830s, and HP Sauce both carry tamarind as their sour backbone — for generations of people in Britain and America, their first tamarind came in a brown sauce, unnamed.

    Craft

    • The seed — nothing is wasted for long. The kernels are roasted and eaten as a snack in India, and ground as a coffee substitute in Thailand; in hard times the seeds have served as emergency food. The kernel's gum is the industrial story: powdered, it sizes cotton and jute yarn — India's textile industry adopted it as more efficient and cheaper than cornstarch — and it thickens foods and medicines, the same seed gum that made the eye drops in Health Benefits.
    • The rest of the tree — the pulp, mixed with sea water, polishes silver, copper and brass bright, the acid doing the work; in West Africa an infusion of the whole pods goes into the dye bath for goat hides, and the pulp serves as a fixative with turmeric and annatto in dyeing. The dark heartwood is very hard, heavy, strong and insect-resistant, prized for furniture, panelling, tool handles and the gears of mills, and at times sold under the name "Madeira mahogany"; and the wood burns with an intense heat, yielding a charcoal once used in making gunpowder.
    • Start with the pulp's own numbers, USDA figures for raw tamarind pulp, per 100 g: 239 kcal, carbohydrate 62.5 g, sugars 38.8 g, fibre 5.1 g, protein 2.8 g, fat 0.6 g. The mineral figures are the strong ones: potassium 628 mg, about 13% of the day's need; magnesium 92 mg, about 22%; iron 2.8 mg, about 16%; and thiamin at about a third of the day. Calcium is modest at 74 mg. Two honesty notes belong with the numbers. A hundred grams is a real sitting of sweet tamarind eaten from the pod, but in cooking the pulp is a flavouring — the spoonful that sours a whole pot of curry is a small fraction of these figures. And the pulp is more than a third sugar by weight before anyone adds more: it is a sweet food that tastes sour, not a sour food that happens to be sweet.
    • The sourness itself deserves a plain explanation, because it is not what most people assume. Tamarind's vitamin C is 3.5 mg per 100 g — almost none. The bite is tartaric acid, the same acid that gives grapes their sharpness, and tamarind pulp is the richest natural source of it known: about 8–18% of the dried pulp is tartaric acid, roughly half of it held as its potassium salt — cream of tartar is that same salt, refined. Sweet types are the exception that proves the rule: their acid falls as low as 2–3% while their sugar climbs toward 40%, which is why they can be eaten like dates while the sour types cannot be eaten like anything but a seasoning.
    • Digestion, and the famous laxative reputation, stated at its true strength. The pulp's fibre is real — 5.1 g per 100 g — and fibre is fibre. The bowel-moving tradition is centuries old on four continents. But it has never been properly tested in people: no clinical trial of tamarind for constipation exists, and the one controlled test on record, in mice, for a Caribbean folk-remedy documentation programme, found no significant speeding of the gut. So the honest line is this: tamarind is a pleasant, fibre-carrying food that many people find gently helpful, and it is not a proven remedy. That is all the evidence supports.
    • Cholesterol, blood sugar and weight — the claims most often made for tamarind — have been tested, and the tests disagree in an instructive way. One small study in Bangladesh (Iftekhar et al., 2006; 30 people) reported that dried pulp lowered total and LDL cholesterol and diastolic blood pressure. The stronger test came later: a randomized controlled trial in Iran (Asgary et al., 2020) gave 40 overweight and obese adults 20 g of tamarind pulp a day for six weeks and found no significant effect, against the control group, on body weight, waist size, cholesterol, blood sugar or blood pressure. Studies in animals report anti-diabetic and antioxidant effects; those are animal and laboratory results, not findings in people. On the best evidence available, tamarind does not lower cholesterol or blood sugar, and it is not a slimming food. It is a food with a good mineral profile, and that is a good enough story. Human trials
    • One narrow finding is real and worth its line. In parts of India where drinking water carries too much fluoride — which damages teeth and bones over years — a small randomized diet study (Khandare et al., 2002) gave schoolboys 10 g of tamarind with lunch for 18 days and found significantly more fluoride leaving the body in their urine; the researchers concluded tamarind is likely to help delay fluorosis, the fluoride condition. That is a specific result for a specific problem — not a general claim. Human · small
    • The seed has one tested use of its own, and it is not a food use. Eye drops made from the seed's gum — tamarind seed polysaccharide, a xyloglucan whose structure resembles the mucin that coats the eye — were tested against standard hyaluronic-acid drops in 30 people with dry eye over 90 days (Rolando & Valente, 2007) and gave at least equal relief, and better relief of some symptoms. It is a medicine manufactured from the seed, not a benefit of eating tamarind — eating the fruit does nothing for the eyes. Human · small
    • A caution about aspirin. In a small study in healthy volunteers, tamarind taken with aspirin increased how much aspirin the body absorbed (Mustapha et al., 1996), and drug-interaction references rate the pairing "be cautious"; the same may hold for ibuprofen. Ordinary amounts of tamarind in food are food. But anyone who takes aspirin or similar painkillers daily should treat concentrated tamarind supplements as something to raise with their clinician first. Human · small
    • And the caution this fruit is genuinely known for: lead. The same acid that makes tamarind useful in the kitchen pulls lead out of lead-based glazes. In the 1990s, tamarind candy jam packed in lead-glazed ceramic jars from Mexico poisoned children in California — blood lead levels in the reported families reached the 50s, in units where anything above a few points is a concern — and California health authorities embargoed those products from 1993 while US regulators moved to keep them out. Testing of imported tamarind suckers in Oklahoma found more than half above the Food and Drug Administration's level of concern, with lead-based inks in the wrappers a second route (Lynch et al., 2000), and the Centers for Disease Control reported further California cases tied to tamarind candy in 2002. The fruit is not the poison; the glaze and the inks were. The plain rule that follows: do not keep or cook sour tamarind in old, traditional or unmarked glazed pottery, and be careful with imported tamarind candy sold in little ceramic jars — above all for children.
    • When to plant: Nursery trees go out at the start of the rainy season
    • Sun: Full sun and room — a roadside, field and village-square tree, not a patio tree
    • Soil: Tolerates almost anything — deep alluvial soil, rocky ground, porous limestone — and withstands salt spray close to the seashore
    • Environment: A tree of the tropics and warm subtropics; a hard freeze can kill even a large, established tree
    • Spacing: 10–20 m (33–65 ft) apart — the crown of a mature tree asks for every metre of it
    • When to pick: In Florida, Central America and the West Indies the flowers open in summer and ripening runs from April into June; a pod takes about eight months from setting to ripe

    Garden notes

    • First, what it is: a slow-growing, long-lived evergreen of the dry tropics — 24–30 m (80–100 ft) tall under good conditions, with a crown spreading to about 12 m (40 ft) and a massive, rough-barked trunk. The foliage is a mass of fine, feathery leaves, each a row of small leaflets that fold at night. The small flowers are yellow streaked with orange or red. The branches are strong and supple, and the tree is famously wind-resistant. It bears abundantly to an age of fifty or sixty years, and may live another hundred and fifty after that: a tamarind is planted for grandchildren.
    • Climate: it is a tree of the tropics and warm subtropics. Young trees must be protected from cold; older trees are hardier than many tropical fruits, but a hard freeze can kill even a large, established tree, as one did in Florida in 1884. It also needs dry weather while the fruit is developing — where rain falls heavily at fruiting time, the tree may grow well and refuse to bear.
    • Soil and site: it tolerates almost anything — deep alluvial soil, rocky ground, porous limestone — and withstands salt spray close to the seashore. A deep taproot makes it steady in drought once established. Give it full sun and room: this is a roadside, field and village-square tree, not a patio tree.
    • Spacing and planting: nursery trees go out at the start of the rainy season, spaced 10–20 m (33–65 ft) apart depending on the soil — the crown of a mature tree asks for every metre of it.
    • Season and harvest: in Florida, Central America and the West Indies the flowers open in summer, the green fruit hangs through winter, and ripening runs from April into June; a pod takes about eight months from setting to ripe. Ripe pods may be left on the tree for as long as six months, drying where they hang — a ripe pod is known by its light weight, its hollow sound when tapped, and a shell that cracks under gentle pressure. Pick by clipping the stalk, or shake the branches and gather what falls; the pods are never knocked down with poles, which would wound the leaves and flowers coming on. A mature tree gives 150–225 kg (330–500 lb) of pods in a year, of which the pulp is roughly a third to a half.

    Propagation
