    the seed keeps its life for months and germinates in about a week, and most tamarinds in the world are seedlings. But seedlings vary, and they are slow to fruit — bearing from the fourth or fifth year in the quickest reports, and delayed ten to fourteen years in parts of India. Named varieties are grafted or budded onto seedling roots, and a grafted PKM-1 bears from about its third year. In cold climates the tree can be kept young in a large pot under glass for its foliage, but fruit from a potted tamarind is not a realistic hope.

    Safety

    • Tamarind taken with aspirin increases how much aspirin the body absorbs, and drug-interaction references rate the pairing "be cautious" — the same may hold for ibuprofen. Ordinary amounts of tamarind in food are food, but anyone who takes aspirin or similar painkillers daily should raise concentrated tamarind supplements with their clinician first.
    • The acid in tamarind pulls lead out of lead-based glazes, and tamarind candy in lead-glazed ceramic jars poisoned children in California in the 1990s. Do not keep or cook sour tamarind in old, traditional or unmarked glazed pottery, and be careful with imported tamarind candy sold in little ceramic jars — above all for children. The fruit is not the poison; the glaze and the inks were.

    Sources

    • Kumar & Bhattacharya (2008) — tamarind seed: properties, processing and utilization — the kernel gum and the seed industries

    • Asgary et al. (2020) — tamarind fruit in overweight and obese adults: the randomized controlled trial
    • Khandare et al. (2002) — tamarind ingestion and fluoride excretion in schoolchildren
    • Rolando & Valente (2007) — tamarind seed polysaccharide eye drops for dry eye: the clinical study
    • Mustapha et al. (1996) — tamarind increased the absorption of aspirin in healthy volunteers
    • Lynch et al. (2000) — lead-contaminated imported tamarind candy and children's blood lead levels

    Angelica

    Angelica archangelica

    CulinaryMedicinal

    FreshCooked

    The archangel's herb, and the north's own vegetable. Angelica is a towering plant of cold, wet ground — two metres and more of hollow, fluted stem topped in July with great round heads of greenish flowers. In Norway, Iceland and Greenland its young stems were eaten as a vegetable when little else green could be had, its root was one of the most trusted medicines of the northern world, and its name carries a legend of an angel bringing it down against the plague. But angelica keeps dangerous company: it grows in the same wet places, in the same family, as poison hemlock, water hemlock and giant hogweed, and no wild plant of this family should ever be eaten on a resemblance.

    Cultivars

    Angelica is not a plant of many named cultivars — seed is sold as the plain species. One named cultivated form is real, and it is a treasure of the north.

    ‘Vossakvann’

    The angelica of Voss, in western Norway, kept for centuries in the kvanngardar, the small walled angelica gardens beside the farmhouses. Generations of farmers selected it for thick-walled, juicy leaf stalks that are sweeter than the wild plant — half as much sugar again, by measurement — with a finer aroma. It was first described in 1928 and was already disappearing; four original farm strains, from Elgje, Mestad, Markhusteigen and Olde, were saved, and ‘Vossakvann’ now stands on Slow Food's Ark of Taste, the catalogue of endangered heritage foods. It has to be actively selected, generation by generation, or it slides back toward the bitter wild form.

    The wild forms

    The wild plant itself splits into forms. Subsp. archangelica is the inland and mountain form — the more aromatic, with softer stems — and the parent both of ‘Vossakvann’ and of the commercial crop. Subsp. litoralis is the coastal form of the Baltic and North Sea shores, sharper-smelling, with harder stems. A third form, subsp. himalaica, grows at the far eastern end of the range in the Himalayas.

    Other angelicas

    Other angelicas share the name and nothing else: dong quai (Angelica sinensis), the Chinese medicine plant; Korean angelica (A. gigas), grown in gardens for its dark purple stems; wild angelica (A. sylvestris), the common wild species of European wetlands; and American angelica (A. atropurpurea), the tall species of eastern North America. Each is its own plant, with its own uses and its own evidence.

    • Angelica is a plant of the subarctic north: the riverbanks, damp meadows and coasts of Scandinavia, Iceland and the Faroes, across northern Russia to Siberia, with outposts in Greenland and the high valleys of central Europe. It grows only in wet ground — a streamside, a pond edge, a marsh — and it does not travel south willingly; heat and dry soil finish it.
    • It was a food before it was a medicine. From at least the 900s the Norse grew it in gardens: Old Norse hvönn, Norwegian kvann, Icelandic hvönn. A good angelica patch was property worth protecting — the Gulathing law, written down in the 1000s, dealt with the stealing of angelica from another man's garden, and a tenant farmer kept the right to take his angelica plants with him when he moved farms. In Iceland, where almost nothing green and tall would grow, the stems were one of the settlement's few garden vegetables.
    • The Sámi of the far north gathered and grew it as fádnu: the stems were eaten, cooked into reindeer milk to make gompa, a preserved food for the lean months, and the hollow stems were cut into a flute-like instrument. Linnaeus, travelling in Lapland in the 1700s, recorded the reindeer-milk use himself. In Greenland, kuanneq is still gathered and eaten as a green vegetable.
    • The name is a legend in Latin. Archangelica means “of the archangel”: the story told across Europe was that the archangel Michael — in some tellings Raphael, the healer — appeared in a dream and revealed the plant as a defence against the plague. By tradition it flowered around the archangel's old feast day, the 8th of May in the old calendar. The apothecaries called its root radix Sancti Spiritus, the root of the Holy Ghost, and the German name is Engelwurz — angel-root.
    • Through the late Middle Ages it spread south into monastery gardens and the printed herbals, carrying its plague reputation with it. Gerard's Herball praised it against poisons and pestilence, and in the plague centuries the root was chewed, carried and distilled into angelica water, which stood among the preventives published for London in the plague year of 1665. All of that is history, told as history: angelica never cured or prevented plague, and the centuries that trusted it most knew nothing of its real dangers, which are set out in Health Benefits.
    • In 1602, by the town's own tradition, angelica was brought to Niort in western France in a plague year, and the marshes of the Marais Poitevin around it became the plant's great growing ground. The bright green candied stems of Niort made the plant's second career, in confectionery.
    • As a medicine of the north and centre it was a bitter, warming root: teas and tinctures for the stomach, the chest, the nerves and fevers, and a remedy to bring on delayed periods — a use that matters to the safety notes below. Austria's folk record, gathered from thousands of interviews, lists the root taken as tea or tincture for the gut, the chest, the nervous system, fever, infections and flu.
    • The drinks trade carried angelica further than any garden could. Root and seed became a base note of gin, of Chartreuse and Bénédictine, of vermouths and absinthe — an earthy, musky flavour, compared to juniper and to musk, that holds the other aromatics together.
    • Norway and Iceland — kvann and hvönn: stems eaten fresh, cooked, or cooked down with sour fruit; angelica gardens protected by law a thousand years ago; ‘Vossakvann’ still grown around Voss.
    • Greenland and the Sámi north — kuanneq gathered as a green vegetable; angelica cooked into reindeer milk as gompa to keep it through the lean months; hollow stems cut into flutes.
    • France — the Marais Poitevin around Niort grows the candying crop: bright green candied stems, angelica jam and angelica liqueur, a speciality since the 1600s.
    • Britain — candied angelica was the classic green decoration on trifles and cakes, and went into puddings and sweets, well into the 1900s.
    • Austria and Germany — root teas and tinctures in folk medicine for stomach, chest, nerves and fever; the root is still an official drug of the German tradition.
    • The drinks world — root and seed flavour gin, Chartreuse, Bénédictine, vermouth, Dubonnet and absinthe, prized less as a flavour you notice than as the base note that holds the rest together.
    • What is in the root: a rich essential oil — more than 200 compounds have been found in it — and a family of bitter chemicals called coumarins. Among them are the furanocoumarins: bergapten, xanthotoxin, imperatorin and angelicin. These are the compounds behind both the root's traditional uses and its chief danger, because furanocoumarins make skin react violently to sunlight.
    • Digestion — an old, officially recorded use that has never been put to a proper test. Germany's Commission E approved angelica root in 1990 for loss of appetite and mild digestive complaints — mild cramps, a feeling of fullness, and wind — on the strength of its long record of use. The European Scientific Cooperative on Phytotherapy (ESCOP), in its 2021 monograph, lists the same complaints, and bronchitis, and states plainly that no clinical studies of angelica root on its own were available. That is still the position: no trial has ever tested angelica by itself in people, so every benefit attached to it rests on tradition and laboratory work, not on proof in patients. Traditional use
    • The mixture problem: angelica root is one of nine plant extracts in Iberogast (also called STW 5), a German herbal drop for indigestion that has been tested in people, with helpful results for some. A nine-herb mixture cannot show which of its herbs did the work, so none of that result can honestly be given to angelica alone.
    • Europe's medicines regulator took the opposite path to Commission E. The European Medicines Agency never adopted a monograph for angelica root. Its herbal committee examined the furanocoumarins in 2007 and set strict limits on them, and in 2014 it placed angelica root on a short list of herbal substances with serious safety concerns, judging a positive balance of benefit and risk unlikely. Angelica's true official standing is both halves of that record: an approved-by-tradition digestive in the German books, and a flagged safety concern at European level.
    • Laboratory and animal work — real, and no stronger than that. In cell studies, a root extract calmed inflammation signals (Vogl et al., 2013, screening the drugs of Austrian folk medicine); the root oil kills some bacteria and yeasts in dishes, including Clostridioides difficile, a dangerous gut bacterium; and single compounds such as imperatorin have shown effects in animal studies. None of this shows what eating angelica does in a person, and none of it is a reason to take it. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • Dong quai is a different plant. Angelica sinensis, the Chinese relative sold for menopause and menstrual complaints, is another species, with its own evidence and its own risks, assessed separately by the European regulators. Nothing found for dong quai — good or bad — belongs to garden angelica, and the two should never be swapped for one another.
    • Safety — sunlight. Furanocoumarins react with ultraviolet light on the skin: sap, juice or root preparations on skin that then meets sunshine can raise a blistering, burning rash, called phytophotodermatitis. Commission E warned against prolonged sunbathing and intense sun while taking the root. The European Medicines Agency set a very low no-concern level for furanocoumarin intake, advised a sun warning above it, and advised against medicinal use by children and in pregnancy. One more twist: a root attacked by fungi can hold twenty to two hundred times the usual coumarins, which is another reason wild-dug roots are a gamble.
    • Safety — pregnancy and medicines. Angelica was traditionally used to bring on periods, and medicinal amounts are best avoided in pregnancy. In laboratory work, some of its compounds change how the liver handles certain medicines, so concentrated root products sit badly with regular medication unless a clinician says otherwise. Food amounts are a different matter: in the United States, angelica root, seed and their oils are permitted food flavourings, generally recognised as safe at flavouring levels — a seasoning is not a dose.
    • Safety — the look-alikes, at full strength. Angelica shares its wet ground and its carrot family with poison hemlock (Conium maculatum), water hemlock (Cicuta species) and giant hogweed (Heracleum mantegazzianum). Water hemlock is one of the most poisonous plants in the northern world; people have died after eating its roots, mistaking them for something edible. Giant hogweed's sap blisters skin in sunlight far more fiercely than angelica's own. The differences between these plants are real, but they are small, and they are not differences to learn by eating. Angelica should come from a garden or a named, trusted source — never from a waterside plant that merely looks right.
    • When to plant: Sow ripe seed in autumn where the plants are to grow, or in pots stood outdoors over winter — the seed needs cold, and light, before it will stir
    • Sun: Full sun where summers are cool; some shade where they are hot
    • Soil: Deep, rich soil that is never dry
    • Environment: Cool summers — heat and dry soil finish it
    • Planter or ground: Ground — give each plant a metre of room
    • Spacing and depth: A metre apart
    • Water: Never dry — a streamside, a pond edge, the damp end of the garden
    • When to pick: Stems for candying in late spring of the second year, before the flower stem runs up; roots in the old medicine tradition were dug in the autumn of the first year

    Garden notes

    • A biennial, and a giant one. The first year is a rosette of large, bright green, divided leaves. In the second year a fluted, hollow stem rises 1 to 2.5 metres and opens great globular heads of small yellowish-green flowers in July, followed by pale, oblong fruits. After seeding, the plant dies — but let one plant ripen seed each year and the patch renews itself.
    • Give it the north in miniature: cool summers, and soil that is deep, rich and never dry — a streamside, a pond edge, the damp end of the garden. Full sun where summers are cool; some shade where they are hot. It sulks and shrinks in drought and in thin, dry soil.
    • Sow fresh seed, and expect to be patient. Angelica seed loses its life within a few months, so the old way is best: sow ripe seed in autumn where the plants are to grow, or in pots stood outdoors over winter — the seed needs cold, and light, before it will stir. Spring-bought seed is often dead already; buy from a source selling the current year's harvest.
    • Give each plant a metre of room. Stems for candying are cut in late spring of the second year, before the flower stem runs up; roots in the old medicine tradition were dug in the autumn of the first year.
    • Handle it with gloves on bright days. The sap carries the same sun-reactive compounds as the root; brush against a cut plant and then garden on in sunshine and a rash can follow. Wash any skin the sap has touched and keep it out of strong sun for a day or two.
    • Buy named seed or plants of Angelica archangelica from a nursery, and check what comes up. Because the family holds deadly plants that share the same wet ground, seed should never be collected from an unknown waterside umbellifer.

    Propagation

    Sow ripe seed in autumn where the plants are to grow, or in pots stood outdoors over winter — the seed needs cold, and light, before it will stir. Seed loses its life within a few months, so spring-bought seed is often dead already; buy from a source selling the current year's harvest. Let one plant ripen seed each year and the patch renews itself.

    Safety

    • Safety — sunlight. Furanocoumarins react with ultraviolet light on the skin: sap, juice or root preparations on skin that then meets sunshine can raise a blistering, burning rash, called phytophotodermatitis. Commission E warned against prolonged sunbathing and intense sun while taking the root. The European Medicines Agency set a very low no-concern level for furanocoumarin intake, advised a sun warning above it, and advised against medicinal use by children and in pregnancy. One more twist: a root attacked by fungi can hold twenty to two hundred times the usual coumarins, which is another reason wild-dug roots are a gamble.
    • Safety — pregnancy and medicines. Angelica was traditionally used to bring on periods, and medicinal amounts are best avoided in pregnancy. In laboratory work, some of its compounds change how the liver handles certain medicines, so concentrated root products sit badly with regular medication unless a clinician says otherwise. Food amounts are a different matter: in the United States, angelica root, seed and their oils are permitted food flavourings, generally recognised as safe at flavouring levels — a seasoning is not a dose.
    • Safety — the look-alikes, at full strength. Angelica shares its wet ground and its carrot family with poison hemlock (Conium maculatum), water hemlock (Cicuta species) and giant hogweed (Heracleum mantegazzianum). Water hemlock is one of the most poisonous plants in the northern world; people have died after eating its roots, mistaking them for something edible. Giant hogweed's sap blisters skin in sunlight far more fiercely than angelica's own. The differences between these plants are real, but they are small, and they are not differences to learn by eating. Angelica should come from a garden or a named, trusted source — never from a waterside plant that merely looks right.

    Sources

    • Commission E (1990) — German monograph on angelica root: approved for loss of appetite and mild digestive complaints, with a warning against strong sun while taking it
    • ESCOP (2021) — monograph on angelica root (Angelicae radix): digestive complaints and bronchitis listed; no clinical data for single-herb angelica products
    • European Medicines Agency (2007) — HMPC reflection paper on the risks of the furocoumarins contained in preparations of Angelica archangelica
    • European Medicines Agency (2014) — public statement on herbal substances with serious safety concerns: angelica root listed, a positive benefit-risk balance judged unlikely, and no EU monograph adopted
    • Vogl et al. (2013) — Austrian folk medicine, documented from the VOLKSMED database and screened in the laboratory: angelica root for gut, chest, nerves and fever; root extract active in cell tests
    • Teixidor-Toneu et al. (2021) — “Sweetness Beyond Desserts”: the cultural, symbolic and botanical history of angelica in the Nordic region — Norse law, Sámi use, and the road south
    • Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste entry for Angelica ‘Vossakvann’: the Voss cultivar, its four saved farm strains, its sweetness, and its history

    Anise

    Pimpinella anisum

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Digestive Health

    FreshDried

    Anise is a small annual of the carrot family, grown for one thing: a tiny ribbed fruit, sold whole or ground as aniseed, with a sweet, warm flavour almost everyone knows from liquorice sweets — though no liquorice need be anywhere near it. The flavour comes from a compound called anethole, and anethole turns up in three different plants that are constantly confused. Anise is this one: a Mediterranean herb about knee-high, with white umbrella flowers. Star anise is the woody star-shaped fruit of an unrelated Chinese tree. Fennel is a much bigger cousin in the same family, eaten as a vegetable as well as a seed. The three share a flavour molecule, not a family record, and nothing known about one of them is evidence about another. Anise is also among the oldest spices in the world — Egypt was growing it some four thousand years ago.

    Cultivars

    • Anise is not really grown in named cultivars. Seed catalogues sell the species plain, under its own name; the big horticultural references list no cultivars for it, and commercial production around the world still grows landraces — local populations kept and re-sown by farmers — rather than bred, named varieties.
    • What the trade has instead is grading by origin. The old drug and spice trade esteemed Spanish anise — Alicante anise — above all for pharmacy, and handled Turkish, Egyptian, Syrian and Russian anise as distinct grades differing in seed size, colour and oil strength. Turkish anise is the rakı industry's seed; Egyptian anise comes from one of the oldest growing regions of all. These are origins, not varieties: the same species, shaped by place.
    • The variation underneath is real. Germplasm collections — seed-bank samples gathered worldwide and grown side by side — differ in height (roughly 30–90 cm), seed size and oil content, and researchers are only now sorting that variation with an eye to future breeding. For the gardener, the practical choice is fresh seed from a spice-growing origin, not a variety name.
    • Anise comes from the eastern Mediterranean and Southwest Asia, and was first cultivated in Egypt and the Middle East. It has been grown in Egypt for approximately four thousand years, which makes it one of the oldest cultivated spices anywhere. The ancient Egyptian word inst is equated with anise, and the Ebers papyrus, written about 1550 BCE, names it among medicines for complaints of the belly and the teeth.
    • Greece took it up early. Hippocrates, in the fifth century BCE, recommended it for the symptoms of a cold, and Greek cooks and doctors passed it to Rome. The Roman writer Pliny, in the first century CE, reported that the most esteemed anise came from Crete and from Egypt, praised it for sweetening the breath, and recorded anise mixed with wine as a treatment for the bites of asps. Those uses are history, told here as history; what the studies actually support is in Health Benefits.
    • Rome also put it on the table. The Romans baked anise into cakes called mustacae, eaten at the end of feasts and weddings to settle the stomach — the ancestor of a long line of aniseed cakes and seed cakes after big meals. In the King James Bible, anise stands in the tithe list of Matthew 23:23 — “ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin” — a spice valuable enough to be taxed in kind. (Some translations read “dill” for the same Greek word; the two plants were near neighbours in every ancient garden.)
    • In the early Middle Ages Charlemagne ordered anise grown on the imperial farms, and it spread through the monastery gardens of Europe as both spice and medicine. In England it was precious enough to tax: in the early 1300s a duty on anise and other imported spices helped pay for the upkeep of London Bridge.
    • In European and Middle Eastern traditional medicine the seed was a standing household remedy: above all a carminative — a remedy for wind, bloating and colic — and an expectorant, taken to loosen a cough. It was also traditionally given to nursing mothers to bring in the milk. All of that is the traditional record, told as history; the trial evidence, where it exists, is set out separately below.
    • The seed travelled with trade and empire: east into India and Persia, where it entered the Persian medicine tradition, and west with Spain to the Americas, where it took root in Mexican baking and drinking chocolate. Around the Mediterranean it became the flavour of a whole family of drinks — Greek ouzo, Turkish rakı, Arab arak, French pastis, Italian sambuca — most of them turning milky white when water is added, because anethole dissolves in alcohol but not in water.
    • One odd working use: in England, sacks dipped in aniseed oil were dragged behind a horse to lay a scent line for training packs of foxhounds — the “drag hunt” — because hounds follow the smell eagerly. The seed's scent is strong enough to work as a trail.
    • The names: Greek anison became Latin anisum and then anise in English. Pimpinella is said to refer to the plant's two kinds of leaves — round and simple at the base, finely cut higher up — from a Latin word for “twice-feathered.”
    • Greece — ouzo, the anise spirit, distilled with aniseed and drunk with water and meze; anise also scents Greek Easter breads and rusks.
    • Turkey — anason is the soul of rakı, the unsweetened anise spirit drunk diluted until it clouds — “lion's milk” — and Turkey grows anise on a large scale to supply it.
    • The Levant and Egypt — arak, the anise spirit of Lebanon, Syria and Jordan; and in Egypt anise tea, yansoon, is a household drink in its own right, given for colds and stomach upsets for as long as anyone can remember.
    • France — pastis and anisette in the south, anise in the historical absinthe, and aniseed in spiced breads and biscuits.
    • Italy — sambuca, served with three coffee beans; anise in sausages and processed meats, and in the brines of Apulia.
    • Spain — anís de Chinchón, the anise liqueur of the town of Chinchón, with its sweet and dry grades; aniseed through Christmas baking and the Three Kings cake, roscón de reyes.
    • Mexico — bizcochitos, the anise shortbread that became the state cookie of New Mexico, and anise in champurrado and atole de anís, the warm corn-based drinks.
    • The Netherlands — muisjes, “little mice”: sugar-coated aniseeds scattered on rusks to greet a newborn — pink or blue by the baby.
    • India and Pakistan — anise is taken after meals as a digestive, and appears in spice blends; in Indian kitchens it keeps company with fennel, its bigger cousin, and the two are sometimes sold side by side — the seed in the jar still has to be one or the other, and their records are not interchangeable.
    • Peru — anise flavours picarones, the squash-and-sweet-potato doughnuts served in spiced syrup.
    • The seed first, by the numbers. Per 100 g: 337 kcal, protein 17.6 g, fibre 14.6 g, iron 37 mg — about twice the whole day's value — calcium 646 mg, about half the day's value, and potassium 1,441 mg. But a teaspoon of aniseed weighs about 2 g, so in the kitchen the seed is a flavouring, not a mineral source: that teaspoon carries under a milligram of iron. The figures describe the spice honestly; they do not make a serving of it a supplement.
    • The flavour is chemistry. The fruit holds about 1.5–6% essential oil, and 80–95% of that oil is a single compound, trans-anethole — distinctly sweet in itself, about thirteen times sweeter than sugar. Anethole is also the main flavour of fennel seed and of star anise, which is why the three taste alike. It proves nothing else about them: fennel's trial record and star anise's record belong to those plants, not to anise.
    • Digestion is where anise has its real human evidence. In a double-blind trial in Iran (Ghoshegir et al., 2015), 107 adults with functional dyspepsia — the full, uncomfortable, slow digestion after meals for which no disease can be found — took 3 g of anise powder after each meal for four weeks, or a corn-starch dummy powder. On a standard symptom scale the anise group's average score fell from 10.6 to 2.4, while the dummy group's rose; the gap was still there eight weeks after the powder stopped. That is a clear result, and it is also one trial, from one clinic, testing powder — not tea, and not a pinch of spice in a cake. Human · small
    • A second trial tested the oil for irritable bowel syndrome (Mosaffa-Jahromi et al., 2016): 120 patients took enteric-coated capsules of anise oil — capsules made for the study, coated to pass the stomach — or a dummy capsule, or peppermint oil, a standard remedy for the condition. After four weeks, 75% of the anise-oil group were free of symptoms, against 35% on the dummy and 52.5% on peppermint oil. The same research group reported that low mood lifted along with the bowel symptoms in these patients. Both findings stand on this one trial, from one university, and no other group has repeated them yet; home-dosed oil and anise tea are not what was tested. Human · small
    • For wind, bloating and cough, anise also carries an official traditional-use standing. The European Medicines Agency's herbal committee accepts aniseed as a traditional herbal medicine for mild, spasmodic stomach and bowel complaints including bloating and flatulence, and as an expectorant — a remedy that loosens phlegm — in coughs that come with a cold. “Traditional” there is a defined grade: it rests on at least thirty years of documented use and on plausible laboratory effects, and the agency had no clinical trials of anise alone before it when it made the assessment. It is a long record of use, honestly labelled — not proof from trials. Traditional use
    • Menopausal hot flashes have two small trials. In the first (Nahidi et al., 2012), 72 postmenopausal women took capsules of anise extract (330 mg, three times a day) or starch capsules for four weeks; the anise group's hot flashes fell sharply in frequency and severity while the control group's did not change. A second, multicentre trial from the same research circle (Zare et al., 2022) found the same direction of effect over eight weeks, with the benefit partly fading in the month after the capsules stopped. The proposed reason is that anethole acts a little like oestrogen in laboratory and animal work — at high concentrations. Two small trials from one circle of researchers are a promising signal, not a settled treatment. Human · small
    • Two famous claims do not clear the bar. The milk-supply claim — anise tea to bring in a mother's milk — is tradition only: no good human trial has tested it, and the medicines assessment advises against medicinal anise in breastfeeding precisely because the safety data are missing. And the blood-sugar and cholesterol effects sometimes quoted come from experiments in rats and mice; no human trial supports them for people. Animal studies
    • Safety, plainly: in cooking amounts anise is a safe, ordinary food, eaten for centuries. The concentrated oil is a different substance from the spice. The European assessment restricts anise medicines because the oil also contains a little estragole, a compound that caused liver tumours in mice at high doses: anise oil is not for children or adolescents, medicinal use is kept to about two weeks at a time, and swallowing even 1–5 mL of the neat oil has been followed by nausea, vomiting, seizures and fluid on the lungs. Medicinal anise is not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding, for lack of safety data. People allergic to other carrot-family plants — fennel, caraway, celery, coriander, dill — or to anethole itself can react to anise too. And one poisoning story that follows the word “anise” around belongs to a different plant entirely: the seizures reported in babies given “star anise tea” were traced to the toxic Japanese star anise mixed into the supply — a relative of star anise, not of the plant anise.
    • When to plant: Sow direct once all danger of frost has passed and the soil has warmed to about 60 °F (16 °C)
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Light, well-drained soil, around neutral to slightly alkaline (pH roughly 6–7.5)
    • Environment: Needs a long season — about 120 frost-free days to ripen seed
    • Planter or ground: Ground; a deep pot suits a single plant, for the taproot
    • Spacing and depth: About ¼ inch deep; thin to about 6–12 inches apart, in rows roughly 18 inches apart
    • Water: Water young plants evenly; once established, fairly drought-tolerant, but seeds best without stress at flowering
    • When to pick: Cut the heads when the umbels turn grey-brown and the seeds firm and begin to loosen

    Garden notes

    • Anise is a warm-season annual that stands about 60–90 cm (2–3 feet) tall — the sources vary, and landraces run from about 30 to 90 cm — with round, toothed leaves at the base and feathery leaves up the stem, then loose umbrellas of small white flowers in summer. It needs a long season: about 120 frost-free days to ripen seed, so where summers are short it is grown for its leaves, or not at all.
    • Sow it where it is to grow. Anise grows a taproot and hates being moved, so it is sown directly in the bed once all danger of frost has passed and the soil has warmed to about 60 °F (16 °C), about ¼ inch deep. Short-season gardeners can start it in biodegradable pots indoors and plant the whole pot out without disturbing the root.
    • Germination is slow and uneven — one to three weeks — so keep the seedbed evenly moist and be patient. Thin the seedlings to about 6–12 inches apart, in rows roughly 18 inches apart.
    • Sun and soil: full sun, in light, well-drained soil, around neutral to slightly alkaline (pH roughly 6–7.5). A sheltered spot helps: the slender stems can flop in wind, and growing in a block gives them mutual support. Go easy on nitrogen-rich feeding, which pushes leaf at the expense of the aromatic seed.
    • Water young plants evenly; once established, anise is fairly drought-tolerant but seeds best without stress at flowering. The white umbels are good insect flowers, drawing hoverflies and other beneficial insects into the garden.
    • The leaves are edible all season — mild and liquorice-sweet, chopped into salads, cheese spreads and dips — and the green, unripe seeds are a fresh seasoning in their own right while they last.
    • Harvesting the seed is a matter of timing, because the heads ripen unevenly and ripe seed shatters and falls. Watch for the umbels turning grey-brown and the seeds firming and beginning to loosen; cut the heads into a paper bag, dry them thoroughly in a warm, airy place, then rub and shake the seed free.
    • Stored whole, in a jar away from light, aniseed keeps its scent a year or two; grind only what is needed. Let a few ripe heads drop their seed where they grew and the plant may sow next year's crop itself.
    • In a pot: choose a deep one, for the taproot, sow in place, and keep it watered — a single plant in a 10–12 inch pot does best.
    • A caution about identification: anise's family includes deadly plants — poison hemlock carries similar white umbels — so seed is sown from a packet and garden plants are known by their planting, never gathered on a guess from the wild.

    Propagation

    Sow it where it is to grow — anise grows a taproot and hates being moved. Let a few ripe heads drop their seed where they grew and the plant may sow next year's crop itself. Short-season gardeners can start it in biodegradable pots indoors and plant the whole pot out without disturbing the root.

    Safety

    • Safety, plainly: in cooking amounts anise is a safe, ordinary food, eaten for centuries. The concentrated oil is a different substance from the spice. The European assessment restricts anise medicines because the oil also contains a little estragole, a compound that caused liver tumours in mice at high doses: anise oil is not for children or adolescents, medicinal use is kept to about two weeks at a time, and swallowing even 1–5 mL of the neat oil has been followed by nausea, vomiting, seizures and fluid on the lungs. Medicinal anise is not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding, for lack of safety data. People allergic to other carrot-family plants — fennel, caraway, celery, coriander, dill — or to anethole itself can react to anise too. And one poisoning story that follows the word “anise” around belongs to a different plant entirely: the seizures reported in babies given “star anise tea” were traced to the toxic Japanese star anise mixed into the supply — a relative of star anise, not of the plant anise.

    Sources

    • European Medicines Agency, HMPC — Community herbal monographs on Pimpinella anisum L., fructus (aniseed) and aetheroleum (anise oil) — the traditional-use indications, dose limits, estragole cautions and oil safety

    • Mosaffa-Jahromi et al. (2016) — Efficacy and safety of enteric coated capsules of anise oil to treat irritable bowel syndrome (Journal of Ethnopharmacology) — 120 patients, anise oil against placebo and peppermint oil
    • Nahidi et al. (2012) — The effects of Pimpinella anisum on relief and recurrence of menopausal hot flashes (Iranian Journal of Pharmaceutical Research) — 72 women, anise extract capsules
    • Zare et al. (2022) — The effect of Pimpinella anisum on treatment and recurrence of menopausal hot flashes: a randomized, controlled, multicenter, double-blind trial (Shiraz E-Medical Journal) — 72 women
    • Shojaii & Abdollahi Fard (2012) — Review of pharmacological properties and chemical constituents of Pimpinella anisum (ISRN Pharmaceutics) — the traditional Persian medicine record and the plant's chemistry

    Apricot

    Prunus armeniaca

    Culinary

    Vitamin A

    FreshDried

    A small, golden-orange stone fruit on a small tree — kin to the plum, the cherry, the peach and the almond, all of them in the rose family. The skin is smooth and faintly velvety, the flesh sweet and a little tart, and inside sits a hard stone. Apricots are eaten fresh in early summer, but more of the world's crop is dried than eaten fresh: dried, the fruit keeps for months and travels anywhere. Two name warnings before anything else. The Japanese pickled “apricot,” ume, is a different species, Prunus mume — not this fruit. And the soft kernel inside the stone is not a snack to eat freely: it can release cyanide in the body, and the full account of that is in Health Benefits below.

    Cultivars

    ‘Moorpark’

    Raised at Moor Park in Hertfordshire, England, in the 1700s. Large fruit with a rich flavour, long the standard for eating fresh. Zones 5–8; needs about 600–700 hours of winter chill.

    ‘Blenheim’ (also ‘Royal Blenheim’)

    An English kind named for Blenheim Palace, and the apricot that built California's orchards. Superb fresh, and the favourite for drying and canning. The fruit is soft, bruises easily and ripens from the inside out, so it is often picked still showing a green shoulder. Needs about 400–500 hours of chill.

    ‘Tilton’

    A California kind: firm, tangy fruit, the standard for canning and good dried.

    ‘Goldcot’

    Bred in Michigan and released in 1967. One of the cold-hardiest kinds, to zone 4–5, and it blooms later than most, which helps it dodge spring frost.

    ‘Harcot’

    Bred at Harrow in Ontario, Canada. Cold-hardy, sweet-tart, and bred to resist the cracking that splits ripening fruit after rain.

    ‘Tomcot’

    A modern kind: large, early fruit and heavy crops.

    ‘Hacıhaliloğlu’

    The traditional apricot of Malatya, Turkey, grown above all for drying; most of the world's dried apricots start as this fruit.

    • The apricot was first grown from wild trees in Central Asia and China. Studies of the tree's genes point to at least three separate domestications — one in southern Central Asia, around today's Kyrgyzstan, one in northern Central Asia, around Kazakhstan, and one in China. People in China were growing apricots more than 3,000 years ago, by 1000 BC at the latest, and apricot stones have been found at a site at Garni, in Armenia, older than the Bronze Age.
    • From Central Asia the tree travelled west along the Silk Road, through Persia to Armenia and the Mediterranean. The Greeks called it the Armenian apple, and the Romans had it by about 70–60 BC; the Roman writer Pliny called it the Armenian plum. When Linnaeus gave the tree its scientific name in 1753, he called it Prunus armeniaca — the Armenian plum. The name records the road the fruit travelled, not the land it came from.
    • In China the apricot was tied to learning and to medicine. A story in the Zhuangzi, written in the 300s BC, tells of Confucius teaching his students in an apricot grove, and “apricot altar” is still a Chinese phrase for a place of teaching. The physician Dong Feng, who lived around 200–280 AD, was said to refuse payment from the people he cured: anyone healed of a small illness planted one apricot tree, and anyone healed of a serious one planted five. His grove grew into a forest, and “apricot forest” is still a Chinese name for the medical profession itself.
    • The English word tells the fruit's own story. “Apricot” traces back through Arabic al-barqūq to an old Latin word for “early-ripe” — the apricot ripens early, ahead of the peach it resembles.
    • Turkey grows about a fifth of the world's apricots, more than any other country, and most of the world's dried apricots come from one Turkish province, Malatya, where the fruit is spread out to dry in the summer sun. In Armenia the apricot is a national symbol — its colour is the orange band of the Armenian flag — and the duduk, the country's best-known instrument, is carved from apricot wood.
    • Around the world the fruit took root in the kitchen. In the Levant and Egypt, sheets of dried apricot paste are soaked in water to make qamar al-din, a sweet drink tied to Ramadan. Austria's Wachau valley is known for its Marille, folded into jam and into Marillenknödel, apricot dumplings. Hungary makes apricot jam and distils apricots into pálinka, a fruit brandy. Spanish missionaries carried the tree to California, and most of the United States crop is still grown there.
    • The kernels were food too, in careful amounts. Sweet kernels were eaten like almonds in parts of Central Asia, bitter kernels were ground into persipan — a marzipan-like paste — in Europe, and kernel oil was pressed for cooking and for the skin. Those uses were always small-scale, and for good reason: the kernel carries the cyanide risk set out in Health Benefits below.
    • Travellers once told of the Hunza valley, high in the mountains of what is now Pakistan, where apricots are a staple food and people were said to live to very great ages. The stories were never backed by records — the ages were not verified — and they stand as travellers' tales, not as evidence about the fruit.
    • Fresh apricots, per 100 g: 48 kcal, protein 1.4 g, carbohydrate 11.1 g, sugars 9.2 g, fibre 2 g, fat 0.4 g. The standout is vitamin A at 96 µg — about a tenth of a day's needs — with vitamin C at 10 mg and potassium at 259 mg besides. The orange colour is beta-carotene, a pigment the body turns into vitamin A; a fresh apricot carries 1,094 µg of it per 100 g. Vitamin A is needed for normal eyesight and for the immune system to work as it should — that is a fact about the nutrient, at the amount the fruit gives.
    • Dried apricots are the denser second form. Per 100 g: 241 kcal, protein 3.4 g, fibre 7.3 g, sugars 53.4 g, iron 2.66 mg, potassium 1,162 mg and vitamin A at 180 µg — nearly twice the fresh fruit's, because drying takes the water out and leaves everything else behind. The sugar is concentrated too: a handful of dried apricots carries far more sugar than the same weight eaten fresh.
    • The bright orange dried apricots in most shops were treated with sulfur dioxide, a preservative that holds the colour. Fruit dried without it turns dark brown and tastes a little richer; it is the same fruit. Sulfur dioxide is harmless for most people, but a small share of people with asthma — roughly 3 to 10 in every 100 — are sensitive to sulfites and can react with tightened airways. Labels must declare sulfites when they are present above a trace level, so the packet tells you which kind you are buying.
    • The kernel inside the stone holds a compound called amygdalin. When a kernel is chewed and digested, amygdalin breaks down and releases cyanide, a poison. The European Food Safety Authority set the safety limit in 2016 and measured how fast kernels cross it: an adult goes past the limit with less than half of one large kernel, and up to three small kernels is the most an adult should ever eat. For a small child, even one small kernel is too much. The flesh of the fruit is a different matter — eating apricots as fruit carries no risk from amygdalin.
    • The kernel was sold as a cancer treatment, and that claim has been tested and has failed. In the 1970s an extract of apricot kernels was promoted under the names “laetrile” and “vitamin B17.” It is not a vitamin: the body does not need it, and no illness comes from lacking it — the name was invented in the 1950s by the man promoting it. The United States National Cancer Institute sponsored a trial, published in 1982, in which 178 people with cancer were treated with amygdalin. It did not cure, improve or stabilise the cancer in any patient, it did not relieve symptoms, and it did not help anyone live longer — while several patients were poisoned by cyanide, with blood levels approaching the lethal range. A Cochrane review of all the studies, published in 2015, found the claims of benefit were not supported by sound clinical data and called the balance of risk and benefit unambiguously negative. Apricot kernels are not a cancer treatment, and eating them in quantity can poison. Human trials
    • When to plant: Plant a young tree while dormant, in spring — or autumn in mild districts
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Deep, well-drained soil — little tolerance for wet, heavy ground, where the roots rot
    • Environment: Needs winter cold to fruit well — most kinds want 600 to 900 hours below 45 °F (7 °C); the blossom opens very early, and a late frost after it opens can kill the whole year's crop
    • Planter or ground: Ground
    • Spacing and depth: Thin the young fruit to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches along the branch, when it is about the size of a grape
    • Water: In dry summers, water deeply every two or three weeks
    • When to pick: June to August, depending on the district — pick when the fruit is fully coloured and just beginning to soften

    Garden notes

    • The apricot is a small deciduous tree, usually kept to about 12–15 ft in a garden with pruning. Most kinds grow in zones 5–8; the hardiest kinds manage zone 4, and its Siberian and Manchurian kin grow colder still. The tree needs winter cold to fruit well — most kinds want 600 to 900 hours below 45 °F (7 °C) across the winter, though low-chill kinds manage on about 350–400 hours.
    • The great risk is timing. The apricot blooms very early, before almost any other fruit tree, and a late frost after the blossom opens can kill the whole year's crop. In cold districts a crop comes only in some years — in Utah, about three years in five. Planting where cold air can drain away downhill, or on a north-facing slope that holds the blossom back a few days, gives the tree a better chance.
    • Give the tree full sun and deep, well-drained soil. Apricots have little tolerance for wet, heavy ground, where the roots rot.
    • Nearly all apricots are self-fertile: one tree on its own will fruit. A second, different kind nearby usually improves the set.
    • The fruit grows on short spurs — stubby side shoots — on one-year-old wood, and a spur stays productive for about three to five years. Prune in dry summer weather, finishing at least six weeks before the autumn rains: cuts made in wet weather invite two diseases, Eutypa dieback and bacterial canker, that enter through the wounds.
    • Apricot trees set far more fruit than they can ripen. When the young fruit is about the size of a grape, thin it to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches along the branch, or the harvest is a crowd of small fruit and the tree can exhaust itself.
    • In dry summers, water deeply every two or three weeks. Pick up fallen fruit and any dried, mummified fruit left hanging — brown rot, the tree's main fruit disease, overwinters in them.
    • Harvest runs from June to August, depending on the district. Pick when the fruit is fully coloured and just beginning to soften. An apricot softens after picking but gains no sugar, so fruit picked green and hard never ripens properly — the sweetness is made on the tree or not at all.

    Propagation

    Nearly all apricots are self-fertile, so one tree on its own will fruit; a second, different kind nearby usually improves the set. The fruit grows on short spurs on one-year-old wood, and a spur stays productive for about three to five years.

    Safety

    • The kernel inside the stone holds a compound called amygdalin. When a kernel is chewed and digested, amygdalin breaks down and releases cyanide, a poison. The European Food Safety Authority set the safety limit in 2016 and measured how fast kernels cross it: an adult goes past the limit with less than half of one large kernel, and up to three small kernels is the most an adult should ever eat. For a small child, even one small kernel is too much. The flesh of the fruit is a different matter — eating apricots as fruit carries no risk from amygdalin.
    • The kernel was sold as a cancer treatment, and that claim has been tested and has failed. In the 1970s an extract of apricot kernels was promoted under the names “laetrile” and “vitamin B17.” It is not a vitamin: the body does not need it, and no illness comes from lacking it — the name was invented in the 1950s by the man promoting it. The United States National Cancer Institute sponsored a trial, published in 1982, in which 178 people with cancer were treated with amygdalin. It did not cure, improve or stabilise the cancer in any patient, it did not relieve symptoms, and it did not help anyone live longer — while several patients were poisoned by cyanide, with blood levels approaching the lethal range. A Cochrane review of all the studies, published in 2015, found the claims of benefit were not supported by sound clinical data and called the balance of risk and benefit unambiguously negative. Apricot kernels are not a cancer treatment, and eating them in quantity can poison. Human trials

    Ashwagandha

    Withania somnifera

    Medicinal

    Mental HealthSleep

    Dried

    A modest shrub in the nightshade family — kin to the tomato and the potato — with small green bell-shaped flowers and round berries that ripen orange-red inside papery husks. The root is the famous part. Dried and powdered, it has been one of the great tonic herbs of Ayurvedic medicine in India for well over two thousand years, given for strength, for worn nerves and for sleep. In the last twenty years it has also become one of the world's best-selling herbal supplements, sold above all for stress. Unusually for an old remedy, it has been put through proper clinical trials, and the trials support something narrower than the advertising: real but modest help with stress and sleep, from standardised root extracts, taken over weeks. The warnings are part of the plant too, and they are not fine print: never in pregnancy, care with thyroid trouble, and a rare but documented risk to the liver.

    Cultivars

    Ashwagandha's named varieties are farm varieties, bred in India for the weight and quality of the dried root. They are not sold in garden centres, and seed offered to gardeners elsewhere is sold simply as ashwagandha. The names still matter: they show how seriously India takes the crop.

    Nagori

    The old landrace of the Nagaur district of Rajasthan: thick, starchy roots, and the traditional standard of the herb trade long before breeding stations existed.

    Jawahar Asgandh-20 and Jawahar Asgandh-134

    Bred at the agricultural university in Madhya Pradesh, the biggest growing state. JA-134 is short-growing, suits close planting, and is ready to dig in about 180 days.

    Poshita and Rakshita

    Released by CSIR-CIMAP, India's central institute for medicinal and aromatic plants, at Lucknow. Both were bred for high dry-root yield; Rakshita suits both of India's main growing seasons.

    CIMAP-Pratap

    Also from CIMAP, and in comparative trials the highest-yielding of the released varieties for dry root.

    • Ashwagandha grows wild across a wide, dry belt: from southern Europe and the Canary Islands, across North Africa and the Middle East, to India, Sri Lanka and beyond. It is a plant of dry, open, stony ground — roadsides, scrub, overgrazed pasture, the edges of fields. India is its heartland and its farm: the dry districts of Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan grow most of the world's supply, and the root has been traded through Indian herb markets for centuries.
    • The name is Sanskrit and it is a small poem in two halves. Ashva means horse; gandha means smell. The fresh root genuinely smells of horse — and the tradition read a promise into the smell: the old texts held that the root gives the strength and vigour of a horse. The Latin name pulls the other way: somnifera means “sleep-bringing.” Strength and sleep, in one root — the whole of the plant's history runs between those two poles.
    • The Charaka Samhita, the foundational Ayurvedic text compiled roughly two thousand years ago, lists ashwagandha among the balya herbs — the strength-givers — and counts it a rasayana, one of the prized rejuvenating tonics meant to rebuild a worn or wasted body. In Ayurvedic practice the root powder was stirred into warm milk or ghee and given, over months, for weakness and wasting, for children who failed to thrive, for sleeplessness and anxious nerves, for aching joints, and for men's fertility and vigour. It passed into Unani medicine as well, under the name asgandh. All of that is history, told as history; what the studies support is in Health Benefits.
    • Where the plant grows wild in Africa, it had its own local medicine: in southern Africa the roots and leaves were used for fevers, inflammation and as a general tonic, and in parts of the Middle East it was a folk sedative. Its close cousin Withania coagulans — not this species — is the plant famous in India as a vegetable rennet, its berries used to curdle milk for paneer.
    • For most of the twentieth century, ashwagandha stayed inside Indian and Unani practice. Then it rode a word westward: “adaptogen,” coined by Soviet scientists in the 1940s for substances said to help the body withstand stress. The word is a product of that research programme and of the marketing that followed it — it is not a medical diagnosis, and no medicines regulator recognises it as a class of medicine. Under that banner the root became a global supplement in the 2000s and 2010s, farmed as a cash crop across dry central India and sold abroad as capsules of standardised root extract. Two trade extracts, KSM-66 and Sensoril, account for a large share of the market — and of the trials, a fact worth holding in mind when reading the results.
    • What is in the root: the working compounds are the withanolides, a family of steroid-like plant chemicals named after the plant itself. Commercial extracts are standardised to a set strength of withanolides, commonly about 5%. In laboratory dishes and in animals, withanolides touch inflammation and stress-hormone pathways; what they do in people is a separate question, and only the human trials below answer it.
    • Stress — the strongest evidence the plant has. Several randomised trials, all small and all short. In the best-known (Chandrasekhar et al., 2012), 64 adults with chronic stress took 300 mg of root extract twice a day for 60 days; their stress scores fell far more than the placebo group's, and their blood cortisol — the body's main stress hormone, measured, not self-reported — fell 27.9%, against 7.9% on placebo. A second trial (Salve et al., 2019) gave 60 stressed adults 250 mg or 600 mg a day for eight weeks and found the same direction: lower perceived stress and lower cortisol at both doses. The honest frame: the trials run to dozens of people, not hundreds; none runs past ten weeks; most were run in India; and several were funded by the companies that sell the extracts. The effect looks real and modest. Whether it lasts, nobody has measured. Human · small
    • Anxiety is a step weaker. The stress trials measured stress scores in stressed people, which is not the same as treating an anxiety disorder. The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), reviewing the same trials, concludes that some ashwagandha preparations may help with stress, while the evidence for anxiety is unclear.
    • Sleep — a small, real effect. A meta-analysis (Cheah et al., 2021) pooled five placebo-controlled trials with 400 people in all and found a small but genuine improvement in sleep, clearest in people diagnosed with insomnia, at doses of 600 mg a day or more, taken for at least eight weeks. In the largest single trial (Langade et al., 2019), 60 people with insomnia took 300 mg twice a day for ten weeks and fell asleep faster — about 29 minutes against 34 on placebo, measured by a wrist monitor — and slept for more of their time in bed. A nudge toward sleep, then; no trial has compared it against standard insomnia treatment. Human · small
    • Strength and testosterone — one small trial. In 2015, 57 young men who were new to weight training took 300 mg of root extract twice a day for eight weeks while they trained (Wankhede et al.). The ashwagandha group gained more strength — bench press up 46 kg against 26 kg on placebo — grew more muscle, and their testosterone rose further (+96 ng/dL against +18). One trial, one extract, young untrained men, eight weeks: a striking result that has not been repeated at any scale. Human · small
    • Memory and thinking — one small trial. Fifty adults took the extract for eight weeks and improved more than the placebo group on tests of memory, attention and processing speed (Choudhary et al., 2017). Early, single and small. Human · small
    • Men's fertility — an older study on a lower rung. In 2010, 75 infertile men were given 5 grams a day of plain root powder for three months, and their sperm count and movement improved (Ahmad et al.). But there was no dummy-pill group to compare against, so the result cannot rule out time and expectation doing the work. Human · small
    • The thyroid — an effect that cuts both ways. Fifty people with a mildly underactive thyroid took 600 mg a day for eight weeks; their TSH fell and their thyroid hormones T3 and T4 rose, against placebo (Sharma et al., 2018). A root that pushes thyroid hormones up is a hazard for anyone whose thyroid already runs fast, or whose levels are balanced on thyroid medicine — and doctors have published case reports of people who developed an overactive thyroid while taking ashwagandha, settling once they stopped. Human · small
    • What has not been shown: there is no good human evidence that ashwagandha treats depression, boosts the immune system in any measured clinical sense, or prevents any disease. The cancer and dementia results sometimes quoted for it come from cells in dishes and from animals. Weight-loss claims rest on single small trials in stressed adults. And because no trial runs longer than about three months, the effects of taking it for years — good or bad — are simply unmeasured. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • Safety — pregnancy. Do not take ashwagandha in pregnancy, and not while breastfeeding. The root had a traditional use for ending pregnancies, animal studies support the concern, and NCCIH advises avoiding it outright in pregnancy. There is no dose at which it has been shown safe for an unborn child.
    • Safety — the liver. Rare, but documented and real. In 2020 doctors in Iceland and the United States published five cases of liver injury in people taking ashwagandha supplements (Björnsson et al.): jaundice — yellowing of the skin and eyes — with itching and nausea, starting two to twelve weeks after the first dose. Nobody in that series developed liver failure, and liver tests returned to normal within one to five months of stopping. More cases have been published since, and LiverTox, the US National Institutes of Health database of drug-induced liver injury, rates ashwagandha a likely cause of clinically apparent liver injury; the severe cases have mostly been in people who already had liver disease. Anyone with liver disease should leave it alone, and anyone taking it who develops yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or severe itching should stop and see a doctor promptly.
    • Safety — interactions and the everyday list. Ashwagandha can cause drowsiness, and it adds to sedative medicines and to alcohol. It may add to medicines for diabetes and for high blood pressure, and it can work against medicines that suppress the immune system (NCCIH). The common side effects are mild: stomach upset, loose stools, nausea, drowsiness. It is not recommended before surgery, because of the sedation. Men with hormone-sensitive prostate cancer are advised to avoid it, because it can raise testosterone. Short-term use — up to about three months, the span the trials cover — is the ground the safety record stands on; beyond that, nobody knows.
    • Safety — the Denmark decision. In April 2023, Denmark banned ashwagandha from food supplements, the first country to do so. Its national food institute's risk assessment had concluded that no safe intake could be set, pointing to possible effects on thyroid and sex hormones, to effects on the immune system, and to the root's traditional use for ending pregnancies. The decision is contested: other researchers have criticised the assessment for not separating root preparations from leaf, and for resting the pregnancy point on traditional-use reports rather than clinical cases. In 2024, the heads of Europe's food safety agencies recommended that ashwagandha be put forward for a formal European Union safety review. The ban and the argument are both part of the record; neither changes what the trials above found.
    • When to plant: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost, or sow outside once the soil is warm
    • Sun: The sunniest, driest spot going
    • Soil: Lean, sandy, quick-draining soil, neutral to slightly alkaline
    • Environment: Needs a long, hot season — about 150 to 180 days from sowing to roots worth digging
    • Planter or ground: Ground; a deep pot works if the ground is heavy — expect smaller roots
    • Water: Once established it is properly drought-tolerant; the commonest way to kill it is kindness with the watering can
    • When to pick: Harvest in autumn, when the berries have ripened red and the leaves begin to yellow, and before hard frost

    Garden notes

    • A short-lived perennial shrub where winters are frost-free; everywhere else, a warm-season annual. In most gardens it stands knee- to waist-high, 35–75 cm, bushy and soft-leaved, the stems and leaves faintly downy. Small green bell-shaped flowers sit in the leaf joints from midsummer on, each followed by a round berry wrapped in a papery husk that ripens from green to orange-red — a tiny ground cherry, which is no accident: it is a nightshade, kin to the tomato, the potato and the chilli.
    • Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost, or sow outside once the soil is warm. Seed stirs in warm soil — about 20–30 °C — usually within one to three weeks. Plant out only when nights are reliably mild; cold checks it and frost kills it outright.
    • Give it the sunniest, driest spot going, and lean, sandy, quick-draining soil, neutral to slightly alkaline. Rich soil and generous feeding grow leaves at the root's expense, and wet ground rots it. Once established it is properly drought-tolerant; the commonest way to kill it is kindness with the watering can.
    • It needs a long, hot season: about 150 to 180 days from sowing to roots worth digging. In short-season climates the early indoor start is not optional — a plant sown late makes a handsome shrub and a disappointing root.
    • Harvest in autumn, when the berries have ripened red and the leaves begin to yellow, and before hard frost. Dig the whole plant, wash the roots, cut them into short pieces and dry them. Ripe berries can be saved for next year's seed.
    • Where winters stay frost-free it lives for a few years and may seed itself; elsewhere, save seed or start again each spring. A deep pot works if the ground is heavy — expect smaller roots.
    • Treat the harvest as a medicine, not a food crop: the root is for adults who have read the safety notes above, and the leaves and berries are not food.

    Propagation

    Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost, or sow outside once the soil is warm. Seed stirs in warm soil — about 20–30 °C — usually within one to three weeks. Ripe berries can be saved for next year's seed. Where winters stay frost-free it lives for a few years and may seed itself; elsewhere, save seed or start again each spring.

    Safety

    • Safety — pregnancy. Do not take ashwagandha in pregnancy, and not while breastfeeding. The root had a traditional use for ending pregnancies, animal studies support the concern, and NCCIH advises avoiding it outright in pregnancy. There is no dose at which it has been shown safe for an unborn child.
    • Safety — the liver. Rare, but documented and real. In 2020 doctors in Iceland and the United States published five cases of liver injury in people taking ashwagandha supplements (Björnsson et al.): jaundice — yellowing of the skin and eyes — with itching and nausea, starting two to twelve weeks after the first dose. Nobody in that series developed liver failure, and liver tests returned to normal within one to five months of stopping. More cases have been published since, and LiverTox, the US National Institutes of Health database of drug-induced liver injury, rates ashwagandha a likely cause of clinically apparent liver injury; the severe cases have mostly been in people who already had liver disease. Anyone with liver disease should leave it alone, and anyone taking it who develops yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or severe itching should stop and see a doctor promptly.
    • Safety — interactions and the everyday list. Ashwagandha can cause drowsiness, and it adds to sedative medicines and to alcohol. It may add to medicines for diabetes and for high blood pressure, and it can work against medicines that suppress the immune system (NCCIH). The common side effects are mild: stomach upset, loose stools, nausea, drowsiness. It is not recommended before surgery, because of the sedation. Men with hormone-sensitive prostate cancer are advised to avoid it, because it can raise testosterone. Short-term use — up to about three months, the span the trials cover — is the ground the safety record stands on; beyond that, nobody knows.
    • Safety — the Denmark decision. In April 2023, Denmark banned ashwagandha from food supplements, the first country to do so. Its national food institute's risk assessment had concluded that no safe intake could be set, pointing to possible effects on thyroid and sex hormones, to effects on the immune system, and to the root's traditional use for ending pregnancies. The decision is contested: other researchers have criticised the assessment for not separating root preparations from leaf, and for resting the pregnancy point on traditional-use reports rather than clinical cases. In 2024, the heads of Europe's food safety agencies recommended that ashwagandha be put forward for a formal European Union safety review. The ban and the argument are both part of the record; neither changes what the trials above found.

    Sources

    • NCCIH (2023) — Ashwagandha: usefulness and safety — the US national centre's summary of the stress and sleep evidence and the full safety list, including pregnancy, thyroid and medicine interactions
    • Chandrasekhar et al. (2012) — randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of root extract in 64 adults with chronic stress: stress scores and a 27.9% fall in blood cortisol
    • Salve et al. (2019) — randomised placebo-controlled trial of 250 mg and 600 mg doses in 60 stressed adults over eight weeks
    • Cheah et al. (2021) — systematic review and meta-analysis of ashwagandha extract for sleep: five trials, 400 people, a small effect clearest in insomnia
    • Langade et al. (2019) — randomised placebo-controlled trial in 60 people with insomnia: sleep measured by questionnaire and wrist monitor over ten weeks
    • Wankhede et al. (2015) — randomised placebo-controlled trial in 57 young men in resistance training: strength, muscle size and testosterone over eight weeks
    • Choudhary et al. (2017) — randomised placebo-controlled trial in 50 adults: memory and cognitive function over eight weeks
    • Ahmad et al. (2010) — root powder given to 75 infertile men for three months: semen quality improved, with no placebo group
    • Sharma et al. (2018) — randomised placebo-controlled trial in 50 people with subclinical hypothyroidism: TSH fell and T3 and T4 rose over eight weeks
    • Björnsson et al. (2020) — five cases of liver injury linked to ashwagandha supplements, from Iceland and the US Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network
    • LiverTox, US National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases — ashwagandha rated a likely cause of clinically apparent liver injury, typically appearing two to twelve weeks after starting

    • Khabiya et al. (2023) — review of the released Indian cultivars of ashwagandha: Nagori, the Jawahar varieties, Poshita, Rakshita and CIMAP-Pratap
