    Aspen

    Populus tremuloides

    MedicinalOrnamental

    The tree that will not sit still. Aspen leaves hang on long stalks that are flattened side to side, so the leaf twists and flutters in air too light to feel on skin — a whole hillside shimmers, and whispers, in a near-calm. That trembling gives the tree its everyday names: quaking aspen, trembling aspen, and “quakies” in the West. It is a slim white-barked tree that turns solid gold in autumn, and it is the most widely spread native tree in North America — growing from Newfoundland across Canada to Alaska, and south down the mountain chains into Mexico. Its deepest secret is underground: a grove of aspens is usually not many trees but one plant, its stems rising from a single shared root system. And its bark carries salicin, a close chemical kin of aspirin, which made it a pain and fever remedy across a continent long before aspirin existed — a remedy with a long traditional record behind it, and no clinical trials at all.

    Cultivars

    Aspen is not rich in named varieties — the wild tree is usually sold as itself, grown from root cuttings of a single clone. A few selections stand out.

    Prairie Gold® (‘NE Arb’)

    Found in the 1970s near Leigh, Nebraska, by Allen Wilke. Mountain aspens sulk and sicken in hot, humid lowland summers; this plains-born clone was chosen because it stands up to prairie heat, drought and humidity. A male clone, 30–40 feet at maturity, named for its golden autumn colour.

    Mountain Sentinel® (‘JFS-Column’)

    A narrow column of a tree, about 35 feet tall and only 8 feet wide at maturity, bred for tight spaces where the species' wide crown will not fit. The suckering habit is still the species' own, so the roots need the same room as any aspen's.

    ‘Prairie Skyrise’

    A Canadian prairie selection, upright and narrow, raised for cold-climate planting in the northern plains.

    Swedish columnar aspen (‘Erecta’)

    One name to watch at the nursery: Swedish columnar aspen, sold as ‘Erecta’, is Populus tremula — the European aspen, a different species — and not this tree. The European aspen is a close cousin with the same trembling leaves, but the two are kept apart, in the garden as in the medicine.

    • Aspen is a pioneer: the first tree into burned, logged or cleared ground. It grows fast in full sun, and its light shade shelters the slower spruces and firs that come up beneath it and one day replace it. An aspen stem lives roughly 50 to 150 years, then dies back — while the root system below it lives on and sends up fresh stems. The forest renews itself from underneath.
    • The pale bark is part of the trick. Under its thin white skin the bark stays green and alive, and it can catch light and make a little food even in early spring, before the leaves open — one reason aspen wakes up so fast after winter and after fire.
    • A grove is one plant. Aspen spreads by suckers — shoots that rise from its travelling roots. Fell a stem or burn a stand, and the roots answer with a crowd of new stems: tens of thousands of shoots to the acre have been counted after fire. Every stem in the crowd carries the same genes, turns gold on the same autumn day, and shares one fate with its sisters.
    • The famous grove is Pando, in Utah's Fishlake National Forest, above Fish Lake. In 1976 the foresters Burton Barnes and Jerry Kemperman showed that a whole hillside of aspen there — about 106 acres (43 hectares) of it — was a single clone. In 1992 Michael Grant and his colleagues gave it its name: Pando, Latin for “I spread.” DNA testing in 2008 confirmed it: one plant, about 47,000 stems, every one of them male, weighing an estimated 13 million pounds (about 6,000 tonnes) — the heaviest single living thing known on land. Its age is honestly unknown. The stems are young; the root system is not, and its age can only be guessed from pollen buried in the lake mud and from the slow tick of mutations in its DNA. Guesses run from a few thousand years to tens of thousands. The often-quoted 80,000 years is the far end of a guess, not a measurement.
    • Pando is in trouble. Photographs from the 1930s onward show the grove thinning: the old stems are dying, and mule deer — with cattle helping — eat the young shoots before they can grow into replacements. Where fences keep the deer out, the new stems are rising; where they do not, they are not. A plant that survived the ice ages is being eaten faster than it can renew itself.
    • Long before any of this was written down, the peoples of North America knew this tree well. Moerman's record of Indigenous plant use describes aspen bark prepared for fevers, colds and coughs, stomach pain and wounds, and the roots and leaves put to their own uses — a root preparation to guard against early labour, leaf poultices for bee stings. The inner bark was food as well as medicine: scraped in spring when it runs sweet, eaten fresh as a treat for children, dried into cakes and flour, or boiled down into a syrup taken as a spring tonic. Even the fine white powder that blooms on the bark was gathered — used to stop bleeding, and rubbed on skin as a deodorant.
    • In the 1800s, American doctors of the Eclectic school — the era's herbal physicians — took up the bark their Indigenous teachers had used, listing it in their dispensatories as a bitter tonic for weak appetite, lingering low fevers and general aches after illness. It held a steady place in American folk medicine for a century.
    • One story travelled with the settlers. In Europe, an old tale told of the aspen's cousin there that its wood had been used for the Cross, and that the tree has trembled ever since. The story crossed the ocean and was retold about the American tree — which is why a tree that trembles for the plain reason of its flattened leaf stalks carries a legend about shame and sorrow. It is a story, told as a story.
    • The wood is soft, pale and light — cut for paper pulp, matches, boxes and wood wool, and a mainstay of the Lake States pulp trade. Wildlife values the living tree more: beavers eat the bark and build with the stems, deer and elk browse the shoots, ruffed grouse winter on the flower buds, and woodpeckers hollow the soft trunks for nests. Few North American trees feed so many.
    • What is in the bark: salicin and populin, two related compounds found across the poplar family. The body changes salicin into salicylic acid — the working heart of aspirin. That chemistry is the whole basis of aspen's medicine. The catch is dose: the amount of salicin in aspen bark swings widely from tree to tree and season to season, and no standard aspen preparation or dose exists.
    • The honest position, plainly: no human trial has ever tested quaking aspen bark on its own. Not one. Everything said for it rests on two legs — its long, well-recorded traditional use for pain and fever, and the known chemistry of salicin. That is a real record, and it is a thinner one than proof.
    • Willow is a different tree, with a different record. White willow bark has been through human trials for back pain and holds an official European monograph at the stronger “well-established use” level; salicin itself was first isolated from willow bark, in 1828, and aspirin was built from that chemistry in 1897. That evidence is willow's. It does not transfer to aspen, however close the kinship.
    • The official books do hold one poplar entry, and it is narrower than it sounds. Germany's Commission E approved poplar buds — gathered from several poplar species — as an ointment ingredient for shallow skin injuries, chilblains, sunburn and haemorrhoids. A different part of the tree, a different use, and a traditional approval: it says nothing about drinking aspen bark for pain. A European combination tincture that mixes poplar bark and leaf with goldenrod and ash has been trialled for joint pain, but the poplar in it is the European aspen, and a three-plant mixture cannot hand its results to any one ingredient. Traditional use
    • In the laboratory, aspen bark extracts show the expected salicylate effects and some antimicrobial and antioxidant activity in dishes. That is laboratory strength only — a reason the traditional use is plausible, not a result in people. Lab studies
    • Safety follows the aspirin family, because salicin is in it. The standing warning for aspirin applies to salicylate-bearing barks: never give them to children or teenagers with fever, flu or chickenpox, because of the risk of Reye's syndrome, a rare but dangerous swelling of the brain and liver. Anyone allergic to aspirin should leave aspen bark alone. It can irritate the stomach like its chemical kin, and care is needed alongside blood-thinning medicines. Its safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established. Aspen pollen, shed in spring before the leaves, also sets off hay fever in some people.
    • When to plant: Plant in spring, where a grove is welcome — a wild corner, a windbreak, the back of a big lot — well away from pipes, foundations and neighbours' gardens
    • Sun: Full sun, always
    • Soil: Cool, moist, well-drained ground; it tolerates poor soil better than drought in its first years
    • Environment: Built for cold country, hardy through USDA zones 2 to 6, and it needs a real winter
    • Planter or ground: Ground — never a pot, and never near pipes, paving or drains
    • Water: Give it cool, moist ground; it sulks in hot, humid lowland summers, where sickness usually follows

    Garden notes

    • A fast, slim tree: 50–80 feet tall in the wild (15–25 m), commonly 40–50 feet in gardens, and quick about it — young trees can add two feet or more in a year. It is built for cold country, hardy through USDA zones 2 to 6, and it needs a real winter.
    • Full sun, always. Aspen is a pioneer and casts off shade rather than growing in it — a young tree under other trees simply fails. Give it cool, moist, well-drained ground; it tolerates poor soil better than drought in its first years, and it sulks in hot, humid lowland summers, where sickness usually follows.
    • The suckering warning, at full strength: the roots travel far beyond the trunk and send up new stems in lawns, flower beds, paths and vegetable plots — that is not a fault in the tree, it is the tree, doing what made Pando. Mowing keeps lawn suckers down but never stops them, and the roots can lift paving and find their way into drains and septic lines. Plant aspen where a grove is welcome — a wild corner, a windbreak, the back of a big lot — well away from pipes, foundations and neighbours' gardens, or do not plant it at all.
    • Expect a short, bright life rather than a long one. Garden stems commonly last 20 to 30 years before cankers, borers and leaf diseases thin them — sooner in hot low ground, longer in the cool mountain air the tree is made for. Planting several stems as a grove spreads the risk: as one stem fails, its own roots replace it.
    • Handle the bark gently. It is thin, living and easily wounded, and every mower scar and strimmer cut is an open door to the canker fungi that kill more garden aspens than anything else. And never strip bark from a living tree for tea or any other use — a ring of bark taken round a trunk kills everything above it. The medicine belongs to history and to pruned branches, not to a standing garden tree.
    • Wildlife will find it. Deer browse the shoots, beavers will fell a waterside tree in a night, and grouse, woodpeckers and a long list of songbirds use the grove through the year. Where it has room, few planted trees give so much back.

    Propagation

    Aspen spreads by suckers — shoots that rise from its travelling roots. The wild tree is usually sold as itself, grown from root cuttings of a single clone. Planting several stems as a grove spreads the risk: as one stem fails, its own roots replace it.

    Safety

    • Safety follows the aspirin family, because salicin is in it. The standing warning for aspirin applies to salicylate-bearing barks: never give them to children or teenagers with fever, flu or chickenpox, because of the risk of Reye's syndrome, a rare but dangerous swelling of the brain and liver. Anyone allergic to aspirin should leave aspen bark alone. It can irritate the stomach like its chemical kin, and care is needed alongside blood-thinning medicines. Its safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established. Aspen pollen, shed in spring before the leaves, also sets off hay fever in some people.

    Sources

    • Moerman (1998) — Native American Ethnobotany — Indigenous uses of quaking aspen bark, roots, leaves and inner bark across North America
    • DeWoody et al. (2008) — genetic sampling of 209 stems confirming Pando is a single clone across 43 hectares
    • Rogers & McAvoy (2018) — mule deer and the failure of new stems at Pando; fenced ground regrows
    • Grant et al. (1992) — the naming and first full description of Pando, “the trembling giant”
    • US Forest Service — Fire Effects Information System: Populus tremuloides — range, growth, clonal spread and ecology
    • Commission E (1990) — German monograph on poplar bud (Populi gemma) — external use only, on skin

    Barley

    Hordeum vulgare

    Culinary

    Heart HealthDigestive HealthBlood Sugar Health

    CookedDried

    One of the first grains ever farmed, and for thousands of years one of the grains the world ran on — bread, soup and beer from the same golden head. Barley is a grass, kin to wheat and rye, grown for its seed: rows of grains wrapped in a tight hull, each carrying a long bristle (an awn) that gives a ripe field its feathery look. Most of the world crop now goes to animal feed and to malt for beer and whisky, and the share eaten as food is the smallest of the three — which is a pity, because as a food it carries some of the strongest evidence of any grain in the ground. One warning belongs at the front: barley contains gluten, the protein set that includes its own form, hordein. For anyone with coeliac disease, barley in every form — grain, flour, malt and nearly all beer — is not safe, and nothing below changes that.

    Cultivars

    Barley sorts first by shape, then by name. In two-row barley only the middle grain of each cluster on the head fills out, giving fewer, plumper grains; in six-row barley all the grains in each cluster fill, giving more, smaller grains with somewhat more protein. Either can be hulled — the hull clings to the grain and must be milled off — or hulless (also called naked), where the hull falls away at threshing like wheat's, which is why hulless types are the ones home growers choose for the kitchen. And either can be a spring type, sown in spring and harvested the same summer, or a winter type, sown in autumn, which needs a spell of cold before it will head up and ripens the following early summer.

    Bere

    The Scottish landrace: six-row, hulled, sown in spring and famously fast, able to ripen in the short northern summer. Still grown in Orkney and Shetland, milled there for bere meal, and malted for whisky since 2005. It is a survivor rather than a bred variety — the oldest barley in this list by centuries.

    ‘Maris Otter’

    An English winter two-row released in 1966, bred at Cambridge by Dr G. D. H. Bell and his team. It became the malt that British ale brewers judge others by, prized for an even, rich-flavoured malt, and it is still grown on contract for brewers long after higher-yielding varieties replaced it on most farms.

    ‘Golden Promise’

    A Scottish spring two-row released in the late 1960s, shorter-strawed and easier to harvest than what came before it. It became the benchmark barley of Scotch whisky distilling through the 1970s and 1980s, kept in production for the flavour of its spirit after the industry mostly moved on.

    ‘Optic’, ‘Concerto’ and ‘Laureate’

    The modern succession: spring two-row malting varieties, each replacing the last across British and European farms roughly every ten to fifteen years, each bred for a little more yield and stronger disease resistance than the one before. Most malt bought today comes from varieties in this line rather than from the famous names above.

    Hulless food barleys

    Food varieties are a smaller world. Hulless types bred for eating rather than malting — grown widely in Tibet and the Himalayan region for centuries and now bred in Canada and elsewhere for the health-food trade — are sold more often by type (“hulless”, “black”, “purple”) than by cultivar name; the dark-grained hulless kinds carry their colour in the outer layers of the grain, which is why those layers are worth keeping.

    • Barley was domesticated in the Fertile Crescent — the arc of land across the Near East where farming began — about 10,000 years ago. It is one of the eight founder crops, the short list of plants that started agriculture there: einkorn wheat, emmer wheat, barley, lentil, pea, chickpea, bitter vetch and flax. People had eaten wild barley long before anyone farmed it — starch traces on grinding stones at the Ohalo II site, in what is now Israel, show wild barley being ground about 23,000 years ago. Farming changed the plant in one crucial way: wild barley heads shatter and scatter their seed, while farmed barley holds its grains on the stalk until harvest, which makes it a crop a person can actually gather.
    • In Mesopotamia, barley was money. Workers were paid in it, rations were measured in it, and the accounts were pressed into clay: a cuneiform tablet from Girsu, in what is now Iraq, written around 2350 BCE in the reign of King Urukagina, lists monthly barley rations — 30 or 40 pints for an adult, 20 for a child. Beer brewed from barley was everyday drink and part of wages in both Mesopotamia and Egypt, and barley bread and beer together were the standard ration foods of the ancient world.
    • From the Near East the crop spread in every direction, reaching right across Eurasia by about 2000 BCE, and it travelled well because it is tough: barley ripens faster than wheat, bears dry ground and salty soil better, and grows farther north and higher up than any other cereal of its age. In the Greek and Roman world it was food for the hard-working end of life — Roman gladiators were fed largely on barley and beans and were nicknamed hordearii, “barley men,” and Greek doctors prescribed barley gruel and barley water for the sick, a use that survived in sickrooms for two thousand years.
    • In England the grain got into the language and the law. A barleycorn — the length of one grain — was a unit of measure, three barleycorns to the inch; shoe sizes are still counted in barleycorns today. The old English word for the crop was bere, and in English folklore the grain itself became a person: John Barleycorn, the bearded figure of the ballads, cut down at harvest, threshed, ground and brewed — killed, in the song, so that everyone might drink. Pubs called The Barley Mow (“mow” is the harvest stack) still carry the crop's name over the door.
    • Scotland kept a barley of its own. Bere is a fast, hardy six-row landrace — a variety shaped by centuries of local seed-saving rather than by breeders — grown in Orkney, Shetland and the Highlands since at least the Middle Ages, and by some accounts far longer. It was milled into bere meal for bannocks (flat griddle cakes) and is still grown and milled in Orkney today; since 2005 an Islay distillery has also malted it for whisky, reviving a grain the industry had left behind.
    • At the other end of the old world, barley climbed the mountains. In Tibet, roasted barley flour — tsampa — mixed with butter tea is the staple food, eaten daily at altitudes where little else ripens; barley is the chief grain of the Tibetan plateau. In Japan and Korea the grain is pressed into service as a drink instead: mugicha in Japanese, boricha in Korean, a tea of roasted barley served cold all summer, and barley is also cooked mixed with rice.
    • Malt is barley's second career, and it is an old one. A barley grain that is soaked, allowed to just begin sprouting, then dried with hot air becomes malt: sprouting switches on enzymes that turn the grain's starch into sugars, and those sugars are what yeast ferments into beer — or what a distiller ferments and distils into whisky. The same grain, three foods: cooked whole in soups and stews, ground into flour for breads and bannocks, and malted for the brewer. Today barley stands fourth among the world's cereals, at about 146 million tonnes in 2023, behind maize, rice and wheat — roughly 70% of it feeding animals, and most of the rest going to the maltings.
    • Whole barley, hulled (the inedible outer hull removed, bran and germ left in place), per 100 g dry: 354 kcal, protein 12.5 g, carbohydrate 73.5 g, fat 2.3 g, and fibre 17.3 g — among the highest fibre figures of any grain. It also carries thiamin (vitamin B1) at 0.65 mg, magnesium at 133 mg, selenium at 37.7 µg, potassium at 452 mg and iron at 3.6 mg per 100 g. Cooked pearl barley, per 100 g: 123 kcal, protein 2.3 g and fibre 3.8 g — the drop is mostly the water the grain drinks as it cooks, though pearling (polishing the grain) does strip some bran away. Unusually, barley keeps much of its best fibre even when pearled, because that fibre runs through the whole grain rather than sitting only in the outer layers.
    • The fibre that matters most is beta-glucan, a soluble fibre — one that dissolves in water and turns thick and gel-like in the gut. Whole barley carries roughly 4 to 6 g of it in every 100 g of dry grain, among the richest sources in any food, alongside oats. That gel slows the gut's handling of both cholesterol and sugar, and beta-glucan is where barley's tested benefits live.
    • Cholesterol is the strong claim, and it is a human one. Barley's beta-glucan has been tested in randomised trials in people, and the results were consistent enough that Europe's food safety authority, EFSA, ruled in 2011 that a cause-and-effect relationship is established, on the strength of a pooled analysis of eleven trials plus a further trial, all at doses of at least 3 g of barley beta-glucan a day. The authorised claim reads: “Barley beta-glucans have been shown to lower/reduce blood cholesterol. High cholesterol is a risk factor in the development of coronary heart disease.” The United States FDA allows a similar claim for barley beta-glucan at the same 3 g a day. Three grams is a reachable amount from food — roughly a generous day's eating of whole barley — but it is the tested dose, and smaller amounts are not what the trials proved. Human trials
    • Blood sugar after a meal has its own authorised claim, also from human testing: eating beta-glucans from oats or barley as part of a meal reduces the rise in blood glucose after that meal, provided the food carries at least 4 g of beta-glucans for every 30 g of available carbohydrate in the portion. That is a statement about the meal in front of a person, measured as it happens — barley is not a treatment for diabetes, and no such claim is made for it. Human trials
    • On ordinary digestion the evidence is simpler and the claim plainer: barley grain fibre contributes to an increase in faecal bulk — an authorised claim resting on the grain's 17.3 g of fibre per 100 g doing what fibre does.
    • The safety line is the one at the top, repeated because it is the one that can harm: barley contains gluten. Coeliac disease is an immune reaction to gluten that damages the gut, and for people who have it, barley — whole, pearled, as flour, as malt, and as ordinary beer — is off the table entirely. Barley allergy separate from coeliac disease also exists but is uncommon. For everyone else, barley is a safe, ordinary food grain with a very long record.
    • Two cautions belong here. “Barley grass” powders and juices are made from the young green leaves of the plant, not from the grain; they are a different product, and the grain's trial evidence does not belong to them. And barley water's long career as a sickroom drink is a tradition, told in the history above as history — it is not a tested treatment for anything.
    • When to plant: Sow spring barley outdoors as soon as the soil can be worked in spring; sow winter barley in autumn, about four to six weeks before hard frost
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Well-drained loam around pH 6.5 to 7.0 — it bears alkaline and even somewhat salty ground that would check wheat
    • Environment: A cool-season crop; it needs less nitrogen than wheat — rich feeding grows tall, soft straw that falls over before harvest
    • Planter or ground: Ground
    • Spacing and depth: Sow about 1 to 1½ inches deep, grains an inch or two apart in rows 6 to 8 inches apart, or broadcast at roughly 2 to 3 pounds per 1,000 square feet and raked in
    • Water: Keep the bed watered evenly while the heads fill; it will not bear standing water, which rots the roots
    • When to pick: About 60 to 90 days from a spring sowing — the whole plant, stems and heads together, turns golden and dry, and the grains are hard

    Garden notes

    • Barley is a cool-season annual grass that pollinates itself, so seed saved from your own plants grows out the same — landraces like bere were built by exactly that, centuries of farmers saving seed from the plants that did best on their own ground.
    • Timing is the same race as with peas, run a little earlier. Sow spring barley outdoors as soon as the soil can be worked in spring — the seed will germinate in soil as cold as about 40 °F (4 °C), though slowly, and young plants take a light frost. Winter barley is sown in autumn, about four to six weeks before hard frost, and suits milder-winter country (about zone 6 and warmer); it sits through the cold and ripens weeks ahead of the spring-sown crop.
    • Sow the seed about 1 to 1½ inches deep, thickly — grains an inch or two apart in rows 6 to 8 inches apart, or broadcast at roughly 2 to 3 pounds per 1,000 square feet and raked in. A firm, weed-free bed matters: barley competes well once it is up, but it starts small.
    • Give it full sun and well-drained soil. Barley is happiest in a loam around pH 6.5 to 7.0 and keeps growing across a wider range (about pH 6.0 to 8.5) than most cereals; it bears alkaline and even somewhat salty ground that would check wheat. What it will not bear is wet feet — standing water rots the roots. It needs less nitrogen than wheat; rich feeding grows tall, soft straw that falls over (lodges) before harvest.
    • The plant grows fast and upright, about 2 to 4 feet tall, each seed sending up several stems (tillers). Heads appear in late spring or early summer; the long awns on the grains are the field mark that tells barley from wheat at a glance. Keep the bed watered evenly while the heads fill; dry weather at that stage thins the grains.
    • Harvest comes quickly — about 60 to 90 days from a spring sowing. The sign is colour: the whole plant, stems and heads together, turns golden and dry, and the grains are hard — a ripe grain dents barely, or not at all, under a thumbnail. Cut the stems with a sickle or shears, tie them in small bundles (sheaves) and stand the sheaves under cover for a week or two to finish drying, then thresh — beat or tread the heads to free the grain — and winnow by pouring the grain from one container to another in a breeze, letting the wind carry off the light chaff.
    • For the kitchen, grow hulless barley. A hulled variety's hull is fixed to the grain and needs milling machinery to remove; a hulless variety threshes clean in the garden, and the whole grain goes straight into the pot after a rinse. Grain for storage should be fully dry — around 12% moisture or less, hard and rattling — and kept in a sealed jar away from damp and mice.
    • Barley earns a place even where no grain is wanted. Sown thickly in autumn or early spring it makes a fast cover crop: a green blanket that holds the soil, shades out weeds, and is cut down and dug in, or left as mulch, before the bed's main crop goes in. Cut a cover crop before it sets seed, or it will volunteer in the bed for seasons after.

    Propagation

    Barley pollinates itself, so seed saved from your own plants grows out the same. Cut a cover crop before it sets seed, or it will volunteer in the bed for seasons after.

    Safety

    • The safety line is the one at the top, repeated because it is the one that can harm: barley contains gluten. Coeliac disease is an immune reaction to gluten that damages the gut, and for people who have it, barley — whole, pearled, as flour, as malt, and as ordinary beer — is off the table entirely. Barley allergy separate from coeliac disease also exists but is uncommon. For everyone else, barley is a safe, ordinary food grain with a very long record.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: barley, hulled, raw, and barley, pearled, cooked — the nutrition figures
    • EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies (2011) — Scientific opinion on barley beta-glucans and lowering of blood cholesterol and reduced risk of coronary heart disease — the pooled trials and the authorised claim
    • Commission Regulation (EU) No 432/2012 — the list of permitted health claims — barley beta-glucan and blood glucose rise after a meal; barley grain fibre and faecal bulk
    • Weiss & Zohary (2011) — The Neolithic Southwest Asian founder crops — barley among the eight crops that started farming in the Fertile Crescent
    • Riehl (2019) — Barley in Archaeology and Early History, Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Environmental Science — domestication, spread, rations, beer and the founder-crop record

    Broccoli

    Brassica oleracea var. italica

    Culinary

    Immune HealthDigestive Health

    FreshCooked

    A head of broccoli is a flower that never opened: hundreds of tiny green buds held tight on branching stalks, picked days before they would bloom. It is one vegetable from a very obliging species. Broccoli, cabbage, kale, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts and kohlrabi are all Brassica oleracea — one plant pulled in six directions by growers who selected, in turn, for leaves, for a single wrapped bud, for side buds, for a swollen stem, and, in broccoli's case, for the flower cluster itself. Italy did the selecting, and the name keeps the receipt: broccolo is Italian for a little sprout. Two name warnings before anything else. Broccoli rabe, also called rapini, is a different plant — Brassica rapa, a turnip relative grown for bitter leaves and loose buds — and it is not this broccoli. And the pale-green spiral heads sold as romanesco belong with the cauliflowers, not here.

    Cultivars

    Broccoli sorts first into two habits of growth, and the habit decides how the harvest comes.

    Heading broccoli

    One large central head, then smaller side shoots after it is cut. ‘Calabrese’ — the old Italian type the whole heading kind is named after (for Calabria), blue-green heads of 4–6 inches and a long run of side shoots; the flavour standard. ‘De Cicco’ — an Italian heirloom dating to 1890, a smaller main head followed by side shoots for months; the cut-and-come-again choice. ‘Waltham 29’ — bred in Massachusetts in the 1950s for cold tolerance, large blue-green heads and heavy side shoots; the fall-crop classic, and one whose seed can be saved, since it breeds true. ‘Green Magic’ — a modern hybrid with smooth, tight, domed heads that holds up in warmer weather better than most, the forgiving spring choice. ‘Belstar’ — a sturdy hybrid with dense, heavy heads and good side shoots, reliable across spring, summer and fall plantings. ‘Marathon’ — a cold-tolerant hybrid with big blue-green heads, widely grown by market farmers for fall and winter harvest.

    Sprouting broccoli

    No single head at all; the plant is overwintered and picked as many small spears through late winter and spring, filling the hungry gap before the new season's crops. Purple sprouting is the best known: very hardy, generous with purple spears that turn green in the pan. White sprouting is its paler twin, milder and a little less hardy. Sprouting types ask patience — sown in spring, they crop the following year — and repay it when almost nothing else in the garden is picking.

    Two near-relatives

    Two near-relatives are worth keeping straight, since both borrow the name. Romanesco — the lime-green head of spiralling cones, a pattern of buds repeating at smaller and smaller scales — belongs to the cauliflower branch of the species, bred in Italy; it cooks like a cauliflower and is not a broccoli. Broccolini — long, thin, tender stems with small loose florets — is a deliberate modern cross between broccoli and Chinese broccoli (gai lan), made in Japan in the 1990s and sold under that trademarked name; it is a real hybrid of the two, not a baby broccoli.

    • The wild ancestor is wild cabbage, a loose-leafed plant that still grows on limestone cliffs and coasts around the Mediterranean and along the Atlantic shore of Europe. Growers in Italy began selecting it for its flower clusters roughly 2,500 years ago — the standard account dates the work to about the sixth century BCE — saving seed, generation after generation, from the plants with the thickest stalks and the fullest, tenderest heads of buds.
    • The Etruscans, the people of what is now Tuscany and famed gardeners among the ancients, are often credited with the early shaping of the plant. Rome took to it: the natural historian Pliny the Elder described a cabbage-family vegetable that may have been broccoli, and recipes in the cookbook that carries Apicius's name may describe it too — the Roman evidence is suggestive, not certain, and is best left at that. What is certain is that broccoli stayed an Italian vegetable for well over a thousand years while the rest of Europe did without it.
    • France's first written mention of broccoli dates to 1560. A favourite story says Catherine de' Medici brought it from Florence when she married into the French royal family in 1533; it is a good story, told of half the vegetables in the French kitchen, and the written record starts a generation after her wedding.
    • England was slower still. Philip Miller's Gardener's Dictionary of 1724 treated broccoli as a stranger in England, and through the 1700s the English called it “Italian asparagus” — a foreign food explained by two familiar ones. John Randolph, writing a gardening treatise in Virginia in 1775, was still explaining it the same way: “The stems will eat like Asparagus, and the heads like Cauliflower.”
    • Thomas Jefferson grew it early. His garden book records broccoli planted at Monticello on 27 May 1767, from seed got through his European correspondents, alongside radishes, lettuce and cauliflower. It changed nothing at the time: broccoli stayed a curiosity in American gardens for another 150 years, grown here and there by gardeners who had met it in Italy and by almost nobody else.
    • What finally naturalised broccoli in America was immigration and ice. Stephano and Andrea D'Arrigo, brothers who had come from Messina, in Sicily, made their first plantings at San Jose, California, in 1922, then shipped the crop east packed in ice, under their Andy Boy brand, and advertised it to a country that mostly had never seen it. Italian-American families bought it first; within a decade it was an ordinary American vegetable. California still grows about nine-tenths of the broccoli sold in the United States, much of it around Salinas.
    • Broccoli has one famous enemy. In March 1990, President George H. W. Bush told reporters: “I do not like broccoli. And I haven't liked it since I was a little kid and my mother made me eat it. And I'm President of the United States, and I'm not going to eat any more broccoli.” He had already banned it from Air Force One. California growers answered by sending tons of broccoli to the White House, much of it donated on to food banks — and the argument did the vegetable's fame no harm at all.
    • Italy — the homeland, and still the place that cooks it simplest: broccoli strascinati, “dragged” in a hot pan with olive oil, garlic and chilli until it softens and catches at the edges, and broccoli boiled and dressed with oil and lemon in Sicily, where the D'Arrigo brothers' seed came from. (The famous Puglian dish of orecchiette with cime di rapa uses broccoli rabe — the turnip relative — not this plant.)
    • China — broccoli itself, a late arrival, is stir-fried fast with garlic and goes through the same high-heat treatment as the native Chinese broccoli, gai lan — a leafy, small-flowered member of the same species that China has grown for centuries and that stayed the first choice at home.
    • The United States — beef and broccoli, the American Chinese restaurant standard, was built in America: in China the dish is made with gai lan, and cooks in the United States swapped in the broccoli that was cheap and familiar there. Raw broccoli also anchors the American picnic salad — florets with bacon, red onion, raisins and a sweet dressing — a dish that would puzzle the plant's Italian makers.
    • The world crop — China grows more broccoli than any other country (its crop is counted together with cauliflower in world statistics), with the United States and India behind it; within the United States, California's cool coastal valleys grow about nine-tenths of the national crop, the harvest the D'Arrigo brothers started a century ago.
    • Raw broccoli, per 100 g: 34 kcal, protein 2.82 g, fibre 2.6 g, carbohydrate 6.64 g, sugars 1.7 g, fat 0.37 g. The standout vitamins are vitamin C at 89.2 mg — about a full day's worth — and vitamin K at 101.6 µg, with folate at 63 µg, potassium at 316 mg and calcium at 47 mg besides. Few vegetables give so much vitamin C for so few calories.
    • The vitamin K figure carries one plain caution. Vitamin K is the vitamin the body uses to clot blood, and people who take warfarin are usually told to keep their vitamin K intake steady from week to week rather than to avoid greens. Broccoli is rich in it, so large swings in how much of it a person eats are the thing to avoid — the same advice given for cabbage, and for the same reason.
    • Broccoli's most studied compound is sulforaphane, and it is not in the plant ready-made. Broccoli stores a quieter compound, glucoraphanin, in its cells, and an enzyme, myrosinase, in separate cells; chopping or chewing breaks the walls between them, the two meet, and sulforaphane forms. Three-day-old broccoli sprouts hold ten to a hundred times more glucoraphanin than a mature head, which is why the sprouts, and extracts made from them, are what most studies use.
    • Heat changes the sums. Cooking destroys myrosinase, so well-cooked broccoli forms less sulforaphane than raw or lightly steamed; bacteria in the gut can convert some glucoraphanin without the enzyme, but less reliably. None of this makes broccoli a medicine — it explains why the studies below used sprouts and extracts rather than helpings of the vegetable.
    • In the laboratory, sulforaphane is genuinely interesting: it switches on a set of the body's own defence enzymes — the system scientists call the Nrf2 pathway — and it kills cancer cells in dishes and slows tumours in animals. That is laboratory and animal evidence. It is the beginning of a research story, not a result in people. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • The human trials so far are small, and they tested sprouts or extracts, not the vegetable on a plate. In Qidong, China, 291 people drank a broccoli-sprout drink daily, and their bodies cleared two air pollutants, benzene and acrolein, measurably faster into the urine. A 12-week trial of a concentrated sprout extract in 97 people with type 2 diabetes found better fasting blood sugar, mostly in the heavier patients whose sugar was worst controlled. A small trial in 44 young men with autism reported better behaviour scores on sulforaphane; a later trial in children did not find the same benefit. Each of these is a single small trial, and none has been repeated at scale. Human · small
    • The closest the vegetable itself has come to a trial result is a bred-up version of it. British breeders crossed broccoli with a wild Sicilian relative to make a variety holding about three times the usual glucoraphanin, and in two small trials — 130 people in all — eating it as a soup for 12 weeks lowered LDL cholesterol by about 5 to 7 per cent, a little more than standard broccoli did. A modest effect, in small trials, from a special variety: that is the honest size of it. Human · small
    • On cancer, the claim most often made for broccoli, the evidence is this: studies that follow large groups of people find that those who eat more cruciferous vegetables — the whole cabbage family, broccoli among them — tend to have somewhat lower rates of some cancers, and other studies find no such pattern. Patterns across a whole family of vegetables, seen in people who differ in many other ways, cannot show that broccoli prevents cancer, and no trial has shown that it does. Broccoli is a nutritious vegetable with an interesting chemistry and a short, small, early trial record. It is not a treatment for anything.
    • When to plant: Start seed indoors four to six weeks before the last spring frost and set the plants out two to three weeks before it, once they have four or five true leaves; for the fall crop, sow in midsummer, about 85–100 days before the first fall frost
    • Sun: Full sun — six hours or more of direct light
    • Soil: Rich soil, well dug with compost, around pH 6.0–7.0
    • Environment: Cool-season; grows best between about 60 and 75 °F (16–24 °C), and heads that form in heat come out small, loose and bitter
    • Planter or ground: Ground — about 18 inches apart each way
    • Spacing and depth: About 18 inches apart each way
    • Water: Steady water, about an inch to an inch and a half a week; dry spells followed by flooding make loose, hollow-stemmed heads
    • When to pick: About 50–80 days from transplant; cut the main head while the buds are tight, firm and dark green, usually 4–8 inches across, before a single yellow petal shows — then side shoots follow for four to six weeks or more

    Garden notes

    • Broccoli is a biennial grown as an annual: left to itself it would overwinter and flower in its second year, but the crop is taken in the first. The head is a cluster of flower buds, and everything about growing broccoli is a race to cut it in the few days between “full size” and “open.” Left standing, the buds open into small yellow four-petalled flowers — the cross shape that gives the whole cabbage family its old name, Cruciferae.
    • It is a cool-season crop and timing is the whole game. Heads that form in heat come out small, loose and bitter, and the plant may “button” — make a tiny head and stop — or bolt straight to flower. Plan for the heads to mature in cool weather: a spring crop racing the first heat, or a fall crop ripening as the weather cools, which most gardeners find the better of the two.
    • Harvest the main head in the morning with a sharp knife, taking 5–6 inches of stem at a slant so water runs off the stump — a head can go from perfect to flowering in two warm days, so look every day once it sizes up.
    • Cutting the head is not the end. Most varieties push out side shoots from the leaf joints below the cut — small heads an inch or two across — and will keep offering them for four to six weeks or more if they are picked before they flower. ‘De Cicco’ and ‘Waltham 29’ are grown for this second harvest as much as for the first.
    • Expect the family's usual company. Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on the leaves and their green caterpillars are the standard tax on an uncovered crop; fine mesh or row cover from planting day is the simple answer, and it also stops flea beetles on young plants. Aphids gather in the heads — a hard jet of water knocks most loose.
    • Rotate the beds. Broccoli and all its Brassica oleracea kin share the soil disease clubroot, which swells roots and stunts plants and lingers in the ground for years; give a bed three or four years between cabbage-family crops where you can, and keep the soil nearer neutral, since clubroot is worst in acid ground.
    • A light frost near harvest is a friend: heads ripening into cooling fall weather come out denser and sweeter than spring heads, and established plants shrug off frosts that would kill tender crops. Picked broccoli keeps only a few days in the refrigerator at its best; for the freezer, blanch the florets briefly first, as with peas.

    Propagation

    Start from seed, indoors or sown where it is to grow. ‘Waltham 29’ breeds true, so seed saved from it grows out the same; seed from a hybrid will not grow true. A plant left to stand flowers in its second year and sets seed — broccoli is a biennial, cropped in its first.

    Safety

    • Safety — vitamin K and blood thinners. Vitamin K is the vitamin the body uses to clot blood, and people who take warfarin are usually told to keep their vitamin K intake steady from week to week rather than to avoid greens. Broccoli is rich in it, so large swings in how much of it a person eats are the thing to avoid — the same advice given for cabbage, and for the same reason.

    • Fahey et al. (1997) — Broccoli sprouts: an exceptionally rich source of inducers of enzymes that protect against chemical carcinogens — sprouts hold ten to a hundred times the glucoraphanin of mature heads
    • Egner et al. (2014) — Sulforaphane bioavailability from glucoraphanin-rich broccoli: control of pollutant excretion in Qidong, China — the 291-person sprout-drink trial
    • Axelsson et al. (2017) — Sulforaphane reduces liver glucose production and improves glucose control in patients with type 2 diabetes — the 97-person sprout-extract trial
    • Singh et al. (2014) — Sulforaphane treatment of autism spectrum disorder — the 44-person trial in young men
    • Armah et al. (2015) — A high-glucoraphanin broccoli diet lowers LDL cholesterol — the bred-up broccoli trials
    • National Cancer Institute (2012) — Cruciferous Vegetables and Cancer Prevention — the population-study record, stated at its strength
    • Jefferson, Garden Book (1767 entry) — broccoli planted at Monticello, 27 May 1767

    Buckwheat

    Fagopyrum esculentum

    Culinary

    Digestive HealthBlood Sugar Health

    CookedDried

    First, the thing the name gets wrong: buckwheat is not wheat. It is not a grass at all, and it is no relation of wheat — it belongs to the knotweed family, and its kin are rhubarb and sorrel. The “wheat” half of the name is about the job, not the family: its seeds are milled and cooked exactly like a grain, which makes buckwheat a pseudocereal, a plant used as a cereal without being one. And because it is not wheat, it carries no gluten at all — none, naturally, in the seed itself. What it does carry is a seed shaped like a tiny three-sided pyramid, dark-hulled, with a pale groat inside, and a flavour all its own: earthy, toasty, a little bitter at the edges. It is also one of the fastest crops on Earth — a field can go from sowing to white flower in about a month — and for centuries it was the grain of poor soil and short seasons, the crop that fed people where wheat refused to grow.

    Cultivars

    Buckwheat is usually sold by type rather than by name — seed labelled simply “buckwheat” or “common” is unnamed stock, grown for cover cropping, flour and pancake mixes. Named cultivars exist where buyers contract for grain, and they are bred mostly for large, even seed that hulls cleanly for groats and soba.

    ‘Mancan’ and ‘Manor’

    ‘Mancan’ — a Canadian large-seeded standard of the 1970s, vigorous and widely planted across the northern plains; much unnamed cover-crop seed descends from this era of Canadian breeding. ‘Manor’ — the large-seeded variety that succeeded ‘Mancan’ through the 1990s, grown under contract where whole groats and soba-grade seed were wanted.

    ‘Manisoba’ and ‘Koto’

    ‘Manisoba’ — bred in Manitoba, contracted in the north-eastern United States from 2000; in New York trials it out-yielded ‘Manor’ by about 10 percent, with larger, more even seed. ‘Koto’ — developed by Cornell University with Kade Research and released in 2002; more stress-tolerant than the older varieties, with uniform seed sized for the soba trade.

    ‘Kitawase’

    ‘Kitawase’ (Kitawasesoba) — the standard Japanese soba cultivar, grown in Hokkaido's short northern summer, bred for early maturity and noodle quality.

    ‘Horizon’ and ‘Koma’

    ‘Horizon’ and ‘Koma’ — newer large-seeded grain types trialled in North America, dark-hulled and even-seeded.

    Tartary buckwheat

    Tartary buckwheat (Fagopyrum tataricum) is not a cultivar of common buckwheat but a second species — hardier in cold mountains, self-pollinating where common buckwheat needs bees, far richer in rutin and noticeably more bitter. It deserves a telling of its own; it is named here only so the two are not confused.

    • Buckwheat was domesticated in the mountains of south-western China, in what is now Yunnan province, where its wild ancestor still grows. The genetic evidence points to that corner of China, and the plant spread from there across the high ground of Asia — to Tibet, along the Himalaya, and north and east through Central Asia. The dates are less certain than the place: family-tree studies of the plant suggest farming began there thousands of years ago, possibly around 6000 BC, but the dug-up record is thin and mostly pollen — buckwheat pollen shows up in Japan from about 4000 BC, and the oldest actual seeds found in China date to about 2600 BC. What is certain is that buckwheat travelled early and far, carried along the same mountain and steppe routes as the peoples who grew it.
    • It grew where almost nothing else would. Buckwheat asks little of soil — thin, sour, rocky ground that starves wheat is good enough — and it races: seed to harvest in ten to twelve weeks, inside a single short mountain summer. That made it the insurance crop of high places, sown when the main crop failed or the season came late. It has been called the highest-elevation grain crop in the world, grown on the edge of the Tibetan Plateau at heights where wheat cannot ripen at all.
    • In Japan the plant is ancient — traces reach back to the Jōmon period, thousands of years ago — and the written record starts with hunger. In 722 CE the Empress Genshō ordered buckwheat planted across Japan as an emergency food against drought and failed rice; another edict in 839 fixed its sowing in August and harvest in October, a two-month crop to fill an empty storehouse. For centuries after, country people ate it as porridge and as dumplings of flour and hot water, kneaded and baked in the ashes — food for the places rice would not grow.
    • The noodle came late, and it changed everything. Cut buckwheat noodles — soba-kiri — are first recorded in 1574, served to workmen repairing a temple in the Shinshu mountains. In the 1600s the city of Edo (now Tokyo) filled with a million people, many of them single men building and trading, and soba became their fast food: cheap, quick, filling, and better cold than any other noodle in summer. Soba shops multiplied into the thousands. The habit never left: to this day, Japanese families eat toshikoshi soba, “year-crossing noodles,” on New Year's Eve — the long noodles standing for a long life, and their easy cutting for cutting off the old year's troubles.
    • Westward, the plant picked up names that tell its route. Russian tradition says buckwheat arrived with the Byzantine Greeks in the seventh century, and the Russian name keeps the story: grechka, “the Greek one.” Roasted into kasha, it became the defining peasant food of Russia and eastern Europe — porridge, filling, side dish, soldier's ration — and Russia still grows about half the world's buckwheat. In France it is sarrasin, “the Saracen,” and blé noir, “black wheat,” from the dark flour; in Italy, grano saraceno, the Saracen grain again. The English name came from the Dutch boekweit: “beech wheat,” because the triangular seed looks like a miniature beech nut.
    • In Brittany, buckwheat found its second home. Brought in during the 1500s, it thrived on the region's poor, acid soils where wheat sulked, and its dark flour became the galette — the big savoury buckwheat pancake, crisp-edged, wrapped around ham, egg and cheese, that is still Brittany's signature dish. Bretons tell a story that Anne of Brittany herself championed the crop; that is a story, told with pride, not a documented fact — what is documented is that buckwheat fed Brittany for centuries and kept famine at bay there more than once.
    • Elsewhere it settled into the same role, the stand-in grain: pizzoccheri, buckwheat ribbon pasta, in Italy's Valtellina valley; memil noodles and buckwheat jelly in Korea; buckwheat breads and porridges across the Himalaya, where wheat will not grow at altitude. In India, buckwheat flour — kuttu — is eaten on Hindu fast days precisely because it is not a true grain, so it sits outside the fasting rules that forbid cereals.
    • Europeans carried it to North America early, and in the 1800s the young United States grew more than a million acres of it — pancakes on every farmhouse table, and dark buckwheat honey in the jar beside them. Then it faded: nitrogen fertiliser made wheat and corn yield heavily on good land, and buckwheat, which yields modestly and sulks under heavy feeding, lost its place. What survives is its old strongholds — the groats, the pancakes, the soba — and a second career nobody in 1800 could have foreseen: the cover crop, grown not to eat but to heal the soil itself.
    • Japan — soba: buckwheat noodles in hot broth or cold with a dipping sauce, eaten daily and ritually on New Year's Eve; also soba-gaki dumplings and roasted-groat tea (soba-cha).
    • Russia and Ukraine — grechka: roasted groats boiled into kasha, eaten with butter, mushrooms, onions or milk; a staple so deep in the culture that shortages of it make national news.
    • France — Brittany's galettes de sarrasin, dark buckwheat pancakes wrapped around savoury fillings, with cider alongside; buckwheat flour is blé noir, black wheat.
    • Italy — pizzoccheri of the Valtellina: short buckwheat ribbons layered with potatoes, cabbage, butter and cheese; and polenta taragna, cornmeal enriched with buckwheat flour.
    • Korea — memil-guksu noodles, including the buckwheat noodles in chilled naengmyeon broth, and memil-muk, a mild buckwheat jelly served with soy and vegetables.
    • India — kuttu flour on fast days: pooris and pakoras eaten during Navratri and other vrat fasts, when true grains are set aside.
    • The Himalaya and Tibet — buckwheat breads, porridges and noodles at altitudes where wheat fails, with Tartary buckwheat taking over from the common kind as the land climbs.
    • United States — buckwheat pancakes, the farmhouse breakfast of the 1800s, still on diner menus; and buckwheat honey, dark as molasses, from hives set beside flowering fields.
    • The dry groats, per 100 g: 343 kcal, protein 13.3 g, carbohydrate 71.5 g, fibre 10 g, fat 3.4 g. The minerals are the standouts — magnesium 231 mg, more than half the daily value, with manganese 1.3 mg, copper 1.1 mg, phosphorus 347 mg and potassium 460 mg. Cooked, the groats take up water and everything thins out: roasted groats, cooked, run about 92 kcal per 100 g with protein 3.4 g and fibre 2.7 g.
    • The protein deserves its own word. True cereals are short on lysine, one of the building blocks of protein, and heavy on the ones buckwheat lacks. Buckwheat runs the other way — its protein is unusually well balanced for a plant food and rich in lysine — so buckwheat and true grains cover each other's gaps, which is one reason buckwheat flour has been blended with wheat flour in noodles and pancakes for centuries.
    • On blood sugar, the measured numbers are kind but modest. Boiled buckwheat groats test in the low-to-middle range on the glycaemic index — roughly 45 to 55 across published tests, varying with the form and the cooking — slower than white rice or white bread, faster than beans. Those are measurements of the food. Buckwheat also carries a compound called D-chiro-inositol, rare in other foods, which plays a part in how cells answer insulin; a concentrate of it, fed to diabetic rats, lowered their blood sugar by 12 to 19 percent (Kawa et al., 2003). That is a finding about an extract, in rats. It is a reason researchers keep studying buckwheat — it is not evidence that eating groats treats diabetes. Animal studies
    • The name most often attached to buckwheat is rutin, a plant pigment of the flavonoid family. Buckwheat is one of the richest food sources of it — but the honest detail is where it sits: mostly in the dark hull, the leaves and the flowers, and in much smaller amounts in the pale hulled groat that people actually eat. The related Tartary buckwheat carries far more rutin than the common kind. Rutin was once sold as “vitamin P”; it is not a vitamin. In people, the evidence is early and small — one trial of a rutin supplement (1 gram a day for three months, in 50 people with type 2 diabetes) found blood pressure improved, but that is a supplement dose, many times what a serving of groats provides. Trials of buckwheat foods themselves, on blood pressure and cholesterol, are few, small and short. The early signs are promising; the proof is not there yet. Human · small
    • Allergy is the serious caution, and it is not rare everywhere. Buckwheat allergy is a true food allergy that can cause anaphylaxis — a whole-body reaction that can kill. In Japan, Korea and the buckwheat-eating parts of China, an estimated 0.1 to 0.4 percent of people are allergic, school surveys count cases of buckwheat anaphylaxis in children every year, and both Japan and Korea require buckwheat to be named on food labels. The allergy is to the seed's proteins, which survive cooking, so no form of buckwheat is safe for someone allergic to it. It can also begin without eating: breathing buckwheat flour dust has caused asthma in mill and bakery workers, and sleeping on a pillow stuffed with buckwheat hulls has caused night-time asthma in people who never ate the plant. Buckwheat allergy is not wheat allergy — the plants are unrelated — but the two are easily confused by name, and the confusion matters.
    • The second caution belongs to the green plant, not the seed. The leaves, flowers and sprouts carry fagopyrin, a pigment that makes skin react to sunlight. In livestock the result is well documented and has its own name — fagopyrism: animals that graze green buckwheat, especially pale-skinned ones, break out in burning, blistering skin wherever the sun reaches them, and recover in shade. In people the reports are anecdotes, not studies, and they follow eating or juicing large amounts of buckwheat greens or sprouts — not ordinary servings of groats or flour. A systematic review of the evidence concluded that buckwheat seeds, flour and teas are safe in normal amounts, and that the risk sits with diets built heavily on the sprouts, greens and flowers (Benković & Kreft, 2015). Eat the seed; go easy on the greens.
    • When to plant: Sow after the last spring frost, once the soil has warmed — the seed germinates in three to five days in warm ground and barely stirs in cold; sow again in any frost-free gap of six weeks or more
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Thin, acid soil suits it (about pH 5 to 7); heavy nitrogen makes soft, leafy plants that fall over and set less seed
    • Environment: Likes cool, moist weather and wilts fast in hot drought; in warm climates it is a spring and late-summer crop, avoiding the worst heat — the first frost kills it outright
    • Planter or ground: Ground — it stands 2 to 4 feet tall, reddish-stemmed, with heart-shaped leaves
    • Spacing and depth: Seed about half an inch to an inch deep
    • Water: Keep moist while it grows; it wilts fast in hot drought
    • When to pick: For grain, harvest when about three-quarters of the seeds have turned brown and hard, roughly 70 to 90 days from sowing

    Garden notes

    • Buckwheat is an annual, and a tender one: the first frost kills it outright. From sowing it is in a hurry: flowering starts about three to four weeks after sowing, and the plant can stand 2 to 4 feet tall, reddish-stemmed, with heart-shaped leaves and clusters of small white-to-pink flowers.
    • The flowers need bees, and this is not a detail. Buckwheat is self-incompatible — a plant cannot pollinate itself, and its flowers come in two forms that must cross — so without insects there is no seed at all. Honey bees, bumble bees and hover flies work the blossoms eagerly, mostly in the morning, when the flowers pour out their nectar. A flowering buckwheat patch hums. Beekeepers have planted it for the honey for centuries: buckwheat honey is famously dark, strong and malty, almost like molasses, and nothing like clover honey.
    • For grain, patience at the end: the plant flowers over many weeks and ripens its seed unevenly, green and brown on the same stem. Harvest when about three-quarters of the seeds have turned brown and hard, roughly 70 to 90 days from sowing — waiting for the last seeds means losing the first to shattering.
    • As a cover crop, buckwheat is the fastest summer worker in the garden. Its canopy closes in four to six weeks and smothers weeds by shade; its fine roots loosen the topsoil; and its roots give off mild acids that free phosphorus locked in the soil, taking it up and handing it on to the next crop when the residue rots down — few cover crops match it for that phosphorus work. It does not fix nitrogen: it is not a legume, and it feeds the soil phosphorus and cover, not nitrogen. Sown in any frost-free gap of six weeks or more, it fills beds between spring and fall crops. Cut it seven to ten days after flowering begins if you do not want it seeding itself — left longer, it volunteers cheerfully next year.
    • Go easy on feeding. Buckwheat evolved on poor ground and grows well in thin, acid soil (about pH 5 to 7) that would stunt other crops; heavy nitrogen makes soft, leafy plants that lodge — fall over — and set less seed. It likes cool, moist weather and wilts fast in hot drought; in warm climates it is a spring and late-summer crop, avoiding the worst heat. Where winters are mild it still dies at the first real frost, which is part of its virtue as a cover: it never becomes a weed problem in winter, and its residue breaks down quickly, leaving the bed ready to plant.

    Propagation

    Sow seed where it is to grow, after the last frost, about half an inch to an inch deep. Buckwheat needs bees: its flowers come in two forms that must cross, so a plant cannot pollinate itself and without insects there is no seed at all. Cut a cover crop seven to ten days after flowering begins if you do not want it seeding itself — left longer, it volunteers cheerfully next year.

    Safety

    • Safety — allergy. Buckwheat allergy is a true food allergy that can cause anaphylaxis — a whole-body reaction that can kill. In Japan, Korea and the buckwheat-eating parts of China, an estimated 0.1 to 0.4 percent of people are allergic, and both Japan and Korea require buckwheat to be named on food labels. The allergy is to the seed's proteins, which survive cooking, so no form of buckwheat is safe for someone allergic to it. It can also begin without eating: breathing buckwheat flour dust has caused asthma in mill and bakery workers, and sleeping on a pillow stuffed with buckwheat hulls has caused night-time asthma in people who never ate the plant. Buckwheat allergy is not wheat allergy — the plants are unrelated — but the two are easily confused by name, and the confusion matters.
    • Safety — the green plant. The leaves, flowers and sprouts carry fagopyrin, a pigment that makes skin react to sunlight. In livestock the result is well documented and has its own name — fagopyrism: animals that graze green buckwheat break out in burning, blistering skin wherever the sun reaches them. In people the reports are anecdotes, not studies, and they follow eating or juicing large amounts of buckwheat greens or sprouts — not ordinary servings of groats or flour. Eat the seed; go easy on the greens.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: buckwheat (whole groats, dry) and buckwheat groats, roasted, cooked — the nutrition figures
    • Hunt et al. (2018) — Buckwheat: a crop from outside the major Chinese domestication centres? — the archaeobotanical, pollen and genetic evidence for a south-western Chinese origin, and how thin the dug-up record is
    • Kawa et al. (2003) — Buckwheat concentrate reduces serum glucose in streptozotocin-diabetic rats — the D-chiro-inositol study, in rats

    • Norbäck & Wieslander (2021) — A review on epidemiological and clinical studies on buckwheat allergy — prevalence, anaphylaxis, flour-dust and pillow cases
