    Celery

    Apium graveolens

    Culinary

    Vitamin K

    FreshCooked

    Three vegetables, one plant. The crisp stalks in a salad, the knobbly root under a winter soup, and the dark, strongly flavoured leaves in a Chinese stir-fry are all the same species, bred three different ways from a bitter marsh plant of the Mediterranean shore. Stalk celery is grown for its thick leaf stems; celeriac for its swollen root; leaf celery — the form closest to the wild plant — for its leaves and seed. All three carry the same clean, savoury, unmistakable celery taste, and all three began as a plant people gathered for medicine and ceremony long before anyone ate it for pleasure.

    Cultivars

    Celery is sorted first by the part it is bred for — stalk, root, or leaf — and only then by named variety. The three forms are told apart by shape and use, because an unlabelled photograph cannot honestly prove a named variety.

    Stalk celery (the Dulce group)

    Thick, crisp, upright leaf stems in a tight bunch, the salad and soup celery of North America and Europe. It comes in two kinds: green Pascal types, full-flavoured and stringier, and self-blanching yellow types, paler, milder and more tender, long preferred in Europe. 'Tall Utah 52-70' is the standard green garden variety — tall, crisp, and reliable. 'Golden Self-Blanching' is the classic yellow heirloom, grown since the 1880s. 'Conquistador' and 'Tango' are modern green varieties bred for early harvests and smooth, less stringy stalks.

    Celeriac (the Rapaceum group)

    The same plant bred for a swollen root the size of a grapefruit, rough, knobbly and cream-fleshed, tasting of celery and nuts. It is a winter vegetable of northern and eastern Europe: mashed, roasted, grated raw into salads, and simmered in soups. 'Giant Prague' is the old, large-rooted standard; 'Monarch' and 'Prinz' are modern varieties bred for smoother, rounder roots that are easier to peel.

    Leaf celery (the Secalinum group)

    Thin stalks and a heavy crop of dark, strongly flavoured leaves: the form nearest the wild plant. In China it is a standard cooking green, chopped into soups and stir-fries; in Europe it is grown as a cut-and-come-again herb, used as parsley is used, and its seed is the celery seed of the spice shelf. One name to keep apart: lovage is a different, much bigger plant with a celery-like taste — a kin, not a form of celery.

    • Wild celery — smallage, in the old English word — still grows in salt marshes, damp ditches and coastal ground around the Mediterranean and across Europe and western Asia. It is a slender, strong-smelling plant with thin, hollow stalks and a bitter bite, nothing like the fat mild stalks in a modern salad. Every garden form descends from it, and its home ground never changed: celery is a marsh plant at heart, and it still wants wet feet in the garden.
    • The name carries the marsh with it. Greek selinon named the plant — the same word that named its close kin parsley, and old writings do not always keep the two apart. Latin turned it into apium; graveolens means strong-smelling, which the wild plant certainly is. English "celery" came through French and Italian from a Greek form of the same word.
    • The oldest traces are ceremonial, not culinary. Garlands woven with wild celery leaves were found in the tomb of Tutankhamun, laid there more than 3,000 years ago. In Homer's Odyssey, the meadows around Calypso's cave bloom with violets and selinon. The Greeks held the plant holy: winners at the Nemean Games and the Isthmian Games were crowned with wreaths of wild celery, as Olympic winners were crowned with olive — and like its kin parsley, it was also a plant of funerals and of the dead.
    • For most of its long history, celery was a medicine and a flavouring, not a vegetable. The seed was the part that mattered most: Ayurvedic physicians in India used celery seed for colds, water retention, poor digestion and aching joints, and European herbals carried the seed and root for much the same list. The stalks, when they were eaten at all, were bitter enough to need taming.
    • The taming happened in Italy in the 1600s. Italian gardeners selected plants with solid, mild, fleshy stalks in place of the hollow bitter ones, and learned that growing celery cool and blanching it — heaping earth around the stalks to shut out the light — softened its strength further. The first clear record of celery eaten as a food comes from France in 1623. From Italy the new vegetable spread to France and England, still a luxury and still strongly flavoured by modern standards.
    • Celeriac was bred in the same centuries, in northern and eastern Europe, by selecting the opposite end of the plant: a swollen, turnip-like root under a crown of rough leaves. Leaf celery kept the old form — thin stalks, plenty of leaf, strong taste — and travelled east, becoming a kitchen staple in China and Southeast Asia, where it is chopped into soups, noodles and stir-fries, and where its seed is also gathered.
    • The 1800s made celery fashionable in America. It stood in cut-glass celery vases at the centre of well-set tables, eaten raw with salt as a delicacy and a digestive; it went into the Waldorf salad in New York in the 1890s — celery, apple and walnuts in mayonnaise — and Kalamazoo, Michigan, grew so much of it on its black marsh soils that it called itself Celery City. The fashion faded, but the plant stayed: in the French mirepoix and the Cajun "holy trinity" of onion, celery and pepper, in celery salt on a Bloody Mary, and in the seed that flavours pickles and sausages.
    • France — mirepoix, the chopped onion, carrot and celery base that starts a thousand sauces, soups and braises; and céleri rémoulade, celeriac grated raw and dressed with a mustard mayonnaise, the standing first course of Paris bistros.
    • Louisiana — the "holy trinity" of Cajun and Creole cooking: onion, celery and green pepper, the base of gumbo, jambalaya and étouffée, named in playful echo of the French mirepoix it descends from.
    • China — leaf celery chopped into noodle soups, dumpling fillings and stir-fries, valued precisely for the strong flavour the stalk forms were bred to lose.
    • Germany and Poland — celeriac goes into the soup pot as part of the classic bundle of soup greens, is breaded and fried as a schnitzel in its own right, and anchors winter salads.
    • The United States — celery and peanut butter ("ants on a log," with raisins, is the children's version), celery salt on Chicago hot dogs and Bloody Marys, and the Waldorf salad, still made to its 1890s New York pattern.
    • India — celery seed, ajmoda, is a spice and an Ayurvedic medicine seed, ground into blends and taken for digestion and aching joints — a use that travelled with the plant's seed trade long before its stalks were food.
    • Celery is mostly water, and its numbers say so honestly. Raw stalks, per 100 g: about 14 kcal, fibre 1.6 g, potassium 260 mg, folate 36 µg, and vitamin K at 29 µg — about a quarter of the day's value. Celeriac is the denser food: about 42 kcal per 100 g, fibre 1.8 g, vitamin K 41 µg, potassium 300 mg. Vitamin K is the vitamin the body uses to clot blood normally and to build bone; people who take warfarin or a similar blood thinner are told to keep their vitamin K intake steady, and celery eaten in normal amounts fits that steadiness — it is large, sudden changes in green vegetables that matter, and those are worth mentioning to the clinician who manages the dose.
    • Celery is not a "negative-calorie" food, despite the famous claim. Digesting food does burn some energy, but only a small share of the energy the food itself carries — roughly a tenth for a food like celery. A stalk brings in more than the body spends chewing and digesting it. Celery is a genuinely low-calorie food, and that is enough; it does not need the myth.
    • Blood pressure is the claim with real research behind it. The compound most studied is 3-n-butylphthalide — one of the chemicals that give celery its smell — and most of the work has used celery seed, not salad stalks. In animals, celery seed extracts and that compound lower blood pressure. In people, the trials so far are small and short: in the best-known one, 52 patients with high blood pressure took celery seed extract capsules (1.34 g a day) for four weeks and their blood pressure fell clearly against placebo (Shayani Rad et al., 2022). A 2025 review gathering ten small trials and 511 people found the same direction of effect, and said plainly that the trials were small, short and mixed in quality. So: seed extract capsules have early human evidence; eating stalks has never been put to the same test, and no trial supports celery juice as a treatment. Celery is a good food inside a diet for blood pressure; it is not a medicine for it, and it is no replacement for prescribed treatment. Human · small
    • Celery carries apigenin and other compounds that calm inflammation and protect cells in dishes and in animals — the same early stage of evidence as its kin parsley — and celery extracts kill some microbes in cultures. None of that has been shown to happen in a person eating celery. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • When to plant: Sow indoors ten to twelve weeks before the last frost; set plants out after the last frost, once nights stay mild
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: The richest, wettest ground in the garden — deep soil full of compost that never dries out
    • Water: Water deeply and often; a plant that dries out answers with thin, stringy, bitter stalks, or stops growing altogether
    • Spacing: Stalk celery about 6–10 in (15–25 cm) apart; celeriac a little wider, set carefully shallow with the crown at soil level. Plants stand 12–18 in (30–45 cm) tall
    • When to pick: Take outer stalks one by one from about 90–120 days after transplanting, or cut the whole bunch at the base when the stalks are thick. Celeriac is dug from autumn onward, once the root reaches tennis-ball size or better — it can take 200 days from sowing

    Garden notes

    • Celery is a biennial grown as an annual: a leafy rosette and stalks in its first year, a tall flower stalk and seed in its second, if it lives through a winter. Like its kin parsley, it is famously slow to start, and for the same family reason — small seed, in no hurry.
    • Celery seed takes two to three weeks to sprout and wants light, warmth and constant moisture while it does. Sow it barely covered and keep the tray damp the whole time; many gardeners soak the seed overnight first. A cold snap on young plants can push them to flower early and spoil the stalks.
    • Celeriac's root forms at and above the soil surface through a very long season. Mulch thickly to hold the moisture in, and rub off side shoots and side roots on celeriac as they appear, to keep the root smooth and single.
    • The old self-blanching varieties pale themselves; green types can be left green — modern taste mostly prefers them so — or blanched in the last two to three weeks by wrapping or earthing up, for paler, milder stalks. Celeriac stands in the ground through light frosts, sweetening as the cold comes.
    • The flat-topped flower heads feed the same small parasitic wasps and hoverflies that hunt garden pests, and black swallowtail caterpillars eat the leaves, as they do on parsley and carrot.

    Propagation

    A plant that overwinters flowers in flat-topped heads like its kin in its second year. Seed is ripe when the heads brown; celery seed from the garden is the spice-shelf seed, fresh and strong.

    Safety

    • Celery allergy is one of the serious ones. In continental Europe, celery allergy is common enough that European law puts celery among the fourteen allergens that must be named and highlighted on food labels — stalk, celeriac and seed all count, raw or cooked, and celery powder hides in spice blends, soups, sauces and stock cubes. Many cases begin with pollen: celery holds a protein, Api g 1, close kin to the main birch-pollen allergen, so people with birch or mugwort hay fever may react to raw celery, sometimes only with an itching mouth. But celery also carries tougher proteins that survive cooking, and reactions can run the whole range — hives, swelling, breathing trouble, and anaphylaxis, the severe whole-body reaction that can kill. Celery stands among the leading causes of food anaphylaxis in parts of central Europe. Anyone who reacts to celery should treat it as a true allergy, not a sensitivity, and anyone unsure should be tested rather than test themselves.
    • Celery belongs to the carrot family, several of whose members carry compounds that react with strong sun on skin: people who harvest or handle large amounts of celery in bright weather have developed blistering rashes where the juice touched, and old or diseased celery carries more of these compounds — wash hands after handling a lot of it.
    • The seed is not the stalk: celery seed and its concentrated oil, taken in medicinal amounts, are not for pregnancy.

    Sources

    • Shayani Rad et al. (2022) — Effect of celery (Apium graveolens) seed extract on hypertension: a randomized, triple-blind, placebo-controlled, cross-over clinical trial, Phytotherapy Research — the 52-patient blood-pressure trial
    • Liu et al. (2025) — Effects of celery (Apium graveolens) on blood pressure, glycemic and lipid profile in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, Frontiers in Nutrition — the ten-trial review and its own caution about small, mixed-quality trials
    • European Union (2011) — Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, Annex II — celery among the fourteen allergens that must be declared and highlighted on food labels
    • Encyclopaedia Britannica — Celery: description, uses, history — the three cultivated varieties, the Tutankhamun garlands, the Greek games wreaths, and the 1623 French food record
    • University of Minnesota Extension — Growing celery and celeriac in home gardens — sowing, spacing, moisture and harvest

    Cherry

    Prunus avium and Prunus cerasus

    Culinary

    Vitamin A

    FreshCookedDried

    Two fruits wearing one name, both of them kin to the plum, the peach, the apricot and the almond in the rose family. The sweet cherry is the glossy dessert fruit, eaten fresh by the handful in early summer. The sour cherry — also called the tart or pie cherry — is smaller, sharper and mostly cooked: pies, preserves, dried fruit and juice. Both come from the lands between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea, and both carry the same warning inside the stone: the soft kernel at the centre holds amygdalin, a compound that can release cyanide. One name warning first: the famous flowering cherries of Japan, and the blossom trees around the water in Washington, D.C., are different species, grown for their flowers. They are not either of the fruiting cherries here.

    Cultivars

    Sweet cherries first, then the sour kinds.

    'Bing'

    Raised in Milwaukie, Oregon, in 1875 by the nurseryman Seth Lewelling, from a seedling of 'Black Republican' crossed with 'Napoleon'. Lewelling named it for Ah Bing, his Chinese foreman, who had tended his orchards for years: the cherry was found in Bing's row, and it was a big cherry, as he was. Large, dark, firm and sweet, it became America's standard sweet cherry. It needs a pollinizer, and it cracks badly in rain.

    'Rainier'

    Bred at Washington State University from 'Bing' × 'Van', the cross made in 1952 and the kind released in 1960, named for Mount Rainier. Yellow fruit with a pink blush and cream flesh, very sweet and delicate; it bruises at a touch and birds take it eagerly.

    'Royal Ann' (also 'Napoleon')

    An old French kind: pale yellow fruit blushed red, firm and sweet-tart. Long the standard for brining and cocktail cherries, and a parent of 'Bing'.

    'Black Tartarian'

    An old kind that reached England from Circassia, in the cherry's home country, and America soon after. Early, soft, dark and rich — a home-garden cherry, too tender for shipping.

    'Stella'

    Released by the research station at Summerland, British Columbia, in 1968: the first self-fertile sweet cherry with fruit good enough to sell. Large, dark, heart-shaped fruit on a tree that needs no partner — and nearly every self-fertile kind since descends from it.

    'Lapins'

    Also from Summerland, named for the breeder K. O. Lapins. Self-fertile, late, large and dark, and it resists rain-cracking better than most.

    'Sweetheart'

    A third Summerland kind: self-fertile, firm, and very late, ripening after the main season and stretching the harvest.

    'Montmorency'

    From the Montmorency valley in France, grown since at least the 1600s. An amarelle: bright red skin over pale flesh and nearly clear juice. Self-fertile, cold-hardy and heavy-cropping, it makes up about 95 in every 100 of America's tart cherries, and it is the cherry behind the juice in the sleep and recovery trials.

    'English Morello'

    A morello: dark red skin, flesh and juice, later and sharper than 'Montmorency'. The pie and preserving cherry of northern Europe.

    'Balaton'

    A Hungarian morello kind, brought to Michigan in the 1980s. Darker and a little sweeter than 'Montmorency' — tart-cherry lovers eat it fresh.

    'North Star'

    Bred in Minnesota: a naturally small tree, 6–12 ft, self-fertile and very hardy, made for northern home gardens.

    • The sweet cherry grows wild across Europe and western Asia, from the Balkans through the Caucasus to the Caspian Sea, and wild trees — called gean or mazzard — still stand in European woods. Birds did the spreading: the species name avium means "of the birds," and birds eating the fruit carried the stones far beyond the parent trees. The wild tree is valued for more than fruit: its reddish timber is one of Europe's prized cabinet woods.
    • The sour cherry began as a natural cross. Where the sweet cherry's range met the low, hardy ground cherry (Prunus fruticosa), the two crossed on their own — probably more than once — and the result was a new species with the sweet cherry's fruit and the ground cherry's toughness and tang. Greeks knew sour cherries by about 300 BC, and growers later selected the cultivated kinds from wild trees around the Caspian and Black Seas. Crosses between sweet and sour cherries, called duke cherries, sit between the two in flavour.
    • The Roman writer Pliny recorded how the cherry reached Italy: before the general Lucullus defeated Mithridates, king of Pontus, in the 70s BC, he wrote, there were no cherry trees in Italy — Lucullus brought them from Pontus, on the Black Sea coast of what is now Turkey. The tree was named for Cerasus, a port there — modern Giresun — and the name travelled with the fruit: Latin cerasus, French cerise, English cherry. (The French word was taken for a plural, so a single fruit became "a cherry.") Pliny added that within 120 years the tree had crossed the sea to Britain. Greeks had known cherries for centuries before Lucullus, so what he carried to Rome was most likely choice cultivated kinds, not the first cherry in Europe.
    • Across Europe the sour cherry became the preserving cherry. In France's Montmorency valley it gave the pie cherry that still rules the trade. In Germany's Black Forest, sour cherries were distilled into kirsch, the clear cherry spirit poured into the region's cherry cake. On Croatia's Dalmatian coast, the small dark marasca cherry was steeped in a liqueur distilled from its own fruit, pits and leaves — maraschino — and the preserved cherries took the same name. When the recipe crossed to America, Oregon growers remade it in the 1920s with a salt brine, pale Royal Ann cherries, dye and almond flavouring: the bright-red cocktail cherry is an American factory version of a Croatian original.
    • America's most famous cherry story is not true, and was never claimed by anyone who was there. The tale of the boy George Washington, his hatchet, his father's cherry tree and "I cannot tell a lie" was invented by Mason Locke Weems, a travelling minister and bookseller who wrote one of the first lives of Washington. It did not appear in his book's first edition of 1800; he added it to the fifth edition, in 1806, as a lesson in honesty for young readers. No record from Washington's lifetime supports it. It stands as a story Americans told about their first president — not as something that happened.
    • Japan's blossom cherries are a separate branch of the family, bred over centuries for flower, not fruit — kinds such as Somei Yoshino (Prunus × yedoensis). Tokyo gave Washington, D.C. its famous trees in 1912, and the blossom festivals in both countries celebrate those ornamental species. Their small fruit is not the cherry of the market, and their fame belongs to the flower.
    • Turkey grows more cherries than any other country — about a fifth of the world's crop — which fits: the tree's homeland is on its Black Sea coast. The United States, Chile and Uzbekistan follow. In America, sweet cherries centre on Washington, Oregon and California, while Michigan, around Traverse City, grows the large majority of the country's tart cherries. Spain's Jerte valley is known for its picota cherries, picked and sold without their stems.
    • Sweet cherries, per 100 g: 63 kcal, protein 1.1 g, carbohydrate 16 g, sugars 12.8 g, fibre 2.1 g, fat 0.2 g, potassium 222 mg, vitamin C 7 mg and vitamin A at just 3 µg. There is no standout vitamin here; a sweet cherry is a moderate fruit whose deep red colour comes from anthocyanins, the pigments studied in laboratories for their effects on inflammation. What the fruit itself has been through in human trials is very little — nearly all the cherry trial evidence below belongs to the sour cherry, and to its juice.
    • Sour cherries, per 100 g: 50 kcal, protein 1 g, carbohydrate 12.2 g, sugars 8.5 g, fibre 1.6 g, fat 0.3 g, potassium 173 mg, vitamin C 10 mg and vitamin A at 64 µg — about twenty times the sweet cherry's, from 770 µg of beta-carotene. Most people meet this fruit cooked, dried or as juice, because fresh it is too tart for eating by the handful.
    • Sour cherries carry melatonin, the hormone the body itself makes at night — but in traces, measured in nanograms per gram of fruit, a tiny fraction of what a melatonin tablet holds. The sleep trials used juice, not fruit bowls. In a 2010 pilot study, 15 older adults with insomnia drank a tart cherry juice blend twice a day for two weeks: against a placebo drink, their insomnia scores improved modestly — about 17 minutes less time spent awake after falling asleep — and the study was paid for by the juice's maker. In a 2012 trial, 20 healthy adults drank tart cherry juice concentrate for seven days; melatonin in their urine rose, and their sleep ran a little longer and better. A 2018 pilot with just 8 people, measured in a sleep laboratory, found 84 extra minutes of sleep — the largest result from the smallest study. Small, short trials of juice and concentrate, all pointing the same way, are a reason for interest. They are not proof that tart cherry treats insomnia. Human · small
    • For gout, the largest study is a watching study, not a trial. Boston University researchers followed 633 people with gout for a year and compared each attack with the same person's quiet periods: eating cherries in the two days before was tied to a 35% lower risk of an attack, cherry extract showed a similar link, and cherries taken alongside the gout drug allopurinol were tied to a 75% lower risk. People reported their own eating, so the link could still hide other causes, and no trial has tested cherries as a gout treatment. In one small study of 12 people, a single serving of tart cherry concentrate lowered uric acid in the blood for a few hours — a mechanism, not a treatment. Human · small
    • Tart cherry juice is also sold to athletes. Many small trials have given Montmorency juice or concentrate around hard training and racing; when 14 of those studies were pooled in 2021, the juice showed a small help against muscle soreness and a moderate help in getting strength back, with wide differences between trials. Real human trials, nearly all small and short, with results mixed from study to study. Human trials
    • Sun: Full sun, and ground that drains
    • Soil: Ground that drains freely — roots standing in wet soil rot, and sour cherries tolerate damp only a little better than sweet
    • Environment: Sweet cherries grow in zones 5–8, sour cherries hardy to zone 4. Both need winter cold to fruit well: most sweet kinds want 700 to 900 hours below 45 °F, sour cherries roughly 700 to 1,000
    • Size: A sweet cherry on a standard rootstock makes a large tree, 20–30 ft tall; a sour cherry is a smaller tree, 10–20 ft. Dwarfing rootstocks hold a sweet cherry much smaller
    • When to pick: Sweet cherries do not sweeten after picking, so pick them fully coloured and ripe, with the stems left on — the season is short, late spring into midsummer, June to July in most districts. Sour cherries are picked fully red and used at once: cooked, frozen or juiced

    Garden notes

    • Sweet and sour cherries ask for different gardens. A sweet cherry on a standard rootstock makes a large tree, 20–30 ft tall, in zones 5–8; dwarfing rootstocks hold it much smaller. A sour cherry is a smaller tree, 10–20 ft, hardier to zone 4, and a little more forgiving of heavier soil. Both want full sun and ground that drains: roots standing in wet soil rot, and sour cherries only tolerate damp a little better than sweet.
    • Both need winter cold to fruit well. Most sweet cherries want 700 to 900 hours below 45 °F (7 °C) across the winter, some kinds more; sour cherries want roughly 700 to 1,000 hours, with 'Montmorency' near 700. In mild-winter districts the buds open unevenly and the crop is poor.
    • Pollination divides the two. Most sweet cherries cannot set fruit with their own pollen, and not every kind can pollinate every other — a compatible partner kind, flowering at the same time, must grow nearby, and planting guides list which kinds pair. A few sweet kinds are self-fertile — 'Stella', 'Lapins' and 'Sweetheart' among them — and crop on a single tree. Sour cherries are self-fertile: one tree on its own crops reliably, which is why the sour cherry is the easier cherry for a small garden.
    • The defining pest flies. Birds can strip a ripening cherry tree in a few days, taking the fruit from the top and the outer branches first — the species was named for them. Netting the tree as the fruit colours is the one reliable defence, and a small tree on a dwarfing rootstock is far easier to net than a standard one. Pick promptly: a ripe tree left unnetted is a feast laid out.
    • Rain near harvest is the sweet cherry's other classic loss: ripe fruit drinks in water through the skin and splits. Kinds differ in how badly they crack — 'Bing' is known for it, 'Lapins' resists it better — and sour cherries crack far less.
    • Sweet cherries do not sweeten after picking, so pick them fully coloured and ripe, with the stems left on, which helps them keep. The season is short — late spring into midsummer, June to July in most districts. Sour cherries are picked fully red and used at once: cooked, frozen or juiced.
    • Prune cherries in dry summer weather, after harvest, rather than in winter dormancy: the cuts then meet less of the wet-weather infection that brings bacterial canker and silver leaf into stone fruit. Clear away fallen fruit and any dried, mummified fruit left hanging — brown rot overwinters in them. Sour cherries fruit heavily on young wood, so steady renewal pruning, taking out some older stems each year, keeps the bearing wood coming.

    Propagation

    Buy a named kind as a grafted tree: cherries are budded or grafted onto a rootstock, and a tree grown from a stone grows into a much larger tree and is slower to fruit — growing from seed is not usually worthwhile.

    Safety

    • The stone at the centre of every cherry holds a soft kernel, and the kernel holds amygdalin — the same compound as in apricot kernels. Chewed and digested, amygdalin releases cyanide. The hard shell of the stone is the protection: a pit swallowed whole passes through the body unopened, and poison centres treat that as a low-risk event. The danger comes from cracking the stones and chewing the kernels in quantity, or blending whole fruit with the pits in, which breaks the kernels into the drink. Cherry kernels carry far less amygdalin than bitter apricot kernels, and poisoning from ordinary cherry eating is rare — but the kernels are not food, and the same amygdalin was once sold as "laetrile," a cancer treatment that failed its trial. For small children the everyday risk of a whole pit is simpler: it is the right size to choke on.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture — FoodData Central: cherries, sweet, raw, and cherries, sour, red, raw — the nutrition figures
    • Pliny the Elder — Natural History, Book 15 — Lucullus, Cerasus, and the cherry's arrival in Italy and Britain
    • Pigeon et al. (2010) — tart cherry juice beverage and sleep in older adults with insomnia: a pilot study of 15 people
    • Howatson et al. (2012) — tart cherry juice concentrate, melatonin levels and sleep quality in 20 adults
    • Losso et al. (2018) — pilot study of tart cherry juice and sleep in 8 older adults, measured in a sleep laboratory
    • Zhang et al. (2012) — cherry consumption and the risk of recurrent gout attacks in 633 people with gout
    • Hillman & Chrismas (2021) — systematic review and meta-analysis of tart cherry and recovery from strenuous exercise, 14 studies
    • National Capital Poison Center — cherry pits, amygdalin and cyanide
    • Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2022) — world cherry production — Turkey's share of the crop
    • George Washington's Mount Vernon — the cherry tree myth and Mason Locke Weems
    • Royal Horticultural Society — How to grow cherries — budding and grafting onto rootstocks; growing from seed is not usually worthwhile

    Chestnut

    Castanea spp.

    Culinary

    Vitamin C

    FreshCookedDried

    The chestnut is the nut of a family of trees in the beech and oak family, and it breaks the rule of what a nut is. A walnut or an almond is mostly fat; a chestnut is mostly starch — a food closer to a potato or a loaf of bread than to any other nut, eaten cooked since long before written history. The nuts ripen inside a green burr armoured with needle-sharp spines, one to three glossy brown nuts to a burr, and every true chestnut nut is drawn out to a point at the tip, finished with a small tuft. One warning about a name before anything else, and it matters: the horse chestnut is a different tree in a different family, and its seeds are poisonous. Horse chestnut seeds — conkers — are round, smooth and shiny, with a pale patch on one side, and they sit in a green husk carrying only a few blunt bumps. A true chestnut comes out of a burr packed tight with sharp spines, and its nut ends in a point. Buckeyes, the horse chestnut's American cousins, are poisonous in the same way. Never eat a conker, and never eat any "chestnut" that does not match the spiny burr and the pointed nut. The water chestnut of stir-fries is not a chestnut either — it is the underground stem of a water plant, and harmless.

    Cultivars

    Several species are grown, and the differences between them are the first thing a grower chooses.

    Sweet chestnut (Castanea sativa)

    The European tree: the largest nuts, the classic flavour, the tree of the bread-tree groves; blight-susceptible in eastern North America.

    Chinese chestnut (C. mollissima)

    A smaller, spreading tree with medium nuts and strong natural resistance to the blight; it carries most modern American orchards.

    Japanese chestnut (C. crenata)

    The biggest nuts of all, less sweet, blight-resistant.

    American chestnut (C. dentata)

    The smallest and by many accounts the sweetest nuts, on the mightiest tree; blight-stricken in its home forest.

    Allegheny chinquapin (C. pumila)

    A shrubby small tree with one sweet little nut to a burr, also hit by the blight.

    'Marron de Lyon'

    The classic French marron cultivar, large glossy nuts that peel well, the roasting and candying standard for generations.

    'Bouche de Bétizac'

    A French-bred hybrid of European and Japanese chestnut, bred for resistance to the root disease called ink disease, bearing large early nuts; widely planted in modern French orchards.

    'Marigoule' and 'Marsol'

    French hybrids used heavily as pollinizers and rootstocks, valued for vigour and reliable pollen.

    'Marrone del Mugello' and 'Marrone di Castel del Rio'

    Italy's protected-name marrons, grown in defined hill districts in Tuscany and Emilia-Romagna, large and sweet with skins that peel away cleanly; the names belong to the places as much as to the trees.

    'Colossal'

    The main orchard tree of California: a European–Japanese hybrid with very large nuts. Its own pollen is largely sterile, so it is always planted with a pollinizer beside it.

    'Eaton', 'Qing' and 'Peach'

    American-grown Chinese chestnuts, heavy and reliable bearers of sweet, easy-peeling nuts.

    'Sleeping Giant'

    A hardy American hybrid of mixed parentage.

    'Dunstan' chestnuts

    Florida-bred hybrids raised from a blight-surviving American tree found growing in Ohio, crossed with Chinese stock; widely sold for wildlife plantings.

    'Tsukuba' and 'Ishizuchi'

    Japanese-bred cultivars with very large nuts, the standards of Japan's orchards.

    In France the grading word is marron: a marron is a nut that fills its burr singly, plump and undivided — the premium grade for roasting whole and for candying — while a châtaigne splits into two or three sections inside the burr and goes to flour and purée. Good cultivars are bred to bear marrons.

    • The chestnuts are an old northern family of trees, kin to the oaks and beeches, with species native to Europe, Asia and North America. The sweet chestnut, Castanea sativa, is at home in the hills around the Mediterranean and east into Asia Minor, and it is the chestnut of European history. In Japan, people were tending chestnut trees around their villages more than 5,000 years ago — at the settlement of Sannai-Maruyama, the pollen record and the chestnut wood and nuts dug up there suggest the trees were planted and cared for, making the chestnut one of the oldest managed food trees in Japan.
    • The Greeks grew the sweet chestnut and the Romans carried it everywhere their roads went, grafting the best trees and planting groves across southern and western Europe, probably into Britain as well. The Latin name Castanea comes from the Greek kastanea, most likely taken from a town famous for its nuts. Roman soldiers are said to have carried chestnut porridge as a marching food — the nut was army rations before it was a treat.
    • Where wheat would not grow, the chestnut became the bread. In the mountain country of Corsica, the Cévennes in France, the Apennines in Italy and the hills of northern Spain and Portugal, chestnuts were dried in stone drying houses over slow smoke, ground into flour, and baked into bread and polenta that carried whole villages through the winter. Corsicans called the chestnut the bread tree, and meant it literally: in a good chestnut valley, a family could live on its trees. The same trees fed the pigs that provided the meat.
    • A sweet chestnut can live for many centuries, and the oldest of them all grows on the slopes of Mount Etna in Sicily: the Hundred Horse Chestnut, a vast hollow tree thought to be somewhere between 2,000 and 4,000 years old, among the oldest and largest chestnut trees known. Its name carries its story — a queen, caught in a storm on the mountain with a hundred knights, is said to have sheltered under its branches until the rain passed.
    • The tree worked as well as fed. Sweet chestnut cut back to the stump regrows in straight poles — coppice — and the poles resist rot in the ground, so they were cut on rotation for fencing, for the hop poles of Kent, for vineyard stakes and for charcoal. The wood and bark are rich in tannin, the bitter stuff that tans leather, and chestnut was once a major source of it. A chestnut grove was a farm, a timber yard and a tannery in one planting.
    • North America had its own giant. The American chestnut, Castanea dentata, was one of the great trees of the eastern forest — in the Appalachian Mountains about one hardwood in every four was a chestnut, growing straight and branch-free to heights of 100 feet, its rot-resistant wood built into barns, houses, fences and telegraph poles. Every autumn it dropped nuts beyond counting, feeding bears, deer, turkeys and the now-vanished passenger pigeon, and mountain families gathered the surplus to sell — chestnuts were a cash crop, shipped by the trainload to eastern cities for the Christmas roasting trade. People said a squirrel could travel the chestnut canopy from Georgia to Maine without touching the ground.
    • Then came the blight. The fungus Cryphonectria parasitica arrived from East Asia on imported Japanese chestnut nursery trees, and it was first noticed in 1904, on chestnuts at the Bronx Zoo in New York. It spreads on the wind, enters through wounds, and girdles the tree with cankers. The American chestnut had never met it and had no defence. Within fifty years an estimated four billion American chestnuts were dead — nearly every mature tree in the eastern forest. The species is not quite extinct: its roots survive, and sprouts still spring from old stumps all over the Appalachians. But the blight finds the sprouts as they grow, and it usually kills them before they become great trees again.
    • The same fungus reached Europe in 1938, near Genoa in Italy, and spread through the sweet chestnut groves. Europe's story turned out differently. From the 1950s, some cankers began to heal on their own: the blight fungus itself had caught a virus, and the virus — plant scientists call the weakening it causes hypovirulence — saps the fungus so its cankers stop growing and the tree can wall them off. European chestnuts were badly hurt but never wiped out, and the virus is now spread deliberately as a living control for the disease.
    • The work of bringing the American chestnut back runs on two tracks. Since 1983 the American Chestnut Foundation has bred by backcrossing: crossing American with blight-resistant Chinese chestnut, then crossing the offspring back to American trees again and again, aiming for a tree that is American in almost everything but carries the Chinese resistance. The second track added a single wheat gene to the American tree, a gene that lets the tree neutralise the acid the fungus attacks with; the engineered tree, called Darling 58, was celebrated for years before it came out in 2023 that the trees in the trials had been a sister line, Darling 54, all along, and that they grew poorly. The Foundation withdrew its support that December. The tested line was cleared by United States regulators in 2026, and a study published in Science that year found that real blight resistance is spread across many genes working together — which is why the breeding track, slow as it is, may prove the surer road. No one has yet restored the great forest, and honesty requires saying so.
    • In France the chestnut became a luxury. In the Ardèche, the chestnut country above the Rhône, Clément Faugier set up in 1885 and built a trade on sweetened chestnut purée and marrons glacés — whole chestnuts candied in syrup until they turn translucent and tender, made by hand and sold at Christmas prices. Roasted chestnuts stayed the people's share: sold hot from braziers on winter streets across Europe, and in America fixed in the national ear in 1945, when "The Christmas Song" opened with chestnuts roasting on an open fire.
    • France — marrons glacés at Christmas; crème de marrons, the sweetened purée, spread on crêpes and spooned into the Mont Blanc dessert, where it is pushed into strands over cream like a little mountain; Corsica still mills its chestnut flour and bakes with it through the winter.
    • Italy — castagnaccio, the flat Tuscan chestnut-flour cake with rosemary, pine nuts and raisins; necci, chestnut-flour pancakes cooked between hot irons; chestnut polenta in the mountain villages; and an autumn festival of the chestnut in nearly every town that grows them.
    • Spain and Portugal — the magosto: chestnuts roasted over open fires at the start of November, eaten with new wine and sausages around bonfires in Galicia and the north; in Portugal, roast chestnuts belong to St Martin's Day, 11 November, sold from carts in Lisbon wrapped in paper cones.
    • Japan — kuri: chestnut rice (kuri gohan) in autumn; kuri kinton, the golden chestnut-and-sweet-potato mash of the New Year feast; and amaguri, sweet roasted chestnuts sold hot in paper bags — a Tianjin speciality from Chinese chestnuts, loved across East Asia.
    • China — sugar-fried chestnuts: vendors stir chestnuts in great woks of hot sand and sugar until the shells gloss and crack, and sell them by weight, steaming, on autumn streets.
    • Turkey — kestane kebab, chestnuts roasted over charcoal by street vendors in winter, and Bursa's kestane şekeri, chestnuts candied in syrup, the city's famous sweet.
    • North America — the Christmas trade is a shadow of what it was: before the blight, trainloads of native nuts reached the cities each December; the roasting carts of New York now work with imported Italian, Chinese and Korean chestnuts, and the song keeps the custom alive.
    • Chestnuts, raw, per 100 g: 213 kcal, carbohydrate 45.5 g — nearly all of it starch — protein 2.4 g, fat just 2.3 g, fibre 8.1 g, and potassium 518 mg. Roasting drives off water and concentrates everything: roasted chestnuts run about 245 kcal and 53 g of carbohydrate per 100 g, with fibre at 5.1 g. Set beside any other nut the shape is unmistakable — a chestnut has roughly a third of the calories of a walnut and almost none of its fat. It is a staple food wearing a nut's name.
    • The surprise in the list is vitamin C. No other common nut carries it in real amounts; a raw chestnut carries about 43 mg per 100 g, close to half a day's worth. Cooking and storage wear it down — roasted chestnuts keep about 26 mg per 100 g — but even cooked, chestnuts bring a vitamin that nuts are not supposed to have. The flour is naturally free of gluten, which made chestnut bread a safe staple long before anyone had a word for coeliac disease.
    • On blood sugar, the honest picture is middling and small. Chestnut starch digests more gently than refined flour — published tables put the glycaemic index of chestnuts around 54 raw and higher once cooked, in the middle range — and in one small randomised trial, 14 healthy adults ate bread made with half chestnut flour and showed a blood-sugar rise about 27% smaller over the meal than with wheat bread. One small single-meal study is a hint, not a verdict: a chestnut is still a serving of starch, eaten in portions like bread or potato, and it is not a treatment for diabetes. Human · small
    • Chestnut skins and shells are rich in the bitter plant compounds called tannins and in phenolic antioxidants, and extracts of them behave as antioxidants in laboratory dishes. That is laboratory work on parts of the nut that mostly are not eaten, and there are no human trials showing that eating chestnuts prevents or treats any disease. The heart claims made for oily nuts do not transfer: chestnut eating has not been put through the cholesterol trials that almonds and walnuts have, and its benefit is the plain one of a filling, low-fat whole food. Lab studies
    • Chestnut leaf stood in old remedy books as a cough medicine — it was an official drug in the United States pharmacopoeia in the 1800s, used for whooping cough — and chestnut honey and leaf teas are still sold on that tradition. The tradition is real; the trials are not there. It belongs to the history of the tree, not to its proven benefits. Traditional use
    • Size: This is a tree to plant for grandchildren. A sweet chestnut grows 20–35 metres tall with a broad crown and can live for centuries; Chinese chestnut is smaller, around 12–15 metres, and better suited to an orchard or large garden. Give it room — a mature tree wants a circle of ground 12 metres across or more
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Environment: Sweet chestnut is hardy in about zones 5–8, Chinese chestnut in zones 4–8. The tree flowers late, in early summer, with long cream catkins — a piece of luck, since the blossom misses the spring frosts that ruin earlier-flowering fruit trees
    • Soil: Deep, well-drained, acid soil — about pH 4.5–6.5 — and they fail on chalk and lime. Wet ground is the other killer: a root disease called ink disease, a Phytophthora, rots the roots of trees standing in waterlogged soil. Plant on a slope or a well-drained rise, never in a hollow where water sits
    • When to pick: Through September and October the burrs split and the nuts fall; gather them every day or two, in gloves — the spines are genuinely sharp — because fallen nuts are taken by squirrels and deer, dry out in the sun, and are bored by chestnut weevil grubs, the main pest of the crop. Fresh chestnuts are perishable like a vegetable, not keeping nuts like walnuts: hold them cool and slightly moist in the refrigerator and use them within weeks, or freeze them

    Garden notes

    • The catkins have a heavy, sweet smell that people either love or avoid; keep the tree downwind of the patio if it is the second.
    • Pollination needs two trees. Chestnuts are wind-pollinated and cannot use their own pollen, so a single tree will flower and drop empty burrs. Plant at least two different cultivars or seedlings within pollen range of each other — orchards set a pollinizer tree every few trees in the block. A few cultivars, 'Colossal' among them, make almost no good pollen of their own and depend entirely on their neighbours.
    • Water young trees through dry spells while they establish; an established tree in deep soil rides out ordinary drought.
    • Freshly fallen nuts sweeten as they cure: a week or two of cool storage lets some of the starch turn to sugar, and a cured chestnut roasts sweeter than one cooked the day it fell. Score the shell before roasting or boiling, or the steam can burst it.
    • Disease, honestly: in eastern North America the blight is in the woods, and planting there means planting resistant stock — Chinese chestnuts or the modern hybrids — rather than the European tree, which thrives better on the west coast and in Europe. Everywhere, the tree's own trick is worth knowing: cut down or killed back, a chestnut sprouts again from the stump, which is how the American species still hangs on in its forests and how coppice poles are harvested on rotation.

    Propagation

    Named cultivars come as grafted trees, which bear in about 3–5 years; trees grown from seed take 7 years or more, and crops build as the crown spreads.

    Safety

    • The dangerous confusion is the horse chestnut: its seeds are poisonous raw, and no part of that tree is a food, whatever the supplements made from its processed seed extract may claim — the extract is a factory product with the poison removed, not a nut to eat. Sweet chestnut itself is a tree nut for allergy purposes: chestnut allergy exists, though it is less common than peanut or hazelnut allergy, and reactions can be serious; a link with latex allergy has been reported. Raw sweet chestnuts are tannic and hard to digest, which is why every chestnut culture cooks them. Fresh nuts are perishable and mould quickly — a mouldy chestnut is rubbish, not food.

    Sources

    • Rigling & Prospero (2018) — review of the chestnut blight fungus: its invasion history, biology and control on both continents
    • Heiniger & Rigling (1994) — biological control of chestnut blight in Europe — the hypovirulence story

    • Food & Function (2026) — randomised crossover trial: bread made with chestnut flour and the blood-sugar response in 14 healthy adults

    Chicory

    Cichorium intybus

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Digestive HealthVitamin K

    FreshCookedDried

    A roadside wildflower with sky-blue flowers that has been bred into three different foods, and the three are easy to mix up, so they are kept apart from the first line. Grown for its root, chicory is roasted, ground and brewed — the "chicory coffee" of France and New Orleans, with no coffee and no caffeine in it. Grown for its leaves, it is radicchio, the red, white-veined salad leaf of northern Italy, and its green chicories beside it. Grown for its root and then forced in the dark, it is Belgian endive — also called witloof, "white leaf" — a tight, pale head that never sees the sun. One species makes all three, plus the blue flowers that open on waste ground every summer morning. Two names to keep straight before anything else: true endive is a different species, Cichorium endivia, and the root in a jar of coffee blend is this plant, not a coffee bean.

    Cultivars

    Chicory's named kinds sort by the three foods, and the name on the seed packet tells you which food the plant was bred for.

    'Magdeburger'

    For the root — the classic coffee chicory, bred for a long, thick, smooth root that roasts evenly; older northern European root kinds such as 'Harburger' and 'Slesvig' were grown the same way. Modern inulin chicories are bred for the factories and are sold to farmers rather than gardeners.

    'Rosso di Chioggia'

    Radicchio and the leaf chicories — the round, ball-headed red radicchio of the supermarkets, raised around Chioggia in the early 1900s.

    'Rosso di Treviso Precoce'

    The earlier, elongated red Treviso type.

    'Rosso di Treviso Tardivo'

    The late one, blanched in spring water after harvest into curving red-and-white leaves — the most prized of all.

    'Rosso di Verona'

    A smaller, rounder red head.

    'Variegato di Castelfranco'

    Cream-leaved and speckled rose-red, milder than the reds.

    'Bianco di Mantova'

    A pale, all-cream heading chicory.

    'Pan di Zucchero'

    Sugarloaf — makes tall, pale green, romaine-like heads.

    'Catalogna'

    The kinds grown for stems and shoots: cut young for greens, or left for the hollow winter shoots that Rome turns into puntarelle.

    'Brussels Witloof'

    For forcing — the traditional witloof kind sold for home forcing, grown a full season for its root and then sprouted in the dark; modern farm crops are mostly unnamed F1 hybrids bred to force evenly without soil, in water.

    'Grasslands Puna'

    For animals — the 1980s New Zealand release that started the forage line, still the name met most often in pasture seed.

    • Chicory is an old Mediterranean plant, native around the Mediterranean and east into Asia, and grown since ancient Egypt. Roman writers knew it well — Horace listed chicory among the plain foods he lived on, and Pliny wrote about the plant and its uses. The wild leaves were eaten as a pot herb around the Mediterranean for centuries, boiled and dressed with oil, and in Rome the hollow winter shoots of a tall chicory called catalogna are still cut into the salad called puntarelle.
    • The root was a medicine chest item for just as long. In the traditional medicine of Europe and India the root was used for jaundice, liver enlargement, gout and rheumatism, and bitter root teas were a household remedy for slow digestion and poor appetite. European regulators still carry that record: the European Medicines Agency's herbal committee keeps a monograph on chicory root as a traditional herbal medicine for mild digestive disorders and temporary loss of appetite — a standing given on long use, not on clinical trials.
    • The coffee story starts in Holland. When coffee reached Europe, the Dutch found that roasted chicory root, mixed in, made a dark, bitter drink that stretched the expensive beans, and the mixing seems to have begun there in the 1700s. Prussia pushed it harder: in 1766 Frederick the Great banned coffee imports, and a Brunswick innkeeper, Christian Gottlieb Förster, won a licence in 1769–70 to manufacture chicory coffee in Brunswick and Berlin.
    • Napoleon made it a mass habit. Under his Continental System, from 1806, British trade — and with it coffee — was shut out of Napoleonic Europe, and France turned to the root that grew at home. Chicory growing and roasting became a French industry; by 1860 France was exporting millions of pounds of it. Chicory was also slipped into coffee without telling the buyer, and the scandal over adulterated coffee was one of the things that pushed Britain toward food-labelling law in the 1800s. In France the blend never went away: a mixture of 60% chicory and 40% coffee is still sold there as Ricoré, and in Britain a coffee-and-chicory essence, Camp Coffee, has been bottled since the 1800s.
    • The American chapter runs through New Orleans. French settlers brought the taste to Louisiana, and by the 1840s New Orleans was the second-largest coffee-importing port in the United States. When Union naval blockades cut the port off during the Civil War, Louisianans stretched what coffee they had with roasted chicory root, as Confederate soldiers did across the South. The war ended and the coffee came back, but the flavour stayed: coffee with chicory is still the New Orleans standard, served as café au lait at Café du Monde, which has poured it since 1862. Further afield the same blending lives on in South Indian filter coffee and in parts of South Africa and Southeast Asia.
    • Radicchio is the leaf line, and it comes from the Veneto, the region around Venice and Treviso, where red chicories have been grown since at least the 1500s. The deep red colour and the tight heads were sharpened by selection over the 1800s, and the most prized kind, the late Treviso type, is blanched after harvest — the roots are stood in dark tanks of spring water until the new leaves grow out white-ribbed and wine-red, a technique worked out in the late 1800s.
    • Belgian endive was an accident that became a technique. Around 1850, chicory roots stored in a dark cellar — kept for roasting — were found to have sprouted tight, pale, mild-tasting heads. Two tellings survive: a farmer, named in one version as Jan Lammers, came home to find his stored roots sprouted; in the other, Frans Breziers, head gardener at the Brussels botanical garden, noticed the same thing and worked the method out properly. Either way, by the 1870s the new vegetable was on sale in Paris as Brussels endive, and Brussels added its soil-grown witloof to the region's heritage inventory in 2021.
    • The newest line is the animal one. Chicory's deep taproot pulls minerals up from well below the surface and keeps growing through dry summers, and farmers had long let livestock graze it. In the 1980s New Zealand breeders released 'Grasslands Puna', the first chicory bred purely as forage, and forage chicory is now sown in pastures in many countries.
    • And the root has a second modern career. In the 2000s the food industry settled on chicory root as its main source of inulin, a fibre extracted with hot water and added to foods as a fibre booster and a stand-in for sugar and fat. Most "chicory root fibre" on an ingredients list starts as roots grown in fields in northern Europe.
    • Italy — radicchio country: the red heads of Chioggia, Treviso and Verona, grilled, shredded into risotto and salads, each town's type carrying its own protected name; and in Rome, puntarelle, the catalogna shoots shaved into curls, dressed with anchovy and garlic through the winter.
    • Belgium, France and the Netherlands — witloof country: the pale chicons are braised, wrapped in ham and baked in cheese sauce, or split raw into salads; in the 1970s it was the most-grown vegetable in Belgium.
    • France — the north drinks café à la chicorée and the country buys Ricoré off the supermarket shelf; chicory is a breakfast ingredient, not a substitute, in its own home ground.
    • New Orleans — coffee and chicory, half and half in the city's telling, drunk as café au lait with beignets; the blend is a point of local identity a century and a half after the blockade that forced it.
    • India — in the south, filter coffee is traditionally blended with chicory, which deepens the colour and thickens the decoction.
    • Greece and the wider Mediterranean — the wild plant itself: bitter chicory greens gathered from field edges and boiled into horta, the plate of wild greens dressed with olive oil and lemon.
    • The leaves are the everyday food, and the numbers are for the leaves. Chicory greens, raw, per 100 g: 23 kcal, fibre 4.0 g, protein 1.7 g, folate 110 µg and vitamin K 298 µg. Radicchio, raw, per 100 g: 23 kcal, protein 1.43 g, fibre 0.9 g, vitamin K 255.2 µg, vitamin E 2.26 mg, folate 60 µg and potassium 302 mg. Belgian endive, raw, per 100 g: 17 kcal, protein 0.9 g, fibre 3.1 g, folate 37 µg and potassium 211 mg — a pale leaf is mostly water, 94.5% of it, and its numbers are gentle across the board.
    • Those vitamin K figures are high — a serving of radicchio or greens can carry more than twice a day's reference intake. Vitamin K is the vitamin that blood thinners such as warfarin work against, so anyone on one is usually told to keep their vitamin K intake steady rather than swinging it up and down; the figures are given so the size of a new daily radicchio habit is plain.
    • The root's one proven effect is about fibre, and it belongs to inulin. Inulin is the root's stored carbohydrate — about 15–20% of the fresh root by weight — a chain of fructose units that human digestion cannot break down. It passes to the large intestine, where gut bacteria ferment it. Six human studies, reviewed by the European Food Safety Authority in 2015, found that 12 g a day of native chicory inulin increased stool frequency, and the European Union authorised the claim in those words: "Chicory inulin contributes to normal bowel function by increasing stool frequency." That is the claim, at that dose, for the extracted fibre — it is not a claim about a cup of chicory coffee, which carries far less. Human trials
    • Beyond that one claim, the prebiotic story is promising and unfinished. Inulin feeds bifidobacteria in the gut — that much is shown in human studies — but what that feeding changes for health, beyond the stool-frequency effect, has not been settled in trials strong enough to carry further claims. Human · small
    • The root's medicinal record is tradition, and it is labelled that way by the regulators who keep it. The European monograph allows chicory root tea for mild digestive disorders and temporary loss of appetite on the basis of long-standing use, with bitter substances that may prompt bile flow as the plausible route, and states plainly that the evidence from clinical trials is insufficient. Nothing stronger has been shown. Traditional use
    • The wider claims made for chicory — for the liver, for blood sugar, against cancer — rest on animal studies and laboratory work with root extracts and their bitter compounds, lactucin and lactucopicrin among them. There are no human trials behind them. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • When to plant: Sow in spring, directly where the plants are to grow
    • Sun: Full sun or some shade
    • Soil: Deep, loose, stone-free ground grows long straight roots; stony or freshly manured ground makes them fork
    • Environment: A hardy perennial usually grown as a biennial — a flat rosette of leaves and a deep taproot in its first year, then a branching flower stem, waist-high or taller, in its second
    • Water: Modest — the taproot finds its own depth, and established plants shrug off dry spells that stop shallow-rooted salads
    • When to pick: Lift roots in the autumn of the first year, when the inulin store is at its peak

    Garden notes

    • Chicory is a hardy perennial usually grown as a biennial — a flat rosette of leaves and a deep taproot in its first year, then a branching flower stem, waist-high or taller, in its second. The wild plant of roadsides is the same species, escaped and self-sown; garden kinds are its selected children.
    • For roots, the soil decides the harvest: deep, loose, stone-free ground grows long straight roots, and stony or freshly manured ground makes them fork. Thin the seedlings so each root has room to thicken, and lift roots in the autumn of the first year, when the inulin store is at its peak.
    • The leaves want cool weather. Radicchio sown in high summer for autumn and winter heads colours up best as the nights cool — frost on a heading radicchio improves it, deepening the red and taking the edge off the bitterness. In hot weather the leaf chicories run bitter and bolt; they are spring and autumn crops in most gardens.
    • The flowers are worth a paragraph of their own. Each sky-blue flower opens for a single morning: the heads unfold early, are worked by bees through the morning, and close by the middle of the day, done by the next. Linnaeus used chicory in his flower clock, a garden meant to tell the time by which flowers opened and closed, with chicory among the earliest risers.
    • Forcing witloof at home is a two-season job in miniature. Grow a forcing kind through the summer, lift the roots in late autumn, trim the leaves back to a stub above the crown, and store the roots cold — near freezing — for a few weeks. Then stand them upright, close together, in a deep pot or box of moist sand or compost with the crowns just showing, and keep them in complete darkness at a cool room temperature. The pale heads — the chicons — are ready to cut in about three to five weeks. Light is the enemy: even a little turns them green and bitter.
    • For the coffee root, the work is after harvest: lift, wash, slice the roots, dry the pieces, then roast them until dark and grind. The roast is where the coffee colour and bitterness come from; the raw root tastes of very little.
    • Water and feeding are modest — the taproot finds its own depth, and established plants shrug off dry spells that stop shallow-rooted salads. The honest cautions are spread and persistence: a chicory left to flower seeds itself freely, and a root fragment left in the ground can regrow. Plant it where a permanent, self-renewing patch is welcome.

    Propagation

    Sow in spring, directly where the plants are to grow — the long taproot dislikes being moved.

    Safety

    • Chicory is in the daisy family, and people allergic to that family — ragweed, chrysanthemums, marigolds and their kin — can react to chicory too; the European monograph makes allergy to the family its one firm contraindication for the root medicines.
    • Inulin's side effects are the ordinary ones of a fermentable fibre: gas and bloating, growing with the dose, which is why fibre powders start small.
    • The monograph also does not recommend the root medicines in pregnancy or while breastfeeding, because safety there has not been established — that caution is about medicinal doses of root, not about salad leaves.
    • And the drink itself: chicory coffee contains no caffeine at all, which is a fact about the root, not a health claim.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2019) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: chicory greens, raw; radicchio, raw; chicory, witloof, raw — the nutrition figures
    • European Food Safety Authority (2015) — scientific opinion on native chicory inulin and maintenance of normal defecation, EFSA Journal 13(1):3951 — the six human studies and the 12 g daily dose behind the authorised claim
    • European Commission (2015) — Regulation (EU) 2015/2314 — the authorised claim wording: chicory inulin contributes to normal bowel function by increasing stool frequency
    • European Medicines Agency (2013) — Community herbal monograph on Cichorium intybus L., radix (EMA/HMPC/121816/2010) — the traditional use for mild digestive disorders and temporary loss of appetite, the daisy-family contraindication, and the pregnancy caution
    • Street et al. (2013) — Cichorium intybus: traditional uses, phytochemistry, pharmacology, and toxicology, Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine — the folk-medicine record across Europe and Asia, and the animal and laboratory state of the wider claims

    Cumin

    Cuminum cyminum

    Culinary

    Dried

    Cumin is a small annual of the carrot family, grown for a slim, ridged fruit with one of the warmest, earthiest flavours in the spice cupboard — the backbone of curry powders, chilli and a dozen other famous blends. Three different plants share its shelf and its name, and they are not interchangeable. Cumin is this one: a Mediterranean and Iranian herb about knee-high, with thread-like leaves and small white or pink umbrella flowers. Black cumin is a borrowed name used for two other plants — most often Nigella sativa, an unrelated buttercup-family plant with small black teardrop seeds (the kalonji of Indian cooking), and sometimes Bunium persicum, a wild mountain relative whose dark seed is the kala jeera of Persian and Kashmiri cooking. Caraway is a true cousin in cumin's own family, with darker, curved fruits and a cooler, sharper flavour; in German the two are confused so often that caraway's name, Kümmel, is borrowed from cumin's. The seeds of all three sit side by side in the shops, but their chemistry and their records are their own — and the loudest health headlines under the words "black cumin" belong to nigella, not to cumin.

    Cultivars

    Unlike many spice seeds, cumin does have named, bred varieties — nearly all of them from India, where the crop matters enough to breed. They were selected above all for yield and for resistance to Fusarium wilt, the soil fungus that is cumin's great enemy.

    GC-1, GC-2, GC-3, GC-4 and GC-5 (Gujarat)

    The Gujarat series comes from the Spices Research Station at Jagudan, and its names are plain working labels: GC-1 (released 1988; erect plants, bold seed, some tolerance of wilt), GC-2, GC-3 (resistant to wilt, with a high oil content of about 3.5%), GC-4 and GC-5. GC-4, released in 2006 and resistant to Fusarium wilt, spread so fast that it became the main cumin variety of India — one research estimate credits it with about three-quarters of the national crop. GC-5 is the sprinter of the family, ripe in about 92 days.

    RZ-19, RZ-209, RZ-223, RZ-341 and RZ-345 (Rajasthan)

    Rajasthan's station at Jobner bred the RZ series for its own dry fields: RZ-19, an older variety with bold seed and a long season of 120–140 days; RZ-209 and RZ-223, both tolerant of wilt; and RZ-341 and RZ-345, bred to stand up to wilt, blight and powdery mildew together. An older selection, MC-43, is still named among the improved varieties of the two states.

    Outside India, cumin is traded by origin rather than by variety name — Iranian, Syrian and Turkish cumin are handled as distinct grades — and garden seed catalogues in the West sell the species plain, under its own name.

    • Cumin comes from the dry country running from the eastern Mediterranean through Iran into Central Asia, and it is among the oldest spices in the world. Cumin seeds dug up at sites in Syria date to the second millennium BCE, and by about 1700 BCE the spice appears in writing on Old Babylonian clay tablets as kamûnu — it flavours recipes in the Yale Culinary Tablets, the oldest cookery record that survives. The word itself may be older still: it is traced back through Akkadian kamûnu to Sumerian gamun, which would make "cumin" one of the few English words that reach back to the first written language of all.
    • Egypt grew it early and used it widely. The Egyptians called it tpnn, cooked with it, and prescribed it for complaints of the stomach and gut, for mouth rinses and for driving out worms; the pharaoh Ramesses III is recorded offering cumin to the god Ra, and cumin turns up in Egyptian sites of the New Kingdom age, the era of the great tombs.
    • The Bible names it twice. In Isaiah, a farmer is described sowing cumin and beating the ripe seed out gently with a rod — cumin is too delicate for the heavy threshing tools used on grain, and the harvest method has barely changed since. In Matthew, cumin stands in the tithe list beside mint and anise — "ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin" — a spice valuable enough to be taxed in kind.
    • Greece kept cumin on the dining table, in its own dish, the way salt and pepper are kept now, and Greece also gave it a reputation: cumin stood for greed, and a miser was jokingly said to have eaten cumin; a Roman emperor careful with money earned a cumin nickname. The Roman writer Pliny called it the most agreeable of all seasonings for a delicate appetite and recorded cumin taken in water for stomach ache — and Roman students ate or smoked the seed to make their faces pale, so they would look worn out by study. The poet Horace had a phrase for it: exsangue cuminum, bloodless cumin.
    • In India the seed — jeeraka, jeera — entered the Ayurvedic medical tradition as a digestive: crushed into decoctions, sometimes fermented, made into pills with ghee, and used to stir up appetite and digestion and to treat diarrhoea and fever. Those uses are the traditional record; what the trials support is a separate matter.
    • In medieval Europe cumin was one of the commonest spices grown, precious enough to work as money: in England a pound of cumin could pay a year's rent on some tenancies. Healers of the period mixed it with barley and boiled it in wine as a general cure-all. And cumin carried a superstition of holding fast — it was said to confer "retention." Fed to chickens and pigeons it would keep them from straying; baked into a cake it would keep a departing lover faithful; carried by a bride and groom on the wedding day, it promised a marriage that stayed together.
    • Trade carried the seed in every direction: east along the spice routes into Persia and India, west with Arab traders across North Africa and into Spain. Spain carried it to the Americas. One strand of that journey is unusually well remembered: in 1731, families from the Canary Islands settled San Antonio, in what is now Texas, cooking with a heavy hand of cumin in the North African style of their islands — and food historians trace the signature cumin flavour of Tex-Mex chilli back to their kitchens.
    • Today India grows roughly seventy percent of the world's cumin, nearly all of it in two dry states, Gujarat and Rajasthan, and the Gujarati town of Unjha is the spice's great trading market. Iran, Syria, Turkey and China grow much of the rest.
    • India — jeera is everywhere: whole seeds sizzled in hot oil or ghee to open a dish (the tempering called tadka), ground seed in garam masala, jeera rice, and jal jeera, the cool spiced cumin drink of summer. Unjha in Gujarat, the great cumin market, sets the price for much of the world.
    • Iran — zireh goes into advieh, the warm Persian spice blend, and into rice dishes, where whole seeds are sometimes cooked right through the polo.
    • The Middle East — kammūn seasons falafel, kebabs and bean dishes, and enters baharat, the region's all-purpose blend.
    • North Africa — cumin is ground into ras el-hanout and over grilled meats in Morocco, and in Egypt it seasons dukkah, the seed-and-nut sprinkle, and the lentil-and-rice koshari.
    • Mexico and Tex-Mex — comino is the signature note of chilli con carne and chilli powder, and runs through tacos and enchilada sauces — the Canary Island inheritance, still doing its work three centuries on.
    • China — in Xinjiang, Uyghur cooks dust lamb skewers with whole cumin and chilli, a flavour that has spread far beyond the region's night markets.
    • The Netherlands — Leyden cheese (Leidse kaas) is studded with cumin seeds, a spiced cheese made since the Middle Ages.
    • Spain — comino flavours sausages and blood sausage, and appears in some regional gazpachos.
    • Cuba and Brazil — comino seasons the garlicky mojo sauces and the daily pot of beans.
    • The seed first, by the numbers. Per 100 g: 375 kcal, protein 17.8 g, fibre 10.5 g, iron 66.4 mg — several times the whole day's value — calcium 931 mg, close to the day's value, and potassium 1,788 mg, about half of it. But a teaspoon of cumin weighs about 2 g, so in the kitchen the seed is a flavouring, not a mineral source: that teaspoon carries roughly 1.4 mg of iron, well under a tenth of the day. The figures describe the spice honestly; they do not make a serving of it a supplement.
    • The flavour is chemistry. The fruit holds roughly 2.5–5% essential oil, and the oil's chief component is cuminaldehyde — the warm, earthy, slightly sharp smell that survives cooking and defines the spice. The oil also carries a little safrole, a compound largely broken down by cooking.
    • Digestion is cumin's oldest medical role — a carminative, a remedy for wind and a heavy stomach, across Egyptian, Greek, Ayurvedic and European medicine alike, and it is still how the seed is used in much of the world. That standing is traditional. No modern trial has tested cumin alone for indigestion, and independent drug references, reviewing the whole record, find the clinical evidence thin everywhere except one area: blood fats.
    • The weight and cholesterol trials are real, and they are small. In the best-known (Zare et al., 2014), 88 overweight and obese women in Iran took 3 g of cumin powder a day, stirred into yogurt at two meals, for three months, alongside diet advice given to both groups. The cumin group lost more weight and body fat than the yogurt-only group, and their total cholesterol, triglycerides and LDL cholesterol fell while HDL rose. Fasting blood sugar did not change. It is one trial, in women only, from one university. Human · small
    • A second Iranian trial (Taghizadeh et al., 2015) tested capsules of cumin essential oil — 300 mg a day, a concentrated extract, not kitchen spice — in 78 overweight adults for eight weeks, against the weight-loss drug orlistat and a dummy capsule. The cumin group lost about 1.1 kg, about the same as the drug group, and their insulin measures improved; their blood fats did not change in that trial. The same research circle then tested cumin combined with lime in 72 people for eight weeks, with results in the same direction. Three trials, one country, one circle of researchers, eight to twelve weeks each, dozens of people rather than hundreds. Human · small
    • Blood sugar follows the same pattern. A small trial in people with type 2 diabetes (63 patients, cumin essential oil, twelve weeks) and pooled analyses of the Iranian trials report modest falls in fasting glucose and insulin resistance — while the powder trial above found no effect on fasting sugar at all. The animal evidence for blood sugar is stronger than the human evidence. Cumin is not a diabetes treatment, and nothing in the record supports using it as one. Human · small
    • Two fences belong here. First, the large and loudly quoted "black cumin" trial literature is about Nigella sativa — a different plant in a different family, with a different chemistry — and none of its results can be carried over to cumin. Second, the bone, cancer and antimicrobial claims sometimes attached to cumin come from animal and laboratory work; no human trial supports them.
    • When to plant: Sow directly in spring, once all danger of frost has passed and the soil has warmed
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Light, very well-drained soil, around neutral to slightly alkaline
    • Environment: A plant of dry heat — it needs a long, warm season of roughly 100 to 120 frost-free days, and dry air at flowering time
    • Spacing: Thin the seedlings to about 6 inches apart, in rows roughly a foot to 18 inches apart
    • When to pick: When the plants yellow and the fruits turn brown-grey; cut the whole plants just before the fruits are fully ripe and begin to shatter

    Garden notes

    • Cumin is a small, slender annual, about 30–50 cm (1–1½ feet) tall, with a thin branched stem, leaves cut into thread-like segments, and small white or pink flowers in flat-topped umbrellas in summer. What is sold as the seed is the whole dried fruit — slim, ridged, yellow-brown, about 5 mm long.
    • It is a plant of dry heat. Cumin needs a long, warm season — roughly 100 to 120 frost-free days — to flower and ripen seed, and it does best where the air at flowering time is dry. In India it is grown as a winter crop in arid country; in a temperate garden it is sown in spring and harvested in summer.
    • Sun and soil: full sun, in light, very well-drained soil, around neutral to slightly alkaline. Thin the seedlings to about 6 inches apart, in rows roughly a foot to 18 inches apart. Crowded, damp cumin is unhappy cumin.
    • Water sparingly once the plants are established, and keep water off the foliage where you can: wet soil and humid air invite the crop's two great diseases, Fusarium wilt and blight. Feed lightly — rich feeding pushes soft growth the plant does not need.
    • Harvest is the delicate part, as it has been since Isaiah's farmer took up his rod. Watch for the plants yellowing and the fruits turning brown-grey; cut the whole plants just before the fruits are fully ripe and begin to shatter, dry them heads-down in paper bags in a warm, airy place, then rub and shake the fruit free.
    • Stored whole, in a jar away from light, cumin keeps its scent about a year; grind only what is needed, because ground cumin loses its warmth within weeks.
    • A caution about identification: cumin's family includes deadly plants — poison hemlock carries similar white umbels — so seed is sown from a packet and garden plants are known by their planting, never gathered on a guess from the wild.

    Propagation

    Sow it where it is to grow. Like its cousin anise, cumin grows a taproot and dislikes being moved, so it is sown directly in the bed once all danger of frost has passed and the soil has warmed, about ¼ inch deep. Germination takes about one to two weeks in warm soil.

    Safety

    • In cooking amounts cumin is a safe, ordinary food, eaten for thousands of years, and it is recognised as safe (GRAS) as a spice and flavouring. The concentrated oil is a different substance from the spice: undiluted cumin oil on skin has been reported to make skin sensitive to sunlight, and medicinal doses of cumin may lower blood sugar, which matters alongside diabetes medicines. Drug references also advise care for people with bleeding disorders, because cumin may slow clotting. Allergy to cumin exists, and people sensitive to other carrot-family plants can react. For medicinal amounts in pregnancy, the safety data are simply missing — the kitchen spice is not the question; the capsule is.

    Sources
