    • Taghizadeh et al. (2015) — Effect of the Cuminum cyminum L. intake on weight loss, metabolic profiles and biomarkers of oxidative stress in overweight subjects (Annals of Nutrition and Metabolism) — 78 adults, cumin essential oil capsules against orlistat and placebo for eight weeks
    • Taghizadeh et al. (2016) — The effect of Cuminum cyminum L. plus lime administration on weight loss and metabolic status in overweight subjects (Iranian Red Crescent Medical Journal) — 72 adults, eight weeks
    • Drugs.com — Cumin monograph (Natural Products Database) — the clinical-evidence summary, GRAS standing, oil phototoxicity and interaction cautions
    • AICRP on Spices (Indian Council of Agricultural Research) — Gujarat Cumin 4 technical bulletin (2023) — the released Indian varieties, their wilt ratings, seasons and yields
    • University of California, Davis — Nutritional Geography: Cumin — the Egyptian, Greek, Roman and medieval record, from Darby, Ghalioungui & Grivetti, Food: The Gift of Osiris (1977)
    • Nabhan (2014) — Cumin, Camels, and Caravans: A Spice Odyssey — the word's Sumerian root, the Yale Culinary Tablets, and the spice's travels

    Dill

    Anethum graveolens

    CulinaryMedicinal

    FreshCookedDried

    Dill is a feathery annual of the carrot family that gives the kitchen two different flavourings from one plant. Dill weed is the fresh or dried leaf — soft, thread-like fronds with a bright, grassy taste, at its best raw or added at the very end of cooking, because heat and drying quickly dull it. Dill seed is the dried fruit — small, flat, oval and ribbed — with a warmer, sharper, more lasting flavour that stands up to heat, which is why the seed, and the flowering heads, do the work in pickle jars. The two are not interchangeable: a recipe asking for one will not be rescued by the other. Two neighbours need keeping apart from it. Fennel is the garden mix-up — a cousin with similar threads and umbrellas, but a solid, bulbing stem base and a sweeter, anise-heavy taste; dill's stem is hollow and its flavour is its own. And Indian dill, called sowa, is a close Indian relative of the same species whose seed oil runs to a different chemistry (it carries dillapiole, which European dill oil does not), so the Indian seed and the European seed are cousins, not twins.

    Cultivars

    Dill varieties divide by the job they were bred for: tall kinds grown for seed and flower heads, slow kinds bred to hold their leaf, and short kinds bred for pots. Garden seed is sold by variety name; farm seed for the spice trade is traded by origin, as with cumin.

    'Long Island Mammoth'

    A tall seed kind, one of the pickling dills: the most widely grown dill of all — two to three feet tall with very large flower heads, quick to bolt and sparse of leaf, which is exactly what a pickle crock wants.

    'Mammoth'

    Its close kin, grown the same way.

    'Bouquet'

    The all-rounder: two to three feet, blue-green foliage, large seed heads, and leaves strong enough in flavour to be worth cutting — the one variety that honestly does both jobs.

    'Dukat'

    One of the leaf kinds, bred to delay flowering, because a dill plant in flower stops making leaf. A Danish variety, the flavour pick: vigorous, high in aromatic oil, with abundant, strongly flavoured fronds and large umbels when it does flower.

    'Superdukat'

    Its improved offspring, selected for still higher oil.

    'Tetra'

    Slow to bolt and bushy, bred for the leaf harvest.

    'Fernleaf'

    One of the compact kinds, which fit pots and small beds: stands only about 18 inches, extra feathery and slow to bolt, with blue-green leaves of fine flavour; it won an All-America Selections award in 1992 and is the standard container dill.

    'Compatto'

    About the same height, grown for strongly flavoured seed.

    'Ella'

    The shortest of all, 10 to 16 inches, slow-bolting, and used for baby leaf and microgreens as much as for the herb garden.

    Beyond the garden, India grows dill as a winter seed crop on a large scale — one of the world's main sources of dill seed — and the Indian seed in trade is the sowa kind named in the introduction, sold by origin rather than by variety name.

    • Dill comes from the Mediterranean and the lands running east through Iran, and it is one of the oldest herbs in the written record. Herb histories trace its first mention to Egypt some five thousand years ago, where it was already spoken of as a soothing medicine, and the Babylonians were growing it in their gardens by about 3000 BCE. Dill was found in the tomb of the Egyptian pharaoh Amenhotep II, who died around 1400 BCE — laid in among the grave goods of a king.
    • Greece knew it well. Theophrastus, the first great writer on plants, described it in the fourth century BCE, and the Greeks burned its scented oil in their homes and flavoured some of their wines with it. The plant's Greek name, anēthon, is the root of its scientific name Anethum — and the same Greek word family gives us "anise," which is why the two herbs' names have tangled ever since. Graveolens, the second half of the name, is Latin for "strong-smelling," which no one who has brushed past a dill bed in summer will argue with.
    • The physician Dioscorides wrote that scorched dill seeds were laid on soldiers' wounds, a practice the Romans shared — and Roman gladiators were fed meals covered with dill in the hope that the herb would give them courage. Pliny included dill among the useful plants of his natural history. The English word itself is usually traced to the Old Norse dilla, "to lull" — a name that points straight at the herb's oldest medical job, calming troubled stomachs and fretful babies.
    • The Bible names the plant once, and under a disguise: in Matthew's list of the tithe herbs — "mint and anise and cummin" in the King James wording — the word in the Greek text is anēthon, dill. The seed was worth tithing because it was worth money: like cumin beside it in the list, dill was a small crop with a real price.
    • Through the Middle Ages dill travelled north with the monasteries and the herb gardens, and it settled deepest in the kitchens of northern and eastern Europe — the country of long winters, where a plant that flavours the preserving pot is a plant that feeds people. Dill went into the brine barrels with cucumbers, cabbage and fish, and in that country it has never left the table since.
    • The pickling story deserves its own telling, because dill pickles are where most people meet this herb. Cucumbers have been brined since ancient Mesopotamia, and across eastern Europe families put down barrels of cucumbers each autumn to last the winter — salt brine, not vinegar, because vinegar was dear. Dill, whole stems and flowering heads of it, went into the barrel with garlic, and the brine did the rest, souring slowly by fermentation. When Jewish families from eastern Europe came to New York in the late 1800s and early 1900s, the barrels came with them: pushcart sellers and then delicatessens made the salt-brined, garlic-heavy, dill-packed cucumber famous as the kosher dill — "kosher" first for the Jewish law the makers kept, and in time simply the name of the style, big food companies included. Poland's ogórki kiszone, soured the same way with whole dill stems, are the same tradition at home. A "dill pickle" today, anywhere in the world, is that barrel's descendant.
    • In colonial America the seed had a quieter second job: dill seed was chewed during long church services — to stay awake, and to keep children quiet and stomachs from rumbling — which earned dill, fennel and caraway seed the shared nickname "meetinghouse seeds."
    • The seed's standing traditional use, in every century, is for the stomach: a carminative, a remedy that settles wind and eases a heavy, griping gut. Dill seed tea — a spoonful of lightly crushed seed steeped in hot water — was the household form of it, and dill water, a mild distillation of the seed, was the nursery form, given to babies for colic long before it was ever sold in a bottle.
    • That bottle came in 1851, when William Woodward, a pharmacist in Nottingham, England, built a remedy for babies' "gripes" — the old word for stomach cramps — on dill seed oil, with sodium bicarbonate, sugar and a little alcohol. Woodward's Gripe Water was adopted by doctors, trademarked in 1876, and carried around the world; for generations it was the bottle reached for when a baby would not settle. The alcohol came out of the recipe in the 1990s, and today's licensed British gripe water still carries dill seed oil — a few milligrams in a spoonful. The tradition is genuine and long. It is also tradition only: no trial has ever shown that gripe water settles babies, and a medical review in 2000 found most of its ingredients of little value beyond the sweet liquid itself. The colic use remains tradition, not proven medicine.
    • Germany's herbal regulators gave the seed a formal traditional standing: the Commission E monograph for dill seed, published in 1987, approved it for dyspeptic complaints — the burning, full, unsettled stomach — at an ordinary kitchen dose of about 3 g of seed a day, and recorded its actions as antispasmodic (cramp-easing) and bacteriostatic (holding bacteria in check). That is a regulator's judgment on a long traditional record, not the result of a clinical trial, and the European Medicines Agency has no monograph for dill. The leaf, notably, was not given the same standing.
    • The rest of the traditional record is smaller: the seed was chewed to sweeten the breath; dill was given to nursing mothers to bring in milk, a use recorded across European folk medicine without a trial behind it; and in the folklore of the north the plant was hung up against ill luck and witchcraft — a protective herb as well as a kind one.
    • Scandinavia — dill is the region's defining herb: gravlax, salmon cured under a blanket of it; new potatoes boiled with dill stems; and in Sweden, crayfish cooked in water crowned with great bunches of flowering dill. No herb appears on more northern tables.
    • Russia and Ukraine — ukrop goes over everything: borscht and other soups, salads, potatoes, pickled cucumbers and salted fish, scattered fresh by the handful in summer.
    • Poland — whole dill stems and heads sour the cucumber barrels (ogórki kiszone and the quick, half-salted ogórki małosolne), and a dill sauce, sos koperkowy, dresses eggs, fish and potatoes.
    • Germany — dill is so bound to the cucumber that its folk name is Gurkenkraut, "cucumber herb": cucumber salads, fish dishes, and pickles of every kind.
    • Greece — anithos, the ancient name still in daily use, seasons bean dishes, rice with spinach, salads and the green, herbed dishes of spring.
    • Iran — shevid is cooked into rice with broad beans for baghali polo, one of the country's best-known dishes, and flavours fish across the south.
    • India — the greens, suva bhaji, are cooked as a vegetable in their own right, wilted with garlic and lentils or potatoes, and the sowa seed goes into pickles and spice mixtures.
    • The Middle East — dill seed, called ain jaradeh, "grasshopper's eye," for its shape, seasons cold dishes such as fattoush and enters pickles; in Egypt the weed flavours stuffed cabbage.
    • Vietnam — chả cá, turmeric-marinated fish fried with heaps of dill fronds, is a Hanoi classic that surprises every visitor who thinks dill belongs only to the north.
    • America — the kosher dill pickle above all, and after it ranch dressing, potato salad, and the dill weed folded through tuna and egg salads.
    • The fresh leaf first, by the numbers. Per 100 g of fresh dill weed: 43 kcal, vitamin C 85 mg — close to a full day's value — vitamin A 386 µg, about two-fifths of the day, folate 150 µg, iron 6.6 mg, calcium 208 mg and potassium 738 mg. But dill weed is eaten by the spoonful and the sprig, not by the hundred grams: a generous handful of fronds weighs about 10 g and brings under a tenth of those figures. Eaten the way people actually eat it — scattered over fish, potatoes and salads, often and gladly — the leaf is a small, real contribution of vitamin C and green-leaf goodness, not a supplement.
    • The seed, by the numbers. Per 100 g: 305 kcal, protein 16 g, fibre 21.1 g, calcium 1,516 mg — well over a day's value — and iron 16.3 mg, close to a day's value. The same serving honesty applies, doubled: a teaspoon of dill seed weighs about 2 g, so it carries roughly a third of a milligram of iron and about 30 mg of calcium. The figures describe the spice truthfully; a teaspoon of it is a flavouring, and no one eats the hundred grams.
    • The flavour is chemistry, and the two forms differ in it. The seed holds a few percent of essential oil, and that oil is led by carvone — commonly around half of it — the warm compound dill seed shares with caraway, backed by limonene, the citrus terpene. The leaf's oil runs greener and sharper, with more alpha-phellandrene and much less carvone. That is why the seed tastes warm and keeping, and the weed tastes bright and brief.
    • Digestion is dill's oldest claim, and its honest standing is this: a formal traditional approval (the Commission E monograph above) resting on centuries of use, laboratory evidence that the seed oil eases cramp in gut muscle, and no clinical trial of dill alone for indigestion. In the diabetes trial described below, which asked about gut symptoms as a side question, one complaint — a disordered, sluggish colon — did ease on dill. That is a footnote in a small trial, not a digestive proof. Traditional use
    • The modern trial record is about blood sugar and blood fats, and it is small, single-country and mixed. Nearly every trial comes from Iran, where dill tablets and powders are a stocked herbal medicine. The best of them (Haidari et al., 2020) was a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 42 people with type 2 diabetes who took 3 g of dill powder a day in capsules for eight weeks: fasting insulin and insulin-resistance scores improved, LDL and total cholesterol fell, HDL rose, and fasting blood sugar itself did not clearly move. Human · small
    • Set against that is the largest trial, and it found nothing. In Shiraz, 150 people with high cholesterol were split three ways — garlic tablets, dill tablets (650 mg twice a day), or dummy tablets — for six weeks (Kojuri et al., 2007). The garlic worked. The dill did not: total cholesterol and LDL barely moved, HDL slipped slightly, triglycerides rose slightly, and the authors concluded plainly that dill is not a cholesterol-lowering agent. One earlier Iranian trial of dill tablets reported cholesterol about 18% below the patients' own starting values after two months — a before-and-after reading in about 35 people, the weakest shape a trial can take. Human trials
    • Pooling the whole record (Mousavi et al., 2022: seven randomised trials, 330 people) gives the fairest summary the evidence allows: LDL cholesterol and fasting insulin were lower on dill, insulin resistance improved, and total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL and fasting blood glucose showed no clear change. The reviewers' own closing words were that further research is necessary. Dill is not a diabetes treatment and not a cholesterol treatment; the record is a few dozen-to-a-hundred people at a time, from one country's research groups, pointing in two directions. Human trials
    • Two fences belong here. First, the animal record is much stronger than the human one — dill extracts lower blood sugar and blood fats handsomely in diabetic rats — and none of it can be carried across to people. Second, the cancer and antimicrobial claims attached to dill in the supplement trade rest on laboratory dishes and animal work; no human trial supports them. Animal studies / Lab studies
    • When to plant: Sow directly where it is to grow, after the last frost, about ¼ inch deep; germination takes about ten days to two weeks in warm soil
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Light, well-drained soil around neutral
    • Size: A quick annual, knee- to waist-high — about 40 to 90 cm (1½ to 3 feet) — with one slender, hollow stem, leaves cut into soft green threads, and flat umbrellas of small yellow flowers in summer
    • Spacing: Thin seedlings to about 9 to 12 inches apart; the tall seed kinds may need a stake or a sheltered corner — the hollow stems are brittle in wind
    • When to pick: Harvest the weed fresh, a little at a time, before flowering begins; harvest seed when the heads turn tan-brown

    Garden notes

    • Dill is a quick annual, knee- to waist-high in most gardens — about 40 to 90 cm (1½ to 3 feet) depending on the variety — with one slender, hollow stem, leaves cut into soft green threads, and flat umbrellas of small yellow flowers in summer. What is sold as the seed is the dried fruit, which splits into two flat, oval, ribbed halves about 3–4 mm long.
    • For a steady supply of weed, sow a short row every two to three weeks from spring into early summer: each sowing gives a few weeks of cutting before the plants run to flower, and heat and long days hurry the running. A gardener who wants both leaf and seed lets the last sowing of the year flower and ripen.
    • Sun and soil: full sun, in light, well-drained soil around neutral. Thin seedlings to about 9 to 12 inches apart. The tall seed kinds may need a stake or a sheltered corner — the hollow stems are brittle in wind. Water steadily while plants are young; established dill asks little.
    • Harvest the weed fresh, a little at a time, before flowering begins; the flavour fades in drying more than in almost any other herb, so the surplus is better frozen in oil or water than hung to dry. Harvest seed like its cousins: when the heads turn tan-brown, cut them into a paper bag and let them finish drying in it, then rub the fruit free.
    • Stored whole, the seed keeps its warmth about a year in a jar away from light. Fresh weed keeps only a few days, stood in water in the refrigerator like a bunch of flowers.
    • Two garden friendships worth knowing: black swallowtail butterflies raise their caterpillars on dill, so a few spare plants are a gift to them; and seed savers keep dill and fennel apart, as the two are said to cross and give seed of muddled flavour.
    • A caution about identification: dill's family includes deadly plants — poison hemlock carries similar white umbrellas (dill's flowers are yellow, hemlock's white, but no one should be deciding dinner on that difference) — so dill is grown from a packet and known by its planting, never gathered on a guess from the wild.

    Propagation

    Sow it where it is to grow. Dill grows a taproot and dislikes being moved, exactly like its cousins cumin and anise, so it is sown directly in the bed after the last frost, about ¼ inch deep. Leave a head or two standing and dill will sow itself for next year.

    Safety

    • In cooking amounts dill is a safe, ordinary food, eaten for thousands of years, and dill and its oil are recognised as safe (GRAS) as flavourings. The cautions belong to medicinal amounts. Concentrated dill oil is a drug-strength substance — it is not given undiluted, and the few milligrams in licensed gripe water are a dilution, not a dose of oil.
    • Medicinal amounts are best avoided in pregnancy: the seed has an old traditional reputation for bringing on menstruation, and there are no safety data to argue with it. Because the trials suggest dill can nudge insulin and blood sugar, medicinal doses matter alongside diabetes medicines.
    • Handling large amounts of the fresh plant in sunshine has blistered the skin of harvest workers — a known, mild version of the celery family's sun-rash — and people allergic to carrots, celery or their kin can react to dill. None of this touches the pickle jar or the garnish.

    Sources

    • Kojuri et al. (2007) — Effects of Anethum graveolens and garlic on lipid profile in hyperlipidemic patients (Lipids in Health and Disease) — 150 patients in three arms; dill showed no significant effect
    • Mirhosseini et al. (2014) — dill tablet trial in patients with high cholesterol (Journal of Research in Medical Sciences) — cholesterol reported against the patients' own starting values after two months
    • Mousavi et al. (2022) — The effects of Anethum graveolens (dill) supplementation on lipid profile and glycemic control: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition) — seven trials, 330 people pooled

    Dahlia

    Dahlia × pinnata

    Culinary

    FreshCooked

    Dahlias are the big, late flowers of the garden year — pompons like buttons, spiky cactus heads, and flat-faced "dinner plates" wider than a hand, in every colour except a true blue. The genus Dahlia holds more than forty wild species, all from the highlands of Mexico and Central America, and the garden plants are hybrids raised from a few of them. The garden dahlia's own name, Dahlia × pinnata, carries an × because it is a cross, not a wild species: it appeared in European gardens from the Mexican plants, and it carries eight sets of chromosomes where most plants carry two, which is part of why its children vary so wildly. Like its kin the sunflower and the marigold, a dahlia "flower" is really a head of many small flowers — a centre of tiny tubes ringed by the showy strap-shaped ones. The plants are tuberous perennials: they grow from finger-thick underground tubers, flower from midsummer until the frost cuts them down, and cannot take a freezing winter in the ground. And there is a second dahlia under the showy one. In Mexico this is the national flower, named so by decree in 1963 — and long before it was a flower at all, it was dinner.

    Cultivars

    The register's size is the story: more than 57,000 named dahlia cultivars have been registered, and hundreds more are added every year. No garden flower outside the rose and the tulip has been bred on this scale. To keep the multitude in order, the Royal Horticultural Society and the American Dahlia Society sort every cultivar by size, by form — the shape of the head — and by colour, and the show bench judges each flower against its own class. Size runs across all the forms: from pompons under 5 cm (2 in) to the dinner plates, over 25 cm (10 in) across — a single flower the size of the plate it is named for.

    Single

    One ring of flat straps around an open centre: the closest form to the wild species, and the one bees can actually use. 'Bishop of Llandaff' (1927) is the famous garden kind — scarlet-red heads over near-black leaves, grown as much for the foliage as the flower.

    Collerette

    A single ring of large straps with a collar of smaller ones inside it, around an open centre.

    Anemone

    The centre is built up into a pincushion of long tubes, ringed by one row of flat straps.

    Waterlily

    Broad, shallow heads with gently cupped straps, held flat like a waterlily flower on a pond.

    Decorative

    The big double heads of the shows: fully double, wide flat straps, no centre showing. Formal decoratives are even and symmetrical; informal ones are looser and wavier. 'Café au Lait', creamy coffee-and-milk dinner plates, is the florists' favourite of the age; 'Kelvin Floodlight' (1959), a giant in clear yellow, is still winning prizes more than sixty years on; 'Thomas Edison' (1929) is a rich purple heirloom. The oldest cultivar still shown, 'White Aster', dates to 1879.

    Ball

    Perfectly round heads of tightly furled straps in a spiral, over about 5 cm (2 in) across.

    Pompon

    The same ball in miniature, under 5 cm, every strap rolled into a little tube: the button dahlias.

    Cactus

    The straps are rolled along their length into pointed quills, radiating like spines; semi-cactus kinds are rolled only toward the tip.

    Laciniated

    Each strap is split and twisted at the end, so the whole head looks fringed.

    Three wild relatives worth knowing. Dahlia coccinea, the scarlet wild species of Mexico, is a parent of the garden kinds and is sometimes grown as itself — single red or orange heads on tall stems. The tree dahlia, Dahlia imperialis, grows 3–6 m (10–20 ft) in a season and flowers at the very end of autumn, so in cold countries the frost usually takes the buds before they open. And the species of Oaxaca and the south are the food plants — the living root of the whole genus.

    • Dahlias are mountain plants. The wild species grow in the high country of Mexico and into Central America, and the peoples of Mexico knew them long before Europeans arrived — gathered from the wild, grown in gardens, eaten, and put to work.
    • The Nahuatl names tell the plant's oldest job. Acocotli and acocoxóchitl are built from atl, water, and a word for a pipe or tube, with xochitl, flower: "water-pipe flower." The stems are hollow, and the long hollow stems of the tree dahlia (Dahlia imperialis, a species that grows to the height of a small tree) were cut and used as pipes to carry water.
    • The tubers were food. They were dug, gathered and grown as a root vegetable — a staple in some districts, and a food kept against hard times. The taste never travelled: the tubers store their energy not as starch, like a potato, but as inulin, a chain of fruit-sugar units, and they eat milder and less mealy than a potato. What inulin does in the gut is set out in Health Benefits.
    • The plant was medicine too, in the record the Spanish found. Francisco Hernández, physician to the king of Spain, was sent to Mexico in 1570 to study the natural products of the country, and his account — the earliest European description of the dahlia — recorded the plant among the remedies of the Aztecs: for chronic coughs and colic, and as a medicine that brings out urine and sweat. Later accounts of the early record add its use against epilepsy. All of this is history; none of it is advice, and none of it has been tested in people since.
    • The plant crossed the ocean as food, not as a flower. In 1789 Vicente Cervantes, director of the botanical garden in Mexico City, sent dahlia material to Antonio José Cavanilles at the Royal Gardens in Madrid. Cavanilles flowered the plants over the next two years, and in 1791 he described the new genus and named it Dahlia — for Anders Dahl, a Swedish botanist and pupil of Linnaeus. Dahl had died in 1789, the very year the plants reached Madrid, and never saw one. The first species named were Dahlia pinnata, for its divided, feather-like leaves, and Dahlia rosea; the scarlet Dahlia coccinea followed a few years later.
    • Europe tried the tuber at table and gave it up — the flavour pleased almost nobody — and within a few years the plant had reached Paris and Berlin and was being grown for its flowers instead. Breeders in Belgium, France, Germany and Britain crossed the Mexican species and selected hard: the open, single wild-type flowers were bred double, then doubled again, until heads appeared that no wild dahlia ever made.
    • By the 1830s Britain was in the grip of a dahlia craze — new varieties fetched high prices, growers competed at shows, and the flower became a fixture of the cottage garden and the exhibition bench. A story is still told of the Empress Joséphine guarding the dahlias at her garden at Malmaison so jealously that a Polish count had tubers stolen from the beds to break her monopoly; it remains a story, not documented history. The societies followed the craze: Britain's National Dahlia Society was founded in 1881, Germany's in 1897, and the American Dahlia Society in 1915 — its first show, in New York, drew some 35,000 visitors.
    • The tuber's one European career was in medicine, and it belongs to the inulin. Before insulin was discovered in 1923, people with diabetes were given a sweet substance drawn from dahlia tubers, sold as "Atlantic starch" or "diabetic sugar" — inulin tastes faintly sweet and passes through the body undigested, which made it a sugar that was not, in the ordinary sense, used. Inulin is still used in medicine today, in a standard test of how well the kidneys filter.
    • Mexico kept the whole plant. Tubers are still eaten there — in Oaxaca they belong to the local cooking, some kinds are still grown for their large tubers rather than their flowers, the Mixtec people eat the fresh roots of wild plants, and in parts of the country the petals are eaten too, fresh in salads and soups. An extract of the roasted tubers, called dacopa, flavours drinks in Central America. And in 1963 Mexico closed the circle: by presidential decree of 13 May that year, the dahlia — in all its species and varieties — was named the national flower of Mexico.
    • Mexico — the national flower since 1963, and still a working plant: tubers eaten and grown for the table in Oaxaca and the west, petals in salads and soups, wild roots gathered by the Mixtec, and the flower everywhere in gardens and festivals in its homeland.
    • Britain — the show-bench country. The Victorian craze made the dahlia an exhibition flower, the National Dahlia Society (1881) still runs the standard, and late-summer shows still bench hundreds of blooms, each judged against its class — form, colour and size exact.
    • North America — the American Dahlia Society (founded 1915, first show that autumn to a crowd of 35,000) federates more than seventy local societies across the United States and Canada; trial gardens test new cultivars, and the dahlia is the official flower of San Francisco, where the Dahlia Society of California dates to 1917.
    • Germany and the low countries — Germany's dahlia society dates to 1897, German towns keep whole dahlia gardens (Gera's and Baden-Baden's are famous), and Dutch and Belgian nurseries do much of the world's dahlia breeding and tuber trading, as they have since the first doubles were raised there.
    • What is in the tuber: inulin, and the honest account of it. Inulin is a fibre — a chain of fructose (fruit sugar) units — and the human gut has no tool that can cut it. It travels to the large bowel whole, where the bacteria that live there ferment it: they feed on it, and the feeding makes gas. That is the whole story, in both directions. The fermentation feeds helpful bacteria, which is why inulin is classed as a prebiotic — food for the gut's own bacteria. And the gas is real: in feeding trials, inulin's bloating and wind rise with the dose, mild at a few grams a day and plain uncomfortable at large ones. A serving of dahlia tuber is a serving of this fibre, with this effect, and anyone who eats tubers for the first time should start small.
    • No trials of the dahlia itself. No study in people has tested eating dahlia tubers, or any dahlia preparation, for any condition — not for blood sugar, not for digestion, not for anything else. The old "diabetic sugar" use is history, and it is not evidence: inulin passes through undigested because the body cannot use it, which is not the same as treating diabetes. No benefit is claimed for this plant.
    • Laboratory work stays in the laboratory. Dahlia flowers and tubers have been ground up and tested in dishes — the coloured petals hold pigments of the same broad family as other flower colours, and extracts show the usual test-tube antioxidant activity. That is chemistry, not a benefit in a body. Lab studies
    • The food industry uses the tuber, and that is a fact about inulin, not about health. Inulin drawn from dahlia tubers is used to thicken and body foods and to stand in for fat and sugar in made products, and the flowers are eaten in Mexico as set out above. The tuber is a traditional food, and that is enough.
    • When to plant: Set tubers out after the last frost, into warm soil, about 10–15 cm (4–6 in) deep
    • Sun: Full sun, in ground that drains — tubers rot in cold, wet earth
    • Soil: Ground that drains — tubers rot in cold, wet earth
    • Size: A handful of the squat bedding kinds stand 30 cm (1 ft); border kinds run 90–150 cm (3–5 ft), and the tall ones need a stake put in at planting time
    • When to pick: Flowers come from midsummer onward and improve as the days shorten, until the first frost ends the show overnight; pick off the faded heads to keep new buds coming

    Garden notes

    • Dahlias are tender perennials. Frost blackens them to the ground and a hard freeze kills tubers left in cold, wet soil. In warm districts (roughly USDA zones 8 and up) they can overwinter in the ground under a deep mulch; everywhere colder, the tubers are lifted and stored, or the plants are grown fresh each year.
    • Planting: set tubers out after the last frost, into warm soil, about 10–15 cm (4–6 in) deep, in full sun and ground that drains — tubers rot in cold, wet earth. A handful of the squat bedding kinds stand 30 cm (1 ft); border kinds run 90–150 cm (3–5 ft), and the tall ones need a stake put in at planting time, before the stems need it. Pinching out the growing tip of a young plant makes it branch and carry more, smaller flowers; leaving it makes fewer, larger ones.
    • The season: growth is slow until the soil is properly warm, then fast. Flowers come from midsummer onward and improve as the days shorten, until the first frost ends the show overnight. Water deeply in dry spells, feed moderately — heavy nitrogen makes leaves, not flowers — and pick off the faded heads to keep new buds coming. A spent dahlia head is pointed and cone-like where a bud is round, which is how you tell what to cut.
    • Lifting and storing: after frost blackens the leaves, cut the stems down, fork the tubers up gently, shake off the soil and let them dry a few days under cover. Store them cool, dark and just barely damp — in peat, shavings or vermiculite — and look them over in spring: divide the clump then, making sure every piece carries a bit of the old stem with an eye, the bud the new plant grows from. A tuber with no eye will root and never shoot.
    • Troubles, honestly: slugs and snails take young shoots, earwigs chew the petals of the show kinds, and aphids gather on the buds. Virus is the quiet one — mottled, stunted plants should be dug out and binned, not composted, and new stock is best bought from clean sources. For pollinators, plant the open kinds: singles and collerettes feed bees freely, while the great tight doubles offer them almost nothing behind their walls of straps.

    Propagation

    Divide the clump in spring, making sure every piece carries a bit of the old stem with an eye, the bud the new plant grows from. A tuber with no eye will root and never shoot.

    Safety

    • Dahlias are in the daisy family, and this one has a documented skin record. "Dahlia dermatitis" is on the medical record — an allergic rash on the face, hands and arms of gardeners and growers who handle the plants a great deal, caused by the sesquiterpene lactones, a family of bitter compounds found across the daisy family; the plant's particles can sensitise through the air as well as by touch. Most gardeners handle dahlias for a lifetime with no trouble, but if your skin complains after working among them, gloves are the answer, and people allergic to ragweed, chrysanthemums and their kin should take the same care.
    • On eating: eat only kinds grown for the table, from clean ground — the named show cultivars are bred for flowers, their tubers vary from mild to bitter, and garden tubers may carry whatever the garden was sprayed with.

    Sources

    • Cavanilles (1791) — Icones et Descriptiones Plantarum — the genus Dahlia described and named for Anders Dahl
    • Hernández (1570s; published 1651) — the natural history of New Spain — the earliest European description, recording the Aztec uses
    • Secretaría de Agricultura y Ganadería (1963) — the presidential decree naming the dahlia, in all its species and varieties, the national flower of Mexico
    • Mera-Ovando & Bye (2006) — the dahlia in Mexico: its history and traditional standing
    • Sánchez-Chávez et al. (2026) — Botanical Sciences — ethnobotany of Mexican Dahlia: ornamental, food and medicine uses across Mexico today
    • Lara-Cortés et al. (2014) — the food use of dahlias in Oaxaca: roots and ray florets
    • Bonnema et al. (2010) — feeding trial of inulin in healthy adults: gas and bloating rise with dose
    • Denisow-Pietrzyk et al. (2019) — review of contact allergy to the daisy family — dahlia dermatitis on record
    • American Dahlia Society — the classification of dahlias by size, form and colour, and the register of named cultivars

    Damiana

    Turnera diffusa

    Medicinal

    Dried

    The love herb of old Mexico — and a fame built almost entirely on tradition. Damiana is a small, wiry shrub of dry, rocky hillsides, its stems reddish, its little toothed leaves strongly scented when crushed, its flowers small, bright yellow and open to the morning sun. In Mexico its leaves have been brewed as a calming tea for centuries, and it carries one of the oldest aphrodisiac reputations in the Americas — a reputation so fixed that botanists once named the plant itself Turnera aphrodisiaca, after Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love. That reputation is tradition and advertising, not tested proof: damiana has never been put to a proper trial in people on its own, and everything claimed for it beyond the tea cup rests on animal work and on mixtures of many herbs at once.

    Cultivars

    Damiana has no named cultivars — none at all. Seed and plants are sold as the plain species, and the dried leaf of commerce is gathered overwhelmingly from wild plants in Mexico rather than from any cultivated variety. The plant itself splits into two botanical varieties.

    Var. diffusa

    The widespread form.

    Var. aphrodisiaca

    The form described from the Baja California material in the 1870s — the one that briefly carried Aphrodite's name as a species of its own. The difference between them is a botanist's distinction, not a gardener's choice, and no named garden form of either exists.

    The name to beware in the nursery trade is false damiana, Turnera ulmifolia: a larger-leaved relative with paler, bigger flowers, sold again and again as the real plant. It is a different species, with different chemistry and a different traditional record, and none of what is told of damiana belongs to it.

    • Damiana is a plant of dry country: the rocky hillsides, arroyos and thorn scrub of Mexico above all, running north into the far south of Texas and south through Central America and the Caribbean to Brazil. It is a much-branched shrub, knee-high to about two metres, and the leaf is at its most fragrant where the ground is poorest and the sun hardest — the wild leaf of the harsh hillsides was always the gatherer's prize.
    • The oldest Mexican record is Maya. In the Maya pharmacopoeia the leaf was a remedy for giddiness and loss of balance, and a tonic to restore strength after alcoholic and sexual excess — a restorative, in other words, before it was anything else. Mexico's great atlas of traditional medicine lists it for stomachache, for complaints of the bladder and kidneys, for rheumatism, for diabetes, and even for scorpion stings: a household herb of many small uses, of which the famous one was only one.
    • Spanish missionaries in Mexico recorded the leaf and its uses, and in Baja California a legend grew around it: the Guaycura people of the peninsula, the story says, drank a sweetened damiana tea in their ceremonies, and the mission fathers, alarmed at what the tea was said to encourage, tried to stamp the custom out. It is told as a legend and kept as one — but it is the kind of legend that only attaches to a plant already famous for the thing alleged.
    • The names keep the plant's company. In Mexico it is hierba de la pastora, the shepherdess's herb; hierba del venado, the deer's herb; and oreganillo, the little oregano, for its scent. The name damiana itself is often said to honour Saint Damian, the patron saint of apothecaries. The genus name, Turnera, honours William Turner, the sixteenth-century English clergyman called the father of English botany.
    • In the 1870s the leaf crossed the border and its fame exploded. Leaves reached the United States from Cabo San Lucas, at the tip of Baja California, through the American consul there, and by 1874 damiana was on the American market. The patent-medicine trade seized on it: bottled elixirs and nerve tonics promised restored vigour in language no regulator would allow today. In 1876 botanists working from those very specimens gave the plant its short-lived name Turnera aphrodisiaca — the reputation, written into Latin.
    • The sceptics were there from the start. Pharmacists of the day complained that the sellers would not say where the leaf came from or produce a proper specimen, and one journal dismissed the whole business as a proprietary medicine shrewdly put upon the market. A Mexican scientist of the next century, Alfonso Herrera, doubted the aphrodisiac reputation altogether. The doubt and the fame have travelled together ever since.
    • Damiana even brushed against a more famous drink. In 1885 the Atlanta pharmacist John Pemberton launched Pemberton's French Wine Coca, a coca wine modelled on the French original, and damiana was among its ingredients. When the drink was remade without alcohol — the line that led to Coca-Cola — the damiana was left behind.
    • For all the doubts, the leaf held an official place for sixty years: damiana stood in the United States National Formulary, the official book of drug preparations, from 1888 until 1947, as an elixir and a fluid extract. Then it was dropped, and its modern life began — in tea blends, capsules and smoking mixtures, famous as ever, and still untested.
    • In Mexico the leaf never went away. It is still gathered mostly from wild plants, sold dried in markets, and brewed at home as an evening tea — for the nerves, for low spirits, for the stomach, and, in the village telling, for love. In the 1960s the dried leaf was also smoked abroad as a supposed marijuana-like herb; the celebrated high was never shown to be real, and damiana's honest effects in people, beyond a pleasant aromatic tea, remain unmeasured.
    • The liqueur is Mexico's other damiana tradition. In Baja California Sur the leaves are steeped into a sweet golden liqueur, credited to the Guaycura and first sold commercially in La Paz in the 1860s, often in a bottle shaped like a woman — a fertility figure, in keeping with the leaf's reputation. Around Los Cabos the liqueur goes into margaritas, and local telling claims the very first margarita was mixed with damiana liqueur in place of triple sec. Cocktail historians doubt it; it remains a local story.
    • Mexico — the leaf's home ground: dried damiana in market herb stalls, brewed as an evening tea for the nerves, the stomach and low spirits, and steeped into the golden liqueur of Baja California Sur.
    • Baja California and Los Cabos — damiana liqueur in its woman-shaped bottle, and the damiana margarita, a local speciality carrying the legend of the first margarita with it.
    • The United States — a nineteenth-century patent-medicine star and sixty-year resident of the National Formulary; today a capsule, tea-blend and smoking-blend herb, sold on the same reputation it arrived with in 1874.
    • Central America and the Caribbean — the shrub is native through the region, and the leaf is used in local folk practice as a tea and tonic, in the same Mexican pattern.
    • Europe — damiana reached European herbals as an exotic American stimulant in the late 1800s and stayed a minor herb-trade article, never gaining the official standing it briefly held in America.
    • The plain position, first: no clinical trial has ever tested damiana on its own in people — not for desire, not for calm, not for anything. The professional monographs say so in so many words. Every human study behind damiana's modern reputation used a mixture of several herbs and nutrients at once, and a mixture's result cannot be handed to one of its ingredients. What exists is a long traditional record, animal studies, and laboratory work — each stated at its own strength below.
    • The aphrodisiac claim — animal work only. In rats, a water extract of damiana improved mating performance in males that were sexually sluggish or sexually exhausted, and the effect ran through the nitric oxide pathway, the same signalling route used by the body's own arousal chemistry (Arletti et al., 1999; Estrada-Reyes et al., 2009). In healthy, normally performing rats the extract did nothing. No study has tested damiana alone for sexual function in people, so the most famous claim attached to the plant is also its least tested. Animal studies
    • Calm — animal work only. Damiana extracts eased anxiety-like behaviour in mice, and single compounds from the leaf, such as apigenin, are calming in animal tests. That is the whole of the evidence behind the "calming tea" reputation: a real traditional use, a suggestive animal record, and no human trial. Animal studies
    • Blood sugar — animal work, and the root of a real caution. A water extract of damiana lowered blood sugar in diabetic mice in one study; other animal work found the effects on blood sugar unpredictable. Nothing is proven in people, but the animal signal is strong enough that the safety notes below treat it seriously. Animal studies
    • Laboratory work — fenced at that strength. In dishes, damiana extract and two of its flavonoids, pinocembrin and acacetin, slowed aromatase, an enzyme that turns testosterone into oestrogen (Zhao et al., 2008); the leaf's arbutin showed a protective effect against stomach ulcers in animals; and extracts kill some bacteria in laboratory tests. None of this shows what drinking damiana tea does in a person. Lab studies
    • What is in the leaf: flavonoids — apigenin, acacetin and pinocembrin among them — together with arbutin, a bitter compound named damianin after the plant, a scented oil that gives the crushed leaf its smell, and, less comfortably, cyanogenic glycosides: plant chemicals that can release cyanide. Their presence matters to the safety notes, at the doses where it matters.
    • The mixtures, fenced. ArginMax, a blend of ginseng, ginkgo, L-arginine, vitamins and damiana, was tested in women in small, short trials with favourable results for sexual satisfaction — and in a larger twelve-week trial in cancer survivors it found no difference at all. A second blend, of yerba mate, guaraná and damiana, was tested for weight loss with modest results. Damiana was one voice in each chorus; none of the results, good or null, can be credited to it. Human trials
    • When to plant: Sow seed warm in spring, or grow from cuttings, which take readily
    • Sun: Full sun, in poor, rocky or sandy soil that drains sharply
    • Soil: Poor, rocky or sandy soil that drains sharply — rich soil and generous watering make a soft, weak plant and a less fragrant leaf
    • Size: A much-branched shrub, knee-high to about two metres, with many reddish, wiry stems from a woody base
    • When to pick: The leaf is gathered from flowering plants through the summer, dried in shade, and kept for tea

    Garden notes

    • A shrub of hot, dry places, and tender with it. Damiana is killed by frost and sulks in cold, wet soil; in warm, frost-free climates (the equivalent of USDA zones 9 to 11) it is a permanent small shrub, and everywhere else it is best grown in a pot that comes indoors for winter, or treated as a summer plant.
    • Give it the hillside it came from: full sun, and soil that is poor, rocky or sandy and drains sharply. Rich soil and generous watering make a soft, weak plant and a less fragrant leaf; hardship is this shrub's idea of home. Once settled it is drought-tolerant and asks for little.
    • The plant itself: many reddish, wiry stems from a woody base, half a metre to two metres tall, clothed in small, toothed, grey-green leaves that release their scent when brushed or crushed. The flowers are small, five-petalled and bright yellow, opening in the morning through the warm season — spring to autumn where summers are long — and the shrub is a host plant for the Mexican fritillary butterfly.
    • Buy with care: because the garden trade so often supplies false damiana, Turnera ulmifolia, in its place, order from a source that gives the full botanical name, Turnera diffusa, and check the plant that arrives — the true leaf is small, toothed and strongly scented, the flowers small and a clear, bright yellow.
    • The leaf is the harvest: in Mexico it is gathered from flowering plants through the summer, dried in shade, and kept for tea. A home plant gives a handful of leaves, not a market crop — enough for the occasional cup, which is the scale this herb has always honestly worked at.

    Propagation

    Grow it from seed sown warm in spring, or from cuttings, which take readily.

    Safety

    • Damiana should be avoided in pregnancy and while breastfeeding. There is no safety record to lean on, the leaf carries cyanogenic glycosides, and the standard references advise against its use outright. Tea-strength tradition in Mexico is one thing; concentrated capsules and extracts in pregnancy are another, and no one has shown them safe.
    • Because damiana lowered blood sugar in animals, it may add to the effect of diabetes medicines and insulin and push blood sugar too low. Anyone taking medicine for diabetes should treat damiana as a herb to discuss with their clinician first, not a harmless tea. The same caution applies before surgery, where blood sugar is closely managed.
    • The one dramatic case on record is an old report of a person who took some 200 grams of damiana extract — an enormous quantity, hundreds of times a normal dose — and suffered tetanus-like convulsions, spasms likened at the time to strychnine poisoning. Headache and insomnia are also reported at heavy doses. Ordinary tea amounts have no such record, but the case is a plain warning about concentrated extracts and heroic doses: more is not better, and with this leaf more has, once, been dangerous.
    • Much of the seed and many of the living plants sold in the garden trade as damiana turn out to be Turnera ulmifolia, a different species with different chemistry, known in the trade as false damiana. Leaf bought from a named herbal source is the traditional material; a garden-centre plant labelled damiana may be nothing of the kind.

    Sources

    • Szewczyk & Zidorn (2014) — ethnobotany, phytochemistry and bioactivity of the genus Turnera, with damiana at its centre: the Maya record, the Mexican traditional uses, the National Formulary years, and the animal evidence (Journal of Ethnopharmacology)
    • Arletti et al. (1999) — damiana extract improved mating performance in sexually sluggish male rats; healthy rats were unaffected (Psychopharmacology)
    • Estrada-Reyes et al. (2009) — a water extract of damiana restored mating in sexually exhausted rats, working through the nitric oxide pathway; the same group's work found calming effects in mice (Journal of Ethnopharmacology)
    • Zhao et al. (2008) — damiana extract and its flavonoids pinocembrin and acacetin slowed the aromatase enzyme in laboratory tests
    • Ito et al. (2001) — small trials of ArginMax, a blend of ginseng, ginkgo, L-arginine, vitamins and damiana, in women; a blend's results, not damiana's (Journal of Sex & Marital Therapy)
    • Andersen & Fogh (2001) — a yerba mate, guaraná and damiana preparation tested for weight loss; a blend's results, not damiana's (Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics)
    • Drugs.com (2026) — professional monograph on damiana: clinical trial data lacking for every use; pregnancy to be avoided; the high-dose convulsion record and the cyanogenic glycosides
    • Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — the accepted name Turnera diffusa, its place in the passionflower family, and its native range

    Date Palm

    Phoenix dactylifera

    Culinary

    FreshCookedDried

    The date palm is the fruit tree of the desert oasis, and one of the oldest cultivated trees on Earth. It stands on a single tall trunk ringed with the diamond-patterned bases of old fronds, wearing a crown of long feather-shaped leaves, and it carries its fruit in heavy hanging bunches that can hold hundreds of dates each. Male and female flowers grow on separate trees — a date palm is one sex or the other — so no female tree fruits at all unless pollen reaches her, which is why growers have pollinated this tree by hand for thousands of years. The fruit ripens through stages that are eaten as different foods. At the khalal stage the date is full-sized, crisp and bright yellow or red, eaten fresh and crunchy like an apple. At the rutab stage it softens from the tip, turns amber and becomes melting, honeyed and perishable — a fresh fruit of a few days. Left on the tree it finishes at the tamar stage: dark, wrinkled, dried by the desert sun while still hanging, and able to keep for months. Most of the world knows only the tamar stage, the dried date of the shops. One thing should be said plainly at the start: a dried date is a very sweet fruit, roughly two-thirds sugar by weight. That is its nature and its usefulness — it is stored sunshine and energy — and nothing turns it into something it is not.

    Cultivars

    More than 3,000 named date varieties are claimed across the growing world, and the count is believable: every oasis kept its own seedlings for centuries. What separates the great cultivars from the crowd is that they are not grown from seed at all. A named variety is a clone, carried from place to place as offshoots from one mother tree, so every 'Medjool' palm on Earth descends from trees like the ones in its home oasis.

    'Medjool'

    The king of dates, from the Tafilalet oases of south-east Morocco: very large, soft, dark and rich, eaten at the dried stage but so moist it eats like a fresh fruit. Its modern history is a rescue. In the early 1900s a soil fungus disease called Bayoud — the name comes from the Arabic for white, for the whitening fronds of dying palms — was destroying Morocco's groves, Medjools among them. In 1927 the American plant scientist Walter Swingle, in Morocco to study the disease, bought eleven offshoots from a single healthy palm in a disease-free garden at Bou Denib. The offshoots were quarantined for years in Nevada, far from any other date palm; nine survived, and their offspring went to growers in California and Arizona from 1944. Nearly every Medjool eaten today descends from those nine palms.

    'Deglet Noor'

    The date of light, named for the way light glows through its amber flesh held up to the sun. From the oases of Tolga in Algeria, and Tunisia's great export date: semi-dry, firm, honey-sweet rather than caramel-soft, the standard baking date and, for most of the twentieth century, the main variety of California's groves. It keeps and travels better than the soft kinds, which is why it fills the chopped-date boxes of the baking aisle.

    'Barhi'

    From Basra in southern Iraq, and the fresh-eater's date. Round and small beside a Medjool, Barhi is sold on its branch at the crisp yellow khalal stage, when it crunches like an apple with a sweet, faintly tannic bite, and again at the rutab stage, when it turns soft, golden and syrupy, with a taste growers compare to crème brûlée. It must be eaten fresh or kept frozen — it does not dry into a keeping date — and it is the variety that shows Western readers what the fresh stages taste like.

    'Khalas'

    The golden date of Al-Ahsa in eastern Saudi Arabia, one of the Gulf's prized table dates: amber, soft, with a clean caramel sweetness, traditionally taken with Arabic coffee. It was one of the five varieties in the blood-sugar study, which gives some idea of its standing in its home region.

    'Mazafati'

    Iran's soft, dark, almost black date from Bam, sold boxed and kept cool like a fresh fruit.

    'Ajwa'

    A small dark date of Medina in Saudi Arabia, prized above its flavour for its place in the Prophet's own tradition.

    'Sukkari'

    The crisp, very sweet golden date of Saudi Arabia's Qassim region.

    'Halawy'

    An old Iraqi cultivar among the first planted in California — soft and sweet.

    'Zahidi'

    An old Iraqi cultivar among the first planted in California — firm, drier, and used much like Deglet Noor.

    • Nobody knows the date palm wild for certain. The tree has been planted and tended for so long that its wild ancestor is argued over, but the cultivation is ancient beyond argument: date stones and palm remains appear at farming sites around the Persian Gulf and in Mesopotamia — the land of modern Iraq — by about 4000 BCE, and the tree was grown in the Indus Valley and in Egypt in the same early ages. The Greek name Phoenix was the Greeks' word for the Phoenicians, the trading people they linked with the palm; dactylifera means "finger-bearing," from daktylos, a finger — a date hanging in its bunch looks like a finger, and the word "date" itself comes down from that same Greek word for a finger.
    • The oldest skill of the date grower is the pollination. Because the trees are male or female, Babylonian and Assyrian farmers learned to climb the female trees in spring and tie clusters of male flowers into their crowns. Carved Assyrian palace reliefs show figures at the crowns of palms holding flower clusters — long read as this very work. The law code of Hammurabi, written in Babylon around 1754 BCE, sets out rules for palm orchards and the gardener's duty to pollinate them, including what happened to his share of the crop if he failed. The Greek writer Herodotus described the Babylonians tying male flower clusters to the fruiting trees, and Theophrastus, the first botanist, explained the practice plainly a century later: the male must be brought to the female, or the fruit falls without ripening.
    • In Egypt the palm shaded gardens and temple courts, its fronds stood for life and triumph, and dates were left in tombs as food for the dead. The tree runs through the scriptures of three faiths — the palm of the Bible's oases and of Palm Sunday, and in the Qur'an the palm beneath which Maryam gave birth, told to shake the trunk so ripe fresh dates — rutab — would fall to her. That verse is one root of the custom, still kept across the Middle East, of women eating dates in the last weeks of pregnancy.
    • The tree spread with every power that ruled dry country. Phoenician and Greek traders carried it around the Mediterranean; Roman authors wrote whole chapters on its varieties; and Arab farmers, from the seventh century onward, carried named cultivars across North Africa and into Spain, where the palm grove of Elche still stands. Wherever it went it made the same bargain with the desert: the old grower's saying gives the palm its feet in water and its head in the fire of the sun — deep roots at an oasis water table, a crown in fierce dry heat, and in return a crop that could feed a family and travel by camel.
    • In the Muslim world the date holds a place no other fruit matches. The fast of Ramadan is broken at sunset with dates and water, following the example of the Prophet Muhammad, and through the fasting month dates appear on iftar tables from Morocco to Indonesia. Harvests, prices and whole import trades bend around Ramadan's calendar, and a bowl of dates beside small cups of unsweetened coffee remains the first act of hospitality across the Gulf — the bitter coffee and the sweet fruit taken together.
    • Spanish missionaries planted dates from seed in Mexico and California in the 1700s, but seed-grown palms are a lottery: half come up male, and the females vary. The modern industry began when growers shipped home the tree's other kind of start — offshoots, the young palms that sprout at a mother tree's base and grow into her exact copy — and planted named varieties: Deglet Noor from Algeria reached California around 1900, and the Medjool's rescue from Morocco in 1927 has its own telling under Cultivars below.
    • As a food, the date was eaten at every stage its climate allowed. In the Gulf and Iraq, fresh dates at the crisp khalal stage and the soft, short-lived rutab stage are seasonal delicacies, bought in markets for a few weeks a year and eaten the day they are picked; the dried tamar stage was the traveller's and storehouse form, pressed into skins and jars, sometimes with its stones removed and the space filled with nuts. Date syrup — dibs in Arabic, silan in Hebrew — was boiled down from pressed dates as the desert's honey, and still sweetens baking across the region. Date vinegar, date paste for filled biscuits such as ma'amoul, and a fermented date wine in old Egypt all come from the same fruit.
    • In the traditional medicine of the region — in Unani practice, the Greek-Arab system of medicine still taught in South Asia, and in local custom generally — dates stood as a strengthening food: given to women after childbirth, to the weak and recovering, and in the last weeks of pregnancy. These are customs and traditions. The modern trials that tested the pregnancy custom are told at their true size.
    • The whole tree worked, not just the fruit. In the oasis garden the palm was the roof of a three-storey farm: palms above, fruit trees beneath them, and vegetables, herbs and fodder crops in the shade at the ground, all sharing the same scarce water. Trunks became beams and doors; fronds were woven into roofs, fences, baskets, mats and crates; the fibre around the trunk was twisted into rope; old trees and stones from the fruit fed animals. Almost nothing of a date palm was thrown away.
    • The Gulf and Arabia — dates and Arabic coffee open every visit; at Ramadan the day's fast ends with dates and water or milk before the evening meal, and the finest boxes of the harvest are gifts.
    • Iraq — among the world's oldest date lands and still one of its largest producers; Basra's Barhi and the great palm groves of the Shatt al-Arab were famous for centuries, and date syrup is a kitchen staple.
    • Iran — Mazafati from the Bam oasis, eaten soft and fresh-tasting; the south's palm provinces hold harvest festivals as the fruit colours in late summer.
    • North Africa — Tunisia and Algeria ship Deglet Noor to the world; Morocco guards the Medjool's home oases in the Tafilalet, where the autumn harvest is the year's hinge.
    • Spain — the Palmeral of Elche, a palm grove planted under Muslim rule and still worked today, where palms are also kept for the bleached fronds of Palm Sunday.
    • United States — the Coachella Valley of California and the Bard Valley grow nearly all of the country's dates; Indio's date gardens made the date shake — dates blended into a milkshake — a desert-road institution, and the valley still holds its date festival each winter.
    • South Asia — dates arrive by import and are eaten above all at Ramadan, when markets in Pakistan, India and Bangladesh fill with dozens of varieties for the iftar table.
    • Dates, dried (Medjool), per 100 g: 277 kcal, carbohydrate 75 g — of which sugars 66.5 g — fibre 6.7 g, protein 1.8 g, fat almost none, and potassium 696 mg. Deglet Noor runs close beside it: 282 kcal, sugars 63.4 g, fibre 8.0 g, potassium 656 mg. So the plain statement first: a dried date is about two-thirds sugar, and one large Medjool date of about 24 g carries about 16 g of sugar and 66 kcal. It is one of the sweetest whole fruits there is. Its sugar is its own — nothing is added — but the body meets it as sugar all the same, and portions are the honest way to eat dates.
    • Fresh dates are a lighter food than dried ones, because so much of their weight is still water: at the fresh stages a date runs at roughly half the calories and half the sugar per 100 g of the dried fruit. The fibre and potassium figures below belong to the dried fruit, the form most readers will meet.
    • The fibre is real. At 6.7–8.0 g per 100 g, dried dates carry more fibre than most fruits, fresh or dried, and a small handful gives a useful share of the day's fibre along with its sugar. The potassium is real too, at about 15% of a day's worth per 100 g. These are food-strength facts — the ordinary good of a whole fruit — and they sit beside the sugar figure, not above it: the fibre slows the sugar's arrival somewhat, and it does not cancel it.
    • On blood sugar, the measured picture is more moderate than the sugar figure alone suggests. In a 2011 study from the Emirates, five date varieties were fed to 13 healthy volunteers and 10 people with type 2 diabetes, and their glycaemic index — the speed at which a food raises blood sugar, with pure glucose set at 100 — came out between about 46 and 55, the low-to-middle range, with no large blood-sugar excursions after the test portions in either group. That is a small measurement study of single portions, not a treatment and not a free pass: the varieties tested were eaten at set amounts of about 70 g, and a food can raise blood sugar gently and still be two-thirds sugar. People with diabetes who eat dates do it in counted portions, as these studies did. Human · small
    • The pregnancy custom has been tested, at small size. In a 2011 Jordanian study, 69 women ate six dates a day for the last four weeks of pregnancy and were compared with 45 women who ate none: the date eaters arrived at hospital further dilated (3.5 cm against 2.0 cm), went into labour on their own more often (96% against 79%), needed labour-inducing drugs less often (28% against 47%), and had a shorter early stage of labour. The study was not randomised — the women were not assigned to their groups by lot — and its authors said a proper trial was needed. Later small randomised trials, including a Malaysian trial of 154 women, pointed in a similar direction on some measures, and reviews of the whole set call the evidence promising but not settled. That is the true size of it: an old custom with a handful of small studies behind it, not a proven way to ease labour, and nothing here is advice for a pregnancy. Human · small
    • Dates carry plant compounds called polyphenols, which behave as antioxidants in laboratory tests, and date extracts have been studied in dishes and in animals for effects on inflammation and blood fats. There are no human trials showing that eating dates prevents or treats any disease, and no honest claim of that kind is made here. Lab studies
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Tolerates salty and alkaline soils that defeat most fruit trees, but still needs drainage
    • Size: A palm grows 9–15 metres tall in gardens, and old trees reach 20 metres and beyond, with a crown spread of 6 metres or more
    • Environment: Zone 9–11 warmth, a long fierce summer to ripen fruit, and dry air at harvest — rain on ripening dates splits and sours them
    • When to pick: Bunches for fresh eating are cut at khalal or picked through at rutab, while drying varieties hang on the tree until the tamar stage and come down whole

    Garden notes

    • This is a tree for hot, dry country. The date palm wants zone 9–11 warmth, a long fierce summer to ripen its fruit, and dry air at harvest — rain on ripening dates splits and sours them, which is why the great groves are in deserts with irrigation, not in humid tropics. In cooler climates it is grown as a handsome ornamental palm, but fruit worth eating needs desert heat.
    • Give it full sun and deep room. A palm grows 9–15 metres tall in gardens, and old trees reach 20 metres and beyond, with a crown spread of 6 metres or more. It tolerates salty and alkaline soils that defeat most fruit trees — one reason it owns the oases — but it still needs drainage: the "feet in water" of the saying means deep irrigation at the roots, not a bog at the trunk.
    • You need two trees, and the right two. A fruiting garden needs female trees of a named variety — bought as offshoots, never seedlings, if the fruit matters — plus one male tree, whose pollen a grower carries by hand to many females: a single male can serve a few dozen females with hand pollination. Every spring the grower climbs each female, opens her flower clusters and ties in strands of male flowers, the same work Hammurabi's gardeners were fined for skipping. Without it, the fruit falls unripe.
    • Young palms are slow and patient work. An offshoot planted out takes some four to eight years to bear its first bunch, and a tree is in full bearing nearer ten. The trunk's crown of fronds is armed — the lower leaflets of each frond are true spines, stiff and sharp — and pruning old fronds is glove-and-sleeve work.
    • Through the season the grower thins the bunches, tying them up and often bagging them in mesh or paper against birds, insects and late rain. Harvest is staged by the eating stages: bunches for fresh eating are cut at khalal or picked through at rutab, while drying varieties hang on the tree until the tamar stage and come down whole.
    • Cold sets the map's edge. Green fronds are damaged by frosts around −6 °C and a hard freeze well below that can kill the growing crown, the tree's single heart. In borderline gardens a palm may live for years as an ornament and still never ripen a date — the tree's survival and the fruit's ripening ask for different amounts of summer.

    Propagation

    Buy female trees of a named variety as offshoots, never seedlings, if the fruit matters — an offshoot is a young palm sprouting at a mother tree's base that grows into her exact copy, while a seedling is a lottery: half come up male, and the females vary.

    Safety

    • The cautions are the sugar's cautions: dates are sticky and very sweet, so they are hard on teeth eaten often and alone, and their calories gather quickly — a bowl of Medjools is a meal's worth of energy in a snack's volume.
    • People managing diabetes treat them as a measured food.
    • Beyond that the fruit is a kind one: date allergy is rare, dried dates are usually sold without the sulphur preservatives used on some other dried fruits, and the single long stone in each date is a choking hazard only in the ordinary way of stones — worth a thought with small children.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture — FoodData Central: dates, Medjool, and dates, Deglet Noor — the nutrition figures
    • Alkaabi et al. (2011) — glycaemic indices of five varieties of dates in 13 healthy and 10 diabetic subjects (Nutrition Journal)
    • Al-Kuran et al. (2011) — late-pregnancy date consumption and labour outcomes in 69 women, with 45 comparisons (Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology)
    • Razali et al. (2017) — randomised trial of date consumption in late pregnancy, 154 women, Malaysia
    • Hodel & Pittenger — the Medjool's history in the United States: Swingle's 1927 offshoots, the Nevada quarantine and the California plantings (the standard account, retold in Fungi Magazine, 2020)

    Dragon Fruit

    Selenicereus spp.

    Culinary

    Digestive HealthVitamin C

    FreshCookedDried

    Dragon fruit is the fruit of a climbing cactus — a plant with long, three-sided green stems that scramble up trees, rocks and posts, holding on with small aerial roots, the little roots that grow out of the stems into the air. It makes one of the largest flowers of any food plant, a white, fragrant bloom as long as a forearm that opens for a single night, and the fruit that follows is just as showy: an oval covered in smooth, overlapping scales, pink or yellow outside and speckled inside with tiny black seeds that are eaten with the flesh, like the seeds of a kiwi. The taste is mild and gentle — soft, juicy, lightly sweet, closer to a pear or a kiwi than to anything dramatic — which surprises people who meet the outside first. Three kinds cover nearly everything sold, and they are worth keeping straight. The common one, Selenicereus undatus, has pink skin and white flesh. The red-fleshed kinds, S. costaricensis and its close kin, wear the same pink skin but cut open magenta-red, stained by the same family of pigments that colours beetroot. The yellow kind, S. megalanthus, is smaller, wears real little spines on a yellow skin, and is the sweetest of the three. The plants were long filed under the name Hylocereus, and most labels, seed lists and older books still use it; botanists have since moved them into Selenicereus, so both names are met in the wild. The name dragon fruit itself is an Asian coinage — the fruit's scaly skin read as a dragon's scales — and it stuck around the world.

    Cultivars

    In this crop the species is the first choice, because it fixes the flesh.

    White-fleshed (Selenicereus undatus)

    Pink skin, white flesh, the mildest flavour and by far the most grown; the export fruit of Vietnam and the dragon fruit of most supermarkets.

    Red-fleshed (S. costaricensis and close kin)

    Pink skin, magenta-red flesh, sweeter and stronger-tasting, the pigment kind.

    Magenta hybrids (S. guatemalensis and crosses)

    Pink skin, purple-magenta flesh, bred heavily in California and Florida for flavour.

    Yellow (S. megalanthus)

    Yellow, lightly spined skin, white flesh, the smallest fruit and the sweetest, from Colombia and Ecuador.

    'Vietnamese White'

    The undatus type behind Vietnam's harvest and most of the world's traded fruit: vigorous, heavy-bearing, mild and refreshing rather than sweet.

    'Bien Hoa Red'

    A Vietnamese red-fleshed selection, among the sweetest of the reds in the University of California's San Diego field trial, where it measured the highest sugar of nineteen cultivars tested.

    'American Beauty'

    A magenta-fleshed cultivar of the guatemalensis kind, bred in the United States; self-fertile, which is not true of many, and one of the most planted by home growers for its rich, berry-like flavour.

    'Purple Haze', 'Physical Graffiti' and 'Halley's Comet'

    California-bred magenta hybrids from the breeding work that built the American home-growing scene; large, sweet, strongly flavoured fruit, and the names home growers ask for.

    'Lisa' and 'Rosa'

    Red-fleshed selections from Nicaragua, where the red kinds are a commercial crop in their own right and not a novelty.

    'Palora' (sold as 'Ecuador Palora')

    The yellow megalanthus of Palora in Ecuador: honey-sweet, the premium fruit of the whole group, and slow — months can pass between its flower and a ripe fruit, which is part of its price.

    A word of caution the whole crop needs: cultivar names in dragon fruit are loosely kept. The same plant circulates under several names, the same name is hung on different plants, and a cutting's label is a claim, not a certificate. Buy from a grower who can state the flesh colour and whether the plant can set fruit with its own pollen.

    • The plant is American. Its home is the tropical forest country from southern Mexico through Central America and into the north of South America, where the wild vines climb trees and rock faces and the fruit was eaten long before Europeans arrived — pitayas were a common food in their native lands in pre-Columbian times, gathered and grown around settlements. In Spanish America the fruit is still pitaya or pitahaya, the name it travelled under.
    • The shared name causes real confusion: in Mexico, pitaya also names the fruits of tall, columnar cacti of the genus Stenocereus — upright desert pillars, a different plant giving a different, often sharper fruit. Those are not dragon fruit, and nothing said here about one applies to the other.
    • The plant crossed the oceans in the colonial centuries. The Spanish carried it to the Philippines in the 1500s, and in the mid-1800s a French priest carried it into Indochina. In Vietnam it was planted at first as a garden ornamental, grown for the drama of its night flowers rather than for food — a curiosity in the gardens of the French and of wealthy households.
    • Vietnam is where the fruit's second life began. The Vietnamese name is thanh long, "green dragon." Through the twentieth century the plant sat in home gardens across the south; then, from the 1980s, farmers in Bình Thuận province — dry, sunny coast country a cactus can thrive in — began planting it as a crop in earnest. The planting spread through Long An and Tiền Giang, the rows of concrete posts each carrying a fountain of green stems became the signature of the region, and Vietnam grew into the largest producer and by far the largest exporter of dragon fruit in the world, shipping most of its harvest abroad. About ninety-five in every hundred fruits Vietnam grows are the white-fleshed kind. Growers there hang lamps over the fields at night in the off-season; the light fools the plant into flowering out of its season, and whole districts glow after dark.
    • From Vietnam the crop spread across Asia — Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Taiwan and southern China all grow it now — and back across the Pacific to Hawaii, Florida and California, and to Israel and Australia. China calls it huo long guo, "fire dragon fruit"; in Malaysia and Indonesia it is buah naga, "dragon fruit" again. Few crops have so completely changed their home address: a Central American forest vine that most of the world now meets as a Vietnamese fruit.
    • The flower is food as well as the fruit. In southern China the great blooms of the white-fleshed plant are dried and sold as bawanghua — "overlord flower" — and simmered for hours in the slow Cantonese soups, traditionally served for coughs and dry, irritated lungs; the fresh flowers and unopened buds are cooked as a vegetable in the same region, and in Vietnam the buds thinned from the vines are now dried for tea rather than wasted. Those uses are tradition, told as tradition; what has actually been tested is in Health Benefits.
    • Folk medicine took the plant up in smaller ways. The tiny seeds carry an oil long known as a mild laxative, and in parts of Latin America and Asia the fruit was eaten in folk practice for the digestion and for blood sugar. None of that was ever put to a proper test in its traditional form, and the modern blood-sugar trials, such as they are, are a separate story told at their true size below.
    • Vietnam — thanh long is a national fruit: eaten fresh and in fruit salads, set out on family altars, and given a place in the south's New Year fruit trays, where its dragon name is counted lucky. Bình Thuận calls itself the dragon fruit kingdom, and its lamp-lit off-season fields are a sight in their own right.
    • China — huo long guo is eaten fresh everywhere, and in Guangdong the plant gives twice: the dried flowers go into the slow soups, a tradition centuries older than the fruit trade.
    • Mexico and Central America — at home, where the plant is native, pitahaya is eaten fresh with a squeeze of lime, and in Nicaragua the red-fleshed fruit is blended into a vivid pink fresco, a fresh fruit drink sold wherever the fruit is in season.
    • Indonesia and Malaysia — buah naga is juiced, cut into fruit salads and rojak, and blended into drinks; Malaysia grows its own in quantity, much of it red-fleshed.
    • Ecuador and Colombia — the yellow pitaya is the premium fresh fruit of the Andes trade, eaten with a spoon straight from the skin and exported at prices the pink kinds never reach.
