    • The wider world — in North America, Europe and Australia the fruit arrived as an exotic and stayed as a smoothie-bowl decoration as much as a food; its looks did that work, and the mild flesh is still catching up with its reputation.
    • Dragon fruit, per 100 g of flesh: 68 kcal, carbohydrate 16.2 g of which sugars 12 g, fibre 1.8 g, protein 0.68 g, fat 0.21 g, and water about 82 g — a light, watery fruit. Its best nutrient is vitamin C at 19.8 mg, about a fifth of a day's worth, with a little potassium (206 mg) besides. Read plainly, those are modest numbers: the vitamin C is useful but not remarkable — an orange carries well over twice as much in the same weight — and the fibre is a small helping, not a large one. The figures are the United States Department of Agriculture's survey average across the kinds sold; they are honest food numbers, and the fruit needs no dressing up beyond them.
    • The red flesh is where the colour claims gather. Red-fleshed dragon fruit is coloured by betacyanins, the red-violet pigments of the betalain family — the same pigment family that makes beetroot red. In laboratory tests, extracts of the red-fleshed fruit show antioxidant activity — they neutralise reactive chemicals in a dish — and score higher in those tests than the white-fleshed fruit. That is the whole of the evidence: laboratory work on extracts. No human trial has shown that eating dragon fruit prevents or treats any disease through these pigments, and the colour, pretty as it is, is not a medicine. Lab studies
    • Blood sugar is the one claim with human trials behind it, and they are small enough to state exactly. A 2017 review gathered every randomised trial then published and found four — covering 36 people with prediabetes and 109 people with type 2 diabetes, in total. In the prediabetes group, fasting blood sugar fell by about 15 mg/dL on average against the comparison group. In the people who actually had type 2 diabetes, the pooled result was not significant — the trials, taken together, showed no proven effect. Two of the four trials were student dissertations rather than journal papers, and all were short. So the honest shape is: a hint of an effect in prediabetes, nothing proven in diabetes, and a fruit that still carries 12 g of sugar in every 100 g. Dragon fruit is not a treatment for diabetes. Human trials
    • For the gut, the offering is the plain one: a watery fruit with some fibre and a great many tiny seeds, pleasant and easy to eat. Its sugars include oligosaccharides — short sugar chains that gut bacteria can feed on — which have been studied in the laboratory as a possible prebiotic, a food for the gut's bacteria. That work is early and in dishes, not people; no digestive treatment is claimed. Lab studies
    • Sun: Full sun, with light shade — about a third — for young plants for their first few months; in very hot, dry, high sun the stems can sunburn
    • Soil: Well-drained soil, rich in organic matter if it can get it
    • Size: A vine, not a bush: the three-sided stems can run to about 20 feet (6 m), climbing by aerial roots, and a mature plant is heavy
    • Environment: A tropical cactus: long spells at or below freezing (about 31 °F, −2 °C) damage or kill it; it grows best in gentle warmth, roughly 65–77 °F (18–25 °C), and suffers above about 100 °F (38 °C)
    • When to pick: Fruit follows the flower by roughly a month to six weeks in the pink kinds — the yellow kind takes far longer — and it must ripen on the plant: dragon fruit is picked fully coloured, cut off with clippers

    Garden notes

    • Start with the shape of the plant: this is a vine, not a bush. The three-sided stems can run to about 20 feet (6 m), climbing by aerial roots, and a mature plant is heavy — farms and gardens grow it up a stout post with a frame or ring on top for the stems to pour over, a support built to carry several hundred pounds. Set the support before the plant. Keep it away from house walls it could climb and well clear of power lines, and give a plant room: it becomes a large, sprawling thing.
    • Climate is the hard limit. This is a tropical cactus: long spells at or below freezing (about 31 °F, −2 °C) damage or kill it, though it recovers quickly from a brief light frost. It grows best in gentle warmth, roughly 65–77 °F (18–25 °C), suffers above about 100 °F (38 °C), and in very hot, dry, high sun the stems can sunburn — young plants do better with light shade, about a third, for their first few months. Where winters freeze, grow it in a large pot with its own post and move it under cover for the cold months.
    • Soil and water surprise people who hear "cactus" and think of a desert. The plant wants well-drained soil, rich in organic matter if it can get it, and it has a real thirst for a cactus — but standing water rots its roots, and overwatering is its commonest killer in gardens. A dry rest in winter and early spring helps trigger flowering; once flowering starts, water regularly through to harvest.
    • The flower is the garden event. Through the warm months the buds swell along the stems and open after dark — one night only — into white, heavily scented bells up to about 14 inches (36 cm) long, made for the bats and moths that pollinate them at home. Many cultivars cannot use their own pollen and will drop their flowers unfruited if planted alone; the fix is to grow two or three different kinds together, or to hand-pollinate at night or in the early morning, brushing pollen from one flower onto the centre of another. Some flowers hold open into the early morning, when bees finish the job.
    • Fruit follows the flower by roughly a month to six weeks in the pink kinds — the yellow kind takes far longer — and it must ripen on the plant: dragon fruit is picked fully coloured, cut off with clippers, and gains nothing by waiting on a counter. In Florida the season runs about June to November. Picked fruit keeps four or five days at room temperature, or some weeks bagged in the refrigerator. Wear gloves for the yellow kind; its spines are small and real.
    • Keep the plant pruned. Left alone it tangles into a dense mass that shades itself and harbours rot; a yearly prune after harvest, taking out dead, damaged and ground-touching stems and thinning for light and air, keeps it bearing. A planting is long-lived — about twenty years is the working life of a farm planting, and a garden plant asks for no less commitment of space.

    Propagation

    It is grown from cuttings, not seed. A stem piece 6–15 inches (15–38 cm) long is cut, left in a dry shady place for about a week while the cut end heals over, then set in well-drained soil or a pot to root. Cuttings grow fast and can carry fruit within the first year or two; a plant raised from seed can take up to seven years to fruit, and its fruit is a lottery. Buy a named cutting whose flesh colour and pollination needs are known.

    Safety

    • After eating red-fleshed dragon fruit, your urine and stools can turn pink or red for a day or so. It is the pigment passing through unabsorbed — the same trick beetroot plays — and it is harmless. It has still frightened people into hospital fearing internal bleeding; a published case report describes exactly that, after red dragon fruit, with every test normal. If red colour shows up with pain, or lasts well beyond the fruit, have it checked — but colour that follows a red dragon fruit is the fruit.
    • Dragon fruit allergy is rare but real: a handful of cases are on record, a few of them severe, so anyone who itches or swells after a first taste should stop and treat swelling of the lips or throat as an emergency.
    • A large serving can loosen the stools — the seeds' oil and the fibre together — which is a portion note, not a danger.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture — FoodData Central: dragon fruit (survey record, FDC ID 2709234) — the nutrition figures
    • Poolsup et al. (2017) — PLoS ONE: systematic review and meta-analysis of dragon fruit and blood-sugar control — four small randomised trials, stated at their size
    • Crane & Balerdi — UF/IFAS Extension (HS303), Pitaya (Dragonfruit) Growing in the Florida Home Landscape — the plant, its flowers, pollination, growing and harvest
    • Tarte et al. (2023) — eFood review of dragon fruit and its value — the French introduction to Vietnam and Vietnam's production figures
    • Leong et al. (2022) — Clinical Case Reports Journal: red stools after red dragon fruit — a benign mimic of bleeding

    Durian

    Durio zibethinus

    Culinary

    Vitamin C

    FreshCooked

    The durian is the fruit of a tall rainforest tree of Southeast Asia, and across the region it carries a title no other fruit holds: the king of fruits. The fruit is big — commonly one to three kilograms — and armoured all over with hard, sharp spikes; the name comes from the Malay word duri, meaning a thorn. Inside the husk the fruit divides into sections, each holding a parcel of soft, custard-rich flesh around one large seed. The flesh is loved for its taste and famous for its smell. The smell comes from sulphur compounds the ripe fruit gives off in unusual strength — the same family of chemicals that gives onions, garlic and rotten eggs their smell — and it carries so far, and fades so slowly, that durians are banned from many hotels, from public transport and from aircraft cabins across Southeast Asia, where the no-durian sign stands beside the no-smoking sign. The smell is not an accident: in the wild it calls animals to the fallen fruit — orangutans among them — and the animals carry the seeds away through the forest. One name needs clearing up first: the soursop is called durian belanda, the "Dutch durian", in Malay, but it is a different fruit in a different family, soft and sour where the durian is rich, and the two share nothing but the borrowed name.

    Cultivars

    Malaysia runs the most formal durian naming system in the world: its Department of Agriculture has registered named clones since 1934, each with a number beginning with D, and around two hundred stand on the register. A registered clone is one chosen tree, copied by grafting, so every tree of a clone is the same tree again and again. Thailand grows its own named kinds under Thai names, and Thailand's kinds fill most of the world's export crates.

    'Musang King' (D197)

    The premium kind. It was registered in 1993 from a tree at Tanah Merah in Kelantan, under its first name Raja Kunyit — "king of turmeric", for the deep golden colour of its flesh. The name it conquered under came later, from Gua Musang, the district where a grower promoted it; in Chinese it is Mao Shan Wang, "cat mountain king". The flesh is thick, golden and bittersweet, with the strong smell Malaysia prizes. It is the fruit China's buyers pay the highest prices for, and the kind whose genome was read in 2017.

    'Monthong' (D159)

    Thailand's standard, registered in Malaysia in 1987 from Thai stock. The name means "golden pillow" in Thai, for the plump, pale-gold sections of flesh. The fruit is large — four to six kilograms is common — the flesh thick, sweet and mild, the smell gentler than the Malaysian kinds. It is the durian most of the world outside the region has met: the mainstay of Thailand's export trade and of the frozen and processed trade everywhere.

    'D24'

    One of the oldest registrations of all, made in 1937 from a tree near the Bukit Merah reservoir in Perak, and nicknamed Sultan. The flesh is rich and bittersweet with a slight bitterness durian lovers prize, and for decades this was the premium Malaysian eating durian, before Musang King passed it.

    'Chanee' (D123)

    A Thai kind registered in 1971, with smooth, sweet, deep-yellow flesh.

    'Red Prawn' (D175)

    A Penang kind registered in 1990, with orange-red, curd-soft flesh.

    'Black Thorn' (D200)

    A newer premium kind, registered in 2015, named for the dark tips of its spines, with rich flesh that now rivals Musang King at the top of the market.

    Beyond the one cultivated species, the genus holds other edible kinds eaten close to home — the red-fleshed durian of Sabah, Durio graveolens, among them — but D. zibethinus is the durian of trade, and the only one most eaters will ever meet.

    • The durian's home is the lowland rainforest of Borneo, Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula, where wild durian trees still grow and where the genus Durio holds some thirty species, most of them found nowhere else. People in the region gathered and planted durians around their villages for centuries — the durian was a village tree long before it was an orchard crop, and the finest fruit was always the one that fell ripe in the night and was found in the morning.
    • One of the first European descriptions came in the 1440s, out of the travels of the Italian merchant Niccolò de' Conti, as written down by the scholar Poggio Bracciolini: a green fruit the size of a melon, he reported, holding five parts, each like a long orange, with a texture like thick butter. The butter comparison would follow the fruit for the next four hundred years.
    • The fruit's most famous praise was written by the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace. In an essay of 1856, "On the Bamboo and Durian of Borneo", and again in his book The Malay Archipelago in 1869, Wallace wrote that "a rich butter-like custard highly flavoured with almonds gives the best general idea of it", with wafts of flavour that call to mind cream-cheese, onion-sauce and brown sherry — "it is neither acid, nor sweet, nor juicy; yet one feels the want of none of these qualities, for it is perfect as it is", and "to eat durians is a new sensation, worth a voyage to the East to experience." Wallace came to it honestly: he had first tried the fruit in Malacca, indoors, and the smell had beaten him. In Borneo he found a ripe fruit on the ground, ate it out of doors, and "at once became a confirmed durion eater". The same 1856 essay carried the fruit's other fame: the durian and the Brazil nut, Wallace wrote, are fruits that grow on lofty trees, fall as soon as they are ripe, "and often wound or kill those who seek to obtain them".
    • In the twentieth century the village tree became an industry. Thailand built the largest export trade of all, shipping its Monthong kind around the world. Malaysia registered its named clones from 1934 onward and built its trade on flavour. And in this century China's appetite turned the fruit into one of the region's great money crops: Malaysia won the right to send fresh whole fruit to China only in 2024, after years of sending it frozen.
    • In 2017 scientists in Singapore read the whole genome of a Musang King tree — the first durian genome ever read — and found the smell written into the fruit's inheritance. Where its cousin the cacao tree carries one copy of a gene that builds sulphur smell compounds, the durian carries four, and they switch on hard in the ripe flesh. The same work traced the kinship of durian and cacao back some 65 million years.
    • The flesh is eaten at every stage, and each stage has its cooks. Firm, just-ripe fruit is eaten fresh. Fruit a day past its peak, soft and beginning to ferment, is prized by many as the richest of all. And flesh that has gone further is not wasted: it is salted and fermented into tempoyak, a sour, pungent paste that keeps for months and goes into curries and sauces across Malaysia and Indonesia. The Dayak peoples of Borneo were salting durian pulp as a relish for rice long before the fruit had a trade.
    • Unripe durian is a vegetable. In Borneo it was eaten cooked, and even raw, while still firm, and young fruit still goes into curries and soups in the region today. In parts of Indonesia the flowers and young leaves are cooked as vegetables too. The big seeds are food as well — boiled or roasted until they turn mealy, almost like chestnuts, and eaten as a snack or sliced into dishes. They are always cooked, never eaten raw.
    • In the Malay tradition the tree was medicine as well as food: water boiled with the leaves and roots was a household remedy for fever, and the fruit itself was held to warm the body and stir desire — a reputation kept alive in the old saying that when the durians come down, the sarongs go up. The tradition is real; the trials are not there.
    • In the Chinese food tradition that runs through the region, foods are classed as heating or cooling, and the durian sits at the heating end of the scale. Eating too much is said to bring on "heatiness" — a sore throat, a feverish feeling, a body out of balance — and the set partner for a durian feast is the mangosteen, the "queen of fruits", whose cool flesh is held to settle what the king heated. The same tradition carries the warning against eating durian with alcohol. These beliefs have centuries behind them, and they shape how the fruit is eaten to this day.
    • Malaysia — durian season is a national event: roadside stalls open into the night, fruit is priced by the kilo and eaten on the spot at plastic tables. Raub and Bentong, in Pahang, are the Musang King heartland. Tempoyak goes into gulai tempoyak, a curry of fermented durian, famously cooked with river fish in Pahang and Perak.
    • Thailand — the export engine: Monthong shipped fresh to China and frozen around the world; durian sticky rice, sweet coconut rice under a durian coconut sauce; durian chips, thin slices fried crisp under vacuum; and durian paste worked into cakes and sweets.
    • Indonesia — es durian, durian flesh over shaved ice; dodol durian, a slow-cooked toffee of durian, coconut milk and palm sugar; Medan's durian pancakes, thin crêpes wrapped around durian cream and carried home by the boxful as gifts; and in Sumatra and Kalimantan, tempoyak at the centre of the table.
    • The Philippines — Davao calls itself the durian capital of the Philippines and feasts the fruit at its Kadayawan festival each August. The flesh goes into candies, tarts, ice cream and a local durian coffee.
    • Singapore — the fruit is banned from the underground railway and from hotels, and loved anyway: the stalls of Geylang grade fruit by kind and price through the season, and the Esplanade concert halls on the bay wear spiked domes that every Singaporean calls "the durians".
    • China and beyond — China takes the largest share of the world's traded durians and pays the top prices for Musang King; fresh Malaysian fruit was allowed in only in 2024, after years of frozen shipments. Frozen durian now reaches North America, Europe and Australia, where it is met in Asian groceries, usually frozen and far from home.
    • Durian flesh, raw, per 100 g: 147 kcal, carbohydrate 27.1 g, fat 5.3 g, protein 1.5 g, fibre 3.8 g, potassium 436 mg, vitamin C 19.7 mg, and a spread of B vitamins led by thiamin at 0.374 mg. Set beside other fruits the shape is unmistakable: a banana carries about 89 kcal to the durian's 147, and almost no fat at all. The durian is a rich food, closer in weight to a serving of cake than to a serving of melon, and its nutrients arrive packaged in that richness. There is no health halo here — there is a genuinely nourishing fruit that is also a treat, and it is best eaten knowing it is both.
    • The honest strengths are the B vitamins. Thiamin at 0.374 mg per 100 g is close to a third of a day's worth, a figure few fruits reach, and the fruit adds useful riboflavin, vitamin B6 and folate beside it, with vitamin C at about a fifth of a day's worth. These are contents, not cures: no trial has tested eating durian against any disease, and a good vitamin list does not turn a rich fruit into a medicine.
    • The potassium is real but modest — 436 mg is under a tenth of a day's worth — and claims that durian lowers blood pressure or protects the heart run ahead of the evidence: there are no human trials of durian for either. The fruit's benefit is the plain one of good nutrients inside a high-energy package.
    • Durian flesh carries phenolic antioxidants in laboratory analyses, and it contains some tryptophan, the building block the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin — the root of claims that durian calms, cheers or helps sleep. Both claims stop at the laboratory door. An antioxidant reading in a dish, and a content figure for tryptophan, are not evidence that eating the fruit does any of these things in a person. Lab studies
    • The alcohol warning deserves a straight answer, because it is the strongest health story told about this fruit. The warning itself is old folk advice across the region. In 2009, researchers in Japan and the Philippines tested it in the laboratory: an extract of the fruit slowed down aldehyde dehydrogenase — the enzyme the body uses to clear acetaldehyde, the poisonous middle product left as alcohol is broken down — cutting the activity of the yeast form of that enzyme by up to 70 per cent in the test system, with the sulphur-rich parts of the extract doing the blocking. One sulphur compound in the fruit, diethyl disulfide, is a chemical cousin of disulfiram, the drug given to make drinkers ill if they drink. That is a real mechanism, shown in a laboratory, on a yeast enzyme, with a concentrated extract. It is not a human trial: no study has ever fed people durian and alcohol together and measured what happens, and deaths blamed on the pairing have never been pinned to it by science. The fair statement is that the danger is plausible and unproven — and since leaving drink aside at a durian feast costs nothing, the old advice is easy to keep. Lab studies
    • Sun: Full sun
    • Soil: Deep, rich, well-drained soil, slightly acid — the tree sulks in heavy clay and dies in standing water
    • Size: A mature durian stands 25–40 metres tall, with a straight trunk and a high, heavy crown
    • Environment: Heat all year — days around 24–30 °C — heavy rain of roughly 1,500 mm or more spread through the year, and no frost at all: cold below about 7 °C damages it, and a freeze kills it
    • When to pick: The fruit ripens on the tree and falls, usually in the night or early morning, and it is gathered from the ground each day. Eat a fallen fruit within a day or two: the husk splits, and the flesh ferments fast in tropical heat

    Garden notes

    • This is a tree of the true tropics and nothing less. It wants heat all year — days around 24–30 °C — heavy rain of roughly 1,500 mm or more spread through the year, and no frost at all: cold below about 7 °C damages it, and a freeze kills it. In the United States that means, in practice, the warmest parts of Hawaii and Puerto Rico and the very tip of South Florida, and even there a young tree is a gamble against one cold night. It grows at low elevations, up to about 800 metres near the equator.
    • Give it the room of a forest tree. A mature durian stands 25–40 metres tall, with a straight trunk and a high, heavy crown. It is not a patio tree, and no pruning regime makes it one for long.
    • Soil and water: deep, rich, well-drained soil, slightly acid. The tree sulks in heavy clay and dies in standing water, yet it wants steady moisture and suffers in a long dry season — and a short dry spell is what triggers flowering, which is why the crop comes in seasons rather than all year.
    • Pollination is the tree's oldest partnership. The flowers open in the late afternoon, pale and full of nectar, and through the night they are worked by bats — above all the cave nectar bat, Eonycteris spelaea — which carry the pollen from tree to tree. The flowers mostly cannot use their own pollen, so a lone tree flowers beautifully and bears little. Plant at least two trees, and keep the bats welcome.
    • Bearing: a grafted tree of a named clone can bear in about four to six years. A seedling takes far longer — ten years or more — and may not match the fruit of its parent, which is why orchards are grafted. Seed is the other trap: a durian seed dies within days of leaving the fruit and must be planted almost at once.
    • Harvest is the dangerous part, and it is never done with a ladder. The fruit ripens on the tree and falls, usually in the night or early morning, and it is gathered from the ground each day. In season, orchards string nets under the trees to catch the fall and to protect heads, and workers wear helmets — Wallace's warning of 1856 stands, because a ripe durian falling from high in the crown can kill. Eat a fallen fruit within a day or two: the husk splits, and the flesh ferments fast in tropical heat.

    Propagation

    A grafted tree of a named clone can bear in about four to six years. A seedling takes far longer — ten years or more — and may not match the fruit of its parent, which is why orchards are grafted. Seed is the other trap: a durian seed dies within days of leaving the fruit and must be planted almost at once.

    Safety

    • The seeds are eaten cooked, never raw: raw durian seeds carry cyclopropene fatty acids, an unusual kind of fat the body is better off without, and cooking them is the settled custom everywhere they are eaten.
    • The flesh is sugar-rich and energy-dense, so portions matter for anyone watching blood sugar.
    • At 436 mg of potassium per 100 g, people told to limit potassium for kidney disease should treat a durian feast with the same care they give other potassium-rich foods.

    Eucalyptus

    Eucalyptus globulus

    Medicinal

    Eucalyptus is a giant of a tree from Australia, and the smell of it is one of the best-known smells in the world — sharp, clean and cooling, the smell of cough rubs and steam rooms. The tree here is the blue gum, Eucalyptus globulus, the species the medicine trade has used most: a fast-growing evergreen that can stand taller than a twenty-storey building, its young leaves round and blue-grey, its grown leaves long, curved and leathery, hanging down like green sickles. The leaves are dotted with tiny glands of oil, and that oil — mostly one compound, 1,8-cineole, also called eucalyptol — is what the whole medicine story is about. The oil is poison if swallowed — less than a teaspoon of the pure oil can kill.

    Cultivars

    The blue gum has no named garden cultivars of its own — none at all in the nursery trade. Trees are grown from seed as the plain species, and the timber and oil trades grow it by seed origin, not by cultivar name. What the species does have is four botanical subspecies, told apart by botanists from the shape of the fruit and the bark.

    subsp. globulus

    The Tasmanian and Victorian tree.

    subsp. bicostata

    The southern blue gum of the mainland ranges.

    subsp. maidenii

    Maiden's gum.

    subsp. pseudoglobulus

    The Gippsland blue gum.

    The differences are a botanist's distinction, not a gardener's choice, and no named garden form of any of them exists. The small, round-leaved eucalyptus sold for gardens and flower arranging — the silver dollar gum, Eucalyptus cinerea, and its cut-foliage forms with names of their own — is a different species, not a cultivar of the blue gum. None of what is told of E. globulus belongs to it, and its oil is not the blue gum's oil.

    • Eucalyptus is an Australian tree through and through. The genus holds more than seven hundred kinds, nearly all of them native to Australia, and the blue gum is a tree of Tasmania and the south-east of the mainland, growing in the wet forests along the coasts. The name is Greek: eu — well — and kalyptos — covered — for the little cap that covers the flower bud before it opens and falls away. The species name, globulus, means a little ball, for the round, button-like fruit.
    • Aboriginal Australians knew the tree long before any European saw it. The leaves were bruised and heated and laid on the skin as a poultice, and a sick person was laid on a bed of green leaves over hot stones in a shallow pit to ease rheumatism. An infusion of the leaves was drunk for a cold, steam from heated leaves was breathed in for a headache, and warmed leaves mixed with native honey were given for severe colds and dysentery — the running, bloody gut sickness. The tree was medicine, timber, shelter and firewood all at once, for tens of thousands of years.
    • The first European to collect the blue gum was the French botanist Jacques Labillardière, on Tasmania in 1792, on the expedition sent to look for the lost explorer La Pérouse. He described the tree in 1800, and the Latin name he gave it is the one it still carries.
    • In the 1850s the tree's great champion was Ferdinand von Mueller, the German-born botanist of Victoria, who praised its speed of growth and sent its seed to country after country. Settlers planted it in California, Portugal, Spain, India, Ethiopia and South Africa in great numbers, hoping for quick timber, firewood and railway sleepers, for shade, and because it was believed to dry out swampy ground and so ward off malaria — the fever of marshes. The tree became known in English as the fever tree, and in Tasmania it is the state's flower emblem to this day.
    • The oil trade began in the 1860s. Joseph Bosisto, a pharmacist in Melbourne, began distilling eucalyptus oil in Victoria, and distilleries in Australia, then in Spain, Portugal and China, made the oil for cough remedies, liniments and cleaning products. By the 1870s the tree was famous enough in London for the Royal Botanic Society to hear a whole lecture on it, and the lecturer could already report that its seed had been spread through southern Europe and northern Africa.
    • In folk medicine the leaf and the oil were used for much the same things everywhere they travelled: for coughs and colds, for fever, for aching joints, for wounds and sores, and as a strong-smelling wash. The nineteenth-century American eclectic doctors — the herbal physicians of the day — used it for fevers, laryngitis, asthma, long-lasting bronchitis, whooping cough and ulcers. Much of that use was hope and habit, not tested proof. The tested part stands on its own, under Health Benefits.
    • The tree also fed Australia's most famous animal. Koalas live almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves, and the blue gum is among the trees they eat. The leaves are poor food — low in nourishment and full of strong oils — which is why a koala sleeps for most of the day and eats for most of the rest. The tree's other great partner is fire. Eucalyptus leaves are rich in flammable oil, the bark peels off in long ribbons, and the tree is built for burning: after a fire it sprouts again from buds hidden under its bark and from a woody swelling at its base, and the heat opens its seed capsules so the next generation can grow. That same fire-loving nature is why the tree is now managed as a problem plant in California and Portugal, where its dense stands burn fiercely and crowd out native trees.
    • Australia — the tree's home: the wet forests of Tasmania and south-east Victoria, where the blue gum is the state flower emblem of Tasmania; Aboriginal medicine from the leaf; and the koala's food tree, the fire-adapted giant of the bush.
    • California — planted in huge numbers from the 1850s for timber, firewood and windbreaks, and for the hope it would dry the marshes; now a familiar sight along the coast, and managed as an invasive tree that burns fiercely and drinks deeply.
    • Spain and Portugal — the great plantation countries of Europe: vast stands grown for pulpwood and for oil, and in Portugal a tree at the centre of the argument over wildfire, water use and native forest.
    • India and Ethiopia — planted for fast firewood and timber, and in Ethiopia for poles and fuel around the highland towns, where it has become part of the landscape and part of the argument about water and farmland.
    • China — one of the world's great producers of eucalyptus oil, distilled from plantation leaves for cough drops, rubs and cleaning products.
    • The Mediterranean — the fever-tree hope of the 1800s: planted around marshes in Algeria, Italy and the south of France to dry the ground and ward off malaria, a belief that drove the tree's spread across the whole region.
    • What is in the leaf, first. Dried blue gum leaves hold about 1 to 3.5% essential oil, and most of that oil — commonly 60 to 90% of it — is 1,8-cineole, with smaller amounts of pinene, limonene and other scented compounds. The leaf also carries flavonoids and tannins. The oil sold in bottles is a separate thing: the pharmacopoeia defines eucalyptus oil as oil steam-distilled from the fresh leaves of cineole-rich kinds, mainly E. globulus, E. polybractea and E. smithii, holding at least 70% cineole.
    • The cough and cold use has a formal traditional standing, and that is its true size. The European Medicines Agency accepts eucalyptus leaf and eucalyptus oil as traditional herbal medicines for relief of a cough with a cold, and the oil also for localised muscle pain rubbed on the skin. The agency found no controlled clinical trials of the oil itself, and none of the leaf — the standing rests on long use, not on proof. No trial has tested the leaves as a tea or a steam. That use is tradition, and it is told as tradition. Traditional use
    • The trials that do exist tested capsules of purified cineole — the single compound, made to be swallowed in a coated capsule — and they are the strongest evidence there is. In a placebo-controlled trial of 242 adults with long-lasting bronchitis, 200 mg of cineole three times a day for ten days eased coughing and bronchitis symptoms more than the dummy capsules by the fourth day. In a trial of 152 adults with sinus infection, 200 mg of cineole three times a day eased symptoms more than placebo over seven days. These are real, placebo-controlled trials in people, at a set dose, of a made medicine — not of a cup of leaf tea. Human trials
    • The lung-disease trials are the most striking, and the smallest. In a placebo-controlled trial of 242 adults with COPD — long-term lung disease that narrows the airways — 200 mg of cineole three times a day for six months, alongside their usual treatment, cut flare-ups: 28% of the cineole group had a flare-up against 46% of the placebo group, and lung function and quality of life improved a little. In a much smaller trial, 32 adults with severe asthma who relied on steroid tablets took 200 mg of cineole three times a day for twelve weeks, and more of them were able to lower their steroid dose than on placebo — the cineole group cut their steroid dose by about 36% against 7% on placebo. The COPD trial is one trial of 242 people; the asthma trial is one trial of 32 people. Both tested cineole alongside usual care, never instead of it. Cineole is not a treatment for asthma or COPD on its own, and no one should change their inhalers or tablets on the strength of it. Human trials
    • First, steam breathing for colds has been looked at in a Cochrane review, and it found no clear benefit — the steam habit rests on tradition, not on a trial.
    • Second, the laboratory work — cineole killing germs in dishes, easing swelling in animal tests — is laboratory and animal work, and none of it shows what breathing the oil or drinking the leaf does in a person. Lab studies / Animal studies
    • When to plant: Grow it from seed sown in spring after the last frost, in pots, and plant out while young
    • Sun: Full sun and a long, warm growing season
    • Soil: Deep, well-drained ground — a sandy loam is ideal — around pH 6.0 to 7.5; roots sitting in water invite disease, and heavy wet clay kills more young blue gums than cold does
    • Size: In the open it grows 30 to 55 metres tall — 100 to 180 feet — with a spread of 9 to 15 metres, and it grows fast, several feet a year when young
    • Environment: Warm, mild places — the equivalent of USDA zones 8 to 10; damaged by hard frost when young, though an established tree can take short cold down to about −10 °C (14 °F)

    Garden notes

    • Be honest about the size before anything else. The blue gum is a forest tree, not a garden shrub. In the open it grows 30 to 55 metres tall — 100 to 180 feet — with a spread of 9 to 15 metres, and it grows fast, several feet a year when young. It belongs in a park, a farm or a very large piece of ground, never in a small garden, never near a house, a drain or a power line. Its roots are strong and far-reaching, and its branches can drop without warning in hot, dry weather.
    • Climate: the tree is a tree for warm, mild places — the equivalent of USDA zones 8 to 10. It likes full sun and a long, warm growing season, and it is damaged by hard frost when young, though an established tree can take short cold down to about −10 °C (14 °F). It wants the pattern of its home: mild, wet winters and warm summers.
    • Soil: it grows in many soils but does best in deep, well-drained ground — a sandy loam is ideal — around pH 6.0 to 7.5. It tolerates poor and stony ground better than wet ground: roots sitting in water invite disease, and heavy wet clay kills more young blue gums than cold does. Once settled it is drought-tough by tree standards, but it is also famously thirsty, and in dry country it will take water other plants need.
    • Grow it from seed sown in spring after the last frost, in pots, and plant out while young — the tree grows a deep taproot and dislikes being moved once it is established. Water steadily for the first year or two while it settles; after that it asks for little. Pruning is for safety, not for shape: take out dead wood and crossing branches, and never top the tree, which makes weak, dangerous regrowth.
    • The leaves change as the tree grows. Young trees carry round, blue-grey, stalkless leaves in opposite pairs — the foliage of the florist's bunch. Grown trees carry long, curved, leathery leaves that hang down, dark green on top and paler beneath. The bark peels away in long ribbons, the flowers are creamy white, and the fruit is a small woody ball with a lid — the globulus of the name. The tree flowers in late summer into autumn where it is planted in the northern hemisphere.
    • Fire is the warning that matters most. The leaves are rich in flammable oil, the bark ribbons catch easily, and the tree sheds a deep litter of oily leaves. In fire country it should never be planted close to a house, and the ground beneath it should be kept clear of litter.

    Propagation

    Grow it from seed sown in spring after the last frost, in pots, and plant out while young — the tree grows a deep taproot and dislikes being moved once it is established.

    Safety

    • The oil is never swallowed. MedlinePlus, drawing on the Natural Medicines database, states that taking only 3.5 ml — less than one teaspoon — of the pure oil can be fatal, and poisoning brings stomach pain, dizziness, muscle weakness, feelings of suffocation, drowsiness, fits and coma. In one Australian hospital study, of 109 young children admitted after drinking eucalyptus oil, 28% had depressed consciousness — a dulled, hard-to-wake state. There is no antidote. Anyone who swallows the oil needs a poison control centre straight away.
    • Children carry the greatest risk. The European Medicines Agency says eucalyptus oil medicines must not be used in children under two years old, and leaf preparations not under thirty months, because strong-smelling preparations can trigger a spasm of the voice box in small children. The oil must not be used in any child who has had a fit, with or without fever, and it should not be put on or near the face of infants or children under ten. The trials used coated capsules of purified cineole made to be swallowed — not the oil sold for scent burners, which is how most childhood poisonings happen: children find and swallow the liquid meant for a vaporiser.
    • The oil can irritate the skin if used undiluted; people with asthma can find strong scents trigger a tightening of the airways; the agency does not recommend eucalyptus medicines in pregnancy or while breastfeeding; and eucalyptus is listed as toxic to dogs, cats and horses. A cold that brings breathlessness, fever, discoloured phlegm, or a cough that lasts more than a week needs a doctor, not more steam.
